This study introduces FLVoogd, an enhanced federated learning framework where servers and clients jointly mitigate Byzantine attacks while safeguarding privacy. Specifically, servers employ a hybrid approach combining automatic Density-based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) and S2PC to group benign participants without accessing sensitive personal data. Concurrently, clients construct dual models and utilize test-based distance control to align their local models with the global one, thereby enabling personalization. The proposed framework is fully automatic and adaptive, eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning by servers or clients during training. Furthermore, it relies on Secure Multi-party Computation (SMPC) operations—such as multiplication, addition, and comparison—while avoiding expensive computations like division and square roots. Experiments conducted on standard image classification datasets demonstrate that FLVoogd effectively filters out malicious uploads in most scenarios and prevents data leakage on the server side.

Over the past few decades, extensive research has focused on the fine structures of type III radio bursts observed in metric to decametric wavelengths, with most explanations attributing this emission to electron beams propagating through the strongly inhomogeneous plasma of the low corona. However, studies on single type III bursts exhibiting such fine structures in hecto-kilometric wavelengths have been scarce. This study reports the discovery of numerous structured type III bursts observed during the STEREO era using the WAVES instruments aboard STEREO A, STEREO B, and Wind. The objectives are to report on, classify, and characterize the fine structures of these bursts, ultimately aiming to elucidate the physical mechanisms driving their generation. Utilizing data from STEREO and Wind spacecraft, we applied 1D density models to determine the velocity of the electron beam sources and conducted spectral analyses of the fine structures to compare them with their metric-decametric counterparts. The results reveal similarities between the fine structures of type III bursts across metric-to-decametric and interplanetary wavelengths, suggesting that the underlying physical processes remain consistent from the low corona out to the interplanetary range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the observed structuring and intermittent nature of these bursts can be explained by variations in the level of density fluctuations at different distances from the Sun.

The generalized $k$-connectivity $\kappa_k(G)$, originally defined by Hager in 1985, extends the traditional connectivity $\kappa(G)$, which applies specifically when $k=2$. The total graph serves as a generalized line graph, constructed through the incidence relationships between vertices and edges of the original graph. While T. Hamada and T. Nonaka et al. \cite{Hamada} previously established the connectivity of the total graph $T(G)$ for a graph $G$, this paper aims to determine the generalized $k$-(edge)-connectivity of $T(G)$ specifically for $k=3$.

RNA molecules, which are single-stranded counterparts to DNA, adopt diverse structural configurations that dictate their biological roles within cells. These structures can be represented combinatorially using a specific class of graphs known as RNA diagrams. This paper introduces a novel partially ordered set (poset) of RNA diagrams, denoted as $\mathcal{B}^r_{f,k}$ for parameters $r\ge 0$, $k \ge 1$, and $f \ge 3$, termed the Penner-Waterman poset. Leveraging findings from multitriangulation theory, we demonstrate that this poset is pure with a rank of $k(2f-2k+1)+r-f-1$. Furthermore, when $r=0$, its geometric realization corresponds to the join of a simplicial sphere with dimension $k(f-2k)-1$ and an $\left((f+1)(k-1)-1\right)$-simplex. As a specific corollary for the case where $k=1$, we recover a result by Penner and Waterman regarding the topology of RNA secondary structure spaces. Ultimately, these findings may pave the way for novel approaches to exploring landscapes of RNA $k$-noncrossing structures.

This paper presents and develops the concept of a Manin triple for a Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak g$ over a field with characteristic $p=2$. We derive cohomological necessary conditions under which the pair $(\mathfrak g, \mathfrak g^*)$ constitutes a Manin triple. Furthermore, we define Lie bi-superalgebras in the $p=2$ context and demonstrate the relationship between Manin triples and these structures. Specifically, we investigate Manin triples arising from classical $r$-matrices subject to an additional constraint, termed an admissible classical $r$-matrix. We examine a specific scenario where $\mathfrak g$ possesses an even, invariant, non-degenerate bilinear form; in this setting, admissible $r$-matrices can be generated inductively via double extensions. Additionally, we introduce the notion of double extensions of Manin triples and illustrate how to construct a new Manin triple from an existing one.

A viewing graph consists of unknown camera poses as vertices and observed relative motions as edges. Solving this graph is a critical step in Structure-from-Motion workflows, which derive relative motions from 2D image collections. Most existing approaches solve for rotations separately via rotation averaging and then use these rotations to determine positions. However, determining positions is difficult because translation observations only indicate motion direction. This challenge intensifies when edges represent pairwise translations between cameras at varying distances. This paper introduces an iterative method to address these problems, along with a technique that estimates rotations and positions simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve state-of-the-art performance.

The locomotion of undulating creatures results from a complex interplay involving the central nervous system, muscles, connective tissues, bones, and the surrounding environment. While many prior studies have simplified this by assuming sufficient internal force exists to generate observed kinematics—thereby neglecting the quantification of the relationship between muscle effort, body morphology, and external reaction forces—this dynamic is crucial for the performance of crawling animals, particularly when body viscoelasticity is present. Furthermore, in bio-inspired robotics, internal damping serves as a tunable design parameter, yet its specific effects remain poorly understood. This research investigates how internal damping influences the locomotion of a crawler modeled as a continuous, visco-elastic, nonlinear beam. Muscle actuation is represented as a posteriorly propagating traveling wave of bending moment, while environmental forces are simulated using anisotropic Coulomb friction to mimic the scale properties of snakes and limbless lizards. The findings indicate that adjusting the crawler's internal damping can modify its performance and enable distinct gaits, including reversing the net locomotion direction from forward to backward. The study discusses this bidirectional control mechanism and identifies the optimal internal damping required to maximize crawling speed.

This paper characterizes the expected value of submodular set functions under pairwise independent random inputs, which include mutually independent distributions but are a subset of arbitrarily dependent (correlated) ones. We analyze the ratio between the maximum expected value achievable with arbitrary dependence versus pairwise independence, given identical marginal probabilities. Inspired by the correlation gap ratio defined by Agrawal et al. (2012) and Calinescu et al. (2007), our findings demonstrate that for any monotone submodular set function over $n$ variables, this ratio is bounded above by $4/3$ in two scenarios: (a) when $n$ is small ($n = 2, 3$) with general marginals, and (b) when $n$ is general but marginals are small. This bound is tight for both cases. In contrast, the correlation gap ratio for mutually independent inputs is known to be bounded by $e/(e-1)$, a bound that is tight specifically in case (b). These results highlight a fundamental distinction in how submodular functions behave under weaker independence assumptions. Furthermore, we explore an application in distributionally robust optimization and conclude with a conjecture.

Orthogonal Time Frequency Space (OTFS) is a two-dimensional modulation scheme that transmits data symbols within the delay-Doppler (DD) domain, specifically designed to mitigate the high Doppler shifts encountered in high-speed wireless communications. However, traditional OTFS channel estimation incurs substantial pilot overhead, as guard symbols consume a large portion of the DD grid. This paper introduces a superimposed channel estimation approach capable of fully recovering channel parameters without incurring pilot overhead or performance loss. Leveraging the sparsity of channel state information (CSI) in the DD domain, the method employs an Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) sparse recovery algorithm. Furthermore, the proposed technique avoids high peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) issues. For symbol detection, a message passing (MP) detector is utilized, capitalizing on the sparsity inherent in the DD channel representation.

We introduce a novel approach to explaining the observed Higgs mass within the cosmological relaxation paradigm. This method is distinguished from other scanning models by incorporating a scanning field with a non-canonical kinetic term, which functions to halt the scan near the target Higgs mass. We present a specific implementation of this concept using two new singlet fields: one responsible for scanning the Higgs mass and another that restricts the duration of the scan. Due to particle production friction, the scanning field remains largely static once the Higgs field approaches the Standard Model value, provided the scan occurs within the limited time window established by the second field.

Using a non-relativistic quark model, we compute the magnetic moments for ground-state heavy flavor charm and bottom baryons with $J^P=\frac{1}{2}^+$ and $J^P=\frac{3}{2}^+$ assignments. Our approach incorporates an effective mass concept derived from single gluon exchange interactions coupled to spectator quarks. By leveraging current experimental data in the heavy flavor sector, we estimate the interaction contributions necessary to determine the effective masses of quarks within these baryons. Furthermore, we investigate the transition moments for $\frac{1}{2}^{'+} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}^+$, $\frac{3}{2}^+ \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}^+$, and $\frac{3}{2}^+ \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}^{'+}$ spin transitions. Based on these calculations, we provide robust predictions for the radiative M1 decay widths of singly, doubly, and triply heavy flavored baryons.

Existing software vulnerabilities within computer programs or system functions represent a critical issue. In codebases containing hundreds or thousands of lines, only a small fraction of statements are actually responsible for these vulnerabilities. Currently, experts use machine learning tools to label vulnerabilities at the function or program level; however, extending this granularity to the individual code statement level is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, remaining an unresolved challenge. This paper introduces a novel, end-to-end deep learning method designed to pinpoint the specific code statements within a function that are relevant to vulnerabilities. Drawing inspiration from the structural patterns found in real-world vulnerable code, the approach first employs mutual information to learn latent variables that quantify the relevance of each statement to the function's vulnerability. Subsequently, we propose a new clustered spatial contrastive learning technique to enhance representation learning and robustly select the vulnerability-relevant statements. Experiments on real-world datasets comprising over 200,000 C/C++ functions demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, in an unsupervised setting, our approach achieves improvements of 3% to 14% in VCP, VCA, and Top-10 ACC metrics compared to existing methods. The source code for our solution is publicly available at https://github.com/vannguyennd/livuitcl.

Fairness and robustness are critical priorities for federated learning systems. This study reveals that in statistically heterogeneous networks, robustness against data and model poisoning attacks and fairness—defined by uniform performance across devices—act as competing constraints. To resolve this, we introduce Ditto, a simple and general framework for personalized federated learning that inherently delivers both fairness and robustness, alongside a scalable solver for it. Theoretically, we evaluate Ditto's capacity to simultaneously achieve fairness and robustness on a specific class of linear problems. Empirically, using a diverse set of federated datasets, we demonstrate that Ditto not only matches the performance of recent personalization methods but also produces models that are more accurate, robust, and fair than current state-of-the-art baselines designed for fairness or robustness.

The Marchenko method enables the creation of virtual sources and receivers within the subsurface by utilizing surface seismic reflection data, allowing for enhanced subsurface monitoring. The response between these virtual entities is derived via homogeneous Green's function retrieval, where a homogeneous Green's function represents the superposition of a Green's function and its time-reversal. This paper aims to generate accurate homogeneous Green's functions from field data. While classical retrieval methods demand an unrealistic enclosing recording surface, a recently proposed single-sided retrieval scheme eliminates this constraint. We first validate the principles of single-sided representation using synthetic data, demonstrating its ability to accommodate various source signatures. Given the Marchenko method's sensitivity to recording limitations in reflection data, we analyze five such limitations with synthetic data to illustrate their impact on the final results. Finally, the method is applied to a pre-processed field dataset that meets the criteria for single-sided Green's function retrieval. This scheme holds promise for future applications, including source localization.

Binary clustering systems are intrinsically linked to monotone transit functions. A particularly notable subset comprises pyramidal transit functions, distinguished by the property that their transit sets constitute an interval hypergraph. This study examines attributes of the transit function $R$, including union-closure, which are adequate to guarantee that $R$ is at minimum weakly pyramidal. Necessary criteria for pyramidal transit functions are established by utilizing the five forbidden configurations identified in Tucker's characterization of interval hypergraphs. The initial configuration pertains to $\beta$-acyclicity (also referred to as total balancedness), for which we derive three distinct alternative characterizations. Regarding monotonous transit functions, the final forbidden configuration becomes superfluous, resulting in a characterization of pyramidal transit functions based on four supplementary conditions.

The 2017 observation of a binary neutron star merger via both gravitational waves and electromagnetic signals inaugurated the era of multimessenger astronomy. However, the mechanism driving magnetic field amplification through Kelvin-Helmholtz instability during such mergers remains numerically challenging due to the involvement of very small scales, with initial magnetic topology simplifications being a primary source of uncertainty. This study employs high-resolution, convergent large-eddy simulations to track the newly formed remnant for up to 30 milliseconds, specifically comparing different initial magnetic configurations rather than the commonly used aligned dipoles. Our results indicate that the initial magnetic topology is rapidly erased within a few milliseconds post-merger. Furthermore, at the simulation's conclusion, both the average magnetic intensity ($B\sim 10^{16}$ G) and the spectral distribution of magnetic energy across spatial scales show negligible dependence on the starting configuration. This outcome is attributed to an efficient small-scale dynamo and remains valid provided that: (i) the initial large-scale magnetic field is not unrealistically high, as often assumed in merger studies; and (ii) the turbulent instability is sufficiently resolved numerically, ensuring that amplified magnetic energy spans a broad range of scales and exceeds the initial energy by orders of magnitude.

The 1.5 order formalism, occasionally referred to as a "trick," serves as the foundation of contemporary supergravity. This study employs the free massive Wess–Zumino model as a simplified test case to examine the BRS symmetry within the first, second, and 1.5 order frameworks. The analysis reveals that the 1.5 order formalism is fundamentally flawed across all theories. Although the 1.5 algebra superficially appears to close, a detailed examination within a tractable model demonstrates that it invariably produces an invalid BRS operator that fails to be nilpotent. This deficiency clearly extends to supergravity as well. Consequently, a revised and complete set of nilpotent first-order supergravity transformations is required to accurately comprehend 3+1 dimensional supergravity. Constructing such a set appears straightforward by incorporating two additional auxiliary fields, thereby integrating the spin connection into a super-Yang-Mills multiplet.

Optimal Recovery addresses the deterministic problem of learning functions from observational data by employing a worst-case perspective grounded in explicit model assumptions. Focusing on Hilbert spaces, this article examines an assumption based on approximability, while also accounting for observational inaccuracies modeled as additive $\ell_2$-bounded errors. Although prior research established that regularization yields optimal algorithms in this context without fully specifying the necessary hyperparameter, this work identifies that parameter for both local and global scenarios. In the local scenario, which involves determining Chebyshev centers, the article complements the semidefinite recipe of Beck and Eldar—which applies strictly to complex settings—with a more direct method, provided the observational functionals possess orthonormal representers; in this approach, the target parameter is derived from an equation solvable by standard techniques. Conversely, in the global scenario dominated by linear algorithms, the previously elusive parameter identified by Micchelli et al. is obtained as a byproduct of a semidefinite program. Furthermore, it is surprisingly established that when observational functionals have orthonormal representers, any choice of regularization parameter is optimal.

This study examines the collection of orthogonal vector pairs within Hilbert space, a structure often termed a "cross" due to its resemblance to the union of horizontal and vertical axes in the Euclidean plane when the space is the real line. These nonconvex sets are pivotal in multiple areas of nonsmooth analysis, including feasibility and optimization challenges. We investigate these crosses and demonstrate that within infinite-dimensional contexts, they fail to be weakly (or sequentially) closed. Nevertheless, we establish that crosses are always proximinal, meaning projections onto them exist, and we derive explicit formulas for such projections across all scenarios.

Inspired by research into summatory $k$-free indicators and totient functions within classical number theory, this work explores their counterparts in function fields. Initially, we establish a formula expressing the error terms of these summatory functions using the zeros of the corresponding zeta function. Assuming the Linear Independence hypothesis, we explicitly determine the limiting distributions of these error terms and calculate their occurrence frequency within the interval $[-\beta, \beta]$ for any real $\beta > 0$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these error terms are unbiased, meaning they appear with equal positive and negative frequencies. Finally, we analyze the average behavior of these error terms across families of hyperelliptic curves with a fixed genus. These findings are achieved by adhering to a general framework first proposed by Cha and Humphries.

We establish the structural theory for weakly geometric rough paths with bounded $1 < p$-variation, alongside their controlled paths. Unlike prior methods, our framework avoids reliance on smooth approximations. We derive an explicit combinatorial formula for the rough path lift of a controlled path, leveraging it to prove key identities including the associativity of the rough integral, the adjunction between pushforwards and pullbacks, and a change of variables formula for rough differential equations (RDEs). As applications, we extend the findings of [CDL15] to arbitrary $p$ by defining rough paths, rough integration, and RDEs on manifolds.

This study examines the creation of prompt charged particles during proton-lead and proton-proton collisions at a nucleon-nucleon centre-of-mass energy of ${\sqrt{s_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{NN}}}=5\,\mathrm{TeV}}$ using the LHCb detector. The analysis investigates these particles as a function of pseudorapidity ($\eta$) and transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) relative to the proton beam. The nuclear modification factor for charged particles is calculated across pseudorapidity ranges of ${-4.8<\eta<-2.5}$ (backward) and ${2.0<\eta<4.8}$ (forward), and transverse momenta from ${0.2<p_{\mathrm{T}}<8.0\,\mathrm{GeV}/c}$. Findings indicate that, for $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ exceeding $1.5\,\mathrm{GeV}/c$, proton-lead collisions exhibit suppressed charged particle production in the forward region compared to proton-proton collisions, while showing an enhancement in the backward region. These results provide constraints on nuclear parton distribution functions and saturation models at previously uncharted parton momentum fractions, extending down to $10^{-6}$.

Most research on school choice prioritizes creating mechanisms for assigning students across numerous schools, often utilizing an ad hoc method for individual school admissions policies. In contrast, an alternative strategy centers specifically on the admissions policies of a single institution, a focus that is particularly vital for clearly conveying goals like fostering diversity or executing affirmative action. I contend that this single-school approach remains insufficiently explored and warrants greater scholarly attention moving forward.
We establish conditions for the unitarizability of Harish-Chandra super modules associated with Lie supergroups and superalgebras.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) facilitates cross-domain learning by transferring knowledge from a labeled source domain with a different distribution to an unlabeled target domain, though it does not always succeed and instances of "negative transfer" are well-documented. This study establishes a simple lower bound on target domain error that complements existing upper bounds, demonstrating that merely minimizing source domain error and marginal distribution mismatch is insufficient to guarantee reduced target error because induced labeling function mismatches can increase. This limitation is illustrated through simple distributions where the same UDA approach can succeed, fail, or yield unpredictable results. Inspired by these findings, we introduce novel data poisoning attacks designed to deceive UDA methods into learning representations that cause high target domain errors. Evaluating these attacks on benchmark datasets where UDA previously showed success reveals that poisoning can drastically reduce target accuracy, sometimes to nearly 0%, by adding only 10% poisoned data to the source. These failures highlight the inherent limitations of current UDA methods in ensuring consistent cross-domain generalization as predicted by our lower bound. Consequently, assessing UDA techniques under adversarial conditions like data poisoning offers a more accurate measure of their robustness against data distributions that are unfavorable for adaptation.

This study computes the form factors for the $\Lambda_b\to\Lambda_c(2625)$ and $\Xi_b\to\Xi_c(2815)$ transitions, alongside their associated semileptonic decays and color-allowed two-body nonleptonic decays. Utilizing the three-body light-front quark model, which is reinforced by baryon spectroscopy, we derive the necessary form factors. The spatial wave functions of the relevant baryons, serving as critical physical inputs, are determined via the Gaussian expansion method within a semirelativistic potential framework. For semileptonic transitions, branching ratios for electron and muon channels may reach approximately $1\%$; specifically, our calculated value of $\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_b^0\to\Lambda_c^+(2625)\mu^-\nu_{\mu})=(1.641\pm0.113)\%$ aligns well with existing experimental data. Regarding nonleptonic processes, decays into $\pi^-$, $\rho^-$, and $D_s^{(*)-}$ final states exhibit significant widths, suggesting these modes are potentially observable at the LHCb experiment.

We address the challenge of counting arbitrary semantic categories in images using either a minimal set of labeled examples (few-shot) or none at all (no-shot). Conventional few-shot approaches generate appearance queries from exemplars to match against image features for counting, but existing methods rely on feature pooling and ignore shape data (such as size and aspect ratio), resulting in diminished localization accuracy and count estimates. To overcome this, we introduce LOCA, a Low-shot Object Counting network featuring iterative prototype Adaptation. Our primary innovation is a novel object prototype extraction module that iteratively combines exemplar shape and appearance queries with image features. This module is readily adaptable to zero-shot conditions, allowing LOCA to address the full range of low-shot counting tasks. On the FSC147 benchmark, LOCA surpasses all recent state-of-the-art methods by 20-30% in RMSE for both one-shot and few-shot scenarios, achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot settings, and exhibits superior generalization capabilities.

This paper introduces a volumetric communication system tailored for remote procedural assistance. It enables a distant expert to visually direct a local operator by sharing a spatially identical view; however, the local operator sees the physical object they are working on, whereas the remote expert perceives it as a mixed-reality "hologram." Communication involves voice commands, gestures, and annotations applied directly to either the target object or its holographic representation. At both endpoints, this spatial visualization is experienced through mixed-reality glasses.

Collective cell migration, defined by sustained contact and coordinated movement among multiple cells, is fundamental to embryonic development and cancer progression. New imaging techniques have generated time-resolved trajectories of individual cells, offering a detailed view of tumor spheroid expansion. Utilizing simulations of a minimal cell model, we examined experimental data tracking cell movement within fibrosarcoma spheroids embedded in a collagen matrix. Both experimental and simulated results indicate that core cells display subdiffusive glassy dynamics (mean square displacement $\Delta(t) \approx t^{\alpha}$ where $\alpha < 1$), while peripheral cells show superdiffusive motion ($\alpha > 1$). This superdiffusion in the periphery arises from highly persistent, correlated directional movement. Notably, the $\alpha$ values derived from both experiments and simulations align nearly quantitatively, a surprising result given that no model parameters were adjusted to fit the data. The distinct dynamics of core versus peripheral cells are effectively described by the fourth-order susceptibility, a metric used to characterize metastable states in glass-forming systems. Velocity autocorrelation analyses reveal significant spatial heterogeneity, with no two cells displaying identical behavior. The prediction that $\alpha$ varies based on a cell's position within the tumor is experimentally testable. Furthermore, the highly heterogeneous dynamics observed in tumor spheroids offer a plausible explanation for the origin of intratumor heterogeneity.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of the multivariate spike-and-slab LASSO (mSSL), introduced by Deshpande et al. (2019), which is designed for joint variable and covariance selection. We focus on the sparse multivariate linear regression framework involving $p$ covariates and $q$ correlated responses. The objective is to estimate a sparse matrix $B$ representing marginal covariate effects and a sparse precision matrix $\Omega$ that characterizes the residual conditional dependencies among outcomes. The mSSL approach achieves this by assigning continuous spike and slab priors to every entry in $B$ and to all off-diagonal elements in the lower triangle of $\Omega$. Under mild conditions, we derive the posterior contraction rate for a slightly adjusted mSSL posterior as both $p$ and $q$ grow alongside the sample size $n$. Our findings demonstrate that this modified version of the mSSL procedure proposed by Deshpande et al. (2019) achieves asymptotic consistency.

This study investigates the physics of a novel neutral gauge boson ($Z^\prime$) that interacts exclusively with third-generation particles and has a mass close to that of electroweak gauge bosons. Focusing on a $Z^\prime$ produced by top quarks and decaying into tau leptons, we demonstrate that the Large Hadron Collider possesses significant exclusion capabilities for the $Z^\prime$ parameter space, even during the high-luminosity phase. By employing a straightforward search strategy modeled after current analyses of standard model gauge boson production alongside top quarks, we show that the $t\bar{t}Z^\prime$ process enables the imposition of constraints on right-handed top couplings to a $Z^\prime$ that preferentially targets third-generation fermions—couplings that are currently only weakly restricted.

This article introduces pose-based tactile servo (PBTS) control, a novel method for manipulating robots through soft tactile sensors. The core concept involves integrating a tactile perception model into a servo control loop to estimate sensor pose based on local object features like edges and surfaces. Implemented using a soft curved optical tactile sensor (the BRL TacTip) and a shear-insensitive convolutional neural network, PBTS achieves robust and precise motion control across diverse complex 3D objects. The paper first reviews tactile servoing and its connection to visual servoing before formally defining PBTS control. It then evaluates tactile servoing performance on both regular and irregular objects. Finally, the authors reflect on the relationship with visual servo control and discuss how controlled soft touch facilitates human-like dexterity in robotic systems.

As individuals navigate physical environments like cities, their movements generate mobility records, such as trajectories, via devices like mobile phones and GPS units. These records reflect essential details about users' daily work, living, and leisure activities, making them valuable for diverse applications including user profiling, mobility forecasting, and traffic control. This paper extends existing research by addressing the challenge of inferring users' socioeconomic statuses—using housing prices as a proxy—based on their mobility data, with potential applications in sectors like automotive lending. To tackle this, we introduce DeepSEI, a socioeconomic-aware deep model integrating a deep network and a recurrent network. These components extract mobility features across three dimensions: spatiality, temporality, and activity, operating at both coarse and fine-grained levels. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world mobility, POI, and housing price datasets demonstrate that DeepSEI outperforms current approaches. Furthermore, all datasets utilized in this study will be released to the public.

This study examines 16 Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) that possess both spectroscopic and photometric data taken within 2 to 3 days of first light. The early $B-V$ colors in this sample exhibit a continuous distribution. For objects with normal ejecta velocities (NV), the C~II $\lambda$6580 spectral feature is consistently present in early spectra, whereas it is either absent or very faint in high-velocity (HV) counterparts. Additionally, the velocities of detached high-velocity features (HVFs) associated with the Ca~II NIR triplet (CaIR3) above the photosphere are significantly higher in HV objects compared to NV objects, typically exceeding 30,000 km~s$^{-1}$ at 2 to 3 days. We also investigate the relationship between the maximum velocity of Si~II $\lambda$6355 ($v_{\rm Si,max}$), the velocity shift of late-time [Fe~II] lines ($v_{\rm [Fe~II]}$), and host galaxy mass. Our analysis reveals that all HV objects display redshifted $v_{\rm [Fe~II]}$, while NV objects show both blue- and redshifted values. Notably, objects with redshifted $v_{\rm [Fe~II]}$ are exclusively found in massive galaxies, suggesting that HV objects and a subset of NV objects share similar progenitor metallicities and explosion mechanisms. We propose that a geometric or projected effect within the He-detonation model could explain both the similarities in their birthplace environments and the observed differences, such as $B-V$ colors, the C~II feature, early-time CaIR3 HVFs, and nebular-phase $v_{\rm [Fe~II]}$. However, certain predictions from He-detonation simulations, like rapidly declining light curves, do not match observations, and some NV objects with blueshifted nebular $v_{\rm [Fe~II]}$ may involve alternative explosion mechanisms.

Micro-systems frequently utilize helical structures, necessitating a thorough grasp of their mechanical characteristics. Although helices constructed from cylindrical filaments have been extensively studied, the impact of the filament's cross-section on the helical form remains largely unexplored. This work experimentally examines the force-extension behavior of micro-helices made from ultra-thin PMMA ribbons. By exploiting recent advancements in controlling helix geometry, we quantify the effect of the helical pitch and observe a marked increase in stiffness as the pitch grows. We identify two key phenomena: a mechanical shift from a twisting-dominated regime at low pitches to a bending-dominated regime at high pitches, alongside a purely geometrical effect unique to helical ribbons. These findings align exceptionally well with an existing analytical model for inextensible elastic strips.

This work introduces an iterative algorithm capable of calculating individual Floquet states in many-body systems with high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, overcoming limitations of standard methods. A specific strategy is developed to track these states as the system's Hamiltonian undergoes minor adjustments. When applied to a periodically driven Bose-Hubbard chain, the approach confirms the feasibility of pseudoadiabatic Floquet state tracking. Notably, the study demonstrates that a target Floquet state resembling a Mott insulator, induced by driving, can be efficiently populated provided the driving amplitude is ramped up smoothly yet not excessively slowly. Ultimately, the algorithm is identified as a robust instrument for future research into many-body Floquet systems.

Due to the critical role search engines play in accessing digital information, there has been significant scientific interest in understanding user interactions and modeling this behavior. Many such models, referred to in the literature as click models, are structured as Dynamic Bayesian Networks. While numerous authors have leveraged the similarities between these models to develop estimation procedures—specifically using Expectation Maximization (EM)—this process often demands extensive effort, particularly when deriving the E-step. This paper proposes that such derivation is frequently unnecessary; under specific assumptions, many existing click models can be optimized as Input-Output Hidden Markov Models (IO-HMMs), where the forward-backward equations naturally provide the required E-step. To support this conclusion, we introduce the Generalized Cascade Model (GCM), demonstrate how it can be estimated within the IO-HMM EM framework, and illustrate how two existing click models can be mapped to the GCM. Additionally, our GCM-based approach for estimating click models has been implemented in the Python package gecasmo.

Magill demonstrated that the remainders of two locally compact Hausdorff spaces within their Stone-Čech compactifications are homeomorphic precisely when their lattices of Hausdorff compactifications are lattice-isomorphic. The article explicitly examines Magill's construction for these compactifications via partitions of the Stone-Čech compactification and characterizes the specific partitions that yield Hausdorff compactifications. Additionally, the study constructs embeddings of certain upper semi-lattices of compactifications into the lattices of compactifications.

If a K3 surface possesses an automorphism featuring a Siegel disk, its Picard number must be an even integer ranging from 0 to 18. In reverse, by employing hypergeometric groups, we have successfully constructed K3 surface automorphisms with Siegel disks that achieve every possible Picard number within this range. These constructions rely on comprehensive computer searches to identify suitable Salem numbers, alongside calculations of algebraic numbers derived from holomorphic Lefschetz-type formulas and associated Grothendieck residues.

Deep learning has attained high precision in face recognition through training on extensive 2D image datasets; however, comparable large-scale public 3D face datasets are scarce. Existing public 3D collections typically involve few subjects, often resulting in over-fitting. To address this, this paper introduces two Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models designed to enhance RGB-D face recognition. The first model, DepthNet, is a segmentation-aware depth estimation network that leverages semantic segmentation data to localize face regions more accurately, thereby generating depth maps from RGB images. The second is a novel mask-guided RGB-D recognition architecture comprising three branches: one for RGB recognition, one for depth map recognition, and an auxiliary segmentation mask branch equipped with a spatial attention module. DepthNet is utilized to expand a large 2D dataset into a substantial RGB-D dataset for training robust recognition models. The proposed mask-guided model effectively utilizes both depth and segmentation information, demonstrating superior resilience to pose variations compared to prior methods. Experimental results confirm that DepthNet generates more reliable depth maps when aided by segmentation masks, and the mask-guided recognition model surpasses state-of-the-art approaches on multiple public 3D face datasets.

This introductory course covers fundamental concepts in pseudodifferential operators ($\Psi$DOs) and microlocal analysis. The lecture notes begin with essential notations and preliminaries, followed by an introduction to symbols and $\Psi$DOs. Chapter 3 defines various types of oscillatory integrals, while Chapter 4 focuses on stationary phase lemmas. A distinguishing feature of this course is that the proofs for stationary phase lemmas extend beyond compactly supported functions to include more general functions with specific smoothness and growth conditions at infinity. The subsequent results on $\Psi$DOs, presented in Chapters 5, 6, and 7, rely heavily on the lemmas established in Chapter 4. Similarities between semi-classical and microlocal analysis are also discussed. Chapter 8 introduces the concept of the wavefront set, and Chapter 9 examines the propagation of singularities for solutions to partial differential equations. Key results are highlighted using "black boxes," with important steps marked in red. Each chapter concludes with exercises.

Following the initial development of power normalized cepstral coefficient (PNCC) features for robust speech recognition, they were effectively applied to other domains such as speaker verification. However, given that PNCC involves long-term operations on the power spectrogram, its specific steps for temporal processing and amplitude scaling aimed at environmental compensation may be superfluous. Furthermore, these steps could inadvertently suppress intrinsic speaker variations that are critical for deep neural network (DNN)-based speaker verification. Consequently, this study revisits and optimizes PNCC by removing its medium-time processor and implementing channel energy normalization. Experimental results using a DNN-based speaker verification system demonstrate significant improvements over baseline PNCCs in both in-domain and cross-domain settings, evidenced by maximum lower equal error rates of 5.8% and 61.2% on the VoxCeleb1 and VoxMovies datasets, respectively.

The concept of well-separated pair decomposition (WSPD), introduced by Callahan and Kosaraju in 1995, holds significant importance in computational geometry for addressing distance problems in $d$-space. We introduce an in-browser tool designed to visualize WSPDs and various of their applications within $2$-space. Beyond research purposes, this tool serves as an educational resource for instructors to present WSPDs in classroom environments. The tool will be permanently maintained by the third author at https://wisno33.github.io/VisualizingWSPDsAndTheirApplications/.

This report introduces an algorithm for calculating unknown rates within the sequential processes of a Stochastic Process Algebra model, given the rates of the combined flat model. This rate lifting technique is valuable for model reengineering and repair. The algorithm operates by solving systems of nonlinear equations and, when needed, modifying the model's synchronization structure without altering its transition system. The report includes the complete pseudo-code for this algorithm. The approach leverages specific structural properties of Stochastic Process Algebra systems, which are defined here for the first time and may prove highly useful in other applications.

Estimating the effective reproduction number in near real-time is a critical tool for monitoring pandemic progression and guiding policy decisions and public awareness. Nevertheless, these estimates depend on reported case counts, which often suffer from significant biases. The course of an epidemic is heavily driven by social contact patterns, yet conventional surveillance systems overlook these dynamics because observing them in real time is difficult. In this study, we introduce a framework that integrates online and offline behavioral data to generate daily, age-stratified contact matrices. By modeling the epidemic with these reconstructed matrices, we dynamically calculated the effective reproduction number during the first two waves of the COVID-19 pandemic in Hungary. Our findings illustrate how behavioral data can support alternative monitoring systems that complement existing public health surveillance. These systems are capable of detecting and delivering more reliable signals during periods when official estimates become distorted by observational biases.

A significant portion of chemistry focuses on comprehending, forecasting, and managing strongly localized electrons, with applications ranging from molecular magnetism and luminescence to color centers in crystals, photochemistry, and quantum sensing. Over time, researchers have created a hybrid of robust quantum chemistry techniques, straightforward intuitive frameworks, and phenomenological parameterizations, resulting in increasingly intricate and specialized methods. Despite this growing specialization, a remarkably universal challenge persists: simultaneously describing continuous symmetries, such as spin and orbital angular momentum, alongside discrete symmetries like crystal fields. Accurately modeling these complex systems is becoming increasingly vital for metal ions exhibiting unusual or technologically significant behaviors. Furthermore, developing broad-scope models with physically meaningful parameters offers the potential to enhance interdisciplinary collaboration and enable large-scale meta-analyses. We propose a generalized algorithmic framework called molecular symmetry adapted spin space (mSASS) for localized electronic structure. We derive the Hamiltonian in a symmetry-constrained matrix format, providing an exact accounting of free parameters along with illustrative examples. Although currently in a preliminary implementation stage, a primary advantage of this approach is its ability to handle spatial and spin-orbit symmetries without relying on perturbative approximations. Generally, the mSASS Hamiltonian is large yet finite, allowing for efficient numerical diagonalization. This provides a foundation for conceptual electronic structure models that naturally integrate spin while capitalizing on the intuition and efficiency gains offered by crystallographic symmetry. To facilitate the generation of the mSASS Hamiltonian, we present an implementation within the Mathematica Software Package, GTPack.

Farahat and Higman established the existence of a ``universal'' algebra, denoted $\mathrm{FH}$, which interpolates the centers of symmetric group algebras, $Z(\mathbb{Z}S_n)$. We demonstrate that this algebra is isomorphic to the tensor product $\mathcal{R} \otimes \Lambda$, where $\mathcal{R}$ represents the ring of integer-valued polynomials and $\Lambda$ represents the ring of symmetric functions. This isomorphism, realized through ``evaluation at Jucys-Murphy elements,'' yields character formulae for symmetric groups. Furthermore, we extend this finding to wreath products $\Gamma \wr S_n$ for a fixed finite group $\Gamma$. This extension requires constructing corresponding wreath-product analogues, $\mathcal{R}_\Gamma$ and $\Lambda(\Gamma_*)$, for $\mathcal{R}$ and $\Lambda$, respectively, which possess intrinsic significance (e.g., both are Hopf algebras). We prove that the universal algebra for wreath products, $\mathrm{FH}_\Gamma$, is isomorphic to $\mathcal{R}_\Gamma \otimes \Lambda(\Gamma_*)$ and apply this result to calculate the $p$-blocks of wreath products.

This study aims to enhance the precision of distributed machine learning (ML) models deployed across resource-limited wireless edge devices. It achieves this by jointly optimizing task size allocation and the frequency of local versus global updates to minimize loss, while accounting for the diverse communication and computational capabilities of individual learners. Utilizing established bounds on the gap between current and optimal training loss, the authors formulate the objective function specifically in terms of local update counts. Solving the resulting convex program yields the optimal number of local updates, from which total updates and batch sizes for each learner are determined. The effectiveness of this heterogeneity-aware (HA) approach is demonstrated by comparing its performance against a heterogeneity-unaware (HU) method.

We demonstrate that long-range quantum correlations are sensitive to short-distance physics. Numerical analysis of a discretized, massless scalar field vacuum reveals that two disjoint regions become separable beyond the "negativity sphere," a region that extends infinitely in the continuum limit. The volume of this quantum coherence is dictated by the highest momentum mode present within the identical regions, each having a diameter $d$. More broadly, effective field theories (EFTs) describing a system up to a specific momentum cutoff $\Lambda$ are anticipated to exhibit this trait: vacuum entanglement between regions relies on the ultraviolet (UV) completion beyond a separation distance proportional to $\Lambda$. Extending these calculations to three dimensions, we conjecture that the negativity magnitude at which entanglement becomes sensitive to UV physics in an EFT (whether on a lattice or otherwise) scales approximately as $\sim e^{-\Lambda d}$, regardless of spatial dimensionality. Consequently, it is concluded that vacuum entanglement between two regions at increasing separations depends on the theory's structure at progressively higher momentum scales, a phenomenon that could appear in perturbative QCD processes.

Cross-lingual speech adaptation addresses the challenge of utilizing abundant data from multiple resource-rich languages to develop models for low-resource target languages. Because these target languages have limited training data, speech recognition models are prone to overfitting. This paper introduces the use of adapters to evaluate the efficacy of multiple adapters for parameter-efficient cross-lingual speech adaptation. Building on our prior work, MetaAdapter, which implicitly utilizes adapters, we propose a new algorithm named SimAdapter designed to explicitly learn knowledge from adapters. Our approach leverages adapters that can be seamlessly integrated into Transformer architectures. While MetaAdapter employs meta-learning to transfer general knowledge from training data to the test language, SimAdapter focuses on learning similarities between source and target languages during fine-tuning via adapters. Extensive experiments conducted on five low-resource languages within the Common Voice dataset demonstrate that our MetaAdapter and SimAdapter methods reduce Word Error Rate (WER) by 2.98% and 2.55%, respectively, while using only 2.5% and 15.5% of trainable parameters compared to a strong full-model fine-tuning baseline. Furthermore, we show that integrating these two novel algorithms yields even better performance, achieving up to a 3.55% relative WER reduction.

Stanley's well-known conjecture posits that his chromatic symmetric function can distinguish between all trees. We propose a corresponding quasisymmetric conjecture, asserting that the chromatic quasisymmetric functions defined by Shareshian and Wachs, as well as by Ellzey, distinguish directed trees. This conjecture would follow if the question posed by Hasebe and Tsujie regarding the $P$-partition enumerator distinguishing posets with tree-like Hasse diagrams were answered affirmatively; Hasebe and Tsujie had already established this for rooted trees, and our findings extend their result.

Facial expression recognition (FER) has become a vital element of human-computer interaction. However, despite recent progress, performance frequently degrades when dealing with non-frontal facial images. To address this, we introduce Contrastive Learning of Multi-view facial Expressions (CL-MEx), a method designed to leverage facial images captured from various simultaneous angles for FER. CL-MEx employs a two-stage training process: initially, an encoder is pre-trained using a self-supervised contrastive loss to learn view-invariant embeddings across different perspectives of a subject, followed by fine-tuning in a supervised manner with labeled data. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on two multi-view FER datasets, KDEF and DDCF. Additional experiments confirm the method's robustness against challenging viewing angles and its effectiveness when the amount of labeled data is limited.

Block-structured quadrangular meshes are frequently constructed using cross field generation, where the arrangement of field singularities critically influences the mesh topology. This paper introduces an extension to Ginzburg-Landau cross field generation methods, incorporating a new formulation that enables users to define internal singularities. The cross field is determined by optimizing a linear objective function subject to localized quadratic constraints. This approach involves fixing singularities within small holes created in the computational domain, applying specific degree conditions to the boundaries of these holes to ensure the resulting cross field remains non-singular on the perforated region. Additionally, we propose a method to compute the Ginzburg-Landau energy of these fields on the perforated domain by solving a Neumann linear problem; this energy converges to the standard Ginzburg-Landau functional energy as the parameter epsilon and the hole radii approach zero. To gain insights into the sum of the internal singularity degrees, we provide: (i) an extension of the Ginzburg-Landau energy to piecewise smooth domains, which facilitates the identification of boundary singularity positions and degrees, and (ii) an interpretation of the Poincaré-Hopf theorem specifically centered on internal singularities.

This work examines the division of gapped ground states in (2+1)-dimensional topological liquids into three or more spatially adjacent regions meeting at vertices. By analyzing the reduced density matrix derived from tracing out subsets of these regions, we calculate various correlation metrics, including entanglement negativity, reflected entropy, and their corresponding spectra. Leveraging the bulk-boundary correspondence, we demonstrate that such multipartitions can be realized through vertex states in (1+1)-dimensional conformal field theory; these states, which define interaction vertices in string field theory, serve as a natural generalization of conformal boundary states. This framework enables an explicit construction of the reduced density matrix near entangling boundaries. Our results reveal signatures of topological liquids within these quantities, such as universal scaling components in entanglement negativity and a non-trivial distribution in the spectrum of the partially transposed density matrix. Regarding reflected entropy, we verify a recent hypothesis stating that the difference between reflected entropy and mutual information—after accounting for short-range correlations—equals $(c/3)\ln 2$, where $c$ represents the central charge characterizing ungappable edge degrees of freedom in the topological liquid. As concrete cases, we analyze topological chiral $p$-wave superconductors and Chern insulators. Furthermore, we investigate a specific lattice fermion model that realizes Chern insulator phases, performing numerical calculations of these correlation measures in both gapped phases and at the critical points separating them.

The upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory is poised to detect an order of magnitude more astrophysical transients than any prior survey, creating a photometric data volume that human classifiers alone cannot manage. While recent initiatives have successfully employed machine learning to address astronomical transient classification, transformers—a deep learning architecture originally designed for natural language processing—have recently demonstrated significant potential. This study introduces a novel transformer model centered on multi-head self-attention, specifically tailored for general multi-variate time-series data. This architecture not only accommodates an arbitrary number of additional features but also provides interpretability. Applied to photometric classification, the model reduces dependence on expert domain knowledge for feature selection and matches the performance of current state-of-the-art methods. In a representative setting using data from the Photometric LSST Astronomical Time-Series Classification Challenge (PLAsTiCC), the model achieved a weighted logarithmic loss of 0.507 on imbalanced data. Additionally, it attained a micro-averaged ROC AUC of 0.98 and a micro-averaged PR AUC of 0.87.

Monitoring land use evolution in targeted regions relies heavily on Earth observation. Accurately identifying and defining such changes necessitates the integration of time-series data with pixel-level segmentations. To address this need, we introduce DynamicEarthNet, a dataset comprising daily, multi-spectral satellite imagery from Planet Labs covering 75 globally distributed areas of interest. These observations are paired with monthly semantic segmentation labels at the pixel level for seven land use and land cover (LULC) classes. DynamicEarthNet stands as the inaugural dataset to offer this distinct combination of daily measurements and high-quality annotations. Our experimental evaluation compares various established baselines, including semi-supervised approaches that leverage daily data for additional training and spatio-temporal methods that utilize multiple observations simultaneously, providing a reference for future studies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called SCS, designed to tackle the specific challenges inherent in time-series semantic change segmentation. The dataset is accessible at: https://mediatum.ub.tum.de/1650201.

Determining how UV-faint early galaxies produce and release ionizing photons remains a critical gap in identifying the main agents of reionization. The launch of JWST now allows astronomers to observe rest-frame optical nebular emission from individual sub-L$^*$ galaxies at z > 3, enabling direct measurements of ionizing photon production ($\xi_\mathrm{ion}$). This study analyzes a sample of 380 galaxies at z ~ 3–7, ranging from M$_\mathrm{UV}$ = -23 to -15.5 (median $\approx$ -18), utilizing deep multi-band photometry from HST and JWST/NIRCam that spans the rest-UV to optical wavelengths within the GLASS and UNCOVER surveys. The dataset includes 109 galaxies with detected Lyman-alpha emission from MUSE spectroscopy. By deriving H-alpha fluxes from NIRCam photometry, we estimate the production rate of ionizing photons that are retained within these galaxies, $\xi_\mathrm{ion}(1-f_\mathrm{esc})$. The median value is found to be $\log_{10}\xi_\mathrm{ion}(1-f_\mathrm{esc})=25.33\pm 0.47$, accompanied by a substantial intrinsic scatter of 0.42 dex, indicating diverse properties and ages among these UV-faint systems. Galaxies showing Lyman-alpha emission exhibit $\xi_\mathrm{ion}(1-f_\mathrm{esc})$ values approximately 0.1 dex higher, a trend attributed to their higher H-alpha equivalent width distributions, which signal younger ages, elevated specific star formation rates (sSFR), and a greater abundance of O/B stars. Significant correlations emerge showing that $\xi_\mathrm{ion}(1-f_\mathrm{esc})$ increases with higher H-alpha EW, lower UV luminosity, and flatter UV slopes, suggesting that ionizing photon production is boosted in young, low-metallicity galaxies. Furthermore, based on photometric characteristics, there is no compelling evidence for sources with extremely high ionizing escape fractions ($f_\mathrm{esc}$ > 0.5) in this sample, even among those selected by Lyman-alpha. This research underscores the necessity of examining the full distribution of $\xi_\mathrm{ion}$ across various galaxy properties to properly evaluate the primary drivers of reionization.

Contemporary statistics offers an increasingly vast array of tools for estimating unknown parameters. As a result, applied statisticians often encounter a challenging choice: whether to stick with an estimate from a well-known method or adopt one derived from a newer or more intricate approach. Although comparing estimators via risk is traditional, such comparisons frequently fail to yield definitive conclusions in practical scenarios. To address this, we introduce the "c-value," a metric quantifying the confidence that a new estimate incurs less loss than an existing one on a specific dataset. We demonstrate that it is improbable for a high c-value to coincide with the new estimate suffering greater loss. Consequently, similar to how a small p-value supports rejecting a null hypothesis, a large c-value supports substituting the old estimate with the new. For a broad range of problems and estimators, we detail a method for calculating the c-value by first establishing a data-dependent high-probability lower bound on the loss difference. While the c-value is fundamentally frequentist, we illustrate its utility in validating Bayesian estimates within real-world applications involving hierarchical models and Gaussian processes.

Driven by large-scale datasets and pre-trained architectures, generative modeling has recently seen substantial growth. Nevertheless, the scarcity of datasets for symbolic music poses a constraint on data-driven multimodal models. A promising approach to overcome this limitation is to adapt pre-trained models from other domains, such as natural language, to enhance symbolic music-related multimodal tasks. This paper presents the inaugural investigation into generating complete and semantically coherent symbolic music scores from textual descriptions, evaluating the effectiveness of publicly available natural language processing checkpoints (specifically BERT, GPT-2, and BART) for text-to-music generation. Our experiments demonstrate that utilizing these pre-trained models yields statistically significant improvements in BLEU scores and edit distance similarity. Furthermore, we analyze our model's strengths and weaknesses to gain deeper insights into the potential of language-music integration.

A core challenge in aggregating Markov chains lies in defining the appropriate number of state clusters. An insufficient number of clusters may inadequately represent the dynamics of the original high-order chain, whereas an excessive number results in a non-parsimonious reduced-order model whose complexity nearly matches that of the source. This paper demonstrates that an augmented value-of-information framework effectively determines the optimal count of state groups. This optimum is achieved when the complexity of the reduced-order chain is balanced against the mutual dependence between the dynamics of the original and reduced chains.

This study introduces an end-to-end framework for task-oriented dialog systems based on a Deep Recurrent Q-Network (DRQN) variant. The model interfaces with relational databases to jointly learn policies for language understanding and dialog strategy. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid algorithm that integrates reinforcement learning and supervised learning to accelerate the learning process. Evaluation on a 20 Question Game conversational simulator demonstrates that the proposed method surpasses modular-based baselines and successfully learns a distributed representation of the latent dialog state.

This note presents a partial classification of nearly free conic-line arrangements in the complex plane featuring nodes, tacnodes, and ordinary triple points. Theoretical results indicate that the degree of such arrangements is bounded above by $12$. We demonstrate the existence of examples for degrees $3$ through $7$, while proving that no such arrangements exist for degrees $10$, $11$, and $12$.

Over the past few years, various attitude determination methods leveraging derivative-based optimization algorithms have emerged. However, techniques such as the gradient-descent (GDA), Gauss-Newton (GNA), and Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithms often encounter local optima in practical engineering applications. Recent work \cite{Ahmed2012} briefly addressed the convexity of this issue, concluding that the problem is neither convex nor concave. This paper provides analytical proofs to substantiate these findings. Our results demonstrate that the target loss function is convex under common quaternion normalization practices, thereby ensuring the absence of local optima.

Large-scale medical image analysis (MIA) datasets in real-world settings face three primary challenges: 1) the presence of noisy labels that hinder training convergence and generalization, 2) an imbalanced distribution of samples across classes, and 3) the prevalence of multi-label scenarios where single samples may correspond to multiple diagnoses. While existing methods typically address only a subset of these issues, no current approach simultaneously tackles all three. This paper introduces the Non-Volatile Unbiased Memory (NVUM) module, which utilizes non-volatile storage to maintain running averages of model logits, thereby generating a new regularization loss for noisy multi-label tasks. Additionally, NVUM adjusts classification predictions during its update process to mitigate imbalanced learning. We conducted extensive experiments on novel benchmarks introduced in this study, training on noisy, multi-label, and imbalanced chest X-ray (CXR) datasets derived from Chest-Xray14 and CheXpert, while testing on clean multi-label CXR datasets such as OpenI and PadChest. Our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art CXR classifiers and other approaches capable of handling noisy labels across all evaluations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/FBLADL/NVUM.

A time-changed mixed fractional Brownian motion is defined as an iterated process formed by superimposing mixed fractional Brownian motion with another process. This paper examines a mixed fractional Brownian motion characterized by parameters $a$, $b$, and $H \in (0, 1)$, which is time-changed using gamma and tempered stable subordinators. We outline their primary characteristics, with a specific focus on long-range dependence. Our findings indicate that the resulting time-changed fractional Brownian motion exhibits long-range dependence for all values of $H$ within the interval $(0, 1)$.

This study examines particle generation in the Schwinger model interacting with an external classical source. The issue can be addressed by leveraging the fact that the fully quantized model is solvable and equivalent to a massive gauge field possessing a non-local effective action, or alternatively by employing the standard semiclassical method. The latter involves quantizing the massless Dirac field while treating the electromagnetic field as a classical background. We calculate the energy produced by a general, homogeneous, and time-varying source, finding that the results from both methods align exactly. This provides a direct and efficient validation of the semiclassical approach for the massless Schwinger model, consistent with earlier analyses using linear response equations. Our findings suggest that a comparable study of the massive Schwinger model could serve as a significant testing ground for comparing a fully quantized solvable model against its semiclassical approximation, effectively replicating the enduring comparison between quantum gravity and quantum field theory in curved spacetime.

Utilizing localization techniques, we calculate the partition function for $\mathcal N=2$ supersymmetric mixed-dimensional QED defined on a squashed hemisphere. This abelian gauge theory includes charged matter fields localized at the boundary. The resulting partition function depends on the complex gauge coupling $\tau$, the specific R-symmetry chosen, and the squashing deformation. The 3-dimensional superconformal R-symmetry is identified through F-maximization. By analyzing the free energy's dependence on the squashing parameter, we can derive correlation functions involving the energy-momentum tensor insertion. Specifically, we determine the 2-point correlation function of the boundary energy-momentum tensor by differentiating the free energy with respect to the squashing parameter, and we discuss how this 2-point function evolves as the complex coupling $\tau$ varies.

Conventional methods for detecting magnetic signals in experiments typically involve complex electronic setups to monitor feedback from superconducting transitions induced by external magnetic fields. This direct detection approach is notably time-consuming, particularly in experiments requiring strict conditions such as low temperatures and high vacuums. To streamline the realization of signal detection, we have developed a novel sample stage capable of both positioning and accepting magnetic fields, utilizing the mirror image method. The apparatus comprises two components: drive coils and receiver coils. The drive coils generate the initial magnetic field applied to the superconducting material, while the receiver coils capture the resulting magnetic signal feedback. By requiring only a power supply and a signal amplifier for the coils, our device significantly simplifies the magnetic signal detection process. A key advantage of this design is the use of first-principles numerical simulations to accurately determine the device's dimensions and parameters. Based on these calculated values, a 3D model of the device was constructed using SOLIDWORKS software.

Quantum phase transitions are a pervasive feature of quantum many-body systems, where low-temperature quantum fluctuations drive transitions between different phases as an external control parameter is varied. The XY Hamiltonian with a transverse field serves as a fundamental model exhibiting two distinct quantum phase transitions, notably the spontaneous breaking of $Z_2$ symmetry as the system shifts from an ordered to a disordered state. While programmable quantum devices have proven effective in exploring exotic quantum phases, there is a concurrent effort to leverage machine learning for identifying these phases. This paper presents a numerical investigation into the capabilities of the Born machine, a quantum-inspired generative model, for learning quantum phases. We analyze data from the system under both open and periodic boundary conditions. Our findings demonstrate that a Born machine utilizing matrix product states can accurately capture the quantum state across various phases of the XY Hamiltonian and near critical points, even in the presence of long-range correlations. Furthermore, we apply boundary conditions to the Born machine and find that aligning these conditions with those of the training data enhances performance when limited data and a small bond dimension are used.

As experiments increasingly aim to detect primordial CMB B-modes, the number of potentially significant astrophysical contaminants grows. For instance, thermal radiation from interplanetary dust, known as Zodiacal or interplanetary dust emission (IPDE), has been observed by the Planck satellite. Although the polarization fraction of this emission is anticipated to be low, its total power is sufficiently bright to be detected. This study estimates the magnitude of such effects as they might appear to the LiteBIRD satellite. By combining the COBE IPDE model from Kelsall et al. (1998) with a simulation of LiteBIRD's scanning strategy, we assess potential contamination in both total power and polarization power spectra. LiteBIRD is expected to detect IPDE in temperature across all its frequency bands, ranging from 40 to 402 GHz, and to tighten constraints on the polarization fraction of IPDE at higher frequencies. If the IPDE polarization fraction is around 1%, matching current mid-infrared limits from ISO/CAM, it could generate large-scale polarization B-modes comparable to cosmological models with an r value of approximately 0.001. Under such conditions, the polarized IPDE must be modeled and subtracted. While IPDE will remain a subdominant foreground compared to Galactic emissions, its origin in dust grains closer to Earth means it varies as Earth orbits the Sun, potentially complicating data analysis. However, by leveraging known symmetries in the emission and employing flexible data processing techniques, IPDE should not become a primary obstacle to measuring CMB polarization.

We introduce a novel image restoration framework grounded in minimized surface regularization, which draws a strong parallel to the classical smoothing ROF model \cite{4}. By reformulating the approach as a min-max optimization problem, we solve it via the primal-dual algorithm. Leveraging convex conjugates, we also establish the algorithm's convergence. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the method's efficacy by comparing its CPU efficiency and restoration quality against established techniques.

This study demonstrates that a decaying neutralino within a supergravity unified framework serves as a viable dark matter candidate. This scenario emerges in a hidden sector with ultraweak interactions to the visible sector, allowing the neutralino to decay into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) with a lifetime exceeding that of the universe. We introduce a specific model extending MSSM/SUGRA with a hidden sector featuring $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ gauge symmetries, where the hidden sector LSP is a neutralino lighter than its visible sector counterpart. We calculate the loop-suppressed radiative decay of the visible neutralino into the hidden neutralino, confirming that the resulting lifetime surpasses the age of the universe. This decaying neutralino is detectable through indirect observation, particularly via its signature decay producing a hidden neutralino and an energetic gamma-ray photon. Such gamma rays can be targeted with enhanced sensitivity by Fermi-LAT, the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), and the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). Additionally, we provide several benchmark scenarios that naturally suppress hadronic channels from dark matter annihilation and decays, remaining consistent with antiproton background measurements.

Estimating population size from incomplete lists, known as the capture-recapture problem, has a longstanding presence in various biological and social disciplines. For instance, organizations focused on human rights frequently compile partial and overlapping records of armed conflict victims to infer the total count. Previous statistical approaches for this scenario either relied on restrictive parametric assumptions or suboptimal plug-in nonparametric estimators; both strategies often resulted in significant bias, the former due to model misspecification and the latter due to smoothing issues. Assuming conditional independence between two lists given observed covariates, this study offers several key advances. First, we establish the nonparametric efficiency bound for estimating capture probability, revealing the theoretical limits and optimal performance for any such estimator. Second, we introduce a novel estimator and analyze its finite-sample behavior, demonstrating that it possesses a double robustness property unique to capture-recapture methods and achieves near-optimality in a non-asymptotic framework under mild nonparametric conditions. Third, we provide a procedure for constructing confidence intervals for total population size using generic capture probability estimators, proving their non-asymptotic near-validity. Finally, through simulations and an application to estimating killings and disappearances in Peru during its 1980–2000 internal armed conflict, we evaluate the proposed methods.

Microtubule behavior in motility assays demonstrates that motor-generated piconewton forces are capable of bending filaments. In biological processes like cytoplasmic streaming, motors move along cytoskeletal tracks while transporting cargo that drags surrounding fluid. When numerous such filaments interact hydrodynamically—as seen in specific phases of *Drosophila melanogaster* oocyte development—complex dynamics emerge, though their precise mechanical basis has been elusive. To address this, we examine a foundational model: an elastic filament anchored at one end and subjected to a molecular motor modeled as a point force. Since this force remains tangential to the filament regardless of its curvature, the resulting "follower-force" problem is inherently non-variational and distinct from Euler buckling, where a fixed-direction force yields a stationary, energy-minimizing shape in the low Reynolds number regime. By integrating linear stability analysis, an analytical investigation of a simplified "two-link" system, and numerical simulations of the complete elastohydrodynamic equations, we clarify the Hopf bifurcation that arises as forcing increases. This transition leads to flapping motions similar to the high Reynolds number oscillations observed in a garden hose with a free end.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly transformed numerous facets of daily life, particularly social interactions. Amidst widespread lockdowns in major cities worldwide, there has been a significant surge in both personal and professional engagement on social media platforms. These platforms now play a pivotal role in disseminating news and maintaining connectivity. However, they present a dual nature; while beneficial, they also fuel a concerning "infodemic" regarding the virus, necessitating focused attention and further investigation. This paper introduces a multilingual Instagram dataset focused on coronavirus content, which has been continuously gathered since March 30, 2020. We have made this dataset publicly accessible via Github for the research community. We anticipate that this contribution will aid in understanding the dynamics of the phenomenon on Instagram, a leading social media platform, and will also support studies on the spread of misinformation related to the outbreak.

This study investigates how thermodynamic length can enhance experimental procedures. Specifically, we apply Landauer erasure to a driven electron level within a semiconductor quantum dot, contrasting a standard protocol that linearly increases energy over time against one derived from geometric optimization. This optimized approach is achieved by selecting an appropriate metric structure, where geodesics represent optimal finite-time thermodynamic protocols under slow driving conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that geodesic driving minimizes dissipation in slow protocols, yielding greater improvements as the system approaches perfect erasure. Furthermore, the geometric method reduces dissipation even when protocol duration approaches the system's equilibration timescale, extending benefits beyond the slow driving regime. Additionally, our findings in a single-electron device illustrate a core principle of thermodynamic geometry: optimal finite-time protocols maintain a constant dissipation rate throughout the process.

Introducing magnetic dopants into topological quantum materials offers a promising pathway to investigate time-reversal symmetry breaking. Guided by this motivation, we examined the incorporation of the transition metal Mn into molecular beam epitaxy-grown thin films of the Dirac semimetal Cd3As2. Scanning transmission electron microscopy revealed the formation of Mn-rich phases at the surface of both uniformly and delta-doped Cd3As2 films, indicating that Mn functions as a surfactant during epitaxial growth and induces phase separation. Magnetometry data confirm a ferromagnetic phase with out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy in these samples.
