Electrical magneto-transport measurements, conducted across varying temperatures, magnetic fields, and chemical potentials, demonstrate that the doped films exhibit lower carrier densities and higher electron mobility than pristine Cd3As2 films grown under comparable conditions, suggesting that the surfactant effect may also facilitate the removal of impurities. Furthermore, robust quantum transport phenomena, including Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations and an emerging integer quantum Hall effect, were observed in extremely thin (7 nm) Cd3As2 films, even while in direct contact with a structurally disordered ferromagnetic overlayer.

In recommender systems, data representation techniques are pivotal because they can expose, obscure, or entangle the explanatory factors hidden within datasets, directly impacting recommendation quality. Specifically, Visual Art (VA) recommendation is challenging for machines due to the intricate concepts embedded in paintings, often leading systems to rely on manually curated metadata. While recent efforts aim to utilize visual features from Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), these methods are resource-intensive and lack direct interpretability, which hampers user adoption. To overcome these issues, we propose a personalized Visual Art recommendation approach grounded in learning latent semantic representations of paintings. By training a Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model on textual painting descriptions, we successfully reveal non-obvious semantic connections between artworks while providing explainable recommendations. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms approaches relying on visual features extracted by pre-trained DNNs.

DBpedia stands as one of the earliest and most significant nodes within the Linked Open Data cloud, offering structured data for over 100 Wikipedia language editions and Wikimedia Commons, supported by a mature ontology and a stable, comprehensive Linked Data publishing lifecycle. In contrast, Wikidata has recently emerged as a user-curated source of structured information integrated into Wikipedia. This paper details the integration of Wikidata into the DBpedia ecosystem. Incorporating structured Wikidata data into DBpedia enhances various usage scenarios; we outline these scenarios and describe the architecture and conversion process of the DBpediaWikidata dataset.

MAXI J1816-195, a recently identified accreting millisecond pulsar characterized by frequent thermonuclear bursts, was observed during its June 2022 outburst by Insight-HXMT and NICER. During the peak and decay phases, Insight-HXMT recorded 73 bursts, confirming the system's status as a prolific burst emitter among accreting millisecond pulsars. Analysis of a single burst simultaneously detected by both instruments revealed a slight deviation from the standard blackbody model. Furthermore, stacking the Insight-HXMT lightcurves of 66 bursts with comparable profiles and intensities uncovered a hard X-ray deficit with a significance of 15.7 sigma within the 30–100 keV range. This shortage, amounting to approximately 30% of the persistent flux, is notably lower than that observed in other bursters and exhibits an energy-dependent trend, being more pronounced at higher energies. These characteristics distinguish MAXI J1816-195 as a unique system compared to other millisecond pulsars and atoll bursters. Additionally, utilizing the brightest burst, we established an upper distance limit of 6.3 kpc, leading to an estimated upper limit for the inner accretion disc radius of roughly 40 km. Treating this radius as the magnetospheric boundary yields a derived magnetic field strength of approximately 7.1 × 10^8 G.

This study constructs a phase space framework to facilitate the analysis, classification, and comparison of extensive classes of static, spherically symmetric wormhole solutions in General Relativity, which are supported by isotropic perfect fluids. Within this phase space, we identify the positions of equilibrium points, throats, and curvature singularities. The analysis of throat locations reveals that the spatial variation of gravitational redshift at the throat invariably diverges, thereby generalizing the finding that no such wormhole can exist with zero tidal force. Several specific models are examined; notably, a vanishing density model yields an exact field equation solution that validates the dynamical system formalism and demonstrates its extension to static black holes, specifically determining the Schwarzschild black hole's trajectory. Furthermore, solutions for various isotropic dark energy models (including generalised Chaplygin gas, constant, linear, and Chevallier-Polarski-Linder equations of state) and dark matter models (Navarro-Frenk-White profile) are investigated. These exhibit diverse behaviors far from the throat, such as singularities, spatial flatness, and cyclic dynamics, yet none are asymptotically Minkowski flat, suggesting that static, spherically symmetric, and isotropic wormholes cannot naturally form from these dark fluids. Finally, we present a toy model of an asymptotically Minkowski flat wormhole, serving as a counterexample to a recent theorem asserting that a static wormhole sustained by an isotropic fluid cannot be asymptotically flat on both sides of its throat.

This paper introduces the concept of Bol algebra representations. We establish an analogue of the classical Engel's theorem and extend the Ado-Iwasawa theorem to the context of Bol Algebras. Additionally, we examine the category of Bol algebra representations, demonstrating that it possesses the structure of a tensor category. Furthermore, for regular representations, we provide a comprehensive classification for all two-dimensional Bol algebras.

The hypothesis that millisecond magnetars drive gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) has gained significant traction due to their profound impact on GRB afterglows. This study examines how such a magnetar engine influences the supernova (SN) emission linked to long GRBs, specifically testing the model against the observational data of SN 2006aj/GRB 060218. Distinguished by its striking double-peaked ultraviolet-optical (UV-opt) light curves, SN 2006aj serves as the focal point. Our analysis of these light curves reveals that the initial peak is effectively explained by shock breakout emission driven by the magnetar wind, while the primary supernova emission receives partial power from magnetar energy injection. The derived magnetic field strength of approximately $10^{15}$ G aligns well with standard inferences from long GRB afterglows. Furthermore, we propose that late-time UV excess in the supernova may result from non-thermal pulsar wind nebula (PWN) leakage, provided specific conditions are met. The strong agreement between our model and the SN 2006aj observations suggests that magnetar engines are likely ubiquitous in GRB phenomena and may strengthen the link between GRBs and superluminous supernovae.

While ionization electron diffusion in Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (LArTPCs) has traditionally been addressed during the detector design phase, its influence on calibration and particle identification has largely been overlooked. This study employs a GEANT4-based simulation to investigate how diffusion affects these processes and examines the simulation methodologies involved. Our findings reveal that diffusion introduces a drift-dependent bias into both the median and the Most Probable Value (MPV) of charge deposition per unit length distributions. For typical maximum drift times in currently operating LArTPCs, this bias is estimated at approximately 2.5% for the median and 5.0% for the MPV, prior to accounting for detector-specific factors like electric field non-uniformities. Consequently, these metrics should not be applied to calibration without caution, challenging conventional wisdom. Furthermore, diffusion has a negligible impact on the ability to distinguish muons from protons and is unlikely to cause issues in future detectors. However, it may represent a significant source of systematic uncertainty when separating particles with similar masses, such as muons and pions or kaons and protons. Implementing drift-time dependent particle identification could enhance the separation of such populations.

As laser peak power rises, conventional solid-state optics struggle to generate and manipulate high-power pulses due to their low damage thresholds, making plasma-based optical components—capable of withstanding extreme fields—increasingly attractive. We introduce a plasma waveplate utilizing magneto-optical birefringence under a transverse magnetic field, designed to operate under ultra-high laser intensities. Uniquely, this device not only modifies the polarization state but also amplifies peak laser power. Numerical simulations demonstrate that a centimeter-scale waveplate can convert an initially linearly polarized pulse with 5 petawatts (PW) of peak power into a circularly polarized pulse exceeding 10 PW, achieving approximately 98% energy conversion efficiency for polarization transformation. The required thickness of the waveplate scales inversely with both the plasma electron density ($n_e$) and the square of the magnetic field ($B_0^2$); for conditions of $n_e=3\times 10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $B_0=100$ T, the thickness is roughly 1 cm. This proposed plasma waveplate, alongside other plasma-based optical elements, is poised to be critical for the efficient deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems.

The swift incorporation of variable renewable energy sources (VRES) into electrical grids heightens the variability and uncertainty of net demand, thereby complicating power system operations. To mitigate these challenges, system operators utilize operating reserves. Historically, reserve needs have been established using static rules of thumb, such as NERC Reliability Standards, whereas recent developments include dynamic methods like DynADOR, DRD, and RESERVE currently in the adoption phase. Although these newer tools enhance traditional static approaches, they depend solely on deterministic data (best-case estimates) and overlook probabilistic uncertainty thresholds linked to specific daily weather conditions. This study introduces practical methodologies for calculating operating reserve requirements by harnessing data from probabilistic forecasts. Validated against real-world data from the CAISO system, the results demonstrate that integrating probabilistic forecast information into the reserve dimensioning process yields significant risk reduction benefits.

Q-learning, a model-free approach aimed at discovering the optimal Q-function for a Markov decision process (MDP), is central to reinforcement learning. In the synchronous setting, where independent samples for all state-action pairs are generated in each iteration, significant strides have been made in analyzing Q-learning's sample efficiency. For a $\gamma$-discounted infinite-horizon MDP with state space $\mathcal{S}$ and action space $\mathcal{A}$, current theory suggests that achieving an entrywise $\varepsilon$-approximation of the optimal Q-function demands a sample size on the order of $\frac{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}{(1-\gamma)^5\varepsilon^{2}}$, a figure that does not align with existing minimax lower bounds. This discrepancy raises key inquiries regarding the sharp sample complexity of Q-learning and whether it is provably sub-optimal. This work addresses these issues within the synchronous framework by demonstrating two main results: (1) when $|\mathcal{A}|=1$, reducing Q-learning to temporal difference (TD) learning, the sample complexity is shown to be minimax optimal, scaling as $\frac{|\mathcal{S}|}{(1-\gamma)^3\varepsilon^2}$ (up to logarithmic factors); (2) when $|\mathcal{A}|\geq 2$, the sample complexity is established as approximately $\frac{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}{(1-\gamma)^4\varepsilon^2}$ (up to logarithmic factors). These findings confirm the strict sub-optimality of Q-learning for $|\mathcal{A}|\geq 2$ and formally validate the detrimental effects of over-estimation. Furthermore, the analysis is extended to asynchronous Q-learning utilizing Markovian samples, refining the horizon dependency of its sample complexity to $\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^4}$.

Intermetallic silicides such as LaScSi and Y$_5$Si$_3$, recognized for their potential as hydrogen storage media, are gaining interest as candidates for electrides where anions are replaced by unbound electrons. Muon spin rotation experiments suggest that the local field at the muon site—coincident with the hydrogen site—experiences a significant negative shift under external magnetic fields that remains largely temperature-independent. This anomalous diamagnetism indicates a distinctive characteristic of electride electrons linked to transition metals. Furthermore, the reduction in diamagnetic shift with higher hydrogen content implies that the electride electrons, which exist coherently in hollow interstitial sites, are captured by hydrogen to create hydride ions (H$^-$).

Software Energy Consumption (SEC) is increasingly attracting attention. This paper addresses the challenge of informing developers about their programs' SEC within Continuous Integration (CI) environments. We explore whether CI systems can utilize developers' existing tests to introduce a novel testing category: energy regression testing. Unlike traditional performance regression, which focuses on metrics like execution time or memory usage, energy regression specifically targets energy consumption. We propose an exploratory study to examine the viability of using developer tests for this purpose. First, we investigate if these tests can yield stable SEC indicators. Second, we assess whether comparing the SEC of tests across two versions can accurately detect energy regressions caused by automated program mutations. Finally, we evaluate the capability to identify the specific lines of code responsible for these regressions. Ultimately, this research aims to lay the groundwork for automated SEC regression tools that can be easily integrated into current CI infrastructures to heighten practitioner awareness of energy efficiency issues.

Recent investigations using the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method have explored a single-hole ground state Ansatz for the two-dimensional t-J model, revealing that the doped hole acts as a "twisted" non-Landau quasiparticle with an emergent quantum number, consistent with exact numerical results. Extending this work, we applied VMC to the two-hole ground state and discovered that these holes experience strong mutual attraction, forming a pairing state characterized by a new quantum number that aligns with findings from exact diagonalization and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) studies. A distinctive aspect of this pairing is its symmetry dichotomy: it exhibits d-wave symmetry regarding electron creation operators but s-wave symmetry concerning the new quasiparticles, a feature clearly evident in the ground state wave function. A comparable VMC analysis of a two-hole wave function in the t-J two-leg ladder also demonstrates strong agreement with DMRG outcomes. We establish that the mechanism driving this strong binding is not attributable to long-range antiferromagnetic order or resonating-valence-bond pairing within the spin background; rather, it arises from quantum phase-strings generated by hole hopping. The VMC calculation explicitly visualizes the spin-current pattern that mediates this pairing force, and the physical implications for superconductivity at finite doping are also examined.

This study re-examines the search for a nonzero tau electric dipole form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, by employing optimal observables in $e^+ e^-$ collisions producing $\tau^+\tau^-$ pairs across the center-of-mass energy range from the $\tau$-pair threshold up to approximately $\sqrt{s} \sim 15$ GeV. We outline the general framework of optimal observables and apply it to two $CP$-odd quantities sensitive to the real and imaginary components of $d_\tau(s)$, respectively. Calculations of the expectation values and covariances for these optimal $CP$ observables are performed for $\tau$-pair production at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV, considering subsequent $\tau^\pm$ decays into major leptonic or semihadronic channels. Full kinematic information is utilized for $\tau$ decays involving two pions or three charged pions. Under the assumption that the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator will eventually process data with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$, and applying acceptance cuts on final-state pions, we determine that 1~s.d. sensitivities of $\delta {\rm Re} d_\tau = 6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $\delta {\rm} Im d_\tau = 4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm are achievable using events where both taus decay semihadronically. In an ideal scenario without final-state particle cuts, utilizing 50 ab$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV (equivalent to $4.5 \times 10^{10}$ $\tau^+ \tau^-$ events), we find 1 s.d. sensitivities of $\delta {\rm Re} d_\tau = 5.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $\delta {\rm} Im d_\tau = 3.2 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm for events with semihadronic decays of both $\tau$ leptons. Additionally, we investigate the potential magnitude of the $\tau$ EDM form factor within the type-II two-Higgs doublet model and in two scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model.

We report ALMA Band 5 observations targeting the galaxy GDS24569 at redshift $z=1.91$, aimed at detecting molecular gas through the [C I] $^3$P$_1$-$^3$P$_0$ transition. GDS24569 is a massive ($\log M_*/M_\odot=11$), passively evolving system with a compact morphology and an effective radius of approximately $0.5$ kpc. By applying two blind detection algorithms to the spectral data cubes, we found no significant [C I] signal within or around GDS24569 out to a projected distance of $\sim320$ kpc, aside from a narrow, tentative detection ($4.1 \sigma$) at $+1200$ km/s from one algorithm. The absence of a confirmed [C I] line allows us to set a $3\sigma$ upper limit on the molecular hydrogen mass at $\sim 7.1 \times 10^9 M_\odot$, implying an exceptionally low gas-to-stellar mass fraction of less than $5 \%$. Modeling the spectral energy distribution across optical to far-infrared wavelengths reveals a notably high dust-to-stellar mass ratio of $\sim0.1\%$, which is roughly $10$ to $100$ times greater than that of local early-type galaxies. Combined with prior findings of a lack of surrounding satellite galaxies, these results suggest that GDS24569 has not undergone substantial size evolution through satellite mergers. Finally, we explore potential physical mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in this galaxy.

We introduce LEAR (Lexical Entailment Attract-Repel), an innovative post-processing technique designed to reshape input word vector spaces to highlight the asymmetric nature of lexical entailment (LE), commonly referred to as hyponymy-hypernymy or IS-A relations. By integrating external linguistic constraints, such as WordNet connections, into the original vector space, the LE specialization process draws genuine hyponymy-hypernymy pairs closer within the transformed Euclidean space. Furthermore, the proposed asymmetric distance metric modifies word vector norms to mirror the actual WordNet-style conceptual hierarchy. Concurrently, a shared objective maintains semantic similarity through symmetric cosine distance, resulting in a vector space optimized for both lexical relations simultaneously. LEAR specialization attains state-of-the-art results in hypernymy directionality, hypernymy detection, and graded lexical entailment tasks, underscoring the efficacy and resilience of this asymmetric specialization model.

The importance of detecting hypergraphic planted cliques (HPC) lies in its role in exploring the computational difficulty of various tensor problems. We seek to determine whether further evidence supporting the inherent hardness of HPC detection can be gathered. Specifically, we hypothesize that the computational hardness of HPC detection might be equivalent to that of standard planted clique (PC) detection.

Ensuring the stability of contemporary power grids is growing increasingly challenging due to erratic demand, the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources, and unforeseen incidents ranging from natural disasters to human errors. To address these issues, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been adopted for sequential decision-making in grid management, requiring operations to account for long-term stability impacts. Nevertheless, current approaches often overlook environmental constraints, posing a risk that learned policies may choose actions violating these limits during emergencies. Such violations can exacerbate power line overloads and trigger widespread blackouts. This study introduces a novel solution built upon search-based planning algorithms. During the planning phase, the search space is restricted to actions generated by the policy, with each candidate strictly validated against constraints using the system's simulation function. To overcome the inability to propagate gradients to the policy during training, we integrate Evolutionary Strategies (ES) for black-box policy optimization, directly enhancing the policy to maximize long-term returns. Our approach successfully secured the top rank in both tracks of the NeurIPS 2020 Learning to Run Power Network (L2RPN) competition by safely managing the power grid.

This work introduces the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) equations and the Y-system to determine the exact spectrum of general multi-magnon local operators within the $D$-dimensional anisotropic bi-scalar fishnet conformal field theory. The mixing matrix for these operators is expressed using fishnet planar graphs characterized by multi-wheel and multi-spiral configurations. These graphs investigate the two fundamental components of the TBA method: the magnon dispersion relation and the magnon scattering matrix, both of which are derived by diagonalizing specific graph-building operators. Furthermore, we derive the dual form of the TBA equations, which establishes a correspondence in the continuum limit between $D$-dimensional graphs and two-dimensional sigma models defined on $AdS_{D+1}$. This dual formulation enables the verification of a general expression for the critical coupling originally proposed by A. Zamolodchikov.

The emergence of contextualized language models has significantly improved search performance, not only by re-ranking results from classical methods like BM25 but also by enabling dense retrieval, a technique where models handle passage indexing and retrieval directly. Current research in neural ranking identifies two primary approaches to dense retrieval: single representation, which encodes entire passages into one embedding (often using BERT's [CLS] token, as seen in ANCE), and multiple representation, which generates a unique embedding for each token within a passage (exemplified by ColBERT). Despite their prominence, these two families have not been directly compared. Given the critical role dense retrieval will play in the future, understanding their respective strengths and weaknesses is essential. This paper addresses this gap by providing a direct comparative analysis, identifying scenarios where each method outperforms or underperforms relative to the other and against a BM25 baseline. Our findings indicate that while ANCE is more resource-efficient than ColBERT regarding memory and response time, multiple representations yield statistically superior results for Mean Average Precision (MAP) and MRR@10. Furthermore, multiple representations demonstrate greater improvement over single representations for the most challenging BM25 queries, definitional queries, and those involving complex information needs.

Despite significant advancements in deep face recognition, concerns regarding skin-tone-based discrimination have hindered their practical adoption. This paper presents a systematic and scientific investigation into such biases from both data and algorithmic perspectives. First, we introduce the Identity Shades (IDS) database, a benchmark utilizing the dermatologist-validated Fitzpatrick Skin Type classification and the Individual Typology Angle to quantify existing biases in face recognition algorithms and commercial APIs. Additionally, we offer two skin-tone-aware training datasets, BUPT-Globalface and BUPT-Balancedface, designed to eliminate bias within training data. To address algorithmic bias, we propose Meta Balanced Network (MBN), a novel meta-learning approach that learns adaptive margins for large margin loss, enabling fair performance across individuals with varying skin tones. By optimizing a meta skewness loss on an unbiased meta set and employing backward-on-backward automatic differentiation for second-order gradient descent, our method effectively determines these margins. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MBN successfully reduces bias, achieving more balanced recognition performance across different skin tones. The proposed datasets are accessible at http://www.whdeng.cn/RFW/index.html.
The phenomenology of neutrino oscillations is concisely reviewed, along with an examination of late Professor Masatoshi Koshiba's contributions to this field from a phenomenological perspective.

We present a structural theorem for pseudofinite groups with finite centraliser dimension. Consequently, it follows that no finitely generated pseudofinite group can possess finite centraliser dimension.

Online optimization is a mature framework designed to generate a series of accurate decisions by utilizing information from past correct answers. In contrast, bilevel programming addresses hierarchical optimization where the feasible region of the outer problem is constrained by the solution set mapping of the inner problem. This work unifies these concepts by investigating an online bilevel optimization framework where a succession of time-varying bilevel problems is revealed sequentially. We generalize existing regret bounds for single-level online algorithms to this bilevel context. Specifically, we define novel concepts of bilevel regret, propose an online alternating time-averaged gradient method that exploits smoothness properties, and establish regret bounds dependent on the path-lengths of the inner and outer minimizer sequences.

Recent years have witnessed substantial progress in precision medicine, particularly in developing algorithms for Individualized Treatment Rules (ITR) that map patient characteristics to treatment options to optimize outcomes. While Direct Learning (D-Learning) offers a one-step approach to estimate ITRs by modeling treatment-covariate interactions directly, it fails to account for heterogeneous outcome variance relative to treatments and covariates. To address this, this paper introduces Stabilized Direct Learning (SD-Learning), a method that capitalizes on potential heteroscedasticity in the error term through residual reweighting. This approach models residual variance using flexible machine learning tools like XGBoost and random forests. Additionally, an internal cross-validation framework is established to select the optimal residual model among various candidates. SD-Learning enhances the efficiency of D-Learning estimates in both binary and multi-arm treatment settings. It is straightforward to implement and serves as an effective way to upgrade existing D-Learning algorithms, such as original D-Learning, Angle-based D-Learning (AD-Learning), and Robust D-Learning (RD-Learning). Theoretical properties and justification for the optimality of SD-Learning are provided. Simulation studies comparing SD-Learning head-to-head with D-Learning methods demonstrate superior performance in terms of average prediction error (APE), misclassification rate, and empirical value, further supported by data analysis of an AIDS randomized clinical trial.

This paper introduces a novel method for constructing graph neural networks using framelet transforms, which offer a multi-scale representation for graph-structured data. By decomposing input graphs into low-pass and high-pass frequency coefficients for training, we define a framelet-based graph convolution. This decomposition naturally facilitates a graph pooling strategy that aggregates features into low-pass and high-pass spectra, accounting for both feature values and geometric properties while conserving total information. Graph neural networks employing this proposed convolution and pooling achieve state-of-the-art results in various node and graph prediction tasks. Furthermore, we introduce shrinkage as a new activation function for framelet convolution, which thresholds high-frequency information across different scales. Compared to ReLU, the shrinkage activation enhances performance in denoising and signal compression; it significantly reduces noise in both nodes and structure by accurately eliminating high-pass coefficients from the framelet decomposition, while compressing the signal to less than half its original size with well-maintained prediction accuracy.

We present and analyze "2-roots," defined as symmetrized tensor products of orthogonal roots within Kac–Moody algebras. Our focus is on the scenario where $W$ represents the Weyl group of a simply laced, Y-shaped Dynkin diagram $Y_{a,b,c}$ with $n$ vertices and three branches of arbitrary finite lengths $a$, $b$, and $c$; this framework encompasses types $D_n$, $E_n$ (for $n \geq 6$), and the affine types $E_6$, $E_7$, and $E_8$. We demonstrate that a specific natural codimension-$1$ submodule $M$ of the symmetric square of the reflection representation of $W$ possesses a remarkable canonical basis $\mathcal{B}$ composed entirely of 2-roots. We conjecture that relative to $\mathcal{B}$, every element of $W$ corresponds to a column sign-coherent matrix, a concept from cluster algebras, and we provide proofs for this conjecture in both finite and affine contexts. For finite simply laced Weyl groups, we show that each $W$-orbit of 2-roots contains a highest element, analogous to the highest root, and we compute these elements explicitly. Furthermore, we establish that if $W$ is not of affine type, the module $M$ is completely reducible in characteristic zero, with each nontrivial direct summand being spanned by a $W$-orbit of 2-roots.

This research investigates fairness in dynamic resource allocation using the $\alpha$-fairness criterion, focusing on two distinct objectives: the conventional slot-fairness approach, which ensures equity at each timeslot, and the underexplored horizon-fairness approach, which guarantees fairness across utilities accumulated over a time horizon. We contend that horizon-fairness yields superior social welfare compared to slot-fairness. Evaluating horizon-fairness through the lens of regret, we demonstrate that vanishing regret is unattainable against an unrestricted adversary. However, by imposing realistic constraints on the adversary's capabilities, we develop an online policy that successfully achieves vanishing regret. Finally, we validate the proposed fairness framework by applying it to a representative resource management scenario involving a virtualized caching system where multiple caches collaborate to fulfill content requests.

Structural optimization, encompassing topology, shape, and sizing, serves as a vital instrument for fostering innovative structural design concepts. Conventionally, topology optimization occurs early in the design process, followed by sequential shape and sizing adjustments. Unlike traditional implicit topology methods, explicit approaches have gained significant interest for their ability to streamline expensive CAD/CAE workflows while utilizing a reduced set of design variables compared to techniques like SIMP. This study introduces an adaptation of the Moving Node Approach (MNA) for topology optimization. By decoupling discretization from material distribution, the method seeks to identify the optimal beam assembly while minimizing compliance. This paradigm shift employs novel design variables—including node positions, element dimensions and orientations, and sizes—resulting in fewer variables than pixel-based methods. The proposed methodology is validated through two classic topology optimization benchmarks: the cantilever beam and the L-shaped structure.

This study investigates the spin and lattice dynamics of ferromagnetic nanoparticles using molecular dynamics and semi-classical spin dynamics simulations, coupling spin and lattice degrees of freedom through a dynamic uniaxial anisotropy term. The model is demonstrated to conserve total angular momentum, although individual spin and lattice angular momenta are not conserved. Simulations of the Einstein-de Haas effect were performed on a freely rotating Fe nanocluster containing over 500 atoms using a modified open-source code called SPILADY. Results indicate that the rate of angular momentum transfer between the spin and lattice is directly proportional to the strength of the magnetic anisotropy interaction. Incorporating this anisotropy enables complete spin-lattice relaxation within previously reported timescales of approximately 100 ps, utilizing tight-binding magnetic anisotropy energies comparable to those found in small Fe nanoclusters.

Single photons serve as essential resources within quantum information science, yet practical applications frequently demand that these photons possess a precisely defined spectral (or temporal) modal profile. For instance, a rising exponential pulse can completely excite a two-level atom, whereas a Gaussian pulse cannot. This necessity drives the investigation of continuous-mode single-photon Fock states, which are defined by their specific spectral or temporal pulse shapes. This paper examines the statistical properties of such states. Rather than relying on the standard normal ordering (Wick ordering), we propose utilizing the Wigner spectrum. This approach offers two key benefits: first, it enables simultaneous analysis of these states in both the time and frequency domains; second, its ability to directly handle Dirac delta functions allows it to yield more information than normal ordering, which typically discards such functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how various control techniques, specifically coherent feedback control, can be employed to manipulate the pulse shapes of continuous-mode single-photon Fock states.

Visual text recognition remains a cornerstone of computer vision research. Although significant advancements have been achieved, with recent models increasingly targeting practical "in-the-wild" scenarios, a critical barrier to real-world application persists: existing methods often fail to recognize unseen or infrequent character sequences. To address this specific challenge, we introduce a novel iterative framework. This system leverages predictions from previous iterations to augment the primary network, thereby enhancing subsequent outputs. A pivotal component of our approach is a specialized cross-modal variational autoencoder serving as a feedback module, trained on textual error distribution data. This module converts discrete predicted character sequences into continuous affine transformation parameters, which condition the visual feature maps for the next iteration. Evaluations on standard datasets demonstrate competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods in conventional settings. Crucially, under a disjoint training and testing regime where labels are mutually exclusive, our method achieves superior results, highlighting its robust ability to generalize to previously unseen words.

To understand how magnetic fields influence the interstellar medium's evolution, the birth and development of molecular clouds, and the subsequent formation of stars, it is essential to map their three-dimensional (3D) structures. Measuring only a single magnetic field component—whether along the line of sight or parallel to the sky plane—fails to reveal these complete 3D vectors. Recently, innovative methods have emerged to measure both components individually and combine them with supplementary information, such as models of Galactic magnetic fields or field inclination angles, to reconstruct 3D magnetic field configurations. This review examines these recent advancements, explores their practical applications, and outlines their potential future trajectory.

Metabolism is fundamental to cell physiology as it supplies the molecular mechanisms required for growth. At the genome-wide level, it consists of thousands of interconnected reactions. Deciphering this complexity is essential for understanding cellular responses to genetic, environmental, or therapeutic changes. This discussion examines two complementary strategies for analyzing genome-scale metabolic models: Flux Balance Analysis (FBA) and network science. While FBA predicts metabolic fluxes based on optimization principles, network approaches uncover emergent properties arising from global metabolic connectivity. We emphasize that integrating both methods offers profound insights into the structure and function of metabolic systems, with broad implications for discovery science, precision medicine, and industrial biotechnology.

The classical study of phyllotaxis centers on the orderly placement of leaves on mature stems, often described by common fractions like 1/2, 1/3, 2/5, 3/8, and 5/13. While these phyllotactic fractions are not static and can shift stepwise during a plant's development, this contradicts observations showing that leaf primordia at shoot apical meristems arrange themselves continuously. To date, no mechanism has fully explained these transitions, aside from hypotheses suggesting specific genetic programs at certain stages. This text proposes that the varying length of leaf traces is a critical factor governing these shifts, based on an analysis of Larson's diagram of the procambial system in young cottonwood plants. The transition is viewed as a necessary outcome of geometric constraints: leaf traces cannot conform to a fractional pattern unless their length remains shorter than the product of the denominator and the internode length.

Federated query engines enable users to run queries across federations of Linked Data (LD). However, because these queries are broken down into potentially thousands of subqueries distributed among various SPARQL endpoints, data providers lack visibility into the original federated queries and only process the individual subqueries. Consequently, unlike traditional warehousing methods, LD data providers do not have access to secondary data. This paper introduces FETA (FEderated query TrAcking), a tracking algorithm that deduces the Basic Graph Patterns (BGPs) handled by a federation by analyzing a shared log kept by data providers. The concurrent execution of thousands of subqueries from multiple federated engines makes this tracking process difficult and uncertain. Experimental results using Anapsid demonstrate that FETA can successfully extract BGPs that, even under worst-case conditions, include the BGPs of the original queries.

Recent studies indicate that step-by-step reasoning chains, known as rationales, enhance performance in complex multi-step reasoning tasks. We revisit the application of rationale-augmented prompting within few-shot in-context learning, expanding traditional (input -> output) structures to (input, rationale -> output) formats. We illustrate that current manual prompting methods often rely on sub-optimal rationales, which can degrade performance. To address this fragility, we introduce a unified framework for rationale-augmented ensembles, identifying rationale sampling in the output space as the critical factor for robust performance gains. This approach is versatile and applicable to various natural language processing tasks, including those not typically associated with intermediate steps, such as question answering, word sense disambiguation, and sentiment analysis. Our results show that rationale-augmented ensembles outperform existing methods—including standard prompting and chain-of-thought prompting—in both accuracy and interpretability, providing clearer insights into model predictions through the generated rationales.

This paper establishes an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (EPTAS) for approximating the genus and non-orientable genus of dense graphs, defined as those where $|E(G)|\ge \alpha |V(G)|^2$ for a fixed $\alpha>0$. Although constant-factor approximations are straightforward for this class, achieving factors arbitrarily close to 1 requires complex algorithms and rigorous mathematical proofs. Specifically, the proposed algorithm takes a dense graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a parameter $\varepsilon>0$, returning an integer $g$ such that $G$ embeds into a surface of genus $g$. This $g$ is $\varepsilon$-close to the minimum genus $\mathsf{g}(G)$, satisfying $\mathsf{g}(G)\le g\le (1+\varepsilon)\mathsf{g}(G)$, with a running time of $O(f(\varepsilon)\,n^2)$, where $f$ is an explicit function. Furthermore, the method is extended to output an embedding (rotation system) with genus $g$. This extension operates as an Efficient Polynomial-time Randomized Approximation Scheme (EPRAS) and executes in $O(f_1(\varepsilon)\,n^2)$ time.

Bright millisecond-duration radio transients known as Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) occur approximately 1,000 times daily across the entire sky, provided the fluence threshold is 5 Jy ms at 600 MHz. The underlying physics of FRB emission and the nature of the compact objects responsible remain subjects of intense scientific debate. To refine source models, the Bustling Universe Radio Survey Telescope in Taiwan (BURSTT) has been optimized to detect and precisely locate a large population of rare, high-fluence, nearby FRBs. This specific group is ideal for multi-messenger and multi-wavelength follow-up, facilitating a deeper understanding of the source mechanisms. BURSTT offers horizon-to-horizon sky coverage with a half-power field-of-view of roughly 10$^{4}$ deg$^{2}$, an effective bandwidth of 400 MHz spanning 300–800 MHz, and sub-arcsecond localization accuracy achieved through outrigger stations situated hundreds to thousands of kilometers from the main array. The initial configuration will utilize 256 antennas, with plans to expand to 2048 antennas following tests of various designs and system performance optimizations. It is estimated that the initial BURSTT-256 configuration will detect and localize approximately 100 bright FRBs (≥100 Jy ms) annually. Furthermore, BURSTT's large field-of-view and continuous operation will significantly enhance the monitoring of FRB repetitions; the current scarcity of sensitive all-sky observations likely results in many repeating FRBs being mistakenly cataloged as single events.

This work addresses the challenge of accurately determining the \textit{mode} of a discrete distribution $\mathcal{P}$ with high confidence by analyzing a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from $\mathcal{P}$. When $\mathcal{P}$ has a support size of $K=2$, the task simplifies to estimating a single parameter, a scenario already effectively managed by prior-posterior-ratio (PPR) martingale confidence sequences \citep{waudby-ramdas-ppr}. Building on this, we extend the approach to mode estimation for distributions with $K \geq 2$ possible values. First, we establish that the "one-versus-one" strategy for generalizing from $K=2$ to larger $K$ is more efficient than the "one-versus-rest" approach. Subsequently, we demonstrate that our proposed stopping rule, PPR-1v1, achieves asymptotic optimality as the error probability approaches zero. PPR-1v1 requires no parameter tuning and minimal computation, drawing significantly fewer samples than competing methods even in non-asymptotic settings. We validate these advantages through two practical applications: election forecasting and smart contract verification on blockchains.

This work examines the minimal Two-Higgs-Doublet Model derived from quark-lepton unification, which accounts for low-scale physics. We analyze the connections between the decay widths of the newly predicted Higgs bosons and investigate their phenomenological implications at the Large Hadron Collider. Due to matter unification, the theory forecasts a specific correlation between the decay rates of heavy Higgs bosons into tau leptons and bottom quarks. We outline strategies to test this framework using such relationships and address the associated flavor constraints.

In solid-state physics, crystal energies are typically calculated using plane-wave discretizations of the Kohn-Sham equations; however, Coulomb singularities necessitate large plane-wave cut-offs for accurate results. This paper analyzes the plane-wave convergence of eigenvalues for periodic linear Hamiltonians with Coulomb potentials via the variational projector-augmented wave (VPAW) method. Within the VPAW framework, an invertible transformation is applied to the original eigenvalue problem, operating locally within spheres centered on the singularities. Consequently, a generalized eigenvalue problem must be solved using plane waves. We demonstrate that the VPAW approach significantly mitigates the cusps in the eigenfunctions at nuclear positions, although these functions exhibit higher-order derivative discontinuities at the spheres surrounding the nuclei. By balancing these two error sources, we show that the VPAW method can substantially enhance the plane-wave convergence of eigenvalues with only a minor increase in computational cost. Numerical tests confirm the method's efficiency in handling Coulomb singularities.

Selective evaporation-induced phase segregation can generate intricate physicochemical hydrodynamics within multicomponent systems. Recent studies by Li et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett., 120, 2018) and Kim & Stone (J. Fluid Mech., 850, 2018) documented demixing behaviors in evaporating binary droplets. In this study, we examine the post-segregation flow dynamics through both experimental and theoretical approaches, focusing on the 1,2-hexanediol-water binary system. We first characterize the overall physicochemical hydrodynamics of the evaporation process, encompassing segregative phenomena and the resulting flow structures near the substrate. By quantifying radial flow evolution, we identify three distinct life stages: In Stage I, a Marangoni-driven radially outward flow is observed. During the transition to Stage II, the radial flow partially reverses from the contact line; this asymmetry-breaking flow is driven directly by segregation. In Stage III, as evaporation diminishes, the flow decays because segregation has permeated the entire droplet, allowing the Marangoni effect to regain control. Consequently, this Marangoni flow homogenizes the distribution of the entrapped volatile water across the droplet.

The paper presents the innovative Modular Pipe Climber III, which utilizes a Three-Output Open Differential (3-OOD) mechanism to prevent track slippage caused by varying pipe cross-sections, regardless of the robot's orientation. Unlike previous designs that rely on three-wheel or track modules with independent drive systems to maintain stability—often leading to significant slippage during pipe turns and necessitating substantial active speed control—the proposed climber uses the 3-OOD to mechanically adjust track speeds automatically when navigating turns. Notably, this proposed 3-OOD is the first three-output differential capable of replicating the functional capabilities of a traditional two-output differential.

Voice assistants like Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant have gained global popularity, yet factors such as linguistic diversity, speech variability, and background noise often lead to misinterpretations of user queries. To enhance user experience, retrieval-based query reformulation (QR) systems are employed to correct these errors. While existing QR approaches typically emphasize neural retrieval model training or direct entity retrieval, they seldom address query expansion and entity weighting concurrently, potentially restricting the scope and accuracy of reformulation. This study introduces a novel method called Query Expansion and Entity Weighting (QEEW), which utilizes relationships within an entity catalog—comprising user queries, assistant responses, and associated entities—to boost reformulation performance. Experiments using Alexa-annotated data show that QEEW improves all top precision metrics, achieving a 6% gain in top-10 precision over baselines without query expansion or weighting, and exceeding a 5% improvement in top-10 precision compared to other baselines that do employ both techniques.

We re-examine constraints on annihilating dark matter derived from the global 21cm signal detected by EDGES. To achieve this, we utilized numerical data from a recent high-fidelity N-body simulation to calculate the boost factor at high redshifts ($z$ = 10 - 100), which amplifies dark matter annihilation during structure formation. By analyzing the fraction of injected energy from annihilation that contributes to the ionization, excitation, and heating of the intergalactic medium during the dark ages, we determined the potential magnitude of the global 21cm absorption. Under the assumption of a thermal freezeout scenario, we conclude that $m_{\rm DM} < 15$ GeV and $m_{\rm DM} < 3$ GeV are excluded at 95% C.L. for annihilation channels into $b\bar{b}$ and $e^+ e^-$, respectively.

This study examines spatially covariant modified gravity theories where the scalar degree of freedom is rendered non-dynamical, resulting in exactly two tensorial degrees of freedom, identical to those in general relativity. By analyzing a specific class of such theories defined by three time-dependent functions, we explore the observational and phenomenological means to distinguish them from general relativity. Our analysis confirms that these theories yield predictions indistinguishable from general relativity regarding weak gravitational fields and the propagation speed of gravitational waves, and they do not alter asymptotically flat black hole solutions. Given the flexibility in choosing the time-dependent functions, the homogeneous and isotropic cosmological evolution can be tuned to closely match or exactly replicate the $\Lambda$CDM model. Furthermore, an investigation of cosmological perturbations across both long and short wavelength regimes reveals that modifications to gravity manifest solely through changes in the background evolution. Finally, we note that introducing a Galileon field within the matter sector reactivates the scalar degree of freedom, thereby undermining the core characteristic of this theoretical framework.

Although numerous proposed machine learning (ML)-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDSs) demonstrate near-perfect performance on synthetic benchmarks, it remains undocumented whether these results hold true for real-world networks or other scenarios. This paper examines the generalizability of ML-based NIDSs by rigorously testing seven supervised and unsupervised learning models across four recently published benchmark datasets. Our findings reveal that no single model successfully generalizes across all tested datasets. Notably, generalizability exhibits significant asymmetry; swapping the source and target domains drastically alters classification performance. Furthermore, within the scenarios studied, unsupervised learning methods demonstrate superior generalization compared to supervised models. Utilizing SHAP values to interpret these outcomes, we identify that poor generalizability stems primarily from a strong correlation between specific feature values and Attack/Benign classes in certain dataset-model combinations—a correlation that is absent in other datasets with distinct feature distributions.

Sums structured as $\sum_{N_m=q}^{n}{\cdots
\sum_{N_1=q}^{N_2}{a_{(m);N_m}\cdots a_{(1);N_1}}}$, where the terms $a_{(k);N_k}$ represent either identical or distinct sequences, are frequently encountered in mathematical literature. We designate these as recurrent sums. This paper presents a range of formulas designed to facilitate the manipulation of such sums. Initially, we establish variation formulas that express the change in a recurrent sum of order $m$ using lower-order recurrent sums. Subsequently, we derive theorems, termed inversion formulas, which demonstrate various methods for reordering the summation indices. Furthermore, we introduce a collection of novel partition identities to prove a reduction theorem, enabling the representation of a recurrent sum as a combination of non-recurrent sums. Finally, we apply this reduction theorem to two well-known recurrent sum forms: the $p$-series and the sum of powers.

This study examines a gatemon qubit constructed from a semiconductor nanowire coated with epitaxial aluminum on two surfaces, enabling gate control over wire density. Two specific sections have the aluminum stripped away: one functions as a Josephson junction, and the other acts as a transistor, facilitating in-situ switching between dc transport and qubit operation. Applying a gate to the nanowire alters the bulk potential distribution, whereas gating the Josephson junction modifies the number of junction modes. Both phenomena are evidenced by the qubit frequency's dependence on the parallel magnetic field. A comprehensive model of the wire and junction aligns with experimental observations. Furthermore, in the multi-mode regime, qubit frequency fluctuations are significantly lower than both the theoretical "universal" value and numerical predictions, a result consistent with prior measurements of fluctuating critical current.

We introduce a comprehensive quantum fluctuation theorem concerning entropy production in open quantum systems interacting with multiple, potentially non-equilibrium environments. When applied to the weak-coupling and Markovian limits, this theorem applies to both local and global master equations, thereby confirming the thermodynamic consistency of local quantum master equations. The result is inherently quantum, formulated through the conservation of a Hermitian operator that governs the system's state evolution and the entropy changes within the baths, from which the integral fluctuation theorem derives. This framework remains valid for systems with time-dependent Hamiltonians, encompassing the quantum Jarzynski equality as a specific instance. Additionally, the theorem extends to nonthermal baths provided microreversibility is maintained. We illustrate these exact findings with numerical examples and further generalize the theorem to explicitly account for system-bath interactions. In this extended context, the fluctuation theorem establishes a relationship between the time-reversed dynamics of the global density matrix and a two-time correlation function along the forward trajectory, involving only the baths' entropy.

Quaternions are extensively utilized across various domains of applied science and engineering, including mechanics and wireless communication systems. It is established that there are two non-isomorphic types of generalized quaternion algebras: the quaternion algebra and the coquaternion algebra. This paper provides the necessary formulas to convert between a basis in a generalized quaternion algebra and bases in either the division quaternion algebra or the coquaternion algebra, and vice versa. An analogous result was derived for the generalized octonion algebra. Furthermore, the study highlights the applications of these findings to algebraic equations and De Moivre's formula within both generalized quaternion algebras and generalized octonion division algebras.

The rapid expansion in cellular data usage compels network operators to devise strategies for the precise dimensioning and management of network resources. Forecasting traffic volumes is a foundational element for any proactive management approach, making it a critical area of focus. Unlike existing literature that predominantly addresses short-term traffic prediction, this study focuses on forecasting busy hour traffic, defined as the time series of daily peak volumes. Specifically, we investigate long-term forecasting (one to two months ahead) and evaluate various methodologies, including different algorithms and a cluster-based approach that groups cells with similar traffic profiles before applying per-cluster models. Analysis of a real-world cellular network dataset demonstrates that busy hour traffic can be predicted with errors under 10% for periods extending up to two months. Furthermore, utilizing cluster-based segmentation improves forecasting accuracy by up to 8% for one-month and 5% for two-month look-ahead periods.

Merging black holes generate gravitational waves (GWs) that offer unique opportunities to investigate strong-field gravity. Validating gravitational theories in this domain necessitates precise waveform templates for viable General Relativity extensions. This study focuses on scalar Gauss-Bonnet gravity, a prominent theory arising as the low-energy limit of quantum gravity frameworks. This model incorporates quadratic curvature terms coupled with a scalar field, permitting black hole solutions endowed with scalar charge. By examining inspiralling binary systems, we calculate the leading-order corrections from curvature nonlinearities in both GW and scalar waveforms, demonstrating that these novel contributions, distinct from the scalar field's direct influence, emerge at the first post-Newtonian order. We supply ready-to-use GW polarization patterns and phase evolution data. Utilizing Fourier-domain GW phasing calculations, we conduct a parameter-space analysis to assess the detectability of deviations from General Relativity. These findings establish a crucial groundwork for future high-precision gravity tests using both parametrized and theory-specific search strategies.

We examine crowdsourcing scenarios in which users are tasked with rating items, either directly or to derive a consensus value. Without incentives, users lack motivation to exert effort, often submitting inaccurate responses instead. We introduce incentive mechanisms that are both truthful—ensuring accurate evaluations are the optimal strategy—and cost-effective, achieving truthfulness with minimal overhead. Our approach addresses both discrete tasks, where evaluations are strictly correct or incorrect, and quantitative tasks, involving real numbers where error is the distance from the true value. For both categories, we propose hierarchical incentive schemes that require only a few additional evaluations, scale to arbitrarily large crowds, and maintain consistent incentive strength regardless of hierarchy depth. Notably, our analysis reveals that the sole prerequisite for these schemes to function is that workers know their position within the hierarchy beforehand.

Datasets frequently include weights for rows (cases or objects), which might represent observation frequency or reliability. While various row-wise weighted methods exist, with the weighted average being the most prominent, there are also scenarios where weights are assigned to individual cells within the data matrix. This note outlines an approach for analyzing such data by defining a cellwise weighted likelihood function, which relies on a dataset transformation termed "unpacking." This weighted likelihood enables the application of multivariate statistical techniques, including maximum likelihood estimation and likelihood ratio tests. Special emphasis is placed on estimating covariance matrices, as they form the foundation of much multivariate analysis. An R implementation of the cellwise maximum likelihood estimator is included, utilizing an EM algorithm variant, alongside a proposed faster approximate method that is asymptotically equivalent to the exact approach.

We investigate magnon bands within slab geometries for a spin model defined on the pyrochlore lattice, incorporating Heisenberg exchange, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, and spin-ice anisotropy. Across various model parameters, covering both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic exchange regimes, we calculate spin wave bands for slabs oriented perpendicular to the $[111]$, $[100]$, and $[110]$ axes. Our analysis examines magnon dispersions in the ferromagnetic splay phase, the all-in-all-out phase, and a coplanar phase. For each of these phases, the magnon band structure exhibits non-reciprocity dependent on the specific slab geometry, allowing us to identify non-reciprocal regions within the surface Brillouin zones. Furthermore, we detail the edge-localized magnons present in these phases, linking them to point degeneracies and distinct nodal lines found in the bulk spectra.

The growing intricacy of Machine Learning (ML) techniques has necessitated a simplification of both academic research and industrial development workflows. ML pipelines have emerged as indispensable tools for data scientists and researchers across various fields, enabling them to efficiently integrate multiple models to handle the entire analytical workflow from raw data. Although numerous solutions have been developed to automate ML pipeline construction—primarily focusing on the semantic properties and characteristics of input datasets—there remains a gap in approaches addressing emerging quality concerns such as fairness, interpretability, and privacy. This paper first identifies key quality attributes of ML systems based on existing literature. Subsequently, we introduce a novel engineering methodology for creating high-quality ML pipelines by appropriately extending the Feature Models meta-model. Our approach facilitates the modeling of ML pipelines, their comprehensive and phase-specific quality requirements, and the quality attributes of algorithms employed in each stage. Finally, we validate the expressiveness of our model using a classification problem.

Secure aggregation, a fundamental element of federated learning, combines models trained locally by distributed users at a central server. The term "secure" implies that the server receives only the aggregated model, with no leakage of individual user data. To ensure this security, a key sharing phase distributes keys among users, followed by a model aggregation phase where each user masks its local model before transmission. This work addresses the information-theoretic secure aggregation problem originally defined by Zhao and Sun, aiming to determine the minimum communication cost during the aggregation phase for $K$ users. The system must tolerate the absence of messages from up to $K-U$ users, where $U$ is a specific parameter. While Zhao and Sun characterized the optimal communication cost under the assumption that user keys could be arbitrary random variables, this paper introduces a new constraint: keys must be mutually independent and shared in groups of no more than $S$ users ($S$ being another system parameter). This constraint reflects the practical advantage of uncoded groupwise keys over the coded keys typically used in existing schemes. We demonstrate that if $S > K - U$, a scheme utilizing uncoded groupwise keys can match the optimal communication cost of the best coded-key scheme; however, if $S \leq K - U$, such uncoded groupwise key sharing results in strictly sub-optimal performance.

Assuming $G$ is a topological group and $C$ is a compact subset within it, this paper introduces the concept of group nonexpansive mappings. We then examine a family $\mathcal{S} = \{T_{i} : i \in I\}$ consisting of such mappings defined on $C$. Furthermore, we investigate the existence of group nonexpansive retractions $P_{i}$ from $C$ onto $\text{Fix}(\mathcal{S})$ that satisfy the condition $P_{i}T_{i} = T_{i}P_{i} = P_{i}$.

This work addresses the decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption that the error matrix is symmetric. We establish two primary findings. First, for rates below $1/2$, we demonstrate the existence of a wide class of rank metric codes capable of correcting any symmetric error pattern, regardless of whether it achieves maximal rank; this class notably encompasses Gabidulin codes with rates less than $1/2$. Second, for rates exceeding $1/2$, we introduce a decoder designed to correct symmetric errors with a rank up to $n-k$. Both proposed decoders are deterministic and guarantee worst-case performance.

Building on the work of Qiu et al. (2017), who introduced residual extropy as an analogue to residual entropy for measuring uncertainty in residual lifetime distributions, this paper extends the concept to past lifetime distributions by defining a new metric called past extropy. We examine the properties and applications of this measure and further present a characterization result regarding the past extropy of the largest order statistics.

Although splitting and projection-type algorithms are widely used in optimization due to their efficiency and simplicity, their application to optimal control remains relatively rare. This paper employs four established projection methods—the Method of Alternating Projections, Dykstra, Douglas–Rachford, and Aragón Artacho–Campoy—to address control-constrained linear-quadratic optimal control problems. Rather than discretizing the problem and applying large-scale finite-dimensional numerical optimization, we divide the problem into two components and use projection techniques to identify a solution within the intersection of their respective solution sets. We derive general formulas for the required projections, propose a numerical implementation, and provide analytic closed-form expressions for the projectors associated with pure, under-, critically-, and over-damped harmonic oscillators. The approach is demonstrated through various examples, including a complex machine tool manipulator problem. Furthermore, case studies are conducted to identify optimal ranges for specific algorithmic parameters that minimize the number of iterations required.

This study examines the ABC model interacting with slow or fast reservoirs. In this framework, each site accommodates at most one particle of type $\alpha\in\{A,B,C\}$, which exchange positions within the discrete set $\{1,\cdots, N-1\}$ via a weakly asymmetric rate contingent on the participating particle types. At the boundaries $x=1, N-1$, particles are injected or removed at rates dependent on their types. We establish that the hydrodynamic limit on the diffusive time scale corresponds to a system of non-linear coupled equations with specific boundary conditions, which vary according to the strength of the reservoir's influence.

Origami design principles have demonstrated significant utility across various technological fields. Specifically, origami tessellations represent a category of morphing metamaterials characterized by unique geometric and elastic traits. While theoretically inextensible, the presence of fine creases enables these metamaterials to undergo effective non-isometric deformation. A critical step in understanding and governing the morphing trajectories of these structures involves identifying compatible strains relative to coarse-grained origami kinematics and deriving the associated elasticity functionals. This work addresses this challenge through a unified theoretical framework applied to a broad spectrum of established origami tessellations, ranging from the classic Miura-ori to its more complex oblique, non-developable, and non-flat-foldable derivatives. The analysis reveals two universal characteristics shared by these patterns: first, they possess equal yet opposite in-plane and out-of-plane Poisson's ratios; second, their bending energy becomes decoupled from in-plane strain, relying instead on the strain gradient. These findings are further demonstrated through an examination of the self-equilibrium geometry in origami pillars.

An examination of existing data regarding the decay exponent for kinetic energy in homogeneous and isotropic turbulence (HIT) reveals variations of up to 100%. Frequently, measurements and simulations fail to align with theoretical predictions, which themselves are inconsistent. This discrepancy is problematic, as HIT serves as a fundamental component of turbulence theory and modeling. To address this, we analyzed decaying HIT across various initial conditions using an extensive dataset of direct numerical simulations. Our results indicate that both the Kolmogorov decay exponent and the Birkhoff-Saffman decay can be observed over extended periods, provided the initial conditions are suitably configured. Additionally, we examined other turbulent statistics, including velocity derivative skewness, energy spectra, and dissipation for both scenarios. These findings suggest that decay and growth laws generally align with theoretical expectations, although the wavenumber spectrum near the origin evolves rapidly, implying that invariants may not strictly exist. Finally, we briefly discuss the reasons for the significant variation in decay exponents reported in previous experiments and simulations.

Previous research indicates that Visual Recognition datasets often fail to adequately represent bias groups (e.g., Females) within specific class labels (e.g., Programmers). This inherent dataset bias causes models to learn spurious correlations between class labels and attributes like age, gender, or race. While recent approaches to mitigate this issue typically demand substantial architectural modifications or extra loss functions that require extensive hyperparameter tuning, data sampling techniques from the class imbalance literature (such as undersampling and upweighting) offer a more cost-effective and efficient alternative. These methods are often implementable with minimal code and lack hyperparameters; however, they have notable limitations. Undersampling, for instance, discards a large portion of the input distribution, whereas oversampling repeats samples, leading to overfitting. To overcome these drawbacks, we propose a novel class-conditioned sampling approach called Bias Mimicking (BM). This method relies on the insight that if the bias distribution of a class $c$, denoted as $P_D(B|Y=c)$, is replicated across all other classes $c^{\prime}\neq c$, then $Y$ and $B$ become statistically independent. Through a new training procedure, BM ensures the model encounters the full data distribution without duplicating samples. As a result, Bias Mimicking enhances the average accuracy of underrepresented groups by 3\% across four benchmarks compared to sampling methods, while sustaining or even surpassing the performance of non-sampling techniques. The implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/mqraitem/Bias-Mimicking}.

The DocRED dataset serves as a leading benchmark for document-level relation extraction (RE), utilizing a recommend-revise annotation strategy to achieve large-scale coverage. However, our investigation reveals that the dataset suffers from significant annotation incompleteness, characterized by a high prevalence of false negatives. We examine the causes and impacts of this issue and propose a solution by re-annotating 4,053 documents to restore missed relation triples, creating a new version called Re-DocRED. Extensive experiments using state-of-the-art neural models demonstrate that training and evaluation on Re-DocRED yield performance gains of approximately 13 F1 points compared to the original dataset. Additionally, we provide a thorough analysis to pinpoint areas for future enhancement. The revised dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tonytan48/Re-DocRED.

This paper introduces an Augmented Physics-Based Modeling (APBM) framework that combines neural networks with physics-based modeling for Bayesian nonlinear latent space estimation. The APBM approach enables model adaptation in response to new operating conditions or when the underlying physics model fails to fully capture the latent phenomenon. A key benefit of both the APBM strategy and our estimation method is the preservation of physical interpretability in the estimated states. Additionally, we introduce a constraint filtering technique to regulate the neural network's influence within the overall model. By utilizing assumed density filtering and cubature integration rules, we develop a flexible estimation strategy capable of handling nonlinear models and high-dimensional latent spaces. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of this methodology through a target tracking scenario featuring nonlinear dynamics and incomplete measurement and acceleration models.

Aerospace technology is fundamental to modern society, with space-based infrastructure supporting essential functions such as weather prediction, communications, terrestrial navigation, logistics, planetary observation, and solar monitoring. Extraplanetary exploration, encompassing orbital surveys as well as recent advancements in roving, flying, and submersible unmanned vehicles, represents a critical scientific and technological frontier widely regarded as vital for humanity's long-term survival and prosperity. All aerospace endeavors necessitate reliable craft control and the capacity to record high-precision physical measurements; magnetometers fulfill both requirements and have been instrumental in the success of many missions. This review paper introduces relevant instruments and their applications, examining past and present magnetometers alongside their established and emerging aerospace uses. We also explore recent technological advancements, with a specific focus on optical readout magnetometers, including atomic, diamond quantum defect, and optomechanical variants. These optical systems offer a unique balance of field sensitivity, size, weight, and power consumption, enabling performance levels unattainable by current methods. This capability promises to facilitate new applications across domains ranging from unmanned vehicles to navigation and exploration.

This study presents the $J^{2+}$-invariant applicable to pairs of generic immersions. Similar to Arnold's $J^{+}$-invariant for generic immersions, this new invariant remains unchanged under homotopies involving inverse tangencies and the crossing of triple points, yet it alters when direct tangencies are traversed. Furthermore, the invariant possesses additional characteristics; notably, as demonstrated in Theorem B, the $J^{2+}$-invariant for a pair is entirely independent of the individual $J^{+}$-invariants of the constituent immersions.

Nonlinear topological photonics has garnered growing research attention because it merges the benefits of active all-optical control from nonlinear optics with the distinctive characteristics of topological photonic systems, including defect-immune, topologically protected light propagation. In this study, we show that topological interface modes and trivial edge modes within a specially engineered graphene metasurface can be coupled in a tunable and optically controllable way, offering an efficient method to channel optical power into topologically protected states. This is realized through a pump-signal setup where an optical pump traveling in a bulk mode adjusts the photonic system's band structure, thereby modifying the coupling coefficient and wave-vector mismatch between the edge and topological interface modes. This tunable coupling mechanism is highly efficient, largely due to graphene's large Kerr coefficient. Significantly, we demonstrate that the necessary pump power can be substantially lowered when the device operates in the slow-light regime. Our analysis combines *ab initio* full-wave simulations with coupled-mode theory that encapsulates the primary physics of this active coupler, revealing strong agreement between the two methods. This research could pave the way for designing active topological photonic devices with novel or enhanced functionalities.

Identifying double JPEG artifacts across various image areas is a common technique for detecting and pinpointing local manipulations, such as image splicing. Building on this, our paper introduces an end-to-end system that not only detects and localizes spliced regions but also identifies whether they originate from different source images. Assuming both the spliced segments and the background have undergone double JPEG compression, we utilize a local estimate of the primary quantization matrix to differentiate between spliced areas from distinct sources. This is achieved by clustering image blocks based on the estimated primary quantization matrix and refining the output through morphological reconstruction. The proposed method is versatile, functioning effectively across aligned and non-aligned double JPEG compression scenarios, irrespective of whether the second compression is stronger or weaker than the first. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates that our approach outperforms baseline methods operating under similar conditions.

HD 49798, a hydrogen-depleted subdwarf O6 star with a massive white dwarf (WD) companion, has been proposed as a potential progenitor for Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia). However, it remains unclear whether the companion is a carbon-oxygen (CO) WD or an oxygen-neon (ONe) WD. While a CO WD would explode as an SN Ia upon reaching the Chandrasekhar mass, an accreting ONe WD would likely evolve into a neutron star. Using a Monte Carlo binary population synthesis method, we simulated the formation of ONe WD + He star systems. Our results show that orbital periods as long as that of HD 49798 are virtually absent in these simulated systems, suggesting the companion is probably not an ONe WD. Instead, we propose that the companion is most likely a CO WD that will gain sufficient mass via He-rich accretion from HD 49798 to reach the Chandrasekhar limit. Consequently, HD 49798 and its companion are poised to produce a Type Ia supernova in their future evolution.

Scattered light noise degrades the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors, necessitating its characterization for effective mitigation. The time-varying filter empirical mode decomposition (TVF-EMD) algorithm is well-suited for detecting signals with time-dependent frequencies, such as scattered light noise. We introduce a fully automated pipeline utilizing the pytvfemd library, a Python implementation of the TVF-EMD algorithm, to identify objects causing scattering within the gravitational-wave channel and track their motion. Applying this pipeline to LIGO Livingston O3 data reveals that the majority of scattering noise originates from the penultimate mass at the end of the X-arm (EXPUM), exhibiting motion within the micro-seismic frequency range.

Point set registration involves determining the optimal alignment between two point clouds and is a prevalent task in various fields, particularly automotive and mobile robotics. While numerous methods exist, including the well-known Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm that relies on establishing explicit correspondences, this study focuses on a probabilistic framework that achieves registration without creating such explicit mappings.
