In such scenarios, corrections serve as a vital mechanism for human-in-the-loop control. These corrections can introduce new goals, impose constraints (such as avoiding specific items), or offer planning hints (like visiting particular waypoints). While existing correction techniques—such as joysticks or direct end-effector manipulation—demand full teleoperation or real-time interaction, this paper investigates natural language as a more expressive and flexible alternative. We outline a method to translate natural language sentences into cost function transformations, enabling users to refine goals, adjust robot trajectories to meet new preferences, and recover from planning failures. Our approach achieves 81% and 93% success rates on tasks previously failed by the original planner using one or two language-based corrections. Furthermore, this method allows for the composition of multiple constraints and generalizes effectively to novel scenes, objects, and linguistic inputs across both simulated and real-world environments.

This paper rectifies earlier research concerning magnetic charge combined with a photon mass. We demonstrate that, in contrast to prior assertions, this system admits a straightforward, closed-form solution: the Dirac string potential scaled by an exponentially decaying factor. Notable characteristics of this solution include (i) the emergence of the Dirac string as a tangible physical feature, (ii) the violation of rotational symmetry in the monopole's magnetic field resulting from gauge symmetry breaking due to the photon mass, and (iii) the potential modification of the Dirac quantization condition.

The Single Shot Multibox Detector (SSD) is renowned for its combination of high accuracy and rapid processing speeds; however, its feature pyramid detection approach complicates the fusion of multi-scale features. This paper introduces FSSD (Feature Fusion Single Shot Multibox Detector), an enhanced variant of SSD equipped with a novel, lightweight feature fusion module. This module significantly boosts performance over the original SSD with only a minimal reduction in speed. Within the fusion module, features from various layers and scales are concatenated and processed through down-sampling blocks to create a new feature pyramid, which is then utilized by multibox detectors to generate final predictions. Evaluated on the Pascal VOC 2007 test set with a 300×300 input size on a single Nvidia 1080Ti GPU, the proposed network achieves an 82.7 mAP at 65.8 FPS. Furthermore, our results on the COCO dataset surpass conventional SSD performance by a substantial margin. Overall, FSSD outperforms many state-of-the-art object detection methods in both accuracy and speed. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/lzx1413/CAFFE_SSD/tree/fssd.

This paper details the measurement of track reconstruction efficiencies at LHCb derived from $J/\psi\rightarrow\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decays. Efficiencies exceeding 95% were observed during the data collection periods of 2010, 2011, and 2012. The ratio between muon track reconstruction efficiency in data and simulation aligns with unity, with an uncertainty of 0.8% for 2010 and improved precision of 0.4% for both 2011 and 2012. For hadrons, an additional 1.4% uncertainty is attributed to material interactions. These findings are essential for achieving precise cross-section and branching fraction measurements within LHCb.

Advancements in wearable sensor technology have increased the focus on collecting and analyzing photoplethysmogram (PPG) signals. By applying machine learning, cardiac rhythms derived from PPG can predict various outcomes, including activity recognition, sleep stage classification, and overall health status. Nevertheless, supervised learning is frequently constrained by the scarcity of labeled data, which is costly to acquire. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) approach that utilizes signal reconstruction as a pretext task to develop a generalized and informative PPG representation. We evaluated this proposed SSL framework against two fully supervised baselines. The findings indicate that in scenarios with extremely limited labeled data (10 or fewer samples per class), SSL offers significant advantages; specifically, a simple classifier trained on SSL-derived representations outperforms fully supervised deep neural networks. However, the results also highlight that these SSL representations are overly focused on subject-specific features, leading to high inter-subject variability. This variability complicates data utilization when labels are scarce, suggesting that further improvements in representation learning are necessary. Overall, the study suggests that SSL holds promise for expanding the application of machine learning models to PPG data in environments where labeled data is limited.

This paper establishes Minimal Requirements for Candidate Predictions in quantum field theories, drawing inspiration from the perspective of the standard model as an effective field theory. It then reviews standard regularization procedures within effective field theory to determine whether the vacuum expectation value of energy density ($\langle\rho\rangle$) satisfies these criteria. The analysis yields a negative verdict, concluding that $\langle\rho\rangle$ lacks physical significance within the standard model. Furthermore, rigorous extensions of flat space quantum field theory remove $\langle\rho\rangle$ from their conceptual frameworks, reinforcing the idea that it is not physically significant across the broader domain of quantum field theory. These findings have implications for cosmology and quantum gravity, suggesting that resolving the cosmological constant problem requires a fundamental revision of the vacuum concept in quantum field theory.

The energy dependence of the total hadroproduction cross section for pseudo-scalar quarkonia is determined by combining Next-to-Leading Order (NLO) Collinear-Factorisation (CF) outcomes with resummed higher-order corrections, which scale as $\alpha_s^{n}\ln^{n-1}(1/z)$. In this context, $z$ represents the ratio $M^2/\hat{s}$, where $M$ denotes the quarkonium mass and $\hat{s}$ is the squared partonic center-of-mass energy. This resummation utilizes High-Energy Factorisation (HEF) within the Doubly-Logarithmic (DL) approximation, a subset of the leading logarithmic $\ln (1/z)$ framework. This approach ensures strict consistency with the NLO and NNLO DGLAP evolution of Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs). By refining the small-$z$ asymptotic behavior of the CF coefficient function, the resummation eliminates the unphysical results inherent in the standard NLO CF calculation. The matching is executed directly in $z$-space for the first time using the Inverse-Error Weighting (InEW) procedure. Additionally, as a by-product of this study, the HEF calculation predicts the NNLO term of the CF hard-scattering coefficient proportional to $\alpha_s^2\ln(1/z)$.

Precise models describing how dark matter subhaloes evolve as they orbit larger structures are essential for grasping the current detailed distribution of dark matter. Numerical simulations indicate that mass loss due to tidal stripping is best conceptualized in energy space, where the least tightly bound particles are removed first. Building on this premise, we previously introduced a zero-parameter "energy-truncation model" for subhalo evolution. By testing this model against simulations of satellites with initial NFW profiles undergoing tidal stripping, we demonstrated that it accurately forecasts both mass loss and density profiles. In this study, we extend the model to Hernquist, Einasto, and King profiles. Our results show that the model aligns closely with simulation outcomes across all tested cases, suggesting it could function as a universal framework for describing tidally stripped collisionless systems. A crucial prediction of the energy-truncation model is that the central density of dark matter subhaloes remains constant even as they lose mass; this finding holds significant implications for dark matter annihilation computations and other observational dark matter tests.

We demonstrate that the orthogonal root number associated with a tempered L-parameter factors into the product of two distinct components: the orthogonal root number of the principal parameter and the evaluation of a specific involution of Langlands's central character on that parameter. This formula confirms a conjecture proposed by Gross and Reeder and enables the calculation of root numbers for Weil-Deligne representations that emerge in the research of Hiraga, Ichino, and Ikeda concerning the Plancherel measure.

While the concept of strong electronic correlations emerged in $d$-metal oxides like NiO, it can also be illustrated in simple systems such as the H$_2$ molecule. This work examines correlation effects in B$_6^{2-}$ clusters within $M$B$_6$ hexaborides, demonstrating that B 2$p$ valence electrons exhibit significant correlation. Computed excitation energies for the B$_6$-octahedron in CaB$_6$ and YbB$_6$ align with resonant inelastic x-ray scattering peak positions, offering a robust explanation for the latter material. These results classify these substances as unique $p$-electron correlated systems, necessitating advanced many-body studies across the entire hexaboride family—including both alkaline and rare-earth compounds—to address not only $N$-states but also ($N\pm1$)-states, such as those defining band gaps.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial formula for the Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold. We present an extended version of their discussion, emphasizing the roots of combinatorial differential manifolds within their research.

Principal component analysis (PCA) is arguably the most popular technique for reducing data dimensionality. A critical aspect of PCA decomposition is determining the appropriate number of factors to keep. This paper introduces a novel method for automatically selecting the count of principal components using the Bayesian minimum message length framework for inductive inference. Furthermore, we derive a new estimate for isotropic residual variance and show through numerical experiments that it outperforms the standard maximum likelihood method.

The ratio of FeII to MgII line fluxes serves as a proxy for the iron-to-magnesium abundance ratio within the broad line region (BLR) of active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Utilizing archival rest-frame ultraviolet spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we analyzed FeII/MgII ratios in type 1 AGNs with redshifts less than 2. Across a broad spectrum of AGN characteristics—including black hole mass, luminosity, and Eddington ratio—we established that the FeII/MgII ratio exhibits a strong correlation with the Eddington ratio, showing no significant dependence on black hole mass, luminosity, or redshift. These findings indicate that BLR metallicity is intrinsically linked to AGN accretion activity rather than the host galaxy's global properties, such as its mass and luminosity. Furthermore, we propose that the relationship between BLR metallicity and accretion rate involves metal cooling, which likely enhances gas inflow into the galactic center, thereby driving high accretion rates in AGNs.

Quantum walk dynamics adhere to quantum mechanical laws subject to an additional locality constraint, requiring the evolution operator to act locally by moving the walker to adjacent sites before reaching distant ones. Typically, the Hamiltonian is derived from a graph's adjacency or Laplacian matrix, causing the walker to transition between neighboring vertices. This study introduces a continuous-time quantum walk variant where the walker can hop between vertices and edges interchangeably. Applying this framework, we examine a spatial search algorithm on a complete bipartite graph by augmenting the new Hamiltonian with a term dependent on the marked vertex or edge, mirroring the standard continuous-time approach. We demonstrate that the optimal time required to locate either a vertex or an edge scales as $O(\sqrt{N_e})$ with a success probability of $1-o(1)$, where $N_e$ denotes the total number of edges in the complete bipartite graph.

This study introduces a thermodynamically consistent phase-field model designed to simulate multicellular deformation and aggregation under flow conditions. Specifically, within this phase-field framework, a Lennard-Jones type potential is developed to represent cell-cell and cell-wall interactions. To solve the governing equations, a second-order accurate $C^0$ finite element method is employed, ensuring precision in both space and time. Numerical tests validate the scheme's convergence, energy stability, and ability to capture nonlinear mechanical properties of cells. Furthermore, the model utilizes vesicles with varying adhesion levels to elucidate the pathological risks associated with sickle cell disease.

This paper introduces an analogue of G\"{o}del's second incompleteness theorem tailored for systems of second-order arithmetic. While G\"{o}del demonstrated that sufficiently strong theories which are $\Pi^0_1$-sound and $\Sigma^0_1$-definable cannot establish their own $\Pi^0_1$-soundness, we show that sufficiently strong theories which are $\Pi^1_1$-sound and $\Sigma^1_1$-definable similarly fail to prove their own $\Pi^1_1$-soundness. Our approach avoids constructing a self-referential sentence, instead relying on ordinal analysis.

We propose a novel approach to enhance current multilingual sentence embeddings by incorporating Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). Unlike raw text, AMR offers a structured semantic format that explicitly and unambiguously captures a sentence's core concepts and relationships, thereby mitigating surface-level variations across diverse languages and expressions. Moving beyond prior studies that primarily assess semantic similarity metrics, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of both existing multilingual embeddings and our AMR-enhanced variants across five distinct transfer tasks in various downstream applications. Experimental findings demonstrate that integrating AMR into multilingual sentence embeddings yields superior state-of-the-art results in both semantic textual similarity and transfer learning tasks. Our codebase and evaluation scripts are available at \url{https://github.com/jcyk/MSE-AMR}.

In 1968, V.I. Oseledets posed the question of convergence within the Birkhoff and multiplicative ergodic theorems for measurable cocycles over flows, assuming integrability for every individual time $t$. In 2016, A.M. Stepin and the author demonstrated that convergence occurs along time subsets with density 1. This note further establishes that convergence holds modulo time subsets of finite measure.

Following unsupervised pre-training, fine-tuning transformer models yields high performance across numerous natural language processing tasks. However, the prolonged inference times associated with transformers significantly increase production costs. Knowledge distillation offers a potential remedy by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, thereby maintaining high performance while achieving substantial compression. Despite these benefits, the student model's size remains fixed post-pre-training, preventing individual adjustments for specific downstream tasks to optimize the performance/speedup ratio. An alternative approach involves pruning layers after pre-training, which offers a more granular and computationally efficient reduction in model size. The drawback is that traditional layer-wise pruning techniques often fail to match the performance of state-of-the-art knowledge distillation methods. This paper introduces Greedy-layer pruning, which (1) surpasses current state-of-the-art results in layer-wise pruning, (2) narrows the performance gap relative to knowledge distillation, and (3) enables dynamic adaptation of model size to achieve a desired performance/speedup tradeoff without requiring additional pre-training. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/deepopinion/greedy-layer-pruning.

**Context.** A recent statistical analysis of 79 active sunspot regions revealed that the average vertical magnetic field component ($B_\text{ver}$) along the umbral boundary does not vary with sunspot size, leading authors to conclude that this field's absolute value is uniform across all spots.

**Aims.** This study examines the temporal changes in the average $B_\text{ver}$ along the umbral boundary of a single, long-lived sunspot during its stable phase.

**Methods.** Data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) were analyzed. The umbral boundary was identified using continuum intensity contours at $I_\text{c}=0.5I_\text{qs}$ (where $I_\text{qs}$ is the quiet sun average) to extract magnetic field values. The analysis accounted for projection effects arising from the differing formation heights of the Fe I 617.3 nm spectral line and the continuum, and restricted observations to heliocentric angles below $60^{\circ}$ to eliminate limb artifacts.

**Results.** During the first disk passage of NOAA AR 11591, $B_\text{ver}$ remained stable at 1693 G with an rms deviation of 15 G. In contrast, the magnetic field strength exhibited significant variation (mean 2171 G, rms 48 G) and long-term trends. Adjusting for formation height had minimal impact on the mean value along individual contours but reduced variations away from the disk center, resulting in a closer alignment between the $B_\text{ver}=1693$ G contours and the $I_\text{c}=0.5I_\text{qs}$ contours.

**Conclusions.** For a stable sunspot during a disk passage, the umbral boundary can be equivalently defined by either the continuum intensity ($I_\text{c}$) or the vertical magnetic field component ($B_\text{ver}$). However, contours of constant magnetic field strength do not accurately delineate the umbral boundary.

In distributed learning, a central server trains a model using updates from nodes with local data. When faced with malicious servers (Byzantine adversaries) sending erroneous information, standard training algorithms like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) fail to converge. This paper offers a streamlined convergence theory for the generic Byzantine Resilient SGD method first introduced by Blanchard et al. [NeurIPS 2017]. Unlike prior analyses, we demonstrate convergence to a stationary point in expectation under standard assumptions regarding the (potentially nonconvex) objective function and flexible conditions on stochastic gradients.

This work addresses the challenge of unbiasedly estimating expectations relative to a general probability measure $\pi$ on $(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))$, which is absolutely continuous with respect to a standard Gaussian measure. Our focus lies on simulations utilizing a specific class of diffusion processes, known as the Schrödinger-Föllmer Sampler. This technique approximates the law of a diffusion bridge process $\{X_t\}_{t\in [0,1]}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d\in \mathbb{N}_0$) designed such that, beginning at $X_0=0$, the terminal state satisfies $X_1\sim \pi$. Typically, the diffusion's drift is intractable; even if computable, exact sampling of the diffusion remains impossible. Consequently, prior works \cite{sf_orig,jiao} employ a stochastic Euler-Maruyama scheme to generate biased estimators for expectations under $\pi$. We demonstrate that for this approach to attain a mean square error of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)$ for any $\epsilon>0$, the computational cost scales as $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-5})$. We subsequently propose an alternative methodology yielding unbiased estimates of expectations with respect to $\pi$, thereby eliminating biases arising from time discretization and drift approximation. We prove that achieving a mean square error of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)$ via this new method incurs a cost of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}|\log(\epsilon)|^{2+\delta})$ with high probability, for any $\delta>0$. Finally, we apply our proposed method to various examples, including Bayesian inverse problems.

We outline the construction of generalized string-net models, a class of exactly solvable lattice models capable of realizing a broad spectrum of two-dimensional topologically ordered phases. The ground states of these systems represent superpositions of distinct "string-net configurations," defined as trivalent graphs with labeled edges situated in the $xy$ plane. The primary distinction of this generalized approach is the relaxation of two key assumptions present in the original framework: tetrahedral reflection symmetry and the requirement that the ground state wave function $\Phi$ be "isotropic." Consequently, in this extended setup, string-net configurations $X_1$ and $X_2$ that are continuously deformable into one another may possess different ground state amplitudes, such that $\Phi(X_1) \neq \Phi(X_2)$. This flexibility enables the realization of topological phases unreachable by the original construction. In this work, we offer a more comprehensive treatment of ground state wave functions, Hamiltonians, and the minimal self-consistency conditions required for generalized string-net models compared to prior literature. Furthermore, we demonstrate the construction of string operators that generate anyon excitations and detail the computation of their braiding statistics. Finally, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which generalized string-net models exhibit isotropic ground state wave functions on either the plane or the sphere—a property that holds potential utility for various applications.

This paper investigates the theory of inner and outer capacities on locally compact spaces concerning general function kernels, with a primary focus on deriving alternative characterizations of these capacities and their associated measures for arbitrary sets. The analysis relies heavily on the interplay between capacity theory and balayage. As a secondary contribution, the work offers a rigorous validation of Fuglede's theories regarding inner and outer capacitary measures and capacitability (Acta Math., 1960). The findings present significant novelty even when applied to logarithmic, Newtonian, Green, $\alpha$-Riesz, and $\alpha$-Green kernels.

Although EEG has been explored as a biometric modality for roughly ten years, its viability in real-world settings remains unconfirmed due to challenges in data collection and reproducibility. To address this, we introduce a deployable EEG biometrics system utilizing a `one-fits-all' viscoelastic generic in-ear sensor, which eliminates the need for skilled assistance or complex preparation. Unlike prior research, our study evaluates data spanning multiple days and subjects to ensure reproducibility, rigorously separating training and testing segments across different recording sessions. Our robust methodology employs the resting-state eyes-closed paradigm, combining parametric (autoregressive) and non-parametric (spectral) features, and utilizes efficient classifiers including cosine distance, linear discriminant analysis, and support vector machines. We examine both verification and identification scenarios, achieving performance comparable to studies relying on impractical on-scalp recordings. A comprehensive analysis across various subjects, configurations, and feature sets confirms the feasibility of our ear-EEG biometrics system and its potential to overcome the critical issues of collectability, robustness, and reproducibility inherent in current EEG biometrics.
Assuming $(X, B)$ is a klt pair where $B$ is a boundary divisor on a projective toric variety $X$, we prove the Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing theorem for this pair.

The thermodynamics of four-dimensional Kerr-AdS black holes is re-examined using a recently introduced restricted phase space formalism. This framework treats the central charge $C$ of the dual CFT and the chemical potential $\mu$ as thermodynamic variables, while omitting pressure and its conjugate volume. Under this approach, the Euler relation is satisfied naturally, and the specific homogeneity orders of the mass (first order) and intensive variables (zeroth order) are clearly demonstrated. A detailed analysis of thermodynamic processes involving each pair of conjugate variables reveals significant scaling properties within the equations of state. The resulting thermodynamic behavior closely mirrors that previously observed in RN-AdS black holes. Specifically, first-order supercritical phase equilibrium occurs in $T-S$ processes when angular momentum is non-zero, whereas vanishing or fixed angular velocities lead to non-equilibrium transitions from small, unstable black holes to large, stable ones. Additionally, a Hawking-Page phase transition emerges in $\mu-C$ processes. Although the complexity of the Kerr metric restricts the explicit calculation of the exact critical point and Hawking-Page temperature to the slow-rotating limit, the fundamental thermodynamic characteristics remain independent of this approximation.

Algorithms exhibiting uniform convergence relative to initial conditions, known as fixed-time stable, are gaining significant traction for addressing control and observer design challenges under strict time limits. Nevertheless, a comprehensive approach for designing such algorithms for high-order perturbed systems with a specified upper bound on settling time remains absent. This study bridges that gap by presenting a methodology to transform a class of asymptotically, finite-, and fixed-time stable systems into non-autonomous fixed-time stable systems with a user-defined settling time ceiling. The proposed approach achieves this by incorporating time-varying gains. Unlike conventional methods where these gains diverge toward infinity near the origin, we establish sufficient conditions to ensure the gains remain bounded. We demonstrate the efficacy of this methodology by constructing fixed-time online differentiators that feature both a user-defined settling time upper bound and bounded gains.

We introduce a non-local framework describing contact guidance and steric hindrance based on a single external cue: the extracellular matrix, which influences both cell polarization and motility velocity. Beginning with a microscopic characterization of the stochastic processes driving cell re-orientation and changes in speed and direction, we formally derive a kinetic model that precisely replicates these microscopic dynamics. From this model, we deduce the macroscopic limit within the relevant regime. Furthermore, we validate the model across various scenarios by numerically identifying the minimal microscopic mechanisms required to reproduce observed cell dynamics, comparing our results with experimental data on breast cancer cell migration. This process not only confirms the validity of our modeling approach but also demonstrates its ability to predict qualitative cellular behaviors in diverse, heterogeneous microenvironments.

Space weathering significantly impacts the surfaces of airless bodies, such as asteroids, in the Solar System. Although experiments simulating this process are crucial for analyzing its effects on meteorites, they only replicate the phenomenon in a fraction of the actual time required. In December 2010, the T-type asteroid 596 Scheila was struck by an impactor tens of meters in size. A decade later, researchers utilized visible spectrophotometry and near-infrared spectroscopy to observe how the asteroid's surface had evolved since the impact. The resulting spectrum aligns with observations made shortly after the 2010 event, indicating that space weathering has not noticeably altered the surface color of dark asteroids over ten years. This marks the first investigation into space weathering-induced color changes on a real asteroid surface. Given that collisions frequently expose fresh layers on asteroids, the study proposes a genetic connection between D/T-type asteroids and dark (low albedo) X-complex asteroids, as well as very red objects like 269 Justitia, 732 Tjilaki, and 203 Pompeja. Recent findings confirm that 203 Pompeja possesses an X-type-like surface, though certain localized areas display a distinctly red spectrum.

This study investigates the low-frequency Drude response of bulk-insulating Bi$_2$Se$_3$ topological insulator films. Using time-domain terahertz spectroscopy, we simultaneously measured the frequency and field dependencies of carrier density and mobility. These films, grown on buffer layers and capped with selenium, had been exposed to air for several months. Under magnetic fields reaching 7 Tesla, we detected distinct cyclotron resonances (CRs). We attribute these sharp CRs to topological surface states (TSSs) originating from both film surfaces. Furthermore, we observed that the CRs sharpen at high fields due to electron-impurity scattering. Magneto-terahertz spectroscopy confirmed the bulk-insulating nature of these films, establishing their potential for applications in topological spintronics and quantum computing that rely on intrinsic topological insulators free from bulk carriers.

We report findings regarding in-medium interactions between static quark-antiquark pairs derived from realistic 2+1 flavor HISQ lattice QCD. The study emphasizes extracting spectral data from Wilson line correlators in Coulomb gauge through four distinct complementary techniques. Our results demonstrate that on HISQ lattices, the location of the dominant spectral peak linked to the real part of the interquark potential remains invariant with temperature, contrasting with earlier quenched QCD studies; consequently, we provide comparative analyses using newly generated quenched ensembles.

The potential of deep learning suggests that new particle discoveries at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) could be on the horizon. After detecting a new Beyond the Standard Model particle in an all-hadronic channel, deep learning methods can effectively determine its quantum numbers. Specifically, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) utilizing jet-images can substantially outperform current techniques in identifying both the quantum chromodynamic (QCD) color and the spin of two-prong resonances based on their substructure. Furthermore, jet-images help pinpoint which aspects of the jet radiation pattern are most valuable for classification, potentially inspiring future taggers. These advancements enhance the categorization of new particles and serve as a crucial addition to the expanding jet substructure toolkit for both current and future LHC searches and measurements.

Although rewriting systems are well-established, abstract tools for Probabilistic Rewriting remain scarce. This paper investigates the uniqueness of the final outcome (specifically, a unique limit distribution) and introduces proof techniques to evaluate and compare reduction strategies. The objective is to provide tools that facilitate the operational analysis of probabilistic calculi—such as probabilistic lambda-calculi—where evaluation involves multiple possible reduction choices leading to different paths.

This paper introduces a straightforward approach to approximately estimate the convergence point by averaging the elite sub-population. Building on this concept, we develop two methods: an ordinary averaging strategy and a weighted averaging strategy. Furthermore, we design a Gaussian sampling operator centered at the estimated convergence point with a specific standard deviation. When integrated with the traditional differential evolution (DE) algorithm, this operator accelerates convergence. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposal effectively speeds up DE across most of the 28 low-dimensional test functions in the CEC2013 Suite, and the method can be readily adapted to other population-based evolutionary algorithms with minimal modification.

SATNet functions as a differentiable constraint solver equipped with a bespoke backpropagation algorithm, enabling its integration as a layer within deep-learning architectures. It represents a significant step toward unifying deep learning with logical reasoning, having already demonstrated success in learning the rules of complex logical puzzles, such as Sudoku, directly from image-based input-output pairs. This paper introduces SymSATNet, an enhanced variant of SATNet that leverages symmetries inherent in the rules of a logical puzzle or formula. SymSATNet translates these symmetries into specific constraints on the solver's parameters, enforcing a particular parametric structure that ensures compliance. By imposing these requirements, the number of learnable parameters is drastically reduced for symmetric rules, rendering the learning process significantly more efficient than with standard SATNet. Furthermore, we outline a method for automatically identifying rule symmetries from example data. Empirical evaluations on Sudoku and the Rubik's Cube confirm that SymSATNet achieves substantial performance gains over the baseline SATNet.

This study theoretically examines the microscopic mechanism converting electron spin into the local microscopic rotation of atoms within crystals. In phonon modes possessing angular momentum, atoms rotate around their equilibrium positions. Utilizing a simple phonon-based toy model and the adiabatic series expansion, we compute the spin expectation value. Our findings demonstrate that microscopic local atomic rotations generate time-averaged spin magnetization through spin-orbit interaction. Conversely, in systems exhibiting only simple atomic vibrations, time-averaged spin magnetization vanishes due to time-reversal symmetry. Furthermore, the magnitude of this magnetization is inversely proportional to the difference in instantaneous eigenenergy; consequently, it diminishes in band insulators characterized by larger energy gaps.

Migration, particularly irregular migration, presents a significant challenge for border authorities and society at large. Various elements, including perceptions of specific routes and destination countries, shape migration-related scenarios and decisions. Systematically analyzing media and social media content, including videos and images, offers a way to deepen understanding of these influencing factors. However, the complexity of migration and the diverse visual representations of its aspects render the automated detection and analysis of relevant multimedia difficult. To address this, we introduce a novel method that connects established domain knowledge—defined through migration-specific semantic concepts—with their visual manifestation in video, utilizing an advanced video analysis and retrieval technique.

This paper investigates typical distances within a geometric random graph defined on the hyperbolic plane. Originally proposed by Krioukov et al.~\cite{ar:Krioukov} to model complex networks, the framework involves placing $N$ vertices randomly within a bounded region of the hyperbolic plane, connecting any pair whose hyperbolic distance falls below a specific threshold. By selecting parameters appropriately, the resulting graph remains sparse while displaying both a power-law degree distribution and local clustering. We demonstrate an additional characteristic: the distance between two randomly selected vertices in the same connected component scales doubly logarithmically with $N$, characterizing the graph as an \emph{ultra-small world}. Specifically, we prove that when this distance is rescaled by $\log \log N$, it converges in probability to a constant determined by the power-law exponent. This same constant appears in a related setting involving the well-established \emph{Chung-Lu} model, which also features a power-law tail in its degree distribution.

Understanding the decision-making processes of effective deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on images enhances the success of deep learning models. However, current methods are limited to interpreting specific decision logic for individual or very few images. To improve human interpretability and generalization, it is crucial to develop representative interpretations that capture the common decision logic of a CNN across a large set of similar images, thereby revealing the shared semantics that contribute to many related predictions. In this paper, we introduce a novel unsupervised approach to generate highly representative interpretations for numerous similar images. We formulate the task of finding these representative interpretations as a co-clustering problem, transforming it into a submodular cost submodular cover problem based on a sample of the CNN's linear decision boundaries. Additionally, we provide a visualization and similarity ranking method. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our method performs excellently.

This work investigates the energetic cost of erasing information by applying the Jarzynski equality. We demonstrate that the Landauer bound, $\langle W \rangle \geq kT \ln 2$, which governs the average dissipated work $\langle W \rangle$ during erasure, directly arises from Kelvin's formulation of the second law, $\langle W \rangle \geq 0$. This emergence occurs as a result of the spontaneous breaking of Crooks-Tasaki fluctuation symmetry, a phenomenon linked to logical irreversibility. We support this finding through numerical simulations of information erasure conducted on a 2D Ising ferromagnet.

Effective emergency evacuations are crucial for saving lives and alleviating suffering. Nevertheless, decision-makers face significant challenges in establishing optimal evacuation strategies due to the chaos, uncertainty, and ethical considerations inherent in such crises. We introduce and evaluate a decision support tool designed for pre-crisis training of teams preparing for civilian evacuations, applying it to the 2021 U.S.-led evacuation from Afghanistan as a case study. Our approach utilizes various classes of Markov decision processes (MDPs) to model three compounding layers of uncertainty: (1) the priority category of the next individual at the gate, (2) the population-level distribution of priority categories, and (3) the accuracy of individuals' claimed priorities. We compare the number of evacuees by priority status across eight heuristic policies, demonstrating that the optimized MDP policy outperforms all heuristic baselines. Furthermore, we find that accounting for these compounding levels of model uncertainty increases complexity without yielding better policy performance. Practical heuristics derived from the optimized policies can guide human decision-makers. Finally, we release all tools as open-source to foster robust discussions regarding the trade-offs, limitations, and potential of integrating algorithms into high-stakes humanitarian decision-making.

Driven by the goal of understanding the internal dynamics of stars and planets, we conducted direct numerical simulations of rotating, internally heated Boussinesq convection within a full sphere. These simulations examined scenarios with both stress-free, fixed-temperature boundaries and no-slip, fixed heat flux boundaries, with a specific emphasis on the emergence of large-scale coherent structures and mean zonal flows. At a Prandtl number of one, increasing the thermal forcing (Rayleigh number) beyond the onset threshold revealed a sequence of regimes: a relaxation oscillation phase followed by geostrophic turbulence. Notably, we observed for the first time the formation of large-scale coherent vortices along the rotation axis within this system. All regime transitions were effectively characterized by critical values of the convective Rossby number ($Ro_c$), occurring at approximately $Ro_c \approx 0.2$ for the shift from oscillation to geostrophic turbulence, and $Ro_c \approx 1.5$ for the transition to the large-scale vortex regime. The direction of the zonal flow, governed by $Ro_c$, reverses during the shift from geostrophic turbulence to the large-scale vortex state. Furthermore, while inertial scaling accurately describes non-zonal flow speeds and heat transfer in the geostrophic turbulence regime, the emergence of large-scale vortices appears to diminish both the non-zonal flow velocity and the efficiency of convective heat transfer.

This thesis aims to investigate the singularities of the exponential map on Riemannian and Finsler manifolds—a topic linked to caustics and catastrophes—as well as the cut locus (also referred to as the ridge, medial axis, or skeleton). The study seeks to enhance current understanding of its structure, offer novel perspectives, and establish applications regarding the Ambrose conjecture and Hamilton-Jacobi equations.

Pedestrian dynamics represents an interdisciplinary research domain where psychologists, sociologists, traffic engineers, physicists, mathematicians, and computer scientists collectively seek to comprehend crowd movement. While computer simulations theoretically facilitate this understanding, a universally accepted locomotion model for crowd dynamics remains elusive, unlike in many classical physics systems. Instead, numerous approaches with distinct characteristics vie for dominance, often requiring specialized expertise within a specific model type to evaluate their impact on simulation outcomes. Consequently, researchers from diverse fields aiming to utilize simulations for pedestrian analysis require a tool capable of comparing these competing methodologies. Similarly, developers would benefit from an accessible means to explore alternative modeling strategies. Vadere addresses this cross-disciplinary need by providing a lightweight, open-source simulation framework featuring a user-friendly interface and pre-implemented versions of the most prevalent models.

This brief communication demonstrates how fundamental techniques from Malliavin calculus can be utilized to derive the two-point function for the slope of the one-dimensional KPZ equation. Starting with an arbitrary two-sided Brownian motion, we express this function using the polymer end-point annealed distribution linked to the stochastic heat equation. Furthermore, we establish that this distribution corresponds to the derivative of the variance of the KPZ equation's solution.

We introduce new ALMA Band 7 data concerning the edge-on debris disc surrounding the M1V star GSC 07396-00759. Approximately 20 million years old and a member of the beta Pictoris Moving Group, this star joins AU Mic as one of the few low-mass M-dwarfs with its disc resolved at sub-millimeter wavelengths. Combining these findings with prior VLT/SPHERE scattered light measurements, we offer a multi-wavelength perspective on the dust distribution within the system, accounting for stellar wind influences. Our results indicate that millimeter-sized dust grains are well-modeled by a Gaussian torus located at 70 au with a full width at half maximum of 48 au, and no CO emission was detected. The radius derived from our ALMA model is notably smaller than that inferred from polarimetric scattered light data, suggesting complex scattering phase function behavior. Furthermore, the brightness asymmetry visible in scattered light does not appear in the ALMA images, implying that the underlying physical mechanism primarily impacts smaller grain sizes. High-resolution follow-up observations are necessary to further examine these unique dust characteristics and to establish a true coeval comparison with its well-studied sibling, AU Mic, among M-dwarf systems.

We investigate electron transport within a Kitaev chain coupled to normal metallic leads at distinct temperatures and chemical potentials. Typically, this system is analyzed using either the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism or the scattering approach. The NEGF method calculates steady-state currents and properties via Green's functions incorporating wire characteristics and lead-induced self-energy corrections, whereas the scattering approach describes transport through plane wave amplitudes incident from the reservoirs. In this work, we explicitly demonstrate that both methods yield identical conductance results for the Kitaev chain. Furthermore, we reformulate the NEGF conductance expression to establish a direct one-to-one mapping between its terms and the scattering amplitudes associated with normal transmission, Andreev transmission, and Andreev reflection, thereby deriving closed-form expressions for these amplitudes. We also derive the wavefunctions for zero-energy Majorana bound states (MBS) in the wire connected to leads, confirming they exist within the same parameter regime as in an isolated wire. These bound states induce perfect Andreev reflection, resulting in a quantized conductance peak at zero bias. We examine how the width of this peak varies with Hamiltonian parameters and relate these variations to the properties of the MBS wavefunctions. Specifically, we find that the peak broadens as the MBS weight in the reservoirs increases, and narrows as it decreases.

We introduce a noise deconvolution method designed to eliminate a broad spectrum of noise during arbitrary measurements on qubit systems. Specifically, we derive the inverse maps for the most prevalent single-qubit noisy channels and apply them during data processing to recover noise-free estimates of observables in qubit systems affected by known noise. We also demonstrate a self-consistency check to verify the accuracy of noise characterization, supported by simulation results for deconvolving a general Pauli channel and experimental validation of decoherence noise deconvolution on Rigetti quantum hardware.

This research utilizes Monte-Carlo simulations to examine the interaction of laser-driven $\gamma$-photons and high-energy charged particles with high-Z materials. The input particles originate from particle-in-cell simulations modeling the collision of a tightly focused, ultra-intense laser pulse with a titanium target. Lead is selected as the secondary high-Z target due to its substantial cross-section for giant dipole resonance and electron-positron pair production. The study identifies an ultra-short, ultra-relativistic, collimated positron population, detailing their energy spectra, angular distribution, and temporal characteristics. Additionally, the influence of target thickness on the total counts and kinetic energies of various emitted particle species is analyzed, with separate investigations for irradiation by laser-generated $\gamma$-photons and charged particles. The production of residual high-Z nuclides in the lead target is also charted. Given the brief pulse duration, these $\gamma$-photon, electron-positron, and neutron sources offer potential applications in material science, nuclear physics, laboratory astrophysics, and as injectors for laser-driven charged particle accelerators.

The "periodic table" for strongly coupled gauge theories is still only partially understood. Holography has advanced sufficiently that bottom-up approaches can model the spectra of specific gauge theories (relying on assumptions regarding their running), incorporating quarks across various representations and higher-dimensional operators. I illustrate this methodology using a refined AdS dual of QCD and present findings for composite Higgs models featuring two quark representations. Furthermore, this approach prompts inquiries into how separable energy scales are in generic gauge theories, specifically questioning whether confinement and chiral symmetry breaking are inherently connected.

We investigate how right-handed neutrinos influence the stability of the electroweak vacuum within high-scale supersymmetric two-Higgs-doublet models. Assuming supersymmetry breaking occurs at $M_S = 2 \times 10^{16}$ GeV, the effective theory below this scale is a type-II two-Higgs-doublet model incorporating three generations of singlet neutrinos. These singlets generate small masses for standard model neutrinos via the type I seesaw mechanism, and we examine both high-scale and low-scale implementations of this mechanism. Our analysis demonstrates that right-handed neutrinos with Yukawa couplings of ${\cal O}(1)$ or larger significantly enhance electroweak vacuum stability. However, this scenario is heavily restricted by measured Higgs properties, Higgs couplings, and flavor physics constraints on the charged Higgs mass. Consequently, achieving a stable or metastable electroweak vacuum alongside an experimentally viable low-energy scalar spectrum necessitates $\tan\beta \lesssim 2.5$ and neutrino Yukawa couplings smaller than ${\cal O}(1)$. Under these conditions, the findings remain qualitatively consistent with scenarios excluding right-handed neutrinos.

We uncover the microscopic mechanism behind electric polarization ($\vec{P}$) generated by noncollinear magnetic ordering. In Mott insulators, this polarization arises from all combinations of position operators $\hat{\vec{r}}_{ij} = (\vec{r}_{ij}^{\, 0},\vec{\boldsymbol{r}}_{ij}^{\phantom{0}})$ and transfer integrals $\hat{t}_{ij} = (t_{ij}^{0},\boldsymbol{t}_{ij}^{\phantom{0}})$ within bonds, where the components $\vec{r}_{ij}^{\, 0}$ and $t_{ij}^{0}$ are independent of spin in the Kramers doublet basis, whereas $\vec{\boldsymbol{r}}_{ij}^{\phantom{0}}$ and $\boldsymbol{t}_{ij}^{\phantom{0}}$ originate exclusively from spin-orbit coupling. Specifically, the term $t_{ij}^{0} \vec{\boldsymbol{r}}_{ij}^{\phantom{0}}$, which links to the spin current, stays finite even in centrosymmetric bonds, thereby producing a finite $\vec{P}$ when spins are arranged noncollinearly. The magnetoelectric coupling, governed by $\vec{\boldsymbol{r}}_{ij}^{\phantom{0}}$, exhibits a rich structure that extends beyond the phenomenological rule $\vec{P} \sim \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{ij} \times [\boldsymbol{e}_{i} \times \boldsymbol{e}_{j}]$, where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{ij}$ denotes the bond vector between spins $\boldsymbol{e}_{i}$ and $\boldsymbol{e}_{j}$. Employing density-functional theory, we demonstrate the operation of this mechanism in spiral magnets such as CuCl$_2$, CuBr$_2$, CuO, and $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, offering a consistent account of existing experimental findings.

A recent investigation revealed that standard accelerometer-based gait authentication systems ($v$ABGait) are vulnerable to random-vector attacks, prompting the proposal of a beta noise-assisted variant ($\beta$ABGait) as a countermeasure. This paper evaluates the efficacy of random-vector attacks against both $v$ABGait and $\beta$ABGait across three distinct accelerometer datasets. Furthermore, we introduce $i$ABGait, an alternative approach leveraging a Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network, and test its robustness against both traditional zero-effort and random-vector attacks. The findings indicate that $i$ABGait effectively reduces the impact of random-vector attacks and surpasses $\beta$ABGait in the majority of experimental scenarios.

This study introduces two novel Bayesian approaches for estimating and forecasting home team win probabilities in games. The initial method utilizes a prior that evolves based on the lead differential and the duration of the match. The second approach refines this by combining the Bayesian estimator with a time-weighted pre-game win probability through a linear function. Comparative analysis against established methods demonstrates that these new techniques outperform existing ones in both estimation and prediction accuracy. The practical value of these methods is highlighted through their application to the 2016 NCAA Division 1 Championship game.

Monitoring complex systems through time-series data to identify anomalous exogenous events for timely action is often essential yet difficult, as determining abnormality requires learning an extrapolative probabilistic model from historical data and classifying based on limited current observations. This work leverages recent advancements in long-term probabilistic forecasting, specifically Deep Probabilistic Koopman, to develop a general approach for anomaly classification in multi-dimensional time-series. Additionally, we demonstrate how incorporating domain knowledge into these models can minimize both Type I and Type II errors. We apply this method to the critical real-world challenge of global atmospheric pollution monitoring by integrating it with NASA's Global Earth System Model. The resulting system effectively detects localized air quality anomalies caused by events such as wildfires and COVID-19 lockdowns.

Although the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is central to photonic quantum information, scaling it to high dimensions relies heavily on the chosen physical encoding, leaving emerging platforms like frequency bins without practical implementation methods. This Letter demonstrates that d-point frequency-bin DFTs can be achieved using a fixed three-component quantum frequency processor (QFP) by incorporating one additional radio-frequency harmonic into the electro-optic modulation signals for every incremental increase in d. Numerical simulations confirm a gate fidelity F > 0.9997 and success probability P > 0.965 up to d = 10, while experimental implementation for d = 3 utilizes parallel DFT measurements to quantify entanglement and perform full tomography of multiple two-photon frequency-bin states. These findings open new avenues for high-dimensional frequency-bin protocols in quantum communications and networking.

This work examines coarse-graining in classical statistical physics through the lens of the symplectic non-squeezing theorem. We discuss the implications of this theorem for the BBGKY hierarchy and demonstrate that the emergence of cubic cells during coarse-graining is a direct result of the uniqueness of Hofer's metric on the group of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of phase space.

This study explores the use of deep learning autoencoders to unsupervisedly identify phase transitions in lattice-based physical systems. The investigation centers on the two-dimensional ferromagnetic Ising model before extending the approach to the anti-ferromagnetic variant. Spin configurations for both models are generated under zero external magnetic field conditions. For the ferromagnetic case, we numerically examine the correlation between a single latent variable derived from the autoencoder and the critical temperature ($T_c$). The autoencoder successfully distinguishes between ordered and disordered spin phases, illustrating the restoration of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry as temperature rises. We conduct a finite volume analysis across an increasing sequence of lattice sizes. In the largest system studied, the observed phase transition aligns closely with the theoretically predicted critical temperature. We introduce a "quasi-order parameter," defined as the absolute average latent variable ($\tilde{z}$), which facilitates the prediction of $T_c$. Furthermore, by defining a latent susceptibility, we quantify the critical temperature $T_c(L)$ at various lattice sizes, observing only minor finite scaling effects. We demonstrate that $T_c(L)$ extrapolates to the established theoretical limit as $L \to \infty$, indicating that the autoencoder can accurately extract the critical temperature of the phase transition. Finally, we apply the autoencoder to the anti-ferromagnetic Ising model, confirming that the network effectively detects the phase transition in a comparable manner.

This paper outlines a methodology for specifying and verifying flow security properties defined within the opacity framework. We introduce OpacTL, a logic designed to express these properties clearly in systems modeled as partially observable labelled transition systems. Additionally, we develop verification techniques to analyze opacity concerning various observation notions. By incorporating a probabilistic operator into the specification language, we enable quantitative analysis and verification, which has been implemented as an extension to the PRISM model checker and demonstrated through several examples. Finally, we sketch an alternative method for quantifying the opacity property using entropy.

Observations of exoplanet orbital distributions reveal a concentration of super-Earth-sized planets near their host stars within compact systems. If inward migration driven by the protoplanetary disc is responsible for their formation, these planets may have halted at the disc's inner edge or been driven through the inner cavity by a resonant chain, a scenario that requires further investigation. Utilizing numerical simulations, this study examines whether outer planets can push inner members of a resonant chain into the disc's inner cavity. We conducted both hydrodynamical and N-body simulations of planetary systems within nascent discs, modeling the inner disc edge in two distinct ways: as a dead zone inner edge (DZ) or a disc inner boundary (IB). The primary distinction between these models is the steepness of the surface density profile. In all cases, the innermost planet has a mass of 10 Earth masses, with additional outer planets of equal or greater mass. Our results indicate that steeper profiles halt planetary chains more effectively than shallower ones. Consequently, final configurations in DZ models are typically more tightly packed and thus more susceptible to instability than those in IB models. We derived analytical expressions for stopping conditions based on power equilibrium and demonstrated that final eccentricities arise from torque equilibrium. Furthermore, for thinner discs, our hydrodynamical simulations revealed, for the first time, clear evidence of over-stable libration, resulting in extremely compact systems. Additionally, we found that popular N-body simulations may overestimate the number of planets that end up within the disc's inner cavity.

Deep Neural Networks are notoriously resource-intensive regarding both computation and memory. Given the growing prevalence of mobile and embedded devices with constrained budgets, creating low-complexity models that retain strong predictive accuracy has become increasingly vital. This study examines and contrasts several established techniques for reducing neural network parameters. Furthermore, we contextualize these methods within recent research on how Receptive Fields (RF) influence model performance, empirically demonstrating that high-performing, low-complexity architectures can be achieved by combining specific RF restrictions with parameter reduction strategies. Additionally, we introduce a filter-damping technique designed to regularize RFs without modifying the network architecture or parameter count. We demonstrate that integrating this approach enhances performance across various low-complexity scenarios, including pruning and decomposed convolutions. Ultimately, our proposed filter-damping method secured the first-place rank in the Low-Complexity Acoustic Scene Classification task at the DCASE-2020 Challenge.

This brief essay demonstrates how computer simulations, particularly visualization, facilitated the discovery of phenomena that might otherwise have gone undetected. We also emphasize the significance of interactivity between the user and the computer. By examining various historical cases from mathematics and the physical sciences, we illustrate these points. The text includes numerous images and hyperlinks to online interactive numerical experiments. Naturally, we do not claim exhaustiveness; the selected examples reflect both our personal preferences and our limited knowledge. Additionally, links to several other interactive digital experiments are included.

Advances in computing and algorithms have enabled applications that can tolerate imprecision. However, these applications generate vast amounts of data that surpass the processing capabilities of current systems, prompting researchers to seek solutions to this challenge. One promising approach is Approximate Computing, which balances precision with efficiency. Another solution involves Acceleration, utilizing specialized logic to perform computations more power-efficiently. Additionally, Data Compression is employed in memory systems to conserve capacity and bandwidth.

Streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) models typically underperform compared to non-streaming counterparts due to the lack of future context. To address this and lower computational costs, this paper introduces a frame-level model for streaming ASR that utilizes an efficient augmented memory transformer block and a dynamic latency training approach. This system stores long-range historical context in an augmented memory bank to supplement the encoder's limited history. Additionally, a caching mechanism preserves key and value pairs for reuse in subsequent chunks, thereby reducing computation. A proposed dynamic latency training method further enhances performance while accommodating both low and high latency inference requirements. Evaluated on the 960-hour LibriSpeech benchmark, the model achieves an average latency of 640ms, delivering a relative word error rate (WER) reduction of 6.0% on test-clean and 3.0% on test-other compared to the truncate chunk-wise Transformer.

High-energy heavy-ion collisions are predicted to generate the chiral magnetic effect (CME) through the interaction between quark chirality imbalance and intense magnetic fields, resulting in charge separation along the magnetic field lines. Although the search for the CME continues at RHIC and the LHC, it is essential to carefully analyze CME-sensitive observables to eliminate non-CME background contributions. This study investigates how globally spin-aligned $\rho$ mesons affect the $\gamma_{112}$ correlator, the $R_{\Psi_2}(\Delta S)$ correlator, and signed balance functions using both a toy model and the AMPT multiphase transport model. Such global spin alignment in vector mesons, quantified by the spin density matrix component $\rho_{00}$, may stem from non-CME mechanisms. Our findings indicate that CME observables exhibit a similar dependence on $\rho_{00}$; specifically, pion decays from $\rho$ mesons contribute positively (negatively) to these observables when $\rho_{00}$ exceeds (falls below) 1/3. Given that pions are the most plentiful particles produced in these collisions, measuring the $\rho_{00}$ of $\rho$ mesons is vital for accurately interpreting CME experimental data.

R Coronae Borealis (RCB) and dustless Hydrogen-deficient Carbon (dLHdC) stars are thought to originate from the mergers of low-mass white dwarfs. These supergiants exhibit unique chemistries characterized by hydrogen deficiency, carbon richness, and significant excesses of $^{18}$O. While RCB stars experience dust formation events causing large photometric fluctuations—a phenomenon absent in dLHdC stars—the known Milky Way population of dLHdC stars has recently expanded by more than five times following the identification of 27 new members. This study presents medium-resolution (R$\approx3000$) near-infrared spectra for 20 newly found dLHdC stars. Our analysis confirms that, unlike RCB stars, dLHdC stars lack strong blueshifted ($>200$ km s$^{-1}$) He I 1.0833 $\mu$m absorption, indicating the absence of powerful, dust-driven winds. Additionally, we provide medium-resolution (R$\approx3000-8000$) $K$-band spectra for 47 RCB stars. We determined $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios for 7 dLHdC and 31 RCB stars displaying $^{12}$C$^{16}$O and $^{12}$C$^{18}$O absorption bands, compiling the most extensive dataset of these ratios for both classes to date. Our findings reveal that six of the seven dLHdC stars possess $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios below 0.5, whereas 26 of the 31 RCB stars exhibit ratios exceeding 1. Consequently, most dLHdC stars display lower $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O values than most RCB stars, validating a key spectroscopic distinction between the two groups. These results disprove the hypothesis that RCB stars represent an evolved phase of dLHdC stars. Instead, we propose that the final nature of a white dwarf merger remnant—as either a dLHdC or RCB star—depends on the specific mass ratios, masses, and compositions of the merging progenitors.

This study examines the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) of the solid solution Nb$_{5}$Ir$_{3-x}$Pt$_{x}$O, which crystallizes in the Ti$_{5}$Ga$_{4}$ structure. Both end members, Nb$_{5}$Ir$_{3}$O and Nb$_{5}$Pt$_{3}$O, are established superconductors with $T_c$ values of 10.5 K and 3.8 K, respectively; notably, Nb$_{5}$Ir$_{3}$O is classified as a two-gap superconductor. Throughout the alloy series, the Ti$_{5}$Ga$_{4}$ structure is retained, and lattice parameters exhibit a linear dependence on $x$. Conversely, the $T_c$ versus $x$ relationship is nonlinear, indicating that $T_c$ is not solely governed by lattice parameters. These findings are analyzed using the Matthias rule and contrasted with other two-gap superconductors, including MgB$_{2}$, Mo$_{8}$Ga$_{41}$, and Nb$_{3}$Sn.

This study reports direct numerical simulation results examining the power spectral densities of kinetic energy, convective entropy, and heat flux for unsteady Rayleigh-Bénard magnetoconvection within the frequency domain. For higher frequencies, the power spectral densities of all global quantities exhibit a variation proportional to $f^{-2}$. This scaling exponent remains invariant with respect to the Rayleigh number, Chandrasekhar's number, and the thermal Prandtl number.

Reservoir computing frameworks utilize driven dynamical systems where external inputs modify the system's evolving states, enabling applications in computation, machine learning, and information processing. A core issue within this paradigm involves determining the statistical link between inputs and system states. This paper establishes conditions ensuring the existence and uniqueness of asymptotically invariant measures for such driven systems and demonstrates that these measures depend continuously on the input process when both input and output spaces are equipped with the Wasserstein distance. The primary method employed involves characterizing these invariant measures as fixed points of naturally defined Foias operators, which have been extensively analyzed in this context. These fixed points are derived by enforcing a newly proposed stochastic state contractivity condition on the driven system, a criterion that is easily verifiable in specific examples. Notably, stochastic state contractivity can hold even in systems lacking state contractivity—a condition often required to ensure the echo state property in reservoir computing. Consequently, this new condition may be satisfied even when the echo state property itself is absent.

Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) offers a promising solution for real-time applications by enabling Roadside Units (RSUs) to cache content, allowing vehicles to retrieve requested data quickly. However, RSU storage is constrained, and the dynamic nature of high-mobility vehicles causes content popularity to fluctuate rapidly, making it crucial to predict and cache trending items in advance. While RSUs could train models using Vehicle User (VU) data for accurate predictions, privacy concerns often deter VUs from sharing raw data. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by enabling vehicles to train local models on their own data and upload only the model updates to the RSU for global aggregation, thereby safeguarding privacy. Traditional synchronous FL requires waiting for all vehicles to finish training and upload models, leading to significant delays in global model updates. In contrast, asynchronous FL updates the global model immediately upon receiving a local model, but varying vehicle dwell times can unevenly impact model accuracy. To address this, we propose an Asynchronous FL-based Mobility-aware Edge Caching (AFMC) scheme that accounts for vehicle mobility to achieve a precise global model, subsequently using this model to predict popular content. Experimental results demonstrate that the AFMC scheme outperforms other baseline caching approaches.

This document details a numerical investigation into how high-density pycnonuclear reactions influence the evolution of white dwarfs accreting material from companion stars. Our primary goal is to identify observable properties that change when these reactions are included under various microphysical assumptions, such as effective nucleon-nucleon interactions, lattice structures, and crystal polarization. Our findings show that while there are notable variations in pycnonuclear reaction rates, these do not lead to detectable differences in white dwarf evolution. Additionally, we compare observable properties when pycnonuclear reactions are assumed to occur versus when they do not. Our calculations suggest that this distinction can result in observable variations in radius ($R$) and effective temperature ($T_{eff}$) at the simulation stopping condition, defined as a total nuclear fusion energy release rate exceeding $10^{8}$ solar luminosities ($L_{nuc} > 10^{8}\thinspace \rm{L}_{\odot}$). Finally, we examine the frequently overlooked impact of temperature enhancement on pycnonuclear rates.

The study investigates the non-adiabatic quantum dynamics of charge transfer reactions involving H+H$_2^+$ $\rightarrow$ H$_2$+H$^+$, along with various isotopic forms, employing a precise wave packet methodology. This analysis utilizes a newly formulated $3\times3$ diabatic potential model derived from highly accurate {\it ab initio} computations, incorporating long-range interactions for both ground and excited states. Results indicate that for initial H$_2^+$(v=0), the quasi-degenerate H$_2$(v'=4) non-reactive charge transfer product is significantly enhanced, leading to increased reaction probabilities and cross-sections. From collision energies exceeding 0.2 eV, this channel becomes dominant, with the ratio of v'=4 products to others rising until 1 eV. In contrast, the H+H$_2^+$ $\rightarrow$ H$_2^+$+H exchange reaction channel is almost negligible, while reactive and non-reactive charge transfer channels are comparable in magnitude, except for the H$_2$(v'=4) case; below 0.2 eV, these two charge transfer processes compete. This enhancement is anticipated to exert significant vibrational and isotopic effects that require further evaluation. Additionally, regarding the three-proton system, the issue of permutation symmetry is addressed when utilizing reactant Jacobi coordinates.

In the single-winner selection scenario involving $n$ voters and $m$ candidates, each voter $j$ experiences a cost $c(i, j)$ if candidate $i$ is selected. The goal is to select the candidate that minimizes the expected aggregate cost for all voters; however, since we only observe voters' preference rankings rather than their true costs, some efficiency loss is unavoidable. This inefficiency is measured by distortion. We present a specific instance of the metric single-winner problem demonstrating that any randomized social choice function exhibits a distortion of at least 2.063164. This finding refutes the longstanding conjecture that a randomized social choice function with a worst-case distortion of at most 2 exists.

Snyder's relativistic, Lorentz-covariant quantum space-times can be characterized using the coset generators of (anti) de-Sitter algebras. In a similar fashion, Yang's Lorentz-covariant quantum phase spaces, which incorporate quantum curved four-momenta and a quantum-deformed relativistic Heisenberg algebra, are defined through appropriately selected coset generators of conformal algebras. This algebraic framework is extended to corresponding superalgebras, yielding quantum Lorentz-covariant superspaces (the SUSY Snyder model) and outlining the derivation of quantum relativistic phase superspaces (the SUSY Yang model). The final section briefly reviews alternative methods for constructing quantum phase (super)spaces and compares spinorial Snyder-type models that define either bosonic or fermionic quantum-deformed spinors.

Sparsity has emerged as a key technique for compressing and speeding up Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Within this domain, structured sparsity has attracted significant interest because it enables efficient execution on contemporary hardware accelerators. Specifically, N:M sparsity is highly appealing since existing accelerator architectures can exploit certain N:M structures to achieve superior compute efficiency. This work concentrates on N:M sparsity, conducting an extensive evaluation of various training strategies to analyze the trade-off between model accuracy and computational cost (FLOPs). Based on these findings, we introduce two novel decay-based pruning techniques: "pruning mask decay" and "sparse structure decay." Our assessments demonstrate that these methods consistently achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy on a Transformer-based translation model, matching the performance of unstructured sparsity. While the enhanced accuracy of the sparse models achieved through these new training recipes involves a slight increase in total training compute (FLOPs), the benefits remain substantial.

This work examines Gushel-Mukai (GM) varieties of dimension 4 and 6 within characteristic $p$. The primary achievement is establishing the Tate conjecture for all such varieties defined over finitely generated fields where $p \geq 5$. For GM sixfolds, we adopt the strategy employed by Madapusi Pera to prove the conjecture for K3 surfaces. To support this, we first establish fundamental properties of GM sixfolds, including the absence of nonzero global vector fields. Regarding GM fourfolds, we prove the Tate conjecture by reducing the problem to the sixfold case, utilizing the concept of generalized partners alongside the fact that these partners possess isomorphic Chow motives in the middle degree when considered in characteristic 0. Various stages of our proofs depend on results from characteristic 0, which are detailed in a companion paper.

Numerous investigations have examined the neural distinctions between encoding and retrieval in working memory (WM) tasks, yet the specific impact of re-encoding on brain activation remains uncertain. This study aimed to contrast three distinct brain states—rest, encoding, and re-encoding—within the context of a WM task. Data were collected from thirty-seven participants via electroencephalography (EEG), with subsequent calculations of power spectral density (PSD) and phase-locking value (PLV) across various frequencies. Furthermore, the study analyzed variations in phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) between encoding and re-encoding phases. Results indicated that alpha PSD diminished as learning advanced, while theta, beta, and gamma PLV exhibited inter-regional differences. Additionally, a statistically significant divergence in PAC was observed. These outcomes imply that understanding the neural correlations associated with learning could enhance the efficiency of re-encoding processes.

This study investigates persistent currents and low-field magnetic susceptibility in single-channel normal metal rings subjected to a magnetic flux $\phi$, utilizing a tight-binding model that incorporates long-range electron hopping along the shortest path. Higher-order hopping integrals are introduced to mitigate disorder effects by delocalizing energy eigenstates, resulting in current amplitudes in disordered rings that approach those of ordered rings. Furthermore, our analysis of low-field magnetic susceptibility indicates that the sign of persistent currents can be precisely determined in mesoscopic rings with a fixed electron count, even when impurities are present. While perfect rings exhibit exclusively diamagnetic behavior in low-field currents regardless of the total electron number $N_e$, disordered rings display a dependence on parity: they show diamagnetic characteristics for odd $N_e$ and paramagnetic behavior for even $N_e$.

We investigate the distribution of unpolarized quarks within an unpolarized pion as a function of the quark's transverse momentum, utilizing unpolarized Transverse Momentum Distributions (TMDs). By analyzing existing data on unpolarized pion-nucleus Drell-Yan processes—specifically focusing on the differential cross section with respect to the lepton-pair transverse momentum—we extract these pion TMDs. In this analysis, the pion TMDs are convoluted with nucleon TMDs derived from our prior research, yielding a satisfactory agreement with experimental results. Additionally, we provide predictions for pion-nucleus scattering currently under measurement by the COMPASS Collaboration.

Ultra-reliable low-latency communications (uRLLC), a key feature of 5G mobile networks, is designed to support mission-critical applications requiring high reliability and minimal latency. Leveraging established multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) information theory, uRLLC in the upcoming 6G era is anticipated to offer superior capabilities for extreme connectivity. Because latency constraints can be equivalently expressed through blocklength, finite block-length channel coding theory is essential for the theoretical analysis of uRLLC. Building upon the asymptotic results by Polyanskiy and Yang, this study first derives exact closed-form expressions for the expectation and variance of channel dispersion. Subsequently, it establishes a bound for the average maximal achievable rate in massive MIMO systems operating under ideal independent and identically distributed fading channels. This research uncovers the fundamental relationships among key MIMO transmission parameters through a concise and complete closed-form formula. Most significantly, the observed inverse proportionality indicates that latency can be further reduced at the cost of spatial degrees of freedom.

The unit distance graph $G_{\mathbb{R}^d}^1$ consists of an infinite set of nodes representing points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where an edge connects any two points separated by a Euclidean distance of 1. While the two-dimensional case, $G_{\mathbb{R}^2}^1$, is primarily investigated regarding its chromatic number within the context of the Hadwiger-Nelson problem, other attributes of such graphs remain underexplored. This study examines the restriction of $G_{\mathbb{R}^d}^1$ to closed convex subsets $X$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$. We demonstrate that the induced subgraph $G_{\mathbb{R}^d}^1[X]$ is connected if and only if the radius $r(X)$ of $X$ is 0, or if $r(X) \geq 1$ and the affine dimension of $X$ is at least 2. Furthermore, for hyperrectangles, we establish bounds on the graph diameter specifically for the critical scenario where the radius equals 1.

Large swarms of agents are prevalent across various engineering and biological domains, where dynamic bi-stability of co-existing spatio-temporal patterns is frequently observed in population models. However, common reduced analytical frameworks, such as mean-field theory, often fail to represent the bifurcation structure underlying this bi-stable behavior. This study introduces a novel model for large swarms incorporating delayed coupling.
