We utilize a transformer-based architecture enhanced by three pretext tasks, optimized during pre-training without requiring labeled data, where each task is specifically aligned with the downstream objectives. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of these selected pretext tasks. Notably, our approach overcomes the limitations of previous state-of-the-art methods relying on contrastive losses while achieving convergence with significantly fewer data samples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing supervised and self-supervised state-of-the-art techniques in handwritten and scene text recognition, as well as document image enhancement. The source code and trained models will be made publicly available at http://Upon_Acceptance.

Electric circuits containing both capacitive and inductive elements exhibit resonances that manifest in admittance measurements based on circuit parameters and AC driving frequency. This study examines the impedance behavior of nontrivial topolectrical circuits (TEs), specifically 1D and 2D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) models, demonstrating that finite $LC$ circuits inevitably display size-dependent anomalous impedance resonances. Utilizing the method of images, we investigate how resonance modes in multi-dimensional circuit arrays are uniquely altered by current reflection and interference from lattice boundaries and the structure itself. Furthermore, we derive analytic formulas for the impedance between two corner nodes across various lattice networks featuring both homogeneous and heterogeneous components. Additionally, we establish the irregular relationship between lattice size and impedance resonance, while offering integral and dimensionally reduced expressions for impedances in three dimensions and higher.

This tutorial is designed to introduce the core principles of adversarial robustness in deep learning, offering a structured review of current methods for evaluating how vulnerable different deep learning models are to adversarial examples. It will specifically emphasize state-of-the-art approaches to adversarial attacks and the verification of robustness in deep neural networks (DNNs). Additionally, we will present effective countermeasures to enhance model robustness, with a special focus on adversarial training. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive overview of this emerging field, highlighting the urgency and importance of developing robust deep learning models for safety-critical data analytics, thereby fostering trust among end-users in deep learning classifiers. Finally, we will outline potential research directions regarding adversarial robustness and its role in creating accountable and trustworthy data analytical systems based on deep learning.

This research addresses the challenge of automatically creating piano scores from audio recordings and raw sheet music images. Unlike prior studies that rely on synthetic, cleaned data, this work develops a system capable of handling the complexity of unprocessed PDF sheet music sourced from IMSLP. The study evaluates the performance of current systems when faced with real scanned music, filler pages, unrelated excerpts, and structural discontinuities such as jumps and repeats. Results indicate that accurately managing jumps and repeats is a major performance bottleneck; specifically, the previously suggested Jump DTW algorithm lacks robustness when jump locations are not known beforehand. To address this, we introduce a new alignment method called Hierarchical DTW, which effectively handles jumps and repeats without prior knowledge of their positions. This approach conducts an initial alignment at the feature level for each line, followed by a segment-level alignment that incorporates domain knowledge regarding the likelihood of specific jumps. Experiments on unprocessed IMSLP PDFs demonstrate that Hierarchical DTW significantly surpasses Jump DTW in managing various jump scenarios.

Rising electricity demand and the increasing complexity of power systems are causing short-circuit fault currents to escalate, threatening grid security because these currents often exceed the interruption capacity of circuit breakers. To mitigate this, series-connected limiting impedances can be introduced into transmission lines to cap fault currents at acceptable levels. Saturated Core Fault Current Limiters (SCFCLs) serve as a critical solution for restraining fault current surges in power networks, offering superior performance. Under normal operating conditions, SCFCLs have a negligible impact on the system but effectively suppress short-circuit currents when faults occur. This chapter examines various SCFCL structures with differing arrangements of AC and DC windings, evaluating and comparing the currents flowing through the limiters during both normal and faulty states. Additionally, the flux density distribution across different core regions for these configurations is analyzed. The study utilizes COMSOL Multiphysics 5.4, a finite element software package, to simulate and provide a rigorous comparison of these protective devices across their various configurations.

This study evaluates two orthogonal semi-supervised learning methods—tri-training and pretrained word embeddings—within the context of dependency parsing. We investigate language-specific FastText and ELMo embeddings alongside multilingual BERT embeddings, with a primary focus on low-resource scenarios where semi-supervised learning yields the most significant benefits. Based on treebank availability and existing ELMo models, we selected Hungarian, Vietnamese, and Uyghur (the latter serving as a zero-shot case for mBERT), while also incorporating English under simulated low-resource conditions. Our findings indicate that pretrained word embeddings leverage unlabeled data more effectively than tri-training, although these two approaches can be successfully integrated.

The dynamics and diagnostic outcomes of core-collapse supernovae are highly sensitive to the characteristics of their stellar progenitors; however, previous research has predominantly examined only one-dimensional, spherically symmetric massive stars. This study introduces some of the earliest three-dimensional simulations of core-collapse supernovae, utilizing 12.5 and 15 solar mass models evolved from collapse through bounce to explosion via the radiation-hydrodynamic code F{\sc{ornax}}. We contrast these results with three-dimensional simulations of spherically symmetric, one-dimensional progenitors of identical mass. Our findings indicate that models evolved in three dimensions during the final stages of massive star evolution exhibit a higher susceptibility to explosion. Specifically, the turbulence present in these multi-dimensional initial configurations acts as seed turbulence that facilitates shock revival. Consequently, the detection of gravitational waves and neutrino signals may uncover signatures of pre-bounce turbulence.

Semantic segmentation is a core capability for agricultural robots to interpret their surroundings within natural orchards. Recent advancements in LiDAR technology now allow robots to capture precise range data in these unstructured environments. Unlike RGB images, 3D point clouds offer distinct geometric attributes; therefore, integrating LiDAR with cameras yields comprehensive information regarding both geometry and texture. This study introduces a deep learning approach designed to execute accurate semantic segmentation on fused data from LiDAR-camera sensors. We address and resolve two key challenges: the efficient fusion of texture and geometric features from multi-sensor inputs, and the effective training of 3D segmentation networks under conditions of severe class imbalance. Furthermore, we provide a detailed implementation overview of 3D segmentation in orchards, covering data fusion, collection, labeling, network training, and model inference. Experimental analysis focuses on the network configuration when processing highly unstructured and noisy point clouds from an apple orchard. In total, the proposed method achieves an 86.2% mIoU for fruit segmentation on high-resolution point clouds (100k-200k points). Results demonstrate that the method enables accurate segmentation within real-world orchard settings.

Recent research has focused on the spectra and dynamical roles of excited states in the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain under longitudinal magnetic fields, specifically concerning Bethe strings. These strings represent bound states of elementary magnetic excitations characterized by complex, non-real Bethe-ansatz rapidities. While earlier investigations were limited to finite-size systems, this study examines the thermodynamic limit for the isotropic spin-1/2 Heisenberg XXX chain in a longitudinal field. We confirm that in this limit, Bethe strings provide the dominant spectral weight, resulting in gapped continua within the spin-flip ($S^+$) and transverse ($S^{xx}$) dynamical structure factors. Conversely, the contribution of Bethe strings to the longitudinal ($S^{zz}$) dynamical structure factor is minimal at low spin densities and becomes negligible when the density exceeds 0.317; for the $S^{-+}$ factor, this contribution is negligible at any finite magnetic field. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for the line shapes of the $S^{-+}$, $S^{xx}$, and $S^{zz}$ factors near singularities situated at and slightly above the gapped lower thresholds of Bethe-string spectra. Additionally, to establish a comprehensive physical picture encompassing the relative positioning of all significant spectral components, we revisit the general line-shape problem for transverse and longitudinal spin dynamical structure factors at finite fields and excitation energies near other singularities, including those at and above the lower thresholds of spectra arising from excited states defined solely by real Bethe-ansatz rapidities.

This study generalizes fractional Sobolev spaces with variable exponents, $W^{s,p(x,y)}$, to encompass the broader fractional setting $W^{K,p(x,y)}$, where $p$ denotes a variable exponent, $s$ lies in the interval $(0,1)$, and $K$ represents an appropriate kernel. We examine key qualitative characteristics of the space $W^{K,p(x,y)}$, including its completeness, reflexivity, separability, and density properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate a continuous and compact embedding theorem mapping these spaces into variable exponent Lebesgue spaces. In terms of applications, we analyze the existence of nontrivial solutions for a nonlocal $p(x, \cdot)$-Kirchhoff type problem and establish both the existence and uniqueness of solutions for a variational problem governed by the integro-differential operator of elliptic type, $\mathcal{L}^{p(x, \cdot)}_K$.

This work introduces an architecture for a versatile NMR spectrometer utilizing software-defined radio (SDR) technology, specifically tailored for dynamically controlled pulsed magnetic fields. While pulse-field technology remains the sole method for accessing magnetic fields exceeding 50 T, traditional NMR experiments in such environments have been challenging due to the continuously varying field strength. Our approach employs dynamically controlled field pulses to establish a quasi-steady field condition, creating a brief period of constant magnetic field strength near the peak of the pulse. We validated the reproducibility of these field pulses by using NMR spectroscopy as a high-precision magnetometer. Leveraging this high reproducibility, we successfully measured the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate ($1/T_1$), a quantity previously unattainable in pulse-field NMR experiments lacking dynamic field control. Additionally, we implemented spectrum measurements in both frequency-sweep and field-sweep modes, discussing the optimal selection of each mode based on the specific magnetic properties of the sample. This advancement, with potential future improvements for longer-duration field pulses, promises to revolutionize microscopic measurements in extremely high magnetic fields.

The $\mathbb{Z}$-scheme $\operatorname{Q}_{2n}$ is defined by the equation $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i = z(1-z)$. We demonstrate that $\operatorname{Q}_{2n}$ serves as a homogeneous space for the split reductive group scheme $\operatorname{SO}_{2n+1}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$. It is already established that $\operatorname{Q}_{2n}$ possesses the $\mathbb{A}^1$-homotopy type of a motivic sphere; however, identifying it as a homogeneous space enables an affine representability statement for motivic spheres that holds independently of the characteristic. This result facilitates characteristic-independent comparisons among Chow--Witt groups, motivic stable cohomotopy groups, and Euler class groups.

Social media platforms allow users to share content across diverse subjects, distinguished by the ability of others to respond through comments, replies, and retweets—a dynamic known as community feedback. We posit that the volume of such feedback shapes the topics users choose to post about. However, isolating this effect is difficult due to user heterogeneity and external confounders. In this study, we employ a predictive framework utilizing an interpretable model to analyze an author's likelihood of continuing a topic from a previous post. By optimizing predictive accuracy, we account for confounding variables, including inherent topic preferences and unobserved external influences like news cycles and social events. This method allows us to pinpoint which users are sensitive to community feedback. Our findings indicate that 33% of active Reddit users and 14% of Twitter users are influenced by such feedback. Furthermore, the model suggests that community feedback can shift the probability of topic continuation by as much as 14%, varying by user and feedback volume.

Determining minute spatial or temporal gaps between two optical sources represents a significant metrological hurdle, as conventional intensity-based measurements become ineffective when these separations approach zero. In contrast, it has been proven that suitable coherent mode projections can achieve quantum-limited precision regardless of how small the separation becomes. Nevertheless, it remains debated whether optical coherence itself provides a metrological benefit to these projections. In this work, we address this issue by experimentally examining how varying degrees of coherence influence the estimation of temporal separation between two single-photon pulses. We demonstrate that accurately interpreting these results requires carefully normalizing the quantum Fisher information to reflect signal strength. Our findings indicate that coherent mode projections remain optimal across all levels of coherence.

This study explores the extension of the Hilbert-Einstein action to investigate specific theoretical characteristics. Specifically, the Lagrangian is modified from $f(R)$ to $f(R, L_m)$ within the action, where $R$ represents the Ricci scalar and $L_m$ denotes the matter Lagrangian. We derive the equations of motion for a test particle within a flat, homogeneous Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime and establish the corresponding energy conditions. Furthermore, we employ cosmographic parameters—including the Hubble, deceleration, jerk, and snap parameters—to constrain the model's parameters. Our results indicate that, given the constrained parameter ranges, the model successfully reproduces the observed accelerated expansion of the universe.

The operator-theoretic examination of nonlinear dynamical systems has garnered significant interest across diverse scientific and engineering domains, particularly due to practical estimation techniques like dynamic mode decomposition. This paper introduces a lifted representation of nonlinear dynamical systems incorporating random noise via transfer operators and proposes a new Krylov subspace method for estimating these operators from finite data, specifically addressing operator unboundedness. To achieve this, we initially examine Perron-Frobenius operators utilizing kernel-mean embeddings. We subsequently adapt the classical Arnoldi method, a standard Krylov subspace technique, for application in this context. However, since the standard Arnoldi method presupposes operator boundedness—a condition often violated by transfer operators in nonlinear systems—we develop a shift-invert Arnoldi method tailored for Perron-Frobenius operators to circumvent this limitation. Furthermore, we outline a strategy for assessing predictive accuracy based on estimated operators using maximum mean discrepancy, a technique suitable for anomaly detection in complex systems. Finally, we evaluate the empirical performance of these methods using both synthetic and real-world healthcare datasets.

We establish that the threshold for the binomial random 3-partite, 3-uniform hypergraph $G^{3}((n,n,n),p)$ to contain a Latin square is $\Theta(\log{n}/n)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate analogous findings for Steiner triple systems and proper list edge-colorings of complete bipartite graphs with random lists. These findings address multiple related inquiries posed by Johansson, Luria-Simkin, Casselgren-H\"aggkvist, Simkin, and Kang-Kelly-K\"uhn-Methuku-Osthus.

Directly measuring reaction or capture (fusion) cross sections is challenging because it necessitates determining individual cross sections for numerous reaction channels, many of which can only be accessed through specific experiments. This approach would require diverse experimental setups that are not always available at a single facility, demanding extensive beam time and likely several years to complete. Consequently, researchers have traditionally relied on measuring elastic scattering angular distributions across full ranges and performing optical model analysis to derive reaction cross sections. This conventional method involves fitting complex optical potential parameters to experimental elastic scattering data and then calculating the predicted reaction cross sections. However, both the experimental execution and the analysis of this method remain complex. In contrast, this work introduces a significantly simpler approach to determine reaction and capture (fusion) cross sections by measuring only elastic or quasi-elastic scattering at a single backward angle, from which these cross sections can be readily extracted.

Over the past few decades, the detection of subtle environmental changes through exceptional points—special degeneracies within non-Hermitian systems—has become a rapidly growing field. Despite the vast body of research dedicated to parity-time (PT) symmetric systems, the distinctive features of anti-PT symmetric systems are only now starting to be explored. Recent findings indicate that a unique resonance in anti-PT symmetric systems, characterized by a vanishing linewidth, displays exceptional sensitivity to inherent nonlinearities. Considering the central role of sensing in non-Hermitian physics and the current prominence of anti-PT symmetry, this study examines the fundamental statistical limits of measurement sensitivity for arbitrary perturbations within dissipatively coupled, anti-PT symmetric systems. By employing quantum Fisher information and the long-time solution of the complete master equation, we analytically determine the Cramér-Rao bound for system parameters such as detunings and couplings. Furthermore, we apply this theoretical framework to a specific case, validating the significance of long-lived resonances in dissipatively interacting systems for practical sensing applications.

Barium (Ba) stars are contaminated by material rich in slow neutron-capture (s-process) elements created within the interiors of their former asymptotic giant branch (AGB) companions, which have since evolved into white dwarfs. We compare the abundance patterns of individual Ba stars with AGB nucleosynthesis models to determine if the model-derived masses align with independently estimated AGB masses. Our study focuses on a sample of 28 Ba stars for which consistent spectroscopic data and stellar mass determinations—based on Hertzsprung-Russell diagram positioning and evolutionary tracks—are available. We utilized both previously and recently determined elemental abundances for these stars to conduct a detailed comparison against s-process models from the Monash and FRUITY theoretical datasets. To simplify the analysis of binary mass transfer, we calculated dilution factors to match the [Ce/Fe] ratios of each star across various AGB models before comparing the resulting diluted abundances against the full Ba-star abundance patterns. Our findings confirm that low-mass, non-rotating AGB models utilizing 13C as the primary neutron source account for the enrichment in the majority of the examined Ba stars. In 21 of the 28 cases, the models align well with both the observed abundances and the independently derived AGB masses, though 16 stars exhibit higher observed abundances of Nb, Ru, Mo, and/or Nd and Sm than predicted. For three stars, a match in abundances is achieved only by employing models with masses lower than those independently determined. Finally, four stars display significantly higher first s-process peak abundances than model predictions, potentially indicating a physical or nucleosynthetic process absent from the current model set.

This paper investigates minimal supersymmetric AdS$_3$ solutions on $G_2$-orientifolds within type IIA and IIB supergravity, utilizing the bispinor formalism. A direct argument is presented demonstrating that no AdS$_3$ solutions exist in massless type IIA string theory on these $G_2$ backgrounds. Additionally, it is established that certain AdS$_3$ solutions in massive type IIA allow for a separation of scales, a property not shared by type IIB vacua. The study also provides a formula for the 3d superpotential in the bispinor framework, applicable to both type IIA and IIB setups, and confirms that the supersymmetry conditions of this superpotential reproduce the bispinor equations.

Cosmic rays (CRs) serve as indicators for both solar phenomena, such as solar flares, and extragalactic events originating outside our solar system. Solar Energetic Particles (SEPs) correlate with the 11-year solar cycle, whereas Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) exhibit an anti-correlation due to their interactions with the heliospheric magnetic field and solar wind. Our objective is to independently quantify how the magnetic field's amplitude and geometry influence the propagation of CRs across various energies within the inner heliosphere, with a specific focus on diffusion along and across magnetic field lines. To achieve this, we utilize data from 3D Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wind simulations extending from the lower corona to 1 AU. These simulations employ a polytropic approximation for the wind, while turbulence is represented using fits and power laws. Based on these results, we calculate the parallel and perpendicular diffusion coefficients for the Parker CR transport equation, producing 3D maps of CR diffusion in the inner heliosphere. We demonstrate that varying the magnetic field amplitude scales the diffusion amplitude by the same factor and alters radial gradients by modifying the current sheet spread. Similarly, adjusting the magnetic field geometry modifies latitudinal diffusion gradients by shifting current sheet positions. Furthermore, we show that SEP value distributions are more peaked than those of GCRs when varying energy levels. For realistic solar configurations, we find that diffusion is highly non-axisymmetric due to current sheet structures, with peak values drifting significantly as distance from the Sun changes. This research illustrates that numerical simulations and theoretical models can better quantify the impact of magnetic field parameters on CR propagation, serving as an initial step toward generating synthetic CR rates from simulations.

Curating large-scale, fully labeled medical datasets is challenging due to the significant human effort required for annotation. A more practical approach involves aggregating multiple smaller datasets with partial labels from diverse sources, where images may only be annotated for a subset of relevant classes. This paper investigates the under-explored issue of partially supervised multi-label classification (PSMLC), focusing on training multi-label classifiers using only partially labeled medical images. Unlike fully supervised methods, the partial supervision resulting from data scarcity can significantly degrade model performance. While augmenting partial labels offers a potential solution, and vicinal risk minimization (VRM) has shown promise in enhancing generalization, its application to PSMLC remains unresolved. To address this gap, we present the first VRM-based solution for PSMLC. Our empirical findings also offer valuable insights for future research into partially supervised learning scenarios constrained by data scarcity.

State-of-the-art (SOTA) scene graph models often produce suboptimal results because the long-tail distribution of relationships and their parent object pairs skews training toward majority classes. Consequently, once training converges, the object-conditional distributions for minority relationship pairs are lost, leading to models that excel on frequent relations like `on` or `wearing` but struggle with rare ones like `eating` or `hanging from`. To address this, we introduce a virtual evidence-based within-triplet Bayesian Network (BN) designed to maintain object-conditional relationship distributions and eliminate bias stemming from marginal relationship probabilities. However, the scarcity of minority relationship samples hinders the learning of this BN. We resolve this by employing embedding-based triplet augmentation, which borrows samples from neighboring triplets in the semantic space to enrich minority classes. Experiments across two datasets demonstrate a significant boost in mean relationship recall, alongside improved balance between recall and mean recall compared to existing SOTA de-biasing methods for scene graphs.
We introduce a formula for the convolution of two circle impulses, $\delta_{C_1}*\delta_{C_2}$, with the derivation relying on a classical addition theorem for Bessel functions.

This research examines heat fluxes associated with both contributors and mitigators of urban heat islands by integrating thermal imagery with meteorological data. Thermal images were captured between November 2021 and April 2022 using an observatory located on a building rooftop, while an automatic weather station network simultaneously recorded weather conditions at various points across a university campus in Singapore. Utilizing data from both sources, a methodology was established to estimate heat emissions from building facades, vegetation, and traffic. Prior to analyzing urban heat fluxes, a sensitivity analysis revealed that surface temperatures recorded by the observatory are influenced by specific variables; consequently, the thermal images were calibrated against outdoor surface temperature measurements. The study subsequently analyzed several factors influencing urban heat islands based on the assessed heat fluxes. Results from the rooftop observatory indicate that concrete walls significantly contribute to urban heat islands by emitting longwave radiation at night. Conversely, vegetation acts as an effective mitigator due to latent heat fluxes produced through evapotranspiration. Furthermore, traffic appears to be a negligible heat source when examined over small road segments. Future research could focus on improving the estimation of heat released by air-conditioning systems using thermal imagery.

We introduce StyleBabel, a novel open-access dataset comprising natural language captions and free-form tags that characterize the artistic styles of more than 135,000 digital artworks. This data was gathered using an innovative participatory approach involving experts from specialized art and design institutions. The collection process employed an iterative methodology inspired by "Grounded Theory," a qualitative framework that facilitates annotation while simultaneously developing a shared vocabulary for describing fine-grained artistic style attributes. We evaluate StyleBabel across several downstream tasks by adapting the recent ALADIN architecture for fine-grained style similarity to train cross-modal embeddings for: 1) generating free-form tags; 2) describing artistic styles in natural language; and 3) performing fine-grained text-based style search. To achieve this, we enhance ALADIN with recent advancements in Visual Transformers (ViT) and cross-modal representation learning, resulting in state-of-the-art accuracy for fine-grained style retrieval.

Accurate motion estimation is critical for all mobile autonomous systems. Although seemingly straightforward, it is frequently complicated by varying environmental factors that degrade odometry data from vision, LiDAR, or wheel encoders. Radar sensors offer a robust alternative, as they remain reliable despite adverse lighting and weather. Typically, automotive radars generate sparse point clouds of the surroundings; however, leveraging this data for motion estimation is difficult due to unstable and phantom measurements that produce a high volume of outliers. We present a robust, probabilistic method for estimating ego-motion based on these challenging radar inputs, designed for integration into a loosely-coupled sensor fusion framework. When evaluated on the nuScenes dataset and others, our algorithm demonstrates superior reliability compared to existing solutions, all without relying on explicit correspondence calculations.

This work examines the dynamics of an inertial active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle that self-propels within a confined harmonic potential. We analyze transport properties by scrutinizing particle trajectories, steady-state correlations, and mean square displacement (MSD). Using various approaches, we derive exact expressions for steady-state correlation functions of both position and velocity. Our investigation explores the impact of inertia on dynamical behavior in two scenarios: when the particle is free versus when it is trapped in a harmonic well. Based on the exact MSD calculations, we observe that while both free and confined particles exhibit ballistic motion at short times, their long-time behavior diverges: free particles become diffusive, whereas confined particles display non-diffusive dynamics. A key finding is that as the self-propulsion or activity time increases, the harmonically confined particle becomes increasingly restricted, eventually becoming permanently trapped for sufficiently large activity times. For free particles, velocity correlations decay through a complex interaction between the inertial time scale and the self-propulsion time scale. Furthermore, velocity decorrelation occurs only when these two time scales are comparable in magnitude.

Many automatic speech recognition (ASR) datasets rely on a single pre-defined test set containing speakers absent from the training data, a strategy known as "hold-speaker(s)-out." However, this approach may be suboptimal for datasets with a very limited number of speakers. This study evaluates ten distinct data partitioning methods across five languages with scarce ASR training resources. The findings reveal that (1) model performance fluctuates significantly based on the specific speaker chosen for testing; (2) the average word error rate (WER) across all held-out speakers is comparable to both the average WER over multiple random splits and the WER of any single random split; (3) WER remains generally consistent whether data is split heuristically or adversarially; and (4) utterance duration and intensity are more predictive of variability than the data splitting method itself. These results indicate that the commonly used hold-speakers-out strategy for ASR data partitioning can produce outcomes that fail to accurately reflect model performance on unseen speakers or data. Consequently, random splits offer more reliable and generalizable estimates in scenarios involving data sparsity.

After decades of research dedicated to game-playing programs for titles like Chess and Go, this paper examines Tetris Link, a board game that has yet to receive scientific analysis. The game's extensive branching factor complicates traditional heuristic planning methods. We investigate three strategies: heuristic planning, Reinforcement Learning, and Monte Carlo tree search, documenting our methodology and reporting on their comparative performance in a tournament. Interestingly, the heuristic approach outperformed the planning and learning methods; however, experienced human players easily defeated the heuristic AIs in most matches. This suggests that Tetris Link is more challenging than anticipated. We present these findings to the community as a challenge for future improvement.

Fermi J1544-0649 was first identified as a transient GeV source during flares observed in 2017. Multi-wavelength data from that period revealed variability and a spectral energy distribution (SED) characteristic of blazars. However, outside of these flare episodes, the source remained inactive in the GeV band for approximately a decade, resembling the quiet galaxy 2MASX J1541967-0649156. Alongside broad absorption line features, these observations support the "misaligned blazar scenario." By analyzing Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) and East Asian VLBI Network (EAVN) data from 2018 to 2020, we identified four jet components and constrained the viewing angle between 3.7° and 7.4°. The lower bound of this angle suggests an extremely low duty cycle for gamma-ray emission, while the upper bound lends further credibility to the misaligned blazar hypothesis. Subsequent multi-wavelength monitoring after 2018 confirmed continued quiescence in the GeV, X-ray, and optical bands. Additionally, a multi-messenger search for neutrinos detected an excess with a significance of 3.1 σ for this source.

The ALICE detector reports measurements of anisotropic flow coefficients ($v_n$) and their cross-correlations via two- and multi-particle cumulant techniques in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, p-Pb at $\sqrt{s_{_{\rm NN}}} = 5.02$ TeV, Xe-Xe at $\sqrt{s_{_{\rm NN}}} = 5.44$ TeV, and Pb-Pb at $\sqrt{s_{_{\rm NN}}} = 5.02$ TeV. The study examines how $v_n$ depends on multiplicity across a broad spectrum from 20 to 3000 particles in the mid-rapidity region ($|\eta|<0.8$) for transverse momenta between $0.2$ and $3.0$ GeV/$c$. An ordering of $v_2 > v_3 > v_4$ is identified in pp and p-Pb collisions, mirroring trends in larger systems, whereas a weak multiplicity dependence of $v_2$ is noted compared to nucleus-nucleus collisions within the same range. Employing a new subevent method, $v_{2}$ derived from four-particle cumulants aligns with results from six-particle cumulants in pp and p-Pb events. Symmetric cumulants SC$(m,n)$ reveal that correlations between $v_2^2$ and $v_4^2$ remain positive across all multiplicities, while those between $v_2^2$ and $v_3^2$ are negative but flip sign below a multiplicity of 100, suggesting distinct fluctuation patterns in low-multiplicity regimes. Furthermore, long-range multi-particle azimuthal correlations observed in high-multiplicity pp and p-Pb collisions cannot be reproduced by PYTHIA 8 or IP-Glasma+MUSIC+UrQMD models, offering fresh perspectives on collective phenomena in small collision systems.

This paper presents an elementary, combinatorial proof demonstrating the equivalence between the rational link defined by the continued fraction $[a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m]$ (where $a_i \in \mathbb{N}$) and the two-bridge link of type $p/q$, with $p/q$ being the rational number represented by that same continued fraction. While existing proofs depend on the two-fold cover of a link and the classification of lens spaces, our approach is more direct: it identifies a specific sequence of moves to transform the rational link into the corresponding two-bridge link.

Precisely estimating anthropometric body dimensions from RGB imagery holds significant promise for fields such as industrial design, e-commerce, medical diagnostics, and ergonomics. However, current research is constrained by the scarcity of data, relying solely on synthetic datasets derived from fitting 3D body meshes to the commercial CAESAR 3D scans, which only produce 2D silhouettes. To address this data limitation, we present a novel 3D scan collection comprising 2,675 female and 1,474 male subjects, alongside a smaller dataset of 200 RGB images with tape-measured ground truth. Leveraging these resources, we develop a part-based shape model and a deep neural network designed to estimate anthropometric measurements from 2D images. All datasets will be released to the public.

Disseminating data is a core challenge in distributed computing. This paper investigates broadcast issues across several novel models where the communication network linking $n$ processes is dynamic (for instance, due to mobility or failures) and managed by an adversary. In the initial model, processes exchange their identifiers transitiveively within synchronous rounds along a rooted tree assigned each round by an adversary aiming to delay the time until every process knows at least one identifier. Prior studies established a lower bound of $\lceil{\frac{3n-1}{2}}\rceil-2$ and an upper bound of $O(n\log\log n)$. This work presents the first linear upper bound for this scenario, specifically $\lceil{(1 + \sqrt 2) n-1}\rceil \approx 2.4n$. The findings are extended to a setting where the adversary provides $k$-disjoint forests each round, seeking to maximize the duration until a set of $k$ identifiers exists such that every process recognizes at least one. We establish a lower bound of $\left\lceil{\frac{3(n-k)}{2}}\right\rceil-1$ and an upper bound of $\frac{\pi^2+6}{6}n+1 \approx 2.6n$ for this variant. Finally, we examine a setting where the adversary supplies a directed graph with $k$ roots per round, intending to maximize the time until $k$ identifiers are known by all processes. We provide a lower bound of $\left\lceil{\frac{3(n-3k)}{2}}\right\rceil+2$ and an upper bound of $\lceil {(1+\sqrt{2})n}\rceil+k-1 \approx 2.4n+k$ for this problem. Notably, no upper or lower bounds were previously established for these last two problems.

This paper details the final outcomes of the Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) 2022 challenge, which addresses a critical yet underexplored aspect of Optical Character Recognition (OCR): recognizing scene text instances that were not present during training. The competition utilizes a public dataset containing 326,385 images and 4,864,405 text instances, ensuring broad coverage of data distributions. A novel, independent validation and test set was created specifically with text instances absent from the training vocabulary. Structured into two tasks—end-to-end and cropped scene text recognition—the challenge featured a comprehensive analysis of results from both baseline models and participants. Notably, even current state-of-the-art models exhibited a substantial performance gap within this new setting. We conclude that the OOV dataset introduced in this challenge represents a vital area for future research, essential for developing scene text models with greater robustness and generalization.

This paper presents simplified design equations and charts for modeling the in-plane expansion of thermally pre-stressed glass panes after fracturing. The methodology employs the Equivalent Temperature Difference (ETD) method combined with a thermal expansion analogy for strains. It originates from a theoretical framework integrating linear elastic fracture mechanics with stochastic geometry to forecast 2D macro-scale glass fragmentation. This approach relies on two key glass parameters: (i) fragment particle size and (ii) fracture particle intensity, both linked to the strain energy density induced by pre-stress prior to fracture. Additionally, Finite Element (FE) analysis of individual cylindrical glass particles establishes functional relationships between fragment dimensions, pre-stress levels, and the resulting maximum in-plane deformation. By synthesizing the two-parameter fracture pattern model with FE results on fragment expansion, this study derives formulas and engineering charts to quantify in-plane expansion via the ETD approach. Two engineering examples demonstrate the calculation of equivalent temperature differences, internal forces, and deformations using this method. Furthermore, the approach provides a foundation for estimating secondary effects—such as deformations and stresses on support structures or remaining glass laminate parts—by converting them into manageable ETD load cases suitable for both analytical and FE analyses.

Computed tomography (CT) imaging is increasingly gaining attention in academic disciplines beyond medical imaging and industrial inspection, such as biology and cultural heritage research. However, the specific requirements of these fields often necessitate on-site imaging, whether in fieldwork or within museum collections, where commercial scanners are frequently unusable, making custom solutions the only viable alternative. To ensure high-quality images under such challenging conditions, reliable calibration and precise trajectory reproduction are typically essential for any bespoke CT system. This paper presents the development of a low-cost, disassemblable CT scanner capable of calibration even when trajectory reproduction is impossible due to project-specific constraints. By utilizing 3D-printed in-image calibration phantoms, we calculate a projection matrix directly from each captured X-ray projection. We provide a detailed description of this methodology and demonstrate its efficacy through successful tomographic reconstructions of various specimens.

Random fields serve as mathematical frameworks for modeling the spatiotemporal interactions of random variables, finding applications across statistical physics, thermodynamics, systems biology, and complex system simulations. Although investigated since the 19th century, the relationship between random field dynamics and the geometric characteristics of their parametric spaces remains largely unexplored. Specifically, challenges persist in quantifying the similarity between random fields operating under different regimes via intrinsic metrics. This paper introduces a numerical approach to calculating geodesic distances within Gaussian random field manifolds. The methodology begins by deriving the metric tensor of the underlying parametric space, specifically the 3x3 first-order Fisher information matrix, followed by the derivation of the 27 Christoffel symbols necessary to formulate the non-linear differential equation system whose solution defines a geodesic curve from given initial conditions. A fourth-order Runge-Kutta method is employed to numerically solve this non-linear system iteratively. The results demonstrate the method's capability to estimate geodesic distances across various initial conditions. Furthermore, the findings reveal a notable pattern: in multiple instances, reversing the differential equation system over time yields a geodesic curve that diverges from the original, indicating the presence of irreversible geometric deformations along the trajectory of a moving reference point.

The classical Cauchy--Davenport inequality establishes a lower bound on the cardinality of the sum of two subsets within ${\mathbb Z}_p$, where $p$ denotes a prime. This paper aims to significantly strengthen this result by considering sums formed from only a limited number of elements selected from each of the two subsets. We demonstrate that there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that for subsets $A$ and $B$ of ${\mathbb Z}_p$ with $|A|=|B|=n\le p/3$, one can find subsets $A'\subset A$ and $B'\subset B$ satisfying $|A'|=|B'|\le c\sqrt{n}$ and $|A'+B'|\ge 2n-1$. Furthermore, we establish that arbitrary sizes are permissible provided $c_1$ and $c_2$ satisfy the condition $c_1c_2 \ge cn$, allowing us to set $|A'|=c_1$ and $|B'|=c_2$. Additionally, we extend these findings to general abelian groups.

This study demonstrates that frustration induces transient chaotic dynamics, even within a basic array of coupled limit cycle oscillators. The combination of these transient chaotic dynamics and the multistable characteristics of frustrated systems enables the formation of intricate basin structures, including fractal and riddled basins. Specifically, transient chaos emerges near the chaotic itinerancy region, where the basin of attraction adjacent to the chaotic zone becomes riddled and transitions into a fractal basin as one moves further away. Although complex basin structures are typically associated with oscillatory states, they surprisingly also appear in oscillation death states. Furthermore, the research reveals the emergence of super persistent transient chaos in coupled limit cycle oscillators, which manifests as stable chaos in larger networks.

Experiments utilizing the OMEGA EP laser system investigate Biermann battery magnetic field generation resulting from high-power laser-solid interactions. By employing proton deflectometry, researchers monitor variations in the strength, spatial distribution, and temporal evolution of these self-generated fields as laser intensity and target materials are adjusted. These magnetic flux measurements assist in validating extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. The findings indicate that kinetic effects suppress the Biermann battery mechanism in laser-plasma scenarios pertinent to both direct and indirect-drive inertial confinement fusion. Additionally, experiments reveal that increasing the target's atomic number leads to greater magnetic flux generation, a result that contradicts standard MHD predictions.

Observations indicate that Titan's stratosphere exhibits superrotation, rotating significantly faster than its surface, alongside a characteristic thick haze layer. This study utilizes a General Circulation Model (GCM) to investigate how the haze layer influences stratospheric superrotation. We implemented a semi-gray radiation model based on McKay et al. (1999), incorporating sunlight absorption by haze particles, while excluding methane phase changes and seasonal variations. With radiation parameters adjusted for Titan, our model generated global eastward equatorial winds that intensified at higher altitudes, except near 70 km, after $10^5$ Earth days. Although the system did not reach equilibrium, the resulting zonal wind profiles closely matched observations. Our analysis suggests that quasi-stationary stratospheric superrotation is sustained by a balance between a meridional circulation decoupled from the surface and eddies transporting angular momentum toward the equator. This mechanism differs from, yet resembles, the Gierasch mechanism, which relies on momentum supplied from the surface, and may account for the observed wind-free region at approximately 80 km altitude.

This study examines statistical complexity to characterize the classical kicked top model, a system crucial for qubit dynamics and the chaotic behavior of entanglement. By analyzing the probability distribution in phase space, we can differentiate between regular, random, and structural complexities within finite simulations of this driven dynamical system. Furthermore, we explore how the kicked top and kicked rotor models vary with excitation strength, all within the framework of statistical complexity.

This study reports experimental findings on the nodal domains—regions of definite sign—within the electric field distributions of a chaotic half-circular microwave rough billiard operating in the Shnirelman ergodicity regime. Wave functions ($\Psi_N$) were measured up to level $N=435$, allowing us to determine the dependence of the nodal domain count $\aleph_N$ on the level number $N$. Our analysis shows that as $N \to \infty$, a least squares fit to the data yields an asymptotic ratio $\aleph_N/N = 0.058 \pm 0.006$, which aligns closely with the theoretical prediction of $\aleph_N/N = 0.062 \pm 0.006$. Furthermore, we observed that the distributions of nodal domain areas ($s$) and perimeters ($l$) follow power laws, $n_s \sim s^{-\tau}$ and $n_l \sim l^{-\tau'}$, with scaling exponents $\tau = 1.99 \pm 0.14$ and $\tau' = 2.13 \pm 0.23$, respectively. These findings are consistent with percolation theory predictions. Finally, for higher levels ($N = 220\text{--}435$), we demonstrate that the signed area distribution oscillates around the theoretical limit $\Sigma_A = 0.0386 N^{-1}$.

We present evidence that VPMS J170850.95+433223.7 is a notable weak line quasar (WLQ). Although it was tentatively identified as a probable quasar two decades ago with significant uncertainty, the Gaia early data release 3 has confirmed this classification through its negligible proper motion and parallax. Utilizing previously unpublished spectra, we establish that the object is a WLQ at a redshift of z = 2.345, characterized by broad emission lines in the rest-frame ultraviolet that are too faint to measure. Preliminary estimates indicate it harbors a supermassive black hole of approximately 10^9 M_sun accreting near or potentially exceeding the Eddington limit. Furthermore, we detect two absorber systems exhibiting blueward velocity offsets of 0.05c and 0.1c, likely representing high-velocity outflows associated with the quasar's elevated accretion state.

Models such as CLIP have demonstrated the ability to learn robust image representations that encapsulate both semantic content and stylistic attributes. To exploit these representations for image synthesis, we introduce a two-stage framework comprising a prior that produces CLIP image embeddings from text captions, and a decoder that synthesizes images conditioned on those embeddings. We demonstrate that explicitly generating image representations enhances image diversity with negligible compromise in photorealism or caption alignment. Furthermore, decoders operating on these representations can generate variations that retain an image's semantics and style while altering non-essential details omitted from the embedding. Additionally, the unified embedding space of CLIP facilitates zero-shot, language-guided image manipulation. We employ diffusion models for the decoder and evaluate both autoregressive and diffusion architectures for the prior, concluding that diffusion-based priors offer superior computational efficiency and generate higher-quality samples.
We establish S. Takahashi's interpolation condition for the Nevanlinna-Pick-Caratheodory problem through the application of Sarason's theory.

In recent years, corporate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) engagement has gained significant public interest. Driven by mandatory reporting mandates and investors integrating sustainability into their strategies, the need for dependable and transparent ESG ratings is growing. Despite this, automated methods for forecasting these ratings remain limited. This study introduces a model that predicts ESG scores from news articles by combining multivariate time-series construction with deep learning. Additionally, we have compiled and released a dataset containing news and rating data for approximately 3,000 U.S. companies to facilitate training. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods and offers practical utility for supporting manual ESG rating analysis and determination.

The growing prevalence of machine learning (ML) has driven research into explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), aiming to clarify ML models and their predictions. Despite numerous surveys and debates, the true capabilities and objectives of XAI remain poorly understood. We contend that this confusion stems from a flawed reasoning pattern in the literature: XAI methods are described as adding desirable traits like "interpretability" to ML models, which are then assumed to foster "trust." However, these traits often lack precise definitions, and their link to such goals is unclear. This vague reasoning obscures research findings and fails to answer a critical question: what can we realistically expect from XAI? In this article, we reframe the goals and capabilities of XAI from the user's perspective. We argue that explaining models is only necessary when users have specific inquiries. While users can pose diverse questions, current XAI algorithms can only address one of them. The difficulty of answering this core question varies by application, ranging from trivial to impossible. Based on these insights, we delineate the reasonable expectations for policymakers, researchers, and society regarding XAI capabilities.

This paper investigates the inverse spectral problem associated with Jacobi-type pencils, defined as $J_5 - \lambda J_3$. In this context, $J_3$ represents a Jacobi matrix, while $J_5$ is a semi-infinite, real symmetric matrix featuring five diagonals, with positive entries located on its second subdiagonal. Specifically, when dealing with a particular perturbation of orthogonal polynomials defined over a finite interval, the corresponding spectral function admits an explicit formulation.

Active liquid droplets are frequently viewed as simplified models of living cells attached to a solid surface. In this study, we introduce a model for shallow, three-dimensional active free-surface drops featuring mean polar order parallel to the substrate and a polarization-surface (PS) coupling. This framework reveals a motility mechanism where active stresses propel the drop via spatial gradients in polarization intensity. Notably, this induces motion even in liquid ridges (two-dimensional drops), differing from previously reported mechanisms reliant on splay and bend configurations. Remarkably, stable polar moving and axisymmetric resting states can coexist, mirroring the interconversion between moving and resting keratocytes triggered by external stimuli. This newly identified motility mode arises from a competition between elastic bulk energy and the orientational control imposed by the drop's surface, breaking parity symmetry even in passive drops. This resulting back-and-forth asymmetry allows active stresses to effectively pump the liquid, leading to drop motion.

We introduce a framework for systematically and quantitatively extending Bell's theorem through the lens of causal networks. Initially, we address a multi-objective optimization task that aligns observed data while reducing the causal impact of nonlocal variables, thereby deriving an inequality for the optimal region that both strengthens and generalizes Bell's theorem. Rather than merely bounding this problem, we devise a new genetic algorithm where causal networks serve as individuals. Applying this algorithm to a photonic Bell experiment illustrates the trade-off between quantitatively relaxing one or more local causality assumptions and the capacity of data to reproduce quantum correlations.

In honeycomb Mott insulators characterized by pseudospin-$\frac{1}{2}$ and strong spin-orbit coupling, two bond-dependent exchange interactions, the Kitaev ($K$) and $\Gamma$ terms, generate significant frustration. Although the Kitaev model's ground state is a quantum spin liquid featuring fractionalized excitations, the ground state of the $\Gamma$ model remains debated. Consequently, the phase diagram of the $K\Gamma$ model, specifically with ferromagnetic $K$ and antiferromagnetic $\Gamma$ interactions, has been extensively investigated due to its applicability to materials like $\alpha$-RuCl$_{3}$. Previous numerical work also explored the impact of varying bond strengths, such as distinguishing the $z$-bond strength from others. Despite this, a unified consensus on the overall phase diagram has not yet been achieved. In this study, we employ Monte Carlo simulations to examine the classical $K\Gamma$ model with anisotropic bond strengths, aiming to elucidate the phases arising from the competition between these two frustrated limits. We further investigate how bond anisotropy influences the phase diagram and the magnitude of quantum fluctuations. Our results reveal various large unit cell phases stemming from competing frustrations, and we analyze their intrinsic degeneracy through Hamiltonian symmetry. Additionally, using linear spin wave theory, we demonstrate that anisotropic bond strengths amplify quantum fluctuations within the $\Gamma$-dominated regime, correlating with the observation of a small reduced moment. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the corresponding quantum model.

Analyzing dynamical processes on networks has long been a primary focus for understanding contagion phenomena. Research has shown that contagion dynamics can reveal how nodes are embedded in Euclidean space; specifically, activation times from threshold contagions allow for the construction of "contagion maps" as a method for manifold learning. However, a significant limitation of these maps is their high computational expense. In this study, we demonstrate that truncating threshold contagions can substantially accelerate the generation of contagion maps. Furthermore, we illustrate that these maps can identify insightful low-dimensional embeddings for single-cell RNA-sequencing data, represented as cell-similarity networks, thereby uncovering biological manifolds. Ultimately, our findings enhance the feasibility of employing contagion maps as manifold-learning tools on empirical network data.

To quantitatively and intuitively investigate the generalization capabilities of pre-trained language models (PLMs), we have devised several tasks involving arithmetic and logical reasoning. We analyze both in-distribution generalization, where test data matches the training data, and out-of-distribution generalization, for which we created a specific cross-distribution test set alongside the standard in-distribution set. Our experiments utilize BART, one of the most advanced publicly available generative PLMs. The results indicate that while PLMs readily generalize within the same distribution, they struggle significantly when generalizing across different distributions.

We forecast the presence of a pair-liquid phase within lattice fermion systems featuring finite-range attractive forces. This unique state exists in a competitive balance between a standard Fermi liquid of unpaired fermions and a phase-separated regime where fermions form macroscopic clusters. We demonstrate that this phase does not occur in bosonic systems, indicating that its existence relies on the exclusion principle. Unlike zero-range attractive systems where multi-fermion clustering is strictly forbidden, here quantum statistics operates dynamically and subtly; because many-fermion wave functions must possess nodes, the energy threshold for forming clusters exceeds that for forming pairs. By numerically solving the four-body Schrödinger equation on one- and two-dimensional lattices, we delineate the stability limits of these pairs. This pair liquid phase is expected to be detectable in cold atom experiments, and we further explore its relevance to the preformed-pair mechanism underlying high-temperature superconductivity.

This essay posits that the adoption of Internet communication platforms, including blogs, will give rise to a novel democratic model termed "Emergent Democracy." It examines the historical evolution of democracy alongside contemporary experiments, analyzing how these digital tools can facilitate democratic processes. Furthermore, the essay addresses potential drawbacks associated with this technological shift, highlighting concerns regarding privacy, as well as the exploitation of these tools by corporations, totalitarian regimes, and terrorist organizations for detrimental societal ends.

We re-examine the production of associated $Z$ bosons with charm or beauty jets at the LHC, focusing specifically on the dynamics governing the formation of heavy jets. Two distinct theoretical frameworks are investigated: the first, utilizing the PEGASUS Monte-Carlo generator, assumes heavy quarks are created within the hard scattering subprocesses; the second, employing MadGraph5_aMC@NLO for NLO hard scattering calculations and CASCADE3 for the TMD parton shower, incorporates a different production scenario. We compare the predictions from both approaches against the most recent experimental data regarding associated $Z + b$ production cross-sections and the relative production rate $\sigma(Z + c)/\sigma(Z + b)$, as gathered by the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations at $\sqrt{s} = 13$~TeV. Furthermore, we define two kinematic observables, $z_b$ and $p_T^{\rm rel}$, capable of distinguishing between heavy jet production mechanisms. By applying these variables to trace the simulated $b$-jet event distributions, we recommend their inclusion in future experimental analyses.
We provide a concise overview of key mathematical structures and findings in significant Quantum Mechanics domains involving partial differential equations, while also proposing open questions.

This study introduces a methodology for generating distributed algorithms for consensus-based optimization and network resource allocation, applicable to switching networks with or without synchronous protocols. The findings demonstrate that first-order gradient distributed consensus-based optimization algorithms can effectively solve distributed resource allocation problems under synchronous protocols, even when operating under weaker assumptions than those required for non-switching (static) networks in existing literature. Conversely, first-order gradient distributed resource allocation algorithms can be employed to determine optimal solutions for distributed consensus-based optimization. These results are applicable to time-varying and random directed networks, regardless of synchronous protocols or initial conditions. Consequently, several algorithms can now be leveraged to develop distributed solutions for both consensus-based optimization and resource allocation, surpassing the limitations of prior research. Although the primary focus is on first-order gradient algorithms, the derived results remain valid for second-order gradient algorithms as well.

We propose a theoretical framework describing a continuous metal-insulator transition at a fixed fractional electron filling, evolving from a metal with a generic Fermi surface to a "Wigner-Mott" insulator that spontaneously breaks crystalline space-group symmetries. Crossing the quantum critical point, the system exhibits two key features: (i) the electronic Fermi surface vanishes abruptly when approached from the metallic phase, and (ii) the insulating charge gap and order parameters linked to the broken symmetries disappear continuously when approached from the insulating phase. Furthermore, the insulating state contains a Fermi surface composed of neutral spinons. We outline a general approach for characterizing such continuous transitions and examine a specific case of a bandwidth-tuned transition at a filling of $\nu=1/6$ for spinful electrons on a triangular lattice. By extending this theory to a large-$N$ limit, we construct a concrete model of such a continuous MIT and explore potential experimental signatures near the critical point. Finally, we relate our findings to recent experimental observations in moiré transition metal dichalcogenides.

The impact of energy absorption during the binary evolution of Exotic Compact Objects (ECOs) has been thoroughly investigated. This review examines the fundamental mechanism responsible for energy dissipation in material bodies—tidal friction. We demonstrate that, unlike in standard astrophysical objects where viscous absorption is negligible, ECOs may exhibit absorption that mimics the tidal heating effect typically associated with black holes (BHs). We analyze both the distinctions and parallels regarding energy dissipation during the inspiral phase. Drawing inspiration from the membrane paradigm and recent research, we illustrate how viscosity serves as a key metric for quantifying the proximity of ECO absorption to that of classical black holes. Furthermore, we show that for ECOs, viscosity can cause substantial alterations to the gravitational wave (GW) waveform. In favorable scenarios involving equal-mass, spinning supermassive binaries, these modifications could enable the detection of ECO absorption in future high-precision GW observations. Finally, we explore the implications for the ECO reflection coefficient and its connection to the universal bound on viscosity relative to volume entropy.

X-ray binaries (XRBs), which are variable or transient in nature, dominate the X-ray point sources within galaxies, though it remains debated whether their variability impacts the X-ray luminosity functions (XLF). We present NGC 7331 as a case study for this investigation, utilizing seven Chandra observations. With a detection threshold of 7$\times10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$ in the 0.3–8.0 keV band—calculated using a power-law spectral model with a photon index of 1.7—we identified 55 X-ray sources. Among these, 13 exhibit variability, including three transients, and several display a bimodal luminosity-hardness ratio characteristic of XRBs. Our study reveals nine additional ultra-luminous X-ray sources compared to prior research, with eight likely classified as low-mass or high-mass XRBs. While Hubble Space Telescope images yielded 21 potential optical counterparts, positional coincidence cannot be entirely excluded. Spectral analysis of SN 2014C indicates a trend of increasing soft photons and decreasing hydrogen column densities as the outer shell expands. Employing a Bayesian method for the first time in XLF fitting, we modeled the seven incompleteness-corrected XLFs using both power-law (PL) and power-law with exponential cut-off (PLC) functions. The hierarchical PLC model provided the best fit for NGC 7331's XLF, yielding a slope of approximately 0.5 and a luminosity cut-off near 8$\times10^{38}$ erg s$^{-1}$. This research demonstrates that multi-epoch observations effectively reduce deviations in XLFs caused by variable luminous sources.

Manual testing serves as a crucial complement to automated GUI testing, acting as the final safeguard for application quality, particularly in identifying usability and accessibility problems. However, its reliance on repetitive actions and the risk of overlooking certain functionalities often render it time-consuming, labor-intensive, and inefficient. Drawing inspiration from the game Candy Crush, where flashing candies suggest the next moves for players, we developed NaviDroid, a tool designed to guide human testers by highlighting subsequent operations for improved efficiency and effectiveness. NaviDroid constructs an enriched state transition graph (STG), using trigger actions as edges between states. Leveraging this STG, it employs a dynamic programming algorithm to plan exploration paths and overlays visualized hint moves onto the runtime GUI. This enables testers to rapidly explore untested states and prevent duplication. Automated experiments confirm NaviDroid's high coverage and efficient path planning, while a user study demonstrates its practical value: participants using the tool covered more states and activities, detected more bugs, and did so in less time compared to a control group. For a demonstration video, please visit: https://youtu.be/lShFyg_nTA0.

This research investigates quasiparticle dynamics within the two-dimensional (2D) integrable Kitaev honeycomb model, examining scenarios both with and without external periodic driving. We identify light-cones in wavefunction propagation as indicators of quantum caustics—bright structures arising during quantum dynamics that mirror imperfect focusing in geometrical optics. Our findings demonstrate that this propagation depends on spatial angle and exhibits anisotropy regarding model parameters. By analyzing the coalescence of critical points, we derive an exact solution for the caustic envelope, which aligns with the 2D Lieb-Robinson bound. Additionally, when the system is subjected to periodic driving, we observe that the caustic structure undergoes a complete transformation in the presence of the external time-dependent force.

This paper investigates how electron screening impacts the Bohr-Weisskopf (BW) effect within many-electron atoms. Since the BW effect represents the contribution of finite-nucleus magnetization to hyperfine structure, we conducted relativistic atomic many-body calculations for $s$ and $p_{1/2}$ states across several systems relevant to atomic parity violation and time-reversal-violating electric dipole moment research: Rb, Cs, Fr, Ba$^+$, Ra$^+$, and Tl. Our findings indicate that electron screening effects are negligible for $s$ states, resulting in similar relative BW corrections for both hydrogenlike ions and neutral atoms. We establish a connection between the ground-state BW effect in H-like ions—which can be precisely isolated experimentally—and the BW effect in $s$ and $p_{1/2}$ states of neutral or near-neutral atoms by introducing an electronic screening factor. This methodology enables the application of BW effects derived from H-like ion measurements to neutral atomic calculations using screening factors, thereby eliminating the need for modeled nuclear structure inputs. Consequently, this approach facilitates unprecedented accuracy in accounting for the BW effect in heavy atoms, a capability validated by existing experimental data for both H-like and neutral $^{203}\text{Tl}$ and $^{205}\text{Tl}$.

The relative simplicity of detecting and characterizing small planets around M dwarf stars has established them as central pillars in exoplanet research. The current scarcity of long-period planets orbiting these stars makes them especially valuable for understanding system formation and evolution. This study reports the discovery of TOI-2257 b (TIC 198485881), a sub-Neptune with a 35-day orbit around an M3 star located 57.8 parsecs away. With a transit depth of approximately 0.4%, this object is detectable using medium-sized ground-based telescopes. The extended transit duration indicates a highly eccentric orbit ($e \sim 0.5$), potentially making it the most eccentric known transiting planet around an M dwarf. By combining TESS observations with data from the 1.0-m SAINT-EX, 0.60-m TRAPPIST-North, and 1.2-m FLWO telescopes, we determined the planet's radius to be 2.2 $R_{\oplus}$ and its orbital period to be 35.19 days. Our planetary interpretation is further supported by archival data, high-resolution imaging, and vetting procedures. TOI-2257 b occupies a unique region of parameter space due to its long period and high eccentricity. Although its equilibrium temperature is low ($\sim$ 256 K), the host star's small radius ($R_* = 0.311 \pm{0.015}$) and relatively bright infrared magnitude (K$_{mag}$ = 10.7) render it an ideal target for atmospheric studies via transmission spectroscopy.

In graph theory, an independent set comprises a collection of nodes with no adjacent pairs. A maximal independent set is one where no additional external node can be included without violating the independence condition. Within network applications, particularly in ad hoc and wireless sensor networks, these maximal independent sets serve as cluster heads. To address potential network failures, self-stabilizing algorithms have been developed to compute maximal independent sets under various assumptions. This paper introduces a self-stabilizing algorithm designed to calculate a maximal independent set where selected nodes maintain a minimum distance of 3 from one another. We demonstrate both the correctness and convergence of this proposed algorithm. Simulation results indicate that our method effectively reduces the number of nodes required in large-scale networks, thereby enabling robust network control.

Integrating a suitable discrete expansion into special relativity, thereby removing the constraint against gravitational acceleration, reveals previously unknown phenomena. This modification accounts for the effects of a slight fluctuation in the limiting velocity over vast time scales, coupled with space-time expansion. It establishes a natural threshold between systems of high and low kinetic energy, offers fresh perspectives on Earth's revolution since its inception, identifies a new mechanism preserving primordial Earth heat, suggests that the self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction driving Earth's primary heat is intensifying alongside space-time expansion, proposes a novel approach to the missing mass problem in galaxies, demonstrates the entanglement of time with space and expansion, and yields a revised interpretation of these characteristics.

Accurate identification of slot values, including domain-specific terms and named entities, is fundamental to Goal-oriented Dialogue Systems. While this step is crucial for downstream tasks like language understanding, general-purpose ASR systems often struggle with rare or domain-specific vocabulary. Although error correction systems are commonly employed, neural models frequently fail to directly output such infrequent entities. To overcome this, we introduce a k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) search mechanism that retrieves domain-specific entities from an explicit datastore. We enhance the error correction rate by integrating this k-NN search into inference for a pre-trained joint phoneme and text transformer sequence-to-sequence model. Our approach was evaluated across five domains featuring long-tail slot entities, such as full names, airports, street names, cities, and states. Our top-performing model achieved a 7.4% relative reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) for rare words compared to the baseline, and demonstrated a 9.8% relative WER improvement on an Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) test set.

This study investigates the robustness of entanglement generated between Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) via quantum nondemolition (QND) measurements. The proposed experimental setup involves routing two BECs through a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, where a QND interaction establishes entanglement between coherent light and the atomic systems. We examine the two primary decoherence mechanisms affecting the resulting entangled states: atomic dephasing and photon loss. Our analysis evaluates how dephasing influences spin operator variances and expectation values, as well as entanglement measures and correlation criteria. Notably, our approach avoids the Holstein-Primakoff approximation, enabling the modeling of extended light-atom interaction times and the generation of non-Gaussian states that extend beyond two-mode squeezed states. Under dephasing conditions, the entangled states remain robust in the macroscopic limit provided the dimensionless interaction time remains below $1/\sqrt{N}$, with $N$ representing the atom count in the BEC. Furthermore, regarding photon loss, entangled states produced by prolonged interaction times exhibit significant robustness, suggesting the scheme's potential for diverse quantum information applications.

A concise derivation of the Jordan structure in finite-dimensional quantum theory emerges from a few foundational postulates regarding abstract probabilistic models, which consist of basic measurements and a convex set of states. The central premise posits that any system $A$ can be paired with an isomorphic conjugate system, $\overline{A}$, via a non-signaling bipartite state $\eta_A$. This state perfectly and uniformly correlates every basic measurement on $A$ with its corresponding measurement on $\overline{A}$. For a quantum system defined by a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, the conjugate system corresponds to the conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$, and $\eta_A$ represents the standard maximally entangled EPR state on $\mathcal{H} \otimes \overline{\mathcal{H}}$. A second essential component is the concept of a "reversible filter," defined as a probabilistically reversible process that independently reduces the sensitivity of detectors linked to a specific measurement. Beyond providing greater flexibility than many existing reconstructions of finite-dimensional quantum theory, this approach avoids reliance on the "no restriction" hypothesis. Consequently, it does not presuppose that arbitrary effects are physically measurable, nor that any collection of measurable effects summing to the unit effect constitutes a physically accessible observable. Furthermore, an appendix demonstrates how a variant of Hardy's "subspace axiom" can substitute for several assumptions native to this paper, albeit with the trade-off of excluding superselection rules.

Forward-swept wings provide distinct aerodynamic benefits for air vehicles, yet their behavior at low Reynolds numbers has remained largely uninvestigated. This study employs numerical simulations to examine laminar separated flows over forward-swept wings with semi-aspect ratios ($sAR$) ranging from 0.5 to 2 at a chord-based Reynolds number of 400. Results indicate that the wakes produced by forward-swept wings differ markedly from those of backward-swept configurations. Specifically, low-aspect-ratio forward wings exhibit steady wakes driven by strong downwash from tip vortices. Conversely, as the aspect ratio increases, downwash effects diminish over the inboard sections, permitting unsteady vortex shedding. At even higher aspect ratios, highly swept wings can develop streamwise vortices that stabilize the flow. Additionally, forward-swept wings demonstrate superior lift generation at high angles of attack compared to unswept or backward-swept designs, albeit with increased drag. Force element analysis reveals that this lift enhancement stems from a vortical structure sustained by tip-vortex-induced downwash across the wing's outboard region. These findings deepen the understanding of how sweep influences laminar separated flows on forward-swept wings and pave the way for innovative high-lift device designs.

We introduce a holographic quantum simulation algorithm designed to variationally generate thermal states of $d$-dimensional interacting quantum many-body systems, requiring only sufficient hardware qubits to encode a ($d$-1)-dimensional cross-section. This method approximates the thermal state by decomposing the quantum matrix-product density operator (qMPDO) into a stochastic mixture of quantum matrix product states (sto-qMPS). The parameters for both the quantum circuits producing the qMPS and the probability distribution forming the mixture are optimized variationally. We provide a small-scale proof-of-principle implementation on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum processor, successfully simulating thermal properties of correlated spin-chains across a broad temperature range using just a single pair of physical qubits. Furthermore, via classical simulations, we investigate the representational capabilities of two sto-qMPS ansatz variants for larger, deeper circuits, deriving empirical correlations between circuit resources and the accuracy of the variational free-energy.
