Additionally, we characterize connected graphs where $dem(G)=2$.

Regarding computational complexity, we prove that determining $dem(G)$ is NP-complete, even when restricted to apex graphs. While a polynomial-time algorithm with a logarithmic approximation factor exists, it is NP-hard to achieve an asymptotically better approximation, even for bipartite graphs with small diameters or subcubic bipartite graphs. For these specific instances, the problem is also unlikely to be fixed parameter tractable when parameterized by the solution size.

Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are routinely employed to identify cardiac anomalies, including atrial fibrillation, bradycardia, and various irregular complexes. Although prior research has successfully classified these conditions using standard 12-lead ECGs, there is scarce evidence supporting the diagnostic capability of reduced-lead ECGs across a broad spectrum of information. Furthermore, the generalizability of classification models across diverse recording sources has not been thoroughly explored. Participating in the PhysioNet Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2021, our team, HaoWan AIeC, introduced the Mixed-Domain Self-Attention Resnet (MDARsn) to detect cardiac abnormalities from reduced-lead ECGs. Our classifiers achieved scores of 0.602, 0.593, 0.597, 0.591, and 0.589 (ranking 54th, 37th, 38th, 38th, and 39th, respectively) for the hidden validation sets comprising 12-lead, 6-lead, 4-lead, 3-lead, and 2-lead configurations, evaluated according to the challenge's metrics.

This paper introduces an implicit dynamic dictionary featuring the working-set property, which executes insert(e) and delete(e) operations in O(log n) time. It supports predecessor(e) and successor(e) queries in O(log l_{p(e)}) and O(log l_{s(e)}) time, respectively, and performs search(e) in O(log min(l_{p(e)},l_{e}, l_{s(e)})) time. In these formulas, n denotes the total number of stored elements, l_{e} represents the count of distinct elements accessed since the last search for e, and p(e) and s(e) refer to the predecessor and successor of e. All time complexities are worst-case bounds. The structure maintains elements within an array of size n without requiring extra space. Within the cache-oblivious model, the logarithm base is B, and the model's obliviousness stems from leveraging an existing cache-oblivious implicit dictionary as a black box. This work marks the first implicit dictionary to support predecessor and successor searches under the working-set bound, whereas earlier implicit structures were limited to O(log n) time for such operations.

The minimax theorem for zero-sum games can be readily derived from the strong duality theorem of linear programming. However, the standard proof for the converse direction by Dantzig (1951) is recognized as incomplete. This paper presents a correct alternative proof by integrating classical results regarding the solution of linear equations with nonnegative variables, offering a more direct approach than Adler (2013). Furthermore, we generalize Dantzig's game to ensure that any max-min strategy yields either an optimal linear programming solution or demonstrates that no such solution exists.

As the High Luminosity LHC comes online soon, event generators must produce vast event samples to align with experimental precision. Currently, the projected cost of generating these events surpasses the LHC experiments' computing budgets. To tackle this challenge, enhancing the computational efficiency of event generators is essential. Various strategies are being pursued to meet this objective. This discussion will cover current efforts in porting event generators to GPUs, utilizing machine learning for matrix elements and phase space, and reducing the count of negative weight events.

This study examines reflection-asymmetric thin-shell wormholes within the framework of Palatini $f(\mathcal{R})$ gravity by joining two electrovacuum spacetime regions at a hypersurface through appropriate junction conditions. We establish the criteria required for these wormholes to be linearly stable and supported by positive-energy matter. Furthermore, we identify specific parameter sets that position the shell radius between the event horizon (if it exists) and the photon sphere on both sides. Using a concrete example, we demonstrate that the presence of two photon spheres enables an observer on one side to detect a secondary circular shadow, in addition to the primary one from their own photon sphere. This phenomenon occurs because photons traverse the throat after passing the effective potential maximum on one side and reflecting off the higher effective potential on the other. Finally, we discuss how these double shadows could serve as a method to detect signatures of gravitational physics extending beyond General Relativity.

Botnets represent a major online threat, inflicting billions of dollars in losses on global economies. As the number of Internet-connected devices grows, analyzing vast amounts of network traffic has become essential. This study aims to enhance botnet traffic classification performance by identifying features that maximize detection rates. To achieve this, we applied two feature selection methods—Information Gain and Gini Importance—to create three pre-selected subsets containing five, six, and seven features, respectively. These subsets were evaluated using three classification models: Decision Tree, Random Forest, and k-Nearest Neighbors. To assess the performance of these feature vectors and models, we generated two datasets, QB-CTU13 and EQB-CTU13, derived from the CTU-13 dataset. Performance was measured by the macro-averaged F1 score relative to the computational time needed for classification. The findings indicate that the Decision Tree model utilizing a five-feature set achieved the highest performance, reaching a mean F1 score of 85% with an average classification time of 0.78 microseconds per sample.

Accurate cancer subtyping is essential for comprehending tumor characteristics and determining appropriate treatments. Nevertheless, current labeling approaches are often medically contentious and have steered subtyping efforts away from utilizing informative teaching signals. Furthermore, cancer genetic expression profiles are characterized by high dimensionality, data scarcity, and complex dependencies, which significantly challenge existing subtyping models to generate meaningful clusters. To address these issues, this study introduces a novel unsupervised clustering method designed to leverage genetic expression profiles for subtype differentiation. This approach adaptively learns categorical mappings between the latent representations of expression profiles and the subtypes identified by the model. By maximizing problem-agnostic mutual information between input profiles and output subtypes, the method automatically determines an optimal number of subtypes. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method refines existing controversial labels, and subsequent medical analysis confirms that these refined subtypes exhibit a strong correlation with cancer survival rates.

This paper introduces a tightly coupled, multi-modal Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) framework named VIRAL (Visual-Inertial-Ranging-Lidar), which fuses data from IMUs, cameras, multiple LiDARs, and Ultra-wideband (UWB) range measurements. Implementing such a comprehensive sensor fusion system requires addressing significant challenges, including data synchronization, multi-threading, bundle adjustment (BA), and resolving conflicting coordinate frames between UWB and onboard sensors to guarantee real-time localization and smooth state estimation. We address these issues with a two-stage approach. Initially, a core odometry thread processes LiDAR, camera, and IMU data within a local sliding window to generate a local graph, from which candidate key frames are selected for inclusion in the global map. Visual feature-based loop closure further enriches the global factor graph with loop constraints. Once the global factor graph meets spatial diversity criteria, the BA process is activated to refine the coordinate transformation between UWB and the onboard SLAM system. Subsequently, the system transitions seamlessly to the second stage, where all sensors are tightly integrated into the odometry thread. The effectiveness of our system is validated through experiments conducted on high-fidelity graphical-physical simulations and public datasets.

Historically, predicting local Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs) has depended primarily on forecasting the rate of change of the magnetic field (dB/dt) as a surrogate, with minimal focus on directly predicting GICs or geoelectric fields. This study employs machine learning, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, using solar wind data as input to forecast two distinct outputs: geoelectric field components (Ex and Ey) and GICs at specific Austrian substations. Models were trained on 26 years of modeled geoelectric field and GIC data derived from one-minute geomagnetic measurements, with performance evaluated against recent GIC measurements. While LSTMs trained on data from individual substations generally outperformed other approaches, they failed to accurately predict a significant portion of the largest GIC events. The model achieved a correlation coefficient of approximately 0.6 and a root-mean-square error of 0.7 A. Detection probabilities were estimated at roughly 50% for mild GIC activity and 15% for larger events.

This work examines the geometry of $\mathcal{L}(X)_w$, the collection of bounded linear operators on a Banach space $X$ equipped with the numerical radius norm, specifically when this norm is well-defined. We determine the structure of the extreme points within the unit ball of the dual space of $\mathcal{L}(X)_w$. Leveraging this framework, we investigate Birkhoff-James orthogonality and best approximation problems to derive distance formulas within $\mathcal{L}(X)_w$. Particular focus is placed on operators that satisfy specific smoothness conditions. Ultimately, we establish an equivalence between Birkhoff-James orthogonality in $\mathcal{L}(X)_w$ and that in the underlying space $X$.

This study details transit observations of the exoplanet HD 149026b conducted using the Spitzer Space Telescope at 8 microns. At this wavelength, stellar limb-darkening has minimal impact on transit light curves, facilitating a more straightforward and precise calculation of planetary parameters. Our analysis yields a planet-to-star radius ratio of Rp/Rs = 0.05158 +/- 0.00077. When combined with ground-based data and independent constraints on stellar mass and radius, we determine an orbital inclination of i = 85.4 +0.9/-0.8 degrees and a planetary radius of Rp = 0.755 +/- 0.040 R_jup. These findings provide additional evidence supporting models suggesting the planet possesses a significantly high heavy-element enrichment.

Neutrino-cooled accretion flows surrounding black holes, generated by compact binary mergers, offer a compelling framework for understanding the central engines of short gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and kilonovae associated with the GW170817 gravitational wave event, specifically regarding jet formation and magnetic-driven winds. In this scenario, Magnetorotational Instability (MRI) turbulence and the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) mechanism are anticipated to be crucial for establishing thermal equilibrium against neutrino cooling and for driving accretion and jet production. Employing the open-source GRMHD HARM-COOL code, we investigate the magnetically-driven evolution of an accretion disk utilizing a realistic equation of state within a fixed curved space-time background. Our analysis highlights the impacts of neutrino cooling and magnetic fields, with a specific focus on the dynamical, thermal, and compositional evolution of both the disk and the resulting outflows.

This study introduces a new unsupervised machine learning method designed to estimate the degradation rate of photovoltaic (PV) systems, a process often called energy-yield degradation analysis. The technique relies solely on measured power signals, eliminating the need for irradiance data, temperature readings, or system configuration details. By applying this approach to a dataset previously examined by NREL using RdTools, we validate its accuracy and demonstrate its enhanced resilience to data anomalies, all while lowering the data requirements necessary for the analysis.

This paper establishes the existence and uniqueness of globally weak solutions for the Cauchy problem associated with the weakly dissipative Camassa-Holm equation within time-weighted $H^1$ spaces. First, we introduce new variables to transform the equation into an equivalent semi-linear system, thereby demonstrating the existence of globally conservative solutions in the specified space. Second, we verify that peakon solutions function as conservative weak solutions within $H^1$. Finally, by defining a specific set of auxiliary variables adapted to a conservative solution, we prove that these variables satisfy a particular semi-linear system with unique solutions, which subsequently guarantees the uniqueness of the conservative solution in the original variables.

Robotic manipulators are integral to contemporary manufacturing, yet deploying them in unstructured settings remains a significant challenge. Addressing the diversity, intricacy, and unpredictability of real-world tasks requires a flexible framework that minimizes assumptions about environmental characteristics. While reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved notable success in single-arm manipulation, research into dual-arm systems is still scarce. Traditional control methods for such tasks demand complex modeling of interactions between two robots, objects, and the coupling mechanisms at the control level. In contrast, this work investigates the potential of model-free RL for dual-arm assembly. Aiming to develop a broader approach for general dual-arm manipulation rather than just assembly, we minimize modeling efforts by avoiding the simulation of interactions between the robots and assembly tools. Instead, we propose a modular architecture featuring two decentralized single-arm controllers linked by a single centralized learned policy. By relying solely on sparse rewards, we further reduce modeling requirements. This architecture facilitates successful assembly and straightforward simulation-to-real-world transfer. We validate the framework's effectiveness using a dual-arm peg-in-hole task, analyzing sample efficiency and success rates across various action spaces. Additionally, we test performance under different clearances, demonstrating disturbance recovery and robustness against position uncertainties. Finally, we achieve zero-shot transfer of policies trained in simulation to the physical world and assess their real-world performance.

We contend that numerous characteristics of fully-connected feedforward neural networks (FCNNs), or multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), can be elucidated by examining a specific sequence of two operations: projecting data randomly into a higher-dimensional space followed by a sparsification step. Following Dasgupta's terminology, we refer to this combined process as "expand-and-sparsify." We demonstrate how this mechanism accounts for various phenomena documented in the literature, including the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, the unexpectedly strong performance of randomly initialized and untrained networks, the effectiveness of Dropout during training, and, most significantly, the enigmatic generalization capabilities of overparameterized models first noted by Zhang et al. and later observed in non-neural architectures by Belkin et al.

Collisions involving heavy ions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (BNL) and the Large Hadron Collider (CERN) offer compelling proof of quark-gluon plasma creation, with temperatures derived from relativistic viscous hydrodynamic simulations exceeding the hadron-to-quark-gluon transition threshold. Significant unresolved challenges in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) include understanding the formation of this strongly correlated matter, its non-equilibrium properties, and the thermalization mechanism within the plasma. This review examines theoretical advancements in weak-coupling QCD effective field theories and strong-coupling holographic methods utilizing gauge-gravity duality. We map the interdisciplinary links between various thermalization stages and non-equilibrium dynamics in diverse systems spanning energy scales from inflationary cosmology and strong-field QED to ultracold atomic gases, highlighting the universal behavior of non-thermal and hydrodynamic attractors. Furthermore, we analyze heavy-ion collision data sensitive to early non-equilibrium phases and evaluate prospects for future experiments. Finally, we outline the current frontiers in thermalization research and pinpoint promising directions for future progress.

Upcoming short and long-duration space missions necessitate advanced monitoring and diagnostic technologies to overcome communication barriers and constraints regarding specialized personnel and hardware. Machine learning-assisted diagnostic frameworks offer a promising remedy for both medical and technical contexts. This discussion examines the challenges and potential applications of these systems within the context of forthcoming missions, while also detailing a prototype use case for a next-generation medical diagnostic tool for future space operations. Furthermore, we provide strategic recommendations and identify key constraints essential for the effective development and deployment of machine learning models on spacecraft.

Hyperspectral Imaging (HSI) is widely applied in various real-world scenarios due to the rich spectral details available at every pixel. However, the intricate nature of HSI data, specifically the nonlinear relationship between captured spectra and their corresponding objects, poses significant classification challenges for conventional methods. In recent years, Deep Learning (DL) has proven to be a potent feature extractor capable of effectively handling nonlinear issues common in computer vision, thereby encouraging its adoption for HSI classification (HSIC) with promising results. This survey provides a systematic review of DL applications in HSIC and compares leading strategies. We begin by outlining the primary limitations of traditional machine learning for HSIC and then demonstrate how DL overcomes these obstacles. Furthermore, the survey categorizes state-of-the-art DL frameworks into spectral, spatial, and combined spatial-spectral approaches to systematically evaluate their performance and future research directions. Additionally, addressing the challenge of DL's heavy reliance on large labeled datasets—which are time-consuming and costly to acquire for HSIC—this review explores techniques to enhance the generalization capabilities of DL models, offering valuable guidance for future work.

Understanding 3D scenes semantically is vital for robotics. Although spatial perception has advanced significantly, robots still lack the common-sense knowledge regarding household objects and locations that humans possess naturally. To address this, we explore using large language models to endow robots with such common sense for scene interpretation. Specifically, we present three paradigms for utilizing language to classify indoor rooms based on their constituent objects: (i) a zero-shot method, (ii) a feed-forward classifier, and (iii) a contrastive classifier. These techniques process 3D scene graphs generated by contemporary spatial perception systems. Our analysis reveals that these approaches exhibit strong zero-shot generalization and transfer abilities derived from their reliance on language. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these methods can infer building labels from contained rooms and validate our zero-shot approach in a real-world setting. All code is available at https://github.com/MIT-SPARK/llm_scene_understanding.
We employ two non-Riemannian curvature tensors, the $\chi$-curvature and the mean Berwald curvature, to define a specific class of Finsler metrics that possess first integrals.

Building upon the classical Lorentz model for the index of refraction, a novel approach is introduced to derive the complex index of refraction from the extinction efficiency of both homogeneous and layered dielectric spheres. This technique simultaneously eliminates scattering contributions and adjusts measured extinction spectra to account for baseline shifts, tilts, curvature, and scaling factors. Unlike traditional methods, it requires no reference spectrum and inherently satisfies the Kramers-Kronig relations, thereby generating pure absorbance spectra for the unambiguous analysis of chemical properties. For homogeneous spheres, the method additionally calculates the particle radius, while for layered spheres, it determines both the radii of individual layers and the composition of the substances within them. The process relies solely on a single-element detector. Validation using simulated $Q_{ext}$ data for polymethyl-methacrylate (PMMA) and polystyrene spheres demonstrates that the reconstruction algorithm is robust and accurately recovers pure absorbance spectra from $Q_{ext}$ measurements. Furthermore, applying the method to a published, experimentally obtained raw absorbance spectrum confirms its effectiveness in handling uncorrected data; it reliably removes scattering effects and, provided shape information is available, simultaneously corrects for various spectral distortions.

Detecting object states within images (State Detection - SD) holds significant theoretical and practical value, closely linked to other key computer vision tasks like action recognition and affordance detection. Furthermore, this capability is crucial for any entity required to reason and act within dynamic environments, including robotic systems and intelligent agents. Despite its importance, research into this area has historically been limited. This paper presents a systematic investigation of the SD problem. First, we introduce the Object State Detection Dataset (OSDD), a new public resource featuring over 19,000 annotations across 18 object categories and 9 state classes. Second, employing a standard deep learning framework for Object Detection (OD), we perform several tailored experiments to conduct an in-depth analysis of the SD problem's behavior. This study establishes a performance baseline for SD and compares its efficacy relative to OD across various scenarios. Overall, the experimental results confirm that SD is more challenging than OD, indicating that specialized SD methods are necessary to effectively address this significant challenge.

Universities in the UK and globally face growing demands to assess the impact of their research, specifically regarding its role in boosting public scientific engagement. Because the necessity for such evidence often emerges months or years after a discovery, obtaining proof of genuine behavioral shifts within target audiences can be challenging. This article outlines several strategies for retrospectively documenting research engagement and demonstrates their application to case studies of discoveries made as recently as five years ago.

The event-driven characteristics of spiking neural networks render them both biologically realistic and more energy-efficient compared to artificial neural networks. This study demonstrates object motion detection within a two-dimensional visual field. The proposed architecture is biologically plausible, leveraging CMOS analog leaky integrate-and-fire neurons alongside ultra-low-power multi-layer RRAM synapses. Comprehensive transistor-level SPICE simulations confirm that this structure can accurately and reliably identify complex object motions in a two-dimensional visual field.

The magnetar SGR 1935+2154 has been observed to exhibit an anti-glitch alongside fast radio bursts and transient pulsed radio emission. According to the wind braking model, this sequence of events indicates that: (1) SGR 1935+2154 lacks a robust particle wind, allowing it to be modeled using magnetic dipole braking during its persistent phase; (2) The anti-glitch results from an intensified particle wind, consistent with previous magnetar anti-glitches; (3) The transient pulsed radio emission likely stems from a narrowing emission beam during the outburst; and (4) enhanced particle acceleration potential and the pulsar death line are not the primary governing factors.

By leveraging data from a comprehensive year-long campaign focused on bright stars, we investigated crosstalk mechanisms within the GPC1 camera. Our analysis generated a dataset evaluating source stars across nearly every CCD in each chip against all potential crosstalk destinations. We identified probable crosstalk events using a clustering algorithm and subsequently verified all hardware-layout-driven combinations through visual inspection. This process yielded 640 rules, with flux attenuation factors spanning from 2.5x10$^{2}$ at the bright end to 2.5x10$^{4}$ at the faint end. The mean difference of m$_{cross}$-m$_{src}\approx$-10.25 translates to an attenuation factor of 1.25x10$^{4}$, resulting in crosstalk ghosts with an average signal-to-noise ratio of 0.64$\pm$0.1 for bright images. Furthermore, no crosstalk signals were detected between CCDs that lack a hardware connection. We also observed that attenuation factors vary with crosstalk movement, specifically showing a clear dependence on cell column offsets, which aligns with the hypothesis that source star charge diminishes progressively as it traverses cell readout lines. Although these trends are visible, current uncertainties in aperture magnitude measurements remain significant.

Although numerous studies within both relativistic and non-relativistic nuclear many-body frameworks have substantiated the empirical parabolic law governing the Equation of State (EOS) of isospin asymmetric nuclear matter (ANM), the underlying physical basis for the symmetry energy's quartic term being significantly smaller than its quadratic term—even near pure neutron matter—remains obscure. This study investigates the impact of relativistic kinematics, spatial dimensionality, nuclear interactions, and Short-Range Correlations (SRC) on the ratio $\Psi(\rho)$ of quartic to quadratic symmetry energies. Utilizing Free Fermi Gas (FFG) models in arbitrary dimensions $d$ (with and without SRC) alongside non-linear Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) models, we observe that in the FFG framework, $\Psi(\rho)$ exhibits a strong dependence on dimensionality $d$. Although already minimal in standard 3D space, this ratio could be even lower in reduced-dimensional spaces relevant to heavy-ion reaction subsystems or neutron stars, influenced by constraints, collectivities, or symmetries. Theoretically, $\Psi(\rho)$ could only surge to very large values in the ultra-relativistic limit at densities exceeding those found in neutron stars. Conversely, nuclear interactions, both directly and via SRC-induced high-momentum nucleons, exert a substantial influence on the density dependence of $\Psi(\rho)$ relative to relativistic FFG predictions. While SRC significantly alters the kinetic energy of symmetric nuclear matter and the $\Psi(\rho)$ ratio, relativistic corrections were found to be negligible. These findings may enhance our understanding of the EOS for dense, neutron-rich matter.

Providing effective information disclosure in databases with extensive conceptual schemas is a complex challenge, particularly when formulating ad-hoc queries. Current solutions to this issue include graphical interfaces, query by navigation, query by construction, and point-to-point queries. This report introduces an adaptation of the query by navigation method, specifically tailored for the InfoAssistant product. Drawing on information retrieval principles and stratified hypermedia architecture, our approach involves two distinct phases. Initially, during the explorative phase, users define simple queries that represent linear paths through the information structure. Subsequently, in the constructive phase known as query by construction, these linear paths are combined to create more sophisticated queries using operations such as concatenation, union, intersection, and selection.

Recent advances in image captioning have relied on neural models capable of producing varied, high-quality descriptions for images that share the same distribution as their training data. Nevertheless, these models struggle to generate pertinent captions when presented with out-of-distribution (OOD) images, such as those that are corrupted or contain unseen objects. This paper addresses OOD detection within the context of image captioning by defining the problem and proposing an evaluation framework to measure model performance on this task. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of using a caption's likelihood score to identify and reject OOD images, indicating that the degree of alignment between an input image and its generated description is reflected in this score.

Optimizing random structures is a prevalent challenge across various scientific and engineering disciplines, including machine learning, artificial intelligence, and statistical physics. While efficient algorithms for finding optimal solutions are often unknown or considered unlikely for these structures, formal proofs of computational hardness, such as NP-hardness, are frequently absent. This introductory article introduces a novel framework for understanding algorithmic intractability in random structures, grounded in the topological disconnectivity of the set of pairwise distances among near-optimal solutions, known as the Overlap Gap Property (OGP). The article illustrates how this property: a) arises in most models displaying apparent algorithmic difficulty; b) aligns with the phase transitions between tractable and hard regimes observed in numerous analyzed models; and c) provides a mathematically rigorous method to exclude large categories of algorithms, specifically those characterized by input stability.

We offer a novel perspective on the techniques developed by Boccato, Brennecke, Cenatiempo, and Schlein regarding the trapped Bose gas, providing a conceptually straightforward and succinct proof of BEC in the Gross-Pitaevskii limit for small interaction potentials.

This study analyzes the polarizability of twisted bilayer graphene, which arises from the collective influence of electron-hole pairs, plasmons, and acoustic phonons. Through the mechanism of screened Coulomb interactions, Cooper pairs can form, enabling superconductivity across a broad spectrum of twist angles and fillings. This propensity for superconductivity is further amplified by the coupling between longitudinal phonons and electron-hole pairs. Additionally, scattering processes characterized by large momentum transfers, specifically Umklapp processes, are essential for the creation of Cooper pairs. Finally, the size of the superconducting gap varies depending on the different pockets of the Fermi surface.

Over the past twenty years, our understanding of neutrino cross sections at the GeV scale has expanded significantly; these measurements are crucial for testing CP symmetry violation within the leptonic sector. However, current precision and theoretical comprehension remain insufficient for modern neutrino physics requirements. Today, uncertainties in neutrino cross sections at the $O(10\%)$ level constitute the primary systematic error in oscillation experiments, thereby limiting their scientific potential. This paper outlines the prospects for a new generation of cross-section experiments designed to operate alongside DUNE and HyperKamiokande. By analyzing the theoretical and experimental constraints of previous studies, we pinpoint key physics objectives. Furthermore, we emphasize the urgent need to improve theoretical models of GeV-scale cross sections and address the experimental hurdles inherent in these upcoming facilities.

Recent precise measurements of the gravity fields of Jupiter and Saturn have constrained the properties of zonal flows within their outer envelopes. A simplified dynamic equation, often referred to as the thermal wind or thermo-gravitational wind equation, connects these zonal flows to associated buoyancy perturbations, which can subsequently be used to determine dynamic gravity perturbations. The necessity of explicitly incorporating the Dynamic Self Gravity (DSG) effect into this equation remains a subject of significant debate. We demonstrate that, under reasonable assumptions, the equation can be solved semi-analytically. This approach enables us to quantify the DSG's influence on each gravity harmonic independently of the specific zonal flow or the details of the planetary interior model. The impact diminishes as the spherical harmonic degree $l$ increases. For degrees ranging from $l=2$ to approximately $l=4$, DSG represents a first-order effect and must be included when inverting gravity data to determine zonal flow characteristics. For degrees between roughly $l=5$ and $l=10$, the relative DSG impact is approximately 10%, making its inclusion worthwhile, especially given the minimal additional computational cost of the method presented. For even higher degrees, it is questionable whether gravity measurements or interior models will ever achieve the precision necessary to resolve DSG effects, which amount to only a few percent or less.
Using the Dirac formalism within the potential model and incorporating a Martin-like potential, we have computed the mass spectra for $D$ and $D_s$ mesons.

Suppressing multi-user interference through precoding is a standard approach for enhancing spectral efficiency in multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) systems, driving a decade-long pursuit of methods that balance high performance with low complexity. However, conventional techniques like zero-forcing (ZF) and weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) have struggled to offer an optimal trade-off between these two factors. This paper introduces a low-complexity precoding framework for MU-MIMO systems by leveraging deep learning. The core strategy involves converting the MIMO precoding challenge into a multiple-input single-output (MISO) problem, which allows for the derivation of an optimal precoding structure in closed form. A tailored deep neural network is employed to map channel conditions to the precoding matrix. Additionally, computational efficiency is enhanced through input dimensionality reduction, network pruning, and recovery module compression. The study also explores the application of this method in practical MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed scheme delivers performance comparable to the WMMSE algorithm while maintaining significantly lower computational complexity.

This work examines the (in)dependence of additivity and homogeneity conditions within the definition of linear mappings between vector spaces sharing the same scalar field. Distinguishing itself from studies restricted to specific fields such as the real or complex numbers, this research addresses the general case, yielding a nearly comprehensive understanding. Specifically, over prime fields, the conditions are dependent, as additivity entails homogeneity. Conversely, for non-prime fields with a characteristic other than 2, the conditions are independent. However, the question remains unresolved for non-prime fields of characteristic 2.

We demonstrate that for any simple graph $G$, the choice index $c'(G)$—also known as the edge-list chromatic number—is bounded above by $\Delta(G)+2$, where $\Delta(G)$ denotes the maximum degree. As a direct consequence of this finding, we establish that both the total chromatic number $\chi_T(G)$ and the total choice number $c_T(G)$ satisfy the inequality $\chi_T(G) \leq \Delta(G)+4$ and $c_T(G) \leq \Delta(G)+4$, respectively. Furthermore, we connect these upper bounds to the Hall index and Hall condition index of a simple graph, as well as to the total Hall number and total Hall condition number.

Cropping is a foundational operation in computer vision, supporting applications from data augmentation and translation invariance to computational photography and representation learning. This study examines the subtle artifacts left by this process. Although modern camera optics have improved, lenses still imprint specific markers such as chromatic aberration and vignetting. Additionally, photographers introduce cues related to image aesthetics and scene composition. We analyze methods for detecting these traces and explore how cropping alters image distributions. Beyond dissecting the fundamental effects of spatial cropping, our research has practical applications, including identifying deceptive photojournalism and aiding neural network researchers in understanding shortcut learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/basilevh/dissecting-image-crops.

We examine normal forms through an abstract lens, establishing a functorial framework for functional analysis, constructing a functional calculus, and demonstrating a comprehensive versal deformation theorem.

This study employs autoencoder-based deep learning to simultaneously optimize geometric and probabilistic constellation shaping for optical coherent communication. The resulting optimized shaping surpasses the 256 QAM Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, achieving an additional 0.05 bits of mutual information per 4D-symbol at 64 GBd over a 170 km single-mode fiber link.

This study examines a thermodynamic limit chain of spin-1/2 particles featuring XX and three-spin interactions (TSI). Through fermionization, the Hamiltonian for the chain under periodic boundary conditions is exactly diagonalized. The ground-state phase diagram reveals a quantum critical point distinguishing between Luttinger liquid and chiral phases. Treating one spin as an open quantum system with the remaining spins acting as its environment, we analyzed entanglement dynamics by varying initial states. Specifically, the initial setup involved a superposition of up and down states for the open system and a polarized environment. Entanglement revival was observed across the entire interaction range, signaling non-Markovian dynamics. Our exact calculations demonstrate that this non-Markovian behavior is independent of the initial state. Furthermore, adjusting the initial state allows the system to achieve complete entanglement with the environment at a specific moment, termed the entanglement-time ($t_E$); this time decreases as TSI increases. Finally, the signature of the quantum critical point is validated by analyzing the long-time average of entanglement and employing trace distance as a witness for non-Markovianity.

Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can handle generation and manipulation tasks using only a single video, their training times are prohibitively long, rendering them nearly impractical. This paper challenges the need for GANs in single-video generation by introducing a non-parametric baseline capable of performing various generation and manipulation tasks. We adapt classical space-time patch nearest-neighbor methods into a scalable, unconditional generative model that requires no learning. Surprisingly, this straightforward baseline surpasses single-video GANs in both visual quality and realism, as verified by quantitative and qualitative evaluations, while being significantly faster—reducing runtime from days to mere seconds. Our method scales effortlessly to Full-HD videos and can also demonstrate video analogies and spatio-temporal retargeting. These findings indicate that traditional approaches often outperform complex deep learning systems for these specific tasks. Consequently, we establish a new benchmark for single-video generation and manipulation, making diverse generation from a single video practically feasible for the first time.

Recent years have seen large-scale contextual representation models significantly propel NLP forward, enabling unprecedented semantic understanding of text. However, achieving high-quality outcomes requires processing vast datasets, which poses considerable challenges when aggregating and accessing data from diverse sources due to privacy and regulatory constraints. Federated Learning offers a solution by enabling distributed model training that leverages the hardware of data-generating devices. This study demonstrates the feasibility of applying the Federated Learning protocol to NLP tasks, specifically using Word2Vec. We examine a scenario involving a limited number of organizations, each possessing a substantial corpus. Our findings indicate that Federated Word2Vec yields results in both quality and convergence speed that are comparable to those of centralized Word2Vec.

With the growing interest in 3D point cloud analysis, challenges such as limited dataset sizes and poor network generalization have become increasingly evident. To address these issues, we introduce PointCutMix, a straightforward yet effective augmentation technique for point cloud data. This method identifies optimal correspondences between two point clouds and creates new training samples by substituting points in one dataset with their optimally matched counterparts from another. We propose two replacement strategies to cater to varying task requirements for accuracy or robustness: one involves randomly selecting all replacement points, while the other selects the $k$ nearest neighbors of a single randomly chosen point. Both approaches consistently and significantly enhance the performance of various models on point cloud classification tasks. Furthermore, incorporating saliency maps to guide point selection yields additional performance gains. PointCutMix also demonstrates improved model robustness against point-based attacks, outperforming state-of-the-art defense algorithms when applied as a mitigation strategy. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/cuge1995/PointCutMix

Diffusion occurs universally whenever a gradient or potential difference exists in a given quantity, continuing until equilibrium is achieved. This quantity can represent concentration or voltage, with electric current serving as an example driven by voltage differences. During the COVID-19 pandemic, variations in incidence rates between low and high areas may be attributed to local population density; specifically, populous urban centers often exhibit higher infection rates compared to rural regions. This paper aims to apply diffusion concepts to explain one aspect of COVID-19 propagation, focusing on the German context by analyzing the distinct incidence data across its various federal states.

This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for weakly nonlinear and monotone operators defined on Banach lattices of multivariate functions. The findings address convergence almost everywhere, convergence in measure, and convergence in $L^{p}$-norm, with several examples provided to demonstrate the theoretical framework.

This paper introduces a learning-based approach to predict dense depth maps from monocular omnidirectional images. Unlike perspective images, omnidirectional images offer a complete field-of-view, providing more comprehensive scene descriptions. However, existing fully-convolutional networks struggle to capture rich global context from panoramas and suffer from the distortions inherent in equirectangular projection. To overcome these challenges, we propose Cubemap Vision Transformers (CViT), a transformer-based architecture capable of modeling long-range dependencies and extracting distortion-free global features. We demonstrate that CViT provides a global receptive field at every stage, ensuring globally coherent predictions for spherical data. Furthermore, to retain critical local details, we incorporate a convolution-based branch named GLPanoDepth and fuse global features from the transformer at multiple scales. This global-to-local strategy enables the full utilization of both global and local features within the panorama, resulting in state-of-the-art performance for panoramic depth estimation.

Research into the clustering of distant Kuiper Belt objects in the outer solar system has suggested the potential presence of a trans-Neptunian planet known as Planet Nine (P9). Recent work has narrowed down the orbital parameters of P9, enabling the generation of a synthetic catalog of hypothetical candidates. Analyzing how well such a catalog can be retrieved from various sky surveys allows for further refinement of P9's parameter space, guiding more focused observational efforts. This study evaluates the capability of the full six-year Dark Energy Survey (DES) dataset to detect the synthetic Planet Nine population described by Brown and Batygin (2021a) [arXiv:2108.09868]. Results indicate that 11,709 out of 100,000 simulated objects traverse the extensive DES survey area, with 10,187 (87.0%) successfully recovered. Consequently, this analysis excludes an additional 5% of the parameter space when accounting for Planet Nine candidates that would have been identified by both the Zwicky Transient Facility and DES.

Both the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the Casimir effect are computed within an FRW universe of zero curvature using Thermo Field Dynamics (TFD), with the gravitational energy-momentum tensor defined via the Teleparallel Equivalent to General Relativity (TEGR). Each effect yields predictions consistent with cosmological observations: one establishes a minimum value for the deceleration parameter, while the other suggests that any cosmological constant must be of a very small magnitude.

A generalized low-density parity-check (GLDPC) code modifies standard low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes by substituting their single parity check nodes with linear codes featuring stricter parity constraints. This paper presents a novel construction method for GLDPC codes that introduces generalized check nodes through a process termed "partial doping." Unlike conventional protograph GLDPC codes, which replace check nodes entirely, the proposed partially doped GLDPC (PD-GLDPC) code adds generalized check nodes while selectively increasing the degrees of specific variable nodes. This approach offers finer doping granularity relative to the protograph and facilitates more precise extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) analysis. Additionally, we establish a constraint for the typical minimum distance of PD-GLDPC codes, demonstrating that codes meeting this condition exhibit linear minimum distance growth. We also derive threshold-optimized protographs for both regular and irregular ensembles over the binary erasure channel (BEC). Specifically, construction algorithms are provided for regular and irregular protograph-based PD-GLDPC codes, enabling the creation of GLDPC codes with superior rates compared to traditional variants. Performance evaluation reveals that the proposed PD-GLDPC codes achieve excellent waterfall performance with a minimal error floor, outperforming other LDPC codes with identical code rates, lengths, and degree distributions.

This study reveals that numerous existing PDF redaction methods are vulnerable because they retain positional data for non-redacted characters. Specifically, minute horizontal subpixel shifts between redacted and non-redacted text can be extracted to successfully recover first and last names, a flaw that impacts redactions where the underlying text is deleted from the PDF file. To substantiate these findings, we conducted a thorough vulnerability assessment of prevalent PDF redaction mechanisms. Our evaluation of 11 widely used tools, including Adobe Acrobat, confirmed that they inadvertently expose redacted content. Furthermore, we successfully de-redacted hundreds of real-world instances, such as those in OIG investigation reports and FOIA responses. To address these issues, we have published open-source algorithms capable of correcting simple redactions and minimizing data leakage in non-excising redactions (where the hidden text remains copy-pastable). Additionally, we have informed the developers of the examined tools. Notifications were also sent to the Office of Inspector General, the Free Law Project, PACER, Adobe, Microsoft, and the US Department of Justice. We are currently collaborating with several of these organizations to ensure our findings are not exploited for malicious ends.

This work details the implementation of a machine-learning-enhanced particle flow algorithm for CMS. The standard particle flow method reconstructs stable particles by combining calorimeter clusters and tracks, achieving global event reconstruction that leverages data from multiple detector subsystems to significantly improve measurements of jets and missing transverse energy. We investigated the transition of particle flow to heterogeneous computing platforms, specifically GPUs, by employing a graph neural network. The resulting machine-learned particle flow model identifies particle candidates using the complete set of tracks and calorimeter clusters from an event. To validate the approach, we assessed its physics performance within the CMS software framework by interfacing the proposed algorithm with offline jet and missing transverse energy reconstruction. Additionally, we report on the algorithm's computational efficiency, noting that both runtime and memory consumption scale approximately linearly with the input size.

This study applies Volume-Averaged Navier-Stokes equations to analyze fluid dynamics around stationary or moving solids, including packed and fluidized beds. We construct a high-order finite element solver utilizing both Form A and Form B of these equations. To address sharp gradients, satisfy the Ladyzhenskaya-Babuska-Brezzi inf-sup condition, and improve local mass conservation and formulation robustness, we implement specific stabilization strategies. The void fraction is determined via the Particle Centroid Method, while drag forces exerted by solids on the fluid are computed using various drag models. We employ the method of manufactured solutions to verify the solver and confirm that it maintains the convergence order of the underlying finite element discretization. Furthermore, we validate the model by simulating gas flow through a randomly packed bed and examining its pressure drop and mass conservation characteristics.

The convergence of eigenfunction expansions for the Laplacian on planar domains within $L^p$ spaces remains largely unresolved for $p \neq 2$. Following an overview of classical Fourier series on the 2-torus, the discussion shifts to the disc, where eigenfunctions can be explicitly calculated as products of trigonometric and Bessel functions. We summarize a finding by Balodis and C\'ordoba (1999) concerning the $L^p$ convergence of Bessel--Fourier series in the mixed norm space $L^p_{\mathrm{rad}}(L^2_{\mathrm{ang}})$ on the disk, valid for $\tfrac{4}{3}<p<4$. Furthermore, we outline how to adapt their result to achieve $L^p(\mathbb{D}, r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}t)$ norm convergence within the subspace $L^p_{\mathrm{rad}}(L^q_{\mathrm{ang}})$ (where $\tfrac{1}{p}+\tfrac{1}{q}=1$) for the restricted interval ${2\leq p < 4}$.

Domain adaptation generally necessitates access to source domain data to leverage its distribution for aligning with target data. However, privacy constraints often prevent such access during target domain adaptation. This paper investigates the challenging yet practical scenario of source-free unsupervised domain adaptation, where only a pre-trained source model and unlabeled target data are available. We introduce a novel denoised pseudo-labeling approach that effectively utilizes the source model and target data to facilitate self-adaptation through pseudo-labels. Crucially, acknowledging that domain shifts inevitably introduce noise into pseudo-labels generated by the source model, we propose two complementary denoising strategies at the pixel and class levels. These schemes employ uncertainty and prototype estimation to filter out noisy labels and retain reliable ones, thereby enhancing pseudo-labeling effectiveness. Experiments on cross-domain fundus image segmentation demonstrate that our method, which requires no source images or modifications to the source training, achieves performance comparable to or superior to state-of-the-art source-dependent unsupervised domain adaptation techniques.

We demonstrate that measuring the source-to-solution map at a single point for the semilinear wave equation on an a-priori unknown Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ allows for the determination of its topological, differential, and geometric structures.

This study focuses on measuring the similarity between pairs of news articles written in various languages. The dataset includes seven distinct objective similarity metrics for each pair. Building upon a pre-trained embedding model, we established a baseline using cosine similarity and subsequently enhanced these results by training a feed-forward neural network. Additionally, we constructed separate pipelines to extract features specific to each similarity metric. The integration of feature extraction with the neural network yielded significant improvements over the baseline performance.

For the past ten years, research has demonstrated that deep neural networks produce sensory representations akin to the mammalian brain, with their activations linearly corresponding to cortical responses for identical sensory stimuli. Yet, it is unclear whether these artificial systems learn in a manner comparable to the brain. To investigate this, we examined fUS recordings of auditory cortices in two ferrets exposed to 320 distinct 10-second audio clips, comparing these biological responses to the activations of Wav2vec 2.0, a self-supervised model pretrained on 960 hours of speech using the same audio set. Crucially, we tested Wav2vec 2.0 in two configurations: (i) "Pretrained," utilizing the fixed model for all inputs, and (ii) "Continuous Update," which adjusts the model's weights via back-propagation after each sound in the exact sequence presented to the ferrets. Our findings indicate that the Continuous-Update mode generates activations more closely resembling brain activity than either a static Pretrained Wav2vec 2.0 or other control models with different training protocols. These results imply that trial-by-trial adjustments in self-supervised algorithms driven by back-propagation mirror the corresponding fluctuations in cortical responses to sound. Consequently, our study offers empirical evidence of a shared learning mechanism between self-supervised models and the mammalian cortex during auditory processing.

This paper reports on the study of $\Lambda_b^0$ baryon decays into the $DpK^-$ final state, utilizing a proton-proton collision dataset with an integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb detector. The analysis focuses on two decay channels: $\Lambda_b^0\to DpK^-$ where $D$ decays to $K^-\pi^+$ or $K^+\pi^-$. In this context, $D$ denotes a superposition of $D^0$ and $\overline{D}^0$ states. While the process involving $D\to K^+\pi^-$ is anticipated to be suppressed compared to the $D\to K^-\pi^+$ mode, it is observed here for the first time. The study measures the ratio of branching fractions between these two decays and reports the $C\!P$ asymmetry of the suppressed channel, a quantity sensitive to the CKM angle $\gamma$.

q-Matroids serve as the q-analogue to classical matroids. This paper introduces several types of mappings between q-matroids; while these maps are not strictly linear, they transform subspaces into subspaces and maintain specific aspects of the q-matroid structure. These distinct mapping types generate various categories of q-matroids. We demonstrate that only one such category admits a coproduct: the category consisting of linear weak maps, where the rank of a subspace's image does not exceed the rank of the subspace itself. In this specific category, the coproduct corresponds to the recently defined direct sum of q-matroids.

Let $G$ be a profinite group. An $S[[G]]$-module is defined as a $G$-spectrum $X$ meeting specific criteria, and for such a module $X$, the homotopy orbit spectrum $X_{hG}$ is introduced. If the components of $X$ fulfill a particular finiteness requirement, we construct a homotopy orbit spectral sequence where the $E_2$-term corresponds to the continuous homology of $G$ with coefficients in the graded profinite $\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}[[G]]$-module $\pi_\ast(X)$. To demonstrate this finding, we establish that under suitable conditions on $G$ and various spectra $Z$, the equivalence $(Z[[G]])_{hG} \simeq Z$ holds. Additionally, further instruments for advancing this area are provided.

Historically, Embedded Systems (ES) development has prioritized functionality over security, a trend that persists across many sectors. However, the growing number of security threats against ES poses significant risks, as successful attacks on systems controlling critical applications can lead to economic, physical, or human casualties. To address this, there is a need for a standardized and widely accepted security testing framework that offers guidance, uniform reporting formats, and the ability to track results over time. This can be accomplished by integrating security metrics into the evaluation process. When carefully selected and designed, these metrics can deliver quantitative, repeatable, and reproducible values that accurately reflect an ES's level of security protection. This paper examines the characteristics of effective security metrics, proposes a taxonomy for their classification, and conducts a literature review on metrics used for ES security evaluation. The review collected and analyzed over 500 metrics, narrowing them down to 169 with potential for application in ES security assessment. As anticipated, 77.5% of these metrics pertain exclusively to software, while only 0.6% address hardware security specifically. Ultimately, this work seeks to establish the groundwork for a security evaluation methodology that utilizes metrics to quantify the security posture of an ES.

Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) are frequently analyzed to probe the scrambling behavior of quantum systems. We demonstrate that local conserved quantities typically induce, at minimum, an algebraic decay of the OTOC, provided that the dynamics are local and the system adheres to the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. This finding depends on the algebraic growth of the infinite-time OTOC with system size, a characteristic of thermalizing systems possessing local conservation laws, alongside the finite speed of correlation propagation in systems with finite-range interactions. Furthermore, we establish that a time-independent Hamiltonian is not a prerequisite, as these conditions can be met in time-dependent systems, whether periodic or aperiodic. Finally, we note that our conclusions extend to systems exhibiting power-law interactions.

We present novel smoothing estimators for complex graph signals, leveraging a recently explored Determinantal Point Process (DPP). These estimators are constructed using subsets of edges and nodes selected via the DPP to form trees and unicycles, which are connected components with precisely one cycle. Additionally, we offer a Julia implementation of these estimators and evaluate their effectiveness in solving a ranking problem.

A major obstacle in developing automatic extraction models for visually complex documents, such as invoices, is the expense of gathering the thousands of high-quality labeled documents required to train models with satisfactory accuracy. We introduce Selective Labeling, which streamlines the annotation process by generating "yes/no" labels for candidate extractions suggested by a model trained on partially labeled data. By integrating this approach with a tailored active learning strategy to identify the model's most uncertain predictions, we demonstrate through experiments across document types from three distinct domains that selective labeling can lower the cost of acquiring labeled data by a factor of 10 while causing negligible accuracy loss.

This paper investigates the application of reinforcement learning for controller design, with a detailed focus on quadcopter attitude control. We supply comprehensive details necessary to replicate our methodology, beginning with a dynamic model of a Crazyflie 2.0 under diverse scenarios, including nominal conditions, partial motor failures, and wind gusts. We introduce a robust variant of signal temporal logic to quantitatively assess vehicle behavior and gauge controller performance. The study meticulously outlines the selection of training algorithms, neural network architectures, hyperparameters, and observation spaces, all tailored to the specific performance metrics developed. Furthermore, we examine the robustness of the resulting controllers against single-rotor power loss and wind disturbances, concluding with insights into practical controller design via reinforcement learning.

Within a completed Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Snapshot initiative, we conducted high-resolution observations of six nearby core-collapse supernovae (SNe): SN 2012A, SN 2013ej, SN 2016gkg, SN 2017eaw, SN 2018zd, and SN 2018aoq. By observing these sites at sufficiently late evolutionary stages, we confirmed the disappearance of massive-star progenitor candidates previously identified in pre-explosion images, establishing them as the most likely actual progenitors. However, for SN 2016gkg, we determined that the candidate was likely a blend of the vanishing progenitor and a closely neighboring star. Consequently, we provide a revised characterization of this progenitor as a binary system featuring a hydrogen-stripped primary star at the time of explosion, with an effective temperature of ~6300--7900 K, a bolometric luminosity of ~10^{4.65} L_sun, a radius of ~118--154 R_sun, and an initial mass between 9.5--11 M_sun. Additionally, by utilizing late-time archival HST data nearly contemporaneous with our observations, we demonstrate that SN 2017eaw exhibited a luminous ultraviolet excess, best explained by ongoing interaction between the supernova shock and pre-existing circumstellar matter. We also note a caveat, particularly regarding SN 2013ej, that obscuration from supernova dust may undermine some of our conclusions. Ultimately, this sample contributes to the expanding catalog of confirmed or probable core-collapse supernova progenitors.

Neutrino telescope experiments are increasingly competitive in the indirect search for dark matter, with signals from dark matter annihilation typically attributed to the hadronization and decay of Standard Model particles. We present the BLSSMIS supersymmetric model, which satisfies current experimental constraints while generating a potentially detectable non-standard neutrino spectrum resulting from dark matter annihilation.

Utilizing devices and sensors to identify individuals prone to falling enables the implementation of preventive measures, fostering independent living among the elderly while lowering long-term care expenses. This study sought to evaluate the accuracy of the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test for fall risk detection by fusing features derived from accelerometer data. A sample of 36 community-dwelling healthy older adults (18 fallers matched with 18 non-fallers), calculated to achieve 94% statistical power, performed both single-task and dual-task (manual and cognitive) TUG trials while wearing a single triaxial waist-mounted accelerometer sampling at 200Hz. By segmenting the TUG trials and conducting comparative analysis, the study demonstrated superior discrimination between fallers and non-fallers compared to conventional functional tests. Furthermore, feature fusion enhanced discriminatory power, yielding an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.84 (with Sensitivity and Specificity both at 0.83; 95% CI 0.62-0.91), thereby confirming the study's clinical significance. The authors conclude that extracting features from segmented TUG trials during dual-task performance holds potential to boost faller identification accuracy via accelerometer sensors, ultimately improving the utility of the TUG test for clinical and epidemiological purposes.

This research investigates the relationship between error and compression within the non-parametric multiclass classification framework, specifically through prototype learning rules. Our primary focus is on OptiNet, a recently introduced compression-based algorithm (Kontorovich, Sabato, and Urner 2016; Kontorovich, Sabato, and Weiss 2017; Hanneke et al. 2021). Beyond its computational advantages, OptiNet has recently been proven to be universally consistent across any metric instance space that supports a universally consistent rule, marking it as the first algorithm to possess this trait. Nevertheless, the specific rates for its error and compression remained unresolved. In this work, we determine these rates for scenarios where data instances exist in Euclidean space, assuming standard smoothness and tail conditions on the distribution. We demonstrate that OptiNet attains non-trivial compression rates alongside near minimax-optimal error rates. Subsequently, we examine a new general compression scheme for prototype rules that locally adjusts to noise levels without compromising accuracy. When applied to OptiNet, this scheme yields additional improvements in compression rates under a geometric margin condition. Finally, we present experimental results comparing the performance of these various methods.

Improving urban air quality and safeguarding public health are paramount priorities for governments, prompting the implementation of strategies to curb critical atmospheric pollutants, including the establishment of Low-Emission Zones (LEZs). Madrid Central represents a key initiative by the Madrid City Council designed to diminish motor traffic and associated pollution in the city center; it expanded upon a prior, smaller restricted zone. Although launched at the end of 2018, the zone became fully operational in the second quarter of 2019. Beyond environmental benefits, LEZs generate social and economic effects, necessitating impact assessments to verify the reduction of pollutant levels as committed. This study proposes two metrics to evaluate Madrid Central's effect on nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentrations, utilizing data from the Plaza del Carmen monitoring station between 2010 and 2019. Additionally, two other monitoring stations surrounding the restricted area are examined to detect any adverse impacts resulting from increased traffic near the zone's boundaries. Consequently, the paper presents two pollutant-independent methodologies for assessing LEZ impacts and their evolution, along with an analysis of the impact during Madrid Central's inaugural year.

We investigate $Z_N$ symmetry within $SU(N)$ gauge theories containing fundamental matter fields by constraining the lattice partition function to uniform spatial matter configurations and gauge fields with zero spatial components. Under this approximation, the interaction between gauge and matter fields simplifies to an effective one-dimensional gauged chain, enabling analytical computation of the matter field's contribution to the Polyakov loop free energy. We demonstrate that as the number of temporal sites grows large, the explicit breaking of $Z_N$ symmetry in this free energy disappears, a phenomenon driven by the dominance of the density of states. Furthermore, we contend that the spatial links and spatial modes of the matter fields dictate the boundaries between regions where $Z_N$ symmetry is realized and the remaining areas of the phase diagram.

We apply the Maxwell equations within curved spacetime to anisotropically expanding Kasner metrics. By utilizing vector identities, we derive second-order differential wave equations for electromagnetic field components; this explicit derivation reveals that these equations are not uncoupled across different components, contrary to previous assumptions. Instead, anisotropic expansion directly generates gravitational coupling between electric and magnetic field components. The absence of such coupling terms in earlier studies may suggest a generally incomplete understanding of electromagnetic energy evolution in anisotropic cosmologies. To decouple the field components, a fourth-order wave equation is required, which we derive for Kasner-like metrics featuring generalized expansion or contraction rate indices. In the axisymmetric Kasner case defined by $(p_{1}, p_{2}, p_{3}) = (1,0,0)$, we obtain exact field solutions for general propagation wavevectors, half of which were previously unreported. For the alternative axisymmetric Kasner case, $\{p_{1}, p_{2}, p_{3}\} = \{(-1/3),(2/3),(2/3)\}$, numerical methods demonstrate an explicit violation of the geometric optics approximation at early times. This shows that the physical phase velocity of the wave is inhibited toward the initial singularity, approaching zero as $t \rightarrow 0$.

Integrating pretrained language models (PLMs) with textual patterns has proven effective in both zero-shot and few-shot scenarios. For zero-shot tasks, it is logical to construct patterns that mimic the text encountered during self-supervised pretraining, as the model lacks exposure to other data. However, supervised training offers greater flexibility; by permitting tokens beyond the PLM's standard vocabulary, patterns can be more adaptively tuned to the model's specific characteristics. We distinguish between patterns utilizing continuous vector tokens and those requiring discrete selections from the vocabulary, designating our approach as CONtinuous pAtterNs (CONAN). We assessed CONAN on two prominent benchmarks for lexical inference in context (LIiC), also known as predicate entailment—a difficult natural language understanding task characterized by limited training data. Compared directly with discrete pattern methods, CONAN consistently achieved superior results, establishing a new state-of-the-art. Furthermore, our experiments provide meaningful insights into the types of patterns that boost PLM performance on LIiC and highlight critical questions about our comprehension of how PLMs utilize textual patterns.

This study addresses survival data involving a cure fraction, where certain individuals will never experience the event of interest. We employ a mixture cure framework comprising two components: an incidence model for the probability of being uncured and a latency model for the survival of those uncured subjects. While various methods, including parametric and nonparametric approaches, have modeled covariate effects on incidence—with the logistic model being predominant—we propose a monotone single-index model for incidence estimation. Our new method utilizes maximum likelihood techniques combined with isotonic regression. This monotone single-index structure relaxes the rigid parametric assumptions of the logistic model while retaining the interpretability of regression coefficients. We demonstrate the estimator's consistency and, via a simulation study, show that when the monotonicity assumption holds, it outperforms the single-index/Cox mixture cure model. To demonstrate practical application, we apply this method to analyze survival data from melanoma patients.

For a unital $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal A$ and a subspace $\mathcal B \subseteq \mathcal A$, a characterization of the best approximation of an element from $\mathcal A$ within $\mathcal B$ is derived. As a consequence, a formula for the distance between an element of $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ is established, provided that a best approximation exists. Additionally, a characterization for Birkhoff-James orthogonality of an element in a Hilbert $C^*$-module with respect to a subspace is obtained.

Current dominant trackers define a fixed-size rectangular search area derived from prior predictions or initial bounding boxes as input. Although this approach enhances tracking efficiency, the rigid search region lacks adaptability, often resulting in failure scenarios such as rapid motion or interference from distractors. Consequently, trackers may lose the target due to insufficient search coverage or become misled by excessive search areas. To address these issues, we introduce Search Region Regulation Tracking (SRRT), a new paradigm that employs a specialized regulator to dynamically estimate an optimal search region for each frame. Additionally, to accommodate appearance variations, we develop a reference frame updating strategy governed by the object's locking state. Our SRRT framework is straightforward in design yet delivers significant performance gains over baseline methods and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art trackers across seven challenging benchmarks. Specifically, on the LaSOT benchmark, SRRT improves SiamRPN++ and TransT by 4.6% and 3.1% in AUC, respectively.

This work investigates two core challenges in distributed computing—consensus and approximate agreement—using a fresh methodology for establishing lower bounds and impossibility results, termed the asynchronous speedup theorem. For any $n$-process task $\Pi$ and computational model $M$, we introduce a derived task known as the closure of $\Pi$ relative to $M$. The asynchronous speedup theorem posits that if a task $\Pi$ is solvable within $t\geq 1$ rounds in $M$, its closure with respect to $M$ can be solved in $t-1$ rounds within the same model. We demonstrate this theorem for iterated models, provided they support solo executions. To showcase the theorem's utility, we offer novel proofs for the wait-free impossibility of consensus using read/write registers, as well as the wait-free impossibility of achieving consensus with registers and test\&set objects when $n>2$. These proofs rely on demonstrating that, in each scenario, the closure of consensus (relative to the specific model) is identical to consensus itself. Our primary application involves examining the capabilities of additional objects, specifically test\&set and binary consensus, in accelerating wait-free solutions to approximate agreement. By analyzing the closure of approximate agreement under both models, we reveal that although these objects surpass read/write registers in terms of computability, they do not offer any advantage in solving approximate agreement more rapidly.

Fluid-structure interactions involving flexible fibers and viscous flows are fundamental to numerous industrial applications, medical challenges, and biological processes. This study specifically examines particles freely transported within time-dependent flows, focusing on the dynamics and morphologies of actin filaments subjected to oscillatory shear. By integrating microfluidic experiments, numerical simulations, and theoretical modeling, we demonstrate that unlike steady shear flows—where minor orientational fluctuations from a flow-aligned state trigger tumbling and deformation—periodic flow reversal enables filaments to explore a wide range of configurations at the start of each cycle. Analyzing motion during the half-periods of oscillation underscores the pivotal influence of initial orientation on resulting dynamics. This tight coupling between orientation and deformation generates novel deformation regimes and higher-order buckling modes not observed in steady flows. Our primary finding is the potential to suppress buckling instabilities for specific combinations of oscillation frequency and initial orientation, even under extremely strong flow conditions. We attribute this counterintuitive behavior to a weakly nonlinear Landau theory of buckling, modeling the filaments as inextensible Brownian Euler-Bernoulli rods with hydrodynamics described by local slender-body theory.

The Tur\'an number $ex(n, H)$ represents the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex graph that does not contain $H$ as a subgraph. Let $P_{\ell}$ be the path on $\ell$ vertices, $S_{\ell-1}$ the star on $\ell$ vertices, and $k_1P_{\ell}\cup k_2S_{\ell-1}$ the path-star forest consisting of the disjoint union of $k_1$ copies of $P_{\ell}$ and $k_2$ copies of $S_{\ell-1}$. Lidick\'y and colleagues first investigated the Tur\'an number of $k_1P_4\cup k_2S_3$ for large $n$ in 2013. Subsequently, Zhang and Wang proposed a conjecture regarding the Tur\'an number of $k_1P_{2\ell}\cup k_2S_{2\ell-1}$ in 2022. This paper determines the Tur\'an numbers for $P_{\ell}\cup kS_{\ell-1}$, $k_1P_{2\ell}\cup k_2S_{2\ell-1}$, and $2P_5\cup kS_4$ when $n$ is sufficiently large, thereby confirming Zhang and Wang's conjecture. Furthermore, all corresponding extremal graphs are fully characterized.

This study examines optical orientation, polarization pinning, and depolarization within optically trapped semiconductor exciton-polariton condensates. We comprehensively map the condensate's polarization across varying incident nonresonant excitation powers and polarization states. By employing a ring-shaped excitation pattern, we create an exciton-induced potential that spatially confines the polariton condensate to a single mode. Our observations indicate that circular polarization formation in the condensate remains stable even with a weakly cocircularly polarized pump. Adjusting the diameter of the excitation ring allows us to transition from a regime where condensate polarization is pinned along cavity-strain axes dependent on coordinates, to a state characterized by zero condensate polarization. Analysis using the driven-dissipative stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii equation demonstrates that this depolarization arises from a competition between sample-induced in-plane polarization splitting and condensate-reservoir overlap. As the influence of the latter increases, the fixed-point phase space attractors of the condensate weaken, leading to enhanced random phase space walks, the emergence of limit cycle trajectories, and a consequent reduction in the degree of time-integrated polarization.

This study addresses the characterization of an inner bound for the capacity region of a three-user classical-quantum interference channel (3-CQIC). The most effective existing coding schemes for CQICs rely on unstructured random codes combined with message splitting and superposition coding. In contrast, for classical three-user interference channels, it has been demonstrated that coset codes, which possess algebraic closure properties, strictly outperform those based on unstructured codes. In this work, we introduce analogous coset code-based techniques for the 3-to-1 CQIC subclass. We evaluate the performance of these methods and derive a novel inner bound for the 3-to-1 CQIC capacity region that encompasses the current largest known bound and strictly improves upon it for specific identified examples.

A graph with $n$ vertices is defined as pancyclic if it includes a cycle of every length $l$ where $3 \le l \le n$.
