In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that for a Hamiltonian graph on $n > 4k^4$ vertices with an independence number of $k$, the graph is necessarily pancyclic. He subsequently proposed that the condition $n = \Omega(k^2)$ would be sufficient to ensure pancyclicity. Building upon his findings and subsequent research, we establish that there exists a constant $c$ such that $n > ck^{7/3}$ is adequate to guarantee this property.

From 2013 to 2019, the MINERvA experiment gathered an accelerator-based neutrino interaction dataset that is uniquely suited to the energy scale of DUNE. These represent the only existing data at intermediate and high momentum transfers for multiple nuclear targets within a single beam. MINERvA is initiating efforts to archive this data and ensure public access, allowing analysis to continue beyond the collaboration's conclusion. The community is urged to explore the creation of centralized resources to guarantee long-term availability of these datasets and associated analysis tools for the broader High Energy Physics community.

Detecting small objects remains a significant challenge within the field of object detection due to their susceptibility to occlusion by larger objects and their inherent lack of distinctive feature information. Specifically, the YOLOv3 network struggles with small object detection because it fails to account for the contextual semantic relationships among them, resulting in low accuracy. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel small object detection network that integrates multi-level feature fusion and feature augmentation. First, a feature enhancement module is embedded into the deep layers of the backbone extraction network to enrich the feature representation of small objects within the feature maps. Second, a multi-level feature fusion module is designed to more effectively capture the contextual semantics of small objects. Furthermore, the study employs a combined strategy of Soft-NMS and CIOU to mitigate missed detections of occluded small objects. Ablation experiments conducted on the MS COCO2017 task validate the efficacy of the proposed modules. Results across the MS COCO2017, VOC2007, and VOC2012 datasets demonstrate that the Average Precision (AP) of this method exceeds that of YOLOv3 by 16.5%, 8.71%, and 9.68%, respectively. These findings confirm that the proposed approach yields superior performance for small object detection.

The EuS/InAs interface has recently garnered interest due to its potential to generate magnetic exchange correlations within a semiconductor exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling, a feature valuable for topological quantum applications. Employing density functional theory (DFT) enhanced by a machine-learned Hubbard $U$ correction [npj Comput. Mater. 6, 180 (2020)], we investigated how the interface's bonding configuration influences the electronic structure. Across all examined configurations, the EuS valence band maximum (VBM) remains lower than that of InAs. Furthermore, new dispersed states appear at the top of the InAs VBM at the interface—states absent in the isolated materials—which are primarily derived from the InAs layer nearest the boundary. These localized states likely result from charge transfer from EuS to InAs. While the interface configuration dictates both the relative positioning of the VBMs and the dispersion of these interface states, the induced magnetic moment in InAs remains negligible for all studied cases. Consequently, this coherent interface configuration does not appear promising for establishing equilibrium magnetic properties in InAs.

We investigate scenarios involving two spatially separated observers, Alice and Bob, who aim to identify a quantum state drawn from a set of possibilities. Specifically, we analyze their strategies to maximize both the probability of correctly guessing the state and the information gained regarding it. While it is established that allowing Alice and Bob to use LOCC can sometimes yield better results than requiring simultaneous measurements, and that access to a Bell pair can also improve outcomes in certain cases, we demonstrate how LOCC enables the optimal distinction between two product states. Furthermore, we find that for distinguishing product states, LOCC is nearly always more advantageous than utilizing a Bell pair.

Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success across various domains in Natural Language Processing. Consistently delivering exemplary results, these models are pretrained on language modeling tasks and subsequently fine-tuned for downstream applications like Text Classification, Question Answering, and Neural Machine Translation. This study introduces a Multitask Fine-tuning approach that integrates Bilingual Machine Translation with an auxiliary Causal Language Modeling task to enhance performance on the former, specifically for Indian Languages. We empirically evaluate this method against standard fine-tuning using the mBART50 model across three language pairs: Marathi-Hindi, Marathi-English, and Hindi-English. Our findings suggest that multitask fine-tuning outperforms standard fine-tuning and can effectively improve Bilingual Machine Translation across these language pairs.

Recent research indicates that Information Retrieval (IR)-driven bug localization struggles when bug reports lack detailed structured data, such as relevant program entity names, and that an overabundance of structured data, like stack traces, can also hinder automated localization. To address this, we introduce BLIZZARD, a new approach that automatically identifies buggy entities within project source code by employing effective query reformulation and information retrieval strategies. Specifically, BLIZZARD assesses whether a bug report contains an excessive number of program entities and subsequently applies tailored query reforms to enhance localization. Evaluations on 5,139 bug reports demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline techniques, achieving 7%–56% higher Hit@10, and 6%–62% higher MAP@10 and MRR@10. Furthermore, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods and their variants reveal improvements of 19% in MAP@10 and 20% in MRR@10, alongside a 59% success rate in handling noisy queries and a 39% success rate in addressing poor-quality queries.

Electromagnetic systems are widely utilized for controlling magnetically actuated objects, particularly in fields like microrheology and microrobotics, making their design optimization highly desirable. However, many existing designs lack compactness, portability, and versatility. Portability is critical for biomedical applications where *in vivo* or *in vitro* testing occurs outside the laboratory microscope. This document details the design, fabrication, and implementation of the ModMag, a compact, affordable, versatile, and user-friendly device capable of managing multiple electromagnetic setups. These include a traditional two-dimensional four-coil configuration, a three-dimensional Helmholtz setup, and a three-dimensional magnetic tweezer arrangement. All electronic circuitry and power systems are housed within a compact 10"x6"x3" unit featuring a 10-inch touchscreen. A graphical user interface further enhances usability. Additionally, the system supports remote control, offering greater flexibility and the ability to interface with proprietary camera software on a remote computer. Beyond the software and electronics, the document outlines the design of the electromagnetic coil setups and provides examples of the ModMag's application in experimental contexts.

This paper aims to integrate the real component of the Riemann-Roch-Grothendieck theorem for complex flat vector bundles into $K$-theory. Specifically, for any submersion $\pi:X\to B$ featuring closed fibers $Z$, we introduce an analytic index $\textrm{ind}^{a, \Lambda}_{\widehat{K}}:\widehat{K}(X)\to\widehat{K}(B)$ linked to twisted de Rham operators, without requiring the twisting bundles to be flat within differential $K$-theory. We demonstrate that when this index's restriction to $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ $K$-theory, denoted as $\textrm{ind}^{a, \Lambda}_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}:K^{-1}(X; \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})\to K^{-1}(B; \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$, acts on the element corresponding to a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded complex flat vector bundle $(F, \nabla^F)$ of virtual rank zero equipped with a Hermitian metric, it yields a canonical representative associated with the cohomology bundle of $(F, \nabla^F)$. Furthermore, we establish a Riemann-Roch-Grothendieck theorem for $\textrm{ind}^{a, \Lambda}_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}$ in $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ $K$-theory at the level of differential forms. These findings provide a novel proof of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded real part of the Riemann-Roch-Grothendieck theorem applicable to complex flat vector bundles.

In Japanese-to-English translation, the absence of explicit pronouns in Japanese presents a significant challenge, as the model must infer and generate the appropriate pronoun for the English output. Although resolving these zero pronouns typically relies on broader discourse context, local cues within a single sentence can sometimes provide sufficient information for inference. This study introduces a data augmentation technique designed to offer additional training signals, enabling the translation model to learn the relationship between local context and zero pronouns. Experimental results in the conversational domain demonstrate that this approach substantially enhances the accuracy of translating zero pronouns.

This paper investigates spatial central configurations in an N+4-body problem where N bodies occupy the vertices of a regular N-gon $T$, and four additional bodies are symmetrically positioned on the line perpendicular to $T$'s plane and passing through its center. We establish the necessary mass conditions required for these bodies to form a central configuration and demonstrate the existence of such configurations within the Newtonian framework.

Achieving low phase noise in THz oscillators created by multiplying microwaves remains challenging. While photonics-based methods—where THz waves are generated by converting two optical tones via opto-electronic conversion—show promise, they require stringent suppression of relative phase noise between those tones. This study demonstrates a low phase noise THz wave (approximately 560 GHz) generated using a frequency-stabilized dissipative Kerr microresonator soliton comb. By locking the comb's repetition rate to a long fiber within a two-wavelength delayed self-heterodyne interferometer, the phase noise of the resulting THz wave is markedly reduced. Furthermore, a novel measurement technique is introduced to evaluate THz phase noise beyond the limits of frequency-multiplied microwaves, confirming that this approach yields superior phase noise performance compared to all other photonic THz oscillators operating above 300 GHz.

This paper introduces various correspondence types, including weakly naturally quasiconvex, *-weakly naturally quasiconvex, weakly biconvex, and those with *--weakly convex graphs, and establishes fixed point theorems for each. Consequently, by applying a variant of W. K. Kim's quasi-point theorem, we demonstrate the existence of equilibria in quasi-games.

Optimizing the weight of frame structures using continuous cross-section parametrization presents a difficult non-convex challenge, which has historically been addressed through local optimization methods. In this work, we leverage the problem's intrinsic semi-algebraic nature and employ the Lasserre hierarchy of relaxations to identify global minimizers. Although this hierarchy naturally provides a sequence of lower bounds, we demonstrate, under mild conditions, how to project relaxed solutions onto the original feasible set to establish feasible upper bounds. Utilizing these bounds, we formulate a straightforward sufficient condition for global $\varepsilon$-optimality. Furthermore, we prove that the optimality gap vanishes as the limit approaches zero, provided the set of global minimizers is convex. These findings are validated through two academic examples.

Calculating the potential energy surface is fundamental to the theoretical modeling of nuclear fission. Within the constrained self-consistent framework, the nuclear shape evolves smoothly from the ground state to a highly elongated form featuring a narrow neck. In standard microscopic models, the neck rupture at scission corresponds to a significant redistribution of nuclear matter density and a swift drop in energy. This study demonstrates, however, that applying multi-constrained calculations with a neck constraint reveals no discontinuity in the potential energy surface at scission. We examine an alternative scenario where the neck ruptures earlier at reduced quadrupole and octupole moments, presenting a competitive fission path to the conventional one. Our analysis of the neck in the scission configuration indicates that in asymmetric fission, the neck radius cannot fall below 2 fm, nor can the nuclear matter density drop beneath saturation levels. Conversely, in the compact fission mode, the nuclear density may decrease to half of the saturation density prior to neck rupture.

Self-adaptive autonomous robots can adjust their actions to environmental changes, enabling efficient resource management and appropriate responses to unforeseen issues like system faults. Designing such robots requires complex architectures that incorporate automatic mechanisms for dynamically configuring behavioral control elements. To streamline the development of these architectures, general software tools applicable across various robotic systems are beneficial. This paper introduces an original algorithm designed for the dynamic configuration of control architectures in self-adaptive autonomous robots. Utilizing a constraint-based approach, the algorithm determines which fundamental behaviors to activate in reaction to both reactive and deliberative events. It employs specialized search heuristics and initialization procedures to meet the performance demands of robotic applications. Implemented as the open-source, ROS-based Behavior Coordinator (CBC), this tool is publicly available and has proven successful in developing multiple autonomous aerial robot applications.

This paper introduces a family of high-order asymptotic preserving (AP) discontinuous Galerkin (DG) schemes designed for nonlinear, time-dependent gray radiative transfer equations (GRTEs). Building upon the stability-enhanced high-order AP DG methods for linear transport equations presented in \cite{Peng2020stability}, we apply a micro-macro decomposition framework to nonlinear GRTEs by incorporating a weighted linear diffusive term. In the diffusive regime, this approach yields a hyperbolic time step constraint of $\Delta t=\mathcal{O}(h)$, surpassing the parabolic restriction of $\Delta t=\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ and remaining independent of the photon mean free path. A key innovation is the use of a Picard iteration coupled with a predictor-corrector strategy, which decouples the global nonlinear system into a linear system featuring local nonlinear algebraic equations within an outer iterative loop. The proposed method is demonstrated to be both asymptotic preserving and asymptotically accurate. Numerical experiments on one- and two-dimensional problems confirm that the scheme achieves high-order accuracy while maintaining effectiveness and computational efficiency.

We demonstrate that integrating relational inductive bias into a deep learning model enhances sample efficiency without the need for extensive data augmentation. This proposed one-shot classification framework utilizes local and pairwise attention to perform relational matching between input pairs. Our method achieves a perfect solution to the Omniglot one-shot image classification challenge, surpassing both human-level accuracy and prior state-of-the-art results without employing data augmentation.

This research investigates how spontaneous emission and incoherent atomic pumping influence the nonlinear semiclassical dynamics of the unbalanced Dicke model, which extends the standard model by allowing independent coupling strengths for co- and counter-rotating interaction terms. Beyond the well-established superradiant phenomenon, the combination of spontaneous emission with significant counter-rotating terms induces a laser-like state known as "counter-lasing," which manifests in the semiclassical framework as stable periodic orbits. We conduct a thorough dynamical analysis of counter-lasing emergence in the unbalanced Dicke model under strong cavity dissipation, enabling the adiabatic elimination of the cavity field to derive an effective Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) model. When co-rotating coupling is weak, the counter-lasing phase arises through a Hopf bifurcation of the de-excited state; however, with low spontaneous emission rates, this can trigger resurgent superradiant pulses. Conversely, stronger co-rotating coupling necessitates the emergence of the counter-lasing phase from the steady-state superradiant regime. This transition reflects the competition between coherent and incoherent processes driving superradiance and counter-lasing, respectively. We identify a remarkably complex transition between these states, characterized by the formation of a chaotic attractor within a narrow transitional parameter region.

We demonstrate that Floquet chiral topological superconductivity emerges naturally within Josephson junctions constructed from magnetic topological insulator-superconductor sandwich structures. Applying a bias voltage across the junction modulates the Josephson phase, propelling the system into an anomalous Floquet chiral topological superconductor state. This state features chiral Majorana edge modes within the quasienergy spectrum, while the bulk Floquet bands maintain zero Chern numbers. The bias voltage serves as a tuning parameter that facilitates novel dynamical topological quantum phase transitions, guiding the system through various exotic Majorana-carrying Floquet topological superconducting phases. Our theoretical framework establishes a new paradigm for achieving Floquet chiral topological superconductivity in solid-state systems, one that should be readily accessible for experimental verification.

We introduce a novel and efficient classification for all Borel Wadge classes of subsets within Baire space, leveraging the true stage machinery first formulated by Montalbán. Utilizing this framework, we provide an alternative proof of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem regarding Borel Wadge classes, which subsequently establishes Borel Wadge determinacy within the subsystem $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I of second-order arithmetic.

We introduce ROME, a system designed to generate realistic one-shot mesh-based human head avatars. Given a single photograph, our model predicts a personalized head mesh along with a corresponding neural texture that captures both local geometric and photometric specifics. The generated avatars are rigged and rendered via a neural network, which is jointly trained with the mesh and texture estimators on a dataset of real-world videos. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance in head geometry recovery and rendering quality, particularly in cross-person reenactment scenarios. See results at https://samsunglabs.github.io/rome/

This paper introduces a new method for deriving non-homogeneous hydrodynamic equations from what we term quasi-Stäckel systems—non-commutatively integrable systems built upon appropriate maximally superintegrable Stäckel systems. We outline the connections between Poisson algebras formed by quasi-Stäckel Hamiltonians and the Lie algebras of vector fields associated with these non-homogeneous hydrodynamic systems. Furthermore, we utilize the Stäckel transform to generate novel non-homogeneous equations of this specific type.

To accurately characterize photomultiplier tube responses, the relationship between quantum efficiency and the incident photon's angle and polarization must be established. A simplified one-step photoelectron emission model, adapted from Spicer's three-step framework, was developed to describe quantum efficiency in the visible spectrum for thin multi-alkali (NaKSbCs) photocathodes. This theoretical expression was validated through photocurrent measurements using linearly polarized light at different incident angles. These measurements simultaneously determined the complex refractive indices and thicknesses of both the stratified photocathode and its antireflection coating. The results indicate that the angular variation in quantum efficiency is governed by the photocathode's optical properties, which are analyzed in detail using the derived parameters.

The size-dependent behavior of energy transport and the impact of reduced dimensionality on transport coefficients are crucial for grasping nonequilibrium properties of nanoscale matter. In this study, we conduct both equilibrium and nonequilibrium simulations of heat conduction within a three-dimensional fluid using multiparticle collision dynamics, bounded by two thermal walls. Our findings indicate that a bulk 3D fluid conserving momentum exhibits a finite, non-diverging thermal conductivity. However, in simulation boxes with large aspect ratios, a transition occurs from 3D characteristics to one-dimensional (1D) anomalous thermal conductivity behavior. We demonstrate this shift from normal to anomalous transport through an appropriate decomposition of the energy current. These results not only offer direct validation of Fourier's law but also reinforce the accuracy of current theories for 3D fluids. Furthermore, they suggest that anomalous heat transport remains prevalent in nearly 1D fluids across a wide range of dimensions.

Monocular 3D object detection is crucial for autonomous driving because it offers a simpler setup than conventional multi-sensor configurations. The primary hurdle in this task is accurately estimating object depth without direct range measurements, relying instead on scene and object cues. While many approaches attempt direct depth estimation, they often struggle with performance due to inaccuracies. Our proposed method, the Categorical Depth Distribution Network (CaDDN), addresses this by predicting a categorical depth distribution for every pixel, which maps rich contextual features to the correct depth intervals in 3D space. We then employ a computationally efficient bird's-eye-view projection and a single-stage detector to generate the final bounding boxes. Designed as a fully differentiable, end-to-end system, CaDDN jointly performs depth estimation and object detection. Evaluated on the KITTI 3D object detection benchmark, our method ranks first among existing monocular approaches. Additionally, we present the first monocular 3D detection results on the recently released Waymo Open Dataset. The source code for CaDDN is also made publicly available.

We present the first demonstration of m-CAP modulation in a real-time Visible Light Communication (VLC) experimental setup, utilizing off-the-shelf LEDs and Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) based on Universal Software Radio Peripherals (USRPs). Our results show that transmission speeds reaching approximately 30 Mb/s are achievable, which is sufficient to support high-definition television streaming.

This thesis investigates the "Unum" concept for representing machine numbers using interval arithmetic and contrasts it with IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic, assessing scenarios where Unums offer advantages over standard floating-point numbers. Additionally, the work establishes theoretical underpinnings for IEEE 754 floating-point representations, interval arithmetic grounded in projectively extended real numbers, and the Unum system.

Paired image-text datasets have grown in popularity for developing generic representations in vision and vision-language domains. However, existing datasets, often sourced from search engines or HTML alt-text, suffer from web noise and necessitate intricate filtering pipelines to ensure quality. We investigate alternative sources to gather high-quality data with minimal filtering requirements. We present RedCaps, a large-scale collection of 12 million image-text pairs derived from Reddit. The images and captions on Reddit cover a diverse array of objects and scenes. Our data comes from a manually selected set of subreddits that provide coarse image labels, enabling us to guide dataset composition without labeling individual items. We demonstrate that captioning models trained on RedCaps generate rich, varied captions favored by humans and learn visual representations that effectively transfer to numerous downstream tasks.

Although numerous moons have been discovered orbiting planets within our own Solar System, none have been unambiguously confirmed around verified exoplanets. This study evaluates the viability of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) for distinguishing exomoon transits from stellar variability and instrumental noise in photometric transit light curves. While CNNs have historically enhanced classification accuracy, network optimization often overlooks the impact of noise on the training phase. In this work, we design and optimize a 1D CNN specifically for classifying photometric transit light curves, employing total variation loss regularization to eliminate unwanted data variations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our network yields results equal to or superior to standard solutions, and most notably, it significantly outperforms classical exoplanet science methods in identifying moon-like signals. Consequently, this proposed network represents a promising tool for the future analysis of real transit light curves.

Recent years have witnessed rapid advancements in image inpainting, with learning-based methods achieving impressive results in reconstructing missing image regions. However, most deep learning approaches are heavily constrained by the resolution of their training data; even minor increases in image size often result in severe artifacts and poor filling quality, rendering these methods unsuitable for interactive processing. This paper introduces a novel solution capable of inpainting images of arbitrary sizes. Additionally, we propose a technique to enhance the restoration of texture fragments within the filled areas by leveraging information from neighboring pixels through shifting the original image in four directions. This approach is compatible with existing inpainting models, granting them near-resolution independence without requiring retraining. Furthermore, we have developed a GIMP plugin that implements this technique, with the plugin, source code, and model weights available at https://github.com/a-mos/High_Resolution_Image_Inpainting.

The NLP community has leveraged the relationship between the maximum spanning tree in a directed graph and the optimal dependency tree of a sentence. However, a critical constraint in many dependency parsing schemes requires the spanning tree to have exactly one edge originating from the root. While efficient solutions exist for identifying the single best dependency tree under this constraint, no prior research has extended these methods to find the $K$-best dependency trees. This extension is arguably more significant because a larger fraction of decoded trees do not strictly adhere to the root constraint. Indeed, our findings indicate that the frequency of root constraint violations increases by an average of 13 times when decoding with $K\!=\!50$ compared to $K\!=\!1$. In this paper, we offer a streamlined version of the $K$-best spanning tree algorithm proposed by Camerini et al. (1980), achieving a constant time speed-up over the original method. Additionally, we introduce a novel adaptation of this algorithm to decode $K$-best dependency trees that satisfy the root constraint.

Epidemic models are essential for comprehending infectious diseases, yet their growing size and complexity often render them computationally unmanageable. Recent methodological advances indicate that surrogate models can effectively emulate complex epidemics, even within high-dimensional parameter spaces. This study demonstrates that deep sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models act as precise surrogates for complex epidemic models utilizing sequence-based parameters, successfully replicating both seasonal and long-term transmission patterns. After training, these surrogates predict scenarios thousands of times faster than the original models, rendering them highly suitable for policy analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate that substituting a traditional epidemic model with a learned simulator enables robust Bayesian inference.

ALMA has detected polarized dust continuum emission in a growing number of deeply embedded protostellar systems, typically revealing a sharp transition from the envelope to the disk scale. During this transition, the polarization fraction generally declines from approximately 5% to 1%, while inferred magnetic field orientations align more closely with the system's major axis. This study quantitatively examines these trends using Perseus molecular cloud protostars and compares them with non-ideal MHD simulations of disk formation. The analysis indicates that gas density rises more rapidly than magnetic field strength as one moves from the envelope to the disk, complicating magnetic grain alignment. Specifically, to achieve the observed ~1% polarization at ~100 au via B-field-aligned grains, even small 1 μm grains require their magnetic susceptibility to be enhanced by a factor of ~20, likely through superparamagnetic inclusions. This requirement becomes increasingly stringent for larger grains, with the necessary enhancement factor scaling linearly with size up to ~2×10^4 for millimeter-sized grains. However, even if such enhancement occurs, the simulated magnetic field orientations do not favor the major axis, contradicting observations. Consequently, we conclude that the observed trends are best explained by a model where envelope-scale polarization is dominated by magnetically aligned grains, whereas disk-scale polarization is driven by scattering.

The Th$_{7}$Fe$_{3}$ family of superconductors serves as a valuable system for studying unconventional superconductivity. This study investigates La$_{7}$Ni$_{3}$, the newest addition to this family, using thermodynamic and muon spin rotation and relaxation techniques. Our specific heat results suggest the existence of two separate, roughly isotropic superconducting gaps. The larger gap exhibits a value marginally exceeding that predicted by weak-coupling BCS theory, signaling strong correlations. These findings are corroborated by transverse-field muon-rotation experiments. Additionally, zero-field measurements detect small internal fields within the superconducting state, appearing near the superconducting onset and suggesting that the order parameter violates time-reversal symmetry. We examine two potential microscopic mechanisms—an unconventional $E_{2}(1,i)$ state and an $s+i\,s$ superconductor formed via two sequential transitions—and analyze the interactions that would favor each phase. Ultimately, our results identify La$_{7}$Ni$_{3}$ as the first member of the Th$_{7}$Fe$_{3}$ family to exhibit both time-reversal-symmetry breaking and multigap superconductivity.

Utilizing polarization-resolved electronic Raman spectroscopy combined with density functional theory, we investigate the interplay between primary and secondary order parameters within the charge density wave (CDW) state of the kagome metal AV3Sb5. Prior x-ray diffraction measurements at 15K revealed that the CDW order in CsV3Sb5 adopts a 2x2x4 structure, consisting of a single inverse-star-of-David layer followed by three consecutive star-of-David layers. By analyzing lattice distortions within this 2x2x4 framework, we determined that the U distortion serves as the primary order parameter for vanadium displacements, whereas M and L distortions act as secondary parameters. This finding is corroborated by bare susceptibility calculations, which exhibit a broad peak near qz=0.25 along the central line of the hexagonal Brillouin zone face (the U-line). Furthermore, we identified several phonon modes characteristic of the CDW state, involving vibrations of V, Sb, and alkali atoms. The temperature-dependent evolution of these modes' frequencies, half-width at half-maximum (HWHM), and integrated intensities supports a phase diagram featuring two successive structural transitions in CsV3Sb5: an initial transition with a primary order parameter at TS=94K, followed by a second isostructural transition near 70K.

This study examines the problem-dependent regime of the stochastic Thresholding Bandit problem (TBP) under specific shape constraints. In TBP, the learner's goal is to identify, upon completion of a sequential process, all arms with means exceeding a designated threshold. While the unstructured version of this problem is well-established, we focus on scenarios where the sequence of arm means $(\mu_k)_{k=1}^K$ is either monotonically increasing (MTBP) or concave (CTBP). Analyzing both settings within the problem-dependent regime, we evaluate the error probability, defined as the likelihood of misclassifying at least one arm. Under a fixed budget, we establish matching upper and lower bounds for this error probability in both the monotone and concave cases, accompanied by corresponding algorithms, with the bounds differing only by universal constants within the exponential term.

Order statistics are central to numerous statistical tasks, including risk assessment, outlier identification, and multiple hypothesis testing, as well as logistical systems involving ranks such as mechanism design, queuing, and load balancing. While calculating the \textit{exact} values from the joint distribution of $d$ order statistics is desirable, this challenge is computationally demanding even when dealing with $n$ independent random variables, a condition often not met in practice. Current approaches derive cumulative distributions indirectly by aggregating marginal distributions after computation. This paper introduces a more direct and efficient algorithm for computing cumulative joint order statistic distributions of dependent random variables. By employing dimensionality reduction, our method enhances an existing dynamic programming approach, delivering an $O(\frac{d^{d-1}}{n})$ and $O(d^{d})$ improvement in time and space complexity, respectively, compared to prior techniques.

The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) seeks to improve services across sectors like manufacturing and product processing, yet it faces significant hurdles, with security being paramount. Specifically, authentication and access control represent critical challenges for IIoT deployments. In an Industry 4.0 environment, networks often connect hundreds of small-scale devices, including sensors, actuators, fog nodes, and gateways; therefore, establishing a robust authentication protocol between these sensing devices or between a sensor and a user is fundamental to IoT security. This paper begins by analyzing a certificate-based scheme proposed by Das et al. for similar contexts, demonstrating its vulnerability to traditional attacks such as device anonymity breaches, Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) assaults, and Denial of Service (DoS). Subsequently, we introduce a lightweight yet highly secure inter-device authentication scheme based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). We validate the security of this proposed approach through both a formal analysis using the Random Oracle Model (ROR) and an informal analysis within the Dolev-Yao channel model. Finally, we compare our proposed EBAKE-SE scheme with existing solutions regarding communication and computation costs and security metrics, confirming its superior efficiency, reliability, and trustworthiness. The paper concludes with an implementation of the EBAKE-SE scheme utilizing the MQTT protocol.

This paper outlines neural models created for the DAGPap22 shared task at the Third Workshop on Scholarly Document Processing, which aims to automatically identify generated scientific papers. Our research compares various transformer-based architectures and employs supplementary datasets and methods to address class imbalance. The final submission utilized an ensemble of SciBERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa, fine-tuned with random oversampling, achieving an F1-score of 99.24% and securing third place in the official evaluation.
This thesis introduces fuzzy sets and fuzzy numbers, explores fractional derivatives, and addresses the solution of first-order fuzzy hybrid equations.

Mapping glaciers is essential for ecological surveillance in the HKH region, where climate change threatens the livelihoods of communities relying on these ecosystems. This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to aid ecological monitoring, specifically targeting glaciers through a semi-automated mapping method derived from satellite imagery. By leveraging accessible remote sensing data, we developed a model capable of detecting and delineating both pristine ice and debris-covered glaciers. Additionally, we have released the associated data and created a web platform that enables experts to visualize and refine model outputs, aiming to expedite the glacier mapping workflow.

Building upon Part 1 (Hernández et al., arXiv:2108.12395, 2021), this study investigates a generalized quasilinear (GQL) approximation within turbulent channel flow. The approach employs a flow decomposition based on spanwise Fourier modes, separating the flow into low-wavenumber and high-wavenumber groups. This separation creates a nonlinear low-wavenumber group capable of sustaining the self-sustaining process within specific integral length scales, while the linearized high-wavenumber group cannot do so, contrasting with the GQL models in Part 1 that offered a minimal mathematical description of self-sustenance across all scales. Despite these physical distinctions, the current GQL models exhibit similarities to those in Part 1, specifically regarding reduced multi-scale behavior and anisotropic turbulent fluctuations. Additionally, although the high-wavenumber group fails to support the self-sustaining process, the models successfully reproduce key statistical features in this group through the `scattering' mechanism previously proposed. Finally, numerical experiments were conducted to suppress specific triadic nonlinear interactions, leveraging the nature of the GQL approximation. These experiments revealed the critical roles of certain triadic interactions, including the energy cascade and inverse energy transfer in the near-wall region. Notably, inhibiting inverse energy transfer in the spanwise direction results in the suppression of large-scale positive turbulent transport near the wall.

This paper examines the directed flow of light hadrons generated in Au+Au, Ru+Ru, and Zr+Zr collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}= 200$ GeV. Using the viscous hydrodynamic model CLVisc, we systematically analyze the evolution of tilted energy density, pressure gradients, and radial flow along the $x$-axis. By comparing experimental data for identified light charged hadrons ($\pi$, $K$, $p$) from Au+Au and isobar collisions at RHIC, we determine that a counter-clockwise tilt of the initial fireball is a crucial origin of the directed flow observed in final-state light hadrons. This tilted initial medium configuration generates positive or negative forces via the average pressure gradient along the impact parameter ($x$) direction at backward or forward rapidities, respectively. Consequently, this results in a negative slope for the $x$-component of the QGP flow velocity relative to rapidity ($\eta_{s}$), as well as a corresponding feature in the directed flow $v_{1}$. Furthermore, our investigation into nuclear structure effects reveals that the directed flow $v_{1}$ of light hadrons remains insensitive to nuclear deformation.

Rydberg excited states of $^{87}{\rm Rb}$ atoms are characterized by their longevity, tunable excitation parameters (detuning), and robust repulsive van der Waals interactions ($V_{{\bf r} {\bf r'}}$) between excited atoms at positions ${\bf r}$ and ${\bf r'}$. This study examines these atoms within a two-leg ladder configuration subjected to both uniform detuning ($\lambda$) and staggered detuning ($\Delta$). We demonstrate that when the interaction strength $V_{{\bf r r'}}$ is significantly larger (or smaller) than $\Delta$ and $\lambda$ for nearest-neighbor ($|{\bf r}-{\bf r'}|=1$) versus distant ($|{\bf r}-{\bf r'}|>1$) pairs, the system exhibits a plateau across a broad spectrum of $\lambda/\Delta$ ratios. Within this plateau, the ground state is determined by a quantum order-by-disorder mechanism, selecting configurations from a macroscopically degenerate manifold of Fock states with a fixed Rydberg excitation density of $1/4$. Furthermore, our analysis reveals an emergent Ising transition stabilized by this order-by-disorder effect within the plateau. We identify the competing terms driving this transition and estimate a critical detuning ratio of $\lambda_c/\Delta=1/3$, a result consistent with numerical exact-diagonalization studies. Additionally, we investigate the transition's persistence under a realistic interaction potential $V_{{\bf r} {\bf r'}} = V_0 /|{\bf r}-{\bf r'}|^6$, showing it remains robust over a wide range of $V_0$ values. We provide an analytic expression for $\lambda_c$ as a function of $V_0$, suggesting that this transition can be directly verified in standard experiments, as discussed.

This study introduces a method for examining controllable qubit-resonator interactions within a driven Dicke model featuring a biased term. The nonlinearity of the spectrum, arising from these interactions, is central to achieving such control. To elucidate the underlying mechanism of this nonlinearity, we apply a unitary transformation to the Hamiltonian. Our findings indicate that the nonlinearity of the transformed Hamiltonian is contingent upon the qubit-resonator coupling strength. We provide a detailed discussion of the effective Hamiltonians' general forms using the frequency modulation approach. By tuning modulation parameters, the dynamical evolution can be toggled on and off. Leveraging these controllable interactions, we explore the generation of Dicke states and arbitrary superpositions thereof. Furthermore, we analyze the energy level nonlinearity in the limit of large qubit numbers. In the thermodynamic limit, a Kerr-type nonlinearity emerges from "magnon"-resonator coupling, enabling the investigation of selective preparation for "magnon" Fock states within the "magnon" regime.

The Doppler Imaging technique is standardly employed to map the non-uniform surface temperatures of rotating active stars. Surface inhomogeneities manifest as wavelength-shifting features in high-resolution spectra, varying according to their location on the visible hemisphere. While previous work has systematically addressed the inversion problem using maximum a-posteriori methods that assume smoothness or maximum entropy, this study aims to solve the full Bayesian inference problem by accessing the complete posterior distribution of stellar surface temperatures. We employ amortized neural posterior estimation to construct a model that approximates this high-dimensional posterior for selected spectral ranges at any rotation phase. This approximation utilizes conditional normalizing flows, which offer flexible, tractable, and easily samplable representations of arbitrary distributions; when conditioned on spectroscopic data, they enable highly efficient posterior sampling. Transformer encoders facilitate this conditioning, accommodating arbitrary wavelength sampling and rotation phases. The model generates thousands of posterior samples per second. Validation against very high signal-to-noise observations confirms that the model accurately approximates the posterior, albeit with some overestimation of broadening. Applied to the moderately rapid rotator II Peg, this approach yields the first Bayesian map of its temperature inhomogeneities. We conclude that conditional normalizing flows represent a highly promising tool for performing approximate Bayesian inference in complex stellar physics problems, such as constraining magnetic properties.

The adaptive spectral Koopman (ASK) method was developed to numerically solve autonomous dynamical systems, which serve as the basis for many applications in science and engineering. While ASK delivers high accuracy, it remains computationally intensive for multi-dimensional systems when compared to traditional time integration methods such as Runge-Kutta. This study proposes integrating sparse grids with ASK to enhance computational efficiency for multi-dimensional problems. The resulting sparse-grid-based ASK (SASK) method employs the Smolyak structure to generate multi-dimensional collocation points and corresponding polynomials for approximating the eigenfunctions of the system's Koopman operator. Consequently, this approach significantly reduces the number of required collocation points compared to the tensor product rule. Numerical experiments demonstrate that SASK effectively balances accuracy and computational cost, thereby accelerating ASK performance. Furthermore, we show that SASK is applicable to solving partial differential equations through their semi-discrete formulations.

Blockchain has proven to be a robust solution for data-sensitive sectors, including finance and healthcare, owing to its core attributes of immutability, non-repudiation, and availability. Consequently, its adoption across various domains has surged, with the healthcare supply chain being a prominent application area. While advancements in treatment methods continue, current healthcare supply chain management remains inefficient and fails to meet necessary standards. Traditional systems are often time-intensive and hinder collaboration among supply chain stakeholders. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a framework utilizing blockchain smart contracts and decentralized storage to link all participants in the supply chain. Within this framework, smart contracts govern and visualize interactions and transactions, thereby automating processes, enhancing transparency, boosting efficiency, and reducing service duration. Preliminary findings indicate that the proposed framework offers superior efficiency, security, and economic viability.

We investigate the non-invertible symmetries arising in class $\mathcal{S}$ theories, which emerge from compactifying the 6d (2,0) theory of type $\mathfrak{a}_{p-1}$ on a genus $g$ Riemann surface without punctures. Following the establishment of a general framework, we detail the classification of these symmetries for genera up to 5. A primary focus of our study is determining whether a non-invertible symmetry is "intrinsic," meaning it cannot be derived from an invertible symmetry via discrete gauging. We further elucidate the higher-dimensional origins of our findings, demonstrating how the Anomaly and Symmetry Topological Field Theories (TFTs), along with $N$-ality defects, of class $\mathcal{S}$ theories arise from the compactification of a 7d Chern-Simons theory. Notably, we discover that the Symmetry TFT for theories possessing intrinsically non-invertible symmetries can be realized only by coupling the 7d Chern-Simons theory to topological gravity.

We investigate classical dimers on two-dimensional quasiperiodic Ammann-Beenker (AB) tilings. Although these tilings lack periodicity, we demonstrate that every infinite instance possesses "perfect matchings" where each vertex is covered by exactly one dimer. To facilitate this analysis, we define an auxiliary "AB*" tiling derived from the original AB structure by removing all vertices with eight-fold coordination. This resulting AB* tiling remains two-dimensional, infinite, and quasiperiodic, consisting of a single connected component that supports perfect matchings. Our findings indicate that within these matchings, dimers on the AB* tiling align along disjoint one-dimensional loops and ladders, which are partitioned by "membranes"—regions devoid of dimers. Consequently, the partition function for the AB* tiling decomposes into the product of partition functions associated with these distinct structures. Employing an analytic transfer matrix method, we calculate the partition function and the free energy per edge for the AB* tiling. When applied to the original AB tiling, these membranes transform into "pseudomembranes," defined as edge sets that collectively accommodate at most one dimer. This transition induces a notable discrete scale-invariance in the matching problem. The resulting structure implies that the AB tiling should display highly inhomogeneous connected dimer correlations that decay slowly. Monte Carlo simulations provide evidence for this hypothesis, revealing connected dimer correlations that align with power-law behavior. Furthermore, among the perfect matchings, we identify quasiperiodic counterparts to the staggered and columnar phases typically observed in periodic systems.

In the geometric framework for defining complexity, operator complexity corresponds to the distance within the operator space. Drawing an analogy to circuit complexity, this paper adopts operator size as the metric for this space, where complexity is represented by path length. The typical sectional curvatures of this geometry are found to be positive, and it is proven that they remain positive whenever the metric is an arbitrary function of operator size. Although complexity geometry is generally anticipated to reside on negatively curved manifolds, an analysis of sectional curvature distributions in $N$-qubit systems reveals that surfaces generated by Hamiltonians with sizes below the typical threshold can exhibit negative curvature. Furthermore, in the large $N$ limit, requiring sectional curvatures to scale as $1/N^2$ uniquely constrains the form of the complexity metric, up to constant corrections. Accounting for state information necessitates modifying operator size to account for redundant actions, leading to a state-dependent generalization. This state-dependent operator size serves as the metric for Hilbert space to define state complexity. Additionally, it is demonstrated that within the Hilbert space, 2-surfaces created by operators significantly smaller than the typical size acting on typical states also display negative curvatures.

This work includes a brief historical overview of quantum mechanics, specifically addressing the theoretical challenges associated with ionization. We outline the fundamentals of resonance theory and detail the exterior complex scaling method used to derive resonance parameters within the Schrödinger equation framework. This approach is implemented numerically using the finite element method applied to the scaled variable. As validation of the theory's independence from the scaling angle, we present resonance parameters for a one-dimensional hydrogen model subjected to a direct current (DC) electric field. Furthermore, we apply the methodology to the real hydrogen atom in a DC field, yielding results consistent with existing literature, and also report resonance parameters for singly ionized helium. Additionally, using a model potential energy for the water molecule, we calculate energy eigenvalues and determine resonance parameters for the molecule in a DC field. Our calculated widths for the water molecule's valence orbital demonstrate strong agreement with values obtained from the "coupled-cluster singles and doubles with perturbative triples excitations" method.

As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and permeates everyday life, it is crucial to comprehend and regulate its influence on human decisions and existence. Contemporary machine learning systems frequently alter user behavior, such as personalized recommenders that learn preferences to modify online actions. A key consequence of this behavioral shift is the alteration of preferences themselves. This paper advocates for a multidisciplinary field dedicated to analyzing how AI systems transform preferences, termed "Preference Science." We define preference by integrating concepts from multiple disciplines, emphasizing the roles of meta-preferences and preferences regarding preference changes, while proposing an initial framework for understanding these shifts. Furthermore, we distinguish between preference change, permissible preference change, and outright preference manipulation, noting that insights from diverse disciplines enrich this framework.

Kagome metals AV$_3$Sb$_5$ (where A represents K, Rb, or Cs) represent newly identified systems characterized by distinctive charge-density-wave (CDW) ordering and superconductivity. The electronic band structure inherent to a kagome lattice supports both flat bands and Dirac-like bands, creating conditions favorable for stabilizing diverse quantum states. In this study, we investigate the band structure of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$ through Shubnikov-de Haas quantum oscillations measured in both bulk single crystals and thin flakes. While our frequency spectra generally align with previously published findings, we definitively identify new frequencies in thin flakes with large values spanning approximately 2085~T to 2717~T when the magnetic field is oriented along the $c$-axis. These quasi-two-dimensional frequencies account for roughly 52% to 67% of the volume of the CDW-distorted Brillouin zone. Furthermore, Lifshitz-Kosevich analysis reveals unexpectedly low cyclotron effective masses, approximately 0.1~$m_e$, associated with these frequencies. This indicates the presence of a significant population of high-velocity carriers within the thin flakes of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. By comparing these experimental results with band structure calculations, we propose that an orbital-selective modification of the band structure is occurring. Our findings offer critical insights into the fermiology of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$, opening pathways to understand how an orbital-selective mechanism can effectively tune its electronic properties.

The optoelectronic characteristics of van der Waals homostructures can be precisely tuned by adjusting the twist angle between their layers. This study investigates twist-angle-dependent moiré coupling in MoSe₂ homobilayers. At small angles, we observe a significant redshift in both K-K and Γ-K excitons, along with a shift in emission from K-K to Γ-K. These phenomena originate from the underlying moiré pattern in the MoSe₂ homobilayers, a conclusion supported by a low-energy continuum model applied to various moiré excitons. We distinguish two specific intralayer moiré excitons for R-stacking, whereas H-stacking produces two degenerate intralayer excitons due to inversion symmetry. In both configurations, bright interlayer excitons appear at higher energies. Our calculations align closely with experimental results, enabling the characterization of observed exciton resonances and offering insights into the layer composition and stacking configurations of different moiré exciton species.

We introduce advancements in creating a Finite State Transducer (FST) driven morphological analyzer and generator for Skolt Sami. As with other minority Uralic languages, Skolt Sami features complex morphology but lacks substantial gold-standard data, making Natural Language Processing approaches challenging without robust morphological analysis. Given the language's severe endangerment, this work contributes to broader revitalization initiatives. Additionally, our description incorporates facilitation and description practices that are not well documented in existing infrastructure. Presently, the analyzer encompasses more than 30,000 Skolt Sami words across 148 inflectional paradigms and over 12 derivational forms.

We anticipate that the phase-dependent error distribution inherent in locally unentangled quantum states directly influences the precision of quantum parameter estimation. Consequently, we utilize the displaced squeezed vacuum (DSV) state as a probe to explore phase-sensitive nonclassical properties within DSV-based metrology. Our findings indicate that the limit of parameter estimation accuracy depends on the phase-sensitive variable $\phi -\theta /2$, exhibiting a periodicity of $\pi$. Specifically, when $\phi -\theta /2$ falls within the interval $\left[ k\pi/2,3k\pi /4\right)$ for any integer $k$, employing a DSV state with enhanced displacement and squeezing strengths allows the estimation accuracy to approach the ultimate quantum limit. Conversely, in the interval $\left(3k\pi /4,k\pi \right]$, the optimal accuracy is achieved only when the DSV state reduces to a squeezed-vacuum state.

This study details the manipulation and dynamics of gold nanorod ensembles suspended in air under standard temperature and pressure conditions by utilizing external electric fields to control both their orientational and positional order, effectively creating an active aerosol. The demonstration of light filtering, valving, and gradient responses positions active aerosols as a distinct optical component, which we define as component-less optics.

This research develops novel tools to distinguish between dynamical and static dark energy. It generates precise evolutionary templates for dynamical cosmological parameters and fundamental constants, expressed as analytic functions of the scale factor. These templates are engineered to substitute standard parameterizations in likelihood calculations with models rooted in the physics of specific dynamical cosmologies and dark energy potentials, a method termed Cosmology and Potential Specific (CPS) templates. The study calculates a suite of CPS templates for a flat quintessence cosmology featuring a Higgs-inspired, polynomial dark energy potential; this potential yields a diverse range of evolutionary behaviors compared to typical monomial potentials. By employing a recently developed beta function formalism that defines the scalar field's differential function in terms of the scale factor, the research establishes an analytical framework for creating CPS templates for various dark energy potentials and cosmologies. This methodology facilitates the determination of likelihoods for dynamical cosmologies relative to Lambda CDM. Additionally, the study investigates the evolution of fundamental constants, including the proton-to-electron mass ratio and the fine structure constant, highlighting an intersection between particle physics and cosmology. Appendix A presents an abbreviated collection of CPS templates for flat quintessence with the HI dark energy potential.

Since diffusion maintains the positivity of concentrations, multicomponent diffusion becomes nonlinear whenever non-diagonal terms are present. The extensive range of such nonlinear equations requires a structured classification and specialized methods to systematically construct diffusion models for multicomponent mixtures with significant inter-component interactions. This work introduces an approach to nonlinear multicomponent diffusion by adapting the concept of reaction mechanisms from chemical kinetics. Chemical kinetics has historically provided fundamental tools for modeling processes through stoichiometric algebra combined with kinetic laws; these innovations now influence diverse scientific fields, from particle physics to sociology. This study extends that application to nonlinear multicomponent diffusion. We demonstrate how this mechanism-based framework integrates into the general thermodynamic system and establish the associated dissipation inequalities. To comply with thermodynamic constraints, kinetic laws for elementary processes cannot be arbitrary; specific conditions are derived for the generalized Mass Action Law. Furthermore, the cell-jump formalism offers an intuitive depiction of elementary transport processes while generating kinetic finite elements for numerical simulation.

Driven by the need for higher prediction accuracy and analysis quality, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are evolving to become deeper, wider, and more non-linear. However, these expanded architectures demand substantial computing resources and processing time. While prior research has largely focused on model pruning to enhance inference speed, few studies have addressed the effective reduction of training costs. This paper introduces ClickTrain, an efficient and precise end-to-end framework designed for both training and pruning CNNs. Unlike existing methods that prune during training, ClickTrain achieves superior model accuracy and compression ratios through fine-grained, architecture-preserving pruning. By utilizing pattern-based pruning coupled with novel weight importance estimation, dynamic pattern generation and selection, and compiler-assisted optimizations, ClickTrain produces highly accurate and fast pruned models ready for immediate deployment without incurring additional time overhead compared to baseline training. Furthermore, it reduces the end-to-end time cost of the pruning-after-training approach by up to 2.3X while maintaining comparable accuracy and compression. Additionally, when benchmarked against state-of-the-art pruning-during-training techniques under similar training time constraints, ClickTrain delivers significant improvements in both accuracy and compression ratio across tested CNN models and datasets.

The performance of deep neural networks relies heavily on network architecture design and parameter selection. Although Genetic Algorithms (GA) have previously been employed to determine network parameters, they are limited by their finite search over discrete, pre-defined candidates and generally cannot generate unseen configurations. To bridge the gap between exploration and exploitation, this paper introduces a novel, systematic approach that autonomously and concurrently optimizes multiple parameters of any deep neural network using a Genetic Algorithm enhanced by a Bi-generative Adversarial Network (Bi-GAN). This proposed Bi-GAN enables the autonomous exploitation and selection of neuron counts for fully-connected layers and filter counts for convolutional layers across a broad spectrum of values. The method employs two generators where distinct models competitively and iteratively refine one another through a GAN-based strategy to optimize the network throughout the GA evolution process. This approach facilitates the autonomous refinement of convolutional and dense layer counts, kernel dimensions and quantities, neuron numbers for dense layers, activation function types, and the inclusion or exclusion of dropout and batch normalization to enhance accuracy across various architectures. Evaluated on the ModelNet database for generality and compared against ShapeNets and two GA-only methods, the results demonstrate that the proposed method can successfully and simultaneously optimize multiple neural network parameters, achieving superior accuracy even with shallower network structures.

This study tackles the challenge of efficiently measuring how groups of variables within a dynamical system convey information about its future. Specifically, we aim to pinpoint clusters of variables that exhibit redundancy or synergy and monitor how the scale and makeup of these groups shift as the system's collective dynamics evolve. To achieve a parsimonious representation of shared information while accounting for lagged interactions and common effects, we introduce a dynamical, conditioned variant of O-information. This framework, recently developed to quantify high-order interdependencies through the multivariate extension of mutual information, yields an expansion of transfer entropy that distinctly separates synergistic and redundant effects. We applied this approach to a dataset of spiking neurons recorded from a monkey executing a perceptual discrimination task. The results successfully identified synergistic multiplets comprising neurons that, individually, were previously classified as having minimal relevant information.

Clarification is becoming an essential component in various information retrieval domains, including modern web search engines and conversational search. Soliciting user clarification during a search session significantly benefits the system, as explicit feedback greatly enhances retrieval accuracy. However, this approach carries a substantial risk of user frustration if the system poses poor clarifying questions. Consequently, determining the optimal timing and method for requesting clarification is critical. This study addresses this challenge by framing search clarification prediction as a user engagement problem, operating on the premise that superior clarifications yield higher user engagement. We introduce a Transformer-based model to solve this task, which demonstrates its effectiveness when compared against competitive baselines using large-scale, real-world engagement data. Furthermore, our analysis of result page elements reveals that the ranked list of search engine results contributes notably to performance improvements. Finally, our comprehensive examination of task-specific features provides valuable guidance for future research.

Ranking (or top-k) and skyline queries are the two most prevalent methods for extracting meaningful data from large datasets. The former relies on a scoring function to evaluate and rank tuples; while computationally efficient, it is highly dependent on the specific evaluation function chosen. In contrast, skyline queries utilize the concept of dominance to identify the set of all non-dominated tuples. Although this approach is conceptually compelling, it lacks control over the cardinality of the results. Recent studies have introduced additional techniques to mitigate these limitations, with this paper specifically examining the flexible skyline approach.

Consider a one-dimensional, real-valued Lévy process $X_t$ starting at $X_0=0$, characterized by a nonnegative jump measure $\nu$ satisfying $\int_{\Bbb R}\min\{1,x^2\}\nu(dx)<\infty$ and a stopping time $\tau(q)$ that follows either a geometric or an exponential distribution with parameter $q$, independent of both $X_t$ and $\tau(0)=\infty$. This study utilizes the Wiener-Hopf Factorization (WHF) to derive an $L^{p^*}({\Bbb R})$ approximation (with $1/{p^*}+1/p=1$ and $1<p\leq2$) for the distributions of the extrema of $X_t$. As a direct application, the finite and infinite-time ruin probabilities are approximated. The article further investigates estimation bounds for this method, presents two specific approximation procedures, and provides several illustrative examples.

Recent research by Bello indicates that training and scaling approaches often outweigh model architecture in importance for visual recognition. This note investigates effective scaling and training methods tailored for video recognition. We introduce a straightforward scaling technique for 3D ResNets, paired with enhanced training protocols and slight architectural adjustments. The resulting 3D ResNet-RS models achieve competitive results of 81.0 and 83.8 on Kinetics-400 and Kinetics-600, respectively, without pre-training. When pre-trained on a large Web Video Text dataset, our top model reaches 83.5 and 84.3 on these benchmarks. Additionally, the proposed scaling rule was tested in a self-supervised contrastive learning environment, yielding further performance gains. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/tensorflow/models/tree/master/official.

This paper establishes Morse index theorems for a broad range of constrained variational problems defined on graphs, which hold significant utility in physical and geometric contexts. The derived formulas determine the discrepancy in Morse indices between two Hessians associated with either distinct graphs or varying boundary conditions. Furthermore, the study demonstrates several applications, including iteration formulas and lower bounds for the index.

We introduce a technique for visualizing the directionality of periodic materials. By accepting dispersion (hyper-) surfaces derived from Bloch analysis as input, this method generates curves or surfaces that encode bulk directionality. Although the provided examples are situated within elastodynamics, the approach remains applicable without requiring specific consideration of the underlying physical phenomena.

This work examines type systems and programming abstractions designed to ensure the safe utilization of resources. Specifically, we explore how types can be used to modularly define and verify the conditions under which programs may access resources, such as ensuring that painted components have sufficient drying time before being assembled by a robot arm on a production line. To model these temporal resources, we introduce a time-graded variant of Fitch-style modal type systems, construct a corresponding modally typed core calculus with effects, and provide it with a graded-monadic denotational semantics demonstrated through a concrete presheaf model. Furthermore, our calculus incorporates temporally-aware graded algebraic effects and effect handlers. These features utilize a new temporal approach where operation specifications explicitly include execution durations, and continuations are aware that the required time has elapsed before proceeding, thereby enabling safe access to subsequent temporal resources while enforcing strict adherence to this temporal discipline within effect handlers.

Digital twins have gained significant traction for their capacity to monitor and optimize machines and processes throughout their operational lifespan by leveraging simulations and sensor data. This paper specifically tackles the challenge of implementing accurate, real-time simulations for digital twins within the domain of electrical machines. Achieving this generally requires more than just computational models for electromagnetic behavior; it also necessitates the inclusion of mechanical and thermal dynamics. We explore mathematical tools capable of executing these simulations based on physical laws, alongside surrogate or data-driven approaches. A key tool discussed is a hierarchy of models ranging from highly detailed to coarse approximations, along with model reduction techniques essential for real-time performance. Furthermore, we examine in depth the coupling of electromagnetic, mechanical, and thermal models to create a simulation framework that captures the interactions among these distinct physical components. In this regard, energy-based formulations within the port-Hamiltonian framework offer a particularly promising approach, an area that has garnered considerable attention recently for multiphysics modeling. We present specific port-Hamiltonian formulations for the individual electromagnetic, mechanical, and thermal models, as well as for the integrated coupled system.

In reference [5], Elnitsky established three refined bijections linking reduced word classes for Type A, B, and D Coxeter groups with specific polygon tilings. This paper extends that idea to encompass all finite Coxeter groups by utilizing embeddings within the Symmetric Group.

[5] Elnitsky, Serge. Rhombic tilings of polygons and classes of reduced words in Coxeter groups. PhD dissertation, University of Michigan, 1993.

This study examines the stability characteristics of a class of equations developed by Moffatt to describe magnetic relaxation. These models maintain the topological structure of magnetic streamlines, incorporate a cubic nonlinearity, and possess a beneficial $L^2$ energy framework. We analyze both local and global-in-time well-posedness for these systems and demonstrate a distinction in their long-term behavior as $t \to \infty$ when comparing weak and strong norms.

It is established that the category of affine Lagrangian relations, AffLagRel_F, over a field F defined by integers modulo a prime p (where p > 2), is isomorphic to the category of stabilizer quantum circuits for p-dits. Additionally, electrical circuits—generalized for the field F—are recognized as a natural subcategory of AffLagRel_F. This paper aims to characterize the relations within this subcategory, along with significant subcategories, using parity-check and generator matrices common in error detection. Specifically, we define the subcategory of Kirchhoff relations as those (affinely) Lagrangian relations that conserve total momentum or satisfy Kirchhoff's current law. Maps in this subcategory are generated by electrical components generalized for F: resistors, current dividers, and current and voltage sources. The "source" components impart the affine nature of the maps, while current dividers introduce a quasi-stochastic aspect. We characterize these Kirchhoff relations via parity-check matrices and further define two key subcategories: deterministic Kirchhoff relations and lossless relations. As electrical circuits, deterministic Kirchhoff relations are generated by resistor networks. Lossless relations, which are a subset of deterministic Kirchhoff relations, provide the fundamental hyper-categorical structure for these settings.

Measurements were conducted at the Beam Test Facility of Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati and various test stands to evaluate the efficiency, light yield, and time resolution of different scintillating tile configurations equipped with direct Silicon Photomultiplier readout and custom front-end electronics. The findings for these various setups are detailed in this work. Specifically, tiles covering an area of approximately 225 cm² achieved a time resolution near 300 ps, a light yield exceeding 230 photo-electrons, and an efficiency surpassing 99.8%. This technology is well-suited for diverse high-energy physics applications, particularly for large-area muon and timing detectors.

We present comprehensive measurements of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) propagating along nearly ideal air-gold interfaces created by atomically smooth surfaces of chemically synthesized gold monocrystals. Using amplitude- and phase-resolved near-field microscopy, we determined the propagation length and effective mode index at visible wavelengths (532, 594, 632.8, 729, and 800 nm). These experimental values were compared against literature-reported dielectric functions for gold. Notably, dielectric data for monocrystalline gold predicts propagation lengths approximately 1.5 times shorter than those we observed, whereas data for properly fabricated polycrystalline gold yields SPP propagation lengths that align with our findings. We contend that the propagation lengths measured in this study represent the ultimate limit of optical losses in gold, thereby motivating further detailed characterization of the optical properties of pure gold and other plasmonic materials.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is the leading approach for addressing the Schrödinger problem; it converges whenever a solution exists and achieves linear convergence if the solution shares the same support as the reference coupling. Driven by recent applications involving structured stochastic processes that create degenerate scenarios with potential non-existence of solutions, we demonstrate that the Sinkhorn algorithm yields exactly two limit points in such cases. These points enable the computation of a solution to a relaxed version of the Schrödinger problem, which emerges as the $\Gamma$-limit when marginal constraints are substituted with marginal penalizations. Furthermore, these findings facilitate a theoretical framework for characterizing the support of solutions in both the original and relaxed problems across various reference couplings and marginal constraints. We illustrate the utility of these results through promising numerical applications in a cell biology model.

Analyzing single-particle trajectories is crucial for understanding dynamics in complex settings like living cells. However, characterizing intracellular motion is frequently complicated by the confinement of particles within intricate subcellular geometries. This study specifically examines particles undergoing Brownian motion inside tubular networks, such as those in certain organelles. We introduce an unraveling algorithm designed to separate particle movement from the confining network structure, enabling precise determination of the diffusion coefficient and distinguishing between standard Brownian and fractional Brownian dynamics. The algorithm is validated using simulated data and then applied to a specific case: tracking membrane proteins confined within the tubules of the peripheral endoplasmic reticulum in mammalian cells. Our results demonstrate that these proteins exhibit diffusive motion with a well-defined diffusivity. Overall, our method offers a broadly applicable solution for disentangling geometric morphology from particle dynamics in networked systems.

The inclusive cross-section for top-quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) production, denoted as $\sigma_{t\bar{t}}$, was determined from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV. This analysis utilized 257 pb$^{-1}$ of data gathered in 2017 by the ATLAS detector at the LHC. Measurements were performed in both the single-lepton and dilepton channels of the $t\bar{t}$ system before being merged. The combined result is given by \begin{equation} \sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 67.5 \pm 0.9\text{(stat.)} \pm 2.3 \text{(syst.)} \pm 1.1\text{(lumi.)} \pm 0.2\text{(beam)} \text{ pb } \end{equation}, where the individual uncertainties correspond to the small data sample size, experimental and theoretical systematic variations, and uncertainties in the integrated luminosity and beam energy, respectively. This totals a 3.9% uncertainty. The outcome aligns with next-to-next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamic predictions that incorporate the resummation of next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic soft-gluon terms and provides constraints on the proton's parton distribution functions at high Bjorken-$x$.

This article introduces GrowliFlower, a georeferenced, image-based UAV time-series dataset comprising two monitored cauliflower fields (0.39 and 0.60 ha) captured in 2020 and 2021. The collection includes RGB and multispectral orthophotos from which approximately 14,000 individual plant coordinates have been extracted and made available. These coordinates allow users to retrieve complete or partial time-series image patches for specific plants. Additionally, the dataset provides phenotypic data for 740 plants, covering developmental stages and dimensions for both the plants and the cauliflower heads. Since the harvestable heads are obscured by foliage, the dataset supplies plant IDs and coordinates to facilitate the extraction of pre- and post-defoliation image pairs, aiding in head size estimation. It also offers pixel-accurate instance segmentations for leaves and plants, along with stem annotations, to support various computer vision tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation.
