Aimed at advancing and evaluating machine learning methods, the dataset specifically targets the analysis of cauliflower growth and phenotypic trait derivation to promote agricultural automation. Two baseline instance segmentation results at the plant and leaf levels are presented, and the full dataset is publicly accessible.

Accurately understanding the environment is fundamental for autonomous vehicle navigation, making the online segmentation of surroundings into moving and static components a critical capability. While deep learning methods are commonly employed for Moving Object Segmentation (MOS), their efficacy relies heavily on the volume and variety of annotated training data, which is often expensive to acquire manually. This paper introduces an automated labeling pipeline for 3D LiDAR data designed to reduce manual effort and enhance the performance of learning-based MOS systems by generating synthetic labeled datasets. Our offline batch-processing approach first performs coarse detection of dynamic objects using occupancy-based removal, followed by segment extraction and trajectory tracking via a Kalman filter. These tracked paths are then used to classify driving cars and pedestrians as moving, while parked vehicles, infrastructure, and buildings are categorized as static. We demonstrate that this method labels LiDAR data with high efficiency, outperforming or matching other label generation techniques. When training a deep neural network with our auto-generated labels, we achieve performance comparable to models trained on manually annotated data, with superior results when leveraging additional datasets processed by our pipeline. Furthermore, evaluations across multiple datasets and sensor types indicate that our approach effectively generates labels in diverse environments.

In 1977, Thouless, Anderson, and Palmer (TAP) formulated a consistent set of equations based on effective magnetization to analyze the free energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glass model. The solutions to these equations were anticipated to reveal crucial details regarding the SK Hamiltonian's energy landscapes and the TAP free energy, while also linking directly to Parisi's replica symmetry breaking ansatz. This study seeks to assess the validity of the TAP equations within the broader context of generic mixed $p$-spin models. Leveraging the ultrametric structure of overlaps, we demonstrate that the TAP equations are asymptotically satisfied by the conditional local magnetizations defined on asymptotic pure states.

Face anti-spoofing (FAS) is essential for protecting face recognition systems against various presentation attacks. While prior research has utilized auxiliary pixel-level supervision and domain generalization to tackle unseen spoof types, these methods often overlook the local characteristics of image captures, specifically the capturing devices and presentation materials. We contend that incorporating this information is vital for networks to effectively distinguish between live and spoofed images. To address this, we introduce PatchNet, which reframes face anti-spoofing as a fine-grained patch-type recognition task. Specifically, our framework identifies the combination of capture devices and presentation materials by analyzing patches extracted from undistorted face images. This reformulation significantly enhances data variation and compels the network to learn discriminative features from local capture patterns. Furthermore, to bolster the generalization of spoof features, we introduce two novel loss functions: Asymmetric Margin-based Classification Loss and Self-supervised Similarity Loss, which regularize the patch embedding space. Experimental results validate our hypothesis, demonstrating that the model robustly recognizes unseen spoof types by focusing solely on local regions. Additionally, this fine-grained, patch-level reformulation of FAS surpasses existing methods across intra-dataset, cross-dataset, and domain generalization benchmarks. Finally, the PatchNet framework supports practical applications such as Few-Shot Reference-based FAS and paves the way for future investigations into intrinsic spoof-related cues.

Extensive research indicates that streaming has become the dominant method for consuming multimedia, a trend supported by the rapid expansion of service providers and their subscriber numbers. Leveraging advancements in affordable electronics, high-speed connectivity, and inexpensive data, Over-The-Top (OTT) music streaming has become the industry standard, generating substantial revenue. This shift is particularly evident in India, where major players utilize freemium models to attract millions of active monthly users. Services such as Gaana, Airtel Wynk, and JioSaavn draw significantly larger audiences than their fully subscription-based counterparts like Amazon Prime Music and Apple Music. Due to their widespread presence and market dominance, it is essential to systematically evaluate these platforms to determine their susceptibility to piracy. This study examines the resilience of content protection systems in India's four largest music streaming services by subscriber count: Airtel Wynk, Gaana, JioSaavn, and Hungama. Using Spotify's Digital Rights Management (DRM) system as a benchmark, the research assesses platform security by attempting to efficiently extract streamed content. The work concludes with a comprehensive analysis of identified security flaws and proposes potential mitigation strategies. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural attempt to analyze the security of Indian OTT music services. Our findings reinforce the established notion that security through obscurity is unsustainable, leaving these platforms vulnerable to piracy and resulting in revenue losses for all stakeholders.

The paper outlines the BUT Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems entered for the OpenSAT evaluations across two domains: low-resourced languages and public safety communications. The initial domain presented significant challenges due to insufficient training data, necessitating the use of diverse architectures and multilingual strategies that ultimately yielded superior results. The second domain proved difficult because of recordings captured under extreme conditions, including specific channel constraints, stressed speakers, and high noise levels, making data augmentation essential to achieve acceptable performance.

We introduce a novel approach to calculate thermal activation rates—applicable to phenomena like bubble nucleation, topology transitions, and similar processes—by employing four-dimensional Euclidean techniques. This framework enables nonperturbative investigations on the lattice. Subsequently, we examine the strong sphaleron rate in pure-glue QCD across a temperature range from 1.3 $T_\mathrm{c}$ to 1000 $T_\mathrm{c}$. Our findings align with prior studies while extending the analysis down to temperatures near the critical point. Applying this method to full QCD will be a direct extension.

Automatic molecule generation has become a pivotal component of drug discovery, garnering significant attention in recent years due to the successful application of deep learning. Currently, graph-based neural networks represent the state-of-the-art approaches for this task. However, generating molecules with specific desired properties remains a core yet challenging objective in drug discovery. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a Controllable Junction Tree Variational Autoencoder (CJTVAE), which incorporates an extractor module within the VAE framework to characterize molecular properties. Our method enables the generation of molecules similar to an input structure while possessing the desired properties, and experimental results indicate promising performance.

Magnetic fields produced within the Sun by the solar dynamo mechanism drive solar activity across various time scales. Although direct space-based observations of the solar corona are limited to just a few decades, sunspot records extend back several centuries, and variations in solar open flux and cosmic ray flux can be reconstructed using cosmogenic isotopes over thousands of years. While these reconstructions suggest extreme solar activity fluctuations occurred in the past, the causal connections between millennium-scale dynamo processes, the resulting coronal fields, solar open flux, and cosmic ray modulation remain unclear. By employing a stochastically forced solar dynamo model, we conduct long-term simulations to reveal how dynamo-generated magnetic fields shape the solar corona and heliospheric state, as reflected in open flux and cosmic ray modulation variations. We identify differences in large-scale coronal structuring during grand maximum, minimum, and regular activity phases and simulate temporal variations in open flux and cosmic ray modulation potential across these cycles. Furthermore, we show that the power spectra of simulated and reconstructed solar open flux align. This study offers a theoretical framework for interpreting long-term solar cycle variability based on cosmogenic isotope reconstructions, linking internal solar variations to the forcing of the heliospheric state.

Although most massive stars exist in multiple systems, the mechanisms driving their high multiplicity remain poorly understood. To constrain potential formation theories, it is essential to examine the low-mass end of the companion mass function for these stars. However, detecting (sub-)solar mass companions at angular separations below 1 arcsecond (equivalent to 1000–3000 AU in nearby young clusters and OB associations) is difficult due to the extreme brightness contrast with the central star. The Carina High-contrast Imaging Project of massive Stars (CHIPS) aims to address this by statistically determining the presence and characteristics of low-mass companions at a previously inaccessible observing window ($\Delta \mathrm{mag} \gtrsim 10$ at $\rho \lesssim$ 1"). This second paper in the series focuses on the Trumpler 14 cluster, home to some of the Milky Way's youngest and most massive O-type stars. Using the IRDIFS_EXT mode on VLT-SPHERE, we observed seven O-type objects in Trumpler 14, enabling a search for companions down to a magnitude contrast of greater than 10 mag in the near-infrared at separations exceeding 0."15 (approx. 360 AU). By employing angular and spectral differential imaging alongside PSF fitting, we identified 211 sources with near-infrared magnitude contrasts ranging from 2 to 12. The closest companion, located at 0."26, is a 1.4M$_{\odot}$ star with an age of 0.6 Myr, consistent with prior age estimates for Tr 14. Furthermore, the derived mass function peaks near 0.4M$_{\odot}$ and shows a notable deficit of stars between 0.5 and 0.8M$_{\odot}$ compared to previous initial mass function estimates for Tr 14.

The main barrier to advancing technology for low-resource languages is the scarcity of usable data. This paper details the implementation and deployment of four technology-driven data collection strategies for Gondi, a vulnerable language spoken by approximately 2.3 million tribal individuals across central and southern India. Beyond data acquisition, our efforts contributed to the language's revival by enhancing access to information through the creation of community resources, including a dictionary, children's stories, a multi-source content app, and an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) mass awareness platform. Following these interventions, we gathered nearly 12,000 translated words and/or sentences and identified over 650 community members available for future translation initiatives. The overarching objective of this project is to accumulate sufficient Gondi data to develop and deploy functional language technologies, such as machine translation and speech-to-text systems, thereby enabling the language to participate in the digital realm.

Geodesic paths encode essential details regarding the curved space defined by a proper metric; for example, in general relativity, they generalize straight lines to curved spacetime. Conversely, within the geometry of quantum evolutions, a geodesic represents a trajectory of minimal statistical length between two pure quantum states, characterized by the minimum number of statistically distinguishable states along the path. This paper offers an explicit geodesic analysis of trajectories arising from the quantum evolution of a single-qubit state, driven by a Hermitian Hamiltonian that facilitates the fastest possible unitary transition between specified initial and final pure states. Beyond treating geodesics in ray space as paths of minimal length, we confirm their geodesic nature through unit geometric efficiency and a vanishing geometric phase. Finally, our analysis briefly outlines the primary challenges in extending the geometry of quantum evolutions to open quantum systems involving mixed states.

How might we obtain world models that accurately reflect external reality, capturing both the state of the environment and the consequences of our actions? Can interaction with the world yield such models, and can we formulate mathematical criteria describing their relationship to an objective external reality? As machine learning shifts toward representations that encode not only observations but also interventional knowledge, we address these challenges using tools from representation learning and group theory. Assuming our actuators influence the world, we propose methods to learn internal representations of sensory data alongside actions, ensuring these representations align with actual world dynamics and transitions. We employ an autoencoder featuring a group representation that acts linearly on its latent space, trained via 2-step reconstruction to enforce a specific homomorphism property. Unlike prior work, our approach requires fewer assumptions regarding the group representation and the set of transformations the agent can sample. We provide theoretical motivation for the method and empirically demonstrate its ability to learn correct group representations and environmental topology. Furthermore, we evaluate its trajectory prediction performance against existing methods.

This paper introduces a global reactive motion planning framework designed for robotic manipulators operating within complex dynamic environments. Specifically, it extends the Circular Field Predictions (CFP) planner proposed by Becker et al. (2021) to guarantee that the entire manipulator structure avoids obstacles. To achieve this, a new framework is developed that utilizes global insights regarding promising avoidance directions from various configuration space planners. This approach yields enhanced global trajectories, enables reactive evasion of dynamic obstacles, and reduces computational demands. The proposed framework has been validated through multiple simulations involving intricate and dynamic obstacles, demonstrating significant advantages over existing motion planning methods.

Leverage score sampling, a robust method rooted in theoretical computer science, accelerates solutions to numerous core problems, including linear regression, linear programming, semi-definite programming, cutting plane methods, graph sparsification, maximum matching, and max-flow. Recent studies have demonstrated its utility in speeding up kernel methods [Avron et al., 2017]. This paper extends those findings to a wider range of kernels and introduces leverage score sampling to deep learning theory. Specifically, we establish:
*   The relationship between neural network initialization and the approximation of the neural tangent kernel using random features.
*   The equivalence between regularized neural networks and neural tangent kernel ridge regression when initialized via either classical random Gaussian or leverage score sampling.

This work investigates meromorphic actions of unipotent complex Lie groups on compact Kähler manifolds through moment map methods. We establish natural stability criteria, demonstrating that the sets of semistable points form Zariski-open subsets which possess geometric quotients equipped with compactifiable Kähler structures derived from symplectic reduction. Furthermore, we provide a detailed discussion connecting our complex-analytic framework to the Geometric Invariant Theory of unipotent group actions on projective varieties developed by Doran and Kirwan.

The diffusive motion of molecules carrying spin is significantly altered when confined. In Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) experiments utilizing magnetic field gradients, this motion is encoded into spin phase, allowing for the assessment of signal attenuation caused by diffusion. This study examines both normal and anomalous diffusion effects using the Langevin stochastic model under the Gaussian phase approximation (GPA) with a constant gradient temporal profile. The phenomenological framework demonstrates the occurrence of fractional-order exponential decay in the NMR signal and recovers the classical findings associated with the Hahn echo.

This paper examines the design of robust and secure transmission within intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-assisted wireless systems. Specifically, we consider a scenario where a multi-antenna access point (AP) transmits to a single-antenna legitimate user in the presence of multiple single-antenna eavesdroppers, utilizing artificial noise (AN) to bolster security. We further assume that the cascaded AP-IRS-user channels are imperfect due to channel estimation errors. To minimize transmit power, we jointly optimize the transmitter's beamforming vector, the AN covariance matrix, and the IRS phase shifts, subject to outage probability constraints under a statistical cascaded channel state information (CSI) error model. To address the resulting non-convex optimization problem, we first approximate the outage probability constraints using Bernstein-type inequalities. Subsequently, we propose a suboptimal algorithm leveraging alternating optimization, penalty-based techniques, and semidefinite relaxation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly lowers transmit power compared to existing benchmark approaches.

We address the challenge of scaling automated reply suggestions for Outlook emails to support multiple languages. Confronted with rising computational demands and limited resources for expanding language coverage, we developed a single universal model to enhance quality and lower production runtime costs. Since data transfer restrictions between regional centers hinder joint training, we introduced a multi-task continual learning framework utilizing auxiliary tasks and language adapters to capture universal language representations across regions. Experimental findings demonstrate successful cross-lingual transfer while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Online evaluations on real user traffic reveal substantial improvements in click-through rates and characters saved, alongside a 65% reduction in training costs compared to per-language models. Consequently, we have successfully deployed this feature across multiple languages, including low-resource markets.

This research examines bifurcation and chaotic dynamics within one-dimensional chains of small particles, focusing on two distinct scenarios. The first involves a fourth-order potential model previously analyzed; we revisit this system to introduce new findings regarding three-armed star behavior and its associated Lyapunov exponent. The second scenario introduces a novel system where particles are modeled by an eighth-order potential. Using the same analytical framework, we explore this new system with a focus on orbital behavior, the bifurcation profile, and the corresponding Lyapunov exponent.

This study establishes a comprehensive formula for quantized fractional corner charges in two-dimensional $C_n$-symmetric higher-order topological insulators. Our approach relies on the description of electronic states via Wannier functions and assumes charge neutrality at the edges, without requiring the bulk electric polarization to vanish. By addressing broader surface conditions—including those with higher Miller indices and surface reconstruction—we extend the corner charge formulas derived in earlier research. This theoretical framework remains valid even when electronic states are significantly modulated near boundaries and applies to insulators with non-zero bulk polarization. Notably, in such scenarios, the corner charge value is contingent upon the specific surface termination, even for identical bulk crystals possessing $C_3$ or $C_4$ symmetry, due to variations in the Wyckoff position of the $C_n$-symmetric crystal center.

Over the past decade, deep learning has emerged as the most potent machine learning approach, yet the efficient training of deep neural networks remains an unsolved challenge. The widely adopted minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) requires acceleration, and the Information Bottleneck (IB) theory offers a valuable framework for understanding its dynamics by positing that optimization comprises an initial fitting stage followed by a compression stage. Leveraging this principle, we investigate typicality sampling, an efficient data selection technique, and provide a novel explanation for its role in accelerating deep network training. We demonstrate that appropriately applying typicality sampling enhances the fitting phase by increasing the signal-to-noise ratio of gradient approximation. This insight further suggests that prior information within the training set is pivotal to optimization, and effectively utilizing the most critical data can expedite information flow through the bottleneck. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets support these conclusions.

We reconstruct finite-dimensional quantum theory using categorical principles. Specifically, we establish properties that guarantee a physical theory, modeled as a dagger compact category where objects can be discarded, is equivalent to a generalized finite-dimensional quantum theory over an appropriate ring $S$. These principles echo those proposed by Chiribella, D'Ariano, and Perinotti. However, our axioms and proof are entirely categorical, notably avoiding the need for tomography assumptions found in prior reconstructions. When applying this result to probabilistic theories, we derive either standard quantum theory with $S$ as the complex numbers or quantum theory over real Hilbert spaces with $S$ as the reals.

Inspired by the finding that the zero forcing number of a tree's complement on $n$ vertices is typically $n-3$ or $n-1$, except in one unique case, we investigate the zero forcing numbers of complements for broader classes of graphs, especially those lacking induced complete bipartite subgraphs. Furthermore, we extend our analysis well beyond trees by thoroughly characterizing the possible zero forcing numbers for complements of unicyclic graphs and analyzing specific multi-cyclic graph families.

Time-of-flight (ToF) 3D imaging supports diverse applications, ranging from industrial quality control to motion tracking and gesture recognition. Typically, these systems retrieve depth data by measuring the round-trip time of laser pulses, necessitating projection and collection optics several centimeters in diameter. This study reduces that size requirement by two orders of magnitude, achieving near video-rate 3D imaging via multimode optical fibers (MMFs)—devices as thin as a human hair. Unlike traditional systems, MMFs display highly complex light transport akin to that of a strongly scattering medium. To address this, we employ high-speed aberration correction through wavefront shaping synchronized with a pulsed laser, facilitating random-access scene scanning at approximately 23,000 points per second. By utilizing non-ballistic light, we successfully image moving objects several meters beyond the tip of a ~40 cm, 50$\mu$m core-diameter MMF, achieving millimeter-level depth resolution at frame rates of ~5Hz. This research extends far-field depth resolution capabilities to ultra-thin micro-endoscopes, promising broad utility in clinical and remote inspection contexts.

We present a model-independent method to isolate static, spherically symmetric wormhole solutions by leveraging the general relativistic Poynting-Robertson effect and extending ray-tracing techniques within generic static and spherically symmetric wormhole metrics. By simulating flux emitted from the Poynting-Robertson critical hypersurface—a stable equilibrium between gravitational and radiation forces—or from an alternative X-ray source within these geometries toward a distant observer, we can locally reconstruct wormhole solutions consistent with high-energy astrophysical observations. This methodology is contingent upon the prior detection of wormhole evidence; as demonstrated in our previous work, Poynting-Robertson critical hypersurfaces in strong gravitational fields serve as effective astrophysical probes for searching for wormholes. As illustrative applications, we utilize this approach on selected wormhole solutions across various extended theories of gravity to generate lightcurves, spectra, and images of accretion disks. Furthermore, this technique offers a means to test gravitational theories. We conclude by discussing the findings and drawing final conclusions.

We introduce a model designed to investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of biocrust and vegetation on sand dunes. Comprising two coupled nonlinear partial differential equations, the model incorporates diffusion and advection terms to represent the dispersal of biocrust and vegetation, as well as the influence of wind. Without spatial variability, the system displays self-sustained relaxation oscillations and bistability, characterized by two distinct states: one dominated by biocrust and the other by vegetation. Focusing on one-dimensional dynamics, we demonstrate that the front connecting these states propagates primarily through wind advection. Within the oscillatory regime, front propagation becomes intricate; at low drift potential (DP) values, the advancing front generates a sequence of spatially oscillatory domains resulting from oscillations in the homogeneous states away from the front. Conversely, at higher DP values, the dynamics become highly complex and sensitive to initial conditions, producing irregular spatial patterns as small domains are repeatedly formed and destroyed during advancement. This irregular behavior correlates with temporal fluctuations in dune cover. Furthermore, similar dynamics can arise in other models featuring temporal oscillations and bistability.

Clustering artworks presents significant challenges due to the difficulty of identifying meaningful patterns through domain expertise and visual perception, as well as the ineffectiveness of traditional clustering and feature reduction methods when applied to high-dimensional pixel data. To overcome these obstacles, this paper introduces DELIUS (DEep learning approach to cLustering vIsUal artS). This method leverages a pre-trained convolutional network to extract features, which are then processed by a deep embedded clustering model. In this framework, the optimization of mapping input data to a latent space is performed jointly with the identification of cluster centroids within that space. Both quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DELIUS, highlighting its utility for various art analysis tasks, specifically visual link retrieval and historical knowledge discovery within painting datasets.

Automatic term extraction is crucial for domain-specific language understanding and various downstream natural language processing tasks. This paper presents a comparative analysis of how Transformers-based pretrained language models perform in extracting terms across multiple languages and domains. In addition to assessing monolingual models for single- and multi-word term identification, we explore ensembles of mono- and multilingual models by intersecting or uniting their respective term output sets. Our experiments utilize the ACTER corpus, which spans four specialized fields (Corruption, Wind energy, Equitation, and Heart failure) across three languages (English, French, and Dutch), as well as the RSDO5 Slovenian corpus covering four additional domains (Biomechanics, Chemistry, Veterinary, and Linguistics). Results indicate that using monolingual models surpasses state-of-the-art multilingual approaches for all languages except Dutch and French when named entity extraction is excluded. Additionally, merging the outputs of the two top-performing models yields significant performance gains.

Healthcare inequities rooted in sex and gender lead to divergent health outcomes. This study examines the time to diagnosis (TTD) through two extensive, complementary analyses involving 195,000 patients across 29 phenotypes. Our initial findings reveal that women consistently face longer TTDs than men, even when presenting with identical conditions. We then investigate how these TTD disparities influence diagnostic performance between genders over time and across varying levels of diagnostic information by assessing gender-agnostic disease classifiers. Both fairness evaluations indicate that the diagnostic process favors men over women, which contradicts earlier observations suggesting women might exhibit relevant symptoms sooner. These results imply that TTD is a critical yet intricate factor in studying gender disparities, necessitating further research.

Measurements of differential invariant cross sections for light neutral mesons have been conducted in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 8 TeV and in p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}}$ = 8.16 TeV, extending to very high transverse momentum ($p_{\text{T}}$). By merging independent reconstruction methods from the ALICE experiment—specifically those utilizing the EMCal and PHOS calorimeters alongside central barrel tracking detectors—the resulting spectra for $\pi^{0}$ mesons span nearly two orders of magnitude in $p_{\rm T}$. The nuclear modification factor $R_{\text{pPb}}$ was determined for both $\pi^{0}$ and $\eta$ mesons, showing consistency with NLO pQCD, CGC, and energy loss models. Furthermore, comparisons with previous $R_{\text{pPb}}$ measurements for $\pi^{0}$ at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}}$ = 5.02 TeV suggest an increasing suppression at low $p_{\rm T}$ as collision energy rises.

We introduce a new approach utilizing time-of-flight data to investigate dark matter (DM) interactions with Standard Model particles, specifically neutrinos ($
u$). Upon a supernova (SN) explosion within a galaxy, dark matter particles with masses $m_\chi \lesssim \mathcal{O}$(MeV) located in the halo can be accelerated to relativistic velocities by SN neutrinos ($
u$). Most of this boosted dark matter (BDM) reaches Earth with a time delay that depends exclusively on $m_\chi$, remaining independent of the interaction cross section. These BDM particles can subsequently interact with targets in both neutrino and DM detectors, generating afterglow events following the initial SN$
u$ detection. The distinct time-dependent signatures of BDM events enable the determination of $m_\chi$. Using data from the Kamiokande and Super-Kamiokande experiments regarding SN1987a in the Large Magellanic Cloud, we establish new constraints on $\sqrt{\sigma_{\chi e} \sigma_{\chi
u}}$. We also project potential sensitivities for future Galactic supernovae observed by Hyper-Kamiokande. Our findings enhance current limits on $\sigma_{\chi e}$ by 1–3 orders of magnitude for $m_\chi\lesssim \mathcal{O}(100\,{m keV})$, particularly in scenarios where $\sigma_{\chi
u}$ and $\sigma_{\chi e}$ are comparable in strength.

This study illustrates how differentiable stochastic sampling methods, originally designed for deep Reinforcement Learning, can facilitate efficient parameter inference for stochastic, simulation-based forward models. Specifically, we address the estimation of parameters for Halo Occupancy Distribution (HOD) models, which link galaxies to their dark matter halos. By combining continuous relaxation with gradient parameterization, we derive well-defined gradients with respect to HOD parameters from discrete galaxy catalog realizations. Access to these gradients enables the use of efficient sampling algorithms like Hamiltonian Monte-Carlo, significantly accelerating the inference process. Applying our method to a mock galaxy catalog from the Bolshoi simulation using the Zheng et al. 2007 HOD model, we achieved posteriors nearly identical to those from standard Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques but with an approximately 8-fold improvement in convergence speed. Furthermore, our differentiable HOD framework offers wide-ranging applications for full forward model approaches in cosmic structure and cosmological analysis.

The geometric renormalization group has emerged as a promising framework for analyzing structural symmetry and functional invariance within complex networks. Building on this approach, we conducted a systematic examination of the finite-size scaling of both structural and dynamical observables during geometric renormalization flows in synthetic and real evolutionary networks. Our findings indicate that these observables are effectively described by specific scaling functions. Notably, the critical exponent derived from these functions remains constant across different observables, depending solely on the network's small-world characteristics. Specifically, all networks within the small-world phase exhibit a uniform scaling exponent, whereas those in the non-small-world phase and its critical regions display a distinct uniform scaling. Furthermore, extensive experiments on real evolutionary networks possessing small-world traits confirm that their observables also demonstrate uniform scaling under geometric renormalization flows. Consequently, this exponent serves as a robust metric for categorizing universal small-world versus non-small-world network models.

We offer a high-resolution perspective on bubbles inside the Phantom Galaxy (NGC 628), a nearby (~10 Mpc), face-on (~9° inclination), star-forming (~2 M☉/yr) grand-design spiral. Utilizing new data from the PHANGS-JWST treasury program, we conduct an in-depth case study of two key areas: one hosting the galaxy's largest and most prominent bubble (The Phantom Void, exceeding 1 kpc in diameter) and another smaller region potentially serving as its precursor (The Precursor Phantom Void). Comparisons with Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Hα data at matched resolution reveal that ionized gas is most intense within the shells of both bubbles, aligning with the youngest (~1 Myr) and most massive (~100,000 M☉) stellar clusters. Additionally, an older generation (~20 Myr) of stellar associations exists within The Phantom Void. Kinematic analysis of HI, H₂ (CO), and HII gas across this region indicates an expansion velocity between 15 and 50 km/s. The substantial size and rapid expansion of The Phantom Void imply that sustained stellar feedback, driven by multiple mechanisms, is responsible; early feedback initially cleared the bubble (as seen in The Precursor Phantom Void), while subsequent supernovae within the cavity have since accelerated the shell. Finally, our JWST observations strikingly resemble simulations, suggesting that such large-scale, stellar feedback-driven bubbles are likely common in other galaxies.

The large-scale architecture of the universe, known as the cosmic web, is composed of galaxies, diffuse gas, and dark matter. We have constrained the joint distribution of these components by cross-correlating stellar mass-binned galaxy samples from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey CMASS catalogue with Planck mission maps of lensing convergence and the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) effect. By fitting a halo-based model to our measured angular power spectra (galaxy-galaxy, galaxy-lensing convergence, and galaxy-tSZ) at a median redshift of $z=0.53$, we identified variations in galaxy satellite fractions and spatial distributions within host halos dependent on stellar mass. Our analysis reveals a tSZ-halo hydrostatic mass bias, $b_h$, where $(1-b_h)=0.6\pm0.05$, with a suggestion of increased bias at the high stellar mass end. Furthermore, the normalization of the galaxy-lensing convergence cross-power spectrum indicates that galaxies trace the matter distribution without evidence of stochasticity ($A=0.97\pm 0.09$). We predict that upcoming cosmic microwave background experiments will refine constraints on hydrostatic bias by a factor of two and enable tighter limits on small-scale dark matter distribution, thereby providing crucial insights for theoretical models of feedback processes.

Regret-based methods are particularly effective for locating approximate Nash equilibria in sequential games like poker; however, most, including counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) and its derivatives, depend on iterate averaging to ensure convergence. Drawing inspiration from recent breakthroughs regarding the last-iterate convergence of optimistic algorithms in zero-sum normal-form games, we investigate this behavior within sequential games. Specifically, we offer a thorough analysis of last-iterate convergence for zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect recall (EFGs) by employing diverse optimistic regret-minimization algorithms across treeplexes. These algorithms incorporate both standard entropy and squared Euclidean norm regularizers, alongside their dilated counterparts, which facilitate more efficient execution. Unlike CFR, we demonstrate that all these algorithms achieve last-iterate convergence, with certain variants converging at an exponential rate. Furthermore, we present experimental evidence to corroborate our theoretical findings.

This study investigates magnetic catalysis of chiral symmetry breaking within quantum chromodynamics using the logarithmic quark sigma model framework. Thermodynamic quantities—including pressure, entropy density, energy density, and interaction measure—are computed via the mean-field approximation. Results indicate that pressure, entropy density, and energy density all rise with increasing temperature and external magnetic field strength. Furthermore, the critical temperature escalates as the external magnetic field intensifies. When explicit symmetry breaking is incorporated and baryonic chemical potential is absent, the chiral phase transition remains a crossover in the presence of an external magnetic field. Comparisons are drawn against the original sigma model and related studies, leading to the conclusion that the logarithmic quark model amplifies the magnetic catalysis effect.

Mobile technology is reshaping human-computer interaction, making speech-based interfaces increasingly vital. Although recently published Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems demonstrate high accuracy, they typically depend on specialized hardware like GPUs for inference, rendering them unsuitable for standard devices, particularly in streaming scenarios. Motivated by the strong performance yet slow inference times of the baseline Kazakh ASR model from (Khassanov et al., 2021) when operating without a GPU, we developed a new baseline acoustic model and three language models for the Coqui STT framework, training them on the same dataset used in the cited paper. While the initial results are encouraging, achieving production-grade accuracy requires additional training epochs, parameter optimization, or potentially restricting the vocabulary supported by the system.

The holographic entropy cone defines the constraints on entanglement entropies across spatial divisions of the boundary spacetime within a holographic CFT, applicable to any state corresponding to a classical bulk geometry. We contend that this cone, regardless of the number of subsystems, can be derived from more fundamental information rooted exclusively in the subadditivity of quantum entropy. We introduce specific conjectures regarding graph models of holographic entanglement, offering substantial evidence for them and rigorously demonstrating that they collectively guarantee the feasibility of this reconstruction. Furthermore, these conjectures (with the exception of the least restrictive one) suggest that the required data is surprisingly straightforward: essentially, reconstructing the holographic entropy cone demands only a specific subset of the extreme rays of this simpler "subadditivity cone," specifically those realizable in holography. This reformulation, which translates the complex entanglement architecture of geometric states into primary building blocks, facilitates a clearer understanding of holography's core principles in the emergence of classical bulk spacetime.

This paper investigates the learning problem within contextual search, driven by real-world applications like first-price auctions, personalized medicine trials, and feature-based pricing experiments. Specifically, given a stream of context vectors, each linked to an intrinsic value, a decision-maker must choose either to query a specific point or skip the context. Upon querying, the decision-maker receives binary feedback regarding the relationship between the queried point and the context's value. Operating within a PAC learning framework, the objective is to estimate the underlying mean value function using the fewest possible queries. To tackle this, we introduce a tri-section search strategy integrated with a margin-based active learning technique. We demonstrate that our algorithm requires only $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ queries to reach an $\epsilon$-estimation accuracy, a significant improvement over the passive setting, which demands at least $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^4)$ samples.

The ATLAS experiment at CERN operates the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) by measuring proton-proton (p-p) collision energies at a 40 MHz repetition rate. As part of the Phase-II upgrade for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), the readout electronics of liquid-argon (LAr) calorimeters are being optimized to handle a projected pileup of up to 200 simultaneous p-p interactions. This surge in interactions causes signals from as many as 25 consecutive collisions to overlap, thereby complicating energy reconstruction. To meet HL-LHC objectives, Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are employed to process 40 MHz digitized pulses in real time, while various machine learning techniques are explored to mitigate signal pileup. Both convolutional and recurrent neural networks have demonstrated superior performance compared to the current optimal signal filter, particularly in assigning reconstructed energy to the correct proton bunch crossing and improving energy resolution. These improvements specifically target energy extraction from overlapping pulses. Since these neural networks are deployed on FPGAs, a careful analysis of parameter count, resource consumption, latency, and operating frequency is essential. Results show excellent agreement between the neural network implementations running on FPGAs and those executed in software.

We establish a geometric Riemann-Hilbert correspondence relevant to Jimbo and Sakai's derivation of the $q$-PVI equation from "isomonodromy" conditions. This work represents a progression in ongoing efforts to apply $q$-isomonodromy and $q$-isoStokes phenomena to $q$-Painlev\'e equations.

We examine a $\Gamma(\alpha, \theta)$ Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process to construct a continuous-path Variance-Gamma (VG) process characterized by five parameters: location ($\mu$), symmetry ($\delta$), volatility ($\sigma$), shape ($\alpha$), and scale ($\theta$). Our analysis of the associated Lévy process demonstrates that its Lévy density falls within the KoPoL family, defined by order $\nu=0$, intensity $\alpha$, and steepness parameters given by $\frac{\delta}{\sigma^2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{\delta^2}{\sigma^4}+\frac{2}{\theta \sigma^2}}$. Furthermore, we establish that this Lévy process converges in distribution to another Lévy process driven by a Normal distribution with mean $(\mu + \alpha \theta \delta)$ and variance $\alpha (\theta^2\delta^2 + \sigma^2\theta)$. Illustrative data derives from fitting the five-parameter VG model to daily SPY ETF prices, as detailed by Nzokem (2021). Subsequently, the five-parameter VG process is employed to evaluate its performance against the Black-Scholes model in pricing European options. We show that the Esscher martingale of the VG model corresponds to another VG model with adjusted parameters and provide the closed-form solution for VG option prices. Using the Fractional Fast Fourier (FRFT) algorithm for numerical computation, our results indicate that, compared to the Black-Scholes model, the VG option is overvalued for deep out-of-the-money (OTM) options. Conversely, the valuation error reverses for deep in-the-money (ITM) options and those with long maturities, where the VG option is undervalued.

PINSKY is a framework designed for open-ended learning via neuroevolution within game environments. It extends the Paired Open-Ended Trailblazer (POET) system, which initially investigated learning and environment creation for bipedal walkers, by adapting these concepts to the General Video Game AI (GVGAI) platform. Prior research demonstrated that co-evolving levels and neural network policies can generate scenarios where successful policies emerge only through evolution rather than optimization alone. Within the field of Artificial Life, Minimal Criteria (MC)-based selection serves as a gradient-based fitness alternative to promote diversity in evolutionary populations. This paper investigates the mechanics of open-ended learning, with a specific focus on policy transfer between distinct evolutionary branches, or "species." The study analyzes system dynamics by constructing phylogenetic trees, tracing policy evolutionary trajectories, and categorizing transfers temporally by species type. Additionally, it examines how the minimal criterion influences level diversity and inter-species transfer. The key finding reveals that although inter-species transfer occurs infrequently, it is essential for the system's overall success.

Standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) exhibit translation equivariance through their convolutional layers, yet their convolution and fully-connected components lack invariance or equivariance regarding other affine geometric transformations. Recent advancements have introduced a new category of CNNs that substitute conventional layers with equivariant versions of convolution, pooling, and batch normalization. In these equivariant networks, the final classification layer achieves invariance to various affine transformations—such as rotation, reflection, and translation—by either reducing spatial dimensions via convolution and down-sampling or by averaging filter responses. This study proposes incorporating orthogonal moments, which capture high-order function statistics, as a robust method for encoding global invariance to rotation, reflection, and translation within fully-connected layers. Consequently, the network's intermediate layers maintain equivariance while the classification layer ensures invariance. The approach evaluates Zernike, pseudo-Zernike, and orthogonal Fourier-Mellin moments, which are the most prevalent options for this purpose. The efficacy of the proposed method is assessed by integrating invariant transitions and fully-connected layers into the architecture of group-equivariant CNNs (G-CNNs), tested on rotated MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets.

When interactions link a central degree of freedom with a bath, the bath's phase should influence the central system's evolution. Recent studies have investigated this phenomenon in systems featuring many-body localized (MBL) baths coupled to a central qubit or single cavity mode, areas of increasing experimental interest. While these models connect to Floquet MBL through the quantization of external drives, this specific link remains underexplored. In this work, we apply the multilayer multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree (ML-MCTDH) method—a tree tensor network algorithm—to numerically simulate a $d$-level system (qudit) coupled to a disordered, interacting 1D spin bath. This approach enables simulations of approximately $10^2$ lattice sites, surpassing the limits of exact diagonalization or kernel polynomial methods. Upon appropriately rescaling the system-bath coupling, we observe a well-defined thermodynamic limit in the qudit's intermediate-time dynamics. The spin system exhibits comparable scaling collapse in both the Edward-Anderson spin glass order parameter and entanglement entropy at relatively short times. At longer times, entanglement grows slowly, potentially due to dephasing in the localized system or long-range interactions facilitated by the central degree of freedom. Notably, similar localization signatures persist even without scaling the system-bath coupling.

This paper introduces a rapid, model-agnostic approach for reconstructing Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) datastreams that contain missing entries and noise. The process begins by converting measurements into a Page matrix, followed by signal reconstruction via low-rank matrix estimation using optimal singular value thresholding. The study demonstrates two algorithmic variations: an offline block-processing technique for imputing historical data and an online method for forecasting future values. Recovery leverages both temporal correlations within individual PMU channels and spatial correlations across multiple channels in a network. Because the method is fast and requires no prior knowledge of the system model or noise distribution, it offers significant practical advantages. Validation using both simulated data from the IEEE 39-bus test system and real-world data from an anonymized U.S. electric utility confirms the algorithm's efficacy. Comprehensive numerical tests indicate that the original signals can be accurately restored even when subjected to additive noise, consecutive data drops, and simultaneous erasures across multiple PMU channels.

This study searches for massive long-lived particles within a 20–60 GeV mass range and lifetimes spanning 5 to 100 picoseconds. The analysis utilizes 0.62 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data recorded by the LHCb detector at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. These particles are hypothesized to be produced in pairs via the decay of a Higgs-like boson with a mass between 80 and 140 GeV. No significant excess above the expected background was observed, leading to constraints on the production cross-section as a function of the long-lived particle's mass, lifetime, and the mass of the parent Higgs-like boson.

Persistent homology (PH) is a topological data analysis (TDA) method used to calculate multi-scale, topologically invariant features of high-dimensional data, offering robustness against noise. Although PH has identified valuable patterns in diverse fields, its computational demands have historically restricted its use to small datasets containing only a few thousand points. We introduce Dory, an efficient and scalable algorithm capable of computing persistent homology for large-scale datasets. Dory consumes significantly less memory than existing published algorithms and achieves substantial reductions in computation time compared to most others, enabling it to process datasets with millions of points. As a practical demonstration, we applied Dory to calculate the persistent homology of the human genome at high resolution using a genome-wide Hi-C dataset. The results indicate that the genome's topology undergoes significant changes upon auxin treatment—a molecule that degrades cohesin—thereby supporting the hypothesis that cohesin is essential for DNA loop formation.

While general machine translation models are trained on diverse documents, models specialized for specific document characteristics typically yield superior results. Fine-tuning serves as a method to adapt neural machine translation (NMT) models to particular domains. This study employs that technique to tailor a model to a specific test set, utilizing transductive data selection algorithms that leverage test set information to extract sentences from a larger parallel corpus. When the model is accessible during the translation phase (i.e., when the test set is available), it can be fine-tuned using a small data subset, resulting in performance that surpasses both generic models and those adapted to a specific domain.

We investigate a gas of interacting ultracold bosons confined within a parabolic trap alongside an optical lattice potential. By modeling the system as a discretized Gross-Pitaevskii framework, we demonstrate that Floquet engineering—achieved by rapidly oscillating the lattice—transforms the system's ground state into a series of bright solitons by reversing the sign of the hopping energy. Our analysis examines how the count of generated solitons varies with the system's nonlinearity and trap curvature, illustrates the technique's applicability across both high and low driving-frequency regimes, and confirms the phenomenon's robustness against noise. Ultimately, we conclude that the Floquet method offers a stable and effective means for preparing solitons in cold atom systems.

This paper underscores the critical role of formulating the appropriate query when interpreting learning model decisions. We extend the theoretical framework established by Janzing et al. (2020) to shift the focus from the direct question, "Why did my model predict a person has cancer?" to the more comprehensive inquiry, "What caused my model to predict a person has cancer?" While the initial question measures direct variable effects, the latter incorporates indirect effects, offering valuable insights aligned with human causal reasoning. We introduce three distinct interpretation categories—observational, model-specific, and causal—each holding independent significance. Additionally, we quantify feature relevance by integrating various interpretation types and measures as characteristic functions for Shapley symmetrization. Beyond the standard expected value, we explore statistical uncertainty and dispersion as informative metrics for generating point-specific explanations, introducing several of these measures to this domain for the first time. These metrics facilitate the analysis of both variable influence on model outputs and overall predictive performance, supported by novel characteristic functions also presented here for the first time.

We introduce a parameter estimation approach for nonlinear mixed effect models based on ordinary differential equations (NLME-ODEs), designed to regularize estimation challenges arising from model misspecification, practical identifiability constraints, and unknown initial conditions. Our estimator is defined as the minimizer of a cost function that accounts for discrepancies between the assumed population-level model and individual-specific dynamics. Calculating this cost function requires formulating and solving optimal control problems at the subject level. This control-theoretic framework eliminates the necessity of estimating initial conditions for each subject and stabilizes the estimation process when parameters are poorly identifiable. Compared to maximum likelihood estimation, simulation studies demonstrate that our method enhances accuracy in partially observed systems, particularly when dealing with unknown initial conditions or poorly identifiable parameters, whether or not model error is present. We conclude with a real-world application analyzing antibody concentration data from phase 1 Ebola vaccine trials, utilizing estimated subject-level model discrepancies to investigate potential model misspecification.

We report 2,241 exoplanet candidates discovered by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) throughout its two-year primary mission. These candidates are compiled in the TESS Objects of Interest (TOI) Catalog, which encompasses both newly identified planet candidates and previously known planets detected by TESS. We outline the methodology for identifying TOIs, analyze the properties of the new candidates, and highlight significant discoveries. The TOI Catalog features a record number of small planet candidates orbiting nearby bright stars, making them ideal for intensive follow-up studies. Data products from the Prime Mission (Sectors 1–26), including the TOI Catalog, light curves, full-frame images, and target pixel files, are accessible to the public via the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes.

We introduce a graph-based variational approach for classifying high-dimensional data, extending the binary diffuse interface model to handle multiple classes. Inspired by total variation methods, the technique minimizes an energy functional composed of three components. The first two components encourage a stepwise continuous classification function with sharp transitions between classes while maintaining symmetry across class labels, and the third component serves as a data fidelity term that enables the integration of prior information within a semi-supervised setting. Experiments on synthetic data, along with the COIL and MNIST benchmark datasets, demonstrate that the algorithm's performance is competitive with leading state-of-the-art graph-based multiclass segmentation methods.

This work establishes a conjecture by Guo and Poznanovi\'{c} regarding chains within specific 01-fillings of moon polyominoes. Central to our proof is a mapping between words $w$ and pairs $(\mathcal{W}(w), \mathcal{M}(w))$ of increasing tableaux, where $\mathcal{M}(w)$ encodes the lengths of the longest strictly increasing and decreasing subsequences for every subinterval of $w$. We construct this correspondence via Thomas and Yong's K-infusion operator, subsequently leveraging it to derive the bijections required to confirm the Guo and Poznanovi\'{c} conjecture. Furthermore, the development of these bijections necessitates the introduction of novel variants of the RSK correspondence and Knuth equivalence.

We explore the application of quantum algorithms to lattice $\Phi^4$ theory within circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) platforms. In this framework, the field is encoded on qudits using a discretized amplitude basis. A key benefit of qudit architectures lies in their multi-level nature, which enables field interactions to be executed exclusively via diagonal single-qudit gates. By utilizing a universal gate set comprising single-qudit phase and displacement operations, we investigate variational approaches for preparing initial states and synthesizing single-qudit gates.

This study investigates the production of heavy vector-like quarks ($T\bar T$ or $B\bar B$) decaying into final states containing jets but no reconstructed leptons. A deep neural network classifies these jets as originating from hadronically decaying $W/Z$ bosons, Higgs bosons, top quarks, or background processes. The analysis utilizes data from the ATLAS experiment, comprising 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV by the Large Hadron Collider during 2015 and 2016. No significant deviation from Standard Model predictions is found. Interpreting the results under the assumption that these quarks decay into a Standard Model boson and a third-generation quark ($T\rightarrow Wb, Ht, Zt$ or $B\rightarrow Wt, Hb, Zb$) across various branching ratios, the study establishes lower mass limits at 95% confidence. For a weak-isospin doublet ($B, Y$), the observed (expected) lower limit on the $B$-quark mass is 950 (890) GeV. Additionally, for the pure decay channels $B\rightarrow Hb$ and $T\rightarrow Ht$, where constraints are most stringent, the lower limits on the masses are 1010 (970) GeV and 1010 (1010) GeV, respectively.

Although stars originate with magnetic fields, the specific distribution of their initial field strengths remains unclear. By integrating observational data with theoretical models of magnetic field evolution, we have inferred the initial field distribution for AB stars with masses between 1.6 and 3.4 solar masses. We evaluated various distribution shapes and determined that a distribution with a mean of approximately 800 G and a full width of roughly 600 G best aligns with the observed mass-dependent fraction of strongly magnetized stars. Our preferred model is a Gaussian distribution characterized by a mean ($\mu$) of 770 G and a standard deviation ($\sigma$) of 146 G. However, independent methods estimating typical field strength yield values near 2–3 kG; this discrepancy may indicate a mass-dependent, bimodal initial field distribution or point to an alternative theoretical framework for the origin of these magnetic fields.

This study traces the evolution of employer labour market power in the United States and Peru throughout the 2010s. Utilizing a structural estimation model of labour market dynamics, we quantify disparities in the market power workers encounter based on their sector, age, gender, location, and education. Our analysis reveals that cross-sectional differences in market power are substantial and exceed temporal variations across the decade. Unlike patterns observed in developed nations like the US, we find significant employer power in Peru specifically regarding tertiary-educated workers, irrespective of age or industry. Conversely, for those with primary education, market power is pronounced in the private service and manufacturing sectors. Among secondary-educated workers, only the mining sector exhibits moderately higher monopsonistic characteristics. Additionally, we demonstrate that labour market power in Peru declined during the 2010s. In contrast, our estimates for the US indicate sharp increases in market power within specific sectors, such as agriculture and entertainment/recreational services, as well as in geographic regions where these industries dominate. Furthermore, we show that US labour market power has gradually risen over the past decade, consistent with broader trends in inequality. Crucially, we find that the persistent gender pay gap cannot be attributed to differential market power, as men actually face higher levels of market power than women. Finally, we explore potential explanations for these results, including the reasons behind the polarization of market power across different skill levels, sectors, and locations.

Our previous research on Semantic Storytelling utilized text analytics methods such as Named Entity Recognition and Event Detection. This paper presents our long-term vision for the field, detailing both our current technical and conceptual strategies. The project driving this research focuses on creating AI technologies that are validated by industry partners. A primary long-term objective is to establish a robust approach with broad coverage for Semantic Storytelling. We present initial findings from experiments involving discourse parsing applied to a specific use case, "Explore the Neighbourhood!", which utilizes a semi-automatically collected dataset of documents regarding notable figures in a Berlin district. Although deriving coherence relations from plain text presents a significant challenge, our preliminary results are encouraging. We anticipate integrating our approach with additional features, including NER, coreference resolution, and knowledge graphs.

While it is generally anticipated that an autoencoder (AE) trained on a specific dataset will assign low likelihood scores to out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs—a method often used for OOD detection—recent research indicates this intuition fails when comparing FashionMNIST and MNIST. This paper attributes such failures to the use of Bernoulli likelihood, offering an analysis of the underlying causes and proposing two remedies: first, estimating likelihood uncertainty through a Bayesian autoencoder, and second, adopting alternative probability distributions to model the likelihood.

This study examines the stability of equilibrium manifolds within hyperbolic shallow water moment equations. These equations model shallow flows with complex vertical velocity variations, serving as extensions of standard shallow water models. Since equilibrium stability is a critical characteristic of balance laws—dictating linear stability near equilibrium states and acting as a prerequisite for stable numerical simulations—we first analyze the hyperbolic nature of these models. This analysis reveals three distinct stability manifolds, corresponding to different limits of the friction term: water-at-rest, constant-velocity, and bottom-at-rest profiles. Our results indicate that structural stability conditions are met for both water-at-rest and constant-velocity equilibria; however, the bottom-at-rest equilibrium may produce unstable modes contingent on the specific velocity profile. Finally, we numerically investigate the relaxation process toward these equilibrium manifolds across various models.

This study derives the Heisenberg representation of the ultrafast inverse Faraday effect, detailing the temporal evolution of magnetic vectors within a system interacting with a laser pulse. We establish a time-dependent effective magnetic operator defined in the Hilbert space of total angular momentum, which characterizes the nonthermal excitation of magnetic precessions in an electronic system driven by a circularly polarized laser. This operator isolates the laser's influence on the magnetic system from other magnetic interactions and yields the equations of motion for magnetic vectors during excitation. We demonstrate that magnetization dynamics derived from these equations are equivalent to those obtained via the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, which incorporates the interaction between the electronic system and the light's electric field. Furthermore, we model and compare laser-induced precessions in the magnetic sublattices of easy-plane and easy-axis antiferromagnetic systems. These models reveal how the ultrafast inverse Faraday effect generates a net magnetic moment in antiferromagnets and highlight the critical roles of crystal field environments and exchange interactions in laser-induced magnetization dynamics, even while the pump pulse is active. Finally, our approach shows that light-induced precessions can initiate during the pump pulse—despite its duration being tens of times shorter than the precession period—and significantly influence the final positions of magnetic vectors after the pulse concludes.

Although quantum computing is typically linked to discrete quantum states and physical quantities with discrete eigenvalue spectra, the broader definition encompasses any computation leveraging quantum properties, whether discrete or continuous. Research has demonstrated that physical quantities featuring continuous eigenvalue spectra are equally viable for quantum computing. Currently, continuous variable quantum computing is an area of rapid theoretical and experimental advancement. This pedagogical overview introduces the fundamental theoretical concepts and algorithmic tools associated with this field. The paper is specifically designed for readers who possess a background in discrete quantum computing but are new to continuous variable approaches.

Although Spanish is one of the world's most widely spoken languages, it is not consistently written or spoken in the same manner across different nations. Grasping these regional linguistic variations can enhance model performance on specific tasks, improving both the interpretation of local structures and the quality of message content. For example, a machine learning engineer automating language classification for a specific area or a social scientist analyzing regional events reflected on social media can leverage dialect-specific models to gain deeper contextual insights and greater precision. This manuscript introduces a collection of regionalized Spanish resources constructed from four years of geotagged public Twitter messages across 26 Spanish-speaking countries. We present FastText-based word embeddings, BERT-based language models, and distinct corpora for each region. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive comparison of lexical and semantic similarities between regions, along with demonstrations of how to apply these regional resources to message classification tasks.

Drawing upon the definition of tense operators on distributive lattices established by Chajda and Paseka in 2015, this paper introduces and examines the variety of tense distributive lattices with implication. We demonstrate that this variety is categorically equivalent to a specific full subcategory of the category of tense centered Kleene algebras with implication. Furthermore, we utilize this equivalence to characterize the congruences of algebras within each variety through the lens of tense 1-filters and tense centered deductive systems.

Floquet-Bloch lattices exhibit rich dynamics through wave packets subjected to periodic spatial and temporal modulations. Although challenging to realize in solid-state physics, optical systems offer ideal platforms for investigating these phenomena, revealing effects such as anomalous Floquet topological insulators and the funneling of light into localized interface modes. Despite the critical role of band dispersion in photon dynamics and topological characteristics, the direct experimental measurement of Floquet-Bloch bands has historically remained elusive. In this work, we present the direct measurement of these bands in a photonic lattice using a single-shot technique. Our approach employs a system of two coupled fiber rings to construct a time-multiplexed Floquet-Bloch lattice. By Fourier transforming the lattice's impulse response, we derive the band structure alongside a precise characterization of lattice eigenmodes, specifically the amplitudes and phases of Floquet-Bloch eigenvectors across the entire Brillouin zone. These findings pave the way for observing topological effects within both linear and nonlinear regimes of Floquet systems.

This study addresses the Schrödinger equation for the Bohr Hamiltonian incorporating Coulomb and Hulthén potentials under the minimal length formalism, utilizing the asymptotic iteration method to derive analytical expressions for energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. These derived formulas for the energy spectrum and wave functions are then applied to compute excitation energies and transition rates for $\gamma$-rigid nuclei at the shape phase critical point X(3), with results compared against experimental data.

We establish the existence of normal forms for certain local real-analytic Levi-flat hypersurfaces featuring an isolated line singularity. Furthermore, we provide sufficient conditions under which a Levi-flat hypersurface possessing a complex line singularity can be expressed as the pullback of a real-analytic curve in C through a holomorphic function.

Although the direct Gaussian copula model with discrete marginals is a valuable analytical tool, its intractable likelihood creates significant computational hurdles. Various approximations have been developed, notably the continuous extension (CE) and distributional transform (DT) methods. While CE achieves exactness up to Monte Carlo error, it suffers from poor scalability. Conversely, DT enables efficient computation but lacks theoretical assurance of exactness. However, in practical applications, the DT-based approximate likelihood is often sufficiently accurate for specific model variants to support valid maximum likelihood or Bayesian inference. This study demonstrates the exactness of the DT objective function for two particular model variants and introduces a diagnostic metric to evaluate exactness in observed data. This metric allows practitioners to determine whether genuine Bayesian inference or standard maximum likelihood inference using the DT likelihood is feasible for a specific dataset.

Open-domain question answering (QA) systems typically utilize a retriever-reader architecture that fetches a few pertinent Wikipedia passages and then analyzes them to generate answers. Nevertheless, even the most advanced readers often struggle to grasp the intricate connections between entities in the questions and the retrieved texts, resulting in factually inconsistent responses. To address this, we introduce Grape, a novel passage reader enhanced by knowledge graphs, designed to boost performance in open-domain QA. Specifically, for every question-passage pair, we build a localized bipartite graph using entity embeddings derived from the reader model's intermediate layers. Subsequently, a graph neural network learns relational knowledge by merging graph structures with contextual representations into the reader's hidden states. Experiments across three open-domain QA benchmarks demonstrate that Grape improves state-of-the-art results by up to 2.2 in exact match score with minimal computational overhead, using the same retriever and passages. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jumxglhf/GRAPE.

Defocus blur arises as a physical limitation of optical sensors in most cameras. While it can serve as an artistic photographic style, it is typically regarded as image degradation, mathematically modeled as the convolution of a sharp image with a spatially-varying blur kernel. Building on recent advancements in blur estimation techniques, we propose a non-blind deblurring approach capable of handling spatially-varying kernels. Our architecture employs two encoder-decoder sub-networks: one processes the blurry input image, while the other utilizes the estimated blur map, with both producing the final deblurred (deconvolved) output. Each sub-network incorporates multiple skip connections to facilitate data flow across distant layers, alongside inter-subnetwork connections that enhance communication between the modules. The network is trained using synthetically generated blur kernels augmented to mimic the outputs of current blur estimation methods. Experimental results demonstrate that our method performs effectively when integrated with various existing blur estimation techniques.

We analyze how a uniformly rotating star reacts to tidal forces exerted by a companion, examining both general periodic orbits and parabolic flybys. By summing contributions from normal modes that account for dissipation, we calculate the rates of energy and angular momentum transfer. We specifically address scenarios where the response is driven by a distinct regular spectrum of low-frequency modes, such as gravity modes, evaluating these under conditions of very weak dissipation. This framework applies to Sun-like stars featuring radiative cores and convective envelopes, as well as more massive stars with convective cores and radiative envelopes. We derive general expressions for energy and angular momentum transfer applicable to orbits of any eccentricity.

Detailed computations focus on Sun-like stars in the slow-rotation regime, neglecting centrifugal distortion in equilibrium and employing the traditional approximation for normal modes. We utilize both the WKBJ method and direct numerical evaluation, finding strong agreement between them in the relevant regimes.

Finally, we apply our formalism to estimate evolution timescales for an object in a low-eccentricity orbit around a Sun-like star undergoing tidal response. We consider systems with either no rotation or synchronous rotation, incorporating only rotationally modified gravity modes under the assumption that wave dissipation occurs near the stellar center.

This paper introduces a nonlinear inversion approach for the steady-state model of an active dual-bridge series resonant converter. The resulting control strategy enables cycle-averaged regulation of the output current and ensures waveform alignment to reliably achieve zero-voltage switching (ZVS) and synchronous rectification. This control method is applicable to both voltage buck and boost modes, as well as low-power fixed-frequency operations. The robustness of the control scheme is evaluated through simulations incorporating external linear control loops.

Simon's problem serves as a canonical illustration of a challenge that requires exponential resources classically but can be solved in polynomial time using quantum algorithms. The problem involves a function $f$ guaranteed to possess a unique non-zero vector $s$ such that $f(x) = f(x \oplus s)$ for all inputs $x$, where $\oplus$ denotes the exclusive-or operation; the objective is to identify $s$. The classical exponential lower bound typically relies on the assumption that $f$ is accessible only as a black box. This paper, however, examines classical complexity when $f$ is provided via standard representations, such as circuits. Specifically, we concentrate on determining the vector space comprising all vectors $s$ that satisfy the condition $f(x) = f(x \oplus s)$ for a given $f$. Our findings yield two primary results: (1) for any circuit representation of $f$, verifying whether this vector space contains a non-zero element is NP-hard, and (2) if $f$ is represented by an ordered Binary Decision Diagram (BDD), a basis for this vector space can be computed in polynomial time.

This paper investigates modal logics defined on bounded distributive residuated lattices within a noncommutative framework, specifically incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$ operators. We present relational semantics for these substructural modal logics and demonstrate that any canonical logic achieves Kripke completeness through the use of discrete duality and canonical extensions. Specifically, we establish that a modal extension of the distributive full Lambek calculus corresponds to the logic of its frames whenever its associated variety is closed under canonical extensions. Furthermore, we develop a Priestley-style duality connecting residuated distributive modal algebras with topological Kripke structures grounded in Priestley spaces.

This paper outlines a methodology for identifying symmetric quadrature rules within triangles, quadrilaterals, tetrahedra, prisms, pyramids, and hexahedra. The approach requires no manual intervention and can generate an ensemble of rules specified by a particular strength and point count. We also introduce polyquad, an implementation of this methodology, which we use to derive a comprehensive set of symmetric rules for the listed domains. All derived rules feature strictly positive weights and internal points. Many of these rules appear to be novel and offer improvements over those previously tabulated in the literature.

This research introduces a new framework for forecasting COVID-19 severity that integrates both data-centric and model-centric strategies. Initially, we develop a data-centric pre-training method tailored for scenarios with extremely limited data within the target dataset. Subsequently, we present two hybrid neural architectures combining convolutional layers with attention mechanisms, utilizing self-attention from Transformers and Dense Associative Memory (Modern Hopfield networks). Our proposed methodology yields substantial performance gains compared to conventional baselines.
