We present the Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton (FSMSN) algorithm, which operates in two phases: initially, a preconditioning step nonlinearly updates pressure and saturation by sequentially solving two approximate subproblems; subsequently, a global step performs a Newton update by linearizing the system based on the preconditioned state. Evaluated against challenging test cases, FSMSN is benchmarked against an existing field-split preconditioner (MSPIN) and standard strategies like the Sequential Fully Implicit (SFI) and Fully Implicit (FIM) methods. These comparisons underscore the influence of upwinding schemes on algorithmic performance and the necessity of dynamically adjusting subproblem tolerances during the preconditioning phase. Our findings indicate that the two-step nonlinear preconditioning approach, specifically FSMSN, achieves faster outer-loop convergence compared to both SFI and FIM. However, an analysis of the preconditioners' impact on computational performance, measured by wall-clock time, is reserved for a future publication.

Vision-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers a compelling solution for control problems where images serve as primary inputs. However, current state-of-the-art RL algorithms face significant challenges regarding sample efficiency, particularly when processing visual data. This limitation has driven a focus on embedding state representation learning (SRL) techniques into RL frameworks, which has proven to substantially enhance sample efficiency and offer additional advantages. To fully leverage this paradigm, the quality of training samples is critical; specifically, sample diversity influences both the efficiency and generalization capabilities of vision-based RL. This study introduces a method designed to improve sample diversity within the SRL framework. By exploiting the SRL setup, our approach strengthens the exploration capabilities of RL algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that this method increases the visitation of difficult-to-reach states, refines the learned state representations, and surpasses baseline performance across all tested environments. These improvements are most pronounced in scenarios where baseline methods fail. Furthermore, even in simpler environments, our technique stabilizes training, lowers reward variance, and fosters greater sample efficiency.

Strong gravitational lenses enable astronomers to observe distant regions of space by refracting light from background sources around foreground massive objects. However, their scarcity makes manual identification in astronomical surveys laborious and inefficient, necessitating an automated detection approach that functions even with a near-total absence of confirmed examples. To facilitate model training, we generate realistic lens simulations to create positive training samples. Training a standard ResNet model directly on these simulations yields low precision despite high recall, as the network inadvertently learns artifacts present in the synthetic data. This study introduces a detection framework integrating simulations, data augmentation, semi-supervised learning, and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), achieving a tenfold performance improvement. Through ablation studies and scalability analyses regarding the ratio of non-lenses to simulated lenses, we demonstrate that researchers can effectively classify strong gravitational lenses with high precision and recall, even when conducting surveys with minimal prior knowledge.

Let $1 < p \neq q < \infty$ and consider the probability space $(D, \mu) = (\{\pm 1\}, \frac{1}{2}\delta_{-1} + \frac{1}{2}\delta_1)$. We define the sequence of Banach spaces recursively by setting $X_0 = \mathbb{C}$ and $X_{n+1} = L_p(\mu; L_q(\mu; X_n))$. This paper establishes the existence of constants $c_1 = c_1(p, q) > 1$, depending solely on $p$ and $q$, and $c_2 = c_2(p, q, s)$, depending on $p$, $q$, and $s$, such that for all $1 < s < \infty$, the $\text{UMD}_s$ constants of the spaces $X_n$ grow exponentially, satisfying $c_1^n \leq C_s(X_n) \leq c_2^n$. Analogous results are demonstrated for the analytic $\text{UMD}$ constants. While Bourgain previously constructed the first super-reflexive non-$\text{UMD}$ Banach lattices, our findings provide an additional elementary construction via the inductive limit of the sequence $X_n$, which represents the infinite iteration of the $L_p(L_q)$ operation.

This study employs a general static, cylindrically symmetric metric to derive $U(1)$ local cosmic string solutions within the scalar-tensor representation of hybrid metric-Palatini gravity. Following the derivation of the dynamical equations for this specific scenario, we applied boost invariance along the $t$ and $z$ axes, which streamlined the equations of motion until only the single metric component $W^2(r)$ remained. For any arbitrary potential $V(\phi)$, the resulting solutions can be expressed in closed parametric form using $\phi$ as the parameter. We examined several specific potential cases, yielding results ranging from simple analytical expressions to those requiring numerical methods. Using this methodology, we identify a broad spectrum of new stable stringlike solutions in hybrid metric-Palatini gravity, where parameters such as the scalar field, metric components, and string tension are fundamentally determined by the boundary values of the scalar field and its derivative at the $r(0)$ circular axis.

Object detection in low-quality images critically relies on image restoration algorithms, particularly super-resolution (SR), as essential pre-processing steps. However, most existing methods operate under the assumption that image degradation is fixed and known beforehand. In real-world scenarios, the actual degradation patterns or the optimal up-sampling ratios are often unknown or deviate from these assumptions, causing performance degradation in both the pre-processing stage and subsequent high-level tasks like object detection. To address this, we introduce a novel self-supervised framework designed for object detection in degraded low-resolution images. This approach employs downsampling as a transformation to generate self-supervised signals, fostering equivariant representations capable of handling various resolutions and degradation types. The proposed Auto Encoding Resolution in Self-supervision (AERIS) framework leverages advanced SR architectures, utilizing an arbitrary resolution restoring decoder to recover original correspondences from degraded inputs. Both representation learning and object detection are optimized jointly through an end-to-end training process. The versatile AERIS framework is compatible with various mainstream object detection architectures and different backbone networks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches under diverse degradation conditions. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/cuiziteng/ECCV_AERIS.

Nonlocal diffusion models effectively capture solute diffusion within complex media, a task where classical partial differential equation (PDE) theories fall short. However, the nonlocal nature of the operators in these models results in dense or full stiffness matrices during numerical discretization, creating substantial computational and memory burdens. This paper introduces a spectral collocation approach for nonlocal diffusion, accompanied by a rigorous error analysis that theoretically validates the spectral convergence rate, assuming sufficient smoothness of the kernel and source functions. By leveraging high-order convergence, spectral collocation methods significantly reduce numerical costs compared to finite difference and finite element techniques. Numerical experiments confirm that the method achieves exponential convergence.

Organizations handling sensitive data in machine learning systems must ensure robust protection. Specifically, Article 35 of the GDPR requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for projects involving personal data. Beyond the risks of unauthorized access via security breaches, machine learning models introduce distinct privacy concerns by inadvertently exposing information through their predictions and parameters. Regulatory guidance from the UK's Information Commissioner's Office and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology highlights these model-based threats, urging organizations to assess and mitigate such risks to adhere to data protection laws. Consequently, there is an urgent requirement for a tool capable of quantifying the privacy risks posed by models. This paper addresses the issue of indirect data leakage from machine learning models by introducing "ML Privacy Meter." This tool utilizes state-of-the-art membership inference attack techniques to measure privacy risk. Furthermore, we explain how practitioners can leverage this tool to ensure compliance with data protection regulations when deploying machine learning models.

A growing agreement within the scientific software community holds that research advancement relies on "quality and accessibility of software at all levels." This progress requires adopting both established and emerging software engineering practices, particularly agile methodologies that blend with formal engineering traditions. As an initial phase of a broader exploratory study on in-process quality metrics for Computational Science and Engineering (CSE) projects, we created the Metrics Dashboard. This platform mines GitHub open-source repositories to generate and visualize metrics. Unlike systems such as GitHub that track individual performance indicators like commits, the Metrics Dashboard emphasizes metrics reflecting team progress and project health. Users can submit a repository URL for batch analysis, with results stored in a cache. Once complete, users can interactively examine various metrics over time at different levels of granularity, both numerically and visually. The initial version is currently available as a public cloud service (SaaS) and supports measurements for project size (KLOC), defect density, defect spoilage, and productivity. Although our system is not the first to offer software metrics, we believe it stands as one of the first community-focused, extensible resources accessible to any hosted project.

Fast and secure voltage regulation strategies are essential for integrating renewable energy into modern distribution grids. To address the challenges of uncertain grid models and rapidly varying power injections, model-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been introduced to optimize inverter reactive power and voltage profiles. However, these data-driven approaches often fail to ensure strict adherence to hard operational limits, such as keeping voltages within specified bounds of the nominal value. To resolve this, we introduce SAVER (SAfe VoltagE Regulator), which combines an RL learner with a computationally efficient, custom-designed safety projection layer. This framework offers a plug-and-play solution compatible with various DRL algorithms, guaranteeing that system voltages remain within safe limits. Real-world data simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.

We provide a statistical examination of the kinetic energy spectrum within the dissipative scales of fully developed three-dimensional turbulence. Our analysis combines data from grid turbulence experiments conducted in the Modane wind tunnel with high-resolution direct numerical simulations of the forced Navier-Stokes equations, focusing specifically on wave-number scales in the near-dissipative region. We observe that spectra in this domain follow a stretched exponential profile with an exponent of $\alpha = 0.68 \pm 0.19$. This finding supports earlier DNS research indicating that a stretched exponential with $\alpha<1$ best describes the near-dissipative spectrum. Furthermore, our estimated value for $\alpha$ aligns precisely with the theoretical prediction of $\alpha=2/3$ derived from non-perturbative renormalization group theory.

We present findings on nanosecond-scale, nanometer-sized heterogeneous dynamics within a free-flowing colloidal jet, as observed using ultrafast x-ray speckle visibility spectroscopy. The Linac Coherent Light Source's free-electron laser, operating in a nanosecond double-bunch mode, generated pairs of femtosecond coherent hard x-ray pulses. By analyzing the anisotropic summed speckle visibility, which corresponds to correlation functions, we determined not only the mean particle flow rate in the colloidal nanoparticle jet but also characterized the heterogeneous flow field inside it. This methodology lays the groundwork for investigating nano- and atomic-scale heterogeneous fluctuations in complex matter via x-ray free electron laser sources.

Defects are a common characteristic of ordered media, possessing universal traits that stem from their topological nature and remain independent of the specific physical system. Although these topological properties are robust, defects manifest as `unphysical' singularities with non-integrable energy densities in coarse-grained macroscopic descriptions. We propose a rigorous framework that integrates sufficient `micro-physics' into coarse-grained theories to produce thermodynamically consistent and well-posed models capable of analyzing defect dynamics and interactions in extended systems. Furthermore, we introduce corresponding numerical methods suitable for calculating energy-driven defect behaviors across the spectrum of amorphous, soft, and crystalline materials. These approaches accommodate order parameters with head-tail symmetry, such as director fields, within systems exhibiting continuous translation symmetry (e.g., nematic liquid crystals) as well as those with broken translation symmetry (e.g., smectics and convection patterns). We demonstrate the efficacy of these methods through explicit computational examples.

We detail the calculation of NNLO QCD corrections for Higgs boson production in association with a $W$ boson at the LHC, where the Higgs subsequently decays into a $b\bar{b}$ pair. Unlike prior NNLO QCD analyses of this process, our approach incorporates massive $b$ quarks. A key benefit of this method is the elimination of the need for flavor-specific jet algorithms, enabling the use of standard jet algorithms to identify $b$ jets. We compare NNLO QCD predictions for associated $WH(b\bar{b})$ production using both massive and massless $b$ quarks and contrast these with parton shower results. Our findings reveal approximately ${\cal O}(5\%)$ discrepancies in fiducial cross sections between the massive and massless treatments. Furthermore, we note that significantly larger deviations can emerge in specific kinematic distributions when comparing massless versus massive results, as well as when contrasting fixed-order calculations with parton showers.

Muon identification performance at LHCb is derived from data involving muons and hadrons generated in J/\psi->\mu\mu, \Lambda->p\pi, and D^{\star}->\pi D0(K\pi) decays. The identification algorithm relies on hit patterns within the muon chambers. A momentum-dependent binary criterion is applied to suppress hadron misidentification to 1% while maintaining a muon efficiency between 95% and 98%. Subsequently, a likelihood is constructed to distinguish between muon and non-muon hypotheses. Imposing a cut on this likelihood achieves a total muon efficiency of 93% with hadron misidentification rates reduced to below 0.6%.

The underwater acoustic channel represents one of the most difficult environments for communication. Because of periodic fluctuations in tidal and daily climatic conditions, underwater noise varies cyclically, causing long-term periodic changes in channel quality. These time-varying conditions often lead to routing failures. To address this, recent underwater channel-aware routing protocols incorporate acoustic channel estimation to sustain routing performance. However, the estimation algorithms used in these protocols are predominantly linear and seldom account for the periodic nature of acoustic channels. This paper presents a nearest neighbor regression approach for acoustic channel estimation in underwater networks. We extend this method for predicting Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) time series, achieving exceptional accuracy even for complex, periodically fluctuating SNR data. Furthermore, we introduce a rapid search algorithm and employ statistical storage compression to optimize the algorithm's time and space complexity. Compared to linear methods, our approach significantly enhances prediction accuracy—by up to three times—on both simulation and sea trial datasets. Leveraging this estimation technique, we develop the Depth-Based Channel-Aware Routing (DBCAR) protocol. By utilizing depth-greedy forwarding and channel-aware reliable communication, DBCAR demonstrates superior network performance in terms of packet delivery ratio, average energy consumption, and average transmission delay, as confirmed by extensive simulations.

Current state-of-the-art digital circuit design tools predominantly utilize pure and inertial delays for timing simulations. Although these methods offer reasonable estimations with low execution times in typical scenarios, their capacity to capture complex signal traces remains constrained. Research has introduced the Dynamic Involution Delay Model (IDM) as a compelling alternative, demonstrating that it (i) more accurately reflects real-world behavior and (ii) integrates well with modern simulation environments. This paper expands on these findings by experimentally assessing the behavioral coverage of the IDM in more sophisticated circuits. Specifically, we apply the IDM to three basic circuits—a combinational loop, an SR latch, and an adder—to interpret outcomes and evaluate performance overhead in realistic contexts. Comparisons with digital (inertial delay) and analog (SPICE) simulations indicate that the IDM produces highly detailed results that closely align with analog simulations. Furthermore, our simulations expose significant limitations of inertial delay, particularly its inability to represent various malicious behaviors. Consequently, the Involution Delay Model emerges as a viable enhancement for delay models in contemporary digital timing simulation tools.

The majority of consumer IoT devices rely on vertical integration with cloud infrastructure, creating significant risks for user data due to vendor fragmentation and the lack of transparency regarding cloud-side operations. A superior alternative involves utilizing local hardware, thereby granting users authority over data processing and the conditions under which data is shared with other devices or the internet. Karl is a novel smart-home framework that orchestrates IoT computation and storage on user-selected devices. Its modular programming model is built on the insight that a familiar, serverless-inspired interface can unify most modern cloud-based IoT components into a single framework capable of executing modules regardless of their physical location. Although local hosting removes many data flows, modularity ensures that all remaining flows can be validated using fine-grained primitives. We propose two security mechanisms for IoT: pipeline permissions, which allow data sharing only when justified, and exit policies, which prevent data flows unless specific criteria are satisfied. We validate Karl using two comprehensive end-to-end applications.

This demonstration paper presents the BLAB Reporter, a robot-journalist dedicated to covering the Brazilian Blue Amazon. Built upon a pipeline architecture for Natural Language Generation, the system delivers daily reports, news summaries, and intriguing facts in Brazilian Portuguese. By gathering, storing, and analyzing structured data from public sources, the robot-journalist leverages domain expertise to generate and publish content on Twitter. Both the code and the corpus are available to the public.

A query game consists of a set $Q$ of queries and a set $\mathcal{F}$ of functions, referred to as code words $f:Q\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$. This structure is modeled as a two-player game where one player, Codemaker, selects a hidden code word $f\in\mathcal{F}$, while the other, Codebreaker, attempts to identify $f$ by posing a sequence of queries $q\in Q$, receiving the response $f(q)$ from Codemaker after each. The objective for Codebreaker is to determine the code word using the minimum number of queries. Two well-known examples of such games are coin-weighing with a spring scale and Mastermind, both of which are significant as recreational pastimes and for their relevance to information theory. This paper introduces a general framework for deriving concise solutions to query games. As applications, we provide new, self-contained proofs regarding the query complexity of various coin-weighing problems and establish new results showing that the deterministic query complexity of Mastermind is $\Theta(n \log k/ \log n + k)$ when only black-peg feedback is available, and $\Theta(n \log k / \log n + k/n)$ when both black- and white-peg feedback are used. In the deterministic setting, these represent the first solutions to Mastermind that are optimal up to constant factors for any $k\geq n^{1-o(1)}$.

Quantum electrodynamics theory suggests that the vacuum acts as a polarizable medium, creating effective nonlinear interactions between electromagnetic fields and phenomena such as light-by-light scattering. We investigate the collision of two optical laser pulses within a pump-probe configuration, utilizing beams with both circular and elliptic cross-sections, to estimate the quantity of signal photons generated by these quantum vacuum nonlinearities. Our analysis explores methods to maximize the detectability of the quantum vacuum signal against the background noise of the driving lasers. A primary finding is that colliding two maximally focused lasers does not yield the optimal signal; rather, broadening the focal point generally enhances the signal-to-background ratio in the far field.

Scrambling and thermalization are subjects of significant research in both condensed matter and high-energy physics, with random unitary dynamics serving as a straightforward framework for theoretical investigation. This study derives precise formulas for the large $q$ asymptotic behavior of various $n$-point correlation functions, out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs), and their moments. Furthermore, we identify a universal principle that decomposes OTOCs into smaller, computationally tractable components, a method that is likely applicable in broader contexts.

We introduce a lightweight and precise approach for video anomaly detection. While previous methods relied on multiple-instance learning (MIL) to classify each video segment as normal or abnormal, recent studies emphasize the importance of capturing temporal relationships between segments rather than analyzing them in isolation. Our analysis of successful recent approaches reveals that although processing all segments collectively is crucial, maintaining their specific temporal order does not enhance accuracy. Consequently, we discard the MIL framework in favor of a lightweight model incorporating a self-attention mechanism, which automatically extracts key features across all input segments to determine anomaly status. This results in a neural network with only 1.3% of the parameters found in existing methods. Evaluations on three benchmark datasets (UCF-Crime, ShanghaiTech, and XD-Violence) demonstrate that our method achieves accuracy comparable to, or superior to, state-of-the-art techniques at the frame level.

We examine a four-dimensional Hamiltonian designed to model the band structure of single-Dirac-cone topological insulators under a uniform perpendicular magnetic field. The analysis reveals surface Landau level (LL) states that remain decoupled from bulk levels and adhere to the quantized energy dispersion characteristic of a purely two-dimensional surface Dirac Hamiltonian. A minor hybridization gap breaks the degeneracy of the central n=0 LL, with a dependence on film thickness and magnetic field strength that can be derived analytically. Explicit calculations of spin and charge densities indicate that these surface LL states are confined to approximately one quintuple layer from the surface termination. Furthermore, the study identifies new surface-bound LLs existing at higher Landau level indices.

This study presents a calculation approach for the local stress tensor tailored for non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (MD) systems, utilizing the Method of Plane (MoP). By establishing a connection between the macroscopic velocity distribution function and the microscopic molecular flux across a stationary control plane, we derived a technique to compute fundamental properties of the macroscopic momentum conservation law. This includes determining density, velocity, momentum flux, and both interaction and kinetic components of the stress tensor defined on a surface of finite area. Within the MoP framework, any component of the streaming velocity can be extracted on a control surface, allowing the kinetic momentum flux to be separated into advection and stress terms. We validated this method by analyzing density, velocity, and stress distributions in two scenarios: a quasi-1D steady-state Couette flow and a quasi-2D steady-state system featuring a moving contact line. Unlike the volume average method, our approach defines density, mass, and momentum fluxes on a surface, a feature essential for maintaining consistency with mass and momentum conservation laws in dynamic systems.

With the increasing adoption of cloud-based pre-trained language models, privacy concerns are escalating, primarily due to the exposure of sensitive plain-text data such as search histories, medical records, and bank details. Consequently, privacy-preserving inference for transformer models is highly sought after by cloud users. While performing computations solely on ciphertext using Homomorphic Encryption (HE) is an appealing solution for safeguarding privacy, it remains challenging to execute inference on pre-trained transformers because their complex operations within transformer blocks are currently unsupported by existing HE tools. This work introduces $\textit{THE-X}$, an approximation method designed for transformers that facilitates privacy-preserving inference for models built with popular frameworks. $\textit{THE-X}$ outlines a workflow to handle intricate computations in transformer networks, addressing non-polynomial functions including GELU, softmax, and LayerNorm. Experimental results demonstrate that $\textit{THE-X}$ enables encrypted data inference for various downstream tasks, achieving negligible performance degradation while providing theory-guaranteed privacy benefits.

Multimodal learning represents a burgeoning yet demanding field of research. This study addresses the detection of sarcasm and humor within conversational videos and image-text pairs. Given that sarcasm is a transient action manifested across various modalities, detection is particularly difficult, especially due to the scarcity of large-scale datasets in existing literature. Consequently, our work prioritizes resource-constrained training scenarios where training data is limited. To address this, we introduce MuLOT (Multimodal Learning using Optimal Transport), a novel system that leverages self-attention to capture intra-modal relationships and optimal transport to establish cross-modal correspondences. Furthermore, we employ multimodal attention fusion to integrate these modalities and capture their interdependencies. We evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets—MUStARD (video, audio, text), UR-FUNNY (video, audio, text), and MST (image, text)—achieving accuracy improvements of 2.1%, 1.54%, and 2.34%, respectively, surpassing state-of-the-art performance.

This work investigates the simple Bershadsky-Polyakov algebra $\mathcal W_k = \mathcal{W}_k(sl_3,f_{\theta})$ at positive integer levels, classifying its irreducible modules to validate the conjecture proposed in arXiv:1910.13781. We further examine the specific case where $k=1$, revealing that this vertex algebra possesses a Kazama-Suzuki-type dual isomorphic to the simple affine vertex superalgebra $L_{k'} (osp(1 \vert 2))$ with $k'=-5/4$. Leveraging the free-field realization of $L_{k'} (osp(1 \vert 2))$ detailed in arXiv:1711.11342, we derive corresponding free-field realizations for $\mathcal W_k$ and their highest weight modules. Future research will address the fusion rules of $\mathcal W_k$.

The comment presents primary arguments demonstrating that the claims and conclusions stated in the title of the reviewed paper are incorrect for several key reasons, with an atomistic simulation provided as an illustrative example.

Future cellular networks leveraging millimeter wave signals offer significant advancements in positioning and situational awareness. The combination of extensive bandwidths and substantial antenna arrays delivers exceptional delay and angle resolution, enabling both high-precision localization and environmental mapping. However, even fundamental filters designed for simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) incur high computational costs due to their reliance on sigma-point or particle-based approximations. This paper proposes a first-order Taylor series-based Gaussian approximation of the filtering distribution. It demonstrates that the resulting Extended Kalman Probability Hypothesis Density (PHD) filter is highly computationally efficient. Furthermore, the findings indicate that this efficiency does not compromise estimation accuracy, as the method approaches the position error bound.

This paper investigates a class of non-Markovian forward-backward doubly stochastic systems. Employing functional It\^o (or path-dependent) calculus, it establishes a connection between these systems and associated path-dependent quasi-linear stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs). Furthermore, the study extends the classic nonlinear stochastic Feynman-Kac formula by Pardoux and Peng [Backward doubly stochastic differential equations and systems of quasilinear SPDEs, Probab. Theory Relat. Fields 98 (1994), pp. 209--227] to accommodate non-Markovian contexts. Additionally, the work derives the differentiability of solutions for the forward-backward doubly stochastic systems and examines various properties of solutions to the path-dependent SPDEs.

Over the last few decades, topological phases of matter have driven significant scientific activity. These materials are categorized using topological invariants, which serve as non-local order parameters for any given symmetry and condition. Consequently, they display quantized phenomena in both bulk and boundary regions, inspiring applications that remain robust against perturbations. This review examines the topological classification within quasiperiodic systems and outlines recent experimental developments in the field.

This paper investigates the real-time dynamics of the $O(4)$ scalar theory using the functional renormalization group on the Schwinger-Keldysh closed time path. We derive flow equations for the effective action and $n$-point correlation functions in terms of "classical" and "quantum" fields, providing a concise diagrammatic framework. An analytic formula for the four-point vertex flow is established, and spectral functions are computed across various temperatures and momenta. Additionally, we determine the dynamical critical exponent for the phase transition near the critical temperature in $3+1$ dimensions, finding a value of $z\simeq 2.023$.

Majorana zero modes are typically regarded as a key outcome of one-dimensional topological superconductivity; however, we demonstrate the reverse: zero modes arising from dynamical instanton events can significantly strengthen, and in certain instances even facilitate, superconductivity. Our analysis reveals that the dynamics of a one-dimensional topological triplet superconductor are controlled by a $\theta$ term within the action. Specifically, isotropic triplets utilize this term to achieve algebraic charge-$2e$ superconductivity, a state that remains robust against fluctuations that would otherwise destroy non-topological superconductors. In contrast, for anisotropic triplets, these zero modes inhibit quantum phase slips, thereby stabilizing superconductivity across an extensive portion of the phase diagram. Finally, we provide predictions regarding the correlation functions and thermodynamic properties associated with these topologically enhanced superconducting states.

Digital editions of historical texts, frequently created by historians, textual scholars, and archivists, often employ markup standards like EpiDoc and the Text Encoding Initiative. These schemes capture both the semantic structure (e.g., figures, notes) and physical layout (e.g., page and line breaks) alongside the transcribed content. This research outlines techniques for leveraging such semantic markup as a form of distant supervision to train and assess layout analysis models. Experiments conducted across half a million pages within the Deutsches Textarchiv (DTA) demonstrate a strong correlation between region-level evaluation metrics and traditional pixel- and word-level measures. Furthermore, the discussion covers strategies to enhance accuracy through self-training and evaluates how models trained on the DTA perform when applied to other historical printed books.

We provide a refined analysis of the classic Count-Sketch algorithm for streaming heavy hitters [CCF02]. Count-Sketch employs O(k log n) linear measurements of a vector x in R^n to produce an estimate x'. While standard analysis guarantees that ||x'-x||_infty^2 < ||x_tail||_2^2 / k (where x_tail comprises all coordinates except the largest k), our primary contribution demonstrates that most coordinates of x' exhibit significantly lower error. Specifically, for any c < O(log n), we prove that with probability 1-2^{-Omega(c)}, each coordinate i satisfies (x'_i - x_i)^2 < (c/log n) ||x_tail||_2^2/k, assuming fully independent hash functions. This result improves upon and subsumes the previous bound, proving optimality for all c. Leveraging these enhanced point estimates, we establish a stronger concentration property for set estimates by first examining the covariance matrix and subsequently applying a median-of-median-of-medians technique to amplify failure probability bounds. Furthermore, these findings yield improved l_2 recovery results for exactly k-sparse estimates x^* when x originates from distributions with appropriate decay, such as power law or lognormal distributions. We validate our theoretical contributions with simulations of Count-Sketch on a power law distribution, showing that the empirical data aligns closely with our bounds: the asymptotics hold, and the constants are small. Additionally, our proof reveals that any symmetric random variable with finite variance and positive Fourier transform concentrates around zero at least as effectively as a Gaussian. This finding, potentially of independent interest, ensures robust concentration even when noise does not converge to a Gaussian.

Transcription factors are proteins that control gene activity by either activating or repressing transcription. A specific category of transcriptional repressors functions through a short-range mechanism that renders local DNA regions inaccessible to activators, thereby exerting indirect repression on target genes. While this mechanism is often modeled under the assumption of thermodynamic equilibrium for repressor-DNA interactions—while ignoring certain gene regulatory configurations—we propose a more comprehensive nonequilibrium framework utilizing graph formalism to describe transitions between gene states. We apply analytical calculations to compare this new model with the traditional equilibrium approach regarding repression strength and expression noise. Unlike the equilibrium method, our nonequilibrium model distinguishes two fundamental mechanisms of short-range repression: one involving the recruitment of factors that drive chromatin condensation, and another involving the inhibition of factors that facilitate chromatin loosening. When tested against published gene expression data for transcription factors regulating Drosophila development, the nonequilibrium model demonstrates superior performance and suggests that the chromatin-condensing mechanism is the most advantageous in this system. Furthermore, this scalable approach can be extended to larger gene networks to infer specific regulatory modes and parameters from gene expression data.

Under strong Floquet driving, coupled electron-nuclear dynamics experience a significant failure of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. This article presents a derivation of a Fokker-Planck equation designed to model non-adiabatic molecular dynamics incorporating electronic friction within Floquet-driven systems. We begin by offering a novel derivation of the Floquet quantum-classical Liouville equation (QCLE) for such driven electron-nuclear dynamics. Subsequently, we convert the Floquet QCLE into a Fokker-Planck equation, providing explicit expressions for both the frictional and random forces. By reformulating electronic friction using Floquet Green's functions, we enable its explicit evaluation. Our results demonstrate that the Floquet electronic friction tensor contains antisymmetric terms even at equilibrium for real-valued Hamiltonians, indicating the presence of a Lorentz-like force in Floquet-driven non-Born-Oppenheimer dynamics, even in the absence of spin-orbit coupling.

We experimentally confirm the existence of Majorana-like bound states (MLBSs) in quasi-one-dimensional metamaterials, which serve as mechanical analogues to Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in the Kitaev chain. Using a mechanical spinner ladder, we observed a topological phase transition accompanied by spectral-gap-protected edge MLBSs. We analyzed the oscillatory and decaying characteristics of these MLBS pairs along with their phase-dependent hybridization. Our results demonstrate that this hybridization can be adjusted to mimic parity switching in MZMs, a fundamental component for topological qubits, showing strong consistency with theoretical predictions.

Recent research utilizing end-to-end trainable neural networks has achieved state-of-the-art performance in dialogue state tracking by estimating probability distributions over all potential slot values. However, these methods struggle to scale with the large value sets found in real-world scenarios and fail to effectively track values absent from the training data. To address these limitations, candidate-generation-based approaches have emerged, which identify a subset of plausible values per turn based on conversation history and language understanding outputs. While these methods successfully handle unseen values and large domains, they underperform compared to distribution-based models. This study evaluates both paradigms and introduces HyST, a hybrid framework that dynamically selects the optimal method for each slot type. Validated on the recently released MultiWOZ-2.0 multi-domain dataset, our experiments demonstrate that HyST effectively scales to complex applications. Our best model achieves a relative improvement of 24% over the previous state-of-the-art and a 10% gain over the best baseline.

Data-centric AI represents an emerging and promising area within the AI research community, yet numerous organizations already operate diverse "data-centric" systems designed to generate high-quality data. These systems span from conventional business data processing tasks—such as determining customer pricing strategies—to production machine learning infrastructure like recommendation engines. Over the past few years, the disciplines of data and ML engineering have evolved to oversee these applications, introducing a wealth of innovative tools and methodologies. Drawing on our experience constructing data and ML platforms that support thousands of applications across various organizations, this paper explores several insights from these engineering fields that hold significant potential for advancing data-centric AI.

Integrating real-time, complex social signal processing into robotic systems, particularly within real-world, multi-party interactions, presents a significant challenge for the Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) community. This difficulty is exacerbated by the absence of a standard model for human representation, which hinders the development and interoperability of social perception components and pipelines. This paper introduces a set of conventions and standard interfaces for HRI scenarios designed for use with the Robot Operating System (ROS). These tools aim to enhance the interoperability and reusability of core functionalities across various HRI-related software tools, ranging from skeleton tracking and face recognition to natural language processing. Importantly, these interfaces are applicable to a wide spectrum of HRI applications, including high-level crowd simulation, group-level social interaction modeling, and detailed human kinematics modeling. We demonstrate these interfaces by providing a reference pipeline implementation that is packaged for easy download and evaluation by the community.

Data assimilation algorithms aim to estimate the most probable state of a dynamical system by integrating observational data with prior models. Variational methods, including the weak-constraint four-dimensional variational approach examined here, can be fundamentally viewed as minimization tasks. A primary difficulty in this framework involves solving large linear systems that emerge during the inner linear step of the nonlinear solver used. Depending on the specific method, these systems are either saddle point problems or symmetric positive definite (SPD). Both types can be addressed using preconditioned Krylov subspace methods, such as GMRES or CG, to guarantee rapid convergence. This paper introduces novel, efficient preconditioning operators based on solving specific Stein matrix equations. Beyond enhancing computational efficiency, these techniques enable the derivation of tighter eigenvalue distribution bounds for the preconditioned system in certain scenarios. Numerical experiments across diverse cases demonstrate the superiority of this proposed methodology over existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Utilizing the local-$\delta{f}$ gyrokinetic code GS2, we investigated how flux-surface shaping influences two highly-shaped equilibria relevant to JT-60SA, covering both low- and high-$\beta$ regimes, alongside a validation benchmark using the GKV code. Our analysis reveals a new mechanism where electrostatic fluctuations become destabilized as elongation increases, specifically in plasmas characterized by strongly peaked pressure profiles. We attribute this phenomenon to a balance between local magnetic shear and finite-Larmor-radius (FLR) stabilization. Electromagnetic simulations demonstrate that kinetic ballooning modes benefit from increased shaping through enhanced sensitivity to FLR effects compared to the ion-temperature-gradient instability. However, at sufficiently high $\beta$ levels, increased elongation undermines the local magnetic shear stabilization required to reach the second-stability region of ballooning modes.

Using density functional theory and semi-classical Boltzmann theory, we examined the structural, elastic, electronic, optical, and thermoelectric characteristics of rhodium-based half-Heusler alloys with 18 valence electrons, specifically RhTiP, RhTiAs, RhTiSb, and RhTiBi. The structural stability of these systems is confirmed by the lack of imaginary frequencies in their phonon dispersion curves. While RhTiP exhibits ductility, the remaining alloys are brittle. All materials demonstrate semiconducting behavior with indirect band gaps between 0.94 and 1.01 eV. Our results indicate high optical conductivity and absorption coefficients in both the ultraviolet and visible spectra. Regarding thermoelectric performance, $p$-type doping proves more effective for enhancement, yielding power factors comparable to existing half-Heusler compounds. The figure of merit ($\zt$) reaches approximately 1 for RhTiBi, identifying it as a strong candidate for thermoelectric applications, whereas RhTiP, RhTiAs, and RhTiSb, with $\zt$ values ranging from 0.38 to 0.67, are also viable options for thermoelectric devices.

This research investigates the dynamics of an infinite chain of nonlinear dimer oscillators linearly coupled according to the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. The ratio of intra-cell to inter-cell coupling in the SSH model delineates distinct phases: topologically trivial and topologically non-trivial. We initially examine the regime of weak inter-cell coupling, characteristic of the topologically trivial phase in linear SSH. Under non-resonance and non-degeneracy conditions for a prescribed isolated dimer frequency, $\omega_b$, we demonstrate the existence of discrete breather solutions for sufficiently small inter-cell coupling. These solutions exhibit $2\pi/\omega_b$ temporal periodicity and exponential spatial localization. We subsequently analyze the global continuation of these states with respect to the coupling parameter. Specifically, we consider cases where $\omega_b$, the initial discrete breather frequency, lies within the phonon gap of the underlying linear infinite array. As coupling increases, the phonon gap narrows and approaches zero at the linear SSH topological transition. In this limit, the discrete breather's spatial extent expands while its amplitude diminishes, signaling a transition to the weakly nonlinear long-wave regime. Asymptotic analysis reveals that in this regime, the discrete breather envelope is governed by a vector gap soliton of the limiting envelope equations. Utilizing envelope theory, we characterize discrete breathers for SSH coupling parameters in both topologically trivial and, via an emergent symmetry, topologically non-trivial regimes where the spectral gap is small. Our asymptotic framework yields results that align closely with extensive numerical simulations across a broad parameter range.

Recent studies indicate that synthetic datasets generated via game engines enhance performance across various computer vision tasks. Nevertheless, these datasets are usually limited to specific game-like environments, such as urban settings featuring vehicles and pedestrians. This paper introduces a novel method for creating synthetic datasets tailored for object counting in any domain, eliminating the requirement for photo-realistic assets manually crafted by costly teams of 3D artists. We propose a domain randomization strategy that leverages synthetic data produced quickly and at low cost. By intentionally avoiding photorealism and significantly boosting dataset variability through random textures and 3D transformations, we achieve improved generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields strong performance on real-world object counting benchmarks across multiple domains, including people, vehicles, penguins, and fruit. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/enric1994/dr4oc

Ranking algorithms often face computational intractability as the dataset size increases, a limitation caused by the intricate geometric structures inherent in rankings. This problem is further complicated by partial rankings, where preferences are defined only for a subset of objects. Consequently, current state-of-the-art techniques fail to scale effectively for real-world applications like recommender systems. To overcome these hurdles, we leverage the geometric properties of ranked data alongside supplementary object information to construct a ranking kernel based on the graph cut function. This approach integrates the computational efficiency of submodular optimization with the robust theoretical framework of kernel-based methods.

We introduce a universal, physically realizable adversarial attack targeting cascaded multi-modal deep learning networks (DNNs) within the self-driving domain. Although DNNs excel at 3D object detection, they remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. While these threats have been extensively studied in both RGB imagery and point clouds individually, this paper addresses the critical gap in simultaneous attacks across both modalities. By leveraging a single 3D mesh and differentiable rendering, we investigate how geometric and textural perturbations can compromise DNN robustness. Specifically, we target the Frustum-Pointnet model, a prominent cascaded architecture. Experiments on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that our proposed universal multi-modal attack significantly degrades the model's car detection capability by approximately 73%. Ultimately, this research enhances our understanding of what cascaded RGB-point cloud DNNs learn and highlights their specific vulnerabilities to adversarial manipulation.

Intense rotation induces a quasi-two-dimensional state in the underlying turbulent flow, driving energy toward larger scales. Recent numerical simulations indicate that under specific conditions, this energy accumulates at the system's largest scales, creating coherent vortex structures termed condensates. We analytically examine the interaction between a strong condensate and weak small-scale turbulent fluctuations, deriving an equation to calculate the radial velocity profile $U(r)$ of these coherent vortices. Under rapid external rotation, the velocity profiles of cyclones and anticyclones are identical and follow the relationship $U(r) \propto \pm r \ln (R/r)$, where $R$ represents the vortex's transverse dimension. As external rotation weakens, this symmetry breaks: cyclones exhibit higher maximum velocities with peaks located closer to the vortex axis compared to anticyclones. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that an anticyclone's size $R$ is constrained by a critical value dependent on the Rossby and Reynolds numbers, whereas cyclone size is limited only by the system's dimensions under the same conditions. These predictions rely on the linear evolution of turbulent pulsations superimposed on the coherent vortex flow and are supported by estimates derived from the nonlinear Navier-Stokes equation.

A canine lymphoma blood test measures two acute phase proteins, C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and Haptoglobin, serving diagnostic, screening, and remission monitoring purposes. The study analyzes clinical data to evaluate various machine learning techniques, selecting the optimal approach through a comparison of decision trees, k-nearest neighbors (including adaptive variants), and radial basis function-based probability density evaluation for classification and risk assessment. Several preprocessing strategies were tested and integrated into the final diagnostic system. For differential diagnosis, the best model achieved 83.5% sensitivity and 77% specificity using CRP, Haptoglobin, and standard clinical symptoms. In screening tasks, a decision tree yielded superior results with 81.4% sensitivity and over 99% specificity using the same features. When clinical symptoms like lymphadenopathy are unknown, a decision tree relying solely on CRP and Haptoglobin maintains 69% sensitivity and 83.5% specificity. The lymphoma risk evaluation problem was formulated and resolved, with the selected models forming a system for computational diagnosis and risk assessment. These methods are deployed in specialized web-based software designed to monitor post-treatment dogs, successfully detecting lymphoma recurrence up to two months before clinical signs appear. Additionally, a risk map visualization offers an accessible tool for explanatory data analysis.

Galaxy mergers are anticipated to create supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries that eventually merge via anisotropic gravitational wave emission, potentially imparting a recoil velocity of 100–1000 km/s to the resulting black hole and causing it to oscillate within its host galaxy's gravitational potential. The quasar E1821+643, identified as a potential recoil candidate through spectropolarimetry, exhibits Doppler shifts in its broad emission lines across both direct and scattered light, indicating a relative velocity of approximately 2100 km/s between the nucleus and the host. This study aims to detect the predicted spatial offset by combining optical spectroastrometry with Hubble Space Telescope (HST) narrow-band imaging. The spectroastrometry data reveal a spatial displacement of roughly 130 mas (~580 pc) toward the North-West between the quasar nucleus and the gas producing the [OIII] 4959,5007 lines. HST images resolve the [OIII] emission on sub-arcsecond scales, displaying an asymmetric distribution that extends 0.5–0.6 arcseconds radially from the nucleus in a broad arc spanning from the North-East to the West. Simulations based on the HST [OIII] image suggest that only a minor portion of the observed displacement stems from this asymmetry. Consequently, the displacement likely represents a genuine spatial offset of the quasar nucleus relative to the narrow-line region, presumed to be centered on the host galaxy, thereby reinforcing the hypothesis that a post-merger gravitational recoil has occurred in E1821+643.
This survey paper examines recent advancements and associated open problems within additive combinatorics, with a specific focus on sumsets in finite abelian groups.

English Wikipedia has historically served as a critical resource for research and natural language machine learning. However, driven by the expansion of non-English editions, increased computational power, and demands for equitable model performance, datasets and models now incorporate a broader range of language versions. Developing superior multilingual and multimodal models necessitates more than just access to larger datasets; it also demands a deeper comprehension of data composition and its generation processes. This paper aims to equip researchers with the necessary background to anticipate variations across different language editions and their impact on models. It outlines three primary sources of content divergence—local context, community governance, and technology—along with best practice recommendations for utilizing multilingual and multimodal data in research and modeling.

We develop a scalar field theory within Snyder non-commutative space-time. While the symmetry of Snyder geometry undergoes deformation solely at the co-algebraic level, its Poincaré algebra remains undeformed. Specifically, the Lorentz sector stays undeformed at both algebraic and co-algebraic levels, though the momentum co-product—which defines the star-product—is non-co-associative. Consequently, the Snyder-deformed Poincaré group is characterized by a non-co-associative Hopf algebra, casting doubt on defining an interacting theory via this non-associative star-product. To circumvent non-associativity, we adopt a space-time approach grounded in the realization of non-commutative geometry. Our primary findings are: (i) a general construction of the co-algebraic sector supporting Snyder geometry, applicable to any realization, and (ii) a well-defined, unambiguous self-interacting scalar field theory on this space-time. We explicitly calculate the first-order correction terms of the resulting Lagrangian and also explore the derivation of Noether charges for Snyder space-time.

Understanding the behavior of quantum liquids is a captivating area of physics. Although linear response theory, grounded in equilibrium two-body correlations via fluctuation-dissipation relations, suffices for strongly correlated systems under external fields, investigating nonlinear non-equilibrium dynamics requires uncovering the influence of higher-order correlations, beginning with three-body effects. This study experimentally examines a tunable quantum liquid within a Kondo-correlated quantum dot, demonstrating the significance of three-body correlations in nonlinear conductance under finite magnetic fields, thereby supporting an extension of Fermi liquid theory to non-equilibrium conditions.

We examine a simplified Pennington, Shenker, Stanford, and Yang model for the Hawking radiation density matrix, extended to incorporate dynamics of End-of-the-World (EOW) branes situated behind the horizon. This extension facilitates interactions that scatter interior states and permits EOW loops. At strong coupling, we observe that EOW states lose their randomness; the ensemble collapses, with coupling constants representing the microscopic matrix elements of Hawking radiation. This implies that robust interior dynamics are crucial for comprehending evaporating black holes, eliminating the need for ensemble averaging. Within this specific framework, the radiation density matrix diverges from a thermal state: small off-diagonal fluctuations signify equivalences between ostensibly orthogonal states and cap the entropy from above. For nearly evaporated black holes, these off-diagonal terms grow to match the diagonal ones, ultimately yielding a pure state. Furthermore, we derive a unique analytic expression for all Renyi entropies.

This study examines the Selmer groups of Jacobians for curves possessing a non-trivial automorphism group, applying these findings to analyze the parity of Selmer ranks. Assuming the Shafarevich-Tate conjecture, we derive a formula expressing the parity of the Mordell-Weil rank for any Jacobian using purely local invariants; these invariants serve as an arithmetic counterpart to local root numbers, which, under the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, dictate the parity of ranks for abelian varieties. The paper's primary focus is establishing the theory of Brauer relations and regulator constants within the framework of Galois covers of curves.

This lecture series introduces readers to recent mathematical tools and findings regarding the mean-field limit in statistical dynamics. To begin, Lecture 1 revisits the classical mechanics approach to the mean-field limit, drawing on the work of W. Braun, K. Hepp, and R.L. Dobrushin, with a focus on phase space empirical measures, Klimontovich solutions, and Monge-Kantorovich-Wasserstein distances between probability measures. Lecture 2 explores a quantum dynamics equivalent of the Klimontovich solution and details its role in Pickl's method for addressing interaction potentials featuring a Coulomb-type singularity at the origin. In Lecture 3, the series demonstrates how to simultaneously apply the mean-field and classical limits to quantum $N$-particle dynamics, resulting in the Vlasov equation. These lectures synthesize findings from collaborative research conducted with C. Mouhot and T. Paul.

We calculate the relationship between the pole mass and the kinetic mass of a heavy quark up to three-loop order. By leveraging the established connection between the pole and $\overline{\rm MS}$ masses, we derive precise conversion formulas between the $\overline{\rm MS}$ and kinetic masses. The kinetic mass is characterized by the moments of the spectral function associated with scattering processes involving a heavy quark near threshold, necessitating the calculation of the imaginary part of a forward scattering amplitude to three-loop precision. This work details the expansion methodology and the reduction to master integrals, providing analytic solutions for the latter. Our findings are applied to both charm and bottom quark masses; for the bottom quark, we incorporate finite charm quark mass effects. Additionally, we determine the large-$\beta_0$ approximation for the conversion formula at four-loop order. For the bottom quark, we estimate the uncertainty in converting between $\overline{\rm MS}$ and kinetic masses to be approximately 15 MeV, representing a two- to three-fold improvement over the two-loop formula. This enhanced precision is essential for extracting the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix element $|V_{cb}|$ at Belle II.

Within the Inert Higgs Doublet model (IHDM), we examined neutral Higgs-boson pair production ($e^+ e^- \rightarrow H^0 A^0$) in the center-of-mass frame, considering an intense, circularly polarized laser field at the lowest order. Utilizing the scattering matrix method, we derived the analytical formula for the differential cross section, which was subsequently integrated over the solid angle to determine the total cross section. We then analyzed the dependence of this total cross section on the outgoing particle masses across various numbers of exchanged photons. Furthermore, we illustrated its behavior as a function of the center-of-mass energy for different neutral Higgs-boson masses. Finally, we demonstrated how the cross section varies with laser field amplitudes, considering both different photon exchange counts and distinct neutral Higgs-boson masses.

The near-horizon region of magnetically charged black holes hosts extremely intense magnetic fields. A practical low-energy effective framework for describing field fluctuations interacting with electrically charged particles is force-free electrodynamics. This theory supports numerous low-energy collective excitations, specifically Alfvén wave modes that follow a massless dispersion relation along field worldlines. We aim to build traversable wormhole solutions by leveraging the negative Casimir energy of these Alfvén modes, mirroring recent approaches utilizing charged massless fermions. However, the behavior of massless scalars within this near-horizon region imposes strict limitations on wormhole dimensions, preventing them from becoming large, despite the broader validity of the force-free description.

We calculate the modular data, specifically the $S$ and $T$ matrices, for the center of the extended Haagerup subfactor. Although the complete structure—namely the associativity data or $F$ matrices (also referred to as 6-$j$ symbols)—remains elusive, we demonstrate that knowing only the count of simple objects and their dimensions (derived via a combinatorial approach in arXiv:1404.3955) allows for a remarkably straightforward derivation of the full modular data by utilizing the representation theory of $SL(2, \mathbb Z)$. Additionally, we examine the potential character vectors linked to this modular data.

Addressing sequential decision-making in operations management to minimize costs under constraints often involves Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). Solving CMDPs to establish effective operational policies faces two primary hurdles: the immense size of the state and action spaces, and the difficulty in calculating the transition kernel. This paper introduces a sampling-based primal-dual algorithm designed to tackle CMDPs. The method alternates between regularized policy iteration to refine policies and subgradient ascent to uphold constraints. Under mild regularity assumptions, the algorithm achieves a convergence rate of $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$ over $T$ iterations. Furthermore, for CMDPs with weakly coupled structures, the proposed approach leverages embedded decomposition to significantly lower problem dimensionality. Applied to two key scenarios with such structures—multi-product inventory management and multi-class queue scheduling—the algorithm demonstrates that its generated controls surpass existing state-of-the-art heuristics.

**Pursuing Stacks (*A la poursuite des Champs*): First Episode – The Modelizing Story**

Alexander Grothendieck's work, *Pursuing Stacks*, originated from a series of letters written in early 1983. These correspondences, addressed to Daniel Quillen as a starting point and later expanded with an appendix and outline for Lawrence Breen, aimed to systematically explore the foundations of non-commutative (co)homological algebra, its coefficients, and homotopical algebra. Written in English based on exchanges with R. Brown and D. Quillen, the title reflects the intuition that stacks serve as a unifying concept for synthesizing homotopical and non-commutative cohomological algebra.

The initial episode, titled "The Modelizing Story," offers a comprehensive reflection on foundational issues in homotopy theory. Shortly after its inception, the focus shifted away from stacks to center on the various methods for modeling homotopy categories. Grothendieck continued this reflection until November of that year. In June, he drafted the first words of an introduction, which he revisited in February 1984 after the main reflection had concluded; during this interim, he also contemplated pseudo-lines and penned *L'Esquisse d'un Programme*. This introduction adopted a more personal tone before transitioning to French. The subsequent months marked the beginning of *Récoltes et Semailles*. Although the entire project was intended for inclusion in a volume of *Réflexions mathématiques*, the series was never published.

The 2015 edition by "thescrivener" is in the public domain. It represents an extended and revised version prepared by Mateo Carmona with the collaboration of Ulrik Buchholtz.

Achieving deep decarbonization in the energy sector demands the widespread integration of stochastic renewable resources and extensive coordination of grid assets, presenting a formidable challenge for operators tasked with preserving grid stability and security amidst these shifts. Machine learning (ML), capable of extracting insights from complex datasets and delivering rapid predictive solutions, is uniquely suited to address these obstacles as power systems evolve over the coming decades. This study identifies five critical hurdles—dataset generation, data pre-processing, model training, model assessment, and model embedding—in developing trustworthy ML models trained on physics-based simulation data. We illustrate how sequentially linking individual modules designed to tackle each specific challenge can significantly improve the overall training process. Specifically, we employ methods that establish feedback connections between various pipeline components, effectively "closing the loop" among model training, performance evaluation, and re-training. The efficacy of this framework, along with its individual modules and feedback mechanisms, is validated by learning the N-1 small-signal stability margin for a detailed model of a proposed North Sea Wind Power Hub system.

Recent research has identified "quasi-symmetries"—approximate symmetry operations that, despite existing only in lower-order approximations of an effective model, are sufficient to dictate a system's physical behavior. In this study, we uncover the hierarchical structure of these quasi-symmetries and the associated nodal structures they enforce within the chiral crystal CoSi, utilizing two distinct perturbation expansion methods for the effective model. In the first approach, the spin-independent linear momentum ($k$) term serves as the zero-order Hamiltonian, yielding four-fold degenerate energy bands protected by an $SU(2)\times SU(2)$ quasi-symmetry. By treating both $k$-independent spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and full quadratic-$k$ terms as perturbations, the first-order correction results in a model governed by a self-commuting "stabilizer code" Hamiltonian possessing a $U(1)$ quasi-symmetry that safeguards nodal planes. The second approach defines the zero-order Hamiltonian using the SOC-free linear-$k$ term and the $k$-independent SOC term, which exhibit an $SU(2)$ quasi-symmetry reducible to a $U(1)$ quasi-symmetry depending on the quadratic terms selected. Consequently, the initial two-fold band degeneracy arising from $SU(2)$ symmetry is transformed into two-fold nodal planes protected by the $U(1)$ symmetry. In both scenarios, incorporating higher-order perturbations breaks the $U(1)$ quasi-symmetry, opening a minimal gap of approximately 1 meV for the nodal planes. These quasi-symmetry-protected near-degeneracies are crucial for interpreting recent quantum oscillation experiments in CoSi.

This paper investigates asynchronous programming through the lens of algebraic effects. It extends the standard synchronous approach by naturally integrating asynchrony, achieved by separating the invocation of operations from their execution and allowing running computations to be interrupted by operation results, which can then trigger interrupt handlers. These concepts are formalized in a minimal core calculus named $\lambda_{\text{ae}}$. The flexibility of $\lambda_{\text{ae}}$ is illustrated through diverse examples, including multi-party web applications, preemptive multi-threading, remote function calls, and a parallel version of algebraic effect runners. Furthermore, the work includes a formal verification of $\lambda_{\text{ae}}$'s type safety using Agda and a prototype implementation written in OCaml.

Krylov complexity represents a new metric for operator complexity, demonstrating universal characteristics and serving as an upper bound for many other measures. This study extends Krylov complexity from closed systems to open systems interacting with a Markovian bath, substituting Hamiltonian dynamics with Lindbladian evolution. We demonstrate that Krylov complexity within open systems can be mapped to a non-Hermitian tight-binding model situated on a semi-infinite chain. Our analysis of the non-Hermitian terms reveals that their strengths grow linearly with the Krylov basis index $n$. This non-Hermitian model supports localized edge modes that dictate the long-term dynamics of Krylov complexity. Consequently, dissipation suppresses the growth of Krylov complexity, causing it to saturate at a finite value significantly lower than that observed in a closed system governed by the same Hamiltonian. Numerical simulations on various models, including the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and interacting fermion models, validate these findings. Our results offer valuable perspectives for exploring complexity, chaos, and holography within the context of open quantum systems.

Collections of self-propelled particles (SPPs) display coherent motion and establish genuine long-range order in two-dimensional settings, though inhomogeneity typically disrupts the long-range order characteristic of polar SPPs. We investigate a system of polar SPPs featuring either inhomogeneous interaction strengths or bond disorder, focusing on the region near the order-to-disorder transition across varying disorder magnitudes. As the disorder strength is adjusted, the phase transition shifts from a discontinuous to a continuous nature. Furthermore, bond disorder promotes ordering near the transition by facilitating a homogeneous flocking state under conditions of high disorder. This phenomenon accelerates information propagation within the system and increases its information entropy. Our research provides novel insights into how intrinsic inhomogeneity influences self-propelled particle systems.

In the recent publication, Phys. Rev. B 102, 144420 (2020), Cabrera-Baez et al. present a study of the effects of Cd-substitution for Zn in the ferromagnetic compound GdFe2Zn20. As part of this paper, they claim that for GdFe2Zn18.6Cd1.4 the effective moment of Gd is reduced by 25% and the saturated moment of Gd is reduced by over 40%. We regrew representative members of the GdFe2Zn(20-x)Cdx series and did not find any such reductions. In addition, we measured several crystals from the growth batch that was used by Cabrera-Baez et al. and did not see such reductions. Although there is a modest increase in TC with Cd substitution, there is no significant change in the Gd effective moment or the saturated moment associated with the low temperature ferromagnetic state.

Large-scale text corpora are becoming essential for numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, making automatic language identification (LangID) a critical technology for assembling multilingual datasets. Although the literature often treats LangID as a solved problem, citing models with over 90% average F1 scores across up to 1,366 languages, we trained models on 1,629 languages with comparable test performance. However, we discovered that the actual accuracy of human-verified LangID on web-crawl corpora generated by these models is merely around 5% for many low-resource languages, highlighting a critical gap in current evaluation methods. Our analysis identified various error patterns stemming from domain mismatches, class imbalance, linguistic similarity, and limited model expressiveness. To address these issues, we propose two strategies: wordlist-based tunable-precision filters (for which we provide curated lists for approximately 500 languages) and transformer-based semi-supervised LangID models. These approaches raise the median dataset precision from 5.5% to 71.2%. Consequently, we have created an initial dataset containing over 100,000 relatively clean sentences for more than 500 languages, laying the groundwork for a future 1,000-language web text corpus.

Barely set-valued tableaux represent a variation of Young tableaux where a single box can hold two numbers. Recent findings have established product formulas that count specific classes of these tableaux. This work introduces a major index variant for such tableaux to derive q-analogs of those product formulas. Additionally, we present both product formulas and their q-analogs for barely set-valued plane partitions. The proofs rely on various probability distributions defined on the order ideals of a poset, parameterized by a real number q > 0, which we believe may hold independent significance.

This study investigates the extent to which genuine synonym substitution attacks (SSAs) are feasible. By analyzing how SSAs substitute words within original sentences, we demonstrate that significant barriers remain, causing current SSAs to produce invalid adversarial examples. Specifically, we find that four common word substitution techniques result in a high proportion of invalid replacements that are either ungrammatical or fail to maintain the source sentence's meaning. Furthermore, we reveal that the semantic and grammatical constraints employed in SSAs to identify invalid word changes are largely inadequate for detecting flawed adversarial samples. Our findings serve as a crucial foundation for developing more robust SSAs in the future.

When a vector field's singular point undergoes resonance, a formal invariant cone emerges. During the 1970s, Pyartli demonstrated that in the case of $(-1,1)$-resonance, this cone is analytic and represents the degeneration of a family of invariant cylinders. Stolovitch, in his thesis, introduced a novel normal form and showed that for simple resonances subject to arithmetic conditions, the cone constitutes the germ of an analytic variety. This paper presents a versal deformation theorem for analytic vector fields featuring an isolated singularity over Cantor sets. Our findings indicate that, under arithmetic conditions, the resonant cone degenerates into a set of invariant manifolds, mirroring Pyartli's scenario. Furthermore, regarding the multi-Hopf bifurcation (specifically $(-1,1)^d$-resonance), our results establish the existence of vanishing tori that support quasi-periodic motions, thereby extending prior work by Chenciner and Li.

This work presents a machine learning framework for deriving effective interactions in condensed matter systems through scattering techniques. Using colloidal suspensions as a case study, we demonstrate that the effective potential can be probabilistically reconstructed from scattering spectra without relying on restrictive model assumptions. When compared to existing parametric methods, our approach exhibits superior performance in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and applicability. Ultimately, this methodology facilitates the quantification of interactions within highly correlated systems by leveraging scattering and diffraction experiments.

This study examines the thermodynamic behavior of a one-dimensional spin-crossover molecular chain under constant external pressure, utilizing an effective compressible degenerate Ising model as the theoretical basis. Through the application of transfer matrix formalism, we derive analytic results for the low-spin to high-spin transition. Specifically, we obtain exact expressions for the fraction of molecules in the high-spin state, the correlation function, and heat capacity. Furthermore, we analyze the parameter regime governing the spin crossover and illustrate the influence of pressure on the transition's location.

Global games represent a category of incomplete information games characterized by strategic complementarity in payoffs, which motivates agents to coordinate their decisions. While these games are frequently applied to socioeconomic phenomena assuming agents receive Gaussian private signals, this study examines a variant where agents observe Poisson random variables. This observation model draws inspiration from microbiology applications, where information is transmitted through discrete molecular signals instead of continuous ones. Despite this model violating key technical assumptions inherent to the Gaussian framework, we provide preliminary findings on the existence of Bayesian Nash equilibria using pure threshold strategies for two specific state-of-the-world scenarios: an arbitrarily distributed discrete binary state and a continuous state following a uniform distribution.

Skew Dyck paths resemble Dyck paths but permit an extra south-west step $(-1,-1)$, as long as the path remains non-self-intersecting. In contrast, lattice paths featuring catastrophes can descend from any height directly to the origin in a single move. This study merges these two concepts, employing a strictly generating function-based approach and utilizing the kernel method for analysis.

K-FAC (arXiv:1503.05671, arXiv:1602.01407) serves as a practical implementation of Natural Gradient (NG) for Deep Learning (DL), yet it is hindered by the computational cost of inverting the "Kronecker-Factors" (K-factors). RS-KFAC (arXiv:2206.15397) enhances K-FAC by offering an efficient method to estimate these inverses. This paper leverages the exponential-average construction of K-factors and applies online numerical linear algebra techniques to introduce an even more cost-effective (though less precise) approach for estimating K-factor inverses in Fully Connected layers. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating our proposed update into RS-KFAC reduces inversion error with negligible CPU overhead. Building on this procedure, along with its correction and RS-KFAC, we develop three practical algorithms for optimizing generic Deep Neural Networks. Numerical evaluations indicate that two of these algorithms surpass RS-KFAC across all target test accuracies on CIFAR10 classification using a slightly modified VGG16_bn. Furthermore, our proposed methods achieve 91% test accuracy more rapidly than SENG (the state-of-the-art empirical NG implementation; arXiv:2006.05924), although they fall short of SENG when targeting higher accuracy levels.
