This reliance yields strong results on standard benchmarks but causes poor generalization and unintuitive failures in difficult scenarios, a phenomenon known as "shortcut learning." In the domain of text recognition, we identify a specific shortcut where models excessively depend on local image statistics. To address this, we propose a method that regulates this dependency to enhance recognition performance.

Named TextAdaIN, our technique introduces local distortions into feature maps to prevent overfitting to these statistics. It treats each feature map as a sequence and intentionally mismatches fine-grained statistics across elements within a mini-batch. Despite its simplicity, extensive experiments demonstrate that TextAdaIN outperforms more complex alternatives. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on standard handwritten text recognition benchmarks, generalizes across various architectures and scene text domains, and improves robustness under challenging conditions. The official PyTorch implementation is available at https://github.com/amazon-research/textadain-robust-recognition.

This study demonstrates that propositional modal logic products, which include the logic of reflexive frames T as a component, can be embedded within their single-variable fragments. The provided proof is a streamlined adaptation of a forthcoming result concerning similar embeddings for products and expanding relativized products that feature KTB—the logic of reflexive and symmetric Kripke frames—as a factor.

This paper introduces a novel metric, the vulnerability index (VuIx), designed to evaluate how susceptible power system measurements are to data integrity attacks. By utilizing information theoretic measures, the VuIx assesses the impact of such attacks on the fundamental tradeoff between disruption and detection. Calculating the VuIx for a system's measurements generates a ranking that reflects their relative exposure to these attacks. Applying this framework to the IEEE 9-bus and 30-bus test systems reveals that power injection measurements are significantly more vulnerable to data integrity attacks than power flow measurements, with a detailed numerical analysis of the VuIx values provided for these test systems.

Space-based gravitational wave detection holds the promise of opening a new observational window into the strong-field dynamics of gravity within astrophysics and cosmology. This article serves as an excerpt from a feasibility report commissioned nearly ten years ago by the National Space Science Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). The study aimed to investigate various mission concepts for detecting gravitational waves in space as alternatives to the (e)LISA mission, while also examining necessary technological requirements. By evaluating the balance between scientific potential and technical feasibility, the report analyzed several representative mission options and ultimately recommended a specific mission design to guide future research and development within the CAS. This design was subsequently adopted as the baseline for the current TAIJI mission. Constrained by current technological capabilities, the TAIJI mission's baseline parameters were optimized to enhance the detector's ability to probe high-redshift light seeds and intermediate-mass black holes, thereby providing crucial insights into the formation of structure in the early universe.

This study introduces an efficiently computable lower bound for quantum Fisher information (QFI), suitable for near-term quantum hardware. The bound holds intrinsic value as it meets the fundamental criteria for a QFI metric; specifically, it functions as a QFI measure for subnormalized states, thereby extending the standard definition. This approach utilizes generalized fidelity on a truncated state, formed by selecting the $m$ largest eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors from the probe state $\rho_{\theta}$. By examining unitary families of exact states, we evaluate the characteristics of this proposed lower bound and illustrate its effectiveness in enabling efficient QFI estimation.

The Dynamic State Index (DSI) is a scalar metric intended to detect atmospheric phenomena, including fronts, hurricanes, and distinct weather patterns. Defined as the Jacobian determinant of three components characterizing three-dimensional fluid flows—the Bernoulli stream function, potential vorticity (PV), and potential temperature—this study investigates two key questions: whether the DSI's mathematical formulation can be simplified without losing essential information, and if such simplification varies across spatial scales. Utilizing principal component analysis, we determine that only three of the six terms comprising the Jacobian determinant are necessary for future DSI computations.

As urban underground infrastructure ages, maintenance and repair have become increasingly critical challenges. Cities struggle with planning upkeep, anticipating and reacting to infrastructure failures, and achieving their smart city goals largely due to an incomplete grasp of their current infrastructure status. Accurate and comprehensive digital records of subterranean systems—such as electricity, water, and natural gas—are scarce, creating significant obstacles for those designing and executing construction projects. To tackle these problems, we present GUIDES, a novel framework for converting and managing data on urban underground infrastructure. This system empowers city administrators, workers, contractors, and the general public to access digitized, integrated information for more informed decision-making. This demo paper outlines the GUIDES architecture and details two core components: (i) the mapping of underground infrastructure systems and (ii) the integration of diverse geospatial data.

Conversational agents often struggle to detect implicit assumptions in user instructions, a capability that humans effortlessly possess through common sense. To address this, we introduce a zero-shot commonsense reasoning system designed for conversational agents. Our reasoner identifies these unstated premises by mapping user commands to a general "if-(state), then-(action), because-(goal)" framework. Leveraging a state-of-the-art, transformer-based generative commonsense knowledge base (KB) as its background knowledge source, the system employs a novel iterative knowledge query mechanism. This mechanism extracts multi-hop reasoning chains from the neural KB and utilizes symbolic logic rules to substantially narrow the search space. Acknowledging that existing commonsense KBs often lack certain information, we propose a dynamic question generation strategy to conversationally elicit missing knowledge from human users by presenting contextualized queries. In a user study, our model demonstrated a 35% higher success rate compared to the state-of-the-art.

Low-rank tensors exhibit linear dependencies among their entries, which can be formulated as multi-linear polynomials known as generating polynomials. These polynomials serve as a tool for calculating tensor rank decompositions and approximations with low rank. It is demonstrated that this approach yields a quasi-optimal low-rank approximation when the input tensor is sufficiently near to a low-rank tensor.

Program synthesis and rewrite-based optimization frequently involve searching through vast spaces of programs. Current methods typically depend on specialized data structures—such as version-space algebras, finite tree automata, or e-graphs—to represent these programs compactly. These existing structures leverage the independence of subterms to achieve compactness but suffer from exponential growth when subterm choices are interdependent. We propose Equality-Constrained Tree Automata (ECTAs), a generalized framework capable of efficiently representing large program spaces even when subterms are entangled. We also provide efficient algorithms for extracting programs from ECTAs, which have been implemented in a high-performance Haskell library named \texttt{ecta}. Leveraging \texttt{ecta}, we developed \textsc{Hectare}, a type-driven program synthesizer for Haskell. \textsc{Hectare} achieves an average speedup of 8x compared to the state-of-the-art synthesizer Hoogle+, despite its implementation being roughly ten times smaller.

The ALICE detector at the CERN LHC measured the production of $\pi^{\pm}$, $\rm{K}^{\pm}$, $\rm{K}^{0}_{S}$, $\rm{K}^{*}(892)^{0}$, $\rm{p}$, $\phi(1020)$, $\Lambda$, $\Xi^{-}$, $\Omega^{-}$, and their antiparticles in inelastic proton-proton (pp) collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, focusing on midrapidity ($|y|<0.5$) and transverse momentum ($p_{\rm{T}}$). Additionally, this report presents the first-ever single-particle $p_{\rm{T}}$ distributions for $\rm{K}^{0}_{S}$, $\Lambda$, and $\overline{\Lambda}$ in inelastic pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 7 TeV. These distributions were analyzed within the $0\leq p_{\rm{T}}\leq20$ GeV/$c$ range at midrapidity, varying by particle type. The study examines $p_{\rm{T}}$ spectra, integrated yields, and yield ratios across different collision energies, comparing them with lower-energy measurements and general-purpose QCD-inspired Monte Carlo models. Results indicate a hardening of spectra at high $p_{\rm{T}}$ as collision energy rises, a trend consistent across all studied species. Furthermore, the scaling properties regarding transverse mass and $x_{\rm{T}}\equiv2p_{\rm{T}}/\sqrt{s}$ were investigated. When collision energy increased from 7 to 13 TeV, the yields of non- and single-strange hadrons normalized to pion yields stayed roughly constant with respect to $\sqrt{s}$, whereas multi-strange hadron ratios showed enhancements. Finally, the $p_{\rm{T}$-differential cross sections for $\pi^{\pm}$, $\rm{K}^{\pm}$, and $\rm{p}$ ($\overline{\rm{p}}$) were compared against next-to-leading order perturbative QCD calculations, revealing that these calculations overestimate cross sections for $\pi^{\pm}$ and $\rm{p}$ ($\overline{\rm{p}}$) at high $p_{\rm{T}}$.

This study numerically examines how distinct network structures impact epidemic dynamics within the contact process. We first observe that the variability difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is minimal, despite heterogeneous structures leading to lower prevalence rates. Unlike networks without communities, strong community structures can trigger secondary outbreaks and produce two distinct peaks in variability. Specifically, within local communities, the exceptionally high variability during the early outbreak stage complicates epidemic prediction. Crucially, bridgeness significantly affects predictability; as the distance between the initial seed and the bridgeness increases, prediction accuracy decreases. Furthermore, we analyzed how different disease reaction mechanisms influence variability, finding that these mechanisms result in distinct variability outcomes by the end of the epidemic.

Maintaining posture and balance are fundamental prerequisites for humanoid robots executing motor functions such as locomotion and environmental interaction; consequently, posture control is a key metric in assessing humanoid performance. This study presents and analyzes a performance indicator that compares the body sway of a robot standing on a moving surface against that of healthy humans performing the same task, aiming specifically to evaluate human-likeness. The proposed measure was validated using three human-inspired posture control systems: independent channel (IC), disturbance identification and compensation (DEC), and eigenmovement (EM). Finally, the advantages and constraints associated with these human-inspired control mechanisms are discussed.

This study elucidates the characteristics of sound spectra in subsonic jets by addressing three problems of escalating complexity. Initially, an analytical solution is derived for the sound field generated by a point source within a two-dimensional plug flow. Subsequently, the sound field is determined by solving the linearized Euler equations for a point source situated in a diverging axisymmetric jet. Finally, the paper examines acoustic waves propagating through a turbulent jet using data from direct numerical simulations. Across all three scenarios, the pressure and density fields are analyzed within the frequency-wavenumber domain. The results indicate that acoustic waves can be categorized into three primary frequency-dependent groups, supported by a physical rationale for this classification. The primary finding is that at low Strouhal numbers, acoustic waves adhere to the d'Alembertian dispersion relation.

We report simultaneous, multi-colour optical light curves of the companion star to the black-widow pulsar PSR J2051-0827, acquired roughly a decade apart with ULTRACAM and HiPERCAM. The ULTRACAM data reaffirm a previously noted asymmetry where the companion's leading hemisphere is brighter than its trailing one. Conversely, the HiPERCAM observations reveal no such asymmetry, indicating that the underlying mechanism varies on timescales of ten years or shorter. By fitting the symmetrical HiPERCAM curves with a direct-heating model, we derived system parameters, including an orbital inclination of $55.9^{+4.8}_{-4.1}$ degrees, which aligns well with radio-eclipse limits. We determined that roughly 50% of the pulsar's spin-down energy is converted into optical luminosity, yielding temperatures of approximately $5150^{+190}_{-190}$ K on the day side and $2750^{+130}_{-150}$ K on the night side. The companion nearly fills its Roche lobe ($f_{\rm RL} =0.88^{+0.02}_{-0.02}$), possesses a mass of $0.039^{+0.010}_{-0.011}$ M$_{\odot}$, and exhibits a mean density of $20.24^{+0.59}_{-0.44}$ g cm$^{-3}$ with an apsidal motion constant between $0.0036$ and $0.0047$. While these mass and density values are consistent with brown dwarfs, the apsidal motion constant suggests a significantly more centrally condensed internal structure than typically observed in such objects.

The Lightning Network (LN) represents a leading off-chain scaling solution for Bitcoin, allowing transactions that bypass the blockchain's inherent scalability constraints. This paper presents CLoTH, a simulator designed for Hashed Time-Locked Contract (HTLC) payment networks, with the Lightning Network serving as its primary real-world implementation. CLoTH models payments and network structures defined by their inputs, generating performance metrics such as payment completion times and failure probabilities. By simulating these scenarios, the tool aids in anticipating potential development challenges and evaluating the impact of proposed optimizations prior to deployment. Future publications will detail the outcomes of these simulations.

To address the global health crisis posed by the Covid-19 pandemic, decision-makers must act on extensive health data, with actions carrying significant implications for patients. Due to the perceived benefits of processing large datasets, automated decision-making (ADM) systems have been adopted to replace human decision-making (HDM). This study examines a specific ADM application—vaccine allocation for the public—comparing it with HDM. We specifically investigate how trust and social group preferences impact the perceived legitimacy of these allocation strategies. A survey employing a 2x2 randomized factorial design was conducted with 1,602 German participants, manipulating decision-making agents (human vs. algorithm) and social group prioritization (teachers vs. prisoners). Results indicate that general trust in ADM and preferences for specific social groups significantly influence the legitimacy of vaccine distribution. However, contrary to expectations, trust in the decision agent did not moderate the relationship between social group preference and legitimacy. Furthermore, the type of decision-maker (human versus algorithm) also failed to moderate this effect. We conclude that the mere trustworthiness of an ADM system does not guarantee its legitimacy.

The Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) posits that within a sufficiently large, randomly initialized neural network, there exists a subnetwork capable of approximating a target network without requiring training. We expand the theoretical foundations of the strong LTH to align more closely with the original hypothesis by generalizing weight modifications during pre-training to include perturbations around initialization. Specifically, we address two open questions: Does permitting an $\varepsilon$-scale perturbation on random initial weights lower the over-parameterization threshold required for the candidate network in the strong LTH? Additionally, does the weight adjustment resulting from SGD correspond to an effective set of such perturbations? To resolve the first query, we extend subset sum theory to accommodate perturbations among candidates and demonstrate that applying this to neural networks confirms that $\varepsilon$-perturbations indeed reduce the over-parameterization demand of the strong LTH. Regarding the second question, experimental results indicate that weights modified via projected SGD yield superior performance when subjected to strong LTH pruning.

This paper examines rigid matter shells and black hole-like configurations on expanding bubbles that realize de Sitter space, as introduced in arXiv:1807.01570. We derive explicit solutions for both the matter shell and the black hole scenarios, with the latter offering a method to construct Randall-Sundrum braneworld black holes in four dimensions.

We construct three-terminal hybrid devices featuring a nanowire segment proximitized by a superconductor, equipped with two tunnel probe contacts on either side of the segment. Simultaneous tunneling measurements are conducted at both ends. Our analysis identifies certain states as delocalized above-gap states appearing on both terminals, alongside states localized near a single tunnel barrier. These delocalized states persist from zero up to finite magnetic fields exceeding 0.5 T. Within the parameter regime of these delocalized states, we investigate correlated subgap resonances predicted by the Majorana zero mode hypothesis. Although both sides display ubiquitous low-energy features at high fields, no correlation is detected. Simulations based on a one-dimensional effective model indicate that delocalized states likely correspond to lower one-dimensional subbands, whereas localized states arise from higher subbands. Consequently, to prevent localization in higher subbands and realize Majorana zero modes, further reduction of disorder may be necessary.

The Probabilistic Solar Particle Event foRecasting (PROSPER) model estimates both the likelihood of occurrence and the anticipated peak flux for Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) events. These predictions, calculated for integral proton energies exceeding 10, 30, and 100 MeV, are based on solar flare attributes (such as longitude and magnitude), coronal mass ejection parameters (including width and speed), and combinations of these factors. This paper outlines the PROSPER methodology for generating SEP forecasts and presents a validation of the model using archived data through selected case studies. Furthermore, the PROSPER model has been integrated into the new operational Advanced Solar Particle Event Casting System (ASPECS) to deliver nowcasting (short-term forecasting) of SEP events as a component of ESA's future SEP Advanced Warning System (SAWS). In addition, ASPECS offers a "run on demand" feature that allows users to query PROSPER for historical event analysis.

Entity Resolution is a fundamental data integration challenge that depends on blocking strategies to mitigate its quadratic time complexity. Schema-agnostic blocking offers high recall without requiring domain knowledge, making it applicable to data with varying structures and schemas; however, it generates numerous irrelevant candidate pairs. Meta-blocking techniques address this by leveraging co-occurrence patterns within blocks to significantly reduce comparisons: they first assign scores to candidate pairs based on their likelihood of matching and then prune those with the lowest scores. Supervised Meta-blocking enhances this by aggregating multiple scores into feature vectors for a binary classifier. Generalized Supervised Meta-blocking further improves upon this by employing probabilistic classifiers to generate scores for pruning algorithms, while also testing new weighting schemes as features. Extensive experiments identify the most effective pruning algorithms, optimal feature sets, and the minimum training set size required, with the resulting approaches demonstrating excellent performance across established benchmark datasets.

To achieve a more realistic classical description of natural quantum systems, we introduce a two-dimensional tensor network algorithm designed to analyze finite-temperature behaviors in frustrated quantum models and real materials. Central to this approach is the infinite projected entangled simplex operator ansatz, which enables the investigation of thermodynamic properties. We generate state-of-the-art benchmark results by examining the highly complex spin-1/2 Heisenberg anti-ferromagnet on the Kagome lattice, specifically focusing on the melting of magnetization plateaus under varying magnetic fields and temperatures. Furthermore, by closely aligning with experimental data from actual quantum materials, we analyze the finite-temperature characteristics of Ca$_{10}$Cr$_7$O$_{28}$. We compare the magnetization curve of this compound under an external magnetic field at finite temperature against classically simulated data. As a pioneering theoretical framework that integrates both thermal fluctuations and quantum correlations for this specific material, our work helps resolve the ongoing controversy between experimental observations and prior theoretical predictions regarding its magnetization process.

To date, observations have identified over 1,500 DBZ or DZ white dwarfs (WDs), many of which exhibit polluted atmospheres containing metal elements. The surface abundances of heavy elements in these known WDs follow a distinct evolutionary sequence. Utilizing the Modules for Experiments in Stellar Evolution, we generated DB WD models to simulate element diffusion driven by strong gravitational fields and the accretion of metal-rich material from disrupted planets. Our results indicate that input parameters ($\alpha_{\rm MLT}$, $\alpha_{\rm th}$, and $Z$) exert a negligible influence on DB WD structures, including internal temperatures, chemical profiles, and convective zones. Instead, heavy element abundances are governed by the mass-accretion rate and the effective temperature. The evolutionary sequence of calcium observed in approximately 1,500 DB or DBZ WDs cannot be accounted for by a model assuming a constant mass-accretion rate; however, it aligns well with a model where the accretion rate declines by a power law when $T_{\rm eff}>10$ kK and rises slightly by another power law when $T_{\rm eff}<10$ kK. Ultimately, the observed evolutionary sequence of heavy element abundances in DB WDs arises from the combined effects of WD cooling and variations in the mass-accretion rate.

Pre-trained models have demonstrated significant efficacy in advancing task-oriented dialogue systems. Nevertheless, existing pre-training approaches primarily concentrate on improving dialogue understanding and generation, often overlooking the optimization of dialogue policies. To address this, we introduce GALAXY, a new pre-trained dialogue model that leverages semi-supervised learning to explicitly learn dialogue policies from both limited labeled data and extensive unlabeled corpora. Specifically, our approach incorporates a dialogue act prediction task to facilitate policy optimization during pre-training and utilizes a consistency regularization term to enhance representations using unlabeled dialogues. Additionally, we implement a gating mechanism to appropriately weight selected unlabeled samples. Experimental findings indicate that GALAXY significantly boosts the performance of task-oriented dialogue systems, establishing new state-of-the-art benchmarks on the In-Car, MultiWOZ2.0, and MultiWOZ2.1 datasets by improving end-to-end combined scores by 2.5, 5.3, and 5.5 points, respectively. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that GALAXY exhibits superior few-shot capabilities compared to existing models across various low-resource scenarios.

In recent years, there has been a surge in user-centric applications that demand effective knowledge transfer across tasks within data-scarce environments. A prime example is personalization, which involves adapting a pre-trained system using limited labeled data from a specific user. This scenario necessitates high accuracy with minimal computational overhead, making the Pareto frontier between accuracy and adaptation cost a critical factor. This paper advances that frontier in few-shot image classification by introducing a novel adaptive module called Contextual Squeeze-and-Excitation (CaSE). CaSE enhances performance by adjusting a pre-trained neural network to a new task using just a single forward pass of user data. By employing meta-trained CaSE blocks to conditionally adapt the network body and a fine-tuning procedure for a linear head, we propose a method named UpperCaSE. On the 26 VTAB+MD datasets and the challenging ORBIT real-world personalization benchmark, UpperCaSE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy among meta-learners. It narrows the performance gap with leading fine-tuning approaches while reducing adaptation costs by orders of magnitude.

We (almost) finalize the time complexity for computing vertex fault-tolerant (VFT) spanners with optimal sparsity, up to polylogarithmic factors. VFT spanners are sparse subgraphs that maintain distance metrics within a small multiplicative stretch even when vertex failures occur. Introduced by [Chechik et al., STOC 2009], these structures have garnered significant attention. We present algorithms for calculating nearly optimal $f$-VFT spanners for any $n$-vertex graph with $m$ edges, achieving near-optimal runtime across various models:
*   **Randomized Sequential:** An algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(m)$ runtime, independent of the fault count $f$. This surpasses the previous best bound of $\widetilde{O}(f^{1-1/k}\cdot n^{2+1/k}+f^2 m)$ established by [Bodwin, Dinitz and Robelle, SODA 2021].
*   **Distributed Congested Clique:** An algorithm completing in $\widetilde{O}(1)$ rounds, improving on [Dinitz and Robelle, PODC 2020], which required $\widetilde{O}(f^{2})$ rounds for spanners with near-optimal sparsity.
*   **PRAM (CRCW):** An algorithm utilizing $\widetilde{O}(m)$ work and $\widetilde{O}(1)$ depth. This improves upon prior bounds derived from [Dinitz and Krauthgamer, PODC 2011], which relied on $\widetilde{O}(f^3m)$ work and $\widetilde{O}(f^3)$ depth to achieve sub-optimal results.

As a direct consequence, we introduce the first nearly-optimal PRAM algorithm for computing nearly optimal $\lambda$-\emph{vertex} connectivity certificates using near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth. This advances the state-of-the-art parallel bounds of $\widetilde{O}(1)$ depth and $O(\lambda m)$ work, previously set by [Karger and Motwani, STOC'93].

Foundation models promise to disrupt the future of AI by expanding deep learning through increased model scale and broader, larger datasets. These systems deliver state-of-the-art results across diverse fields, including natural language processing and computer vision, often via additional fine-tuning. They display unique emergent capabilities, such as in-context learning, which allows models to generate answers based on a few examples provided in the prompt without prior specific training. Furthermore, the trend toward model homogenization could consolidate a vast array of specialized tools into a handful of massive models managed by a few corporations, thereby altering power dynamics and control within the AI landscape. This paper offers a concise introduction to foundation models, distinguishing them clearly from earlier deep learning approaches, tracing the historical evolution of machine learning toward this paradigm, exploring socio-technical dimensions like organizational challenges and user interaction, and outlining directions for future research.

Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is usually optimized for average loss, often leading to estimators that are vulnerable to outliers, suffer from poor generalization, or exhibit unfairness toward specific subgroups. Although numerous approaches tackle these issues in isolation, this paper introduces a unified solution called Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization (TERM). Specifically, we demonstrate that a simple hyperparameter extension to ERM, known as the "tilt," allows for flexible control over the impact of individual losses. We offer multiple interpretations of this framework: TERM can either dampen or amplify outlier influence to enhance robustness or fairness, possesses variance-reduction characteristics that improve generalization, and serves as a smooth approximation of superquantile methods. We also develop both batch and stochastic first-order optimization algorithms for TERM, proving it can be solved efficiently compared to standard alternatives. Furthermore, we illustrate TERM's versatility across various tasks, including subgroup fairness enforcement, outlier mitigation, and class imbalance handling. TERM not only matches the performance of specialized existing methods but also facilitates novel applications, such as simultaneously addressing outliers and promoting fairness.

In spherical space, a regular tetrahedron supports only a finite set of simple closed geodesics. For every pair of coprime integers $(p,q)$, specific values $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ have been identified as functions of $p$ and $q$, adhering to the condition $\pi/3 < \alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < 2\pi/3$. It is established that if the face angle $\alpha$ of the regular tetrahedron lies within the interval $(\pi/3, \alpha_1)$, exactly one simple closed geodesic of type $(p,q)$ exists, unique modulo rigid motions of the tetrahedron. Conversely, when the face angle $\alpha$ falls in the interval $(\alpha_2, 2\pi/3)$, no simple closed geodesic of type $(p,q)$ exists on the regular tetrahedron.

This paper examines the existence and uniqueness of fixed points for the product of two nonlinear operators within a Banach algebra. Furthermore, it establishes an approximation technique for fixed points associated with hybrid nonlinear equations in Banach algebras, applying this method to two distinct and significant types of functional equations. Finally, numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the practical applicability of the obtained results.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning (RL) is extensively applied across diverse robotic control tasks. By interpreting actor-critic RL through the lens of variational inference (VI), the policy network learns to approximate the posterior distribution of actions based on optimality criteria. Nevertheless, practical implementations often result in suboptimal policies due to the amortization gap and inadequate exploration. Drawing inspiration from the application of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) in VI, this work introduces the integration of HMC with the actor-critic policy network, a method named {\it Hamiltonian Policy}. In this approach, actions are evolved from the base policy using HMC, offering several advantages. First, HMC refines the policy distribution to more accurately approximate the posterior, thereby mitigating the amortization gap. Second, it directs exploration toward action space regions with higher Q-values, boosting exploration efficiency. Furthermore, rather than directly applying HMC to RL, we introduce a novel leapfrog operator to simulate Hamiltonian dynamics. Additionally, in safe RL scenarios, the proposed method not only increases the achieved return but also decreases safety constraint violations by filtering out potentially unsafe actions. Comprehensive empirical evaluations on continuous control benchmarks, including MuJoCo and PyBullet Roboschool, demonstrate that our approach offers a data-efficient and straightforward enhancement over existing actor-critic techniques.

In recent years, numerous low-threshold dark matter (DM) direct detection experiments have reported unexplained excesses at low energies. For instance, the CRESST experiment has identified unidentified events below approximately 200 eV, a finding that complicates the search for GeV-scale DM by degrading detector performance. This study evaluates how nuclear recoil timing information influences DM signal discovery and model selection in a low-threshold experiment constrained by a background resembling these low-energy unidentified events. Focusing on the CRESST collaboration's Al₂O₃ target—which achieved an energy threshold as low as 19.7 eV—we assess the experiment's capacity to detect a signal above a specific background or to reject spin-independent (SI) interactions in favor of magnetic dipole (MD) coupling, quantified by p-values. We calculate these p-values under two conditions: 1) incorporating timing information, and 2) assuming its absence. Comparing these approaches reveals that while timing data has a marginal effect on the potential for DM discovery, it yields significantly stronger results for distinguishing between the SI and MD models. For the parameters examined, the p-value for rejecting SI interactions in favor of MD coupling is approximately 0.11 for an exposure of 460 g·year, dropping to about 0.06 when timing information is utilized. This qualitative conclusion regarding the utility of timing information holds true even for exposures as high as 1 kg·year. Concurrently, our findings indicate that achieving a 90% confidence level rejection of SI interactions in favor of MD coupling is feasible with an upgrade to the CRESST experiment.

Variational quantum algorithms offer a promising avenue for addressing partial differential equations. While standard numerical techniques typically rely on finite difference schemes reducible to linear algebra, this work explores three distinct quantum strategies for solving the heat equation. The direct variational method seeks the solution by minimizing a Hamiltonian's expectation value, where the ground state corresponds to the problem's solution; however, the exponential number of Pauli terms in the Hamiltonian usually precludes quantum speedup. Although the Hadamard test-based approach mitigates this issue, simulations have not yet definitively demonstrated that its Ansatz circuit scales with polynomial depth relative to the qubit count. In contrast, the Ansatz tree method leverages an explicit matrix representation, enabling a clear advantage over classical algorithms. Numerical simulations involving up to $n=8$ qubits confirm that this approach achieves exponential speedup.

An $n \times n$ matrix composed of $\pm 1$ entries that functions as a scaled isometry on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is known as a Hadamard matrix; however, these only exist for specific dimensions. By integrating number-theoretic and probabilistic methods, we develop a construction of $\pm 1$ matrices that serve as approximate scaled isometries in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for every $n$. Specifically, the resulting matrices possess condition numbers bounded by a constant that does not depend on $n$. Leveraging this construction, we demonstrate a phase transition regarding the likelihood that a random frame includes a Riesz basis. We prove that a random frame in $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of $N$ vectors with independent, identically distributed coordinates from a non-degenerate symmetric distribution contains numerous Riesz bases with high probability whenever $N \ge \exp(Cn)$. Conversely, if the entries follow a subgaussian distribution, we show that a random frame is unlikely to contain a Riesz basis when $N \le \exp(cn)$, where $c$ and $C$ are constants determined by the specific entry distribution.

We introduce a novel stock market index designed to quantify market chaos by analyzing mutual shifts in asset prices. Leveraging a tensor-based embedding of market data, this index overcomes the limitations of conventional value- or capitalization-weighting methods found in popular indexes. We demonstrate that our index serves as a robust estimator of market volatility, facilitating reliable market segmentation. Furthermore, by employing a time-dependent dynamical system model, we examine the dynamics and kinematics of realized volatility in relation to implied volatility. Computational analysis spanning January 1990 to December 2019 reveals a bidirectional causal relationship between the processes driving realized and implied volatility. Notably, implied volatility exerts a stronger causal influence on realized volatility than vice versa, indicating that implied volatility plays a pivotal role in characterizing the market's actual volatility.

This study focuses on identifying and categorizing stellar flares and potential coronal mass ejection (CME) indicators within optical spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 14. The analysis targets over 630,000 main-sequence stars of spectral types F, G, K, and M, utilizing individual spectral exposures. An automated flare detection method was employed by measuring significant amplitude shifts in the $H\alpha$ and $H\beta$ lines following Gaussian profile fitting to the line cores. CMEs were sought by detecting asymmetries in Balmer lines attributed to Doppler shifts from plasma motion along the line of sight.

We found 281 flares on late-type stars (spectral types K3 to M9) and identified six potential CME candidates characterized by excess flux in the Balmer line wings. Flare energies in $H\alpha$ and CME candidate masses were subsequently calculated. The $H\alpha$ flare energies span from $3 \times 10^{28}$ to $2 \times 10^{33}$ erg; these energies rise with earlier spectral types, whereas the frequency of flaring increases with later types. Estimated masses for the CME candidates fall between $6 \times 10^{16}$ and $6 \times 10^{18}$ g, with maximum projected velocities ranging from approximately 300 to 700 km/s. Our low CME detection rate aligns with prior research, indicating that the occurrence rate of CMEs on late-type main-sequence stars detectable via optical spectroscopy is minimal.

This paper introduces a novel deep neural network classifier that leverages polyhedral conic classification functions to simultaneously enhance inter-class separation and reduce intra-class variation. The approach utilizes two distinct loss terms: one to maximize margins for better class separation, and another to regulate the compactness of class acceptance regions. This method offers a clear geometric interpretation grounded in polyhedral conic function geometry. We evaluated the classifier on diverse visual tasks, including closed and open set recognition as well as anomaly detection. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method generally surpasses other state-of-the-art techniques, making it a superior option, particularly for open set recognition scenarios.

The presence of quantum tricriticality and exotic phases has been identified in a Dicke triangle (TDT) system, consisting of three cavities housing ensembles of three-level atoms and coupled via an artificial magnetic field. In this setup, the conventional superradiant (SR) phase transitions into the normal phase along first- and second-order boundaries that intersect at tricritical points. Beyond the standard SR phase, adjusting the artificial magnetic field reveals a chiral superradiant (CSR) phase, distinguished by a nonzero photon current and bounded by chiral tricritical points (CTCPs). By analyzing various critical exponents, researchers can distinguish the universality classes of the CTCP and standard tricritical points (TCP) from those of second-order critical points, as well as identify unique critical behaviors separating the two superradiant phases. The TDT framework is applicable across diverse platforms, such as atoms in optical cavities and circuit QED systems, facilitating the investigation of numerous critical manifolds.

We have identified a spin integral of motion for neutrinos traveling through moving, polarized matter. This newly derived operator enables a consistent classification of neutrino states within such environments and facilitates a systematic analysis of associated physical phenomena. Leveraging this operator, we derive the neutrino dispersion relation and examine specific instances of it.

Enceladus stands as a key astrobiological target, largely because of the salty plume material detected by the Cassini spacecraft and the hypothesized subsurface ocean maintained by tidal heating. While one theory posits that these plumes originate from a direct conduit linking the ocean to the surface through a full-shell fracture spanning approximately 10 km, this study investigates an alternative mechanism. We propose that shear heating within the shallower "tiger stripe" fractures causes partial melting of the ice shell, enabling interstitial fluid to erupt as geysers. Utilizing a two-dimensional multiphase reactive transport model, we simulated the thermomechanics of a mushy region created by localized shear heating in a saline ice shell. Our results predict the temperature, porosity, melting rate, and liquid volume of this intrashell mushy zone surrounding the fracture. We found that the brine volume within this zone is sufficient to sustain geysers for roughly 250,000 years without further melting, and the internal melting rate aligns with observed ice ejection rates. However, the composition of the brine in the mushy zone differs from the ocean due to the partial melting process. This shear heating mechanism for geyser formation is applicable to Enceladus and other moons, offering new insights into the geophysical processes and astrobiological potential of icy satellites.

Recently, extending transfer learning to cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has garnered significant interest. Unlike single-agent scenarios, the coordination essential in cooperative MARL restricts individual agent policies; however, current transfer approaches focus solely on agent policies, neglecting coordination knowledge. We introduce a novel architecture that enables robust transfer of coordination knowledge by decomposing overall coordination into multiple coordination patterns. This framework employs a new mixing network, the Level-Adaptive QTransformer (LA-QTransformer), to facilitate agent coordination that accounts for credit assignment, alongside a dedicated Level-Adaptive Transformer (LA-Transformer) to transfer coordination knowledge across appropriate patterns for different agents. Furthermore, we utilize a novel agent network called the Population Invariant agent with Transformer (PIT) to achieve coordination transfer across diverse scenarios. Extensive experiments on StarCraft II micro-management demonstrate that the combination of LA-QTransformer and PIT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

Collaborative inference has recently gained attention as a promising approach for deploying deep learning in Internet of Things (IoT) environments by partitioning a DNN into components executed locally on resource-limited devices and remotely in the cloud. Although the raw input data remains private within this framework, the intermediate outputs of the local model components still pose significant privacy risks. While differential privacy offers a theoretical solution, its practical viability across different scenarios remains uncertain. Specifically, it is unclear how setting the privacy budget (epsilon) influences both protection strength and model accuracy when facing advanced reconstruction attacks, and whether an optimal balance between privacy and utility can be achieved. This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study evaluating the effectiveness of differential privacy against reconstruction attacks in collaborative inference across multiple datasets. Our findings demonstrate that differential privacy is viable for this purpose, offering valuable insights into privacy-utility trade-offs. Across the tested datasets, we identified a specific range of the privacy budget (notably 100 ≤ epsilon ≤ 200) that effectively balances utility and security. A key takeaway from our research is that differential privacy performs more effectively when the dataset exhibits smaller intraclass variations, providing what we believe is the first practical and easily adoptable guideline for this application.

Accurately predicting registration error is vital for assessing registration procedures, a key factor in their clinical implementation, and can also aid in enhancing registration quality. However, this task is challenging due to the scarcity of ground truth data in medical imaging. This paper introduces a novel automatic approach for quantitatively predicting registration error, specifically applied to chest CT scans. The method employs a random regression forest to estimate local errors, utilizing features derived from the transformation model and post-registration dissimilarity. The model was trained and evaluated using manually annotated corresponding points from two experimental setups: one on the SPREAD database (training and testing on the same data) and another inter-database study involving SPREAD, DIR-Lab-4DCT, and DIR-Lab-COPDgene. Results indicate mean absolute regression errors of $1.07 \pm 1.86$ mm for SPREAD and $1.76 \pm 2.59$ mm for the inter-database experiment. Additionally, the classification accuracy for three categories (correct, poor, and wrong registration) reached 90.7% and 75.4%, respectively, for the SPREAD and inter-database cases. The robust performance of this method supports significant applications, such as automatic quality control in large-scale image analysis.

In graph-based community detection, the semi-supervised learning task involves determining the true community membership of every node based on the network's connectivity and a sparse set of known labels. Since different configurations of revealed labels can vary in their information content and impact reconstruction accuracy, we utilize statistical physics techniques within the dense stochastic block model framework to perform a large deviation analysis in the high-dimensional limit. This approach characterizes fluctuations around typical behavior, accounting for correlations among label selections to estimate their informativeness and rarity within subsets of equal size. Our findings provide theoretical evidence of a non-monotonic link between reconstruction accuracy and the free energy of the inference problem's posterior measure. Finally, we explore potential implications for active learning strategies in community detection.

Neutrino geophysics is an emerging interdisciplinary discipline that investigates the Earth's interior by measuring the flux of geologically generated neutrinos at the surface, combining principles from geology, geophysics, and particle physics. Geoneutrinos, which are antineutrinos emitted by long-lived natural isotopes driving the Earth's radiogenic heat, offer critical insights into models of the planet's chemical composition. This overview discusses theoretical calculations of expected geoneutrino signals alongside experimental detection challenges, including background sources and suppression techniques. Currently, only the Borexino and KamLAND detectors possess the necessary sensitivity to observe geoneutrinos; together, they have recorded approximately 190 events while continuing data collection. The text details these experiments, their detection results, and their implications for geophysics. Looking ahead, several new detectors are planned or under construction, including the SNO+ detector, which is being filled with liquid scintillator, and the 20-kiloton JUNO detector, the largest of its kind. The review also examines the physics potential of these upcoming facilities, along with other proposals and innovative methods for future geoneutrino detection.

This paper examines the optical characteristics of a thin accretion disk within the Simpson-Visser spacetime, contrasting them with the Schwarzschild black hole scenario. We compute and visualize the red-shift and observed flux distributions as seen by distant observers from different inclination angles. Images of Novikov-Thorne accretion disks generated by the Simpson-Visser metric family closely resemble those of a Schwarzschild black hole. Additionally, we analyzed the embedding diagram and electromagnetic properties, including the disk's temperature, radiation flux, and accretion efficiency. Our findings indicate that, relative to the Schwarzschild black hole, the disk's temperature, radiation flux, and luminosity all rise as the regularization parameter '$l$' increases. We conclude that astrophysical observational signatures within the electromagnetic spectrum allow us to distinguish wormhole geometries from both regular black holes (black-bounce) and standard Schwarzschild black holes.

This research investigates the two-dimensional water wave problem within an infinitely deep domain subject to a nonzero constant vorticity. The primary objective is to characterize how uniform shear flow influences the modulation of weakly nonlinear, quasi-monochromatic surface gravity waves. By employing Hamiltonian transformation theory on the Hamiltonian formulation of the system, we derive a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation governing the temporal evolution of the wave envelope. Consistent with prior findings, our results indicate that the impact of uniform shear flow on the modulational instability of Stokes waves varies based on the flow's direction and magnitude, either enhancing or suppressing the instability. Furthermore, our approach offers a non-perturbative method to reconstruct surface elevation from the wave envelope, utilizing a Birkhoff normal form transformation to remove all non-resonant triads. The validity of this model is confirmed through comparisons with direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and with a recently developed Dysthe equation by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch (J. Fluid Mech. 855, 2018) addressing constant vorticity, demonstrating excellent agreement across a range of vorticity values.

Machine learning holds the potential to facilitate the automated creation of test oracles. To analyze this developing domain, we conducted a systematic literature review focusing on oracle categories, researcher objectives, utilized machine learning methods, evaluation metrics, and current open challenges. Our analysis covered a sample of 22 relevant studies, revealing that machine learning algorithms primarily generate expected output, test verdict, and metamorphic relation oracles, with expected output being the most frequent. The vast majority of these studies rely on supervised or semi-supervised learning, trained on labeled system executions or code metadata using techniques such as neural networks, support vector machines, adaptive boosting, and decision trees. Evaluation of these oracles typically involves metrics like mutation scores, classification accuracy, and ROC curves. While current research demonstrates significant promise, substantial challenges remain concerning training data requirements, the complexity of modeled functions, the selection and application of ML algorithms, benchmark standards, and study replicability. We aim for these findings to act as a guiding roadmap and source of inspiration for future researchers in this area.

By periodically modulating system parameters, Floquet engineering generates intriguing synthetic gauge fields and complex collective behaviors within quantum systems. Applying a Floquet drive to magnon mode frequencies enables chiral state transfer in a cavity-magnonic setup, thereby breaking time-reversal symmetry in a platform highly suitable for coherent information processing. Specifically, in the large-detuning regime, the photon mode is adiabatically eliminated, allowing magnon modes subjected to conditional longitudinal drives to couple indirectly via phase-modulated interactions. Utilizing the resulting effective Hamiltonian facilitates the generation of chiral currents in a circular loop, with the loop's dynamics assessed to quantify the symmetry of the system Hamiltonian. Furthermore, this protocol extends beyond fixed-excitation manifolds to encompass continuous-variable systems with arbitrary states and demonstrates robustness against systematic errors in both photon-magnon coupling strength and Kerr nonlinearity.

This chapter begins by introducing a principal-agent game-theoretic framework to model the dynamics between a single insurer and a single user. In this setup, the insurer acts as the principal who lacks complete information regarding the user's security measures. The user, defined as either an infrastructure operator or a customer, establishes local defenses and pays an insurance premium. The insurer constructs an incentive-compatible mechanism comprising both the premium and coverage terms, whereas the user decides on participation and the level of defensive effort exerted against attacks. Additionally, the chapter examines an attack-aware cyber insurance model by integrating adversarial actions into the system. The attacker's behavior dictates the nature of cyber threats, such as denial of service (DoS), data breaches, phishing, and spoofing. These distinct threat categories influence the resulting losses and shape the coverage policies. Specifically, data breaches can cause financial harm alongside reputational damage, and the insurance coverage may only reimburse an agreed-upon percentage of the financial losses.

This work extends the investigation of hyperspaces and function spaces from classical topology into the realm of digital topology. It introduces the concepts of digital hyperspaces and digital function graphs, examining their interconnections and graphical characteristics.

Particle robots represent a new class of biologically inspired systems capable of robust, collective locomotion, though they cannot move independently. Although current control relies on hand-crafted policies for basic movement, these multi-robot systems could be managed more efficiently across various tasks using Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). However, particle robots pose unique challenges for DRL compared to traditional swarm robotics, specifically due to the low degrees of freedom per unit and the heightened need for inter-robot coordination. We introduce a 2D particle robot simulator built with the OpenAI Gym interface and Pymunk physics engine to explore underutilized DRL applications in this domain, alongside new tasks and challenges. Additionally, we employ Stable-baselines3 to establish benchmarks for these tasks. While current baseline DRL algorithms show promise in completing the tasks, they have not yet matched the performance of hand-crafted policies, indicating that further development of DRL methods is essential to achieve the proposed goals.

A major hurdle in creating resilient machine learning models is covariate shift, which arises when input distributions between training and test sets diverge, even though conditional label distributions stay consistent. Although covariate shift is common in practical applications, theoretical insights regarding modern machine learning have been scarce. This study investigates the precise high-dimensional asymptotics of random feature regression under such shifts, offering a detailed characterization of the limiting test error, bias, and variance. Our findings introduce a natural partial ordering of covariate shifts, establishing sufficient conditions to predict whether a shift will degrade or potentially improve test performance. We demonstrate that overparameterized models display increased robustness against covariate shift, providing a theoretical basis for this notable phenomenon. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers an exact linear correlation between in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization, explaining a recent surprising empirical observation.

Dynamical processes in complex systems frequently involve spreading events occurring on networks with evolving structures, known as temporal networks. The susceptibility of such systems to facilitate spreading, termed "spreading vulnerability," is often hypothesized to depend on the network's temporal topology. However, directly deriving this vulnerability from topological data remains difficult. To address this, we introduce "entropy of temporal entanglement," a new metric that quantifies the topological complexity of temporal networks using diverse real-world data. This parameter-free measure enables meaningful topological comparisons across vastly different systems. Furthermore, simulations of three distinct stochastic dynamical processes on temporal networks reveal that the entropy of temporal entanglement effectively captures the systems' spreading vulnerability, regardless of specific process details. Consequently, this entropic metric provides a quantitative method to extract spreading proneness from topology, offering broad applications across natural, social, biological, and engineered domains.

Let $\left\{ Z_{n},n=0,1,2,...\right\} $ denote a critical branching process within a random environment, and let $\left\{ S_{n},n=0,1,2,...\right\} $ represent the corresponding random walk. It is established that if the increments of this random walk fall (without centering) into the domain of attraction of a stable law, then there exists a sequence $a_{1},a_{2},...,$ that varies slowly at infinity, such that the conditional distributions \begin{equation*} \mathbf{P}\left( \frac{S_{n}}{a_{n}}\leq x\Big|Z_{n}>0\right) ,\quad x\in (-\infty ,+\infty ), \end{equation*} converge weakly, as $n\rightarrow \infty $, to the distribution of a strictly positive and proper random variable. In this study, we extend this finding by characterizing the asymptotic behavior of the probability \begin{equation*} \mathbf{P}\left( S_{n}\leq \varphi (n);Z_{n}>0\right) , \end{equation*} provided that $\varphi (n)\rightarrow \infty $ as $n\rightarrow \infty $ while satisfying the condition $\varphi (n)=o(a_{n})$.

Although the angular momentum formalism offers a robust method for classifying atomic states, its reliance on initial spherical symmetry limits its direct application to periodic systems, despite the common practice of labeling cubic semiconductor states using atomic notation. It has gone unnoticed that an analog of orbital angular momentum can be defined solely based on the potential experienced by electrons. Consequently, the spin-orbit interaction in crystals adopts the $\mathbfcal{\hat{L}}\cdot \hat{\vS}$ form, where $\mathbfcal{\hat{L}}$ simplifies to $\hat{\vL}=\vr\times\hat{\vp}$ under spherical symmetry. This establishes the necessary theoretical foundation for utilizing the eigenvalues of $\mathbfcal{\hat{L}}$ and $\mathbfcal{\hat{J}}=\mathbfcal{\hat{L}}+\hat{\vS}$ as quantum indices for cubic semiconductor states. Crucially, these indices govern the phase factor relating valence electron and hole operators, mirroring the relationship between particles and antiparticles, even though holes are not true antiparticles of valence electrons. Since these ($\mathbfcal{\hat{L}},\mathbfcal{\hat{J}}$) analogs of the ($\hat{\vL},\hat{\vJ}$) angular momenta stem from a broader definition, distinct terminology is required: we propose "spatial momentum" for $\mathbfcal{\hat{L}}$, which operates in real space, and "hybrid momentum" for $\mathbfcal{\hat{J}}$, which additionally acts on spin, with the potential symmetry designated as "cubic spatial momentum." This framework would categorize $\hat{\vJ}$ as "spherical hybrid momentum," a term that, while slightly cumbersome, is necessary given the novelty of the concept.

This paper details the QMUL-SDS team's approach to Task 1 of the CLEF 2020 CheckThat! shared task, which aims to evaluate the fact-checking value of COVID-19 related tweets to prioritize those requiring verification. The broader goal is to bolster public protection against misinformation and facilitate access to trustworthy information. We present and analyze our submission outcomes, demonstrating that a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) enhanced with numeric expressions and trained on COVID-Twitter-BERT (CT-BERT) significantly improves upon baseline performance. Additionally, we examine the effects of data augmentation using rumors from other topics. Our top-ranked system placed fourth in the competition, yielding promising results that suggest potential for future enhancements.

Optimal Transport (OT) has become a vital computational instrument in machine learning and computer vision, offering a geometric approach to analyzing probability measures. However, OT is hindered by the curse of dimensionality and necessitates regularization for practical application, with entropic regularization being a favored method that yields an 'unbiased' Sinkhorn divergence. This study investigates the convergence of estimating the 2-Sinkhorn divergence between Gaussian processes (GPs) via their finite-dimensional marginal distributions. We demonstrate almost sure convergence when marginals are sampled based on a specific base measure. Additionally, we establish that employing $n$ marginals results in an estimation error scaling dimension-independently as $\mathcal{O}\left(\epsilon^{-1}n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes the entropic regularization magnitude.

This paper establishes the convergence of Nörlund means for Vilenkin-Fourier series with monotone coefficients applied to integrable functions at both Lebesgue and Vilenkin-Lebesgue points. Furthermore, we examine pointwise convergence and convergence in $L_p$ norms for these specific means.

Effective image representation is vital for numerous visual applications. Rather than relying on discrete 2D pixel arrays, the recent Local Implicit Image Function (LIIF) approach models images as continuous functions where pixel values are derived by expanding upon input coordinates. This continuous framework enables LIIF to handle arbitrary-scale image super-resolution, creating a unified and efficient model for diverse up-scaling factors. Nevertheless, LIIF frequently exhibits structural distortions and ringing artifacts near edges, primarily because its single shared model neglects local image properties. To address this, we introduce Adaptive Local Image Function (A-LIIF), a novel method designed to mitigate these issues. Our A-LIIF comprises two key components: an encoder that extracts cross-scale features, and an expansion network that constructs the continuous up-scaling function through a weighted fusion of multiple local implicit image functions. Consequently, A-LIIF achieves more accurate reconstruction of high-frequency textures and structures. Experimental results across various benchmark datasets confirm the method's efficacy. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/LeeHW-THU/A-LIIF}.

Over recent years, the frequency and intensity of extreme weather phenomena have risen markedly due to human-induced climate change, yet their global statistical properties and fundamental physical drivers remain incompletely understood. This study employs a methodology rooted in statistical physics and probability theory to analyze extreme weather, with a specific focus on the statistics of daily air temperature fluctuations. Our results demonstrate that the magnitudes of these extreme events conform to a universal \textit{Gumbel} distribution, whereas their waiting times adhere to a universal \textit{Gamma} function. Analysis of finite-size effects confirms robust scaling behaviors. Furthermore, we reveal that the cumulative distribution of logarithmic waiting times between record-breaking events follows an \textit{Exponential} distribution, indicating a directional evolution of the climate system driven by a decelerating release of tension. These universal scaling laws prove remarkably stable and remain unaffected by global warming. Contrary to typical expectations for record dynamics, the number of extreme temperature variability "quakes" does not decay inversely with time but instead exhibits deviations linked to large-scale climate extremes. This theoretical framework offers a novel perspective on the interplay between universality, scaling, and climate systems, providing new insights into weather variability that may enhance the forecasting of extreme events.

Machine learning has recently become a potent instrument for forecasting the properties of quantum many-body systems. While generative models can accurately reconstruct ground states of gapped Hamiltonians from measurements of a single state to predict local observables, kernel methods achieve similar goals by learning from measurements across various related states. This study integrates the strengths of both methodologies by introducing conditional generative models capable of representing an ensemble of states simultaneously; these models identify shared structural patterns across different quantum states through measurement data. The resulting trained model enables the prediction of arbitrary local properties of ground states, including those absent from the training set, without requiring additional training for new observables. We provide numerical validation of this approach using simulations of up to 45 qubits applied to two distinct quantum many-body problems: 2D random Heisenberg models and Rydberg atom systems.

Many real-world systems are best understood through multi-layered networks, where various theories have been proposed to explain how these connections influence synchronization stability. However, the resulting equations are often computationally prohibitive, making them difficult or impossible to solve for large-scale systems. To address this, we introduce a mean-field theory of synchronization for multi-layer networks. By assuming quasi-identical layers, our method yields accurate stability assessments that closely match exact results. Notably, our theory maintains high accuracy even when layers are highly dissimilar, raising broader questions about the mean-field nature of synchronization stability in such networks. Furthermore, our approach requires only quadratic computational complexity relative to the number of nodes, enabling the analysis of systems that were previously intractable.

We introduce a novel optical transmission spectrum (400–950 nm) for the hot Jupiter WASP-31b (M=0.48 MJ; R=1.54 RJ; P=3.41 days), derived by merging four transit observations conducted with the IMACS instrument on the Magellan Baade Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory under the ACCESS project. This study examines the presence of upper-atmospheric clouds or hazes and evaluates the impact of stellar activity on observed spectral features. Specifically, we search for absorption signatures of the alkali metals Na I and K I, focusing on K I due to conflicting prior results: while HST/STIS observations indicated its presence, both low- and high-resolution ground-based studies did not. By combining our optical data with existing near-infrared measurements, we employed both equilibrium and non-equilibrium chemistry retrievals to explore the system's planetary and stellar parameters. Our best-fit model indicates a scattering slope consistent with Rayleigh scattering ($\alpha = 5.3^{+2.9}_{-3.1}$), high-altitude clouds at a pressure of $-3.6^{+2.7}_{-2.1}$ bars, and potentially muted H2O features. These findings support previous ground-based assertions regarding the absence of K I, suggesting that clouds are responsible for the suppression of H2O signals and the non-detection of Na or K. Finally, we compare our Magellan/IMACS spectrum with data from VLT/FORS2, HST/WFC3, HST/STIS, and Spitzer to further constrain the planet's atmospheric characteristics across the optical and infrared ranges. We conclude that a steeper scattering slope ($\alpha = 8.3 \pm 1.5$) is supported by STIS data blueward of 400 nm, and only the original STIS observations reveal a significant potassium signal.

We introduce Reddit Health Online Talk (RedHOT), a dataset comprising 22,000 richly annotated social media posts from Reddit covering 24 distinct health conditions. The annotations identify spans representing medical claims, personal narratives, and inquiries, with additional granular labeling applied to these claims to highlight Patient Populations, Interventions, and Outcomes (PIO elements). Leveraging this corpus, we define the task of retrieving reliable evidence pertinent to specific social media claims. We propose a novel approach to automatically generate (noisy) supervision for this objective, which trains a dense retrieval model that surpasses baseline performance. Manual evaluation by medical professionals suggests that while the system shows promise, significant improvements are still possible. The collected annotations and scripts for assembling the dataset are accessible at https://github.com/sominw/redhot.

Building upon Demidovich's framework for convergent systems, we investigate the optimal nonlinear damping control recently introduced [1] for second-order dynamics. Addressing output regulation and the tracking of $\mathcal{C}^1$-trajectories, we demonstrate that all solutions of the controlled system exhibit global uniform asymptotic stability. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a unique limit solution at the origin for both the control error and its time derivative, adhering to Demidovich's criteria for convergent dynamics. This analysis is supported by explanatory numerical examples.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have transformed deep learning, yet recent studies reveal their limitations in generalizing across diverse conditions. Consequently, the concept of capsules was introduced in 2011, with significant research momentum emerging from 2017 onward. This paper reviews recent advancements in capsule architectures and routing mechanisms. We observe that current literature predominantly focuses on modifying the overall architecture or routing procedures, while neglecting finer components, particularly the squash function. Therefore, this work offers new insights into how squash functions influence capsule network performance. Finally, we conclude by discussing and suggesting future opportunities within the field of capsule networks.

We demonstrate that specific Riordan arrays possess generating functions expressible as Jacobi and Thron continued fractions. We examine the inverses of these arrays, noting that under certain conditions, their generating functions can also be represented via continued fractions. Connections to orthogonal polynomial moment sequences and Laurent biorthogonal polynomials are established. Furthermore, we illustrate how continued fractions can define particular Riordan group involutions. Additionally, we show that simple transformations of Jacobi continued fractions yield exponential Riordan arrays. Finally, for comparison, we analyze certain combinatorially significant non-Riordan arrays, such as the Narayana numbers.

As laboratory technology advances, low-order correlation functions are no longer sufficient to capture the primary effects of decoherence in quantum many-body systems, making the investigation of higher-order correlation functions essential. This paper analytically examines how correlation functions evolve under decoherence and determines the conditions under which low-order functions suffice versus when third-order or higher functions are required within the 1D transverse Ising model. The findings indicate that under strong coupling and long coherence times, high-order correlation effects cannot be neglected, and the classical Markov approximation becomes limited. Conversely, in scenarios involving weak coupling and short coherence times, low-order correlation functions provide an adequate description.

Microscale 3D printing has garnered significant attention in both research and industry, yet fabricated structures frequently deviate from intended designs due to physico-chemical changes occurring during and after printing. This study introduces preliminary steps toward a simple, rapid, and easily implementable algorithm designed to predict the final topography of structures created via multi-photon lithography (Direct Laser Writing or DLW). By approximating the three primary DLW stages—photo resin exposure, cross-linking, and subsequent shrinkage—using mathematical operations, the method demonstrates strong alignment with experimental data. For instance, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) between a predicted topography and an unmodified radial-symmetrically chirped 3D print is merely 0.46 $\mu$m, significantly lower than the 1.49 $\mu$m error observed between the print and its target. These robust predictions can be applied before printing to reduce unwanted discrepancies between target and final structures. Furthermore, employing a Downhill-Simplex algorithm to identify optimal parameters allowed us to decrease the RMSE from 4.04 $\mu$m to 0.33 $\mu$m within just two correction loops in the best-case scenario (achieving 0.72 $\mu$m after a single loop). Ultimately, this approach aims to eliminate the necessity for extensive structural optimization cycles, facilitating the future production of highly conformal, high-quality microstructures.

Evaluating node influenceability is a core challenge in social network analysis and mining, with critical applications such as viral marketing, identifying key influencers, and online advertising. This study focuses on assessing influenceability using the widely adopted Independent Cascade model. Although this problem is #P-complete, leading most prior research to rely on Naive Monte-Carlo (
mc) sampling, the 
mc estimator often suffers from high variance, limiting its effectiveness. To address this, we introduce two families of estimators grounded in stratified sampling principles. First, we define two basic stratified sampling ( ss) estimators— ssi and  ssii—which partition the population into $2^r$ and $r+1$ strata, respectively, by selecting $r$ edges. Second, to further minimize variance, we observe that both  ssi and  ssii can be applied recursively within each stratum, resulting in two recursive stratified sampling (ss) estimators: ssi and ssii. Theoretically, all proposed estimators are unbiased and exhibit significantly lower variance than the 
mc estimator. Finally, comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the efficiency and accuracy of our new methods.

Group lasso is a prevalent regularization technique in statistical learning that removes parameters based on predefined groups. However, handling overlapping groups creates non-separability, making optimization computationally expensive for large-scale problems and thereby hindering its application in modern tasks like gene pathway selection and graphical model estimation. To address this, we introduce a separable penalty that approximates the overlapping group lasso penalty. Due to its separable nature, computing regularization with our proposed method is significantly faster than with standard overlapping group lasso, particularly for high-dimensional and large-scale datasets. We demonstrate that this penalty represents the tightest separable relaxation of the overlapping group lasso norm within the family of $\ell_{q_1}/\ell_{q_2}$ norms. Furthermore, we establish that the resulting estimator achieves statistical equivalence to the overlapping group lasso estimator regarding error bounds and rate-optimal performance under squared loss. Simulation studies and a cancer tumor classification task utilizing gene expression and multiple pathways confirm both the improved computational efficiency and statistical parity of our approach compared to the traditional overlapping group lasso.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) are expected to serve as a cost-effective innovation for enhancing future wireless networks. This study examines a practical RIS-assisted multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) system subject to transceiver hardware impairments, RIS phase noise, and imperfect channel state information (CSI). The primary focus is on jointly optimizing the MIMO transceiver and the RIS reflection matrix to minimize the total average mean-square-error (MSE) across all data streams. Due to these practical imperfections, the resulting optimization problem is non-convex and difficult to resolve. To address this, we first derive the total average MSE by accounting for the effects of these system flaws. Subsequently, to manage the tightly coupled variables and non-convex, NP-hard constraints, we propose an efficient iterative algorithm grounded in an alternating optimization (AO) framework with guaranteed convergence; each subproblem yields a closed-form optimal solution utilizing the majorization-minimization (MM) technique. Additionally, by capitalizing on the unit-modulus constraint structure, we introduce a modified Riemannian gradient ascent (RGA) algorithm for discrete RIS phase shift optimization. The algorithm's optimality is confirmed under line-of-sight (LoS) channel conditions, and we demonstrate an irreducible MSE floor caused by hardware and CSI imperfections in high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scenarios. Numerical results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms benchmark schemes in terms of MSE and reveal that increasing the number of RIS elements does not always yield benefits under these specific system imperfections.

Over 3 billion individuals do not have access to dermatological care. While AI diagnostic tools offer potential for early skin cancer detection, most existing models have not been evaluated on images representing diverse skin tones or rare conditions. To resolve this gap, we created the Diverse Dermatology Images (DDI) dataset, which is the first publicly accessible collection of pathologically verified images featuring varied skin tones. Our analysis reveals that leading dermatology AI models perform significantly worse on the DDI dataset, with ROC-AUC scores declining by 29 to 40 percent compared to their baseline performance. Specifically, dark skin tones and uncommon diseases, which are well-represented in DDI, drive these performance deficits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that current robust training techniques fail to mitigate these biases without access to diverse training data. These findings highlight critical weaknesses and biases in dermatology AI that must be addressed to ensure reliable application across all patient demographics and disease types.

We examine $\mu$-proximal, stationary actions—referred to as boundary actions—for a non-elementary hyperbolic group $\Gamma$ equipped with a probability measure $\mu$. Our focus lies on the spectrum of Furstenberg entropies associated with $(\Gamma,\mu)$-boundaries and the topological and lattice-theoretic structure of the boundary set $\mathcal{BL}(\Gamma,\mu)$.
