This paper presents Pareto Estimation to Pick the Perfect Precision (PEPPP), which utilizes matrix factorization to identify non-dominated configurations—forming a Pareto frontier—with minimal network evaluations. For any specific memory constraint, the optimal precision that minimizes error lies on this frontier, enabling practitioners to effectively balance memory against error to select the most suitable precision for their specific objectives.

Coalescing compact binaries represent the most promising and well-understood targets for detecting gravitational waves (GWs) using the complete network of operational ground-based observatories. Anticipating the initial detections, understanding the expected distribution of these GW sources within the local universe is of significant interest. This study examines the full phase space distribution of merging compact binaries at $z = 0$ by utilizing dark matter simulations of structure formation. Because these binary systems are born with substantial barycentric velocities, known as "kicks," their merger locations are spread more diffusely relative to their host galaxies, with mergers occurring several megaparsecs away from the host halo. Consequently, redshift estimates derived solely from the nearest galaxy in projection may be inaccurate. Conversely, significant offsets from the host galaxy could facilitate the identification of faint optical counterparts and should be factored into strategies for follow-up observations. The study finds that the isotropy of projected sky distributions of GW sources increases with higher kick velocities and is markedly enhanced if progenitor systems exhibit the large kicks inferred from the known populations of pulsars and double compact binaries. Furthermore, even without observed electromagnetic counterparts, GW observatories, particularly advanced LIGO with additional interferometers, should be able to distinguish between sky distributions generated by different kick-velocity models within expected detection rates and accuracy limits.

We investigate the fractional porous medium equation proposed by Caffarelli-Vazquez, deriving local existence, uniqueness, and blow-up criteria for smooth solutions. The proof relies on deriving a commutator estimate that incorporates fractional Laplacian operators.

This study introduces an efficient and robust technique for accurately resolving the electric field in multi-material scenarios. The approach utilizes the finite element method enhanced by hat-type shape functions within elements intersected by material interfaces. A key advantage of this method is its direct use of hat-functions, which necessitate only one additional degree of freedom per cut element to capture the discontinuity in the electric potential gradient and, consequently, the electric field. This extra degree of freedom is statically condensed at the element level before assembling the global system, ensuring that the system matrix graph remains identical to that of the standard finite element method. To ensure robustness across a broad spectrum of electrical material property ratios, the method also addresses potential discontinuities between adjacent cut elements caused by the fully local nature of the added degrees of freedom. Validated through various examples on both structured and unstructured grids, this approach establishes a foundation for enriched finite element methods applicable to diverse electromagnetic problems.

Fine-tuning a pre-trained deep learning model on new classes often leads to the network acquiring new concepts while gradually losing knowledge of previous training, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. In practical scenarios, it is crucial to learn new classes without compromising the ability to recognize old ones. While this challenge is commonly studied using 2D image recognition, this paper extends the investigation to 3D point cloud data in light of advancing depth camera technology. Addressing this problem in the 3D domain is particularly difficult due to the scarcity of large-scale datasets and robust pre-trained backbone models. To mitigate forgetting, we explore knowledge distillation techniques applied to 3D data and enhance this process by incorporating semantic word vectors for object classes. Our findings indicate that analyzing the interconnections between old and new knowledge during training facilitates the acquisition of new concepts while retaining old ones. By evaluating three 3D point cloud backbones (PointNet, DGCNN, and PointConv) across synthetic (ModelNet40, ModelNet10) and real-world scanned (ScanObjectNN) datasets, we establish new baselines for learning without forgetting in the 3D realm. This research aims to inspire further developments in this field.

Valvular heart diseases represent a growing concern in impoverished regions, such as Southern Africa, accounting for over 31% of cardiovascular-related deaths. Modeling the impact of regurgitant and obstructive lesions on the valve body can aid clinicians in developing personalized treatment plans. This study develops a multi-compartment lumped parameter model of the human cardiovascular system, incorporating a novel valve modeling approach that considers geometry and flow-regime-dependent pressure drops alongside valve cusp motion. The model is applied to analyze various degrees of aortic stenosis using standard human cardiovascular parameters. The results generated by this proposed model are compared against predictions from previously published valve modeling approaches, with both sets of data evaluated against typical local and global physiological parameters found in literature, including left-ventricular systolic pressures, peak and mean aortic valve pressure drops, and vena contracta velocities. The findings indicate that previously published valve models underestimate peak and mean transvalvular pressure drops in severely stenosed cases by approximately 47% and 30%, respectively. In contrast, the newly proposed model underestimates the peak pressure drop by 20% while overestimating the mean pressure drop by 7%.

Supervision constraints, specifically the difficulty of determining when an instruction has been successfully executed, limit the training of reinforcement learning agents on natural language tasks. We address this by adapting the CLEVR visual question answering dataset to produce intricate natural language navigation commands paired with scene graphs, thereby creating an environment-agnostic supervised dataset. To illustrate the utility of this data, we map the generated scenes to the VizDoom environment and employ the architecture described in \citet{gatedattention} to train an agent capable of following these more sophisticated language instructions.

Training contemporary large language models (LLMs) relies heavily on large batch sizes and long sequences to optimize throughput and accuracy. To accommodate variable-length sequences on hardware accelerators, it is standard to pad sequences, ensuring uniform length within a batch. This paper demonstrates that sequence length variation in typical NLP datasets can result in padding accounting for up to 50% of all tokens, with ratios reaching as high as 89% in less common but significant cases, such as the GLUE-cola dataset with a sequence length of 128. Current solutions to mitigate this inefficiency are hindered by the necessity to prevent cross-contamination in self-attention mechanisms, potential accuracy drops due to the loss of sequence ordering, or reliance on specialized kernel implementations limited to specific accelerators. This study introduces a novel formalization of sequence packing by framing it within the well-established bin packing problem, presenting new algorithms that achieve a 2x speedup for BERT phase 2 pre-training. Furthermore, we illustrate how existing models can be adapted to maintain mathematical equivalence between original and packed sequences, allowing packed models to be trained using standard pre-training and fine-tuning workflows.

Meta-learning is a widely adopted framework for learning from limited data, where an algorithm is trained across numerous few-shot tasks. In classification scenarios, these tasks usually involve sampling a small number of support and query examples from a subset of classes. Although it is commonly believed that greater task diversity enhances meta-learning performance, this study presents evidence to the contrary. We introduce a modification to standard meta-learning methods that keeps support sets constant across tasks, thereby reducing task diversity. Surprisingly, this adjustment does not negatively impact results; instead, it consistently improves performance across various datasets and meta-learning algorithms. Additionally, we offer preliminary analyses to explain this phenomenon. Our contributions include: (i) a deeper investigation into how support set construction affects meta-learning, and (ii) the proposal of a simple, general, and competitive baseline for few-shot learning.

Due to limited spatial resolution, numerical simulations of atmospheric and geophysical flows depend on parameterizations for subgrid-scale processes. Although significant advancements have been made in creating closure models based on physical intuition and mathematical approximations, these models remain imperfect and often yield inaccurate results. Recently, machine learning has excelled at identifying complex patterns in high-resolution spatio-temporal data, enhancing parameterization models and improving coarse-grid predictions. However, challenges such as failing to adhere to known physical laws and poor generalization limit their practical application. This study introduces a frame-invariant closure approach that boosts the accuracy and generalizability of deep learning-based subgrid-scale models by integrating physical symmetries directly into the neural network architecture. Specifically, we employ specialized layers within the convolutional neural network to theoretically guarantee desired constraints without relying on regularization terms. We validate this framework using a two-dimensional decaying turbulence test case dominated by the forward enstrophy cascade. Our results demonstrate that the proposed frame-invariant SGS model (i) accurately predicts subgrid-scale source terms, (ii) upholds physical symmetries including translation, Galilean, and rotation invariance, and (iii) maintains numerical stability in coarse-grid simulations while generalizing across various initial conditions and Reynolds numbers. By bridging extensive physics-based theories with data-driven modeling, this work marks a promising step toward developing physically consistent, data-driven turbulence closure models.

Utilizing simple digital cameras for collision avoidance could facilitate the secure integration of small UAVs into congested, low-altitude spaces. This study introduces an obstacle avoidance framework for small UAVs that combines a monocular camera with a hybrid neural network and path planning controller. The architecture includes a vision network for depth estimation from imagery, a high-level control network, a collision prediction network, and a contingency policy. The system was tested on a simulated UAV traversing an obstacle course within a restricted flight pattern. Results indicate that the proposed approach achieves minimal collision rates while sustaining operationally significant flight speeds.

Developing efficient techniques for uncertainty quantification in kinetic equations is challenging due to the models' high dimensionality, which often leads to prohibitive computational costs. Conversely, this "curse of dimensionality" has driven significant research into creating simplified models that offer approximate solutions at a fraction of the computational expense. Various researchers have explored such approximations through suitable closures of moment equations or by employing simplified collisional models. Consequently, within the realm of uncertainty quantification, it is logical to leverage these models in a multi-fidelity framework, where the original kinetic equation serves as the high-fidelity reference and the simplified versions act as low-fidelity surrogates. This article surveys recent advancements in multi-fidelity methods for kinetic equations designed to accelerate uncertainty quantification by integrating evaluations from both high- and low-fidelity models, with specific focus on compressible and incompressible hydrodynamic limits. The discussion primarily centers on two strategic classes: multi-fidelity control variates and bi-fidelity stochastic collocation. These approaches are examined based on the surrogate models employed and the associated numerical techniques. Given the critical impact of surrogate model selection, the presentation adopts an application-oriented perspective.

This work presents an expanded version of a rapid communication by the author (Phys. Rev. B, v76, 041402(R), 2007) concerning the simulation of water's wetting transition on graphite. Its primary goal is to offer greater detail regarding the methodology, parameters, and findings for the benefit of interested readers. We computed water adsorption isotherms on graphite via grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations enhanced with multiple histogram reweighting. These calculations utilized the SPC/E empirical potentials for water, a 10-4-3 van der Waals model, and a newly developed induction and multipolar potential for the water-graphite system. Our findings indicate that the wetting transition occurs between 475 K and 480 K, while the prewetting critical temperature falls within the 505–510 K range. The calculated wetting transition temperature aligns quantitatively with a prior prediction derived from a simple model. Furthermore, the observation of stable and metastable state coexistence at temperatures between the wetting transition and prewetting critical points confirms that the transition is of the first order.

The charge-$q$ Schwinger model represents $(1+1)$-dimensional quantum electrodynamics (QED) featuring a Dirac fermion with charge $q$. This system possesses both $\mathbb{Z}_q$ $1$-form symmetry and $\mathbb{Z}_q$ chiral symmetry in the chiral limit, exhibiting a mixed 't Hooft anomaly between them. We investigate this model numerically using the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) within a lattice Hamiltonian framework. In this approach, the Jordan-Wigner transformation maps the Schwinger model to a spin chain with nonlocal interactions, and we employ open boundary conditions to ensure a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. Our calculations of energy density and chiral condensate reveal that utilizing local operators substantially mitigates boundary effects compared to deriving results from extensive quantities divided by volume. To address the implications of the 't Hooft anomaly, we rigorously handle the renormalization of chiral condensates, ultimately verifying that Wilson loops induce discrete chiral transformations as the continuum limit is approached.

Although recent LIGO and Virgo gravitational wave detections permit tests of general relativity in strong-field regimes, they remain insensitive to many phenomena beyond their sensitivity limits. Future observatories like LISA will extend our reach to longer-duration, lower-frequency events, specifically enabling the study of non-linear dynamics in extreme mass-ratio inspirals involving small compact objects and supermassive black holes. This paper investigates test particle motion around rotating black holes within two quadratic gravity frameworks: scalar Gauss-Bonnet and dynamical Chern-Simons theories. We demonstrate that geodesic paths in these theories likely lack a fourth constant of motion. Specifically, Poincaré sections of the orbital phase space reveal chaotic characteristics that could influence the inspiral process. However, these chaotic regions are extremely small in scale and situated very near the event horizon. Consequently, detecting such chaos with LISA is likely to be exceedingly difficult, if feasible at all.

A defining characteristic of integrable systems is their capacity to yield exact analytical solutions. This work demonstrates the construction of novel models by generalizing established nonlinear partial differential equations with PT-symmetries while maintaining integrability. We then adapt known methodologies to derive exact analytical soliton solutions for these new systems. Our initial PT-symmetric generalizations involve extensions to complex and multicomplex fields; consistent with the reality properties observed in PT-symmetric non-Hermitian quantum systems, we identify that PT-symmetry is crucial for the reality of conserved charges in this context. We further investigate degenerate multi-soliton solutions for the sine-Gordon and Hirota equations, discovering that, unlike non-degenerate cases, the time delays associated with degenerate soliton scattering are time-dependent. Additionally, we present a universal formula for calculating exact time-delay values for N-soliton scattering. Further PT-symmetric extensions explored include nonlocal systems featuring spatial and/or temporal nonlocalities of the time-crystal type. In developing solution construction methods for these systems, we uncover new solution types with distinct parameter dependencies and qualitative behaviors, even in the one-soliton limit. We also leverage gauge equivalence between the Hirota system and the continuous Heisenberg and Landau-Lifschitz systems to trace how nonlocality is transferred between them. Finally, extending our inquiry to the quantum regime, we generalize the Darboux transformation scheme for fully time-dependent non-Hermitian quantum systems, thereby generating an infinite hierarchy of solvable models.

Recent years have seen a strong focus on multi-view clustering due to its superior performance; however, traditional approaches still suffer from limitations regarding the elimination of redundant data, effective integration of diverse views, and feature fusion. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel method: adaptive graph regularization-based low-rank subspace multi-view clustering. By unifying two new data matrix decomposition models into a single optimization framework, we introduce novel low-rank and sparse constraints on the sparse subspace matrix to capture both shared cross-view knowledge and unique per-view information. Furthermore, adaptive graph regularization and unsupervised clustering constraints are integrated into the model to maintain the internal structural integrity of the data and ensure effective sparse representation. Comparative experiments against several state-of-the-art algorithms across five standard multi-view benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing techniques.

Mapping entities and relations within a knowledge graph into a low-dimensional space has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in predicting missing entity links. Despite these advancements, current approaches remain largely heuristic, lacking a robust theoretical foundation. This study extends the random walk model originally applied to word embeddings (Arora et al., 2016a) to Knowledge Graph Embeddings (KGEs) to formulate a scoring function that assesses the strength of a relation R between a head entity h and a tail entity t. Furthermore, we demonstrate that marginal loss minimization—a prevalent objective in prior KGE research—emerges naturally from maximizing the log-likelihood ratio based on probabilities estimated via our theoretical framework. Consequently, we introduce a learning objective grounded in this theoretical analysis for training KGEs on given knowledge graphs. Empirical validation on the FB15K237 and WN18RR benchmark datasets confirms that models trained with this objective achieve high accuracy, thereby supporting the proposed theory.

Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$. The Seidel matrix of $G$ is an $n \times n$ matrix where diagonal elements are zero, the $(i,j)$-th entry equals $-1$ if $v_i$ and $v_j$ are adjacent, and $1$ otherwise. The Seidel energy of $G$, denoted by $\se{G}$, is defined as the sum of the absolute values of all eigenvalues of this matrix. In \cite{aekn}, it was established that the Seidel energy of any graph of order $n$ is at least $2n-2$. This study enhances that previously proven lower bound specifically for tree graphs.

Analyzing predicate-argument structures is fundamental to representing the meaning of text. Ambiguity in language comprehension and challenges for machine interpretation often arise because certain arguments are not explicitly stated in sentences. Currently, few resources explicitly represent these implicit roles for Natural Language Understanding, and existing NLP research typically makes only broad distinctions regarding omitted argument categories. This paper introduces a fine-grained typology for annotating implicit arguments, built upon the foundational layer of Universal Conceptual Cognitive Annotation (UCCA). Driven by theories of implicit role interpretation, this categorization system defines six specific types: Deictic, Generic, Genre-based, Type-identifiable, Non-specific, and Iterated-set. To demonstrate this framework, we re-analyze a portion of the UCCA EWT corpus with this new refinement layer, creating an updated dataset and offering a comparative evaluation against other annotation schemes.

This work examines parity games on infinite graphs where states are defined by control-states and integer vectors. This model encompasses two well-known game types: parity games on vector addition systems with states (VASS) and multidimensional energy parity games. We demonstrate that multidimensional energy parity games are inter-reducible with a specific subset of single-sided parity games on VASS, where one player exclusively modifies counters while the other alters only control-states. Our primary finding is that the minimal elements within the upward-closed winning set of these single-sided VASS parity games are computable. Consequently, this establishes that the Pareto frontier of the minimal initial credits required to win multidimensional energy parity games is also computable, resolving a longstanding open problem. Furthermore, our main result proves the decidability of weak simulation preorder and equivalence for finite-state systems against VASS, as well as the decidability of model checking VASS using a substantial portion of the modal mu-calculus.

Detecting lanes is a critical but difficult component of autonomous driving, complicated by various elements such as lighting variations, occlusions from other vehicles, distracting road markings, and the naturally elongated and narrow nature of lanes. Traditional approaches typically frame lane detection as semantic segmentation, assigning a class label to every pixel; however, this method relies on the restrictive assumption that the lane count is fixed and static, which is often unrealistic. To ensure the model handles an arbitrary number of lanes and dynamic lane-changing events, we employ an instance segmentation strategy that first separates lanes from the background before categorizing each lane pixel into its specific instance. Additionally, we implement a multi-task learning framework to leverage structural information and a feature pyramid network to identify extremely thin lanes. The proposed algorithm's efficacy is validated across three established benchmarks: TuSimple, CULane, and BDD100K.

This study utilizes relativistic many-body theory to evaluate the viability of the ground-state TlF+ molecular ion for detecting the electron electric dipole moment. By employing high-quality basis sets alongside configuration interaction and coupled cluster approaches, we calculated the molecular permanent electric dipole moment and the effective electric field, subsequently analyzing the impact of electron correlation on these properties. Our results indicate that TlF+ exhibits a substantial effective electric field of approximately 163 GV/cm, a value roughly 1.5 times greater than those of HgF and HgH, which currently hold the record for the largest effective electric fields among non-superheavy systems.

In *Journal of Symbolic Logic*, 51(4): 957-968 (1986), Pawlikowski demonstrated that if $r$ is a random real over $\mathbf{N}$ and $c$ is a Cohen real over $\mathbf{N}[r]$, then: (a) the model $\mathbf{N}[r][c]$ contains a Cohen real over $\mathbf{N}[c]$, and (b) the set $2^\omega \cap \mathbf{N}[c]$ is not in $\mathcal{N} \cap \mathbf{N}[r][c]$, implying that no random real over $\mathbf{N}[c]$ exists within $\mathbf{N}[r][c]$. To establish these results, Pawlikowski introduced a specific concept: for two ZFC models $\mathbf{N} \subseteq \mathbf{M}$ and a continuum cardinal characteristic $\mathfrak{x}$, he defined a sentence $\mathfrak{x}_\mathbf{N}^\mathbf{M}$ asserting that in $\mathbf{M}$, the reals belonging to $\mathbf{N}$ form a family satisfying the cardinal's requirements. Consequently, proving (a) and (b) reduces to verifying the implications: (a') $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M})_{\mathbf{N}[c]}^{\mathbf{M}[c]} \Rightarrow \mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})_{\mathbf{N}}^{\mathbf{M}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})_{\mathbf{N}}^{\mathbf{M}}$, and (b') $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M})_\mathbf{N}^\mathbf{M} \Rightarrow \mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})_{\mathbf{N}}^{\mathbf{M}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})_{\mathbf{N}[c]}^{\mathbf{M}[c]} \Rightarrow \mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})_{\mathbf{N}[c]}^{\mathbf{M}[c]}$. This paper presents the notion of Tukey-order with models, an extension of Vojtáš's Tukey-order (Israel Math. Conf. Proc. 6: 619-643, 1991), designed to prove implications of the form $\mathfrak{x}_\mathbf{N}^\mathbf{M} \Rightarrow \mathfrak{y}_\mathbf{N}^\mathbf{M}$. Specifically, we utilize Tukey-order with models to demonstrate both (a') and (b').

We elaborate on the Berry phase origin of the recently discovered planar spin Hall effect, which exhibits current-induced spin polarization within the plane of Hall deflection. By uncovering a spin-repulsion vector that governs this effect, we provide a clear criterion for identifying intrinsic planar spin Hall materials. Our findings reveal that a finite spin-repulsion vector is allowed in 13 crystalline point groups, indicating a large number of previously unexplored planar spin Hall systems. These results enable quantitative calculations of the planar spin Hall effect, thereby aiding future material discovery and experimental research.

Atomic nuclei function as composite systems that can undergo dynamic excitation during nuclear reactions. These excitations influence various reaction mechanisms, including inelastic scattering, as well as elastic scattering and fusion. The coupled-channels approach provides a unified framework to describe these processes by expanding the system's total wave function in terms of the ground and excited states of the colliding nuclei. By solving the coupled Schrödinger equations, this method yields the S-matrix, which is then used to calculate various cross sections. As a standard tool for analyzing experimental nuclear reaction data, this approach is the focus of the present review, which examines its current status and recent advancements. Key topics include the microscopic coupled-channels method applied to cluster physics, the continuum discretized coupled-channels (CDCC) method for breakup reactions, semi-microscopic treatments of heavy-ion subbarrier fusion, the impact of channel coupling on nuclear astrophysics and superheavy element synthesis, and inclusive breakup and incomplete fusion reactions involving weakly-bound nuclei.

We have observed that Marek et al. (2021) attempted to replicate our work, "Zheng et al. (2020a)," in their paper "OodGAN: Generative Adversarial Network for Out-of-Domain Data Generation." Our approach introduces a model designed to generate pseudo OOD samples that closely resemble IN-Domain (IND) input utterances. These samples enhance OOD detection performance by optimizing an entropy regularization term during the construction of the IND classifier. However, Marek et al. (2021) reported significant discrepancies between their re-implementation results and ours on the CLINC150 dataset (Larson et al., 2019). This discussion highlights several key factors likely responsible for this gap, drawing primarily from our experiments since Marek et al. (2021) have not made their code available. A primary insight is that stronger IND classifiers generally demonstrate more robust OOD detection capabilities. We hope these findings assist researchers, including Marek et al. (2021), in developing superior OOD detectors for their specific applications.

Although Gaia has mapped the phase space coordinates of over a billion Galactic stars, it has successfully captured only five of the six dimensions in most cases, leaving radial (line-of-sight) velocity unmeasured. By employing a realistic simulated dataset, we demonstrate that Bayesian neural networks can effectively learn to predict these missing radial velocities based on the remaining five coordinates. Unlike standard point predictions, our network outputs complete posterior distributions that account for the intrinsic scatter in the stellar phase space, observational errors in the input data, and epistemic uncertainty arising from incomplete knowledge of the distribution. When applied to actual Gaia data, this approach generated and released a catalogue of radial velocity posteriors (with a median width of 25 km/s) for 16 million stars in the Gaia DR2/EDR3 dataset within the magnitude range 6 < G < 14.5. While upcoming Gaia DR3 data will likely fill many of these gaps and serve as a test for our blind predictions, the primary value of our current catalogue lies in validating our methodology, thereby justifying its future application to produce updated posterior catalogues for radial velocities absent in Gaia DR3.

We present a theoretical investigation into the thermoelectric characteristics of graphene quantum dot arrays (GQDAs) featuring line- or surface-contacted metallic electrodes. These structures are constructed from zigzag graphene nanoribbons (ZGNRs) containing periodic vacancies, resulting in the formation of gaps and minibands that enable both metallic and semiconducting phases. Electronic states within the first conduction (valence) miniband, characterized by nonlinear dispersion, exhibit extended coherent lengths along the zigzag edge. When armchair edge atoms of the ZGNRs connect to line-contacted metal electrodes, the system behaves like serially coupled quantum dots (SCQDs); conversely, coupling the zigzag edge atoms yields properties akin to parallel quantum dots. At room temperature, SCQDs with line contacts made of Cu, Au, Pt, Pd, or Ti achieved maximum thermoelectric power factors comparable to or exceeding $0.186 \text{ nW/K}$, with corresponding figures of merit surpassing three. Overall, GQDAs utilizing line-contacted metal electrodes demonstrate significantly superior thermoelectric performance compared to those with surface contacts.

Optimal transport (OT) theory offers robust methods for comparing probability distributions, yet it is restricted to nonnegative measures with identical total mass and faces significant challenges regarding computational efficiency and statistical properties. Consequently, recent research has explored various regularized OT variants. This study introduces an *entropy partial transport* (EPT) framework designed for nonnegative measures on a tree structure where masses may differ. We demonstrate that EPT is mathematically equivalent to a standard complete OT problem on an extended tree with a single node. By deriving a dual formulation, we propose a novel regularization scheme for EPT that ensures both rapid computation and negative definiteness. To our knowledge, this regularized EPT is the first unbalanced OT variant to provide a *closed-form* solution. For scenarios lacking prior knowledge of the tree structure, we introduce tree-sliced variants of the regularized EPT, calculated by averaging results across random tree metrics constructed adaptively from support data points. Leveraging the negative definiteness of our approach, we define a positive definite kernel and assess its performance against baseline methods on benchmark tasks, including document classification using word embeddings and topological data analysis. Furthermore, empirical results confirm that our regularization yields effective approximations.

This study introduces a two-level distributed algorithmic framework designed to solve the AC optimal power flow (OPF) problem with assured convergence. The highly nonconvex constraints inherent in OPF present substantial hurdles for distributed methods relying on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), particularly because convergence cannot be guaranteed for nonconvex network optimization tasks like AC OPF. To address this, we develop a novel distributed reformulation of AC OPF alongside a two-level ADMM algorithm that extends beyond conventional ADMM structures. We demonstrate the global convergence and iteration complexity of this proposed approach under mild assumptions. Furthermore, extensive numerical experiments on large-scale test cases from NESTA and PGLib-OPF (including systems with up to 30,000 buses) reveal that our algorithm outperforms existing ADMM variants in convergence, scalability, and robustness. Additionally, when implemented in parallel, the method achieves rapid convergence that matches or exceeds the performance of leading centralized solvers.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has recently garnered significant attention, yet a critical and often overlooked issue persists: noise. Stochastic elements inherent in network initialization, training processes, and data splits render single-run performance evaluations unreliable, an effect that is magnified with limited datasets. To mitigate this, we propose assessing architectures by averaging performance across multiple training runs with varied random seeds and cross-validation techniques. Our experiments explore a combinatorial optimization framework for NAS, adjusting noise reduction levels while maintaining a constant computational budget; consequently, increasing the number of training runs per architecture necessitates fewer total architecture evaluations. We evaluate several search algorithms, including evolutionary methods known for their efficacy in NAS, using two public medical image segmentation datasets characterized by limited size and high sample variability. Our findings demonstrate that reducing noise in architecture evaluation consistently enables the discovery of superior architectures across all tested search algorithms.

A recently proposed approach to achieving a "natural hot-ion mode" involves leveraging ion viscous heating within a rotating plasma confined by a fixed boundary. By examining the steady-state solutions of the Braginskii equations, we identify the specific parameter range that allows for a sustained significant temperature disparity between ions and electrons in a driven steady state. This effect becomes feasible when the ion Larmor radius satisfies $\rho_i\gtrsim0.1R$. Our analysis includes an analytic solution at leading order for low flow velocities, alongside a numerical investigation of moderate Mach numbers up to $M\lesssim2$, revealing that the primary limitation arises at these moderate Mach numbers.

We examine the Laplacian on a metric graph, subject to Robin ($\delta$-type) conditions at specific vertices and Neumann-Kirchhoff conditions at the remainder. The resulting spectrum consists of Robin eigenvalues, distinct from Neumann eigenvalues which arise when Neumann-Kirchhoff conditions apply universally. The sequence of differences between these paired eigenvalues is defined as the Robin-Neumann gap. We demonstrate that the limiting mean of this sequence exists and corresponds to a geometric invariant, mirroring findings for planar domains. Additionally, we establish that the sequence is uniformly bounded and derive explicit upper and lower bounds. Our analysis further investigates the potential accumulation points of the sequence and connects them to the associated probability distribution of the gaps. To substantiate these primary findings, we establish a local Weyl law and determine explicit formulas for the second moments of eigenfunction scattering amplitudes.

This paper investigates the combinatorial aspects of free Borel actions of the group $\mathbb Z^d$ on Polish spaces. Drawing on recent findings by Chandgotia and Meyerovitch, we define property $F$ for $\mathbb Z^d$-shift spaces $X$, characterized by the existence of an equivariant map from any free Borel action to the free component of $X$. Assuming additional entropic constraints, we demonstrate that any subshift $Y$ (excluding periodic points) can be Borel embedded into $X$. Notable examples satisfying property $F$ include the space of proper $3$-colourings, tilings by rectangles (subject to a specific arithmetic condition), proper $2d$-edge colourings of $\mathbb Z^d$, and the space of bi-infinite Hamiltonian paths. These findings address inquiries posed by Seward and Gao-Jackson, while also recovering results established by Weilacher and those announced by Gao-Jackson-Krohne-Seward.

Blind quantum computing enables secure cloud interactions between quasi-classical clients and complete quantum servers. A recently introduced protocol mandates that clients perform solely measurements. We present a proof-of-principle realization of this measurement-only approach for blind quantum computing, utilizing a photonic system to create four-qubit cluster states essential for computation and verification. The technological feasibility for both the client and the device-independent security guarantees render this scheme highly suitable for future secure quantum networks.

Human perception and behavior are significantly influenced by situational context, especially during social interactions. Recent research indicates that humans process visual stimuli differently when performing tasks alone versus alongside a robot; specifically, the central tendency effect is more pronounced in social settings compared to non-social ones. However, the specific nature of these behaviorally induced changes and the underlying cognitive mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper addresses this gap by training an artificial neural network, grounded in predictive coding theory, on the aforementioned behavioral dataset. Using this computational model, we examine whether the context-driven behavioral shifts observed in human experiments can be explained by continuously adjusting a parameter that reflects the relative weight of sensory versus prior information in perception. We show that replicating human behavioral data across both individual and social contexts is achievable by modulating the precision of sensory and prior signals, suggesting that social and non-social tasks may exist on a continuum. Furthermore, an analysis of the neural activation patterns within the trained networks reveals that information is encoded in fundamentally different ways under individual versus social conditions. These findings highlight the value of computational replications for formulating hypotheses about the cognitive mechanisms of shared perception and may inspire future neuroscience research.

Twisted transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) homobilayers have recently become a prominent system for investigating correlated insulating states. In the strong correlation regime, we develop an effective spin Hamiltonian defined on a honeycomb lattice for the Mott-insulating phase at half-filling. This Hamiltonian incorporates the Heisenberg interaction alongside nonsymmetric terms, specifically the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and the Kane-Mele coupling. For these twisted TMD systems, the spin-orbit coupling within the Hubbard model—which drives the antisymmetric exchange couplings in the effective spin description—is a highly tunable parameter accessible via applied electric fields. Utilizing both analytical and numerical approaches, we explore the classical and quantum phase diagrams of this effective Hamiltonian. Our results reveal a complex classical landscape featuring antiferromagnetic (AFM), planar spiral (with high degeneracy), $z$-AFM, noncoplanar, noncollinear, and 120$^{\circ}$-AFM phases. In the quantum analysis, we employ linear spin-wave theory and density matrix renormalization group techniques to compute the ground state energy, static spin structure factor, and low-energy magnon spectra, thereby constructing the quantum phase diagram. Beyond the standard Heisenberg term, we identify that these antisymmetric couplings are the driving force behind the emergence of quantum spin liquid, $z$-AFM, noncoplanar, and 120$^{\circ}$ phases. Consequently, twisted TMD homobilayers serve as versatile platforms for realizing diverse matter phases, including quantum spin liquids and noncollinear orders, mediated by spin-orbit coupling.

Strong interactions generate a diverse array of resonances decaying into three or more hadrons. To understand their phenomenology, a theoretical framework is essential for deriving parameters from experimental data and Lattice QCD simulations of hadron scattering. Currently, two classes of relativistic three-body methods are being explored: those based on Effective Field Theory (EFT) and those based on unitarity. This work examines a model of relativistic three-body scattering featuring an S-wave bound state within a two-body sub-channel, employing both formalisms. We present and analyze numerical solutions for multi-hadron scattering amplitudes across various kinematic regions, derived from the integral equations of the EFT-based approach. We also highlight the relevance of our findings to the ongoing efforts in computing the three-body spectrum via the lattice. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to extend the unitarity-based framework to encompass all pertinent open channels, address nonphysical singularities near the physical region, and illustrate a method to eliminate these singularities in a specific case.

While conventional iterative methods often surpass data-driven deep learning in image registration accuracy, particularly with limited training data, we introduce VR-Net to bridge this gap without sacrificing the speed of deep learning inference. VR-Net is a novel cascaded variational network designed for unsupervised deformable image registration. By applying variable splitting optimization, the generic variational formulation of image registration is decomposed into two sub-problems: one solvable via a point-wise closed-form solution and another framed as a denoising task. To address these, we propose two neural layers—a warping layer and an intensity consistency layer—to represent the analytical solution, alongside a residual U-Net acting as a generalized denoising layer. These components are cascaded to constitute VR-Net. Comprehensive experiments across three cardiac magnetic resonance imaging datasets (two 2D and one 3D) demonstrate that VR-Net achieves superior registration accuracy compared to existing deep learning methods while retaining both the rapid inference capabilities of deep learning and the data efficiency characteristic of variational models.

Drawing inspiration from feedforward multilayer perceptrons (FF-MLP), decision trees (DT), and extreme learning machines (ELM), this study introduces a novel classification framework known as the subspace learning machine (SLM). The SLM initially identifies a discriminant subspace, denoted as $S^0$, by evaluating the discriminative capability of individual input features. It then employs probabilistic projections of features within $S^0$ to generate one-dimensional subspaces and determines the optimal partition for each, which is mathematically equivalent to dividing $S^0$ using hyperplanes. A specific criterion is formulated to select the most effective $q$ partitions, resulting in $2q$ distinct subspaces. The subspace $S^0$ is designated as the root node of the decision tree, while the intersections of these $2q$ subspaces form the child nodes at depth one. This partitioning procedure is applied recursively to every child node to construct the SLM tree. The process halts at leaf nodes when samples achieve sufficient purity, at which point predictions are made. This methodology can be extended to regression tasks, creating the subspace learning regressor (SLR). Additionally, ensembles composed of SLM/SLR trees can produce more robust predictors. Comprehensive experiments were conducted to benchmark the performance of SLM/SLR trees, their ensembles, and traditional classifiers/regressors.

Extrapolating from brief to extended problem instances represents a vital form of out-of-distribution generalization for reasoning, particularly when training data contains few long examples, as seen in theorem proving, quantitative math, and novel reading/summarization. This paper presents rigorous empirical investigations into the length generalization capabilities of transformer-based language models. We first demonstrate that naive fine-tuning on length generalization tasks yields significant performance deficits regardless of model size. Subsequently, we show that integrating in-context learning from pretrained large language models with scratchpad prompting—where models output solution steps before final answers—leads to a substantial enhancement in length generalization. Finally, we conduct detailed failure analyses across these learning approaches to pinpoint common error sources, thereby revealing avenues for improving models' ability to handle longer problems.

Curating extensive fully supervised datasets has emerged as a significant obstacle in machine learning. Weak supervision offers an alternative by utilizing inexpensive, noisy, and potentially correlated labeling functions from diverse sources. The primary difficulty in weakly supervised learning lies in integrating these disparate signals while managing misleading error correlations. This paper introduces a straightforward, data-free technique for merging weak supervision signals by establishing a constrained space for potential labels and employing random labeling within that framework. Our approach is both efficient and stable, achieving convergence after only a few gradient descent iterations. We provide theoretical proofs demonstrating that the worst-case error of randomized labels diminishes as the rank of linear constraints increases. Experimental results confirm that our method surpasses other weak supervision techniques across various text and image classification tasks.

This survey paper explores rainbow sets, also known as choice functions, by distinguishing between two categories: those with a large image (defined by membership in a specific filter, namely a closed-up set of sets) and those characterized by a large domain paired with a small image, where "smallness" refers to belonging to a specified complex (a closed-down set). The work introduces several new findings, including theorems regarding scrambled versions where sets are re-ordered prior to selection, as well as results on weighted and cooperative variants.

We introduce JECL, a technique for clustering image-caption pairs that employs parallel encoders trained with regularized clustering and alignment objectives to jointly learn representations and cluster assignments. This approach addresses scenarios common in high-value applications where structured training data is costly, yet free-text descriptions are abundant. JECL operates by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the distributions of images and text toward a unified joint target distribution, while simultaneously optimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence regarding their soft cluster assignments. To avoid trivial solutions, regularizers are integrated into the JECL framework. Experimental results demonstrate that JECL surpasses both single-view and multi-view methods on large-scale benchmark datasets and exhibits remarkable robustness to missing captions and fluctuations in data volume.

We introduce a randomized algorithm operating in polynomial time to approximate the permanent of any real $M \times M$ matrix $A$ within an additive error margin. This approach models the permanent of $A$ as the expected value of a product of centered joint Gaussian variables, defined by a covariance matrix termed the Gaussian embedding of $A$. The algorithm generates an estimate, denoted as $S_{N}$, by calculating the empirical mean of this product over $N$ samples drawn from the corresponding multivariate distribution. Specifically, with a failure probability bounded by $\frac{3^{M}}{t^{2}N}\alpha^{2M}$ (where $\alpha \geq \|A \|$), the procedure completes in $O(MN)$ time after $N$ samples.

This study presents the discovery of KIC 6382916 (J19480292+4146558), a rapidly evolving high-amplitude $\delta$ Scuti star currently traversing the Hertzsprung gap. Analysis of archival data reveals three independent pulsation modes whose frequencies and amplitudes exhibit distinct variations over a four-year period. The linear period variation rates for the first two modes are approximately 3 to 4 times greater than those predicted by the best seismic model derived from standard evolutionary theory, whereas the rate for the third mode is roughly eight times larger than that of the first two. Notably, in the frequency domain, nearly all combinations of the third mode display frequency peaks shifted by $0.0815\ \mathrm{c\ d}^{-1}$ from the original peaks. To explain the exceptionally large variation rates in frequency and amplitude observed in the third mode, we propose a framework utilizing a newly identified pulsation mode—the resonating integration mode—arising from the resonance between a radial p-mode and a nonradial mixed mode. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of interactions among the three independent pulsation modes and their harmonics or combinations is conducted using interaction diagrams of amplitudes and phases, offering a valuable tool for future asteroseismological research.

The Universal Extra Dimension (UED) framework is a robust and extensively analyzed theoretical scenario, primarily motivated by the existence of a dark matter candidate known as the lightest level-1 Kaluza-Klein (KK) particle within its spectrum. The minimal UED (mUED) variant is particularly predictive, relying on just two parameters—the compactification radius and the cut-off scale—to define its phenomenology. Consequently, precise measurements of the universe's dark matter relic density by WMAP and PLANCK impose strict constraints on this model. At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the production and decay of level-1 quarks and gluons in UED scenarios manifest as multijet final states. This study examines the ATLAS search for multijet events accompanied by missing transverse energy using 13 TeV collision data with an integrated luminosity of 139 inverse femtobarns. Given that the region of mUED parameter space compatible with dark matter relic density has already been excluded by ATLAS multijet results, the analysis extends to a less constrained version, the non-minimal UED (nmUED), which incorporates non-vanishing boundary-localized terms (BLTs). These BLTs substantially modify both the dark matter properties and collider signatures of nmUED, leading to the derivation of stringent limits on the BLT parameters based on the ATLAS multijet plus missing transverse energy search.
A method is introduced that derives Williamson matrices of order $2n$ from those of odd order $n$. This approach is fully constructive, relying solely on three basic sequence operations.

We introduce a new method for automatically colorizing grayscale images that integrates a U-Net model with Fusion Layer features. This strategy enables the model to acquire colorization capabilities from a pre-trained U-Net. Additionally, the Fusion layer combines local information derived from small image patches with global priors across the entire image for each class, yielding more visually appealing results. Finally, our approach is validated through a user study and compared against state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating significant improvements.

Current object detection models rely on the assumption that training and testing data originate from the same domain, a condition rarely met in real-world deployments where detectors face new visual environments. To counter the negative impacts of domain shift, Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) techniques are typically utilized; however, most existing approaches function offline, adapting the model before deployment. This static strategy is ill-suited for practical applications where models must continuously handle emerging domain shifts. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a UDA method capable of generalizing to shifts encountered during operation in a continuous, online fashion. To address this, we introduce a novel unified framework designed to adapt and enhance generalization within online settings. Specifically, we present MemXformer, a cross-attention transformer-based memory module that leverages domain shifts to capture prototypical patterns of the target distribution. Additionally, MemXformer generates robust positive and negative pairs to guide a new contrastive loss function, thereby strengthening target-specific representation learning. Experiments across various detection benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in both online and offline scenarios. To our knowledge, this is the first study to tackle object detection adaptation in both online and offline contexts. Code is available at https://github.com/Vibashan/memXformer-online-da.

Recent studies on interpretability in natural language processing frequently employ feature scoring techniques to pinpoint the most critical input components for model predictions (i.e., explanations or rationales). However, prior work indicates that no single scoring method universally outperforms others across diverse text classification tasks, and practitioners often face arbitrary decisions regarding rationale characteristics, such as length and continuity. Motivated by these challenges, we introduce a straightforward yet adaptable method capable of optimizing, for each individual data instance, three key parameters: the feature scoring technique, the rationale length, and the rationale type. Drawing inspiration from input erasure approaches, our method operates on the premise that the most faithful explanation is the one yielding the greatest disparity between the model's output distribution on the full text versus the text after the rationale is removed. Experiments across four standard text classification datasets demonstrate that our approach generates explanations that are more faithful, comprehensive, and sufficiently detailed than those derived from fixed scoring methods, lengths, and types. Crucially, we show that practitioners can extract faithful rationales using our method without needing to make any ad-hoc selections.

The CASH problem has been extensively researched within automated machine learning pipeline configurations, with numerous solvers and toolkits currently available. Nevertheless, existing CASH solvers fail to natively manage black-box constraints like fairness, robustness, or other domain-specific requirements. We introduce our recent methodology [Liu, et al., 2020], which utilizes the ADMM optimization framework to break down CASH into smaller sub-problems, illustrating how ADMM enables the integration of black-box constraints.

A key component of the Phase-II Upgrade for the ATLAS detector involves replacing the existing Inner Detector with the ATLAS Inner Tracker (ITk), an all-silicon system composed of pixel and strip trackers. The sensors for the ITk strip tracker have been engineered to endure the intense radiation environment anticipated after the High Luminosity Upgrade at CERN, which will drastically increase collision rates and particle tracks. During operation, these sensors are projected to accumulate fluences reaching 1.6 x 10^15 n_eq/cm^2 (including a 1.5 safety margin), significantly impacting their performance. A critical characteristic for such highly irradiated sensors is the uniformity and configuration of the electric field within their active regions. The study presented here involves irradiating diodes with edge geometries mirroring full-scale ATLAS sensors up to fluences comparable to those expected in the ITk strip tracker, then mapping their electric fields using a micro-focused X-ray beam with a 2x3 {\mu}m^2 diameter. These results illustrate the shape and extent of the electric field inside heavily irradiated diodes across various bias voltages. Furthermore, by measuring the outlines of the depleted sensor areas, researchers can compare leakage current measurements at different fluences against expectations for the corresponding active areas.

We introduce a novel Bayesian optimization framework designed to learn user preferences within high-dimensional spaces, specifically targeting the optimization of black-box functions. The core premise is that the objective function cannot be directly evaluated; instead, the system queries minimizers along specific projections, termed "projective preferential queries." This query structure facilitates natural, interactive feedback from humans. Our approach is validated through a user experiment where feedback consists of the optimal position and orientation of a molecule adsorbing to a surface. Results demonstrate that our framework successfully identifies the global minimum of a high-dimensional black-box function, a task that remains infeasible for existing preferential Bayesian optimization methods relying on pairwise comparisons.

Self-organized criticality refers to dynamical systems that sustain an attractor state lacking intrinsic scales of time or length. Fundamentally, this framework necessitates a mechanism for local instability that can trigger cascading instabilities through dissipative processes. This theory has been applied to explain nonlinear phenomena, including the featureless energy spectra observed in earthquakes, avalanches, and solar flares. If this interpretation holds, it suggests the solar coronal magnetic field remains in a critical state through a precise equilibrium between dynamo-driven energy injection and energy release via flares. All-sky, high-cadence missions such as the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) offer the data required to compare flare energy distributions across stars of various spectral types against those of the Sun. Utilizing TESS observations at a 2-minute cadence, we identified approximately $10^6$ flaring events across roughly $10^5$ stars. By fitting flare frequency distributions within different mass bins, we found that all main-sequence stars display flare distributions comparable to the Sun's, regardless of mass or age. This implies that stars universally maintain a critical state in their coronal structures via magnetic reconnection. If this view is correct, we could potentially deduce properties of magnetic fields, internal structures, and dynamo mechanisms for stars that otherwise appear as unresolved point sources.

We construct a series of perfect quantum error-correcting codes designed to rectify phase errors occurring on any qubit at any moment throughout a flawless state transfer process. These codes enable the identification of the optimal operational conditions for corrected state transfer. Furthermore, for a particular class of systems, we demonstrate that while dephasing noise can be mitigated, depolarizing noise remains uncorrectable.

This paper investigates the Mellin transform of the weight 2, level $N$ polar harmonic Maass form $H_{N,z}^*(\tau)$, examining its behavior as an (generalized) $L$-function when $\mathrm{Im}(z)$ approaches infinity. Along the way, we derive the Fourier expansion of $H_{N,z}^*(\tau)$ at any cusp of $\Gamma_0(N)$, and we establish a functional equation and factorization into local components for the $L$-function associated with weight 2, level $N$ Eisenstein series at the cusps $i\infty$ and $0$.

Stochastic parameterizations address uncertainties in unresolved sub-grid processes by sampling from the distribution of potential sub-grid forcings. While some current stochastic methods employ data-driven techniques, they often rely on heavy structural assumptions that hinder scalability. Conversely, machine learning models, particularly neural networks, can model diverse distributions and establish optimized mappings between numerous inputs and sub-grid forcings. Although recent work on machine learning parameterizations has largely focused on deterministic approaches, this study introduces a stochastic parameterization based on the generative adversarial network (GAN) framework. We train and assess this GAN-based parameterization using outputs from the Lorenz '96 model, a standard benchmark for evaluating parameterization and data assimilation methods. The study examines various strategies for characterizing input noise and conducts model runs across both weather and climate timescales. Results indicate that certain GAN configurations outperform a baseline bespoke parameterization at both scales, closely replicating the spatio-temporal correlations and regimes of the Lorenz '96 system. Furthermore, we observe that models generating skillful forecasts also tend to produce the most accurate climate simulations.

Currently, the pharmaceutical sector relies on manual inspection by trained personnel to screen opaque vaccines containing suspensions. This study demonstrates that deep learning can effectively automate this procedure. To differentiate anomalies from surface reflections, dust, and other particles, a moving contrast technique is employed. We trained 3D-ConvNets to assess the probability of anomalies within 20-frame video sequences. Our baseline dataset comprises manually labeled samples recorded using vials supplied by the HAL Allergy Group. We evaluated ten randomly initialized 3D-ConvNets as a benchmark, achieving mean AUROC scores of 0.94 for positive (anomalous) samples and 0.93 for negative (anomaly-free) samples. By utilizing Frame-Completion Generative Adversarial Networks, we: (i) developed an algorithm to generate saliency maps, confirming that the 3D-ConvNets correctly identify anomalies; and (ii) introduced a novel self-training method using these maps to ensure consensus on anomaly locations across multiple networks. This self-training strategy enabled the augmentation of our dataset with 217,888 additional labeled samples. Consequently, 3D-ConvNets trained on this augmented dataset outperformed those trained solely on the original unaugmented data.

The Transit Timing Variation (TTV) method serves as a robust dynamical approach for determining exoplanet masses by analyzing transit light curves. We evaluated the transit timing capabilities of the Ariel Fine Guidance Sensors (FGS1/2) using simulated light curves from both bright (55 Cnc) and faint (K2-24) planet-hosting stars. Through Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo analysis, we quantified transit time uncertainties at the nominal 1-second cadence, alongside comparisons for 30 and 60-second cadences. Our results indicate that at the nominal cadence, Ariel can achieve a transit timing precision of approximately 12 seconds for 55 Cnc and 34 seconds for K2-24. Subsequent dynamical simulations, incorporating Ariel's timing errors, revealed a 20–30% enhancement in planetary mass measurement accuracy via TTVs for systems resembling K2-24. Additionally, we simulated conditions enabling the detection of TTV signals caused by a hypothetical external perturber, with masses ranging from Earth to Neptune, using just 10 transit light curves from Ariel.

This paper introduces a new Bayesian learning approach grounded in pessimism, designed for optimal dynamic treatment regimes within offline environments. Since existing methods often yield sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition is violated—a frequent occurrence in offline datasets—the proposed method leverages the pessimism principle to avoid recommending under-explored actions relative to the current state. While most current pessimism-based techniques depend on a sensitive hyper-parameter to control the degree of pessimism, our approach integrates this principle with Thompson sampling and Bayesian machine learning to automatically optimize this degree. We construct a credible set whose boundary uniformly lower-bounds the optimal Q-function, thereby eliminating the need for manual tuning of the pessimism parameter. The resulting general Bayesian framework is compatible with various models, ranging from Bayesian linear basis functions to Bayesian neural networks. Furthermore, we implement a computationally efficient and scalable algorithm using variational inference. We provide theoretical assurances for the method and demonstrate through simulations and a real-world data application that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art solutions.

We report measurements of the azimuthal dependence of charged jet production in central and semi-central $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 2.76 TeV Pb-Pb collisions relative to the second harmonic event plane, expressed as $v_{2}^{\mathrm{ch~jet}}$. Jets are reconstructed using the anti-$k_{\mathrm{T}}$ algorithm with a resolution parameter $R$ = 0.2 based on charged tracks from the ALICE tracking system. The event-by-event azimuthal anisotropy of the underlying event is accounted for, while remaining statistical region-to-region fluctuations are eliminated on an ensemble basis by unfolding jet spectra for various event plane orientations separately. A significant non-zero $v_{2}^{\mathrm{ch~jet}}$ is detected in semi-central collisions (30-50\% centrality) for charged jet transverse momenta between 20 and 90 ${\mathrm{GeV}\kern-0.05em/\kern-0.02em c}$. The azimuthal variation in charged jet production mirrors that observed for jets containing both charged and neutral fragments and aligns with high $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ single charged particle $v_2$ measurements. In semi-central collisions, the data show good agreement with JEWEL event generator predictions, which simulate parton shower evolution within a dense QCD medium.

Directly detecting and characterizing exoplanets via extreme adaptive optics (ExAO) represents a primary scientific objective for future extremely large telescopes (ELTs), yet wavefront errors constrain the sensitivity of such missions. Ground-based observatories face limitations stemming from both quasi-static and residual AO-corrected atmospheric disturbances; the latter produce short-lived aberrations that accumulate into a halo during long exposures. To address these challenges, we developed and validated the Fast Atmospheric SCC Technique (FAST), a framework utilizing the self-coherent camera (SCC) designed for ground-based applications. This paper details recent and ongoing advancements in FAST, covering both numerical simulations and laboratory experiments. Our simulations demonstrate FAST's scientific promise, showing that current 10-meter telescopes could detect reflected light from exoplanets and thermal emission from exo-Jupiters, while future ELTs might identify habitable worlds. Additionally, we present initial laboratory characterizations of the proposed coronagraphic masks, which have now been manufactured.

This study introduces a controller designed to achieve stable grasping of objects with unknown shapes using two robotic fingers equipped with tactile sensors. Stability is maintained by rolling the fingertips along the contact surfaces while applying a target grasping force to attain equilibrium. The approach is validated through both simulations and experiments on a fully-actuated robot hand (the Shadow Modular Grasper) outfitted with custom optical tactile sensors derived from the BRL TacTip architecture. The controller relies on the orientations of contact surfaces, which are inferred by a deep convolutional neural network that regresses data from tactile images. The system successfully demonstrates stable equilibrium poses across objects of varying shapes and softness, exhibiting robustness against perturbations and measurement inaccuracies. Furthermore, this methodology shows potential for extension to stable in-hand manipulation involving multiple fingers.

Inequalities are fundamental to both pure and applied mathematics, with Jensen's inequality, a particularly renowned result, being central to analyzing the existence and uniqueness of initial and boundary value problems in differential equations. This paper establishes several novel Jensen-type inequalities for $m$-convex functions and applies them to generalized Riemann-Liouville-type integral operators. Notably, setting $m=1$ yields new inequalities specifically for convex functions.

This report details a search for previously unobserved beauty baryon decays into the final states $K^0_{\mathrm{S}}p\pi^-$ and $K^0_{\mathrm{S}}pK^-$, utilizing a dataset from $pp$ collisions with an integrated luminosity of $1.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. For the first time, the $\Lambda^0_b \rightarrow K^0_{\mathrm{S}}p\pi^-$ decay is observed with a significance of $8.6\,\sigma$, and the measured $CP$ asymmetry is consistent with zero. No significant signals were detected for $\Lambda^0_b \rightarrow K^0_{\mathrm{S}}pK^-$ decays, $\Xi^0_b$ decays to either $K^0_{\mathrm{S}}p\pi^-$ or $K^0_{\mathrm{S}}pK^-$ final states, nor for the $\Lambda^0_b \rightarrow D^-_s (K^0_{\mathrm{S}}K^-)p$ decay; consequently, upper limits on the branching fractions for these channels are provided.

We examine a smooth $2n$-manifold $M$ equipped with a bi-Lagrangian structure $(\omega,\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2})$, where $\omega$ denotes a symplectic form and $(\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2})$ represents a pair of transversal Lagrangian foliations on $(M, \omega)$. These structures feature a significant geometric entity known as the Hess Connection, which plays a crucial role in classifying affine bi-Lagrangian structures. In this study, we demonstrate that a bi-Lagrangian structure on $M$ can be elevated to a bi-Lagrangian structure on its trivial bundle $M\times\mathbb{R}^n$, and specifically, the lifting of an affine bi-Lagrangian structure retains its affine nature. We introduce a dynamic within the symplectomorphism group and the set of bi-Lagrangian structures (an action of the symplectomorphism group on these structures). This dynamic is compatible with Hess connections, maintains affine bi-Lagrangian structures, and admits a lift to $M\times\mathbb{R}^n$. This lift can be further extended to $\left(M\times\mathbb{R}^{2n}\right)\times\mathbb{R}^{4n}$, where it coincides with the original dynamic on $M\times\mathbb{R}^n$ for certain bi-Lagrangian structures. Furthermore, these results remain valid when replacing $M\times\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with the tangent bundle $TM$ or the cotangent bundle $T^{*}M$ of $M$, applicable to specific manifolds $M$.

By integrating concepts from non-equilibrium thermodynamics with the energetic variational framework, we establish a general model describing the evolution of non-isothermal chemical reactions governed by arbitrary mass kinetics. Based on this framework, we derive a linearized approximation for systems near equilibrium and investigate the global-in-time well-posedness of the system for small initial data within a critical Besov space.

We begin an investigation into quantum algorithms designed to escape saddle points with provable guarantees. For a function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$, our proposed quantum algorithm produces an $\epsilon$-approximate second-order stationary point by utilizing $\tilde{O}(\log^{2} (n)/\epsilon^{1.75})$ queries to the quantum evaluation oracle (zeroth-order). In contrast, the current classical state-of-the-art method by Jin et al. requires $\tilde{O}(\log^{6} (n)/\epsilon^{1.75})$ queries to the gradient oracle (first-order). Consequently, our quantum approach achieves a polynomial improvement over classical methods regarding the $\log n$ term while maintaining identical complexity in terms of $1/\epsilon$. Our primary technical contribution involves substituting classical perturbations used in gradient descent with simulated quantum wave equations, which drives the enhancement in quantum query complexity by $\log n$ factors for saddle point escape. Additionally, we demonstrate how to leverage Jordan's quantum gradient computation algorithm to convert classical gradient queries into quantum evaluation queries without increasing complexity. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments that corroborate our theoretical results.

The recent discovery of hidden charm and open strangeness ($c\bar c q\bar s$) states by BESIII and LHCb offers new prospects for constructing a comprehensive model of heavy-quark exotics. This study extends the dynamical diquark model to include these states, retaining Hamiltonian parameters previously derived from nonstrange and hidden-strange sectors. The significant mass difference between $Z_{cs}(4000)$ and $Z_{cs}(4220)$ indicates considerable SU(3)$_{\rm flavor}$ mixing among all $J^P \! = \! 1^+$ states, while their mean mass relative to other sectors provides a direct test of flavor octet-singlet mixing within the exotic sector. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of $\eta$-like exchanges and determined their influence to be minimal. Finally, employing the same diquark-mass parameters, we demonstrate that $P_c(4312)$ and $P_{cs}(4459)$ serve as well-fitting models for nonstrange and open-strange pentaquarks, respectively.

Mental and emotional well-being is a pressing concern in modern urban environments. Living in a metropolis impacts psychological health due to heightened stressors, including overcrowding, pollution, elevated violence, and diminished social support. It is crucial to recognize that a truly smart city is composed solely of healthy citizens. This paper introduces a fuzzy-based method for evaluating individual well-being by monitoring daily activities and performance. We categorize the factors influencing wellness into three dimensions: physical, productive, and social. By utilizing these parameters, we generate a coefficient representing a person's overall well-being.

In recent times, end-users have accumulated vast amounts of decentralized data across numerous edge devices, yet aggregating this data for machine learning tasks remains challenging due to legal and regulatory constraints. Federated Learning (FL) offers a viable solution by enabling collaborative global model training without exchanging sensitive raw data; however, the scheduling of devices for multiple concurrent FL jobs remains a critical, unresolved issue. This paper introduces a novel multi-job FL framework designed to facilitate parallel training. The framework comprises a system model and two distinct scheduling strategies. Within the system model, we define a parallel training process for multiple jobs and develop a cost model that accounts for training duration and data fairness across diverse devices. To optimize device scheduling and minimize costs, we propose two methods: one based on reinforcement learning and another on Bayesian optimization. Extensive experiments involving multiple jobs and datasets demonstrate that our proposed approaches significantly surpass baseline methods, achieving training speeds up to 8.67 times faster and accuracy improvements of up to 44.6%.

Emerging advanced Human-Vehicle Interactions depend on the Internet-of-Vehicles (IoV) paradigm to facilitate large-scale data synchronization and communication. Because IoV operates similarly to a distributed system—where vehicles act as nodes connected to a central server—it raises critical data privacy concerns, as these nodes collect, process, and share personal statistics such as multi-modal driving statuses. Consequently, understanding how contemporary privacy-preserving methods align with IoV is essential. This paper presents the most comprehensive analysis to date of privacy-preserving techniques for IoV, focusing specifically on Differential Privacy (DP), a set of mathematically guaranteed mechanisms for protecting sensitive data during processing and sharing. Our objective is to clarify the tradeoffs involved in deploying DP regarding service quality. We begin by characterizing representative privacy-preserving processing mechanisms facilitated by advanced DP approaches. Subsequently, we conduct an in-depth study of an emerging in-vehicle application driven by Deep Neural Networks, evaluating the pros and cons of DP across various data streams. Our research yields 11 key findings, with five highlighted as the most significant observations. We conclude that while substantial challenges remain, there are also numerous opportunities for future work to enable privacy-preserving IoV with minimal overhead to service quality.

This work introduces various highness notions for degrees concerning the computation of isomorphisms between structures, assuming such isomorphisms are present. We examine different variations across dimensions of uniformity, the incorporation of negative information, and other isomorphism-related challenges. These additional challenges encompass Scott analysis (specifically through back-and-forth relations), jump hierarchies, and the calculation of descending sequences within linear orders.
This paper presents a concise proof of the linear nested Artin approximation property for algebraic power series rings.

Algorithmic stablecoins (AS) represent a unique class of stablecoins that operate without collateral backing. While they have the potential to transform sovereign fiat systems, current implementations often suffer from poor stabilization, frequently deviating from their price targets or triggering catastrophic collapses known as "death spirals," which leads many to dismiss them as Ponzi schemes. However, does this narrative capture the full reality? This paper aims to uncover the truth and dispel misconceptions surrounding these instruments. We identify that a Ponzi scheme is essentially a financial protocol where payouts to existing investors are funded by new capital inflows. Crucially, operating such a scheme does not inherently mean participants lose value, provided the system can be sustained indefinitely; economists refer to this sustainable scenario as a *rational Ponzi game*. Consequently, we propose a rational model within the context of algorithmic stablecoins and establish the conditions required for its validity. Using this framework, we investigate whether algorithmic stablecoins qualify as rational Ponzi games. Furthermore, we analyze two distinct AS mechanisms—Rebase and Seigniorage shares—and evaluate the historical market performance of two prominent projects, Ampleforth and TerraUSD, to validate our model.

This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to forecast peak-stress clusters within heterogeneous polycrystalline materials.
