While previous machine learning applications in mechanics have primarily targeted effective responses and general stress field structures, the prediction of peak stresses—critical for failure analysis—remains unexplored due to the small spatial volume of these clusters relative to the total domain, which necessitates computationally intensive training. To address this, the research develops a deep learning-based Convolutional Encoder-Decoder architecture focused on identifying peak-stress clusters, specifically their size and other attributes, under the framework of heterogeneous linear elasticity. This approach utilizes convolutional filters to capture local spatial relationships between microstructures and stress fields via spatially weighted averaging. Initially, the model is trained on linear elastic stress calculations derived from synthetically generated microstructures under applied macroscopic strain, serving as ground truth. Subsequently, the trained model predicts stress fields for new synthetic microstructures and detects peak-stress clusters within those fields. Prediction accuracy is evaluated using cosine similarity metrics and by comparing the geometric features of the clusters against ground-truth data. Results indicate that the model successfully learns and predicts the geometric details of peak-stress clusters, demonstrating superior performance for higher normalized peak stress values compared to lower ones. These findings confirm that the proposed method is highly effective for predicting the characteristics of peak-stress clusters.

This paper introduces a Fourier series defined in fractional dimensional space for an arbitrarily periodic function $f(t;\alpha)$, which we term the fractional Fourier series of order $\alpha$. By extending the basis functions of a linear space via rotation transformations into the fractional domain, we define both real and complex Fourier series and derive their respective coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fractional derivative of a periodic function can be realized using (fractional) Fourier series with adjusted coefficients.

Hybrid logic serves as an extension of modal logic, and its many-dimensional product is known as Hybrid Product Logic (HPL). We developed a sound and complete tableau calculus for two-dimensional HPL. Furthermore, we constructed a tableau calculus for Hybrid Dependent Product Logic (HdPL), in which one dimension relies on the other. We also introduced a specific rule to the HdPL calculus and demonstrated that it remains sound and complete. However, none of these systems guarantee termination.

Cluster Editing is an NP-complete problem aimed at converting a static graph into a collection of disjoint cliques by minimizing edge modifications. We propose a temporal graph interpretation of this problem, where edge sets evolve over time. While the problem remains NP-complete even for temporal graphs with a path as their underlying structure, we present two polynomial-time algorithms for specific restricted scenarios. Although it is established that a static graph consists of disjoint cliques if and only if it lacks an induced $P_3$, we show that no such characterization using sets of at most four vertices exists for temporal graphs. Instead, we derive a complete characterization based on forbidden configurations involving at most five vertices. This characterization enables the development of a Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) algorithm parameterized by both the allowed number of modifications and the temporal graph's lifetime.

Over the past ten years, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have been increasingly deployed across diverse platforms, ranging from data centers to embedded systems, including low-power processors and, more recently, FPGAs. Neural Networks (NNs) are poised to become ubiquitous in Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, transforming a wide array of real-world applications, particularly within safety-critical and security-sensitive sectors. Nevertheless, hardware security vulnerabilities inherent in embedded NN implementations remain largely unaddressed. Specifically, embedded DNNs are susceptible to Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) attacks, a concern that is especially acute in IoT and edge computing environments where attackers often possess physical access to the target device. Consequently, a rapidly expanding research field has emerged, focusing on SCA techniques such as timing, electromagnetic, and power analysis to target embedded NN implementations. Since 2018, scholarly work has demonstrated that SCA allows attackers to recover inference model architectures and parameters, expose intellectual property, and compromise data confidentiality and privacy. Lacking a comprehensive review of this emerging domain in existing literature, this paper surveys state-of-the-art physical SCA attacks against embedded DNNs implemented on microcontrollers and FPGAs to offer a thorough analysis of the current landscape. It presents a taxonomy and detailed classification of contemporary attacks, discusses mitigation strategies, and offers insights for future research directions.

We present a computationally efficient, data-driven framework designed to quantify uncertainty in both physical parameters and the model formulations of computer models based on differential equations. This approach constructs physics-informed priors utilizing multi-output Gaussian process (GP) priors that embed the model's structure within the covariance function. We extend this into a comprehensive Bayesian framework to assess uncertainties in physical parameters and model predictions. Acknowledging that physical models may imperfectly represent real-world processes, we incorporate a discrepancy function to account for deviations between the model and observed data. Posterior distributions are derived using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. We validate our method through a simulation study involving hemodynamical models, which are time-dependent differential equations; in this study, data are generated from a more complex model than ours, aiming to infer physical parameters based on established mathematical relationships. To showcase the method's flexibility, we also include an example using the Heat equation, a space-time dependent differential equation, under a scenario of biased data acquisition. Finally, we apply the hemodynamic model fitting to real-world data collected from a medical trial.

For functions within the classes $C^{2}[0, 1]$ and $C^{3}[0, 1]$, we derive a lower bound with an explicit constant for Bernstein polynomial approximation, expressed via the second-order Ditzian-Totik modulus of smoothness. Additionally, several applications to specific function examples are provided.

In probabilistic learning tasks, organisms frequently employ a sub-optimal "probability-matching" strategy, aligning their choice frequencies with reward probabilities, instead of the optimal "maximization" strategy, which consistently selects the option with the highest reward probability. Although decades of research have investigated the origins of probability-matching, the underlying mechanisms remain debated, with no prior findings linking these behavioral differences to specific brain activities. This study presents a theoretical proof for a computational model that accounts for the full spectrum of behaviors ranging from pure maximization to pure probability-matching. When this model was fitted to the data of 60 participants performing a probabilistic reinforcement learning task while undergoing fMRI scanning, it supported the prediction that probability-matching correlates with heightened integration of negative outcomes during learning. This was evidenced by a stronger coupling between the midbrain's BOLD signal and negative prediction errors. Furthermore, since the degree of probability-matching remained consistent within individuals across nine different conditions, the results suggest that the propensity to adopt a specific learning strategy is a trait-like characteristic of the individual.

Free-free opacity is essential for comprehending energy transport within stellar interiors and for inertial confinement fusion studies. Yet, theoretical predictions in the difficult dense plasma regime remain contradictory, and a lack of precise experimental data hinders direct model verification. In this work, we report time-resolved transmission measurements of solid-density aluminum heated by an XUV free-electron laser. By employing a new functional optimization method, we derived the temperature-dependent absorption coefficient from an oversampled set of single-shot data, revealing a significant increase in opacity as the plasma reaches temperatures comparable to the Fermi energy. Both the plasma heating and the associated opacity enhancement occur on ultrafast timescales, confined within the femtosecond XUV pulse duration. We attribute additional opacity increases observed on picosecond timescales to melting and the creation of warm-dense matter.

Elliptic curves play a significant role in contemporary number theory, often analyzed by constructing $L$-functions from local data, specifically the count of solutions modulo $p$. The properties of these global $L$-functions are intimately linked to two of the Clay Millennium Problems: the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This research focuses on one-parameter families defined over $\mathbb{Q}(T)$ in the form $y^2=x^3+A(T)x+B(T)$, characterized by a non-constant $j$-invariant. The $r$-th moment of an elliptic curve is defined as $A_{r,E}(p) := \frac1{p} \sum_{t \bmod p} a_t(p)^r$, where $a_t(p)$ represents $p$ minus the number of solutions to $y^2 = x^3 + A(t)x + B(t) \bmod p$. Rosen and Silverman previously demonstrated that biases in the first moment correspond to the rank of the Mordell-Weil group of rational points. Michel established that $pA_{2,E}(p)=p^2+O(p^{3/2})$. Drawing on special families with closed-form solutions, Miller conjectured in his thesis that the leading non-vanishing lower-order term in the second moment exhibits an average negative bias, a phenomenon he linked to the distribution of zeros of the elliptic curve $L$-function near the central point. Although evidence for this conjecture remains confined to specific families, this study extends the analysis to additional closed-form families and systematically examines families of varying ranks. These represent the first broad tests of the conjecture; while general closed-form solutions are unattainable, computational results are presented that either support or refute the hypothesis. Furthermore, the investigation is extended to higher moments, revealing evidence that this negative bias persists in even moments.

We construct four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric nonlinear sigma models on Hermitian symmetric spaces, incorporating higher-derivative terms via gauged linear sigma models to eliminate auxiliary field issues and Ostrogradski ghosts. Our investigation focuses on Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield equations that preserve 1/2 or 1/4 supersymmetry, revealing two distinct solution branches: a canonical branch where the auxiliary field $F$ vanishes, and a non-canonical branch where $F \neq 0$. Specifically for the ${\mathbb C}P^N$ model, the canonical branch yields a supersymmetric ${\mathbb C}P^N$ Skyrme-Faddeev model, whereas the non-canonical branch results in a Lagrangian containing only the Skyrme-Faddeev term, lacking a standard kinetic term. These findings extend to the Grassmann manifold $G_{M,N} = SU(M)/[SU(M-N)\times SU(N)\times U(1)]$. For other Hermitian symmetric spaces, such as the quadric surface $Q^{N-2}=SO(N)/[SO(N-2)\times U(1)]$, we apply F-term (holomorphic) constraints to embed them into ${\mathbb C}P^{N-1}$ or Grassmann manifolds. We observe that while these constraints remain consistent in the canonical branch, they impose further restrictions on dynamical fields in the non-canonical branch, effectively reducing the target spaces.

We provide an elementary, self-contained folkloristic proof that utilizes limits of primitives of Bernstein polynomials to demonstrate the existence of primitive functions for continuous functions defined on the unit interval.

The LHCb experiment has measured the cross-section for inelastic proton-proton collisions requiring at least one prompt, long-lived charged particle with transverse momentum $p_{\rm T}>0.2$ GeV/$c$ in the pseudorapidity interval $2.0<\eta<4.5$, at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. Within the spectrometer's acceptance, this cross-section is found to be $\sigma_{\rm inel}^{\rm acc} = 55.0 \pm 2.4$ mb, where the uncertainty is primarily systematic. Extrapolating to the complete phase space using PYTHIA 6 results in $\sigma_{\rm inel} = 66.9 \pm 2.9 \pm 4.4$ mb, with the first error representing experimental uncertainty and the second arising from the extrapolation process.

Historically, annotated data have served as the primary input for training supervised machine learning (ML) models. However, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing (NLP) models possess embedded linguistic knowledge that can guide the annotation workflow. This study leverages the BERT neural language model to reintegrate information into an annotation task focused on semantically labeling dialog behaviors within "Emotion Twenty Questions" (EMO20Q), a question-asking game. We begin by outlining the background of BERT, the EMO20Q dataset, and assisted annotation processes, followed by a description of the methods used to fine-tune BERT for verifying annotated labels. Specifically, we employ a paraphrase task to ensure that all utterances sharing the same label are correctly identified as paraphrases of one another. We demonstrate that this approach effectively assesses and revises annotations of complex, utterance-level semantic labels in textual user data.

This study examines the immediate and long-term operational status of an n-node blockchain that is subject to constant surveillance by a corporate IT department while simultaneously enduring relentless cyber attacks from a solitary hacker. The system remains functional provided no stored data is altered, removed, or locked. Upon detecting the hacker's intrusion, the IT department instantly resets the blockchain, nullifying the hacker's prior attempts. The attacker persists until the blockchain becomes non-functional. For any given distributions of attack and detection intervals, we calculate the limiting and instantaneous functional probabilities, as well as the mean functional duration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these metrics increase with the number of nodes, confirming the intuitive notion that larger blockchain networks are more resistant to successful cyber attacks.

Leveraging mathematical tools from noncommutative geometry, this work investigates Connes spectral distances applied to one- and two-qubit states. We build a spectral triple representing $2D$ fermionic phase spaces and compute the Connes spectral distance for single qubits. Utilizing this distance metric, we establish a coherence measure for quantum states and determine the coherence of one-qubit systems. Furthermore, we examine specific cases involving two-qubit states, demonstrating that their corresponding spectral distances adhere to the Pythagorean theorem. Our findings reveal that Connes spectral distances differ from quantum trace distances, suggesting that the former serves as a valuable complement to trace distances within quantum information science. These insights hold significance for understanding the physical relationships and geometric structures of qubits and other quantum states.

Over recent years, research into quantum phenomena at both mesoscopic and macroscopic scales has grown significantly. Within this field, the 2019 paper *Entropy* 21, 705 introduced a formalism known as the Reduced State of the Field (RSF) to describe macroscopic quantum fields. Although the original study derived a specific entropy concept for these fields along with their dynamical equations, this work extends the thermodynamic analysis of the RSF. It examines the definition of heat, solves the dynamical equations across various relevant regimes, and explores the thermodynamic consequences of these solutions.

T Aurigae, an eclipsing old nova that erupted in 1891, is classified as a relatively nearby system based on Gaia EDR3 distance measurements ranging from 815 to 871 pc. Utilizing precise Gaia distance data alongside ultraviolet spectral modeling, we determined that the HST/STIS spectrum aligns with an accretion disk characterized by a mass transfer rate ($\dot{M}$) of approximately $10^{-8} M_{\odot}$/yr. This model assumes a white dwarf mass of roughly $0.7 \pm 0.2 M_{\odot}$, an inclination of about $60^{\circ}$, and a refined Gaia distance of $840_{-25}^{+31}$ pc. The sharp metal absorption lines are unlikely to originate within the disk itself; instead, they likely form in material above the disk (such as from stream overflow), in circumbinary regions, or within the ejected shell from the 1891 explosion. Furthermore, the saturated hydrogen Ly$\alpha$ absorption feature indicates a substantial interstellar hydrogen column density of order $10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$ toward T Aur, a finding supported by its reddening value of $E(B-V)=0.42 \pm 0.08$.

Thioacetamide (CH3CSNH2) serves as the sulfur counterpart to acetamide (CH3CONH2) and represents a promising target for astronomical observation, particularly in regions where other sulfur-bearing molecules and acetamide itself have been identified. Confirming its presence would not only broaden the understanding of molecular complexity in space but also clarify the formation mechanisms of such species. Researchers investigated the rotational spectrum of CH3CSNH2 up to 650 GHz. By utilizing the newly refined spectral data for CH3CSNH2 alongside additional information on the related molecule CH3CONH2, an extensive search was conducted across various astronomical sources using data from three major surveys: PRIMOS with the Green Bank Telescope (GBT), EMoCA with ALMA, and ASAI with the IRAM 30m Telescope. In total, 1428 transitions from the ground vibrational state (vt=0) were assigned, covering maximum quantum numbers of J=47 and Ka=20 up to 330 GHz, and J=95 and Ka=20 between 400–660 GHz. Additionally, 321 transitions from the first excited vibrational state (vt=1) with maximum values of J=35 and Ka=9 were assigned up to 330 GHz. The final spectral fit employed the rho-axis-method (RAM) Hamiltonian model, incorporating 40 parameters. Despite this comprehensive search based on the new spectroscopic data, no transitions of CH3CSNH2 were detected toward any of the surveyed sources. Consequently, upper limits for the column densities of CH3CSNH2 were calculated for each source, utilizing the specific telescope capabilities and physical parameters applicable to those environments.

Current deep learning-based 3D object detectors predominantly depend on individual object appearances, often neglecting the rich contextual details of the surrounding scene. To address this, we introduce the Contextualized Multi-Stage Refinement for 3D Object Detection (CMR3D) framework. This approach ingests a 3D scene and aims to explicitly incorporate multi-level contextual information to predict object bounding boxes and their semantic labels. Specifically, we employ a context enhancement network to capture context at varying granularities, followed by a multi-stage refinement module that iteratively improves box localization and class predictions. Extensive experiments on the ScanNetV2 benchmark demonstrate the efficacy of our method, achieving a 2.0% absolute improvement over the baseline. Beyond 3D detection, we also evaluate the CMR3D framework's performance on 3D object counting. Our source code will be made publicly available.

English serves as the primary medium for database instruction across nearly all South African universities and many other nations. Consequently, novice programmers with native backgrounds are typically taught Structured Query Language (SQL) using English. This linguistic barrier often hinders native learners who lack proficiency in English, making it difficult for them to comprehend SQL syntax. To address this challenge, this study introduces Local-Nar-SQL, a tool that leverages a Finite Machine—specifically a Jumping Finite Automaton—to convert local language narratives into executable SQL queries. The system generates these queries to extract data from a sample database and display the results to the learner. This paper expands upon previous research in this area, supported by a survey of 145 participants who found Local-Nar-SQL effective in understanding SQL through their native tongues. By adopting this tool as a learning aid, native speakers can more easily engage with SQL, thereby removing many obstacles associated with English proficiency in programming education.

We develop an anomaly-preserving compactification of four-dimensional gauge theories—including $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills, $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills, and QCD—reducing them to two dimensions via the activation of 't Hooft flux through a torus ($T^2$). This approach offers a novel framework for analytically determining nonperturbative characteristics such as confinement, chiral symmetry breaking, and the multi-branch structure of vacua. We present a semiclassical description of these phenomena utilizing center vortices and demonstrate that this model satisfies the same anomaly matching conditions as the original $4$d gauge theory. We conjecture that the weak-coupling vacuum configuration on a small $T^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2$ is adiabatically linked to the strong-coupling regime on $\mathbb{R}^4$ without undergoing any phase transitions. Furthermore, in QCD with fundamental quarks, 't Hooft flux can be implemented either by applying an $SU(N_f)_{\mathrm{V}}$ symmetry twist for $N_f=N$ flavors or by introducing a baryon number $U(1)_{\mathrm{B}}$ magnetic flux for arbitrary $N_f$. In both scenarios, the weak-coupling center-vortex theory yields predictions consistent with the chiral Lagrangian of $4$d QCD.

Using computer simulations, we examine the evolutionary dynamics of systems composed of continuously moving Active Brownian Particles. These findings are compared with results from the passive 2D Ising model. We analyze far-from-steady-state dynamics following sudden quenches of uniform configurations to states within the miscibility gap, at critical points, and elsewhere. This investigation involves calculating metrics related to structure and characteristic length scales. Furthermore, we explore aging phenomena during quenches into the miscibility gap, offering a quantitative description of the scaling behavior of the two-time order-parameter correlation function. The observed overall structure and dynamics align with expectations derived from the Ising model. This consistency extends to specific active lattice models, for which we also present results concerning quenches to critical points.

Accurately predicting movements is crucial for effectively collaborating with intelligent systems. We introduce a model that incorporates organized spatial data derived from the skeletal structure of a moving body. By applying Graph Convolutions to this inherent structure, our approach transforms spatial information into highly competitive predictions using a lightweight architecture that demands a relatively low parameter count.

The Casimir effect, which forecasts an attractive force between two parallel, highly reflective plates in a vacuum, is crucial across multiple physics disciplines, including quantum field theory, cosmology, nanophotonics, and condensed matter physics. However, Casimir forces remain lacking an intuitive explanation, and existing derivations depend on regularization techniques to eliminate infinities. By beginning with special relativity and treating spatial and temporal coordinates equivalently, this paper circumvents quantum electrodynamics no-go theorems to derive a local relativistic quantum description of the electromagnetic field in free space. When applied to cavities, this methodology allows for the direct calculation of Casimir forces in position space, eliminating the need for cut-off frequencies.

Wakamatsu tilting bimodules are shown to characterize dualities within resolving subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras. When these dualities are restricted to resolving subcategories of such modules that possess finite projective or Gorenstein-projective dimensions, they yield Miyashita's duality, Huisgen-Zimmermann's correspondence regarding tilting modules (along with their Gorenstein variants), and related results. Key applications involve establishing triangle equivalences between the derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules and demonstrating the invariance of higher algebraic $K$-groups and semi-derived Ringel-Hall algebras for these modules under tilting operations.

Person re-identification remains a persistent and demanding challenge. This paper details our approach for the re-identification track in the VIPriors Challenge 2021, where the primary difficulty lies in training a model from scratch without utilizing any pretrained weights. Our methodology demonstrates that by employing state-of-the-art data processing techniques, innovative model architectures, and post-processing ensemble strategies, it is feasible to surmount data scarcity and achieve competitive outcomes. Specifically: (1) Advanced image augmentation and a novel pre-processing technique for occluded images enable the model to extract more discriminative features. (2) The integration of robust backbone networks and diverse loss functions facilitates the learning of highly representative features. (3) Post-processing mechanisms such as re-ranking, automatic query expansion, and ensemble learning substantially enhance final performance. Our team (ALONG) achieved a final mAP score of 96.5154%, securing the first-place position on the leaderboard.

Combinatorial challenges found in puzzles, origami, and (meta)material design often possess sparse solution sets that establish intricate, sharply defined boundaries within configuration space. Conventional statistical and numerical techniques struggle to identify these boundaries. This study demonstrates that convolutional neural networks can detect these boundaries for combinatorial mechanical metamaterials with high precision, even when trained on heavily undersampled datasets, while maintaining successful generalization. This indicates that the network deduces the underlying combinatorial rules from sparse data, thereby enabling new avenues for the complex design of (meta)materials.

For a specified combinatorial class $\mathcal{C}$, we examine the class $\mathcal{G} = \mathrm{MSET}(\mathcal{C})$, defined by the multiset construction where every element in $\mathcal{G}$ is uniquely identified by a collection of $\mathcal{C}$-objects along with their respective multiplicities. A notable instance is $\mathrm{MSET}(\mathbb{N})$, which corresponds to the class of integer partitions, a well-established and significant case. The multiset construction is fundamental in analyzing unlabelled structures, such as graphs or other forms related to number partitions. Our primary finding determines the asymptotic magnitude of the set $\mathcal{G}_{n,N}$, comprising all multisets in $\mathcal{G}$ with total size $n$ and consisting of $N$ elements from $\mathcal{C}$, as both $n$ and $N$ approach infinity under the condition that $\mathcal{C}$'s counting sequence exhibits subexponential growth—a critical scenario for combinatorial applications. Furthermore, we investigate the component distribution of random elements within $\mathcal{G}_{n,N}$ and identify a phenomenon termed \emph{extreme condensation}: after removing the largest component and all components of the minimal size, the remaining structure converges in distribution as $n,N\to\infty$, and we derive the distribution of this limiting object. Notably and surprisingly, unlike analogous results for labelled objects, our findings hold uniformly with respect to $N$.

This paper introduces the dataset employed in the data challenge organized by the Conference on Sound and Music Technology (CSMT). The challenge tasks participants with determining whether a specific melody was created by a computer or composed by a human. The dataset consists of two components: a development set and an evaluation set. The development set includes exclusively computer-generated melodies, whereas the evaluation set comprises both computer-generated and human-composed melodies. The objective of this dataset is to investigate the feasibility of distinguishing computer-generated melodies by learning their inherent features.

This paper presents two newly constructed symmetric designs with parameters 2-(176,50,14), which remain invariant under specific subgroups of the full automorphism group of the Higman design. One of these designs is self-dual and possesses an automorphism group of size 11520, whereas the other is not self-dual and has an automorphism group of size 2520.

Human-robot interaction influences humans, frequently altering their behavior. This paper investigates a specific consequence of such behavioral shifts: changes in preference. Building on prior research regarding preference modification in AI, it examines how a robot's adaptive, user-specific behavior can leverage social interactions to shift a user's preferences. The article contends that this risk is particularly elevated due to the robot's distinct capacity to influence behavior compared to other pervasive technologies, thereby raising concerns that Persuasive Robotics could become manipulative.

This analysis examines the social welfare achievable through a constant function market maker (CFMM). With ample liquidity, a CFMM can closely approximate optimal social welfare by executing all user transactions. However, when a block proposer faces scarce blockspace, they can achieve higher expected utility compared to otherwise identical agents, thereby establishing a lower bound on the maximal extractable value that arises under conditions of limited blockspace.

The structure of wavefunctions in dense, interacting many-boson systems is investigated using a Hamiltonian $H$, composed of a one-body term $h(1)$ and an embedded Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) of $k$-body interactions $V(k)$ scaled by strength $\lambda$. The initial analysis provides a full analytical expression for the variance of the strength function as a function of $\lambda$ and $k$, identifying the threshold $\lambda_t$ that marks the onset of thermalization. In the strong coupling regime ($\lambda > \lambda_t$), a conditional $q$-normal density characterizes the transition from Gaussian to semi-circular distributions in strength functions as the interaction rank $k$ increases. The second analysis applies this interpolating strength function form to model fidelity decay following a $k$-body interaction quench and to derive a smooth approximation for the number of principal components, which quantifies chaos in finite many-particle systems. This smooth form accurately captures embedded ensemble results across all values of $k$.

As web data grows exponentially, hashing has gained prominence as a technique for approximate nearest neighbor search. Earlier supervised hashing approaches relied on similarity or dissimilarity matrices to extract semantic information, yet constructing these matrices is challenging for new datasets. Instead of reconstructing such matrices, we introduced a straightforward CNN-based hashing method that binarizes the activations of a fully connected layer using a threshold of 0, treating the resulting binary output as hash codes. This approach achieved top-tier performance on CIFAR-10 and matched state-of-the-art results on MNIST. Furthermore, our CIFAR-10 experiments indicated that activation signs may convey more information than the relative values of activations across samples, highlighting the importance of co-adapting feature extractors with hash functions for effective hashing.

Building on the success of curriculum learning in speech enhancement, which improves performance by decomposing spectrum estimation into simpler sub-tasks, we introduce DB-AIAT, a dual-branch attention-in-attention transformer designed to process both coarse and fine spectral regions concurrently. Complementary to this, a magnitude masking branch provides a rough estimate of the overall magnitude spectrum, while a complex refining branch meticulously recovers missing spectral details and implicitly reconstructs phase information. Within each branch, we replace standard RNNs and temporal convolutional networks with a novel attention-in-attention module for temporal sequence modeling. This module comprises adaptive temporal-frequency attention blocks and an adaptive hierarchical attention component, enabling the capture of long-term temporal-frequency dependencies and the aggregation of global hierarchical context. Experiments on the Voice Bank + DEMAND dataset confirm that DB-AIAT achieves state-of-the-art results (3.31 PESQ, 95.6% STOI, and 10.79 dB SSNR), outperforming prior advanced systems with a compact model size of 2.81M parameters.

Retrieving evidence from both tabular and textual sources is crucial for open-domain question answering (OpenQA) as it offers more comprehensive information. However, training an effective dense retriever for table-text data is challenging due to discrepancies between the two modalities and data sparsity. To overcome these issues, we introduce the Optimized OpenQA Table-Text Retriever (OTTeR), designed to jointly retrieve tabular and textual evidence. First, we enhance mixed-modality representation learning through two mechanisms: modality-enhanced representation and a mixed-modality negative sampling strategy. Second, to mitigate data sparsity and improve general retrieval capabilities, we perform retrieval-centric mixed-modality synthetic pre-training. Experimental results show that OTTeR significantly boosts table-and-text retrieval performance on the OTT-QA dataset, with comprehensive analyses validating the effectiveness of each proposed mechanism. Furthermore, integrating OTTeR into our OpenQA system achieves state-of-the-art results on downstream QA tasks, delivering a 10.1% absolute improvement in exact match scores compared to the previous best system. All code and data are accessible at https://github.com/Jun-jie-Huang/OTTeR.

Using ALICE data from the Large Hadron Collider at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV, we analyze and compare charged-particle pseudorapidity densities across a broad range (${-3.5 <\eta <5}$) for pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb collisions. Centrality-dependent distributions are derived for p-Pb and Pb-Pb systems, whereas pp results correspond to inelastic events containing at least one charged particle at midrapidity. Under straightforward and reliable assumptions, these pseudorapidity densities are converted into rapidity densities. This conversion enables the evaluation of rapidity distribution widths and establishes a lower limit for the Bjorken energy density as a function of participant number across all three collision types. Our findings reveal that while particle production width decreases, the energy density increases by approximately a factor of ten as the system size expands.

With the rising prevalence of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), researchers have increasingly focused on its detection and treatment. Current MDD recognition algorithms typically rely on single time-frequency domain methods, which are considered too simplistic to effectively simulate the complex relationships within brain function. To address this limitation, this study introduces a recognition approach based on Multi-Layer Brain Functional Connectivity Networks (MBFCN) for MDD, accompanied by cognitive analysis. The analysis reveals that the Alpha-Beta1 frequency band is a critical sub-band for MDD identification. Additionally, the study indicates that in Brain Functional Connectivity Networks (BFCN) derived from the Phase Lag Index (PLI), connections between the right prefrontal lobe and the temporal lobe are notably deficient in individuals with extremely depressed disorders (EDD). Finally, the research identifies potential biomarkers through significance analysis of depression features and the PHQ-9 scale.

Existing tabling systems experience heightened space and/or time complexity when processing sequences, primarily due to the data structures used for tabled subgoals and answers, as well as the overhead of copying terms between the table and the main area. This issue affects not only B-Prolog, which relies on hash tables, but also systems utilizing tries like XSB and YAP. This paper introduces the application of hash-consing to structured data within B-Prolog. Although hash-consing effectively lowers space usage through sharing, it does not inherently improve time complexity. To address this, we augment hash-consing with two techniques—input sharing and hash code memoization—to reduce time complexity by bypassing hash code computations for specific terms. The resulting system removes the additional linear factor present in previous sequence processing methods, thereby significantly boosting scalability for applications such as language parsing and bio-sequence analysis. Experimental results validate these improvements.

In $\mathcal{N}$=1 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, the gluon's superpartner is the gluino, a spin 1/2 Majorana fermion residing in the adjoint representation of the gauge group. By combining three gluinos, one can construct color-neutral bound states that are analogous to baryons in QCD. The correlation functions of these baryonic operators include contributions from a "sunset diagram" and, distinct from QCD, an additional contribution from a "spectacle diagram." This paper presents initial results derived from numerical simulations of supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, which implement and calculate these specific diagrammatic objects.

This work introduces a method for the non-parametric reconstruction of statistical properties for penetrable, isotropic, two-dimensional randomly rough surfaces using in-plane, co-polarized light scattering data. By utilizing Kirchhoff approximation expressions for diffuse scattering from such surfaces, an analytic formula for the normalized surface height correlation function is derived as an integral over the scattering data, requiring only a few additional approximations. The inversion process involves two primary stages: first, estimating the surface roughness; second, determining the functional form of the height correlation function without presupposing a specific shape. To validate this approach, in-plane and co-polarized scattering data were generated through computer simulations or experiments for various correlation functions on dielectric and metallic surfaces. The results demonstrated excellent agreement between the reconstructed roughness and correlation functions and the original parameters used to generate the input data, covering both p- and s-polarized light and different incidence angles. Ultimately, this proposed method offers an accurate, efficient, robust, and contact-less technique for characterizing the statistical properties of isotropic two-dimensional randomly rough dielectric and metallic surfaces based on in-plane and co-polarized scattering data.

This work introduces entanglement-assisted concatenated quantum codes (EACQCs), which are formed by concatenating two quantum codes. These EACQCs offer several benefits compared to standard concatenated quantum codes (CQCs). The study derives multiple families of EACQCs that surpass the nondegenerate Hamming bound for entanglement-assisted quantum error correction codes (EAQECCs), a capability standard CQCs lack. Additionally, numerous EACQCs are constructed with superior parameters relative to the best-known standard quantum error correction codes (QECCs) and EAQECCs. Specifically, several catalytic EACQCs are built that outperform the best known QECCs of identical length and net transmission, each utilizing only one or two ebits. The research demonstrates that EACQCs enable entanglement-assisted quantum communication even when ebits are noisy. Furthermore, EACQCs achieve higher entanglement fidelity than CQCs over depolarizing channels when ebits are less noisy than qubits, and they exhibit a higher threshold error probability under similar conditions. Consequently, EACQCs are not only competitive in quantum communication but also suitable for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

A key component of urban planning involves assessing crowd density across different areas, a task that traditionally relies on physical sensors. However, deploying these sensors on a large scale can be both expensive and time-intensive. To overcome this limitation, this study leverages publicly available social media data to address two urban sensing challenges: event detection and crowd level estimation. A primary contribution of this work is the compilation of a dataset derived from Twitter and Flickr, paired with verified ground truth events. The utility of this dataset is demonstrated through two initial supervised learning methods: first, a series of neural network models designed to classify whether a social media post pertains to an event, and second, a regression model that utilizes post frequencies to forecast actual crowd sizes. The paper presents preliminary findings from these experiments and outlines the associated challenges.

The Witting configuration, comprising 40 complex rays, was proposed as a geometric reformulation of the Penrose model involving two spin-3/2 systems based on the dodecahedron's structure to analyze quantum nonlocality and contextuality. This work introduces an alternative configuration featuring 120 quantum states. Although the two configurations differ in their state counts, both can be derived from the complexification of the 240 minimal vectors of the 8D real lattice associated with the $E_8$ Lie algebra root system. The analysis of the proposed quantum state configuration draws upon numerous analogies with the properties of the Witting configuration.

The absence of detailed annotations impedes the implementation of automated diagnostic systems, which necessitate human-understandable rationales for their decisions. This paper tackles the challenge of weakly supervised detection and localization of anomalies in chest X-rays. To achieve this, we propose a new loss function for training convolutional neural networks that enhances \emph{localization confidence} and supports \emph{disease identification}. By utilizing both image-level and patch-level predictions to create auxiliary supervision, this loss function generates targets in a tailored manner rather than enforcing strict binary classifications as prior methods do. This customization enables the loss to accommodate potential misclassifications. We demonstrate that the supervision introduced by our learning framework yields superior performance and more accurate predictions compared to existing loss functions, specifically on multiple-instance learning datasets and the NIH ChestX-Ray14 benchmark for disease recognition.

Model studies are essential for elucidating and understanding the nonperturbative characteristics of transverse momentum dependent parton distribution functions (TMDs). The parton model frequently serves as a useful initial framework for investigating TMD properties and describing deep-inelastic processes where these functions become accessible. Through a systematic examination of the parton model concept, we reconcile conflicting literature claims regarding the number of independent structures within the quark correlator (two versus three) by clarifying the underlying assumptions driving these differing conclusions. Additionally, we systematically analyze the antiquark correlator and, to our knowledge, derive model expressions for all T-even leading and subleading antiquark TMDs for the first time. Finally, we demonstrate the internal consistency of this framework, which offers a basis for future studies to develop more sophisticated TMD models.

This study examines how temperature influences the magnetoplasmon spectrum in an electrically modulated graphene monolayer and a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG). Using the Self Consistent Field (SCF) method, we analyze the intra-Landau-band magnetoplasmon spectrum for both systems. The results reveal both Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) and commensurability (Weiss) oscillations, which vary periodically with the inverse magnetic field. Our findings indicate that both SdH and Weiss oscillations exhibit larger amplitudes and demonstrate greater resilience to temperature changes in graphene than in conventional 2DEGs. Additionally, a $\pi$ phase shift exists between the magnetoplasmon oscillations of the two systems, a phenomenon attributed to the Berry's phase acquired by Dirac electrons in graphene as they traverse a closed loop within a magnetic field.

We investigate a dynamic non-bipartite matching scenario featuring a fixed collection of agent types, where agents of each type arrive and leave based on specific Poisson processes, with departures occurring without prior notice. Match values depend on the types of the paired agents. We introduce an online algorithm that achieves a (1/8)-competitive ratio against the optimal-in-hindsight policy for any weighted graph. This approach handles agent heterogeneity by blending immediate and delayed matching strategies, thereby expanding market depth while still capturing valuable opportunistic matches.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in developing embodied intelligent agents capable of interacting with 3D indoor environments. While existing research predominantly addresses single-object capabilities or agent-object affordances, this work introduces the study of a critical yet underexplored visual relationship: inter-object functional connections. These relationships describe how one object influences another, such as a wall switch controlling a light or a remote operating a television. Humans effortlessly infer these dynamics upon entering a new room by leveraging strong prior knowledge or through minimal exploratory interactions when faced with uncertainty. This paper marks the initial step toward building AI systems that learn these inter-object functional relationships within 3D indoor settings. Our key technical contributions include modeling prior knowledge through training on large-scale scenes and designing interactive policies that enable effective exploration and rapid adaptation to novel environments. We established a new benchmark utilizing the AI2Thor and PartNet datasets and conducted extensive experiments demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. The results confirm that our model successfully acquires priors and strategies for fast interactive adaptation when exploring inter-object functional relationships in complex 3D scenes. Additionally, several ablation studies further validate the utility of each proposed module.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) enhance standard Neural Networks (NNs) by leveraging graph structure through a relational inductive bias (edge bias), instead of treating nodes as independent and identically distributed (\iid) samples. While GNNs are generally expected to surpass basic NNs in practical applications, they occasionally show minimal performance gains or even underperform graph-agnostic NNs in specific scenarios. To pinpoint these instances, we introduce two metrics grounded in graph signal processing and statistical hypothesis testing that evaluate situations where edge bias in both features and labels offers no benefit. Utilizing these metrics allows for the establishment of a threshold value to forecast the potential performance superiority of graph-aware models compared to graph-agnostic ones.

Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) provides an effective means to lower the computational expenses and memory demands associated with numerical simulations utilizing computational meshes. This paper presents a new, intelligent approach to AMR that integrates classical techniques with machine learning to overcome limitations inherent in traditional methods. We outline a specific algorithm for adaptive refinement, followed by the development of a modular, object-oriented framework to implement this smart AMR strategy. Next, we detail the procedures employed to train the smart AMR model. The research then demonstrates preliminary numerical experiments that validate the feasibility of applying adaptive mesh refinement to several representative problems within the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) field. The work concludes with observations regarding potential future directions.

This study highlights the utility of network embedding in analyzing vaccine skepticism, a contentious issue with deep historical roots that has regained critical importance following the late 2019 onset of the Covid-19 pandemic. Despite rapid vaccine development and successful clinical trials within a year of the first international cases, significant hurdles remain regarding logistics, testing, and development. Beyond these challenges, public hesitancy and outright refusal of vaccination represent a pivotal factor in the pandemic's management. The discourse is generally divided into two camps: "pro-vaxxers," who advocate for vaccination, and "vax-skeptics," who doubt vaccine efficacy or the necessity of widespread Covid-19 immunization. Accurately quantifying the size of these groups and understanding the drivers behind the rising popularity of skeptical views remain complex tasks. Consequently, this research aims to create techniques capable of efficiently distinguishing between pro-vaxxer and vax-skeptic content. Following extensive data preprocessing, we examined both tweet text and the structural patterns of user interactions on Twitter. We implemented various node embedding and community detection models designed to scale effectively across graphs containing millions of edges.

Within the field of statistical modeling, the Akaike information criterion (AIC) remains a widely recognized and frequently applied instrument for model selection. In contrast, the $\phi$-divergence test statistic represents a recently introduced approach for this purpose. However, the adoption of divergence-based criteria is often limited by their documented lack of robustness when sample sizes are small. This paper examines penalized minimum Hellinger distance statistics, establishing several of their properties. It derives the limiting distributions of both the estimates and test statistics under null and alternative hypotheses, alongside deducing approximations for power functions. Furthermore, a model selection criterion based on these divergence measures is formulated for parametric inference. The study specifically addresses the challenge of selecting between two models using informational statistics when independent samples are drawn from a discrete population. Consequently, the asymptotic properties and performance of these new testing procedures are analyzed, with a particular focus on their behavior in small samples.

This study examines signed graphs, which feature edges labeled as positive or negative. We identify the permissible parameters for $\{5,6,\ldots,10\}$-regular signed graphs that possess exactly two distinct eigenvalues and supply specific examples for each derived parameter. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to construct infinitely many signed graphs for every listed valency that exhibit only two distinct eigenvalues. Furthermore, we prove that for any $k\geq 5$, there exist infinitely many connected signed $k$-regular graphs with a maximum eigenvalue of $\sqrt{k}$. Additionally, for each $m\geq 4$, we construct a signed $8$-regular graph with the spectrum $[4^m,-2^{2m}]$. These results generate an infinite family of Ramanujan graphs that are $k$-regular for every $k$.

Building upon paper [3], this work examines the implications of the Hahn-Banach theorem for bounded b-linear functionals within linear n-normed spaces and outlines the concept of reflexivity in such spaces relative to these functionals. Furthermore, it introduces the ideas of strong and weak convergence for sequences of vectors based on bounded b-linear functionals in linear n-normed spaces and explores several of their associated properties.

The novel coronavirus variant, commonly known as COVID-19, poses a widespread threat to humanity globally. Consequently, leveraging advanced machine learning for its effective detection is a pressing necessity. Despite numerous sophisticated methods proposed recently, they continue to face challenges in accurately identifying COVID-19 from chest X-ray images, often relying on complex, time-consuming pre-processing steps. In contrast, deep networks have demonstrated promising, end-to-end capabilities in image-based recognition tasks over the last decade. This study evaluates several widely adopted state-of-the-art deep networks for detecting COVID-19 using chest X-ray images from a publicly available dataset. The results indicate that these deep networks can effectively identify COVID-19 from such images, with the EfficientNetB7 architecture outperforming other existing techniques.

It is clear that relying solely on a single user with a strong password fails to fully resolve security challenges. Research demonstrates that passwords remain vulnerable to various attacks, often due to human factors, despite existing protection mechanisms. The primary obstacle to adopting more robust authentication methods across different sectors is balancing security with usability. To address the gap between user-friendly interfaces and advanced security, the Fast Identity Online (FIDO) alliance established several authentication protocols. Although biometric authentication based on FIDO is not a new idea, it continues to intimidate both end-users and developers, potentially hindering FIDO's total market dominance. This paper examines the evolution of FIDO protocols by analyzing their technical characteristics and security requirements across various versions, while offering a comprehensive study of their applicability, ease of use, extensibility, and future security implications in different markets such as digital banking, social networks, and e-government. Based on this analysis, we conclude that no single FIDO protocol version currently dominates the landscape, and notably, earlier FIDO protocols remain applicable to emerging vertical services.

We demonstrate that the Fibonacci quantum representations $\rho_{g,n}:\rm{Mod}_{g,n}\to \rm{PU}(p,q)$ for $(g,n)\in\{(0,4),(0,5),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1)\}$ function as holonomy representations of complex hyperbolic structures on compactifications of the associated moduli spaces $\mathcal{M}_{g,n}$. Consequently, the forgetful map linking the compactifications of $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{1,2}$ establishes a surjective holomorphic mapping between compact complex hyperbolic orbifolds of distinct dimensions exceeding one, thereby resolving a question posed by Siu. Our proof involves calculating these Toledo invariants; we further generalize this approach by substituting Fibonacci representations with any Hermitian modular functor and extending the Toledo invariant into a comprehensive series of cohomological invariants originating from the signature $p-q$. Additionally, we establish that these invariants adhere to the axioms of a Cohomological Field Theory and determine the $R$-matrix to the first order (yielding the standard Toledo invariants) for $\rm{SU}_2/\rm{SO}_3$-quantum representations at all levels.

Unets and fully convolutional networks (FCNs) have established themselves as the standard approaches for medical image semantic segmentation. To address specific limitations inherent in Unets and FCNs, Unet++ was developed as an enhanced variant. By integrating an ensemble of variable-depth Unets, Unet++ removes the necessity for experts to manually determine the optimal network depth for a given task. Although Unet and its derivatives, including Unet++, aim to facilitate effective training with limited annotated data, none have sought to completely eliminate the requirement for pixel-wise annotations. Acquiring such data for every diagnostic condition is prohibitively expensive, resulting in scarcity. Consequently, this paper employs contrastive learning to train a Unet++ architecture for medical image segmentation—utilizing diverse sources such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT)—without relying on pixel-wise labels. We detail the proposed model's architecture and training methodology here; however, as this work is ongoing, results are excluded. The trained model and experimental outcomes will be released upon publication or in future versions of this paper on arXiv.

Semantic Web (SW) technology has been extensively utilized across various fields, including medicine, healthcare, finance, and geology. Currently, researchers primarily depend on personal experience and preferences to develop and assess SW initiatives. Despite the long-standing and well-established general architecture, such as Tim Berners-Lee's Semantic Web Layer Cake, there remains a lack of a concrete guideline for standardizing SW development. To address this gap, this paper introduces an SW technology index designed to standardize development processes, ensuring high-quality design and enabling the quantitative evaluation of SW work. This index comprises 10 criteria that assign a quality score ranging from 0 to 10. Each criterion is elaborated upon through three specific dimensions: the definition of the criterion, the rationale for its inclusion, and an analysis of how existing studies align with it. Furthermore, the paper validates the index by demonstrating its application through specific case studies. Ultimately, the study concludes that this index serves as a valuable standard for guiding and evaluating work within the Semantic Web domain.

Let $D=(V,A)$ denote a digraph with $n$ vertices, where $S$ is a subset of $V$ with cardinality $k$ ($2\le k\leq n$). An $S$-strong subgraph $H$ of $D$ is defined as a strong subgraph containing $S$. Two $S$-strong subgraphs, $D_1$ and $D_2$, are considered arc-disjoint if they share no common arcs, meaning $A(D_1)\cap A(D_2)=\emptyset$. The value $\lambda_S(D)$ represents the maximum count of such arc-disjoint $S$-strong subgraphs within $D$. Consequently, the strong subgraph $k$-arc-connectivity, denoted by $\lambda_k(D)$, is defined as the minimum of $\lambda_S(D)$ across all subsets $S \subseteq V(D)$ of size $k$. This parameter serves as an extension of the classical edge-connectivity found in undirected graphs.

In this study, we derive a formula for the arc-connectivity $\lambda(G\Box H)$ of the Cartesian product of two digraphs, $G$ and $H$, thereby extending a similar result for undirected graphs established by Xu and Yang (2006). Furthermore, we investigate the strong subgraph 2-arc-connectivity, $\lambda_2(G\Box H)$, establishing the inequality:
$$ \min\left \{ \lambda \left ( G \right ) \left | H \right | , \lambda \left ( H \right ) \left |G \right |,\delta ^{+ } \left ( G \right )+ \delta ^{+ } \left ( H \right ),\delta ^{- } \left ( G \right )+ \delta ^{- } \left ( H \right ) \right \}\ge\lambda_2(G\Box H)\ge \lambda_2(G)+\lambda_2(H)-1. $$
The upper bound for $\lambda_2(G\Box H)$ is proven to be sharp and directly follows from the aforementioned formula for $\lambda(G\Box H)$. The lower bound is either sharp or nearly so, differing by at most 1 from the optimal value. Additionally, we determine precise values for $\lambda_2(G\Box H)$ for specific families of digraphs.

In a recent study [I. H. Kim, Phys. Rev. X, 11, 021039], we presented a solution to the quantum marginal problem for two-dimensional quantum many-body systems, originally requiring that marginals exhibit internal translational invariance. We demonstrate that this requirement can be substituted with a less stringent condition: the local consistency of the marginals. This refinement broadens the solution's scope to encompass any two-dimensional quantum many-body states adhering to the entropy scaling law, regardless of whether they possess symmetry. Furthermore, we greatly streamline the proof by employing the maximum-entropy principle.

The study demonstrates that the Constant Temperature (CT) model for nuclear level density arises directly from a symmetrized Poisson distribution of level spacings. However, the standard CT model for total level density is fundamentally flawed because discontinuities at Yrast energies and the emergence of new $J^{\pi}$ sequences disrupt the exponential formula, rendering the back shift parameter unphysically negative. To address this, a new CT-JPI model is introduced, featuring a constant temperature and distinct back shift parameters for each $J^{\pi}$ sequence. This model is further constrained to match the spin distribution predicted by Ericson's function at the neutron separation energy. A fitting procedure is outlined to extract the temperature $T$, back shifts $E_0(J^{\pi})$, and spin cutoff parameters $\sigma_c$ from nuclear structure and resonance data. The CT-JPI model successfully predicts level densities across a broad spectrum of spins and parities for 46 nuclei spanning $Z=7$ to $92$. Contrary to previous findings, the spin cut-off parameters exhibit no mass dependence but instead show significant variation across all mass regions.

We provide a fresh characterization of computads for weak globular $\omega$-categories through an explicit inductive definition of free words. This approach offers novel insights into computads and enables a redefinition of $\omega$-categories that bypasses the need for globular operads. Our framework facilitates direct proofs of significant results using structural induction, allowing us to demonstrate that every $\omega$-category is equivalent to a free one and that the category of computads equipped with variable-to-variable maps forms a presheaf topos, thereby offering a direct description of the index category. Furthermore, we establish that our definition of $\omega$-category aligns with those proposed by Batanin and Leinster, and show that the induced cofibrant replacement for $\omega$-categories matches that of Garner.

We introduce a protocol to emulate the dynamics of a two-level system interacting with a classical light field. Driven transversely by two microwave tones, the system's Hamiltonian matches that of the general semi-classical Rabi model, which we implement using a superconducting transmon qubit. By adjusting the amplitude, phase, and frequency of these driving fields, we reproduce quantum dynamics spanning from weak to extremely strong coupling regimes. As the driving strength increases, the observed evolutions progressively depart from standard sinusoidal Rabi oscillations, aligning with theoretical predictions of the general semi-classical Rabi model well beyond the weak-driving approximation. This methodology offers a robust means to explore the exceptionally strong interactions between a two-level system and a classical light field, a regime typically unattainable in experimental settings.

The CREMA collaboration aims to measure the ground-state hyperfine splitting (HFS) in muonic hydrogen ($\mu$p) with 1 ppm precision using pulsed laser spectroscopy, specifically targeting a $2\times10^{-4}$ relative accuracy for the two-photon-exchange contribution. The proposed setup involves laser-exciting a $\mu$p atom from the singlet to the triplet hyperfine state, followed by inelastic collisional quenching back to the singlet state via interaction with an H$_2$ molecule. This process generates a kinetic energy increase that serves as the signature of a successful transition. This paper calculates the joint probability of a $\mu$p atom, starting in the singlet state, undergoing laser excitation to the triplet state and subsequently returning to the singlet state through collisional deexcitation. These calculations employ optical Bloch equations that incorporate both elastic and inelastic collisions. Neglecting decoherence effects arising from laser bandwidth and collisions would result in an overestimation of the transition probability by more than a factor of two under experimental conditions. Furthermore, the study accounts for Doppler effects and provides the matrix element, saturation fluence, and rates for both elastic and inelastic collisions for the singlet and triplet states, along with the resonance linewidth. Consequently, this calculation quantifies a critical unknown in the HFS experiment, enabling precise laser system requirements and optimizing the hydrogen gas target for muonic hydrogen formation and spectroscopy.

Given the scarcity of high-quality annotations in medical imaging, semi-supervised learning has become highly prized for image semantic segmentation tasks. This paper introduces an advanced self-ensembling method grounded in consistency-aware pseudo-labeling, designed to fully leverage the capabilities of both Vision Transformers (ViT) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The proposed framework features a feature-learning module enhanced by the mutual strengths of ViT and CNN, alongside a guidance module optimized for consistency awareness. Within the feature-learning module, pseudo-labels are generated and applied iteratively and independently across CNN and ViT views to expand the dataset, fostering mutual benefit. Additionally, a perturbation scheme is implemented for the feature-learning module, while network weight averaging drives the guidance module. This integration combines the feature extraction power of CNNs and ViTs, boosts performance through dual-view co-training, and facilitates consistency-aware supervision in a semi-supervised context. Comprehensive validation of various supervision modes using CNN and ViT confirms the method's optimal performance and configuration for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art outcomes on public benchmark datasets across multiple metrics, with the source code made publicly available.

Contemporary software architectures are becoming more configurable, which enhances flexibility but complicates development, testing, and analysis, particularly regarding how specific settings lead to desired behaviors or bugs. We present GenTree, a dynamic analysis tool that automatically discovers a program's configuration interactions by generating logical formulas that map option settings to code coverage. GenTree employs an iterative refinement process: it executes the program with a limited set of configurations to gather coverage data, applies a custom classification algorithm to construct decision trees representing potential interactions, and then analyzes these trees to generate new configurations for further refinement in subsequent iterations. Experimental results across 17 configurable systems in four different languages demonstrate that GenTree efficiently identifies precise interactions by exploring only a small fraction of the total configuration space.

The need for scalable algorithms in hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) is critical given the enormous scale of real-world datasets, yet efficiently parallelizing HAC remains challenging due to its inherently sequential structure. This paper introduces ParHAC, the first efficient parallel HAC algorithm achieving sublinear depth for the widely used average-linkage function. Specifically, we present a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for this problem on $m$ edge graphs that utilizes $\tilde{O}(m)$ work and poly-logarithmic depth. Furthermore, we demonstrate that achieving comparable bounds for exact average-linkage HAC is infeasible under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions. Complementing these theoretical findings, we conduct a thorough evaluation of ParHAC regarding its scalability, performance, and result quality, comparing it against several state-of-the-art sequential and parallel benchmarks. Across a diverse collection of large, publicly available real-world datasets, ParHAC achieves an average 50.1x speedup over the best sequential baseline while maintaining quality comparable to exact HAC. Additionally, we show that ParHAC can cluster one of the largest publicly available graph datasets, containing 124 billion edges, in slightly over three hours using a standard commodity multicore machine.

We forecast a series of anomalous quantum acoustic effects arising from sound-matter interactions within a completely tunable solid-state system. This platform couples an array of diamond-based solid-state spins to quantized acoustic waves in a one-dimensional optomechanical crystal. By employing a spatially varying laser drive that imposes a position-dependent phase on the optomechanical coupling, we can adjust the mechanical band structure in real time, thereby generating unconventional quantum sound-matter interactions. Specifically, when spins resonate with these bands, quasi-chiral interactions emerge, with tunability ranging from bidirectional to quasi-unidirectional. Furthermore, if the spin frequency falls within the acoustic band-gap, we observe the formation of an exotic polariton bound state capable of mediating long-range, tunable, odd-neighbor, and complex spin-spin interactions. This research broadens the current scope of quantum phononics and holds significant potential for applications in quantum simulation and quantum information processing.

OpenPodcar is an affordable, open-source research platform for autonomous vehicles, utilizing a hard-canopy mobility scooter as its base. It offers comprehensive hardware and software build instructions to transform the donor vehicle into a fully autonomous system. The open platform includes: (a) hardware elements such as CAD designs, a bill of materials, and assembly guides; (b) Arduino, ROS, and Gazebo software files that provide standard ROS interfaces and vehicle simulation; and (c) advanced ROS implementations for autonomous planning and control, featuring the move_base interface with a Timed-Elastic-Band planner to navigate from a current to a desired pose while avoiding obstacles. Capable of carrying a human passenger or comparable loads at speeds up to 15 km/h, the vehicle is suitable for applications like last-mile autonomous taxi services or transporting delivery containers within city centers. Its compact and safe design allows it to be stored in a standard research lab, facilitating realistic human-vehicle interaction studies. As of 2022, the total system build cost using new components is approximately USD 7,000, offering an optimal balance between practical utility, safety, affordability, and research convenience.

The susceptibility of high-performance machine learning models introduces significant security risks in applications where real-world impacts are possible. Investigating adversarial attacks serves a dual purpose: it guides the improvement of machine learning systems and aids in developing targeted defenses. Currently, most adversarial attacks rely on gradient or logit information to craft perturbations. In contrast, decision-based attacks, which generate perturbations solely by observing a model's output labels without access to internal details, remain uncommon and predominantly depend on gradient-estimation techniques. This paper introduces a pixel-wise decision-based attack algorithm that utilizes reinforcement learning to determine an adversarial perturbation distribution, termed Decision-based Black-box Attack with Reinforcement learning (DBAR). Experimental results demonstrate that DBAR surpasses existing state-of-the-art decision-based attacks, achieving both a higher success rate and improved transferability.

Exotic nuclear properties within neutron-rich isotopes of Ca, Ni, Zr, and Sn are investigated using the continuum Skyrme Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory, which incorporates the Green's function method. The approach successfully reproduces experimental data for both one-neutron ($S_{\rm n}$) and two-neutron ($S_{\rm 2n}$) separation energies, although the $S_{\rm n}$ calculations predict significantly shorter drip lines than those derived from $S_{\rm 2n}$. Systematic analysis of neutron pairing energies ($-E_{\rm pair}$) reveals that odd-$A$ nuclei exhibit much lower values than their neighboring even-even counterparts, a discrepancy attributed to the lack of pairing energy contribution from the unpaired neutron. Furthermore, examinations of single-particle structures, rms radii, and density distributions suggest the existence of halo structures in neutron-rich Ca, Ni, and Sn isotopes. These predictions are characterized by abrupt increases in rms radii that deviate markedly from the conventional $r \propto A^{1/3}$ scaling, alongside highly diffuse spatial density profiles. An analysis of partial wave contributions to the total neutron density indicates that orbitals near the Fermi surface, particularly those with low angular momentum, are the primary drivers of the extended nuclear density and enlarged rms radii. Finally, the discussion on the number of neutrons ($N_{\lambda}$ or $N_0$) occupying states above the Fermi surface (in the continuum) demonstrates behaviors consistent with pairing energy trends, thereby reinforcing the critical role of pairing correlations in halo phenomena.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have recently gained significant traction for learning representations within non-Euclidean feature spaces. Current research emphasizes stacking multiple GCN layers, akin to Convolutional Neural Networks, to enhance expressive capabilities. However, simply stacking these layers often results in challenges such as vanishing gradients, overfitting, and over-smoothing. These issues are notably reduced in shallower architectures, although they come at the cost of lower expressive power. To address this, we introduce a novel Multipath Graph Convolutional Neural Network that integrates the outputs of several distinct shallow networks. We evaluated our model across various benchmark datasets for node property prediction. The results demonstrate that our proposed approach not only achieves higher test accuracy but also converges with fewer training epochs. The complete implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/rangan2510/MultiPathGCN.

Nuclei facilitate the import and export of proteins, including those regulating the cell cycle. These trafficking processes are periodically modulated by the cell cycle, partly due to the rhythmic assembly and disassembly of the nuclear envelope. Consequently, replicated DNA is partitioned into daughter cells, while nuclear proteins are released to diffuse throughout the cytoplasm. This study employs a mathematical import-diffusion model to demonstrate how proteins, specifically cell cycle regulators, can be redistributed within the cytoplasm by nuclei oscillating between interphase and mitosis. We find that when the cell cycle duration is dependent on the local concentration of these regulators, the model generates mitotic waves. Furthermore, we analyze how the velocity and spatial origin of these waves vary with different model parameters. This research is inspired by recent in vitro experiments involving cycling cell-free extracts from *Xenopus laevis* frog eggs containing multiple nuclei sharing a common cytoplasm. These experiments indicate that nuclei function as pacemakers for the cell cycle, thereby playing a crucial role in collectively determining the spatial origin of mitotic waves.

We investigated an X1.6 solar flare from NOAA AR 12602 that occurred on October 22, 2014. Because the entire event was observed by RHESSI, IRIS, and Hinode/EIS, we were able to analyze how the chromosphere reacted to a driver of nonthermal electrons. Using RHESSI spectral fitting, we calculated the energy of these nonthermal electrons and correlated their time-varying parameters with changes in Doppler velocity, density, and nonthermal width across a wide temperature spectrum. The injection of energy, totaling $4.8\times10^{30}$ erg over 352 seconds, triggered explosive chromospheric evaporation. This process showed distinct patterns in both Doppler and nonthermal velocities at the flow reversal temperature, ranging from 1.35 to 1.82 MK. The peak electron injection occurred at 14:06 UT, coinciding with the maximum velocities; at this moment, we detected 200 km s$^{-1}$ blueshifts in the core of Fe XXIV, an ion typically considered stationary. Just prior to this peak, the nonthermal electron population exhibited its shallowest spectral index (approximately 6), which aligned with the highest nonthermal velocities in Si IV and Fe XXI. Conversely, nonthermal velocities in Fe XIV, formed near the flow reversal temperature, remained low and showed no correlation with density or Doppler shifts. However, nonthermal velocities in ions with similar temperatures increased and correlated with Doppler velocities, suggesting the presence of unresolved flows around the flow reversal point. This research offers a detailed, time-resolved set of chromospheric diagnostics for a major X-class flare, including a time-resolved profile of energy injection, making it highly suitable for future modeling efforts.

The recent discovery of low-temperature superconductivity in V-based Kagome metals has generated significant interest. This study presents the synthesis and physical characterization of high-quality single-crystalline thin films of the Kagome metal KV$_3$Sb$_5$. For a film approximately 15 nm thick, resistance measurements as a function of temperature exhibit Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) behavior, confirming the existence of two-dimensional superconductivity. Relative to bulk samples, the onset critical temperature ($T^{onset}_{c}$) and the out-of-plane upper critical field ($H_{c2}$) are improved by 15% and by more than an order of magnitude, respectively. Furthermore, the zero-resistance state is suppressed by a magnetic field as low as 50 Oe. Additionally, a wide range of magnetic fields exhibits temperature-independent resistance, a signature characteristic of a quantum metallic state. These findings offer compelling evidence for unconventional superconductivity in this material.

This paper introduces a higher-order time-discretization scheme for the stochastic semilinear wave equation with multiplicative noise, featuring general drift and diffusion terms. Using a variational approach for error analysis, we establish an enhanced convergence order of 3/2 for the solution approximates. The analysis primarily relies on Hölder continuity in time and moment bounds for both the continuous and discrete solutions, alongside the presentation of computational experiments.

Electronic edge states in topological insulators represent a fundamental concept in physics.
