Experimental results confirm the efficacy of operating within the RGB image space for grasping transparent objects.

This study addresses the general issue of projecting onto a polyhedral convex cone defined by a finite set of generators. By reformulating this as a projection onto a polytope created through the simple truncation of the original cone, the problem can be resolved using two closely related projections onto the same bounded polytope. The computational efficiency of this method relies heavily on the effectiveness of the core algorithm used to determine the least-norm element within the convex hull of a finite set of points. In our numerical experiments, we employed a specialized finite algorithm from the open-source matrix-vector calculation system, Octave. This algorithm proved largely insensitive to the ratio between the number of generators and the problem's dimensionality, significantly outperforming Octave's built-in general-purpose active-set quadratic programming solver when the number of points surpassed the dimensionality of the original problem.

Applying stochastic resetting to a process typically drives its dynamics toward a time-independent stationary state, with the optimal resetting rate minimizing the mean time to reach a target. While these phenomena have been extensively researched in ordinary diffusive systems over the past ten years, this paper investigates the impact of stochastic resetting on diffusive motion governed by a non-linear differential equation. This non-linearity arises from the power-law dependence of the diffusion coefficient on the probability density function (or particle concentration). We first outline this concept to establish the necessary foundations. Subsequently, we derive an exact expression for the mean squared displacement and show how it converges to a steady-state value under exponential resetting; this mechanism also causes the spatial support of the probability density function, which is initially confined to a finite measure in free non-linear diffusion, to expand across the entire real domain. Furthermore, we analyze the first-passage properties of non-linear diffusion subjected to exponential resetting, deriving analytical formulas for the mean first-passage time and numerically identifying the optimal resetting rate that minimizes the time required for a particle to reach a specific target. Finally, we verify the universal property stating that the relative fluctuation in the mean first-passage time for optimally restarted non-linear diffusion equals unity.

Supermassive black holes linked to cosmic strings may aid in cosmic structure formation and become captured by galaxies if their velocities are low, implying that their acceleration is likewise minimal. This slow acceleration does not significantly alter the shadow of these black holes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for such slowly accelerating black holes, the angular positions of images in gravitational lensing remain largely unchanged. We propose a detection method based on gravitational lensing, which relies on the fact that differential time delays between images differ substantially from those observed in non-accelerating black holes.

The Scotogenic framework serves as a radiative mechanism for generating Majorana neutrino masses at the one-loop level while also accommodating a dark matter candidate. This study extends the original Scotogenic model to accommodate any number of generations of Scotogenic states. Subsequently, we detail the light neutrino mass matrix, outlining its derivation and offering a practical approximate formula. Finally, we numerically solve the Renormalization Group Equations to investigate the model's behavior at high energy scales.

New antineutrino spectra for fissile isotopes ($^{235}$U, $^{238}$U, $^{239}$Pu, and $^{241}$Pu) present in nuclear reactor fuel have been derived. This achievement employed a combined approach involving the calculation of antineutrino spectra and their fitting to experimental data from the Rovno NPP in the 1980s. Cross sections for these fissile isotopes, calculated using these spectra, align well with experimental results from the Double Chooz experiment. For the same reactor core composition, the calculated cross section is $\sigma_{f} = (5.82 \pm 0.12)\times10^{-43}$ cm$^2$/fission, representing the closest prediction among all available results. Furthermore, the derived spectra exhibit the same "bump" feature as experimental observations within the 5 MeV energy region.

When humans operate robot arms, the robots must infer the user's intended task. Previous research on shared autonomy and assistive teleoperation has investigated how robots can deduce desired tasks from joystick inputs. Typically, this inference relies on an internal mapping between specific inputs and discrete tasks; for instance, moving the joystick left might signal a desire to grasp a plate, while moving it right indicates a cup. While this method functions effectively once users understand the robot's interpretation, inexperienced operators must still learn these mappings through trial and error. We propose recognizing that the robot's input-to-task mapping is merely a convention, noting that multiple equally efficient conventions exist. Instead of passively waiting for users to adapt, we introduce a shared autonomy approach where the robot actively demonstrates its chosen convention. Through repeated interactions, the robot exaggerates its arm movements to highlight more efficient inputs while simultaneously assisting with the current task. We compare this method against a state-of-the-art baseline requiring users to self-identify the convention, as well as against written instructions. Our user study results show that modifying the robot's behavior to reveal its convention outperforms both baselines and significantly reduces the time humans spend controlling the robot. You can view videos of our user study here: https://youtu.be/jROTVOp469I

This study empirically investigates the link between the reopening of K-12 schools and colleges and the dissemination of COVID-19, utilizing county-level panel data from the United States. By leveraging foot traffic data alongside K-12 reopening plans, we evaluate how increased school visits and the implementation of various instructional modes (in-person, hybrid, and remote) correlate with the two-week forward growth rate of confirmed cases. Our debiased panel regression, incorporating county dummies, state-week interactions, and additional controls, reveals that higher visitation rates at both K-12 institutions and colleges correspond to subsequent increases in case growth. Specifically, fully reopening K-12 schools for in-person learning is estimated to raise the case growth rate by 5 percentage points (SE = 2). Furthermore, the positive correlation between K-12 attendance or in-person openings and case growth is more pronounced in counties where mask mandates for staff are not enforced. These findings support a causal interpretation within a structural model accounting for unobserved county and temporal confounders, and sensitivity analyses confirm that the baseline results remain robust across different timing assumptions and model specifications.

Neural Style Transfer (NST) generates remarkable art by applying a reference style to a content image. However, existing image-to-image NST approaches lack the fine-grained control necessary for detailed artistic editing. To address this gap, we introduce an interactive style transfer (IST) method inspired by drawing, allowing users to collaboratively create harmonious-style images. This IST approach functions like a digital brush, enabling users to sample styles from any location and apply them to specific regions of the target content. To define the area of influence, we integrate a fluid simulation algorithm that treats styles as pigments around the brush's position, spreading them based on similarity maps within either the style or content images. By expanding the creative potential of NST, our method allows a single style image to generate thousands of unique and striking works through simple dip-and-paint interactions. A demonstration video is included in the supplementary materials or accessible at http://mmcheng.net/ist.

Traditional few-shot experiments focus on quickly classifying previously unseen samples. However, we argue that few-shot learning must be a long-term process that assimilates new knowledge for the future without discarding previously learned concepts. In the mammalian brain, the hippocampus is critical for this mechanism, enabling rapid learning and the incremental consolidation of information into the neocortex. This research investigates whether an Artificial Hippocampal Algorithm (AHA) can be integrated with a standard Machine Learning model—acting as an incremental neocortex—to achieve both short-term and long-term one-shot learning. The results indicate that incorporating the AHA allows the system to learn from single examples and retain that knowledge over time, avoiding catastrophic forgetting. This study represents one of the earliest applications of a Computational Hippocampus model for memory consolidation and marks a significant step toward few-shot continual learning.

Statistical research has extensively addressed multiple testing, yet controlling false discoveries remains difficult when test statistics are dependent. Various methods have been developed to estimate the false discovery proportion (FDP) under arbitrary dependence, primarily by reducing such dependence to a weaker form to prove the strong consistency of both FDP and the false discovery rate (FDR). Consequently, FDPs converge to the same asymptotic limit within weak dependence frameworks. However, we observe that the asymptotic variance of the FDP can be heavily influenced by the specific dependence structure of the test statistics, even under weak dependence. Quantifying this variability is practically significant, as it serves as an indicator of the estimate's quality. Current literature on this aspect remains limited. In this paper, we derive the asymptotic expansion of the FDP under mild regularity conditions and investigate how its asymptotic variance changes across different dependence structures through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. Based on these findings, we recommend that when employing an FDP procedure for multiple testing, researchers should report both the mean and variance estimates of the FDP to provide a more comprehensive study outcome.

Data on proton form factors within the time-like region, gathered by the BaBar, BESIII, and CMD-3 Collaborations, are analyzed to provide a coherent understanding of proton structure. Oscillations in the annihilation cross section, previously noted, are now established with improved precision. This study discusses the moduli of individual form factors, determined here for the first time, along with their ratio and the angular asymmetry of the $e^+e^-\to\bar p p$ annihilation reaction. By fitting available data on the cross section, effective form factor, and form factor ratio, a description of the electric and magnetic time-like form factors is proposed, covering the range from the threshold to the highest momenta.

Modified $r$-matrices, which serve as solutions to the modified classical Yang-Baxter equation introduced by Semenov-Tian-Shansky, are pivotal in mathematical physics. This paper first establishes a cohomology theory for these matrices and subsequently examines three distinct types of deformations—algebraic, geometric, and linear—based on this framework. We identify the differential graded Lie algebra that controls algebraic deformations. Regarding geometric deformations, we demonstrate a rigidity theorem and analyze the conditions under which a neighborhood of a modified $r$-matrix remains smooth within the space of all such structures. In the context of trivial linear deformations, we define the concept of a Nijenhuis element for a modified $r$-matrix. The work concludes with applications to the deformation of the complement of the diagonal Lie algebra and compatible Poisson structures.

Recently, continual learning (CL) has attracted considerable attention for its ability to allow deep learning models to master new concepts without losing previously acquired knowledge. However, the majority of current approaches rely on knowing task identities and boundaries, a requirement that is often impractical in real-world scenarios. This paper tackles a more realistic and demanding CL scenario known as Task-Free Continual Learning (TFCL), where models must be trained on non-stationary data streams without explicit task information. To solve TFCL, we propose an evolved mixture model featuring a network architecture that dynamically expands to accommodate shifts in data distribution. This expansion is executed by calculating the probability distance between knowledge stored in each mixture component and the current memory buffer via the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC). Additionally, we incorporate two straightforward dropout mechanisms to selectively discard stored examples, thereby preventing memory overload while maintaining memory diversity. Empirical findings indicate that the proposed method delivers outstanding performance.

This work investigates the local finiteness properties within specific varieties of nonassociative coalgebras and presents the Gelfand-Dorfman construction for Novikov coalgebras alongside the Kantor construction for Jordan super-coalgebras. Several examples are provided, including non-locally finite instances of differential coalgebras, Novikov coalgebras, Lie coalgebras, Jordan super-coalgebras, and right-alternative coalgebras; notably, the dual algebras associated with each of these examples satisfy stringent additional identities. Furthermore, examples of infinite-dimensional simple differential coalgebras, Novikov coalgebras, Lie coalgebras, and Jordan super-coalgebras are constructed over fields of characteristic zero.

We investigate a sensor network comprising distributed Mach-Zehnder interferometers (MZIs) designed for the simultaneous estimation of any number $d \geq 1$ of phase shifts. This approach utilizes a squeezed-vacuum state distributed across $d$ modes via a quantum circuit (QC), where each QC output feeds one MZI alongside a coherent state. Specifically, ${\it i})$ we determine the optimal network configuration for maximizing sensitivity when estimating any linear combination of the $d$ phases. This protocol surpasses the shot-noise limit, achieving Heisenberg scaling relative to the total average particle count in the probe state while relying solely on local photocounting for multiphase estimation. Moreover, this parallel strategy outperforms optimal separable methods for estimating linear phase combinations, offering a sensitivity gain of up to a factor of $d$. Conversely, ${\it ii})$ for a given QC, we identify the specific linear combination of phases that yields maximum sensitivity and demonstrate that these results remain robust against random variations in the QC. Our framework opens avenues for diverse applications in distributed quantum sensing.

Biological complex networks frequently exhibit substantial structural variety, ranging from the three-dimensional configurations of allosteric proteins to the micro-scale variations in cerebral vasculature, making it challenging to discern structure-function relationships. This study presents a methodology for analyzing these relationships within flow networks optimized for specific tasks. By employing persistent homology, we investigate networks designed for complex multifunctional roles to determine how local structural modifications align to generate global functionality. Our analysis reveals that the response of these networks encodes concealed topological characteristics—specifically, sectors of uniform pressure—that are not immediately visible in the network's architecture. Despite variations in local connectivity, these features offer a universal topological framework for all networks executing such functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these characteristics strongly correlate with the tuned response, establishing a distinct topological link between structure and function while providing insight into the boundaries of multifunctionality.

Simulations are essential for accurately modeling observables from galaxy surveys, yet they become costly when a vast dynamic range is needed. This work outlines a method to integrate Lagrangian perturbation theory with N-body simulations, utilizing the control variates technique to mitigate the impact of finite computational volumes on ensemble average predictions. Specifically, we leverage the strong correlation between Zel'dovich displacements—calculated during initial condition setup—and the final density field. Because correlators for biased tracers can be determined with high precision using these displacements, pairing a Zel'dovich "simulation" with an N-body realization reduces sample variance by a factor of one hundred for power spectrum and correlation function estimates. Consequently, Zel'dovich control variates enable matter and tracer field emulators to reach larger scales than previously feasible and enhance statistical measurements in simulations constrained to small volumes, such as hydrodynamical models of galaxy formation and reionization.

This study proposes an investigation into $d_{N\Omega}$ dibaryon production via the reaction $K^- p \rightarrow d_{N\Omega} \bar{\Xi}^0$, utilizing kaon beams with typical momenta near 10 GeV, which are accessible at facilities such as COMPASS, OKA@U-70, and SPS@CERN. We estimate the cross sections for this process, noting that for three distinct form factors, values at $P_{K}=20$ GeV reach approximately 577.20, ~5625.51, and $251.11 \mathrm{\mu b}$, respectively. Given that $d_{N\Omega}$ primarily decays into $\Xi \Lambda$ and $\Xi \Sigma$, we further calculate the cross sections for the final states $K^- p \to \Xi^0 \Lambda \bar{\Xi}^0$ and $K^- p \to \Xi^- \Sigma^+ \bar{\Xi}^0$ at $P_{K}=20$ GeV. In these channels, the dibaryon $d_{N\Omega}$ can be identified through the invariant mass distributions of $\Xi^0 \Lambda$ and $\Xi^- \Sigma^+$, respectively.

Quantum nonlocality without entanglement represents a remarkable phenomenon within quantum theory, rooted in the task of locally distinguishing quantum states. Recently, Bandyopadhyay and Halder [Phys. Rev. A 104, L050201 (2021)] investigated whether any set of orthogonal states can be locally distinguishable yet yield locally indistinguishable sets upon any orthogonality-preserving local measurement; they defined such sets as possessing hidden nonlocality. Furthermore, if this phenomenon cannot be attributed to discarding subsystems, it is termed genuine hidden nonlocality. In their work, they demonstrated several sets of entangled states exhibiting genuine hidden nonlocality, yet they questioned whether such a phenomenon could exist without entanglement. This paper resolves that doubt by constructing a series of unentangled sets capable of genuinely activating nonlocality. Additionally, we develop a method to address the local irredundancy problem, which is particularly challenging for systems with composite local dimensions. As Bandyopadhyay and Halder noted, sets with genuine hidden nonlocality have potential applications in data hiding.

Multi-task learning (MTL) seeks to enhance overall performance by fully leveraging knowledge from multiple supervision signals, yet determining how to appropriately share knowledge across tasks remains an unresolved challenge. While most current deep MTL models rely on parameter sharing, designing a suitable mechanism is difficult due to the complex inter-task relationships. This paper introduces Multi-Task Neural Architecture Search (MTNAS), a general framework designed to efficiently identify an optimal sharing route for specific MTL problems. MTNAS decomposes the sharing component into multiple sub-network layers, enabling sparse connections between them and facilitating soft sharing via gating mechanisms for selected routes. This architecture allows each candidate in the search space to define a dynamic, sparse sharing path, offering greater flexibility than the rigid full-sharing strategies of prior methods. We demonstrate that conventional sharing approaches are merely sub-graphs within our proposed search space. Extensive experiments on three real-world recommendation datasets show that MTNAS consistently outperforms both single-task models and standard multi-task methods while maintaining high computational efficiency. Additionally, in-depth analysis confirms that MTNAS can learn appropriate sparse routes to effectively mitigate negative transfer.

Venture capital distribution plays a pivotal role in determining market entry, startup viability, and the broader composition of our economy. Although gender diversity enhances startup success, funding disproportionately favors male-only teams. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, 2020 witnessed a significant reduction in capital directed toward female and mixed-gender groups, highlighting an urgent necessity to examine and rectify entrenched gender biases in investment allocation. This study performs a comprehensive analysis of over 48,000 entities on Crunchbase, evaluating funding outcomes based on the gender makeup of founding teams and presenting detailed insights across various industries and regions. Additionally, we develop machine learning models to forecast a startup's likelihood of securing an equity round, uncovering the unexpected result that a CEO's gender is the dominant predictor of funding success. Finally, the paper addresses policy recommendations to tackle this critical issue.

Building on the generalized Polya theorem, which characterizes the Gaussian distribution on the real line through the equidistribution of monomials and linear forms of independent identically distributed random variables, we provide a comprehensive description of the $a$-adic solenoids that admit an analogous theorem. The proof of our primary result relies on resolving a specific functional equation within the class of continuous positive definite functions defined on the character group of an $a$-adic solenoid.

Multi-modal fusion represents a core challenge for autonomous driving perception, a topic that has recently drawn significant research attention. However, attaining high performance remains difficult due to noisy raw data, the underutilization of information, and sensor misalignment. This paper presents a literature review of existing multi-modal methods for autonomous driving perception. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of over 50 papers utilizing sensors such as LiDAR and cameras to address object detection and semantic segmentation. Departing from traditional fusion categorizations, we introduce an innovative taxonomy that classifies these methods into two major and four minor categories based on the fusion stage. Furthermore, we examine current fusion techniques in depth, highlighting unresolved issues and exploring potential research opportunities. Ultimately, this paper aims to propose a novel taxonomy for multi-modal fusion in autonomous driving perception and to stimulate future advancements in fusion-based techniques.

Detection heterogeneity is an intrinsic feature of ecological data, stemming from variables like diverse terrain, weather fluctuations, uneven sampling efforts, or individual variability. While adding covariates to statistical models is one strategy to mitigate this, it does not guarantee that measurable factors will fully capture the heterogeneity, and unmodeled variation can lead to biased inferences. Alternative solutions include random effects or finite mixtures of homogeneous subgroups. This study introduces a non-parametric method for modeling detection heterogeneity within a Bayesian hierarchical framework, utilizing a Dirichlet process mixture that offers flexible subgroup numbers without requiring pre-specification, unlike finite mixtures. We outline this approach and apply it to two prevalent ecological contexts: capture-recapture and occupancy modeling. For each context, we evaluate a homogeneous model, finite mixture models, and the proposed non-parametric method. Using two simulation studies, we compare these techniques and find the non-parametric approach to be the most reliable across varying levels of heterogeneity. Additionally, we present two real-data examples to compare inferences across the different modeling strategies. All analyses were conducted using the \texttt{nimble} package for \texttt{R}, which supports Bayesian non-parametric modeling.

To investigate $\mathbf{M}(R,C)$, the collection of binary matrices with specified row and column sums $R$ and $C$, we examine sub-matrices of the forms $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, referred to as positive and negative checkerboards, respectively. We construct a directed graph $G(R,C)$ where vertices represent matrices in $\mathbf{M}(R,C)$, and a directed edge from $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{A'}$ signifies that $\mathbf{A'}$ can be obtained from $\mathbf{A}$ by converting a negative checkerboard into a positive one. We demonstrate that $G(R,C)$ is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and determine specific matrix classes that serve as unique sinks and sources within this graph. For any $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A'} \in \mathbf{M}(R,C)$, we establish both necessary and sufficient conditions on the difference matrix $\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{A'}-\mathbf{A}$ that guarantee the existence of a directed path from $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{A'}$. We further analyze the special case of $\mathbf{M}(\mathcal D)$, comprising adjacency matrices of graphs with a fixed degree distribution $\mathcal D$. In this context, $G(\mathcal D)$ is defined by performing positive switches on symmetric pairs of negative checkerboards. We prove that $Z_2$, an approximation of the spectral radius $\lambda_1$ derived from the second Zagreb index, does not decrease along the arcs of $G(\mathcal D)$. Additionally, the quantity $\ll$ attains its maximum value in $\mathbf{M}(\mathcal D)$ at a sink of $G(\mathcal D)$. Finally, simulation results indicate that sequentially applying positive switches to an Erd\H os-R\'enyi graph can substantially increase $\lambda_1$.

This paper investigates standard discrete-time slotted ALOHA featuring a finite set of terminals equipped with infinite buffers. Our research jointly analyzes the system's stability and physical layer security across two configurations: a dominant system, where every terminal perpetually holds a packet, and an original system, which does not enforce this condition. For the case of N = 2, we derive the secrecy-stability regions for both setups. Additionally, we determine transmission probabilities that maximize system throughput. Finally, this work introduces a novel methodology for calculating joint stability and secrecy regions.

We examine global-in-time solutions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier system, which models the behavior of a general compressible fluid that is both viscous and heat-conducting, operating far from equilibrium. By introducing a novel definition of weak solutions designed to handle inhomogeneous, time-dependent Dirichlet boundary conditions, we establish sufficient criteria ensuring that these global weak solutions remain ultimately bounded.

It is widely established that modeling the underlying asset price to replicate vanilla option market prices requires incorporating both diffusion and jump components. In this study, we assume the asset price process $S$ is Markovian with cadlag paths and introduce a method to compute the distribution of realized variance for log returns accumulated while the asset trades within a predefined range. Consequently, we develop an algorithm for pricing and hedging volatility derivatives and derivatives based on corridor-realized variance in such markets. The framework is broad, covering jump-diffusion models and Lévy processes. We demonstrate the weak convergence of the proposed scheme and provide a detailed implementation guide for specific scenarios: the CEV process (continuous paths), the variance gamma process (jumps with independent increments), and infinite activity jump-diffusion models (discontinuous paths with dependent increments).

We introduce a variational quantum algorithm designed to generate ground states for one-dimensional lattice quantum Hamiltonians, optimized for programmable quantum devices utilizing Quantum Data Buses (QDB) for qubit interactions. Specifically addressing trapped ions where the axial Center-Of-Mass (COM) vibrational mode serves as the single QDB, our approach employs resonant sideband optical pulses as the primary operations; these are potentially more rapid than off-resonant couplings and consequently less susceptible to decoherence. The separation of the QDB from the qubits emerges naturally as a result of the variational optimization process. Through numerical simulations of ground state preparation for the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model in ionic systems, we demonstrate that our method is scalable and robust against finite temperatures in the COM mode.

In Markov-chain Monte Carlo simulations, determining statistical errors or confidence intervals for computed values is a critical step. This paper reviews various error estimation techniques, including basic empirical approaches using multiple independent runs, the blocking method, and the stationary bootstrap method. We evaluate their effectiveness by applying them to a real Monte-Carlo time series. Our findings indicate that the stationary bootstrap method provides reliable and stable estimates for any quantity using just a single time series. Conversely, simple estimation methods relying on a limited number of independent runs can yield demonstrably incorrect results. We also explore the potential applications of the stationary bootstrap method in numerical simulations.

The exceptional stability of MoSi2N4 against air, water, acid, and heat has sparked significant interest in this class of two-dimensional (2D) materials. Within this family, NbSi2N4, VSi2N4, and VSi2P4 stand out as easy-plane ferromagnetic semiconductors featuring negligible in-plane magnetic anisotropy, thereby fulfilling a key requirement for a dissipationless spin superfluid mode. Monte Carlo and density functional theory calculations indicate that the Curie temperatures of monolayer VSi2N4 and VSi2P4 exceed room temperature. Furthermore, the magnetic moments of VSi2N4 can be reoriented from an in-plane to an out-of-plane configuration through the application of tensile biaxial strain or electron doping.

Identifying shifts within data streams is a fundamental goal in stream analysis, with applications ranging from predictive maintenance and fraud detection to healthcare. A rigorous method for detecting these shifts involves comparing distributions observed across the stream. However, data streams often present high-dimensional challenges, and changes may be intricate, appearing only in higher-order moments. Furthermore, the streaming environment imposes strict limitations on memory and computational resources. We introduce Maximum Mean Discrepancy Adaptive Windowing (MMDAW), an algorithm that utilizes the established Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) two-sample test to enable efficient online computation on windows with flexible sizing. Since MMD is sensitive to any underlying distributional change, MMDAW serves as a versatile, non-parametric change detector that meets the demands of streaming contexts. Experimental results demonstrate that MMDAW outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in detection quality.

We present findings on how hydrogenation modulates the spin Seebeck effect (SSE) in Pd/YIG bilayers. When exposed to 3% hydrogen gas, the SSE voltage drops by over 50% compared to measurements taken in pure argon. Although this modulation of the SSE voltage is reversible, restoring the voltage to its pre-hydrogenation level requires several days due to the slow time constant associated with hydrogen desorption. Furthermore, we observe a significant reduction in the spin Hall magnetoresistance of the same sample upon hydrogen exposure, confirming that the detected changes in spin current signals stem from the hydrogenation of the Pd/YIG interface.

This paper surveys the methods and concepts developed for evaluating dialogue systems, a crucial component of their development. While dialogue systems are frequently assessed through human evaluations and questionnaires, these approaches are often costly and time-consuming. Consequently, significant research has focused on developing techniques that minimize the need for human labor. This survey presents the primary concepts and methods in this field, categorized by different classes of dialogue systems: task-oriented, conversational, and question-answering systems. For each class, we introduce the core technologies and subsequently outline the specific evaluation methods applied.

Broadcasting reliable data to multiple receivers over lossy wireless channels is difficult because of varying link conditions. While Automatic Repeat-reQuest (ARQ) retransmission schemes suffer from bandwidth inefficiency caused by data duplication at receivers, Network Coding (NC) offers a promising solution by combining multiple lost packets to improve efficiency. However, disrupted feedback channels make it hard to identify which lost packets should be combined. To address this, this paper introduces an adaptive encoding scheme at the transmitter that integrates Network Coding with Machine Learning (NCML) for retransmitting lost packets. The proposed NCML system analyzes historical feedback signals to train a classifier, which then predicts the status of transmitted packets at various receivers based on corrupted feedback to facilitate effective data mixing. Extensive simulations demonstrate the approach's efficiency. Results indicate that the machine learning algorithm trains efficiently and accurately, correctly classifying the state of transmitted packets for different receivers 90% of the time on average. Furthermore, compared to ARQ and traditional NC schemes across various terrains, power levels, and transmitter-receiver distances, the proposed NCML method achieves significant bandwidth gains.

In Novel Class Discovery (NCD), the task involves training clustering models on unlabeled data from unseen classes, given labeled data from seen classes. However, the underlying assumptions of NCD remain ambiguous. This study clarifies these assumptions, revealing that high-level semantic features must be shared between seen and unseen classes. Based on this insight, NCD is theoretically solvable under specific conditions and aligns naturally with meta-learning, which operates under identical assumptions. Consequently, we can empirically address the NCD problem using slightly adapted meta-learning algorithms. This approach significantly lowers the amount of unlabeled data required for training, enhancing practicality as shown in experiments. The efficacy of using minimal data is further supported by the NCD application context: since labeling only seen classes is unrealistic, NCD represents a sampling process rather than a labeling one in a causal sense. Therefore, unseen-class data is naturally collected alongside seen-class data; their novelty arises precisely because they require initial clustering.

To enhance sustainability and energy efficiency, optimizing the control of Heating, Ventilating, and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) systems has garnered significant attention; however, analyzing thermal and HVAC signatures and evaluating optimization strategies remains inefficient and cumbersome due to the scarcity of public datasets. This paper introduces the Subway station Energy and Environment Dataset (SEED), derived from a Beijing subway line, which offers minute-level data on environmental dynamics (including temperature, humidity, and CO2), HVAC operational states and energy usage (covering ventilators, refrigerators, and pumps), and hourly passenger flow statistics. We detail the sensor deployment and HVAC configurations used for data collection and environmental control, alongside an initial investigation into energy disaggregation for HVAC systems, as well as the signatures associated with thermal loads, cooling supply, and passenger flows using this dataset.

In a mechanical system featuring a rotator and pendulum linked by a weak, time-periodic Hamiltonian perturbation, the Arnold diffusion problem posits that "diffusing orbits" exist where the rotator's energy increases by an amount independent of the coupling parameter's magnitude, provided the coupling is sufficiently small. Extensive research has been dedicated to proving Arnold diffusion in such contexts. This study examines a scenario where a further dissipative perturbation is introduced to the coupled rotator-pendulum system, rendering it conformally symplectic rather than symplectic. We establish explicit criteria regarding the dissipation parameter under which the system continues to display energy growth. Although Chirikov conjectured that Arnold diffusion could influence systems with minor dissipation, this work involves a specifically chosen coupling; however, the underlying mechanism is adaptable to general couplings, which will be addressed in future research.

This work examines rank 2 vector bundles on a curve $C$ that arise as specializations of the trivial bundle. A full classification is achieved when $C$ is either Brill-Noether generic or hyperelliptic; in these scenarios, every limit vector bundle is decomposable. Furthermore, we provide instances of indecomposable limit bundles occurring on certain specific curves.

The Metaheuristic Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm has become a leading technique for addressing highly constrained, non-linear, and non-convex optimization challenges across various electrical engineering domains. Within the field of power system economic operation, PSO has proven particularly effective in resolving practical system issues. This paper presents an extensive survey of research utilizing different PSO variants to tackle diverse aspects of Economic Load Dispatch (ELD) in power systems. The study categorizes published ELD papers based on PSO into five key areas: (i) single-objective economic load dispatch, (ii) dynamic economic load dispatch, (iii) economic load dispatch incorporating non-conventional energy sources, (iv) multi-objective environmental/economic dispatch, and (v) economic load dispatch for microgrids. Each section concludes with a summary table outlining the primary features of the reviewed papers. Finally, the review concludes by highlighting promising directions for future research.

This study examines the multilevel algorithm's efficacy near criticality using the Ising model across various temperatures. Numerical findings indicate that the algorithm's performance degrades as the correlation length grows relative to the lattice size. Specifically, within a multilevel framework, the statistical error of the longest correlator decreases only when the correlation length remains below one-tenth of the lattice size; beyond this threshold, the multilevel method underperforms compared to a single-level algorithm with equivalent computational cost. A theoretical model describing this performance scaling is presented, demonstrating remarkable agreement with the numerical data. This model can be extended to systems with more complex spectra to forecast whether multilevel techniques will enhance statistical accuracy.

Spin-squeezing criteria, which rely on first and second moments, serve as entanglement witnesses for detecting particle entanglement through collective measurements, while modified uncertainty relations function similarly for identifying mode entanglement or steering. By establishing a correspondence between these approaches, we demonstrate that metrologically valuable spin squeezing indicates multimode entanglement within symmetric spin states distributed across addressable modes. Additionally, we derive tight, state-independent bounds for the spin-squeezing coefficient regarding multipartite entanglement and highlight their relationship to established entanglement criteria based on polarization. These findings are particularly significant for advanced experiments involving symmetric entangled states partitioned into multiple addressable modes, such as split spin-squeezed Bose-Einstein condensates.

The $n$th $r$-extended Lah-Bell number represents the count of partitions of a set containing $n+r$ elements into ordered blocks, where $r$ specific elements must reside in distinct ordered blocks. This paper introduces both incomplete and complete $r$-extended Lah-Bell polynomials as multivariate extensions of the $r$-Lah numbers and $r$-extended Lah-Bell numbers, respectively, and examines their properties and identities. Through this analysis, we derive finite sum expressions for the $r$-Lah numbers and the $r$-extended Lah-Bell numbers.

To comprehend how binary star systems evolve dynamically and influence their stellar and planetary companions, astronomers need well-defined binary populations spanning various stellar ages. However, identifying and characterizing these binaries demands costly observational resources. The advent of high-precision Gaia astrometry has introduced the re-normalized unit weight error (RUWE) statistic as a tool to detect binary systems; typically, RUWE values exceeding 1.2 suggest a stellar companion within approximately 1 arcsecond. This study aims to determine if this diagnostic, originally calibrated for field-age systems older than 1 Gyr, remains valid for younger systems hosting circumstellar disks. By comparing RUWE values between disk-bearing and disk-less systems within the Taurus and Upper Scorpius star-forming regions—using a control sample of single stars identified via high-contrast imaging—we demonstrate that protoplanetary disks alone can artificially inflate RUWE readings. Consequently, we propose a more conservative threshold for distinguishing single stars from binaries in the presence of disk material, setting the cutoff at the 95th percentile of the RUWE distribution for disk-bearing single stars, which corresponds to RUWE = 2.5.

A user's browsing history often reveals sensitive details, including health status, political views, and financial standing. Recent research shows that website fingerprints can be inferred from usage metrics such as network traffic, cache and memory consumption, CPU activity, power usage, and hardware performance counters (HPCs). However, current fingerprinting attacks suffer from significant drawbacks: they require high sampling rates that lead to substantial performance overhead and network traffic, or they necessitate the user visiting a malicious site, which cannot always be guaranteed. These limitations make existing attacks more conspicuous to users and easier to detect. To address these issues, we introduce Leaked-Web, a novel, accurate, and efficient machine learning-based website fingerprinting attack leveraging processor HPCs. Leaked-Web collects HPC data at a low monitoring granularity and transmits samples to a remote server for classification. The system analyzes browser microarchitectural features using advanced machine learning techniques, including classical, boosting, deep learning, and time-series models. Experimental results demonstrate that Leaked-Web, utilizing a LogitBoost classifier with only the top four HPC features, achieves 91% classification accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art attacks by nearly 5%. Additionally, the proposed method incurs negligible performance overhead (less than 1%), representing approximately a 12% reduction compared to existing hardware-assisted fingerprinting attacks.

We have derived an analytic solution for charged, rotating black strings within four-dimensional Einsteinian quartic gravity (EQG) that approaches Anti-de Sitter space asymptotically. By analyzing the near-horizon limit of these solutions, we have independently and analytically determined their thermodynamic characteristics. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of the first law of thermodynamics for rotating black strings in both charged and uncharged scenarios, serving as a consistency check.

The widespread success of neural networks (NNs) across various domains has spurred greater interest in comprehending their internal learning mechanisms. This paper advances beyond simple descriptions by adopting a graph-based approach to examine the correlation between NN graph structures and their performance. Specifically, we introduce three key contributions: (1) modeling the NN learning process as a time-evolving graph composed of static snapshots across epochs, (2) condensing the structural transformations of NNs during training into a concise temporal summary, and (3) utilizing this summary to forecast the accuracy of NNs in classification or regression tasks. Regarding the dynamic graph representation, we investigate structural features for both fully-connected and convolutional layers, which are fundamental to robust NN models. Our analysis demonstrates that a straightforward summary of graph statistics, such as weighted degree and eigenvector centrality, derived from merely a few epochs, can accurately predict NN performance. For instance, a weighted degree-based summary of a time-evolving graph built from the first five training epochs of the LeNet architecture achieves a classification accuracy exceeding 93%. These results remain consistent across diverse NN architectures, including LeNet, VGG, AlexNet, and ResNet.

Grasping thermodynamics in liquids at the atomic scale is difficult due to intense atomic interactions and an absence of symmetry. Previous theoretical studies have attempted to model liquid heat capacity using phonon-like excitations but frequently depend on fitted parameters and arbitrary assumptions. This study conducts a microscopic analysis of instantaneous normal modes and velocity autocorrelations through molecular dynamics simulations of single-element systems across extensive temperature ranges (up to $10^8$ K) and pressures (up to 1 TPa). Our findings indicate that liquid heat capacity can be explained by a blend of solid-like and gas-like degrees of freedom, thereby establishing a unified framework applicable to the heat capacity of all three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas.

Recent debates concerning entangled systems shared among various Wigner's friend setups allegedly demonstrate that the premise of definite experimental outcomes by friends contradicts quantum predictions, leading to the conclusion that measurement results lack objectivity. In this work, I argue that these arguments rely on an erroneous assumption about the correlations (specifically "mixed" correlations) between the friends' results and those of the Wigners, which generates invalid predictions. Consequently, the problem does not stem from assuming definite outcomes, but rather from comparing such assumptions against flawed predictions. Furthermore, I examine the more renowned no-go theorems proposed by Frauchiger and Renner and by Brukner, which motivate these recent discussions. Regarding the former, I show that despite its different formulation, it also hinges on the same mistaken assumption regarding "mixed" correlations, thereby rendering it invalid. As for Brukner's theorem, I highlight that it relies on the highly unappealing assumption of locality, which significantly undermines its impact. Throughout this analysis, I support my assertions with explicit calculations based on pilot-wave theory.

This study focuses on developing positive definite functions on the Cartesian product of quasi-metric spaces by utilizing generalized Stieltjes and complete Bernstein functions. The established findings align with T. Gneiting's well-known methodology for constructing space-time positive definite functions, along with its various extensions. Furthermore, when the spaces are metric, the paper provides necessary and sufficient conditions to ensure the strict positive definiteness of the proposed models.

Although common sense has long intrigued Artificial Intelligence, it has seldom been a primary focus. Despite references in John McCarthy's early work and decades of research by committed scholars, no AI system with substantial general common sense has yet materialized. The reasons for this gap remain unclear, yet numerous examples of AI failures highlight a tendency to prioritize specialized expertise over common sense, leading to brittleness. Efforts to overcome this limitation, even within modern deep learning, often involve aggregating vast quantities of small commonsense facts. However, compiling such fragments does not yield a system that exhibits human-like common sense. We propose a broader perspective: common sense should be studied as an integral part of a complete cognitive system encompassing history, goals, desires, and drives, rather than through isolated instances. A new approach is necessary to recognize that common sense deserves dedicated scientific inquiry.

We examined the connection between stellar mass and absolute Gaia G magnitude, derived from theoretical models by \cite{2012MNRAS.427..127B} across various luminosity classes. For subgiants and main-sequence stars, we established approximate analytical direct and inverse relationships using the most probable G magnitude values during their evolutionary phases. Comparisons with limited observational data indicate that these results are effective for estimating stellar masses between 1 and 10 solar masses using Gaia photometry. However, we contend that deriving similar relations for other luminosity classes would yield little value.

We examine stellar elemental abundance patterns at redshift zero within eight low-mass ($M_* = 10^6 - 10^9 M_{\odot}$) galaxies simulated using the Feedback in Realistic Environments (FIRE-2) cosmological model. Employing magnesium (Mg) as a proxy for alpha-elements, we analyze the relationship between $[\text{Mg/Fe}]$ and $[\text{Fe/H}]$, which exhibits a general monotonic trend evolving gradually over cosmic time. Additionally, we identify three distinct secondary enrichment features observed in specific case studies, driven by galaxy mergers or sporadic star formation episodes. First, a secondary track with sub-standard $[\text{Mg/Fe}]$ ratios appears; at $z=0$, stars in this track reside 2–6 kpc from the center and were accreted during a 1:3 mass-ratio merger approximately 0.4 Gyr ago. Second, a clear bimodal distribution in elemental abundances emerges following a vigorous star formation burst in a galaxy roughly 10 Gyr ago; this event temporarily halted star formation for ~0.66 Gyr, permitting Type Ia supernovae to enrich the system with iron before star formation restarted. Third, we observe enrichment stripes oriented roughly perpendicular to the primary $[\text{Mg/Fe}]$ versus $[\text{Fe/H}]$ trend, representing short-lived star formation bursts where core-collapse supernovae rapidly enriched the medium with magnesium and iron. Detecting these signatures would validate the power of elemental abundances in reconstructing the assembly and star formation histories of dwarf galaxies. We assess the feasibility of observing these features in future spectroscopic surveys. Our findings indicate that precise measurements of elemental abundance patterns can uncover pivotal events in the formation histories of low-mass galaxies.

Massive Internet of Things (IoT) networks support diverse applications, notably the swift dissemination of emergency and disaster alerts. While existing benchmark algorithms address message delivery in these scenarios, they face practical limitations such as poor network coverage and excessive redundant transmissions required to expand reach, leading to significant energy drain on individual IoT devices. To address these issues, we introduce a new performance metric called "forwarding efficiency," defined as the ratio of coverage probability to the average number of transmissions per device, to better assess data dissemination. Subsequently, we propose Fishbone Forwarding (FiFo), a novel and efficient method designed to enhance forwarding efficiency while maintaining manageable computational complexity. The FiFo method accomplishes two key tasks: first, it clusters devices using the unweighted pair group method with arithmetic average; second, it constructs main and sub-axes for each cluster by applying the expectation-maximization algorithm for Gaussian mixture models alongside principal component analysis. Utilizing a real-world dataset, we demonstrate the method's superiority. Extensive and comprehensive simulations confirm that the proposed FiFo approach outperforms benchmark algorithms regarding forwarding efficiency.

Patient-centered care necessitates that patients comprehend upcoming dental procedures, a step that also mitigates fear and anxiety. However, the expertise gap between patients and dentists often renders traditional education methods ineffective for detailing surgical steps. To address this, we introduce \textit{OralViewer}, the first interactive application allowing dentists to demonstrate surgeries in 3D, thereby enhancing patient understanding. \textit{OralViewer} reconstructs patient-specific 3D tooth structures from a single 2D panoramic X-ray and integrates them with registered gum and jaw bone models to create a complete oral cavity representation. During demonstrations, dentists can utilize virtual instruments to animate surgical effects on the 3D model in real-time. Technical evaluation indicates that our deep learning-based model achieves a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.771 for 3D tooth reconstruction. A study involving 12 patients demonstrates that \textit{OralViewer} improves their comprehension of surgical procedures, while a separate assessment by three board-certified dentists confirms the system's clinical validity.

**Objective:** This study investigates transitions to low-lying excited states in both the residual and ejectile nuclei resulting from the 76Se(18O, 17O) 77Se one-neutron stripping reaction at an incident energy of 275 MeV. The analysis aims to clarify the contributions of single-particle and core excitations to the observed cross sections and assess the sensitivity of calculated results to various nuclear structure models. **Methodology:** Using the MAGNEX large acceptance magnetic spectrometer, we measured excitation energy spectra and differential cross-section angular distributions for the ejectiles, while reaction kinematics were reconstructed via the missing mass technique. These experimental data were compared against theoretical predictions derived from the distorted-wave Born approximation, coupled-channels Born approximation, and coupled reaction channels models. The latter utilized spectroscopic amplitudes for projectile and target overlaps obtained from large-scale shell-model and interacting boson-fermion model calculations. **Outcomes:** The energy spectra revealed peaks corresponding to groups of unresolved transitions to 77Se and 17O. Extracted experimental cross sections showed remarkable agreement with theoretical calculations without the need for scaling factors, indicating that the employed nuclear structure and reaction models accurately capture the essential physics of the process. Furthermore, the primary transitions contributing to the cross section of each identified peak were determined.

Repetition serves as a fundamental element of musical organization. This research presents novel algorithms designed to detect musical phrases through the lens of repetition, which then combine to create sections, forming a two-tiered hierarchical framework. The automatically identified hierarchical repetition patterns uncover substantial relationships between structure and elements such as chord progressions, melody, and rhythm. Because different hierarchical levels interact in distinct ways, this provides evidence that structural hierarchy is crucial to music, extending beyond basic concepts of repetition or similarity. Consequently, our findings point toward new possibilities for music generation and evaluation.

Presence-absence data consists of binary vectors or matrices where ones signify presence at specific locations. Such data is common in studies of species geographical distributions, genetic profiles, and term occurrences within texts. Clustering these data types has numerous applications, including the identification of biotic elements, which are groups of species that frequently co-occur geographically. Various clustering techniques can be employed, including latent class mixture models assuming local independence, distance-based hierarchical clustering utilizing the Jaccard distance, and methods adapted for continuous data applied to a multidimensional scaling representation of distances. Because these approaches are conceptually distinct, theoretical comparisons are difficult. Consequently, their performance was evaluated through an extensive simulation study grounded in species distribution models. This work has been accepted for publication in the volume "Innovations in multivariate statistical modelling: navigating theoretical and multidisciplinary domains," edited by Ferreira, J., Bekker, A., Arashi, M., and Chen, D., as part of the Springer Emerging Topics in Statistics and Biostatistics series.

The study investigates the excitation of hydrogen ($1s-2s$) via electron impact, examining scenarios both with and without a laser field using the first Born approximation. It presents the angular dependence of the laser-assisted differential cross section (DCS) for atomic hydrogen across various incident electron kinetic energies. Employing the Darwin wave function as a semirelativistic representation of atomic hydrogen yields significant insights when the condition $z/c\ll1$ holds. Comparisons with non-relativistic theory and experimental data demonstrate strong agreement. It was noted that beyond 2700 eV—the threshold separating the two approaches—the non-relativistic theory fails to match the results closely and may deviate by several orders of magnitude in certain energy ranges. Furthermore, the sum rules established by Bunkin and Fedorov and by Kroll and Watson \cite{22} have been confirmed in both non-relativistic and relativistic regimes.

P-hacking involves researchers employing various tactics to boost the likelihood of obtaining statistically significant findings. This practice undermines the utility of hypothesis testing by artificially inflating the frequency of significant results beyond what would occur without genuine effects. Although widespread, current hypothesis testing theory fails to account for p-hacking, as standard critical values are calculated under the assumption that it does not exist. To resolve this, we develop a model of p-hacking to derive new critical values that maintain the desired frequency of significant outcomes even when researchers adapt their behavior to these standards. These robust critical values, which accommodate p-hacking, are consequently higher than traditional ones. Using evidence from social and medical sciences, we calibrated the model and discovered that the robust critical value for any test corresponds to the classical critical value at one-fifth of the original significance level—a type of Bonferroni correction. For example, in a one-sided $z$-test at the $5\%$ level, the robust critical value is $2.31$ rather than $1.65$, and for a two-sided test, it is $2.57$ instead of $1.96$.

Two-dimensional transition metal trichalcogenides (TMTCs) consist of covalently bonded metal-chalcogen layers separated by van der Waals gaps. Like transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), TMTCs frequently exhibit charge density waves (CDWs) and superconductivity; however, unlike TMDCs, the atomic chains within their crystal structure facilitate quasi-one-dimensional conduction. Specifically, ZrTe$_3$ displays a charge density wave below $T_{\textrm{CDW}}$ = 63 K and filamentary superconductivity below 2 K, both of which can be strengthened through pressure or chemical substitution. This study reveals that ZrTe$_3$ crystals contain mixed valence states of Zr$^{2+}$ and Zr$^{4+}$, a condition that diminishes upon doping in ZrTe$_{3-x}$Se$_x$ and Zr$_{1-y}$Hf$_y$Te$_3$. Superconductivity is boosted by disorder within the Te2-Te3 atomic chains, which are linked to CDW formation. Substituting Hf for Zr raises $T_{\textrm{CDW}}$ by maintaining the periodicity of the Te2-Te3 chains and increasing electron-phonon coupling. Conversely, weak electronic correlations observed in ZrTe$_{3-x}$Se$_x$ appear to be driven by lattice contraction.

We introduce a hybrid partitioned deep learning framework designed for the reduced-order modeling of fluid-structure interaction. By utilizing the discretized Navier-Stokes equations within an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian framework, we produce full-order flow snapshots and point cloud displacements to serve as target data for learning and inferring fluid-structure dynamics. This approach integrates two data-driven models for fluid and solid subdomains through deep learning-based reduced-order models (DL-ROMs). The framework features partitioned data-driven drivers for unsteady flow and moving point cloud displacements, with force information exchanged between the subdomain solvers at the fluid-structure interface. The first component employs a proper orthogonal decomposition-based recurrent neural network (POD-RNN) as a DL-ROM procedure to infer point clouds with moving interfaces, using POD basis modes to reduce dimensionality and evolve them temporally via RNNs. The second component utilizes a convolution-based recurrent autoencoder network (CRAN) as a self-supervised DL-ROM procedure to infer nonlinear flow dynamics at static Eulerian probes. These probes are introduced as spatially structured query nodes within the moving point cloud to resolve Lagrangian-to-Eulerian conflicts and facilitate the training of the CRAN driver. To establish these Eulerian probes, we develop a novel snapshot-field transfer and load recovery algorithm. We evaluate the proposed methodology's efficacy across various reduced velocities using a canonical fluid-structure interaction problem involving flow past a freely oscillating cylinder. The framework successfully tracks the interface description with acceptable accuracy and predicts nonlinear wake dynamics over the selected test data range.

Rare decays involving $B$, $D$, and $K$ mesons offer valuable insights into the Standard Model (SM), often possessing greater sensitivity to New Physics (NP) than more frequent decay modes. However, measuring these processes experimentally is difficult, and interpreting them theoretically demands a precise understanding of low-energy QCD within the non-perturbative (hadronic) domain. The diverse $b$, $c$, and $s$ decay channels enable various SM tests across different experimental environments, some of which may show correlated anomalies in New Physics models.

This study investigates the one-dimensional dynamics of identical discrete units that integrate the characteristics of Newtonian mechanical particles and cellular automata. It is demonstrated that the movement of a cluster of these combined discrete elements—the model's most basic observable entity—results in the Feynman chessboard model, whose continuous approximation yields the Dirac equation.

This paper investigates the exponential Diophantine equation $L_n + L_m = 3^a$ within the set of nonnegative integers $n, m,$ and $a$, where $(L_n)_{n\geq 0}$ denotes the Lucas sequence defined by $L_0 = 2, L_1 = 1$, and the recurrence relation $L_{n+2} = L_{n+1} + L_n$. The primary objective is to determine all instances where the sum of two Lucas numbers yields a power of three. The proof of our central result relies on lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms, properties of continued fractions, and a variation of the Baker-Davenport reduction method applied to Diophantine approximation.

This paper investigates resonant leptogenesis within a radiative seesaw framework, specifically focusing on a scenario involving two quasi-degenerate right-handed neutrinos. In this model, the required CP violation arises from the phases inherent in the neutrino mixing matrix. Our numerical analysis utilizes the best-fit values for three neutrino mixing angles and two mass-squared differences derived from current global data. We demonstrate the dependence of the predicted baryon asymmetry on both Dirac and Majorana CP phases. Furthermore, with specific mass parameter choices, the model favors a normal neutrino mass hierarchy to match the observed baryon asymmetry. Finally, we calculate the effective neutrino mass, pertinent to neutrinoless double beta decay, using these constrained CP phases.

This study examines a sensor-receiver link operating over a wireless channel subject to potential denial-of-service attacks from a jammer. We model this interaction as a zero-sum game involving a coordinator, which optimizes both transmission and estimation strategies, and the jammer. The analysis covers two scenarios based on the jammer's ability to sense the channel. When the jammer lacks sensing capabilities, we derive a saddle-point equilibrium for symmetric and unimodal probability density functions. Conversely, if the jammer can detect channel usage, we propose an efficient algorithm that cycles between Projected Gradient Ascent and the Convex-Concave Procedure to approximate First-order Nash-Equilibria. Numerical simulations indicate that, in specific instances, the jammer may choose to execute a denial-of-service attack aimed at deceiving the receiver, even when the sensor refrains from transmitting.

Excess astrometric noise (AEN), surpassing that attributed to parallax and proper motion, may indicate the orbital wobble of individual stars within binary systems. Consequently, combining X-ray selection with AEN analysis offers a robust method for identifying accreting binaries in extensive surveys. This study analyzes the Gaia EDR3 catalogue to find Galactic sources exhibiting significant AEN within the parameter ranges typical of known and candidate X-ray binaries (XRBs). Cross-matching this selection with the Chandra Source Catalogue yields a primary sample of approximately 6,500 X-ray sources showing notable AEN. These objects demonstrate an X-ray detection efficiency roughly 4.5 times higher than a control sample with low AEN. In colour-magnitude space, the primary sample deviates significantly from the main sequence compared to controls and contains a greater proportion of known binaries, variable stars, and young stellar objects. However, current Gaia pipeline AEN values often exceed theoretical expectations for individual XRBs based on known semi-major axes and system parameters. It is probable that other factors, such as attitude and modelling uncertainties alongside source variability, currently dominate the observed excess noise in these systems. Therefore, definitive characterization must await future Gaia releases, though the full X-ray matched catalogue is provided here to facilitate legacy follow-up observations.

When evaluating dynamical systems, nonlinearity must be considered. While modern computing power now allows analyses that were once too complex to run on standard hardware, specific applications like high-precision real-time simulation or uncertainty quantification still face significant computational hurdles. To address this, reduced-order modeling (ROM) techniques are essential for lowering the computational burden of nonlinear assessments. This study introduces a reduction strategy that utilizes an autoencoder to derive a latent space from output-only data. This latent space effectively approximates the system's nonlinear normal modes (NNMs) and functions as an invertible basis for reducing the nonlinear system. Furthermore, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are integrated within this reduced space to construct a nonlinear ROM capable of reproducing the full system's dynamic response to known inputs.

The primary objective of [1] was to examine specific sets of continuants that arise in practical applications and to determine their maximal and minimal values. The original work outlined four distinct approaches for locating these extrema: the method of basic substitutions (section 4.1), the method of quadratic irrationalities (section 4.2), the use of majorizing inequalities (section 4.3), and the method of unit variation (section 4.4). However, the original text was plagued by numerous typographical errors, rendering it difficult to read. The current work addresses these defects by correcting the errors and providing more detailed justifications for several of the original statements.

Optical techniques operating at terahertz and mid-infrared frequencies are becoming essential for investigating the nonlinear dynamics of collective modes within correlated many-body systems and their interaction with electromagnetic radiation. Recent studies have revealed unexpected optical behaviors in transient states generated by external driving forces, such as photo-induced edges in the reflectivity of cuprate superconductors, detected both above and below their equilibrium transition temperatures. Additionally, reflection coefficients exceeding unity have been recorded in other driven materials. This paper argues that these anomalous optical characteristics in photoexcited systems can be explained through the lens of Floquet systems, defined by periodically modulated parameters resulting from pump-induced oscillations of collective modes. We introduce a general phenomenological framework for calculating reflectivity in Floquet materials that incorporates the parametric generation of excitation pairs. Our analysis yields a universal phase diagram of drive-induced reflectivity features, highlighting a competition between driving forces and dissipation. To validate this general approach, we apply our formalism to two specific cases inspired by recent experimental data: a single plasmon band representing Josephson plasmons in layered superconductors, and a phonon-polariton system describing upper and lower polaritons in materials like insulating SiC. Finally, we show that our model accurately reproduces results from phonon-pump, terahertz-probe experiments on the high-temperature superconductor $\rm{YBa_2Cu_3O_{6.5}}$. Specifically, the model accounts for the emergence of a pump-induced edge at energies higher than the equilibrium Josephson plasmon edge, even when the pump pulse suppresses the interlayer Josephson coupling.

A positive monoid is defined as an additive submonoid within the nonnegative cone of the real line. Recent scholarly focus has centered on positive monoids composed of rational numbers, also termed Puiseux monoids, as well as those generated by geometric sequences. This survey aims to highlight recent developments in the study of positive monoids, offering extensive examples to demonstrate the intricate nature of their atomic and arithmetic properties.

Against the backdrop of gravitational collapse, we calculate the transition amplitudes for particle creation as seen by distant observers, accounting for both Hawking radiation and higher-derivative interactions. These amplitudes increase exponentially over time, reaching an order of unity when the collapsing matter is approximately one Planck length from the horizon. Consequently, the effective theory fails at the scrambling time, rendering its predictions for Hawking radiation invalid. Ultimately, physics at the Planck scale determines the outcome of black-hole evaporation.

Thirty-eight years after its discovery, the origin and destiny of the Leo ring—the most extensive extragalactic neutral cloud identified in the local Universe—remain a subject of debate. Researchers have proposed two competing explanations: the gas is either residual primordial material with minor metal contamination or enriched gas stripped away during a galaxy-galaxy collision. Utilizing MUSE on the VLT for optical integral field spectroscopy of three HI clumps within the ring that exhibit ultraviolet continuum emission, we detected ionized hydrogen for the first time and identified four star-forming nebulae powered by massive stars. Analysis of multiple metal emission lines ([OIII], [NII], [SII]) yielded reliable metallicity measurements, indicating values at or exceeding solar levels. Because the diffuse stellar sources are extremely faint, less than 3% of the observed heavy elements could have formed locally within the main body of the ring, and no more than 15% in the HI clump directed toward M96. These findings, combined with the chemical uniformity across the regions, strongly indicate that the ring's gas is not primordial; rather, it was pre-enriched in a galaxy disk before being stripped and sculpted by tidal forces, where it now sustains a sparse population of stars.

We introduce FiLex, a stochastic process designed to mathematically model lexicon entropy within deep learning-driven emergent language systems. By establishing a formal mathematical framework, FiLex enables the generation of precise, testable predictions. Our empirical validation across four distinct environments confirms that FiLex accurately predicts the relationship between hyperparameters—specifically training steps, lexicon size, learning rate, rollout buffer size, and Gumbel-Softmax temperature—and emergent language entropy in all 20 tested combinations. Additionally, our experiments highlight that varying environments exhibit diverse correlations between hyperparameters and entropy, underscoring the necessity for a model capable of delivering well-defined predictions at a high level of granularity.

Source extension reframes inverse problems in wave propagation into computationally manageable iterative approaches. The fundamental subproblem within these methods involves solving a linear inverse problem for the source term (the right-hand side of wave equation systems) by minimizing data misfit in a least-squares manner, while simultaneously applying physical constraints on the source through an additive quadratic penalty. A variation of the time reversal technique used in photoacoustic tomography offers an approximate solution that serves as a preconditioner for Krylov space iterations, enabling rapid convergence toward the solution of this subproblem. An acoustic 2D case study featuring surface-supported sources with a soft constraint enforcing point support demonstrates the efficacy of this preconditioning strategy.

The attributable fraction among the exposed (\textbf{AF}$_e$), also referred to as attributable risk or excess fraction among the exposed, represents the proportion of disease cases within an exposed group that could be prevented by removing the exposure. Gaining insight into \textbf{AF}$_e$ across various exposures is essential for directing public health strategies. Traditional inference methods for \textbf{AF}$_e$ typically assume no unmeasured confounding and remain vulnerable to hidden biases from unobserved variables. This paper introduces a novel method to mitigate sensitivity to such hidden bias when performing statistical inference on \textbf{AF}$_e$ by utilizing case description information, such as specific cancer subtypes. Since exposures may impact certain case types more significantly than others, we investigate how incorporating these details can lessen sensitivity to unmeasured confounding using asymptotic tools like design sensitivity, supported by simulation studies. We also account for the potential introduction of additional selection bias by including an extra sensitivity parameter. The proposed approach is demonstrated by re-analyzing the link between alcohol consumption and the risk of postmenopausal invasive breast cancer, utilizing case description data on hormone-sensitive versus insensitive subtypes from the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) Observational Study.

A recent study by Weidner et al. [2021] introduces a technique for deriving graph characteristics that predict the dynamic behavior of multivariate, discrete biochemical regulation models. Essentially, this approach relies solely on structural features of network interactions to identify the nodes most critical to automata network dynamics. However, the authors assert that analyzing the dynamics of large automata networks is "not even feasible." To prevent discouraging others from tackling this challenge, it is crucial to clarify that effective dynamical analysis of automata networks is indeed possible. Contrary to the article's suggestion, graph-based analysis of static features is not the exclusive analytical path for large-scale systems biology models of regulation and signaling, as scalable dynamical methods do exist.

We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for Alt's system to be represented by a continuous utility function, alongside a corresponding necessary and sufficient condition for that function to be concave. This concavity condition serves as an extension of Gossen's first law, offering a meaningful economic interpretation. In conjunction with these findings, we also derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Alt's utility function to be continuously differentiable.

Identifying attitudes within texts, referred to as stance detection, is crucial for systems designed to uncover false information online, whether it be unintentional misinformation or intentional disinformation. This task has been conceptualized in two primary ways: either as an integral part of fact-checking, rumor identification, and the verification of previously analyzed claims, or as a standalone objective. Although previous studies have compared stance detection with related fields like argumentation mining and sentiment analysis, no comprehensive survey has yet explored its connection to the detection of mis- and disinformation. This paper aims to fill that void by reviewing and analyzing current research focused on mis- and disinformation, while also highlighting key insights and future challenges in this domain.

This study presents findings from experiments evaluating data transmission and signal stability using two distinct wide-band multiplexing (MUX) schemes in point-to-point configurations. These schemes employed electromagnetic waves carrying Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) to operate effectively in noisy, real-world environments. Each radio link successfully transmitted two high-definition wide-band analog TV channels within the same frequency band, utilizing FM-carriers centered at 2.414 GHz with a 27 MHz bandwidth. The channels were encoded with different OAM modes while maintaining the same polarization state and operated continuously for five months during the "Globale-Digitale" world exhibition at ZKM in Karlsruhe, followed by an additional two months across various time slots over the subsequent four years, running 24 hours a day.
