For example, these agents can collaborate to answer queries like "Who achieved the longest javelin throw from the USA?" by utilizing text and table QA capabilities. Our findings indicate that black-box models fail to learn this task from scratch, achieving accuracy below 50% even when provided with each agent's knowledge and gold fact supervision. Conversely, models trained to communicate with agents surpass black-box performance, reaching 100% accuracy when given gold decomposition supervision. However, we demonstrate that mastering the art of solving complex tasks via agent communication remains a significant hurdle when no auxiliary supervision or data is available. We release CommaQA, including a compositional generalization test split, to foster further research in this area. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/allenai/commaqa.

The development of user simulators (USs) for reinforcement learning (RL) in task-oriented dialog systems (DSs) has attracted increasing attention, yet it continues to confront significant fundamental hurdles. First, it remains uncertain whether pretrained language models, such as GPT-2 based USs, can match the capabilities of recently advanced GPT-2 based DSs in design and interaction. Second, while effectively incorporating and tracking user goals is a crucial component of a US, creating a flexible, end-to-end trainable US capable of handling multi-domains remains a persistent challenge. To address these issues, this work introduces a generative user simulator (GUS) featuring a GPT-2 architecture and goal state tracking. We conducted extensive experiments on the MultiWOZ2.1 dataset, training various DSs via RL using the GUS, the traditional agenda-based user simulator (ABUS), and other ablation simulators for cross-model, corpus-based, and human evaluations. The GUS demonstrated superior performance across all three evaluation metrics.

An integer $n$ is classified as practical if every integer from 1 to $n$ can be written as a sum of distinct divisors of $n$. This paper investigates practical numbers that follow a specific polynomial structure. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition regarding coefficients $a$ and $b$ to ensure the existence of infinitely many practical numbers of the form $an+b$. Additionally, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for a quadratic polynomial to yield infinitely many practical numbers, which allows us to resolve the first part of a conjecture cited in [9]. Finally, we demonstrate that any integer of the form $8k+1$ can be expressed as the sum of a practical number and a perfect square. Conversely, we prove that for every $j \in \{0,\ldots,7\} \setminus \{1\}$, there exist infinitely many natural numbers of the form $8k+j$ that cannot be represented as the sum of a practical number and a square.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) offer a viable approach to creating programmable wireless transmission environments. Due to the vast quantity of controllable reflecting elements, RIS can achieve significant passive beamforming gains. Current research predominantly focuses on the modeling, design, performance analysis, and optimization of systems assisted by a single RIS. While some studies have examined multiple RISs serving individual users separately, the cooperation between multiple RISs remains underexplored. To address this gap, this paper investigates cooperative beamforming design for multi-RIS-assisted downlink communication systems. We begin by modeling the general channel from a base station to users, accounting for an arbitrary number of reflection links. Subsequently, we formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the sum rate for all users. However, analysis reveals that the problem is challenging to solve due to its non-convex nature and the interdependencies among decision variables. To resolve this effectively, we decompose the problem into three disjoint subproblems. By introducing suitable auxiliary variables, we derive closed-form expressions for the decision variables and propose a low-complexity cooperative beamforming algorithm. Simulation results validate the algorithm's effectiveness through comparisons with various baseline methods. Additionally, these findings demonstrate that distributing reflecting elements across multiple RISs yields superior sum rate performance compared to concentrating them on a single RIS.

We present Cohort Comfort Models, a novel framework designed to forecast how new occupants will perceive their thermal environment. By utilizing historical data from a reference group with shared underlying preferences, this model predicts the thermal responses of new individuals. The framework effectively integrates available background information—including physical attributes, one-time onboarding surveys (such as the Satisfaction with Life Scale, Highly Sensitive Person Scale, and the Big Five personality traits)—alongside paired physiological and environmental sensor measurements with thermal preference data. We validated our approach using two public datasets featuring longitudinal records from 55 participants, encompassing over 6,000 individual thermal comfort surveys. Our results indicate that while incorporating background information yields minimal improvement in prediction performance compared to models with no historical data, utilizing Cohort Comfort Models significantly enhances accuracy for many users. Specifically, for half and one-third of the occupants in each dataset, the model improved thermal preference prediction by 8% and 5% on average, respectively, and reached increases of up to 36% and 46% for certain individuals, outperforming general-purpose models trained on the entire population. Designed to be data and site-agnostic, the framework's components can be easily adapted to match specific data availability in different buildings and for various occupants. Ultimately, Cohort Comfort Models represent a significant step toward personalization, enabling tailored predictions without the necessity of developing a unique model for every new occupant.

Sharpened dimensionality reduction (SDR), a recent multidimensional projection technique designed to address challenges in exploring and visualizing high-dimensional data, has been successfully applied to diverse real-world datasets, including human activity and astronomical data. However, manually labeling samples in these generated projections remains costly. To mitigate this, we propose integrating clustering algorithms—specifically k-means, Hierarchical Clustering, DBSCAN, and Spectral Clustering—to facilitate the labeling of 2D projections from high-dimensional data. Our pipeline, combining SDR with these clustering methods, was evaluated on various synthetic and real-world datasets, featuring two public human activity datasets derived from smartphone accelerometer and gyroscope recordings. We utilized clustering to assess the visual separability of SDR projections both qualitatively and quantitatively. Our findings indicate that applying clustering to SDR results produces superior labeling outcomes compared to clustering standard dimensionality reduction techniques, with k-means emerging as the optimal choice for SDR due to its high accuracy, ease of use, and computational scalability.

The global education system underwent a dramatic transformation during the COVID-19 pandemic, necessitating an immediate transition to distance learning. Physics instruction, including lectures, tutorials, and lab sessions, was rapidly converted to online formats, creating a blend of synchronous, asynchronous, and hybrid learning activities. To understand students' perceptions of this abrupt shift, we administered a survey to 578 physics students across five universities in Germany, Austria, and Croatia. This study examines the adaptation of problem-solving sessions (recitations) and laboratories, evaluates student judgments regarding various course formats, and assesses their perceived utility and effectiveness. These findings are analyzed in relation to self-efficacy ratings, behavioral indicators such as self-regulated learning skills, and demographic factors. A companion paper will address online physics lectures and compare simultaneous versus asynchronous teaching methods. Our results indicate that strong communication skills and self-organization abilities are positively linked to perceived learning outcomes. Additionally, the duration of prior study significantly influenced perceived overall achievement, the acquisition of experimental skills in labs, and the assessment of recitation effectiveness; specifically, first-year students consistently scored lower than more advanced peers. Regarding physics laboratories, collecting real data was identified as essential for developing experimental skills and reinforcing content, while for recitations, submitting personal solutions for feedback correlated with higher perceived effectiveness. We conclude with implications for the future design of online physics classes.

For a Galois extension $L/K$, the regular subgroup defining an induced Hopf Galois structure is formed by the direct product of the regular groups associated with the inducing subextensions. This text details the corresponding Hopf algebra and action for such induced structures, demonstrating that they result from the tensor product of the objects in the inducing subextensions. Furthermore, to address the associated orders, we introduce a general technique for calculating bases and free generators using matrices derived from the representation theory of Hopf modules. Specifically, when dealing with an induced Hopf Galois structure where the inducing subextensions are arithmetically disjoint, this method enables the decomposition of the associated order.

We contend that the majority of scientific and technological advancements from the past two centuries depend heavily on modern physics concepts originating in the early 20th century. This dependence is so fundamental that efforts to improve science and technology literacy fail without these concepts in physics curricula. Although some literature has noted that modern topics are often overlooked in textbooks \cite{cht}, we confirm this assertion and further argue that omitting discussions on the limitations of classical concepts and the necessity for paradigm shifts in physics education fosters serious misconceptions and presents a distorted view of science.

The $Y$--$M$ relation, linking the integrated thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich ($tSZ$) $y$-decrement to halo mass, offers a potential means to test galaxy formation models, provided that both theoretical and observational systematics are adequately addressed. We examine this relation within the SIMBA and IllustrisTNG-100 cosmological hydrodynamic simulations, specifically quantifying the impacts of feedback mechanisms, line-of-sight projection, and beam convolution. Our findings indicate that AGN jet feedback in SIMBA causes significant departures from self-similar predictions for the $Y$--$M$ relation, particularly for halos with $M_{500}<10^{13}M_{\odot}$. In SIMBA, this deviation stems from reduced in-halo $y$ contributions resulting from lower baryon fractions within the halos. The IllustrisTNG results, lacking these specific jet effects, align more closely with a SIMBA simulation without jets. While line-of-sight projections slightly mitigate these model discrepancies, the differences remain substantial, especially at group and lower halo masses. Conversely, beam smearing at $\textit{Planck}$ resolution renders the models indistinguishable, causing both to agree well with $\textit{Planck}$ observations down to the lowest probed masses. We demonstrate that the anticipated arcminute resolution of upcoming facilities would preserve the distinctions between model predictions, thereby offering robust constraints on AGN feedback.

We introduce a new method for storing three-nucleon (3N) interaction matrix elements, which are crucial for the normal-ordered two-body approximation widely used in ab initio nuclear calculations. This approach reduces memory requirements by roughly two orders of magnitude, enabling the generation of 3N matrix elements with a standard truncation of $E_{\rm 3max}=28$, significantly surpassing the previous ceiling of 18. We show that this level of truncation is adequate to converge the ground-state energy of $^{132}$Sn within a few MeV regarding the $E_{\rm 3max}$ cutoff. Furthermore, we analyze asymptotic convergence trends and extrapolate results to the un-truncated limit. We also examine the effects of truncations applied during the similarity renormalization group evolution of free-space 3N interactions. Our findings indicate that for relative angular momentum blocks with $J_{\rm rel}>9/2$, the contribution to the ground-state energy is primarily a basis-truncation artifact that disappears in the large-space limit; thus, these computationally intensive components can be safely ignored. For the two nuclear interaction sets utilized, the calculated binding energy of $^{132}$Sn matches experimental data within theoretical uncertainties. This study facilitates converged ab initio calculations for heavy nuclei.

Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $V(G)$ and edge set $E(G)$, where $d(u,w)$ represents the length of a shortest path between vertices $u$ and $w$. For any vertex $v \in V(G)$ and edge $e=xy \in E(G)$, define $d(e,v)$ as $\min\{d(x,v), d(y,v)\}$. For distinct edges $e_1, e_2 \in E(G)$, let $R\{e_1,e_2\} = \{z \in V(G) : d(z,e_1) \neq d(z,e_2)\}$. Kelenc et al. [Discrete Appl. Math. 251 (2018) 204-220] defined the edge dimension of a graph: a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ is an edge resolving set if $|S \cap R\{e_1,e_2\}| \ge 1$ for every pair of distinct edges $e_1, e_2 \in E(G)$. The edge dimension, denoted $edim(G)$, is the minimum size of such a set.

Given a real-valued function $g$ on $V(G)$ and a subset $U \subseteq V(G)$, let $g(U) = \sum_{s \in U} g(s)$. A function $g: V(G) \to [0,1]$ is an edge resolving function if $g(R\{e_1,e_2\}) \ge 1$ for all distinct $e_1, e_2 \in E(G)$. The fractional edge dimension, $edim_f(G)$, is the minimum value of $g(V(G))$ over all edge resolving functions. Note that $edim_f(G)$ coincides with $edim(G)$ if the range of the function is restricted to $\{0,1\}$.

This paper introduces and investigates the fractional edge dimension, deriving general results regarding edge dimension. We demonstrate that non-isomorphic graphs can share the same vertex set and identical edge metric coordinates. Furthermore, we construct graphs $G$ and $H$ with $H \subset G$ such that the differences $edim(H)-edim(G)$ and $edim_f(H)-edim_f(G)$ can be arbitrarily large. We prove that any graph $G$ with $edim(G)=2$ cannot contain $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$ as subgraphs, yet we also provide a non-planar graph $H$ with $edim(H)=2$. For any connected graph $G$ of order $n \ge 3$, it holds that $1 \le edim_f(G) \le \frac{n}{2}$; we characterize graphs where $edim_f(G)=1$ and analyze specific graph classes where $edim_f(G)=\frac{n}{2}$. Finally, we determine the fractional edge dimension for several graph classes.

This study offers a microscopic investigation into dissipation during fission dynamical evolutions using the time-dependent Hartree-Fock+BCS approach, analyzing both energy and pairing dependencies. Friction coefficients and dissipation energies were derived by mapping the symmetric fission of $^{258}$Fm onto a classical equation of motion, with dynamical potentials obtained through density-constrained calculations. The resulting friction coefficients exhibit a pronounced dependence on deformation and align, on average, with those used in statistical models. Dissipation is observed to increase with higher initial excitation energies or reduced pairing. Additionally, the research highlights the significant contribution of post-scission dissipation. These identified characteristics of dissipation are expected to aid in calibrating various fission models.

Temporal data refers to information captured within a temporal framework. This contextual structure offers essential elements for data exploration and serves as the foundation for interactive plotting features. In multivariate time series, one anticipates temporal dependencies, long-term and seasonal patterns, and cross-correlations, whereas longitudinal data also exhibits both within-subject and between-subject dependencies. Although time series and longitudinal data require distinct analytical approaches, they are frequently visualized using similar methods. We present a taxonomy of plot interactions designed to facilitate the exploration of temporal components in these datasets, detailing how to construct such interactions through data transformations. Furthermore, since temporal data often coexists with other data types, we explain how to connect temporal plots with alternative visualizations. These concepts are organized into a data pipeline for temporal analysis and implemented within the R package `cranvas`. This package offers a variety of interactive graphics that can be combined to either explore data or diagnose model fit.

Recent research has identified a label alignment property within supervised learning, noting that the dataset's label vector predominantly lies within the span of the top few singular vectors of the data matrix. Drawing inspiration from this finding, we propose a regularization technique for unsupervised domain adaptation. Unlike conventional domain adaptation approaches that regularize representation learning, our method regularizes the classifier to ensure target domain predictions partially align with the top singular vectors of the target domain's unsupervised data matrix. In the context of linear regression, we provide theoretical justification for the label alignment property and establish the optimality of our regularization solution by bounding its distance to the optimal solution. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively addresses label shift problems where traditional domain adaptation methods typically fail. Furthermore, we observe modest improvements over baseline domain adaptation techniques on standard MNIST-USPS adaptation tasks and cross-lingual sentiment analysis benchmarks.

We provide a summary of significant findings from a recent series dedicated to non-Hermitian quantum field theories, where we methodically adjust fundamental symmetries. Our focus centers on the relationship between the continuous symmetry group—transitioned from global to local, Abelian to non-Abelian, and rank one to generic rank N—and discrete anti-linear modified CPT-symmetries. These modified symmetries ensure a real mass spectrum within specific parameter ranges. We examine the extension of Goldstone's theorem and the Higgs mechanism, showing that they function conventionally under CPT-symmetric conditions but require technical modifications at standard exceptional points in the mass spectrum. Furthermore, they completely fail at zero exceptional points and within the broken CPT-symmetric regime. In the complete non-Hermitian non-Abelian gauge theory, we identify t'Hooft-Polyakov monopoles using a fourfold Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield (BPS) limit. We further explore this limit across other non-Hermitian field theories in 1+1 dimensions featuring complex super-exponential and inverse hyperbolic kink/anti-kink solutions, as well as 3+1 dimensional Skyrme models, where we discover novel complex solutions characterized by real energies thanks to various CPT-symmetry types.

Systematic errors in time-delay cosmography most frequently stem from inaccuracies in the lens mass distribution model, which can potentially skew the $H_0$ value. To address this, a Bayesian hierarchical framework has been developed that integrates lens systems with kinematic data to constrain mass profile shapes at a population level. While previously validated on a limited set of hydro-simulation galaxies, this study aims to test the framework against a broader collection of lenses resembling observed systems and to verify its ability to merge two distinct populations: those with time delays and those without, the latter exhibiting systematically different image radii. We achieve this by generating analytic lens mass distributions (baryons plus dark matter) and fitting the resulting mock images with standard power-law models, while also emulating corresponding kinematic data. Applying this hierarchical approach to an ensemble of time-delay lenses corrects the $H_0$ bias linked to model selection, yielding results within $1.5\sigma$ of the fiducial value. Furthermore, combining this ensemble with a set of non-time-delay lenses—characterized by lower source redshifts and smaller image radii relative to their effective radii—allows the framework to account for these differences. This combined approach recovers an $H_0$ value that is both more precise ($\sim2\%$ uncertainty) and more accurate ($0.7\%$ median offset) than using time-delay lenses alone. These findings confirm that non-time-delay lenses provide significant constraining power for determining $H_0$ through kinematic constraints, provided they belong to the same global population as the time-delay set.

We explore the implications of time reversal symmetry for the thermoelectric effect within nonequilibrium coherent quantum transport. By deriving from a quantum formulation of the fluctuation theorem, we demonstrate universal connections between the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients in general mesoscopic systems featuring Coulomb interactions, even under nonlinear conditions. This extended Kelvin-Onsager relation allows researchers to infer properties of heat current, such as the nonlinear Peltier coefficient—which is challenging to measure in standard experimental configurations—solely through the measurement of electric current.

We introduce a technique for acquiring neural representations of flow maps derived from time-varying vector field data. Flow maps are fundamental to flow visualization, serving as the basis for various methods such as pathline and streakline integral curve computations, as well as the identification of separation and attraction structures. However, the numerical integration required to compute these maps often creates bottlenecks that hinder their application in interactive visualization contexts. To address this, our work proposes neural representations of flow maps that are both computationally efficient and scalable in terms of optimization costs and data needs. A pivotal element of our approach is framing representation learning through a self-consistency criterion applied to flow map derivatives, which removes the necessity for flow map samples and numerical integration entirely. This is achieved via a specialized neural network architecture for flow maps paired with an optimization strategy that requires only the time-varying vector field, encoded as instantaneous velocity, for training. We demonstrate that our method surpasses prior approaches in accuracy and efficiency across diverse 2D and 3D time-varying vector fields, and we illustrate how our neural flow map representations enhance unsteady flow visualization techniques, including streaklines and the finite-time Lyapunov exponent.

The rise of large pretrained models has allowed language models to outperform earlier static word representation techniques on standard NLP tasks, such as language modeling and question answering. Combining these models with a retriever to fetch relevant documents as explicit supporting knowledge offers a more interpretable approach to solving NLP problems, as it injects information directly rather than embedding it within the model's parameters. Despite recent advancements, our analysis indicates that retriever-augmented language models still struggle to reason effectively over retrieved documents. This paper evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of various models in this category—including REALM, kNN-LM, FiD, ATLAS, and Flan-T5—regarding their ability to reason about selected documents across different tasks. Specifically, we investigate the reasoning failures of each model and examine how these shortcomings originate from both the retriever component and the underlying language model.

The vast amount of information accessible to the general public makes it difficult to isolate meaningful and reliable content. Trustworthiness and the sheer number of news sources present the primary obstacles in identifying authoritative figures. Furthermore, the failure of news providers to disseminate quality content on social media creates a void that young people struggle to fill with trustworthy information. This article introduces an automated system designed to extract key news stories and republish them in novel formats across social media networks.

Calculating global radial basis function (RBF) approximations involves solving a linear system that can become ill-conditioned depending on the selected RBF parameters. This study investigates the stability and accuracy of Gaussian RBF methods across all scaling regimes of the shape parameter. The approach employs discrete least squares with function samples on a bounded domain, utilizing RBF centers both within and outside the domain to form a rectangular linear system. For one-dimensional cases, we demonstrate that linearly scaling the shape parameter with the degrees of freedom is optimal, maintaining constant overlap between neighboring RBFs regardless of their quantity, and we suggest an explicit value for the proportionality constant. Numerical results confirm that highly accurate approximations for smooth functions on bounded domains in multiple dimensions are achievable using linear scaling relative to the degrees of freedom per dimension. Furthermore, we extend the least squares framework to a collocation-based method for solving elliptic boundary value problems, showing that combining external centers, oversampling, and optimal scaling can yield accuracy near machine precision, even when addressing highly ill-conditioned linear systems.

Designed as an introductory resource for undergraduates and novice graduate students, this work offers a pedagogical overview of one-dimensional topological phases, with a specific focus on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. We explore key concepts such as entanglement—analyzed via both correlator and von-Neumann density-matrix methods—as well as geometric phases, polarization, transport signatures, and the impact of electron-electron interactions. Accompanied by accessible numerical experiments whose code is available at $\href{https://github.com/hnoend/SSH_codes}{codes}$, our goal is to demonstrate how simulating quantum electronics with topological toy models serves as a vital repository for uncovering profound physical insights.

The Skolem Problem investigates whether a linear recurrence sequence $(u_n)$ contains a zero term at some index $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This paper examines a specific variant of this problem: given an additional natural number $c$, we determine if there exists an index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ of the form $n=lp^k$, where $k,l \leq c$ and $p$ is any prime, such that $u_n=0$.

Point clouds are a prevalent method for representing and storing three-dimensional geometric information. While numerous approaches have been developed for point cloud processing, techniques like PointNet and FoldingNet have demonstrated significant potential for tasks such as 3D shape classification and segmentation. This study introduces a tree-structured autoencoder framework that leverages hierarchical data via graph convolution to create robust point cloud embeddings. Multiple experiments were conducted to evaluate the quality of these embeddings, with t-SNE visualizations employed to underscore the model's capacity to differentiate between object classes. Furthermore, the framework's utility is demonstrated in applications including 3D point cloud completion and single-image-based 3D reconstruction.

Rosetta serves as a scientific platform designed for resource-heavy, interactive data analysis by executing user tasks within software containers. It operates on a unique architecture that treats user tasks as microservices—autonomous, self-contained units—enabling full support for custom software packages, libraries, and environments. This includes both standard analysis environments like Jupyter Notebooks and complete remote desktop applications with graphical user interfaces. Built upon Open Container Initiative standards, Rosetta ensures safe, efficient, and reproducible code execution. It is compatible with various container engines and runtimes while seamlessly integrating with multiple workload management systems, allowing containerized workloads to run across diverse computing resources. Although originally developed for astronomy and astrophysics, Rosetta is versatile enough to support virtually any science or technology field requiring resource-intensive, interactive data analysis.

Neutron powder diffraction has been used to study the ground-state magnetic configurations of Eu$^{2+}$ spins in the newly identified RbEu(Fe$_{1-x}$Ni$_{x}$)$_{4}$As$_{4}$ superconductors. The results indicate that increasing Ni doping suppresses superconductivity and reduces the magnetic propagation vector of the Eu sublattice, which reflects a smaller rotation angle between magnetic moments in adjacent Eu layers. Both the ferromagnetic superconductor RbEu(Fe$_{0.95}$Ni$_{0.05}$)$_{4}$As$_{4}$ and the superconducting ferromagnet RbEu(Fe$_{0.93}$Ni$_{0.07}$)$_{4}$As$_{4}$ exhibit ferromagnetic Eu layers that are helically modulated along the $\mathit{c}$ axis with an incommensurate propagation vector. This helical arrangement evolves into a purely collinear ferromagnetic structure in the non-superconducting RbEu(Fe$_{0.91}$Ni$_{0.09}$)$_{4}$As$_{4}$, where all Eu$^{2+}$ spins align along the tetragonal (1 1 0) direction. First-principles calculations corroborate this transition from helical to collinear ferromagnetic order as Ni concentration rises. Furthermore, the changes in the rotation angle between neighboring Eu$^{2+}$ layers are effectively explained by variations in magnetic exchange couplings driven by the indirect Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction.

This study establishes the local-in-time existence and uniqueness of solutions to the Degasperis-Procesi equation within the space $B^1_{\infty,1}(\R)$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the data-to-solution mapping for this equation is continuous, yet lacks uniform continuity in $B^1_{\infty,1}$.

We introduce a high-precision radial velocity (RV) survey covering 719 FGKM stars, which contain 164 confirmed exoplanets alongside 14 newly identified or revised exoplanets and substellar companions. This catalog refines the orbital parameters of existing exoplanets and long-period candidates, extending observational baselines for some by decades beyond their initial detection. The newly discovered planets span warm sub-Neptunes and super-Earths to cold gas giants. We detail the sample selection criteria and present over 100,000 RV measurements obtained using the Keck-HIRES, APF-Levy, and Lick-Hamilton spectrographs. Additionally, we unveil RVSearch, the novel RV search pipeline employed to create this catalog, which is now publicly available as an open-source Python package. This work serves as the inaugural study in a planned series aimed at measuring exoplanet occurrence rates and comparing populations, including investigations into giant planet occurrence beyond the water ice line and eccentricity distributions to probe formation mechanisms. All radial velocities and associated data utilized in this catalog have been made public.

Aguilera, Gafni, and Lamport addressed the Mailbox Problem in their 2010 Distributed Computing paper by presenting an algorithm utilizing two flag registers, each holding 14 values. They posed the question of whether an algorithm with smaller flag values exists. We affirmatively answer this by introducing a mailbox algorithm that employs two flag registers containing only 6 and 4 values, respectively.

Driven by evolving energy sector trends like renewable integration and vehicle electrification, smart grids have become increasingly vital to the electric power industry. A core component of smart grids is the high-speed, secure, and reliable data network that facilitates information flow, enabling the intelligent and effective management of complex power systems. Unlike traditional grids that rely on one-way communication, smart grids operate using bidirectional data exchange. Because communication needs and optimal techniques vary across different environments and scenarios, this paper offers a comprehensive and current survey of communication technologies in smart grids. It covers communication requirements, physical layer technologies, network architectures, and existing research challenges, aiming to assist readers in identifying future research opportunities in smart grid communications.

Vertical Axis Wind Turbine (VAWT) arrays can generate more power per unit of land area than Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine (HAWT) farms, primarily due to the beneficial synergy between closely spaced turbines. To maximize energy output through reliable array design, theoretical wake models must accurately capture driving wake dynamics. VAWTs produce highly complex wakes governed by two length scales—the rotor diameter and height—which define a rectangular cross-section with unique expansion rates. This paper introduces analytical VAWT wake models that account for asymmetric wake expansion using both top-hat and Gaussian velocity deficit distributions. The proposed analytical Gaussian model improves initial wake expansion predictions, setting the wake width ($\varepsilon$) behind the rotor to $(\beta/4 \pi)^{1/2}$, where $\beta$ represents the ratio of initial wake area to the turbine's frontal area; this resolves limitations in earlier models that underestimated the wake onset area. Velocity deficit predictions were validated through numerical benchmarks involving a single turbine and an array of four in-line VAWTs. Comparisons against field data and large-eddy simulations demonstrate that the models accurately represent mean wake distributions, maximum velocity deficits, and momentum thickness, with the Gaussian model delivering the superior results. These models are expected to enhance the design of VAWT arrays and accelerate the adoption of this technology.

Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is extensively employed in numerous digital communication systems because of its benefits, including high bit rates, robust resistance to multipath interference, and superior spectral efficiency; however, it is hindered by a high Peak-to-Average Power Ratio (PAPR) in the transmitted signal. Addressing PAPR reduction is crucial for preventing signal degradation within OFDM frameworks. As the PAPR challenge remains a prominent focus of research, this paper introduces and mathematically analyzes several techniques, listing their respective advantages and disadvantages to give readers a comprehensive view of the current state of the PAPR problem.

The neutron and proton densities for the doubly-closed shell nuclei ⁴⁰Ca, ⁴⁸Ca, and ²⁰⁸Pb were investigated using a Hartree-Fock framework with the SAMi, SAMi-J27, and SAMi-T energy density functionals. Additionally, ground state correlations (GSC) driven by isoscalar and isovector phonons were assessed via second-order perturbation theory combined with a self-consistent random phase approximation (RPA). Results indicate that GSC reduces the interior region of the ground state densities, aligning with experimental observations. Conversely, GSC increases the neutron skin thickness in ⁴⁸Ca and ²⁰⁸Pb. The impact of GSC on total binding energy was further examined using the quasi-boson approximation, revealing that the tensor interaction has a negligible effect on both density distributions and binding energies.

This work presents a representation of polymer self-consistent field theory, analogous to quantum density functional theory, utilizing non-orthogonal basis sets. It details molecular integrals and self-consistent equations for spherically symmetric systems employing Gaussian basis functions, subsequently calculating binding energies and radial electron densities for neutral atoms ranging from hydrogen to krypton. The study incorporates an exact electron self-interaction correction and enforces the Pauli-exclusion principle by applying concepts of polymer excluded-volume. Specifically, atoms from hydrogen to neon are further analyzed without certain approximations that allow for error cancellation. For both scenarios, electron correlations are omitted to maintain simplicity, with results compared against Hartree-Fock theory. The paper discusses the implications of both the approximate and exact forms of the Pauli-exclusion potential and analyzes the Pauli model using scaling theory for uniform electron density, demonstrating the recovery of the correct Thomas-Fermi quantum kinetic energy and Dirac exchange correction forms.

This paper outlines ongoing research into heat spreader properties and their relevance to architectural studies. Specifically, we performed two experiments to quantify thermal distribution across the spreader's surface during standard operation. The first utilized T-type thermocouples to measure temperature variations at different locations, revealing an average differential of approximately 6 degrees Celsius. The second experiment attempted to capture temperature gradients using an infrared camera but yielded inconclusive results due to practical limitations, primarily the spreader's low emissivity. We conclude that accurate modeling of the spreader requires detailed finite element simulations. Furthermore, we present a method for precisely measuring the heat spreader's thermal conductivity to facilitate the calculation of steady-state temperature distributions.

This research examines an energy market featuring competing producers seeking to maximize profits by supplying energy across various markets. The market structure is represented as a graph modeling a constrained power network, where nodes denote markets and edges represent physical transmission lines with finite capacities. Producers engage in a networked Cournot game alongside a centralized entity, the market maker, which facilitates trade between geographically distinct markets via the power network while optimizing a specific welfare function. We initially establish a general theorem linking the market maker's optimal actions to the capacity constraints of the power network. Under mild assumptions, we analyze the existence and uniqueness of Nash equilibria and utilize our general result to demonstrate a connection between power network capacity bottlenecks and the emergence of price disparities between markets separated by saturated lines, a phenomenon frequently observed in actual power grids.

Ram pressure stripping (RPS) is a critical mechanism in galaxy evolution that rapidly expels the interstellar medium (ISM). While earlier studies often simplified the ISM as a single phase or lacked the resolution to model its full multiphase nature, this work utilizes the TIGRESS framework to introduce a self-consistent, inflowing hot intracluster medium (ICM) within a local patch of star-forming galactic disks. Our simulations demonstrate that RPS operates not only through the direct acceleration of the ISM by ICM ram pressure but also via mixing-driven momentum transfer, which involves substantial phase transitions and radiative cooling. In this process, the hot ICM penetrates the porous, low-density channels of the multiphase ISM, fragmenting the cool gas and generating mixing layers. Momentum is transferred through these layers as the ICM populates intermediate-temperature gas and dissipates thermal energy. Consequently, the mixed gas extends beyond the galactic disk, forming stripped tails that cool unless the ICM flux is sufficiently high to delay cooling until the gas escapes the simulation domain. The mixing-driven mechanism predicts an anti-correlation between outflow velocity and the gas metallicity of the stripped ISM, as greater mixing accelerates the ISM. Furthermore, while ICM ram pressure compresses the ISM disks and boosts star formation rates by up to 50% relative to models without ICM, star formation is ultimately quenched within approximately 100 Myr once the ICM ram pressure exceeds the disk's anchoring pressure.

This paper investigates the conditions under which a product of ideals results in a Golod ring. We demonstrate that in a $3$-dimensional regular local ring (or polynomial ring in three variables) $(R, \mathfrak{m})$, the product $I\mathfrak{m}$ yields a Golod ring for every proper ideal $I \subset R$. Furthermore, we establish that non-Golod ideal products are common; specifically, for any proper ideal with grade at least $4$, there exists an ideal $J \subseteq I$ such that $IJ$ is not Golod. Finally, we prove that if $I$ is a proper ideal in a $3$-dimensional regular local ring and $\mathfrak{a} \subseteq I$ is a complete intersection, then $\mathfrak{a}I$ is Golod.

We introduce a factorization method for numbers utilizing two interacting bosonic atoms within a central potential, where the single-particle spectrum exhibits a logarithmic dependence on the radial quantum numbers of zero-angular-momentum states. Initially prepared in the ground state, the bosons are driven by a sinusoidally time-varying interaction into a state defined by quantum numbers that correspond to the factors of a number encoded in the perturbation's frequency. Additionally, we examine the complete single-particle spectrum and address limitations arising from decoherence.

Captioning involves generating a natural language sentence that describes the fine-grained differences between two similar images. In this task, viewpoint shifts are the most common distractors, as they alter object scale and position, often overshadowing genuine changes. This paper introduces the Relation-embedded Representation Reconstruction Network (R³Net) to effectively separate real changes from significant amounts of clutter and irrelevant variations. First, a relation-embedded module is developed to identify potential changed objects within cluttered scenes. Subsequently, a representation reconstruction module (RRM) is designed to learn reconstruction representations and model differences based on semantic similarities at corresponding locations in both images. Additionally, a syntactic skeleton predictor (SSP) is incorporated to strengthen the interaction between change localization and caption generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on two public datasets.

Krylov subspace methods serve as a fundamental component of numerical simulation software, yet efficiently leveraging modern hardware remains a significant challenge in their development. This study presents Krylov subspace methods designed to solve linear systems with multiple right-hand sides, specifically optimized for high-performance computing environments. We examine an innovative block Krylov framework that balances computational and data-transfer costs to align with hardware capabilities. Utilizing this framework, we reformulate standard Krylov methods. For the CG and BiCGStab algorithms, we propose a new stabilization technique as an alternative to deflation, which preserves the block size to facilitate a simpler and more efficient implementation. Additionally, we enhance these methods for distributed memory systems by reducing communication overhead. Regarding the CG method, we investigate strategies to overlap communication with computation and offer multiple variants distinguished by their communication characteristics. We also introduce optimizations for the GMRes orthogonalization process, including a pipelined Gram-Schmidt variant that overlaps global communication with inner product calculations, and a novel orthonormalization method based on the TSQR algorithm, which offers both communication optimality and stability. Finally, we provide test results demonstrating the superior performance of all optimized methods in a distributed setting.

This study examines the ground-state phase diagram of the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg-$\Gamma$ model on a honeycomb lattice using dimer series expansion and exact diagonalization. We analyze how interaction anisotropy influences the system, which transitions between isolated dimer and spin-chain regimes by adjusting coupling constants. In the spin-chain limit, three distinct states emerge: a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid and two magnetically long-range-ordered phases. While infinitesimal interchain interactions drive all three into two-dimensional long-range order, an exception occurs when the Heisenberg interaction is significantly weaker than the off-diagonal symmetric ($\Gamma$) interaction. Beginning from the isolated dimer limit, a triplet dimer phase persists across a large portion of the phase diagram—specifically where Heisenberg and $\Gamma$ interactions are ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic, respectively—until the system becomes isotropically interacting. Conversely, if these conditions are not met, a transition to a magnetically ordered phase precedes isotropy. These findings suggest that the quantum spin liquid proposed in the $\Gamma$ model (Catuneanu et al., npj Quantum Mater. 3, 23 (2018)) is unstable under interaction anisotropy.

To comply with recent privacy regulations such as the GDPR and CCPA, online websites employ cookie notices to obtain user consent. Previous research indicates that these notices often utilize dark patterns to coerce users into selections that favor the website, thereby compromising privacy. This study introduces CookieEnforcer, a novel system designed to automatically detect cookie notices and determine the specific options necessary to disable all non-essential cookies. The system first employs an automated detector that identifies notices by analyzing the rendering patterns of HTML elements. Subsequently, CookieEnforcer analyzes these notices and predicts the required actions to opt out of unnecessary cookies by framing the challenge as a sequence-to-sequence task, where the input is a machine-readable notice and the output is the sequence of clicks needed. An end-to-end accuracy evaluation demonstrates that CookieEnforcer successfully generates the required steps in 91% of cases. Furthermore, a user study reveals that the system significantly reduces the effort required from users. Finally, the system was applied to analyze the top 5,000 websites from the Tranco list (accessed from both the US and the UK) to draw large-scale comparisons and observations.

The dynamical interplay between minor bodies (such as comets and asteroids) and planets is fundamental to the formation and evolution of planetary systems, leading to the creation of structures like the Oort cloud and the Kuiper belt. Specifically, collisions between these minor bodies and planets can significantly alter a planet's internal development and orbital trajectory. This paper introduces an analytical framework to calculate the impact timescale of a minor body striking a planet across various geometric configurations. By benchmarking this formulation against extensive N-body simulations and existing analytical collision timescale methods within the solar system, we validated its accuracy. As a demonstration, we applied the method to estimate the collision rate of minor bodies randomly distributed around a Jupiter-like planet, simulating a Kuiper belt-like disk. Our results demonstrate strong agreement with numerical simulations, confirming that this analytical approach offers a concise and reliable alternative to computationally intensive numerical calculations.

The production of a $\mathrm{J/}\psi$ vector meson via coherent photonuclear processes at the LHC has been calculated using two distinct sets of solutions to the impact-parameter dependent Balitsky-Kovchegov equation. The nuclear dipole scattering amplitudes were derived either ($i$) by applying a Glauber-Gribov prescription to solutions for proton targets or ($ii$) from solutions initialized with nuclear conditions. These methods yield differing cross-section predictions, which have been contrasted against existing data from ultra-peripheral collisions at the LHC; the second approach appears to align more closely with current measurements. Future LHC datasets are expected to possess sufficient precision to definitively determine which of the two theoretical frameworks is correct.

The energy sustainability of Proof-of-Work blockchains is a subject of intense debate, driven by the mining process required to validate crypto-asset transactions. Mining involves solving cryptographic puzzles for rewards, and as the number of miners increases, so does the blockchain's total electricity usage, creating a negative environmental externality. This study investigates whether individual miner incentives can align with the collective goal of reducing energy consumption. We introduce the "Crypto-Asset Game," an Evolutionary Game Theory model where agents choose between acting as miners or crypto-asset users. In this framework, mining energy costs reduce miners' payoffs and serve as an environmental factor for users. Numerical simulations of the model indicate that under certain conditions, the agent population can evolve toward a strategy profile that optimizes global energy consumption by maintaining a low density of miners. Ultimately, our findings suggest that blockchain protocol parameters play a significant role in determining the energy sustainability of Proof-of-Work technologies.

The count of particles observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions is highly sensitive to the impact parameter. Consequently, fluctuations in multiplicity and rapidity correlations of these multiplicities are primarily driven by variations in the impact parameter. This paper introduces a Bayesian inference-based approach capable of robustly reconstructing fluctuations and correlations at a specific impact parameter. Applying this method to ATLAS data regarding charged multiplicity and transverse energy distributions, we demonstrate that multiplicity fluctuations are less pronounced at large rapidities compared to those near central rapidity. We propose straightforward new analyses to verify this phenomenon.

When analyzing a finite admixture model with unknown components and weights, where the count of identifiable components depends on the volume of data, we apply stochastic convex geometry to determine the expected growth rate of this count. Furthermore, by imposing a Dirichlet process prior on densities defined over the unit simplex, we recover the Dirac measure corresponding to the Choquet measure on the identifiable components, thereby yielding the identifiable admixture weights. Consequently, we introduce a new algorithm that estimates the model's complexity using the minimal number of components required to capture the data's intricacies.

Regional differences in social app adoption lead to significant imbalances in the volume and quality of check-in data, posing a major obstacle for effective location recommender systems. This paper introduces Axolotl (Automated cross Location-network Transfer Learning), a new approach designed to transfer location preference models from data-abundant areas to substantially enhance recommendation quality in data-poor regions. Axolotl primarily utilizes two transfer channels: (1) a meta-learning procedure trained on both location recommendations and social predictions, and (2) a lightweight, unsupervised, cluster-based transfer mechanism that connects users and locations with similar preferences. These components work synergistically to improve recommendation accuracy in data-scarce environments without requiring overlapping users or extensive fine-tuning. Built upon a twin graph-attention neural network, Axolotl captures user- and location-specific influences within a user-mobility graph for each region. Extensive experiments were conducted on 12 user mobility datasets from the U.S., Japan, and Germany, using three regions as sources and nine data-sparse regions as targets. Empirical results demonstrate that Axolotl outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by up to 18% across all metrics.

We have created a hybrid galactic chemical evolution model that integrates a multi-ring calculation of chemical enrichment with a framework for stellar migration and vertical population distribution, based on a cosmological hydrodynamic disc galaxy simulation. Our primary model utilizes empirically driven star formation laws and histories, adjusting the outflow mass loading gradient to match the observed metallicity gradient. This approach successfully replicates numerous key qualitative characteristics of the Milky Way disc's abundance structure: (i) the variation of the [O/Fe]-[Fe/H] distribution with galactic radius ($R_\text{gal}$) and midplane distance ($|z|$); (ii) the evolving shapes of [O/H] and [Fe/H] distributions across $R_\text{gal}$ and $|z|$; (iii) a wide [O/Fe] distribution at sub-solar metallicities that shifts with $R_\text{gal}$, $|z|$, and [Fe/H]; (iv) a strong correlation between [O/Fe] and stellar age for [O/Fe] > 0.1; (v) a group of young and intermediate-age $\alpha$-enhanced stars resulting from migration-driven fluctuations in the Type Ia supernova rate; and (vi) non-monotonic age-[O/H] and age-[Fe/H] relationships featuring significant scatter and a median age of approximately 4 Gyr near solar metallicity. Models incorporating observationally motivated enhancements to the star formation rate around 2 Gyr ago align better with observed age-[Fe/H] and age-[O/H] trends but fail to match the age-[O/Fe] data. Furthermore, none of our simulations produce the distinct bimodal [O/Fe] distribution seen in observations, indicating that more extreme evolutionary scenarios are necessary. All code and tables associated with these models are publicly accessible via the Versatile Integrator for Chemical Evolution (VICE; https://pypi.org/project/vice).

Euclid represents the inaugural space mission to map the majority of the extragalactic sky within the 0.95–2.02 $\mu$m wavelength range, achieving a median point-source depth of 24.4 AB magnitudes at a $5\sigma$ confidence level. This distinctive photometric dataset is expected to have extensive applications beyond Euclid's primary scientific objectives. This study details precise calculations of the Euclid NISP instrument's Y$_E$, J$_E$, and H$_E$ passbands and their corresponding photometric system. Special emphasis is placed on passband variations across the field of view, incorporating factors such as spatially dependent filter transmission and changes in the angle of incidence on the filter substrate via optical ray tracing. The cut-on and cut-off wavelengths of the response curves, along with their field-of-view variations, are determined with 0.8 nm precision, a requirement critical for the photometric redshift accuracy needed by Euclid. Following the computation of AB magnitude zeropoints, we provide linear conversion equations to and from standard ground-based near-infrared systems for normal stars, red and brown dwarfs, and galaxies individually. Additionally, a Python utility is offered to calculate accurate magnitudes for custom passbands and spectral energy distributions. We examine various potential causes for gradual shifts in Euclid's spectral response, ranging from space weathering to material outgassing. At the absolute flux level, the in-flight calibration program links the NISP photometric system to Hubble Space Telescope spectrophotometric white dwarf standards, while at the relative flux level, the chromatic evolution of the response is monitored at the milli-mag level. Through these efforts, we establish a highly accurate photometric system that remains fully controlled throughout the duration of the Euclid mission.

This study evaluates the sky localization and early warning capabilities of third-generation gravitational wave detector networks, featuring various configurations of the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE) across sites in Europe, North America, and Australia. Employing a Fisher matrix approach that accounts for Earth's rotation, we calculate sky localization uncertainties for $1.4\text{M}\odot$-$1.4\text{M}\odot$ binary neutron star (BNS) mergers at distances ranging from $40\text{Mpc}$ to $1600\text{Mpc}$, as well as for an astrophysical population extending to a redshift of 2. Our results indicate that for BNS mergers at $200\text{Mpc}$, a 2ET1CE network (two ET-like detectors and one CE) achieves a 90% credible region upper limit of $0.25\text{deg}^2$ for the best 90% localized signals, with an astrophysical distribution upper limit of $91.79\text{deg}^2$. In contrast, a 1ET2CE configuration (one ET-like and two CE-like detectors) yields an upper limit of $0.18\text{deg}^2$ at $200\text{Mpc}$ and $56.77\text{deg}^2$ for the astrophysical distribution, while detecting 7.2% more of the simulated population than the 2ET1CE setup. Regarding early warning performance, both network configurations can provide alerts approximately one hour before merger with sky localization uncertainties of $30\text{deg}^2$ or less. Ultimately, we conclude that the 1ET2CE network offers an optimal balance between BNS detection rates, sky localization precision, and early warning potential.

This study introduces a two-stage framework for conducting techno-economic analyses of demand-side flexibility services within distribution networks. The first stage employs optimization-based modeling to generate a generic problem formulation that establishes offer curves, defining both the available flexible capacity and its marginal cost for assets connected to the distribution grid. These curves serve as inputs for the second stage, which utilizes a multi-agent iterative game framework to assess the benefits of demand-side flexibility for both the Distribution System Operator (DSO) and service providers. By integrating the objectives of flexibility providers, technical asset constraints, customer preferences, market clearing mechanisms, and strategic bidding behaviors, this combined framework ensures comprehensive analysis, as omitting any of these factors could yield inaccurate results. The framework was validated through a real-world case study in North East England, evaluating four market mechanisms and three bidding strategies. Findings indicate that flexibility markets utilizing discriminatory pricing, such as pay-as-bid and Dutch reverse auctions, are susceptible to manipulation, particularly in low-competition environments. Conversely, uniform pricing via pay-as-cleared auctions offer significantly fewer opportunities for manipulation, even when competition is limited.

This paper presents an investigation into indirect CP violation in $D^0$ mesons by measuring the parameter $A_\Gamma$, utilizing a dataset of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions recorded by the LHCb detector at the LHC's center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The $A_\Gamma$ parameter quantifies the asymmetry in effective lifetimes between $D^0$ and $\bar{D}^0$ decays into the CP eigenstates $K^-K^+$ and $\pi^-\pi^+$. Analysis of the data yields $A_\Gamma(KK)=(-0.35\pm0.62\pm0.12)\times 10^{-3}$ and $A_\Gamma(\pi\pi)=(0.33\pm1.06\pm0.14)\times 10^{-3}$, with the first uncertainties being statistical and the second systematic. These findings constitute the most precise measurements of these parameters to date. The results indicate no variation in $A_\Gamma$ across the two final states and provide no evidence for CP violation.

Neutron-deficient calcium isotopes remain a focal point of research due to their significance in validating isospin symmetry and their role in nuclear capture reactions relevant to nova nucleosynthesis and the light curves of Type I X-ray bursts. While existing spectroscopic data on $^{38,39}$Ca primarily covers low-spin excited states, this study presents in-beam $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy of complementary higher-spin, complex-structure states in $^{39}$Ca. These states were populated via fast-beam-induced, momentum-dissipative processes involving neutron pickup onto excited projectile configurations in the reaction $^{9}$Be($^{38}$Ca, $^{39}$Ca + $\gamma$)X. This dissipative mechanism was previously identified in the inelastic scattering of $^{38}$Ca off $^{9}$Be. The paper also provides further analysis and discussion on the nuclear structure of $^{38}$Ca. Additionally, an explanation is offered for the more complex states that appear in the tails of longitudinal momentum distributions and are populated with low cross sections in one-nucleon knockout reactions.

We address the inference challenge in high-dimensional linear models where covariates exhibit spatially organized correlations, a common scenario in high-resolution imaging where adjacent pixels are highly similar. In settings with many more covariates than samples and strong inter-covariate correlations, obtaining precise point estimates and confidence intervals becomes infeasible. Consequently, we reformulate statistical inference to incorporate this spatial structure: when covariates are locally correlated, detection is considered valid within a specified spatial uncertainty. We introduce the $\delta$-FWER, defined as the probability of a false discovery occurring at a distance exceeding $\delta$ from any true positive. Focusing on this metric, we analyze ensembled clustered inference algorithms that integrate spatially constrained clustering, statistical inference, and ensembling to aggregate multiple clustered solutions. Our findings demonstrate that these algorithms control the $\delta$-FWER under standard assumptions when $\delta$ matches the largest cluster diameter. Additionally, empirical results complement the theoretical analysis, confirming both accurate $\delta$-FWER control and satisfactory power for these inference methods.

This study examines the emergence of quantum signatures in a single-atom heat engine, where an atom trapped in a tapered potential interacts with hot and cold thermal reservoirs—a setup previously demonstrated experimentally in Ref.[1]. By employing a quadratic optomechanical model, we identify an effective Otto cycle within the system's dynamics and assess the engine's performance by comparing power dissipation between quantum and classical regimes. Our results indicate that merely lowering the temperature is inadequate to transform the engine from Ref.[1] into a genuinely quantum-enhanced device. Instead, we demonstrate that achieving power output enhancement through quantum correlations requires increasing the trap's asymmetry and confinement.

Data artifacts encourage machine learning models to rely on non-transferable shortcuts within the data, with increasing evidence linking these artifacts to the high performance of deep learning models on recent natural language processing benchmarks. This paper examines task-oriented dialogue to determine if widely used datasets like MultiWOZ contain such artifacts. Our findings indicate that state-of-the-art models achieve performance comparable to those trained on full datasets when only frequent phrases are retained in the training set, implying they exploit these spurious correlations to complete the task. Driven by this observation, we introduce a contrastive learning framework designed to compel models to disregard these cues and prioritize generalizable patterns. Additionally, we explore adversarial filtering to eliminate "easy" training instances, forcing the model to learn from more challenging examples. Through various generalization tests, including cross-domain/dataset and adversarial evaluations, we demonstrate that our approach yields exceptional robustness.

Language Models (LMs) serve as critical elements in various Natural Language Processing frameworks. Among these, Recurrent Neural Network LMs utilizing LSTM units—particularly those enhanced with external memory—have attained state-of-the-art performance. Nevertheless, these architectures face challenges when handling long sequences, which often involve long-distance dependencies, due to issues like information decay and a bias toward recent data. This paper introduces a robust retrieval mechanism for memory-augmented LSTM LMs that prioritizes memory content based on the duration the LSTM gating mechanism retained the information.

This study extends the investigation into the bifurcations of critical points within a symmetric Caldera potential energy surface. Specifically, it examines how potential depth affects trajectory dynamics both prior to and following these bifurcations. Two distinct trajectory behaviors are identified: dynamical matching and the absence of dynamical matching. Dynamical matching describes a phenomenon that restricts trajectory exit paths based exclusively on entry conditions. Additionally, the work explores two varieties of symmetric Caldera potential energy surfaces and the transitions between them driven by critical point bifurcations.

This work investigates the compactness of composition operators acting on Bergman spaces over specific bounded convex domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$ that possess non-trivial analytic discs within their boundaries. As a result, we provide a characterization for the compactness of composition operators with continuous symbols (extended to the closure) defined on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

Belle II is a next-generation B-factory experiment focused on investigating new physics beyond the Standard Model within the flavor sector. Data collection began in April 2018 utilizing a synchronous data acquisition (DAQ) system governed by pipelined trigger flow control. Designed to manage a 30-kHz trigger rate with roughly 1% dead time under a 1 MB raw event size assumption, the DAQ system achieved an overall data-taking efficiency of 84.2% during the January 2020 to June 2020 run period. However, the existing readout infrastructure lacks the maintainability required for a 10-year operational lifespan and hinders high-speed data transmission. To address these limitations, an upgrade employing a PCI-express-based readout module capable of up to 100 Gb/s throughput was implemented. This initiative prioritized the development of firmware and software for the new PCIe40 readout board, which utilizes an Altera Arria 10 field-programmable gate array. Key design elements included 48 GBT serial links, a PCI-express hard IP-based DMA architecture, and interfaces for timing, trigger distribution, and slow control systems to ensure integration with the current DAQ. This paper details the performance results from data readout and slow control tests conducted on a test bench and via on-site demonstrations involving Belle II TOP and KLM sub-detectors.

Tensor factorization has gained significant attention for its capacity to uncover latent factors within multi-dimensional data, finding widespread use in recommender systems and Electronic Health Records (EHR) mining. To handle irregular tensors where one mode lacks alignment—such as varying record lengths among users or patients—methods like PARAFAC2 and its variants have been developed. While PARAFAC2 has proven effective in extracting meaningful medical concepts (phenotypes) from EHRs, current models often fall short in predictability and interpretability, hindering their utility for downstream analysis. To address this, we introduce MULTIPAR, a supervised irregular tensor factorization framework utilizing multi-task learning. MULTIPAR flexibly integrates both static tasks (e.g., in-hospital mortality prediction) and dynamic or continuous ones (e.g., ventilation requirements). By supervising the factorization process with downstream prediction tasks and leveraging information across multiple related tasks, MULTIPAR generates more meaningful phenotypes while enhancing predictive performance for downstream applications. Extensive experiments on two real-world temporal EHR datasets demonstrate that MULTIPAR is scalable, achieves superior tensor fitting, identifies more meaningful subgroups, and delivers stronger predictive results compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Although deep learning (DL) language models excel at Natural Language Inference (NLI) benchmarks, symbolic approaches have garnered less recent attention. While both DL and symbolic methods offer distinct strengths and limitations, no existing system integrates them to address NLI. To bridge this gap, we introduce NeuralLog, an inference framework that combines a monotonicity-based logical inference engine with a neural network for phrase alignment. By modeling NLI as a classic search problem and employing beam search to identify optimal inference paths, our joint logic and neural system enhances accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that NeuralLog achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SICK and MED datasets.

This work outlines a comprehensive approach to retrieving phases ab initio using spatial intensity triple correlations. Simulations confirm that this method accurately recovers phases for clusters of classical incoherent sources.

A mutilated model is developed to approximate the collision term in the spin Boltzmann equation, specifically incorporating newly identified collisional invariants such as total angular momentum. Utilizing degenerate perturbation theory, we derive the dispersion relations for hydrodynamic modes, noting that spin modes drive spin equilibration. Our findings indicate that while non-locality leaves the sound speed unchanged, it reduces the propagation speed of spin waves. Furthermore, within a reasonable range of parameters, the damping rates of spin modes are comparable to those of spinless modes. These results suggest that a unified transport framework must treat both spin and momentum simultaneously. Additionally, an analysis of the short-wavelength behavior of normal modes in the nonrelativistic limit reveals a critical point for each distinct discrete mode, beyond which only quasiparticle modes contribute.

To investigate how edge states influence the phase diagram of a spinless Falicov-Kimball model (FKM) on a Haldane lattice, researchers analyzed a ribbon configuration featuring zigzag edges. By adjusting the ribbon widths, the study distinguishes between effects stemming solely from the existence of edges and those arising from interference among edge states. It is demonstrated that local doping induced by the edges creates a topologically trivial bulk insulator with metallic edges and generates a charge density wave (CDW) phase characterized by mixed subband properties across different regions of the phase diagram. The impact of this local doping on CDW instability is also examined. Furthermore, two additional gapless phases are identified, which are driven by the edges and whose stability depends on the ribbon's width.

We demonstrate that for percolation games on $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ characterized by site trap probability $p$ and target probability $q$, the likelihood of a draw is zero whenever $p+q > 0$. Specifically, for any fixed $p$ and $q$, a draw occurs with probability zero if and only if the associated one-dimensional probabilistic cellular automaton $F_{p,q}$, which features a size-3 neighborhood, is ergodic. This equivalence enables the conclusion that $F_{p,q}$ is ergodic for all $p+q > 0$, thereby rigorously proving ergodicity for a significant class of such automata.

The resilience of object detection algorithms is critical in real-world scenarios, particularly within uncontrolled settings where image acquisition introduces distortions. It is well-established that such in-capture distortions significantly degrade the performance of detection methods. This study introduces an evaluation framework for state-of-the-art object detection techniques using a specialized dataset featuring images with diverse distortions at varying severity levels. Additionally, we propose a novel strategy for generating image distortions on the MS-COCO dataset, integrating both local and global distortions to achieve superior results. Our findings demonstrate that training with this proposed dataset enhances object detection robustness by 31.5%. Finally, we release a custom dataset comprising naturally distorted images derived from MS-COCO to facilitate more reliable assessments of robustness against common distortions. The dataset and the source code for generating these distortions are made publicly available.

This paper outlines the PUM team's participation in SemEval-2020 Task 12. Our approach utilized two prominent pretrained NLP models, BERT and XLNet, known for achieving state-of-the-art performance across various tasks. We fine-tuned these models individually for each subtask, aggregated features extracted from their hidden layers, and processed them through a fully connected neural network. This architecture, leveraging combined Transformer features, proves highly effective for identifying offensive language. In Sub-task C (Offense target identification), our team secured the 7th place out of 40 participants with a macro F1-score of 64.727%, and placed 64th out of 85 in Sub-task A (Offensive language identification), achieving an F1-score of 89.726%.

We outline the construction of the two-loop amplitude for four-graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5\times$S$^5$. Beginning with a preamplitude ansatz, we derive the complete amplitude by applying a specific Casimir operator. This ansatz aligns with a recent proposal by Huang and Yuan, which we validate using comparable constraints. Our findings suggest that all ambiguities reside within the preamplitude, thereby fixing the result up to tree-level uncertainties. We identify a specific class of four-dimensional `zigzag' integrals ideally suited for describing the leading logarithmic discontinuity to all orders. Furthermore, we note that a bonus crossing symmetry of the preamplitude arises from the transformation properties of the Casimir operator; combined with the zigzag integrals, this enables the construction of a crossing-symmetric function possessing the correct leading logarithmic discontinuities across all channels. From this two-loop result, we derive an explicit formula for the two-loop correction to the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin, incorporating dependencies on (alternating) nested harmonic sums up to weight three. Additionally, we re-examine the prescription for the bulk-point limit of AdS amplitudes, demonstrating how it recovers the full flat-space amplitude rather than merely its discontinuity. Utilizing this extended definition of the bulk-point limit, we successfully reproduce the scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms characteristic of type IIB string theory in flat space.

This study presents a solution-growth technique for synthesizing single crystals of Y$_2$Co$_3$, detailing their structural and magnetic characteristics. The material adopts an orthorhombic La2Ni3-type structure (space group Cmce, No. 64), featuring distorted kagome lattices formed by cobalt. Antiferromagnetic ordering occurs below a Néel temperature ($T_N$) of 252 K. Magnetization data indicate that magnetic moments are predominantly oriented along the b-axis, accompanied by some canting. While band-structure calculations suggest that ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states are nearly degenerate—contradicting experimental findings—pressure-dependent magnetization up to 1 GPa shows the Néel temperature dropping at a rate of -1.69 K/GPa. Furthermore, a field-induced spin-flop transition was detected at 1.5 K under a 21 T field applied along the b-direction. The absence of magnetization saturation even at 35 T demonstrates the robustness of the antiferromagnetic ordering in Y$_2$Co$_3$, an unexpected feature for such a cobalt-rich intermetallic.

The widespread integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed every facet of human existence, with radio positioning serving as a tangible illustration of this influence. This article introduces a novel approach by leveraging AI to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) using 5G New Radio (NR) fingerprints derived from beamformed Channel State Information (CSI). Since monitoring CSI allows for the characterization of the multipath channel between a transmitter and receiver, it offers valuable spatiotemporal data for determining User Equipment (UE) locations. We gathered ray-tracing-based 5G NR CSI within an urban setting, collecting signal data from a single Base Station (BS) at reference points with known coordinates to train the CNN. The study evaluates the model through two primary metrics: a) the robustness of the trained network in estimating positions for new measurements taken at the same reference points, and b) the accuracy of CNN-based position estimation when the UE is located at points distinct from the training references. The findings demonstrate that the trained network, tailored to a specific urban environment, can estimate UE positions with a minimum mean error of 0.98 meters.

Neural networks represent a promising approach for simulating quantum many-body systems, with recent findings indicating that enforcing correct symmetry properties enhances their accuracy. This paper demonstrates how to construct maximally expressive models for quantum states with specific symmetries by leveraging insights from the machine learning community. By implementing group equivariant convolutional networks (G-CNNs) \cite{cohen2016group}, we show that performance gains can be achieved without increasing memory consumption. Furthermore, we establish that G-CNNs attain high accuracy for Heisenberg quantum spin models across both ordered and spin liquid phases, while also surpassing other variational Monte-Carlo methods in ground state accuracy on triangular lattices.

In network dynamics research, moment closure is a prevalent technique for deriving low-dimensional evolution equations suitable for analysis. These equations involve variables representing the mean counts of subgraph states, termed moments. Because neighbor interactions cause each moment equation to depend on higher-order moments, an infinite hierarchy of equations emerges. Consequently, derivation necessitates truncating the hierarchy at a specific order and approximating the highest-order moments using lower-order ones via a closure formula. While recent systematic approaches have either focused exclusively on closed moment equations for SIR epidemics or unclosed equations for general dynamics, this paper introduces a general procedure that automates both the derivation and closure of arbitrary-order moment equations for nearest-neighbor interactions on undirected networks. This automation is achieved through a generalized closure scheme that systematically decomposes the largest subgraphs into smaller components. We demonstrate that this decomposition is exact under conditions of tree-like component formation, independence beyond the graph diameter, and spatial homogeneity.
