Testing the method on SIS epidemic spreading across lattices and random networks reveals that biases are more pronounced in networks with numerous short cycles within regimes exhibiting long-range dependence. A Mathematica package automating this moment closure process is available for download.

Online social networks struggle with misinformation, a challenge often tackled by machine learning systems that automatically detect false posts after they are published. In contrast, we propose a proactive approach that predicts whether a user will interact with misinformation before it happens, utilizing a graph neural network classifier built on ego-graphs. However, the dynamic nature of social networks—characterized by shifting user behaviors and evolving content—poses a significant issue for machine learning models trained on static datasets, leading to performance degradation over time. Drawing inspiration from continual learning techniques, we introduce EgoCL, an ego-graph replay strategy that leverages graph neural networks to overcome this obsolescence. We assessed our method's effectiveness in predicting user engagement with misinformation across nineteen conspiracy and misinformation topics using two Twitter datasets. Our experimental findings demonstrate that EgoCL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.

The independent chromatic vertex stability, denoted as $\ivs(G)$, and the chromatic vertex stability, $\vs(G)$, are defined as the smallest sizes of an independent set $S\subseteq V(G)$ required to reduce the chromatic number by exactly one, such that $\chi(G-S)=\chi(G)-1$. This paper presents an infinite family of graphs $G$ where the maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ is 4, the chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is 3, $\ivs(G)$ equals 3, and $\vs(G)$ equals 2. These results provide a partial negative response to the question raised in \cite{ABKM}.

This paper introduces psc2code, a method designed to clean up the extraction of source code from programming screencasts. Initially, psc2code employs Convolutional Neural Network-based image classification to filter out frames containing non-code or noisy code. Subsequently, it utilizes edge detection and clustering-based segmentation to identify sub-windows within code frames, allowing the system to pinpoint and crop the specific screen areas most likely to represent a code editor. Finally, the method invokes a professional OCR tool's API to extract source code from these cropped regions and corrects OCR errors by leveraging cross-frame information from the screencast alongside a statistical language model trained on a large corpus of source code. We evaluated our approach on 1,142 programming screencasts sourced from YouTube. Our results demonstrate that the CNN-based classification effectively eliminates non-code and noisy frames, achieving an F1-score of 0.95 for valid code frames. Utilizing the denoised source code, we developed two applications: a programming screencast search engine and an interaction-enhanced viewing tool. Experiments using the extracted code from the 1,142 screencasts indicate that our search engine attains precision@5, 10, and 20 scores of 0.93, 0.81, and 0.63, respectively.

Contemporary machine learning classification methods, such as deep neural networks, support vector machines, and AdaBoost, rely on surrogate loss functions to avoid the computational burdens of directly minimizing empirical classification risk. These methods are equally applicable to causal policy learning, where deriving individualized treatment rules can be framed as a cost-sensitive classification task. However, the consistency of surrogate loss approaches discussed by Zhang (2004) and Bartlett et al. (2006) depends heavily on the assumption of correct specification—that the chosen classifier set is sufficiently rich to include an optimal solution. This assumption becomes questionable when classifier sets are restricted by requirements for interpretability or fairness, leaving the performance of surrogate loss algorithms in these "second-best" contexts unclear. This study investigates the consistency of surrogate loss procedures under constrained classifier sets without relying on the correct specification assumption. We demonstrate that when constraints apply only to the prediction set, hinge losses (specifically $\ell_1$-support vector machines) are the exclusive surrogate losses that maintain consistency in second-best scenarios. Conversely, if constraints also limit the functional form of the classifier, consistency is not assured even with hinge loss. Consequently, we identify the conditions under which a constrained classifier set can ensure the consistency of hinge risk minimization. Leveraging these theoretical findings, we construct robust and computationally efficient hinge loss-based procedures tailored for monotone classification problems.

Existing literature provides analytical formulas for calculating the probability that a receiver successfully decodes a source message encoded via random linear network coding. This study examines the likelihood of decoding at least a fraction of the source message and derives an exact solution for both systematic and non-systematic network coding approaches. Leveraging these derived expressions, we analyze the capabilities of these two coding implementations regarding information-theoretic security and progressive data recovery.

Although the quantum spin Hall effect (QSHE) has been detected in topological insulators via spin-orbit coupling, it remains unobserved in metals. This paper proposes an experiment to detect the QSHE of electrons or holes within a two-dimensional (2D) metal by leveraging a relativistically induced 2D quantum spin Hall Hamiltonian, distinct from traditional spin-orbit coupling approaches. The setup involves a long cylindrical solenoid positioned perpendicularly through the inner radius of a 2D metallic Corbino disk. An azimuthal current $I_S$ flowing around the solenoid creates a magnetic vector potential in the disk without generating a magnetic field. Simultaneously, a radial electric field is established by applying either (a) a voltage difference $\Delta v$ or (b) a radial charge current ${\bm I}$ between the disk's inner and outer edges. By modulating both $I_S$ and the radial parameter ($\Delta v$ or ${\bm I}$), the system spontaneously produces quantized azimuthal charge and spin currents, which the experiment aims to measure consistently. Exact solutions for the quantum Hamiltonians corresponding to both experimental configurations are provided. Furthermore, a technique for managing Joule heating is introduced, potentially enabling room-temperature QSHE measurements. Expanding this design into an array of thermally controlled solenoids surrounded by stacks of 2D metallic Corbino disks could create a room-temperature quantum computer.

Compartmental models are commonly utilized to analyze and forecast the propagation of infectious diseases, requiring the estimation of unknown parameters from available data. In scenarios where certain model variables cannot be directly observed—such as asymptomatic COVID-19 carriers—these must be derived as model outputs. This study presents a framework designed to measure how data uncertainty influences both parameter estimation and the trajectory of unmeasured variables within a specific model. We demonstrate the method's capability to characterize various identifiability regimes, even in models with limited compartments. Finally, we examine how identifiability issues in a realistic COVID-19 model can hinder the generation of reliable epidemic forecasts.

Vibropolaritonic chemistry has emerged as a promising area within synthetic chemistry, offering enhanced mode selectivity and a purer method for controlling reaction kinetics. Notably, numerous studies have demonstrated altered reactivity by conducting reactions within optical microcavities without the need for optical pumping. These optimal conditions are characterized by (1) resonance between the cavity and reactive modes at normal incidence ($k=0$) and (2) a steady increase in the observed effect as emitter concentration rises. Despite these experimental successes, conceptualizing the underlying mechanisms has presented significant theoretical hurdles. This perspective reviews key theoretical approaches, highlighting both their contributions and unresolved challenges. We anticipate that this manuscript will guide future research toward establishing a definitive formalism for vibropolaritonic chemical kinetics.

We re-examine specific complexities in renormalization that emerge when constructing a low-energy effective action by integrating out heavy fields from a more comprehensive theory. While these issues are typically avoided by matching physical observables like scattering amplitudes, a more sophisticated approach is necessary for deriving the effective theory to all orders in light fields, provided the derivative expansion remains at a fixed order. As a specific case, we investigate the $U(1)$ Goldstone low-energy effective theory representing the spontaneously broken phase of a complex scalar $\phi^4$ theory. Calculating to the lowest order in the derivative expansion but to all orders in the Goldstone fields, we integrate out the radial mode at one loop and formulate the low-energy effective action using the renormalized couplings of the ultraviolet completion. This process produces the one-loop equation of state for the superfluid phase of complex $\phi^4$. We apply the same methodology to a renormalizable scalar $SO(N)$ theory at finite chemical potential, integrating out the gapped Goldstones as well, and verify that the resulting effective theory for the gapless Goldstone modes shows no clear indication of the original $SO(N)$ symmetry.

We present CoLN (Combined Learning of Neural network weights), a new approach for securely merging Machine Learning models across sensitive datasets without exchanging raw data. Under the CoLN framework, local nodes employ identical neural network architectures and initial parameters to train models exclusively on their local data. These locally trained models are then transmitted to a central combining agent, which synthesizes them into a unified model. The resulting parameters can be redistributed to the hosts to serve as initialization for subsequent training rounds. CoLN supports the aggregation of multiple distributed neural networks of the same type but remains agnostic to specific architectural constraints. This paper outlines the combination algorithm and reports experiments using feed-forward, convolutional, and recurrent networks, demonstrating that the CoLN-generated model closely matches the performance of an ideal centralized model trained on the aggregated local datasets. CoLN offers a solution for secure collaborative research, particularly in the medical field, where privacy regulations prohibit data sharing yet local data limitations necessitate insights derived from larger, combined datasets.

This study examines the performance of various cross-validation (CV) methods under algorithmic stability, particularly emphasizing K-fold. We establish a general upper bound for risk estimation error that applies to a broad range of CV strategies. This bound guarantees the consistency of leave-one-out and leave-p-out procedures but does not constrain the error associated with K-fold. We substantiate this limitation by deriving a lower bound for K-fold error that fails to approach zero as sample size increases. Consequently, we introduce a debiased variant of K-fold that achieves consistency for any uniformly stable learner. Finally, we apply these findings to model selection and empirically validate the efficacy of the proposed method using real-world data.

The Eclipse framework is a widely adopted platform that has evolved for more than ten years, offering both stable APIs and unstable non-APIs. Although Eclipse discourages their use, developers frequently rely on non-APIs, which often lead to system failures during upgrades to newer framework versions. Prior research indicates that applications utilizing older non-APIs tend to maintain better compatibility with new releases than those depending on recently introduced ones. Additionally, a previous study on the stability of Eclipse's internal interfaces identified 327,000 stable non-API methods across the framework's evolution. That same study suggested promoting these 327,000 stable non-API methods to official interfaces; however, because non-APIs are unsupported and may harbor bugs, it is essential to first assess them for defects before promotion. This study employs the SonarQube quality tool to empirically investigate these stable non-APIs for potential bugs. The findings reveal that over 79.8% of classes containing legacy stable non-API methods have zero bugs. These results serve as a valuable starting point for both interface providers and users to evaluate which interfaces are well-tested and to estimate the effort required for bug fixing in upcoming Eclipse releases.

We present concise and straightforward proofs for two folklore results: * the largest possible size of the intersection between a lattice cube and an affine subspace, and * the smallest number of affine subspaces required to cover a lattice cube.

We examine recoil corrections in the superallowed beta decays of $T=1$, $J^P=0^+$ nuclei by determining the mean square charge weak radius without relying on specific models, utilizing data from multiple charge radii within the nuclear isotriplet. Through comparison with theoretical estimates, we contend that the current uncertainty in the statistical rate function $f$ may have been significantly overlooked. Furthermore, we explore the consequences of our suggested approach for high-precision Standard Model validations, potentially resolving the first-row CKM unitarity deficit, and we advocate for new experiments focused on measuring charge radii.

We investigate how thermodynamic observables evolve following an instantaneous temperature quench. By integrating stochastic thermodynamics with large-deviation theory, we construct a robust framework for calculating the large-deviation statistics of these quantities. This approach naturally formulates a dynamical Landau theory, a flexible instrument for analyzing finite-time dynamical phase transitions. The topology of the resulting Landau potential enables a clear determination of the dynamical order parameter and the corresponding phase diagram. As a direct application, we demonstrate that the heat distribution exchanged between a mean-field spin model and its surroundings displays a singularity, or kink, resulting from a finite-time dynamical phase transition. Leveraging our Landau theory, we perform an in-depth analysis of this transition. While the observable signature of this new transition resembles a previously identified finite-time transition in magnetization, their underlying properties and dynamical origins are fundamentally distinct.

This research examines the performance of continuous phase modulation (CPM) capable of producing a single-sideband (SSB) spectrum directly. The analysis investigates how modulation indices, pulse lengths, and pulse widths influence error probability, bandwidth, SSB characteristics, and receiver complexity. Error probability is estimated using an approximation of the minimum Euclidean distance, and a numerical calculation of the power spectral density for this specific SSB modulation is provided as a function of the modulation index. To achieve significant improvements in bit error rate (BER), spectral efficiency, and complexity while maintaining the SSB property, the study proposes reasonable design tradeoffs through multi-objective optimization. Finally, the proposed scheme is compared against established CPM methods, such as Gaussian Minimum Shift Keying (GMSK) and Raised Cosine-based CPM (RC).

Advanced sports analysis techniques have sparked diverse strategies to enhance player performance and fan engagement. Nevertheless, current methods are limited to offline evaluation, as real-time testing during matches is prohibitively expensive and difficult to replicate. To enable safe and reproducible experimentation, we concentrate on turn-based sports and present a badminton environment that simulates rallies from various perspectives, defining specific states, actions, and training protocols. This approach aids coaches and players by allowing the simulation of past matches for tactical analysis, while also enabling researchers to rapidly assess new algorithms.

We introduce Homo Entropicus, an agent constructed using a neural network whose learning process is refined by entropic dynamics, an information-theoretic approach. At a macroscopic scale, this algorithm operates through aggregate variables that function as quantitative indicators of proto-emotions. By assembling systems of these interacting neural networks, we establish a framework for simulating societies exhibiting complex emergent behaviors. Several applications demonstrate how interactions regarding multidimensional opinions and trust in information sources influence the state of the agent society. These include scenarios involving a class of $N$ agents learning from a static teacher, two dynamical agents, and panels of three agents modeling US Court of Appeals decisions, where we measure political bias, inter-judge trust, and adherence to a shared legal understanding. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which ideological polarization precedes or follows affective polarization in large societies and explore how simplified versions of the learning algorithm might alter these dynamics.

We investigated $^4$He droplets doped with magnesium atoms using density functional theory, discovering that solvation characteristics are highly sensitive to droplet size. In small droplets, magnesium occupies a deep surface state, whereas in larger ones, it becomes fully solvated yet radially delocalized within the interior. We analyzed the $3s3p$ $^1$P$_1 \leftarrow 3s^2$ $^1$S$_0$ transition of the dopant and compared our findings with laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) experimental data, explicitly accounting for line broadening caused by the coupling between dynamical helium deformations and the impurity's dipole excitation. Our results suggest that radial delocalization of Mg in large droplets can resolve apparent contradictions between LIF and electron-impact ionization experiments regarding magnesium's solvation. Additionally, we examined systems with two magnesium atoms to interpret resonant two-photon-ionization (R2PI) and LIF results. We found that two solvated Mg atoms do not readily form a dimer; instead, an energy barrier imposed by the helium environment maintains them approximately 9.5 Å apart, resulting in a weakly bound state that prevents Mg$_2$ molecule formation. Based on this, we propose that Mg atoms in $^4$He droplets may form a soft, foam-like aggregate under suitable conditions rather than coalescing into a compact metallic cluster, a prediction that aligns qualitatively with recent R2PI evidence. Conversely, we predict that Mg atoms adsorbed in $^3$He droplets will not form such metastable aggregates.

Unlike methods relying on metadata like keywords, content-based information retrieval focuses on the actual information within documents, typically utilizing either text or images. This study examines the utility of multimodal features for cross-lingual news search across five domains: politics, health, environment, sports, and finance. We evaluated five distinct feature types combining text and image data, comparing retrieval performance across various combinations. The experimental findings indicate that integrating both visual and textual information enhances retrieval outcomes. Furthermore, among textual features, entity overlap proved superior to word embeddings, while geolocation embeddings yielded better results than other visual features in the retrieval task.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have reached state-of-the-art levels in node classification, yet most current research assumes access to perfectly accurate training labels. There remains a significant gap in understanding how to enhance GNN robustness when label noise is present. While label noise learning has been extensively explored in image classification, these methods fail to translate directly to graph data due to unique challenges like label sparsity and dependency. This paper introduces UnionNET, a novel framework designed for semi-supervised learning with noisy labels on graphs. UnionNET offers a unified approach that simultaneously enables robust GNN training and label correction. The core methodology involves aggregating labels to estimate node-level class probability distributions, which then guide sample reweighting and the correction process. Compared to prior work, UnionNET offers two distinct benefits: it eliminates the need for additional clean supervision or explicit noise transition matrix estimation, and it provides an end-to-end unified learning framework. Experimental findings demonstrate that UnionNET effectively boosts model robustness against various noise types and intensities, while delivering substantial performance gains over existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Although there is ongoing debate regarding the advantages of proprietary versus open-source algorithm development, we contend that open-source approaches should become the standard in high-stakes areas impacting human lives. This preference is driven by the benefits of transparency and collaboration, which enhance predictive accuracy while offering cost savings. To support this argument, we examine criminal sentencing algorithms, a domain of profound societal and individual consequence. The urgency of this issue has intensified following recent research revealing racial biases, overfitting, and excessive model complexity within proprietary sentencing tools, problems that are often worsened by their high costs and closed nature. By replicating a significant algorithm using real criminal data and applying three penalized regressions, we demonstrate that open-source, computationally efficient alternatives can achieve superior predictive power. Consequently, our findings provide a data-driven recommendation: judges seeking to formulate accurate and cost-effective sentences should prioritize open-source options.

We examine the weakly asymmetric exclusion process on a $d$-dimensional torus. We establish a large deviations principle for the time-averaged empirical density and current, considering the simultaneous limit where both the observation time and the particle count tend to infinity. This proof is achieved by analyzing the variational convergence of the Donsker-Varadhan functional for the empirical process as the number of particles grows, alongside an investigation into the large-time behavior of the hydrodynamical rate function. Subsequently, the large deviations asymptotics for the time-averaged current are derived via the contraction principle. The structure of the minimizers in this variational problem reflects the potential occurrence of dynamical phase transitions.

The richness of information within Electronic Health Records (EHRs) makes mining them a highly promising area. By leveraging EHR data, machine learning models can assist medical professionals in decision-making, thereby enhancing healthcare quality. While recent advancements have introduced sequential and graph-based models to achieve this, EHRs—characterized by multiple entities and relations—can effectively be modeled as heterogeneous graphs. Despite this, prior research has often overlooked EHR heterogeneity. Furthermore, existing heterogeneous graph neural networks are not directly applicable to EHR graphs due to the presence of hub nodes. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), a novel approach for analyzing EHRs. Our framework comprises two components: a preprocessing stage and an end-to-end GNN. The preprocessing phase normalizes edges and partitions the EHR graph into several homogeneous graphs, each retaining partial information from the original structure. Subsequently, the GNN processes these homogeneous graphs as inputs, fusing them into a unified representation to generate predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that HSGNN surpasses other baselines in diagnosis prediction tasks.

Contact inhibition restricts the proliferation and migration of cells within colonies. This study employs a multiphase field model to examine the growth dynamics of proliferating cell colonies, incorporating local mechanical interactions that drive both contact inhibition of locomotion and proliferation. By contrasting non-migrating and migrating cells, the research offers a quantitative assessment of these dynamics and analyzes the velocity of the colony boundary in both scenarios. Furthermore, the study quantifies single-cell velocities, neighbor distribution counts, and the effects of stress and age on individual and relative cell positions. Finally, the results are compared against experimental data derived from Madin-Darby canine kidney cells.

Building upon our findings in arXiv:2111.02429, we introduce a comprehensive new category of gravitational observables situated in asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space, defined across general codimension-zero bulk regions. By applying specific limits, these observables converge to established holographic complexity concepts, such as the volume of the maximal slice and the action or spacetime volume of the Wheeler-DeWitt patch. Similar to the codimension-one family detailed in arXiv:2111.02429, these new observables exhibit two fundamental universal characteristics for the thermofield double state: linear growth at late times and the reproduction of the switchback effect. Consequently, we contend that any member of this expanded class serves as a viable gravitational dual for complexity. Furthermore, utilizing the Peierls construction, we demonstrate that variations in both codimension-zero and codimension-one observables are captured by the gravitational symplectic form on the semi-classical phase-space, which can subsequently be mapped to the CFT.

For $0 < p, q, r < \infty$ with $q < r \leq \infty$, we examine the natural embedding $\ell_{p,q} \hookrightarrow \ell_{p,r}$ between Lorenz sequence spaces. We demonstrate that this non-compact embedding is invariably strictly singular, yet it fails to be finitely strictly singular.

Paleomagnetic analyses of chondrules within CO carbonaceous chondrites, alongside astronomical data and meteorite isotopic records, support the presence of disk substructures in the early solar nebula. Our study investigates these features by examining chondrules from CO carbonaceous chondrites. We find evidence of a magnetic field measuring $101 \pm 48\ \mu\text{T}$ in the outer solar nebula (approximately 3 to 7 AU from the Sun). This field's intensity is significantly higher than that inferred from meteorites originating in the inner solar system ($\lesssim$3 AU), implying a disparity in nebular accretion rates between the two regions by a factor of roughly 5 to 150. Such a discrepancy points to substantial mass loss from the disk, likely driven by a major substructure such as a magnetized disk wind.

Although large pre-trained models excel in numerous natural language processing tasks, they face significant hurdles when deployed in specialized domains due to domain shift, alongside challenges related to fine-tuning and the latency and capacity constraints of online serving. To address these issues, we introduce a general framework for creating compact, rapid, and high-performance pre-trained models tailored to specific domains. Our method adapts existing general-purpose models through task-agnostic knowledge distillation within target domains. Specifically, we implement domain-specific vocabulary expansion during the adaptation phase, utilizing corpus-level occurrence probabilities to automatically determine the optimal size for the incremental vocabulary. Furthermore, we systematically investigate various strategies to compress large pre-trained models for domain-specific applications. Experiments conducted in the biomedical and computer science sectors reveal that our approach outperforms the BERT BASE model on domain-specific tasks, while being 3.3 times smaller and 5.1 times faster. The accompanying code and pre-trained models can be accessed at https://aka.ms/adalm.

This study extends and generalizes recent findings from the literature, adapting them to include nonlinear effects and logistic perturbations. Previously, criteria for boundedness were established for an attraction-repulsion Keller-Segel system with double saturation under linear conditions without logistic terms.

Pre-editing involves adjusting the source text (ST) to improve the quality of output from machine translation (MT). Despite the inherent unpredictability of black-box neural MT (NMT), pre-editing remains widely used in practical applications. While numerous studies confirm the effectiveness of pre-editing in specific contexts, a comprehensive understanding of its mechanics regarding black-box NMT is still missing. To address this gap, we conducted an extensive investigation into human pre-editing practices. We established a protocol to capture the minimal necessary edits for each ST, gathering 6,652 instances across three translation directions, two MT systems, and four text domains. These instances were analyzed from three angles: the nature of the pre-edited ST, the variety of editing operations, and the resulting impact on NMT outputs. Our findings reveal that (1) increasing the explicitness of meaning and syntactic structure in the ST yields better translations than merely shortening or simplifying the text, and (2) while the effect of pre-editing on NMT is generally unpredictable, certain editing operation types exhibit consistent tendencies in altering NMT outputs.

Semiconductor-superconductor hybrid nanowires represent a primary platform for realizing Majorana zero modes, with prior research focusing predominantly on InAs and InSb. This study demonstrates induced superconductivity in a PbTe nanowire epitaxially coupled to a Pb superconductor. The resulting Josephson junction device exhibits gate-tunable supercurrent in the open regime and a hard superconducting gap in the tunneling regime. By confirming the superconducting proximity effect, these findings pave the way for Majorana searches and applications such as gate-tunable qubits within a novel semiconductor system.

Optical lattice clocks represent promising tools for investigating subtle physical phenomena, such as fluctuations in the fine structure constant ($\alpha_e$). Achieving this requires measuring atomic clock frequency ratios with extraordinary precision. Contrary to previous claims identifying the most sensitive transition to $\alpha_e$ in Ytterbium (Yb) [Phys. Rev. Lett. {\bf 120}, 173001 (2018)], our findings indicate that the $4f^{14}6s6p\,(^3P_2) - 4f^{13}5d6s^{2}\,(^3P_2^*)$ transition offers the highest sensitivity coefficient ($K \approx -25(2)$). Furthermore, we propose a method to achieve simultaneous magic trapping conditions for this transition alongside two other candidate transitions—$4f^{14}6s^2\,(^1S_0) - 4f^{14}6s6p\,(^3P_2)$ and $4f^{14}6s^2\,(^1S_0) - 4f^{13}5d6s^{2}\,(^3P_2^*)$—all of which exhibit large $K$ values. This magic condition is attainable by applying a bias magnetic field at a specific polarization angle relative to the quantization axis within the experimental apparatus. Once implemented, this approach establishes Yb as the most viable optical lattice clock for detecting variations in $\alpha_e$.

Classical maximal superintegrable systems in $n$ dimensions are Hamiltonian systems possessing $2n-1$ globally defined, independent constants of motion, representing the theoretical maximum. These systems are particularly notable for their algebraic solvability. This paper explicitly demonstrates, primarily through examples of second-order superintegrable systems in two dimensions, how trajectories can be precisely determined using elementary algebraic, geometric, and analytic techniques applied to the closed quadratic symmetry algebra of the system. We examine a family of second-order degenerate systems, including oscillator analogies on flat spaces, spaces with nonzero constant curvature, and Darboux spaces, which are interrelated via contractions and adhere to Kepler's laws. Additionally, we analyze two second-order nondegenerate systems: a caged Coulomb problem on a 2-sphere and its contraction to a Euclidean caged Coulomb problem. In every instance, the structure of the symmetry algebra yields detailed insights into the trajectories. A particularly intriguing case involves "metronome orbits"—trajectories restricted to an arc rather than a full loop—which are readily identified through structure equations but might be missed by conventional methods. We also address the Post-Winternitz system, a classical fourth-order superintegrable system that resists solution via separation of variables. Furthermore, we study a superintegrable system linked to the addition theorem for elliptic functions, where constants of motion are rational in momenta; this system is of special interest because its constants generate a closed polynomial algebra. Although this paper presents numerous new findings, the material is presented accessibly to facilitate entry into the theory of superintegrability for nonexperts.

This technical note outlines a collection of baseline tools designed for the automated processing of Danish text. These machine-learning-driven tools utilize natural language processing models trained on previously annotated documents. Hosted by ITU Copenhagen, they will remain permanently free to access.

Classical-quantum hybrid algorithms have recently attracted considerable interest by integrating classical and quantum computing protocols to extract results from specific quantum circuits. Building on a 2019 study by Lubasch et al., which demonstrated readout capabilities for the Schrödinger and Inviscid Burgers equations using a novel variational quantum algorithm (VQA) to find the ground state of a cost function defined by variational parameters and a superposition of expectation values, this work examines further computational opportunities. We investigate whether the VQA can reliably solve other partial differential equations (PDEs) to an accuracy comparable to noiseless classical simulations. To assess the algorithm's capacity to handle nonlinearities in various initial value problems (IVPs), we analyze several PDEs, starting with the Navier-Stokes equations and extending to those modeling electromagnetism, gravitation, and wave propagation. This includes simulations of the Einstein, Boussinesq-type, Lin-Tsien, Camassa-Holm, Drinfeld-Sokolov-Wilson (DSW), and Hunter-Saxton equations. Supplementary sections provide the cost functions required for the VQA's optimization routines to numerically approximate solutions via quantum circuit readout, following simulations using hundreds of ZGR-QFT ansätze.

We generate infinite families of abstract regular polytopes with type $\{4,p_1,\ldots,p_{n-1}\}$ by extending centrally symmetric spherical abstract regular $n$-polytopes. Furthermore, utilizing the halving operation, we derive infinite families of regular hypertopes that are both locally spherical and locally toroidal, featuring the type $\left\{{p_1 \atop p_1},\ldots,p_{n-1}\right\}$.

This paper introduces both centralized and decentralized methodologies for analyzing and synthesizing networked systems consisting of interconnected non-linear subsystems, relying exclusively on subsystem dissipativity properties. Building upon recent work that formulated dissipativity-based centralized analysis as linear matrix inequality (LMI) problems, we first address four specific networked system configurations (NSCs) by providing centralized stability and dissipativity analysis techniques in the form of LMIs. Second, we demonstrate that centralized interconnection topology synthesis for these NSCs can also be formulated as LMI problems, allowing for the optimization of specific stability and dissipativity measures by designing the subsystem interconnections. Furthermore, we illustrate that the proposed analysis and synthesis frameworks can be executed in a decentralized and compositional fashion, facilitating the convenient addition or removal of subsystems. Finally, we present numerical examples to validate our contributions.

This work introduces a variant of contextual linear bandits inspired by routing tasks in navigation engines and recommendation systems. The objective is to infer a hidden $d$-dimensional vector $w^*$. In each round, a set of candidate actions $\mathcal{X}_t \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is provided. Selecting an action $x_t$ yields a utility of $\langle x_t, w^* \rangle$, but the learner only observes the index of the optimal action, defined as $\arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{X}_t} \langle x, w^* \rangle$. We propose algorithms achieving $O(d\log T)$ regret and $\exp(O(d \log d))$ complexity. These methods employ novel cutting-plane algorithms with minimized "regret," measured as the cumulative distance between $w^*$ and the hyperplanes supplied by the separation oracle. Additionally, we address a scenario allowing multiple recommendations, presenting an algorithm with $O(d^2 \log d)$ regret and a list size polynomial in $d$. Furthermore, we develop nearly tight algorithms for a weaker setting where feedback indicates only whether an action outperforms the recommendation. Our findings leverage new techniques in convex geometry, such as a variation of Steiner's formula for the centroid of a convex set, which hold independent significance.

We begin by deriving the Hamilton-Jacobi framework for continuous-time Markov processes and subsequently utilize this construction to formulate a variational algorithm for estimating escape paths—defined as the least improbable or first-passage trajectories—in generic stochastic chemical reaction networks featuring multiple fixed points. Our algorithm's design ensures independence from the system's dimensionality, employs discretization parameters that converge toward the continuum limit, and includes a readily calculable metric to verify solution accuracy. We demonstrate the algorithm's utility through several applications, validating its results against computationally intensive benchmarks such as the shooting method and stochastic simulation. Although our approach integrates theoretical methods from mathematical physics, numerical optimization, and chemical reaction network theory, we aim for practical relevance to an interdisciplinary audience encompassing chemists, biologists, optimal control theorists, and game theorists.

Extensive research indicates that multi-task learning leverages the assumption that various tasks share a low-rank, latent common subspace, making joint learning superior to independent approaches. This paper introduces two new multi-task learning frameworks utilizing specific regularization terms designed to identify the optimal shared latent subspace by minimizing exactly the $k$ smallest singular values. These regularization terms offer tighter approximations to rank minimization than the trace norm; however, solving exact rank minimization is an NP-hard challenge. To address this, we develop a novel iterative strategy based on re-weighting, which tactically manages the exact rank minimization issue by employing a large penalizing parameter. Experiments on benchmark datasets confirm that our methods successfully recover the low-rank structure shared across tasks and outperform existing multi-task learning techniques.

This document serves as a reproducibility report for "FDA: Fourier Domain Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation," presented at CVPR 2020 within the ML Reproducibility Challenge 2020. The original code was provided by the author. A thoroughly commented version, incorporating all ablation studies from the original work and featuring WANDB integration, can be found at <github.com/thefatbandit/FDA>, complete with detailed README instructions for running the experiments.

This paper details the enhancements and performance of Gator, a high-purity germanium counting facility designed for low-background $\gamma$-ray spectrometry. Located at the Gran Sasso Underground Laboratory in Italy at an average depth of 3600 meters water equivalent, Gator supports material screening and selection for ultra-low background experiments in astroparticle physics. The detector features a passive shield composed of copper, lead, and polyethylene layers, with the sample cavity flushed with pressurized gaseous nitrogen to suppress radon. Following an upgrade to its enclosure, the background rate decreased by 20% to (82.0$\pm$0.7) counts/(kg$\cdot$day) within the 100 keV to 2700 keV energy range. We present the temporal stability of various operational parameters, outline the sample analysis protocol, and validate Gator's sensitivity by analyzing a candidate photosensor for the DARWIN experiment.

Ensuring safety is essential for deploying reinforcement learning (RL) in safety-critical environments. Although current safe exploration techniques offer safety guarantees under regularity assumptions, they struggle to scale to large real-world problems. We introduce SPO-LF, a new algorithm that optimizes agent policies by learning the relationship between locally sensed features and environmental rewards or safety via generalized linear function approximations. We establish theoretical guarantees regarding both safety and optimality. Experimental results demonstrate that SPO-LF outperforms prior safe RL methods with theoretical guarantees by requiring fewer samples and less computational effort, while also being more scalable. Furthermore, it achieves comparable sample efficiency and superior safety when compared to existing advanced deep RL approaches with safety constraints.

Three primary segregation and pattern formation mechanisms have been identified in granular mixtures within a rotating cylindrical drum: radial segregation, axial banding, and the long-term coarsening of these band patterns. While the causes of radial segregation are well-established and several models exist for axial banding, the mechanism driving long-term coarsening has remained elusive. We show that unidirectional flow between bands in axially segregated patterns arises from slight size variations among small beads located at the band edges. This size difference becomes effective across all experiments involving polydisperse beads due to an unrecognized process of microsegregation within each band of small particles. Consequently, the stability of individual bands can be readily controlled through minor adjustments to their composition. These findings indicate that a new mechanism must be identified as the driving force behind axial particle flow, and we propose several potential hypotheses for this phenomenon.

In stereoscopic display systems that utilize polarization to separate channels for each eye, the screen is a critical component. The overall image quality is dictated by two factors: crosstalk, which reflects the screen's ability to maintain the polarization of the incoming signal, and the scattering rate, which indicates how effectively the screen directs light to the viewer. Both of these metrics vary depending on the viewing angle. This study evaluates the performance of three silver screens and three rear-projection screens, alongside measurements of their surface textures using white-light interferometry. Although some optical results can be attributed to surface roughness, further research is required to fully understand the screens' optical properties through a microscopic model.

A core challenge in the physics of living systems involves identifying how a few macroscopic variables arise from numerous microscopic components. During evolution, gene regulatory networks were shaped to ensure that the expression of target genes remains stable against environmental fluctuations. Subsequently, the expression levels of the remaining genes increased autonomously as a plastic response. An inverse relationship was detected between the average changes in target and residual genes, illustrating a reciprocity between the macroscopic robustness of homeostatic genes and the plasticity of regulator genes. This reciprocity adheres to the lever principle, which has been maintained throughout evolutionary history, thereby establishing a specific evolutionary constraint.

Utilizing ab initio calculations, we investigate the electronic structure at the interface of the BiTeI/MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ heterostructure, which combines the polar semiconductor trilayer BiTeI with the anti-ferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi$_2$Te$_4$. Our results reveal distinct electronic characteristics depending on the contact configuration between the substrate and the overlayer. In the Te-Te interface scenario, the Dirac cone states are primarily located within the polar overlayer region and experience minor exchange splitting, effectively representing a natural extension of the substrate. Conversely, the Te-I contact generates a four-band state arising from the combination of the substrate's Dirac cone and the Rashba-type state of the polar trilayer. Due to magnetic proximity effects, the Kramers degeneracy of this state is lifted, resulting in a Hall response during transport. We conclude that these findings offer promising avenues for developing novel spintronic devices.

This research investigates the electric double layer adjacent to a charged soft surface using a mean-field framework that accounts for non-uniform size effects and solvent polarization. By employing a free energy model, we numerically determine the electrostatic potential and the number densities of water and ions by solving a system of coupled differential equations that incorporate Poisson's equation. Our findings indicate that solvent polarization substantially influences the electrostatic potential, ion concentrations, and permittivity within an electrolyte solution near a charged soft surface. We demonstrate that including solvent polarization amplifies the magnitude of the Donnan potential. Furthermore, we show that within the fixed charge layer, the number densities of both counterions and coions are marginally lower when solvent polarization is considered compared to when it is ignored. Additionally, increasing ionic size intensifies the impact of solvent polarization on the electrostatic properties inside the fixed charged layer of the charged soft surface. Finally, in regions characterized by high surface charge density, water polarization causes a significant reduction in both permittivity and the number density of water dipoles.

Multiband superconductors support collective excitations that differ significantly from those in single-band systems. We initially examine the spectrum of collective amplitude fluctuations in a clean two-band superconductor, demonstrating that the spectral weight of the Higgs mode diverges quickly from the simple extension of the single-band scenario once interband coupling is introduced. These findings are then applied to critically evaluate the non-linear optical response in MgB$_2$, offering an explanation for conflicting recent experimental results by highlighting the selective importance of either the Leggett mode or amplitude fluctuations at twice the lower gap. Employing exact numerical simulations alongside realistic disorder estimates, we calculate the relative contributions of quasiparticle, amplitude, and phase fluctuations to the non-linear optical response. We demonstrate that at low pumping frequencies, only the resonance at twice the smaller gap appears due to the BCS response, whereas the Leggett mode prevails only within a narrow band of higher pumping frequencies corresponding to its low-temperature value. Our results offer a new perspective on the utility of non-linear THz spectroscopy for detecting collective modes in other multiband systems, such as iron-based superconductors.

A crucial permutation is defined as one that evades a specific set of prohibitions, yet any permissible extension of it inevitably introduces a violation. This paper introduces five distinct categories of crucial permutations relative to monotone patterns, with a particular focus on quadrocrucial permutations, which bear a strong resemblance to Erd\H{o}s-Szekeres extremal permutations. The definitions provided for right-crucial and bicrucial permutations align with those found in existing literature concerning other types of prohibitions. For each of the five categories, we offer a characterization utilizing Young tableaux through the RSK correspondence. Leveraging these characterizations, we demonstrate that the count of such permutations of length $n$ increases as $n$ approaches infinity, and we enumerate minimal crucial permutations in all cases except one. Additionally, we present further enumerative findings.

This study bridges the gap between language model adaptation and machine learning theory. It examines a training scenario involving a large out-of-domain dataset paired with a small in-domain one, deriving how the advantages of training on either set vary based on their respective sizes and the divergence between their underlying distributions. The analysis demonstrates that out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain fine-tuning yields superior generalization compared to using either dataset alone. Furthermore, it establishes a unified framework for adaptation techniques rooted in data selection—including importance sampling, intelligent data selection, and influence functions—thereby illuminating both their shared characteristics and nuanced distinctions.

Addressing communication bottlenecks and data privacy in federated multi-armed bandit (MAB) scenarios—such as wireless-connected vehicle decision-making and recommendation systems—this paper proposes a communication-efficient, privacy-preserving algorithm. We investigate the interplay between privacy, communication overhead, and learning performance, measured by regret. Specifically, we develop privacy-aware learning algorithms and communication protocols, deriving regret bounds for online bandit learning by networked private agents across master-worker, decentralized, and hybrid architectures. Our approach relies on epoch-wise sub-optimal arm elimination at individual agents, with knowledge exchange occurring between agents and the server at the conclusion of each epoch. To ensure data privacy during information exchange, we employ differential privacy (DP), while reducing communication costs by limiting the frequency of updates and the number of participating agents. Through theoretical analysis of the proposed framework in all three structures, we demonstrate the trade-offs among regret, communication costs, and privacy. Finally, empirical results confirm these theoretical trade-offs, aligning with our analytical findings.

Tor, an anonymity network relying on onion routing, has proven susceptible to Website Fingerprinting (WF), a technique that de-anonymizes users by examining unique patterns in encrypted traffic. While numerous defensive measures have been suggested, most have either been simulated or lack real-world deployment, raising concerns that synthetic simulations may not accurately reflect actual performance. To address this, we introduce WFDefProxy, a versatile platform designed to implement WF defenses on Tor via pluggable transports. We present the first complete real-world implementations of three specific defenses: FRONT, Tamaraw, and Random-WT. By comparing simulation results with our practical deployments, we determined that simulations accurately predict the efficacy of these defenses against attacks. However, our findings confirm that Random-WT is ineffective in both environments, reducing the strongest attacker's accuracy by merely 7%. We also observed minor discrepancies in overhead between simulated and real implementations, likely stemming from simulation assumptions regarding packet delays, queuing, or the soft stop condition we implemented in WFDefProxy to detect page load completion. Specifically, FRONT's real-world implementation incurred approximately 23% more data overhead than predicted, whereas Tamaraw's implementation required 28% to 45% less data overhead. Furthermore, Tamaraw's actual time overhead was only 21%, significantly lower than the 242% to 51% range estimated in prior simulated studies.

We project the number of galaxy clusters detectable through thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) signals by upcoming cosmic microwave background (CMB) missions, focusing on CMB-S4's extensive wide-area survey, its deep delensing survey, and the proposed CMB-HD experiment. Our predictions indicate that CMB-S4 will identify 75,000 clusters across a 50% sky coverage ($f_{\rm sky}$) in its wide survey and 14,000 clusters in its 3% sky coverage ($f_{\rm sky}$) deep survey. Among these, roughly 1,350 clusters will reside at redshifts $z \ge 2$, a range challenging for optical and X-ray observations. Assuming CMB-HD covers the same area as CMB-S4's wide survey, we estimate it will detect three times as many total clusters and ten times as many clusters at $z \ge 2$ compared to CMB-S4. These forecasts account for atmospheric and instrumental noise, as well as galactic and extragalactic foregrounds. By leveraging CMB-cluster lensing to calibrate the tSZ-mass scaling relation, we combine cluster counts with primary CMB data to constrain a two-parameter extension of the standard model ($\Lambda$CDM + $\sum m_{\nu}$ + $w_{0}$). In addition to limiting $\sigma(w_{0})$ to less than 1%, both surveys could achieve a $2.5$ to $4.5\sigma$ detection of $\sum m_{\nu}$, significantly enhancing CMB-only limits. Furthermore, modeling cluster virialization ${\rm v}(z)$ allows us to study intracluster medium evolution, yielding tight constraints from CMB-S4 and improvements by factors of 3 to 4 with CMB-HD. Associated products, including binned cluster counts and Fisher matrices, are available for download at https://github.com/sriniraghunathan/tSZ_cluster_forecasts.

We introduce a size-consistent Gr\"uneisen-quasiharmonic approach (GQA) designed to compute lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa_l$), where Gr\"uneisen parameters—quantifying phonon anharmonicity—are derived directly via first-principles calculations. This method involves identifying and adjusting two equations linked to the Slack formulae for $\kappa_l$, which previously exhibited size-inconsistency issues in non-monoatomic primitive cells (where the atom count $n$ exceeds one). Alongside other thermal parameters like the acoustic Debye temperature ($\theta_a$), obtainable within the GQA framework, we predicted $\kappa_l$ across various materials including diamond, zincblende, rocksalt, and wurtzite structures. Our predictions were benchmarked against experimental data and the quasiharmonic Debye model (QDM). Generally, the GQA, experiments, and QDM yielded consistent results for $\theta_a$. However, while the QDM tended to overestimate Gr\"uneisen parameters and consequently underestimate $\kappa_l$ for most materials, the GQA aligned more closely with experimental trends for both Gr\"uneisen parameters and $\kappa_l$. We anticipate that the GQA, utilizing modified Slack formulae, will serve as an efficient and practical tool for predicting $\kappa_l$, particularly in crystals with large $n$.

This study analyzes the impact of introducing political outsiders into the nomination process preceding an election. To achieve this, we construct a sequential game in which politicians—both insiders and outsiders—submit platform proposals to a party, which then decides which offer to accept; this sequence ultimately shapes the voting ballot. Central to evaluating the compatibility between a party and a candidate is "partisan affect," a variable reflecting voters' attitudes toward the party that can positively or negatively bias the electorate's assessment of a match. We identify the conditions under which an outsider is nominated and assess whether their inclusion as a potential candidate influences the winning policy and voter welfare. Our findings indicate that an outsider's victory typically results in policy polarization, and that partisan affect exerts a more substantial influence on welfare than ideology extremism.

Variational (or parameterized) quantum circuits are architectures incorporating real-valued parameters that require optimization to achieve specific computational goals, where analytic derivatives are preferable to numerical ones for this training process. While parameter shift rules have been widely studied as a method for obtaining these derivatives through statistical estimators, this paper employs Fourier Analysis to characterize the complete set of shift rules capable of computing a fixed partial derivative within a multi-parameter VQC. Furthermore, by applying Convex Optimization, we demonstrate that identifying the shift rule with the minimal standard deviation results in a primal-dual pair of convex optimization problems. We provide a theoretical analysis of these problems, establish a strong duality theorem, and utilize it to derive optimal dual solutions for various VQC families. These findings not only confirm the optimality of certain existing shift rules but also resolve an outstanding open question. Additionally, as a secondary contribution, we illustrate how optimal shift rules can be efficiently computed and how known optimal dual solutions facilitate this process.

Modern Autonomous Vehicle (AV) systems incorporate machine learning and probabilistic methods, introducing substantial complexity to conventional verification and validation processes. Consequently, scenario-based testing has gained widespread acceptance within both industry and academia over the past few years due to its ability to target critical road situations and streamline testing efforts. Effectively evaluating the System Under Test (SUT) in this framework requires accurately encoding real-world traffic behavior, which necessitates extracting scenario parameters from actual data to ensure realistic simulations. This paper primarily focuses on identifying a set of meaningful parameters that adequately model real-world lane-change events. Utilizing these parameters enables the construction of a parameter space capable of efficiently generating a diverse range of challenging scenarios for AV evaluation. We validate our methodology by comparing generated scenarios against real-world trajectory data using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Furthermore, we demonstrate that minor perturbations to specific parameters can yield distinct scenarios and apply the Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS) metric to assess the associated risks.

Although particle paths contain information about the underlying forces, robustly recovering these forces from the paths is difficult. Positional measurement errors can distort data, and sparse sampling often restricts information in high-energy zones like barriers. We propose a Bayesian framework capable of inferring potentials of any shape while accounting for measurement noise. Replacing Gaussian process priors, we introduce structured kernel interpolation to the natural sciences, enabling the analysis of large datasets. This approach is validated using one- and two-dimensional experimental trajectories of particles confined by a feedback trap.

Functional dependencies (FDs) and multi-valued dependencies (MVDs) serve as cornerstones in database schema design, just as probabilistic conditional independences (CIs) are vital for analyzing multivariate probability distributions. The implication problem determines whether a set of antecedent constraints entails a consequent constraint, a topic explored in both database and AI fields under the premise that constraints are strictly exact. However, contemporary applications often deal with constraints that hold only approximately. This paper introduces the concept of approximate implication as a linear inequality relating the satisfaction degrees of antecedents and consequents, focusing on the relaxation problem: identifying when an exact implication yields an approximate one. Utilizing information theory to quantify satisfaction, we establish several key findings. First, we demonstrate that any implication derived from data dependencies (MVDs and FDs) can be relaxed into a simple linear inequality with a factor no greater than quadratic relative to the number of variables; this factor drops to 1 if the consequent is an FD. Second, we prove that while some CI implications admit no relaxation, all CI implications eventually relax "in the limit." Third, we show that the implication problem regarding differential constraints in market basket analysis also permits a relaxation with a factor of 1. Finally, we illustrate how these results can be derived using I-measure theory, which connects information-theoretic metrics with set theory. Our findings not only recover but occasionally extend prior knowledge, confirming that MVD and FD implications can be verified by examining only 2-tuple relations.

This work introduces the concept of convolution metrics within Finslerian geometry, defined as a function derived from a specific mathematical operation applied to two Finslerian metrics. The study examines fundamental properties of these convolution metrics and characterizes those that correspond to Riemannian, Minkowskian, and Randers types. Additionally, several examples of Finslerian convolutions are provided.

Although Bayesian optimization is a widely used formalism for global optimization, its high computational costs restrict its application to functions that are expensive to evaluate. In contrast, optimistic optimization offers a computationally more efficient alternative that leverages prior knowledge of the search space geometry through a dissimilarity function. This study explores how to merge the conceptual strengths of Bayesian optimization with the efficiency of optimistic optimization. By transforming a kernel into a dissimilarity measure, we develop an optimistic optimization algorithm tailored for Bayesian optimization that achieves a runtime of up to $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$. Our key findings indicate that for objectives with relatively low evaluation costs and stationary kernels, optimistic optimization is often significantly preferable to Bayesian optimization. However, for strongly coupled and parametric models, well-implemented Bayesian optimization can outperform optimistic approaches even when evaluation costs are low. We propose that a new research area exists between geometric and probabilistic search, characterized by methods that operate much faster than traditional Bayesian optimization while maintaining essential Bayesian functionalities.

Recent investigations into the Magellanic Clouds have identified a unique class of Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars characterized by WN3/O3 spectra that display both WR-like emission and O3 V-like absorption, yet at significantly lower luminosities than typical O3 V or WN stars. An analysis of the projected spatial distribution of these WN3/O3 stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) compared to O-type stars reveals a surprising result: they are among the most isolated massive stars. Their distribution closely resembles that of red supergiants, which are dominated by initial masses between 10 and 15 solar masses ($M_{\odot}$), making them far more dispersed than classical WR stars or luminous blue variables (LBVs). This lack of association with O-type star clusters strongly indicates that WN3/O3 stars are not evolved single massive stars (30 $M_{\odot}$ or greater). Instead, they likely originate from interacting binaries with lower initial masses (10–18 $M_{\odot}$). Binary evolution models suggest these stars were once primaries in this mass range that lost their hydrogen envelopes via non-conservative mass transfer from a low-mass secondary. We demonstrate that theoretical models of stripped binary stars align with the observed spectra and Hertzsprung-Russell diagram positions of WN3/O3 stars. Furthermore, monitoring radial velocities using high-resolution spectra can help detect low-mass companions or runaway motions. Given their lower initial masses and environments distinct from those of very massive stars, WN3/O3 stars are consistent with being the progenitors of Type Ib and potentially Type Ibn supernovae.

After three and a half years of operation, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has identified approximately 5000 planets and candidates. As a second Extended Mission covering Years 5 through 7 approaches, it is timely to update forecasts for the TESS exoplanet yield. This study presents simulations estimating the number of detectable planets among 9.4 million AFGKM stars listed in the TESS Input Catalog Candidate Target List v8.01 over a seven-year mission duration. These simulations leverage enhanced models for photometric performance and temporal window functions, alongside a detection model refined using inject-and-recovery test results from the Kepler team. We estimate that the Prime Mission (Years 1–2) will yield 4719 ± 334 detectable planets, while the current Extended Mission (Years 3–4) will contribute an additional 3707 ± 209 planets. Under a proposed pointing scenario for the second Extended Mission (Years 5–7), we predict a further 4093 ± 180 planets, resulting in a total yield of 12519 ± 678. Additionally, we provide these yield predictions as functions of host star spectral type, planet radius, orbital period, follow-up feasibility, and habitable zone location, and we compare our estimates to the actual Prime Mission results, observing strong agreement.

This study investigates double-gluon charmonium ($\bar{c}ggc$) and bottomonium ($\bar{b}ggb$) hybrids with $1^{--}$ quantum numbers using QCD sum rules. Our calculations, which incorporate contributions up to dimension eight at leading order of $\alpha_s$ within the operator product expansion, estimate the hybrid charmonium mass ($M_{H_c}$) to be between 5.33 and 5.90 GeV, and the hybrid bottomonium mass ($M_{H_b}$) to lie in the range of 11.20 to 11.68 GeV. The predicted $\bar{c}ggc$ hybrid meson is expected to decay into pairs of charmed mesons or charmed mesons accompanied by a light meson. Specifically, we recommend searching for the $I^G(J^{PC})= 0^-(1^{--})$ $\bar{c}ggc$ hybrid in $D \bar{D}/D^* \bar{D}/D^{*} \bar{D}^{*}$ final states via P-wave transitions, and in $D^* \bar{D}^{*} \pi/D^* \bar{D}^*\eta/D \bar{D}\rho/D \bar{D}\omega$ channels via S-wave transitions. These decay modes are potentially accessible through experiments at Belle II, PANDA, Super-B, GlueX, and LHCb.

This study utilizes mimetic $f(R,T)$ gravity, incorporating a Lagrange multiplier and a mimetic potential, to generate inflationary cosmological solutions that align with recent Planck and BICEP2/Keck Array data. We introduce three viable solutions for the Hubble parameter ($H$), defined as $H(N)=\left(A \exp \beta N+B \alpha ^N\right)^{\gamma }$, $H(N)=\left(A \alpha ^N+B \log N\right)^{\gamma }$, and $H(N)=\left(A e^{\beta N}+B \log N\right)^{\gamma }$, where $A$, $\beta$, $B$, $\alpha$, and $\gamma$ are adjustable parameters and $N$ denotes the number of e-foldings. The analysis employs the minimal $f(R,T)$ model given by $f(R,T)= R + \chi T$, with $\chi$ serving as the model parameter. We demonstrate that viable cosmologies consistent with observational data are achieved within this $f(R,T)$ framework by appropriately selecting the Lagrange multiplier and the mimetic potential.

We examine autonomous conservative dynamical systems restricted to a fixed total energy level. A theorem is established that derives quadratic first integrals (QFIs)—both autonomous and time-dependent—from the symmetries, specifically conformal Killing vectors and tensors, of the kinetic metric. The analysis identifies three distinct types of QFIs and provides explicit computational formulas for each. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that considering autonomous QFIs yields results consistent with prior literature. In the case of a zero potential, corresponding to constrained geodesics, specific formulas for computing QFIs are derived. The theorem is applied in two scenarios: first, to identify potentials supporting the second type of QFI, recovering an Ermakov-type superintegrable potential and discovering a new integrable potential with circular trajectories at zero energy and zero QFI; second, to integrate constrained geodesic equations for a family of two-dimensional conformally flat metrics.

As the Internet has evolved, individuals have established numerous personal profiles on social media platforms, and recent interactions within these networks have increasingly included location data. This study examines user engagement across Facebook and Twitter to identify the factors influencing retweets and likes. Beyond analyzing named entities, lexical errors, and expressed sentiments, we also evaluate the influence of shared user locations on interaction patterns. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that user geolocations significantly impact which posts or tweets receive likes or retweets. We believe these insights will assist researchers in determining how to enhance the visibility of social network content.

This document outlines the ALICE Collaboration's strategy for a significant detector upgrade, designated ALICE 3, intended for use during LHC Run 5 and subsequent operations. ALICE 3 will facilitate a comprehensive initiative to maximize the LHC's potential for investigating the properties of strongly interacting matter through high-energy nuclear collisions. The proposed detector configuration, utilizing advanced silicon sensors, offers exceptional pointing resolution, superior tracking and particle identification across a wide acceptance range, and high readout rates. Furthermore, this document examines the suggested physics program, the detector concept, and its performance capabilities regarding a series of benchmark measurements.

This research examines a cluster Ising model featuring a non-Hermitian external field, which admits an exact solution using free fermions. By analyzing the second derivative of energy density and fidelity, we tentatively identify potential new critical points. Subsequently, string order parameters and staggered magnetization are employed to uncover emergent phases with unique characteristics. To classify the exotic phases and transitions arising from non-Hermiticity, we compute the variation modes of the spin correlation function and string parameter, which reveal distinct decay patterns and critical exponents for these emergent states. Leveraging string order parameters and staggered magnetization, we identify four distinct phases introduced by non-Hermiticity: the cluster, gapless, paramagnetic (PM), and antiferromagnetic (AF) phases. We present a phase diagram that visually depicts the formation of three critical lines as non-Hermitian strength increases, corresponding to two "KT-like" transitions and one Ising transition. This theoretical framework is anticipated to be experimentally realized in ultra-cold atom systems, thereby advancing the exploration of novel phases and transitions.

Typically, conventional superconductivity and magnetism act as competing phenomena, a dynamic that in certain alloys depends on elemental concentration. This study demonstrates that in palladium alloys of the form Pd$_{1-c}$(H/D/T)$_{c}$ (Pd-ides), increasing the concentration $c$ of hydrides (hydrogen, deuterium, or tritium) progressively suppresses the predicted magnetism of amorphous palladium ($a$-Pd). This suppression enables superconductivity to emerge when $c \approx 40\%$. The presence of this magnetism accounts for the absence of superconductivity at lower concentrations ($c \leq 40\%$). Furthermore, these findings indirectly corroborate our prior predictions regarding magnetism in amorphous/porous palladium ($a/p$-Pd). Gaining insight into the interplay between magnetism and superconductivity could enhance our understanding of magnetic behaviors in materials, particularly in high $T_{c}$ superconductors, with significant implications.

High-harmonic generation (HHG) in solids offers a novel approach to investigating ultrafast electron dynamics at the attosecond level. This study examines HHG in both monolayer and bilayer graphene, specifically analyzing bilayer configurations with AA and AB stacking. Results indicate that the harmonic spectra of monolayer and bilayer graphene differ markedly, a distinction primarily attributed to interlayer coupling. Furthermore, both intraband and interband contributions significantly influence the total harmonic spectrum. Additionally, distinct polarization and ellipticity dependencies are observed in the total harmonic spectra for both monolayer and bilayer graphene.

We introduce a novel solution within Einstein-Maxwell theory, representing the magnetized counterpart of the Kerr-Taub-NUT solution. This study examines various properties of the resulting spacetime and calculates the entropy of an extremal black hole residing therein by applying the Kerr/CFT correspondence framework.

The so-called 3-3-1 models have been extensively explored in the literature; however, in nearly every instance, along with other frameworks, only simplified variants have been examined. Meanwhile, the LHC has neither confirmed nor ruled out any specific model. In this paper, we address several aspects of 3-3-1 models that require theoretical investigation and potential experimental re-analysis. Some of these issues are universal, remaining independent of the specific representation content or the value of the $\beta$ parameter, whereas others are highly dependent on the particular model under consideration.

Accurately estimating the rotation of known rigid objects is crucial for robotics tasks like dexterous manipulation. While most current approaches rely on intermediate representations—such as templates, feature descriptors, or object coordinates—necessitating multiple inference steps, we propose a method that directly regresses a pose vector from raw point cloud segments using a convolutional neural network. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods while demonstrating greater robustness to occlusion. Furthermore, our method eliminates the need for post-processing steps, such as refinement via the iterative closest point algorithm.

We establish an infinitesimal rigidity result for the strain tensor of surfaces exhibiting sign-changing curvatures. As a direct application, we determine that the optimal constant in the first Korn inequality for such mixed-type shells scales proportionally to $h^{4/3}$.

Object-oriented programming (OOP) has historically been viewed as inefficient for SIMD high-performance computing (HPC), even though many critical HPC applications naturally possess an object-based structure. On SIMD accelerators like GPUs, this limitation stems primarily from memory allocation and access issues. Although a few libraries offer parallel memory allocation for accelerator devices, they all suffer from uncoalesced memory accesses.

We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over raw (de)allocation speed. Benchmark results show that DynaSOAr accelerates application code by up to 3x compared to current state-of-the-art allocators. Furthermore, its superior heap memory management allows programmers to execute problem sizes up to 2x larger within the same memory constraints.

Due to varying training backgrounds and clinical experiences, radiologists often generate diverse segmentation annotations for lung nodules. While conventional studies typically select a single annotation as the learning target, this approach discards valuable insights found within the consensus or disagreements among multiple annotations. To address this, we propose the Uncertainty-Guided Segmentation Network (UGS-Net), which extracts rich visual features from regions prone to segmentation uncertainty to improve overall performance. Equipped with an Uncertainty-Aware Module, the network generates a Multi-Confidence Mask (MCM) that highlights areas with varying levels of segmentation uncertainty. Additionally, a Feature-Aware Attention Module is introduced to strengthen the learning of nodule boundaries and density variations. Experimental results on the LIDC-IDRI dataset demonstrate that our method can effectively predict nodule regions across different uncertainty levels while achieving superior performance.

We demonstrate that the three-dimensional asymptotically linear dilaton background, emerging in the near-horizon decoupling region of NS5-branes compactified on $T^4$, supports boundary conditions yielding an infinite spectrum of symmetries. The resulting conserved charges, which enact field-dependent coordinate transformations, are identical to the corresponding generators in a symmetric product orbifold of $T\bar T$-deformed CFTs. Their algebra represents a non-linear deformation of the $\mathrm{Virasoro \times Virasoro}$ algebra, matching exactly the algebra of the ``unrescaled'' symmetry generators in $T\bar T$-deformed CFTs. This result further reinforces a previously suggested connection between the single-trace $T\bar T$ deformation and compactified little string theory.

Component-based program synthesis typically involves generating a program using a library of functions, yet existing synthesizers struggle with loops and other control structures and often depend on costly formal component specifications. We introduce FrAngel, a novel approach that synthesizes short Java functions containing control structures given only a target signature, input-output examples, and a library set, without requiring formal specs. FrAngel seeks to discover programs with diverse behaviors by integrating two core strategies.
