First, it extracts code fragments from partially successful programs that satisfy only a subset of examples, leveraging a concept termed "special-case similarity" to find these fragments useful for synthesis. Second, FrAngel employs angelic conditions as placeholders for control structure logic, allowing for optimistic evaluation of program sketches. This use of angelic conditions breaks the synthesis process into two stages: initially identifying promising partial programs and subsequently filling in their missing conditions. Our results show that FrAngel can generate various programs involving combined control structures within seconds, significantly surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods.

Recent studies utilizing deep neural networks (DNNs) to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) have shown that spatiotemporal function approximators based on auto-differentiation are highly effective for nonlinear problems, including the Burgers' equation, heat conduction, Allen-Cahn, other reaction-diffusion equations, and the Navier-Stokes equation. Concurrently, researchers have employed automatic differentiation within physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to address nonlinear hyperbolic systems with highly discontinuous transitions, such as Riemann problems, by formulating inverse problems through data-driven methods. However, forward methods relying on DNNs without prior knowledge of the solution struggle to resolve discontinuities in nonlinear conservation laws. To overcome this, the present study integrates first-order numerical schemes into DNNs to construct the loss functional approximator, replacing the traditional auto-differentiation approach used in frameworks like TensorFlow, thereby enhancing the model's ability to capture discontinuities in Riemann problems. Specifically, this work introduces the 2-Coarse-Grid neural network (2CGNN) and the 2-Diffusion-Coefficient neural network (2DCNN). These networks utilize two solutions from a converging sequence of a conservation law, calculated via a low-cost numerical scheme, as inputs within the domain of dependence of a space-time grid point to predict the high-fidelity solution at that point. Despite receiving smeared input solutions, the networks produce sharp approximations for solutions containing shocks and contacts and remain efficient once trained.

This paper investigates the Degrees-of-Freedom (DoF) in a wireless scenario where K Transmitters (TXs) jointly serve K users. The analysis focuses on a distributed Channel State Information (CSI) setup where each TX designs its transmit coefficients using its own multi-user imperfect channel estimate. These estimates are characterized by both acquisition imperfections and imperfect sharing among the TXs. Our primary contributions include deriving a genie-aided upper bound for the DoF in this setting and proposing a novel robust transmission scheme that exploits the varying qualities of available CSI to enhance DoF performance. We demonstrate that in a specific regime termed the "Weak-CSIT regime," the proposed scheme achieves the genie-aided upper bound. Notably, within this regime, the optimal DoF relies exclusively on the CSI quality of the most informed TX, remaining independent of the CSI quality at all other transmitters.

High-Mass X-ray Binaries (HMXBs) emerge following the initial supernova in a massive binary system. These systems are inherently young and often experience substantial natal kicks, suggesting their progenitors likely originated far from their current X-ray emitting locations. Our objective is to identify the birthplaces of known Galactic HMXBs, specifically investigating whether their formation correlates with open stellar clusters or Galactic spiral arms to estimate the time elapsed since the first supernova. Utilizing astrometric data from Gaia EDR3, we initialized the positions and velocities of all known Galactic HMXBs and integrated their trajectories backward in time. Simultaneously, we applied identical calculations to a sample of 1,381 Gaia-detected open clusters and four modeled Galactic spiral arms. We report all past encounters between HMXBs and clusters or spiral arms within the last 100 Myr. Among our sample of 26 HMXBs, we deduced that 7 were born in clusters, 8 near a spiral arm, and 7 likely formed in isolation. The origins of the remaining 4 remain uncertain due to their great distance, limited astrometric precision, and the absence of nearby known clusters. We have determined kinematic ages for 15 HMXBs. Our results demonstrate that Gaia astrometry combined with orbit integration effectively locates HMXB birthplaces in the Milky Way. After accounting for data and methodological biases, we conclude that HMXB progenitors preferentially formed alongside other massive stars within open clusters.

The growing prevalence of offensive language on social media has become a significant societal concern, necessitating automated solutions to manage the vast daily volume of content. While existing research has predominantly addressed this issue in English, the challenge is inherently multilingual. We introduce a novel Danish dataset comprising user-generated comments from Reddit and Facebook; to our knowledge, this is the first of its kind. The dataset is annotated to identify various types and targets of offensive language. We developed four automatic classification systems capable of operating in both English and Danish. For English offensive language detection, the top-performing system achieved a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.74, whereas the best Danish system reached 0.70. Regarding the detection of whether a post is targeted, the leading English system scored 0.62, while the Danish counterpart achieved 0.73. Furthermore, in classifying the target type within targeted offensive posts, the best English system attained an F1-score of 0.56, compared to 0.63 for the Danish system. Our work provides automatic methods for identifying different forms of offensive language, such as hate speech and cyberbullying, for both languages by capturing their types and targets.

This work investigates Besov-type decomposition spaces, which form scales linked to specific coverings of Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ or its open subsets. A key, yet poorly understood issue in this field is determining when distinct coverings generate identical scales of decomposition spaces. We introduce a coarse geometric framework to address this problem, demonstrating its application to wavelet coorbit spaces tied to a specific class of matrix groups $H < GL(\mathbb{R}^d)$ that act through dilations. Recognizing this class as a subset of decomposition spaces, we show that the equivalence of coorbit spaces for two dilation groups $H_1$ and $H_2$ can be resolved by examining whether a suitably defined map $\phi: H_1 \to H_2$ constitutes a quasi-isometry relative to appropriate word metrics. Furthermore, we apply this criterion to a broad category known as {\em shearlet dilation groups}, where the quasi-isometry condition admits an algebraic characterization. The paper concludes with an analysis of selected examples.

We report findings from a broad-field ALMA mosaic covering approximately 60 x 90 parsecs, mapping CO(2-1) and $^{13}$CO(2-1) emission within the molecular cloud linked to the 30 Doradus star-forming region. This analysis resolves three primary emission complexes into intricate filamentary networks; two of these form a bowtie shape extending northeast and southwest from the central R136 cluster. Aligning with prior research, we observe that the cloud's central region exhibits higher line widths at fixed sizes compared to both the remainder of the cloud and other Large Magellanic Cloud clouds, signaling intensified turbulent activity. Nevertheless, no distinct correlation emerges between gravitational boundedness (quantified by the virial parameter) and distance from R136. Structures detected in $^{13}$CO align spatially with filaments and reside near virial equilibrium. Conversely, CO structures display significant variation in virialization: low surface brightness features outside the main filamentary network are largely unbound. These faint structures, accounting for roughly 10% of the total measured CO luminosity, may represent shredded remnants of former star-forming clumps or the CO-emitting components of more massive, CO-dark entities.

This study examines the stability and collapse of fundamental unstaggered bright solitons within the discrete Schrödinger equation featuring nonpolynomial on-site nonlinearity, a model representing a nearly one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate in a deep optical lattice, specifically under the influence of long-range dipole-dipole interactions. Both attractive and repulsive scenarios for contact and dipole-dipole interactions are analyzed. Stability and collapse diagrams mapping the model's parametric space reveal that attractive dipole-dipole interactions enhance soliton stability and mitigate collapse, while the mobility of these discrete solitons is also briefly addressed.

A recent study derived and examined an explicit Robinson--Trautman solution featuring a minimally coupled free scalar field. The analysis revealed that this solution contains a curvature singularity that is initially naked before becoming hidden by a horizon. While the original work focused on the general case where all free constants are non-zero, interesting special cases emerge when certain parameters are set to zero; in most of these instances, the scalar field remains present. Notably, one such case yields a static solution representing a parametric limit of the Janis--Newman--Winicour scalar field spacetime. Furthermore, we compute the Bondi mass to clarify the interpretation of the general solution and, through a complex rotation of the parameter governing the scalar field's strength, derive a dynamical wormhole solution.

This study addresses lossy neural image compression (NIC). Existing state-of-the-art approaches utilize a uniform posterior to model quantization noise and a single-sample pathwise estimator to approximate the gradient of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). In contrast, this paper introduces training NIC using a multiple-sample importance weighted autoencoder (IWAE) target, which offers a tighter bound than ELBO and converges to the log likelihood as the sample size grows. Initially, we observe that the uniform posterior in NIC possesses unique characteristics that influence the variance and bias of both pathwise and score function estimators for the IWAE target. Additionally, we offer a gradient variance-based perspective on a common technique used in NIC. Leveraging these insights, we propose MS-NIC, an enhanced IWAE target specifically designed for NIC. Experimental outcomes indicate that MS-NIC outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, MS-NIC is plug-and-play and can be readily adapted to other neural compression applications.

Quantum algorithms tailored for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices typically necessitate extensive repeated measurements to estimate observable expectation values within many-qubit states. To mitigate this substantial measurement overhead, various advanced schemes have emerged by leveraging principles such as importance sampling, observable compatibility, and classical shadows. However, since the underlying mechanisms for reducing costs differ across these approaches, systematically identifying the optimal strategy remains a significant theoretical hurdle. This work addresses that challenge by introducing a unified quantum measurement framework that encompasses existing advanced methods as specific instances. Within this framework, we propose a general "overlapped grouping measurement" scheme that simultaneously capitalizes on the strengths of current techniques. We demonstrate that an optimal strategy involves partitioning observables into groups where members are mutually compatible, providing explicit strategies for such grouping and numerically validating performance across various molecular Hamiltonians. Our results indicate substantial improvements over existing methods, thereby establishing a foundation for efficient quantum measurements on near-term hardware.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a broad class of sublinear operators $T_\alpha$, where $\alpha\in[0,n)$, encompassing both Calderón-Zygmund operators (when $\alpha=0$) and fractional integral operators (when $\alpha>0$), within the framework of generalized mixed Morrey spaces $M^\varphi_{\vec{q}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Additionally, the study examines the boundedness of the commutators associated with $T_\alpha$ on these same spaces. As applications, the authors establish the boundedness properties for the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator, Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, fractional integral operators, fractional maximal operators, and their respective commutators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

It has been demonstrated that radially symmetric solutions to the repulsive Euler-Poisson equations with a non-zero background, representing cold plasma oscillations, exhibit blow-up in numerous spatial dimensions, excluding $\bd=4$, for almost all initial conditions. The specific initial data that allow solutions to avoid blow-up are associated with simple waves. Furthermore, any solution that remains globally smooth over time must either be affine or asymptotically approach an affine state as $t\to\infty$.

This paper investigates the minimal norm tensors for both general third and fourth covariant tensors, providing a novel interpretation of the Weyl and Cotton tensors: the Weyl tensor represents the minimal norm component of the Riemannian curvature tensor, while the Cotton tensor corresponds to the minimal norm component of the divergence of the Riemannian curvature tensor. Furthermore, we derive several useful inequalities by calculating the norms of these minimal norm tensors.

This work introduces the jet schemes associated with a holomorphic foliation, providing an alternative characterization of simple singularities for codimension-1 foliations that does not rely on any normal form. Consequently, we establish an equivalent criterion for the existence of a desingularization within the non-dicritical context. Finally, we present several results and conjectures regarding the conditions under which this criterion holds.

This paper introduces a new formulation of Shannon and Weaver's "effectiveness problem" [2] within a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) context, focusing on agents coordinating and cooperating over noisy channels. We model this scenario as a multi-agent partially observable Markov decision process (MA-POMDP) where agents interact with an environment and communicate with one another via a noisy channel. By explicitly integrating the noisy channel into the environmental dynamics and treating transmitted messages as agent actions, the framework enables agents to learn both collaboration and effective communication strategies despite channel noise. This approach generalizes traditional reliable communication problems and recent "learning to communicate" MARL models that assume error-free channels. Empirical examples demonstrate that the joint policies derived from this framework outperform those where communication is treated separately from the MA-POMDP. This robust framework holds significant real-world potential, ranging from autonomous vehicle planning to drone swarm control, while leveraging deep reinforcement learning to advance multi-user communication system design.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have recently demonstrated remarkable success in creating photo-realistic images from low-dimensional random noise. However, the capacity to produce high-quality content on a massive scale introduces significant risks, as generated samples can be used to spread misinformation, causing severe hazards in social, political, health, and business domains. We introduce SubsetGAN, a method designed to detect synthetic content by identifying specific subsets of anomalous node activations within the inner layers of pre-trained neural networks. These nodes collectively maximize a non-parametric divergence metric relative to the expected activation distribution of real data, allowing for the identification of synthesized images without requiring prior knowledge of their specific distribution. SubsetGAN efficiently evaluates node subsets and returns the group within a pre-trained classifier that yields the highest score. This classifier may be a general fake detector trained on multi-source samples or the discriminator network from various GANs. Our approach demonstrates consistently superior detection performance compared to existing methods across several state-of-the-art GAN architectures (PGGAN, StarGAN, and CycleGAN) and across varying proportions of generated content.

The CMS Collaboration at CERN's LHC reports a measurement of single top quark and W boson associated production from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=$ 13 TeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on events containing one electron and one muon in the final state, accompanied by at least one jet originating from a bottom quark. To distinguish the signal from the primary $\mathrm{t\overline{t}}$ background, a multivariate discriminant leveraging event kinematic properties was employed. The resulting cross section of $63.1 \pm 1.8$ (stat) $\pm 6.4$ (syst) $\pm 2.1$ (lumi) pb aligns with standard model predictions.

Node embedding stands as a core area within graph representation learning. Methods relying on full-graph computations often face significant hurdles regarding computational efficiency and scalability. To address this, we introduce sampling strategies for node embedding—whether explicitly modeling feature vectors or not—that are designed to capture meaningful information from both the graph Laplacian's eigenvectors and the associated node values.

Assuming the $K_0^\ast(1430)$ represents the ground state of $s\bar{q}$ or $q\bar{s}$, we investigate its leading-twist distribution amplitude, $\phi_{2;K_0^\ast}(x,\mu)$, utilizing QCD sum rules within the background field theory framework. We propose a more robust sum rule formula for the $\xi$-moments $\langle\xi^n\rangle_{2;K_0^\ast}$, specifically to mitigate issues arising from the inability to normalize the sum rule for $\langle\xi^0_p\rangle_{3;K_0^\ast}$ across the entire Borel region. Using this approach, we compute more precise values for the first ten $\xi$-moments ($n = 1, 2, \dots, 10$). Furthermore, we introduce a novel light-cone harmonic oscillator (LCHO) model for the $K_0^\ast(1430)$ leading-twist DA for the first time; by applying the least squares method to the calculated moments, we determine the DA's behavior under this model. Finally, employing light-cone QCD sum rules, we evaluate the transition form factors and branching fractions for the semileptonic decays $B_s, D_s \to K_0^\ast(1430) \ell \nu_\ell$. These numerical results are expected to facilitate the extraction of Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix elements when combined with future experimental data.

This study introduces novel algorithms for signomial programming, an extension of geometric programming, utilizing the MM algorithm, a universal optimization principle. By employing both the geometric-arithmetic mean inequality and a supporting hyperplane inequality, the approach constructs a surrogate function with decoupled parameters, thereby transforming unconstrained signomial programming into a series of one-dimensional minimization tasks. Illustrative examples show that the derived MM algorithm can converge to a boundary point or a single point within a continuum of minima. The paper also establishes conditions for the uniqueness of the minimum point or its occurrence within the parameter space interior for geometric programming, noting that convergence to an interior point happens at a linear rate. Furthermore, the MM framework readily integrates equality and inequality constraints of signomial type. Notably, for the critical special case of constrained quadratic programming, the MM algorithm requires only straightforward updates.

Multi-modal entity alignment seeks to identify equivalent entities across two distinct multi-modal knowledge graphs, which are composed of structural triples and entity-associated images. While prior research primarily focuses on encoding and utilizing information from various modalities, leveraging multi-modal knowledge for entity alignment remains challenging due to modality heterogeneity. To address this, we introduce MCLEA, a Multi-modal Contrastive Learning based Entity Alignment model designed to generate effective joint representations for multi-modal entity alignment. Unlike previous approaches, MCLEA accounts for task-oriented modalities and models inter-modal relationships within each entity representation. Specifically, MCLEA first learns multiple individual representations from various modalities and subsequently employs contrastive learning to jointly model intra-modal and inter-modal interactions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MCLEA surpasses state-of-the-art baselines on public datasets under both supervised and unsupervised settings.

Although hierarchical variational autoencoders (VAEs) excel at image modeling density estimation, their prior-generated samples often appear less realistic compared to models with equivalent log-likelihoods. We identify this issue as stemming from learned representations that excessively prioritize compressing visually imperceptible image details. To resolve this, we propose a KL-reweighting method to regulate information within each latent group and utilize a Gaussian output layer to mitigate sharpness in the learning objective. Furthermore, to balance image diversity against fidelity, we implement a classifier-free guidance strategy specifically for hierarchical VAEs. Our experimental results validate the efficacy of these approaches, with the code accessible at https://github.com/tcl9876/visual-vae.

We present a minimal toy model of unresolved irreducible uncertainty within a system utilizing hierarchical inference, consisting of a chain of unidirectionally coupled adaptive excitable elements driven stochastically from one end and open at the other. Threshold potentials adjust gradually to balance sensitivity with efficiency. Energy and activity manifest as intermittent pulse avalanches exhibiting a discrete scaling distribution that remains largely unaffected by the external input's form. Both subthreshold activities and threshold potentials display Lorentzian temporal spectra, where the power-law range depends on the element's position in the chain. The observed subthreshold bistability mirrors empirical data on intracellular membrane potentials. We propose that critical cortical cascades arise from balancing metabolic costs against performance needs in a critical environment, and that the temporal scaling patterns seen in brain electrophysiological recordings result from weighted linear combinations of subthreshold activities and pulses across various hierarchical levels.

This work presents the first theoretical development of neutrino-electron excitation at low energies within semiconductor detectors, incorporating screening effects under both the Standard Model and scenarios involving a neutrino magnetic moment. Utilizing linear response theory, we investigate how semiconductor screening influences excitation rates and provide corresponding numerical calculations. Our findings demonstrate that the screening effect dramatically amplifies excitation rates arising from the neutrino magnetic moment, thereby significantly enhancing sensitivity to levels as low as $10^{-13}\,\mu_{\rm B}$, which far surpasses existing laboratory and astrophysical constraints.

Null linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is a competitive dimensionality reduction technique, though its standard implementation is computationally intensive. To address this, a recent fast approach utilizing random matrix multiplication with scatter matrices was introduced. However, arbitrary selection of the random matrix can result in a rank-deficient orientation matrix, leading to the loss of valuable discriminant information. This paper examines the proper selection of the random matrix to ensure that the two theoretical criteria of null LDA are met. Furthermore, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition to guarantee that the orientation matrix maintains full column rank and provide a corresponding geometric characterization of this condition.

Gathering and sustaining precise world knowledge within the RoboCup 3D Soccer Simulation—a dynamic, intricate, adversarial, and stochastic setting—presents a significant challenge, particularly given the requirement for real-time learning under time pressure. To address this, we employ recently developed Off-Policy Gradient Descent algorithms within Reinforcement Learning to create learnable knowledge representations that facilitate dynamic role assignments. Our findings demonstrate that these agents have mastered competitive strategies against top-tier teams from the RoboCup 2012 competitions across 3v3, 5v5, and 7v7 matches. Furthermore, by utilizing specific subsets of agents, we identified the underlying dynamics and semantics that enable agents to maximize performance metrics and acquire knowledge regarding various objectives. This approach ensures that all agents contribute effectively and efficiently to the collective group.

Monitoring Earth's transformations, including urban expansion, deforestation, and natural disasters, is a rapidly growing research area. While satellite imagery offers a promising solution to these challenges, the massive storage requirements force users to predefine Areas of Interest, a limitation that hinders the detection of potential disaster or development zones. To address this issue, we developed GRASP EARTH, a novel, user-friendly change detection application built on Google Earth Engine. This tool simplifies the processing of satellite imagery and is designed for applications in disaster monitoring and tracking urban development.

In this study, we demonstrate that numerous fractal sets arising from specific dynamical systems comprise exclusively irrational numbers. As a practical application, we explicitly build several overlapping self-similar sets that contain solely irrationals.

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are increasingly utilized in music information retrieval tasks such as genre classification, mood detection, and chord recognition. Nevertheless, the mechanisms behind their learning and prediction processes remain poorly understood, especially when applied to spectrograms. This study introduces the concept of "CNN auralization" to elucidate these underlying mechanisms, utilizing a deconvolution method referenced in [2]. CNN auralization involves transforming convolutional features derived from deconvolution into audible audio signals. Through experimental analysis and discussion, we examine the trained features of a 5-layer CNN by analyzing both deconvolved spectrograms and their corresponding auralized outputs. Furthermore, we investigate pairwise correlations across layers with varying musical attributes to trace the evolution of learned features. Results indicate that in deeper layers, the network learns to capture textures and patterns of continuous distributions rather than distinct line shapes.

New invariants for 2-dimensional cell complexes are introduced, interpretable as curvature constraints. Their rationality and computability are established in a related paper. This document serves as a survey that compiles theorems regarding these invariants, calculates specific examples, and outlines a research agenda of conjectures.

Although image outpainting technology can generate visually plausible content, it remains unreliable for practical use due to concerns about authenticity, even when augmented with additional modalities like sketches. Given that sparse depth maps are commonly acquired alongside RGB images in robotics and autonomous systems, we integrate sparse depth into image outpainting to achieve more dependable results. Specifically, we introduce the Depth-Guided Outpainting Network (DGONet), which differentially models feature representations across modalities and learns structure-aware cross-modal fusion. This is achieved through two key components: 1) a Multimodal Learning Module that generates distinct feature representations for depth and RGB based on their unique characteristics, and 2) a Depth Guidance Fusion Module that utilizes the complete depth modality to steer RGB content generation via progressive multimodal feature fusion. Additionally, we implement a specialized constraint strategy comprising Cross-modal Loss and Edge Loss to refine ambiguous contours and accelerate the creation of reliable content. Extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset confirm our method's superiority over state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating more reliable content generation.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have become a cost- and energy-effective approach to boosting wireless communication capacity. However, recent research indicates that RIS-assisted systems often require excessively large surfaces to outperform conventional relays, and their performance gains are frequently diminished by hardware limitations, such as low-resolution phase shifters. To address these issues, we introduce a hybrid relay-reflecting intelligent surface (HR-RIS) concept. This architecture deploys one or a few elements equipped with power amplifiers (PAs) as active relays, while the remaining elements function solely as passive reflectors. We propose two architectures: fixed and dynamic HR-RIS. Using alternating optimization and power allocation strategies, we derive the coefficient matrices for these systems, offering insights into the fundamental trade-offs between RIS and relaying-based approaches. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed schemes significantly enhance both spectral efficiency (SE) and energy efficiency (EE) compared to traditional RIS-aided systems, with the dynamic HR-RIS yielding particularly favorable outcomes. Furthermore, the optimal design and deployment of HR-RIS are both analytically derived and numerically validated.

The global proliferation and ongoing mutation of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) make it essential to develop systems capable of detecting both established and emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants. Accurate variant identification is vital for modeling transmission dynamics, formulating effective containment measures, averting future outbreaks, evaluating vaccine efficacy, and predicting breakthrough infections. Notably, the spike protein harbors the majority of the genetic variation associated with these variants. This study leverages spike sequences to classify human coronavirus variants, demonstrating that maintaining the original amino acid order enhances classifier performance. Furthermore, we illustrate that our model can surpass baseline algorithms even with a minimal dataset (representing just 1% of the total data). Finally, we highlight the significance of specific amino acids in variant identification, confirming their alignment with the variants reported by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

We introduce an explicit sech-squared-soliton solution linked to the optical Pockels effect, which arises from frequency comb generation through parametric down-conversion in quadratic nonlinear optical microresonators. This soliton differs from the parametric sech-soliton that characterizes the half-harmonic field under large index mismatch conditions and is associated with the cascaded-Kerr effect. We forecast variations in the spectral profiles and power levels between Pockels and cascaded-Kerr solitons, and confirm that the pump power threshold for the Pockels soliton aligns with recent experimental findings.

Teichmüller space ($Teich$) is defined as the quotient of the space of all complex structures on a manifold $M$ by the connected components of its diffeomorphism group, while the mapping class group ($\Gamma$) of $M$ consists of those connected components themselves. Moduli problems can be interpreted as assertions regarding the action of $\Gamma$ on $Teich$. This presentation describes the mapping class group and Teichmüller space specifically for hyperkähler manifolds, demonstrating that the associated action is ergodic. Leveraging this ergodicity, I establish that a hyperkähler manifold cannot be Kobayashi hyperbolic. This submission, prepared for the ICM, includes a review of my work on Teichmüller spaces and moduli, with sketched proofs, new observations, and a discussion of open problems.

Multiple scattering can disperse a perfectly collimated beam, generating a speckle pattern and expanding the system's etendue. Since standard optical systems conserve etendue, they cannot reverse this process to convert a speckle pattern back into a collimated beam or a sharp focus. Wavefront shaping, however, allows for the manipulation of a light beam's amplitude and/or phase to control its propagation through such media. By enabling this control, wavefront shaping can circumvent etendue conservation and theoretically reduce it. This study investigates the maximum fraction of energy within a fully developed speckle pattern that can be transformed into a high-quality (low M²) beam. Furthermore, we examine the benefits and constraints of this method, focusing specifically on the inherent variability in output quality caused by multiple scattering.

We introduce a registration algorithm that simultaneously estimates motion and the ground truth image from noisy frames under conditions of rigid, constant translation. This non-iterative method requires no hyperparameter tuning and executes a fixed count of FFT, multiplication, and downsampling operations for any given input size. These characteristics facilitate rapid deployment on embedded systems, such as cubesats, where on-board image fusion significantly reduces the demand on scarce downlink bandwidth. Theoretically, the algorithm achieves maximum likelihood optimality for additive white Gaussian noise and non-stationary Gaussian approximations of Poisson noise. Furthermore, it delivers accurate registration even at extremely low SNR levels, successfully operating when visible features fall below the noise floor.

This study examines the impact of the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) on the equilibrium between baryon asymmetry and the surplus of stable quarks from a new generation. By conserving SU(2) symmetry and other quantum numbers, the research facilitates sphaleron transitions that interconvert baryons, leptons, and new generations of leptons and quarks. Consequently, a specific relationship linking this excess to the baryon asymmetry is derived. Additionally, it is demonstrated that sphaleron transitions cause a minor, though negligible, dilution of the pre-existing dark matter density.

Neutral atom arrays have recently become a leading candidate for quantum information processing. However, a major hurdle for scaling these systems is the implementation of error-corrected quantum operations. Typically, qubits are entangled by exciting atoms to Rydberg states, a process that can lead to decay and correlated errors difficult to handle with conventional fault-tolerant methods. This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of these error sources in neutral-atom quantum computers and introduces hardware-efficient, fault-tolerant schemes designed to mitigate them. Specifically, we devise a novel and highly efficient approach to address critical errors arising from atomic qubit decay into states outside the computational subspace. These advancements substantially lower the resource requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computation compared to standard general-purpose protocols. Furthermore, our protocols are feasible for near-term deployment on cutting-edge neutral atom platforms utilizing both alkali and alkaline-earth atom qubits.

Weighted flow time is a fundamental and extensively researched objective function in scheduling. This paper examines a single-machine environment allowing preemptions, where the input comprises jobs defined by processing times, release times, and weights, with the goal of generating an optimal (potentially preemptive) schedule to minimize the total weighted flow time (the duration between a job's release and completion). Finding a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for this scenario was a longstanding open challenge. While Batra, Garg, and Kumar (FOCS 2018) achieved such an algorithm for polynomially bounded integers and Feige, Kulkarni, and Li (SODA 2019) provided a black-box reduction, the resulting approximation ratio was an unspecified constant of at least 10,000. We improve this ratio to $2+\varepsilon$. Unlike the approach by Batra et al., which reduces the problem to Demand MultiCut on trees solved via LP-rounding and dynamic programming, our method first reduces the problem to a distinct geometric problem with only a $1+\epsilon$ loss. We then solve these instances to within a factor of $2+\varepsilon$ using a dynamic program. Our reduction guarantees specific structural properties, rendering LP-rounding unnecessary. We believe this advancement significantly progresses the search for a PTAS for weighted flow time on a single machine.

Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) have emerged as a primary metric for assessing solar activity, particularly regarding their transient impacts on the heliosphere. While CMEs correlate with sunspot numbers (SSN), they also originate from other closed magnetic areas, such as quiescent filaments, making them a more comprehensive indicator of solar dynamics. Sunspots primarily reflect the toroidal magnetic component, whereas quiescent filaments—and the CMEs they generate—link both toroidal and poloidal components through the rush-to-the-pole (RTTP) phenomenon. By treating the conclusion of the RTTP in each hemisphere as a marker for solar polarity reversal, studies reveal that north-south reversal asymmetry exhibits a quasi-periodicity spanning 3 to 5 solar cycles. Regarding geospace effects, maximum CME speeds averaged over Carrington rotation periods demonstrate a strong correlation with geomagnetic activity indices like Dst and aa.

A defining characteristic of human daily interaction is the capacity for empathy, making the integration of this trait essential for creating dialogue systems that feel authentically human. While prior research has primarily concentrated on identifying user emotions to craft empathetic replies, empathy encompasses both affective and cognitive dimensions. Consequently, we contend that effective empathetic generation requires not only emotion detection but also a cognitive grasp of the user's circumstances. To address this, we introduce a novel method for generating empathetic responses that utilizes commonsense reasoning to infer additional context about the user's situation, thereby enriching the empathy expressed in the output. We assess this approach using the EmpatheticDialogues benchmark, a standard dataset for such tasks. Our empirical findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses baseline models in both automated and human evaluations, producing responses that are more empathetic and informative.

Using cryogenic magnetic force microscopy, we examined ferromagnetic domains in van der Waals single crystals of MnSb2Te4 obtained from two distinct sources. The observed dependence of these domains on magnetic field indicates extremely weak pinning of domain walls within MnSb2Te4, leading to a nearly negligible magnetic hysteresis loop. Furthermore, the temperature-dependent variation in domain contrast exhibits mean-field-like behavior, which aligns well with results from bulk magnetization measurements.

Codebook design for code-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (CD-NOMA) is fundamentally equivalent to autoencoder (AE)-based constellation design for multi-user multidimensional modulation (MU-MDM). However, current AE architectures yield suboptimal bit-error-rate (BER) performance because they operate within a constrained design space, such as fixed resource mapping and uniform power allocation across all codebooks. To address this, we introduce a novel MU-MDM AE architecture and a corresponding training methodology designed for the joint optimization of resource mapping and constellation design with bit-to-symbol mapping. Our goal is to achieve BER performance comparable to single-user MDM (SU-MDM) AE models while maintaining identical spectral efficiency. The proposed AE's core features include dense resource mapping and a new power allocation layer that normalizes the total user codebook power across all resources. This approach expands the design domain by facilitating flexible resource mapping and power distribution, thereby enabling the AE-based training to converge toward globally optimal MU-MDM constellations for CD-NOMA. Comprehensive BER simulations confirm that the proposed design surpasses existing CD-NOMA solutions and reaches within 0.3 dB of the BER performance achieved by the equivalent SU-MDM AE over an additive white Gaussian noise channel.

In the field of artificial intelligence, knowledge constitutes the information essential for intelligent systems to execute tasks. Although traditional knowledge bases rely on discrete, symbolic formats, there has been a growing focus on identifying knowledge embedded within continuous representations derived from data. This study introduces a method for constructing a Continuous Knowledge Base (CKB) capable of aggregating knowledge from multiple, varied neural networks. The core strategy involves defining an interface for each network and reframing knowledge transfer as a function simulation task. Text classification experiments demonstrate promising outcomes: the CKB successfully imports knowledge from one model and exports it to another, matching the original model's performance. More notably, when importing knowledge from several models into the CKB and subsequently exporting this fused knowledge to a single model, the system achieves superior accuracy compared to the original models. Furthermore, the CKB facilitates knowledge distillation and transfer learning with ease. Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing a universal continuous knowledge base to gather, store, and organize the continuous knowledge encoded across diverse neural networks trained for various AI applications.

Quasiparticles are a fundamental concept for describing interacting particles, characterizing electron-electron interactions in metallic Fermi liquids and electron pairing in superconductors. Although this framework simplifies complex many-body problems into a one-particle picture with residual effects, it often struggles to separate many-body contributions from experimental signatures, thereby obscuring intrinsic low-energy dynamics. This challenge is evident in ongoing debates regarding the Dirac-band anomaly in graphene and dispersion kinks in high-temperature superconductors. To address this, we propose Bayesian modelling of quasiparticles. Using the topological insulator $\mathrm{TlBi(S,Se)_2}$ as a model system, we formulated an inverse problem for quasiparticle spectra using semiparametric Bayesian analysis, successfully isolating both one-particle and many-body characteristics, specifically the intrinsic energy gap and anomalous lifetime of Dirac-quasiparticle bands. This method offers broad applicability for elucidating quasiparticle dynamics in quantum materials.

Standard reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically aim to autonomously master tasks from scratch, enabling repeated performance. In contrast, many real-world scenarios require success in a single attempt rather than repeated execution. Consider a disaster relief robot retrieving an item from a collapsed building without human guidance; it must succeed in one trial while navigating unknown obstacles, though it can use pre-existing knowledge of the structure. We define this scenario as single-life reinforcement learning (SLRL), where an agent must complete a task within one episode without external intervention, relying on prior experience while facing novel challenges. SLRL offers a framework for studying autonomous adaptation to unfamiliar situations; however, we observe that standard episodic RL algorithms often fail to recover from out-of-distribution states in this context. Addressing this limitation, we introduce $Q$-weighted adversarial learning (QWALE), an algorithm that uses a distribution matching strategy to leverage prior experience as a guide in novel situations. Experiments on various single-life continuous control tasks demonstrate that methods based on our distribution matching approach achieve 20–60% higher success rates by recovering more quickly from novel states.

Tractograms serve as virtual models of the brain's white matter fibers, playing a critical role in presurgical planning, the study of neuroplasticity, and the investigation of neurological disorders. Each tractogram consists of millions of 3D polylines representing these fibers. However, a significant fraction of these fibers lack anatomical validity and are merely artifacts generated by tracking algorithms. While common filtering techniques rely on signal reconstruction—a principled method that fails to incorporate anatomical knowledge—this work reframes tractogram filtering as a supervised learning task. We leverage ground truth annotations from a recent heuristic approach, which classifies fibers as plausible or implausible based on established anatomical criteria. The core concept involves modeling fibers as point clouds to determine if and how geometric deep learning can identify their anatomical characteristics. Our contribution is an enhanced Dynamic Edge Convolution model that utilizes the sequential relationships between points within a fiber to achieve high-accuracy discrimination between plausible and implausible fibers.

Within a nonlinear gyrokinetic framework, we derive two-field equations that describe the fully nonlinear dynamics of drift waves (DW) and geodesic acoustic modes (GAM) in toroidal geometry. Our analysis identifies and examines two distinct stages. During the linear growth phase, the nonlinear equations simplify to the well-known parametric decay instability (PDI), which explains the spontaneous resonant excitation of GAM by DW. Numerical solutions of these two-field equations successfully reproduce key findings from prior research on spontaneous GAM excitation, including the significantly enhanced GAM group velocity and the nonlinear growth rate. In the fully nonlinear stage, soliton structures emerge due to a balance between the self-trapping effect of the spontaneously excited GAM and the kinetic dispersiveness of the DW. These solitons facilitate turbulence spreading from linearly unstable regions into stable ones, demonstrating convective propagation rather than typical linear dispersion, and are therefore anticipated to drive core-edge interactions and nonlocal transport.

We introduce a new, large-scale emotional dialogue dataset comprising 1 million dialogues sourced from the OpenSubtitles corpus. These dialogues are annotated with 32 distinct emotions and 9 empathetic response intents, utilizing a BERT-based fine-grained dialogue emotion classifier. The study details the intricate pipeline for preprocessing movie subtitles and selecting high-quality dialogues for annotation, as well as the semi-supervised learning approach employed to train the emotion classifier. Despite managing a vast array of labels, the classifier attained a $65\%$ accuracy rate and successfully annotated the 1 million dialogues. This work represents a unprecedented scale in emotional dialogue classification, both regarding dataset volume and the granularity of emotion and intent categories. Furthermore, visualization methods applied to evaluate the resulting dataset indicate that it aligns with the patterns observed in human social interaction.

Multicore architectures feature on-board memory hierarchies and communication networks that significantly impact the performance of shared-memory parallel applications. Understanding how specific hardware configurations affect different codes is crucial, yet characterizing these influences remains complex. Previous research has leveraged runtime data from hardware counters to profile individual thread behavior, specifically measuring floating-point operations per second, operational intensity, and memory access latency. This study proposes utilizing such metrics to direct thread migration strategies, thereby enhancing execution efficiency through improved locality and affinity. The efficacy of these strategies was validated using various configurations of NAS Parallel OpenMP benchmarks on multicore systems. Results indicate that the proposed methods can yield up to a 70% performance boost in scenarios with low locality and affinity, while incurring only a minor performance drop for codes already exhibiting high locality and affinity.

This paper introduces a novel Python library designed for anomaly detection within unsupervised learning frameworks, specifically targeting univariate time series data representing specific phenomena. The system identifies anomalous epochs—time intervals where observations exceed a defined percentile of a baseline distribution established via a dissimilarity metric. By utilizing time-evolving graphs, the library capitalizes on inter-dependencies among data points to enhance detection. Currently, it supports 28 distinct dissimilarity metrics and is architected for seamless extension with additional metrics. Through a comprehensive API, the library provides full functionality for executing anomaly detection. To the best of our knowledge, this is the only publicly available library that combines dynamic graph-based detection with the extensibility to incorporate other state-of-the-art techniques. Experimental results indicate promising performance in both algorithm execution times and detection accuracy. Furthermore, the paper offers parameter tuning guidelines to optimize detector performance and prediction precision.

Researchers spanning computer science, network science, and mathematics have dedicated significant effort to curbing Internet misinformation outbreaks that jeopardize social systems and societal well-being. While most existing studies model interpersonal connections as static, these links are inherently dynamic, meaning social networks function as temporal networks. To date, no theoretical framework exists for containing misinformation within such temporal structures. Consequently, we introduce a novel theoretical approach alongside a specific misinformation spreading model designed for temporal networks. We further propose a heuristic-containing (HC) strategy, which optimizes the final outbreak size and demonstrates superior performance compared to simplified methods like random-containing (RC) and targeted-containing (TC). Through extensive numerical simulations and theoretical analyses on both synthetic and real-world networks, we validate the efficacy of the HC strategy. Our findings indicate that this approach significantly raises the outbreak threshold and reduces the final outbreak size.

This brief note revisits the `shift-desingularization' formulation of the $[Q,R]=0$ theorem applied to potentially singular symplectic quotients. Beginning with the refined proof by Szenes and Vergne regarding the quasi-polynomial nature of multiplicity in relation to the tensor powers of the prequantum line bundle, we employ the Berline-Vergne index formula alongside stationary phase expansion. This approach allows us to calculate the quasi-polynomial, drawing upon an earlier methodology proposed by Meinrenken.

Explaining "black box" models is a critical challenge in advancing deep learning, particularly for networks processing visual data where identifying and visualizing dominant input pixels or regions is both fundamental and difficult. While current research largely addresses single-image inputs, it often overlooks the temporal dynamics inherent in videos. Consequently, developing a user-friendly visual explanation method adaptable to diverse video understanding architectures remains an unsolved problem. This paper introduces a generic perturbation-based approach for explaining video networks, augmented by a novel loss function that enforces result smoothness across both spatial and temporal dimensions. This technique facilitates comparative analysis across different network structures and prevents the generation of pathological adversarial explanations for video data. Experimental results confirm the method's effectiveness.

Automating the identification or extraction of requirements from text is a laborious and error-prone process that many researchers advocate for. We manually annotated the PURE dataset to create a novel collection comprising both requirements and non-requirements. Leveraging this dataset, we fine-tuned a BERT model and benchmarked its performance against several baselines, including fastText and ELMo. To assess the model's capability on semantically complex documents, we compared the PURE dataset outcomes with experiments conducted on Request for Information (RFI) documents, which frequently contain software requirements in a less standardized format. The fine-tuned BERT model yielded promising results on the binary sentence classification task within the PURE dataset. When compared to prior and recent studies involving constrained inputs, our approach exhibits high performance in precision and recall metrics while remaining agnostic to unstructured textual input.

This paper details our submission to the Simultaneous Speech Translation task at IWSLT 2022. We investigate methods for applying an offline model in a simultaneous translation scenario without altering the original architecture. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed onlinization algorithm achieves performance nearly equivalent to the offline setting while reducing latency by a factor of three on the test set. Furthermore, the onlinized offline model surpasses the top-performing IWSLT 2021 simultaneous system in medium and high latency conditions and performs comparably in low latency scenarios. Finally, we have made our system publicly accessible.

Video represents a powerful information source, with online and offline consumption reaching unprecedented heights in recent years. A core challenge in extracting insights from video is that viewers must process the entire sequence to grasp context, unlike images where information can be derived from a single frame. Beyond contextual understanding, creating a universally appealing video summary is nearly impossible due to individual biases regarding keyframes. For instance, in a soccer match, a coach may prioritize frames showing player positioning and techniques, whereas a novice might focus on goals and the scoreboard. Consequently, addressing video summarization via supervised learning would necessitate extensive personalized data labeling. This paper proposes solving video summarization through unsupervised learning by leveraging traditional vision-based algorithms for precise feature extraction. We further introduce a deep learning-based feature extraction pipeline followed by various clustering techniques to effectively summarize videos by identifying interesting keyframes. Performance evaluations on the SumMe dataset demonstrate that deep learning-based feature extraction outperforms other approaches, particularly for videos with dynamic viewpoints.

Decaying Cold Dark Matter (DCDM) is currently being studied, primarily to address the $S_8$ tension between cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations and specific large-scale structure measurements. In this model, the decay of a parent particle into one massive and one or more massless daughters suppresses the late-universe power spectrum; this suppression relies on the relative mass splitting $\epsilon=(1-m^2/M^2)/2$ and the particle lifetime $\tau$. This work examines how the BOSS DR14 one-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest flux power spectrum constrains the DCDM model, employing a conservative effective model to handle astrophysical uncertainties. Because the power suppression accumulates at low redshifts, we determine that parameter regions capable of resolving the $S_8$ tension remain largely consistent with Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data. However, for degeneracy parameter values of $\epsilon\sim 0.1-0.5\%$, where suppression occurs within the scales probed by BOSS Lyman-$\alpha$ data, we derive tighter constraints than previous CMB and galaxy clustering studies, yielding $\tau\gtrsim 18$ Gyrs for small mass splittings. Additionally, our analysis of the BOSS Lyman-$\alpha$ flux power spectrum permits values such as $\tau\sim 10^2$ Gyrs and $\epsilon\sim 1\%$, which were previously favored by combined Planck and galaxy clustering data with a KiDS $S_8$ prior, and we even identify a marginal preference for this regime.

Charge transport is fundamental to the diverse applications of two-dimensional materials, such as field-effect transistors, solar cells, and transparent conductors. However, at typical operating temperatures, this transport is often impeded by carrier scattering caused by lattice vibrations. Consequently, accurately evaluating intrinsic phonon-limited carrier mobility is critical for identifying viable candidates for next-generation devices. This work presents a framework for efficiently calculating the drift and Hall mobility of two-dimensional materials via the Boltzmann transport equation, utilizing Fourier-Wannier interpolation. Expanding upon a recent method for long-range contributions to dynamical matrices and phonon dispersions [Phys. Rev. X 11, 041027 (2021)], we extend this approach to include electron-phonon coupling effects involving dynamical dipoles and quadrupoles. By analyzing a broad range of monolayers—from SnS$_2$ and MoS$_2$ to graphene, BN, InSe, and phosphorene—we demonstrate the necessity of this strategy for properly addressing the unique long-range electrostatics inherent to two-dimensional systems. Notably, we uncover a complex temperature dependence in the Hall hole mobility of InSe, where mobility rises above 150 K due to the "mexican-hat" structure of its valence bands. Ultimately, our findings indicate that dynamical quadrupoles are indispensable, capable of altering carrier mobility by more than 40%.

We introduce a family-universal $U(1)_X$ model framework incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, where the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry is constructed as a linear combination of the $U(1)_Y$ and $U(1)_{\chi}$ factors originating from $SO(10)$. To ensure compatibility with quantum gravity effects, we incorporate a Dirac fermion $\chi$ as a dark matter candidate; this particle remains odd under a gauged $Z_2$ symmetry following the breaking of $U(1)_X$. This setup naturally yields isospin-violating dark matter with a ratio of $f_n/f_p = -0.7$, thereby satisfying constraints from LUX, PANDAX, and XENON1T experiments. Furthermore, we analyze the mass spectra and mixing patterns of Higgs and gauge bosons, examine LHC limits on the $Z'$ boson mass, and simulate constraints from both direct and indirect dark matter detection experiments to identify viable parameter spaces. In investigating LHC $Z'$ mass bounds across generic $U(1)_X$ models, we evaluate four distinct scenarios, noting that Scenario II—characterized by zero $U(1)_X$ charge for right-handed up-type quarks—offers a slight relaxation of the $Z'$ mass lower limit.

The paper establishes an equality linking the spectral flow of a family $A$ of self-adjoint Fredholm operators to the index of the associated differential operator $\frac{d}{dt}-iA$, subject to Atiyah-Patodi-Singer-style boundary conditions. This finding extends a result by C.B\"ar and A. Strohmaier, which they employed to prove their Lorentzian formulation of the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer Index Theorem.

We propose an alternative interpretation of fermion mass matrix elements. Since the complete rotational freedom inherent in gauge-kinetic terms generates an infinite set of "weak bases," any basis-dependent features like mass matrices are unphysical. Conversely, matrix invariants offer basis-independent objects of greater significance. We utilize one such invariant to create a novel parametrization of the mass matrices, thereby gaining control over their implicit structural implications. Central to this approach is the trace invariant, which geometrically resembles a hypersphere with a radius defined by the mass matrix's Frobenius norm. Through the concepts of alignment and misalignment, we can associate texture zeros with specific alignments, while Froggatt-Nielsen structures in the matrix elements arise from misalignment. This methodology provides deeper insights into the underlying flavor geometry found in traditional approaches.

Reduced-precision floating-point arithmetic is now standard in short-term numerical weather forecasting, yet its viability for long-term climate simulations—particularly those modeling dynamic climate change—remains uncertain. To address this, we utilized the global atmospheric SPEEDY model to simulate a climate system under rising $\text{CO}_2$ levels over a century. Although double precision is the conventional standard for climate modeling, our results demonstrate that reduced precision formats (Float32 and Float16) yield sufficient accuracy. Notably, employing stochastic rounding instead of the standard "round-to-nearest" method significantly enhances the performance of reduced-precision simulations. After 100 years, the mean bias error (MBE) for global mean surface temperature and precipitation relative to double precision was $+2 \times 10^{-4}$ K and $-8 \times 10^{-5}$ mm/6hr for single precision, and $-3.5 \times 10^{-2}$ K and $-1 \times 10^{-2}$ mm/6hr for half precision. However, incorporating stochastic rounding reduced the half-precision error to $+1.8 \times 10^{-2}$ K and $-8 \times 10^{-4}$ mm/6hr. Analysis of climatic distributions after a century shows that, when using half precision with stochastic rounding, the difference in the expected value of global surface temperature relative to double precision is $\leq 5 \times 10^{-3}$ K, while precipitation differences amount to $8 \times 10^{-4}$ mm/6h. The study further explores and discusses specific model regions where stochastic rounding offers marked improvements over deterministic rounding. [abridged]

Hydride Vapor Phase Epitaxy (HVPE) represents a promising approach for lowering the costs of manufacturing III-V materials and devices, with significant potential for high-efficiency solar cells used in both space and terrestrial settings. However, recent demonstrations achieving ultra-fast growth rates (approximately 500 $\mu$m/h) using uncracked hydrides are not adequately explained by current growth models. Consequently, there is a critical need to elucidate the growth kinetics and their interaction with transport phenomena to facilitate rapid and uniform epitaxial deposition. This study derives a kinetic model based on experimental data and incorporates it into a computational fluid dynamics simulation of an HVPE reactor. Additionally, we refine an existing hydride cracking model, validating it against both numerical simulations and experimental results. Our findings demonstrate that the newly developed growth model and the enhanced cracking model successfully replicate experimental growth measurements of \ce{GaAs} within an established HVPE system.

We introduce the Fuzzy Jaccard Index (FUJI), a scale-invariant metric designed to evaluate the similarity between two ranked or ordered lists. By integrating a membership function that accounts for specific rank positions, FUJI enhances the traditional Jaccard index, yielding more stable and precise similarity estimates. Our work offers theoretical analysis of the FUJI score's properties, proposes an efficient computation algorithm, and provides empirical validation across various synthetic scenarios. Furthermore, we illustrate its practical application in a standard machine learning context by comparing feature ranking lists pertinent to specific tasks. In real-world, high-dimensional domains where only a fraction of the feature space is relevant, robust feature ranking is crucial for achieving interpretability, computational efficiency, and strong predictive performance. In such settings, FUJI effectively differentiates between existing feature ranking methods while demonstrating superior robustness and efficiency compared to benchmark similarity scores.

In soccer, known as association football, player status fluctuates rapidly between hero and zero. Since performance is inherently dynamic rather than static, analyzing it as a time series is essential for informed decision-making. This study introduces and examines I-VAEP and O-VAEP models to assess player actions, intentions, and execution. By tracking these ratings longitudinally, we propose specific use cases that support treating player evaluation as a continuous process. Consequently, we identify top performers and trace their performance trajectories, establish volatility metrics to gauge consistency, and construct player development curves to aid strategic choices.

The orbital angular momentum (OAM) technique introduces a novel dimension for data transmission within millimeter wave communications. Leveraging the spatial properties of OAM beams, a new OAM spatial modulation (OAM-SM) system is introduced for upcoming mobile networks. Analytical expressions are developed to evaluate the capacity, average bit error probability, and energy efficiency of these OAM-SM millimeter wave systems. When compared to traditional multi-input multi-output (MIMO) millimeter wave systems, the proposed OAM-SM approach achieves a 36% increase in maximum capacity and a 472.3% boost in energy efficiency. Additionally, numerical findings demonstrate that OAM-SM systems exhibit greater resilience to path-loss attenuation than conventional MIMO systems, rendering them well-suited for long-distance transmission. Consequently, OAM-SM millimeter wave communication systems offer significant potential for the evolution of future mobile networks.

Colorectal cancer remains a primary cause of mortality among both genders. Consequently, histopathological analysis of colorectal polyps serves as the pathologist's principal tool for assessing actual cancer risk and determining necessary follow-up actions. This diagnostic process involves evaluating the polyp type and, crucially, the dysplasia grade, which is a pivotal factor in clinical management. The proposed deep learning classification framework utilizes a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network, trained with specific strategies to address whole slide image (WSI) high resolution and significant data imbalance. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that adenoma dysplasia grading can be accurately classified with 70% precision, a result that aligns with pathologist agreement.

With the expanding intersection of traditional computational mechanics and machine learning, there is a rising need for simple methods to connect Python workflows with C++-based OpenFOAM. This paper presents a general solution that enables running Python code directly inside an OpenFOAM solver, eliminating the requirement to translate Python scripts. The method relies on the lightweight pybind11 library, which facilitates data exchange by sending OpenFOAM information to an embedded Python interpreter for processing and returning results as required. After reviewing existing solutions, the article details this approach, emphasizing data transfer mechanisms, script execution, and implementation specifics within OpenFOAM. Three complementary test cases illustrate the system's capabilities and compare various data transfer strategies: a Python-defined velocity profile boundary condition, a Python-based solver for prototyping purposes, and a machine learning constitutive law class for solids4foam that executes field calculations.

This paper presents efficient techniques for optimizing metrological performance within bipartite quantum systems governed by local Hamiltonians. For any specific quantum state, our approach identifies the optimal local Hamiltonian that maximizes the state's metrological advantage over separable states. We demonstrate that this task can be reformulated as maximizing the quantum Fisher information (QFI) across a defined set of Hamiltonians. By expressing the QFI in a bilinear form, we solve the optimization problem using an iterative see-saw algorithm where each step relies on semidefinite programming. Additionally, we apply the method of moments, which proves highly effective for smaller systems. Finally, we extend these strategies to other quantum information theory challenges, such as identifying bound entangled states that most severely violate the Computable Cross Norm-Realignment (CNNR) criterion.

Scattering and refraction of low-frequency radio waves can significantly alter the apparent size and location of solar coronal radio sources, phenomena attributed to electron density fluctuations driven by turbulence. Consequently, accurately measuring the true source size offers a method to probe coronal plasma turbulence. Nevertheless, the scarcity of high spatial resolution low-frequency radio interferometric data, such as that from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), has historically hindered precise determination of these source dimensions and scattering levels. In this study, we directly model the visibilities from a LOFAR observation of a Type IIIb burst using an elliptical Gaussian function to derive the source's size and position. This approach avoids the spurious effects associated with imaging followed by deconvolution of the point spread function. At a frequency of 34.76 MHz and a heliocentric distance of 1.75 R$_\odot$, we determined the full width at half maximum (FWHM) to be $18.8^\prime \pm 0.1^\prime$ along the major axis and $10.2^\prime \pm 0.1^\prime$ along the minor axis. Our findings indicate that density fluctuations in the solar corona are the primary driver of radio wave scattering, leading to substantial source sizes, although the derived magnitude of $\varepsilon$ appears smaller than values obtained from previous tied-array image studies of radio wave scattering.

Let $\vec C_m$ and $\vec C_n$ denote directed cycles of lengths $m$ and $n$ respectively, where $m,n \ge 3$. Define $P(\vec C_m \mathbin{\Box} \vec C_n)$ as the digraph derived from the Cartesian product $\vec C_m \mathbin{\Box} \vec C_n$ by selecting a vertex $v$ and reversing the direction of all four incident edges (an operation known as "pushing" at $v$). Utilizing a specific case of unpublished research by S.X. Wu, we establish elementary number-theoretic necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle in $P(\vec C_m \mathbin{\Box} \vec C_n)$. As a corollary, if $P(\vec C_m \mathbin{\Box} \vec C_n)$ contains a Hamiltonian cycle, then $\gcd(m,n) = 1$, which further implies that the original product $\vec C_m \mathbin{\Box} \vec C_n$ is not Hamiltonian. This result confirms a conjecture proposed by J.B. Klerlein and E.C. Carr.

This research addresses the challenges of modeling light scattering and estimating scattering parameters within homogeneous translucent materials. Among these parameters, the scattering phase function plays a critical role in determining the distribution of scattered radiation, yet it remains the most difficult to model accurately. Consequently, practitioners often rely on empirical functions like the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) model or its variants, which are typically restricted to specific material types. This limitation creates significant difficulties for inverse rendering tasks where the target material is unknown, necessitating a more versatile phase function. While general polynomial-based functions using bases such as Legendre polynomials have been proposed, their application in inverse rendering is problematic because the constituent polynomials can yield negative values, whereas a valid phase function must remain non-negative. This study introduces a novel, general phase function designed to overcome this constraint and facilitates an inverse rendering application based on it. The proposed function has been validated across a broad spectrum of materials simulated using Mie scattering theory. Furthermore, the accuracy of scattering parameter estimation using this new function has been confirmed through both simulations and real-world experiments.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a novel machine learning paradigm that leverages local devices. At the server level, FL periodically aggregates models trained locally by distributed clients to create a more generalized model, thereby preventing private data from traversing the network and minimizing communication costs. However, existing approaches depend on clients having substantial stored data to fine-tune server-sent models, a requirement that is often unrealistic in mobile pervasive computing environments where storage capacity is limited and data distributions shift significantly. To address this variability, a common strategy involves using the data continuously gathered by clients to progressively adapt received models; yet, this straightforward method leaves clients vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. This paper aims to illustrate this issue within the context of mobile human activity recognition on smartphones.

Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has become a leading platform for nanophotonics and quantum sensing due to its optically active defects, which exhibit exceptional brightness and significant spectral tunability. Historically, the precise, deterministic positioning of these emitters remained a challenge, hindering their effective characterization and integration into hybrid devices. Recently, focused ion beam (FIB) systems have demonstrated utility in creating various spatially defined emitters with distinct structural and photophysical characteristics. This study systematically investigates the physical mechanisms behind FIB-induced defect formation in hBN, identifying beam-substrate interaction as a critical factor. These conclusions are validated by transmission electron microscopy, which reveals local mechanical degradation and amorphization within the ion-irradiated hBN regions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that exposure to water triggers a structural and optical transition between two defect types with unique emission profiles in the amorphized material. By combining super-resolution optical microscopy with atomic force microscopy, we precisely locate emitters within defect sites, confirming that defected edges serve as the primary sources of fluorescence. These findings establish a foundation for FIB-assisted engineering of optically active defects in hBN with high spatial and spectral precision, enabling applications in integrated photonics, quantum sensing, and nanofluidics.

Recent interest in probabilistic time series forecasting has surged across diverse dynamic system contexts, such as system identification and prognostic health management. To address this, we integrate advancements in deep generative models and state space models (SSMs) to develop a novel, data-driven deep probabilistic sequence model. Adopting a widely used encoder-decoder framework, we construct an RNN-assisted variational sequence model within an augmented recurrent input space, capable of capturing rich stochastic sequence dependencies. Furthermore, to resolve posterior inconsistency between training and inference phases and enhance the extraction of dynamic patterns, we (i) introduce a lagged hybrid output as input for the posterior at subsequent time steps, thereby aligning training and prediction processes; and (ii) design a generalized auto-regressive strategy that encodes all historical dependencies for the posterior. Following an investigation of the model's methodological characteristics using toy datasets, we comprehensively demonstrate its superiority over existing deep probabilistic SSMs through extensive numerical experiments on eight system identification benchmarks from various dynamic systems. Finally, we apply the proposed sequence model to a real-world centrifugal compressor forecasting task, further validating its exceptional performance by quantifying the time series predictive distribution.

This study introduces a multi-agent actor-critic reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed to speed up multi-level Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) sampling. In this setup, the agents' policies (actors) generate proposals for MCMC steps, while a centralized critic estimates long-term rewards. We validate the proposed approach by tackling an inverse problem characterized by multiple scales. Traditional MCMC methods face significant hurdles in this context: first, calculating the posterior distribution requires a forward solver that is computationally expensive for heterogeneous problems; consequently, we employ a multi-level strategy, specifically using the Generalized Multiscale Finite Element Method (GMsFEM) as the forward solver within the multi-level rejection procedure. Second, constructing a function capable of producing meaningful samples is challenging; to address this, we utilize a learned RL policy as the proposal generator. Experimental results demonstrate that our method substantially enhances the sampling process.

We investigate how antisymmetric tensor unparticle mediation contributes to the Higgs boson's diphoton production rate to address the discrepancy between the measured decay width of the newly discovered resonance and the Standard Model Higgs prediction. Our analysis reveals that the tree-level contribution from antisymmetric unparticle mediation serves as a viable candidate for explaining the observed diphoton decay rate.

In a graph $G=(V,E)$, a dominating set $D$ is a collection of vertices where every vertex in $V(G) \setminus D$ is connected to at least one member of $D$. The size of the smallest such set defines the domination number, denoted as $\gamma(G)$. A set $D$ is termed a $k$-isolating set if the subgraph $G - N_{G}[D]$ lacks any $k$-cliques. The minimum size of a $k$-isolating set is the $k$-isolation number, represented by $\iota_{k}(G)$. It is evident that $\gamma(G) = \iota_{1}(G)$. A set $I$ is irredundant if, for each non-isolated vertex $v$ within the induced subgraph $G[I]$, there is a vertex $u$ outside $I$ such that its neighborhood in $G$ intersects $I$ exactly at $\{v\}$. An irredundant set $I$ is maximal if adding any vertex from $V(G) \setminus I$ destroys its irredundancy. The minimum cardinality of a maximal irredundant set is the irredundance number, denoted $ir(G)$.
