Over the past few decades, the 3D morphable model (3DMM) has become a standard approach for photorealistic 3D face reconstruction from images. Nevertheless, face images are frequently compromised by severe occlusions from non-face objects such as hands, masks, and eyeglasses. These obstructions hinder the accurate capture of landmarks and shading data, rendering the resulting 3D face models largely unusable. This paper introduces a novel technique to restore de-occluded face images by leveraging the inverse application of 3DMMs and generative adversarial networks (GANs). The method employs 3DMM priors within a proposed adversarial framework, integrating both global and local adversarial convolutional neural networks to learn a de-occlusion model. In this setup, the 3DMM functions not only as a geometric prior but also defines the face region for the local discriminator. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness and robustness in eliminating various challenging occlusions across different head poses and lighting conditions. Additionally, the proposed method successfully reconstructs accurate 3D face models with restored textures.

We examine thermal emission and extinction from dust linked to the nearby superluminous supernova (SLSN) 2018bsz. Our dataset features daily sampling and simultaneous optical and near-infrared observations extending to approximately 100 days, supplemented by late-time mid-infrared (MIR) data at +1.7 years. By 230 days post-peak, the supernova remains undetected in the optical band but exhibits a remarkable near-infrared excess, characterized by r - J > 3 mag and r - Ks > 5 mag. Analyzing the infrared light curve's evolution allows us to determine whether the mid-infrared emission originates from newly formed dust within the ejecta, a pre-existing circumstellar envelope, or interstellar material heated by the supernova's radiation. We conclude that the latter two scenarios are invalid, whereas a model where new dust forms in the ejecta beyond 200 days consistently reproduces the observed flux evolution. The spectral energy distribution at +230 days is well-fitted by 5 x 10^-4 solar masses of carbon dust, which grows to 10^-2 solar masses by +535 days. SN 2018bsz marks the first SLSN to provide evidence for dust formation within the ejecta, producing roughly ten times more dust than typical core-collapse supernovae at comparable epochs. Combined with their tendency to reside in low-mass, low-metallicity host galaxies, we propose that SLSNe may play a significant role in dust formation during the early Universe.

It is well-established that ensembles of predictions yield superior results compared to individual models; however, training separate learners for each member of such an ensemble is often computationally prohibitive, particularly in resource-intensive tasks like semantic segmentation. This work introduces a self-ensemble approach designed to harness the performance gains of ensemble methods for semantic segmentation without incurring the traditional heavy training costs. By utilizing multi-scale features generated by feature pyramid networks to feed multiple independent decoders, our method effectively constructs an ensemble within a single unified model. The final output is derived by aggregating the predictions from each decoder, mirroring the standard ensemble strategy. Unlike prior approaches, our model supports end-to-end training, thereby eliminating the cumbersome multi-stage training procedures typically associated with ensembles. This self-ensemble technique surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on the Pascal Context and COCO-Stuff-10K benchmarks for semantic segmentation and remains competitive on ADE20K and Cityscapes. The code is accessible at github.com/WalBouss/SenFormer.

This paper investigates the challenge of covering an environment using an energy-limited robot operating alongside multiple charging stations. Due to restricted onboard power, the robot cannot traverse the entire area on a single charge and must intermittently recharge at these stations. The system enforces a strict energy constraint, ensuring the robot never attempts to visit a location with insufficient remaining energy. To address this, we introduce a deep Q-learning framework designed to generate a policy that maximizes coverage while minimizing budget violations. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a recurrent neural network (RNN) to enhance its ability to handle this multi-objective optimization task. We evaluated the proposed method in a 16x16 grid environment featuring charging stations and diverse obstacle layouts. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully identifies feasible solutions and surpasses the performance of comparable existing techniques.

Recently, there has been growing interest in animal diets, specifically regarding how pasture-based feeding affects milk and dairy product quality, driven by the rising availability of grass-fed options in markets. However, the lack of effective verification methods makes these products vulnerable to fraud and adulteration, necessitating statistical tools to distinguish between milk samples from different feeding systems and thereby enhance product authenticity. Infrared spectroscopy is commonly employed to gather milk data and predict traits; although routinely used for macro-component composition, each spectrum contains untapped information. Interpreting this data is challenging due to its high dimensionality and the complex interrelationships among spectral variables. This study proposes a modified factor analysis to create a concise summary of spectroscopic data, mapping observations into a low-dimensional latent space while simultaneously clustering variables. This approach identifies data redundancies and clarifies complex wavelength relationships. A flexible Bayesian estimation procedure is utilized for model fitting to determine an appropriate number of latent factors and clusters. Applied to mid-infrared spectroscopy data from dairy cows on varying pasture and non-pasture diets, the method successfully models data correlations, clusters variables, and reveals differences between milk samples from different dietary groups.

CAPTCHAs are intended to stop malicious bots from exploiting websites. While many online services offer audio CAPTCHAs as an accessible alternative to text and image versions for visually impaired users, previous studies have revealed that these audio systems are highly susceptible to automated attacks utilizing Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). To strengthen audio CAPTCHAs against such automation, this paper introduces the design and implementation of aaeCAPTCHA, a system that leverages audio adversarial examples to thwart ASR-based solutions. We performed a rigorous security assessment of this new design against five state-of-the-art deep neural network (DNN) ASR systems and three commercial Speech-to-Text services. Our experiments confirm that aaeCAPTCHA remains highly secure against these recognition technologies, even if attackers possess full knowledge of current adversarial techniques. Additionally, we evaluated the usability of our proof-of-concept implementation, finding that it maintains high robustness with only a moderate impact on user experience compared to standard audio CAPTCHAs. Ultimately, our comprehensive analysis indicates that aaeCAPTCHA can significantly bolster the security and resilience of traditional audio CAPTCHA systems without compromising usability.

Using ab initio methods, the free energy, equation of state, and elastic constants for AgBr in NaCl-, KOH-, and CsCl-type configurations were determined, with the latter calculated via the stress-strain relationship. Notably, the shear elastic constant $C_{44}$ was found to be unusually soft. At zero temperature, the phase transition from the low-pressure NaCl-type to the high-pressure CsCl-type structure proceeds through a monoclinic KOH-type intermediate phase. Free energy analysis reveals that this monoclinic phase is stable between 8 and 35 GPa.

This study introduces the first clustering analysis of Strong Blended Lyman $\alpha$ (SBLA) absorption systems, achieved by measuring their cross-correlation with the Lyman $\alpha$ forest. SBLAs represent a newly identified population of absorbers located within the Lyman $\alpha$ forest. Our results indicate a bias of $2.329\pm0.057$, which aligns with the bias observed in Damped Lyman $\alpha$ absorbers (DLAs). For DLAs, we derive a bias of $2.331\pm0.057$, a value higher than previously reported by P\'erez-R\`afols et al. (2018b). Additionally, we determine a redshift space distortion parameter of $\beta=0.417\pm0.010$, consistent with the DLAs' recovered value of $\beta=0.416\pm0.010$. These findings suggest that both SBLA and DLA systems trace different regions of the circumgalactic medium within a broadly similar galaxy population. Leveraging these shared clustering characteristics, we combined the datasets to conduct a cross-correlation of galaxies in absorption with the Ly$\alpha$ forest. We find that the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) scale uncertainty for this new measurement is $1.75\times$ greater than that of Ly$\alpha$ auto-correlation and $1.6\times$ greater than that of the quasar cross-correlation with the Ly$\alpha$ forest. We also note that the currently preferred metal contamination model for fitting correlation functions relative to the Ly$\alpha$ forest may not be sufficiently realistic for SBLA systems, likely because they serve as high-precision, high-metal-enrichment sites at high redshifts. Consequently, mock spectra incorporating SBLA systems and their associated metal absorption are necessary for a complete understanding of this sample. We conclude that SBLAs hold the potential to complement standard Ly$\alpha$ cosmological analyses in future surveys.

This study investigates how chirped laser pulses influence transmission and ion acceleration within sub-wavelength targets. In chirped pulses, the temporal variation of frequency relative to the fundamental frequency induces a corresponding time-dependent critical density ($n_c$). We employed a chirp model that extends beyond linear approximations. Specifically, negatively (positively) chirped pulses initially interact with the target via their high (low) frequency components, followed by low (high) frequencies. Our findings indicate that the threshold plasma density required for pulse transmission is elevated for negatively chirped pulses compared to unchirped or positively chirped ones. At higher densities ($6n_c$), the improved transmission of negatively chirped pulses facilitates efficient electron heating, generating a stable, persistent longitudinal electrostatic field behind the target. This creates an electron void that drives ions to expand in both directions, yielding a broad energy spectrum. Furthermore, we introduced a thin, low-density ($< n_c$) secondary layer behind the primary target. Ions from this secondary layer are accelerated as a mono-energetic bunch by the electrostatic field established by the primary layer upon interaction with the negatively chirped pulse. Under optimal conditions, proton energies reach approximately 100 MeV using a 10 fs (intensity fwhm), circularly polarized, Gaussian, negatively chirped laser pulse with a peak intensity of $\sim 8.5\times 10^{20}$ W/cm$^2$.

The NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS) serves as a vital research resource for the astrophysics community, aiming to foster an inclusive and accessible environment for exploring astronomical literature. A key component of this mission is developing a digital platform that accommodates all users, including individuals with disabilities who require alternative information presentation methods. NASA ADS adheres to the official Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) to ensure its applications are accessible, often striving to surpass these standards. By conducting both internal audits and external expert reviews aligned with these guidelines, we have identified numerous opportunities to enhance accessibility within our current web application and have subsequently implemented several user interface updates. This overview presents current trends in web accessibility, shares our experiences integrating these trends into our application, and outlines the lessons learned along with recommendations for future projects.

Recent studies indicate that Transformer-based neural models can be enhanced by either expanding input length or increasing model size. This paper introduces LongT5, a new model designed to investigate the combined effects of scaling both dimensions simultaneously. We achieve this by integrating attention mechanisms from long-input transformers (ETC) and adopting pre-training strategies from PEGASUS into the scalable T5 architecture. This integration yields a novel attention mechanism named {\em Transient Global} (TGlobal), which replicates the local/global functionality of ETC without needing extra side inputs. Consequently, LongT5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on various summarization tasks and surpasses the original T5 models in question answering.

This paper examines hermitian operators and isometries defined on spaces of vector-valued Lipschitz maps equipped with the sum norm $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}+L(\cdot)$. The study presents two primary results: first, it demonstrates that any hermitian operator acting on $\operatorname{Lip}(X,E)$, where $E$ is a complex Banach space, constitutes a generalized composition operator. Second, it provides a comprehensive characterization of unital surjective complex linear isometries on $\operatorname{Lip}(X,\mathcal{A})$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is a unital factor $C^{*}$-algebra. These findings represent advancements over prior work by the author.

This study examines soliton self-compression and photoionization phenomena within an argon-filled antiresonant hollow-core photonic crystal fiber pumped by a commercial Yb:KGW laser. Prior to the initiation of photoionization, we achieve the self-compression of a 220-fs pump pulse down to 13 fs in a single, compact stage. Leveraging the plasma-driven soliton self-frequency blueshift, we establish a tunable light source ranging from 1030 to approximately 700 nm. Furthermore, we comprehensively characterize the compressed pulses using sum-frequency generation time-domain ptychography, providing the first experimental visualization of complete time-frequency plasma-soliton dynamics inside hollow-core fibers.

In fibrous paper, fluctuations in moisture content induce alterations in both geometric and mechanical characteristics. These shifts are significantly influenced by inter-fibre bonds, which facilitate the transmission of hygro-mechanical responses across the network, leading to macroscopic sheet deformation. While most existing literature models assume perfect bonding between fibres, real-world 3D scenarios exhibit some flexibility within bond regions due to deformation gradients through the fibre thickness. Conversely, earlier 2D idealizations posited perfect bonding, effectively imposing full kinematic constraints across the entire sheet thickness. This study aims to evaluate the implications of such assumptions. Employing a homogenization technique, a random fibre network with varying coverages is generated and simulated via finite elements. To elucidate the impact of bonding on hygro-expansive behavior, a specialized bond model is created. In this framework, fibres are represented by 2D regular bulk finite elements, while bonds are modeled as interfacial elements with finite stiffness situated between bonded fibre pairs. These embedded interfacial elements link adjacent fibres, permitting relative displacement between their mid-planes. The hygro-elastic response of networks utilizing this bond model is examined by adjusting bond stiffness and network coverage under mechanical loads and moisture variations. Additionally, the model analyzes how inter-fibre bonds influence the anisotropic behavior of the paper fibre network.

Real-world conjectures lack explicit guidance on whether they should be proven or refuted. However, it is now clear that regardless of the outcome, the resulting argument must be not only persuasive but rigorously verifiable to the extent necessary to mitigate risk. For those without direct access to mathematical truths, the modern discipline of formalized mathematics offers valuable insights. We should consider its lessons regarding: the significance of strategic proof methods; precise automation control in analyzing proof structures; reasoning both forward from premises and backward from objectives when crafting proof scripts; discerning when definitions and identities are or are not applicable; and viewing proofs and refutations as dynamic entities rather than the static derivation trees emphasized by Proof Theory. I believe the current primary challenge for educators and learners lies less in the availability of generic tools than in their wise integration aligned with specific educational paradigms and pedagogical goals, potentially aided by intelligent interactive tutoring systems. As a proof of concept, a computerized proof assistant is introduced here; it leverages several existing free tools and incorporates findings on teaching and learning logic. While additional technology might enhance our intuitions, no major breakthrough is required: the necessary tools are already within our reach to develop through collaborative effort.

The global medical ultrasound (US) sector, valued in the billions, maintains steady annual growth. Its advantages—including non-ionizing radiation, real-time imaging capabilities, and lower costs relative to alternative modalities—have expanded its utility across diverse domains such as cardiology, angiography, obstetrics, and emergency care. Driven by continuous innovation, ultrasound is fundamentally reshaping standards for patient screening, diagnosis, and surgical procedures. This robust and promising market is propelled by advancements in imaging and processing methodologies. Evolving from 3D visualization to sophisticated software, hardware, and portable designs, ultrasound is firmly established as a premier medical imaging technology for the foreseeable future. However, as systems advance, new engineering hurdles arise. All ultrasound-based modalities face the common challenge of acquiring, transmitting, and processing vast data volumes. Furthermore, there is a persistent demand for higher resolution to enhance the visualization of deep tissues, organs, and blood vessels for improved diagnostic accuracy. This article aims to stimulate interest and research into emerging processing techniques and their applications in medical ultrasound, leveraging recent breakthroughs in signal processing algorithms and deep learning. We examine key challenges and potential solutions from a signal processing standpoint, utilizing the inherent structure of received ultrasound signals.

We present energy renormalizations arising from electron-phonon and electron-magnon interactions within spin minority surface resonances on Ni(111). These distinct interactions are separated and quantified by their coupling strength ($\lambda$), utilizing the unique forms of their complex self-energies and the significantly different binding energies at which they manifest. The detected electron-magnon interactions exhibit a pronounced dependence on both momentum and energy band position across the bulk Brillouin zone. Conversely, electron-phonon interactions originating from these same bands are found to be nearly independent of momentum and symmetry. Furthermore, a moderately strong electron-phonon interaction ($\lambda>0.5$) is identified in a "buried," near-parabolic spin majority band that remains below the Fermi level.

This study investigates the impact of pairing fluctuations on three-dimensional spin-orbit coupled Fermi gases at finite temperatures by employing a $T$-matrix approach under the $G_0G$ approximation for pair susceptibility. We calculate the critical temperatures marking the superfluid-to-normal phase transition across three distinct spin-orbit coupling (SOC) regimes: (1) extreme oblate (EO) or Rashba SOC, (2) extreme prolate (EP) or equal Rashba-Dresselhaus SOC, and (3) spherical (S) SOC. For both EO and S-type SOC, the critical temperature exhibits a crossover from the BCS to the BEC regime; notably, in the strong SOC limit, these temperatures converge with those of ideal BEC of rashbons. Additionally, pairing fluctuations generate a pseudogap in the fermionic excitation spectrum within both the normal and superfluid phases. Our findings indicate that for EO- and S-type SOC, sufficiently strong SOC can produce a significant pseudogap even at weak coupling. Consequently, this research implies that spin-orbit coupled Fermi gases offer a promising avenue for exploring pseudogap formation in fermionic systems.

We demonstrate that determining whether a query is equivalent to one with tree-width $k$ is decidable for the class of Unions of Conjunctive Regular Path Queries with two-way navigation (UC2RPQs). While Barceló, Romero, and Vardi previously established decidability for $k=1$, we prove that this property extends to any arbitrary $k>1$. Our algorithm operates within 2ExpSpace; however, for the practically significant restricted case where all regular expressions take the form $a^*$ or $(a_1 + \dotsb + a_n)$, the problem's complexity reduces to $\Pi_2^p$. Furthermore, we explore the related task of approximating a UC2RPQ using queries of small tree-width. We present an algorithm that, for any fixed $k$, constructs the maximal under-approximation of tree-width $k$ for a given UC2RPQ. This maximal under-approximation, denoted $q'$ for a query $q$, is a tree-width $k$ query contained in $q$ in a maximal and unique manner, meaning that if any tree-width $k$ query $q''$ is contained in $q$, it is necessarily also contained in $q'$.

Nevanlinna demonstrated that two non-constant meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$ are connected by a Möbius transformation if they possess identical inverse images with multiplicities for four distinct values. Subsequently, Gundersen extended this result to cases where two meromorphic functions share two values ignoring multiplicity while sharing two others with multiplicities truncated at 2. Previously, the first author established that for $n\ge 2$, there exist at most two linearly nondegenerate meromorphic mappings from $\mathbb C^m$ into $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ that share $2n+2$ hyperplanes in general position ignoring multiplicity. In this paper, we prove that if two meromorphic mappings $f$ and $g$ from $\mathbb C^m$ into $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ share $2n+1$ hyperplanes ignoring multiplicity and an additional hyperplane with multiplicities truncated by $n+1$, then the product mapping $f\times g$ is algebraically degenerate.

Driven by the rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) and the surging demand for connected devices, there is a pressing need for more efficient storage and processing frameworks to handle the resulting data volume. This study examines various data processing and storage paradigms—specifically Cloud, Fog, and Edge computing—and evaluates their compatibility with IoT integration. Additionally, it explores the low-latency and high-connectivity demands of future cellular networks in the context of machine-type communication (MTC). Finally, the paper addresses the necessity of enabling internet connectivity for IoT devices through a standardized protocol stack that facilitates data transmission, all while accounting for the inherent resource limitations of these devices.

We introduce a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to generate probabilistic reconstructions of hydroclimatic variability across Queensland, Australia. This framework offers a standardized methodology for integrating multiple palaeoclimate proxies from natural archives, including tree rings, ice cores, and speleothems. By merging time-series analysis with inverse prediction, the approach quantifies the link between specific hydroclimate indices and their corresponding proxies during the instrumental era to subsequently reconstruct historical trends. We apply this method to the Brisbane and Fitzroy catchments, examining the Rainfall Index (RFI) and the Standardised Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). The probabilistic output enables the estimation of the likelihood that a hydroclimate index in any reconstructed year exceeded or fell below the instrumental record's observed minimum and maximum values. In Brisbane, the RFI is unlikely (probability < 20%) to have surpassed the extremes recorded between 1889 and 2017. Conversely, the Fitzroy reconstruction indicates several years where the RFI likely (probability > 50%) exhibited behavior beyond the instrumental range. Regarding the SPEI, the probability of observing such extremes since 1889 remains below 50% for all reconstructed years in both catchments.

Investigating how noise affects quantum circuits is crucial for advancing Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) computing. This paper presents a pulse-level simulation of noisy quantum circuits using the Quantum Toolbox in Python (QuTiP). We present novel tools within the qutip-qip package, which utilizes QuTiP's quantum dynamics solvers and control optimization capabilities to simulate circuits at the pulse level. The study demonstrates compiling quantum circuits on simulated processors where control pulses act upon a target Hamiltonian governing the unitary evolution of physical qubits. Noise can be modeled through various physical frameworks, such as Lindblad density-matrix dynamics or Monte Carlo quantum trajectories. Specifically, users can define environment-induced decoherence at the processor level and incorporate noise simulations directly into control pulses. We illustrate the compilation and execution of the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm on superconducting-qubit and spin-chain processors, as well as using control optimization techniques. Additionally, we show how to replicate experimental results regarding cross-talk noise in ion-based processors and model Ramsey experiments using Lindblad dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate the integration of these features with other software frameworks.

We will investigate the properties of "hypergeometrization," an operator that modifies analytic functions near the origin by incorporating two Pochhammer symbols into their Taylor expansions. Fundamentally, this operator transforms elementary functions into hypergeometric ones. The primary objective is to generate numerous "change of variable" formulas for this operator, which can subsequently be utilized to derive a wide variety of transformations for multivariate hypergeometric functions.

In applied mathematics, particularly within optimization, functions are frequently available only as "black-box" software modules or highly intricate algorithms, rendering automatic differentiation impractical or impossible. Consequently, researchers rely on numerically approximating derivatives. However, numerical differentiation is inherently challenging and prone to instability. While numerous studies address this issue, often employing global Chebyshev approximations, these methods offer rapid convergence for smooth functions but face significant practical limitations. Specifically, real-world functions often lack global smoothness, and achieving a global approximation typically demands a high number of function evaluations. Despite these hurdles, a solution exists: real-world functions are typically smooth except at a finite number of singularities, corners, or edges. This observation motivates a local Chebyshev approach, which approximates the function locally to maintain the speed of Chebyshev convergence while mitigating the drawbacks of global methods. This work investigates such an approach and presents a numerical example.

This study introduces a planning and perception framework for a robot agent operating in a partially observable environment to tackle image classification tasks. The proposed three-layer architecture comprises a meta-layer responsible for determining intermediate objectives, an action-layer that chooses local movements during navigation toward these goals, and a classification-layer that assesses rewards and generates predictions. These layers are developed and executed using deep reinforcement learning, with a generalized policy gradient algorithm employed to optimize the parameters by maximizing expected rewards. The methodology is evaluated on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, offering enhanced interpretability by clarifying the agent's intermediate goals and navigational path.

The study investigates photoinduced charge dynamics in dimerized systems using exact diagonalization and the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. This analysis covers a one-dimensional spinless-fermion model at half filling and a two-dimensional model for $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$X at three-quarter filling. Upon applying a single-cycle electric field pulse with specific polarization, charge densities at half the sites oscillate in phase, while those at the remaining half oscillate out of phase. Under weak field conditions, the Fourier transform of the post-photoexcitation charge density time profile exhibits peaks in finite systems that align with the steady-state optical conductivity spectrum. However, strong fields suppress these peaks and introduce a new high-energy peak, resulting in charge densities oscillating primarily at a single frequency before eventual damping. In the absence of intersite repulsion for the 2D case and for the 1D case, this frequency reflects charge-transfer processes involving all bonds connecting the two site classes, manifesting as an electronic breathing mode. The connection between this new peak and a recently observed reflectivity peak in $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$X following photoexcitation is also examined.

This study introduces an extension to the wave packet framework for quantum plasmas, allowing packets to elongate along arbitrary directions. A generalized Ewald summation is developed to handle long-range Coulomb interactions within these models, while fermionic effects are approximated using specialized Pauli potentials that remain self-consistent with the wave packets. The numerical implementation is demonstrated to offer robust parallel performance and near-linear scaling with particle count, facilitating comparisons against conventional models utilizing isotropic wave packets. Comparisons of ground state and thermal properties reveal differences mainly within the electronic subsystem. Notably, investigations into the electrical conductivity of dense hydrogen show a 15% increase in DC conductivity when using this wave packet model relative to alternative approaches.

Non-parametric episodic memory enables rapid identification of high-reward experiences within reinforcement learning tasks. Unlike parametric deep reinforcement learning methods, which require repeated discovery of solutions, non-parametric approaches identify the solution once and can reuse it subsequently. However, existing episodic control strategies rely on discrete tables and have been limited to discrete action spaces. To address this, this paper presents Continuous Episodic Control (CEC), a new non-parametric episodic memory algorithm designed for sequential decision-making in environments with continuous action spaces. Experimental results across various sparse-reward continuous control settings demonstrate that CEC learns faster than current state-of-the-art model-free and memory-augmented reinforcement learning algorithms while sustaining strong long-term performance. Ultimately, CEC offers a rapid learning solution for continuous control tasks and serves as a valuable component for hybrid approaches combining parametric and non-parametric methods.

The phase diagram for motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) within a system of interacting self-propelled disks is investigated via Langevin dynamics simulations, focusing specifically on disk wall softness and the interaction range between disks. We highlight significant alterations in the MIPS phase diagram resulting from disk softness and inertia. Specifically, we demonstrate that softer disks in an overdamped regime undergo phase separation, whereas MIPS occurs only in the inertial limit for harder disks. Contrary to most prior MIPS studies that assume hard-core disks, our results are directly relevant to soft active matter across various biological contexts.

Using chiral effective field theory at next-to-leading order, we investigate $DN$ and $D^\ast N$ interactions to explore the internal structure of $\Sigma_c(2800)$ and $\Lambda_c(2940)$. Our analysis incorporates contact terms, along with one- and two-pion-exchange contributions, to describe short-, long-, and mid-range forces within the $D^{(\ast)}N$ systems. The low-energy constants for these systems are linked to those of the $N\bar{N}$ interaction via a quark-level Lagrangian inspired by the resonance saturation model, and $\Delta(1232)$ degrees of freedom are integrated into the loop calculations. We find that the attractive potential in the $[DN]_{J=1/2}^{I=1}$ channel is insufficient to form a bound state, suggesting that $\Sigma_c(2800)$ is better described as a compact charmed baryon. Conversely, the isoscalar channel potentials are sufficiently deep to support molecular states. Our calculations predict masses of $2792.0$ MeV for $[DN]_{J=1/2}^{I=0}$, $2943.6$ MeV for $[D^\ast N]_{J=1/2}^{I=0}$, and $2938.4$ MeV for $[D^\ast N]_{J=3/2}^{I=0}$. Given its low mass, $\Lambda_c(2940)$ is likely an isoscalar $D^\ast N$ molecule; furthermore, its signal may comprise both spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ and spin-$\frac{3}{2}$ structures, offering a qualitative explanation for its significant decay ratios to $D^0p$ and $\Sigma_c\pi$. Additionally, we examine $\bar{B}^{(\ast)}N$ systems and predict potential molecular states in their isoscalar channels. We encourage experimentalists to search for open-charm molecular pentaquarks in the $\Lambda_c^+\pi^+\pi^-$ final state.

In \cite{[Et]} and \cite{Kukin}, we present Gr\"obner-Shirshov bases for the Drinfeld-Kohno Lie algebra $\textbf{L}_{n}$ and the Kukin Lie algebra $A_P$, where $P$ denotes a semigroup. Leveraging these bases, we demonstrate that $\textbf{L}_{n}$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module and provide an explicit $\mathbb{Z}$-basis. Additionally, we offer an alternative proof of Kukin's Theorem, which states that if the semigroup $P$ possesses an undecidable word problem, then the Lie algebra $A_P$ shares this property.

The Baldwin, Phillips, & Terlevich (BPT) diagram, plotting [O III]/H$\beta$ against [N II]/H$\alpha$ (N2-BPT), has traditionally served as a classification tool for galaxies based on their primary ionization sources. Recent data indicates that galaxies at redshifts around $z\sim2$ occupy a distinct region in N2-BPT space compared to local galaxies. This study employs controlled numerical experiments to identify the physical mechanisms behind this offset. Using the CLOUDY photoionization code, we modeled nebular line emission from H II regions in a large sample of galaxies from the SIMBA cosmological hydrodynamic simulation. Our results show that the observed shift toward elevated [O III]/H$\beta$ and [N II]/H$\alpha$ ratios at high redshift is driven by sample selection; specifically, when focusing on massive galaxies ($M_* \sim 10^{10-11} M_\odot$), the offset emerges naturally due to their high metallicities. We predict that deeper surveys targeting lower-mass galaxies will uncover populations aligning with the locus seen in $z\sim 0$ observations. Even after correcting for selection effects, a minor discrepancy remains between simulations and observations. To address this, we examined the influence of varying ionization parameters, H II region densities, gas-phase abundance patterns, and radiation field hardness on N2-BPT diagrams. We conclude that either lowering the ionization parameter or increasing the N/O ratio at a fixed O/H can shift galaxies along a self-similar arc in N2-BPT space, matching the distribution of high-redshift galaxies.

A Josephson parametric amplifier (JPA) is implemented within a three-dimensional microwave cavity by connecting it to a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) integrated into a two-dimensional resonator. This JPA operates using a three-wave mixing setup, triggered by injecting AC magnetic flux at twice the frequency of the 3D cavity into the SQUID. Measurements on an 8.3 GHz cavity, configured for non-degenerate phase-insensitive operation, demonstrate gains exceeding 40 dB. Specifically, a 20 dB gain provides a 0.4 MHz bandwidth, while the 1 dB compression point reaches -115 dBm with an added noise level of half a quantum.

Boelen et al. (2010) derived a $q$-discrete Painlev\'e equation governing the recurrence coefficients of orthogonal polynomials and proposed that this equation possesses a unique positive solution. We confirm this conjecture and examine related research, emphasizing a methodological approach that may offer a unifying framework.

Two spatial birth-and-death Markov processes coupled in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are established as unique weak solutions to their corresponding Fokker-Planck equations. These solutions are built upon a sequence of correlation functions that adhere to the Ruelle-bound. By employing the general framework of Vlasov scaling, we derive a set of non-linear, non-local mesoscopic equations that characterize the effective particle density. These findings are subsequently applied to various ecological and biological models.

We announce the detection of a new outburst from the recurrent nova M31N 2017-01e, which occurred on January 11, 2012. This event was identified by Pan-STARRS and preceded the January 31, 2017 eruption (designated M31N 2017-01e) by 1847 days, or approximately 5.06 years. To date, four eruptions have been recorded for this nova: M31N 2012-01c, M31N 2017-01e, M31N 2019-09d, and M31N 2022-03d. These events exhibit a mean recurrence interval of $929.5\pm6.8$ days ($2.545\pm0.019$ yr), representing the second shortest period known for any nova. Additionally, we identify a blue variable source located at the nova's position with a mean magnitude of $\langle V \rangle = 20.56\pm0.17$ and a color index of $B-V\simeq0.045$, which displays a 14.3-day periodicity. While several system models have been proposed, none fully satisfy the observations.

We present a novel syntactic proof demonstrating that every function $(\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}) \to \mathbb{N}$ definable in G\"odel's System T is continuous. Unlike standard syntactic techniques, our method begins by translating System T into itself, where natural numbers are mapped to functions of type $(\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}) \to \mathbb{N}$. We then inductively define a continuity predicate for these translated elements and prove that the translation of any System T term adheres to this predicate. By employing a parametrized logical relation to connect original terms with their translations, we derive the continuity result. Both our constructions and proofs have been formalized in the Agda proof assistant; since Agda functions as a programming language, we can execute the proof to compute the moduli of continuity for functions definable in System T.

The growing computational demands of deep learning models hinder their training and deployment across diverse cloud and edge environments. To address this, replacing floating-point arithmetic with low-bit integer arithmetic offers a viable strategy to reduce energy consumption, memory usage, and latency, drawing significant research interest through quantization. However, a comprehensive study of constructing a fully functional integer training pipeline—encompassing the forward pass, back-propagation, and stochastic gradient descent—remains limited. Our empirical and mathematical findings indicate that integer arithmetic alone is sufficient for training deep learning models. Unlike recent approaches that rely on quantization, our method directly alters the number representation used in computations. This novel technique establishes a complete integer training pipeline that maintains the same loss trajectory and accuracy as floating-point methods, without requiring special hyper-parameter tuning, distribution adjustments, or gradient clipping. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across a broad spectrum of tasks, including classification (such as vision transformers), object detection, and semantic segmentation.

In cross-device federated learning (FL), clients like mobile devices collaborate with a server to train a global machine learning model while keeping their data local. However, recent studies indicate that adversaries can still extract private information by simply eavesdropping on the communication between clients and the server. For instance, an attacker might deduce whether a client possesses a specific data sample, a technique known as a passive membership inference attack. This paper introduces a novel passive inference attack that demands significantly lower computational resources and memory compared to current methods. Our experimental results demonstrate that this attack achieves superior accuracy on the CIFAR100 dataset (improving by over 4 percentage points) while utilizing three orders of magnitude less memory and five orders of magnitude fewer calculations.

Within the broad context of Metric-Affine gravity theories, where the metric and connection are treated as independent, we examine actions that are quadratic in both the Ricci scalar and the Holst invariant (the contraction of the Riemann tensor with the Levi-Civita tensor), coupled non-minimally to a scalar field. We investigate the profile of the resulting effective metric theory, which includes an additional dynamical pseudoscalar degree of freedom, demonstrating that it simplifies to an effective single-field inflationary model. A detailed analysis of the inflationary predictions reveals that they align with the most recent observational constraints across a wide parameter range, permitting a higher tensor-to-scalar ratio. Furthermore, the spectral index may either increase or decrease, contingent upon the specific location within the parameter space.

Determining whether and how treatment effects differ among individuals is essential for guiding clinical practice and recommendations. Consequently, evaluating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE) based on pre-specified effect modifiers has become a standard objective in modern randomized trials. However, if one or more potential effect modifiers are missing, relying on complete-case analysis can result in bias, under-coverage, inflated type I errors, or reduced statistical power. Although statistical approaches for handling missing effect modifier data have been developed and evaluated for individually randomized trials, few guidelines address the cluster-randomized context, where intracluster correlations in effect modifiers, outcomes, or missingness mechanisms may further compromise accurate HTE assessment. This paper neutrally compares the performance of common missing data methods—including complete case analysis, single imputation, multiple imputation, multilevel multiple imputation (MMI), and Bayesian MMI—through a simulation study of cluster-randomized trials with missing effect modifier data. Subsequently, we apply controlled missing data scenarios to an effect modifier from the Work, Family, and Health Study to further evaluate these methods using real-world data. Our simulations and data application indicate that MMI and Bayesian MMI outperform other available methods, with Bayesian MMI demonstrating superior bias reduction and coverage when model specification or compatibility issues arise. We also offer practical recommendations for researchers and identify areas for future investigation.

Makespan, defined as the total duration from the start to the completion of a sequence of jobs or tasks, is a critical metric in scheduling, particularly for traversing belt conveyor systems. Manufacturing firms frequently utilize this metric to enhance operational efficiency by optimizing job processing sequences. It is established that a machine's performance relies on specific timing details, even when the job order remains constant; consequently, system performance in flowshop environments is heavily dependent on scheduling procedures. This study first explores the relationship between makespan and various scheduling methods using a small-scale example and introduces an algorithm to calculate makespan. Subsequently, numerical experiments based on this algorithm investigate the correlation between typical makespan behavior and the location of the fiducial machine across different processing time distributions. Additionally, the study analyzes makespan behavior through the lens of shape function properties within percolation theory. The primary contributions include a detailed examination of makespan universality in flowshop problems and the derivation of three novel properties: (1) makespan exhibits universality, meaning it is minimally impacted by changes in the probability distribution of processing times; (2) makespan can be expressed as the sum of two shape functions; and (3) makespan is more sensitive to the scheduling procedure than to the dispatching rule.

Practical domains including gene expression analysis, multi-task learning, image recognition, signal processing, and medical data analysis often seek sparse solutions for feature selection, specifically preferring non-zero elements that are evenly distributed across various groups. To address this, the exclusive sparsity norm has been extensively adopted. Nevertheless, systematic research regarding the optimization of this norm remains limited. This paper makes two primary contributions from an optimization standpoint: 1) We introduce several efficient algorithms for minimizing the exclusive sparsity norm under both smooth and hinge (non-smooth) loss functions, all of which attain the optimal convergence rate of $O(1/k^2)$, where $k$ represents the iteration count. To our knowledge, this represents the first guarantee of such a convergence rate for general exclusive sparsity norm minimization. 2) In scenarios where group information is absent to define the exclusive sparsity norm, we propose a random grouping scheme to construct groups. We demonstrate that if the number of groups is suitably selected, true features will be grouped ideally with high probability. Empirical results confirm the efficiency of our algorithms and the efficacy of the random grouping scheme within the proposed exclusive SVM framework.

Let $f:X\to X$ denote an invertible Lipschitz map on a compact metric space $X$. For a given $f$-invariant ergodic measure and a H\"{o}lder continuous invertible operator cocycle acting on a Banach space, this work demonstrates that the Oseledets subspaces are H\"{o}lder continuous over a compact set of arbitrarily large measure. This finding generalizes a result from \cite{Simion16} concerning invertible operator cocycles on Banach spaces. Furthermore, the paper establishes H\"{o}lder continuity in the non-invertible setting.

This article outlines the Auslander-Reiten quivers for certain posets equipped with an involution, designated as types $\mathfrak{U}_n$ and $\mathfrak{U}_\infty$, which were introduced in the differentiation III section of Zavadskij [12]. We adhere to the classical Auslander-Reiten theory framework established by Auslander, Reiten, and Smal\o{} [1]. To achieve this, we establish a natural exact structure on the category of representations for a partially ordered set with an involution, thereby describing both the projective and injective representations.

To explain fermion mass hierarchies and flavor mixings, a minimal flavor structure is proposed for both quarks and leptons using the bi-unitary decomposition of the fermion mass matrix. The real matrix ${\bf M}_0^f$ fully accounts for family mass hierarchies through a nearly flat structure. Meanwhile, the left-handed unitary phase ${\bf F}_L^f$ serves as the source of CP violation in mixing, interpreted as a quantum interplay between Yukawa and weak gauge states. This minimal framework is defined by exactly 10 non-redundant parameters: 6 fermion masses, 3 mixing angles, and 1 CP-violating phase within the quark/lepton sector. Crucially, this approach offers a universal flavor structure independent of specific flavor data, a validity confirmed by successfully reproducing observed masses and mixings. Additionally, potential scenarios that generate this flavor structure are explored.

Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), along with its constrained (CDTW) and weighted (WDTW) variants, serves as a versatile distance metric for time series analysis by minimizing costs associated with non-linear alignments. While CDTW and WDTW were developed to address DTW's excessive flexibility, CDTW relies on a simplistic step function that permits unrestricted warping only within a specific window, whereas WDTW applies multiplicative weights based on the distances between aligned points rather than the degree of warping itself. This paper presents Amerced Dynamic Time Warping (ADTW), an intuitive new variant that imposes a fixed additive penalty for warping. Although ADTW, like its predecessors, limits warping, it eliminates the abrupt discontinuities found in CDTW and the constraints of multiplicative penalties used in WDTW. The authors formally define ADTW, demonstrate its key properties and parameterization, illustrate its intuitive configuration through a simple example, and validate its effectiveness on a standard time series classification benchmark. Additionally, a C++ implementation is provided.

Reinforcement learning (RL) stands as one of the three fundamental machine learning paradigms, showcasing remarkable success in complex domains such as Go and StarCraft, while gaining traction in applications like autonomous driving and smart manufacturing. Despite these achievements, RL faces the persistent challenge of the exploration-exploitation dilemma. This paper addresses the issue of enhancing exploration by introducing intrinsically-motivated RL. Unlike traditional exploration strategies, this approach leverages intrinsic learning motivation to generate sustainable exploration incentives. We provide a detailed classification of existing intrinsic reward methods, highlighting their practical limitations. Furthermore, we propose a novel intrinsic reward mechanism based on Rényi state entropy maximization, which overcomes the shortcomings of prior approaches and offers robust exploration incentives. Extensive simulations confirm that the proposed module achieves superior performance, characterized by greater efficiency and robustness.

Multi-access edge computing (MEC) is considered a vital component of next-generation wireless networks, designed to accommodate applications with strict latency and reliability demands. However, ensuring ultra-reliable and low-latency MEC (URLL MEC) remains difficult due to wireless channel uncertainties, constrained communication and computing resources, and fluctuating network traffic. Achieving URLL MEC requires analyzing the statistical distributions of end-to-end (E2E) latency and reliability throughout both wireless and edge computing systems. This paper introduces a novel framework to enhance MEC network reliability by modeling the distribution of E2E service delays, which includes both over-the-air transmission and edge computing times. Leveraging correlated variational autoencoders (VAEs), the framework estimates the complete E2E service delay distribution. Based on this estimation, an optimization problem rooted in risk theory is formulated to maximize reliability by minimizing the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the E2E delay. To address this problem, a new algorithm is developed for efficiently assigning user tasks to edge servers across the network, utilizing the delay statistics learned by the VAEs. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses several baselines that fail to incorporate risk analysis or E2E delay statistics.

Symmetry is fundamental to the topological states of quantum matter. While Carten originally identified three symmetry classes, Altland and Zirnbauer expanded this framework to a ten-fold classification for mesoscopic systems. In this study, we identify the emergence of a novel symmetry class specifically within BdG Hamiltonians set against a spinful background. Notably, we find no evidence of Kramers degeneracy in this BdG model, regardless of whether the background is spinless or spinful. We designate this additional symmetry class as X, thereby extending the established ten-fold symmetry classification for topological quantum matter. Consequently, these BdG systems exhibit numerous new, intriguing, and insightful phenomena.

This research investigates a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) scenario where agents operate within a specific network structure. The objective is for these agents to collaboratively maximize the average of their entropy-regularized long-term rewards. To address the curse of dimensionality and minimize communication overhead, we introduce the Localized Policy Iteration (LPI) algorithm, which provably converges to a near-globally-optimal policy using exclusively local data. Specifically, we demonstrate that even when each agent limits its focus to a $\kappa$-hop neighborhood, the resulting policy achieves an optimality gap that decreases polynomially with respect to $\kappa$. Furthermore, we establish the finite-sample convergence of LPI to the global optimum, explicitly characterizing the trade-off between solution quality and computational cost involved in selecting $\kappa$. Empirical simulations confirm the efficacy of the proposed LPI approach.

Advancements in digitalization and autonomous driving have positioned on-demand ride pooling as a disruptive force in urban mobility; however, its successful deployment relies on efficient fleet management algorithms, particularly for solving real-time assignment problems at scale. This study highlights the necessity of advanced algorithms by contrasting a rapid yet simplistic insertion heuristic with a state-of-the-art multi-step matching approach. Utilizing private vehicle origin-destination data from Munich, Germany, the results demonstrate that the multi-step algorithm can serve up to 8% more requests and reduce total driving distance by 10% in tested scenarios. Despite these benefits, the advanced algorithm's computational time grows too quickly to remain practical as problem sizes increase. To address this, the study introduces several optimizations to minimize redundant checks within the multi-step process and presents a refined vehicle selection heuristic based on three specific rules. In the scenarios tested, this heuristic accelerates the most computationally expensive step by a factor of over 8, maintaining nearly the same number of served requests and preserving approximately 70% of the distance savings. When integrated across all algorithmic stages, these improvements yield an overall speedup of 2.5x.

This study measures the production of a top quark-antiquark pair alongside a W boson ($\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$W) in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The data, collected by the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC, covers an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis selects events containing two or three leptons (electrons or muons) accompanied by additional jets. For two-lepton events, a multiclass neural network discriminates between signal and background processes, while three-lepton events are classified according to jet counts, the number of jets from b-quark hadronization, and lepton charge configurations. The inclusive $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$W cross section across the full phase space is determined to be 868 $\pm$ 40 (stat) $\pm$ 51 (syst) fb. Additionally, the $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$W$^+$ and $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$W$^-$ cross sections are measured at 553 $\pm$ 30 (stat) $\pm$ 30 (syst) fb and 343 $\pm$ 26 (stat) $\pm$ 25 (syst) fb, respectively, yielding a ratio of 1.61 $\pm$ 0.15 (stat) $^{+0.07}_{-0.05}$ (syst). These findings align with Standard Model predictions within two standard deviations and constitute the most precise measurements of these cross sections available to date.

Generally, the splitting operation on binary matroids fails to maintain their graphic and cographic properties. This paper presents a characterization of graphic matroids where splitting with respect to a three-element set yields cographic matroids. Additionally, we offer an alternative proof for the case where the set contains two elements, which was previously established by Borse et al.

This study re-examines the anomalous multiwavelength lightcurves of GRB 101225A under the hypothesis that it originated from an off-axis gamma-ray burst powered by a newly formed magnetar. By modeling the optical afterglow with a forward shock framework and describing the jet structure as a Gaussian function with a core half-opening angle of $1.67^{\rm o}$, we determine an initial Lorentz factor ($\Gamma_0$) of 120 and a viewing angle of $\theta_v=3.7^{\rm o}$. Analysis of X-ray flares within the $[4900,\ 7500]$ second interval reveals tentative quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) signatures at periods of $P=488$ seconds and $P=250\sim 300$ seconds, both with 90% confidence. These findings, along with the global gamma-ray and X-ray lightcurve, are explained using a magnetar dipole radiation (DR) model that incorporates magnetar precession, assuming gravitational wave (GW) emission dominates the magnetar's spindown. The bulk Lorentz factor of the DR ejecta is constrained to 8, significantly lower than $\Gamma_0$. When comparing GRB 101225A with the highly off-axis event GRB 170817A, we propose that the two-component jet in GRB 170817A consists of a co-axial GRB jet combined with DR ejecta. Furthermore, GRB 101225A is identified as a potentially bright member of the CDF-S XT2-like population of magnetar-driven X-ray transients, and the paper concludes with a discussion on the detectability of its associated gravitational wave emission.

Recent findings demonstrate that general policies across numerous classical planning domains can be defined and acquired through a feature pool derived from domain predicates via description logic grammar. Since most description logics map to a fragment of $k$-variable counting logic ($C_k$) with $k=2$—a fragment proven to tightly characterize the expressive capacity of graph neural networks (GNNs)—this work leverages these insights to explore the capabilities and constraints of GNNs in learning optimal general policies for various tractable planning domains where such policies are guaranteed. We trained a simple GNN in a supervised setting to approximate the optimal value function $V^{*}(s)$ for a set of sample states $s$. Consistent with theoretical predictions, the results indicate that general optimal policies emerge in domains where $V^{*}$ can be expressed using $C_2$ features but fail to appear in domains requiring more expressive $C_3$ features. Furthermore, the learned features align closely with those necessary to define $V^{*}$ in closed form. By combining theoretical analysis with domain-specific insights, we identify which features can and cannot be acquired through this method, thereby enabling a principled transition from combinatorial optimization strategies to a potentially more robust and scalable deep learning approach for learning general policies.
We demonstrate that a complete minimal immersion cannot possess a specific type of epitrochoid as a geodesic.

District cooling energy plants (DCEPs), which integrate chillers, cooling towers, and thermal energy storage (TES) systems, incur significant electricity costs. Effectively scheduling TES and chiller operations to leverage fluctuating electricity prices presents a complex optimal control challenge. Traditional Model Predictive Control (MPC) struggles here, as it must solve a computationally intensive high-dimensional mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) due to the discrete on/off nature of chillers and the continuous charging/discharging cycles of TES. Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a promising alternative by reducing real-time control to a low-dimensional optimization task that is straightforward to solve. However, RL performance is highly sensitive to various design parameters. This paper introduces a Q-learning-based RL controller tailored for this application. Numerical simulations indicate that the proposed controller lowers energy expenses by roughly 8% compared to a rule-based baseline, a saving rate comparable to MPC results found in existing literature for similar DCEPs. The study details critical design elements of the RL framework, such as basis functions, reward shaping, and algorithm parameters. Distinct from prior RL research on DCEPs, this controller is specifically engineered to handle continuous state and action spaces.

Complex networks composed of FitzHugh-Nagumo units display rare, high-amplitude extreme events, which are often preceded by proto-events characterized by the excitation of a specific subset of units. While it is established that a critical mass of excited units is necessary to escalate a proto-event into an extreme one, the mechanism by which the remaining units are recruited remains unclear. To address this gap and simulate typical experimental conditions, we analyzed the centrality of edges within time-dependent interaction networks derived from the units' dynamics using standard bivariate analysis. By applying recently developed edge centrality metrics alongside an edge-based decomposition method, we found that recruitment is chiefly driven by specific sets of edges that lack counterparts in the underlying topology. These insights may enhance our comprehension of how extreme events emerge in natural networked dynamical systems.

Comparison-Based Optimization (CBO) represents an optimization framework that operates with minimal access to the objective function f(x). Although CBO is increasingly significant for practical applications, it has garnered far less attention than the related field of Zeroth-Order Optimization (ZOO). This paper introduces a straightforward technique to transform ZOO algorithms into CBO algorithms, substantially expanding the repertoire of available CBO methods. Using PyCUTEst, we evaluated these algorithms across a collection of unconstrained problems. Furthermore, we employed hyperparameter tuning to identify optimal settings for specific algorithms and applied visualization techniques, including heat maps and line graphs, to facilitate interpretation. The complete codebase is accessible on GitHub.

This paper explores potential applications of stroboscopic tomography (also referred to as stroboscopic observability) within specific decoherence models for 2-level quantum systems. Our approach rests on the premise that the system's time evolution follows a master equation defined as $\dot{\rho} = \mathbb{L} \rho$, where macroscopic data is derived from the mean values $m_i (t_j) = Tr(Q_i \rho(t_j))$ of specific observables $\{Q_i\}_{i=1} ^r$ measured at discrete time points $\{t_j\}_{j=1}^p$. The primary objective of stroboscopic tomography is to determine the optimal conditions for system observability, specifically identifying the minimal requirements for the number of observables ($r$) and measurements ($p$), along with the necessary characteristics of the observable set $\{Q_i\}_{i=1} ^r$.

Interior modeling of Jupiter and Saturn has evolved to generate thousands of configurations spanning vast parameter uncertainties, necessitating rapid computation methods for gravity fields and planetary shapes. Following the delivery of gravitational harmonics up to J12 by the Cassini and Juno missions, we present an extension of the Theory of Figures (ToF) to its 7th-order version (ToF7), enabling calculations up to J14. We validated ToF7 against three different codes using polytropic models and applied it to interior models of both planets with the CMS-19 H/He-EOS. For Jupiter, the J6 harmonic is best reproduced by a transition from a helium-depleted to helium-enriched envelope occurring between 2 and 2.5 Mbar. However, achieving an atmospheric metallicity of 1x solar requires either perturbing the adiabat toward lower densities or increasing the surface temperature by approximately 14 K above the Galileo-derived value. Saturn models suggest a largely homogeneous envelope with 1.5 to 4x solar metallicity sitting atop a small core; perturbing the adiabat in these models produces metallicity profiles featuring an extended, heavy-element enriched deep interior (a diffuse core) reaching 0.4 RSat, similar to Jupiter. While classical models featuring compact, dilute, or absent cores remain viable provided the deep interior is enriched in heavy elements, representative models for both planets that include a thermal wind fitted to observed wind speeds are consistent with all measured Jn values.

As quantum computers scale up, noise becomes increasingly detrimental. When devices are too small or noisy to support error correction, error mitigation serves as an alternative. While this approach does not enhance the fidelity of quantum states, it seeks to minimize approximation errors in key metrics, such as observable expectation values. Nevertheless, it remains uncertain which circuit architectures and device characteristics yield the greatest benefits from error mitigation. This work introduces a methodology for evaluating the performance of these techniques using volumetric benchmarks executed across various superconducting hardware platforms, complemented by extensive classical simulations. These benchmarks help distinguish between predicted and actual performance, identifying specific scenarios where mitigation is advantageous. To support these experiments and assist the broader community, we present Qermit, an open-source Python package for quantum error mitigation. Qermit accommodates a diverse array of mitigation strategies, offers high extensibility, and features a modular, graph-based architecture that simplifies the composition of mitigation protocols and subroutines.

Supervised learning approaches typically depend on vast quantities of labeled data, a resource that is both costly and labor-intensive to acquire. Currently, annotated datasets for COVID-19 imaging remain scarce. While self-supervised learning allows training to begin with unlabeled data, existing generic methods for natural images fail to adequately integrate contextual information. In the medical domain, an effective method must be sensitive to anomalies within specific anatomical regions, where anatomy serves as the critical context. We propose a novel framework utilizing two-tiered self-supervised learning objectives: one focused on regional anatomy and another on the patient level. To capture relationships between different anatomical areas, we employ graph neural networks, with graph structures derived from anatomical correspondences between individual patients and a standard atlas. Furthermore, this graph-based representation effectively processes images of arbitrary sizes at full resolution. Evaluations on extensive lung CT datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline methods lacking contextual awareness. Additionally, the learned embeddings successfully quantify the clinical progression of COVID-19, exhibiting strong generalization across patients from various hospitals. Qualitative analyses indicate that the model can accurately pinpoint clinically significant regions within the images.

Automatic language identification presents a significant challenge, particularly when distinguishing between closely related tongues. This paper introduces a machine learning methodology for identifying Nordic languages, which are frequently misclassified by current state-of-the-art systems. Specifically, the study concentrates on differentiating among six Nordic languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian (Nynorsk), Norwegian (Bokmål), Faroese, and Icelandic.

Reactive synthesis involves automatically generating operational system models that satisfy high-level formal behavioral specifications. However, these specifications are frequently unrealizable, meaning no valid system can be derived from them. To address this, we propose a search-based method for repairing unrealizable specifications formulated in Linear Temporal Logic (LTL). Our approach targets the creation of solutions that remain similar to the original specifications by introducing both syntactic and semantic similarity metrics. Syntactic similarity evaluates the structural resemblance between specifications, whereas semantic similarity quantifies the behaviors retained or discarded by a potential repair. To approximate semantic similarity, we develop a novel heuristic utilizing model counting. Empirical evaluation across 26 case studies from various benchmarks demonstrates that our method successfully repairs all unrealizable specifications. Furthermore, compared to existing techniques, our approach generates hundreds of distinct solutions and applies to a broader range of LTL formulas.

Designing parametric quantum circuits (PQCs) for efficient variational quantum simulations (VQS) involves balancing two opposing requirements. First, the PQC must generate a sufficiently large state space to encompass the target solution; failing to do so limits the result to the best possible approximation within the circuit's restricted state set. Second, the PQC should utilize the minimum number of parametric gates necessary to reduce noise from quantum hardware, which necessitates eliminating redundant parameters. The dimensional expressivity analysis presented in these proceedings addresses this trade-off by identifying independent versus redundant parameters. By removing superfluous parameters and calculating the dimension of the generated state space, one can determine if the PQC is capable of reaching all physical states. This analysis can be efficiently executed via a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm with low overhead for both components. Consequently, it is well-suited for future on-the-fly circuit construction, enabling the use of optimized circuits in every iteration of a VQS rather than relying on a static PQC throughout the process. These proceedings review and extend the work detailed in references [1, 2].

Mathematical ecology employs diverse methodologies and analytical tools, with the Jacobian of Lotka-Volterra models serving as a longstanding cornerstone for investigating system stability. In this framework, instability is identified when an eigenvalue of the community matrix resides in the right half-plane. The coefficients of the characteristic polynomial derived from these matrices reveal insights into specific matrix elements that exert the strongest destabilizing influence. However, the destabilizing circuits formed by combining these elements represent only a fraction of the total feedback loops within a system. This study examines destabilizing feedback loops across predator-prey, mutualistic, and competitive systems by analyzing sets of matrix elements to understand how sign structure influences elemental contributions to instability. Consequently, as the set size increases within the characteristic polynomial's coefficients, a complex combinatorial structure emerges among the destabilizing cycle sets.

We constructed and examined a network comprising the hundred most-cited nodes (research papers and books from Google Scholar, with citation strengths ranging from approximately 44,000 down to 100) spanning from the early 1980s to the most recent year. These publications, centered on Quantum Annealing Computation and Information, were classified into four distinct categories based on their titles or abstracts: A) Quantum/Transverse Field Spin Glass Model, B) Quantum Annealing, C) Quantum Adiabatic Computation, and D) Quantum Computation Information. We fitted the annual growth of publications ($n_p$) in each category (A through D) to the exponential form $n_p \sim\exp{(t/\tau)}$, where $t$ represents the year. Our analysis revealed that the scaling time $\tau$ is approximately 10 years for categories A and C, while it is roughly 5 years for categories B and D.

Knowledge distillation serves as a powerful machine learning approach for transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a more compact student model, particularly when utilizing unlabeled data. This study examines knowledge distillation specifically for RNN-T models, which are integral to state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition systems. We evaluated both hard and soft target distillation methods for training large-scale RNN-Ts on the LibriSpeech/LibriLight public dataset (60k hours) and proprietary in-house data (600k hours). Our findings indicate that hard targets yield superior results when the teacher and student possess different architectures, such as pairing a large teacher with a small streaming student. Conversely, soft target distillation proves more effective in self-training scenarios, including iterative large teacher training. Using a large model with 0.6B weights and applying Noisy Student Training with soft target distillation, we achieved a new state-of-the-art word error rate (WER) on LibriSpeech, marking an 8% relative improvement on the dev-other set. Furthermore, this approach enables our production teacher to continuously adapt to new data domains.

The extragalactic background light represents the accumulated radiation from all galaxies throughout cosmic history. However, the angular power spectrum of anisotropies in this background at near-infrared (IR) frequencies remains incompletely understood, exhibiting a robust excess that cannot be readily accounted for by known sources. Axion-like particles (ALPs), a form of dark matter with masses near the electronvolt scale, could decay into two photons within the near-IR band, potentially contributing to this background intensity. We calculate the near-IR background angular power spectrum, incorporating emissions from galaxies, intra-halo light, and ALP decay, and compare these results with data from the Hubble Space Telescope and Spitzer. Our findings indicate that the ALP mass and photon coupling values required to explain the observed excess are in conflict with constraints derived from star cooling processes and observations of dwarf spheroidal galaxies.

We report new spectroscopic and imaging data for the exoplanet host star $\gamma$ Cep A and its low-mass companion, $\gamma$ Cep B. Utilizing the AstraLux/CAHA instrument, we tracked the companion's orbital motion around the primary, while its radial velocity was measured using FLECHAS spectra acquired at the University Observatory Jena. By measuring the relative astrometry of $\gamma$ Cep B across all AstraLux images and analyzing its apparent SDSS i'-band photometry (determined to be $i'=9.84\pm0.17$ mag), we applied stellar evolutionary models and the Gaia parallax to estimate the companion's mass at $0.39\pm0.03$ M${_\odot}$. This result aligns well with literature values derived from NIR photometry. Based on the detection limits of our AstraLux images, we investigated the potential for additional companions within the $\gamma$ Cep system. In the background-limited region beyond an angular separation of 5 '' (approximately 69 au projected separation), companions as low as $0.11$ M$_\odot$ are detectable around $\gamma$ Cep A. Although the radial field of view in our images spans 11.2 '', allowing for the detection of companions up to 155 au in projected separation, no additional companions were imaged besides $\gamma$ Cep B. We subsequently recalculated the orbital solution for the $\gamma$ Cep binary by integrating our new AstraLux astrometry of $\gamma$ Cep B, fresh radial velocities of $\gamma$ Cep A from our FLECHAS observations, and existing literature data. These refined orbital elements were used to derive updated system parameters and generate specific future ephemerides for this fascinating exoplanet host binary.

The efficacy of neural code search hinges heavily on the quality of the training data used to develop these models. Establishing an accurate mapping between natural language and programming language requires a substantial corpus of high-quality query-code pairs. However, due to scarcity, most prevalent datasets rely on compromises, such as substituting code comments for actual queries. Our empirical analysis of a prominent dataset reveals that over one-third of its queries contain noise, causing them to diverge from genuine user intent. Consequently, models trained on such contaminated data suffer significant performance drops when deployed in real-world settings. To enhance practical utility, it is essential to improve dataset quality and ensure queries are semantically equivalent to authentic user inputs. This paper introduces a data cleaning framework comprising two sequential filters: a rule-based syntactic filter and a model-based semantic filter. This represents the first framework to apply semantic query cleaning to code search datasets. Experimental evaluations across two widely-used code search models and three manually annotated retrieval benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Specifically, training the popular DeepCS model on the filtered dataset yields an average performance boost of 19.2% in MRR and 21.3% in Answer@1 across the validation benchmarks.

While NLP interpretability has primarily relied on attention visualization and gradient-based saliency maps to analyze individual predictions, we introduce a k-nearest neighbor (kNN) approach to identify the training instances driving model outputs, thereby achieving a corpus-level perspective. Beyond interpretability, our method effectively reveals spurious correlations, flags mislabeled data, and enhances fine-tuned model performance. Using Natural Language Inference (NLI) as our case study across multiple datasets, we apply a backoff kNN strategy for BERT and RoBERTa on low-confidence predictions without altering model parameters. Our findings demonstrate that this kNN integration increases the model's robustness against adversarial inputs.

A graph $G$ is termed edge-magic if there exists a bijective mapping $f:V(G) \cup E(G) \rightarrow \{1, 2, \ldots, |V(G)| + |E(G)|\}$ such that the sum $f(u) + f(v) + f(uv)$ remains constant for every edge $uv \in E(G)$. The graph $G$ is classified as super edge-magic when $f(V(G)) = \{1, 2, \ldots, |V(G)|\}$. Additionally, the super edge-magic deficiency $\mu_s(G)$ of a graph $G$ is defined as the smallest nonnegative integer $n$ such that $G \cup nK_1$ becomes super edge-magic, or $+\infty$ if no such integer exists. In this study, we define the parameter $l(n)$ as the minimum size of a graph $G$ with order $n$ such that all graphs of order $n$ and size at least $l(n)$ satisfy $\mu_s(G) = +\infty$, and we establish lower and upper bounds for $l(G)$.
