This study draws inspiration from the gravitational wave observations of the GW190814 event, which indicate that the signal originates from a compact binary coalescence involving a black hole with a mass between 22.2 and 24.3 $M_{\odot}$ and a compact companion object ranging from 2.50 to 2.67 $M_{\odot}$. The present work focuses specifically on modeling the lower-mass component of this system. By employing $f(\mathcal{Q})$ gravity in conjunction with the Minimum Geometric Deformation (MGD) technique, we construct compact stellar objects whose masses correspond to those observed in the GW190814 event. Utilizing the Tolman IV ansatz for one metric function and an MIT Bag model equation of state, we simplify the description of the gravitational behavior of the seed solution into a quadrature. Through the MGD method, anisotropy is introduced by deforming the radial component of the gravitational potential. This approach yields two novel classes of solutions dependent on the metricity parameter, $\cal Q$, and the deformation constant, $\beta$. We demonstrate that these parameters are pivotal in governing the thermodynamic properties and stability of the models. Specifically, we show that the interaction between the metricity parameter and the deformation constant predicts a progenitor mass consistent with the secondary component of the GW190814 event.

We establish the regularity of solutions to the strain tensor equation on degenerated hyperbolic surfaces $S$, where the Gauss curvature vanishes on a portion of the boundary. Additionally, we demonstrate that smooth infinitesimal isometries are dense within the space of $W^{2,2}({S},\R^3)$ infinitesimal isometries, and we prove the matching property. These findings serve as essential tools for deriving recovery sequences (specifically the $\Ga$-lim sup inequality) in dimensionally-reduced shell theories of elasticity.

A recent study by Ahmed and Devanbu demonstrated that fine-tuning multilingual Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) using code corpora from multiple languages outperforms using monolingual corpora. However, their work did not examine the fine-tuning of monolingual PLMs. Additionally, because programming languages often have distinct structures—such as the significant differences between Ruby and Java—code written in one language cannot always be substituted for another. To better understand the impact of monolingual versus multilingual PLMs across various languages, this study investigates: 1) the performance of PLMs on Ruby for two key Software Engineering tasks, Code Summarization and Code Search; 2) an effective strategy for selecting programming languages when fine-tuning multilingual PLMs for Ruby; and 3) the performance of these fine-tuned models across varying code lengths.

Our analysis covers over a hundred pre-trained and fine-tuned models. The findings indicate that: 1) multilingual PLMs exhibit a lower Performance-to-Time Ratio (defined as BLEU, METEOR, or MRR scores relative to fine-tuning duration) compared to monolingual PLMs; 2) the proposed strategy for selecting target languages for fine-tuning multilingual PLMs is effective, reducing fine-tuning time while improving performance in both Code Summarization and Code Search; and 3) this strategy consistently delivers strong performance across different code lengths.

Let $G$ be a finite group, $A$ an infinite-dimensional stably finite simple unital C*-algebra, and $\alpha \colon G \to \operatorname{Aut} (A)$ a tracially strictly approximately inner action of $G$ on $A$. In this setting, the radius of comparison of $A$ is bounded above by that of the crossed product $C^*(G, A, \alpha)$, i.e., $\operatorname{rc} (A) \leq \operatorname{rc} \big( C^*(G, A, \alpha) \big)$. If the crossed product is simple, the inequality extends to $\operatorname{rc} (A) \leq \operatorname{rc} \big( C^*(G, A, \alpha) \big) \leq \operatorname{rc} (A^{\alpha})$. Additionally, the inclusion map from $A$ to $C^*(G, A, \alpha)$ induces an isomorphism between the purely positive part of the Cuntz semigroup $\operatorname{Cu} (A)$ and its image within $\operatorname{Cu} \left(C^*(G, A, \alpha)\right)$. Specifically, when $\alpha$ is strictly approximately inner, this induced map constitutes an ordered semigroup isomorphism onto its range. Furthermore, for any finite group $G$ and any $\eta \in \left(0, \frac{1}{\operatorname{card} (G)}\right)$, we demonstrate the existence of a simple separable unital AH algebra $A$ with stable rank one, along with a strictly approximately inner action $\alpha \colon G \to \operatorname{Aut} (A)$, satisfying:
(1) $\alpha$ is pointwise outer and lacks the weak tracial Rokhlin property.
(2) $\operatorname{rc} (A) =\operatorname{rc} \left(C^*(G, A, \alpha)\right)= \eta$.

Adapting transducer models to text-only scenarios remains difficult for end-to-end speech recognition because these models lack clearly distinct acoustic, language, and blank components. This study introduces the Modular Hybrid Autoregressive Transducer (MHAT), which features a shared acoustic encoder alongside structurally separated decoders for labels and blanks to predict their respective distributions. Outputs from the encoder and label decoder are projected into acoustic model and internal language model scores, which are then summed to determine label posteriors. We train MHAT using both an internal language model loss and a HAT loss to ensure the internal language model functions as an independent neural network capable of effective text adaptation. Furthermore, adapting MHAT to text enables superior language model fusion compared to methods relying on internal language model subtraction. On Google's extensive production dataset, a multi-domain MHAT adapted with 100 billion sentences achieved relative Word Error Rate reductions of up to 12.4% without language model fusion and 21.5% with fusion, starting from a HAT model trained on 400,000 hours of data.

We introduce an updated version of the TRQS package designed for the Mathematica computing environment. This tool enables the utilization of quantum random number generators (QRNG) to analyze the statistical characteristics of quantum states and includes various functions for creating random states. The latest iteration enhances functionality by integrating access to an online QRNG service and introducing new capabilities for retrieving lists of random numbers. These improvements facilitate faster access to high-quality random sources, making the package suitable for simulations that demand extensive volumes of random data.

The emergence of COVID-19 has made mitigating and containing its spread a critical challenge for governments. Consequently, the Department of Public Health requires robust models to forecast the trajectory and magnitude of such pandemics, as well as to assess the impact of public policies. A primary shortcoming of current models is their reliance on calculating $R_0$ only after infections occur, rather than providing observable indicators. To address this, we introduce a novel Spatial-Temporal-Susceptible-Infected-Removed (STSIR) framework based on the transmission dynamics of COVID-19. This approach integrates intra-city and inter-city mobility indices with traditional SIR dynamics to create a dynamic system. We demonstrate that the STSIR system is closed, ensuring its self-consistency. Furthermore, we developed a Multi-Stage Simulated Annealing (MSSA) algorithm to determine optimal system parameters. Experimental results using the Baidu Mobility dataset and the China pandemic dataset from Dingxiangyuan show that our model can effectively predict the total scale of the pandemic and offer clear policy analysis through observable metrics.

This study proposes two central hypotheses. The first posits the existence of random phenomena or experiments where individual events generally lack definite probabilities, yet admit a class of nearly certain events; these are termed "typicalistic" rather than probabilistic. While probabilistic experiments are modeled using probability spaces, typicalistic experiments are represented by "typicality spaces." A typicality space functions similarly to a probability space but replaces the probability measure with a less structured typicality measure, denoted as $T$. In this framework, typical sets are defined by the condition $T(A) \approx 1$, and a typicality space corresponds to a typicalistic experiment by mapping these typical sets to the experiment's nearly certain events. The initial section of the paper outlines various components of a mathematical theory of typicality, including the formal definition of typicality spaces.

The second hypothesis asserts that the evolution of a single quantum particle or a system of particles can be viewed as a typicalistic phenomenon, allowing it to be described through a synthesis of typicality theory and quantum mechanics. This approach yields a novel formulation of quantum mechanics that resolves the measurement problem and appears to circumvent certain limitations associated with Bohmian mechanics and the Many-Worlds Interpretation. The remainder of the paper elaborates on this subject.

The Galois lattice serves as a visual tool for depicting knowledge structures. This paper's primary objective is to present a novel category known as graded Galois lattices. Consequently, this work introduces the concept of graded closed itemsets, thereby broadening the traditional definition of closed itemsets. A second major aim is to establish a constructive approach for calculating both graded formal concepts and graded closed itemsets; by "constructive," we refer to a technique that generates a complete solution from the ground up by iteratively expanding a partial solution until it is finalized. Beyond computational considerations, our methodologies rely on significant findings derived from specialized mappings within domain theory. To achieve these fruitful outcomes and develop corresponding constructive algorithms, it is necessary to extend the investigation into the structures of Banach lattices.

We introduce a new technique for identifying cosmic magnification signals by cross-correlating foreground convergence fields derived from galaxy shear measurements with background galaxy number densities, a method known as shear-number density correlation. This approach is applied to data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Utilizing 27 non-independent data points with their complete covariance matrix, we obtain $\chi_0^2\approx 34.1$ and $\chi_T^2\approx 24.0$ when comparing against the null hypothesis and a cosmological model based on HSC shear correlation parameters from Hamana et al. (2020), respectively. Assuming equal prior probabilities for both models, the resulting Bayes factor is $\log_{10}B_{T0}\approx 2.2$, indicating a robust detection of magnification signals. Theoretically, the ratio between shear-number density and shear-shear correlations offers a way to constrain the effective multiplicative shear bias $\bar m$ using only internal data. We validate this concept using signals from HSC-SSP mock simulations and scale the statistical uncertainties to a survey area of $15000\deg^2$. For two-bin analyses involving background galaxies brighter than $m_{lim}=23$, the combined results yield a forecasted constraint of $\sigma(\bar m) \sim 0.032$, which is 2.3 times tighter than the constraint derived from shear-shear correlations alone. Consequently, the uncertainty on $S_8$ (defined as $\sigma_8(\Omega_\mathrm{m}/0.3)^{0.5}$) is improved by a factor of approximately 2.1. Crucially, the joint constraint on $\bar m$ remains nearly independent of cosmological parameters. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating shear-number density correlation into weak lensing analyses, as it enables valuable consistency checks of observational data and strengthens the reliability of derived cosmological constraints.

Convex optimizers are frequently employed as differentiable layers within deep neural networks, notably for projecting points onto a convex set. However, the computational cost of both forward and backward passes for these layers is significantly higher than that of standard neural network components. This paper investigates whether an inexact yet computationally efficient projection can effectively guide a descent algorithm to an optimum. We introduce an interpolation-based projection method that is both cheap and straightforward to compute given a convex domain-defining function. Furthermore, we propose an optimization algorithm that tracks the gradient of the composition between the objective function and the projection, demonstrating its convergence for linear objectives under arbitrary convex, Lipschitz inequality constraints. Beyond these theoretical contributions, we empirically validate the practical utility of the interpolation projection when integrated with neural networks in both reinforcement learning and supervised learning contexts.

This study explores applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to create spatial assemblies by integrating concepts from Procedural Generation, specifically the Wave Function Collapse (WFC) algorithm, with RL techniques used for Game Solving. WFC, a Generative Design method rooted in Constraint Solving, takes a defined set of tiles, blocks, and constraints to produce assemblies that adhere to them. We formulate the challenge of generating spatial assemblies as a Markov Decision Process where state transitions are governed by WFC, proposing a novel algorithm that leverages Reinforcement Learning and Self-Play to develop a policy capable of generating assemblies that optimize designer-defined objectives. Ultimately, we showcase the application of this Spatial Assembly algorithm within the field of Architectural Design.

Accurate scene perception is vital for ensuring traffic safety and making informed driving decisions. However, fog—a frequent weather condition, particularly in mountainous regions—obscures the surrounding environment, hindering clear observation. Consequently, precisely estimating visibility during foggy conditions is crucial for enhancing traffic management and safety. While existing approaches typically rely on costly and inflexible professional instruments installed at fixed roadside locations to measure visibility, this paper introduces a novel end-to-end convolutional neural network framework. This proposed method leverages exclusively image data and Koschmieder's law to estimate visibility by integrating a physical model into the network architecture, rather than relying on direct prediction. Furthermore, unlike previous methods that output a single visibility value for the entire image, our approach generates a pixel-wise visibility map. This provides richer information, especially in uneven fog distributions, which supports the development of more accurate early warning systems. Such systems can better safeguard and advance intelligent transportation infrastructure. To validate the framework, we created the FACI dataset, a virtual collection of 3,000 foggy images with varying concentrations generated via the AirSim platform. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces an Isogeometric Boundary Element Method (IgA-BEM) designed for numerically solving Helmholtz problems across three-dimensional bounded and unbounded domains, provided their finite boundary surfaces admit a smooth, conformal multi-patch representation. The discretization employs $C^0$ inter-patch continuous basis functions; when restricted to a single patch, these reduce to the span of tensor product B-splines mapped by the patch parameterization. For both regular and singular integration tasks, the proposed model applies a numerical procedure defined over the support of each trial B-spline, enabling a function-by-function approach to matrix assembly. Spline quasi-interpolation serves as the foundational element for all quadrature rules considered. In cases involving singularities, this is combined with B-spline recursion over the degree and a singularity extraction technique, which represents the first extension of such methods to a multi-patch environment. A threshold selection strategy is introduced to automatically differentiate between nearly singular and regular integrals. Numerical experiments on key benchmarks demonstrate that the anticipated convergence rates are attained using uniform discretization with a modest count of uniformly spaced quadrature nodes.

Absorbing a focused femtosecond X-ray pulse from a Free-Electron Laser (FEL) can induce extreme electronic excitations within solids. These excitations drive transformations in the electronic system throughout the pulse duration, making the total pulse absorption dependent on fluence. Consequently, fluence-dependent non-linear X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) offers sensitivity to valence excitation dynamics near the Fermi level on a few-femtosecond timescale. This work introduces a simplified rate model grounded in established physical mechanisms to describe the evolution of the electronic system.

We formulate temporal and spatial differentials for key processes, including resonant absorption, stimulated emission, non-resonant absorption, Auger decay, valence band thermalization, and scattering cascades of free electrons. The phenomenological rate model approach provides direct insight into how each physical process contributes to the fluence-dependent variations observed in XANES data. Even without accounting for fluence-dependent changes in the density of states, the model achieves good agreement with experimental results on metallic nickel across more than three orders of magnitude in fluence. This confirms that electron redistribution is the primary driver of non-linear absorption changes at high fluences. While more complex approaches are required to address remaining discrepancies in the immediate vicinity of the resonance, the demonstrated ability to describe spectral changes up to extreme fluences yields fundamental insights into the complex dynamics following intense core excitation. Furthermore, this serves as a vital tool for designing and evaluating future FEL experiments, particularly for advancing non-linear X-ray spectroscopy.

Multitask learning posits that models trained on multiple tasks can attain superior quality and efficiency through knowledge transfer, mirroring a fundamental aspect of human cognition. However, current state-of-the-art machine learning models typically depend on extensive task-specific customization and scale based on data volume rather than the number of tasks. Furthermore, while continual learning introduces a temporal dimension to multitask scenarios, research has predominantly focused on addressing issues like catastrophic forgetting, neglecting its potential as a large-scale component for next-generation AI. We introduce an evolutionary approach designed to generate large-scale multitask models that accommodate the dynamic incorporation of new tasks. These models utilize sparse activation and a task-based routing mechanism, ensuring bounded computational costs and minimizing the addition of parameters as the model grows. By employing knowledge compartmentalization, the proposed method achieves immunity against catastrophic forgetting and other common challenges such as gradient interference and negative transfer. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach can jointly address and yield competitive performance on 69 public image classification tasks; notably, it improves upon the state of the art on the CIFAR10 benchmark by achieving a 15% relative error reduction compared to the best publicly trained models.

This study details a search for generic, short-duration gravitational-wave transients within the third observing run of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo. The analysis targeted signals lasting from milliseconds to several seconds across a 24–4096 Hz frequency band, without imposing constraints on signal direction, polarization, or morphology. While the search successfully detected gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences previously identified by other targeted analyses, it found no statistically significant evidence for other gravitational wave bursts.

The paper reports sensitivities to various signal types, including updated upper limits on source rate-density as a function of characteristic frequency, which are approximately ten times more stringent than prior limits. This search can detect sources radiating roughly $10^{-10} M_{\odot} c^2$ in gravitational waves at $\sim$70 Hz from a distance of 10 kpc, achieving a 50% detection efficiency at a false alarm rate of one per century. Additionally, the study estimates the search's sensitivity to two plausible astrophysical sources: neutron star f-modes potentially excited by pulsar glitches and specific core-collapse supernova models.

Conventional LHC searches utilizing leptons, jets, and missing transverse momentum have found it difficult to detect doubly-charged Higgs bosons (with masses between 84 and 200 GeV) that decay into W-boson pairs. However, these bosons, along with slightly heavier singly-charged and neutral counterparts organized in an $SU(2)_L$ triplet as predicted by the type-II see-saw model, have recently been demonstrated to align with the CDF collaboration's measurement of the W-boson mass. When produced in a highly Lorentz-boosted state, these particles often appear as a single fat-jet or as a pair of adjacent same-sign leptons accompanied by missing transverse momentum. We first employ a multivariate analysis to distinguish these exotic jets from standard model jets. Subsequently, we introduce a novel search targeting the final state consisting of an exotic jet, two same-sign leptons, and missing transverse momentum. Our results indicate that low-mass doubly-charged Higgs bosons can be directly investigated using the existing Run 2 LHC data.

Techniques such as pruning and quantization significantly enhance the efficient deployment of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on edge devices, yet these models remain susceptible to adversarial examples—subtle inputs crafted to deceive them. Specifically, Universal Adversarial Perturbations (UAPs) represent a potent attack class capable of generating perturbations that generalize across diverse inputs. This study investigates how various compression strategies, including distinct pruning and quantization methods, influence UAP attacks. We assess the robustness of compressed models against both white-box and transfer attacks, contrasting them with uncompressed versions on the CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets. Our findings highlight notable distinctions between pruning approaches, particularly Soft Filter and Post-training Pruning. We observe that UAP transfer attacks between pruned and full models are restricted, indicating that their systemic vulnerabilities differ. This insight holds practical value, as selecting specific compression techniques can mitigate the efficacy of black-box transfer attacks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quantization can sometimes induce gradient-masking, creating a misleading impression of security. Ultimately, our results indicate that conclusions regarding the robustness of compressed models against UAPs are context-dependent, with varying phenomena observed across the two datasets.

Originally introduced by~\citet{capsule} and subsequently refined by~\citet{emrouting}, Capsule Networks (CapsNet) have demonstrated effectiveness in modeling spatial features using a significantly reduced number of parameters. Nevertheless, the routing mechanisms in these existing approaches are not seamlessly integrated into the overall training pipeline, requiring the optimal number of routing iterations to be determined manually—a cumbersome process. To address these limitations, we propose Generalized CapsNet (G-CapsNet), which embeds the routing procedure directly into the network's optimization process by rendering all coupling coefficients trainable alongside other parameters. We have implemented both "convolutional" and "fully-connected" variants of G-CapsNet. Our experiments on the MNIST dataset show performance comparable to the original methods. Additionally, we evaluated two capsule packing strategies from prior convolutional layers (cross-feature map and with-feature map) and observed no significant performance differences. We also investigated the feasibility of stacking multiple capsule layers. The implementation code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/chenzhenhua986/CAFFE-CapsNet}{CAFFE-CapsNet}.

Identifying unique characteristics and their interconnections within data facilitates the extraction of essential knowledge for tasks such as classification. In the field of neuroimaging, such features are instrumental in diagnosing, categorizing, and potentially preventing brain disorders. While introspecting highly effective, overparameterized deep learning (DL) models can reveal these patterns, achieving such performance typically demands a large volume of labeled training samples ($n$), which are often scarce in many domains. This study introduces a pre-training approach utilizing graph convolutional/neural networks (GCNs/GNNs) that maximizes the mutual information between two high-level embeddings derived from an input sample. Unlike recent methods that pre-train a single network within an architecture, our approach leverages the ensemble nature of most DL models by extracting embeddings from two distinct components: a convolutional network and a graph network. The resulting graph-based latent representations enhance performance on downstream graph classification tasks while reducing the dependency on extensive labeled datasets. We validated this method on a neuroimaging dataset designed to distinguish between healthy controls (HC) and individuals with schizophrenia (SZ). Experimental results demonstrate that the pre-trained model significantly surpasses its non-pre-trained counterpart, achieving comparable performance with 50% less data.

We present a comprehensive thermodynamic solution for a one-dimensional hopping model under a random potential by deriving the density of states. Since the partition function is a Laplace transform of the density of states, the latter fully dictates the system's thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transfer matrix method, also known as dynamic programming, which calculates the density of states in this 1D model, can be extended to address a persistent challenge in statistical significance assessment for a critical proteomic task: peptide sequencing via tandem mass spectrometry.

We introduce and analyze StkTokens, a novel calling convention designed for capability machines that guarantees well-bracketed control flow and local state encapsulation through provable means. This convention relies on linear capabilities, which hardware prevents from duplication. Beyond designing and formalizing the convention, we also provide a method to formally verify its effectiveness in enforcing these safety properties using a fully abstract overlay semantics. This document serves as a technical report for the paper of the same title and authors, published at POPL 2019, offering proofs and additional details that were excluded from the original publication due to constraints on space and presentation.

The Kalman filter is a widely used algorithm for estimating hidden variables in linear Gauss-Markov dynamical systems. Recently, its Bayesian interpretation has gained significant traction in neuroscience, robotics, and machine learning. Within neuroscience, frameworks such as predictive coding, optimal feedback control, active inference, and the broader Bayesian brain hypothesis have extensively utilized concepts derived from the Kalman filter. Specifically, active inference, which operates under the free energy principle, employs approximate Bayesian inference to explain neural computation and behavior through gradients of variational free energy. Consequently, numerous studies have explored the connections between free energy minimization and standard Kalman filters. However, with rare exceptions, these studies typically highlight only qualitative similarities or rely on disparate comparisons that emphasize differences between the two approaches. This paper provides a direct derivation of Kalman filters that aligns with active inference by applying a variational treatment of free energy minimization via gradient descent. This methodology establishes a more immediate connection between gradient descent models of neural dynamics and traditional probabilistic accounts of perception and decision-making, thereby narrowing the divide between hypotheses on neural implementation and computational principles in brain and behavioral sciences.

We outline the large $N$ saddle point and the fluctuation structure of a theory featuring a sharp, critical Fermi surface in two spatial dimensions. This framework models the emergence of Ising order within a Fermi liquid, with analogous applications to other systems possessing critical Fermi surfaces. Utilizing random flavor-space couplings between fermions and the bosonic order parameter, yet maintaining spatial homogeneity, we express the $G$-$\Sigma$ path integral using spacetime-bilocal fields. The critical exponents derived from the large $N$ saddle point match those of the established non-random RPA theory; notably, the entropy density approaches zero as temperature vanishes. We provide a comprehensive numerical solution to the large $N$ saddle-point equations, confirming consistency with the analytically derived critical behavior. Inspired by studies of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev models, we identify scaling operators originating from fermion bilinears near the Fermi surface. This enables a systematic examination of time reparameterization symmetry and the scaling of Cooper pairing and $2k_F$ operators, which signal potential instabilities in the critical Fermi surface. Our analysis reveals no scaling violations induced by time reparameterizations. Furthermore, we extend this model to include spatially random couplings, thereby constructing a systematic large $N$ description of a marginal Fermi liquid characterized by Planckian transport.

Inspired by recent breakthroughs in solving symmetry breaking issues like maximal independent set (MIS) and maximal matching within the low-memory Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) framework (see Behnezhad et al., PODC 2019; Ghaffari-Uitto, SODA 2019), we examine the complexity of ruling set problems under these constraints. The MPC model is widely adopted for large-scale distributed computing, characterized by a memory-per-machine limit that is strongly sublinear relative to the input size. While extremely efficient MPC algorithms exist for graph problems assuming $\tilde{\Omega}(n)$ memory per machine—such as the $O(\log\log n)$ MIS algorithm by Ghaffari et al. (PODC 2018)—designing fast algorithms for the low-memory regime remains challenging. In this setting, memory-per-machine is restricted to $O(n^\eps)$ where $0 < \eps < 1$.

This paper introduces an algorithm for the 2-ruling set problem that executes in $\tilde{O}(\log^{1/6} \Delta)$ rounds with high probability (whp) within the low-memory MPC model. We further generalize this approach to $\beta$-ruling sets for any integer $\beta > 1$. Specifically, we demonstrate that a $\beta$-ruling set can be computed with $O(n^\eps)$ memory-per-machine in $\tilde{O}(\beta \cdot \log^{1/(2^{\beta+1}-2)} \Delta)$ rounds whp. Consequently, for $\beta = \Omega(\log\log\log \Delta)$, a $\beta$-ruling set can be solved in just $O(\beta \log\log n)$ rounds whp. These results assume a total memory of $\tilde{O}(m + n^{1+\eps})$. Additionally, we provide algorithms for $\beta$-ruling sets in the low-memory MPC model under the stricter constraint that total memory across all machines is limited to $\tilde{O}(m)$.

We present a ``user-friendly'' algorithm designed to systematically and rapidly derive exact planar black hole solutions within the Einstein-Maxwell framework, specifically when deformed by the most general shift- and reflection-symmetric Horndeski sector (where the standard Galileon is substituted with a scalar tuple featuring coordinate-linear profiles on the transverse manifold). Under specific conditions, these axion backgrounds disrupt the system's translational invariance, leading to momentum dissipation in the holographically dual field theory. The method's efficacy stems from the straightforward observation that bulk equations of motion are significantly more manageable when expressed via axion kinetic terms rather than the radial coordinate. By demonstrating this highly efficient approach, we obtain novel asymptotically AdS black holes and prove that their extremal versions invariably flow to an $\mathrm{AdS}_2\times \mathbb{R}^2$ infrared fixed point. Furthermore, we introduce a new family of asymptotically Lifshitz black hole solutions characterized by $z>1$. Lastly, we examine the DC transport properties of the corresponding dual relativistic field theories, highlighting potential applications in condensed matter physics.

For the first time, the U.S. decadal particle-physics community is addressing Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics (HEP); until recently, this was not a mainstream subject. This inclusion reflects the rapid expansion of the subfield over the last few years, driven by breakthroughs in Quantum Information Sciences (QIS) and related technologies during the past decade, alongside substantial investments from both government and private sectors in the U.S. and globally. High-energy physicists have swiftly pinpointed critical issues essential to understanding nature at both the smallest scales and cosmological levels—problems that are unsolvable with classical computers but offer potential for quantum advantage. Consequently, they have launched and are sustaining a robust initiative focused on the co-design of theory, algorithms, and hardware for simulations pertinent to the HEP mission. This community whitepaper aims to highlight this dynamic yet demanding research area, detailing the promises, requirements, challenges, and potential solutions expected over the coming decade and beyond.

Natural language processing for emotion classification typically assigns emotional labels to entire sentences or paragraphs. However, this sentence-level approach overlooks the distinct emotional perspectives of the individuals involved, such as the speaker ("I") and another person ("he") in a statement like "I felt guilty when he cried," who may experience different affective states. While emotion semantic role labeling partially addresses the emotions of various entities by linking them to cue words, we propose a refined task that specifically targets the experiencers of events to assign an emotion to each one. Our method represents emotions both categorically and through appraisal variables to capture the psychological mechanisms behind emotional development. Experimental results on an event description corpus demonstrate that our experiencer-aware models for emotions and appraisals significantly outperform experiencer-agnostic baselines, proving that ignoring event participants is an oversimplification in emotion detection.

The ATLAS experiment presents an overview of the analyses that enabled the observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top quark pair ($t\bar t H$). This significant achievement was realized using up to 80 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

**Context.** Sulfur (S) remains one of the less-explored $\alpha$-elements, with existing research primarily concentrating on individual local stars and a limited number of Milky Way clusters. This study targets the globular cluster Ruprecht 106, which has never been analyzed for sulfur content but is noted for its low [$\alpha$/Fe] ratio, alongside the open cluster Trumpler 5. Previous investigations into Trumpler 5 identified only a single star with an anomalously low sulfur abundance.

**Aims.** Our objectives are to determine the first sulfur abundance measurements for Ruprecht 106 and to examine the sulfur content of Trumpler 5 using an expanded stellar sample, utilizing the open cluster Trumpler 20 as a comparative reference.

**Methods.** We conducted standard abundance analyses using 1D model atmospheres under local thermodynamical equilibrium (LTE), incorporating high-resolution, high signal-to-noise UVES-slit and UVES/FLAMES spectra, along with non-LTE corrections. Metallicities were derived from equivalent widths, while sulfur abundances were calculated from multiplets 1, 6, and 8 via spectrosynthesis.

**Results.** We determined metallicities of [Fe/H] = -1.37 +/- 0.11 for Ruprecht 106 and [Fe/H] = -0.49 +/- 0.14 for Trumpler 5. Ruprecht 106 exhibits lower sulfur enrichment than other Galactic clusters at comparable metallicity; its low sulfur content ([S/Fe]$_{NLTE}$ = -0.52 +/- 0.13) aligns with its $\alpha$-element deficiency, supporting an extra-galactic origin. For Trumpler 5, we established a more robust sulfur abundance of approximately [S/Fe]$_{NLTE}$ = 0.05 +/- 0.20, indicating it follows the Galactic disk trend in the [S/Fe]$_{LTE}$ versus [Fe/H] diagram. Our findings for Trumpler 20, yielding [Fe/H] = 0.06 +/- 0.15 and [S/Fe]$_{NLTE}$ = -0.28 +/- 0.21, are consistent with existing literature.

Breaking down a density function over a domain into the fewest possible unimodal parts is a core statistical challenge that defines the unimodal category, a key topological invariant. This paper presents an efficient algorithm to generate such a minimal unimodal decomposition for tame density functions defined on a finite metric tree.

This paper investigates the concept of $C^{(n)}$-supercompactness, as defined by Bagaria in \cite{Bag}, and demonstrates the identity crises phenomenon within this class. Specifically, we establish that it is consistent for the least supercompact cardinal to be strictly below the least $C^{(1)}$-supercompact cardinal, while also showing that the least supercompact cardinal can be $C^{(1)}$-supercompact (and even $C^{(n)}$-supercompact). Additionally, under appropriate hypotheses, we prove that the ultimate identity crises scenario is attainable. These findings resolve several open questions raised by Bagaria and Tsaprounis.

We examine the hypergraph bootstrap percolation process defined on a fixed $r$-uniform hypergraph $H$, where, starting from an initial hypergraph $G_0$, every edge forming a new copy of $H$ is added in each iteration. The objective is to maximize the duration of this process until it stabilizes. For $H=K_{r+1}^{(r)}$ with $r\geq3$, we present a novel construction of $G_0$ demonstrating that the process can run for $\Theta(n^r)$ steps, thereby addressing a recent inquiry by Noel and Ranganathan. To illustrate that varying running times are possible, we establish that if $H$ is $K_4^{(3)}$ with one edge removed, the maximum runtime equals $2n-\lfloor \log_2(n-2)\rfloor-6$. Conversely, when $H$ is $K_5^{(3)}$ missing an edge, the process may persist for $\Theta(n^3)$ steps.

Effective generation of dense positrons via laser-solid interactions in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime has been established, yet their polarization status remained unreported, constraining potential applications. This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 30% and a charge greater than 30 nC, with a flux of $10^{12}\,{\rm sr}^{-1}$. The degree of polarization varies with deflection angles, reaching up to 60% at specific energies and angles. This angular dependence stems from the asymmetrical laser fields experienced by positrons within the skin layer of the overdense plasma, where radiative spin-flip and radiation reaction are critical factors. Furthermore, this positron polarization is robust and is expected to occur in future 100-PW-class laser-solid experiments, offering diverse application possibilities.

Observations of isolated young exoplanets and brown dwarfs offer rare insights into atmospheric dynamics within a previously unexplored regime, yet questions regarding global circulation mechanisms persist. Earlier research indicated that small-scale, stochastic thermal fluctuations arising from convection-stratification interactions can generate zonal jets, waves, and turbulence. In this study, we refine our general circulation model by implementing a two-stream grey radiative transfer scheme to better simulate realistic heating and cooling processes. We investigate the genesis and temporal evolution of zonal jets, alongside the vertical mixing of passive tracers such as clouds and chemical species. Under conditions of weak radiative and frictional dissipation, robust zonal jets with velocities reaching several hundred meters per second are commonly produced. While off-equatorial jets show little dependence on pressure, equatorial jets display substantial vertical wind shear. Conversely, models featuring strong dissipation suppress jet formation and result in isotropic turbulence away from the equator. Quasi-periodic oscillations in equatorial flow, with periods spanning tens of days to months, are frequently observed at lower atmospheric temperatures. Sub-micron cloud particles can be lifted several scale heights above condensation levels, whereas larger particles create thinner layers; additionally, cloud decks exhibit inhomogeneity near their tops. Chemical tracers with timescales exceeding $10^5$ seconds are driven out of equilibrium. Our models yield global-mean vertical diffusion coefficients ($K_{\mathrm{zz}}$) for tracers typically ranging from $1$ to $10^2\,\rm m^2\;s^{-1}$, and we provide an analytic estimation of $K_{\mathrm{zz}}$ for various tracer types under relevant conditions.

Orthogonality optimization has proven valuable for training deep neural networks (DNNs), where both computational efficiency and stability are crucial. However, current approaches face a trade-off: methods relying on Riemannian optimization or hard constraints guarantee stability but lack efficiency, whereas those using soft constraints improve efficiency at the expense of stability. This paper introduces Feedback Gradient Descent (FGD), a novel technique to our knowledge that simultaneously achieves high efficiency and stability. FGD enforces orthogonality through the Euler discretization of a continuous-time dynamical system defined on the tangent bundle of the Stiefel manifold. Specifically, adapting the concept of Feedback Integrators—a numerical integration technique for manifolds—we apply it for the first time to the tangent bundle of the Stiefel manifold. Extensive image classification experiments demonstrate that FGD comprehensively surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, efficiency, and stability.

This study integrates energy conservation principles into the Daala video codec by employing gain-shape vector quantization. This method encodes a vector of AC coefficients into a magnitude (gain) and an orientation (shape), a technique originally adapted from the CELT mode of the Opus audio codec to maintain the spectral envelope of audio signals. In video processing, conserving energy offers the advantage of preserving textures instead of applying low-pass filtering. By explicitly quantizing the gain, the approach enables a straightforward contrast masking model without incurring any signaling overhead. Furthermore, vector quantizing the shape maintains the same number of degrees of freedom as scalar quantization, thereby eliminating representational redundancy. The paper illustrates that predicting the vector via a transformation of its encoding space—rather than subtracting a predictor—makes energy conservation feasible. Additionally, an encoding scheme for the vector-quantized codewords is derived that leverages their non-uniform distribution. Results indicate that this method surpasses scalar quantization by an average of 0.90 dB on still images, corresponding to a 24.8% bitrate reduction at equivalent quality, while achieving an average improvement of 0.83 dB and a 13.7% bitrate reduction for video content.

Earlier works introduced $q$-analogues of alien derivations for linear analytic $q$-difference equations featuring integral slopes, establishing both a density theorem within the Galois group and a freeness theorem. This paper fully characterizes the wild fundamental group and utilizes this characterization to address the inverse problem in $q$-difference Galois theory. Additionally, this revised edition includes an appendix on pronilpotent completion and refines the main result concerning the direct problem. (Submitted for publication)

This paper introduces a new Image Fusion Model (IFM) designed for ECG heart-beat classification, addressing the limitations of current machine learning approaches that depend on manual feature extraction or direct processing of 1D raw ECG signals. The IFM converts heart beats into three distinct images using Gramian Angular Field (GAF), Recurrence Plot (RP), and Markov Transition Field (MTF), which are subsequently fused into a single imaging modality. We utilize AlexNet for feature extraction and classification, implementing an end-to-end deep learning framework. Experiments were conducted on the PhysioNet MIT-BIH dataset for five arrhythmias following the AAMI EC57 standard and on the PTB diagnostics dataset for myocardial infarction (MI) classification. Our results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in prediction accuracy, precision, and recall.

Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) is a widely utilized technique in pattern recognition that seeks to approximate nonnegative data $M$ with a low-rank product of two nonnegative matrices, $W$ and $H$. Although solving NMF is generally NP-hard, it becomes computationally efficient under the separability assumption, which stipulates that the columns of the factor matrix correspond exactly to columns in the input matrix. This paper extends the separability assumption to a three-factor NMF model defined as $M = P_1 S P_2$, where $S$ is a sub-matrix of the input. We term this approach Co-Separable NMF (CoS-NMF). The study examines the mathematical properties of CoS-NMF and elucidates its connections to related factorizations, including CUR decomposition, generalized separable NMF (GS-NMF), and bi-orthogonal tri-factorization (BiOR-NMF). An optimization framework for CoS-NMF is introduced and solved using an alternating fast gradient method. Experimental evaluations on synthetic data, document collections, and facial image databases demonstrate the model's efficacy. Results indicate that CoS-NMF outperforms state-of-the-art methods in co-clustering tasks while maintaining a high-quality approximation of the original data matrix.

For robots to effectively collaborate with humans in realistic settings, they must be capable of identifying and manipulating various tools. Currently, no existing dataset or study tackles this specific challenge in real-world scenarios. To address this gap, this paper introduces METU-ALET, an extensive dataset designed for detecting tools across diverse domains, including farming, gardening, office work, stonemasonry, vehicle maintenance, woodworking, and workshops. The dataset features complex scenes that may or may not include humans using the tools. These scenarios present significant hurdles for object detection, such as the small size of tools, their articulated structures, occlusions, and visual similarities between different tool classes. Furthermore, we evaluate several state-of-the-art deep learning detectors—specifically Faster R-CNN, Cascade R-CNN, RepPoint, and RetinaNet—on this dataset. Our results reveal that these models struggle particularly with small-scale tools and those that resemble parts of other tools, underscoring the value of our contribution. By providing the dataset, source code, and trained models, this work establishes a foundation for future research into tool detection and its application in robotics.

Machine learning pipelines, which are used to train and assess models, are susceptible to bugs similar to those found in any other code. Data leakage between training and test sets can artificially inflate accuracy metrics during offline testing, potentially resulting in the deployment of subpar models in production. Such leakage often occurs inadvertently through errors or the adoption of poor practices and is difficult to identify manually due to its complexity. We propose a static analysis method designed to detect prevalent forms of data leakage within data science code. Our evaluation demonstrates that this analysis effectively identifies leakage issues, which were found to be widespread across more than 100,000 public notebooks. Furthermore, we explore how this static analysis approach can assist both developers and educators, and discuss strategies for integrating leakage prevention directly into the development workflow.

This work investigates morphism complexes arising from differential graded lifts of Rouquier complexes. We reconstruct the transitive system of homotopy equivalences linking distinct lifts that correspond to the same braid, alongside the Rouquier formula. Furthermore, we establish a large-scale variant of Gaussian elimination tailored for complexes, applying it to simplify morphism spaces of the form $\text{Hom}^\bullet(\mathbf{1},F_{\underline{w}})$, where $F_{\underline{w}}$ denotes the Rouquier complex tied to a Coxeter word $\underline{w}$.

Scene graph generation (SGG) is a core task focused on identifying visual relationships between objects within an image. However, current dominant SGG approaches mandate that all object categories present in the training data, creating a closed-set scenario that restricts real-world utility. This paper presents open-vocabulary scene graph generation, a new, practical, and demanding framework where a model learns from base object classes but must predict relationships for unseen target classes. We introduce a two-stage approach that initially pre-trains on extensive coarse-grained region-caption datasets and subsequently refines the pre-trained model using two prompt-based strategies without altering its parameters. Furthermore, our method enables inference on entirely novel object classes, a capability absent in existing techniques. Through comprehensive evaluations on three benchmark datasets—Visual Genome, GQA, and Open-Image—our approach significantly surpasses recent, robust SGG methods in both the open-vocabulary (Ov-SGG) and traditional closed-set configurations.

For an element $r$ in a ring $R$, a Diophantine $D(r)$ $m$-tuple is defined as an $m$-tuple $(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_m)$ of elements from $R$ where the condition $a_ia_j+r$ yields a perfect square in $R$ holds for every pair of distinct indices $i$ and $j$. This article calculates and estimates the measures of the sets containing such $D(r)$ $m$-tuples within the ring of $p$-adic integers, $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and its associated residue field, $\mathbb{F}_p$.

This paper introduces Directional Analytic Discrete Cosine Frames (DADCFs) as block-based structures designed for sparse image representation. Unlike traditional overlapped frames, DADCFs offer significantly lower computational complexity, reduced memory consumption, and decreased global memory access, making them ideal for high-resolution image processing tasks. We present two specific DADCF variants derived from Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) and Discrete Sine Transform (DST). The first variant utilizes parallel separable transforms where the DST is row-permuted, while the second variant employs a customized DST that eliminates DC leakage—a critical feature for image processing. Both frameworks exhibit strong directional selectivity with distinct characteristics and can be implemented as non-overlapping block transforms that form Parseval block frames with minimal redundancy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these DADCFs in image recovery when compared against conventional directional block transforms.

We demonstrate that centrosymmetric antiferromagnets with broken time-reversal symmetry and nonrelativistic spin-splitting can be effectively characterized by the ferroic ordering of magnetic octupoles. As the lowest-order ferroically ordered magnetic quantity in this context, these octupoles serve as the natural order parameter for the transition to a magnetically ordered state. They offer a unified framework for explaining both the broken time-reversal symmetry and non-relativistic spin splitting, acting as a platform for manipulating the latter, while also accounting for associated phenomena like piezomagnetism typical of this antiferromagnetic class. Unusually for antiferromagnets, we show that magnetic octupoles induce non-zero magnetic Compton scattering, establishing a direct experimental detection method. These concepts are illustrated through density-functional and model calculations applied to rutile-structure manganese difluoride (MnF₂), a prototypical non-relativistic spin-split antiferromagnet.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in various Internet of Things (IoT) domains, particularly in computer vision and machine listening. To fully leverage these capabilities within IoT ecosystems, these models must be deployed directly on edge devices. However, a significant challenge arises because deep learning can only function on strictly resource-limited edge hardware if models are drastically reduced in size. This necessitates the use of compression strategies such as network pruning, quantization, and the emerging XNOR-Net architecture. This research investigates the viability of these methods for audio classification tasks on microcontrollers. We introduce an application of XNOR-Net for end-to-end raw audio classification and conduct a thorough empirical comparison against pruning-and-quantization approaches. Our findings indicate that XNOR-based raw audio classification achieves performance comparable to full-precision networks for a small number of classes, while simultaneously reducing memory usage by 32-fold and computational demands by 58-fold. Conversely, as the class count increases substantially, performance declines, making pruning-and-quantization the superior choice; these methods meet identical space constraints but require roughly 8x more computation. We demonstrate that these conclusions hold true for both raw audio and image classification using standard benchmarks. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to apply XNOR to end-to-end audio classification and assess it against alternative techniques. All source code is publicly accessible on GitHub.

Behavioral cloning has been widely employed to train agents, recognized as a rapid and robust method for imparting general behaviors derived from expert trajectories. Operating under the supervised learning paradigm, this technique is highly sensitive to data distribution. In our paper, we demonstrate that integrating behavioral cloning with human-in-the-loop training mitigates several of its limitations, enabling task-specific agent corrections that handle complex scenarios while accelerating training and reducing resource demands. To achieve this, we present a novel framework allowing an expert to intervene and guide the agent at any point during a simulation to resolve problematic situations with optimal solutions. Our experimental results indicate that this approach yields superior policies, improving both quantitative performance and human-likeness.

This paper extends the development of Aubry-Mather and weak KAM theories for contact Hamiltonian systems $H(x,u,p)$ that depend on the contact variable $u$. In cases of Lipschitz dependence, we derive specific properties of the Ma\~{n}\'{e} set. For non-decreasing dependence, we characterize the Aubry set by establishing a comparison property, the graph property, and a partially ordered relationship among all projected Aubry sets relative to backward weak KAM solutions. Additionally, we identify a new flow-invariant set, $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_s$, composed of strongly static orbits, which aligns with the classical Aubry set $\tilde{\mathcal{A}}$ in standard Hamiltonian systems. However, counterexamples demonstrate that in the contact setting, $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_s$ is a proper subset of $\tilde{\mathcal{A}}$. These findings reveal novel phenomena that arise even when the strict increasing dependence of $H$ on $u$ fails at a single point, and they highlight a discrepancy between minimal and non-minimal viscosity solutions regarding the vanishing discount problem approached from the negative direction.

We conducted a radio survey of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) to search for WIMP dark matter. This study utilized a recent deep image of the LMC acquired via the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) as part of the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey. The LMC is an ideal candidate for radio-frequency WIMP searches due to its high J-factor and significant magnetic field. Our analysis found no evidence of emission resulting from WIMP annihilations, leading to strict constraints on the annihilation rate across various WIMP masses and channels. Specifically, this work rules out the thermal cross section for WIMP masses below 480 GeV annihilating into quarks.

Astronomers have identified several exoplanets with rocky compositions that orbit so closely to their host stars that their surfaces are at least partially molten. These "lava planets" are expected to possess a rock-vapor atmosphere on their daysides that rapidly flows toward the airless nightside. While this partial atmosphere is essential for interpreting observations, it transports negligible heat, resulting in surface magma ocean temperatures ranging from approximately 3000 K at the sub-stellar point to 1500 K near the day-night terminator. Using simple models that integrate the thermodynamics and geochemistry of partial melting, we predict the physical and chemical characteristics of the magma ocean as a function of distance from the sub-stellar point. Our two primary conclusions are that 1) the dayside magma ocean is significantly deeper than previously believed, potentially reaching the core-mantle boundary in certain areas, and 2) a large portion of the dayside exists in a partially molten state, creating gradients in surface chemistry. These findings carry significant implications for the dynamics of the magma ocean, as well as the composition and behavior of the atmosphere.

Effectively communicating the dangers of natural hazards to stakeholders and policymakers requires visualizing landslides at a regional scale. Conventional visualization methods are confined to post-processing small subsets of simulation data and cannot scale to render regional models. In contrast, in situ visualization renders simulation data in real-time, synchronizing visuals with the active simulation. This study introduces a scalable N:M interface architecture designed for visualizing regional-scale landslides. We validate the architecture's scalability by simulating the long runout of the 2014 Oso landslide using the Material Point Method, coupled with the Galaxy ray tracing engine to render 4.2 million material points as spheres. Our results show that in situ visualization incurs only a 2% amortized increase in runtime compared to non-visualized simulations. Consequently, this approach enables the real-time visualization of regional-scale landslides with minimal disruption to the simulation process.

We re-emphasize the substantial complementarity between low-energy experiments and high-energy colliders in investigating new physics related to neutrino properties and the mechanisms generating their masses. Signals from this new physics across both energy scales may stem from a shared underlying dynamic. We illustrate this complementary relationship by outlining the discovery reach for Type I, II, and III Seesaw models, as well as general neutrino interactions within an effective field theory framework and a $Z'$ model.

Increasingly, organizations are adopting cloud environments to deliver services to their clients. Although configuring such environments is straightforward, it is equally critical to monitor runtime behavior and detect anomalies. Recently, utilizing Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for runtime anomaly detection has become a popular trend; however, the interpretability of these models and their ability to explain decision-making processes remain unclear. In contrast, state machine models offer a more intuitive way to interpret modeled behavior. This study proposes a method for learning state machine models to capture the runtime dynamics of cloud environments hosting multiple microservices. To our knowledge, this is the first application of state machine models to microservice architectures. We employ these models to identify various attacks launched against the cloud environment. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively detects these attacks, achieving a balanced accuracy of 99.2% and an F1 score of 0.982.

The effectiveness of variational quantum algorithms depends on the synergistic integration of quantum and classical computing resources. This study examines the interplay between these components, specifically focusing on MaxCut combinatorial optimization algorithms and the relationship between classical optimization landscapes and the quantum circuits evaluating the MaxCut objective. To analytically assess how quantum characteristics influence the critical points of these landscapes, we analyze a family of quantum circuit ansätze built from mutually commuting elements. We identify multiqubit operations as a crucial resource and demonstrate that overparameterization leads to favorable landscapes. Specifically, we prove that ansätze within this family, containing an exponentially large number of variational parameters, produce landscapes devoid of local optima for generic graphs. However, we also establish that such ansätze do not provide superpolynomial advantages over purely classical MaxCut algorithms. Finally, we present numerical experiments showing that noncommutativity and entanglement are essential features for enhancing algorithmic performance.

For a finite group $G$ with a generating set $S \subseteq G$, the diameter $diam(G,S)$ denotes the smallest integer $n$ such that every element of $G$ can be expressed as a product of at most $n$ elements from $S$. In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes.

We establish that the differential Galois group for the entire family of regular singular differential equations defined on the Riemann sphere is the free proalgebraic group generated by a set with cardinality equal to that of the complex numbers, $|\mathbb{C}|$.

The paper "Does the weak trace show the past of a quantum particle?" (arXiv:2109.14060v2) contends that null weak values for spatial projectors fail to indicate a quantum particle's presence at intermediate times between preparation and detection. This stance rests on two points: (i) the disturbance caused by weak measurements and (ii) the imposition of classical-like attributes, such as continuous paths, as necessary evidence of particle presence. In this work, we first demonstrate that point (i) stems from a misinterpretation of null weak values by presenting a counter-example showing that vanishing amplitudes, rather than the wavefunction, are the critical factors. Furthermore, we argue that attempting to enforce classical prerequisites to explain quantum behavior during unitary evolution is unlikely to yield a consistent understanding of quantum phenomena.

This study examines a specific problem involving a right-angled Pythagorean triangle $BCA$ (with the right angle at $C$). Let $P$ be a point on the hypotenuse $BA$, and let $D$ and $E$ denote the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to sides $BC$ and $CA$, respectively. The central question is determining when either of the resulting right triangles, $BDP$ or $PEA$, is itself Pythagorean. According to Theorem 1, these two triangles share the same property: they are either both Pythagorean or neither is. When they are both Pythagorean, the paper provides a full parametric description of these triangles based on the parameters of the original triangle $BCA$. The work subsequently analyzes three specific scenarios: when $P$ is the midpoint $M$ of the hypotenuse, when $P$ is the foot $I$ of the angle bisector from $C$, and when $P$ is the foot $F$ of the altitude from $C$. Further investigation covers additional cases, including a scenario where not only are $BDP$ and $PEA$ Pythagorean, but the four surrounding right triangles ($DCP$, $DEP$, $DCE$, and $CEP$) are also Pythagorean; precise conditions for this occurrence are established in Theorem 7. Finally, Theorem 2, part (i), demonstrates that if triangle $BCA$ is a primitive Pythagorean triangle, no such point $P$ exists on the hypotenuse $BA$ that would make both $BDP$ and $PEA$ Pythagorean.

A Cascadia Subduction Zone (CSZ) earthquake is expected to inflict extensive damage on the lifelines and infrastructure of the northern US west coast. This research aims to offer a bottom-up assessment of the impact on and recovery timeline for the US western power grid following a CSZ event, thereby complementing and refining existing expert-based estimates. The study's scope is restricted to evaluating shaking-induced damage to utility substation equipment within a power system model. The analysis employs probabilistic models for asset damage and recovery, graph theory to represent connectivity, and Monte Carlo quasi-steady-state power flow calculations. Results indicate that a conservative estimate of initial damage and resulting load loss amounts to approximately 4,000 MW, with a projected recovery period of 230 days.

Acquiring well-annotated chest radiograph (CXR) datasets is challenging due to the high expenses associated with labeling. Consequently, there is a strong need to develop robust, transferable representations through unsupervised learning to assist tasks where labeled data is scarce. Unlike natural images, medical imaging possesses distinct domain priors; for instance, pulmonary conditions like COVID-19 typically manifest as alterations in lung tissue texture rather than changes in anatomical structure. Based on this, we hypothesize that isolating texture features from structural variations offers significant advantages for downstream prognostic and predictive modeling. This paper introduces the Lung Swapping Autoencoder (LSAE), a generative framework designed to learn factorized CXR representations that disentangle texture from structure. Through adversarial training, LSAE optimizes the generation of hybrid images that retain the lung shape of one source while adopting the lung texture of another. To validate the efficacy of the disentangled texture representation, we evaluated the LSAE's texture encoder ($Enc^t$) on the ChestX-ray14 dataset (N=112,120) and our proprietary multi-institutional COVOC COVID-19 outcome prediction dataset (N=340 Subset-1 + 53 Subset-2). On both datasets, fine-tuning the LSAE $Enc^t$—which is 77% smaller than a baseline Inception v3—achieved or exceeded state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, in semi-supervised and self-supervised scenarios with comparable model budgets, LSAE $Enc^t$ remains competitive with the state-of-the-art MoCo. By "re-mixing" texture and shape factors, we create meaningful hybrid images for data augmentation, which further enhances COVOC prediction accuracy. This improvement remains consistent even when the model trained on Subset-1 is directly evaluated on Subset-2 without any additional fine-tuning.

This study introduces a traffic management framework designed to mitigate congestion within networks of interconnected, signal-controlled roads. The approach prioritizes emergency vehicles by ensuring efficient and prompt routing. It employs model predictive control to regulate incoming traffic flows via network gates and to configure traffic signals throughout the system. The paper evaluates two distinct strategies: a centralized approach and a decentralized one. In the centralized model, a single central unit manages the entire network, yielding optimal results, though it may struggle to meet real-time computational demands in large-scale systems. Conversely, the decentralized model assigns individual control units to each intersection, which transmit local data to a central aggregator. This aggregator consolidates information from all control units and the emergency vehicle, processes it, and redistributes it to the units. Given that decision-making in the decentralized scheme is local and the aggregator must complete its tasks within a potentially long traffic cycle, this approach is better suited for large networks despite potentially offering sub-optimal outcomes. Comprehensive simulations were conducted to validate and assess these schemes. The results indicate that emergency vehicle travel times can be reduced by approximately 50% using the centralized method and by about 30% using the decentralized method, all without inducing congestion in other lanes.

We introduce a novel algorithm designed to automatically bound Taylor remainder series. Specifically, for a scalar function $f: \mathbb{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$, the algorithm accepts a reference point $x_0$, a trust region $[a, b]$, and an integer $k \ge 0$, outputting an interval $I$ where $f(x) - \sum_{i=0}^k \frac {f^{(i)}(x_0)} {i!} (x - x_0)^i \in I (x - x_0)^{k+1}$ holds for every $x \in [a, b]$. Similar to automatic differentiation, $f$ must be supplied in symbolic form and constructed from known elementary functions.

The algorithm operates in two primary stages. First, we establish precise polynomial upper and lower bounds for the Taylor remainder of frequently used elementary functions, such as $\exp$ and $\log$. Second, we recursively merge these bounds using an interval arithmetic adaptation of Taylor-mode automatic differentiation. This approach efficiently leverages machine learning hardware accelerators, and an open-source implementation is available in JAX.

Regarding applications, we primarily utilize this framework to develop the first universal majorization-minimization optimization algorithms. These algorithms iteratively minimize any loss function by automatically deriving a majorizer, eliminating the need for manual derivation. In machine learning contexts, this results in architecture-specific optimizers capable of training deep networks from any initialization point without hyperparameter tuning. Experimental results indicate that for certain optimization tasks, these hyperparameter-free optimizers surpass tuned variants of gradient descent, Adam, and AdaGrad. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the automatically generated bounds facilitate verified global optimization, numerical integration, and the proof of tighter versions of Jensen's inequality.

Hybrid semiconductor-superconductor nanowires are theoretically expected to harbor Majorana zero modes, which appear as zero-bias peaks (ZBPs) in tunneling conductance. However, ZBPs by themselves do not constitute conclusive proof because Andreev bound states (ABS) commonly occur within these systems as well. In this study, we utilized InAs-Al nanowire devices equipped with a highly resistive normal lead to demonstrate that the majority of anticipated ZBPs—originating from zero-energy ABS—can be suppressed through environmental Coulomb blockade. This work marks the first experimental observation of such a dissipative interaction effect on Andreev bound states and offers a viable filtering mechanism to refine the ZBP phase diagram in future investigations for Majorana modes.

As the cerebellum undergoes morphogenesis, it transitions from a smooth, convex surface to a folded structure. In this process, the cortical layer becomes thinnest at the fold crests (gyri) and thickest at the fold troughs (sulci), a pattern that standard elastic buckling theories fail to explain. A recent minimal model, proposed by Engstrom et al. (PRX 2019), accounts for this by treating the developing cortex as a growing fluid constrained by radially spanning elastic fibers, a pliable membrane, and a non-growing sub-cortex. This "minimal buckling without bending morphogenesis" (BWBM) framework originally assumed linear elasticity for the fibers. This study investigates the impact of nonlinear elasticity on shape formation within the BWBM model. We find that nonlinear elasticity introduces a quadratic term into the system's governing differential equation, resulting in sharper troughs and broader crests—features characteristic of mature cerebellar folds. Furthermore, since developing organs are rarely isolated, we examine the influence of steric confinement, which causes crest flattening. Finally, using the developing cerebellum as a paradigmatic case, we introduce a hierarchical BWBM variant that naturally gives rise to a novel branching morphogenesis mechanism, accurately predicting the later-stage morphology of the organ.

Approximately 80% of the Universe's matter exists as dark matter, forming the structural backbone of the large-scale Cosmic Web. Since this web governs the gravitational motion of matter within galaxies and the intergalactic medium, understanding its distribution is vital for analyzing large-scale structures. However, the web's precise configuration remains elusive because it is dominated by dark matter and warm-hot intergalactic gas, both of which are difficult to observe directly. This study demonstrates that the Cosmic Web can be reconstructed from galaxy distributions using a deep-learning algorithm based on convolutional neural networks. By leveraging results from the advanced Illustris-TNG cosmological simulations, we established a mapping between galaxy positions and velocities and the underlying Cosmic Web. This mapping was validated using the EAGLE simulation. Furthermore, applying this method to the local galaxy sample from Cosmicflows-3 yielded a dark-matter map of the local Universe. We anticipate that this map will enhance research into the nature of dark matter and the formation and evolution of the Local Group. Future improvements in high-resolution simulations and precise distance measurements to nearby galaxies will further refine the accuracy of this dark-matter map.

Distributed optimization involves a network of agents collaborating to find a parameter that minimizes the average of their individual cost functions. Although numerous algorithms exist for this task, they are often susceptible to "Byzantine" agents that deviate from the protocol. Existing solutions to this vulnerability typically handle only single-dimensional functions or rely on specific statistical assumptions about the cost functions. This paper introduces two resilient and scalable algorithms capable of addressing multi-dimensional functions. These methods employ two distinct filters—a distance-based filter and a min-max filter—to eliminate extreme neighborhood states at every iteration. We demonstrate that these algorithms can withstand up to F (where F is unknown) Byzantine agents within the vicinity of each normal agent. Specifically, under certain network topology conditions, we prove that the states of all regular agents will converge to a bounded region that includes the minimizer of the average of their respective functions.

Emotional dimensions are integral to how we engage with music, yet modeling them within Music Information Retrieval (MIR) systems has historically proven difficult. This challenge stems from emotion being an inherently abstract and subjective phenomenon, which complicates both its quantification and the interpretation of any resulting predictions. To address this, we introduce a VGG-style deep neural network designed to forecast the emotional attributes of a musical piece by leveraging human-interpretable, mid-level perceptual features. When compared to an identical network that predicts emotion directly without these intermediate features, our approach shows only a surprisingly minor reduction in predictive accuracy. Because our architecture enables the visualization of how perceptual features influence specific emotion predictions, we contend that the slight compromise in performance is well worth the substantial increase in the explainability of the results.

Creating, manipulating, and detecting pure spin currents—defined as the transport of spin angular momentum independent of charge flow—offers promising pathways for developing next-generation spintronic devices with ultra-low power consumption. Traditionally, conventional ferromagnetic electrodes like Co and NiFe have served as spin injectors for generating these currents in nonmagnetic channels. However, their generation efficiency remains extremely low at room temperature, presenting a significant barrier to practical device applications. In this study, we demonstrate the production of giant pure spin currents at room temperature within lateral spin valve devices utilizing a highly ordered Heusler-compound, Co$_2$FeSi, as the spin injector. The efficiency of pure spin current generation using Co$_2$FeSi injectors is approximately one hundred times greater than that of NiFe injectors, suggesting that Heusler-compound spin injectors can enable high-performance lateral spin devices. This research represents a major technological advancement in spintronics and highlights the immense potential of ferromagnetic Heusler compounds exhibiting half-metallicity for generating pure spin currents.

We examined site and bond percolation on two-dimensional lattices using the random rule and the product rule, respectively. Under the random rule, sites or bonds are incorporated into the lattice stochastically. Conversely, the product rule involves selecting between two random candidates and adding the site or bond that results in the smaller product of the sizes of the two connected clusters. Our analysis focused on both the size of the largest cluster and its size jump to characterize the percolation universality class.
