We proposed finite-size scaling forms for the giant cluster size and size jump to extract critical exponents from Monte Carlo simulations. Results indicate that the critical exponents for both the cluster size and size jump in random site percolation match those in random bond percolation, implying they belong to the same universality class under the random rule. However, we calculated the critical exponents for site percolation under the product rule and found them to differ from those of random percolation and bond percolation under the same rule. Consequently, the universality class of site percolation diverges from that of bond percolation when the product rule is applied.

We introduce an algorithm grounded in online convex optimization designed for the control of discrete-time linear dynamical systems. This data-driven approach eliminates the need for an explicit system model and accommodates cost functions that are both unknown beforehand and time-varying. By leveraging a single persistently exciting input-output sequence alongside insights from behavioral systems theory, the method effectively manages unknown linear time-invariant systems. Furthermore, the framework operates with noisy output feedback rather than requiring full state measurements and supports general economic cost functions. Our closed-loop analysis demonstrates that the algorithm achieves sublinear regret, with measurement noise contributing only a constant term to the regret upper bound. This performance is enabled by a data-driven characterization of the steady-state manifold for unknown systems, allowing the algorithm to asymptotically estimate measurement noise with exactness. Finally, a comprehensive simulation on thermal control illustrates the method's effectiveness and practical applicability.

The growing capacity to engineer two-dimensional (2D) systems through materials, photonic lattices, or cold atoms has spurred a quest for structures exhibiting unique properties, such as flat bands. Conventionally, achieving these flat bands necessitates long-range hoppings, precise adjustments of nearest-neighbor interactions, or the breaking of time-reversal symmetry via staggered flux distributions within the unit cell. We present a method that utilizes projections from a parent system to construct various flat band configurations. By establishing the criteria required to sustain flatness, we identify a novel path-exchange symmetry in these systems that renders the flat band degenerate with other dispersive bands. Disrupting this symmetry lifts the degeneracy while maintaining the band's flatness. Unlike previous suggestions, this approach avoids altering topology or breaking time-reversal symmetry. Furthermore, it eliminates the need for fine-tuning; however, the resulting projected systems still inherit the specific fine-tuning conditions previously identified in the literature for isolating flat bands. As demonstrations, we apply this prescription to derive the flat band conditions for well-known systems, including the Kagome, Lieb, and Dice lattices.

Since its inception in 1963, the Hubbard model has emerged as a leading framework in the literature for investigating cooperative phenomena in narrow-band metals, including ferromagnetism, metal-insulator transitions, charge-density waves, and high-T$_c$ superconductivity. Of these phenomena, the issue of itinerant ferromagnetism within the Hubbard model possesses the most extensive historical context. Despite significant research efforts over the years, the microscopic mechanisms responsible for stabilizing itinerant ferromagnetism in this model (and narrow-band metals generally) remain poorly understood. This review details our numerical findings on this topic, derived from small cluster exact diagonalization, density matrix renormalization group, and quantum Monte Carlo simulations across various extensions of the Hubbard model. We focus specifically on the key interactions that facilitate the stabilization of the ferromagnetic state: (i) long-range hopping, (ii) correlated hopping, (iii) long-range Coulomb interactions, (iv) flat bands, and (v) lattice structure. While most results are based on one-dimensional systems, the impact of increasing system dimensionality on the ferromagnetic state is also thoroughly examined.

Standard inference regarding a scalar parameter of interest usually depends on the asymptotic normality of typical likelihood pivots, including the score, Wald, and signed likelihood root statistics. However, these methods often fail when nuisance parameters have a large dimension relative to the sample size or when parameter information is scarce. In such situations, applying asymptotic normality to analytical adjustments of the signed likelihood root can restore inferential accuracy. This paper demonstrates that bootstrapping standard likelihood pivots parametrically yields inference as precise as those analytical adjustments do in stratified models featuring stratum-specific nuisance parameters. The analysis specifically addresses the difficult scenario where the number of strata grows as rapidly as or faster than the sample size within each stratum. Furthermore, the study establishes that this equivalence remains valid whether constrained or unconstrained bootstrap methods are employed. This contrasts with cases where the number of strata is fixed or grows more slowly than the stratum sample size; in those instances, constrained bootstrap provides higher-order correction to inference compared to the unconstrained approach. Supporting simulations confirm these theoretical results and highlight the superior performance of bootstrap methods in extreme conditions.

Characterizing Low Surface Brightness (LSB) stellar structures, such as tidal debris from past or ongoing galactic collisions, is vital for constraining models of galaxy evolution. Our objective is to derive quantitative measurements of LSB structures identified in deep images of hundreds of galaxies. To achieve this, we created an online annotation tool that allows contributors to outline diffuse extended stellar structures, along with artifacts or foreground elements. All parameters are automatically saved in a database that can be queried for specific quantitative data. We applied this tool to annotate LSB structures around 352 nearby massive galaxies using deep CFHT images from the MATLAS and UNIONS/CFIS programs. Each structure was delineated and classified based on its probable nature, including stellar shells, streams from disrupted satellites, tails from major mergers, ghost reflections, or cirrus. From a database of 8,441 annotations, we calculated the area, size, median surface brightness, and distance to the host for 228 structures. These results confirm that tidal streams are thinner than tails, as predicted by numerical simulations. Additionally, tidal tails show a higher surface brightness than streams (approximately 1 magnitude), which may reflect different survival times for these types of collisional debris. We detected no tidal features fainter than 27.5 mag.arcsec$^{-2}$, despite our survey limits ranging between 28.3 and 29 mag.arcsec$^{-2}$; this discrepancy must be considered when assessing the sensitivity of future surveys. Our database of observed LSB structures serves as a resource for quantitative analysis and as a training set for machine learning algorithms.

Identifying regions with similar climatological behavior helps reveal long-range spatial relationships, such as teleconnections. However, the global landscape of interdependence patterns among extreme rainfall events (EREs) remains underexplored. To address this, we introduce a top-down, complex-network-driven clustering workflow that integrates consensus clustering with mutual correspondences. While consensus clustering establishes a dependable community structure within individual datasets, mutual correspondences create matching links between the community structures derived from different datasets, thereby ensuring robustness when multiple data sources are used. Applying this method to two satellite-derived precipitation datasets during boreal summer reveals consistent, synchronized ERE structures globally. Two of these structures exhibit independent spatiotemporal traits, highlighting the core components of distinct monsoon systems. These findings explicitly demonstrate primary intraseasonal variability within the global monsoon framework, specifically the "monsoon jump" in East Asia and West Africa, and the mid-summer drought in Central America and southern Mexico. A case study on the Asian summer monsoon (ASM) confirms that intraseasonal variations in upper-level atmospheric conditions are maintained through significant connections within this global synchronization structure. Ultimately, our work advances network-based clustering methodologies for (i) deciphering the spatiotemporal configuration of natural variability interdependence patterns and (ii) comparing these patterns, particularly their spatial distributions across different datasets.

This study examines Dust-ion-acoustic rogue waves (DIARWs) within a three-component dusty plasma consisting of inertialess electrons with a non-thermal non-extensive distribution, inertial warm ions, and negative dust grains. By applying the reductive perturbation method, a nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) was derived to describe the modulational instability (MI) of Dust-ion-acoustic waves (DIAWs). Numerical analysis of this NLSE reveals that the plasma system exhibits two distinct regimes: a stable domain where the dispersive and nonlinear coefficients share the same sign, and an unstable domain where these coefficients have opposite signs; notably, DIARWs are generated exclusively within the unstable domain. Furthermore, the fundamental characteristics of these waves—including stability, MI behavior, growth rate, amplitude, and width—are substantially influenced by key plasma parameters such as dust charge state, electron and ion number densities, the non-extensive parameter $q$, and the non-thermal parameter $\alpha$. These findings offer valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of DIARWs in both laboratory and space environments characterized by mixed distributions of inertialess electrons alongside inertial ions and dust grains.

By examining octet baryons within relativistic mean field theory at an entropy per baryon of $S=1$, we analyze the impact of the U boson on the equation of state, mass-radius relations, moment of inertia, and gravitational redshift of massive protoneutron stars (PNS). The effective coupling constant $g_{U}$ between U bosons and nucleons is varied from 0 to 70 GeV$^{-2}$. Our findings indicate that U bosons stiffen the equation of state (EOS). Specifically, the bosons exert a more pronounced effect on pressure at low densities, whereas their influence on energy density is more significant at high densities. Consequently, U bosons substantially enhance both the maximum mass and radius of PNS. As $g_{U}$ increases from 0 to 70 GeV$^{-2}$, the maximum mass of massive PNS rises from 2.11 $M_{\odot}$ to 2.58 $M_{\odot}$, and the radius corresponding to PSR J0348+0432 expands from 13.71 km to 24.35 km. Additionally, U bosons increase the moment of inertia while reducing the gravitational redshift of PNS. For the massive PSR J0348+0432, the radius and moment of inertia scale directly with $g_{U}$, whereas the gravitational redshift varies inversely with it.

Organizing information using a taxonomy involves assigning objects, such as documents or images, to suitable taxonomic categories. The adaptability of zero-shot learning makes it attractive for this purpose, as it enables classifiers to naturally adjust to changes in the taxonomy. This study investigates zero-shot multi-label document classification using fine-tuned language models within realistic expansion scenarios in the human resources sector. Experimental results indicate that zero-shot learning is highly effective in this context. When controlling for training data constraints, zero-shot classifiers outperform traditional multi-label classifiers trained on all classes by achieving a 12% relative increase in macro-AP. Surprisingly, these findings suggest that in certain situations, it is advantageous to employ zero-shot methods and allocate annotation resources to a larger volume of documents with an incomplete class set, rather than distributing the labeling budget evenly across all classes with traditional techniques. Further experiments reveal that integrating the well-established filter/re-rank framework from recommender systems literature can substantially lower the computational demands of high-performance zero-shot classifiers, yielding a 98% reduction in computational overhead with only a 2% relative drop in performance. The presented evidence underscores the potential of zero-shot learning to enhance taxonomy flexibility and points toward promising avenues for future research.

Materials with a phase refractive index near zero (NZI), including epsilon-and-mu near-zero (EMNZ), epsilon-near-zero (ENZ), and mu-near-zero (MNZ) types, are recognized for their ability to either enhance or suppress light-matter interactions. While most theoretical frameworks for fundamental radiative processes focus on energy and detailed balance rather than momentum, this study incorporates momentum exchange into models across the three NZI categories. Addressing the Abraham-Minkowski debate within dispersive media, we find that the Minkowski-canonical momentum of light vanishes in all NZI materials. Conversely, Abraham-kinetic momentum is zero in ENZ and MNZ materials but remains nonzero in EMNZ materials. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that momentum recoil, field-to-atom momentum transfer, and Doppler shifts are inhibited within NZI materials. Furthermore, we explain the suppression of fundamental radiative processes in three-dimensional NZI materials through these momentum considerations. Finally, the absence of diffraction patterns in slit experiments is attributed to zero Minkowski momentum. These insights offer significant value for comprehending fundamental light-matter interactions at the nanoscale and advancing lasing applications.

We introduce a model describing the adaptation of a phenotypically structured population within an $H$-patch environment linked by migration, where each patch features a distinct phenotypic optimum, followed by a rigorous mathematical analysis. Our findings indicate that the long-term dynamics of the solution—specifically whether the population persists or goes extinct—are determined by the sign of a principal eigenvalue, $\lambda_H$, and we examine how $\lambda_H$ varies with $H$. This investigation offers novel insights into how increasing the number of patches influences population persistence, with significant implications for agroecology and the study of zoonoses, where the population consists of pathogens and patches represent different host species. The resulting effects, ranging from a "springboard" effect that enhances persistence to a detrimental impact from adding patches, rely on a complex interplay involving the specific locations of optimal phenotypes within the phenotypic space. Mathematically, the primary challenge in analyzing cases where $H \ge 3$, as opposed to $H=1$ or $H=2$, stems from the absence of symmetry. Utilizing a fixed point theorem, comparison principles, integral estimates, variational arguments, rearrangement techniques, and numerical simulations, our results deepen the understanding of these dependencies. Notably, we offer a precise characterization of the conditions under which adding a third patch alters the probability of persistence compared to a two-patch scenario.

This study numerically explores turbulent Rayleigh-Bénard convection in two immiscible fluid layers to determine how layer thickness and fluid properties influence heat transfer, quantified by the Nusselt number ($Nu$), in two-layer configurations. Simulations in both two and three dimensions were conducted at a fixed global Rayleigh number ($Ra=10^8$), Prandtl number ($Pr=4.38$), and Weber number ($We=5$). The relative thickness of the upper layer ($\alpha$) was varied from $0.01$ to $0.99$, and the ratio of thermal conductivity coefficients ($\lambda_k$) ranged from $0.1$ to $10$. Two distinct flow regimes were identified: the first, occurring when $0.04 \le \alpha \le 0.96$, features convection in both layers with $Nu$ showing little sensitivity to $\alpha$. The second regime, found at $\alpha \le 0.02$ or $\alpha \ge 0.98$, exhibits convection only in the thicker layer while the thinner layer remains in a pure conduction state; here, $Nu$ is highly sensitive to $\alpha$. To predict $Nu$ for a system separated by a single interface, we applied the Grossmann-Lohse theory to each layer individually and enforced heat flux conservation at the boundary. These predictions, made without any free parameters, align well with our numerical findings and prior experimental data, including both $Nu$ and interface temperature.

In a 2006 paper, Jin demonstrated that Kalantari's bounds for polynomial zeros, denoted as $L_m$ and $U_m$ for indices $m \leq 2$, approach sharpness as $m$ tends to infinity. Specifically, for a degree $n$ polynomial $p(z)$ that does not vanish at the origin and any error tolerance $\epsilon > 0$, Jin showed there exists an $m$ such that $\frac{L_m}{\rho_{min}} > 1-\epsilon$, where $\rho_{min}$ represents the minimum modulus of the polynomial's roots. This paper presents a formula to determine such an $m$, offering a constructive proof of Jin's theorem. Furthermore, we establish a stronger result showing that this convergence is uniform, with its rate determined solely by $n$ and a few other parameters. Experimental findings suggest an optimal $m$ of approximately $O\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon^d}\right)$ for some $d \ll 2$. Proving these results would confirm that Jin's method operates in $O\left(\frac{n}{\epsilon^d}\right)$ time, rendering it efficient for isolating zeros of high-degree polynomials.

We calculate the masses of isovector mesons—including vectors, scalars, and pseudoscalars with their established resonances—using a novel approach to finite energy QCD sum rules. This technique relies on selecting an optimal integration kernel that minimizes the integral over the cut in the complex energy-squared plane. Our results are notably stable across a broad range of R, representing the integration contour's radius. The predictions align closely with experimental data within anticipated accuracy limits, demonstrating that QCD effectively describes single resonances.

This paper introduces a general framework for defining a many-valued preferential interpretation within gradual argumentation semantics. By verifying graded (strict or defeasible) implications against a preferential interpretation, the approach facilitates conditional reasoning over arguments and their boolean combinations across various classes of gradual semantics. As a proof of concept, we propose an Answer Set Programming method for conditional reasoning in many-valued argumentation semantics applied to weighted argumentation graphs, specifically within the finitely-valued context. Furthermore, the paper develops and examines a probabilistic semantics for gradual argumentation that extends the many-valued conditional semantics.

The Kondo lattice model is essential for comprehending quantum materials, yet its analysis has been hindered by the absence of small parameters for an extended period. We introduce a three-dimensional $S = 1/2$ Kondo lattice model that depicts a spin liquid immersed in an electron sea. By treating strong spin-liquid correlations exactly, we achieve a controlled analytical framework. Similar to Peierls or BCS phases, a logarithmically divergent susceptibility triggers an instability toward a new phase even at infinitesimally small Kondo coupling. Our solution elucidates a wide range of emergent phenomena, such as odd-frequency pairing, pair density wave formation, and order fractionalization. The resulting ground state is a pair density wave characterized by a fractionalized charge $e$ and an $S = 1/2$ order parameter, arising from the interplay between electrons and Majorana fermions.

Quantum backflow is typically characterized as an interference effect where the probability current of a particle flows opposite to its momentum. This work quantifies backflow across arbitrary momentum distributions, facilitating future experimental validation. We present cases involving gravitational and harmonic potentials and outline the necessary procedures for demonstration using atomic gravimeters. Successfully executing such an experiment would demonstrate that, for specific quantum states with predominantly downward momentum, the probability of locating a freely falling particle above its starting position can increase.

Random circuit sampling has emerged as a key method for proving quantum computers' superiority over classical supercomputers. Although quantum hardware advances quickly, classical sampling techniques are also improving. The primary hurdle remains generating bitstrings with XEB fidelity exceeding that of current quantum chips. This work introduces a classical algorithm capable of producing the probability distribution for any random quantum circuit with rigorously bounded fidelity. The method combines a recently developed multi-tensor contraction algorithm with rejection sampling. Fidelity is managed by partially contracting dominant tensor network paths and tuning the number of rejection sampling batches. As proof of concept, we generated one million samples with a fidelity bounded at 0.2% for a 20-cycle Sycamore 53-qubit circuit. While this task was previously estimated to require 10,000 years on the Summit supercomputer, our algorithm completed it in approximately 14.5 days using a modest 32-GPU cluster (Tesla V100 16GB). Additionally, we project that the Selene supercomputer (4480 Tesla A100 80GB GPUs) could produce one million samples with 0.066% fidelity for the Zuchongzhi 56-qubit 20-cycle circuit in roughly four days.

Privacy is becoming increasingly critical across various fields, particularly within street-view imagery. Traditionally, this is managed by automatically identifying and blurring sensitive content; however, processing expenses rise as image resolutions increase. We introduce a cost-efficient system capable of maintaining performance even when resolution scales by 2.5 times. By leveraging LiDAR-derived depth data to narrow the search area for detection, we substantially lower computational costs. Furthermore, we evaluate multiple detectors within this constrained space, offering a superior alternative to the current HoG-SVM-Deep framework. This new approach, built on state-of-the-art deep learning, delivers both faster processing and enhanced performance.

In Petri net synthesis, the core question is whether a transition system $A$ can be realized by a Petri net $N$. Depending on the required precision, there are three implementation modes: an embedding, which is the least accurate and preserves only the state diversity of $A$; a language simulation, which maintains $A$'s exact language; and a realization, the most accurate form that replicates $A$'s behavior precisely. However, a corresponding net does not always exist for a given system. In such cases, the input behavior is suggested to be modified minimally. Since transition systems comprise states, events, and edges, these elements are natural candidates for modification. This paper demonstrates that converting an unimplementable system into an implementable one by removing the fewest possible states, events, or edges is NP-complete, regardless of the specific implementation type sought. Furthermore, the associated parameterized problems are $W[2]$-hard when the number of removed components is the parameter. Finally, we establish that no polynomial-time $c$-approximation algorithm exists for either problem for any constant $c \geq 1$.

We establish criteria derived from a calibration argument utilizing discrete partial differential equations and semidiscrete optimal transport. These criteria aim to determine sharp isoperimetric inequalities of the form $(\sharp \Omega)^{d-1} \le C (\sharp \overrightarrow{\partial\Omega})^d$, where $\Omega$ represents a subset of vertices within a graph and $\overrightarrow{\partial\Omega}$ denotes its oriented edge-boundary, alongside identifying the optimal isoperimetric shapes. This approach serves as a discrete analogue to the Optimal Transport and AB method proofs established in the continuum, addressing a query raised by Hamamuki \cite{hamamuki}. It extends his findings, which were originally limited to rectangular grids, to a broader spectrum of graphs, including those dual to simplicial meshes of uniform volume. Furthermore, we link this problem to the theories of Voronoi tessellations and Aleksandrov solutions arising from semidiscrete optimal transport. In this discrete context, the geometric-arithmetic inequality, previously central to continuum cases and $\mathbb{Z}^d$-graph scenarios, is replaced by a geometric cell-optimization constant, where the optimization process mirrors Minkowski's proof of his classical theorem for convex polyhedra. Finally, we investigate the optimal constant associated with the related discrete Neumann boundary problem and outline several potential avenues for the future classification of discrete edge-isoperimetric constants and their corresponding shapes.

We have derived *ab initio* low-energy effective Hamiltonians (LEH) for several high-temperature superconducting (SC) cuprates, including Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_6$ (Bi2201, $N_{\ell}=1$, $T_c^{\rm exp} \sim 10$ K), Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_8$ (Bi2212, $N_{\ell}=2$, $T_c^{\rm exp} \sim 84$ K), HgBa$_2$CuO$_4$ (Hg1201, $N_{\ell}=1$, $T_c^{\rm exp} \sim 90$ K), and CaCuO$_2$ (Ca11, $N_{\ell}=\infty$, $T_c^{\rm exp} \sim 110$ K), which exhibit varying experimental optimal SC transition temperatures and numbers of laminated CuO$_2$ planes ($N_{\ell}$). Utilizing the most recent multiscale *ab initio* methodology for correlated electron systems (MACE), we concentrate on the LEH defined by a single antibonding (AB) Cu$3d_{x^2-y^2}$/O$2p_{\sigma}$ orbital per Cu atom. Key findings include: (1) The ratio $U/|t_1|$, representing onsite effective Coulomb repulsion (ECR) relative to nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude, rises with both $T_c^{\rm exp}$ and $N_{\ell}$, aligning with the anticipated growth of the $d$-wave SC correlation function $P_{dd}$ as $U/|t_1|$ increases. This rise in $U/|t_1|$ may stem from neighboring CuO$_2$ planes substituting apical oxygen atoms when $N_{\ell}$ grows, alongside reduced effective screening (ES) from external electrons due to increased Cu-apical O distances. (2) In Hg1201 and Ca11, $U/|t_1|$ diminishes as hole doping ($\delta$) per AB orbital increases, potentially explaining the loss of superconductivity when $\delta$ surpasses the optimal experimental value. (3) For $N_{\ell} \geq 2$, off-site ECR between CuO$_2$ planes is comparable to that within the planes, and we analyze how inter-plane ECR influences both $P_{dd}$ and the stability of the SC state.

We investigated thermal gyro-synchrotron radio emission in five radio-loud stars possessing X-ray coronae with hot ($T_e>10^7$ K) thermal components. Utilizing the JVLA, we measured Stokes I and V/I spectral energy distributions (SEDs) across the 15--45 GHz range, fitting the data with both power-law and thermal gyro-synchrotron emission models. For the three chromospherically active binaries (Algol, UX Arietis, HR 1099), the SEDs were accurately described by a power-law gyro-synchrotron model, showing no signs of a thermal component. In contrast, the SEDs of the two weak-lined T Tauri stars (V410 Tau, HD 283572) exhibited a circularly polarized excess above 30 GHz that a pure power-law distribution could not explain. These spectra were successfully modeled by combining emission from an extended coronal volume of power-law gyro-synchrotron radiation with a smaller region containing thermal plasma and a significantly stronger magnetic field producing thermal gyro-synchrotron emission. We employed Bayesian inference to estimate physical plasma parameters—such as characteristic size, electron density, temperature, power-law index, and magnetic field strength and direction—using independently measured radio sizes, X-ray luminosities, and magnetic field strengths as priors where applicable. The resulting parameters were well-constrained yet somewhat degenerate. We conclude that the power-law and thermal volumes in pre-main-sequence stars are likely not co-spatial, speculating that they originate from two distinct regions: a tangled-field magnetosphere where reconnection takes place and a recently identified axisymmetric toroidal magnetic field.

This research investigates the electronic states within an intermediate band created by interstitial titanium in silicon. Our single-site approach integrates electronic correlations, described by dynamical mean-field theory, with disorder, represented through the coherent potential approximation and typical medium mean-field theory. Across all examined concentrations, we find an extended metallic state featuring a significantly depleted density of states at the Fermi level. The resulting self-energy exhibits Fermi-liquid characteristics and, at specific temperatures, indicates the presence of coherent quasi-particles.

Predicting how proteins physically interact is a fundamental challenge in computational biology. While new end-to-end learning algorithms are being developed—typically trained on large, complex structures from the Protein Data Bank—these datasets are often cumbersome for prototyping and lack the interpretability found in image or natural language data for non-experts. To address this, we introduce Dock2D-IP and Dock2D-IF, two simplified "toy" datasets designed for selecting algorithms that predict protein-protein or other molecular interactions. These datasets utilize two-dimensional shapes as input: Dock2D-IP ("interaction pose") examples depict the specific interaction pose of two known interacting shapes, while Dock2D-IF ("interaction fact") examples indicate whether two shapes form a stable complex. We propose several baseline solutions and demonstrate that a single underlying energy function can be learned to solve both the interaction pose task (framed as an energy-minimization docking problem) and the interaction fact task (framed as a binding free energy estimation problem).

This study tackles the difficult challenges of writer identification and retrieval within document analysis and recognition. The authors propose a new pipeline utilizing a unified neural network architecture that combines ResNet-20 for feature extraction with a NetVLAD layer in the head, drawing inspiration from locally aggregated descriptors. This setup employs a triplet semi-hard loss function to directly learn embeddings for individual image patches, followed by generalized max-pooling to aggregate descriptors for each handwritten image. Additionally, a novel re-ranking strategy based on $k$-reciprocal nearest neighbors is introduced to enhance both identification and retrieval tasks, yielding significant performance improvements. Experiments conducted on three public datasets—ICDAR 2013, CVL, and KHATT—demonstrate that while the method performs comparably to state-of-the-art results on KHATT, it achieves superior mean Average Precision (mAP) on the ICDAR 2013 and CVL datasets.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have revolutionized neural dialogue modeling. Although these models are initially trained on vast text corpora, they are typically fine-tuned on limited, domain-specific dialogue data. However, effectively leveraging the extensive prior knowledge within PLMs while adapting them to specific dialogue contexts remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces DialogPrompt, a novel framework that reframes dialogue generation as a prompt-learning task. Rather than relying on scarce fine-tuning data, DialogPrompt learns continuous prompt embeddings optimized for specific dialogue contexts, thereby eliciting relevant knowledge from the large pre-trained model. To maximize the utility of these embeddings, the prompt encoders are dynamically generated based on the current dialogue context. Experiments on major conversation datasets demonstrate that DialogPrompt significantly outperforms both traditional fine-tuning baselines and generic prompt-learning methods. Additionally, human evaluations confirm the superior quality of responses generated by DialogPrompt.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC performed an invariant differential cross-section measurement of inclusive $\pi^{0}$ and $\eta$ meson production at mid-rapidity in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=8$ TeV. The transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) ranges covered were $0.3 < p_{\rm T} < 35$ GeV/$c$ for $\pi^{0}$ and $0.5 < p_{\rm T} < 35$ GeV/$c$ for $\eta$ mesons. Next-to-leading order perturbative QCD calculations utilizing DSS14 fragmentation functions for $\pi^{0}$ and AESSS for $\eta$ overestimate the cross sections for both neutral mesons, though they remain consistent with the observed $\eta/\pi^{0}$ ratio within uncertainties. Comparisons with PYTHIA 8.2 predictions showed that the Monash 2013 tune provided the best fit to the measured neutral meson spectra. These findings support a universal behavior of the $\eta/\pi^{0}$ ratio across ALICE, PHENIX, and NA27 data for pp collisions spanning $\sqrt{s}=27.5$ GeV to 8 TeV, consistent with experimental errors. Additionally, $m_{\rm T}$ scaling describes the relationship between $\pi^{0}$ and $\eta$ production cross sections for $p_{\rm T} > 3.5$ GeV/$c$, whereas a significant deviation ($6.2\sigma$) from this empirical rule is observed in the $\eta/\pi^{0}$ ratio for $p_{\rm T} < 3.5$ GeV/$c$.

The spaces $BV(\sigma)$ and $AC(\sigma)$ were originally developed within a framework aimed at establishing a unified theory for both well-bounded and trigonometrically well-bounded operators on Banach spaces. However, it has since become evident that their definitions can be refined for greater simplicity. This paper offers a self-contained presentation of the primary characteristics of these spaces, utilizing this streamlined methodology.

Various flavor physics observables exhibit significant discrepancies from Standard Model predictions, specifically in leptonic flavor-changing neutral current processes and ratios of semi-leptonic branching fractions across different lepton generations, with deviations reaching approximately four standard deviations. Should these findings be validated, they would strongly suggest the existence of new physics. This manuscript evaluates the current experimental landscape of these phenomena and, for the first time, quantifies the projected impact of future datasets from the Belle II and LHCb experiments on existing tensions with the Standard Model by scanning new physics contributions to Wilson coefficients. Furthermore, the text investigates the current and future sensitivities of tree-level CKM parameters, providing orthogonal tests of the Standard Model. Direct comparisons of estimated sensitivity are made across three distinct benchmark time points. A high degree of complementarity is observed between Belle II and LHCb, stemming from their respective strengths and limitations. We project that by the conclusion of data collection at Belle II and the LHCb upgrade, all anomalies under consideration will be either confirmed or excluded by both experiments independently with very high statistical significance.

The persistent muon g-2 anomaly may be resolved by heavy new physics particles via chirally enhanced contributions. Recently, it was suggested that a muon collider operating at multi-TeV center-of-mass energies could test these scenarios in a model-independent manner by examining high-energy processes like $\mu^+\mu^- \to h\gamma$. In this study, we confirm these results using effective field theories, analyzing specific renormalizable simplified models and calculating this one-loop process in full generality. Additionally, we investigate how direct and indirect high-energy searches interact to precisely determine the characteristics of the new physics model that accounts for the muon g-2 anomaly.

The proposed Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC), operating at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 240$ GeV, is designed mainly as a Higgs factory. Simultaneously, it provides promising avenues for investigating low-energy new physics phenomena that are difficult to detect at hadron colliders but are theoretically supported by models explaining aspects such as dark matter relic abundance. This study conducts sensitivity analyses for chargino pair production across two scenarios: one where the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) is Bino-like and another where it is Higgsino-like, utilizing comprehensive Monte Carlo (MC) simulations. Assuming systematic uncertainties of 5%, the CEPC can discover chargino pair production up to the kinematic limit of $\sqrt{s}/2$ in both cases. The findings show only a slight dependence on the reconstruction model and detector geometry. Furthermore, these results serve as a valuable benchmark for analogous searches at other proposed electron-positron colliders, including the Future Circular Collider ee (FCC-ee) and the International Linear Collider (ILC), given their comparable facilities, detectors, energies, and luminosity targets.

This note presents the classification of all symmetric 2-(36,15,6) designs that possess an automorphism of order 2 and whose incidence matrices generate an extremal ternary self-dual code. We demonstrate that, up to isomorphism, exactly one such design exists, featuring a complete automorphism group of order 24; furthermore, the ternary code derived from its incidence matrix is equivalent to the Pless symmetry code.

The advent of optical coherence tomography (OCT) has enabled the investigation of intricate three-dimensional morphological alterations in optic nerve head (ONH) tissues associated with glaucoma progression. Despite recent proposals of various deep learning (DL) methods for the automated segmentation and quantification of these changes, their clinical implementation is hindered by device specificity and the challenges involved in creating manual segmentation training data. As new manufacturers and next-generation OCT systems enter the market, the complexity of deploying DL algorithms clinically continues to rise. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce a DL-based 3D segmentation framework designed for seamless translation across different OCT devices without requiring manual re-segmentation (a label-free approach). Our solution comprises two DL networks: an "enhancer" that improves image quality and harmonizes characteristics across three distinct OCT devices, and a second network that performs 3D segmentation of six key ONH tissue layers. We determined that the enhancer is essential for achieving device independence; consequently, a segmentation network trained on any one of the three devices successfully segmented ONH layers from the other two with high accuracy (Dice coefficients exceeding 0.92). This methodology allows for the automatic segmentation of images from novel OCT devices without ever needing manual segmentation data from those specific devices.

This study investigates how randomness and magnetic frustration interact within the series of $S = 1/2$ Heisenberg square-lattice compounds, Sr$_2$CuTe$_{1-x}$W$_x$O$_6$. Replacing Te with W drastically changes magnetic interactions, shifting them from dominant nearest-neighbor to next-nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic coupling. Using neutron scattering, we examine the magnetic ground states and excitations across various $x$ values. We introduce a bond-disorder model that successfully replicates ground states exhibiting only short-ranged spin correlations in these mixed systems. The resulting calculated neutron diffraction patterns and powder spectra align closely with experimental data, enabling precise predictions for future studies. Ultimately, we determine that quenched randomness is the primary factor governing the physics of Sr$_2$CuTe$_{1-x}$W$_x$O$_6$, with frustration playing a lesser role.

We prove a congruence relation for sums of central $q$-binomial coefficients. Leveraging this $q$-congruence, we establish the divisibility properties of the $q$-trinomial coefficients originally defined by Andrews and Baxter.

This study investigates the minimization of a continuously differentiable convex function subject to linear equality constraints using a second-order dynamical system characterized by an asymptotically vanishing damping term. The analyzed system represents a time-rescaled variant of a previously established model found in existing literature. We demonstrate that the primal-dual gap, feasibility measure, and objective function value exhibit fast convergence along the resulting trajectories, with rates contingent upon the rescaling parameter, allowing for optimization through appropriate selection of this parameter. When the objective function possesses a Lipschitz continuous gradient, we establish that the primal-dual trajectory converges weakly to an optimal primal-dual solution. Furthermore, we present enhanced convergence rates for the gradient along primal paths and the adjoint of the linear operator along dual paths. Notably, even in the absence of constraints, certain trajectory convergence results appear to be novel. Finally, we validate these theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

Designing precision components for aerospace and other high-tech sectors necessitates simulating physical phenomena governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) that often lack exact solutions. Contemporary design challenges demand simulation resolutions that are difficult to achieve within reasonable timeframes, even when using effectively parallelized solvers. While the gap between problem scale and available computing power remains the primary barrier to accelerating these applications, substantial performance improvements can be realized by optimizing memory communication and access patterns. The swept time-space decomposition rule mitigates inter-subdomain communication by fully exhausting a sub-domain's influence before exchanging boundary data. This paper introduces a GPU implementation of the swept rule, adapted for this architecture by prioritizing private (shared) memory usage, eliminating inter-block communication, and overwriting redundant values. For one-dimensional unsteady PDEs solved via finite-difference methods, this approach yields significant execution time reductions, achieving 2–9× speedups over basic GPU versions and 7–300× speedups over parallel CPU versions across various problem sizes. Conversely, when applied to a more complex one-dimensional system discretized using a second-order finite-volume scheme, the swept rule performs 1.2–1.9× slower than a standard implementation for all tested problem sizes.

This study details the creation of machine-learned potentials for atmospheric gases featuring flexible monomers, intended for molecular simulations. We employ a recently proposed permutationally invariant polynomial neural network (PIP-NN) to model the full-dimensional two-body energy component of dimers. To guarantee an asymptotic zero-interaction limit, we select a specialized subset of the complete invariant polynomial basis and adjust the variables to optimize the fit of long-range asymptotic behavior. This novel method constructs full-dimensional potentials for the two-body interactions of N$_2$-Ar and N$_2$-CH$_4$ by fitting databases of *ab initio* energies derived from coupled-cluster theory calculations. Subsequently, second virial coefficients, fully accounting for molecular flexibility, are computed within a classical framework using these PIP-NN potential surfaces. To demonstrate the benefits of the PIP-NN approach, we evaluate its accuracy and computational efficiency against various kernel-based and neural-network-based methods using the MD17 energy and force dataset for ethanol. With large training sets, PIP-NN models achieve the highest accuracy among those tested, with computation times comparable to PIP regression models and several orders of magnitude faster than the quickest alternatives.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, decision-makers have depended on forecasting models to establish and execute non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). Constructing these models requires continuously updated datasets from diverse stakeholders, including developers, analysts, and testers, to ensure accurate predictions. This study presents the design of a scalable data synchronization pipeline called "where2test," which supports inter-country top-down spatiotemporal observations and forecasting for Germany, Czechia, and Poland. We developed an Operational Data Store (ODS) using PostgreSQL to continuously integrate datasets from multiple sources, enable collaborative work, facilitate high-performance analysis, and track data changes. Beyond storing data for Germany, Czechia, and Poland, the ODS is also designed to accommodate information from other regions. Utilizing a dimensional fact model, a metadata schema synchronizes varying data structures across these areas and is scalable globally. The ODS is populated via batch Extract, Transfer, and Load (ETL) jobs, followed by the creation of SQL queries to minimize the need for user-side data preprocessing. This data infrastructure supports forecasting through a version-controlled Arima-Holt model, various decision-making analyses, risk calculators, and optimization applications. The data synchronization operates on a daily schedule and is accessible at https://www.where2test.de.

Many cosmological models with $\Lambda < 0$ feature big-bang/big-crunch spacetimes that are time-symmetric and possess asymptotically AdS Euclidean continuations, hinting at a holographic interpretation. We contend that these models typically involve time-varying scalar fields, which can produce realistic cosmological scenarios at the homogeneous background level, including an acceleration phase before the universe reaches its maximum expansion and subsequent collapse. First, using explicit effective field theory cases, we show that asymptotically AdS Euclidean continuations can yield accelerated expansion without requiring fine-tuning. Next, we demonstrate that certain highly tuned instances can yield predictions nearly indistinguishable from a $\Lambda$CDM model. Finally, by constructing explicit examples, we prove that the relevant potentials can be derived from a superpotential, suggesting compatibility with an underlying supersymmetric framework.

This paper, honoring the late Prof. Jean Cleymans, examines nuclear modification factors ($R_{xA}$) for pion production in small system collisions using data from the PHENIX experiment at RHIC. The analysis employs the transverse momentum $k_T$-factorization formalism for hard processes at low momentum fractions. It investigates evidence for collective expansion and thermal effects on equilibrium pions through a phenomenological blast-wave parametrization within the relaxation time approximation. The study discusses dependencies on centrality and projectile species, focusing on the Cronin peak behavior and the suppression of $R_{xA}$ at high transverse momentum ($p_T$), while also incorporating particle multiplicity to account for the soft sector of the spectra.

The rise of online education has significantly transformed traditional classroom methods. While recording lectures is a standard practice for digital educators, it has gained renewed importance during the pandemic due to ongoing delays in in-person classes. Graphics tablets have emerged as a portable and computer-compatible alternative to whiteboards; however, their high cost makes them inaccessible for many instructors. To address this, we propose a computer vision-based solution called the "Do-It-Yourself Graphics Tab" (DIY Graphics Tab). This system replicates the functionality of a graphics tablet by utilizing only a pen, paper, and a laptop's webcam. It processes a sequence of images capturing handwriting on paper and displays the resulting content on a screen. Implementing this task is challenging due to various obstacles, including hand occlusion, paper movement, suboptimal lighting, and perspective distortion caused by viewing angles. Our system employs a pipeline that performs instance segmentation and preprocessing to handle these issues and generate the final output. Additionally, this paper presents user experience evaluations conducted with teachers and students to assess the system's performance.

This study focuses on ranking numerous pre-trained deep neural network (DNN) checkpoints for transfer learning to downstream tasks. Given the widespread adoption of DNNs, it is easy to gather hundreds of checkpoints from diverse sources, yet identifying which ones perform best for a specific target task remains a challenge. To address this comprehensively, we introduce the Neural Checkpoint Ranking Benchmark (NeuCRaB) and evaluate several intuitive ranking metrics. These metrics are versatile, functioning across checkpoints with different output types regardless of their pre-training datasets, and they require minimal computational resources, ensuring practical utility. Our findings indicate that the linear separability of features extracted by these checkpoints serves as a robust predictor of transferability. Furthermore, we propose a novel metric named NLEEP, which achieves superior performance in our experimental evaluations.

Since October 2019, Betelgeuse began to dim noticeably, and by January 2020, its brightness had decreased by a factor of roughly 2.5. This caused it to drop from the position of the 11th brightest star to the 21st. Astronomers were excited, viewing this as a calm before the storm, believing Betelgeuse was ready to go supernova. This article serves primarily as a case study demonstrating how scientific arguments and data answered this question. It will also emphasize the importance of supernovae to human existence and provide a brief discussion on the evolution of massive stars. Finally, the article answers the question.

The quadratic phase Fourier transform (QPFT) represents a novel extension of the Fourier transform family, encompassing various signal processing frameworks such as the Fourier, fractional Fourier, linear canonical, and special affine transforms. This paper extends the QPFT to quaternion-valued signals, resulting in the quaternion QPFT (QQPFT). Our study begins by analyzing the QPFT of two-dimensional quaternionic signals before introducing the QQPFT for the same domain. Leveraging the fundamental link between the QQPFT and the quaternion Fourier transform (QFT), we derive the inverse transform along with Parseval and Plancherel identities. Additionally, we examine other key properties, including linearity, shift, and modulation. Finally, we establish several uncertainty principles for the QQPFT, covering Heisenberg, logarithmic, Hardy, Beurling, and Donoho-Stark types. This work serves as an initial step toward applying the QQPFT in practical, real-world scenarios.

The mystery of how classical reality emerges within our quantum universe remains a longstanding enigma. In this study, we investigate a naturally evolving nitrogen vacancy center interacting with its environment to explore quantum Darwinism—the process by which information regarding preferred quantum states proliferates across the world via environmental interactions. This redundantly recorded information explains the perception of objective reality, as it becomes independently accessible to multiple observers without disturbing the system. To witness the emergence of this redundant information, we employ a new dynamical decoupling protocol that allows for the measurement and control of multiple nuclear spins (the environment, E) coupled with a nitrogen vacancy (the system, S). Beyond demonstrating the creation of entangled SE states significant for quantum metrology, we show that under the decoherence of S, redundant information is imprinted onto E, resulting in classical objectivity—a consensus among nuclear spins regarding the state of S. This marks the first laboratory confirmation of an objective classical world arising from an underlying quantum foundation.

This study continues the work presented in [arXiv:2206.13206], which established a geometric characterization of the Eyring-Kramers formula. In this paper, we generalize the capacity estimate from the previous work to accommodate arbitrary configurations of critical points, a necessary step for extending the Eyring-Kramers formula to a broader context. This extension is achieved through the discretization of the problem and its connection to Kirchoff's theorem in graph theory.

This work examines the family of Dirichlet $L$-functions associated with all even primitive characters having a conductor no greater than $Q$, where $Q$ approaches infinity. For any positive integer $k$, we estimate the twisted $2k$th moment of this family by employing Dirichlet polynomial approximations for $L^k(s,\chi)$ of length $X$, constrained by $Q < X < Q^2$. Under the assumption of the Generalized Lindelöf Hypothesis, we derive an asymptotic formula for these approximated twisted moments. Our findings align with the prediction made by Conrey, Farmer, Keating, Rubinstein, and Snaith for this specific family of $L$-functions and constitute the first rigorous proof supporting terms beyond the diagonal in their conjectured asymptotic formula for the general $2k$th moment.

Video Question Answering (VideoQA) inherently depends on visual data to address general inquiries, yet videos frequently contain substantial redundant information unrelated to the specific task. For instance, if the objective is merely to determine whether someone is laughing, all other visual details can be disregarded. This paper explores the minimum number of bits required for effective VideoQA by proposing a novel Few-Bit VideoQA challenge, which aims to answer questions using extremely limited video information, such as just 10 bits. To address this, we introduce a straightforward yet effective task-specific feature compression method. This approach integrates a lightweight Feature Compression Module (FeatComp) into a VideoQA framework, enabling the model to extract minimal, task-relevant features—down to 10 bits—that are optimal for specific queries. Our results demonstrate over 100,000-fold storage efficiency compared to MPEG4-encoded videos and a 1,000-fold improvement over standard floating-point features, achieving only a 2.0% to 6.6% absolute drop in accuracy. This represents a significant and novel achievement. Furthermore, we analyze the content of these compressed features, showing they successfully filter out non-task-specific data, and present a Bit Activation Map to visualize the retained information. This process mitigates privacy risks by offering k-anonymity and resilience against feature-inversion attacks, thereby enabling secure data storage with privacy guarantees while maintaining task performance.

Large pre-trained language models have demonstrated significant success across diverse tasks, including narrative generation, question answering, and machine translation. Concurrently, recent research has prioritized the control of salient text properties—such as sentiment, topic, and coherence—to enhance human-likeness. This paper introduces Uniform Complexity for Text Generation (UCTG), a challenge aimed at compelling existing models to produce text with complexity levels matching their input prompts. For instance, if a prompt is tailored to low-level learners (e.g., A2 CEFR), the generated output should maintain that same readability level. In a controlled narrative generation study, we evaluated over 160 linguistic and cognitively driven features to assess text readability, discovering that both GPT-2 models and humans often fail to preserve the linguistic complexity of the input prompts. Finally, we outline potential strategies and methodologies that can be integrated into general frameworks to steer language models toward solving this critical challenge.

The effectiveness of facial super-resolution techniques hinges on their capacity to accurately reconstruct facial structures and prominent features. Although convolutional neural networks and generative adversarial networks have achieved remarkable results in face hallucination, their utilization of attributes derived from low-resolution images remains inadequate. To address this, we introduce an Attribute Guided Attention Generative Adversarial Network (AGA-GAN) that utilizes novel Attribute Guided Attention (AGA) modules to direct the generation process toward specific facial characteristics. By stacking multiple AGA modules, the framework successfully recovers both high-level and low-level facial structures. Furthermore, we design a discriminator to capture discriminative features by leveraging the correlation between high-resolution images and their facial attribute labels. Additionally, we integrate a U-Net architecture to refine predictions and synthesize additional facial details. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our AGA-GAN and AGA-GAN+U-Net frameworks surpass several state-of-the-art face hallucination methods across various metrics. Finally, we validate the method's robustness in scenarios where not all attribute descriptors are available, confirming its suitability for real-world applications.

This paper introduces a fully integrated CMOS temperature sensor designed for dense thermal monitoring in systems on chip that support dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. The sensor's front-end utilizes a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to transform local temperature into two biasing currents, which subsequently determine two oscillation frequencies. The ratio of these frequencies corresponds directly to the absolute temperature. The back-end then converts this frequency ratio into a digital temperature code. Benefiting from its low-complexity architecture, the design offers a compact footprint, low power usage, and high accuracy across a broad temperature spectrum. Additionally, an embedded line regulation mechanism enables voltage scalability. Prototyped in 180nm CMOS, the sensor operates within a 0°C to 100°C detection range, supports a supply voltage from 0.6V to 1.8V, and occupies a minimal silicon area of 0.021mm². Experimental results from 20 test chips demonstrate competitive performance metrics, including a resolution of 0.24°C, an inaccuracy of ±1.4°C, a sampling rate of approximately 1.5kHz, and an energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion at 30°C.

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) faces substantial hurdles in reconstructing and modeling black-hole images due to its sparse interferometric coverage. PRIMO, a novel algorithm grounded in principal components analysis, addresses this by utilizing high-fidelity general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of low-luminosity accretion flows as its training data. This approach ensures reconstructed images align with interferometric observations while remaining within the subspace defined by the simulations. By employing Monte Carlo Markov Chains, PRIMO fits a linear combination of principal components extracted from an ensemble of simulated images to the observed data. Our findings demonstrate that PRIMO can efficiently and accurately reconstruct synthetic EHT datasets for various simulated images, even when the underlying simulation parameters differ significantly from those used to generate the principal components. The resulting reconstructions attain resolution commensurate with the array's capabilities and avoid introducing notable biases in image features, such as the emission ring's diameter.

Creating efficient, easy-to-adopt, and maintainable low-power wide-area network (LPWAN) solutions is essential for smart city development. However, unlicensed LPWANs suffer from poor quality of service, while LTE-M and NB-IoT are hindered by high costs. Combining licensed and unlicensed LPWANs offers a way to leverage the strengths of both while mitigating these drawbacks. Despite this advantage, a concatenated architecture inevitably introduces additional latency, which could affect user quality of experience (QoE). To assess the practical viability of such a system, we propose a concatenated LPWAN framework and experimentally analyze end-to-end (E2E) latency statistics. We determine the acceptable delay margin by benchmarking three schemes: standalone unlicensed IoT (LoRa), standalone cellular IoT (LTE-M), and a concatenated setup (LoRa interfaced with LTE-M). Through extensive testing involving 30,000 data points, we find that the extra delay caused by interfacing averages less than 300 milliseconds. These proof-of-concept results indicate that for smart city applications where human perception and decision-making are involved, the latency introduced by combining unlicensed LPWAN with cellular IoT is negligible.

This report details the advancement of X-ray sources utilizing laser-plasma accelerators at ELI beamlines. A primary goal of ELI Beamlines is to supply users across diverse research disciplines with beams of ultrashort particles and complex X-ray sources. Currently, two hard X-ray betatron sources characterized by high photon flux, driven by laser-plasma acceleration (LPA), are undergoing commissioning. The first, known as the Gammatron beamline in Experimental Hall E2, delivers X-ray pulses ranging from 1-100 keV via betatron radiation and up to 1 MeV using a Compton scheme. We have also designed new X-ray optics to serve as focusing elements for these hard X-ray sources in user applications. The second LPA-based hard X-ray source is being developed within the ELI plasma physics platform (P3), where it will support active diagnostics for high-energy density (HED) physics, laboratory astrophysics, multi-beam experiments, and fundamental research; we will present initial experimental results from its ongoing commissioning. Furthermore, we propose a novel method to enhance X-ray flux by exploiting betatron oscillations amplified through nonlinear resonances caused by interaction with a two-color laser field. Additionally, we will introduce a new optical probing technique offering high sensitivity for characterizing low-density gas targets in laser-plasma accelerators. This technique was realized by utilizing multiple passes of the probe beam through the target and employing relay imaging of the object between each pass.

The LHCb Experiment is preparing a comprehensive detector upgrade designed to fully leverage the flavour physics capabilities of the LHC. The entire detector will be read out at the full collision rate, with online event selection handled by a software trigger. This approach will boost event yields by a factor of 10 for muonic and a factor of 20 for hadronic final states. Research for this upgrade has commenced, with the goal of installing the detector in 2018.

Automatic sequences possess several characteristics that are not guaranteed in other sequences, especially non-uniformly morphic ones. This paper reviews various techniques for demonstrating that a specific sequence is not automatic. Furthermore, when these sequences are defined over the finite field ${\mathbb F}_q$, these methods also allow for proving that their associated formal power series are transcendental over ${\mathbb F}_q(X)$.

We enhance an established finding regarding the strong consistency of M-estimates for regression parameters within a linear model featuring independent and identically distributed random errors, subject to certain mild assumptions.

Since the Internet's emergence, determining the relative significance of web pages has been central to search engine methodologies. The PageRank algorithm models the global web structure using a Google matrix, where the principal eigenvector's components assign numerical rankings to pages. However, calculating this dominant eigenvector for an exponentially expanding web has become a computationally demanding task that challenges the limits of Moore's Law. This study demonstrates that specialized optical hardware, including networks of optical parametric oscillators, lasers, and gain-dissipative condensates, can accelerate the reliable reconstruction of principal eigenvectors for real-world web graphs. We evaluate the viability of simulating the PageRank algorithm on massive Google matrices using these non-traditional systems. Additionally, we present alternative ranking methods derived from minimizing spin Hamiltonians. Our projections indicate that these dedicated optical machines could achieve substantial reductions in power consumption compared to classical computing architectures.

We build a sequence of Calabi-Yau manifold examples across arbitrary dimensions and calculate their primary invariants, specifically offering a higher-dimensional extension of Borcea-Voisin Calabi-Yau threefolds. Furthermore, we present a technique for determining the local zeta function via the Frobenius morphism applied to Rose's orbifold cohomology, and we derive the Hodge numbers of these constructed examples using orbifold Chen-Ruan cohomology.

Quantum entanglement forms the foundation of quantum information science and technology. Within the optical realm, polarization entanglement is the predominant form, yet it is typically generated through postselection involving destructive photon detection, which limits its utility for applications requiring accessible entanglement resources. This study introduces a heralded scheme for preparing multipartite entangled states of polarized photons, eliminating the need for postselection. By applying the quantum scissors technique, we truncate existing continuous-variable entanglement to produce target states that are either hybrid discrete-continuous or purely discrete. We examine two implementations of this technique: a modified version of the original quantum scissors method utilizing single photons and linear optics, and a newly designed approach employing a type-II two-mode squeezer. We analyze the advantages and limitations of both implementations while addressing practical considerations for entanglement preparation. Ultimately, this work demonstrates an interface between different types of optical entanglement, suggesting that the proposed quantum scissors methods offer viable alternatives for the heralded generation of polarization entanglement.

We investigate cosmological models incorporating two extra free parameters, $N_\mathrm{eff}$ and $\xi_e$, alongside the standard $\Lambda$CDM parameters. These models include additional radiation sources, such as hot axions or sterile neutrinos, combined with neutrino energy densities featuring significant degeneracy. A higher $N_\mathrm{eff}$ becomes viable without compromising Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) because a positive neutrino degeneracy ($\xi_e$) can enhance the BBN fit. Analysis of data from Planck, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), BBN, and type-Ia supernovae (SNeIa) suggests that the Hubble tension can be alleviated when $\xi_{e}\simeq 0.04$ and $0.3 \lesssim \Delta N_\mathrm{eff} \lesssim 0.6$.

We present a simplified toy model for polarized synchrotron images from an equatorial source orbiting a Kerr black hole, utilizing a semi-analytic solution to the null geodesic equation alongside the conservation of the Penrose-Walker constant. Building upon Narayan et al. (2021), who focused on Schwarzschild black holes with a fully analytic approximation, our framework extends these results to include arbitrary observer inclinations, black hole spin, local boosts, and various local magnetic field configurations. By examining the geometric impacts of black hole spin on photon parallel transport, we isolate these effects from the complex interplay of relativistic, gravitational, and electromagnetic processes within the emission zone. Our findings confirm an analytic approximation for the subleading geometric influence of spin on face-on polarization rotation in direct images, expressed as $\Delta {\rm EVPA} \sim -2a/r_{\rm s}^2$ (where $a$ denotes spin and $r_{\rm s}$ the emission radius). Additionally, we demonstrate that spin induces an order-unity effect on face-on subimages, given by $\Delta {\rm EVPA} \sim \pm a/\sqrt{27}$. Furthermore, this model facilitates the analysis of polarization "loops" seen during flares from orbiting hotspots, offering valuable insights for both polarimetric simulations and observations of black holes by facilities such as the EHT and GRAVITY.

System identification for nonlinear dynamics is crucial due to its extensive applicability. Conventional methods encompass Volterra series, nonlinear autoregressive with exogenous inputs (NARX), block-structured, state-space, and neural network (NN) models. Among these, NNs stand out as a potent black-box technique, leveraging universal approximation capabilities and minimal reliance on prior knowledge. Nevertheless, NNs present specific hurdles. First, determining an optimal network architecture is difficult; overly simple structures fail to capture system characteristics, whereas complex ones risk overfitting. Second, sufficient training data is often scarce for certain nonlinear systems, necessitating strategies for effective identification with limited datasets. Additionally, quantifying the uncertainty of NN parameters would enhance subsequent analysis. This paper introduces a sparse Bayesian deep learning framework to tackle these issues. By incorporating sparsity-inducing priors, the Bayesian approach strengthens regularization within neural networks and facilitates the computation of parameter uncertainty. We also propose an efficient iterative re-weighting algorithm. The method's efficacy is evaluated across various dataset ratios, with one-step-ahead predictions on a Cascaded Tank System demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, simulations on this benchmark confirm that our algorithm surpasses other methods even under more challenging conditions.

Currently, the primary benchmark for assessing AI algorithm performance is model accuracy, where higher scores equate to superior quality. Pursuing new state-of-the-art achievements has driven a massive, exponential rise in computational requirements. Although this surge has yielded remarkable results, it is unsustainable. This paper introduces tensor networks (TNs)—an established concept from multilinear algebra—as a viable solution for sustainable, or "Green," AI. TNs can enhance efficiency without sacrificing accuracy, making them ideal for reducing computational costs. We demonstrate these efficiency gains within both kernel machine and deep learning frameworks. Furthermore, we argue that algorithms should be evaluated based on both accuracy and efficiency, discussing various efficiency metrics and analyzing them through an experimental setup for kernel ridge regression. Our goal is to highlight the benefits of Green AI for sustainability and research. Our main contribution is proving that TNs facilitate efficient algorithms, thereby advancing the cause of Green AI and enabling the development of superior AI models.

This study addresses the challenging and under-explored task of clustering survival data. We propose a new semi-supervised probabilistic framework that utilizes recent advancements in stochastic gradient variational inference. Unlike prior approaches, our method leverages a deep generative model to reveal the underlying distributions of both explanatory variables and censored survival times. Through extensive experiments on diverse synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets—including medical imaging data—we benchmark our model against existing clustering and mixture models for survival analysis. Our approach demonstrates superior performance in cluster identification and competitive accuracy in survival time prediction. By relying on novel generative assumptions, the proposed model provides a holistic view of survival data clustering and offers potential for discovering subpopulations governed by distinct generative mechanisms.

CMOS sensors acquire images row-by-row, a process that often introduces rolling shutter (RS) distortions due to scene motion. Current single-image RS correction techniques typically rely on algorithms designed for specific scene types requiring known intrinsic camera parameters, or on learning-based frameworks that depend on known ground-truth motion data. This paper introduces an end-to-end deep neural network to address the difficult problem of single-image RS rectification. The proposed architecture includes a motion block, a trajectory module, a row block, an RS rectification module, and an RS regeneration module utilized solely during training. The motion block estimates the camera pose for each row of the distorted input, while the trajectory module fits these motion parameters to a third-order polynomial. Subsequently, the row block determines the camera motion required for every pixel in the corrected target image. Finally, the RS rectification module warps the input image using the motion trajectory and row block outputs to produce a distortion-free result. To accelerate training convergence, the RS regeneration module compares the input RS image against a ground-truth image distorted by the estimated motion parameters. Because the end-to-end formulation does not restrict estimated motion to match ground-truth values, the model effectively rectifies RS images involving complex real-world camera movements. Experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our network surpasses existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative metrics.

Our calculations demonstrate that a negative refractive index (NRI), previously thought to exist exclusively in metamaterials, can also occur in Dirac semimetals (DSM). Since electrons in DSM possess zero effective mass, the system lacks a nominal energy scale; consequently, the electromagnetic responses of these electrons are not dominated by mass-related physical effects as they are in conventional materials. This NRI arises from the interplay between vacuum polarization quantum effects and their finite-temperature corrections, which scale with $T^4$ at low temperatures. The phenomenon represents a resonance between incident light and the distinctive structure of Dirac cones, enabling numerous states to contribute to electron-hole pair production through a dispersion relation similar to that of the cones. In DSM, the NRI effect spans a broad range of photon frequencies and wave numbers, potentially observable in the giga Hertz range at temperatures slightly above room temperature.

This paper's primary contributions are twofold. First, we establish Bernstein-type inequalities for geometric and algebraic irregularly-spaced NED random fields, of which time series are a specific instance. By incorporating the concept of "effective dimension" into the random field's index set, our findings demonstrate that the sharpness of these inequalities depends solely on this dimension. To our knowledge, this is the first study to highlight this phenomenon, effectively updating the foundational work of \citeA{xu2018sieve}. As a direct consequence, we also derive a Bernstein-type inequality for geometrically irregularly-spaced $\alpha$-mixing random fields. Second, leveraging these inequalities, we determine the $L_{\infty}$ convergence rates for various kernel-based nonparametric estimators. This requires deriving two deviation inequalities for the supremum of the empirical process under NED and $\alpha$-mixing conditions. Specifically, for irregularly-spaced NED random fields, we prove that the local linear estimator in nonparametric regression achieves the optimal rate, advancing upon the earlier work of \citeA{jenish2012nonparametric}. We further examine the uniform convergence rate of uni-modal regression under identical NED assumptions. Following the framework of \citeA{rigollet2009optimal}, we also show that the kernel-based plug-in density level set estimator attains optimality up to a logarithmic factor. Additionally, when data originates from $\alpha$-mixing random fields, we establish the uniform convergence rate for a simple local polynomial density estimator \cite{cattaneo2020simple}.

We introduce a multi-scale modeling and simulation framework designed for low-Reynolds number hydrodynamics involving shape-changing immersed objects, such as biological microswimmers and active surfaces. The core concept involves treating principal shape changes as generalized coordinates and establishing corresponding conjugate hydrodynamic friction forces. Advantageously, these generalized friction coefficients can be pre-calculated and reused to efficiently solve the dynamic equations of motion. This approach extends the Lagrangian mechanics of dissipative systems to active surfaces and microswimmers, where shape dynamics are driven by internal forces. As a practical application, we demonstrate the prediction of both in-phase and anti-phase synchronization in cilia pairs using an experimentally measured beat pattern.

While established deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch offer efficient interfaces for training models on single devices or via data parallelism, they often lack the flexibility and performance required for training emerging large-scale models across distributed systems that demand advanced parallelism strategies. Although plugins and wrappers have been created to extend these frameworks for model or pipeline parallelism, they often introduce unnecessary complexity. To address this, we introduce OneFlow, a streamlined distributed training framework designed to support various parallelism paradigms through a novel SBP (split, broadcast, and partial-value) abstraction and the actor model. The SBP abstraction simplifies the programming of both data and model parallelism compared to existing solutions, while the actor model offers a concise runtime mechanism to manage complex dependencies arising from resource constraints, data movement, and computation in distributed environments. Extensive experiments and case studies demonstrate OneFlow's efficiency and broad applicability for training diverse large DNN models, with results showing it outperforms many custom libraries built atop current state-of-the-art frameworks. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Oneflow-Inc/oneflow.

We performed 3D radiative hydrodynamic simulations modeling dust and gas to study planet formation. Our investigation covered a parameter space including Neptune-, Saturn-, Jupiter-, and 5-Jupiter-mass planets located at 5.2, 30, and 50 AU from their host stars. We discovered that meridional circulation \citep{Szulagyi14,FC16} generates a powerful vertical flow for dust, preventing even mm-sized grains from settling in the midplane.
