This circulation transports both dust and gas vertically into the circumplanetary region, effectively bridging the gap. Dust accretion rates within the Hill sphere range from $\sim10^{-8}$ to $10^{-10}$ $\rm{M_{Jup}/yr}$, rising with increasing planet mass, while gas accretion rates span $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-8}$ $\rm{M_{Jup}/yr}$. As planetary mass decreases, the disparity between gas and dust accretion rates diminishes. Near the planet, mm-grains are more easily trapped than gas, suggesting the circumplanetary disk could be solid-enriched relative to the circumstellar disk. We computed the local dust-to-gas ratio (DTG) throughout the circumstellar disk to determine altitudes where DTG equals 1, 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001. Larger planets deliver mm-sized dust to higher altitudes and lift a greater fraction of the dust disk. Furthermore, mm-dust stirring is negligible for planets with masses at or below that of Neptune but becomes significant for those exceeding Saturn's mass.

This study examines dust characteristics and star-formation indicators in early-universe galaxies by stacking 111,227 sources from the newly released COSMOS catalogue onto maps spanning wavelengths around the peak of warm dust emission. Our results reveal an elevated far-infrared luminosity density extending to redshift 8, signaling a prevalence of dust in the early cosmos. Additionally, we observe a rise in dust temperature with increasing redshift, peaking at approximately 100 ± 12 K near z ~ 7; this suggests either silicate-rich dust from Population II stars or heating mechanisms beyond those provided by young, hot stars. Finally, we analyze why these objects were overlooked in prior surveys and propose strategies for future observations. All code, data links, and reproduction instructions are available at https://github.com/marcoviero/simstack3/.

This paper investigates the online Euclidean spanner problem for point sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given a sequence of $n$ points $(s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n)$ arriving sequentially, the goal of an online algorithm is to maintain a geometric $t$-spanner on the current set $S_i = \{s_1, \ldots, s_i\}$ at each step $i$. First, we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n / \log \varepsilon^{-1})$ for the competitive ratio of any online $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner algorithm operating on 1-dimensional point sequences. We demonstrate that this bound is tight by presenting an algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n / \log \varepsilon^{-1})$. Next, we develop online algorithms for sequences in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \ge 2$) under the $L_2$ norm. While existing incremental algorithms yield a competitive ratio of $O(\varepsilon^{-(d+1)}\log n)$, we show that allowing the use of Steiner points significantly improves the dependence on $\varepsilon$. Specifically, we propose an online Steiner $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner algorithm with a competitive ratio of $O(\varepsilon^{(1-d)/2} \log n)$. Conversely, we establish that the dependence on $n$ cannot be removed for dimensions $d \ge 2$; specifically, any online spanner algorithm in $\mathbb{R}^d$ under the $L_2$ norm must have a competitive ratio of $\Omega(f(n))$, where $\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}f(n)=\infty$. Finally, we present improved lower bounds for the $L_1$ norm: $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}/\log \varepsilon^{-1})$ in two dimensions and $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-d})$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \ge 3$.

Given a lacunary sequence of integers $n_k$ satisfying $n_{k+1}/n_k > \lambda > 1$, we construct a new sequence $\{m_k\}$ consisting of all possible $l$-wise signed sums $\pm n_{k_1} \pm \ldots \pm n_{k_l}$. We demonstrate that if $\lambda > \lambda_l$, then any series of the form $\sum_k c_k e^{im_k x}$ with $\sum_k |c_k|^2 < \infty$ converges almost everywhere regardless of the rearrangement of its terms, where $1 < \lambda_l < 2$ is a specific critical threshold. This result is established by proving a novel Khintchine-type inequality, $\|S\|_p \le C_{l,\lambda,p} \|S\|_2$ for $p > 2$, where $S$ represents a finite sum of the type in equation (1). For $\lambda \ge 3$, we determine a sharp growth rate of $p^{l/2}$ for the constant $C_{l,\lambda,p}$ as $p \to \infty$; a similar estimate for Rademacher chaos sums was previously derived independently by Bonami and Kiener. Additionally, when $\lambda \ge 3$, we prove inverse convergence properties for series (1): first, that almost everywhere convergence implies $\sum_k |c_k|^2 < \infty$, and second, that convergence to zero almost everywhere necessitates $c_k = 0$.

Acquiring discriminative features across categories and clustered features within classes is central to numerous computer vision tasks, particularly in large-scale recognition systems that must handle unseen test identities among millions of classes. This paper tackles this challenge using the intuition that features within a single class should exhibit small cosine distances in high-dimensional space, while those from different categories should be far apart. To achieve this, we introduce the Congenerous Cosine (COCO) algorithm, which simultaneously optimizes cosine similarity among data points. COCO retains the softmax property for inter-class discrimination and incorporates concepts from metric learning regarding class centroids. Unlike prior methods where the center acts as a transient, statistical variable within a mini-batch, our formulated centroid is dedicated to clustering intra-class features to enforce their aggregation around the network trunk. COCO is integrated with discriminative training, enabling stable, end-to-end learning. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate the method's effectiveness in both small-scale classification and large-scale human recognition.

This paper examines a family of non-autonomous scalar parabolic PDEs defined on a general compact and connected flow. The presence or absence of a zero neighborhood where the problems are linear influences the analytical methods employed and the dynamics of the resulting skew-product semiflow; consequently, the study distinguishes between linear-dissipative and purely dissipative cases. In both scenarios, the structure of global and pullback attractors is analyzed using principal spectral theory. Additionally, within the purely dissipative framework, a straightforward condition is established—incorporating aspects of the underlying linear dynamics and characteristics of the nonlinear term—to identify the nontrivial sections of the attractor.

We provide a complete classification of scalar-flat toric K\"ahler 4-manifolds subject to two asymptotic regimes: either slow (or non-existent) decay of the action fields, or quadratic decay of the curvature. This includes a full categorization of instantons with ALE-F-G-H asymptotic types. Since the momentum functions obey a degenerate elliptic equation, and the moment map image remains closed under these conditions, we utilize a recent Liouville theorem for such equations to determine all feasible momentum functions, thereby establishing the set of all possible metrics.

We conduct a numerical investigation of quenches transitioning from a fully ordered state to the ferromagnetic phase of the chiral $\mathbb{Z}_3$ clock model, a system characterized by sparse domain walls with six flavors. Consistent with earlier models, the propagation of entangled domain wall pairs created by the quench results in a linear entropy increase over time within bulk subsystems of size $\ell$, persisting until $t = \ell/2v_g$, where $v_g$ represents the maximum group velocity of these walls. In small bulk subsystems, entropy continues to rise toward $\ln 3$ as domain walls cross the region and populate the two oppositely ordered states, thereby restoring $\mathbb{Z}_3$ symmetry. A similar entropy growth is observed in small subsystems near an open boundary in non-chiral clock models. However, in the chiral model, entropy in such boundary subsystems saturates. We attribute this divergence in behavior to the distinct scattering properties of domain walls at open boundaries within the chiral framework. Additionally, we provide empirical data on entropy growth, correlation spread, and the energies of bound states formed by domain wall pairs induced by longitudinal fields in the chiral model.

We examine the lateral van der Waals (vdW) force acting on an anisotropic polarizable particle near a perfectly conducting plane featuring a hemispherical bump of radius $R$. Through exact calculations, we predict a sign reversal in this lateral force: under specific conditions, the force directs away from the protuberance rather than toward it. Previous literature attributed such sign inversions to perturbative solutions applicable only when the bump's height is negligible compared to the particle-plane distance $z_0$. In contrast, our approach utilizes exact formulas to analyze how this nontrivial geometric effect varies with the $R/z_0$ ratio, as well as how particle orientation and anisotropy influence the occurrence of this sign inversion.

Cloze-style reading comprehension has recently emerged as a key benchmark for evaluating advancements in natural language understanding. This paper introduces a novel multi-perspective framework that functions through the joint training of heterogeneous experts, effectively aggregating contextual information from various angles, where each perspective is handled by a straightforward aggregation module. The final answer is derived by feeding the outputs of these multiple modules into a one-timestep pointer network. Additionally, to address the challenge of limited labeled data, we propose an efficient sampling mechanism that automatically generates additional training examples by aligning the candidate distributions between labeled and unlabeled datasets. Experiments were conducted on the recently released CLOTH dataset (Xie et al., 2017), which contains approximately 100,000 questions curated by professional teachers. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous strong baselines.
This paper aims to establish a Cayley-Hamilton-Ziebur Theorem for non-autonomous semilinear matrix differential equations and demonstrates the relevance of such findings to ODE theory.

Blazars exhibit rapid, luminous non-thermal flares that demand an effective mechanism for particle acceleration and energy dissipation within the relativistic jets of active galactic nuclei (AGN). Kinetic numerical simulations are currently investigating particle acceleration via relativistic magnetic reconnection. In highly magnetized environments (where magnetization $\sigma = B^2/(4\pi w) \gg 1$), this process generates hard power-law electron spectra characterized by an index $p \to 1$ and an exponential cutoff at a Lorentz factor $\gamma_{\text{max}} \sim \sigma$. Furthermore, reconnection in electron-proton plasmas can enhance $\gamma_{\text{max}}$ by the proton-to-electron mass ratio ($m_p/m_e$). Consequently, achieving $\gamma_{\text{max}} \sim 10^6$ for BL Lacs necessitates reconnection in plasma with extremely high magnetization, $\sigma_{\text{max}} \gtrsim 10^3$. Conversely, magnetic bulk acceleration of relativistic jets requires moderate average magnetization, $\sigma_{\text{mean}} \sim \Gamma_j \lesssim 20$, where $\Gamma_j$ is the jet's bulk Lorentz factor. I propose that the observed "blazar sequence"—the systematic variation of $\gamma_{\text{max}}$ across luminosity classes—stems from corresponding trends in $\sigma_{\text{max}}$, driven by homogeneous lepton loading via pair creation regulated by external high-energy radiation fields. Simultaneously, relativistic AGN jets must be highly inhomogeneous due to filamentary proton loading, which sets $\sigma_{\text{mean}}$ largely independent of the specific blazar class.

The Atiyah-Hitchin manifold represents the moduli space of parity-inversion symmetric charge-two SU(2) monopoles within Euclidean space. This work introduces a hyperbolic counterpart by determining the boundary metric for the moduli space of such monopoles in hyperbolic space. Utilizing a twistor description of the moduli space, the metric calculation is executed, with the final result expressed through standard elliptic integrals.

For a Fell bundle $\mathscr C\overset{q}{\to}\Xi$ defined over the discrete groupoid $\Xi$, we investigate the symmetry properties of the associated Hahn algebra $\ell^{\infty,1}(\Xi\!\mid\!\mathscr C)$ by analyzing the isotropy subgroups of $\Xi$. We establish that $\Xi$ possesses symmetry (respectively, hypersymmetry) if and only if every isotropy subgroup within it is symmetric (respectively, hypersymmetric). Furthermore, we characterize hypersymmetry through Fell bundles with constant fibers, demonstrating that in the context of discrete groupoids, 'hypersymmetry' is equivalent to 'rigid symmetry'.

This study examines the kinematic correlations between pairs of beauty hadrons generated in high-energy proton-proton collisions. The analysis utilizes a data sample from the LHCb experiment, acquired at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$. The measurement focuses on inclusive $b\rightarrow J/\psi X$ decays within the rapidity interval $2<y^{J/\psi}<4.5$. The observed correlations align well with theoretical predictions.

This research is driven by the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and aims to introduce a previously overlooked method for non-adaptive group testing, formulated through residuated pairs on partially ordered sets. A significant benefit of this approach is that it naturally generates an efficient decoder for any specific testing scheme, capable of identifying numerous infection patterns. Additionally, we propose constructing effective group testing schemes using incidence matrices from finite partial linear spaces. The core strategy involves leveraging the structural properties of these matrices to serve as test matrices, which can be customized for various estimated disease prevalence rates. We illustrate this with schemes based on generalized quadrangles. Currently, our findings are limited to error-free scenarios; however, extending this work to noisy environments is a priority for future research.

This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a planar conductivity inclusion. The objective is to analytically reconstruct a homogeneous inclusion with arbitrary constant conductivity using generalized polarization tensors (GPTs) derived from exterior measurements. The main result is an inversion formula, expressed in terms of GPTs, that determines the conformal mapping coefficients associated with the inclusion. To validate this formula, we demonstrate matrix factorizations of the GPTs.

The article establishes almost global existence for Dirac Equations on Tori, assuming high regularity and small initial data. Additionally, global existence is proven under conditions of low regularity with small initial data. These results are primarily achieved using Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Moser estimates and the Bernstein-Type Lemma.

By applying a unified framework that utilizes a homogeneous Lippmann-Schwinger-type equation for resonance functions alongside fundamental properties of Riesz potentials, this work examines the non-existence of threshold resonances in Dirac and Schrödinger operators under sufficiently short-range interactions across general spatial dimensions. Specifically, assuming potentials decay according to a sufficient power law, we establish the absence of zero-energy resonances for massless Dirac operators in dimensions $n \geq 3$, the lack of resonances at $\pm m$ for massive Dirac operators (where $m > 0$) in dimensions $n \geq 5$, and reiterate the established result regarding the absence of zero-energy resonances for Schrödinger operators when $n \geq 5$.

This study examines the roles of Cartan generators within static potentials across different representations, utilizing the domain model of center vortices for SU(3) gauge theory. Employing center domains based solely on the H8 generator, as previously proposed, results in concavities in potentials for higher representations and causes the fundamental string tension to remain identical under both Casimir scaling and N-ality regimes. By incorporating the contributions of the second Cartan generator, H3, into the potentials, these deficiencies are resolved. Nevertheless, we observe that at intermediate distances, potentials driven exclusively by H8 align more closely with Casimir scaling than those derived from the combined influence of both Cartan generators.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating the probability of significant losses in a financial portfolio, where future loss is defined as a conditional expectation. Because this conditional expectation is often computationally intractable, nested simulation is a common approach. To mitigate the complexity associated with nested simulation, we introduce a hybrid method integrating Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) and Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC). Specifically, the outer simulation generates financial scenarios using standard Monte Carlo techniques, while the inner simulation estimates portfolio losses within each scenario using QMC. We demonstrate that incorporating QMC accelerates convergence rates for both crude and multilevel nested simulations. Under specific conditions, the combination of MLMC and QMC reduces computational complexity to $O(\epsilon^{-2}(\log \epsilon)^2)$. Furthermore, we identify that standard MLMC suffers from a catastrophic coupling issue caused by indicator functions. To resolve this, we propose a smoothed MLMC approach that approximates these indicator functions with logistic sigmoid functions. Numerical experiments indicate that the near-optimal complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ is achieved using QMC in both standard and smoothed MLMC frameworks, even in moderately high-dimensional settings.

Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) have become a standard component of software engineering research, though their quality remains inconsistent. To enhance future research and industry applications, these reviews must meet high-quality standards. Consequently, the study's objective was to evaluate the quality of SLRs in software engineering by developing a dedicated appraisal instrument. This tool is designed for appraisers to evaluate reviews, though authors can also utilize it as a checklist during the design and documentation phases. The methodology involved adapting a well-established healthcare appraisal instrument for software engineering by integrating domain-specific guidelines, checklists, and experiences. Validation was conducted by having four external experts review the initial version and provide feedback for updates. The research resulted in a quality assessment instrument comprising 16 items, each rated on a two- or three-grade scale to capture specific quality aspects. These items can be consolidated into groups to determine the overall quality of an SLR. The conclusion is that this instrument serves as a valuable support tool for appraisers assessing the quality of systematic literature reviews in software engineering.

Acquiring visual concepts directly from raw images without robust supervision remains a difficult endeavor. This study demonstrates the benefits of utilizing prototype representations to interpret and refine the latent space within neural concept learners. To achieve this, we propose interactive Concept Swapping Networks (iCSNs), a new framework designed to learn concept-based representations through weak supervision and implicit prototypes. By exchanging latent representations between paired images, iCSNs associate conceptual data with designated prototype slots. This creates a discrete, semantically anchored latent space that enhances both human comprehension and human-machine collaboration. We validate these findings through experiments on our newly created "Elementary Concept Reasoning" (ECR) dataset, which concentrates on visual concepts common to geometric shapes.

This study examines the $L^p$ boundedness of the maximal function associated with the averaging operator $f\to \mathcal{A}_t^s f$ across a two-parameter family of tori, denoted as $\mathbb{T}_t^{s}$, where the parameters satisfy $c_0t>s>0$ for a constant $c_0\in (0,1)$. We establish that the corresponding two-parameter maximal function is $L^p$-bounded precisely when $p>2$. Additionally, we derive $L^p$--$L^q$ estimates for the local maximal operator within a sharp range of $p$ and $q$. The analysis further proves sharp smoothing estimates, including local smoothing results for the operators $f\to \mathcal A_t^s f$ and $f\to \mathcal A_t^{c_0t} f$. These results rely on the application of Bourgain--Demeter's decoupling inequality for the cone and the local smoothing estimates for the two-dimensional wave operator provided by Guth--Wang--Zhang.

Monaural speech enhancement (SE) offers a flexible and economical solution by relying on single-microphone recordings; however, its performance trails behind multi-channel SE because single-channel inputs lack spatial cues, thereby restricting its practical utility. To overcome this limitation, we integrate spatial information into monaural SE models using a knowledge distillation strategy. This approach allows the monaural model to learn binaural speech characteristics from a binaural SE model, enabling the reconstruction of enhanced speech with superior intelligibility and quality even under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed monaural SE model, which incorporates spatial information via knowledge distillation, outperforms other monaural SE models in terms of performance while utilizing fewer parameters.

This work addresses the challenge of collaboratively estimating Gaussian processes within multi-agent systems. In this setting, each agent gathers a limited set of measurements to jointly reconstruct a shared estimate from the collective data. The agents operate under constraints of restricted computational power and communication bandwidth, collecting a total of $M$ noisy measurements at input locations independently sampled from a known common probability density. While the optimal approach necessitates exchanging all $M$ locations and measurements to invert an $M \times M$ matrix—a task that is not scalable—we introduce two suboptimal methods. These methods utilize the first $E$ orthonormal eigenfunctions derived from the Karhunen-Loève (KL) expansion of the selected kernel, where typically $E \ll M$. Consequently, both computational and communication complexities scale with $E$ rather than $M$, and the necessary statistics can be computed using standard average consensus algorithms. We derive probabilistic, non-asymptotic bounds that allow for the a priori determination of the desired estimation accuracy. Furthermore, we propose novel distributed strategies based on Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE) for tuning regularization parameters; these strategies are applicable to generic basis functions, not just kernel eigenfunctions, and can also be executed via average consensus. Finally, the proposed estimators and theoretical bounds are validated using both synthetic and real-world field data.

This study investigates the semi-leptonic transitions $\bar B^0/D^0 \to (a_0(980)^{\pm}\to\pi^{\pm}\eta) l^{\mp} \nu$ employing light-cone sum rules. The analysis utilizes the two- and three-body light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) for the $B$ meson, alongside the sole existing two-body LCDA for the $D$ meson. To account for the finite width of the $a_0(980)$, a scalar form factor is employed to model the final-state interactions between the $\pi\eta$ system, a quantity previously derived via unitarized Chiral Perturbation Theory. The predicted branching fraction for the $D^0$ decay aligns well with recent measurements from the BESIII Collaboration, whereas the branching fraction for the $\bar B^0$ decay offers a target for future experimental verification.

The free metaplectic transformation (FMT) has recently become widely popular due to its diverse applications in signal processing, paraxial optical systems, digital algorithms, and optical encryption. However, the FMT falls short when analyzing non-transient signals locally, necessitating the introduction of a specialized localized transform known as the short-time free metaplectic transform (STFMT). This paper explores the STFMT by first defining it and presenting its time-frequency analysis within the FMT domain. Secondly, we examine the transform's fundamental properties, including the reconstruction and Moyal formulas. The introduction of the STFMT and its associated properties significantly advance the theoretical framework for time-frequency representations of higher-dimensional signals. Finally, we extend several uncertainty principles (UP) from quantum mechanics—specifically those of Lieb, Pitts, Heisenberg, Hausdorff-Young, Hardy, Beurling, logarithmic, and Nazarov—which have previously been established in the FMT domain.

This research examines non-Gaussianity and secondary Gravitational Waves (GWs) arising from the production of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) during inflation. Specifically, we analyze the $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, where a small bump in the inflaton potential amplifies curvature perturbation amplitudes at certain scales, triggering PBH formation across various mass ranges. Utilizing the BINGO computational code to evaluate the non-Gaussianity parameter across diverse triangle configurations, our findings indicate that non-Gaussianity is significantly enhanced in the equilateral configuration at scales where the scalar perturbation power spectrum experiences a sharp drop. These non-Gaussian signatures could be detected in the frequency ranges associated with Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) and $\mu$-distortion events, or at smaller scales; future observations of such signals would either validate or refute our PBH generation model. Additionally, we investigate secondary GWs within this framework, demonstrating that the peak present fractional energy density, $\Omega_{\rm GW0}$, reaches approximately $10^{-8}$ across various frequencies dependent on model parameters. These values fall within the sensitivity bands of several GW detectors, allowing forthcoming data to assess the model's observational viability. Finally, we estimate the spectral tilts of the induced GWs across different frequency intervals, confirming that the spectrum adheres to a power-law relationship, $\Omega_{\rm GW0}\sim f^{n}$, within those bands.

This study examines the extraction of randomness from generic partially entangled pure states of two qubits within a device-independent framework, utilizing Bell tests to verify apparatus functionality. We demonstrate that for any such state, two bits of randomness are consistently achievable, whether through projective measurements generating global randomness or nonprojective measurements generating local randomness. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum randomness achievable via nonprojective measurements globally is bounded between approximately 3.58 and 3.96 bits. This upper limit excludes the possibility of reaching the four-bit threshold potentially available with extremal qubit measurements. We attribute this restriction to the limited degree of self-testing possible for four-outcome nonprojective qubit measurements in Bell experiments.

Magnetic fields in Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars are recognized for their long-term stability, yet the internal physical conditions enabling these states remain an active area of research. While it has been analytically shown that purely toroidal or purely poloidal fields inevitably develop instabilities, numerical simulations confirm that roughly axisymmetric configurations within stably stratified stars can remain stable. These stable setups involve twisted torus structures where toroidal and poloidal components mutually reinforce one another. Previous investigations have estimated approximate upper and lower limits for the ratio of magnetic energy between these two components. To explore the parameter space governing the stability of such configurations, we employed the Pencil Code to conduct 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations of magnetic field evolution in non-rotating, non-degenerate stars, where viscosity serves as the sole dissipation mechanism. Our simulations covered stars with both uniform (barotropic) and radially increasing (stably stratified) specific entropy, varying conditions for the degree of stratification and the magnetic energy distribution. These results broadly corroborate the previously proposed stability boundaries for the magnetic field.

Repeated idempotent elements are frequently employed to model iterable behaviors within abstract computational frameworks. Consequently, for a given monoid $M$, it is natural to inquire about the minimum sequence length required to guarantee the existence of consecutive idempotent factors. This inquiry is formalized via the Ramsey function $R_M$ associated with $M$, which maps each positive integer $k$ to the smallest integer $R_M(k)$ such that any word $u$ in $M^*$ of length $R_M(k)$ contains $k$ consecutive non-empty factors representing the same idempotent element of $M$. In this study, we examine the behavior of $R_M$ by analyzing the regular $D$-length of $M$, defined as the maximum size $L(M)$ of a submonoid in $M$ isomorphic to the set of natural numbers $\{1, 2, \dots, L(M)\}$ under the Max operation. We demonstrate that the regular $D$-length of $M$ dictates the degree of $R_M$ by establishing the bounds $k^{L(M)} \leq R_M(k) \leq (k|M|^4)^{L(M)}$. To facilitate the application of these findings, we determine the regular $D$-length for various monoids. Notably, we prove that the full monoid of $n \times n$ Boolean matrices—utilized to represent transition monoids of non-deterministic automata—possesses a regular $D$-length of $\frac{n^2+n+2}{2}$.

Over-the-air computation (AirComp) unifies communication and computation by leveraging the superposition principle inherent in multiple-access channels. While prior research primarily addresses AirComp transceiver design in static networks, this study investigates an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted AirComp framework where a flying base station collects data from mobile sensors. By optimizing the UAV's flight path, the system gains an extra degree of freedom to enhance performance. The objective is to minimize the time-averaged mean-squared error (MSE) through the joint optimization of the UAV trajectory, receive normalizing coefficients, and sensor transmit power. To achieve this, we introduce a novel problem transformation using intermediate variables, which converts the issue into a convex subproblem whenever any two variable blocks are fixed. This structure facilitates efficient algorithm development using block coordinate descent and alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Specifically, we derive closed-form optimal solutions for the normalizing factors and intermediate variable subproblems. Additionally, the convex trajectory design subproblem is reformulated for ADMM, yielding closed-form update expressions for all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly lowers the time-averaged MSE and reduces computational time by orders of magnitude compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Accurate 3D tooth segmentation is crucial for digital orthodontics, with numerous deep learning approaches developed to automatically segment teeth from 3D intraoral scans or dental models. However, these methods typically depend on annotated 3D scans, and manual annotation is time-consuming. One potential solution is to develop self-supervised techniques to minimize the need for manual labels. Given that 3D tooth point clouds possess a highly regular structure and robust shape priors, distinct from other point cloud types like scene or shape data, we investigate the extent of representational information that can be extracted from a single 3D intraoral scan. Quantitatively, we assessed this using ten different methods: six generic point cloud segmentation techniques and four specialized for tooth segmentation. Surprisingly, our results indicate that training on a single scan yields a Dice score of up to 0.86, compared to 0.94 with the full training dataset. This suggests that segmentation models can acquire significant knowledge from a solitary 3D tooth scan under appropriate conditions, such as data augmentation. To our knowledge, this study provides the first quantitative evaluation demonstrating the representation learning capacity of deep learning methods from a single 3D intraoral scan. These findings can facilitate the creation of self-supervised tooth segmentation methods for scenarios with extreme data scarcity by maximizing the utility of available data.

This paper determines the asymptotic behavior of the count of pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms conjugate to a given pseudo-Anosov map $\gamma$, where the axis of their action on Teichmüller space intersects the ball of radius $R$ centered at a point $X$ in the Teichmüller space of a genus $g$ surface, as $R$ approaches infinity.

Can leveraging descriptions of actions and their quality enhance performance in action quality assessment (AQA)? While existing AQA and skills evaluation methods typically learn features dedicated solely to predicting final scores, this paper introduces a strategy to learn spatio-temporal features that simultaneously address three interconnected tasks: fine-grained action recognition, commentary generation, and AQA score estimation. To validate this approach, we assembled a new multi-task AQA dataset, currently the largest of its kind with 1,412 diving clips, available at https://github.com/ParitoshParmar/MTL-AQA. Our results demonstrate that the proposed multi-task learning (MTL) framework surpasses single-task learning (STL) methods across two distinct architectures, C3D-AVG and MSCADC. Specifically, the C3D-AVG-MTL configuration establishes a new state-of-the-art benchmark, achieving a rank correlation of 90.44%. Comprehensive experiments further reveal that MTL provides superior generalization compared to STL and indicate that representations derived from action recognition models are inadequate for AQA; instead, task-specific features must be explicitly learned.

This study outlines a threat model revealing that split-network federated learning systems are vulnerable to model inversion attacks launched by malicious computational servers. We demonstrate that such attacks can succeed even when the adversary possesses only limited knowledge of the underlying data distribution. To counter this, we propose a straightforward additive noise technique that significantly diminishes attack effectiveness while maintaining an acceptable trade-off in accuracy on the MNIST dataset. Additionally, our analysis indicates that NoPeekNN, a current defense mechanism, shields different types of information from exposure, implying that a combined defensive strategy is essential for comprehensive protection of private user data.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) serves as a versatile method for investigating diverse systems, spanning statistical physics, strong interaction theory, and gravity. Its utility depends on deriving flow equations that track the evolution of the quantum effective action as a coarse-graining parameter varies. This study details a new strategy for solving these equations by leveraging the fact that renormalization group (RG) equations can be reformulated to mirror fluid dynamics conservation laws. This analogy enables two main advancements: first, it permits the use of robust numerical methods from fluid dynamics to solve RG equations, ensuring reliable handling of nonanalytic behaviors in the effective action's flow, such as those arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the fluid dynamics parallel offers fresh perspectives on interpreting RG flows and their inherent irreversibility. We demonstrate this connection using zero-dimensional quantum field theory models, with a discussion of extending it to higher dimensions. These results are anticipated to enhance future FRG investigations of quantum field theories in higher dimensions, improving both qualitative understanding and quantitative accuracy.

This study utilizes blockchain technology to authenticate drone nodes within the Internet of Drone Things (IoDT), verifying credentials during the authentication process to eliminate malicious actors. In IoDT, drones collect and relay data to cluster heads (CHs) for processing; however, the computational burden on CHs causes their energy reserves to deplete rapidly. To mitigate this, we propose R2D, a low-energy adaptive clustering hierarchy protocol that selects new CHs based on residual energy, node degree, and distance from the base station (BS). Since storing large datasets on the blockchain is costly, we integrate the Interplanetary File System (IPFS) for data storage, which further secures user data using industry-standard AES-128 encryption. Additionally, to reduce the high computational overhead associated with Proof of Work consensus mechanisms, our approach employs Proof of Authority (PoA). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed system operates effectively and efficiently, and a formal security analysis confirms the smart contract's resilience against attacks.

Decentralized algorithms achieve global objectives through local interactions among directly connected agents, utilizing low-cost communication. In large-scale optimization with distributed data, these algorithms often outperform centralized approaches. Recently, applying decentralized methods to deep learning has gained significant interest as a low-communication alternative to parameter servers or Ring-Allreduce protocols. However, the absence of accessible and efficient software tools has largely confined these algorithms to theory. To address this, we present BlueFog, a Python library designed for straightforward and high-performance implementation of various decentralized algorithms. Built on a unified abstraction of communication operations, BlueFog provides intuitive interfaces supporting a range of methods, from synchronous operations on static, undirected graphs to asynchronous ones on dynamic, directed graphs. Additionally, it incorporates system-level acceleration techniques to optimize performance for deep learning tasks. On mainstream DNN training workloads, BlueFog achieves significantly higher throughput, delivering a 1.2x to 1.8x speedup compared to Horovod, a state-of-the-art distributed deep learning package based on Ring-Allreduce. The library is open source at https://github.com/Bluefog-Lib/bluefog.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of small eigenvalues on Riemann surfaces as the genus increases. We demonstrate that for any positive integer $k$, the $k$-th smallest eigenvalue of Riemann surfaces within any thick region of the moduli space for genus $g$ scales uniformly as $\frac{1}{g^2}$ when $g$ approaches infinity. In establishing the upper bound, we show that for any constant $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a closed Riemann surface of genus $g$ located in the $\epsilon$-thick part of moduli space that possesses a pants decomposition where all boundary curves have length $\epsilon$, and the count of separating systole curves is uniformly comparable to $g$.

Andrew Pitts' framework for the relational properties of domains offers a robust approach to defining predicates or relations, with uses spanning program equivalence reasoning to proofs that bridge denotational and operational semantics. Its primary strength lies in managing recursive definitions that lack obvious well-foundedness; provided the domain itself is defined recursively and its recursion aligns with the relations, the framework ensures their existence. While Pitts' original work relied on the Knaster-Tarski fixed-point theorem, these notes demonstrate how his construction also fits within the scope of other fundamental fixed-point theorems, including the inverse limit, Banach, and Kleene theorems. This connection highlights how Pitts' method is deeply intertwined with the techniques used to build recursive domains, as well as with recent approaches involving guarded recursion or step-indexing.

We examine the optical characteristics of silicon-vacancy (SiV) and germanium-vacancy (GeV) color centers within nanodiamonds subjected to hydrostatic pressures reaching 180 GPa. The nanodiamonds, synthesized via Si or Ge-doped plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, were compressed using a diamond anvil cell. Under these conditions, we detected blue-shifts in the zero-phonon lines for both SiV and GeV centers, amounting to 17 THz (70 meV) and 78 THz (320 meV), respectively. These experimentally observed pressure-induced shifts align well with ab initio calculations that incorporate lattice compression derived from the diamond equation of state and are extrapolated to the tin-vacancy (SnV) center. This study offers insights into utilizing group-IV-vacancy centers as quantum sensors in extreme pressure environments, leveraging their unique optical and spin properties arising from their intrinsic inversion-symmetric structure.

We calculate the antiproton-deuteron level shifts, widths, scattering lengths, and volumes for the lowest hydrogenic states by solving the Faddeev equations for the $\bar{p}$pn system. The resulting $\bar{p}$d annihilation densities are derived and contrasted with the nuclear density of deuterium. Furthermore, we examine the applicability of the Trueman relation to composite particles. The strong $\bar{N}N$ interaction is modeled using two distinct optical approaches that account for $\bar{p}p$-$\bar{n}n$ coupling and the neutron-proton mass difference, whereas several realistic interactions are employed for the $NN$ system.

This study examines matrix bi-orthogonal polynomials relative to the sesquilinear form $\langle P(x),Q(x)\rangle_W=\int P(x) W(x)\operatorname{d}\mu(x)(Q(x))^{\top}$, where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ belong to $\mathbb R^{p\times p}[x]$ and $\mu(x)$ denotes a matrix of Borel measures supported on an infinite subset of the real line. The work establishes connection formulas linking these matrix bi-orthogonal polynomials to those orthogonal with respect to $\mu(x)$. Specifically, when the perturbation matrix polynomial $W(x)$ possesses nonsingular leading coefficients, a generalized Christoffel formula is derived using the Jordan chains of $W(x)$. Additionally, several examples by Durán et al. regarding perturbations with singular leading coefficients are revisited. The research concludes by extending these findings to the non-Abelian 2D Toda lattice hierarchy.

This study introduces a new approach for synthesizing distributed controllers in homogeneous interconnected systems composed of identical subsystems. The controller aims to minimize the L2-gain within the performance channel. By extending the Full Block S-Procedure (FBSP) with an extra set of variables, the method relaxes the block-diagonal structural constraints on Lyapunov and multiplier matrices typically needed for distributed control. This relaxation significantly reduces conservatism compared to most current methods. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how to break down this extended FBSP into compact synthesis conditions, each corresponding in size to a single subsystem.

The Automatic Dependent Surveillance Broadcast (ADS-B) protocol represents a mandatory evolution in air traffic monitoring. Although it facilitates the tracking of an increasing volume of aircraft, it simultaneously introduces cybersecurity vulnerabilities, such as false data injection attacks where adversaries transmit fabricated surveillance data. Leveraging current data sources and tools for retrieving flight records, researchers can construct datasets and train Machine Learning models to identify anomalies within En-Route trajectories. In this study, we introduce a novel multivariate anomaly detection framework named the Discriminatory Auto-Encoder (DAE). This model adapts a standard LSTM-based auto-encoder by incorporating multiple decoders, each trained on data specific to distinct flight phases like climbing, cruising, or descending. To demonstrate the DAE's effectiveness, we developed an evaluation dataset comprising both real-life and synthetically generated anomalies. Comparative testing against three existing anomaly detection models revealed that the DAE outperforms them in both detection accuracy and speed. The dataset, model implementations, and evaluation outcomes are publicly accessible in an online repository to ensure reproducibility and support future research.

Several fourth-generation synchrotron light sources incorporate a Higher Harmonic Cavity (HHC) to extend bunch length and thereby enhance Touschek lifetime. However, achieving the desired bunch lengthening is complicated by necessary gaps within the bunch train. In a recent study, the author and Venturini investigated the impact of different fill patterns by computing equilibrium charge densities using coupled H\"aissinski equations, assuming the sole collective force stemmed from the lowest-mode wake field of the harmonic cavity. The current work refines the notation and organization of these equations to facilitate the incorporation of multiple resonator wake fields. This enhancement enables the analysis of beam loading effects from the main accelerating cavity, higher-order cavity modes, and short-range geometric wakes modeled by low-$Q$ resonators, with specific explorations conducted for ALS-U. The practical compensation of induced voltage in the main cavity via a feedback system is simulated here by adjusting the generator voltage through a novel iterative method. Except under complete fill conditions, compensated beam loading in the main cavity significantly influences bunch profiles and Touschek lifetimes. Furthermore, a $Q=6$ resonator, representing realistic short-range wakes, also substantially affects bunch formation.

Addressing the persistent challenge of mitigating privacy risks in distributed or federated learning without compromising training speed or model accuracy, this paper introduces TextHide, a solution tailored for natural language understanding. TextHide mandates a straightforward encryption step for all participants, which thwarts eavesdropping attempts aimed at recovering private text data; this process is highly efficient and incurs only a minimal impact on task performance. Furthermore, TextHide is compatible with the widely used framework of fine-tuning pre-trained language models, such as BERT, for various sentence and sentence-pair tasks. Evaluated on the GLUE benchmark, our experiments demonstrate that TextHide effectively defends against attacks targeting shared gradients or representations while reducing averaged accuracy by merely 1.9%. Additionally, we provide a security analysis of TextHide based on the conjectured computational intractability of a specific mathematical problem. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Hazelsuko07/TextHide.

The upcoming launch of NASA's Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) is set to reveal new insights into the high-energy universe through X-ray polarimetry. Currently, polarimeter performance is constrained by track reconstruction algorithms that rely on linear estimators and often ignore the quality of individual events. This study introduces a modern deep learning approach designed to enhance the sensitivity of X-ray telescopic observations with imaging polarimeters, specifically targeting the gas pixel detectors (GPDs) aboard IXPE. By employing a weighted maximum likelihood combination of predictions from a deep ensemble of ResNets trained on Monte Carlo simulations, we establish and apply optimal event weighting to maximize the polarization signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) during track reconstruction. For typical power-law source spectra, this method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, reducing the required exposure times by approximately 40% to achieve a specific SNR.

Multi-Task Learning (MTL) serves as an effective paradigm for enhancing generalization through knowledge sharing, yet existing research indicates it can occasionally degrade performance, particularly when tasks exhibit low correlation. A primary culprit for this decline is spurious correlation, where models erroneously rely on non-causal associations that fail when those correlations shift. Within the MTL context, spurious correlations present distinct challenges: first, the likelihood of incorporating non-causal knowledge increases because a shared model must encode information from diverse tasks, meaning causal features for one task may be spurious for another. Second, correlations between task labels introduce a unique form of spurious dependency. We theoretically demonstrate that MTL is more susceptible to adopting non-causal knowledge from other tasks compared to single-task learning, leading to inferior generalization. To address this, we introduce the Multi-Task Causal Representation Learning framework, which utilizes disentangled neural modules to represent multi-task knowledge and employs MTL-specific invariant regularization to identify causally linked modules. Experimental results indicate that this approach improves average MTL performance by 5.5% across Multi-MNIST, MovieLens, Taskonomy, CityScape, and NYUv2 datasets by mitigating the issue of spurious correlations.

Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) has emerged as a significant trend in radiology, aiming to minimize excessive X-ray exposure to patients. While reducing radiation lowers health risks, it simultaneously increases image noise, thereby compromising image quality and diagnostic utility. A potential solution involves training deep learning denoising models on paired low-dose and high-dose CT projections; however, such paired data are seldom available in real-world settings. This paper introduces a novel self-supervised method for CT denoising that differs from existing approaches by requiring only noisy CT projections and leveraging correlations between adjacent images. Experimental results on an LDCT dataset indicate that this method achieves accuracy nearly comparable to supervised techniques while outperforming other considered self-supervised denoising methods.

We extend the Standard Model by introducing a new fermion $\chi$ possessing a minimal baryon number of 1/3. The decay of neutrons into three non-relativistic $\chi$ particles ($n \to \chi\chi\chi$) offers an explanation for the neutron decay anomaly, consistent with constraints derived from neutron stars. This particle $\chi$ is a viable Dark Matter candidate, with its cosmological abundance potentially established via freeze-in mechanisms around the temperature scale $T \sim m_n$. Furthermore, related processes—including $n \to \chi\chi\chi \gamma$, hydrogen decay (${\rm H}\to \chi\chi \chi\nu(\gamma)$), and Dark Matter-induced neutron disappearance ($\bar\chi n \to \chi \chi (\gamma)$)—occur at rates lower than current experimental limits, presenting promising targets for future investigations.

We frame grasp learning as a neural field and introduce Neural Grasp Distance Fields (NGDF). In this approach, the system takes a 6D robot end-effector pose as input and outputs the distance to a continuous manifold of valid grasps for a given object. Unlike existing methods that predict discrete sets of candidate grasps, the NGDF's distance-based representation is intuitively interpretable as a cost function; minimizing this cost yields a successful grasp. This grasp distance metric can be seamlessly integrated into a trajectory optimizer to jointly optimize with other factors like trajectory smoothness and collision avoidance. During the optimization process, as these competing costs are balanced and minimized, the target grasp pose smoothly adjusts, leveraging the continuity of the learned grasp field. Simulation benchmarks using a Franka arm demonstrate that joint grasping and planning with NGDF surpasses baseline methods by 63% in execution success, while effectively generalizing to novel object shapes and unseen query poses. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/neural-grasp-distance-fields.

Estimating Remaining Useful Life (RUL) faces significant challenges due to data imbalance, specifically the scarcity of samples from machines nearing failure, and the fact that data can only be labeled post-failure. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) offers a solution by leveraging the abundant unlabeled data generated by operational machines. However, prior SSL research has been limited by unrealistic evaluation settings where near-failure data remained accessible, yielding only modest performance gains. This paper introduces a novel SSL framework utilizing self-supervised pre-training. Under realistic conditions on the NASA C-MAPSS dataset, this method surpasses both established SSL approaches and supervised baselines.

The electronic bandstructure of Au$_2$Pb features a Dirac cone that opens a gap upon transitioning into a low-temperature superconducting phase. This indicates that the superconducting state ($T_c=1.1$ K) may exhibit topological characteristics at the surface. Consequently, we performed Scanning Tunneling Microscopy investigations on the surface of superconducting Au$_2$Pb. Our measurements of the superconducting gap reveal a significant superconducting density of states at the Fermi level. We explore potential explanations for this observation by considering superconductivity induced in surface states.

Simplicial synchronization highlights how topology and geometry dictate the dynamical behaviors of simplicial complexes. The geometric and topological structures of these networks are inherently captured by the spectral characteristics of both standard graph Laplacians and higher-order Laplacians. This study demonstrates that the geometry of simplicial complexes generates spectral dimensions within the complex Laplacians, which fundamentally alter the phase diagram of the Kuramoto model. Specifically, simplicial complexes with non-trivial network geometry fail to maintain a synchronized state in the infinite limit if their spectral dimension is four or less. This theoretical finding is validated using the "Network Geometry with Flavor" generative model, which exhibits emergent hyperbolic geometry. Furthermore, simplicial topology is shown to govern the dynamics of the higher-order Kuramoto model. This model describes the synchronization of topological signals, where phases are assigned not only to nodes but also to higher-order simplices such as links and triangles. When topological signals of varying dimensions are coupled adaptively—specifically through their solenoidal and irrotational projections—the model exhibits discontinuous synchronization transitions.

We demonstrate that the Littlewood conjecture holds true for a specific subset of pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ consisting of badly approximable numbers. Our approach involves localizing the roots of a cubic equation, where the coefficients are determined by the diophantine characteristics of the pair $(\alpha,\beta)$. The resulting root estimates are derived from the properties of the denominators associated with the convergents in the continued fraction expansions of both $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

This paper primarily investigates the local deformations of Calabi-Yau $\partial\bar{\partial}$-manifolds that are co-polarized by a Gauduchon metric, focusing on a specific subfamily of co-polarized fibers defined by the Aeppli/De Rham-Gauduchon cohomology class of the Gauduchon metric established on the central fiber. In the latter section, we demonstrate that the $p$-SKT $h$-$\partial\bar{\partial}$-property is deformation open by introducing and analyzing a novel concept known as the $hp$-Hermitian symplectic ($hp$-HS) form.

Liquid drop transport within fibrous media plays a critical role in numerous engineering applications, including textile cleaning and fog harvesting. Enhancing system efficiency and facilitating novel applications relies on the capacity to regulate or adjust liquid movement. This study experimentally examines the manipulation of partially wetting drops on individual fibers through fiber vibration. We demonstrate that standing waves can induce either a sliding motion along the fiber or cause the drop to detach and drip. Furthermore, we determine the specific conditions regarding drop volume, fiber tilt angle, and oscillation amplitude and frequency required to elicit these distinct behaviors. Finally, our experiments illustrate how vibrations can govern the transport and collection of water droplets along a fiber by combining sliding and dripping transitions.

Deep Neural Network (DNN) approaches for automatic modulation classification (AMC) surpass traditional methods, even under difficult wireless channel conditions. Nevertheless, adversarial attacks can degrade the accuracy of DNN-based AMC by injecting carefully crafted perturbations into the channel. To address this, we introduce a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) countermeasure designed to protect DNN-based AMC systems. Our proposed GAN aims to filter out adversarial examples before they reach the DNN classifier. We demonstrate the robustness of our defense GAN against the Fast-Gradient Sign (FGSM) method, a highly effective algorithm for generating perturbed signals. Since existing defense GANs are tailored for image classification and fail in our communication context, our approach utilizes a mixture of generators to resolve mode collapsing issues common in radio signal classification tasks. Simulation results confirm the efficacy of our defense GAN, boosting the accuracy of DNN-based AMC under adversarial attacks to approximately 81%.

Information Extraction (IE) from scientific literature helps readers identify key details, yet narrow IE systems capture only a limited portion of available data, while Open IE systems struggle with the lengthy and intricate sentences common in scientific writing. This study addresses these limitations by merging the outputs of both approaches to introduce Semi-Open Relation Extraction, a novel task investigated within the Biology domain. First, we introduce the Focused Open Biological Information Extraction (FOBIE) dataset, using it to train a state-of-the-art narrow IE system designed to extract trade-off relations and arguments central to biological texts. Next, we apply both the narrow IE system and a top-performing Open IE system to a corpus of 10,000 open-access biological documents. Our results demonstrate that narrow IE extractions can filter out 65% of the erroneous and uninformative outputs from the Open IE system. Additionally, we find that the retained extractions are significantly more informative for readers.

We assess three-loop massive vacuum bubble diagrams using polylogarithms up to weight six and establish a basis of irrational constants composed of harmonic polylogarithms evaluated at arguments $e^{k i \pi/3}$.

We present MJPC, an open-source, interactive framework and application designed for real-time predictive control utilizing MuJoCo physics. This tool enables users to readily define and solve intricate robotics problems, currently offering three shooting-based planners: derivative-based iLQG and Gradient Descent, alongside a simple derivative-free approach termed Predictive Sampling. Although Predictive Sampling was initially created as a pedagogical baseline, it has proven surprisingly competitive against more established algorithms. Rather than introducing algorithmic innovations, this work emphasizes high performance, straightforward code, and the accessibility of model-based methods through an intuitive, interactive software environment. MJPC can be accessed at github.com/deepmind/mujoco_mpc, with a video overview available at dpmd.ai/mjpc.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesions remains a difficult task, prompting the development of various deep-learning approaches in recent years. Yet, many existing methods are static, relying on a single model trained on extensive, specialized datasets that often fail to generalize effectively. Instead, models should adapt sequentially to data from diverse hospitals by continuously learning lesion characteristics. To address this, we investigate experience replay—a recognized continual learning technique—applied to MS lesion segmentation across multi-contrast data from eight distinct hospitals. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields positive backward transfer and mitigates catastrophic forgetting more effectively than sequential fine-tuning. Moreover, experience replay surpasses multi-domain training, positioning it as a promising strategy for MS lesion segmentation. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/naga-karthik/continual-learning-ms

The Sun remains the sole star allowing for the observation of superficial turbulent convection at extremely high spatial resolution. Since July 2010, the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) has monitored the entire Sun from space using multi-wavelength filters. Specifically, the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) captures high-cadence images of continuum intensity every 45 seconds, revealing solar granulation. This study aims to track the evolution of solar granules throughout an activity cycle and identify changes in their spatial characteristics. By segmenting deconvolved SDO/HMI images and defining granules as convex image elements, we measured their density and mean area. Our results indicate an approximately 2% fluctuation in both density and mean area over the cycle; granule density peaks at solar maximum with a correspondingly smaller mean area. Notably, this maximum density lags behind classical activity indicators, such as the sunspot number, by roughly one year. These findings were corroborated by high-resolution observations from the Hinode/SOTBFI instrument, which yielded consistent results. Variations in granulation at the disk center provide direct insight into physical property changes within the upper convective zone during the solar cycle. These shifts likely stem from interactions between convection and magnetic fields, occurring either globally or locally at the granulation scale.

We introduce a novel metric comparison, analogous to Alexandrov's, and demonstrate its significant link to the continuity of optimal transport for regular measures on Riemannian manifolds, especially concerning the MTW condition formulated by Ma, Trudinger, and Wang.

We examine the canonical Grothendieck topology under specific conditions. Initially, we utilize a characterization of the canonical topology to derive a variation of Giraud's Theorem. Next, we investigate the canonical Grothendieck topology within the categories of sets and topological spaces, where we identify a convenient basis for this topology. Finally, we analyze the canonical Grothendieck topology on the category of $R$-modules.

Clustering algorithms, including anti-$k_T$ and soft-drop, have been widely adopted for precision studies like determining the strong coupling $\alpha_s$ and exploring nucleon intrinsic dynamics. Nevertheless, the theoretical precision of these methods is limited by the absence of higher-order QCD corrections in the jet functions within the corresponding factorization theorems, a challenge exacerbated by the complexity of the clustering procedure. This study introduces a novel approach to compute jet functions at higher orders in QCD, utilizing phase space sector decomposition alongside appropriate soft subtractions. Specifically, we demonstrate this method by calculating the quark-jet function employing the anti-$k_T$ algorithm with E-scheme recombination at next-to-next-to-leading order.

Creating data-driven predictive models for dynamical systems is a priority across numerous fields. This work introduces a unified framework that integrates mechanistic insights with machine learning to reconstruct dynamical systems from noisy, partially observed data. We evaluate purely data-driven methods against hybrid models that incorporate imperfect domain knowledge. Our approach remains model-agnostic, applies to both continuous and discrete time, and handles both memoryless and memory-exhibiting model errors.

First, we analyze memoryless linear model errors (regarding parametric dependence) through a learning theory lens, defining excess risk and generalization error. For ergodic continuous-time systems, we demonstrate that both excess risk and generalization error are bounded by terms decreasing with the square root of $T$, the training duration.

Second, we examine scenarios where modeling memory is advantageous, proving universal approximation theorems for two types of continuous-time recurrent neural networks (RNNs) capable of learning memory-dependent errors. Furthermore, we link one RNN class to reservoir computing, connecting the learning of memory-dependent errors to recent supervised learning research in Banach spaces using random features.

Numerical experiments on Lorenz '63 and Lorenz '96 multiscale systems compare purely data-driven and hybrid approaches, revealing that hybrid methods require less data and exhibit greater parametric efficiency. Finally, we numerically illustrate how data assimilation can be utilized to infer hidden dynamics from noisy, partially observed data, while highlighting challenges in representing memory and training such models.

Throughout the software development life cycle, stakeholders make diverse decisions concerning requirements, design, and management. However, these choices are often poorly documented and categorized due to constraints in time, budget, and personnel. Consequently, automated methods offer a viable solution. This study aims to automatically categorize decisions into five distinct types to facilitate better documentation and comprehension by stakeholders. We gathered a dataset from the Hibernate developer mailing list and subsequently tested 270 different configurations involving feature selection, extraction techniques, and machine learning classifiers to identify the optimal setup for decision classification. Specifically, we employed ensemble learning to construct ensemble classifiers, allowing for a performance comparison against base classifiers. Our experimental findings indicate that (1) feature selection significantly enhances classification outcomes; (2) well-constructed ensemble classifiers surpass base classifiers in performance; and (3) the highest accuracy was achieved using a Bag-of-Words representation with 50% selected features and an ensemble of Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machines, yielding a weighted precision of 0.750, recall of 0.739, and F1-score of 0.727. This research benefits various stakeholders in software development by providing an automated mechanism to effectively classify decisions into types relevant to their specific interests.

This note provides the Stiefel-Whitney classes (SWCs) for orthogonal representations of various finite groups of Lie type, specifically $G=\text{SL}(2,q)$, $\text{SL}(3,q)$, $\text{Sp}(4,q)$, and $\text{Sp}(6,q)$ where $q$ is odd. Additionally, we outline the SWCs for $G=\text{SL}(2,q)$ in the case where $q$ is even.

A great sphere fibration is defined as a sphere bundle where the total space is $S^n$ and the fibers are great $k$-spheres. For any smooth great sphere fibration, projecting centrally onto a tangent hyperplane results in a \emph{nondegenerate} fibration of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of pairwise skew, affine copies of $\mathbb{R}^k$ (although not every nondegenerate fibration originates from this process). This work investigates the topology and geometry of nondegenerate fibrations, demonstrating that all such fibrations satisfy a specific "Continuity at Infinity" property and establishing several classification theorems. These findings enable the precise identification, in specific dimensions, of which nondegenerate fibrations correspond to great sphere fibrations under central projection. By leveraging this correspondence, we reprove various recent results regarding sphere fibrations within the more tractable framework of nondegenerate fibrations. Specifically, we prove that every germ of a nondegenerate fibration can be extended to a global fibration and examine the connection between nondegenerate line fibrations and contact structures in odd-dimensional Euclidean space. The paper concludes with several partial results, anticipating that further exploration of nondegenerate fibrations and their link to sphere fibrations will provide fresh perspectives on the unresolved classification challenges for sphere fibrations.

This study expands the persona-driven sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) neural conversation model into a multi-turn dialogue framework by adapting the state-of-the-art hredGAN architecture. The enhanced system, named phredGAN, incorporates a persona-based HRED generator (PHRED) and a conditional discriminator designed to jointly model utterance attributes including speaker identity, dialogue topics, and sentiments. We investigate two implementations of the conditional discriminator: phredGAN_a, which integrates attribute representations as auxiliary inputs to a standard adversarial discriminator, and phredGAN_d, a dual-discriminator setup that not only performs adversarial training but also collaboratively predicts the attributes of the input utterance. To validate phredGAN's superiority over conventional persona Seq2Seq models, we conduct experiments on the Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus (UDC) and TV transcripts from *The Big Bang Theory* and *Friends*. Our evaluation encompasses various quantitative metrics alongside crowd-sourced human assessments. Furthermore, we analyze the performance trade-offs of both phredGAN variants across datasets characterized by numerous but weak attribute modalities (e.g., *The Big Bang Theory* and *Friends*) versus those with fewer but stronger attribute modalities (e.g., customer-agent interactions in the Ubuntu dataset).

These notes outline a path integral method for handling partial differential equations with stochastic initial conditions. We subsequently apply this framework to the dynamics of the spiked tensor model, demonstrating that the large-$N$ saddle point equations are governed primarily by melonic diagrams.

This paper addresses a specific formulation of Hilbert's irreducibility theorem: given a Galois $G$-covering of varieties $\pi: X \to Y$ over a number field $k$ and a subgroup $H \subset G$, it is shown that for all sufficiently large and highly divisible integers $n$, there exists a closed point $y \in |Y|$ of degree $n$ over $k$ such that $k(y)/k$ is an $S_n$-extension, and there is a point $x \in \pi^{-1}(y)$ where $k(x)/k(y)$ forms a Galois $H$-extension. The findings yield significant corollaries when applied to various moduli spaces. For example, for any finite group $G$, there exists a threshold constant $N$ such that for every $n > N$, one can find a degree $n$ extension $F/\mathbb{Q}$ with Galois group $S_n$ over which the inverse Galois problem for $G$ admits a solution.

Renewable energy, particularly wind power, is becoming increasingly vital to modern power grids, making accurate forecasting essential for maintaining grid balance. Although significant research efforts focus on developing new forecasting techniques, there is a notable gap in addressing how to evaluate, replicate, and apply these methods across different scenarios and datasets. This oversight is partly due to the scarcity of open-source data; many existing datasets are proprietary, rendering research non-reproducible. This issue is especially pronounced in commercially lucrative areas like wind power forecasting. To address this, the present paper aims to facilitate method comparison by offering the most comprehensive and current catalog of available open-source wind power datasets, organized into distinct categories for forecasting applications. We demonstrate that sufficient public data exists for these tasks and analyze the characteristics of these data groups, thereby empowering researchers to select appropriate datasets and benchmark their methodologies effectively.

The holographic entropy cone (HEC) defines the entanglement architecture of quantum states possessing geometric bulk counterparts within holographic frameworks. Because of its inherent intricacy, the HEC has only been fully characterized for up to $n=5$ parties; for larger systems, our understanding remains incomplete, particularly regarding its extremal elements. This work introduces a symmetrization method that maps the HEC onto a natural lower-dimensional subspace, enabling the deduction of properties governing its extremal structure for arbitrary $n$. Additionally, by applying this symmetrization to the quantum entropy cone, we quantify the typicality of holographic entropies, revealing that they constitute an exponentially rare subset of all possible quantum entropies as the number of parties increases.

Convolutional networks (ConvNets) have demonstrated high accuracy in diverse anatomical segmentation tasks; however, they remain sensitive to variations in data appearance. Given the significant variability in scans arising from artifacts, pathologies, and differing scanning protocols, developing robust ConvNets is critical for clinical use, yet this area remains underexplored. To address this, we propose enhancing ConvNets by making them aware of inherent anatomical invariances across imaging scans. Specifically, we introduce a fully convolutional Constraint Adoption Module (CAM) that integrates probabilistic atlas priors as explicit constraints within a locally connected Conditional Random Field (CRF). This approach effectively strengthens the anatomical consistency of prediction labels. The CAM is designed to be both flexible for integration with various ConvNets and compact enough for co-optimization with network fusion parameters to achieve peak performance. Our method demonstrates two-fold advantages across two brain parcellation tasks: first, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among ConvNet-based approaches by significantly reducing structural abnormalities in predictions; second, it substantially improves the robustness of existing ConvNets, evidenced by tests on scans with synthetic pathologies and evaluations across different scanning setups from multiple datasets. Ultimately, our method offers an easy-to-implement solution for boosting both accuracy and robustness by fine-tuning existing ConvNets with the integrated CAM.

We examine various swampland constraints, with a particular focus on the swampland distance conjecture, across a wide range of space-time dimensions $D$. Our analysis of Kaluza-Klein (KK) states in the limit of large $D$ reveals that certain KK spectra exhibit a notable dependence on the dimension. Based on these findings, we introduce a new conjecture for large dimensions. Applying this conjecture to KK states arising from compactifications into anti-de Sitter backgrounds yields a predicted upper limit for the space-time dimension as a function of its characteristic radius. Furthermore, we extend our conjecture to black hole spacetimes, noting that their entropies display a $D$-dependence closely mirroring that of the KK spectrum.

In this study, we compute the phase diagram of the Abelian-Higgs model within a (1+1)-dimensional lattice framework. We locate a first-order phase transition line that demarcates the Higgs phase from the confined phase. This line culminates in a quantum critical point; above this point, the two phases merge into a smooth crossover. Upon analyzing the critical point, we find strong evidence characterizing it as the decoupled product of two non-interacting systems: a massless free fermion and a massless free boson. Nevertheless, we also observe unexpected results that defy this simple interpretation, indicating that this newly identified critical point possesses unusual properties.

High-energy physics experiments aiming to achieve their projected physics goals impose rigorous demands on the upcoming generations of vertex and tracking detectors. Consequently, a wide array of silicon pixel sensors has been developed and rigorously tested in both laboratory settings and test-beam campaigns to address the unique requirements of each application. Corryvreckan is a versatile, rapid, and lightweight framework designed for test-beam data reconstruction and analysis, built upon a modular reconstruction chain. It is engineered to meet the challenges of offline event building within complex data-taking environments that integrate detectors employing diverse readout schemes. The framework's modular design isolates the core from specific implementations of reconstruction, analysis, and detector algorithms. This paper offers a concise overview of the software framework and its associated reconstruction and analysis chain. Additionally, it presents an analysis of a dataset utilizing the framework's offline event building features, along with an enhanced event building scheme that improves test-beam data efficiency by leveraging the pivot pixel information of Mimosa26 sensors.

Although predicting grasps for parallel-jaw grippers is well-established and extensively used in robotic manipulation, generating natural human grasps with multi-fingered hands remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a method to generate human grasps based on 3D objects in the environment. Our central insight is the necessity of ensuring consistency between hand contact points and object contact regions; specifically, we prioritize placing prior hand contact points near the object surface while ensuring the object's common contact regions are simultaneously touched by the hand. Leveraging this hand-object contact consistency, we develop novel training objectives for the grasp generation model and introduce a new self-supervised task that enables model refinement even during the testing phase. Experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Notably, optimizing the model via this self-supervised task during testing yields even greater performance gains on unseen and out-of-domain objects. Project page: https://hwjiang1510.github.io/GraspTTA/

Emergent dynamics within joint human-robot systems often defy prediction based solely on knowledge of the individual components. Typically, robotic actions are driven by algorithms optimizing reward functions intended to quantify the system's shared goals. While these functions can be refined to align with human requirements, they do not guarantee the elimination of misalignment given the complexity and variability of human needs. Furthermore, algorithms may inadvertently learn undesirable behaviors when interacting with humans in an inherently unpredictable environment, leading to further divergence from user or bystander expectations. Consequently, humans may act in unanticipated ways, prompting the robot to adapt in ways that generate further undesirable outcomes.
