This paper argues that designing Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) to mitigate such emergent issues requires supplementing algorithmic advancements with human factors expertise. Specifically, we propose a three-part strategy illustrated through the safety-critical example of a driver engaging with a semi-autonomous vehicle. To curb undesirable emergence, we recommend: (1) integrating driver behavioral models into vehicle algorithms and reward structures; (2) employing model-based methods that account for driver adaptations induced by interaction; and (3) adopting a driver-centered design that fosters engagement and ensures transparent communication of actions to facilitate mutual support and adaptation. We offer examples from our recent empirical research, hoping to stimulate further discussion on emergent HRI.

Following the derivation of the fourth post-Newtonian (4PN) gravitational-wave generation for compact binary systems, we examine and compare various constructions of the exterior metric for isolated systems using post-Minkowskian expansions. While the metric in "harmonic" coordinates has been studied previously to calculate tails and memory effects, it suffers from logarithmic powers of the radial distance $r$ as $r\to\infty$ (at constant $t-r/c$). Consequently, the complex calculation of the "tail-of-memory" effect, which appears in the gravitational-wave flux at 4PN order, is more efficiently handled in "radiative" coordinates. These coordinates allow for a (Bondi-type) expansion at infinity in simple powers of $r^{-1}$, free of logarithms. In this work, we present a specific construction performed order by order in the post-Minkowskian expansion that directly produces a metric in radiative coordinates. We establish the relationship between the two constructions and demonstrate their physical equivalence once a specific relation is confirmed between the "canonical" moments parametrizing the radiative metric and those for the harmonic metric. We provide this relation for the mass quadrupole moment at 4PN order, which is essential for deriving the "tail-of-memory" contribution to the gravitational flux.

This paper introduces DD-NeRF, a novel neural radiance field leveraging double diffusion to reconstruct human body geometry and render appearance from novel viewpoints using only sparse input images. Our approach utilizes a double diffusion mechanism to generate expressive representations by fully harnessing human body priors and visual details across two hierarchical levels. At the coarse level, we model general body poses and shapes using an unclothed 3D deformable vertex model as guidance. At the fine level, a multi-view sampling network captures intricate geometric deformations and detailed appearances, such as clothing and hair, by analyzing multiple input views. To address the sparsity of these two-level features, we diffuse them into feature volumes within the canonical space to build the neural radiance fields. Subsequently, a signed distance function (SDF) regression network reconstructs body surfaces from these diffused features. Benefiting from our double-diffused representations, the method is capable of synthesizing novel views for unseen subjects. Experimental results across various datasets confirm that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both geometric reconstruction and novel view synthesis.

This study proposes a principled, unified, and training-free framework for Neural Architecture Search (NAS) that achieves high performance, low cost, and deep interpretability. Although NAS has rapidly advanced to automate the discovery of top-tier neural networks, it remains plagued by heavy resource demands and search biases stemming from truncated training or approximations. While recent efforts have investigated training-free performance predictors, they often rely on limited deep network properties or fail to extend these benefits to broader search methodologies. Through rigorous correlation analysis, we introduce a unified framework that accelerates and clarifies NAS by disentangling the "TEG" characteristics—Trainability, Expressivity, and Generalization—each evaluated without training. These scalable TEG indicators can be integrated with diverse NAS search strategies, encompassing both supernet and single-path approaches. Extensive experiments confirm that our TEG-NAS framework provides effective and efficient guidance, enhancing search accuracy and reducing search time costs by over 2.3x. Furthermore, visualizations of search trajectories across three "TEG" landscapes reveal that while identifying a good local minimum is relatively straightforward on the simple topology of NAS-Bench-201, balancing "TEG" traits is significantly more challenging in the DARTS search space due to its complex landscape geometry. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/VITA-Group/TEGNAS.

The primary obstacles to widespread electric vehicle (EV) adoption are the accessibility and cost of charging infrastructure. Despite significant initiatives in the United States to expand public charging networks, persistent social inequities in EV uptake necessitate targeted interventions. This study examines the current state of EV charging infrastructure in New York City (NYC) to determine which socio-demographic and transportation characteristics correlate with the distribution of charging stations. Our findings reveal that population density does not correspond to the density of EV chargers, a mismatch that impedes New York's decarbonization and EV adoption objectives. Conversely, the placement of EV charging stations is disproportionately concentrated in highways-adjacent zip codes while systematically excluding low-income, Black-identifying, and historically disinvested neighborhoods. These results highlight the urgent need for policy frameworks that integrate equity and justice into the deployment of EV charging infrastructure.

The $\mathcal{Q}$-graph of a graph $G$, represented as $\mathcal{Q}(G)$, is constructed by attaching a new vertex to every edge of $G$ and connecting any two new vertices that correspond to adjacent edges in $G$. This paper investigates the existence of signless Laplacian perfect state transfer (PST) and signless Laplacian pretty good state transfer (PGST) within the $\mathcal{Q}$-graphs of graphs. We demonstrate that if a regular graph $G$ possesses only integer signless Laplacian eigenvalues, then its $\mathcal{Q}$-graph cannot exhibit signless Laplacian PST. Furthermore, we provide a sufficient condition ensuring that the $\mathcal{Q}$-graph of a regular graph admits signless Laplacian PGST, provided that $G$ itself exhibits signless Laplacian PST between two specific vertices.

This study examines two key characteristics of metric measure spaces that adhere to the reduced curvature-dimension condition under negative dimension parameters: the existence of a transport map connecting two appropriate marginals and the local-to-global property.

For a finite Galois extension of number fields $L/K$, the relative Pólya group $\Po(L/K)$ is identical to the group of strongly ambiguous ideal classes in $L/K$. This paper leverages a well-known exact sequence associated with $\Po(L/K)$, previously utilized by Brumer-Rosen and Zantema, to provide concise proofs for several classical results found in the literature. Furthermore, we introduce the "Ostrowski quotient" $\Ost(L/K)$ as the cokernel of the capitulation map into $\Po(L/K)$ and extend established findings regarding $\Po(L/\mathbb{Q})$ to the broader context of $\Ost(L/K)$.

We introduce a new approach to speed up both the training and inference of Recurrent Neural Network Transducers (RNN-T) by leveraging guidance from a co-trained Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) model. Our primary assumption is that if the CTC model classifies an encoder embedding frame as a blank, it is probable that this frame aligns to a blank across all partial alignments or hypotheses within the RNN-T, allowing it to be removed from the decoder's input. We demonstrate that applying this frame reduction in the middle of the encoder yields substantial speedups for both RNN-T training and inference. Additionally, we show that CTC alignment, generated as a by-product of the CTC decoder, can facilitate lattice reduction for RNN-T during training. Evaluated on the Librispeech and SpeechStew datasets, our method accelerates RNN-T inference by a factor of 2.2 while maintaining word error rates (WER) that are comparable to or slightly better than the baseline.

Word embeddings serve as the primary framework for representing words semantically and syntactically, yet they frequently exhibit problematic associations driven by gender, racial, and religious biases. Current post-processing techniques fail to address gender bias concealed within the spatial layout of word vectors. This paper introduces RAN-Debias, an innovative gender debiasing approach that removes bias from individual word vectors while simultaneously adjusting the spatial distribution of neighboring vectors. This dual action creates a bias-free environment with negligible semantic disruption. Additionally, we introduce the Gender-based Illicit Proximity Estimate (GIPE), a novel metric designed to quantify undue closeness in word vectors caused by gender-based preferences. Experimental results across various evaluation benchmarks demonstrate that RAN-Debias significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods in reducing proximity bias (GIPE) by at least 42.02%. Furthermore, the method effectively lowers direct bias with minimal semantic interference and delivers superior performance in downstream tasks, specifically coreference resolution.

Developers face a significant challenge in executing distributed cyber-physical processes on edge devices, as they must balance system resiliency with strict resource limitations. Existing solutions fail to address the issue of deploying software components in a manner that satisfies diverse, developer-defined resilience requirements established during the design phase. This paper presents a resilient deployment framework that accepts user-defined constraints to optimize for either redundancy or cost within a specific application deployment. Experimental results using a microgrid energy management application built on a decentralized software platform demonstrate that the deployment configuration significantly enhances the resilience of distributed applications and reduces resource consumption on individual nodes, all without altering the underlying control logic.

This study employs density functional theory to investigate the electronic structures of various $s-p$ cubic perovskites with the formula $ABX_{3}$. The analysis covers experimentally realized compounds such as SrBiO$_{3}$, BaBiO$_{3}$, BaSbO$_3$, CsTlF$_{3}$, and CsTlCl$_{3}$, alongside hypothetical candidates including MgPO$_{3}$, CaAsO$_{3}$, SrSbO$_{3}$, and RaMcO$_3$. Using tight-binding modeling, we compute the interatomic hopping integrals ($t_{sp\sigma}$) between $B-s$ and $X-p$ orbitals and the charge-transfer energies ($\Delta$), which are the critical parameters governing low-energy electron and hole states. Our findings reveal periodic trends in these parameters, particularly how relativistic effects lower the energy of $B-s$ orbitals in heavy cations, resulting in strongly negative $\Delta$ values. These results are contextualized within the general phase diagram for $s-p$ cubic perovskites (Ref. 26), confirming that parent superconductors SrBiO$_{3}$ and BaBiO$_{3}$ occupy the regime characterized by negative $\Delta$ and large $t_{sp\sigma}$. Building on this, we search for new materials exhibiting similar parameters to potentially identify novel superconductors. Furthermore, we examine potential correlations between specific electronic structures and physical properties, such as the propensity for bond disproportionation and the maximum achievable superconducting transition temperature.

The significance of relationships is continuously reshaped by memory imprints, which strengthen through social interactions and weaken during the intervals between them, thereby altering relationship dynamics. Although the evolution of relationships within social networks is crucial, there has been limited research into how long-term interaction patterns correlate with individuals' internal records of relationship importance. In this study, we model these memory dynamics by adapting a established cognitive science framework. Leveraging two distinct longitudinal datasets, we calibrated the model's parameters to maximize the alignment between predicted relationship strengths—derived from call detail records—and the actual ground-truth rankings of a node's connections. Our findings demonstrate that a model trained on one population can accurately predict outcomes for another, indicating that the memory imprints of social interactions among unrelated individuals are universal. This work establishes a foundation for modeling social interactions as memory traces and highlights their potential as an unobtrusive method for the early detection of memory disorders.

We introduce a simulation algorithm that precisely propagates a pair of molecules using large time steps, eliminating the necessity of computing full exact analytical solutions to the Smoluchowski diffusion equation. Since the method relies exclusively on uniform and Gaussian random numbers, it achieves position updates that are two to three orders of magnitude faster than those of corresponding schemes based on complete solutions, all while maintaining equivalent accuracy. The approach avoids simplifying or ad hoc assumptions inconsistent with the underlying Smoluchowski theory; instead, it faithfully integrates the specific components of the theoretical model. Demonstrating flexibility across one, two, and three dimensions, the method suggests broad utility for various stochastic simulation algorithms. We illustrate the algorithm's performance for non-reactive, irreversible, and reversible reacting molecule pairs.

We utilize the dynamical large-$N$ Schwinger boson method as an impurity solver for dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) simulations of the Kondo lattice model. This approach successfully incorporates hybridization physics via DMFT self-consistency, addressing a limitation in pure Schwinger boson calculations that rely on independent electron baths. The derived thermodynamic and transport characteristics align qualitatively with more rigorous results and accurately reproduce the crossover from the local moment regime to the Fermi liquid across a broad temperature spectrum. Furthermore, this methodology holds potential for extension to density functional theory, enabling efficient material computations.

Local entropic loss functions offer a flexible framework for designing architecture-specific regularization techniques. Beyond their ability to exhibit anisotropy within synaptic space, the local entropic smoothing applied to the loss function can evolve throughout training, enabling adjustable model complexity. A scheduling protocol that applies strong regularization at the onset of training and gradually diminishes it serves as an alternative to standard initialization methods for deep convolutional neural networks, while also demonstrating broader applicability. By examining anisotropic, local entropic smoothenings through the lenses of statistical physics and information theory, we gain deeper insight into their mechanics and interpretation. Additionally, we discuss relevant aspects concerning the physics of renormalization and the spacetime structure inherent in convolutional networks.

We examine the presence of vortex configurations within two gauged-$CP(2)$ models augmented by magnetic impurities, analyzing both Maxwell-$CP(2)$ and Chern-Simons-$CP(2)$ extensions individually. Our study employs a $CP(2)$-field configuration characterized by zero topological charge, applicable to both the simplest free case and scenarios coupled to an Abelian gauge field. Utilizing the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield (BPS) formalism reveals that the effective models for these configurations exhibit a self-dual structure akin to that found in gauged sigma models. Consequently, when coupled to the Maxwell term, the system's total energy features a well-defined Bogomol'nyi bound and quantized magnetic flux. In contrast, under the Chern-Simons gauge scenario, the total electric charge is confirmed to be proportional to the quantized magnetic flux. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that magnetic impurities contribute to the BPS potentials and appear within the BPS equations for both models. We subsequently introduce a Gaussian-type impurity and resolve the self-dual equations using a finite-difference scheme, yielding solutions with nonmonotonic behavior that invert both magnetic and electric fields. Finally, we address topologically trivial solutions in the limit where the impurity reduces to a Dirac $\delta$-function.

We examine the functional equations of Selberg zeta functions associated with Tate motives $f$ on a compact Riemann surface $M$ of genus $g \ge 2$. Our results establish that specific functional equations are valid if and only if $f$ possesses absolute automorphy.

The multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem represents a prevalent decision-making challenge that highlights the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Conventional formulations typically omit risk considerations, yet risk significantly complicates standard reward-maximization goals, largely due to the absence of a universally accepted definition. This paper investigates an entropic risk (ER) metric and evaluates the performance of a Thompson sampling-based algorithm, ERTS, under this framework by deriving regret bounds for ERTS alongside corresponding instance-dependent lower bounds.

This study examines the $k$-essence modified $f(R)$ gravity model, specifically the $f(R,\phi,X)$ theory, with a focus on investigating causality violations within the framework of Gödel-type universes. The analysis allows for both causal and non-causal solutions and determines a critical radius associated with non-causal scenarios. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the occurrence of causality violation is contingent upon the specific matter content.

We introduce a framework utilizing continuous frequency space to characterize and construct solid-state NMR experiments. While this method shares similarities with the established Floquet treatment for NMR, it extends beyond periodic Hamiltonians and facilitates reverse engineering of experimental designs. Built upon perturbation theory within a continuous Fourier domain, the approach yields effective, time-independent Hamiltonians. This enables the derivation of pulse sequences from target effective Hamiltonians as functions of specific spin-system parameters. As a demonstration, we illustrate how to determine the rf irradiation for the MIRROR experiment by back-calculating from the desired chemical-shift offset profile of the sequence.

Gaining insight into network and application performance is crucial for troubleshooting, enhancing user experience, and conducting performance benchmarks. However, modern mobile devices are engineered for energy efficiency, a design choice that can inadvertently constrain network and application capabilities. Recently, various tools have appeared that assess mobile app network performance in real-time using VPN services. Yet, there remains a scarcity of knowledge regarding how these measurement instruments and system-level optimizations influence overall performance. This study first establishes that mobile operating systems utilize energy-aware hardware tuning, which directly impacts application speed and network throughput. Subsequently, we demonstrate that VPN-based measurement tools, including Lumen, PrivacyGuard, and Video Optimizer, contribute to ambiguous network metrics while simultaneously degrading application performance. Our results indicate that achieving accurate performance measurements on Android devices necessitates a comprehensive understanding of the device architecture, network conditions, measurement methodologies, and the applications themselves.

We recently derived an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information of entangled coherent states within a lossy Mach-Zehnder Interferometer, as introduced by J. Joo et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 107, 083601(2011)]. Our analysis shows that under conditions of minimal photon loss, these entangled coherent states can exceed the Heisenberg limit. Additionally, the methodology presented in this work can be extended to investigate the phase sensitivity of multipartite entangled coherent states.

This work reviews findings concerning linear local and 2-local homomorphisms, as well as zero-product preserving operators acting between C$^*$-algebras, integrating novel precise observations and results. We demonstrate that every bounded linear 2-local homomorphism between C$^*$-algebras is necessarily a homomorphism. As a result, it follows that every linear 2-local $^*$-homomorphism between C$^*$-algebras is a $^*$-homomorphism.

Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) serve as a crucial tool for analyzing the dynamic behavior of astrophysical objects during transient phenomena such as gamma-ray bursts, solar flares, and magnetar flares. Standard QPO searches typically employ periodograms and estimate spectral density via the Whittle likelihood function; however, this method is strictly valid only for stationary time series, as non-stationarity causes frequency bins to lose statistical independence. We demonstrate that when analyzing non-stationary data, the statistical significance of QPOs can be severely overestimated, and estimates for central frequencies and widths may become overly constrained. This bias arises specifically when a QPO exists only for a portion of the dataset while the noise level fluctuates across the series, a scenario common when including pre- or post-transient background noise or when low-frequency noise profiles vary significantly. We verify that this bias exists in previously published solar flare data, confirming that reported significances were often exaggerated. Finally, we offer recommendations to help researchers identify whether their analyses are compromised by this specific bias.

This paper presents a generalization of Multi Poly-Euler polynomials and examines several relationships concerning these polynomials. Consequently, deriving a closed-form expression for the generalized Multi Poly-Euler numbers emerges as a natural and significant objective.

The fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) represents a unique form of electronic correlation in two-dimensional systems subjected to a strong perpendicular magnetic field. It emerges from the interplay between intense Coulomb repulsion among electrons within the same Landau level and the specific chirality of their electronic states, a property derived from the classical cyclotron motion dictated by the magnetic field's orientation. In graphene, the FQHE exhibits distinct characteristics due to a four-fold spin-valley degeneracy inherent to the electronic bands near the Fermi level. Since the relevant Coulomb interactions respect this SU(4) symmetry, the system gives rise to a generic four-component fractional quantum Hall effect alongside other correlated four-component phases, such as spin-valley ferromagnetic states. This article focuses on a primarily theoretical exploration of these exotic phases, contrasting them with existing experimental observations.

Thousands of customers daily submit inquiries on Amazon product pages, occasionally receiving responses from informed peers. Recognizing that many of these questions can be resolved using existing product reviews, we introduce the task of review-based question answering. This task involves a QA system that generates answers by synthesizing information from a given set of reviews and a specific question. To address this, we present a novel dataset and a methodology that integrates information retrieval to select pertinent reviews and reading comprehension models to formulate answers. Our dataset comprises 923,000 questions, 3.6 million answers, and 14 million reviews spanning 156,000 products. Expanding upon the established Amazon dataset, we added annotations to classify each question as either answerable or unanswerable based on the available review content. A deployed system could first determine if a question is answerable before attempting to generate a response. Distinct from many standard QA datasets, our collection features questions, passages, and answers derived directly from real human interactions. We evaluated various answer generation models and established robust baselines, highlighting the inherent difficulty of this new task.

Let X denote a smooth, complex Fano variety with Lefschetz defect delta(X). It is established that if delta(X) ≥ 4, then X is isomorphic to a product S × T where dim T = dim X − 2. This paper establishes a structure theorem for the case delta(X) = 3. We demonstrate that there exists a smooth Fano variety T with dim T = dim X − 2 such that X arises from T via two specific constructions. In both scenarios, X is the blow-up of a P²-bundle Z over T along three pairwise disjoint, smooth, irreducible subvarieties of codimension 2. Furthermore, we apply this theorem to Fano 4-folds, the case where X has Picard number 5, and Fano varieties admitting an elementary divisorial contraction mapping a divisor to a curve. Notably, these applications complete the classification of Fano 4-folds with delta(X) = 3.

We examine the merging potential of central Brightest Group Galaxies (BGGs) using a volume-limited sample of 550 groups from the Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) Galaxy Group Catalogue, covering halo masses between $\log[M_h/M] = 12.8$ and $14.2$. Focusing on low-redshift BGGs ($z \leq 0.2$), we utilize spectroscopically confirmed close companions as a proxy for potential stellar mass accretion. We identify 17 such companion galaxies that satisfy criteria of projected separation $r_p < 30$ kpc, relative velocities $\Delta v \leq 300$ km s$^{-1}$, and stellar mass ratios $M_{BGG}/M_{CC} \leq 4$. These companions result in a total pair fraction of $0.03 \pm 0.01$. Consequently, our analysis indicates that BGGs in this sample can increase their stellar mass through mergers at a rate of $2.2 \pm 1.5\%$ per Gyr, a figure that falls below the growth rates predicted by existing galaxy evolution models.

Selecting the relevant data attributes for multivariate decision algorithms, commonly known as feature selection, is a critical phase in addressing machine learning challenges. Although there is a prevailing trend toward training complex deep networks on vast quantities of raw inputs—a practice termed automated feature engineering—many physics applications already possess sets of features that are theoretically sound and well-characterized. Leveraging these pre-existing features offers significant advantages, such as improved interpretability, shortened training and inference times, and increased stability and robustness. We introduce a novel feature selection technique grounded in Distance Correlation (DisCo) and validate its efficacy on boosted top- and $W$-tagging tasks. By applying this method to a collection of more than 7,000 energy flow polynomials, we demonstrate that it is possible to achieve performance comparable to significantly deeper architectures using merely ten features and approximately two orders of magnitude fewer model parameters.

Brown dwarfs serve as vital probes for investigating planetary and sub-stellar atmospheres under diverse thermal and chemical regimes. With ongoing survey advancements and improved observational capabilities, the catalog of known Y dwarfs—the coldest sub-stellar class, defined by effective temperatures under approximately 600 K—is expanding rapidly. These ultra-cool objects possess atmospheric conditions that mirror those of Solar System bodies, making tools derived from studying Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, and similar worlds highly applicable to sub-stellar atmospheres. In response, we created a one-dimensional vertical atmospheric structure model for ultra-cool objects that incorporates moist adiabatic convection, a critical process for many planets in our own system. Applying this model across various effective temperatures (350, 300, 250, and 200 K), metallicities ([M/H] of 0.0, 0.5, 0.7, and 1.5), and gravities (log $g$ of 4.0, 4.5, 4.7, and 5.0) reveals significant effects of water latent heat release on simulated temperature-pressure profiles. At peak metallicities, water vapor mixing ratios attain Earth-like levels of 3%, causing substantial changes to the thermal structure in regions where water condenses. Spectroscopic and photometric indicators of both metallicity and moist convection are expected to be easily detectable at near- and mid-infrared wavelengths, particularly through James Webb Space Telescope observations, offering insights into an object's formation history.

Recent advancements have enabled the accurate prediction of a Deep Neural Network's (DNN) testing performance based on the statistical properties of its topological structure; however, applying this insight practically remains difficult due to prohibitive computational costs regarding time and memory. This work introduces a novel class of topological features that effectively characterize learning progress while remaining computationally efficient during runtime. Furthermore, these features are designed to be compatible with backpropagation, allowing for seamless integration into end-to-end training. By offering a practical topological characterization of DNNs, this approach enables several new applications. First, it allows for performance prediction without requiring a testing set or high-performance computing resources. Second, it demonstrates that these topological features are effective for estimating task similarity. Finally, the study shows that learning can be actively induced by constraining the DNN's topological structure, thereby opening new avenues for controlling underlying network architectures within a meta-learning framework.

Touch serves as the main interaction method for smartphones, yet creating mobile interfaces that function effectively for everyone is challenging due to varying user abilities and preferences. We introduce Reflow, a system that automatically applies small, personalized UI adjustments, termed refinements, to mobile app screens to enhance touch efficiency. By employing a pixel-based approach, Reflow operates within existing applications to boost touch performance while preserving the original design intent with minimal disruption. The system optimizes a user interface through three steps: extracting the layout from a screenshot, refining that layout, and re-rendering the UI to incorporate these changes. A user study involving 10 participants and a heuristic evaluation by 6 experts revealed that Reflow-optimized applications achieved an average 9% reduction in selection time with negligible layout interference. These findings demonstrate that Reflow's refinements provide valuable UI adaptations for improving touch interactions.

Since physical realizations of quantum information processors are rarely unique, selecting the optimal implementation remains a significant challenge. This work examines how sensitive these devices are to fluctuations in their constituent parts. By employing a quantum metrological framework, we demonstrate that a device's sensitivity to component variations follows a notably simple general pattern. We introduce cost functions as a practical metric to evaluate and choose between different physical architectures for the same quantum device, which comprises various components. Specifically, we analyze the sensitivity of two linear optical quantum computing gates—the KLM and Reverse nonlinear sign gates—to changes in beam splitter transmitivities, alongside the enhanced optical Bell detectors proposed by Grice and by Ewert & van Loock. Finally, we briefly contrast this sensitivity measure with the diamond distance, concluding that the latter is less effective for assessing the behavior of components embedded within a larger quantum system.

Recovering object geometry and material properties from multiple viewpoints generally relies on optimization. While differentiable path tracing offers a promising framework for replicating complex visual effects, its high computational cost makes it challenging to implement. This paper investigates the application of differentiable ray tracing to enhance an initial coarse mesh and per-facet material representation. Our simulations demonstrate that fine geometric and material details can be reconstructed from low-resolution inputs, achieving high-quality results within hours despite the computational expense of path tracing. These reconstructions effectively distinguish between shading, shadows, and global illumination phenomena—such as diffuse interreflection—and intrinsic material properties. We evaluate the influence of various geometry initializations, including space carving, multi-view stereo, and 3D neural networks. Furthermore, using smartphone video and a consumer 360-degree camera for lighting estimation, we illustrate how to refine initial reconstructions of real-world objects in unconstrained settings.

Using data from the ATLAS detector at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of 28 nb⁻¹, Bose-Einstein correlations between identified charged pions were analyzed in p+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV. Pion identification relied on ionization energy loss measurements within the pixel detector. The study presents two-particle correlation functions and derived source radii across varying collision centralities, average transverse momenta ($k_{\mathrm{T}}$), and pair rapidities ($y^{\star}_{\pi\pi}$), with pairs selected in the ranges $-2 < y^{\star}_{\pi\pi} < 1$ and $0.1 < k_{\mathrm{T}} < 0.8$ GeV. The impact of jet fragmentation on these correlations was investigated, and a technique utilizing opposite-charge pairs to constrain such contributions was detailed. Results indicate that source sizes are significantly larger in central collisions and diminish as pair $k_{\mathrm{T}}$ increases, with a demonstrated correlation between radii and local charged-particle density. Additionally, the scaling of radii with the mean number of participating nucleons was employed to evaluate various initial-geometry models. Finally, the cross-term $R_\mathrm{ol}$ was measured as a function of rapidity, revealing a nonzero value with a combined significance of 5.1σ for $-1 < y^{\star}_{\pi\pi} < 1$ in the most central events.

This paper introduces a novel task focused on predicting the relational coverage of text documents for relation extraction (RE), specifically determining whether a document contains numerous relational tuples for a specific entity. Such predictions are valuable for identifying optimal documents when constructing knowledge bases from large corpora. To investigate this issue, we introduce a dataset comprising 31,366 diverse documents covering 520 entities. We examine the correlation between document coverage and various features, including document length, entity mention frequency, Alexa rank, language complexity, and information retrieval scores; however, each feature exhibits only moderate predictive capability. We utilize methods that integrate these features with statistical models, such as TF-IDF, and language models, such as BERT. The proposed model, HERB, which combines features with BERT, achieves an F1 score of up to 46%. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of coverage predictions through two use cases: knowledge base construction and claim refutation.

Given the severe adverse effects of particulate matter (PM) on human health, accurately forecasting PM concentrations in South Korea has become critically important. Most traditional statistical and machine learning approaches rely on the assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, such as Gaussian distributions; however, air pollution and weather time series often violate this premise. This study employs the maximum correntropy criterion for regression (MCCR) loss to analyze the statistical properties of these datasets. Due to intricate seasonal patterns and heavy-tailed distributions that persist even after seasonal adjustments, rigorous seasonality correction was applied to both air pollution and weather data. The MCCR loss function was implemented across various models, ranging from standard statistical techniques to advanced machine learning algorithms. The findings indicate that MCCR loss is superior to conventional mean squared error loss when predicting extreme values.

Although neural networks have excelled in computer vision, they remain susceptible to adversarial examples—inputs subtly modified to deceive classifiers while remaining indistinguishable to humans. Building on existing detection research, we introduce a structured approach that integrates a detector subnetwork into a deep neural network (DNN). Central to our method is $\textit{Adversarial Noise Sensitivity}$ (ANS), a new metric that quantifies the adversarial gradient impact across various intermediate layers. We strategically attach a detector to the layer exhibiting the highest ANS value. Unlike previous studies that employed complex detectors which increased computational overhead, our targeted integration reduces model complexity while enhancing adversarial resilience. Extensive white-box and black-box evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that our technique surpasses current state-of-the-art detector robustness. Additionally, we confirm the energy efficiency of our approach through comprehensive hardware analysis on scalable CMOS accelerators and assess the performance impact of quantization on detector-augmented networks.

Every geodesic current defined on a hyperbolic surface possesses a corresponding dual space. When the current represents a lamination, this dual space embeds isometrically into a real tree. We demonstrate that, more broadly, the dual space functions as a hyperbolic metric tree-graded space, with its Gromov hyperbolicity constant expressible through the geodesic current. For geodesic currents lacking atoms and possessing full support—such as those arising from specific higher-rank representations—we establish that their duals are homeomorphic to the surface. Additionally, we examine the dual's completeness and the fundamental group's action upon it, while also endowing the space of duals with a topology that aligns with the natural topology of geodesic currents.

Linear-scaling density functional theory (DFT) methods typically depend on electron localization, a behavior that does not occur in many practically significant large systems, such as semiconductor nanocrystals, until their dimensions become extremely vast. Consequently, numerical scaling often deviates from linearity in these scenarios. This work addresses such systems by introducing a massively parallel, formally quadratic-scaling DFT approach that does not rely on electron localization. Despite its quadratic formal scaling, the method achieves highly efficient linear wall-time performance in the weak scalability regime. Building upon the stochastic DFT framework presented by Fabian et al. (WIRES: Comp. Mol. Science, e1412, 2019), this approach is fully deterministic. It represents electronic wave functions using standard atom-centered Gaussian basis sets while employing Cartesian real-space grids for specific operators and to accelerate Poisson equation solvers. The primary conclusion is that, given access to processor-abundant high-performance computing (HPC) resources, this methodology can enable the investigation of large systems in regimes where quantum confinement or electron delocalization would otherwise render linear-scaling methods ineffective.

The actual degradation of silicon bipolar devices exposed to combined ionization and displacement irradiation is typically estimated by summing the individual damages from each effect. However, recent experimental findings reveal a distinct discrepancy between this summed value and the observed practical damage, highlighting significant irradiation synergistic effects (ISEs). Comprehending the behaviors and mechanisms underlying ISEs is crucial for accurately predicting real-world device performance. This study begins with a critical review of current literature, specifically addressing the challenges previous models face in explaining the dose rate dependence of ISEs. We subsequently present detailed models that elucidate this fundamental phenomenon through three main components. First, we report experimental results on PNP and NPN transistors using a setup with variable neutron fluence and gamma-ray dose; we observe fluence-dependent "tick"-like profiles in PNP transistors and sublinear dose profiles in NPN transistors. Second, we detail our theoretical investigation into the positive ISE in NPN transistors by proposing an atomistic model of the transformation and annihilation of $\rm V_2$ displacement defects in p-type silicon under ionization irradiation. This approach differs fundamentally from the traditional view of Coulomb interactions between oxide trapped charges and carriers in irradiated silicon, and our predicted novel dependencies on dose and fluence are fully confirmed by experimental data. Third, we examine the mechanism behind the negative ISE in PNP transistors using a similar framework. In n-type silicon, $\rm VO$ displacement defects also undergo ionization-induced transformation and annihilation. Our findings indicate that the evolution of displacement defects driven by carrier-enhanced defect diffusion and reaction constitutes the dominant mechanism for these synergistic effects.

Stream-based active learning involves processing a continuous flow of unlabeled data, requiring the system to determine for each instance whether to request a label for training or discard it. Various strategies aim to reduce the number of necessary labeled samples by prioritizing the most informative data points. Predominantly, these approaches are rule-based and depend on uncertainty metrics, which measure how close a data point lies to the classifier's decision boundary. Although recent efforts have sought to derive optimal selection strategies directly from data, many lack broad applicability due to three main constraints: (1) a focus on specific classification scenarios, (2) reliance on rule-based metrics, and (3) the requirement for offline pre-training on related tasks. This work overcomes these limitations by introducing an online, stream-based meta-active learning framework. This method learns an informativeness metric dynamically from the data and applies to a wide range of classification problems without needing prior task-specific pre-training. Built on reinforcement learning, the approach integrates episodic policy search with a contextual bandits framework to train the active learner alongside the model. Empirical results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that this method selects training samples more efficiently than current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines coined quantum walk search and state transfer protocols, specifically targeting complete $M$-partite graphs where each partition contains $N$ vertices. Initially, we demonstrate that introducing a loop to every vertex enables the search algorithm to locate a marked node with unit probability as the graph size approaches infinity. Subsequently, we utilize the search evolution operator involving two marked nodes to facilitate state transfer between a sender and a receiver. Our results indicate that when the sender and receiver occupy different partitions, the transfer fidelity approaches unity for large graphs; however, if they reside within the same partition, the fidelity fails to reach exactly one. To address this limitation, we propose a state transfer algorithm incorporating an active switch, allowing the fidelity to be estimated solely based on the single-vertex search.

Although internet search engines are essential to daily life, users continue to depend on text-based platforms like Google for pop music. We introduce Pied Piper, a meta search engine designed specifically for music. It allows users to query lyrics, song metadata, audio files, or any combination thereof, efficiently delivering relevant results.

Iterative approaches for resolving sparse linear systems and eigenvalue problems are foundational to critical domains within scientific research and engineering. The core computational engine driving these iterative methods is the multiplication of a sparse matrix by a dense vector; consequently, the efficient realization of sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and linear solvers is paramount and has been the subject of extensive investigation across diverse computing architectures and accelerators, including CPUs, GPUs, MICs, and FPGAs. To fully exploit an architecture or accelerator, one must identify the factors influencing an efficient SpMV implementation. This article offers a pioneering, comprehensive survey of more than two hundred state-of-the-art optimization strategies for solving sparse iterative linear systems, with a specific emphasis on SpMV. It introduces a novel taxonomy for iterative solutions and SpMV techniques applicable to all architectures. By reviewing SpMV methods across every architecture, the article consolidates a unified taxonomy to foster cross-architectural and heterogeneous development, though the primary focus remains on GPUs. Using this taxonomy, the article first delineates the major, primary, secondary, and tertiary contributions of SpMV techniques before conducting a qualitative comparison. Furthermore, it separately summarizes the current research landscape for each architecture and concludes by outlining several open problems and key challenges for future research directions.

The diffusive halo, a fundamental aspect of cosmic ray (CR) propagation, enhances our comprehension of CR research and indirect dark matter investigations. However, deriving the halo size typically encounters degeneracy issues, resulting in significant uncertainties. Diffusive gamma rays originating from high-latitude clouds may offer an independent method to constrain the halo size. Given that the spatially dependent propagation (SDP) model aligns more closely with observed CR data than conventional models, this study examines halo thickness using the SDP framework and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray observations of high- and intermediate-velocity clouds. Our findings indicate that to avoid exceeding the relative gamma-ray emissivity in high-latitude clouds, the halo thickness must fall within the range of $\rm ~3.3\sim9~ kpc$. Furthermore, the distinct spatial morphologies of gamma rays predicted by the SDP model under varying halo thicknesses provide a viable tool for determining the halo size. We anticipate that future multi-wavelength observations will allow our model to be tested and refined.

In 1979, K. Okamoto defined the space of initial values for the six Painlevé equations and their corresponding Hamiltonian systems, demonstrating that these constitute regular initial value problems at all points within an augmented phase space—a rational surface excluding specific exceptional divisors. This work establishes that the concept of the space of initial values remains valid for broader classes of second-order complex differential equations and Hamiltonian systems where all movable singularities of their solutions are algebraic poles (a condition some refer to as the quasi-Painlevé property, which extends the Painlevé property). However, unlike the original case, the resulting initial value problems in the extended phase space achieve regularity only following an additional transformation of both dependent and independent variables. Furthermore, this method for constructing the space of initial values functions as an algorithm to identify, within a given class of equations or systems, those that are free from movable logarithmic branch points.

Item categorization is a machine learning process designed to assign e-commerce products, usually described by textual features, to appropriate categories from a fixed list. A precise categorization system is crucial for enhancing both customer experience and corporate operational efficiency. This study addresses scenarios where item descriptions are noisy and brief, and ground-truth labels are absent. To handle these challenges, we introduce a new framework called Ensembled Transferred Embeddings (ETE), built on two core concepts: 1) semi-automatically labeling a small subset of the target data, and 2) utilizing large-scale, labeled datasets from related domains or tasks to derive "transferable embeddings." Testing ETE on a substantial real-world dataset from PayPal demonstrates that it significantly surpasses both traditional and state-of-the-art item categorization techniques.

Advancements in quantum hardware are approaching the scale necessary to execute quantum algorithms in fields like physics and encryption, making quantum addition circuits essential for these applications. Ideally, circuits utilizing fault-tolerant gates and error-correcting codes would mitigate environmental noise; however, current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices lack the resources to support the overhead required for such designs. Consequently, researchers have turned to low-depth architectures, such as quantum carry-lookahead adders (QCLAs), as noise and decoherence risks escalate with circuit depth. This study introduces an out-of-place QCLA constructed from Clifford+T gates, optimized for minimal T-gate usage by employing a novel uncomputation technique. The choice of Clifford+T gates is strategic, as they can transition to fault-tolerant implementations once hardware capabilities improve, with T-gate efficiency being the primary focus due to their high cost in fault-tolerant contexts. Comparative analysis demonstrates that the proposed QCLAs outperform existing methods in both T-count and total gate count. Finally, the practical utility of these adders is illustrated through their application in quantum image processing, specifically via circuits for bilinear interpolation.

Detecting changepoints is a critical task within time series and genomic data analysis. In certain scenarios, it is beneficial to restrict the direction of these changes; for instance, in ChIP-seq data, enforcing an up-down constraint enhances peak detection precision but complicates the optimization process. We demonstrate how a recently introduced functional pruning method can be modified to address these constrained changepoint detection challenges. This adaptation yields a novel algorithm capable of handling problems with arbitrary affine constraints on the means of adjacent segments, featuring an empirical time complexity that scales log-linearly with data size. The algorithm attains state-of-the-art accuracy across a benchmark of various genomic datasets and operates orders of magnitude faster than comparable existing methods. The implementation is accessible as the `PeakSegPDPA` function within the `coseg` R package: https://github.com/tdhock/coseg

The AMS-02 collaboration has recently published cosmic-ray Fluorine-to-Silicon (F/Si) data with previously unmatched precision. Since cosmic-ray Fluorine (CR F) is primarily generated through the fragmentation of heavier parent nuclei, whereas Silicon (Si) is mainly accelerated at the source, this ratio offers exceptional sensitivity to cosmic-ray propagation dynamics. We examine whether the transport parameters derived from the F/Si ratio align with those obtained from lighter ratios such as Li/C, Be/C, and B/C. Additionally, we investigate the CR source abundance of Fluorine, a rare element characterized by a high first ionization potential and moderate volatility, making it a critical probe for understanding cosmic-ray acceleration mechanisms. Utilizing the 1D diffusion model within the USINE code, we conduct $\chi^2$ analyses that incorporate various systematic uncertainties, including energy correlations, nuclear cross-section variations, and solar modulation effects. Leveraging the EXFOR nuclear database, we update production cross-sections for Fluorine's key progenitors—identified as $^{56}$Fe, $^{32}$S, $^{28}$Si, $^{27}$Al, $^{24}$Mg, $^{22}$Ne, and $^{20}$Ne. The transport parameters derived from the AMS-02 F/Si data are consistent with those from the (Li, Be, B)/C measurements. A combined fit of all these ratios yields a $\chi^2/dof \approx 1.1$, requiring only adjustments of less than 10% to the production cross-sections of Boron and Fluorine; the latter, based on sparse nuclear data, would significantly benefit from new measurements. The F/Si ratio is consistent with a purely secondary origin for Fluorine, showing a best-fit relative source abundance of $^{19}$F/$^{28}$Si$_{CRS} \sim 10^{-3}$ and an upper limit of $\sim 5 \times 10^{-3}$. However, this limit is insufficient to constrain global acceleration models of cosmic-ray nuclei, which necessitate values around $\sim 10^{-4}$. Achieving such precision might be possible with F/Si data possessing a few-percent accuracy at energies of a few tens of TV, a goal potentially attainable by next-generation cosmic-ray experiments.

The spectral energy distribution (SED) of galaxies reveals essential details about underlying physical processes, yet it is heavily influenced by dust within the interstellar medium. This dust originates primarily from asymptotic giant branch stars and Type II supernovae, with its mass growing via metal accretion and grain sizes altering through collisions. Since the contribution of these mechanisms and the resulting extinction rely on the size distribution, accurate SED models must account for the evolution of both dust mass and grain sizes. Despite this significance, many prior SED models failed to incorporate the evolution of total mass and size distribution in a physically consistent way. This study presents a new radiative transfer SED model grounded in a dust evolution framework consistent with chemical evolution. To minimize computational demands, we utilized the mega-grain approximation and a one-dimensional plane-parallel galaxy setup. Using a Milky Way-like galaxy as a fiducial case under a closed-box model, we calculated SEDs across various ages. Our results indicate that galaxies younger than 100 Myr do not generate small grains like polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Conversely, after 1 Gyr, there is a sharp rise in infrared emission and attenuation driven by a rapid increase in dust mass—a phenomenon our model addresses for the first time. This approach enables SED fitting for galaxies at any evolutionary stage.

Addressing intricate logical queries on knowledge graphs (KGs) that contain missing edges is a pivotal challenge in KG reasoning. The query embedding approach tackles this by mapping queries and entities into a unified embedding space, subsequently selecting answer entities based on their similarity to the query embedding. However, since answers to complex queries result from logical operations on sub-queries, the resulting entity embeddings often do not conform to a uni-modal distribution. Consequently, retrieving a diverse set of answers from the embedding space using a single, concentrated query representation—such as a vector or hyper-rectangle—is difficult. To address queries with diversified answers, we introduce Query2Particles (Q2P), a method for complex KG query answering. Q2P encodes each query into multiple vectors, termed particle embeddings. This allows candidate answers to be retrieved from various regions of the embedding space by identifying maximal similarities between entity embeddings and any of the particle embeddings. Furthermore, neural logic operations are defined to facilitate reasoning over arbitrary first-order logic queries. Experimental results demonstrate that Query2Particles achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex query answering tasks across the FB15k, FB15K-237, and NELL knowledge graphs.

The P2 experiment is designed to perform high-precision measurements of parity-violating asymmetries in elastic scattering between longitudinally polarized electrons and protons or $^{12}$C nuclei. This study examines the experiment's sensitivity to new physics arising from an extra neutral gauge boson, $Z'$, associated with a new $U(1)'$ symmetry. If the $U(1)'$ charge assignment is chiral, meaning left- and right-handed fermions carry different charges, direct additional parity violation occurs. Conversely, non-chiral charge assignments can induce parity violation through mass or kinetic mixing between the $Z$ and $Z'$ bosons. By comparing P2's sensitivity to current constraints, we demonstrate that the experiment possesses discovery potential across a broad spectrum of $Z'$ masses in both scenarios. Specifically, for chiral models, P2 can detect gauge couplings of order $10^{-5}$ for light $Z'$ bosons and reach up to 79 TeV (90 TeV) for heavy $Z'$ bosons in the proton ($^{12}$C) channel. For non-chiral models involving mass mixing, P2 can constrain mixing angles to values below approximately $10^{-4}$, contingent upon specific model parameters and gauge coupling strengths.

A single-mode silicon bus-waveguide hosts an ultra-compact one-dimensional topological photonic crystal (1D-TPC) engineered to produce Fano resonance. This resonance arises from the interference between the discrete topological boundary state within the 1D-TPC and the continuum high-order leaky mode of the bus-waveguide. Experimental results in the waveguide transmission spectrum demonstrate standalone asymmetric Fano resonance lineshapes, achieving a maximum extinction ratio of 33 dB and a slope ratio of 10 dB/nm against a broadband flat background.

Recent years have seen a surge in discourse surrounding fairness in machine learning, AI ethics, and algorithmic audits, prompting various entities to create framework guidelines that serve as baseline rubrics for accountability. Despite this heightened dialogue and the proliferation of frameworks, practical implementation of algorithm and data auditing remains challenging. Although numerous open-source auditing tools exist, there is often a lack of user awareness regarding their availability, utility, and accessibility. Furthermore, model auditing and evaluation are not frequently prioritized as essential skills within the machine learning domain. Beyond the pursuit of fairness, there are compelling legal imperatives for proactively adopting these tools, alongside significant social benefits related to public perception and goodwill in an increasingly interconnected global society. Enhancing awareness of these tools and the rationale for their active use could benefit the entire ecosystem, including programmers, data scientists, engineers, researchers, and end-users. It is crucial for all stakeholders to comprehend input-output differentials, their origins, and strategies for promoting FATE (fairness, accountability, transparency, and ethics) in machine and deep learning. Free access to open-source auditing tools eliminates fundamental barriers to fairness assessment. Consequently, this paper underscores the urgent necessity of utilizing these tools and offers motivations for doing so, highlighting exemplary open-source solutions with accessible repositories that can be immediately deployed by anyone globally.

The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for conducting Bell experiments with varying levels of complexity. The paper begins by reviewing Bell's foundational argument, specifically the CHSH inequality, to interpret these experiments. It posits that any independent observer faces a cognitive limitation: they cannot simultaneously retain all relevant variables when modeling the experiment. This perspective is contrasted with Tim Maudlin's proposal, which relies on nonlocality. While Maudlin critiques the Nobel committee, this criticism is refuted in the text. Additionally, the authors briefly outline a new approach to the foundations of quantum mechanics and provide references to pertinent literature.

This paper describes the inaugural demonstration of muon acceleration via a radio-frequency accelerator and details the accelerator system employed in the upcoming experiment. Conducted at the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex, this study marks the first experiment to utilize accelerated muon beams for measuring the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and electric dipole moment; construction of the facility is set to commence shortly.

Embedding representations are essential for various machine intelligence applications, such as recommendation systems, yet they demand substantial storage space, often consuming hundreds of gigabytes in large-scale scenarios. To address this significant memory overhead, we investigate mixed dimension embeddings, an architecture where the dimensionality of each embedding vector is adjusted based on its query frequency. Both theoretical analysis and comprehensive experiments reveal that employing mixed dimensions can substantially lower memory requirements without compromising machine learning performance; in fact, performance can be enhanced. Specifically, for the click-through rate prediction task on the Criteo Kaggle dataset, our proposed mixed dimension layers achieve a 0.1% accuracy improvement with half the parameters, or maintain equivalent accuracy with 16 times fewer parameters.

This PhD thesis investigates specific geometric structures defined on Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks, building upon the research presented in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375]. Specifically, [arXiv:1907.00375] explores the relationship between two distinct definitions of gerbes over stacks. The work in [arXiv:2012.08447] establishes the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids that possess a connection. Furthermore, [arXiv:2012.08442] examines connections on principal bundles over Deligne Mumford stacks by utilizing the Atiyah sequence. Finally, [arXiv:2103.04560] introduces the concept of topological groupoid extensions and analyzes the correspondence between Morita equivalent classes of these extensions and gerbes over topological stacks.

The Lyubeznik size of a monomial ideal $I$ in a polynomial ring $S$ serves as a lower bound for the Stanley depth of $I$ minus one. This text addresses a gap in a proof previously provided by Herzog, Popescu, and Vladoiu.

Magnetic fields arising from non-central heavy-ion collisions represent some of the most intense in the universe, with strengths comparable to those of strong interactions. Supported by model simulations, these fields are anticipated to exhibit spatial modulation, differing markedly from the standard assumption of uniformity. To enhance our comprehension of quark and gluon physics under such extreme conditions, we employ lattice QCD simulations featuring $2+1$ staggered fermion flavors at physical quark masses within an inhomogeneous magnetic background across a temperature spectrum spanning the QCD phase transition. Utilizing a $1/\cosh^2$ function to describe the field profile, we vary its intensity to assess effects on computed observables and the transition itself. Our calculations of local chiral condensates and local Polyakov loops, alongside an estimation of lattice artifacts, reveal that both observables display complex spatial characteristics resulting from the interaction between sea and valence effects.

This study explores a higher-degree generalization of the S-lemma, a concept significant for its close connection to Hilbert's 1888 theorem regarding tenary quartics. Specifically, if such a generalization were valid, it would enable a Hilbert-style theorem requiring positivity only over specific semi-algebraic sets. However, we demonstrate that this generalization is unfeasible unless additional constraints are imposed. To substantiate this conclusion, we employ and extend tools originally developed by Netzer ([Ne]). These refined instruments reveal that the impossibility stems from geometric factors. Moreover, we successfully bridge the gap between these geometric and algebraic explanations by operating within the framework of quadratic modules.

Circular colliders offer the benefit of providing collisions at multiple interaction points, enabling the study and optimization of up to four distinct detector designs for FCC-ee. While detectors must adhere to constraints imposed by the invasive interaction region layout, their performance in heavy-flavour tagging, particle identification, tracking, particle-flow reconstruction, and the resolution of leptons, jets, missing energy, and angles must align with the physics programme and the exceptional statistical precision of FCC-ee. During the FCC feasibility study (2021-2025), benchmark physics processes will guide simulations to define detector design and performance requirements, ensuring that systematic uncertainties remain proportional to statistical precision. Additionally, the utilization of data to achieve challenging goals regarding detector stability and alignment, particularly for the Z peak programme, will be investigated. Furthermore, the potential discovery of weakly coupled new particles through Z or Higgs boson decays may drive the development of specialized detector designs to enhance the reconstruction efficiency of these rare signatures. These investigations provide essential input for optimizing the CLD and IDEA concepts outlined in the Conceptual Design Report, as well as for evolving new concepts that could better suit the FCC-ee physics programme.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud (designated as G28.37+0.07 or G28.34+0.06) classifies them into protostellar and starless groups based on their connection to molecular outflows. Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this mass accretion. The implications of this finding for the relationship between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function require further investigation.

This study examines an extended cosmological framework inspired by the asymptotic safety of gravity, where corrections to matter density, radiation density, and the cosmological constant are introduced via parameters $\delta_G$ and $\delta_\Lambda$. These corrections cause slight deviations from standard evolutionary behaviors, interpreted as a scenario of vacuum energy interacting with matter and radiation. We analyze two specific model variants: (i) $\tilde\Lambda$CDM, which includes one additional free parameter $\delta_G$ under the constraint that $\delta_G$ and $\delta_\Lambda$ are linked by a low-redshift relation, and (ii) e$\tilde\Lambda$CDM, which features two independent free parameters, $\delta_G$ and $\delta_\Lambda$. Using two datasets—CMB+BAO+SN (CBS) and CMB+BAO+SN+$H_0$ (CBSH)—we constrain these models. Our results indicate that with CBS data alone, neither $\tilde\Lambda$CDM nor e$\tilde\Lambda$CDM significantly alleviates the $H_0$ tension. However, incorporating CBSH data allows both models to substantially mitigate this tension, with the e$\tilde\Lambda$CDM model reducing it to just 0.71$\sigma$. We conclude that, as an interacting dark energy model, $\tilde\Lambda$CDM outperforms $\Lambda(t)$CDM in both resolving the $H_0$ tension and fitting current observational data.

The LISA Pathfinder mission aims to validate drag-free test mass technology for future space-based gravitational wave detectors, using them as inertial references. To achieve this, the spacecraft executes drag-free flight around a primary test mass while measuring its acceleration relative to a secondary reference mass housed within the same vehicle. Because this reference mass must be actively controlled to maintain its position and orientation relative to the spacecraft, applied forces introduce potential acceleration noise unique to the Pathfinder configuration and absent in the full LISA design. Although the spacecraft was engineered to satisfy its primary objectives despite this noise, recent assessments indicate that "suspension noise" could constrain on-orbit performance. Consequently, drift-mode and free-flight experiments offer a means to mitigate this noise source and better characterize the underlying disturbances relevant to LISA-like instrument designers. This article outlines a high-level overview of these experiments and the analytical methods being developed to process the resulting data.

Federated machine learning enables model training across multiple devices without transferring data between them. Since data stays localized at each compute node, this approach is ideal for sectors with strict data privacy requirements, such as healthcare, or environments facing bandwidth limitations. A primary limitation of current methods is their dependence on a central server for task delegation and the generation of a unified shared model. This paper proposes a flexible framework to decentralize the federated learning paradigm and offers an open-source, reference implementation that is compatible with PyTorch.

While shockwave theory typically derives density, velocity, and pressure jumps from conservation equations, this work reverses the approach to examine weak shock physics. We demonstrate that the density profile of a weak shock in a fluid can be represented as a superposition of linear acoustic modes. This constructed shock travels at the speed of sound with exact mass conservation at the front, though momentum and energy are conserved only to zeroth order in shock amplitude. The resulting jumps in density, velocity, and pressure mirror those of a standard fluid shock, allowing for the definition of an equivalent Mach number. A comparable decomposition applies to magnetohydrodynamics; however, it is unattainable for collisionless shocks due to the dispersive characteristics of ion acoustic waves. Adjusting frequencies via weakly nonlinear corrections fails to resolve this issue. Consequently, weak collisionless shocks may be inherently nonlinear and resist linear superposition, or they might not exist at all, as suggested by recent research.

In general relativity, the flatness of macroscopic spacetime, defined as the lack of curvature, is a well-established concept. However, this understanding does not extend to nonperturbative quantum gravity, where spacetime's microscopic structure cannot be described merely as small deviations from a fixed background. Two-dimensional quantum gravity models present a unique scenario; lacking a classical limit, they represent a state of maximal quantum behavior. This study examines the recently defined quantum Ricci curvature within Causal Dynamical Triangulations (CDT) on a two-dimensional torus, hypothesizing that its quantum geometry might appear flat at coarse-grained scales. Contrary to expectations based on Monte Carlo simulations involving up to 600,000 building blocks, the geometry does not exhibit classical flatness. Instead, the results reveal a scale-independent "quantum flatness" that lacks a direct classical counterpart. Additionally, the research establishes a criterion for differentiating between local and global topological properties within this toroidal quantum system.

The development of heterogeneous photocatalysts has garnered significant attention for their potential in degrading organic pollutants in wastewater and producing carbon-free hydrogen through water splitting. This study reports on the synthesis of a nanostructured LaFeO$_{3}$-MoS$_{2}$ photocatalyst using a straightforward hydrothermal method, evaluating its performance in photodegradation and hydrogen generation. Before these experiments, the composite's structural, morphological, and optical characteristics were thoroughly analyzed via X-ray diffraction, field emission scanning electron microscopy, and UV-visible spectroscopy, respectively. The LaFeO$_{3}$-MoS$_{2}$ nanomaterial achieved a 96% degradation of rhodamine B dye within 150 minutes, outperforming both pure LaFeO$_{3}$ and commercial Degussa P25 titania nanoparticles. Furthermore, it displayed markedly improved photocatalytic efficiency in breaking down the colorless pollutant ciprofloxacin, thereby ruling out dye-sensitization effects. Additionally, the composite exhibited exceptional activity for solar-driven hydrogen evolution from water. Based on band structure analysis and reactive species contributions, a direct Z-scheme mechanism is proposed to explain the superior photocatalytic performance of the LaFeO$_{3}$-MoS$_{2}$ nanocomposite.

A dominating set consists of vertices where every vertex outside the set has at least one neighbor within it. While counting such sets is #P-complete for chordal graphs, it can be solved in polynomial time for the subset of interval graphs. The complexity for directed path graphs—which lie between chordal and interval graphs—remained previously unresolved. This study demonstrates that counting dominating sets is also #P-complete for directed path graphs, though it becomes solvable in polynomial time when restricted to rooted directed path graphs.

Effective co-manipulation robotics requires leveraging both proprioceptive and exteroceptive data to enhance safety and autonomy. Guided by this principle, the study introduces an intuitive task formulation aligned with the human perspective through the integration of visuo-tactile perception. Depth cameras provide visual data to monitor object dimensions and infer human intent, while tactile sensors ensure precise contact to prevent slippage. Experiments conducted on a robot platform with human collaboration in an industrial environment confirm the efficacy and practical utility of this proposed approach.

Traditionally, incorporating real data into classrooms involved using datasets that were pre-cleaned and processed before students accessed them. However, a crucial component of statistics education should involve students actually retrieving data from the internet. Today, numerous sources offer data that is continuously updated by their hosting organizations. Tools within R for downloading such dynamic data have advanced significantly, making access feasible even for introductory statistics courses. This work presents five complete analyses using dynamic data, along with nine additional sources suitable for classroom use. Our objective is to show that mastering dynamic data requires a brief learning curve, even for introductory students or faculty unfamiliar with the field. While these examples will not train expert data scrapers, they aim to inspire both students and instructors to engage more deeply with online data resources.

This study reports on the measurement of inclusive four-jet production in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Jets with transverse momenta extending down to 35, 30, 25, and 20 GeV for the first through fourth leading jets, respectively, are analyzed within the pseudorapidity range $|\eta| < 4.7$. Differential cross sections are determined as functions of jet transverse momentum, jet pseudorapidity, and various other observables characterizing angular correlations between the jets. These measured distributions exhibit sensitivity to different components of the underlying event, parton shower, and matrix element calculations. Specifically, the analysis highlights the significance of the interplay between angular correlations arising from parton showers and double-parton scattering contributions. The double-parton scattering contribution is isolated via a template fit to the data, utilizing single-parton scattering distributions from Monte Carlo event generators and a double-parton scattering distribution derived from inclusive single-jet events in data. Finally, the effective double-parton scattering cross section is computed and discussed in the context of prior measurements and its reliance on models describing the single-parton scattering background.

A recent study successfully constructed a geometric embedding of the classical space and phase space of an n-particle system into the system's state space, demonstrating its physical significance. Specifically, Newtonian particle dynamics were derived from Schrödinger dynamics by restricting the system's state to a classical phase space submanifold within the larger state space. Several theorems concerning this embedding and Schrödinger evolution under a random Hamiltonian were established and demonstrated their relevance to measurement processes in both classical and quantum mechanics. In this work, these findings are utilized to offer a novel perspective on prominent quantum-mechanical thought experiments and paradoxes, providing new insights into wavefunction collapse and the motion of macroscopic objects within quantum theory.

[arXiv Abridged] This study examines novel spatially-resolved measurements of the initial mass function (IMF) for three edge-on lenticular galaxies within the Fornax cluster. By applying existing orbit-based dynamical models that replicate observed stellar kinematics, we constrain new IMF maps within this orbital framework to investigate correlations between intrinsic orbital characteristics and the local IMF. Our results indicate that within each galaxy, both high-angular-momentum disk-like stars and centrally concentrated, pressure-supported orbits display IMFs enriched in dwarf stars. In contrast, orbits at large radii with intermediate angular momentum show IMFs significantly poorer in dwarfs compared to other regions of the same galaxy. Assuming that current-day stars on dynamically hot, large-radius orbits are primarily accreted, we interpret these findings as a link between the dwarf content of a stellar population and the mass of the host galaxy where it formed: deeper gravitational potentials yield more dwarf-rich populations, explaining the relative lack of dwarfs from lower-mass accreted satellites. Conversely, central and high-angular-momentum populations likely consist mainly of in-situ stars formed within the more massive host galaxy. Additionally, global differences of up to $\sim 0.3\ \mathrm{dex}$ in the IMF parameter $\xi$ exist among the three galaxies, with no single local dynamical or chemical property fully accounting for these variations.

This research investigates the holographic renormalization group (RG) flow within $(d+1)$-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert gravity augmented by higher-order curvature corrections and an arbitrary interacting scalar field, utilizing the superpotential method. We identify the critical points of the RG flow corresponding to local minima and maxima of the potential and demonstrate the existence of bounce solutions.
