Unlike standard Einstein-Hilbert gravity, the superpotential in this bulk theory can possess both upper and lower bounds depending on the coupling values. Furthermore, the RG flow dynamics are governed by singular curves, offering insights into the potential existence of a $c$-function under these corrections.

This manuscript was accepted for publication in *Comment. Math. Univ. Carolinae* in 1968 but disappeared during the military occupation of Prague and related upheavals. My personal, long-lost carbon copy was eventually discovered in my Columbia office. The only modifications to the text involve adding a footnote and a few commas.

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the thickness-dependent third-order (\(\chi^{(3)}\)) nonlinear optical characteristics of RF-sputtered WSe2 thin films, utilizing ultrashort pulses at various excitation wavelengths. Single-beam Z-scan measurements across the visible spectrum highlight the significant influence of Pauli-blocking in driving saturable absorption and optical limiting within WSe2 films of differing thicknesses. Additionally, the research examines the dispersion of third-order nonlinear susceptibility (\(\chi^{(3)}\)) in these films. Notably, WSe2 thin films of all thicknesses demonstrate a self-focusing effect, indicating a positive nonlinear refractive index (\(n_2 > 0\)). The frequency-dependent nonlinear absorption (\(\eta\)) shows specific relationships with the film bandgap, a property further explored via density-functional-theory (DFT) simulations. Changes in the band structure are mainly attributed to defect bands caused by selenium deficiency in WSe2 thin films, which significantly affect the material's optical limiting performance.

Turbulent systems display a striking multi-scale complexity where spatial structures generate scale-dependent statistics that deviate significantly from Gaussian distributions. In Fourier space, this manifests as distinct phase synchronization. However, a quantitative link connecting real-space structure, statistical properties, and phase synchronization remains absent. This study tackles that gap using a minimal phase-coupling model, facilitating a thorough analysis through dynamical systems theory and high-resolution multi-scale simulations. We determine that the steepness of the spectral power law, which governs phase coupling, serves as the control parameter for adjusting the system's non-Gaussian characteristics. While both extremely steep and shallow spectra yield nearly Gaussian statistics, the most significant deviations occur at intermediate slopes similar to those found in hydrodynamic and Burgers turbulence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model's non-Gaussian regime aligns with the dynamical system collapsing onto a lower-dimensional attractor and the onset of phase synchronization, thus providing a dynamical-systems framework for understanding turbulent intermittency.

Recently, there has been a surge in research on spoken dialogue systems, particularly open-domain ones designed for casual discussions about popular subjects like movies, books, and music. These systems strive to socially interact with, entertain, and empathize with users. Because measuring these social objectives is challenging, recent studies have relied on dialogue length and human ratings as evaluation metrics, alongside developing automatic methods to calculate novel indicators such as coherence, consistency, relevance, and engagement. In this work, we introduce the PARADISE model to forecast the performance of Athena, a finalist Alexa Prize system that has engaged in thousands of real-user conversations. We employ both user ratings and dialogue length as quality metrics and experiment with predicting them using automatic features that are either system-dependent or system-independent. Our objective is to derive a generalizable objective function capable of optimizing dialogue choices for any Alexa Prize system in real-time and assessing their performance. Our top model for predicting user ratings, based on a DistilBert architecture, achieves an R² of .136, whereas the best model for predicting length using system-independent features reaches an R² of .865, indicating that conversation length may serve as a more dependable metric for the automatic training of dialogue systems.

This paper presents mARC, a novel data modeling technology based on the second quantization formulation of quantum mechanics. It serves as a universal, unsupervised, and incremental system for storing and retrieving data, applicable to both structured and unstructured, textual and non-textual signals. mARC addresses various information classification and retrieval challenges, such as e-Discovery and contextual navigation, and can also be formulated within the artificial life framework known as Conway's "Game of Life" theory. Unlike Conway's approach, mARC allows objects to evolve within a massively multidimensional space. To assess mARC's potential, the authors developed a demonstrator featuring a mARC-based Internet search engine with contextual capabilities. Comparing this demonstrator to Google search in terms of performance and relevance, the study reveals that the mARC engine responds an order of magnitude faster while delivering more relevant results for certain query categories.

We define quasi-antisymmetric Higgs $G$-bundles on curves featuring marked points, equipped with additional structures that substitute the parabolic data found in standard parabolic Higgs bundles. Specifically, while parabolic bundles associate coadjoint orbits to marked points, our modified bundles attach cotangent bundles over specific symmetric spaces instead. Consequently, the moduli spaces of these quasi-antisymmetric bundles also function as phase spaces for complex completely integrable systems, just as those of parabolic bundles do. We demonstrate that the moduli space of parabolic Higgs bundles arises as the symplectic quotient of the moduli space of quasi-antisymmetric bundles under the action of a product of Cartan subgroups. Furthermore, by varying the underlying symmetric spaces, we introduce quasi-compact and quasi-normal Higgs bundles. The fixed point sets of real involutions on their respective moduli spaces correspond to the phase spaces of real completely integrable systems. Several illustrative examples are provided, including integrable extensions of the ${\rm SL}(2)$ Euler-Arnold top, the two-body elliptic Calogero-Moser system, and the rational ${\rm SL}(2)$ Gaudin system along with its real reductions.

Cybersecurity represents a paramount technical challenge in the modern era, making the detection of hostile actions and the safeguarding of intellectual property and customer data critical priorities for global corporations and government bodies. Cyber defenders must scrutinize vast, high-resolution network flows to identify, classify, and neutralize attacks that cross institutional and national borders. Numerous cyber threats can be characterized as subgraph patterns, including insider infiltrations (modeled as path queries), denial-of-service attacks (parallel paths), and malicious propagation (tree queries). This reality drives our investigation into subgraph matching within streaming graphs under continuous conditions. Our work's innovation stems from utilizing subgraph distributional statistics from streaming data to dictate query processing strategies. We present a "Lazy Search" algorithm that determines search tactics on a vertex-by-vertex basis based on the probability of finding a match within a vertex's neighborhood. Additionally, we introduce the "Relative Selectivity" metric to choose between various processing strategies. Experiments conducted on real-world online news data, network traffic streams, and synthetic social network benchmarks demonstrate speedups of 10 to 100 times compared to selectivity-agnostic methods.

Recent proofs have demonstrated that linear codes invariant under a doubly transitive permutation group achieve the capacity of the erasure channel, making the classification of such codes a significant pursuit. This work advances that goal by reviewing the relevant permutation groups and existing findings regarding codes invariant under them. The analysis reveals the existence of capacity-achieving families of algebraic geometric codes.

Categorizing IoT devices is crucial for security and privacy. Although recent studies have successfully used machine learning to fingerprint these devices, they often assume that necessary features are readily available or inexpensive to extract, ignoring the associated costs. This work adopts a more realistic perspective by acknowledging that feature extraction incurs varying costs. Furthermore, we move beyond treating misclassification loss as a simple binary value, instead proposing a framework where losses vary based on performance. More significantly, we introduce the concept of "risk" in IoT device classification. By defining and formulating this as a cost-aware classification problem, we recognize it as a combinatorial optimization challenge. To address this, we developed a novel algorithm that utilizes Cross-Entropy (CE) based stochastic optimization for fast and effective solutions. Using real-world traffic data, we demonstrated that this CE-based approach can select features that minimize misclassification risk while adhering to a specified budget for feature extraction costs.

Fraud involving public funds poses severe risks to the economic, social, and political stability of societies, with procurement-related fraud alone causing billions of euros in annual losses. Consequently, developing analytical frameworks to help public authorities detect firms prone to irregular behavior is critically important. This study applies standard network science techniques to examine co-bidding patterns among companies participating in public tenders across 184 municipalities in the Brazilian state of Ceará from 2015 to 2019. We identified 22 distinct groups of firms characterized by similar procurement activities, defined by their geographic reach and operational scope. By profiling these communities, we can pinpoint groups that are particularly vulnerable to market manipulation and misconduct. Our findings underscore the utility of network analysis in public policy, demonstrating its ability to reveal the intricate relationships between market actors even when data is limited.

Shaping codes are employed to create sequences where symbols adhere to a specific probability distribution. These codes naturally emerge in source coding scenarios involving noiseless channels with varying symbol costs. Recently, they have been suggested to enhance flash memory longevity and shorten DNA synthesis durations. This paper investigates a broad category of shaping codes designed for noiseless finite-state channels dealing with cost constraints and independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sources. We derive the connection between code rate and minimum average symbol cost, subsequently identifying the rate that minimizes the total average cost per source symbol. Furthermore, we demonstrate an equivalence between codes that minimize average symbol cost and those that minimize total cost. Finally, we prove a separation theorem, indicating that optimal shaping can be realized through the concatenation of optimal compression and optimal shaping tailored for a uniform i.i.d. source.

The Linac to End Station A (LESA) beamline, currently under construction at SLAC, is designed to deliver a near-continuous wave (CW) beam of multi-GeV electrons to the SLAC End Station A for particle physics research. The first half of the facility is scheduled for commissioning by the end of fiscal year 2022, with the complete beamline expected to become fully operational in the first quarter of fiscal year 2024. This low-current, multi-GeV electron beam is generated parasitically by the superconducting RF (SRF) linac powering the LCLS-II and LCLS-II-HE X-ray Free Electron Laser. LESA is engineered to accommodate experiments aimed at detecting light dark matter, such as the Light Dark Matter eXperiment (LDMX), along with a diverse array of other projects and test beams that require near-CW electron currents spanning from picoamperes (pA) to microamperes ({\mu}A).

G\"odel modal logics are essentially extensions of intuitionistic modal logics incorporating the prelinearity axiom. This paper investigates the algebraic and relational semantics of G\"odel modal logics by utilizing the duality between finite G\"odel algebras and finite forests, defined as finite posets where principal downsets are totally ordered. We examine various subvarieties of the basic variety of G\"odel algebras with two modal operators (GAOs) and their associated classes of forest frames, featuring either single or dual accessibility relations. These relational structures function as prelinear adaptations of standard relational semantics for intuitionistic modal logic. Specifically, we analyze two primary extensions of finite G\"odel algebras with operators: one derived from adding Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intuitionistic logic fragments, and another based on Fischer Servi axioms. Furthermore, we establish J\'onsson-Tarski-style representation theorems for the distinct types of finite GAOs addressed in this study.

Recently, numerous multimodal networks designed for Visually-Rich Document Understanding (VRDU) have been introduced, demonstrating the benefits of transformers by merging visual and layout data with text embeddings. Nevertheless, most current methods rely on position embeddings to handle sequence information, often overlooking the inaccurate reading orders generated by OCR tools. This paper introduces XYLayoutLM, a robust layout-aware multimodal network that effectively captures and utilizes rich layout information derived from the correct reading orders produced by our Augmented XY Cut technique. Furthermore, we propose a Dilated Conditional Position Encoding module to manage input sequences of varying lengths; this module also extracts local layout information from both textual and visual modalities while generating position embeddings. Experimental results indicate that our XYLayoutLM achieves competitive performance on document understanding tasks.
We demonstrate that the Theorem of Bobadilla and Pełka yields a non-isolated variant applicable to aligned hypersurface singularities.

Current research in Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery (RAMIS) aims to enhance robot autonomy, shifting the surgeon's role to one of supervision. While Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) is a favored method for autonomous systems to acquire expert gestures, it typically demands extensive demonstrations and struggles to generalize across the variable conditions of a surgical setting. This study introduces an LfD framework grounded in Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL) within a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) environment. By integrating generative adversarial networks to model expert trajectory distributions with a DRL structure, GAIL ensures robust generalization and human-like behavior. The research focuses on automating tissue retraction, a prevalent RAMIS task involving the manipulation of soft tissues to expose specific areas. The proposed method acquires a limited set of expert trajectories using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) and trains the LfD algorithm in a simulated environment. Results demonstrate that this approach performs tissue retraction with human-like proficiency and exhibits superior sample efficiency compared to baseline DRL methods. Finally, the study confirms that the learned policies can be effectively transferred to a real robotic platform and successfully deployed for soft tissue retraction on a synthetic phantom.

Thermonanophotonics, which examines photothermal phenomena in optical nanoantennas, has recently gained significant attention. Although thermoplasmonic structures facilitate diverse applications ranging from optofluidics and imaging to medical and photochemical systems, dielectric nanoantennas introduce novel possibilities for thermo-optical modulation and reconfigurable metasurfaces. Nevertheless, calculating both photo-thermal and thermo-optical effects within large-scale arrays of nanoantennas remains a significant challenge. This study presents a rapid numerical approach to determine temperature elevation in multi-dimensional arrays of optical antennas situated in a uniform medium, incorporating self-heating, collective heating, and thermo-optical effects. Specifically, we demonstrate the scalable calculation of temperature in 3D networks containing $10^5$ particles within under one hour. Notably, by explicitly accounting for the influence of discrete nanoparticles on light attenuation and photothermal conversion, this method allows for the optimization of intricate temperature profiles in 3D arrays. Crucially, we present the first computation of thermo-optical effects beyond the single nanoantenna level. Our findings reveal that collective heating amplifies these effects in multi-dimensional arrays of both Silicon and Gold nanospheres, underscoring the necessity of including them in photothermal analyses. In summary, the proposed methodology offers new avenues for the swift evaluation of complex photothermal interactions in optical nanoantenna arrays, thereby supporting the advancement of sophisticated thermonanophotonic functionalities.

The paper investigates perturbations of giant magnons and single spikes within a $2+1$-dimensional $\mathbb R \times S^2$ spacetime. By employing the giant magnon solution in the Jevicki-Jin gauge, we formulate the standard Jacobi equation governing small normal deformations of an embedded time-like surface. Notably, this equation simplifies to a basic wave equation set in a Minkowski background. The analysis subsequently examines the finiteness of these perturbations and the resulting stability of giant magnons under small deformations; it is found that only the zero mode permits finite deformations and maintains stability. Finally, the study shifts focus to the single spike solution within the same gauge, where the perturbation equation is derived, solved numerically, and analyzed regarding stability.

This paper presents a novel four-parameter extension of the flexible Weibull distribution, constructed upon the Beta Generalized (BG) distribution introduced by Eugene et al. \cite{Eugeneetal2002}, which pioneered the use of BG distributions for generating new models. The proposed model, termed the beta flexible Weibull (BFW) distribution, includes derivations of key statistical properties such as the mode, $r$th moments, skewness, and kurtosis, alongside the moment generating function and order statistics. Parameter estimation is performed using the maximum likelihood method, with the corresponding Fisher's information matrix also derived. Finally, the utility of the BFW distribution is demonstrated through an empirical application utilizing a real dataset.

The introduction of laser cooling methods has transformed research into atomic-scale systems, driving advancements in quantum computing through the preparation of trapped ions in their motional ground states and the creation of new matter states via Bose-Einstein condensation. Similar cooling approaches offer a versatile way to prepare macroscopic objects in their motional ground state, effectively extending micromechanics into the quantum domain. Cavity opto- or electro-mechanical systems utilize strong light-motion interactions to achieve sideband cooling. However, reaching the quantum regime—defined as having less than one quantum of motion—has remained elusive because sideband cooling has not adequately countered the coupling of mechanical systems to warm environments. In this work, we demonstrate sideband cooling of a micromechanical oscillator's motion to its quantum ground state. Achieving this requires a substantial electromechanical interaction, realized by integrating a micromechanical membrane into a superconducting microwave resonant circuit. To confirm the membrane's cooling into the quantum regime, we conducted a near quantum-limited measurement of the microwave field, resolving the motion with a factor of 5.1 above the Heisenberg limit. Additionally, our device exhibits strong coupling, enabling the coherent exchange of microwave photons and mechanical phonons. Simultaneously achieving strong coupling, ground state preparation, and efficient measurement paves the way for rapid progress in controlling and detecting non-classical states of motion, potentially allowing tests of quantum theory in previously unexplored regions of larger mass and size.

We report the identification of a charge density wave (CDW) ground state in heavily electron-doped molybdenum disulfide (MoS$_2$), marking the first such observation in any $d^2$ (column 6) transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD). Because the electronic band structure of MoS$_2$ differs from that of the $d^0$ and $d^1$ TMDs where CDWs were previously found, this discovery offers novel perspectives on CDW formation. Our study reveals a metal-insulator transition at 85 K, a 25 meV gap at the Fermi level, and two distinct CDW modulations: a $(2\sqrt{3}\times2\sqrt{3})$R$30^\circ$ pattern driven by Fermi surface nesting (FSN) and a $2\times2$ pattern resulting from electron-phonon coupling (EPC). This coexistence of FSN and EPC-induced modulations is unprecedented in CDW ground state observations, and we analyze it through the lens of band folding. These findings offer a pathway to resolve ongoing debates regarding the origins of CDW modulations in TMDs.

Consider two families of meromorphic functions, F and G, defined on a domain D, and let a, b, and c be three distinct points in the extended complex plane. Assume that G is a normal family in D where every limit function is non-constant. If every function f in F shares the values a, b, and c partially with some function g in G, then F is also normal in D. This finding offers a significant refinement of a theorem by X. J. Liu, S. H. Li, and X. C. Pang, and we additionally establish several other pertinent sharp results.

This study examines the dynamics of a quantum system subjected to repeated measurements when unitary evolution is halted prior to each observation. We begin by analyzing a solitary two-level system coupled to two independent baths of harmonic oscillators, then extend the analysis to an ensemble of such systems, effectively utilizing the large spin-boson model. In this setup, each two-level system experiences strong coupling with one bath and weak coupling with the other. To address the strong-coupling regime, we employ a polaron transformation, enabling the application of perturbation theory. Our results reveal qualitative and quantitative distinctions between the single-system and collective scenarios; however, the overarching impacts of strong and weak couplings mirror those observed when system evolution is present. Consequently, we conclude that system evolution has no practical influence on these effects.

This paper aims to address monocular 3D object detection by learning feature representations that are sensitive to both context and depth. Our key contributions include: (i) introducing a depth-conditioned dynamic message propagation (DDMP) network that effectively merges multi-scale depth data with image context, avoiding the complexity of pseudo-LiDAR methods; (ii) achieving this through adaptive sampling of context-aware nodes followed by the dynamic prediction of hybrid depth-dependent filter weights and affinity matrices for information propagation; (iii) mitigating inaccurate depth priors by incorporating a center-aware depth encoding (CDE) task; and (iv) providing comprehensive validation that demonstrates state-of-the-art performance among monocular-based methods on the KITTI benchmark, specifically securing the first rank in the highly competitive KITTI monocular 3D object detection track on November 16th, 2020. Our code and models are available at \url{https://github.com/fudan-zvg/DDMP}.

We present a novel two-sided stable matching framework modeling the summer internship allocation process at an Australian university. This model bridges two existing frameworks by Kamada and Kojima concerning matchings under distributional constraints. We examine three stability concepts: the strong and weak definitions introduced by Kamada and Kojima, and a newly proposed intermediate concept termed "cutoff stability." While Kamada and Kojima demonstrated that strongly stable matchings can be absent in their most restricted model featuring disjoint regional quotas, our first finding establishes that verifying their existence is NP-hard. Subsequently, we prove that a cutoff stable matching is guaranteed to exist for both the specific summer internship scenario and the broader matching model with arbitrary heredity constraints. We provide an algorithm to compute such a matching for the summer internship case, demonstrating it operates in polynomial time. Conversely, we show that identifying a maximum-size cutoff stable matching is NP-hard, though we offer a Mixed Integer Linear Program formulation to address this optimization challenge.

All-electrical control of spin states is a highly sought-after mechanism for developing energy-efficient spintronic devices. Using rigorous first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that molecular spin interfaces formed by depositing iron tetraphenyl porphyrin (FeTPP) on boron-substituted graphene (B-G) allow for the manipulation and detection of spin properties. Specifically, a gate electrode enables reversible switching between $S=1$ and $S=3/2$ spin states, a phenomenon driven by strong hybridization between Fe-$d_{{z}^2}$ and B-$p_z$ orbitals. By integrating density functional theory with nonequilibrium Green's function formalism, we propose a viable three-terminal experimental configuration to investigate these spin states. Additionally, we illustrate how the FeTPP molecule modifies the inherently non-spin-polarized in-plane quantum transport of B-G, generating substantial transport spin polarization near the Fermi energy (exceeding 10% at typical coverage). This research establishes a foundation for realizing all-electrical spintronics devices through molecular spin interfaces.

We report findings on SARS-CoV-2 infection risk across various scenarios, utilizing data on particle-size-dependent mask penetration, total inward leakage, human aerosol emissions (ranging from 10nm to 1mm), and inhalation re-hydration. Well-mixed room models substantially underestimate infection risk during brief, direct exposures. Consequently, we establish an upper bound for infection risk by assuming a masked susceptible individual inhales the entire exhalation of a masked infectious person. Without masks, social distancing alone—even at 3 meters between speakers—yields an upper bound infection risk of 90% after a few minutes. If both parties wear surgical masks, the risk for the speaker remains below 26% even after 60 minutes. When both wear well-fitting FFP2 masks, this upper bound decreases by a factor of 60 compared to surgical masks. In both scenarios, face leakage is critical; for FFP2 masks, leakage is minimal in the nasal area but directed upward, which can be significantly mitigated by applying double-sided medical tape. Given that these calculated upper bounds greatly overestimate actual risk and that even the upper bound is very low when masks are worn poorly, we conclude that wearing a mask, despite potential leakage, offers excellent protection for both third parties and the wearer.

This study aimed to understand the research process, specifically the production of journal articles, by contrasting preprints with their final published counterparts. Initially, leveraging the recent shift toward open journals, we secured sufficient full-text XML data for both preprints and journal articles, confirming the technical viability of such a comparison. However, within the scope of this trial—which examined differences based on external metrics like word count and reference numbers, as well as basic document similarity—we failed to identify clear distinctions between preprints and journal articles, nor between preprints that were eventually published and those that were not. Even when applying machine learning techniques, classification accuracy remained low at approximately 47%. The finding that no significant difference exists between preprints and journal articles aligns with and replicates previous studies conducted in larger, more recent contexts. Beyond this, our paper introduces new insights: the variations across many external criteria, including the number of authors, are minimal, and the gap between preprints that do not become journal articles and those that do is also negligible.

We analyze 12 ks snapshot Chandra observations of 12 shocked post-starburst galaxies to investigate the unresolved role of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in driving the transition from active star formation to quiescence. Although seven galaxies show statistically significant detections (with two additional marginal ones), the brightest source yielded only 10 photons. Due to the diverse hardness ratios within the sample, we opted for forward modeling to constrain intrinsic luminosity and obscuration rather than employing stacking. This approach utilized total count numbers and spectral shapes—primarily dictated by obscuration—to model obscured power-law intrinsic luminosities, yielding hardness ratios consistent with the data. We also evaluated thermal models; while power-law fits were consistent for all galaxies, one-third were best described as obscured power-laws, another third as thermal emission, and the remainder as power-laws. Assuming these early-transition post-starburst galaxies host AGN, they are predominantly characterized by lower obscuration ($n_H \leq 10^{23}$ cm$^{-2}$) and lower luminosity ($L_{2-10~ \rm keV}\leq10^{42}$erg s$^{-1}$), though two galaxies clearly exhibit significant obscuration. At least half the sample displays evidence of low-luminosity AGN activity, yet none possess the power to radiatively expel the remaining molecular gas. Consequently, these AGN likely accompany the transition rather than driving it, having been fueled by the same processes facilitating the galaxy's evolution.

This work addresses a stochastic bandit problem potentially involving an infinite number of arms, denoting $p^*$ as the fraction of optimal arms and $\Delta$ as the smallest mean gap between optimal and sub-optimal arms. We establish the optimal learning rates for both cumulative regret and best-arm identification in terms of the budget $T$, $p^*$, and $\Delta$. Regarding cumulative regret minimization, we derive a lower bound of $\Omega(\log(T)/(p^*\Delta))$ and present a UCB-style algorithm achieving a matching upper bound within a factor of $\log(1/\Delta)$. This algorithm requires knowledge of $p^*$ for parameter calibration, which we prove is essential, as adapting to $p^*$ is infeasible in this context. For best-arm identification, we establish a lower bound on the error probability of order $\Omega(\exp(-cT\Delta^2 p^*))$, where $c>0$ is a constant, and offer an elimination algorithm with a matching upper bound up to an exponential factor of $\log(T)$ that operates without requiring $p^*$ or $\Delta$. These findings extend directly to three related tasks: competing against the $j$-th best arm, identifying an $\epsilon$-good arm, and locating an arm with a mean exceeding a known-order quantile.

In machine learning, it is standard to utilize abundant information, as models typically achieve higher prediction accuracy with large datasets. However, when data is scarce, Few-Shot Learning (FSL) offers a strategy to develop precise algorithms using minimal training examples. This study introduces a novel, lightweight, end-to-end architecture designed to verify biometric data, achieving competitive accuracy against state-of-the-art FSL methods. Unlike complex deep learning models where dense layers hinder deployment in low-power environments, our approach integrates a shallow network with a conventional machine learning technique that leverages hand-crafted features to authenticate multi-modal biometrics, including fingerprints, iris, periocular regions, faces, and signatures. Furthermore, we implement a self-estimated threshold that rigorously controls the False Acceptance Rate (FAR) while ensuring generalization, thereby removing the reliance on potentially biased, user-defined thresholds derived from local ROC distributions. By combining these elements, the hybrid model effectively compensates for data scarcity in biometric scenarios. Extensive experiments on standard biometric datasets demonstrate that this solution provides an effective framework for biometric verification systems.

This second installment of our two-part series extends the one-dimensional discontinuous Galerkin (DG) scheme introduced previously—characterized by full conservation, positivity preservation, and entropy bounding—to multiple spatial dimensions for chemically reacting Euler equations. Our main goal is to achieve robust and accurate solutions for intricate reacting-flow scenarios using high-order DG methods without necessitating excessively fine resolutions, while accounting for variable thermodynamics and detailed chemical kinetics. This multidimensional framework represents a further generalization of existing positivity-preserving and entropy-bounded DG schemes found in the literature. Notably, the proposed formulation supports curved elements of arbitrary geometry, diverse numerical flux functions, general quadrature rules with positive weights, and mixtures of thermally perfect gases. We also address the preservation of pressure equilibrium between adjacent elements, a critical factor in multicomponent flow simulations. The method accurately computes complex detonation waves in two and three dimensions using high-order polynomials, and we find that enforcing an entropy bound, rather than just positivity, significantly enhances stability. Furthermore, the discretization ensures the conservation of mass, total energy, and atomic elements.

Theta sums are defined as finite exponential sums featuring a quadratic form within their oscillatory phase. This study derives novel upper bounds for these sums under conditions of smooth and box truncations. The findings extend a seminal 1977 result by Fiedler, Jurkat, and K\"orner regarding one-variable theta sums, and in the multi-variable context, they enhance earlier estimates by Cosentino and Flaminio from 2015. Central to our methodology are the automorphic representation of theta functions and their behavior near the cusps of the associated homogeneous space.

This study introduces third-order Lovelock gravity topological black holes situated within a cosmological constant and nonlinear electromagnetic Born-Infeld field framework. The nature of these solutions varies with metric parameters, ranging from black holes possessing inner and outer event horizons to extreme black holes or naked singularities. We examine the thermodynamics of asymptotically flat configurations, demonstrating that their conserved and thermodynamic quantities adhere to the first law of thermodynamics. Additionally, by applying the counterterm method, we assign global rotation to Ricci-flat solutions and determine their finite action and conserved quantities. Using the Gibbs-Duhem relation, we calculate entropy and confirm its compliance with the area law. We derive a Smarr-type mass formula dependent on entropy, angular momentum, and charge, then compute temperature, angular velocities, and electric potential, verifying that these values align with those derived geometrically. Finally, we conduct stability analyses across both canonical and grand-canonical ensembles, concluding that neither the nonlinear electromagnetic field nor higher curvature terms influence the stability of black branes, which remain stable throughout the entire phase space.

We demonstrate that pure, symmetric, three-qubit entangled states which are inequivalent under stochastic local operations and classical communication (SLOCC) display unique geometric configurations represented as spheroids inscribed in the Bloch sphere. Through a detailed examination of the SLOCC canonical forms of the reduced two-qubit states derived from these entangled pure symmetric three-qubit states, we establish two distinct geometric models based on the Lorentz canonical forms: (i) for pure permutation symmetric three-qubit states formed from three distinct spinors, a prolate spheroid centered at the Bloch sphere's origin with its longest semiaxis (aligned with the z-axis) equal to 1; and (ii) for three-qubit pure states generated by symmetrizing two distinct spinors, a spheroid centered at (0,0,1/2) within the Bloch sphere, characterized by fixed semiaxis lengths of (1/√2, 1/√2, 1/2).

Explaining how the distribution of network chains influences the mechanical properties of elastomers remains a persistent challenge in rubber mechanics. Traditional rubber elasticity theory relies on the premise that network strands have uniform lengths and exhibit entropic elasticity. However, kinetic models of vulcanization, computational simulations, and indirect experimental data consistently show that vulcanizate microstructures consist of polymer strands with a random length distribution. This variation in strand length is anticipated to govern mechanical strength because overloaded short strands rupture at low deformations, thereby shifting the load to longer strands. The primary objective of this thesis is to develop simplified rubber mechanics theories that incorporate strand length distributions and their impact on elasticity and the initiation of bulk failure in both filled and unfilled elastomers. In unfilled systems, short chains are identified as the primary agents of damage initiation; during deformation of a polydisperse network, these shorter strands break at significantly lower stretches than longer ones. As deformation increases, the resulting network alterations dictate the onset of mechanical failure. Conversely, in filled networks, the deterioration of mechanical performance is attributed to the adhesive failure of short strands adsorbed onto filler surfaces, where the finite extensibility of these adsorbed strands serves as a critical factor determining overall mechanical strength.

Dibismuth dioxychalcogenides, represented by Bi$_2$O$_2$Ch (where Ch = S, Se, Te), represent a promising class of materials for future electronics and thermoelectric applications, characterized by exceptionally high carrier mobility and superior stability in air. Specifically, Bi$_2$O$_2$S is of particular interest due to the stereochemically active 6$s^2$ lone pair of the Bi$^{3+}$ ion, its heterogeneous bonding nature, and the significant mass disparity among its constituent elements. This study employs first-principles calculations combined with Boltzmann transport theory to systematically examine how hydrostatic pressure influences the lattice dynamics and phonon transport characteristics of Bi$_2$O$_2$S. At ambient conditions, the $Pnmn$ phase displays a low average lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa_l$) of 1.71 W·m$^{-1}$·K$^{-1}$ at 300 K. However, around 4 GPa, the material undergoes a structural phase transition from a low-symmetry ($Pnmn$) to a high-symmetry ($I4/mmm$) structure driven by the centering of Bi$^{3+}$ cations. This compression suppresses the lone pair activity of Bi$^{3+}$, causing $\kappa_l$ to increase nearly threefold to 4.92 W·m$^{-1}$·K$^{-1}$ in the $I4/mmm$ phase at 5 GPa. Furthermore, analyses of phonon lifetimes and Gr\"uneisen parameters indicate that anharmonicity diminishes under increasing pressure due to the suppression of the lone pair and the strengthening of both intra- and intermolecular interactions. Consequently, the average room-temperature $\kappa_l$ rises to 12.82 W·m$^{-1}$·K$^{-1}$ at 20 GPa. In summary, this research offers a thorough understanding of how hydrostatic pressure modulates the stereochemical activity of the Bi$^{3+}$ lone pair and its subsequent impact on the phonon transport properties of Bi$_2$O$_2$S.

This paper presents and investigates V- and CI-semirings, defined as semirings where all simple semimodules and all cyclic semimodules are injective, respectively. We characterize V-semirings within various semiring classes and outline their core properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every Jacobson-semisimple V-semiring qualifies as a V-ring. Additionally, we provide a full description of CI-semirings among bounded distributive lattices, Gelfand, subtractive, semisimple, and anti-bounded semirings. Leveraging these findings, we deliver complete characterizations of congruence-simple subtractive and congruence-simple anti-bounded CI-semirings, thereby resolving two previously open problems concerning these specific categories.

This paper presents Eilmer, an open-source, general-purpose solver for compressible flow created at the University of Queensland, specifically tailored for hypersonic and high-speed aerothermodynamic research. Widely adopted by various university research groups, Eilmer offers extensive capabilities detailed on its website, in reference manuals, and through a comprehensive collection of example simulations. The first section outlines the code's formulation, covering the equations, physical models, and numerical methods essential for basic fluid dynamics, along with several optional multi-physics models frequently used for hypersonic flow analysis. The second section details the development and maintenance processes of the code, highlighting adherence to sound programming practices and endorsing specific techniques beneficial for scientific software. Finally, the paper examines six example simulations that demonstrate Eilmer's full range of capabilities; each includes sample results and a brief explanation of the problem addressed, aiming to guide new users in applying Eilmer to their own research.

Using the Very Large Array (VLA), we analyzed a lengthy, continuous VHF observation of the bright radio source Cygnus A during nighttime to showcase the instrument's capabilities through the midlatitude ionosphere. A related study previously established that the VLA can resolve total electron content (TEC) fluctuations as small as <0.001 TECU and measure TEC gradients with a precision of approximately 0.0002 TECU/km. This paper details two complementary spectral analysis methods for these gradient measurements. The first method tracks individual waves with wavelengths of roughly 20 km (half the array size) or larger; it successfully identified and characterized numerous medium-scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (MSTIDs) occurring intermittently throughout the night, with partial validation provided by concurrent GPS data. Additionally, this technique detects smaller waves at nearly all times, many traveling in directions similar to the MSTIDs. The second method enables the detection and statistical characterization of wave groups moving in similar directions, capable of resolving wavelengths down to 5 km. By integrating results from both techniques, we identified a class of intermediate and small-scale waves likely corresponding to the quasi-periodic (QP) echoes observed within sporadic-E (Es) layers. We distinguish two distinct populations of these waves: one population is temporally coincident with MSTIDs and appears generated within Es layers via E-F coupling instability, while the other population seems more influenced by neutral winds, resembling the predominant QP echo types documented by the Sporadic-E Experiments over Kyushu (Fukao et al. 1998; Yamamoto et al. 2005).

Shoenfield's 1959 completeness theorem asserts that any true first-order arithmetical statement possesses a recursive $\omega$-proof, which can be encoded through recursive applications of the $\omega$-rule. We demonstrate that, under an appropriate encoding of Gentzen-style $\omega$-proofs, this theorem extends to cut-free $\omega$-proofs generated via primitive recursive applications of the $\omega$-rule. Furthermore, we establish that the set of codes for $\omega$-proofs—whether derived from recursive or primitive recursive $\omega$-rule applications—is $\Pi^1_1$ complete. This $\Pi^1_1$ completeness also holds for the codes of cut-free $\omega$-proofs.

Utilizing information-theoretic reductions, this work investigates a framework for fair optimization and learning that employs a black-box optimizer to develop fair models for classification or regression tasks. Our primary objective is to determine the statistical and computational complexity required to ensure these models meet the strict criteria of differential privacy. We address several open questions, demonstrating the approach's utility in fair machine learning, hypothesis testing, and the optimization of non-standard classification loss metrics. Notably, our derived sample complexity bounds are optimal among all strategies that minimize a composition of functions.

The reductions method for fair optimization can be conceptualized as a constrained group-objective optimization problem, where the goal is to optimize an objective function dependent on individual group losses while adhering to specific constraints. We present the first polynomial-time algorithms capable of solving this problem with $(\epsilon, 0)$ or $(\epsilon, \delta)$ differential privacy guarantees, provided the decision set (such as an $\ell_P$ unit ball) and constraints are convex. Alongside these algorithms, we establish corresponding information-theoretic lower bounds. Compared to prior methods that ensured differential privacy under a relaxed equalized odds fairness constraint, our $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differentially private algorithm offers asymptotically superior sample complexity, yielding an exponential improvement in specific parameter regimes. Additionally, we introduce a class of bounded divergence linear optimizers, which holds independent interest and specializes to both pure and approximate differential privacy.

This paper presents a model describing the nonlinear frequency shift of ion acoustic waves (IAWs) in multi-ion species plasmas, incorporating the effects of ion temperature. Since thermal ions are present in both inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and solar wind environments, their influence on the nonlinear frequency shift of IAWs must be accounted for. However, existing models, such as those by Berger et al. and Feng et al., rely solely on cold ion fluid approximations. The proposed comprehensive theory, which includes multi-ion species and thermal ions, offers a more accurate calculation of large-amplitude nonlinear IAW frequencies. This accuracy is particularly significant for the slow mode at high ion temperatures, with broad applicability in space physics and inertial confinement fusion.

This study introduces XBART (Accelerated Bayesian Additive Regression Trees), a new stochastic tree ensemble designed for nonlinear regression. By merging regularization and stochastic search techniques from Bayesian models with the computational efficiency of recursive partitioning, the method achieves state-of-the-art results, often outperforming the widely used XGBoost algorithm in both speed and accuracy. Rigorous simulation studies confirm that XBART delivers precise point-wise estimates of the mean function more rapidly than popular alternatives, including BART, XGBoost, and Keras-based neural networks. The authors also establish key theoretical properties, such as the consistency of the single-tree variant and the stationarity of the Markov chain generated by the ensemble. Additionally, the paper shows that initializing standard Bayesian additive regression trees Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with XBART-fitted trees significantly enhances credible interval coverage and reduces total computation time.

We leverage recent advancements in quantifying neural network robustness against input perturbations to develop and calibrate a model-based anomaly detector, utilizing an autoregressive neural network as the data-driven estimator. During the tuning process, we explicitly establish upper limits on the expected false alarm rate during normal operations. To achieve this, we extend existing theory to enable the propagation of multiple confidence ellipsoids through a neural network; the output ellipsoid resulting from input variations guides the detector's sensitivity and threshold calibration. We validate this methodology on both linear and nonlinear dynamical systems.

The microscopic dynamics of natural processes are often described using random walk models that focus on local particle transitions. This approach is favored because it accurately captures molecular-level dynamics and offers a clear physical interpretation. However, recent theoretical research has surprisingly revealed that in complex systems, the symmetry between forward and backward transition times relative to local dynamic biases can be broken, potentially causing downhill movements to take longer than uphill ones. The underlying physical causes of these phenomena are not yet fully grasped. This study investigates the microscopic details of this symmetry breaking in forward/backward transition times by examining exactly solvable discrete-state stochastic models. Specifically, we analyze a scenario involving two random walkers on a four-site periodic lattice to model general systems with multiple pathways. Our findings indicate that the asymmetry in transition times is influenced by various factors, including the extent of deviation from equilibrium, particle crowding, and the methods used to measure dynamic properties. Consequently, our theoretical analysis suggests that this temporal asymmetry can be probed experimentally to reveal key microscopic characteristics of natural processes by quantitatively assessing local equilibrium deviations and crowding levels.

To achieve and sustain collisions for the proposed International Linear Collider (ILC), a high-resolution intratrain position feedback system has been created. A prototype was commissioned and tested with a beam in the extraction line of the Accelerator Test Facility at KEK in Japan. The system comprises a stripline beam position monitor (BPM) with analog signal-processing electronics, a specialized digital board for feedback calculations, and a stripline kicker powered by a high-current amplifier. With a closed-loop feedback latency of 148 ns, the system successfully stabilized the third bunch of a three-bunch train (with 154 ns spacing) to 450 nm. The kicker response remains linear, maintaining feedback performance across a correction range exceeding $\pm$60 {\mu}m. Correction propagation was verified using an independent downstream stripline BPM. This demonstration confirms that the system meets the ILC requirements for BPM resolution, beam kick, and latency.

Standard oscillators face two primary constraints: their synchronization capabilities are restricted to a finite region, and they lack memory of previous interactions, reverting to their natural frequency once an entraining signal ceases. Previously, we introduced a general method to convert oscillators into adaptive frequency variants capable of learning input frequencies by adjusting their parameters. This approach expands the synchronization region to infinity and allows the oscillator to maintain the learned entrainment frequency even after the driving signal is removed. Although this mechanism has proven effective in applications like robot control and observer design for active prosthetics, a rigorous theoretical understanding of its properties remains elusive. This paper examines the adaptation mechanism within strongly coupled phase oscillators, revealing that non-trivial slow-fast dynamics drive the adaptation. We identify a layered architecture of stable and unstable invariant slow manifolds and demonstrate how input signals compel the system to transition between these manifolds at regular intervals, resulting in exponential frequency convergence. Furthermore, we generalize this concept to networks of oscillators featuring amplitude adaptation, confirming that the structure of slow invariant manifolds remains intact. Numerical simulations corroborate our findings and broaden the analysis to more intricate scenarios.

This research investigates how the spatial coupling parameter between interacting ballistic exciton-polariton condensates changes when photonic spin-orbit coupling, arising from TE-TM splitting in planar semiconductor microcavities, is present. We introduce a method to enhance the coupling strength between next-nearest neighbors beyond that of nearest neighbors, thereby reversing the conventional spatial coupling hierarchy. This approach exploits the predominantly high-momentum components within the ballistic condensates; under TE-TM splitting, these components induce rapid radial precession of the polariton pseudospin. Consequently, condensate pairs undergo distance-periodic screening of their interaction strength, which significantly alters their synchronization and condensation threshold solutions.

Topological statistical theory underpins a contemporary mathematical restructuring of classical statistics, known as Structural Statistics. This framework highlights the structural assumptions inherent in distribution families and the structure-preserving transformations between them, defined as statistical morphisms. The developed language aims to unify complex structured model spaces, such as deep-learning architectures, while bridging the divide toward topology and differential geometry. To ensure alignment with classical statistics, the language incorporates corresponding concepts for standard information criteria, including sufficiency and completeness.

Human collaboration involves both explicit and implicit intention sharing, making mutual intention recognition essential for advancing human-robot teamwork. Current methods depend on extensive sensor arrays mounted on or near robots, which restricts intuitive collaboration to cumbersome systems unsuitable for large-scale, real-world applications due to their high complexity and expense. This paper introduces an intention recognition framework relying solely on a portable head-mounted display, which also supports the visualization of robot intentions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our human goal estimation module and illustrate basic interactions with an industrial robot. The proposed HAIR system aims to enhance human-robot interaction quality rather than causing anxiety or discomfort among human coworkers.

Biochemical processes within living cells frequently take place amidst crowders—non-reactive molecules that alter reaction rates via excluded volume effects. Yet, standard modeling of stochastic intracellular kinetics relies on the chemical master equation (CME), which assumes propensities are unaffected by crowding. This study introduces a machine learning approach using Bayesian Optimization, trained on synthetic data from spatial cellular automata (CA) simulations that explicitly account for volume exclusion, to derive effective propensity functions for CMEs. By applying Gaussian Process regression to a small set of CA training data, we extrapolate these predictions across the full parameter space relevant to physiological crowding levels. The method is validated using an enzyme-catalyzed reaction and a genetic feedback loop, demonstrating strong agreement between the time-dependent molecular distributions predicted by the modified CME and those from CA simulations.

This paper introduces a novel, straightforward, and language-agnostic approach to word alignment that leverages external bilingual resources, such as machine translation systems. We demonstrate that the aligner's few parameters can be trained on a minimal corpus, achieving precision levels comparable to the state-of-the-art GIZA++ tool. Regarding other metrics like alignment error rate and F-measure, the parametric aligner, when trained on a very small gold-standard dataset of 450 sentence pairs, yields results similar to those of GIZA++ trained on an in-domain corpus of approximately 10,000 sentence pairs. Additionally, the findings suggest that the training process is domain-independent, allowing the trained aligner to be applied immediately to any new sentence pair.

Traditionally, federated learning (FL) involves training a single global model collaboratively across multiple clients and a server, yet it faces two inherent challenges: data heterogeneity among clients and the need to accommodate clients with diverse resources. This paper presents QuPeL, a \textit{quantized} and \textit{personalized} FL algorithm designed to enable collective training among heterogeneous clients while respecting their varying resource constraints. To achieve personalization, the method allows clients to train \textit{compressed personalized models} equipped with distinct quantization parameters tailored to their specific capabilities. First, we introduce an algorithm for learning quantized models by addressing a relaxed optimization problem that simultaneously optimizes quantization values. When clients have differing requirements regarding quantized model values and precision, we establish a quantized personalization framework by incorporating a penalty term into local client objectives to foster collaboration with a globally trained model. We develop an alternating proximal gradient update to solve this quantized personalization problem and analyze its convergence. Numerical results demonstrate that optimizing quantization levels enhances performance, and we confirm that QuPeL surpasses both FedAvg and standalone local training within a heterogeneous environment.

This paper presents CMU Informedia Lab's system for the YouTube 8 Million Video Understanding Challenge. In this multi-label video classification task, our pipeline attained 84.675% and 84.662% GAP scores on the evaluation split and the official test set, respectively. We attribute this strong performance to three key components: 1) Refined video representation learning utilizing residual links and hypercolumns, 2) Latent concept mining that captures concept interactions, and 3) Temporal segment learning combined with a weighted multi-model ensemble. We conducted experiments to validate and analyze the contributions of our models. Additionally, we discuss unsuccessful attempts using conventional approaches, such as recurrent neural networks for video representation on this large-scale dataset. All code required to reproduce our results is publicly available at https://github.com/Martini09/informedia-yt8m-release.

This paper demonstrates that the Maxwell superalgebra in four dimensions, which inherently includes a nilpotent fermionic generator, can be understood as a hidden superalgebra within N = 1, D=4 supergravity when extended by a 2-form gauge potential linked to a 2-index antisymmetric tensor. Within this framework, the theory is analyzed using Free Differential Algebras (FDAs), which generalize the Maurer-Cartan equations to incorporate higher-degree differential forms. The investigation is subsequently expanded to D=11 supergravity, revealing the existence of an underlying super-Maxwell algebra in that context as well. Furthermore, the extra spinors dual to the nilpotent fermionic generators—essential for constructing supersymmetric Maxwell algebra extensions in both D=4 and D=11—are shown to be critical components for reproducing the corresponding FDAs on ordinary superspace, defined by the supervielbein basis. Finally, the gauge structure of these supersymmetric FDAs is examined by considering gauge transformations derived from the hidden supergroup-manifold associated with the Maxwell superalgebras.

We present a deep learning framework designed to detect malware families by analyzing function call graphs derived from x86 assembly instructions. While static call graph analysis has been explored previously, few studies apply modern, principled feature learning techniques to this specific challenge. Our proposed system utilizes an executable's function call graph, where function representations are generated via a recurrent neural network (RNN) autoencoder that converts sequences of x86 instructions into dense, latent vectors. These function embeddings serve as graph vertices, with edges representing call dependencies. By effectively capturing both rich node-level representations and global topological properties of the executable, our method significantly enhances malware family detection rates. This approach offers a more rigorous solution that deliberately circumvents the need for laborious feature engineering and specialized domain expertise. We validated our method through experiments on a Microsoft malware classification dataset, achieving excellent separation between malware families with a classification accuracy of 99.41%.

Mechanical relaxation of twisted bilayer graphene creates large moiré patterns that form a triangular lattice. When gating is applied, the electronic Dirac points within each triangular region become gapped, mimicking bulk topological insulators where topological indices vary based on the valley index and stacking configuration. However, because each triangle contains two valleys with opposite charges, the system remains topologically trivial overall. This study investigates edge currents in this system through the analysis and computation of continuum partial differential equation models. First, we derive bulk invariants for a single valley and utilize a bulk-interface correspondence to quantify asymmetric transport along interfaces. Second, we develop a valley-coupled continuum model to demonstrate that valleys remain approximately decoupled under small perturbations via multiscale expansion, yet couple in the presence of larger defects. Third, we establish a method to prove that a quantized asymmetric current is conserved across junctions, such as vertices in a triangular network, for a broad class of continuum (pseudo-)differential models. These theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical simulations employing spectral methods to calculate relevant currents and wavepacket propagation.

Markov decision processes are increasingly popular for modeling diverse applications, from supply chain and queuing network analysis to cognitive science and autonomous vehicle control. However, their numerical tractability diminishes rapidly as model size increases. Although recent machine learning approaches attempt to address this scalability challenge, they lack convergence guarantees. This note offers a concise review of literature on solving large-scale Markov decision processes and their application to key combinatorial optimization problems.

Recently, researchers have highlighted the detrimental impact of unreliable or "fake" news on political systems and democracy. This misinformation, particularly when spread via social media, is widely credited with influencing major events such as the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. This study investigates the individual motivations behind sharing fake news and identifies effective interventions to curb its spread. By developing a model that separates an article's truthfulness from its bias and analyzes how these factors interact with a reader's pre-existing beliefs, we propose specific strategies for both platforms and users. We advise social media companies to promote unbiased, factual content, prioritize fact-checking for mildly to moderately biased articles, suggest friends across the political spectrum, and inform users about the political leanings of their news feeds. Simultaneously, we recommend that individual users verify news that strongly confirms their own biases and actively seek out content with opposing political viewpoints.

Unsupervised anomaly detection with localization holds significant practical value, particularly when data labeling is impractical and anomaly examples are absent from training sets. Although recent models for this specific scenario achieve high accuracy, their complexity hinders real-time processing. This paper introduces a real-time model and analytically establishes its connection to existing methods. Our proposed CFLOW-AD framework utilizes a conditional normalizing flow approach tailored for anomaly detection and localization. Specifically, CFLOW-AD features a discriminator-pretrained encoder followed by multi-scale generative decoders that explicitly estimate the likelihood of encoded features. This approach yields a model that is both computationally and memory-efficient, operating 10 times faster and with a 10 times smaller footprint than prior state-of-the-art models under identical input conditions. Experiments on the MVTec dataset demonstrate that CFLOW-AD surpasses previous methods with a 0.36% improvement in detection AUROC, along with 1.12% and 2.5% gains in localization AUROC and AUPRO, respectively. We have made our code and fully reproducible experiments publicly available.

The spectrum of the Dirichlet Laplacian on any quasi-conical open set typically comprises the entire non-negative semi-axis. However, we demonstrate the existence of a connected quasi-conical open set where the associated Dirichlet Laplacian possesses a positive, embedded eigenvalue. This specific domain is formed by a tower of increasingly large cubes linked by windows of diminishing size. Furthermore, we establish that the dimensions of these windows can be selected such that the absolutely continuous spectrum of the Dirichlet Laplacian vanishes entirely.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RISs) have emerged as a pivotal solution to enhance signal coverage and overcome frequent blockages in millimeter wave (mmWave) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. Nevertheless, acquiring Channel State Information (CSI) remains a significant hurdle for the practical implementation of RIS technology. Passive RISs, which lack baseband processing capabilities, complicate channel estimation (CE) because individual or cascaded channels can only be estimated at the base station (BS) through uplink training or at the mobile station (MS) via downlink training. To address these challenges, this work investigates a hybrid RIS architecture, wherein a limited number of elements are active to receive and process pilot signals directly at the RIS. The CE process occurs in two stages, utilizing atomic norm minimization to recover channel parameters, specifically angles of departure (AoDs), angles of arrival (AoAs), and propagation path gains. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms passive RIS channel estimation under identical training overhead. Additionally, theoretical performance limits regarding mean square error (MSE) are analyzed using Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) assessments.

This paper reports a search for supersymmetric particles generated through vector boson fusion in proton-proton collisions. The analysis focuses on final states characterized by zero or one lepton, substantial missing transverse momentum, and two widely separated jets in rapidity. The dataset comprises 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV in 2016 using the CMS detector at the LHC. The observed distributions for dijet invariant mass and lepton-neutrino transverse mass align with standard model predictions. Consequently, upper limits on the production cross sections for charginos ($\widetilde\chi_1^\pm$) and neutralinos ($\widetilde\chi_2^0$) accompanied by two jets are established. In a compressed mass spectrum scenario where these particles decay via a light slepton and the mass splitting between the lightest neutralino ($\widetilde\chi_1^0$) and the nearly degenerate $\widetilde\chi_1^\pm$ and $\widetilde\chi_2^0$ is 1 (30) GeV, the study sets the current most stringent lower mass limits of 112 (215) GeV on these latter particles.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) frequently suffers from word dropping or repetition in translations. This paper investigates new strategies to resolve this coverage issue by modifying only the attention mechanism. Our method assigns fertilities to source tokens, which limits the attention weight each token can receive. We test several sparse and constrained attention transformations and introduce a novel differentiable and sparse variant called constrained sparsemax. We provide empirical results across three language pairs to validate our approach.

Brooks and Makover constructed a combinatorial model of random hyperbolic surfaces through the gluing of specific hyperbolic ideal triangles. This paper demonstrates that for any $\epsilon>0$, as the count of ideal triangles increases indefinitely, a typical hyperbolic surface within the Brooks-Makover framework exhibits a Cheeger constant smaller than $\frac{3}{2\pi}+\epsilon$.

We present a formulation of the P=W conjecture that connects the Borel-Moore homology of the representation stack of the fundamental group of a genus $g$ Riemann surface with that of the stack of degree zero semistable Higgs bundles on a smooth projective complex curve of the same genus. To articulate this conjecture, we outline a method for constructing a canonical isomorphism between these respective Borel-Moore homology groups. Furthermore, we situate this stacky variant of P=W in relation to the original P=W conjecture regarding the cohomology of smooth moduli spaces of twisted objects, as well as the PI=WI conjecture involving the intersection cohomology of singular moduli spaces for untwisted objects. Finally, we provide proofs for these conjectures in the cases where the genus is zero or one.

Composite minimization serves as a robust framework within large-scale convex optimization, utilizing the decomposition of objective functions into components with distinct structural characteristics to facilitate more adaptable algorithmic strategies. This paper presents a novel algorithmic framework for complementary composite minimization, characterized by the separation of the objective function into a (weakly) smooth component and a uniformly convex term. This specific decomposition is widely prevalent in statistics and machine learning, largely due to its connection to regularization techniques.

The primary contributions of this study are outlined as follows: first, we define the complementary composite minimization problem within general normed spaces; second, we establish a unified accelerated algorithmic framework capable of solving a wide range of such problems; and third, we demonstrate that the algorithms derived from this framework achieve near-optimality across most standard optimization scenarios. Furthermore, we illustrate that our framework effectively addresses the challenge of minimizing gradient norms in general normed spaces. Specifically, we develop a nearly-optimal approach for the standard $\ell_1$ setting (aiming for small gradients in the $\ell_\infty$ norm), which essentially replicates the bound established by Nesterov (2012) for Euclidean spaces. Finally, we demonstrate the broad applicability of our composite methods to various regression problems, yielding complexity bounds that are either novel or equivalent to the best existing results.

This study examines the dynamics and rheology of a vesicle confined within a channel subjected to shear flow at finite temperatures, specifically investigating how thermal effects influence vesicle motion and system viscosity. A detailed analysis was conducted using a two-dimensional numerical model that integrates molecular dynamics with mesoscopic hydrodynamics to account for thermal fluctuations, covering a broad spectrum of Peclet numbers (the ratio of shear rate to rotational diffusion coefficient). Results indicate that suspension viscosity increases monotonically with the viscosity contrast (the ratio of the internal fluid's viscosity to that of the surrounding fluid) across both tank-treading and tumbling regimes, driven by competing temperature-dependent mechanisms. Thermal effects generate shape and inclination fluctuations and facilitate Brownian diffusion of the vesicle across the channel, both of which contribute to increased viscosity; however, these phenomena diminish as the Peclet number rises.

While Einstein's general relativity (GR) has undergone rigorous testing within our solar system, such validations remain scarce on extragalactic scales. This study addresses this gap by utilizing a recently assembled dataset of galaxy-scale strong gravitational lenses to probe GR at kiloparsec distances. To circumvent the circularity inherent in assuming a specific GR-based cosmological model a priori, we apply the distance sum rule within the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric. By integrating data from strong lensing and Type Ia supernovae, we directly derive the parameterized post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma_{\rm PPN}$ and cosmic curvature $\Omega_k$. This marks the inaugural simultaneous measurement of these parameters without relying on assumptions regarding the universe's contents or the underlying theory of gravity. Our findings yield $\gamma_{\rm PPN}=1.11^{+0.11}_{-0.09}$ and $\Omega_{k}=0.48^{+1.09}_{-0.71}$, revealing a significant degeneracy between the two. The measured $\gamma_{\rm PPN}$, which aligns with GR's prediction of unity, offers a precise extragalactic verification of GR with a fractional accuracy exceeding 9.0%. Imposing a prior of spatial flatness ($\Omega_{k}=0$) refines the constraint on $\gamma_{\rm PPN}$ to $1.07^{+0.07}_{-0.07}$, achieving 6.5% precision. Conversely, assuming the GR framework ($\gamma_{\rm PPN}=1$), our results remain marginally consistent with zero curvature ($\Omega_k=-0.12^{+0.48}_{-0.36}$), offering no compelling evidence against a flat universe.

This brief note defines the conditions under which conditioning on Synthetic Control (SC) weights mimics a randomized control trial, ensuring treatment status is independent of potential outcomes. Specifically, it is shown that if SC weights exist such that (i) treatment effects are precisely identified and (ii) these weights are uniformly and cumulatively bounded, then the SC weights function as balancing scores.

This work explores the principles behind creating conformally accurate Euclidean and hyperbolic tilings for compact surfaces, illustrated by a tiling of the Chmutov surface using hyperbolic (2, 4, 6) triangles.

While pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2 spread through forceful actions like coughing, they are also transmitted during routine behaviors including speaking, singing, and breathing. Our study utilizes direct numerical simulations to examine the turbulent transport of infectious aerosols during brief conversations. Results indicate that a two-way dialogue substantially lowers aerosol exposure compared to a monologue by one individual while the other remains silent, as the interaction between opposing mouth jets creates a "canceling" effect. Conversely, unbalanced conversations significantly heighten infection risk for the quieter participant. Notably, a slight height difference between speakers exacerbates transmission compared to face-to-face alignment at the same level; at close axial distances, speech jets exhibit large oscillations that intermittently reach the listener. We propose specific lateral separation distances to minimize transmission risk. Furthermore, a realistic assessment of infection probability is achieved by accounting for exposure via both the eyes and mouth, in addition to the traditional focus on inhaled virions. We anticipate these findings will offer valuable data for epidemiological modeling and disease management strategies.

With the surge of multivariate time series data generated by complex systems in Smart Manufacturing, there is a critical need for enhanced anomaly detection frameworks to mitigate operational risks and lessen the monitoring load on system operators. However, developing these frameworks presents significant challenges, primarily due to the scarcity of defective training data and the necessity for models to simultaneously capture temporal and contextual dependencies across time steps while maintaining robustness against noise. To address these issues, this paper introduces an unsupervised Attention-based Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) Autoencoder with Dynamic Thresholding (ACLAE-DT) designed for anomaly detection and diagnosis in multivariate time series. The proposed framework begins with data pre-processing and enrichment, followed by the construction of feature images that represent system statuses across various time steps by modeling inter-correlations between time series pairs. These feature images are then processed by an attention-based ConvLSTM autoencoder, which encodes the images to capture temporal dynamics, compresses the information, and subsequently decodes it to reconstruct the input feature images. Finally, reconstruction errors are calculated and evaluated using a statistical, dynamic thresholding mechanism to identify and diagnose anomalies. Empirical evaluations using real-world manufacturing data confirm that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse experimental configurations.

Scaling up remains the primary obstacle for quantum computing. Decades ago, classical computers encountered a similar hurdle, which was overcome by very-large-scale integration using silicon. Modern silicon chips contain billions of FinFETs, where wrap-around gates regulate current flow through fin-shaped channels. The semiconductor industry now utilizes fins narrower than 10 nm, a dimension suitable for quantum applications: at cryogenic temperatures, electrons or holes can be confined beneath the gate to function as spin qubits. A significant advantage of silicon's scalability is the potential to integrate both quantum hardware and classical control circuitry within a single package. However, this necessitates qubit operation above 1 K, a temperature regime sufficient to manage heat dissipation. In this study, we demonstrate that silicon FinFETs serve as an exceptional host for spin qubits capable of operating above 4 K. We achieved fast electrical control of hole spins with frequencies reaching 150 MHz and single-qubit gate fidelities meeting fault-tolerance thresholds. At these elevated "hot" temperatures, the number of spin rotations before coherence loss matches or surpasses that of hole spin qubits operating at millikelvin temperatures. Although our devices combine industrial compatibility with high quality, they are produced using a flexible and agile fabrication method to expedite development. This research establishes a foundation for the large-scale integration of all-electrical, ultrafast spin qubits.

Scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) has been employed to investigate and induce the one-dimensional diffusion of cobalt ad-atoms on graphene nanoribbons. By imaging the ribbons and Co atoms before and after applying current pulses via an STM tip in direct contact, we observed the atoms moving along the ribbons.
