This motion aligns with a distribution characteristic of a thermally activated one-dimensional random walk, suggesting that the nanoribbons attain temperatures significantly exceeding 100 K, well above that of the underlying gold substrate. This system offers a promising platform for advancing research into electromigration at the single-atom scale.

This paper investigates a nonlinear Choquard equation governed by a fractional Laplacian, defined as $(-\Delta)^{s}u+ u =(|x|^{-\mu}\ast F(u))f(u)$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$, where $N\geq3$, $s\in(0,1)$, and $\mu\in(0,N)$. Assuming the nonlinearities adhere to general Berestycki-Lions type conditions \cite{BL}, we establish the existence of groundstates for this equation using variational methods.

The submodular over signal (SOS) framework introduces a class of functions that support truthful mechanisms achieving constant approximations of social welfare for agents with interdependent valuations. While the most recognized truthful auction offers a 4-approximation with a proven lower bound of 2, we introduce a novel and straightforward truthful mechanism that attains an approximation ratio of 3.315.

This document presents PyCSP$3$, a Python library designed for modeling combinatorial constraint problems in a declarative way. With PyCSP$3$, users can formulate both Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP) and Constraint Optimization Problems (COP). A key feature is the distinct separation between modeling and solving: users define a model, compile it with data to generate an XCSP$3$ instance, and then solve it using a constraint solver. Alternatively, the solving process can be directly controlled within PyCSP$3$, supporting incremental solving strategies. This guide provides comprehensive instructions on using PyCSP$3$, accompanied by over 50 illustrative models.

Superconducting high-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a novel category of superconducting materials, offering a distinct platform to investigate the intricate relationship between disorder and superconductivity. This study details the synthesis and comprehensive bulk and microscopic analysis of the Nb$_{60}$Re$_{10}$Zr$_{10}$Hf$_{10}$Ti$_{10}$ HEA through transport, magnetization, specific heat, and muon spin rotation/relaxation ($\mu$SR) experiments. The findings confirm bulk superconductivity with a critical transition temperature ($T_{C}$) of 5.7 K, supported by magnetization, resistivity, and heat capacity data. Furthermore, zero-field $\mu$SR results indicate that the superconducting state maintains time-reversal symmetry, while transverse-field measurements of the superfluid density align well with an isotropic s-wave model.

This paper introduces a novel parameter for tournaments known as degreewidth, which quantifies the distance of a tournament from being acyclic. For a tournament $T$, the degreewidth $\Delta(T)$ represents the smallest integer $k$ such that there exists a vertex ordering $\langle v_1, \dots, v_n \rangle$ where each vertex has at most $k$ backward arcs (arcs $(v_i, v_j)$ with $j < i$). Consequently, a tournament is acyclic precisely when its degreewidth equals zero. Notably, the class of sparse tournaments identified by Bessy et al. [ESA 2017] corresponds exactly to those tournaments with a degreewidth of one.

We begin by analyzing the computational complexity of determining degreewidth, proving it to be NP-hard while also presenting a $3$-approximation algorithm. Furthermore, we offer a cubic-time algorithm to determine whether a tournament is sparse. Finally, we investigate the parameterized complexity of classical graph problems, specifically \textsc{Dominating Set} and \textsc{Feedback Vertex Set}, relative to degreewidth. Our findings indicate that \textsc{Dominating Set} is fixed parameter tractable, whereas \textsc{Feedback Vertex Set} remains NP-hard even on sparse tournaments. Additionally, we examine the \textsc{Feedback Arc Set} problem within the context of sparse tournaments.

We introduce FireBERT, a trio of proof-of-concept NLP classifiers designed to resist TextFooler-style word perturbations by generating diverse alternatives to input samples. The first strategy involves co-training BERT on both original training data and synthetic adversarial examples. The second method creates synthetic samples during evaluation by substituting words and perturbing embedding vectors, with the diversified results aggregated via voting. The third approach substitutes evaluation-time word substitution with embedding vector perturbation alone. We assess FireBERT on the MNLI and IMDB Movie Review datasets, testing performance on both standard data and adversarial examples generated by TextFooler. Additionally, we examine whether TextFooler is less effective at creating new adversarial samples against FireBERT compared to unhardened classifiers. Our findings demonstrate that BERT-based model accuracy can be improved against adversarial attacks without significantly compromising performance on regular benchmarks. Specifically, co-tuning with a synthetic data generator proves highly effective, protecting against 95% of pre-manufactured adversarial samples while retaining 98% of original benchmark performance. Furthermore, we highlight evaluation-time perturbation as a promising research avenue, which restores accuracy to up to 75% of benchmark levels for pre-made adversarials and achieves up to 65% (compared to a baseline of 75% original / 12% attack) under active TextFooler attacks.

Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) utilizes an options framework to decompose complex objectives into simpler, reusable tasks and their corresponding policies, thereby enabling action space abstraction. Ideally, these options should be transferable across various high-level goals; such reusability is essential for realizing the potential of continual learning agents that can effectively build upon prior experience. While previous methods have only offered limited mechanisms for transferring pre-learned options to new settings, we introduce a novel Option Indexing approach for Hierarchical Learning (OI-HRL). This method learns an affinity function mapping options to environmental items, facilitating the zero-shot reuse of a large library of pretrained options by restricting goal-directed learning to only those relevant to the current task. Furthermore, we implement a meta-training loop that refines representations of both options and environments across a sequence of HRL problems by incorporating feedback on the relevance of retrieved options to the overarching goal. Evaluated in two simulated environments, CraftWorld and AI2THOR, OI-HRL demonstrates performance competitive with oracular baselines and yields significant improvements over a baseline that grants the entire option pool to the hierarchical policy learner.

Topic models serve as a valuable text-mining instrument for uncovering hidden structures within extensive text collections. While numerous methods have been suggested for topic modeling, the literature lacks a rigorous theoretical examination of the statistical identifiability and precision of estimating these latent topics. This paper introduces a maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for latent topics, derived from a specific integrated likelihood that aligns with the concept of volume minimization in computational geometry. Our theoretical framework establishes a novel set of geometric conditions for topic model identifiability; these conditions are less restrictive than standard separability requirements, which usually depend on the presence of pure topic documents or anchor words. By relaxing these constraints, we enable a broader and potentially more productive area of inquiry. We perform a finite-sample error analysis of the proposed estimator and explore the relationships between our findings and prior research. Finally, we present empirical evaluations using both simulated and real-world datasets.

This work addresses two algorithmic challenges involving sub-semigroups of Heisenberg groups and, more broadly, two-step nilpotent groups. The first challenge, Intersection Emptiness, determines if the intersection of a finite set of finitely generated semigroups is empty; a problem initially explored by Markov in the 1940s. We demonstrate that Intersection Emptiness can be decided in polynomial time (PTIME) for Heisenberg groups $\operatorname{H}_{n}(\mathbb{K})$ over any algebraic number field $\mathbb{K}$, as well as for direct products of such groups. Furthermore, this decidability result is extended to all finitely generated 2-step nilpotent groups. The second challenge, Orbit Intersection, investigates whether the orbits of two matrices under multiplication by two distinct semigroups share any common elements. While Babai et al. (1996) established decidability for commutative matrix groups, we prove that Orbit Intersection is also decidable within the Heisenberg group $\operatorname{H}_{3}(\mathbb{Q})$.

It is well established that the spectrum of a non-relativistic two-body system bound by the Coulomb potential yields the Balmer series, $E_n=\frac{\alpha^2m}{4n^2}$, as derived from the Schrödinger equation. In 1954, Wick and Cutkosky demonstrated within the Bethe-Salpeter framework that when $\alpha>\frac{\pi}{4}$, relativistic effects give rise to additional energy levels beyond the Balmer series. Nevertheless, the physical origin of these new states was ambiguous, leading to skepticism regarding their existence. Our recent findings indicate that these extra states are primarily governed by the exchange of massless particles traveling at the speed of light; this characteristic explains their absence in the non-relativistic Schrödinger framework.

This work introduces the classes of decomposable and bi-decomposable Monge-Ampère systems, which encompass equations for improper affine spheres and hypersurfaces of constant Gauss-Kronecker curvature. These systems are analyzed within the clear geometric framework of Lagrangian contact structures, grounded in the existence of Lagrangian pairs. We demonstrate that, for systems with at least three independent variables, the Lagrangian pair associated with a bi-decomposable system is uniquely determined up to ordering. Furthermore, in the three-variable case, each such system is generated by a non-degenerate three-form in the sense of Hitchin. We also observe that various classes of homogeneous Monge-Ampère systems featuring Lagrangian pairs emerge naturally across different geometries. Additionally, we derive upper bounds on the symmetry dimensions of decomposable and bi-decomposable Monge-Ampère systems in terms of their underlying geometric structures, proving that these estimates are sharp (as detailed in Proposition 4.2 and Theorem 5.3).

Physical experiments and numerical simulations have identified a notable stabilizing effect where a background magnetic field stabilizes and damps electrically conducting fluids. This study aims to rigorously prove this phenomenon within the framework of a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) system featuring anisotropic dissipation. Specifically, the velocity component follows the 3D Navier-Stokes equation with dissipation restricted to the $x_1$-direction, whereas the magnetic field adheres to the induction equation with diffusion occurring in two horizontal directions. We demonstrate that perturbations near the background magnetic field $(0,1,0)$ are globally stable in the $H^3(\mathbb R^3)$ Sobolev space, alongside derived explicit decay rates in $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. In the absence of a magnetic field, the global well-posedness of the 3D anisotropic Navier-Stokes equation for small data remains an open and intriguing question. This work elucidates the mechanism by which the magnetic field induces enhanced dissipation to stabilize the fluid.

We demonstrate that every finite-dimensional quantum system undergoing Markovian (specifically GKLS-generated) time evolution possesses an autonomous unitary dilation capable of dynamic decoupling. However, since autonomous unitary dilations also exist that resist dynamic decoupling, this distinction underscores the significance of dilations in managing quantum noise. Our construction employs a time-dependent adaptation of the Stinespring theorem, integrated with Howland's clock Hamiltonian and specific point-localized states. These states can be viewed as a C*-algebraic counterpart to improper bra-ket position eigenstates, rendering them of independent mathematical and physical relevance.

We present a novel sequential approach for calibrating fixed parameters and tracking stochastic dynamical variables within a state-space system. Building on the nested hybrid filtering (NHF) framework from [1], our method utilizes a dual-layer filter structure to compute the joint posterior distribution of both static parameters and state variables. Specifically, we replace the Monte Carlo methods used in the original procedure with deterministic sampling techniques for Gaussian approximation in the initial layer. This modification lowers computational costs, rendering the algorithm more suitable for high-dimensional spaces of states and parameters. Following a description of a specific implementation, we evaluate the performance and efficiency of the proposed scheme using a stochastic Lorenz 63 model with uncertain parameters.

This paper presents a solution to the widely known Wordle puzzle using novel reinforcement learning techniques that extend to adaptive control in dynamic systems and classes of Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). Grounded in value-space approximation and the rollout method, these approaches are easy to implement and outperform various heuristic strategies. For Wordle, they generate online strategies that approach optimality with relatively low computational cost. These methods are also suitable for more complex Wordle variants and related search tasks where calculating an optimal strategy is infeasible. Furthermore, they apply broadly to adaptive sequential decision-making problems involving environments with unknown or frequently changing parameters that are estimated in real time.

Optimizing water electrolysis, a process heavily influenced by bubble nucleation and growth, is essential for the energy transition. This study combines experimental imaging of in-situ bubble evolution and dissolution with numerical simulations using the immersed boundary method. We demonstrate that accurately modeling observed bubble behavior requires incorporating solutally driven natural convection, a factor often overlooked in previous simulations. Our findings reveal that convective patterns vary based on current density and bubble spacing, resulting in unique bubble growth and shrinkage dynamics. Specifically, bubbles spaced at distances greater than or equal to 4 mm under the tested conditions promote convective instability, while closer inter-bubble distances delay the onset of convection. These insights and our methodology can aid in developing effective mass transfer strategies for gas-evolving electrodes.

We investigate how gravitational waves generated by first-order phase transitions influence structure formation. By conducting a second-order perturbation analysis within the $1+3$ covariant framework, we derive a wave equation showing that, during radiation domination on sub-horizon scales, second-order adiabatic density perturbations in the photon-baryon fluid are sourced by gravitational wave energy density. The characteristic scale of this effect is proportional to the horizon size at the transition time multiplied by the inverse of the transition duration. Consequently, only phase transitions occurring relatively late ($\ge 10^{6}\,\text{s}$) can impact the energy density perturbations of galactic and larger structures. Employing cosmic variance as a constraint, we establish limits on the transition strength $\alpha$ and relative duration $(\beta/H_*)^{-1}$ as functions of occurrence time, creating a new exclusion region for the present-day gravitational wave energy density. Our results indicate that the cosmic variance bound restricts only long-lasting transitions—specifically $\beta/H_*\lesssim 6.8$ for $t_*\approx 5\times10^{11}\,\text{s}$—that involve significant supercooling ($\alpha>20$) capable of altering the matter power spectrum.

This brief note presents and proves a straightforward algorithm for determining a basic feasible solution for the Simplex Algorithm. The approach employs a rule analogous to Bland's rule during the algorithm's initial phase.

We performed laboratory searches for exotic spin- and velocity-dependent interactions using an established experimental protocol. This setup involved two approximately 6 kg heavy source masses rotated at 20 Hz. An array of four identical atomic magnetometers was employed to enhance statistical precision and suppress common-mode noise. Data analysis utilized a high-precision numerical integration method to process the four harmonic signal frequencies. By reversing the rotation direction of the source masses to invert the signal, we implemented a [1,-3,3,-1] weighting technique to eliminate slow drifts. This noise-reduction approach yielded new constraints on Vector-Axial (VA) and Axial-Axial (AA) interactions; specifically, limits on VA interactions improved by over four orders of magnitude, while AA limits improved by two orders of magnitude within the corresponding force range.

End-to-end geometric deep learning has recently achieved initial success in approximating solutions for combinatorial optimization problems. However, generating data for NP-hard or NP-complete tasks presents significant theoretical and practical hurdles, leading to evaluation protocols that are overly optimistic. Specifically, most existing datasets only address simpler subproblems and likely rely on spurious features. To investigate these issues, we examine adversarial robustness—a form of local generalization—to uncover difficult, model-specific instances and identify spurious patterns. In this work, we develop perturbation models tailored for SAT and TSP. Unlike other fields where perturbation models rely on subjective definitions of imperceptibility, our models are both efficient and sound, enabling us to determine the true labels of perturbed samples without requiring a solver. Surprisingly, we find that a sufficiently expressive neural solver does not face the typical accuracy-robustness trade-off observed in supervised learning. Despite the existence of such robust solvers, our empirical results demonstrate that current neural solvers fail to generalize well when subjected to minor perturbations in problem instances.

We introduce an asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm designed to address Nash equilibrium problems that feature combinations of smooth and nonsmooth functions applied to linear combinations of strategies. This approach is fundamentally grounded in monotone operator theory, with a specific emphasis on the use of warped resolvents.

We introduce a three-dimensional (3-D) visualization technique for jet geometry, utilizing numerical methods that combine Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with a limited memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) optimization algorithm. Our objective is to reconstruct the 3-D structure of active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets from inherently two-dimensional (2-D) observational images. Since many AGN jets exhibit complex features such as bends and hotspots, understanding their intrinsic structure is crucial, as these features can appear significantly different in the sky frame due to viewing geometry compared to their actual configuration in the jet's frame. Elucidating this intrinsic structure aids in interpreting the magnetic field configuration and, consequently, the processes of emission and particle acceleration along the jet. We present the $JetCurry$ algorithm, which enables the visualization of a jet's 3-D geometry from its 2-D image, detailing the underlying geometrical framework and the method for decomposing 2-D images. We report findings from applying this visualization to the knot D region of the M87 jet. Our 3-D reconstruction aligns broadly with the anticipated double helical magnetic field structure of that region. Finally, we outline future developments for the $JetCurry$ algorithm.

Safe navigation of urban areas by autonomous vehicles relies on robust real-time detection and motion prediction of traffic participants. This paper introduces RV-FuseNet, a new end-to-end framework that jointly performs detection and trajectory estimation directly from time-series LiDAR inputs. Unlike the commonly adopted bird's eye view (BEV), we leverage the native range view (RV) of LiDAR data. RV maintains full sensor resolution by bypassing the voxelization required for BEV, while its compact structure allows for efficient processing. While prior methods typically project time-series data to a unified viewpoint for temporal fusion—suitable for BEV but problematic for RV as it can cause information loss and distortion when the viewpoint differs from the capture location—we propose a novel and effective architecture called *Incremental Fusion*. This approach minimizes data loss by sequentially projecting each RV sweep into the viewpoint of the subsequent temporal sweep. Our results demonstrate that this method significantly enhances motion forecasting compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions and outperforms other RV-based fusion techniques across multiple datasets.
An overview of hypergeometric motives, emphasizing their source varieties, Hodge numbers, and L-functions.

The rise of generative self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, such as BeiT and MAE, has heightened interest in learning effective representations by masking random image patches and reconstructing the missing data. However, BeiT and PeCo require an initial "pre-pretraining" phase to generate discrete codebooks for these masked patches. While MAE bypasses the need for a pre-training codebook, reconstructing individual pixels can create an optimization gap between pre-training and downstream tasks, as high reconstruction fidelity does not always guarantee strong descriptive capabilities. Addressing these limitations, we introduce SdAE, a simple Self-distillated masked AutoEncoder. SdAE features a student branch with an encoder-decoder architecture to reconstruct missing information, alongside a teacher branch that generates latent representations for masked tokens. From an information bottleneck perspective, we analyze optimal strategies for constructing teacher views to produce these latent representations. Furthermore, we propose a multi-fold masking strategy that provides multiple masked views with balanced information to enhance performance while reducing computational complexity. Our method demonstrates strong generalization: pre-training a vanilla ViT-Base for just 300 epochs yields 84.1% fine-tuning accuracy on ImageNet-1k classification, 48.6 mIOU on ADE20K segmentation, and 48.9 mAP on COCO detection, significantly outperforming other approaches. The code is accessible at https://github.com/AbrahamYabo/SdAE.

Over recent decades, revolutionary advancements in Machine Learning (ML) have led to the swift integration of ML models into diverse software systems. These Machine Learning Software Applications (MLSAs) are increasingly vital in daily life, making their Quality Assurance (QA) critically important. While numerous studies have identified specific challenges associated with adopting ML models into software, there is currently no research offering a comprehensive overview of how these QA challenges are distributed across the various phases of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). This paper presents an in-depth literature review of extensive research concerning ML model QA. By analyzing these studies, we constructed a taxonomy of MLSA QA issues that maps adoption challenges to different SDLC phases. Based on this taxonomy, we offer recommendations and identify research opportunities to enhance SDLC practices. This mapping serves to prioritize QA efforts for MLSAs where ML adoption is essential.

Organ or lesion segmentation within medical imagery is vital for clinical tasks like diagnosis and treatment planning. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) currently lead in automatic segmentation performance, they often struggle with accuracy and robustness in complex scenarios. Consequently, interactive segmentation serves as a viable alternative. However, conventional interactive approaches demand extensive user input, whereas recent CNN-based interactive methods fail to perform well on objects not encountered during training. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel deep learning-driven interactive segmentation framework that combines high efficiency—requiring only click inputs—with strong generalization capabilities for previously unseen objects. Our approach first encodes user-provided interior margin points using a custom exponentialized geodesic distance, enabling the CNN to generate a robust initial segmentation for both familiar and novel objects. Subsequently, a new information fusion technique integrates this initial result with minimal additional user clicks to produce a refined segmentation. We validated our framework through extensive experiments on 2D and 3D medical image segmentation tasks involving diverse objects absent from the training data. The results demonstrate that our method 1) delivers accurate outcomes with fewer interactions and reduced time compared to state-of-the-art interactive systems, and 2) exhibits superior generalization to unseen objects.

Irreversibility represents a fundamental characteristic of non-equilibrium transport phenomena. It has long been argued that the entropy production rate acts as a Lyapunov function across all process types, known as the principle of minimum entropy production. However, this principle relies on stringent assumptions that are seldom met in real-world applications. This study examines the shared characteristics of parabolic-like transport processes and proposes a theorem stating that the scalar product of fluxes and their conjugate forces serves as a Lyapunov function for such processes. These fluxes and forces are defined by their actual constitutive relations, such as Fourier's law and Fick's law. Subsequently, several typical transport processes are analyzed. Specifically, for heat conduction, both theoretical and numerical results indicate that when Fourier's law holds, the Lyapunov function is entransy dissipation rather than entropy production. This work aims to enhance the understanding of irreversibility and provide a mathematical interpretation of non-equilibrium processes.

Primordial black holes (PBHs), hypothesized to form in the early universe, represent a potential candidate for dark matter. Should they exist, their presence could be identified via photometric and astrometric signals generated by the gravitational microlensing of Milky Way stars. PopSyCLE (Population Synthesis for Compact-object Lensing Events) is a simulation tool designed to model microlensing surveys; notably, it is the first to incorporate both photometric and astrometric microlensing effects, which are crucial for detecting and characterizing PBHs. By adapting PopSyCLE to include a dark matter halo populated by PBHs, we estimate the frequency of observable PBH microlensing events. This study outlines our PBH population model and validates our PopSyCLE + PBH framework through simulations of the OGLE-IV and Roman surveys. While serving as a proof-of-concept analysis, our approach includes simplifying assumptions regarding $f_{\text{DM}}$ (the fraction of dark matter made of PBHs) and $\bar{m}_{\text{PBH}}$ (the mean PBH mass). Under the assumption that $\bar{m}_{\text{PBH}}=30$ $M_{\odot}$, we predict approximately $4f_{\text{DM}}$ times more PBH microlensing events than those from stellar evolved black holes, with an average peak Einstein crossing time of roughly 89 days. Furthermore, we estimate that the Roman telescope will detect on the order of $10^3f_{\text{DM}}$ PBH microlensing events during its planned survey.

Determining the nearest separable state to a specific target is an exceptionally challenging problem, often surpassing the difficulty of merely distinguishing between entangled and separable states. To address this, we employ a neural network to parameterize separable states, training it to minimize a differentiable metric—such as trace or Hilbert–Schmidt distance—to a chosen target. Analyzing the algorithm's output yields an upper bound on the target state's entanglement and generates an approximation for its closest separable counterpart. Benchmarks across various well-established bipartite state classes demonstrate excellent agreement, even at local dimensions up to $d=10$, while offering conjectures and analytical insights for isotropic and Werner states. Furthermore, the method proves efficient for multipartite scenarios under different separability definitions. By evaluating three- and four-party GHZ and W states, we recover existing bounds and derive new ones, such as those for triseparability.

Wikipedia stands as a massive entity, driven by the substantial volume of content added or removed every minute across its various projects. This vastness presents a significant opportunity within natural language processing to create automated tools for content moderation and review. This paper introduces the Self Attentive Revision Encoder (StRE), which predicts the quality of new edits by utilizing the orthographic similarity of lexical units. Unlike prior approaches that rely mainly on features such as page reputation, editor activity, or rule-based heuristics, our method focuses on the textual content of edits, which we argue contains superior indicators of quality. Specifically, we use deep encoders to generate representations of edits based on their text, which are then used to infer quality. Additionally, we contribute a novel dataset comprising 21 million revisions across 32,000 Wikipedia pages. Our results demonstrate that StRE significantly outperforms existing methods, with improvements ranging from at least 17% to as much as 103%. Notably, our pretrained model achieves these results after being retrained on as little as 20% of the edits within a single Wikipedia page. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to apply deep language models to the large-scale domain of automated content moderation and review on Wikipedia.

Numerical investigations using Monte Carlo simulations on Euclidean Dynamical Triangulations explore the geometric characteristics of two-dimensional lattice quantum gravity. A novel computational approach is introduced to model gravity interacting with fermions, enabling the analysis of lattice-based interacting theories, including non-Riemannian gravity. This method was validated using Majorana spinors, yielding a Hausdorff dimension of $d_W = 4.22 \pm 0.03$, which aligns with established literature bounds ranging between 4.19 and 4.21.

We introduce a model-free reinforcement learning framework designed to determine an optimal policy for finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) that ensures a specified minimum probability of satisfying signal temporal logic (STL) constraints. Our approach effectively expands the MDP state space to incorporate necessary historical information and reformulates the STL requirement as a reachability goal, thereby converting the planning task into a finite-horizon constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Addressing general finite-horizon CMDPs with unknown transition dynamics, we develop a reinforcement learning strategy capable of utilizing any model-free RL algorithm to derive an approximately optimal policy from the broad space of non-stationary randomized policies. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through robotic motion planning applications involving complex missions subject to uncertainty and specific performance criteria.

This research details the design, simulation, and experimental evaluation of a flexible piezoelectric energy harvester constructed from laser-cut Poly(vinylidene fluoride co-trifluoroethylene)/Polyethylene Terephthalate (PVDF-TrFE / PET). The study explores how ambient vibrations, an ideal source for such devices, can power autonomous sensor systems by harvesting environmental energy. Finite element modeling (FEM) was employed to perform modal analysis and assess von Mises stress, while numerical simulations provided the resonance frequency sweeps, damping ratios, and quality factors for the circular plate. Specifically, for a PVDF-TrFE layer with a thickness of 18 $\mu$m and a radius of 1.5 mm, the calculated damping ratio was 0.117 and the quality factor was 4.284. Furthermore, the maximum output voltage ($V_{max}$) was determined to be 984 mV through wind tunnel testing, with these experimental results compared against the FEM predictions.

This study addresses the challenge of identifying distributional shifts within high-dimensional data sequences. Our methodology integrates two distinct statistics derived from $L_p$ norms; these exhibit comparable behavior under the null hypothesis ($H_0$) but diverge under the alternative hypothesis ($H_A$), resulting in a testing framework adaptable to diverse alternatives. We derive the asymptotic distributions of the proposed test statistics for both weakly and strongly dependent coordinates as $\min\{N,d\}\to\infty$, where $N$ represents the sample size and $d$ the dimension, while also proving the consistency of our testing and estimation procedures under high-dimensional one-change scenarios. Empirical evaluations across single and multiple change point settings indicate that our method surpasses other nonparametric techniques found in the literature for specific high-dimensional alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of our approach through an analysis of Twitter data regarding mentions of U.S. Governors.

Recent investigations into interacting quantum spins, ultracold atoms, and correlated fermions have illuminated how isolated many-body systems can evade rapid equilibration toward thermal states. It has been demonstrated that numerous such systems exhibit "weak" ergodicity breaking: they contain a limited number of non-thermalizing eigenstates and/or show sluggish relaxation from specific initial conditions, whereas most other states equilibrate quickly, akin to conventional thermalizing systems. This chapter offers a pedagogical overview of weak ergodicity breaking, covering Hilbert space fragmentation and quantum many-body scars. These advances rely heavily on tools grounded in quantum entanglement, specifically matrix product states and tangent space techniques, which have enabled the analytical construction of non-thermal eigenstates across various non-integrable quantum models and facilitated the exploration of semiclassical quantization without relying on large-N or mean-field approximations. Furthermore, we examine recent experimental demonstrations of weak ergodicity breaking in systems comprising Rydberg atoms and tilted optical lattices.

The study of rap lyrics serves as a fundamental component for numerous web applications, including music recommendation, automatic categorization, and information retrieval, driven by the vast availability of digital music online. Despite extensive research in this area, current understanding remains insufficient, primarily because key elements like prosodic information and its effective representation, along with the proper integration of diverse features, are often overlooked. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Attention Variational Autoencoder (HAVAE), a framework designed to learn rap lyrics representations by jointly considering both semantic and prosodic features. Specifically, prosodic features are encoded using phonetic transcriptions via a new and effective strategy called rhyme2vec. Additionally, a feature aggregation method is proposed to effectively combine various inputs and produce prosodic-enhanced representations. Comprehensive empirical evaluations show that the proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics in different rap lyrics learning tasks.

This study examined the interaction of Laguerre-Gaussian light, spanning wavelengths from 690 to 810 nm, with a p-type gallium arsenide (GaAs) photocathode device to analyze the generation of photogenerated electrons. Spin angular momentum (SAM) and orbital angular momentum (OAM) were imparted through the use of linear or circular polarization alongside q-plates, with the polarization degree (P) of the resulting electron signal subsequently measured. At an excitation wavelength of 695 nm (corresponding to an energy of 1.78 eV), the measured polarization values were $P_{OAM} \approx 2.1\%$, $P_{SAM} \approx 1.3\%$, and $P_{SAM, OAM (q=1)} \approx 3.4\%$. In contrast, at 800 nm (1.55 eV), which is near the bandgap, the values shifted to $P_{OAM} \approx -14.7\%$, $P_{SAM} \approx -2.6\%$, and $P_{SAM, OAM (q=1)} \approx 4.0\%$.

The mechanism driving high-temperature superconductivity in iron-based materials remains a pivotal unresolved question in condensed matter physics, with the electronic structure—specifically Fermi surface topology—believed to be central to governing this phenomenon. Recent discoveries of unique electronic properties and potential high-temperature superconductivity (Tc > 65 K) in single-layer FeSe films grown on SrTiO3 substrates offer crucial insights into how Fermi surface topology and interfaces influence or enhance superconductivity. In this study, we present high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission measurements on the electronic structure and superconducting gap of a novel bulk FeSe-based superconductor, (Li0.84Fe0.16)OHFe0.98Se, exhibiting a Tc of 41 K. Our findings reveal that this single-phase bulk material displays electronic behaviors strikingly similar to those of the superconducting FeSe/SrTiO3 interface, characterized by comparable Fermi surface topology, band structure, and a nearly isotropic, nodeless superconducting gap. These observations provide vital perspectives for understanding the mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity in the FeSe/SrTiO3 system and, more broadly, within the class of iron-based superconductors.

Buoyant shear layers are a prevalent feature in numerous engineering and environmental contexts, a subject that has been the focus of experimental and theoretical research for many years. These flows frequently exhibit high Reynolds and Richardson numbers, creating prohibitive demands for spatial and temporal resolution in Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) or Large Eddy Simulation (LES). Conversely, critical physical phenomena such as stress anisotropy, wake stabilization, and regime transitions make traditional eddy viscosity-based Reynolds Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) models unsuitable. Consequently, this work employs Second-Moment Closure (SMC), encompassing full Reynolds stress, flux, and variance modeling, for moderate Reynolds number shear layers (both non-stratified and stratified) where DNS remains feasible. Various levels of sub-model complexity were investigated regarding the diffusion of stresses, density fluxes, and variance, as well as pressure strain and scrambling and dissipation. These sub-models were assessed based on their representation in DNS data relative to exact Reynolds-averaged terms and their influence on the overall accuracy of the RANS closure. In non-stratified scenarios, the SMC model accurately predicted shear layer growth rates and Reynolds shear stress profiles, though stress anisotropy and budgets were only captured qualitatively. Comparisons between exact and modeled DNS terms revealed discrepancies in model performance and assumptions, including poor predictions of individual statistics, significant pressure diffusion, and dissipation anisotropy. In stratified cases, the model's accuracy in predicting shear layer and gradient Richardson number growth rates, as well as the decay rates of stress, flux, and variance, was lower than in the non-stratified case. These findings have yielded several recommendations for enhancing the models.
This brief letter aims to specify which Feynman graph components are resummed within a Loop Vertex Expansion and to propose a conjecture regarding $\phi^4$ theory in non-integer dimensions.

Beame et al. [ITCS 2018 & TALG 2021] pioneered the use of Bipartite Independent Set (BIS) and Independent Set (IS) oracles for edge estimation in unknown, simple, unweighted, undirected graphs. This innovation sparked a wave of research, with works by Dell and Lapinskas [STOC 2018], Dell, Lapinskas, and Meeks [SODA 2020], Bhattacharya et al. [ISAAC 2019 & Theory Comput. Syst. 2021], and Chen et al. [SODA 2020] either addressing open problems posed by Beame et al. or generalizing their findings. While edge estimation via BIS requires only polylogarithmic queries, IS queries demand a sub-linear but super-polylogarithmic number. Chen et al. refined Beame et al.'s upper bounds for IS-based edge estimation and established an almost matching lower bound. Addressing one of Beame et al.'s open questions regarding the estimation of higher-order structures like triangles and cliques using BIS, we fully determine the query complexity for estimating triangles via BIS oracles. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the Edge Emptiness (EE) oracle, a more powerful query model recently introduced by Assadi, Chakrabarty, and Khanna [ESA 2021] for testing graph connectivity.

Realistic free-space transmission channels often degrade light's quantum states, frequently causing erasure errors due to issues like coupling inefficiencies between senders and receivers. This study introduces an error correction code designed to safeguard a single-mode quantum state against such erasures. By utilizing a bipartite continuous variable (CV) entangled state, our three-mode code protects a single-mode CV state. In practical applications, this approach can nearly fully recover a single erasure on the encoded state and enhance the fidelity of received states compared to direct transmission when two erasures occur. The encoding employs a bipartite entangled state that can be either Gaussian or non-Gaussian, with the non-Gaussian variant offering superior performance. As the simplest known code for protecting a single mode from erasures, this new method holds significant promise for building practical CV quantum networks based on free-space optics.

How can we account for the dynamical behavior of matter? While some might attribute this to natural laws, the world's geometric architecture, or the smooth topological properties of the spacetime manifold, others find the metaphysical implications of such explanations too mysterious. Consequently, some prefer to invert the direction of explanation, prioritizing dynamics. For example, Lewis's Best Systems Analysis (BSA) treats natural laws merely as summaries of specific patterns within matter's dynamical behavior, and Huggett's Regularity Relationism offers a similar perspective on the world's geometric structure. However, no comparable "dynamics-first" framework currently exists for the spacetime manifold itself. This dissertation proposes exactly such a framework: the spacetime manifold is simply a codification of particular patterns found in the dynamical behavior of matter.

The dissertation establishes robust mathematical tools to explore and reconcile various spacetime settings across different theories. It then introduces a competition among distinct spacetime codifications, mirroring the competition between different law-like codifications in Lewis's BSA. While BSA evaluates law-like codifications based on a balance of simplicity and strength, spacetime codifications are assessed by how effectively they align with a theory's dynamics and kinematics.

Achieving efficient ObjectGoal navigation (ObjectNav) in unfamiliar settings demands a grasp of the spatial and semantic patterns inherent in environment layouts. This paper introduces a simple approach to learning these patterns by forecasting the positions of unseen objects based on partial semantic maps. Unlike prior prediction-driven navigation techniques, such as frontier potential prediction or egocentric map completion, our method directly targets the localization of unseen goals by utilizing global context from all previously explored regions. The proposed prediction model is lightweight and can be trained via supervised learning with a modest amount of passively gathered data. After training, this model integrates seamlessly into a modular ObjectNav pipeline without requiring any reinforcement learning. We evaluated our method on the HM3D and MP3D ObjectNav datasets, where it attained state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, even without leveraging any additional training data.

LiDAR point clouds capture detailed measurements of complex natural environments and support a wide range of applications, including updating digital elevation models, monitoring glaciers, detecting faults and uplift, conducting forest inventories, tracking shoreline and beach volume changes, analyzing landslide risks, mapping habitats, and aiding urban development. A critical application involves classifying these 3D clouds into fundamental categories, such as distinguishing vegetation from man-made structures and water. This paper presents a preliminary comparative study on the classification of LiDAR point clouds that incorporates various feature engineering techniques. Specifically, we demonstrate that enhancing performance by providing context through the augmentation of each point with information about its neighbors improves downstream learning algorithms. Furthermore, we experiment with multiple dimensionality reduction strategies, ranging from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to neural network-based auto-encoders, to evaluate their impact on classification accuracy. Our findings indicate that combining feature engineering with dimension reduction methods like PCA yields higher classification accuracy compared to using raw data directly.

This study introduces a supervised learning framework for frame interpolation in computer vision, a technique particularly beneficial for cartoon animation to reduce the time-consuming process of manually drawing every frame. While current solutions predominantly rely on unsupervised methods optimized for high-frame-rate real-world footage, experimental results indicate their inefficiency when dealing with low frame rates and significant object displacement. This limitation arises because interpolating large motion shifts requires understanding motion structure, causing simple approaches like frame averaging to fail. To address this, the work employs deep convolutional neural networks, demonstrating that integrating prior information, such as optical flow, substantially enhances interpolation quality.

We employed hard-particle Monte Carlo simulations to investigate equilibrium systems formed by monodisperse, wedge-shaped molecules. Each molecule was constructed from six tangent spheres aligned linearly, with diameters decreasing in a linear fashion; consequently, the geometry was defined uniquely by a single parameter, $d$, representing the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameter. The system's phases were examined across varying values of $d$ and packing density ($\eta$). Since interactions were exclusively excluded-volume in nature, the resulting phases were determined entirely by configurational entropy. At densities below 0.5, the systems exhibited an isotropic liquid alongside conventional nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. However, for $\eta > 0.5$, in addition to the standard non-polar hexagonal crystal, two novel frustrated polar crystalline phases featuring splay modulation emerged: the antiferroelectric splay crystal ($\text{Cr}_\text{S}\text{P}_\text{A}$) and the ferroelectric splay crystal ($\text{Cr}_\text{S}\text{P}_\text{F}$). All configurations were characterized using nematic, smectic, and hexatic order parameters, along with the radial distribution function and polarization correlation function.

Multi-object tracking (MOT) stands as a fundamental task within computer vision, benefiting significantly from recent rapid advancements in deep learning. Despite these gains, several persistent challenges endure, including sensitivity to occlusion, instability across varying lighting conditions, and poor robustness when handling deformable objects. To tackle these widespread issues affecting current trackers, this paper introduces a tracklet booster algorithm designed to function as a plug-in for any existing tracker. The core concept is straightforward: identify potential ID-switch locations to split tracklets, then rejoin those segments if they belong to the same object. Consequently, the tracklet booster comprises two primary modules: a Splitter and a Connector. For the splitting position prediction, we utilize an architecture featuring stacked temporal dilated convolution blocks, enhanced by a label smoothing strategy with adaptive Gaussian kernels. Subsequently, a multi-head self-attention based encoder generates tracklet embeddings, which facilitate the connection of tracklets into larger, coherent groups. Extensive experiments conducted on the MOT17 and MOT20 benchmark datasets yield promising results. When integrated with the proposed tracklet booster, existing trackers typically see substantial improvements in IDF1 scores, underscoring the efficacy of this method.

Microcavity-polaritons within two-dimensional lattice structures have facilitated the exploration of diverse physical phenomena. Concurrently, organic materials have emerged as promising candidates for polaritonic devices, driven by the high binding energy of their Frenkel excitons, which enables condensation and lasing at room temperature. Although theoretical frameworks exist for condensation in planar organic microcavities, models addressing lattice geometries remain scarce. In this work, we present a model for the dynamics of lattices composed of zero-dimensional organic microcavities, where condensation is primarily driven by vibrational phonon emission. This vibronic resonance mechanism allows for the targeted excitation of specific system eigenmodes, a capability demonstrated through analyses of a dimer and a dimerized chain. In the dimer case, we identify a double resonance in condensation efficiency resulting from tuning the condensate-reservoir detuning to match either the symmetric or antisymmetric modes. This selective condensation strategy was further applied to the dimerized chain to populate topological edge states under uniform pumping across all cavities. Additionally, we reveal a distinctive signature of nonreciprocal transport when pumping a single cavity within the chain, where the propagation direction is contingent upon the specific sublattice being excited.

Over the last ten years, the concept of Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS) has become prominent in system identification. Within this framework, estimating the impulse response is treated as a regularized optimization task within an infinite-dimensional RKHS composed of stable impulse responses. This estimation problem is rigorously defined under the core premise that convolution operators, when restricted to the RKHS, act as continuous linear functionals. Given this premise, the representer theorem applies, allowing the impulse response to be determined by solving a finite-dimensional optimization problem. Therefore, the property of continuity is crucial for kernel-based system identification. This paper demonstrates that this fundamental assumption holds true in broad scenarios, specifically when the kernel is an integrable function and the input signal remains bounded. Additionally, the strong convexity of the optimization problem combined with the continuity of the convolution operators ensures that kernel-based system identification yields a unique solution. Thus, it is established as a well-defined methodology.

This study addresses the conflict between naturalness expectations and current LHC constraints on superpartner masses. We demonstrate that direct gauge mediation SUSY models exhibit a focusing phenomenon that significantly mitigates the fine-tuning required for a 126 GeV Higgs boson. These models offer high predictivity regarding the mass spectrum, featuring a multi-TeV third generation, an $A_t$ term near 1 TeV, gluino masses exceeding LHC limits, and light neutralinos and charginos below 1 TeV.

This study investigates large-scale composite optimization problems where the objective function consists of two terms, potentially nonconvex. One term possesses a block coordinate-wise Lipschitz continuous gradient, while the other is differentiable but nonseparable. Within this framework, we develop and analyze two novel random coordinate descent approaches. The first, termed the random coordinate proximal gradient method, explicitly accounts for the composite structure of the objective function. In contrast, the second method ignores this composite form, utilizing the partial gradient of the entire objective to create a random coordinate gradient descent scheme equipped with innovative adaptive stepsize rules. We demonstrate that these new stepsize rules ensure the gradient-based scheme functions as a descent method, contingent upon specific assumptions regarding the second term of the objective function. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive worst-case complexity analysis for both methods across convex and nonconvex scenarios. Preliminary numerical experiments further validate the efficiency of these algorithms on practical applications.

Determining microservice boundaries remains one of the most difficult aspects when migrating a monolith to a microservices architecture. Although recent methods for automatically identifying these boundaries follow a similar fundamental process, they differ in how they gather and analyze data from the existing monolith. This paper evaluates decompositions of two monolith systems into candidate microservices, comparing outcomes derived from static versus dynamic data collection techniques. By employing a mix of similarity measures and assessing the results against a complexity metric, we address the research question of whether static or dynamic analysis yields superior decompositions. Our findings indicate that neither technique consistently outperforms the other; however, dynamic data collection demands significantly more effort.

Young core-collapse supernovae (YSNe) serve as prolific sources of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays, generated when shock-accelerated protons interact efficiently with protons in the dense circumstellar medium. This study investigates the detectability of secondary particles from Type IIn, II-P, IIb/II-L, and Ib/c YSNe. Results indicate that Type IIn YSNe generate the highest flux of neutrinos and gamma-rays, with Type II-P events following closely. Both Fermi-LAT and the Cherenkov Telescope Array (alongside IceCube-Gen2) could detect Type IIn YSNe out to distances of $10$~Mpc (or $4$~Mpc for the latter), while other YSNe types would be observable only at closer ranges. Furthermore, YSNe are projected to dominate the diffuse neutrino background, particularly within the $10$~TeV to $10^3$~TeV energy range, although they do not appear to be a major contributor to the isotropic gamma-ray background measured by Fermi-LAT. Concurrently, existing data from IceCube's high-energy starting events and Fermi-LAT already constrain a significant portion of the model parameter space for YSNe, limiting scenarios that were previously suggested by multi-wavelength electromagnetic observations of these transients.

We address the Dirichlet problem for the Monge-Ampère equation involving $(n-1)$-PSH functions, even when the right-hand side is degenerate, by establishing a quantitative boundary estimate based on the existence of $(n-1)$-PSH subsolutions. Furthermore, we validate this subsolution condition for the product of a closed balanced manifold and a compact Riemann surface with a boundary.

This paper introduces a computational framework for estimating the stability domain of quadratic-bilinear reduced-order models (ROMs), which serve as low-dimensional approximations of large-scale dynamical systems. For nonlinear ROMs, it is crucial not only to verify local asymptotic stability at the origin but also to determine whether the operational range of the ROM falls within the region of convergence. Although accuracy and structure preservation are primary development goals for nonlinear ROMs, there has been a lack of computational methods that surpass existing highly conservative analytical bounds. In this study, we first derive an efficient but conservative analytical estimate of the stability domain based on a given quadratic Lyapunov function. To expand this estimate, we formulate and solve a convex optimization problem to obtain an optimal ellipsoidal approximation of the stability domain. These results offer critical insights into the stability characteristics of ROMs, which is essential for predictive simulations. The proposed method does not rely on a specific ROM construction technique, making it particularly valuable for data-driven quadratic-bilinear models where stability properties cannot be inferred from the full-order model. Numerical experiments involving a LQG-balanced ROM for Burgers' equation, a proper orthogonal decomposition ROM for FitzHugh-Nagumo, and a non-intrusive ROM for Burgers' equation demonstrate the scalability and quantitative benefits of the approach. The optimization-based estimates reduce conservatism by up to four orders of magnitude compared to purely analytical estimates.

Recent research has increasingly focused on how strategic or adversarial manipulation of test data can deceive classifiers. While prior studies have largely examined two extreme scenarios—where test points are either fully adversarial or consistently favor the positive label—this paper extends both cases through a unified framework for strategic classification. We introduce the concept of Strategic VC-dimension (SVC) to characterize PAC-learnability within this generalized setting, which provably encompasses the recent adversarial VC-dimension (AVC) proposed by Cullina et al. We apply our framework to the fundamental problem of strategic linear classification, providing a complete characterization of: (1) the statistical learnability of linear classifiers by determining their SVC, and (2) their computational tractability by analyzing the complexity of empirical risk minimization. Notably, the SVC for linear classifiers is always bounded above by their standard VC-dimension. This result also strictly generalizes the AVC bounds for linear classifiers established in arXiv:1806.01471.

Neural implicit representations are rapidly transforming computer vision and graphics, extending their utility from shape generation and image-based rendering to the core challenge of image-based 3D reconstruction. However, current approaches generally rely on controlled environments with consistent lighting and are captured by a limited number of uniformly positioned cameras. We present a novel method capable of efficiently and accurately reconstructing surfaces from internet photo collections despite varying illumination conditions. This is achieved through a hybrid sampling strategy that combines voxel and surface guidance, optimizing ray sampling near surfaces to substantially enhance reconstruction quality. Additionally, we establish a new benchmark and evaluation protocol for assessing performance in uncontrolled, real-world scenes. Extensive experiments confirm that our method outperforms both traditional and neural reconstruction techniques across a broad range of metrics.

The investigation of the nickel-oxide series LaNiO$_3$ (formal Ni$^{d^7}$), La$_2$NiO$_4$ (formal Ni$^{d^8}$), and LaNiO$_2$ (formal Ni$^{d^9}$) utilizes first-principles many-body methods, combining density functional theory with self-interaction correction and dynamical mean-field theory. By adopting a compound-independent approach for local Coulomb interactions, the study uncovers characteristics of these nickelates that align well with experimental data. As the Ni$(3d)$ filling increases across the series, the dichotomy within the low-energy dominant Ni-$e_g$ sector, comprising $\{d_{z^2},d_{x^2-y^2}\}$ states, becomes more pronounced. Furthermore, an intermediate-coupling scheme for spin-polarized calculations is introduced, demonstrating that the infinite-layer compound LaNiO$_2$ exhibits very weak Ni ordered moments, contrasting sharply with the robust-moment system La$_2$NiO$_4$.

This work introduces a new family of explicit stabilized Runge-Kutta-Chebyshev methods of second order designed for advection-diffusion-reaction equations. These methods demonstrate superior performance compared to existing schemes when dealing with relatively high Peclet numbers, attributed to their advantageous stability characteristics and the explicit availability of their coefficients. The development of these schemes relies on stabilization techniques using second-kind Chebyshev polynomials, originally applied in the stochastic integrator SK-ROCK. Additionally, an adaptive algorithm is proposed to facilitate the implementation of the new scheme, capable of automatically determining the optimal step size, number of stages, and damping parameter at every integration step. Numerical experiments are provided to demonstrate the efficiency of this new algorithm.

A primary obstacle in implementing deep neural networks lies in their substantial size, which negatively impacts inference speed and memory consumption. Depth-wise pruning involves removing layers or blocks, while width-wise pruning eliminates filters based on their significance. Typically, width-wise pruning utilizes learnable gates or sparsity regularizers, whereas layer removal has historically relied on manually designing smaller "student" networks without systematic optimization. We introduce a unified pruning framework capable of executing both depth-wise and width-wise reductions. This is accomplished by inserting gates at various levels of granularity—ranging from individual neurons to filters, layers, and blocks—which are regulated by an objective function that orchestrates simultaneous pruning across these scales during every forward pass. Our method is versatile, accommodating diverse architectures regardless of spatial dimensions or connection types, including sequential, residual, parallel, and inception structures. Evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves a compression ratio between 70% and 90% with negligible accuracy degradation.

The prevailing understanding of renormalization in quantum gravity (QG) relies on the premise that ultraviolet divergences within the effective actions of covariant QG models manifest as covariant local expressions. Given that this foundational assertion is pivotal to QG, it is crucial to validate it across the broadest possible spectrum of QG theories. By employing the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism alongside the background field method, we develop a proof demonstrating gauge-invariant renormalizability for a general diffeomorphism-invariant quantum gravity model, one that lacks additional, potentially anomalous symmetries.

Investigating laboratory plasma instabilities, magnetic reconnection, and related turbulent phenomena necessitates high spatial and temporal resolution, achieved through the simultaneous sampling of hundreds to thousands of magnetic sensors at several hundred kHz. While pick-up (Mirnov) coils are standard in experimental pulsed plasma devices due to their simplicity and reliability, their output—proportional to the magnetic field's time derivative ($dB/dt$)—requires time integration to determine the instantaneous field value. Conventional analog or chopped integrators used for this purpose typically restrict bandwidth to the kHz range, are difficult to implement, and necessitate extra fast channels to capture high-frequency plasma dynamics directly. This paper assesses the viability of employing a single-channel precision ADC to simultaneously acquire $dB/dt$ data and perform digital integration for the magnetic field ($B$) measurement on the new RFX-mod2 device. To this end, an existing ADC module was interfaced with a Xilinx Zynq FPGA to evaluate intrinsic noise and determine the feasible integration window. The findings suggest a compact, cost-effective, and reliable acquisition system capable of simultaneous real-time control and transient recording, scalable from tens to thousands of channels for a wide variety of pulsed plasma experimental devices.

This chapter introduces new information-theoretic findings for analyzing stationary time series within the frequency domain. Specifically, it identifies the generalized von Mises spectral distribution as the form associated with the most unpredictable stationary time series when certain autocovariance values are fixed. Consequently, this represents a maximum entropy spectral distribution, and the resulting time series is termed the generalized von Mises time series. While the generalized von Mises distribution is already applied in directional statistics to model multimodal planar directions, this work further introduces the Gaussian-generalized von Mises time series. This variant maximizes entropy in both the frequency and time domains, known respectively as spectral and temporal entropies. Finally, the chapter briefly examines parameter estimation and computational considerations related to this time series.

In their books, M. Tinkham and P. G. de Gennes described an intermediate type-I superconductor arising from external surface effects that modify the traditional classification of superconductors into type-I and type-II. This study examines mesoscopic superconductors, where the small volume-to-area ratio amplifies surface influences. Using standard Ginzburg-Landau theory, we extend the Tinkham-de Gennes scenario to intermediate type-I mesoscopic superconductors. We identify novel characteristics of the transition from genuine to intermediate type-I behavior. The intermediate type-I phase exhibits two distinct transitions: a shift from paramagnetic to diamagnetic response as the magnetic field decreases, and quasi type-II behavior as the critical coupling is approached with an increasing field. These proposed features and their associated transitions reflect intrinsic properties of the superconductor rather than its geometrical characteristics.

This study introduces a novel primal-dual algorithm designed to compute the equilibrium of generalized (continuous) Nash games, known as the Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem (GNEP), in which each player's feasible strategy set is contingent upon the strategies of others. The approach relies on a newly formulated Lagrangian function incorporating a quadratic approximation. Initially, the GNEP is reformulated as a saddle point problem using this Lagrangian, establishing a direct equivalence between the Lagrangian's saddle point and the game's equilibrium. Subsequently, a straightforward algorithm is proposed that converges to this saddle point. Global convergence is further proven under the assumption that the Lagrangian function satisfies the Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz property. A key aspect of the analysis involves utilizing the new Lagrangian as a potential function to direct the convergence of iterates. The method offers two significant innovations compared to existing techniques: (i) it eliminates the need for boundedness assumptions regarding strategy sets, multiplier sets, or the algorithm's generated iterates; and (ii) it yields a Jacobi-type decomposition scheme, representing, to our knowledge, the first distributed algorithm developed for solving a broad class of GNEPs. Finally, numerical experiments on benchmark test problems validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

We introduce a set-valued framework designed to establish the well-posedness of birth-and-growth processes. This model is rigorously formulated as a specific integration of two broad set-valued processes—representing nucleation and growth—utilizing both the Minkowski sum and the Aumann integral. By employing a straightforward geometrical methodology, we circumvent analytical challenges associated with defining front growth, such as issues regarding boundary regularity. Within this framework, growth is typically anisotropic; from a mesoscale perspective, it is non-local, meaning that at any given instant, the growth behavior remains consistent across all spatial points.

While the primary loss mechanism in planar microwave superconducting resonators is recognized as coupling to a two-level system (TLS) bath, the cavity's behavior under an off-resonant pump remains incompletely understood. This study derives a semi-classical model that predicts a power-dependent frequency shift in addition to the established TLS-induced damping. The model is experimentally validated through two-tone spectroscopy on multiple resonators made from different substrates. Alongside the accompanying analytical formulas, this proposed technique serves as a straightforward yet effective method for characterizing various properties of the TLS bath, including their average dephasing rate.

This study investigates the feasibility of incorporating two relatively light top squarks (`stops') within the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM), a configuration that significantly enhances the model's naturalness. We demonstrate that such light stops remain consistent with direct LHC searches, current Higgs sector data, other low-energy electroweak constraints, and recent dark matter (DM) limits. We propose dedicated LHC searches for these light stops using a simplified scenario where the dark matter candidate is either bino-like or singlino-like, highlighting specific final states that reflect their collective presence. In certain cases, this scenario produces atypical final states. Detailed detector-level analyses following the 8 TeV LHC run assess the viability of this scenario and project prospects for the 13 and 14 TeV runs. In favorable regions of the NMSSM parameter space characterized by low-lying spectra, signals achieving a significance of $\gtrsim 5\sigma$ are achievable with integrated luminosities ranging from tens to hundreds of $\text{fb}^{-1}$ across various final states.

Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on updating merely a small fraction of parameters when adapting pretrained models for downstream applications. This paper presents PASTA, a method that adjusts only the representations of special tokens (such as [SEP] and [CLS] in BERT) prior to the self-attention layer in each Transformer layer. PASTA delivers performance comparable to full fine-tuning on natural language understanding tasks, including text classification and NER, while training as few as 0.029% of the total parameters. Beyond offering a straightforward and effective approach to parameter-efficient tuning with broad practical utility for deploying multi-task models, this work highlights the critical importance of special tokens within pretrained language models.

We derive quantum gravitational corrections to the Wald entropy of a four-dimensional, non-extremal Reissner-Nordstr\"om (RN) black hole with a small electric charge, extending prior work by Calmet and Kuipers [1] on Schwarzschild black holes. Starting from an effective action for quantum gravity, we demonstrate that at second order in Ricci curvature, quantum effects modify the RN metric, thereby displacing the classical event horizon. By applying the Wald entropy formula through an integration over the perimeter of this quantum-corrected horizon, we subsequently calculate the resulting quantum gravitational corrections to the black hole's temperature and pressure.

We present observations of the flickering variability of the dwarf nova RX And across five photometric bands (UBVRI) spanning two nights. On October 25, 2019, the star exhibited a brightness of $B\approx 13.9$ mag, with a flickering amplitude of 0.47 mag. We estimated the flickering source temperature to be $T_{fl} = 10700 \pm 400$ K and its radius to be $R_{fl} = 0.046 \pm 0.004$ $R_\odot$. By contrast, on January 2, 2020, the star was approximately 3 magnitudes brighter ($B \approx 10.7$), and the flickering amplitude decreased significantly to 0.07 mag. For this epoch, we derived a flickering source temperature of $T_{fl} = 9600 \pm 700$ K and a radius of $R_{fl} = 0.098 \pm 0.009$ $R_\odot$. These findings suggest that the star's 3-magnitude brightening resulted in a doubling of the flickering source's radius. The data can be obtained from the authors upon request.

This paper presents a search conducted by the CMS experiment using proton-proton collision data from 2016–2017 at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV for long-lived particles that decay into photons and weakly interacting particles. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 77.4 fb$^{-1}$. The findings are interpreted within the framework of supersymmetry featuring gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking, specifically focusing on scenarios where the neutralino is long-lived and decays into a photon and a gravitino. Exclusion limits are established as functions of the neutralino's mass and proper decay length. At a 95% confidence level, masses up to 320, 525, 360, and 215 GeV are ruled out for neutralino proper decay lengths of 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 m, respectively. These results improve upon previous best limits, extending the reach in neutralino proper decay length by up to one order of magnitude and in neutralino mass by up to 100 GeV.

At RHIC, the hydrogen jet target polarimeter (HJET) measures proton beam polarization with a systematic accuracy of $\sigma_P^\text{syst}/P\lesssim0.5\%$ by detecting low-energy (1--10 MeV) recoil protons in left-right symmetric detectors. This capability also enabled precise determination of $pp$ and $p$A (where A denotes any ion stored at RHIC) analyzing powers within the CNI region, and the findings are presented below.

Under the Compressive Sensing (CS) framework, sparse signals can be recovered using a limited number of measurements, where the solution's reliability hinges on the uniqueness condition. Among CS metrics, the coherence index holds significant practical value due to its mathematical tractability and feasible computation. This paper introduces an enhanced coherence-based uniqueness relationship tailored for matching pursuit algorithms. Beginning with an intuitive derivation of the standard uniqueness condition relying on the coherence index, we establish a less conservative lower bound for signal sparsity. Furthermore, these findings are extended to the uniqueness condition of $l_0$-norm minimization for signals represented within two orthonormal bases.

The only expected resonant contributions to $B^+\to D^+D^-K^+$ decays arise from charmonium states within the $D^+D^-$ channel. To evaluate this hypothesis, a model-independent analysis was performed using LHCb proton-proton collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=7, 8,$ and $13$ TeV, with a total integrated luminosity of 9 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis demonstrates that describing the data under the assumption that resonances occur solely in $D^+D^-$ decays is insufficient. This discrepancy provides evidence for an additional contribution to the decay, likely representing one or more new charm-strange resonances in the $D^-K^+$ channel with masses near 2.9 GeV$/c^2$.

This study presents a probabilistic framework incorporating implicit norm regularization to address nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), a technique widely utilized for imputing missing values and uncovering latent patterns where matrix factors serve as latent variables tied to data dimensions. Nonnegativity constraints are enforced by selecting priors defined over the nonnegative subspace, such as exponential densities or functions. The approach utilizes Gibbs sampling for Bayesian inference. Validated across multiple real-world datasets, including the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC $IC_{50}$) and Gene body methylation datasets of varying sizes and dimensions, the proposed Bayesian NMF models (GL$_2^2$ and GL$_\infty$) demonstrate robust predictive performance across diverse data values and effectively mitigate overfitting relative to competing Bayesian NMF methods.

Although image classification has advanced significantly, identifying samples that fall outside the training classes remains a difficult challenge. This area, known as Open-Set Recognition (OSR), has recently garnered substantial attention. The objective in OSR is to simultaneously perform classification and detect out-of-distribution (OOD) samples. While numerous complex techniques have been introduced to improve empirical results, we argue that such intricacy is unnecessary. We demonstrate that Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), a straightforward OSR baseline, achieves surprising performance when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs) trained with non-OOD augmentations. These augmentations preserve the data distribution without altering it significantly. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods on the CIFAR-10 dataset and outperforms most existing approaches on SVHN and MNIST. We further show that augmentation strategies critically impact ViT performance in OSR tasks; while augmented samples should exhibit meaningful diversity, their deviation from the distribution (OOD-ness) must remain constrained.

This study addresses the challenge of sampling and reconstructing continuous-time sparse signals without requiring prior knowledge of sampling instants or rates. The research originates from the problem of recovering multiple light echoes from low-pass filtered, time-domain auto-correlated measurements. Our work aligns closely with sparse phase retrieval, specifically highlighting the benefits of phase-free measurements. Although the problem is inherently ill-posed, physical constraints provide the necessary cues for appropriate regularization. We validate our theoretical framework through experiments using customized optical time-of-flight imaging sensors. A distinguishing feature of our approach is that it enables temporal phase retrieval, contrasting with the more common spatial phase retrieval. Preliminary experiments and results indicate a strong capability of our phase-retrieval-based imaging device.

Intelligent dialogue systems are envisioned as a novel interface connecting humans and machines. To function effectively, such systems must infer a user's internal state (UIS) during conversations and adapt their responses accordingly. This paper models the UIS within dialogues, using movie recommendation scenarios as a case study, to build a system that tailors its replies based on this inferred state. Through dialogue data analysis, the UIS is decomposed into three components: knowledge, interest, and engagement.
