Estimators for these states were trained on a corpus annotated with these specific UIS elements, achieving high accuracy. Furthermore, response modification rules were developed to adjust system outputs based on the detected UIS. Results confirm that incorporating UIS estimation into response generation significantly enhances the naturalness of system utterances, as verified by both dialogue-level and utterance-level evaluations.

The distinction between training and deploying machine learning models means that deployment scenarios cannot always be fully predicted during training, limiting the efficacy of training improvements alone. Consequently, Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection is critical for testing a model's capacity to recognize unseen situations—essentially determining if a model knows when it lacks knowledge. Current OOD detection techniques typically require additional training iterations, extra data, or significant structural changes to the network. In contrast, this paper introduces ASH, an extremely straightforward, post-hoc, on-the-fly activation shaping technique. ASH involves removing a substantial portion (e.g., 90%) of a sample's activation at a late layer while simplifying or slightly adjusting the remainder (e.g., 10%). Applied during inference, this method requires no statistics derived from training data. Experimental results demonstrate that this simple approach significantly enhances the distinction between in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples, achieving state-of-the-art OOD detection on ImageNet without noticeably compromising in-distribution accuracy. Alongside this paper, we provide two calls for explanation and validation to leverage collective efforts in further verifying and understanding this discovery. Resources, including calls, videos, and code, are available at: https://andrijazz.github.io/ash

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) typically learn implicit representations of static scenes from images. Our work extends NeRFs to process dynamic environments in an online manner. We introduce ParticleNeRF, which adapts to real-time geometric changes by learning an updated representation every 350ms. Compared to other NeRF frameworks, ParticleNeRF captures the current state of dynamic scenes with significantly higher fidelity. To accomplish this, we propose a novel particle-based parametric encoding that links intermediate NeRF features to spatial particles, enabling them to move with the evolving geometry. This is achieved by backpropagating the photometric reconstruction loss to the particles' positions; these position gradients are treated as velocities and integrated into the positions using a position-based dynamics (PBS) physics system. Incorporating PBS into the NeRF formulation facilitates the addition of collision constraints and opens avenues for integrating other movement priors, such as rigid or deformable body constraints. Videos demonstrating the results are available at https://sites.google.com/view/particlenerf.

In industrial NLP applications, manually labeled datasets often contain noise. We propose a straightforward approach to identify and manually relabel these noisy instances while simultaneously gathering correction data. Subsequently, we introduce a novel method to integrate this human-derived correction information into deep learning models, leveraging human expertise to refine model performance. We conducted experiments on a proprietary text classification dataset that underwent manual relabeling for industry use. The results demonstrate that our method boosts classification accuracy from 91.7% to 92.5%. Furthermore, the initial accuracy of 91.7%, achieved by training on the corrected dataset, represents a significant improvement over the baseline of 83.3%.

Topological indices serve as scientific descriptors that capture a graph's topology and function largely as graph invariants. In the fields of QSAR and QSPR, these indices—such as the Atom-Bond Connectivity (ABC) and Geometric-Arithmetic (GA) indices—are utilized alongside physico-chemical properties to predict the bioactivity of chemical compounds, highlighting the significant role of graph theory in this domain. This paper focuses on Planar Octahedron networks generated from an n-dimensional honeycomb structure, deriving analytical closed-form results for the first multiplicative topological indices and presenting closed formulas for degree-based indices.

In his various publications, V.V. Sharko has explored functions on manifolds and cobordism, areas deeply intertwined with braid theory. These relationships are manifested through the mapping class groups and fundamental groups of associated discs, alongside other topological and algebraic frameworks. This paper highlights selected algebraic techniques and findings concerning the intersections of braids, links, and cobordism with Sharko's research. The discussion encompasses group-theoretic insights into braids and links, infinitesimal braid group relations, and their connections to coherent sheaves on smooth schemes. Furthermore, it outlines an algorithm for constructing Lazard's one-dimensional universal commutative formal group and presents key results on applying these formal groups to cobordism theory.

This paper introduces a frequency-domain technique for intra-predicting chroma planes using the reconstructed luma plane. It leverages the observation that while RGB-to-YUV conversion decorrelates color planes globally, local correlations persist at the block level. Unlike previous approaches that model the spatial relationship between luma (Y) and chroma (U and V) planes, this method is designed for codecs utilizing lapped transforms, where such spatial modeling is infeasible due to transform support crossing block boundaries and the unavailability of neighboring blocks during prediction. We propose a frequency-domain chroma intra-predictor that maintains low complexity while exploiting this local correlation. Furthermore, we detail a low-complexity algorithm that directly predicts chroma from luma coefficients through gain-shape quantization and band partitioning. Experiments within the experimental Daala video codec demonstrate that this lower-complexity algorithm outperforms the alternative technique as a chroma predictor.

Significant resources have been invested in developing high-performance few-shot learners, which are large-scale pretrained language models (PLMs) capable of excelling with minimal downstream training data. Although training these PLMs is expensive, their massive scale continues to pose challenges for practical utilization. This study addresses the critical question of how to leverage these few-shot learners effectively. We introduce LMTurk, an innovative framework that conceptualizes few-shot learners as crowdsourcing workers. The underlying logic is that crowdsourcing workers function similarly to few-shot learners: they observe a few examples to understand a task before beginning annotation. LMTurk applies this paradigm by using PLM-based few-shot learners as workers. We demonstrate that the annotations generated by these workers can be used to train compact models that perform well on the task and are small enough for real-world deployment. Furthermore, LMTurk incorporates active learning to decrease the number of queries sent to PLMs, thereby reducing the computational costs associated with inference. Collectively, LMTurk represents a significant advancement in effectively harnessing the capabilities of current PLMs.

The advent of Industry 4.0 has led to the generation of vast datasets suitable for modeling as functional data. While conventional profile monitoring techniques focus on assessing the temporal stability of fully observed functional quality traits, real-time evaluation during active processes offers significant potential for enhancing monitoring efficacy. To address this, we introduce Functional Real-Time Monitoring (FRTM), a novel approach designed to capture both phase and amplitude variations through three key stages: registration, dimensionality reduction, and the monitoring of partially observed functional quality characteristics. We conducted an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study to evaluate FRTM's performance against two alternative methods. Additionally, we present a practical application demonstrating the method's utility in real-time monitoring of batches within a penicillin production process.

This paper presents a reorganization and consolidation of research conducted during the author's second and third years of undergraduate mathematics at the University of Toronto, which was previously scattered and disorganized. The primary objective is to construct a family of analytic functions, $\alpha \uparrow^n z$, mapping $(1,e^{1/e}) \times \mathbb{C}_{\Re(z) > 0}$ to $\mathbb{C}_{\Re(z) > 0}$ through fractional calculus methods. This family adheres to the hyper-operator chain property, $\alpha \uparrow^{n-1} \alpha \uparrow^n z = \alpha \uparrow^n (z+1)$, subject to the initial condition $\alpha \uparrow^0 z = \alpha \cdot z$.

Following the rise of deep learning and its integration into steganalysis, the majority of reference studies have relied on small to medium-sized CNNs trained on relatively limited datasets. Consequently, benchmarks comparing various deep learning-based steganalysis algorithms, specifically CNNs, are typically conducted on these smaller scales. This approach overlooks three critical questions: 1) whether performance rankings based on metrics like accuracy remain consistent when the dataset size increases; 2) whether the efficiency of CNNs would degrade significantly if the training data were expanded by an order of magnitude; and 3) the minimum database or network size necessary to achieve results superior to random guessing. In this paper, after thoroughly analyzing the behavior of CNNs in relation to both their architecture and dataset dimensions, we confirm that the error's power-law relationship holds true in steganalysis. This finding is particularly significant as it applies to a borderline case involving a medium-sized network operating on a large, constrained, and highly diverse database.

Differentiable simulations of physical phenomena have garnered significant recent interest. While some initiatives aim to create differentiable robotic physics engines by leveraging the computational advantages of integrating rigid body simulations with modern differentiable machine learning frameworks, this work introduces a library specifically designed to merge data-driven approaches with analytical rigid body calculations. Our library, \emph{Differentiable Robot Models}, provides both \emph{differentiable} and \emph{learnable} representations of robot kinematics and dynamics within Pytorch. The source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/differentiable-robot-model}.

This paper introduces methods for developing a portable, fully C-based vectorized library of standard mathematical functions. To ensure portability without sacrificing performance, we abstract vector extension intrinsics using inline functions or preprocessor macros. Our implementation leverages specific sub-features of vector extensions, including fused multiply-add, mask registers, and mantissa extraction. To maximize the efficiency of SIMD computations, the library minimizes conditional branches and ensures all computational paths are vectorized. Additionally, we developed a variation of the Payne-Hanek argument reduction tailored for trigonometric functions and floating-point remainders, both optimized for vector processing. Finally, we benchmark our library's performance against Intel SVML.

This study examines the spectral convergence of graph Laplacians toward the Laplace-Beltrami operator, given an affinity matrix built from $N$ random points on a $d$-dimensional manifold within a potentially high-dimensional space. Through the analysis of Dirichlet form convergence and the construction of approximate eigenfunctions using manifold heat kernel convolutions, we demonstrate that with a Gaussian kernel, choosing the bandwidth parameter $\epsilon \sim (\log N/ N)^{1/(d/2+2)}$ yields an eigenvalue convergence rate of $N^{-1/(d/2+2)}$ and an eigenvector convergence rate in the 2-norm of $N^{-1/(d+4)}$. Alternatively, if $\epsilon \sim (\log N/N)^{1/(d/2+3)}$, both eigenvalue and eigenvector rates improve to $N^{-1/(d/2+3)}$. These findings, valid up to a logarithmic factor, apply to a finite set of low-lying eigenvalues. The results cover un-normalized and random-walk graph Laplacians for uniformly sampled data, as well as density-corrected graph Laplacians (where the affinity matrix is doubly normalized by the degree matrix) for non-uniformly sampled data. Additionally, we establish new point-wise and Dirichlet form convergence rates for the density-corrected graph Laplacian as an intermediate finding, supported by numerical experiments that validate the theoretical results.

MAXI J1820+070 is a high-luminosity low-mass black hole X-ray binary that exhibits strong optical and X-ray emissions during outbursts. We provide comprehensive photometric data across X-ray, ultraviolet, and optical wavelengths, along with frequently sampled optical spectra, spanning from the onset of the optical outburst to approximately 550 days. During the rebrightening phase, optical emission led the X-ray rise by 20.80 ± 2.85 days. Spectral features include blue continua and emission lines from the Balmer series, He I, He II, and the broad Bowen blend. We observed an anticorrelation between the pseudo equivalent widths (pEW) of emission lines and the X-ray flux at similar phases, attributed to the increasing suppression by the optical continuum. Near the X-ray peak, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of H$_{\beta}$ and He II $\lambda$4686 stabilized at 19.4 Å and 21.8 Å, respectively, indicating line formation regions at 1.7 and 1.3 R$_{\odot}$ within the accretion disk. Analysis of absolute line fluxes revealed positive correlations between H$_{\beta}$ and He II $\lambda$4686 fluxes and the X-ray flux, supporting the irradiation model as the primary driver of optical emission. However, the dramatic X-ray flux decline at t~200 days post-outburst, contrasted with the relatively stable optical flux, implies that additional energy sources, such as viscous dissipation, likely contribute to the optical radiation alongside X-ray irradiation.

Current Domain Adaptation (DA) methods train target models to classify all target domain samples, overlooking the possibility that some target samples resemble the source domain and should instead be handled by source models. This paper introduces a novel unsupervised DA approach called Enforced Transfer. It utilizes an out-of-distribution detection method to determine whether to apply the source or target model for each test instance, effectively employing a divide-and-conquer strategy. Rather than selecting models at the instance level, our approach makes this decision at the layer level within deep neural networks. Experimental results across three types of DA tasks demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

GRB~221009A, the most luminous long gamma-ray burst identified to date by Swift-BAT and Fermi-GBM, offers a unique chance to investigate high-energy mechanisms within extreme transient events. However, standard leptonic models, including synchrotron and synchrotron-self-Compton processes for the afterglow, fail to account for the gamma-ray observations made by LHAASO up to 18 TeV. We analyzed the gamma-ray spectrum within the 0.1–1 GeV range using Fermi-LAT data. Our leptonic models predict that flux is heavily suppressed above 1 TeV due to gamma-gamma pair production with the extragalactic background light, necessitating an additional emission component. We propose that ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays accelerated within the GRB jet generate an electromagnetic cascade as they propagate through the extragalactic medium. The line-of-sight portion of this flux can account for the TeV emission detected by LHAASO, provided a specific fraction of the blastwave energy is invested in these cosmic rays. This finding may represent the first direct proof of ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray acceleration occurring in gamma-ray bursts.

Real Clifford algebras are essential to the eight Altland-Zirnbauer symmetry classes and the classification of topological phases. In this work, we introduce an elegant realization of these algebras within $d$-dimensional spinless rectangular lattices featuring a $\pi$ flux per plaquette. Because of the time-reversal ($T$) invariant flux arrangement, real Clifford algebras emerge as projective symmetry algebras of lattice symmetries. Notably, the value of $d$ modulo $8$ aligns precisely with the eight Morita equivalence classes of real Clifford algebras, reflecting eightfold Bott periodicity and mirroring the eight Altland-Zirnbauer classes. The representation theory of these algebras dictates the degeneracy of band structures at both generic and high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. Specifically, the significant degeneracy at high-symmetry points provides a versatile resource for creating new topological states through various dimerization schemes. These include a 3D higher-order semimetal with double-charged bulk nodal loops and hinge modes, a 4D nodal surface semimetal hosting 3D surface solid-ball zero modes, and 4D Möbius topological insulators characterized by eightfold surface nodal points or fourfold surface nodal rings. Our theoretical framework can be experimentally implemented in artificial crystals utilizing engineerable $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge fields to simulate higher-dimensional systems.

This paper addresses adversarially robust self-supervised learning within graph structures. By employing a contrastive learning framework, we propose a novel approach that enhances the robustness of learned representations through two mechanisms: adversarial transformations and operations that both remove and insert edges. Preliminary experiments on a selected dataset yield encouraging outcomes. We contend that this research represents a significant advancement toward integrating robustness as a practical auxiliary objective in graph contrastive learning.

The Galactic halo is believed to originate from the merging of nearby dwarf galaxies. To investigate various components of the halo, we employed Gaussian Mixture Models on a selected sample of metal-poor stars ([Fe/H] < -0.7 dex) from the APOGEE DR16 catalogue, utilizing four parameters: metallicity, [Mg/Fe] ratio, and spatial velocities ($V_R$, $V_\phi$). This analysis identified nine distinct groups: four belonging to the halo (groups 1, 3, 4, and 5), one from the thick disk (group 6), one from the thin disk (group 8), and one attributed to dwarf galaxies (group 7), based on their distributions across ([M/H], [Mg/Fe]), ($V_R$, $V_\phi$), ($Z_{\text{max}}$, eccentricity), (Energy, $L_z$), and ([Mg/Mn], [Al/Fe]) coordinates. The remaining two groups arise from observational effects (group 9) and the transitional component between the thin and thick disks (group 2). Our findings indicate that in the extreme outer accreted halo (group 1), Milky Way-born stars are indistinguishable from accreted ones based on either chemistry or kinematics. At intermediate metallicities ($-1.6 < \text{[Fe/H]} < -0.7$ dex), the accreted halo is predominantly composed of the Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage substructure (group 5), which is readily separable from the in-situ halo (group 4) in both chemical and kinematic spaces. Additionally, some members of group 4 may originate from the disk, while certain disk stars are scattered to high orbits via resonant effects, as evidenced by the $Z_{\text{max}}$ versus Energy plot. Finally, the spatial distribution of the halo's main components and the ratio of accreted components show no clear correlation with Galactic radius.

Session-based recommendations (SBRs) identify item dependencies within user sessions to predict the next item. Recently, Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based SBRs have become the dominant approach due to their ability to model complex dependencies effectively. However, most GNN-based models rely on a strong assumption that adjacent items in a session are inherently dependent. Given the inherent uncertainty and complexity of user behavior, we argue that adjacency does not guarantee dependency. Consequently, this assumption often fails in real-world scenarios, leading to two major issues: (1) false dependencies arise from adjacent items that lack a true relationship, and (2) genuine dependencies are missed when non-adjacent items are actually related. These limitations impair item representation learning and degrade overall recommendation performance. To overcome these challenges, we introduce RI-GNN, a novel review-refined inter-item graph neural network that leverages topic information extracted from item reviews to enhance inter-item dependencies. Experimental results on two public real-world datasets confirm that RI-GNN surpasses state-of-the-art methods.

This technical report presents our enhancements to YOWO, a real-time framework for spatio-temporal action detection. While retaining the original network architecture—comprising 3D-ResNext-101 and YOLOv2—we improve performance by utilizing superior pretrained weights for our reimplemented YOLOv2 and refining the label assignment strategy. Additionally, we incorporate GIoU loss to optimize box regression for precise action instance detection. These incremental improvements yield a frame mAP of 84.9% and a video mAP of 50.5% on UCF101-24, surpassing the official YOWO, and a frame mAP of 20.6% on AVA using 16 frames. Our optimized version, designated YOWO-Plus, achieves 21.6% frame mAP on AVA with 32 frames while maintaining 25 FPS on an RTX 3090 GPU. Furthermore, we developed YOWO-Nano by substituting 3D-ResNext-101 with the efficient 3D-ShuffleNet-v2 to create a lightweight detector. YOWO-Nano attains 81.0% frame mAP and 49.7% video mAP on UCF101-24 at over 90 FPS, and reaches 18.4% frame mAP on AVA with approximately 90 FPS, establishing it as the fastest state-of-the-art action detector to date. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yjh0410/PyTorch_YOWO.

This paper examines the convergence of Bochner-Riesz means across various Sobolev-type spaces, specifically $L^p$-Sobolev spaces (where $p\geq 1$) and $H^q$-Sobolev spaces (where $0<q<1$). Furthermore, it establishes the connection between the degree of smoothness required for functions and the speed of their almost everywhere convergence under generalized Bochner-Riesz means.

This study utilizes a diffusing transcription factors model to numerically simulate human chromatin topology and transcriptional dynamics. Simulations of short chromatin filaments demonstrate distinct regulatory pathways for transcription, indicating that activity profiles can be modulated by manipulating either the chain's structural characteristics or external variables, such as transcription factor counts. Furthermore, comparisons between GRO-seq experimental data and large-scale simulations of whole chromosomes from human umbilical vein endothelial cells and B-lymphocytes (GM12878) confirm that the model yields reliable, statistically significant predictions of transcription across diverse cell lines.

Let $(X,L)$ denote a Weinstein manifold $X$ containing an exact Lagrangian submanifold $L$, possessing an ideal contact boundary $(Y,\Lambda)$ where $Y$ is a contact manifold and $\Lambda \subset Y$ is a Legendrian submanifold. We examine the Chekanov-Eliashberg differential graded algebra, $CE^{\ast}(\Lambda)$, utilizing coefficients derived from the chains of the based loop space of $\Lambda$, and investigate its connection to the Floer cohomology $CF^{\ast}(L)$ of $L$. Leveraging the augmentation generated by $L$, we represent $CE^{\ast}(\Lambda)$ as the Adams cobar construction $\Omega$ applied to a Legendrian coalgebra, $LC_{\ast}(\Lambda)$. Furthermore, we define a twisting cochain $\mathfrak{t} \colon LC_{\ast}(\Lambda) \to \mathrm{B} (CF^*(L))^\#$ based on holomorphic curve counts, where $\mathrm{B}$ signifies the bar construction and $\#$ represents the graded linear dual. Under assumptions of simple connectivity, we demonstrate that the associated Koszul complex is acyclic, implying that $CE^*(\Lambda)$ and $CF^{\ast}(L)$ are Koszul duals. Specifically, $\mathfrak{t}$ yields a quasi-isomorphism between $CE^*(\Lambda)$ and the cobar construction of the Floer homology of $L$, denoted $\Omega CF_*(L)$. Utilizing this duality, and assuming specific conditions regarding connectivity and local finiteness, we establish that $CE^*(\Lambda)$ is quasi-isomorphic to $C_{-*}(\Omega L)$ for any Lagrangian filling $L$ of $\Lambda$. Our constructions admit interpretations within the framework of wrapped Floer cohomology following variations of Lagrangian handle attachments. Notably, we sketch a proof demonstrating that $CE^{\ast}(\Lambda)$ is quasi-isomorphic to the wrapped Floer cohomology of a fiber disk $C$ situated in the Weinstein domain formed by attaching $T^{\ast}(\Lambda\times[0,\infty))$ to $X$ along $\Lambda$ (or, using the terminology of arXiv:1604.02540, the wrapped Floer cohomology of $C$ in $X$ with wrapping halted by $\Lambda$). Throughout this process, we also provide a definition of wrapped Floer cohomology that does not rely on Hamiltonian perturbations.

While prior research on multi-agent reinforcement learning primarily targets decentralized, cooperative strategies to optimize shared rewards, it seldom addresses the transferability of these policies to novel tasks, thereby hindering their application to more complex scenarios. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a framework that combines hierarchical graph attention networks for multi-agent representation learning with a multi-agent actor-critic approach for policy learning. This hierarchical graph attention network is tailored to capture the complex cooperative and competitive relationships between agents, enabling the development of sophisticated strategic policies. By employing distinct inter-agent and inter-group attention layers, the model effectively manages both individual and group-level interactions. These attention mechanisms have demonstrated their ability to support policy transfer across tasks with varying agent compositions and to enhance the interpretability of learned strategies. Empirical results indicate that our proposed model surpasses current methods in various mixed cooperative and competitive environments.

The concept of mean temperature is fundamental across various disciplines, such as biophysics, fluid dynamics, and climate science. Nevertheless, a valid thermodynamic basis for this concept remains absent or is even considered unattainable. Relying on mathematical averages, such as the arithmetic or geometric mean, is inadequate because they overlook the unique nature of temperature and lack uniqueness. We propose a thermodynamically sound definition grounded in two key premises. First, since the definition must account for equilibration in initially non-equilibrium systems, the mean temperature is bounded by examining the reversible and fully irreversible limits of this process. Second, within this thermodynamic framework, we posit that mean temperature is primarily governed by energy and entropy. When combined with dimensional analysis, these two premises yield a unique definition. For both ideal and non-ideal (van der Waals) gases with temperature-independent heat capacities, this results in a concise, general formula that, in addition to initial temperatures, relies solely on gas concentrations and heat capacities.

This paper aims to identify the most concise representation of a matrix $A \in PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ using continuant matrices, which are fundamental in continued fraction theory. While Morier-Génoud and Ovsienko addressed this issue in Chapter 7 of arXiv:1811.01229 under the constraint of positive coefficients, this work seeks to find the shortest presentation allowing any integer coefficients. To achieve this minimal presentation, specific characteristic transformations are introduced, and the conditions under which such a presentation becomes unique are examined. Furthermore, these findings are extended to conjugacy classes within $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$. For inquiries or correspondence regarding this research, please email christian.streib@online.de.

This study provides projections for anomalous neutral triple gauge couplings ($aNTGC$) derived from $pp \rightarrow ZZ$ production within the 2$\ell$2$\nu$ final state at the 100 TeV "FCC-hh" proton-proton collider. The analysis incorporates realistic "FCC-hh" detector conditions and their associated effects. Focusing on a decay mode where one Z boson produces a pair of same-flavor, opposite-sign leptons (electrons or muons) and the other decays into two neutrinos, the paper establishes new 95% Confidence Level (C.L.) bounds on CP-conserving ($C_{\widetilde{B}W} / \Lambda^{4}$) and CP-violating ($C_{WW} / \Lambda^{4}$, $C_{BW} / \Lambda^{4}$, $C_{BB} / \Lambda^{4}$) couplings. Utilizing the transverse momentum of the dilepton system ($p_{T}^{\ell \ell}$), the resulting constraints are $[-\, 0.042, \,\, +\,0.042]$, $[-\,0.050, \,\, +\,0.050]$, $[-\,0.050, \,\, +\,0.050]$, and $[-\,0.048, \,\, +\,0.048]$ TeV$^{-4}$, respectively.

This paper derives enhanced upper bounds for the indices of character sums of polynomials defined over finite fields. We provide specific examples demonstrating that our new bound surpasses both the classical Weil bound and the index bound established by Wan and Wang. Furthermore, we apply this result to determine the total number of solutions for certain algebraic curves.

We investigate the holographic quantum error correction capabilities of a Sierpinski Triangle-shaped boundary subregion within $AdS_4/CFT_3$. Because existing no-go theorems in topological quantum error correction restrict fractal noise, holographic codes demonstrate a distinct advantage over topological codes in this context. Furthermore, we argue that a boundary subregion shaped like the Sierpinski gasket in $AdS_5/CFT_4$ lacks these holographic quantum error correction properties.

This study reports findings on the branching fraction and effective lifetime of the B$^0_\mathrm{s}\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay, alongside a search for the B$^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay mode. The analysis is based on proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS experiment during 2011, 2012, and 2016, covering center-of-mass energies of 7 TeV (5 fb$^{-1}$), 8 TeV (20 fb$^{-1}$), and 13 TeV (36 fb$^{-1}$). Branching fractions were determined by comparing event yields to B$^+\to$ J/$\psi$K$^+$ decays (where J/$\psi\to\mu^+\mu^-$), a method that significantly reduces systematic uncertainties. The B$^0_\mathrm{s}\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay is observed with a significance of 5.6 standard deviations, yielding a branching fraction of $\mathcal{B}$(B$^0_\mathrm{s}\to\mu^+\mu^-$) = [2.9 $\pm$ 0.7 (exp) $\pm$ 0.2 (frag)] $\times$ 10$^{-9}$. The first uncertainty encompasses experimental statistical and systematic effects, while the second arises from the uncertainty in the fragmentation function ratio between B$^0_\mathrm{s}$ and B$^+$. No significant excess was detected for the B$^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay, resulting in an upper limit of $\mathcal{B}$(B$^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$) < 3.6 $\times$ 10$^{-10}$ at the 95% confidence level. The effective lifetime for B$^0_\mathrm{s}\to\mu^+\mu^-$ is measured as $\tau_{\mu^+\mu^-}$ = 1.70 $^{+0.61}_{-0.44}$ ps. These outcomes align with Standard Model predictions.

We define categories of Harish-Chandra bimodules for affine Lie algebras that mirror the structure of those with infinitesimal characters for simple Lie algebras, thereby resolving a longstanding issue posed by I. Frenkel and Malikov. Assuming an integrality condition, we demonstrate monoidal equivalences between blocks of these affine bimodule categories and specific variants of the affine Hecke category. This achievement relies on introducing a novel singular localization on Whittaker flag manifolds. Furthermore, this approach yields an alternative perspective on regular localization, revealing that the category of Lie algebra representations equipped with a generalized infinitesimal character corresponds to the parabolic induction, within categorical representation theory, of a Steinberg module.

In recent decades, the landscape of applied regression and predictive modeling has evolved significantly. First, the availability of larger datasets and more powerful computing resources has necessitated more flexible model specifications. Second, there is a growing recognition that full probabilistic modeling is essential in many contexts, going beyond the prediction of mere means or expectations. Third, Bayesian inference has gained traction both as an effective tool for regularizing model estimation and as a natural alternative to classical frequentist approaches. Despite extensive research and the development of various software packages in these three areas, no modular solution previously existed to seamlessly integrate them. To address this gap, the R package `bamlss` has been introduced, designed for Bayesian additive models for location, scale, and shape (and beyond). The package's core features highly efficient algorithms for Bayesian estimation and inference applicable to generalized additive models (GAMs) and generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), also known as distributional regression. Its architecture functions like "Lego bricks," offering a modular combination of diverse distributions (e.g., exponential family, Cox, joint models), regression terms (e.g., linear, splines, random effects, spatial fields), and estimators (e.g., MCMC, gradient boosting, lasso). This flexibility allows users to easily recombine these components to enhance classical models or develop custom solutions for specific challenges.

As an emerging discipline, network neuroscience has historically prioritized aggregate brain behaviors averaged across numerous experiments or extended recording periods to build robust models. However, these models struggle to account for spontaneous dynamic state transitions inherent to normal brain function. Recently, Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) trained on neuroimaging time series have emerged as a means to create trainable dynamical models, though they often present challenges in full parametrization and analysis. We introduce an interpretation of these neural HMMs as multiplex brain state graph models, termed Hidden Markov Graph Models (HMGMs). This framework enables the application of comprehensive network analysis techniques to dynamic brain activity. Additionally, we propose a general method for selecting HMM hyperparameters without external data, grounded in the principle of maximum entropy, which determines the number of layers in the multiplex model. We also develop a new tool to identify significant communities of brain regions using a spatiotemporal random walk procedure that leverages the model's inherent Markov structure. Analysis of real multi-subject fMRI data yields novel findings that support the modular processing hypothesis of the resting brain and provide new evidence of functional overlap both within and between dynamic brain state communities. Ultimately, our analysis pipeline offers a means to characterize the dynamic network activity of the brain under novel behaviors or conditions.

The scientific pursuit of extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) faces distinct challenges, primarily the significant uncertainty regarding what data to search for and when to initiate that search. Consequently, researchers have sought to establish fundamental limits and benchmarks for communication between human and extraterrestrial civilizations to predict likely signal types. While prior research framed this as an information-theoretic communication task, we propose viewing it instead as a detection problem, specifically a one-shot asymmetric hypothesis test. Adopting this perspective, we derive fundamental limits and offer straightforward examples of applying this framework to analyze and benchmark potential signals from alien civilizations. Our findings indicate that detecting electromagnetic signals requires substantially less power than establishing communication, that detection capabilities relative to power can exhibit non-linear behavior, and that much of this analysis can be addressed through computationally efficient optimization problems, providing practical tools for future investigation.

This study examines quantum transition amplitudes that involve time zigzags. The analysis is conducted using the Minkowski metric and standard quantum mechanics, without introducing additional postulates. We assert that while time zigzags are not suppressed at the quantum level, their contribution to the amplitude is zero.

The multifractal characteristics of fluid turbulence, as demonstrated by Parisi and Frisch, are directly linked to Leray's weak solutions of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. This connection reveals that the energy-dissipating set, $\mathbb{F}_{m}$, possesses a dimension range of $\Dim=3/m$ for $1 \leq m \leq \infty$. Consequently, the sub-Kolmogorov dissipation inverse length scales, $L\eta_{m}^{-1}$, follow the relation $Re^{3/(1+\Dim)}$, covering a spectrum from $Re^{3/4}$ to $Re^{3}$. In alignment with this, the multifractal model scaling parameter $h$ must satisfy $h \geq h_{min}$, where $-\twothirds \leq h_{min} \leq \third$.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have recently become prevalent in face hallucination tasks, leveraging their capacity to infer high-frequency details from extensive datasets. Nevertheless, most existing approaches struggle to simultaneously address the overall facial structure and fine texture details, which compromises the naturalness and fidelity of the reconstructed images and hinders performance in downstream applications such as face detection and recognition. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel External-Internal Split Attention Group (ESAG), comprising two distinct pathways dedicated to capturing facial structure and texture details, respectively. By integrating features from these pathways, our method simultaneously enhances structural consistency and detail fidelity. Furthermore, we propose a Split-Attention in Split-Attention Network (SISN) that reconstructs photorealistic high-resolution facial images by cascading multiple ESAG modules. Experimental evaluations on face hallucination and recognition demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves image clarity and substantially boosts subsequent face recognition accuracy. The source code is available at https://github.com/mdswyz/SISN-Face-Hallucination.

The study presents a variational approach for the Oseen equations formulated using vorticity and Bernoulli pressure, with velocity fully decoupled via the momentum balance and subsequently recovered through a post-processing step. A finite element scheme is developed employing equal-order Nédélec elements for vorticity and piecewise continuous polynomials for the Bernoulli pressure. Theoretical analysis establishes a priori error bounds in the $\mathrm{L}^2$-norm for velocity, pressure, and vorticity, contingent upon smallness conditions regarding either the convecting velocity or the mesh parameter. Additionally, a robust and efficient a posteriori error estimator is constructed and evaluated using weighted norms. Numerical experiments in both two and three dimensions demonstrate how the error indicator directs adaptive mesh refinement, validating the proposed formulation under typical flow regimes and confirming the theoretical predictions.

This study examines models explaining the origins of intra-strand parity and strand compositional asymmetries in bacterial genomes. Given the specific manner in which these features arise, we treat them as complementary phenomena requiring joint analysis. While most existing models attribute these traits to evolutionary mechanisms, recent proposals suggest they may instead be "relics" of a primordial genome, preserved throughout evolutionary history. We focus particularly on the S-H model, currently the only framework proposed to account for these asymmetries in primordial genomes as a result of randomness under chemical and physical constraints. Specifically, we discuss potential avenues for testing hypotheses within the S-H model and present a possible formulation of the S-H model as an evolutionary process.

Graphs serve as a versatile and broadly applicable representation for nearly all data processing challenges. Spectral graph theory, grounded in robust linear algebra principles, offers powerful algorithms that can be instrumental in creating deep network components with spectral properties. For example, these networks facilitate the design of task-specific optimal graphs or the derivation of a canonical, low-dimensional orthogonal embedding of data. Previous efforts to address this involved minimizing Rayleigh-quotient-based losses. In contrast, we introduce a method that directly learns the eigenspace. However, applying this direct approach in batch learning presents a significant challenge: the inconsistent mapping of features to eigenspace coordinates across different batches. We examine the degrees of freedom inherent in learning this task using batches and propose a stable alignment mechanism capable of handling both batch variations and changes in graph metrics. Our results demonstrate that the learned spectral embedding outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of NMI, ACC, Grassman distance, orthogonality, and classification accuracy, while also offering superior stability during the learning process.

A state on a tripartite quantum system $\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes \mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C}$ constitutes a quantum Markov chain, or exhibits quantum conditional independence, if it can be reconstructed from its marginal on $\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes \mathcal{H}_{B}$ via a quantum operation from $\mathcal{H}_{B}$ to $\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C}$ defined by the Petz map. Specifically, a quantum Markov chain $\rho_{ABC}$ satisfies $\rho_{ABC}=\rho_{BC}^{1/2}(\rho_B^{-1/2}\rho_{AB}\rho_B^{-1/2}\otimes id_C)\rho_{BC}^{1/2}$. This paper investigates the robustness of the Petz map across various metrics, examining whether the proximity of marginals ensures the proximity of Petz map outputs. The derived robustness results are independent of dimension for both infidelity $\delta$ and trace distance $\epsilon$.

Regarding applications, the sample complexity required for quantum Markov chain tomography—the number of copies of an unknown state needed to determine it—is $\tilde{\Theta}(\frac{(d_A^2+d_C^2)d_B^2}{\delta})$ for infidelity and $\tilde{\Theta}(\frac{(d_A^2+d_C^2)d_B^2}{\epsilon^2})$ for trace distance. For quantum Markov chain certification, which determines if a tripartite state matches a fixed Markov chain $\sigma_{ABC}$ or is at least $\delta$-far from it, the sample complexity is ${\Theta}(\frac{(d_A+d_C)d_B}{\delta})$ for infidelity and ${\Theta}(\frac{(d_A+d_C)d_B}{\epsilon^2})$ for trace distance. Additionally, testing whether $\rho_{ABC}$ is a quantum Markov chain or $\epsilon$-far from its Petz recovery state requires $\tilde{O}(\frac{\min\{d_Ad_B^3d_C^3,d_A^3d_B^3d_C\}}{\epsilon^2})$ copies. Finally, we extended the tomography findings to multipartite systems, demonstrating that $\tilde{O}(\frac{n^2\max_{i} \{d_i^2d_{i+1}^2\}}{\delta})$ copies suffice for $n$-partite quantum Markov chain tomography with infidelity $\delta$, where $d_i$ denotes the dimension of the $i$-th subsystem.

Contemporary neuroimaging modalities, including diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), allow researchers to model the human brain as a connectome or network. Grasping the structural details and hierarchical organization of these networks is crucial for deciphering both brain functionality and pathological conditions. Recently, the efficacy of graph neural networks (GNNs) in learning network representations has spurred the development of numerous GNN-based approaches for analyzing brain networks. These techniques typically utilize feature aggregation and global pooling to transform brain network data into compact, low-dimensional representations suitable for downstream tasks. However, current GNN methods often overlook the fact that different subjects' brain networks may necessitate varying numbers of aggregation steps, leading to the use of fixed-layer architectures that fail to adapt. Consequently, fully unlocking the potential of GNNs for brain network analysis remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce BN-GNN, a novel framework that identifies the optimal GNN architecture for each individual brain network. Specifically, BN-GNN leverages deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to train a meta-policy capable of automatically selecting the ideal number of feature aggregation layers for any given network. Comprehensive experiments across eight real-world datasets confirm that BN-GNN outperforms traditional GNNs on various brain network analysis tasks.

This work investigates the $K$-armed contextual dueling bandit problem, a sequential decision-making framework where a learner leverages context to select two actions but receives only \emph{preference-based feedback} indicating which action is superior. We address regret minimization under the realizability assumption, wherein feedback stems from a pairwise preference matrix accurately captured by a specific function class $\mathcal F$. We introduce a novel algorithm that attains the optimal regret rate for a newly defined best response regret metric, which represents a stricter performance criterion than those evaluated in previous studies. Furthermore, the algorithm is computationally efficient, operating in polynomial time given access to an online oracle for square loss regression over $\mathcal F$. This advancement resolves an open issue raised by Dudík et al. [2015] regarding the existence of oracle-efficient, regret-optimal algorithms for contextual dueling bandits.

For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, we investigate two families of large random matrices defined as $\mathcal{L}_n =\sum_{\alpha=1}^m\xi_\alpha \mathbf{y}_\alpha \mathbf{y}_\alpha ^T$ and $\mathcal{A}_n =\sum_{\alpha =1}^m\xi_\alpha (\mathbf{y}_\alpha \mathbf{x}_\alpha ^T+\mathbf{x}_\alpha \mathbf{y}_\alpha ^T)$. In these expressions, for each $n$, the coefficients $(\xi_\alpha )_\alpha$ are independent and identically distributed real random variables independent of the vector sequences $(\mathbf{x}_\alpha,\mathbf{y}_\alpha)_\alpha$. These vectors belong to $\mathbb{R}^n$, consist of independent random vectors (not necessarily independent across the two sequences), possess distinct covariance matrices, and generate bilinear forms that are well-concentrated. We analyze two primary asymptotic scenarios as $n$ and $m(n)$ grow: a standard regime where $m/n\to c$, and a modified regime where $m/n\to\infty$, $\mathbf{E}\xi\to 0$, yet $m\mathbf{E}\xi /n\to c$ for some constant $c\ge 0$. Under the assumption that the vector sequences are normalized and isotropic on average, we demonstrate that the empirical spectral distributions of $\mathcal{L}_n$ and $\mathcal{A}_n$ converge in probability to a specific Marchenko-Pastur law and an effective medium spectral distribution, respectively. Notably, when the coefficients $(\xi_\alpha )_\alpha$ are chosen as normalized Rademacher random variables within the modified regime, the resulting laws include shifted semicircle and standard semicircle distributions. Furthermore, we extend these findings to specific classes of matrices with block structures, previously examined in references [9, 21].

It is contended that merely observing the anisotropic azimuthal distribution of final-state particles is inadequate to determine if the matter created at RHIC exhibits hydrodynamic flow. A more conclusive assessment requires investigating the intrinsic interactions or correlations within the formed matter. Consequently, a spatially dependent azimuthal multiplicity-correlation pattern is proposed. This pattern distinctly reveals two distinct types of interactions occurring in the early stages of Au + Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV, as generated by RQMD with hadron re-scattering and AMPT with string melting, findings that deviate from expectations based on anisotropic expansion driven by elliptic flow.

Cell movement within tissues is a widespread occurrence. Specifically, in vitro monolayered cell colonies exhibit significant collective behavior characterized by swirl-like motion deep within the colony, yet the colony maintains cohesion without any cells escaping at the boundary. Consequently, the colony demonstrates liquid-like properties internally while coexisting with a cell-free "vacuum" externally. This raises questions regarding how strong adhesion can maintain unity without inducing a glassy, jammed state, what minimal model can capture this behavior, and what other activity signatures emerge from internal fluidity. We introduce a novel active Brownian particle model featuring attraction, where the interaction potential possesses a broad minimum, allowing particles sufficient wiggle room to collectively remain in a fluid state. We show that with moderate propulsion, this model reproduces the aforementioned fluid-vacuum coexistence. Furthermore, the interplay between the colony's fluid nature and cohesion results in a preferred outward orientation of cell polarity at the edge, generating tensile stress consistent with experimental observations in epithelial sheets. Higher propulsion levels predict the collective detachment of cell clusters. Finally, incorporating an alignment preference for cell polarity and velocity direction enhances coordinated, swirl-like motion, increases tensile stress, and promotes cell-cluster detachment.

This study derives novel analytic expressions for fixation time within the Wright-Fisher model under selection, addressing the three standard fixation scenarios: fixation at zero, one, or both. By employing a streamlined approach that relies solely on the law of total probability and Taylor expansions, we obtain second-order differential equations for fixation time. The resulting solutions are formulated as combinations of exponential integral functions and elementary functions. Additionally, we present approximate formulas consisting exclusively of elementary functions that are valid for small selection effects. An extensive simulation study evaluates the accuracy of our findings, demonstrating that they closely approximate the discrete problem even for small population sizes (in the hundreds) and large selection coefficients.

Spatio-temporal machine learning is essential for numerous societal uses, including agricultural monitoring, hydrological forecasting, and traffic management. These fields heavily depend on regional characteristics that capture spatial and temporal variations. However, spatio-temporal data presents distinct challenges for machine learning: 1) handling spatial heterogeneity across locations often requires multiple models; 2) models trained on specific regions struggle to generalize to diverse and anomalous areas; 3) the entanglement of spatial and temporal variations demands robust and adaptive solutions; and 4) real-world data scarcity (e.g., annual crop yield records) inherently complicates these problems. To address these issues, we introduce task-adaptive formulations and a model-agnostic meta-learning framework that integrates heterogeneous regional data into location-sensitive meta-tasks. Our approach employs an easy-to-hard task hierarchy, adapting different meta-models to varying difficulty levels. A primary benefit of this method is its ability to enhance adaptation across numerous heterogeneous tasks while improving generalization by automatically selecting the appropriate meta-model for new tasks based on their difficulty. We demonstrate that our framework outperforms diverse baselines and state-of-the-art meta-learning approaches. Extensive experiments using real crop yield data confirm the method's effectiveness in managing spatially heterogeneous tasks within real-world societal applications.

The Grassmann manifold, representing linear subspaces, is pivotal for modeling diverse applications spanning machine learning, computer vision, image processing, low-rank matrix optimization, dynamic decompositions, and model reduction. This work compiles essential geometric facts and formulas for the Grassmann manifold tailored to address these challenges using matrix-based algorithms. We present the geometry of the manifold through two complementary lenses: the representation of subspaces via orthogonal projectors and the quotient space perspective of the orthogonal group, where subspaces are treated as equivalence classes of orthogonal bases. This dual approach unifies related research tracks and facilitates a seamless transition between them. Key contributions include a numerically superior algorithm for the Riemannian logarithm map on the Grassmannian, which also offers a more elementary yet comprehensive characterization of the cut locus and conjugate points. Additionally, we derive formulas for parallel transport along geodesics within the orthogonal projector framework, expressions for the derivative of the exponential map, and formulas for Jacobi fields that vanish at a single point.

This study reports a measurement of the jet mass distribution for hadronic decays of boosted top quarks generated in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV. Using the CMS detector at the LHC, data corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ were analyzed. The analysis focuses on the lepton+jets channel of $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ events, selecting events where the lepton is either an electron or a muon. The hadronic decay products of the top quark ($t \to bW \to bq\mathrm{\bar{q}}'$) are reconstructed as a single jet with transverse momentum exceeding 400 GeV. By unfolding the $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ cross section as a function of jet mass to the particle level, a top quark mass of 172.6 $\pm$ 2.5 GeV was determined. This work introduces a new jet reconstruction technique for the first time at the LHC, achieving a threefold improvement in precision compared to a previous measurement. This result underscores the promise of using boosted top quarks for high-precision studies, with this novel method paving the way for future measurements.

In a seminal 1976 work, Gordon James introduced regularisation maps for integer partitions, which produce specific decomposition numbers for the modular representations of $\mathfrak{S}_n$. We present an extension of James's regularisation map and provide a proven algorithm for implementing these maps using the abacus.

Recurrences involving positive definite functions have found applications across various fields, often linking to the special functions that define the geometry of a given space. Specifically, for the sphere ${\mathbb S}^{d-1} \subset {\mathbb R}^d$, the strict positive definiteness of a zonal function $f(\cos \theta)$ is governed by the signs of the coefficients in its expansion using Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$, where $\lambda=(d-2)/2$. While recent findings indicate that classical differentiation and integration preserve positive definiteness in this setting, these operations shift the space dimension in increments of two. This paper introduces operators for zonal functions on the sphere that maintain (strict) positive definiteness while transitioning between dimensions by steps of one. These fractional operators are specifically designed to act suitably on the Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$.

The close contact between distinct materials creates a complex coupling of quasiparticles, frequently resulting in novel electronic states at their interface. In this study, we reveal a resonance-type many-body ground state in graphene—a non-magnetic two-dimensional Dirac semimetal—when it is grown on SmB6, a Kondo insulator, using thermal decomposition of fullerene molecules. Such ground states are typically found in three-dimensional magnetic materials with correlated electrons. While the electron band structure of pure graphene remains largely unchanged above the substrate's characteristic Kondo temperature, cooling the system causes the graphene Dirac fermions to hybridize with the Sm 4f states. Further cooling and an increase in graphene's charge carrier density lead to a significant boost in both hybridization and Kondo resonance, confirming that the conduction electrons of graphene are screening the local magnetic moments of Sm 4f at the interface. These results demonstrate that the Kondo effect can be induced in graphene through the proximity of SmB6, with its strength modulated by temperature and charge carrier density.

The paper investigates the $GL$-ideal of relations among the generators of the invariant algebra for the dihedral group acting on $m$-tuples of vectors within its standard 2-dimensional representation. It is demonstrated that this $GL$-ideal can be generated by relations involving at most three vector variables. Furthermore, explicit minimal generating sets for this ideal are determined for the case where $m=2$, as well as for the dihedral group of order 8 with any $m$.

In relativistic dynamics, force and acceleration are not necessarily aligned. This article revisits the motion of a particle subjected to a constant force, $\boldsymbol{f}$. For two-dimensional motion, the final velocity along each axis is given by $(f_{i}/f)c$, regardless of initial conditions, resulting in an asymptotic velocity that is always parallel to the force. The scenario where the force acts along a single axis is examined in detail, illustrating the behavior of velocity and acceleration across various configurations. Previous findings in the literature regarding velocity and acceleration are refined and explored more thoroughly. Contrary to earlier claims, this study demonstrates that a negative acceleration component can occur in the direction of the largest force component and that acceleration does not necessarily decrease monotonically toward zero.

Deep learning networks have been integrated throughout every phase of the MRI pipeline, yielding state-of-the-art outcomes. However, this progress entails substantial increases in computational demands and storage needs. Consequently, substituting these networks with compact models at various stages of the MRI workflow can markedly decrease storage requirements and offer significant speed enhancements. While knowledge distillation is a prevalent technique for model compression in computer vision, our study introduces a knowledge distillation (KD) framework tailored for image-to-image tasks within the MRI domain. Our goal is to create compact, low-parameter models that maintain performance levels. We combine an attention-based feature distillation approach with imitation loss and validate its efficacy on the widely used DC-CNN architecture for MRI reconstruction. Through extensive experiments on Cardiac, Brain, and Knee MRI datasets across 4x, 5x, and 8x acceleration factors, we found that student networks trained with our proposed KD-assisted teacher outperformed those trained independently across all datasets and acceleration levels. Specifically, on the Knee dataset, the student network achieved a 65% reduction in parameters, along with a 2x speedup on CPU and a 1.5x speedup on GPU compared to the teacher. Additionally, we benchmarked our attention-based feature distillation against other methods and performed an ablation study to assess the impact of attention-based distillation and imitation loss. Finally, we extended this KD framework to MRI super-resolution, yielding promising results.

We examine how long-range Coulomb interactions influence the low-temperature behavior of a second-order Dirac semimetal using renormalization group methods. Unlike first-order Dirac semimetals, the full rotational symmetry is broken even in the continuum limit; consequently, the low-energy dynamics are governed by two dimensionless parameters: the coupling constant and the ratio of anisotropy parameters. We demonstrate that the coupling constant flows to zero, while the anisotropy ratio approaches a fixed value at low energies, allowing physical quantities to be calculated via renormalized perturbation theory. As an application, we derive the temperature dependence of the specific heat by solving the renormalization group equations. Due to the broken rotational symmetry, a crossover temperature scale $T_c$ (and corresponding length scale $L_c$) emerges. Physical observables resemble those of the first-order Dirac semimetal only when the temperature is significantly lower than $T_c$. Similarly, the screened Coulomb potential becomes anisotropic at distances shorter than $L_c$, whereas its unscreened form is restored at larger distances.

Although imitation learning for vision-based autonomous mobile robot navigation has garnered significant research interest, current methods generally necessitate state-action demonstrations recorded on the specific deployment platform. This presents a challenge when outfitting the platform for data collection is difficult or impossible, or when the demonstrator lacks direct access to the robot. Can imitation learning for this application function under such constraints? This study posits that it can, leveraging recent concepts from Imitation from Observation (IfO) to enable robots to navigate using solely ego-centric video from a demonstrator, despite viewpoint discrepancies. Consequently, we present a novel algorithm called Visual Observation only Imitation Learning for Autonomous navigation (VOILA), capable of learning navigation policies from a single video demonstration captured by a physically distinct agent. Evaluated within the photorealistic AirSim simulator, VOILA demonstrates successful imitation of experts and the ability to generalize navigation policies to new environments. Furthermore, we validate VOILA's efficacy in a real-world scenario, showing that it enables a wheeled Jackal robot to imitate a human walking in an environment using video recorded by a mobile phone camera.

We investigate the connection between the quantum state of a localized matter source and its distant gravitational field. When the source occupies an energy eigenstate, the corresponding graviton state is primarily determined by that energy value at the leading order. Provided there are no accidental degeneracies in energy levels, a unique one-to-one correspondence exists between the graviton states at spacetime's boundary and the states of the matter source. A typical semiclassical source typically generates an entangled asymptotic graviton state. Furthermore, we demonstrate a purely quantum gravitational phenomenon where the subleading asymptotic behavior of the graviton state relies on the source's internal structure. These findings confirm the presence of ubiquitous quantum hair arising from gravitational interactions.

Using the relativistic, gauge-invariant spectral integral approach, we computed the radiative decays $\rho(770) \to \gamma\pi(140)$ and $\omega(780) \to \gamma\pi(140)$ by modeling all mesons ($\pi, \rho, \omega$) as quark-antiquark pairs. The resulting $q\bar{q}$ wave functions for mesons and the photon provide a satisfactory fit to experimental data ($\Gamma^{(exp)}_{\rho^{\pm}\to\gamma\pi^{\pm}}=68\pm 30$ keV, $\Gamma^{(exp)}_{\rho^{0}\to\gamma\pi^0}=77\pm 28$ keV, $\Gamma^{(exp)}_{\omega\to\gamma\pi^0}=776\pm 45$ keV), allowing us to estimate the pion bremsstrahlung coupling constant $g_\pi \equiv g_\pi (u\to d \pi)$. Two solutions for $|g_\pi|$ were identified: $16.7 \pm 0.3 ^{+0.1}_{-2.3}$ (Solution I) and $3.0 \pm 0.3 ^{+0.1}_{-2.1}$ (Solution II). Assuming SU(6)-symmetry for nucleons, Solution I yields a $\pi NN$ coupling range of $16.4 \le g_{\pi NN}^2/(4\pi) \le 23.2$, which qualitatively aligns with $\pi N$ scattering data ($g_{\pi NN}^2/(4\pi)\simeq 14$). For excited states, Solution I predicts partial widths of $\Gamma (\rho_{2S}^\pm\to \gamma\pi)\simeq 10 - 130$ keV, $\Gamma (\rho_{2S}^0\to \gamma\pi)\simeq 10 - 130$ keV, and $\Gamma (\omega_{2S}\to \gamma\pi)\simeq 60 - 1080$ keV. The substantial uncertainties highlight the need for further measurements of radiative meson processes at higher masses.

Let $\{E_{(p,q)}\}$ denote a family of elliptic curves defined over a rational field by the equation $E_{(p,q)} : y^2 = x^3 - p^2x + q^2$, where $p$ and $q$ are prime numbers exceeding five. Previous research established that for all such $p$ and $q$, these curves possess a rank of at least two, featuring two independent points. This study demonstrates that, under specific conditions, two such points can be extended to form a basis for $E_{(p,q)}$ with high confidence that this recovery will be complete.

Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are commonly located at the cores of the majority of massive galaxies. Determining SMBH mass is crucial for comprehending their origins and evolution; however, conventional techniques rely on costly spectroscopic data. We introduce an algorithm that estimates SMBH masses by analyzing quasar light curves, thereby eliminating the necessity for expensive spectra. By training, validating, and testing neural networks on multi-color optical light curves from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Stripe 82 for a sample of 38,939 spectroscopically confirmed quasars, we map the nonlinear relationship between SMBH mass and these light curves. Our findings reveal a $1\sigma$ scatter of 0.37 dex between predicted masses and the standard virial mass estimates derived from SDSS single-epoch spectra, a level of precision comparable to the systematic uncertainties of the latter. These results offer significant implications for optimizing future observations with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The accompanying code, \textsf{AGNet}, is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/snehjp2/AGNet}.

Carl Morris introduced the Finite Selection Model (FSM) in the 1970s to facilitate the design of the RAND Health Insurance Experiment (HIE), a landmark and extensive social science study in the United States (Morris 1979, Newhouse et al. 1993). The FSM operates on the principle that treatment groups take turns selecting units in a fair, random sequence to maximize a shared criterion. Specifically, during each turn, a group chooses the available unit that most significantly enhances the overall quality of its assigned set based on that criterion. Building upon this foundation, we revisit, formalize, and expand the FSM as a versatile instrument for experimental design.

Drawing on D-optimality, we introduce and evaluate a novel selection criterion within the FSM framework. This approach, which utilizes a D-optimal selection function, requires no tuning parameters, maintains affine invariance, and effectively recovers classical designs like randomized block and matched-pair structures when applicable. For experiments involving multiple arms, we develop algorithms to ensure a fair and random ordering of treatment selections. We assess the FSM's efficacy through a case study modeled on the HIE and an analysis of ten randomized studies across health and social sciences. Results indicate that, on average, the FSM achieves 68% superior covariate balance compared to complete randomization and 56% better balance than rerandomization in typical scenarios. Consequently, we recommend adopting the FSM for experimental design due to its conceptual clarity, efficiency, balance, and robustness.

Bus bunching is an inherent issue that compromises the efficiency and stability of public transit. Current solutions involve deliberately extending bus dwell times at specific stops. Existing approaches include conventional formula-based methods for calculating control duration and reinforcement learning (RL) techniques that derive control policies through iterative system interactions. This paper introduces the Integrated Proximal Policy Optimization with Dual-Headway (IPPO-DH) model, which combines conventional headway control with reinforcement learning. By merging these algorithms, IPPO-DH leverages their respective strengths, achieving higher efficiency in standard conditions and greater stability in challenging environments. To validate these benefits, a bus simulation environment was developed to compare IPPO-DH against various RL and conventional methods. The results indicate that the proposed model retains the practical utility of conventional techniques by preventing the instability often seen with RL in specific scenarios, while simultaneously outperforming traditional controls in efficiency. These findings offer new insights for optimizing real-world bus transit systems.

For many decades, identifying the sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major unsolved challenge in high-energy astrophysics. A promising strategy to address this mystery involves correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, as neutrinos directly trace hadronic interactions and remain unaffected by magnetic deflection. This paper outlines three distinct methods for correlating the arrival directions of these particles. Data on neutrinos come from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES, while UHECR data (with energies exceeding ~50 EeV) are sourced from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. Both datasets offer enhanced statistics and refined reconstructions compared to our 2015 findings. The first analysis employs a high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source detection to identify excesses of neutrinos clustering near UHECR trajectories. The second method looks for an excess of UHECRs pointing toward the highest-energy neutrinos, while the third examines excesses of UHECR-neutrino pairs across various angular scales. No significant excesses were detected in any of these analyses, and previously reported over-fluctuations have seen their statistical significance diminished. Consequently, these results allow for tighter constraints on the spatially correlated neutrino flux associated with UHECRs.

Undirected probabilistic graphical models capture the conditional dependencies and Markov properties among a set of random variables. Understanding the sparsity of these models is crucial for effectively modeling multivariate distributions and conducting efficient inference. Although learning graph structures from data has been widely researched for specific parametric distributions, most current methods struggle to consistently reconstruct the graph when dealing with non-Gaussian data. We introduce an algorithm designed to learn the Markov structure of continuous, non-Gaussian distributions. To assess conditional independence, we propose a score derived from integrated Hessian information within the joint log-density, proving that this score serves as an upper bound for conditional mutual information across a broad class of distributions. Our algorithm, SING, computes this score by estimating density through a deterministic coupling generated by a triangular transport map, iteratively leveraging the sparse structure of the map to uncover graph sparsity. We demonstrate that for specific non-Gaussian datasets, our method successfully recovers the graph structure even when using a biased density approximation. Additionally, we apply SING to identify dependencies between states in a chaotic dynamical system characterized by local interactions.

The coupling between a quantum emitter and a topological photonic system causes both components to exhibit unusual behaviors. This study investigates a configuration where a giant atom interacts with two distinct points along a one-dimensional topological waveguide constructed from a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain. We analyze the topological characteristics of this hybrid setup and discover that the giant atom functions as an effective boundary, generating chiral zero-energy modes within the waveguide under periodic boundary conditions. These modes share properties akin to those found in an SSH model with open boundaries. Furthermore, the structured environment of the SSH waveguide induces retardation and non-Markovian dissipation in the giant atom. Our findings are expected to encourage further research into matter-topological environment interactions, and experimental validation using superconducting quantum circuits appears feasible with current technology.

Growing attention has been directed toward multi-modal imaging as a means to derive more reliable estimates of Functional Connectivity (FC) within high-dimensional contexts. We introduce innovative algorithms that adapt graphical methods by integrating diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) with statistically rigorous controls, ensuring both computational efficiency and scalability. Our approach utilizes a graphical random walk on DTI data to establish a novel metric of structural influence, emphasizing relevant connected components. Subsequently, we assess minimum subnetwork sizes and identify subnetwork topologies through permutation testing prior to evaluating the significance of these components. Comprehensive simulations indicate that our method matches the power of existing techniques while offering superior speed, equal or enhanced robustness, and straightforward implementation. To validate our approach, we examined task-based fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project, uncovering new insights into brain interactions during motor tasks. We anticipate that the transparency and flexibility of our method will be highly valuable as the structure-function relationship advances network estimation. Furthermore, scalability will increasingly become critical as neurological data grow more granular and high-dimensional.

Genetic research frequently focuses on quantitative traits, where identifying relevant genetic factors aids in understanding disease origins. Quantile regression analyzes the conditional quantiles of the response variable, offering a more thorough characterization of the regression structure. However, genetic studies typically deal with high-dimensional genomic data, and the regression structure often exhibits heterogeneity in both effect magnitudes and sparsity. To address this potential genetic heterogeneity, including variations in sparsity, a regularized quantile regression approach is proposed. The theoretical properties of this method are explored, and its performance is evaluated via multiple simulation studies. Additionally, a real-world dataset is analyzed to illustrate the method's practical application.

The contextual bandit framework offers a theoretically sound basis for diverse applications. Although prior research typically assumes independence between noise and contexts, our study addresses a more realistic scenario where noise acts as a latent confounder influencing both contexts and rewards. While this confounded setting broadens applicability, it introduces bias in reward estimation that results in significant regret. To mitigate these challenges, we employ dual instrumental variable regression to accurately recover the true reward function. We demonstrate that this method achieves a near-optimal convergence rate within two commonly used reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Consequently, we develop computationally efficient and regret-optimal algorithms grounded in these theoretical assurances for confounded bandit problems. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms in this setting.

Recent advancements have shown promise in automatic stage scoring by extracting spatio-temporal features from electroencephalogram (EEG) data; however, these approaches rely on tedious manual feature engineering and specific domain expertise. To address this, we introduce an adaptive framework that probabilistically encodes, filters, and accumulates input signals, subsequently weighting the derived features based on half-Gaussian probabilities of signal intensities. These adaptive representations are then input into a transformer model to automatically identify the relevance between features and specific stages. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the largest available public dataset, benchmarked against state-of-the-art techniques, confirm the efficacy of our proposed method and highlight potential avenues for future research.

Although temporal data is vital for numerous database applications, existing support for querying such data remains inadequate. To address this, we introduce the RD-index, a structure designed to handle range-duration queries on interval-timestamped relations by constraining both the timeline positions and the durations of tuples. Modeled as a grid in a two-dimensional space—where axes represent timeline position and timestamp duration—the RD-index adapts its cell construction based on data distribution to ensure uniform interval counts per cell. This approach offers provable bounds on operation runtimes, facilitates straightforward implementation, and delivers highly predictable query performance. Evaluations across diverse datasets and workloads, analyzing both aggregate query rates and individual query behaviors, demonstrate that the RD-index surpasses baseline methods for its specific range-duration use case. Additionally, it exceeds the performance of specialized indexes even on workloads involving queries that constrain only duration or only range.

Standard imaging relies on three fundamental components: a light source that illuminates and scatters off a target, the capture of that scattered light, and a detector capable of spatial resolution. However, these essential elements often restrict the use of conventional imaging for sensitive biological specimens due to limitations in low-light detection and the inevitable damage caused by photon interaction. We introduce and experimentally validate a quantum imaging protocol that eliminates all three of these constraints. By integrating a single-photon Michelson interferometer with a nonlinear interferometer based on induced coherence and employing single-pixel imaging, we achieve interaction-free, single-pixel quantum imaging of structured objects using photons that never interact with the target. This approach pushes quantum imaging to its limit, requiring no object-photon interaction and significantly reducing detection needs. Consequently, our work enables the characterization of delicate samples via single-pixel imaging at silicon-detectable wavelengths.

We present a novel method for measuring electric (E) fields, designed to create a compact, broadband, self-calibrating E-field probe with direct SI traceability. This method relies on the interaction between radio frequency (RF) fields and alkali atoms in Rydberg states. Specifically, the RF field induces an energy splitting in these states through the Autler-Townes effect, which is then detected using electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT).
