This study examines the steady-state fingering instability of an elastic membrane dividing two fluids of differing densities under external pressure within a rotating Hele-Shaw cell. We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving mixed modes and circumferentially localized folds, varying with rotation rate and external pressure. The analysis includes both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral configurations, with results illustrated through bifurcation diagrams. Furthermore, the ratio of the system scale to the natural length scale is identified as the key factor governing the sequence of primary bifurcations from the unperturbed circular state, as well as the resulting solution profiles and the initiation of secondary bifurcations.

Our recent arXiv preprints and published works addressing the Riemann-Lanczos and Weyl-Lanczos problems have highlighted the necessity of re-examining the algebraic structure of Bianchi identities within Riemannian geometry. Furthermore, we observed that in our 1978 book, we previously employed a novel approach to analyze compatibility conditions (CC) for operators that are not necessarily formally integrable (FI), utilizing this method to construct canonical, formally exact differential sequences at the jet level. This paper aims to demonstrate that the synthesis of these two insights underscores the critical role of the Spencer operator and Spencer $\delta$-cohomology, which remain notably absent from contemporary mathematical physics. The derived results are inevitable, relying solely on elementary combinatorics and diagram chasing, and they offer the first purely intrinsic interpretation of the counts for successive first, second, third, and higher-order generating CC. While these findings align with the linearized Killing operator over the Minkowski metric, they significantly diverge from recent publications concerning the same operator over Schwarzschild and Kerr metrics. Numerous examples illustrate these new techniques, including the provision of the only known symbol in the literature that is 2-acyclic yet not of finite type, contrasting with the conformal case.

This study examines a dynamical system governed by autonomous differential equations on $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$. Leveraging Mickens' rule for the nonlocal approximation of nonlinear terms, we develop an implicit Nonstandard Finite Difference (NSFD) scheme that, provided existence and uniqueness conditions are met, functions as an explicit time-reversible method. Beyond demonstrating elementary stability, we establish that the scheme is second-order accurate and domain-preserving, thereby resolving an outstanding issue regarding the creation of higher-order nonstandard schemes free from spurious solutions, while also extending the tangent condition to discrete dynamical systems. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is shown to be directly applicable to mass action-based models in biological and chemical processes.

This study numerically investigates solute mass transfer from a rigid, fluid-filled spherical capsule under shear flow, accounting for unsteady, continuous, and non-uniform surface boundary conditions. In this scenario, the capsule functions as a reservoir where the internal solute concentration diminishes over time, distinguishing it from classical models involving constant surface concentration or mass flux. Using fully three-dimensional lattice Boltzmann simulations, the flow and concentration fields are calculated, with fluid-structure two-way coupling implemented via the immersed boundary method. The impact of flow dynamics and boundary conditions on mass transfer efficiency is quantified through the Sherwood number, which rises due to the combined influence of forced convection and shear forces generated by the capsule's rotation. Furthermore, maintaining continuity in both concentration and mass flux at the capsule surface results in a notably lower Sherwood number compared to cases with constant and uniform boundary conditions. These findings are equally applicable to heat transfer problems involving the cooling of an initially hot spherical particle, provided that concentration is substituted with temperature and the Sherwood number with the Nusselt number.

The radiation resilience of J-series silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) has been investigated for their potential use in future space-based scintillation detectors. Multiple SiPM samples were subjected to 101.4 MeV proton irradiation, achieving a 1 MeV neutron-equivalent fluence between 1.27×10⁸ and 1.23×10¹⁰ n/cm². Post-irradiation analysis revealed a significant rise in dark current and noise, raising concerns regarding power usage, thermal management, and the ability to detect low-energy events on extended space missions. Testing with a CeBr₃ scintillator indicated that after exposure to the highest fluence (1.23×10¹⁰ n/cm²) and subsequent room-temperature annealing, the dark noise of a single 6 mm² SiPM at room temperature surged from 0.1 keV to 2 keV. Consequently, the gamma-ray detection threshold for a CeBr₃ system employing a 4-SiPM array rose to roughly 20 keV, while a 16-SiPM array configuration saw its threshold increase to approximately 40 keV. However, proton irradiation exerted only a minimal impact on the average detector signal, implying that SiPM gain and photon detection efficiency remained largely unaffected.

The Vlasov-Schrödinger-Poisson system serves as a kinetic-quantum hybrid framework for modeling quasi-lower dimensional electron gases. Within this context, we establish a broad class of 2D kinetic/1D quantum steady states in bounded domains by identifying them as generalized free energy minimizers. Furthermore, we demonstrate their finite subband structure, monotonicity, uniqueness, and conditional dynamical stability. Although our proof relies on the concentration-compactness principle, the hybrid nature of the system introduces specific challenges due to a lack of compactness (refer to Remark 1.9). To address these issues, we implement a three-step refinement of the minimizing sequence utilizing rearrangement and partial minimization techniques, with the coercivity lemma for free energy (Lemma 5.3) playing a pivotal role.

This study investigates the interplay between speaker and emotion recognition. Initially, we demonstrate that transfer learning allows speaker recognition knowledge to be repurposed for emotion recognition tasks. Conversely, we analyze how emotional states impact speaker recognition accuracy. Regarding emotion recognition, we find that simple linear models achieve strong results using features from pre-trained systems like x-vector, and performance is further enhanced by fine-tuning for specific emotion classification. Our experiments were conducted across three datasets: IEMOCAP, MSP-Podcast, and Crema-D. Fine-tuning yielded absolute performance gains of 30.40%, 7.99%, and 8.61% over non-pre-trained baselines on these respective datasets. Additionally, we examined the influence of emotion on speaker verification, revealing that verification accuracy is sensitive to the emotional state of the test speaker. Notably, trials involving angry utterances resulted in the lowest performance across all three datasets. We anticipate that these findings will spark further research within the speaker recognition community.

The paper primarily investigates the domains of definition through the boundary conditions of minimal and maximal operators, along with the selfadjoint extensions of a minimal operator linked to a fourth-order differential equation. Additionally, it establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for these operators to possess either a purely discrete or continuous spectrum, to admit an extension with a resolvent from the point spectrum, and to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the spectrum in cases of pure discreteness. Finally, it introduces a novel and more generalized approach for calculating regularized traces of operators with discrete spectra associated with a specific class of boundary value problems.

This paper introduces novel general convergence findings regarding the behavior of the Distributed Bellman-Ford (DBF) family of routing protocols, encompassing both distance-vector (e.g., RIP) and path-vector (e.g., BGP) approaches. First, we introduce a fresh algebraic framework for abstract routing challenges that utilizes fewer primitives than earlier models while supporting more expressive policy languages; notably, this is the first model to enable concurrent reasoning about both distance-vector and path-vector protocols. Second, we explicitly illustrate how DBF protocols function as instances of a broader class of asynchronous iterative algorithms, leveraging existing powerful convergence results. Building on Sobrinho's previously established sufficient and necessary conditions for path-vector protocol convergence, we generalize and strengthen these findings in several ways: we demonstrate that with slight adjustments, they also apply to distance-vector protocols; we prove that they ensure a unique final routing solution, thereby ruling out anomalies like BGP wedgies; and we relax the asynchronous communication model to show that the results remain valid even when routing messages are lost, reordered, or duplicated. Third, our model and theoretical results have been completely formalized within the Agda theorem prover. The resulting library serves as a robust tool for rapidly prototyping and formally verifying new policy languages. For instance, we have formally verified the correctness of a policy language featuring numerous BGP characteristics, including communities, conditional policies, path-inflation, and route filtering.

The experimental identification of solvated excess proton signatures in infrared difference absorption spectra, particularly the continuum band situated between water bending and stretching modes, has long been established; however, connecting these spectral features to the microscopic proton-transfer mechanism previously depended on normal-mode analysis. By employing trajectory-decomposition techniques within ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations of aqueous hydrochloric acid, we examine excess-proton dynamics. We demonstrate that the continuum band observed in the 2000–3000 cm$^{-1}$ range arises from normal-mode oscillations of transient H$_3$O$^+$ complexes. Furthermore, a distinct peak at 400 cm$^{-1}$ indicates the coupling between excess-proton motion and the vibrational modes of adjacent water molecules. Actual proton transfer between water molecules, which requires overcoming an energy barrier at larger separations and thus does not constitute a normal mode, is defined by two specific time scales: first, a waiting time of 200–300 fs for the transfer to occur, resulting in a broad, weak shoulder near ~100 cm$^{-1}$ that aligns with experimental THz spectra; second, an average transfer event duration of approximately 14 fs, generating a well-defined spectral contribution around 1200 cm$^{-1}$ that matches the position and width of prior mid-infrared experimental data.

The war in Ukraine, which commenced in February 2022, triggered the most significant refugee crisis in decades, displacing millions internally and forcing millions to cross borders into neighboring nations. This paper explores how Internet measurements can be leveraged to analyze this humanitarian emergency. Utilizing preliminary data from the initial two months of the conflict, we examine how such metrics reveal trends in refugee movements from Ukraine to adjacent countries and subsequently to further destinations. We contend that these findings can substantially support international initiatives aimed at mapping refugee flows to facilitate aid and protection efforts.

Global rates of atrial fibrillation (AFib) are rising alarmingly, prompting the development of an automated deep neural network system for early risk detection. Recognizing that effective signal pre-processing is crucial for accurate classification, this two-part study first proposes an end-to-end model using denoising autoencoders (DAE) to clean electrocardiogram signals. We evaluated three architectures—convolutional neural networks (CNN), dense neural networks (DNN), and recurrent neural networks (RNN)—and found that the CNN-based DAE outperformed the others. Consequently, these denoised signals were used to train deep neural networks for classification, with performance assessed via accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

The proposed end-to-end deep learning model achieved remarkable results, including 99.20% accuracy, 99.50% specificity, 99.50% sensitivity, and a 99.00% true positive rate. This surpasses the average accuracy of 96.26% obtained by the compared algorithms by 3.2%, with the CNN classification network demonstrating superior performance. Furthermore, the model is computationally efficient for real-time use, processing a 24-hour ECG signal in approximately 1.3 seconds. When tested on an unseen dataset with varying arrhythmia proportions to assess robustness, the model achieved a recall of 99.10% and a precision of 98.50%.

Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) is vital for achieving intelligent wireless communications. While numerous deep learning models, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have been developed for AMC, their high computational cost renders them unsuitable for post-5G networks, which demand both high accuracy and low latency. To address these issues, a new AMC scheme leveraging involution within a residual network bottleneck structure is introduced. By replacing convolution with involution and integrating a self-attention mechanism, the model's discriminative power and expressiveness are significantly enhanced. Simulation outcomes indicate that this proposed approach outperforms other benchmark methods in terms of both classification accuracy and convergence speed.

This paper presents LINKS, a comprehensive dataset comprising 100 million one-degree-of-freedom planar linkage mechanisms and 1.1 billion coupler curves. LINKS exceeds the size of any existing planar mechanism database by more than a factor of 1,000 and is not restricted to specific configurations like four-bar or six-bar linkages, which typically dominate current repositories. The dataset includes 100 million mechanisms, their corresponding simulation data, normalized paths, a curated selection of paths, the generation and simulation code, and an interactive web demo. The curated paths serve to mitigate biases inherent in raw mechanism-generated paths, thereby ensuring a more uniform representation of the design space. We detail the methodologies used to create this massive dataset and address the challenges associated with such scale. To achieve this, we introduce a novel operator for generating 1-DOF mechanism topologies. Additionally, we significantly accelerate slow mechanism simulations by vectorizing and parallelizing our simulator across numerous threads, achieving a speedup of 800 times over basic algorithms. This optimization is critical because, on average, only 1 in 500 generated candidates is valid, necessitating billions of simulations to ensure validity. Finally, we demonstrate the dataset's utility through a bi-directional chamfer distance-based shape retrieval study, illustrating its effectiveness in identifying mechanisms capable of tracing paths that closely match desired targets.

This research employs Large Eddy Simulation to investigate Langmuir turbulence within the deep ocean surrounding a substantial macroalgal farm, utilizing wave-averaged equations to model wave-current interactions. The study reveals that hydrodynamic processes over the farm generate a stationary flow pattern resembling Langmuir circulations, which remains fixed in space across the farm. These secondary circulations arise because shear generated cross-stream by rows of canopy elements creates a steady vertical vorticity field; this vorticity is subsequently rotated downstream by the vortex force. As the driving mechanism aligns with the Craik-Leibovich type 2 instability theory, these features are classified as attached Langmuir circulations. A triple decomposition of the flow field was conducted to analyze the kinematics and energy exchange between the mean flow, the secondary flow induced by farm drag, and transient eddies. Visualizations and statistical data indicate that these attached circulations represent the upper ocean mixed layer adjusting to the presence of the macroalgal farm and will diminish or vanish once flow equilibrium is achieved within the farm. Furthermore, energy budget analysis based on triple decomposition shows that the secondary flow derives its energy from the mean flow via canopy drag, whereas transient eddies sustain themselves through energy conversion from the secondary flow and wave energy transported by Stokes drift.

The effective potential of a spinning heavy symmetric top is investigated under conditions where the magnitudes of the conserved angular momenta differ. This analysis examines how the effective potential varies with these conserved quantities. The results indicate that when one angular momentum magnitude exceeds the other, the potential's minimum approaches a constant value determined by these momenta, whereas it diverges to infinity if the other magnitude is larger. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that neither strong nor weak top separation methods provide adequate solutions across all scenarios.

This study examines the interplay between dark matter (DM) constraints and the scalar sector within a scale-invariant (SI) scotogenic model. Motivated by neutrino mass generation and DM stability under a classically SI framework, this model extends the Standard Model (SM) with a real singlet, an inert scalar doublet, and three Majorana singlet fermions, where the lightest fermion ($N_1$) serves as the DM candidate. Beyond annihilation channels involving $N_1N_1\rightarrow\ell_{\alpha}\ell_{\beta},\nu_{\alpha}\bar{\nu}_{\beta}$, the DM can also annihilate through several s-channel processes into SM particles mediated by the Higgs or dilaton. These mechanisms permit the Yukawa interactions responsible for neutrino mass to remain small, thereby avoiding the mass degeneracy between CP-even and CP-odd inert scalars that plagues the minimal scotogenic model. Unlike many Majorana DM scenarios, the DM in this SI-scotogenic framework couples to quarks at tree level, making direct detection constraints crucial for defining the viable parameter space. Consequently, the primary objective of this work is to analyze the correlations between DM requirements and the scalar sector in this specific model.

Single-Image Super Resolution (SISR) is a well-established challenge in computer vision that has been investigated for many years. While recent advancements have shifted the focus toward deep learning methodologies to achieve state-of-the-art performance, most of these approaches rely on models with millions of parameters and layers, hindering their practical deployment. To address this, we introduce XLSR, an extremely lightweight, quantization-robust, real-time super-resolution network designed with awareness of hardware constraints, specifically the Synaptics Dolphin NPU. Drawing inspiration from root modules used in image classification, we adapted these components for SISR tasks. Additionally, to ensure robustness against uint8 quantization, we implemented a Clipped ReLU activation at the network's final layer, successfully balancing reconstruction quality with computational efficiency. Despite containing 30 times fewer parameters than the VDSR model, XLSR outperforms it on the Div2K validation set and secured victory in the Mobile AI 2021 Real-Time Single Image Super Resolution Challenge.

This paper introduces an experimental method for detecting gravitational interactions between milligram-scale masses, utilizing Meissner effect levitation of neodymium magnets. The setup involves two superconducting lead traps, each containing a levitated magnet that functions as a harmonic oscillator. By driving the motion of one magnet into resonance with the other, we demonstrate that measuring the gravitational field of a 4 mg sphere is feasible, with the sensitivity to predictably detect attractions from masses as small as 30 μg within a practical timeframe. We illustrate this acceleration sensitivity by applying it to a specific case, thereby validating the potential to test models of modified Newtonian dynamics.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) may account for some or all of the current dark matter density. Inflation offers a mechanism to generate PBH seeds during a phase where the inflaton field's velocity $\phi$ drops rapidly toward zero. We calculated the primordial power spectra of curvature perturbations arising from Gauss-Bonnet (GB) corrected Higgs inflation, where the inflaton features both a nonminimal gravitational coupling and a GB coupling. When the scalar-GB coupling changes rapidly during inflation, curvature perturbations are significantly amplified due to an effective potential $V_{\rm eff}(\phi)$ exhibiting plateau, bump, and intermediate structures. We identify parameter spaces where PBHs can constitute the entirety of dark matter across all three potential types. Notably, models with bump- and intermediate-type potentials produce primordial scalar and tensor power spectra consistent with recent Planck observations on cosmic microwave background scales. This alignment stems from the fact that the number of e-foldings $\Delta N_c$ around the bump region of $V_{\rm eff}(\phi)$ can be as low as a few, whereas plateau-type models typically require $\Delta N_c$ exceeding ten.

Structured light (SL) systems capture high-precision 3D geometry through active illumination but face difficulties in settings characterized by intense ambient light, global illumination, and cross-device interference. To enhance SL robustness, this paper introduces a versatile technique that projects redundant optical signals alongside standard SL patterns. This approach makes projected signals more distinguishable from noise, facilitating easier geometry recovery via straightforward signal processing and yielding performance "coding gains." The authors present three applications for these redundancy codes: (1) self-error correction for SL imaging in bright ambient conditions, (2) error detection enabling adaptive reconstruction under global illumination, and (3) interference filtering using device-specific projection sequences, particularly for event camera-based SL and light curtain technologies. The study systematically examines the design principles and signal processing algorithms across these scenarios. Hardware prototypes were developed to evaluate the system in real-world complex environments. Experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets confirm significant performance enhancements in SL systems utilizing these redundancy codes.

This paper introduces a simple sparse approximate inverse for triangular matrices, termed SAIT. By employing the Jacobi iteration method, we derive an exact inverse for triangular matrices as a finite series, which serves as the foundation for constructing the SAIT. These matrices are applied within iterative methods alongside ILU preconditioners, where the two triangular solvers in the preconditioning process are substituted with two matrix-vector multiplications capable of fine-grained parallelization. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through experiments solving various linear systems and eigenvalue problems using preconditioned iterative techniques.

This work explores a semi-discrete adaptation of A. S. Fokas's Unified Transform Method, designed to address initial-boundary-value problems for linear evolution partial differential equations with constant coefficients. By applying this semi-discrete approach to various spatial discretizations of first- and second-order linear equations on the half-line ($x \geq 0$), we derive the exact solutions for these semi-discrete systems, contingent upon specified initial and boundary conditions. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how the Unified Transform Method accommodates derivative boundary conditions and the ghost points resulting from different discretization stencils. Finally, we examine the continuum limit of these semi-discrete solutions and present several numerical examples.

Data from the KASCADE air shower experiment rivals modern observatories in both quality and statistical volume. We introduce a new mass composition analysis utilizing archival records from 1998 to 2013, managed by the KASCADE Cosmic ray Data Center (KCDC). This study employs contemporary machine learning algorithms trained on KCDC simulation data to deliver spectra for specific primary nucleus groups, investigate anisotropies in event arrival directions while accounting for mass composition, and identify potential gamma-ray candidates within the PeV energy range.

This study investigates how mimicking the saccade mechanism from biological vision can enhance the efficiency of deep neural networks for classification and object detection. Our method leverages attention-driven visual processing, specifically focusing on saccades, which are miniature eye movements guided by attention. We evaluate our approach through two main analyses: first, assessing the robustness of various deep neural network (DNN) feature extractors against partially sensed images for classification and detection, and second, examining the effectiveness of using saccades to mask image patches for classification and object tracking. Experiments were performed using convolutional networks (ResNet-18) and transformer-based architectures (ViT, DETR, TransTrack) across multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10, DAVSOD, MSCOCO, and MOT17. Results demonstrate that intelligently reducing data by learning to emulate human saccades alongside state-of-the-art DNNs significantly improves efficiency for classification, detection, and tracking. Specifically, classification and detection tasks experienced minimal performance degradation while utilizing only approximately 30% of the original sensor data. Finally, we explore how the saccade mechanism can guide hardware design through "in-pixel" processing.

This paper introduces and investigates a Hom-type generalization of rings, outlining their fundamental properties and essential constructions. Additionally, it examines modules over Hom-rings, characterizing both simple modules and simple Hom-rings. The study also extends classical group concepts and results to the realm of Hom-groups. Specifically, it constructs free regular Hom-groups using Super-Leaf weighted trees and analyzes normal Hom-subgroups, the abelianization of regular Hom-groups, as well as the universality of tensor products involving Hom-groups and simple Hom-groups.

We calculate invariants associated with the two-variable M\"obius transformation. Specifically, our focus lies on partial differential equations involving two dependent and two independent variables that remain invariant under this transformation.

The proliferation of IP cameras across modern road infrastructures presents a significant opportunity to leverage captured data for video analysis and event detection. Historically, identifying moving vehicles relied on classical computer vision methods, but deep learning networks have since driven substantial advancements, although object detection remains a primary challenge in the field. As the landscape evolves with new models and techniques, specific issues regarding the detection of small objects—predominantly vehicles in road scenes—have emerged. Consequently, developing novel solutions to address the low detection rates of these small elements is crucial. Focusing on this emerging research area, this study targets vehicle detection from surveillance imagery. We introduce a novel procedure for small-scale object detection that integrates super-resolution techniques with convolutional neural networks (CNNs). By enhancing image resolution prior to detection, this approach aims to improve overall performance. Tested on a diverse set of traffic images featuring elements at various scales, the results demonstrate that our proposed method effectively achieves robust detection across a wide range of scenarios.

The rise of social and engaging features has made video moderation—specifically the removal of deviant or explicit material from e-commerce livestreams—increasingly common. Nevertheless, this process remains laborious and time-intensive because analyzing multimodal content, such as video frames and audio, presents significant challenges. To address these issues and ensure effective moderation, we introduce VideoModerator, a risk-aware framework that harmoniously combines human expertise with machine learning. This system utilizes advanced models to extract risk-sensitive features from multimodal inputs and identify potentially problematic videos. Additionally, it offers an interactive visualization interface comprising three distinct perspectives: a video view that employs a segmented timeline to highlight high-risk intervals, a frame view featuring a novel visual summarization technique that merges risk-aware features with video context for efficient navigation, and an audio view utilizing a storyline-based design to offer a comprehensive overview of audio content. Finally, we demonstrate the framework's application through a case study and validate its efficacy via experiments and a controlled user study.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) applied to energy-based models exhibits a direct conceptual link to equilibrium thermodynamics, as the softmax layer converts energies into probabilities via a Gibbs distribution. However, the specific mechanisms through which SSL functions as a thermodynamic process remain to be clarified. We demonstrate that certain SSL frameworks operate as thermodynamic composite systems, consisting of representations and self-labels interacting with a nonequilibrium reservoir. Furthermore, these systems undergo standard thermodynamic cycles, including adiabatic expansion and isochoric heating, which lead to the formation of a generalized Gibbs ensemble (GGE). Within this framework, the learning process is interpreted as a demon performing cyclic operations that utilize feedback measurements to extract negative work from the system. We apply this perspective to analyze various SSL algorithms.

We demonstrate that, under broad conditions on the marginals—permitting unbounded densities and supports—the gradients of Schrödinger potentials converge to the Brenier map as time approaches zero. Additionally, we introduce new quantitative stability estimates for the optimal values and couplings in the Schrödinger problem (SP), formulated using a negative-order weighted homogeneous Sobolev norm that captures the linearized behavior of the 2-Wasserstein distance between marginals. Our proofs underscore, for the first time, the critical role of gradient bounds for Schrödinger potentials, established here in full generality, in analyzing the short-time dynamics of Schrödinger bridges. Finally, we examine how these findings extend to the framework of quadratic Entropic Optimal Transport, a variant of SP particularly suited for applications in machine learning and data science.

This study revisits the classic pursuit curve problem originally solved by Pierre Bouguer in the 18th century, incorporating the constraint that information travels at a finite speed. While this adjustment can be interpreted as a relativistic correction, it does not require Einstein's theory of relativity to derive or comprehend. Addressing this generalized pursuit problem offers a valuable pedagogical tool for introducing the concept of retarded time, free from the complexities typically associated with its initial appearance in the study of electromagnetic radiation. We derive the governing differential equation, solve it numerically, compare our results with Bouguer's original findings across various parameter values, and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the pursuer to intercept the pursued, thereby extending upon previous research by Hoenselaers.

Accurately predicting runoff requires a deep understanding of hydrological response dynamics, which can be achieved quantitatively by monitoring shifts in model parameters that reflect physical attributes. This study employs a Bayesian estimation technique to continuously update hydrology model parameters for small watersheds using observed rainfall and runoff data. Coupled with a conceptual hydrology model featuring a Gamma distribution-based Instantaneous Unit Hydrograph, the analytical framework was validated using both synthetic datasets and observational records from the Fall Creek watershed. Findings indicate that the Bayesian approach effectively tracks hidden parameters that vary annually. Furthermore, applying the model to analyze temporal and spatial variations in rainfall-runoff responses revealed: 1) a systematic shift in the Fall Creek watershed's response around 1943, and 2) a statistically significant correlation between rainfall-runoff responses and watershed sizes across selected watersheds in New York. These results highlight the potential of Bayesian estimation as a rapid surveillance tool for monitoring and tracking hydrological response changes in small watersheds.

This study introduces a novel framework to boost the secrecy capabilities of a NOMA-based coordinated direct relay transmission system (NOMA-CDRT) featuring an untrusted relay. By integrating physical-layer network coding with non-orthogonal multiple access, the approach enhances spectrum efficiency. Additionally, the system leverages inter-user interference and friendly jamming to degrade the eavesdropping potential of the untrusted relay while maintaining the quality of service for legitimate users. In this specific configuration, the far user during the first slot and the near user during the second slot function as jammers to secure confidential signal transmissions. The paper evaluates the secrecy performance within NOMA-CDRT systems and derives a closed-form expression for the ergodic secrecy sum rate, followed by an asymptotic analysis at high signal-to-noise ratios to provide deeper insights. Finally, simulation results are provided to validate the efficacy of the proposed scheme and confirm the accuracy of the theoretical findings.

This study examines the dynamics of roll solutions at the zigzag boundary within the planar Swift-Hohenberg equation. Linear analysis reveals that small perturbations decay algebraically at a rate of $t^{-1/4}$, deviating from the classical $t^{-1/2}$ diffusive rate. This anomaly arises from the degeneracy of the quadratic term associated with the continuation of the translational mode of the linearized operator in Bloch-Fourier spaces. The proof utilizes a decomposition of neutral and faster-decaying modes within the Bloch-Fourier space alongside a fixed-point argument, which establishes the irrelevance of nonlinear terms.

Voice-activated assistants like Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant are increasingly integrated into streaming television platforms, enabling users to navigate a growing array of applications via voice commands. Nevertheless, these current systems are limited to basic control and search functions, lacking support for more sophisticated recommendation or exploratory queries. To understand how users interact with voice-driven recommendation features on TV, this study employs research through design to investigate an early prototype movie recommendation system that relies exclusively on voice input. The authors present findings from in-depth qualitative sessions with 11 participants. Key contributions include implications for designers of voice-controlled TV interfaces: addressing the limitations of voice-only interactions, balancing the trade-off between expressiveness and efficiency, and creating voice-driven recommendation interfaces that encourage user exploration.
In this paper, we investigated C3-like Finsler metrics that satisfy both the un-normal and normal Ricci flow equations, demonstrating that these metrics are Einstein.

The surface code, enhanced with lattice surgery, represents a premier approach for scalable quantum computing. However, because fundamental lattice surgery operations—specifically the merging and splitting of logical qubits—act non-unitarily on logical states, they resist representation within standard circuit notation. This limitation creates challenges in designing, verifying, and optimizing lattice surgery protocols, especially within architectures facing complex resource management constraints. This paper establishes that the operations of the ZX calculus, a quantum diagrammatic reasoning framework grounded in bialgebras, correspond precisely to lattice surgery operations. In this correspondence, red and green "spider" nodes represent rough and smooth merges and splits, respectively, while adhering to the axioms of a dagger-special associative Frobenius algebra. Furthermore, lattice surgery operations that necessitate non-trivial corrections are natively captured by the ZX calculus through ensembles of diagrams. By examining two specific operations—the T gate and the generation of a CNOT—we provide an initial demonstration of the calculus's potential as a language for lattice surgery. We illustrate how ZX diagram rewrite rules yield novel, efficient, and highly configurable lattice surgery procedures for these tasks.

This study employs first-principles calculations to assess the energetic stability of two-dimensional (2D) binary compounds ($XY$), where $X$ and $Y$ represent metallic elements ranging from lithium to lead. A total of 1,081 compounds are examined across five structural types: buckled honeycomb (BHC), buckled square, B2, L1$_0$, and B$_h$. For compounds exhibiting negative formation energy within the BHC structure or those capable of adopting the B$_h$ structure, phonon dispersion calculations are performed to evaluate dynamical stability. The results demonstrate that (i) a negative formation energy does not guarantee nor preclude dynamical stability in 2D compounds, and (ii) if a compound in the B$_h$ structure has been experimentally synthesized, its counterpart in the BHC structure is dynamically stable.

We construct a noise-stable sequence of transitive, monotone increasing Boolean functions $f_n: \{-1,1\}^{k_n} \longrightarrow \{-1,1\}$ that possess numerous pivotals with high probability. We demonstrate that this sequence is also volatile, thereby serving as an example of a volatile and noise-stable sequence of transitive, monotone functions.

Repeated Reading (RR) supports learners with minimal fluent reading experience by fostering confidence, enhancing speed, and promoting automatic word processing. The advantages of RR encompass improved fact recall, better identification of main ideas and vocabulary, increased comprehension, accelerated reading rates, higher word recognition accuracy, and a smoother transition from word-by-word decoding to meaningful phrasing for struggling students. Consequently, RR significantly enhances learners' oral fluency and narrative production. Despite these benefits, no open audio datasets currently exist regarding learners' oral responses following RR practice. To address this gap, this paper introduces a new dataset, outlines its characteristics, and proposes a method to evaluate oral fluency and narrative production in English learners using acoustic, prosodic, lexical, and syntactical features. The findings demonstrate that a Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) system can be successfully developed to assess improvements in these areas.

Privacy-preserving neural network inference has recently attracted substantial interest, with various solutions offering distinct latency and bandwidth trade-offs. Many of these rely on homomorphic encryption (HE) to compute over encrypted data; however, even advanced HE schemes remain significantly slower than plaintext operations. While pruning neural network parameters is a standard technique for accelerating inference, methods effective in plaintext settings often yield negligible gains in HE environments, as recent studies have shown. This work introduces a novel set of pruning strategies that reduce both latency and memory usage, effectively extending plaintext pruning benefits to HE contexts. Our approach leverages two core techniques—permuting and expanding packed model weights—to enable the pruning of substantially more ciphertexts and to recover most of the accuracy typically lost during pruning. We validate our method on fully connected layers utilizing "tile tensors," a recent packing technique that facilitates non-interactive deep neural network inference. Evaluations across various autoencoder architectures demonstrate that our approach achieves a mean-square reconstruction loss of 1.5×10⁻⁵ on MNIST while reducing both memory requirements and inference latency by 60% in HE-enabled scenarios.

This study introduces Automatic Chord Estimation (ACE), a statistically grounded semi-supervised technique that effectively processes music signals with or without chord annotations. While conventional ACE methods rely on supervised deep classification models trained solely on annotated data, they largely ignore prior knowledge regarding the sequential nature of chord labels. In contrast, our proposed approach unifies generative and discriminative frameworks through amortized variational inference. Specifically, we develop a deep generative model that simulates the creation of chroma vectors (observed variables) from discrete chord labels and continuous latent features. These latent variables adhere to a Markov model that encourages self-transitions for labels and a standard Gaussian distribution for features. Given observed chroma vectors, approximate posterior distributions for both latent labels and features are derived using deep classification and recognition networks, respectively. Together, these three components constitute a variational autoencoder capable of joint semi-supervised training. Experimental findings demonstrate that incorporating a Markov prior for chord labels and a generative model for chroma vectors enhances ACE performance, even in supervised settings. Furthermore, semi-supervised learning utilizing additional unannotated data yields further performance gains.

Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) involves automatically identifying the optimal pipeline for achieving the best generalization performance on a specific dataset. Over the past decade, this field has garnered significant attention and been tackled using complex black-box optimization methods, including Bayesian Optimization, Grammar-Based Genetic Algorithms, and tree search algorithms. In contrast, we introduce Naive AutoML, a straightforward approach that leverages key meta-knowledge about machine learning issues and employs simplifying yet effective assumptions to rapidly generate high-quality solutions. Although Naive AutoML can serve as a baseline for these advanced black-box solvers, empirical evidence demonstrates that these sophisticated methods fail to outperform it, and in some cases, the opposite occurs. Furthermore, Naive AutoML offers distinct benefits such as interpretability and flexibility, presenting a formidable challenge to existing tools.

Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) offers a low-cost method for generating accurate geographical data, yet its scalability is constrained by the limited availability of volunteers in specific regions, often hindering timely mapping of large areas. The advent of street-view imagery, however, facilitates virtual urban exploration, allowing contributors to map areas from which they are not physically located. This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of the Virtual City Explorer (VCE), a system that leverages paid crowdworkers to identify Point of Interest (PoI) coordinates within a bounded area using a street-view service. Evaluation results indicate that paid workers are highly effective at discovering PoIs and achieve near-complete area coverage. While our method does not capture every PoI identified by experts or VGI communities, it successfully detects unique locations missed by them, demonstrating complementarity. Furthermore, we examined the effect of designating PoIs discovered by a certain number of workers as "taboo" for subsequent contributors; this strategy promotes deeper exploration, increases the total number of detected PoIs, and reduces operational costs.

To fulfill its ambitious scientific objectives, the Webb Space Telescope's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) must satisfy stringent throughput requirements, specifically regarding photon-conversion efficiency (PCE). Through calibration activities conducted during instrument commissioning, we secured the first in-flight PCE measurements and refined the modeling of light losses within NIRSpec slit devices. Overall, the measured PCE for NIRSpec's fixed-slit and multi-object spectroscopy modes meets or surpasses pre-launch predictions. In contrast, the integral-field spectroscopy mode shows more significant deviations from the model, with differences reaching -20% above 4 microns and exceeding +30% below 2 microns. Furthermore, leveraging the high quality of the JWST point-spread function, slit losses at shorter wavelengths are substantially lower than predicted in pre-flight models. These findings, alongside confirmed low detector noise performance, establish NIRSpec as an exceptionally sensitive spectrograph.

We analyze a 700 ks Chandra ACIS-S observation of the Spiderweb Galaxy's environment at z=2.156, emphasizing nuclear activity within the large-scale structure. Unresolved X-ray sources were detected down to flux limits of 1.3×10⁻¹⁶ and 3.9×10⁻¹⁶ erg/s/cm² in the soft and hard bands, respectively. By cross-matching with optical, NIR, and submm data, we identified 107 unresolved X-ray sources within 5 arcmin (2.5 Mpc) of J1140-2629; 13 have spectroscopic redshifts between 2.11 and 2.20, and one has a consistent photometric redshift. Spectral analysis indicates an average intrinsic slope of <Γ>~1.84±0.04. Five protocluster members exhibit intrinsic absorption N_H>10²³ cm⁻², while six others have upper limits around a few×10²² cm⁻². Two sources, requiring very flat spectra (Γ≤1), are candidates for Compton-thick AGN. Their rest-frame 0.5–10 keV luminosities exceed 2×10⁴³ erg/s, far surpassing levels expected from star formation. The AGN X-ray luminosity function (10⁴³<L_X<10⁴⁴·⁵ erg/s) in the Spiderweb protocluster is at least ten times higher and significantly flatter than the field at the same redshift. For galaxies with log(M*/M_sun)>10.5, the AGN fraction is measured at (25.5±4.5)%, representing a 6.0⁺⁹·⁰₋₃·₀ enhancement over the COSMOS field. We conclude that Mpc-scale environmental effects trigger enhanced X-ray nuclear activity in the Spiderweb Protocluster galaxy population.

This study presents a high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission (ARPES) analysis of sodium, a prototypical nearly-free-electron metal. The measured mass enhancement is marginally lower than values obtained in prior research. Additionally, the newly observed lifetime broadening suggests that theories must extend beyond the random phase approximation. Our findings contradict the hypothesis of a significant increase in charge carrier scattering rates caused by spin fluctuation coupling. Furthermore, comparing these results with earlier electron energy-loss data reveals that the mass enhancement associated with dipolar electron-hole excitations is substantially reduced relative to that of monopole hole excitations as determined by ARPES.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) is conducting the first direct investigation of the solar wind within 0.2 astronomical units (au) of the Sun. Early data revealed that magnetic field (B) and velocity (V) fluctuations near the Sun exhibit Alfvénic characteristics, occurring in regions where the magnetic field magnitude $|{\bf B}|$ remains nearly constant, indicating approximate magnetic pressure balance. These regions are periodically disrupted by intense fluctuations, notably radial field reversals termed "switchbacks." A hypothesis suggests that nonlinear Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities arising near magnetic boundaries in the young solar wind generate extensive shear-driven dynamics, powerful turbulent fluctuations such as switchbacks, and mixing layers characterized by approximate magnetic pressure balance. This study identifies and analyzes these domains using data from the first five PSP solar encounters. The filling fraction, serving as a metric for Alfvénicity, drops from a median of 90% inside 0.2 au to 38% beyond 0.9 au, exhibiting significant variability. We observe an inverse relationship between the average duration of these domains and plasma $\beta$. Furthermore, we investigate whether mean domain duration correlates with the crossing time of spatial structures frozen into the solar wind flow for extreme aspect ratios. Our findings contradict the existence of long, thin domains aligned radially or along the Parker spiral, instead supporting the presence of isotropic domains, a conclusion consistent with previous observations of isotropic density fluctuations or "flocculae" in the solar wind.

A deck of $n$ cards is shuffled through a repeated procedure where the top card is removed, flipped with probability $1/2$, and reinserted at a random location. This process defines a Markov chain on the group $B_n$ of signed permutations. We demonstrate that the eigenvalues of the transition probability matrix are $0, 1/n, 2/n, \ldots, (n-1)/n, 1$, with the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $i/n$ corresponding to the count of signed permutations possessing exactly $i$ fixed points. Similar findings are established for colored permutations. Additionally, we prove that the mixing time of this Markov chain is $n\log n$, matching that of the standard 'top-to-random' shuffle without card flipping. Finally, the cut-off phenomenon is examined by leveraging the asymptotic properties of Stirling numbers of the second kind.

Quantum metrology leverages quantum resources and strategies to enhance the precision of measuring unknown parameters, with a key challenge being the preparation of entangled states capable of surpassing the standard quantum limit. This work introduces a method utilizing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to identify optimal pulse sequences that accelerate one-axis twisting dynamics for entanglement generation. The pulse trains consist of $\pi/2$ pulses applied along either a single axis or two orthogonal axes, with operations optimized to maximize quantum Fisher information. Within a constrained evolution time, the resulting entangled states achieve ultimate precision bounds scaling according to the Heisenberg limit. These states serve effectively as inputs for Ramsey interferometry, maintaining Heisenberg-limited scaling in final measurement precision. Although pulse sequences along a single axis offer greater simplicity and efficiency, those employing two orthogonal axes demonstrate superior robustness against variations in atom number. Overall, this DRL-based protocol is both efficient and readily implementable in current state-of-the-art experiments.

Beyond the kinetic and potential energies associated with quarks and gluons, the nucleon's mass encompasses a unique energy derived purely from quantum effects, arising from the anomalous breaking of scale symmetry. We illustrate the impact of this quantum anomalous energy (QAE) within QED and in a toy 1+1 dimensional non-linear sigma model, where it operates non-perturbatively, mirroring the Higgs mechanism responsible for generating masses in electro-weak theory. The contribution of QAE to nucleon mass can be elucidated through a comparable process: a dynamical response of the gluonic scalar field mediated by Higgs-like couplings between nucleons and scalar resonances. Furthermore, the QAE establishes the scale for other nucleonic energies via a relativistic virial theorem and exerts a negative pressure necessary to confine colored quarks.

The dressing approach utilizing the $3\times3$ matrix $\bar{\partial}$-problem has been extended to investigate the long-short wave equation for both $\sigma=\pm1$ scenarios. Soliton solutions for this equation under these conditions are derived through the properties of Cauchy matrices. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the case where $\sigma=1$ yields cusp solitons.

Stochastic reaction networks are extensively employed to model random processes across physics, chemistry, and biology; however, their state space grows exponentially with the number of species, complicating the analysis of the chemical master equation's time evolution. This work introduces a machine learning solution utilizing variational autoregressive networks (VAR) to address the chemical master equation. Grounded in a reinforcement learning framework, this method operates without requiring pre-simulated data from other techniques. Unlike approaches that simulate individual trajectories, the proposed VAR method tracks the time evolution of the joint probability distribution across species count states, facilitating direct configuration sampling and the computation of normalized joint probabilities. Applied to diverse systems in physics and biology, including the genetic toggle switch, early life self-replicator, epidemic models, and intracellular signaling cascades, the approach accurately generates probability distributions over time. The VAR network demonstrates the capacity to represent multi-modal distributions through feedback regulation, adheres to conservation laws, accommodates time-dependent reaction rates, and offers efficiency for high-dimensional networks with flexible upper count limits. These findings indicate that modern machine learning provides a robust general framework for investigating stochastic reaction networks.

Unsupervised domain adaptive classification aims to enhance classification accuracy on an unlabeled target domain. While numerous methods attempt to mitigate domain shift by aligning source and target domains within the feature space, they often treat features as monolithic units for alignment. This approach neglects the explicit role of alignment in serving the classification task, resulting in sub-optimal outcomes. To address this, we introduce Task-oriented Alignment (ToAlign) for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). We investigate which specific features require cross-domain alignment and propose guiding this process to actively benefit classification through feature decomposition. This decomposition is informed by prior knowledge derived directly from the classification task itself. Specifically, we decompose source domain features into two components: a task-relevant, discriminative part that should be aligned, and a task-irrelevant part that should be ignored, based on classification meta-knowledge. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks (including Office-Home, Visda-2017, and DomainNet) under different adaptation settings confirm the efficacy of ToAlign, achieving state-of-the-art performance. The code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/UDA.

Elastic self-scattering events leave the count of dark matter particles unchanged, leading to their usual exclusion from relic abundance calculations. This study identifies scenarios where such self-scattering significantly alters the efficiency of annihilation by modifying the dark matter momentum distribution. We examine various freeze-out cases, including resonant and sub-threshold annihilations, as well as a model featuring dark matter production from the decay of a heavier mediator. Notably, when analyzing the dark matter momentum distribution function, we discover that introducing additional high-energy dark matter particles into the thermal population can actually reduce the final relic abundance.

We investigate the initial-boundary value problem for stochastic Navier–Stokes equations within a half-space, establishing the existence of weak solutions as random processes taking values in a standard Besov space, provided the initial data lie in the corresponding critical Besov space.

Thermodynamic integration (TI) typically computes marginal likelihoods by following an inverse annealing trajectory from the prior to the posterior distribution. However, the resulting estimator often exhibits high variability, primarily driven by the prior regime. When comparing complex models with only a few differing parameters, intrinsic sampling fluctuations can dominate the log marginal likelihood estimates, obscuring meaningful differences. This article introduces a TI scheme specifically designed to target the log Bayes factor. Our approach utilizes a modified annealing path connecting the posterior distributions of the two models being compared, thereby systematically bypassing the high-variance prior region. Furthermore, we integrate this scheme with non-equilibrium TI concepts to minimize discretization errors arising from numerical integration. Empirical results on Bayesian regression models using standard benchmark datasets, as well as a complex hierarchical model for biopathway inference, demonstrate a substantial reduction in estimator variance compared to state-of-the-art TI methods.

This article demonstrates that Federer's work on reach, combined with specific geometric insights, allows for a significant streamlining of the homotopy reconstruction proof originally established by Niyogi, Smale, and Weinberger. Unlike the original authors, who limited their scope to C² manifolds with positive reach, our approach generalizes the result to apply to any set S possessing positive reach. Furthermore, the sample points do not need to reside exactly on S; instead, we assume the one-sided Hausdorff distances (ε and δ) between the sample P and the set S are bounded. We derive explicit bounds for ε and δ that ensure a specific radius r exists, such that the union of r-balls centered at points in P deformation retracts onto S. For manifold cases, we provide even tighter bounds. In both scenarios, our results substantially improve upon existing state-of-the-art methods in nearly all contexts, and we prove that these bounds are optimal.

This study proposes a conceptual framework for quantum heat engines utilizing two coupled double quantum dots (DQDs), where each dot contains an extra electron to serve as the working substance. We introduce a compression ratio defined as the ratio of Coulomb couplings, which governs electron interactions during the isochoric stages of the quantum Otto cycle, and subsequently examine the resulting operational regimes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of an Otto engine that defies classical expectations by accounting for quantum tunneling effects as a single electron moves between individual DQDs.

The relationship between argumentation and belief is complex. On one side, argumentation is essential for forming beliefs, as engaging in a debate can lead an agent to justifiably accept a proposition. Conversely, beliefs serve as a foundation for evaluating arguments; an agent regards arguments with premises they believe as strictly more compelling than those without. Recent literature has introduced an awareness epistemic logic to model these principles in qualified forms. This paper advances that logic in three ways: first, by strengthening its conceptual basis through an analysis of its philosophical underpinnings, a critical review of its design decisions, and an exploration of additional potential; second, by establishing a previously absent completeness theorem for the logic's basic fragment; and third, by utilizing techniques from dynamic epistemic logic to examine how various types of information updates can be represented within the framework.

This paper examines a novel class of solvable nonlinear difference equations defined by the system:
\begin{equation*} x_{n+1}=ax_{n}^{2}y_{n}+bx_{n}y_{n}^{2},\
y_{n+1}=cx_{n}^{2}y_{n}+dx_{n}y_{n}^{2},\ n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}, \end{equation*}
where the initial conditions $x_{0},y_{0}$ and the parameters $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are arbitrary real numbers. The study derives a closed-form general solution for this system using an efficient methodology.

Although graphs offer rich information, they are restricted to modeling pairwise interactions, whereas real-world systems like social and neuronal networks often involve multi-node interactions. Simplicial complexes serve as a robust mathematical framework for capturing these higher-order relationships. While the spectrum of the graph Laplacian is established as a marker for community structure and drives spectral clustering, we propose that the spectrum of the Hodge Laplacian—defined on simplicial complexes—encodes simplicial communities. We present an algorithm to extract these communities across arbitrary dimensions, testing it on both benchmark simplicial complexes and real higher-order data, including social networks and those derived from linguistic or text processing. However, since explicit simplicial complex datasets are rare and most available data only contains pairwise interactions, we develop an inference method to predict the most probable higher-order structure. This approach leverages known data properties to identify the higher-order interactions that maximize adjusted mutual information relative to ground-truth community structures. Finally, we analyze higher-order networks formed by thresholding edge weights in collaboration networks (which encode only pairwise interactions), demonstrating the existence of persistent simplicial communities that remain stable across a broad range of thresholds.

This brief overview begins with the fundamentals of quantum computing, highlighting the distinction between quantum and classical control paradigms. It then surveys the research on quantum control within the lambda calculus, progressing from untyped systems to categorical and realisability models. This summary encapsulates over a decade of advancements in the field, beginning with the foundational work of Arrighi and Dowek and extending to the present day.

Axion-like particles (ALPs) are prevalent in new physics frameworks designed to address significant Standard Model puzzles. Despite their ubiquity, their connection to flavour physics has recently garnered more attention. This study investigates the phenomenology of ALPs that couple exclusively to up-type quarks at the tree level, a feature found in motivated ultraviolet completions like QCD-inspired dark sectors or Froggatt-Nielsen flavour models. Conducted within a low-energy effective theory framework, our analysis highlights these scenarios in a model-independent manner. We compile all current constraints on such models and illustrate how forthcoming experiments at fixed-target facilities and the LHC can explore a vast, currently unconstrained region of parameter space, despite existing cosmological and astrophysical limits. Furthermore, we underscore the potential of a future measurement of the yet-undecayed meson process $D \to \pi + \rm{invisible}$ to complement these searches and probe extensive unexplored regions of the parameter space.

This study investigates and applies a strategy that integrates ring-polymer instanton (RPI) theory with transfer learning (TL) to map a low-level potential energy surface (PES) onto a higher-level electronic structure theory, using malonaldehyde as a test case. Since the RPI method offers a semiclassical estimate of tunneling splitting that is highly sensitive to PES precision, the researchers utilized second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory (MP2) for the low-level model and coupled cluster singles, doubles, and perturbative triples (CCSD(T)) for the high-level model. The results demonstrate that incorporating CCSD(T) data from merely 25 to 50 carefully chosen structures along and near the instanton trajectory is sufficient to achieve high-level accuracy for tunneling splitting. Furthermore, the overall quality of the resulting high-level PES is validated by a mean absolute error of 0.3 kcal/mol for energies up to 40 kcal/mol above the minimum (double the range used during transfer learning) and harmonic frequency errors below 2 cm⁻¹, all compared against computationally intensive CCSD(T) normal mode calculations.

We introduce a new deep metric learning approach that differs from existing methods by defining a novel latent space via an autoencoder. This space, termed S-space, is segmented into distinct regions representing where object pairs are similar or dissimilar, identified by specific markers. We estimate object similarities using a kernel-based t-student distribution to measure distances between these markers and the new data representation. Our method simultaneously determines marker positions within the S-space and represents objects within the same space. Additionally, we propose a new regularization function to prevent similar markers from collapsing. We provide evidence that our approach effectively represents complex spaces, such as those where similar object groups reside in disjoint regions. We evaluated our method against nine other distance metric learning approaches (including four deep-learning-based ones) across 28 real-world heterogeneous datasets. According to four quantitative metrics, our method outperforms all nine existing strategies.
Feuerbach's theorem asserts that for any triangle that is not equilateral, the nine-point circle touches both the incircle and the three excircles. We provide a straightforward proof of this result.

Khan and Lespérance (2021) recently introduced the first account of causal knowledge grounded in a novel action-theoretic formalization of actual cause. Their approach supports epistemic effects, models the dynamics of causal knowledge, and permits sensing actions to serve as causes for observed effects. While no prior research has addressed these specific issues, their formalization lacks the expressiveness required to model explanations derived from analyzing mental states, as it overlooks a critical component of theory of mind: motivations. This paper extends their work to enable causal reasoning regarding conative effects. Our framework allows for the analysis of causes underlying motivational states and treats actions that alter motivation as causes of observed effects. We demonstrate that combining this formalization with a goal recognition model facilitates the explanation of agent behavior within communicative multiagent settings.

During Deep Neural Network (DNN) training, weights are optimized from random initialization to a near-optimal state that minimizes the loss function; however, only this final configuration is typically retained for inference, while the valuable data regarding the weight space geometry gathered during the optimization process is discarded. This study proposes leveraging this overlooked information to calculate weight distributions, which can subsequently be used to estimate epistemic uncertainty by sampling an ensemble of networks. To achieve this, we present a technique for monitoring weight trajectories during optimization that requires no modifications to the network architecture or training protocol. We assess this method on standard classification and regression benchmarks, as well as on out-of-distribution detection tasks for classification and semantic segmentation. Our approach yields competitive performance while maintaining computational efficiency relative to other leading methods.

Current reward learning methods based on human preferences can tackle complex reinforcement learning (RL) tasks without explicit reward functions by establishing a single, fixed preference for trajectory pairs. However, this approach lacks dynamism and necessitates extensive human input across thousands of iterations. This study introduces a weak human preference supervision framework, featuring a scaling model that captures human perception of weak choices between trajectories and a supervised human-demonstration estimator to predict preferences, thereby minimizing the need for human input. The proposed framework effectively solves complex RL tasks and yields higher cumulative rewards in simulated robot locomotion (MuJoCo) compared to methods using fixed human preferences. Additionally, the human-demonstration estimator requires feedback for less than 0.01% of agent-environment interactions, cutting human input costs by up to 30% relative to existing techniques. To demonstrate the approach's flexibility, we have released a video (https://youtu.be/jQPe1OILT0M) comparing agent behaviors trained on various human input types. We believe that our naturally inspired weakly supervised preferences enhance precise reward learning and are applicable to advanced RL systems, including human-autonomy teaming.

Current air traffic complexity metrics are formulated to accommodate the varied objectives of different Air Traffic Management (ATM) layers. In practice, these layers often have conflicting goals, leading to fragmented decision-making processes. This fragmentation, combined with competing Key Performance Areas (KPAs), necessitates transparent and neutral air traffic information to enable explainable actions. This paper introduces the concept of single-aircraft complexity to quantify each aircraft's contribution to overall traffic complexity. Additionally, we present a methodology that extends this concept to identify "complex communities"—groups of interdependent aircraft responsible for the majority of complexity within a specific airspace. To demonstrate this methodology, a visualization tool displaying various algorithmic outputs has been developed. Using synthetic and real historical traffic data, we illustrate that the algorithm can both formalize controller decisions and guide them toward improved outcomes. Furthermore, we examine how the provided data can enhance decision-maker transparency toward various airspace users, thereby promoting fairness and equity. Finally, a sensitivity analysis is performed to systematically evaluate how individual inputs influence the methodology.

This paper investigates the challenge of assessing element addition to a set, a task that is inherently difficult because general cases cannot be reduced to unconditional preferences among options. Consequently, we model preferences based on decision contexts. We examine and compare two distinct Siamese network architectures for this purpose: a twin network that evaluates the two resulting sets and a triplet network that captures each candidate's contribution to the existing set. We assess both approaches on a real-world application involving human card preferences for deck construction in the collectible card game *Magic: The Gathering*. Our results demonstrate that the triplet approach outperforms the twin network, with both methods surpassing previous performance on this task.

Over the past ten years, online social networking services (SNSs) like Facebook, Twitter, RenRen, and LinkedIn have experienced rapid expansion. Although these platforms offer significant advantages, including relationship building, community development, and news dissemination, they have also become targets for unwanted interference. Spammers exploit SNSs to distribute unsolicited content swiftly and extensively, which undermines the trust and dependability of these services. Consequently, identifying spammers has emerged as a pressing challenge. This study specifically addresses follow spam on Twitter, where spammers bypass public messaging by subscribing to legitimate accounts rather than broadcasting content. Assuming that the social connections of spammers differ from those of genuine users, we developed classification methods to detect such behavior. Specifically, we examined cascaded social relationships and created two detection schemes, TSP-Filtering and SS-Filtering, which operate within a two-hop subnetwork centered on each user by leveraging Triad Significance Profile (TSP) and Social Status (SS) metrics, respectively. Additionally, we introduced an ensemble approach called Cascaded-Filtering that integrates both TSP and SS features. Experimental results using real Twitter data indicate that these three methods are highly practical. The proposed schemes are scalable because they analyze user-centered two-hop networks rather than the entire network. Performance evaluations demonstrate that our methods achieve superior results compared to previous approaches, yielding higher true positive rates and lower false positive rates.

Gravitational waves provide insights into the likely distances of their source signals. When aggregated across numerous observations, this data facilitates the modeling of how merger rates evolve with redshift, a critical component of binary black hole population studies that correlates with universal star formation history or the dynamical evolution of star clusters. At minimum, these measurements can investigate the time lag between star formation and the merger of stellar remnants. However, the inherent degeneracy between a binary's inclination angle and its luminosity distance introduces significant uncertainty in measured distances, thereby hindering precise determination of the merger redshift distribution. In this letter, we demonstrate that applying the cosmological principle can mitigate this uncertainty, allowing for more effective discrimination among various models of binary black hole merger rate evolution. Furthermore, by comparing our approach with analyses that do not enforce this principle, we offer a method to test the validity of the cosmological principle itself.

Web3 is spearheading a new generation of web services, attracting interest from many Web2 applications. However, the scarcity of Web3 expertise among Web2 developers creates barriers to seamless adoption and transition. Conversely, Web3 applications require promotion and endorsement from established Web2 entities to expand their currently small market share. This paper introduces "WebttCom," a seamless transition framework designed to bridge Web2 and Web3, developed after analyzing the core concepts of Web3 and the fundamental distinctions between Web2 and Web3 applications. To validate the framework, we present a full-stack implementation as a practical use case, supported by interviews with five participants yielding four positive and one neutral response. Our findings confirm that WebttCom effectively addresses the identified research question, and the implementation demonstrates strong necessity, usability, and completeness in alignment with the proposed framework.

Open quantum systems represent a field of significant theoretical interest. Among the most effective frameworks for modeling a system's evolution under external environmental interactions are master equations. However, experimental capabilities to investigate various open system implementations have historically been constrained, making the development of tools that emulate diverse master equation dynamics and validate open systems theories highly valuable. This paper presents a systematic approach to engineering specific system-environment interactions and simulating particular master equations using classical stochastic noise. Furthermore, we show that non-Markovian noise can serve as a resource to enhance quantum system coherence and mitigate the detrimental impacts of Markovian environments.

This study employs lattice cluster theory (LCT) for polymer fluids to demonstrate the strong interdependence of internal energy, enthalpy, and configurational entropy, aligning with recent findings by Caruthers and Medvedev. Consequently, the generalized entropy theory (GET) of glass formation—which integrates LCT with the Adam-Gibbs model—can be reformulated using any of these thermodynamic variables for practical convenience. To identify which properties most naturally correlate with dynamics, we apply thermodynamic scaling, a density-temperature relationship observed in both dynamic and select thermodynamic behaviors. The origins of this scaling are investigated through direct calculations grounded in GET and molecular dynamics simulations of a coarse-grained polymer system. By synthesizing comprehensive LCT modeling of thermodynamic properties, the predictive capabilities of GET regarding the link between fluid thermodynamics and dynamics, and simulation data that validate these frameworks, we derive new insights into the thermodynamic underpinnings of collective motion and the slow $\beta$-relaxation processes in glass-forming liquids.

A power packet dispatching system has been introduced for smart power management, conceptualizing power as discretized packets. This paper examines the optimization of routing these power packets across a network of power routers. By conducting circuit analysis on the router network, we establish a cost metric for power packet delivery. Leveraging this metric, the optimization challenge is formulated as a general shortest path problem between a source node and a load node. Numerical simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm successfully allocates distributed power sources to meet load demands and determines the optimal path for power delivery.

We introduce a data collection and annotation pipeline designed to extract information from Vietnamese radiology reports to generate precise labels for chest X-ray (CXR) images. This approach supports Vietnamese radiologists and clinicians by creating annotated data that aligns with their region-specific diagnostic categories, which often differ from those in other countries. To evaluate the effectiveness of our labeling method, we constructed a CXR dataset comprising 9,752 studies and tested the pipeline using a subset of this collection. The assessment revealed an F1-score of at least 0.9923, confirming that the labeling tool operates with high precision and consistency across all categories. Following dataset creation, we trained deep learning models that utilize knowledge transferred from large, publicly available CXR datasets. To address the challenges of imbalanced multi-label data, we implemented various loss functions and experimented with multiple model architectures to identify the optimal configuration. Our top-performing model, CheXpert-pretrained EfficientNet-B2, achieved an F1-score of 0.6989 (95% CI 0.6740, 0.7240), an AUC of 0.7912, a sensitivity of 0.7064, and a specificity of 0.8760 for general abnormal diagnoses.
