Joseph regarding parabolic adjoint action, Weierstrass sections, and components of the nilfibre in type $A$ (specifically their work in *Indag Math.* and their 2021 Weizmann preprint). This map defines a composition tableau that reconstructs the "canonical" Weierstrass section $e+V$ originally detailed in their first paper. Notably, it is subsequently demonstrated that $e+V$ constitutes a Weierstrass section without relying on that prior work, yielding a substantial simplification. Furthermore, the composition tableau allows one to identify the "VS quadruplets" from the second referenced paper, thereby characterizing the "canonical component" of the nil-fibre containing $e$, even though the tableau itself does not fully determine this component.

Photophoretic levitation enables the lifting and control of lightweight objects via light interactions. Because these forces on macroscopic items are strongest at low pressures, experiments are often conducted in vacuum chambers near the floor or walls. This study presents experimental data showing that the terrain beneath levitating microflyers—including the chamber floor or launchpad—can significantly amplify photophoretic lift compared to free-space values. To characterize this "ground effect" in vacuum settings, we developed a new miniature launchpad consisting of three J-shaped wires designed to reduce unwanted interactions with underlying surfaces. We compared this design against traditional wire-mesh launchpads using simple levitating Mylar disks with diameters of 2, 4, and 8 cm. Notably, wire-mesh launchpads boosted photophoretic lift forces by up to six times. A pronounced ground effect was also observed at the bottom of the vacuum chamber, especially when the distance to the surface was less than the disk's diameter. We offer guidelines to mitigate this ground effect in vacuum experiments, which is essential for testing photophoretic microflyers destined for high-altitude exploration and surveillance on Earth or Mars.

Meta-surfaces aim to substantially enhance future wireless network performance by manipulating radio wave propagation and shaping signals based on the generalized Snell's law. A prominent application is reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, yet their practical utility is constrained by the need for precise user location data. To address scenarios where user position is unavailable, we propose randomly reconfigurable surfaces (RRSs) designed to scatter incoming waves. An RRS consists of a reconfigurable meta-surface where each element applies a randomly selected, time-varying phase shift to the reflected signal. To enable performance analysis of RRS-assisted systems, we first derive novel closed-form expressions for the probability density function, cumulative distribution function, moments, and characteristic function of the sum of double-Nakagami-m random vectors. These vectors have amplitudes following a double-Nakagami-m distribution (the product of two Nakagami-m variables) and phases following a circular uniform distribution. We also examine a specific instance involving the sum of Rayleigh-Nakagami-m random vectors. Leveraging these mathematical tools, we analyze the RRS-assisted composite channel under the assumption that both links experience Nakagami-m fading and the equivalent phase is circularly uniform. We provide closed-form expressions for outage probability, average received signal-to-noise ratio, ergodic capacity, bit error probability, fading margin, and channel quality estimation index to evaluate system performance. Furthermore, these metrics are derived for a practical special case where one of the two links undergoes Rayleigh fading.

Strong-field Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) represents a vibrant area of research, yet investigating fundamental processes like pair production and photon-electron or photon-photon interactions within the nonlinear QED regime poses significant theoretical and experimental hurdles. Globally, numerous experiments are currently being planned or prepared to explore this strong-field domain. Among them, LUXE (Laser Und XFEL Experiment) is a notable platform designed to collide a high-quality 16.5 GeV electron beam from the European XFEL with a 100 TW-class high-power laser. A distinctive feature of LUXE is its capability to measure critical observables, such as $e^+e^-$ pair production rates, with exceptional accuracy and ample statistics by precisely characterizing both beams. Advanced detector technologies for high-energy particles and photons now allow for precision at the percent level. While state-of-the-art high-power lasers provide superior beam quality, residual shot-to-shot fluctuations combined with the high nonlinearity of the studied processes present a specific challenge; for instance, a mere 5% uncertainty in absolute laser intensity can result in approximately a 40% uncertainty in the pair rate. Consequently, precise control of laser parameters is essential. To address this, a comprehensive suite of laser diagnostics is currently being developed at the JETI40 laser in Jena, aiming to tag shot intensities with better than 1% accuracy. This presentation will detail the laser system and the diagnostic suite designed for single-shot tagging of all laser parameters. Furthermore, it will discuss results from an ongoing campaign focused on accurately imaging the beam without introducing significant distortions to the laser parameters for subsequent diagnosis.

This work introduces a radar detection system designed for orthogonal-frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) transmissions, where the transmitting antenna is colocated with a monostatic radar that knows the transmitted signal and monitors echoes from both stationary and moving targets. Target parameters, specifically range and velocity, are estimated using a 2D-Periodogram. To enhance estimation performance under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, we employ discrete Fourier transform channel estimation (DFT-CE), while demonstrating that Zadoff-Chu precoding (ZCP) used for communication does not compromise radar estimation accuracy in high SNR scenarios. Given that the data matrix dimensions often far exceed the number of targets, we propose a sparse Fourier transform-based Fourier projection-slice (FPS-SFT) algorithm to significantly reduce the computational complexity of the 2D-Periodogram. By optimizing system parameters within the 77GHz industrial, scientific, and medical (ISM) band, the system achieves a range resolution of 30.52 cm and a velocity resolution of 0.67 m/s, while cutting periodogram computation time by approximately 98.84%.

Chemical short-range order (CSRO) in crystalline materials significantly affects their properties, with this influence being especially critical for multicomponent systems. We introduce a scheme for the CSRO $\Delta$-parameter, defined by the count of like and unlike bonds within multicomponent systems. This approach utilizes the OPERA (Order Parameter Engineering for Random Systems) framework, applicable to both semi-canonical and canonical ensembles. The proposed framework offers a high-throughput method for exploring CSRO via the $\Delta$-parameter. We demonstrate the $\Delta$-parameter's utility in characterizing CSRO in multicomponent alloys and oxides, specifically FCC-CoCrNi, BCC-MoNbTaW, and (CoCuMgNiZn)O. Furthermore, we show that the $\Delta$-parameter retains the advantages of the Warren-Cowley order parameter while overcoming its limitations. As a scalar quantity, the $\Delta$-parameter effectively represents chemical order, and the OPERA framework successfully handles both semi-canonical and canonical ensembles.

We investigate nearest-neighbor correlation functions for the ground state of the supersymmetric XYZ spin chain with odd length and periodic boundary conditions. Based on a technical assumption concerning the $Q$-operator of the associated eight-vertex model, we demonstrate that these functions admit exact expressions in terms of the Painlevé VI tau functions $s_n$ and $\bar s_n$ defined by Bazhanov and Mangazeev. Additionally, we provide an interpretation of these correlation functions using the Painlevé VI Hamiltonian.

In standard domain adaptation for person Re-identification (Re-ID), both training and target test images are typically gathered under sunny conditions. Conversely, real-world scenarios often involve retrieving pedestrians under severe weather, such as haze, dust, or snow. To address interference from hazy weather in domain adaptation Re-ID, this paper introduces a novel Interference Suppression Model (ISM). The ISM employs a teacher-student architecture to distill interference information at the feature level by minimizing the discrepancy between intrinsic similarity matrices for clear and hazy images. Additionally, at the distribution level, an extra discriminator is incorporated to help the student model refine the clarity of the interference feature distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on two synthetic datasets. The associated code is available online at https://github.com/pangjian123/ISM-ReID.

We examine the asymptotic expansion as $x\to\pm\infty$ of the entire function defined by
\[F_{n,\sigma}(x;\mu)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\sin\,(n\gamma_k)}{\sin
\gamma_k}\,\frac{x^k}{k! \Gamma(\mu-\sigma k)},\quad
\gamma_k=\frac{(k+1)\pi}{2n},\]
where $\mu>0$, $0<\sigma<1$, and $n=1, 2, \ldots$. When $\sigma=\alpha/(2n)$ for $0<\alpha<1$, L.L. Karasheva recently introduced this function in {\it J. Math. Sciences}, {\bf 250} (2020) 753--759 as a solution to a fractional-order partial differential equation. By representing $F_{n,\sigma}(x;\mu)$ as a finite sum of Wright functions, we apply standard asymptotic methods for hypergeometric-type integral functions to derive its expansion. The resulting asymptotic behavior is shown to be highly sensitive to the parameter $\sigma$, with a secondary dependence on the integer $n$. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the precision of the various derived expansions.

Constructing a quantum counterpart to classical deep neural networks poses a significant hurdle in quantum computing. A central obstacle involves replicating the inherent non-linearity of classical deep learning, which is difficult in the quantum realm because the sequential composition of unitary transformations through quantum gates remains intrinsically linear. Previous literature has tackled this issue primarily by inserting measurements between layers of unitary operations. In this work, we present the Quantum Path Kernel, a framework for quantum machine learning designed to emulate the superior generalization capabilities of classical deep learning, particularly hierarchical feature learning. Our method extends the concept of the Quantum Neural Tangent Kernel, previously utilized to analyze the dynamics of both classical and quantum models. By leveraging the parameter trajectory—the path traced by model parameters during training—the Quantum Path Kernel captures differential layer-wise convergence and hierarchical parametric dependencies within the gradient space of the predictor function. We assess this approach using variants of Gaussian XOR mixture classification, an artificial yet representative task that necessitates multilevel learning for optimal class separation.

We establish the existence of what we term "carousel solutions," which are relative periodic solutions to the planar $N=\sum_{j=1}^n k_j$-body problem. These solutions originate with $n$ bodies situated near a non-degenerate central configuration, where each body is subsequently substituted by a cluster of $k_j$ bodies moving in proximity to a small central configuration. Our demonstration utilizes blow-up techniques adapted from variational methods employed in our earlier research.

Research into age-related genes is crucial for various objectives, including elucidating the mechanisms of aging, extending life expectancy, predicting age, and advancing healthcare applications. Building upon a dataset of 27,142 genes, we introduce an information-theoretic framework to detect aging-associated genes by employing unsupervised and semi-supervised learning on human dermal fibroblast gene expression data. Initially, unsupervised learning combined with information-theoretic metrics is utilized to extract key features that effectively represent transcriptome gene expression values. Subsequently, clustering is performed using these identified features. Finally, semi-supervised learning is applied across the resulting clusters with various distance measures to pinpoint novel genes potentially linked to aging. Performance evaluations of both the unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches demonstrate the efficacy of this framework.

Leveraging XOR clauses, also known as parity constraints, can enable the application of more efficient reasoning methods. This paper introduces a gadget designed to translate SAT clauses into Max2XOR constraints, which are XOR clauses involving at most two variables set to either zero or one. Furthermore, we propose novel resolution rules for the Max2XOR problem, which seeks to determine the maximum number of satisfiable constraints within a given set of 2XOR equations.

The small-scale turbulent dynamo (SSD) is widely believed to generate the interstellar medium (ISM) magnetization observed today. This mechanism efficiently transforms kinetic energy ($E_{\rm kin}$) into magnetic energy ($E_{\rm mag}$), typically explaining how a weak initial field ($E_{\rm mag} \ll E_{\rm kin}$) is amplified and sustained at a level where $E_{\rm mag} \lesssim E_{\rm kin}$. Standard studies usually simulate this by growing a weak seed field via turbulence until saturation. However, utilizing three-dimensional, non-ideal magnetohydrodynamical simulations, we demonstrate that the same saturated state can be reached even when the system starts with $E_{\rm mag} \gg E_{\rm kin}$ or $E_{\rm mag} \sim E_{\rm kin}$. This transition occurs through a two-stage exponential decay: first, a slow backreaction converting $E_{\rm mag}$ into $E_{\rm kin}$, followed by Ohmic dissipation within anisotropic current sheets. We provide an analytical model for this saturated state, implying that temporary local magnetic enhancements (where $E_{\rm mag} > E_{\rm kin}$), such as those caused by compressions, will eventually decay to the SSD-determined saturation level governed by turbulence and dissipation. Nevertheless, by developing analytical models for decay times and applying wait-time statistics from compressive supernovae, we show that if the magnetic field exceeds the saturated state, it will not decay sufficiently before the next supernova event occurs. Consequently, absent a magnetic field destruction mechanism beyond our non-ideal MHD framework, interstellar magnetic field amplitudes may also be... (abridged).

We introduce a graph isomorphism test for graphs with Euler genus $g$ that executes in $2^{O(g^4 \log g)}n^{O(1)}$ time. This algorithm establishes the first explicit upper bound regarding the dependency on $g$ for an fpt isomorphism test parameterized by Euler genus. While the only prior fpt algorithm (Kawarabayashi 2015) ran in time $f(g)n$ for some function $f$, our method also applies to graphs that exclude $K_{3,h}$ as a minor, a scenario for which no fpt isomorphism test had previously been identified. The approach leverages a sophisticated integration of combinatorial, graph-theoretic, and group-theoretic methods. Specifically, we define $(t,k)$-WL-bounded graphs, a concept that serves as a robust mechanism for merging group-theoretic strategies with the standard Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm and may hold independent significance.

This paper investigates the formation of consensus within a finite group of like-minded individuals who possess asymmetric information regarding the true state of the world. After observing private signals, these agents begin exchanging messages. Building upon the classical model of rational dialogues by Geanakoplos and Polemarchakis (1982) and its later extensions, we relax the standard requirement that the state space be a probability space and impose no limits on the cardinality of the state space or the information partitions. We demonstrate that a specific class of rational dialogues invariably results in consensus, contingent upon three primary conditions: first, universal connectivity where every agent can communicate directly or indirectly with every other agent; second, reciprocal communication; and third, the capacity for agents to engage in dialogues of transfinite duration.

Current efforts to formulate a theory of active matter often rely on hydrodynamics, kinetic theory, and non-equilibrium statistical physics. Yet, these methods frequently overlook a defining characteristic of certain active systems, especially biological ones: the presence of purpose and the inherent drive toward maximum utility. We argue that this distinction is fundamental to separating active from passive matter. In this work, we present a new game-theoretic approach called statistical teleodynamics, which explicitly incorporates this element and demonstrates its integration with traditional statistical mechanics to create a unified theory of arbitrage equilibrium for both active and passive matter. We define a spectrum of self-actualizing capabilities, ranging from none to fully strategic decision-making, and position various active matter systems within this range. Furthermore, we illustrate that statistical teleodynamics converges to standard statistical mechanics results when self-actualization is zero. Conversely, in economic contexts, it offers fresh perspectives on the emergence of income distributions and fairness within an ideal free market. For intermediate cases, our theory predicts behaviors in active Brownian particles, the formation of ant craters, and phase equilibria in social segregation dynamics. Finally, we propose that this framework provides a novel systems-theoretic view of emergent phenomena, potentially serving as a foundation for a broader theory of design, control, and optimization via self-organization.

Clinical notes offer valuable data that remains underutilized in predictive modeling relative to structured information. This study introduces Clinical XLNet, a novel text representation designed for clinical notes that additionally incorporates temporal information from the sequence of entries. When evaluated on the task of predicting prolonged mechanical ventilation, our experiments show that Clinical XLNet consistently surpasses the leading baseline models.

We investigate the nonlinear response of non-integrable one-dimensional spin models by employing infinite matrix-product state methods. To validate and illustrate this approach, we initially compute two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy for the analytically solvable ferromagnetic transverse field Ising model, characterized by freely propagating domain-wall excitations. Subsequently, we introduce a longitudinal field to probe the unique signatures of confined bound states, noting the appearance of pronounced non-rephasing-like signals. To elucidate these observations, we apply a two-kink approximation to perturbatively calculate the two-dimensional spectra. Our analysis reveals strong consistency between these results and the exact infinite matrix-product state calculations within the strongly confined regime. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for quasi-one-dimensional Ising spin chain materials, specifically $\mathrm{CoNb}_2\mathrm{O}_6$.

An ideal $I \subset \mathbb{k}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ is defined as having linear powers if the minimal free resolution of $I^k$ is linear for every integer $k$. This paper investigates the Betti numbers of such ideals, calculating them explicitly as polynomials in $k$ for specific cases: the ideal generated by all square-free monomials of degree $d$ where $d \in \{2, 3, n-1\}$, and the product of all ideals generated by $s$ variables where $s \in \{n-1, n-2\}$. Additionally, the study examines the generators of the Rees ideal for ideals with linear powers, with a particular focus on those where the Rees ideal is generated by quadratic elements, a topic connected to a conjecture by White regarding matroids.

This research examines initial value problems for semilinear wave equations in one spatial dimension that incorporate spatial weights. It establishes lifespan estimates for classical solutions with compactly supported data across all polynomial weight scenarios. These findings are categorized into two distinct cases based on the total integral of the initial velocity.

Derivative-based optimization techniques excel at solving optimal control problems in the vicinity of local optima but struggle to converge when derivative data becomes unavailable. Conversely, the inference approach to optimal control imposes fewer constraints on the objective landscape, yet its reliance on sampling results in significantly slower computational speeds. We introduce a novel method that integrates second-order optimization with inference. By employing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) control framework, we formulate an inference problem that derives optimal controls from an adaptive distribution approximating the solution of a second-order method. This approach accommodates both simple convex and non-convex cost functions, thereby streamlining cost function design and capitalizing on the advantages of both inference and second-order optimization. Comparative evaluations against Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) and iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator (iLQG) demonstrate that our method surpasses both in terms of sample efficiency and solution quality for manipulation and obstacle avoidance tasks.

Chinese idioms are predominantly four-character expressions characterized by non-compositionality and metaphorical meaning, making them challenging for children and non-native speakers to comprehend. This study introduces a new task called Chinese Idiom Paraphrasing (CIP), which involves rephrasing sentences containing idioms into non-idiomatic equivalents while maintaining the original meaning. By converting idiomatic sentences into standard language, CIP simplifies processing for Chinese NLP systems, thereby enhancing performance in areas such as machine translation, idiom cloze tests, and idiom embeddings. Treating CIP as a specialized paraphrase generation task, the study addresses annotation scarcity by creating a large-scale dataset through human-machine collaboration, comprising 115,530 sentence pairs. Three baseline methods and two novel approaches were implemented to tackle the CIP challenge, with experimental results demonstrating that the proposed methods outperform the baselines on the established dataset.

Autonomous vehicles inevitably face severe weather conditions where public safety is paramount, with climate change anticipated to increase the frequency of heavy snowstorms, posing a significant threat to safe navigation. Although extensive research aims to enhance navigation resilience in winter, there remains a scarcity of standardized metrics for quantifying lidar visibility loss due to precipitation. This chapter introduces a novel real-time metric for measuring lidar visibility degradation, drawing on meteorological concepts of visibility. Evaluated on the Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions (CADC) dataset, the metric correlates with the performance of a state-of-the-art lidar-based localization system and assesses the advantages of filtering point clouds prior to localization. The analysis reveals that while the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm demonstrates surprising robustness against steady snowfall, sudden events like snow gusts can severely compromise its accuracy. The discussion highlights these abrupt phenomena and underscores the necessity for datasets specifically targeting extreme events to better quantify their impact.

We introduce a self-supervised framework that learns scene representations from video by automatically separating them into background, characters, and animations. This approach leverages the fact that moving characters remain equivariant under frame-to-frame transformations, whereas the background remains invariant. Once trained, the system allows for real-time manipulation of image encodings to generate novel combinations of these separated components. To our knowledge, this is the first method capable of unsupervised extraction and synthesis of interpretable backgrounds, characters, and animations. We validate our approach using three datasets: Moving MNIST with backgrounds, 2D video game sprites, and Fashion Modeling.

In recent years, many efforts have been made to develop efficient methods for representing directivity, whether for sound sources or head-related transfer functions. However, the diversity of programming tools and scripts employed by various researchers has made it difficult to reproduce and compare these representations, thereby hindering progress in the field. This paper proposes an objective-oriented solution to address this challenge. The proposed approach involves defining classes for different directivity models that share common properties of directivity functions, facilitating straightforward comparison between various representations. Additionally, a basic MATLAB toolbox implementing this method is presented, along with example implementations of directivity models based on spherical and hyperspherical harmonics.

This work provides an analytic characterization of the infinitesimal generator defined by Applebaum and Estrade for Lévy flights across a wide range of closed Riemannian manifolds, encompassing negatively curved spaces, the flat torus, and the sphere. Leveraging this enhanced understanding of the generator, we derive key properties of the associated semigroup and analyze the asymptotic behavior of the expected stopping time for Lévy flight-based random searches targeting small objects, a scenario often referred to as the narrow capture problem. Furthermore, our research connects to the Lévy flight foraging hypothesis in biology by calculating the mean time required to locate a small target via Lévy flight random walks. For comparison, a similar analysis involving Brownian motion on surfaces was previously presented in [arXiv:2209.12425].

Speech variation is typically measured by comparing phonetic transcriptions of identical utterances; however, manual transcription is both labor-intensive and susceptible to errors. Consequently, this study explores the extraction of acoustic embeddings from multiple self-supervised neural models as an alternative approach. Utilizing these representations, we calculate word-level pronunciation discrepancies among non-native versus native English speakers and between speakers of various Norwegian dialects. To benchmark our findings against previous research, we assess the alignment between these computed differences and human perception by referencing existing human similarity judgments. Our results indicate that speech representations derived from Transformer-based models align more closely with human perception than earlier methods relying on phonetic transcriptions or MFCC features. Additionally, we observe that the most effective features are generally obtained from middle hidden layers rather than the final layer. Finally, we demonstrate that neural speech representations capture not only segmental variations but also intonational and durational nuances that discrete phonetic symbols fail to adequately represent.

The stochastic generalized linear bandit serves as a well-established framework for sequential decision-making, where numerous algorithms achieve near-optimal regret bounds under immediate feedback. However, this assumption often fails in real-world scenarios where rewards are not observed instantly, leaving standard algorithms theoretically unexplained in such contexts. To address this, we analyze delayed rewards by formally introducing a lag between action selection and reward receipt. We demonstrate that an algorithm grounded in the optimistic principle outperforms existing methods by removing the necessity for prior knowledge of the delay distribution and loosening constraints on the decision set and delay characteristics. Consequently, this approach enhances regret bounds from $\widetilde O(\sqrt{dT}\sqrt{d + \mathbb{E}[\tau]})$ to $\widetilde O(d\sqrt{T} + d^{3/2}\mathbb{E}[\tau])$, where $\mathbb{E}[\tau]$ represents the expected delay, $d$ denotes the dimension, and $T$ is the time horizon (with logarithmic terms suppressed). Finally, we validate our theoretical findings using experiments on simulated data.

This review examines space charge effects within ionization detectors, focusing specifically on liquid argon time projection chambers. It provides both analytical and numerical characterizations of how these effects influence reconstructed coordinates in both drift and transverse dimensions. The analysis covers scenarios involving limited electron lifetime, dual-phase detectors experiencing ion feedback, and systems where the drift length is small and comparable to the width. Finally, two design strategies proposed to mitigate these effects are discussed.

Following the introduction of satellite altimetry, the oceanic circulation has been redefined by the ubiquity of mesoscale eddies, which span tens to hundreds of kilometers [5], function as the oceanic equivalent of atmospheric weather systems, and typically represent the peak of the kinetic energy (KE) wavenumber spectrum [7, 19, 23]. However, prior knowledge of these spatial scales largely relied on Fourier analysis within limited regional domains (e.g., [16, 14, 4]), usually measuring a few hundred kilometers, which failed to encompass the full dynamic range at planetary extents. This study introduces the inaugural global wavenumber spectrum of oceanic circulation derived from satellite observations and high-resolution re-analysis data, employing a coarse-graining technique to investigate scales previously inaccessible. Spectra covering three orders of magnitude in length-scale identify the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC) as the dominant spectral peak for the global extra-tropical ocean at approximately $10 \times 10^3~$km. Additionally, a novel power-law scaling is observed across scales exceeding $10^3~$km. While a secondary peak occurs near $300~$km corresponding to mesoscales, these features, due to their broader distribution in wavenumber space, contribute over 50% of the resolved surface KE globally. Length-scales up to twice this size (up to $10^3~$km) display a characteristic seasonal lag of roughly 40 days; consequently, KE at $100~$km peaks in late spring in both hemispheres, whereas KE at $10^3~$km peaks in late summer. This global spectrum provides a novel perspective for comprehending multiscale oceanic circulation within Earth's climate system, extending to the largest planetary scales.

We have developed an explicit family of 3-XOR problems that remain hard for $\Omega(n)$ levels of the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) semi-definite programming hierarchy. This achievement marks the first explicit construction to surpass brute force search (excluding minor low-order improvements noted by Tulsiani 2021 and Pratt 2021). When combined with standard gap amplification methods, our result achieves the same optimal hardness as random instances, accounting for imperfect completeness (as established by Grigoriev TCS 2001 and Schoenebeck FOCS 2008).

Our approach relies on a novel type of small-set high-dimensional expansion (SS-HDX), drawing inspiration from recent advances in locally testable and quantum LDPC codes. By adapting the framework introduced by Dinur, Filmus, Harsha, and Tulsiani (ITCS 2021)—which derived SoS lower bounds from the Ramanujan complex—to this context, we demonstrate that any bounded-degree SS-HDX can be converted into a highly unsatisfiable 3-XOR instance resistant to refutation by $\Omega(n)$ levels of SoS. Furthermore, we show that the recent qLDPC construction by Leverrier and Zémor (Arxiv 2022) provides the required explicit family of bounded-degree SS-HDX. Notably, this also yields the strongest known form of bi-directional high-dimensional expansion available to date.

Cai, Song, and Kou (2015) established a significant advancement by introducing a unified framework for pricing Asian options, covering both discrete and continuous monitoring scenarios within one-dimensional Markov processes. In this work, we extend their research by explicitly performing inverse Z-transforms and inverse Laplace transforms for the discrete and continuous monitoring cases, respectively, under a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) setting. Our approach yields explicit single Laplace transforms that refine their Theorem 2 (p. 543), and numerical analysis confirms the resulting improvements in computational efficiency.

We introduce an efficient technique for producing twisted gamma rays using highly accelerated helium-like ions. These ions are excited to a specific state via irradiation with two optical lasers and subsequently emit a photon carrying orbital angular momentum during deexcitation. Furthermore, we investigate the emission rate alongside related characteristics, including background effects and photo-ionization processes.

Swarm intelligence is a field dedicated to analyzing collective behaviors arising from local interactions among individuals within a group and their surroundings. Within Computer Science, various swarm intelligence methods are employed to solve optimization problems by efficiently locating optimal solutions across a search space. Gradual pattern mining, another area in Computer Science, could significantly benefit from swarm-based optimization to identify gradual patterns within vast search spaces. A gradual pattern represents a rule-based correlation illustrating the evolving relationship between attributes in a dataset; for instance, with attributes {G, H}, such a pattern might be expressed as "the less G, the more H." This paper introduces a numeric encoding scheme for gradual pattern candidates to establish an effective search space. Furthermore, we provide a systematic evaluation of multiple meta-heuristic optimization techniques as robust solutions for discovering gradual patterns using the proposed search space.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) serves as a unified framework for addressing diverse NLP challenges, including relation extraction, question answering, and summarization. Although the availability of extensive labeled datasets has spurred significant research interest in recent years, most prior work has been confined to sentence-level inference, thereby restricting NLI's utility in downstream applications. To address this, we introduce DocNLI, a newly developed large-scale dataset designed for document-level NLI. Derived from a wide variety of NLP tasks and encompassing multiple text genres, DocNLI maintains premises at the document level while allowing hypotheses to range from single sentences to multi-hundred-word passages. Furthermore, unlike many popular sentence-level NLI datasets, DocNLI exhibits minimal artifacts. Our experiments reveal that a model pretrained on DocNLI achieves promising results on standard sentence-level benchmarks even without fine-tuning and demonstrates strong generalization to out-of-domain tasks requiring document-level inference, with additional gains possible through task-specific fine-tuning. The dataset, code, and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/salesforce/DocNLI.

Standard full and half-harmonic oscillators are converted into field theories and analyzed through both canonical and affine quantization methods. This approach yields a successful affine quantization for the half-harmonic oscillator field theory, suggesting that similar valid quantizations can be achieved for more realistic field theory models.

Exposure to external environments triggers various processes in quantum systems, such as equilibration and decoherence. Since macroscopic objects are observed to be both objective and thermal, it is hypothesized that these two properties can coexist within the quantum realm. However, a critical tension exists because objectivity depends on distributed classical information, which may conflict with thermalization. This study investigates the compatibility between thermal and objective states, revealing that they generally cannot coexist. Nevertheless, specific conditions facilitate their simultaneous presence: the high-temperature limit, the non-degenerate low-temperature limit, and scenarios involving large environments. These findings align with our everyday experience of macroscopic objects being both thermal and objective.

This study examines the $\lambda\phi^4$ model in $0+2$ dimensions at its critical point, implementing a simultaneous scaling of both ultraviolet and infrared regimes. We show that the order parameter $\phi$, the correlation length $\xi$, as well as observables such as $\phi^3$ and entanglement entropy, display valuable double scaling behaviors. These computations utilize boundary matrix product state methods applied to tensor network representations of the partition function, although the approach remains valid beyond tensor network contexts. Our analysis yields a refined critical point value of $\alpha_c=11.09698(31)$, surpassing earlier findings.

We investigate the potential equivalence between 5-dimensional primordial black holes and massive 5-dimensional Kaluza-Klein (KK) gravitons as dark matter candidates within the recently introduced dark dimension framework, which tackles the cosmological hierarchy problem. First, we demonstrate that in the local universe, a population of 5-dimensional black holes with masses around $M_{\rm BH}\sim 7\times 10^{13}~{\rm g}$ is practically indistinguishable from a KK tower of dark gravitons having a mass $m_{\rm DM} \sim 50~{\rm keV}$. Second, we link the increase in 5-dimensional black hole mass and the corresponding drop in temperature to the cooling process of the tower of massive spin-2 KK graviton excitations. Initially produced at masses between $\sim 1 - 50~{\rm GeV}$, the bulk of these dark gravitons shifts down to roughly $1 - 100~{\rm keV}$ in the present day. This system cools through decays into lighter gravitons while retaining most of its total mass density, a mechanism similar to intra-tower decays observed in the cosmological evolution of dynamical dark matter. We associate these intra-tower graviton decays with black hole growth via accretion. Furthermore, we argue that the connection between primordial black holes and the dark graviton gas is well-explained by the bound state picture of black holes composed of gravitons.

This study investigates memory allocation behaviors in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) within large-scale systems. We note that in multi-threaded environments, these allocation patterns suffer from significant latency caused by \texttt{mutex} contention in system memory allocators. Such contention-induced latencies create bottlenecks that degrade user-facing services. To address this, we introduce \texttt{MemoMalloc}, a "memorization" technique designed to optimize overall latency with only a moderate rise in peak memory usage. Our approach comprises two parts: a runtime module that records all allocations and links them uniquely to their high-level source operations, and a static analysis module that generates an efficient allocation plan. We implemented \texttt{MemoMalloc} within the PyTorch framework and evaluated its impact on memory consumption and execution performance across various DNN architectures. Results indicate that \texttt{MemoMalloc} surpasses state-of-the-art general-purpose memory allocators regarding DNN inference latency, achieving improvements of up to 40\%.

The emergence of translational medicine was driven by the widening disparity between advancements in biological understanding and actual improvements in patient health, making the application of new knowledge a core component of research plans. Abramson and Parashar contend that a comparable divide exists between sophisticated computational technologies and increasingly demanding applications, necessitating a parallel field known as translational computer science. In this discipline, the intentional transition of research findings into large-scale practice becomes a primary research objective rather than a secondary consideration. Examining the evolution and deployment of grid computing from the mid-1990s through this lens reveals that a translational framework effectively elucidates both the technology's development and its impact. Specifically, the growth of grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit was facilitated by this translational methodology. Furthermore, the authors highlight key lessons derived from these experiences that can inform future translational computer science endeavors.

During the age of extensive sky surveys, photometric redshifts (photo-z) are essential for advancing research in galaxy evolution and cosmology. This study introduces GaZNet-1, a novel Machine Learning framework leveraging neural networks that integrates both imaging data and multi-band photometry to estimate galaxy redshifts. This approach outperforms conventional photometry-only methods in terms of accuracy, precision, and the reduction of outliers. As an initial application, we applied GaZNet-1 to a galaxy sample from the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS). The model was trained and validated on approximately 140,000 galaxies from KiDS Data Release 4 (DR4) with available spectroscopic redshifts from various surveys. Although the dataset primarily consists of bright (MAG_AUTO < 21) and low-redshift ($z < 0.8$) systems, we utilized roughly 6,500 galaxies within the range $0.8 < z < 3$ to enhance training at higher redshifts. The input features comprise r-band images alongside 9-band magnitudes and colors derived from combined optical (KiDS) and near-infrared (VISTA) catalogs. By fusing image and catalog data, GaZNet-1 achieves exceptional precision, with a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of 0.014 for lower redshifts and 0.041 for higher redshifts, while maintaining low outlier fractions of 0.4% and 1.27%, respectively. Compared to machine learning models relying solely on photometry, GaZNet-1 demonstrates a 10–35% boost in precision across redshifts and a 45% decrease in outlier rates. Furthermore, by effectively distinguishing galaxies from stars and active galactic nuclei, the overall photo-z outlier fraction for galaxies can be reduced to 0.3%.

Based on first-principles calculations, two new two-dimensional carbon allotropes consisting of octagons and pentagons have been proposed, designated as OPG-L and OPG-Z. These materials display distinct characteristics: OPG-L is metallic, whereas OPG-Z is a gapless semimetal. Notably, OPG-Z shows significant electronic anisotropy, featuring highly anisotropic Dirac points at the Fermi level. A tight-binding model has been introduced to characterize the low-energy quasiparticles, elucidating the source of these anisotropic Dirac points. This unique anisotropic electronic behavior in OPG-Z is anticipated to hold broad relevance for nano-electronics.

We introduce a new approach to model hierarchical metrical structures for both symbolic music and audio signals in a self-supervised setting that requires minimal domain expertise. The system trains and infers on beat-aligned music data, generating an 8-layer hierarchical metrical tree spanning from the beat to the measure and section levels. The training process necessitates no hierarchical metrical labels beyond beats, relying instead on metrical regularity and inter-voice consistency as inductive biases. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to supervised baselines across various metrical structure analysis tasks for both symbolic and audio music. All demos, source code, and pre-trained models are openly accessible via GitHub.

We demonstrate that for each integer $n$, there are infinitely many $D(n)$-triples that also satisfy the $D(t)$-property for some integer $t$ where $t \neq n$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of infinitely many triples within $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ possessing the $D(-1)$ property that simultaneously exhibit the $D(n)$ property for two distinct integers $n \neq -1$, with none of these triples being equivalent to any $D(1)$-triple.

We compute energy deposition in alpha-quartz (SiO_2) caused by ultra-short laser pulses to develop systematic rules for forecasting damage and nanoparticle generation. This study utilizes a theoretical framework based on time-dependent density functional theory, executed via the real-time method within a multiscale model. To ensure high realism, we apply a meta-GGA Kohn-Sham potential akin to the Becke-Johnson formulation. Our results indicate that deposited energy can be precisely modeled as a function of local electromagnetic pulse fluence. Furthermore, this energy-deposition function aligns closely with the strong-field Keldysh formula across intensities ranging from below the melting point to well beyond the ablation threshold. We observe reasonable consistency between the calculated damage threshold and the energy needed to melt the substrate. However, the ablation threshold derived from the energy required to transform the substrate into an atomic fluid exceeds experimental measurements, highlighting the nonthermal character of the process. Additionally, our predictions show satisfactory agreement with observed ablation depths.

Cryptocurrency mining demands significant energy, making it an ideal candidate for hardware acceleration. This ongoing project introduces the first coprocessor design tailored for the ASIC-resistant CryptoNight-Haven Proof of Work algorithm. Our hardware accelerator is built as an Xilinx Run Time (XRT) RTL kernel specifically targeting the Xilinx Varium C1100 Blockchain Accelerator Card. The architecture utilizes deeply pipelined computation and High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to manage underlying scratchpad data. Our objective is to benchmark this accelerator against current CPU and GPU miners to demonstrate superior throughput and energy efficiency in hash calculations.

The source of the diffuse gamma-ray background (DGRB)—the residual signal remaining after removing all discrete sources from the observed gamma-ray sky—remains unidentified. This background may arise from various source populations, including star-forming and starburst galaxies, active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts, and galaxy clusters. In this study, we integrate cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulations of galaxy clusters with Monte Carlo simulations of cosmic ray (CR) propagation across redshifts $z\leq 5.0$. Our findings indicate that the cumulative gamma-ray flux from clusters could account for up to $100\%$ of the DGRB flux detected by Fermi-LAT above $100$ GeV, provided CR spectral indices fall between $\alpha = 1.5$ and $2.5$ and energy cutoffs range from $E_{\text{max}} = 10^{16}$ to $10^{17}$ eV. The flux is primarily dominated by clusters with masses between $10^{13}$ and $10^{15}$ solar masses at redshifts $z \lesssim 0.3$. Furthermore, our results suggest that future experiments such as HAWC, LHAASO, and the upcoming CTA have the potential to observe high-energy gamma rays originating from these clusters.

We introduce a novel approach to proving nontermination in linear lasso programs, termed the geometric nontermination argument. This concept provides a finite characterization of infinite executions, specifically those following the pattern $(\vec{x} + \sum_{i=0}^t \lambda^i \vec{y})_{t \geq 0}$. The presence of such an argument can be formulated as a system of nonlinear algebraic constraints. We demonstrate that any linear loop program capable of a bounded infinite execution necessarily possesses a geometric nontermination argument. Additionally, we examine nonterminating programs that lack this specific type of argument.

This paper introduces a new full-duplex non-coherent (FD-NC) transmission framework for massive MIMO (mMIMO) systems utilizing analog beamforming (ABF). The approach employs a structured Grassmannian constellation to enable non-coherent communication without the need for channel estimation. Transmit and receive ABF are designed based on slow time-varying angle-of-departure (AoD) and angle-of-arrival (AoA) data, respectively, with the objective of maximizing desired signal power while mitigating the substantial self-interference (SI) inherent in full-duplex operations. Furthermore, the proposed ABF method requires only a single transmit and receive radio frequency (RF) chain to support extensive antenna arrays, thereby lowering hardware costs and complexity in mMIMO environments. Results demonstrate that the suggested FD-NC scheme achieves significant improvements in bit error rate (BER) compared to both half-duplex non-coherent (HD-NC) and half-duplex coherent methods. Additionally, the proposed FD-NC reduces the error floor caused by residual SI in full-duplex transmission and delivers a lower BER than FD coherent transmission.

To achieve high sensitivity in near-infrared wavelengths, new pixel geometries are emerging for silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). This study evaluates prototypes of tip avalanche photodiodes, which incorporate a quasi-spherical p-n junction and demonstrate high photodetection efficiency across a broad spectral range, alongside an analysis of their performance following neutron irradiation. The observed rise in dark count rate is notably lower than that of SiPMs with conventional designs, indicating that this pixel geometry exhibits superior radiation hardness.

Consider a set $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+2}\}$ within $\mathbb{Z}^n$ containing $n+2$ points, where each coordinate of every point has an absolute value no greater than $d$, and the points are not confined to a single affine hyperplane. Let $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ be an $n\times n$ polynomial system with generic integer coefficients bounded by $H$ in absolute value, such that $A$ comprises the union of the exponent vectors for all $f_i$. We present the first algorithm that, for any fixed $n$, precisely counts the number of real roots of $F$ within a time complexity that is polynomial in $\log(dH)$.

This study examines traces at initial times for functions exhibiting mixed time-space smoothness, a topic frequently required in evolution equation theory. Our findings generalize and consolidate numerous prior results, with a key advancement being the ability to accommodate general interpolation couples. We apply these abstract results to regularity issues in fractional and stochastic evolution equations, establishing uniform trace estimates on the half-line.

We investigate inference within the scalar diffusion model $dX_t=b(X_t)dt+\sigma(X_t)dW_t$, utilizing discrete observations $(X_{j\Delta_n})_{0\leq j \leq n}$ as $n\to \infty$ and $\Delta_n\to 0$, assuming periodic coefficients. With $\sigma$ specified, we establish a general theorem outlining the conditions required for Bayesian posteriors to contract in $L^2$-distance around the true drift $b_0$ at the frequentist minimax rate (modulo logarithmic terms) across Besov smoothness classes. We demonstrate that natural nonparametric priors meet these criteria. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the Bayesian approach adapts to both unknown sampling regimes and unknown smoothness levels.

Low-frequency ionization oscillations, known as breathing modes, represent the most intense disturbances in Hall thrusters used for electric propulsion. Due to their simplicity, researchers frequently employ a zero-dimensional (0-D) predator-prey model consisting of two nonlinearly coupled ordinary differential equations to characterize these oscillations and perform scaling analyses. This study examines the continuum equivalent, a one-dimensional (1-D) system comprising two nonlinearly coupled partial differential equations (PDEs) for plasma and neutral density. This 1-D framework serves as a more general model, with the standard 0-D predator-prey model acting as a specific limiting case. We demonstrate that the 1-D model remains stable and exhibits no oscillations under boundary conditions relevant to Hall thrusters and uniform ion velocity. However, we propose a reduced 1-D model based on two coupled PDEs for plasma and neutral densities that becomes unstable and displays oscillations when utilizing an ion velocity profile featuring a near-anode back-flow region (directed toward the anode). Comparisons between this reduced model and the full model, which accounts for self-consistent plasma responses, indicate that the primary characteristics of the breathing mode are accurately captured. Specifically, the analysis reveals that the frequency of breathing mode oscillations is only weakly dependent on the final ion velocity but exhibits a strong correlation with the width of the ion back-flow region.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in image-based learning largely because of their translation equivariance. Recent advancements have extended traditional convolutional layers to non-Euclidean spaces, demonstrating that generalized convolution operations exhibit group equivariance. This paper introduces a novel higher-order Volterra CNN (VolterraNet) designed for data represented as function samples on Riemannian homogeneous spaces. Similar to standard convolutions, we demonstrate that Volterra functional convolutions are equivariant under the action of the isometry group associated with these spaces. Furthermore, under specific constraints, we show that any non-linear equivariant function can be represented by our homogeneous space Volterra convolution, thereby generalizing the non-linear shift-equivariant characterization of Volterra expansions found in Euclidean space. We also establish that second-order functional convolutions can be modeled as cascaded convolutions, enabling efficient implementation. Additionally, we propose a dilated VolterraNet architecture. These innovations result in substantial parameter reductions compared to baseline non-Euclidean CNNs. To validate the efficacy of VolterraNet, we conduct experiments on real-world datasets—including spherical-MNIST, atomic energy, and Shrec17 for classification, and diffusion MRI for group testing—alongside performance comparisons against state-of-the-art methods.

Most existing distantly supervised datasets for relation extraction concentrate on sentence-level tasks and cover a limited range of relations. This study introduces cross-document relation extraction, where the entities forming a relation tuple are located in separate documents linked by a sequence of shared entities. Building on this concept, we constructed a dataset specifically for two-hop relation extraction, where each chain involves exactly two documents. Our new dataset encompasses a significantly larger variety of relations compared to publicly available sentence-level alternatives. Additionally, we developed a Hierarchical Entity Graph Convolutional Network (HEGCN) model tailored for this task, which achieves a 1.1% improvement in F1 score over several strong neural baselines on our two-hop relation extraction dataset.

This study presents a robust, adaptive, well-balanced, and positivity-preserving central-upwind scheme designed for unstructured triangular grids to solve shallow water equations. Building upon the methodology introduced by Liu et al. in *J. of Comp. Phys*, 374 (2018), pp. 213 - 236, the proposed numerical approach incorporates a local a posteriori error estimator within the adaptive algorithm to facilitate efficient mesh refinement. The scheme's accuracy, high resolution, and computational efficiency are validated through various challenging test cases for shallow water models.

This research examines a real-world scenario where regular and reserve crew schedules are dynamically managed up until their execution day. As each day approaches, sudden personnel unavailability creates disruptions that render the original schedules infeasible. We address the fundamental challenge of repairing this infeasibility in the days leading up to execution, while adhering to labor regulations. Our proposed robust repair strategy maintains flexibility to handle future disruptions, explicitly accounting for reserve-crew usage variability by evaluating expected shortfalls via a Markov chain model. Central to our approach is the Robust Crew Recovery Problem, a set-covering formulation that integrates this flexibility concept. We developed a specialized branch-and-price algorithm to solve this problem optimally, utilizing a newly created pulse algorithm to efficiently address the subproblem. Using data from a medium-sized hub-and-spoke airline, we demonstrate that our approach results in fewer flight cancellations and last-minute changes compared to traditional methods that do not incorporate robust measures.

By comparing Galactic chemical evolution models with observed elemental abundances in the Milky Way, we demonstrate that neutron star mergers can serve as a primary r-process site only if, at low metallicities, they exhibit very short delay times and substantial ejecta masses driven by the properties of the compact objects. Specifically, black hole-neutron star mergers, contingent upon black hole spins, may play a significant role in the early chemical enrichment of the Milky Way. Furthermore, we find that none of the binary population synthesis models examined in this study—COMPAS, StarTrack, Brussels, ComBinE, and BPASS—can currently replicate observed elemental abundance patterns. These discrepancies pose challenges not only for neutron star merger scenarios but also for Type Ia supernovae, suggesting potential deficiencies in binary evolution models.

We introduce a constructive theory of continuous domains designed for program extraction. Our objective is to ensure that programs embody provably correct computation without relying on witnesses of correctness, a goal achieved by stating correctness assertions classically. Methodologically, we begin with a predomain base and build its completion. We subsequently examine continuity under the Scott topology and provide a construction for function spaces. Finally, we elaborate on our primary motivating example, applying our theory to real numbers—conceptualized as the total elements of the completion of the predomain of rational intervals—and establish a representation theorem that exactly defines the class of representable continuous functions.

This paper investigates class incremental learning (CIL), a subset of continual learning (CL), addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting (CF). While many existing methods tackle CF by incrementally building a single classifier head for all tasks, they often rely on replaying a limited set of samples from previous tasks to prevent forgetting. However, this strategy remains ineffective because the network parameters for prior tasks are still forced to adapt to these scarce replay samples. In contrast, this work introduces MORE, a novel approach that employs a transformer-based multi-head architecture, assigning a dedicated classifier to each task. Unlike traditional methods that adjust existing network weights using stored samples, MORE utilizes these samples exclusively to construct new, task-specific classification heads without modifying the parameters learned for earlier tasks. Furthermore, the model for the current task is trained not only to recognize its own classes but also to identify out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Consequently, when a test instance is presented, the classifier corresponding to its true data distribution yields a high score, while classifiers for other tasks produce low scores because the input does not match their distributions. Experimental findings demonstrate that MORE surpasses state-of-the-art baselines and inherently supports OOD detection within the continual learning framework.

Partitioning the set of reactions in a chemical reaction network (CRN) yields a decomposition, generating smaller subnetworks from a parent network. A complex is designated as "common" if it appears in at least two of these subnetworks. A decomposition is termed incidence independent when the image of the parent network's incidence map equals the direct sum of the subnetworks' incidence map images. Recent findings reveal a fundamental connection between the complex balanced equilibria of the parent network and its subnetworks within incidence independent decompositions. This paper employs the set of common complexes and a specific criterion to examine the incidence independence of such decompositions. Additionally, a framework was established to analyze decomposition classes sharing similar structural and incidence independence characteristics. We identified classes defined by their common complexes and investigated their incidence independence, noting that some apply to biological and chemical models. Finally, we derived a sufficient condition for complex balancing in certain power law kinetic (PLK) systems featuring incidence independent and complex balanced decompositions. This condition facilitates a generalization of the Deficiency Zero Theorem for specific PLK systems.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC measured the cross sections of $t\bar{t}Z$ and $t\bar{t}W$ processes through a simultaneous fit applied to 36.1 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. Furthermore, an exclusive fit within the 4$\ell$ channel yielded a cross section of $\sigma_{t\bar{t}Z} = 1.07 \pm 0.26 \,\text{pb}$. This value aligns with the combined fit results and is consistent with Standard Model predictions.

We enhance the understanding of complexity in quantum many-body systems by analyzing $W$-states within a spin chain context. These states exhibit a level of non-stabilizerness, or "magic" (quantified by Stabilizer Rényi Entropy or SRE), that increases logarithmically with the number of qubits or spins. Our investigation targets systems where the Hamiltonian features a classical point characterized by extensive degeneracy. In the vicinity of these points, a Clifford circuit transforms the ground state into a $W$-state, whereas in the broader phase associated with this classical point, the state is augmented with local quantum correlations. Topologically frustrated quantum spin chains provide phases exhibiting this specific phenomenology; we demonstrate that the SRE of their ground states equals the sum of the $W$-state's SRE and an extensive local contribution. Our findings indicate that $W$-states and frustrated ground states possess a non-local complexity degree that serves as a harvestable quantum resource, a feature absent in GHZ states and non-frustrated systems.

Evaluating the uncertainty of camera parameters derived from Structure from Motion (SfM) is essential for assessing reconstruction quality and optimizing the process. However, assessing the accuracy of parameters in large-scale reconstructions has remained uncommon due to significant computational hurdles. We introduce a novel algorithm that leverages the sparsity of uncertainty propagation to accelerate computation by approximately tenfold compared to prior methods. This approach maintains high accuracy without relying on any approximations, enabling the calculation of uncertainties for thousands of cameras within tens of seconds on a standard personal computer. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's scalability to reconstructions of any magnitude by applying it to smaller sub-reconstructions.

The junction between a ferromagnet (FM) or antiferromagnet (AFM) and a heavy metal (HM) generates an antisymmetric exchange interaction called the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI), which promotes non-collinear spin arrangements. This interaction stabilizes non-collinear spin textures, including skyrmions, even in materials lacking bulk inversion symmetry. While iDMI values for FM/HM interfaces have been established through both theory and experiment, this study calculates them for metallic AFM MnPt and insulating AFM NiO, considering HM partners of W, Re, and Au. The analysis evaluates the impact of varying AFM and HM thicknesses. Results indicate that iDMI values in MnPt heterostructures are comparable to those found in standard FM materials, whereas those in NiO are significantly lower.

This work investigates the regularity of the boundary separating the disjoint supports of two nonnegative subharmonic functions. Specifically, the subset of this interface where the Alt-Caffarelli-Friedman (ACF) monotonicity formula approaches a positive limit constitutes an $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-rectifiable set. Furthermore, at $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-almost every point within this set, the functions admit unique blowups; that is, their Lipschitz rescalings converge in $W^{1,2}$ to a pair of nondegenerate truncated linear functions whose supports intersect at the approximate tangent plane. The primary methodologies employed are the Naber-Valtorta framework and our recent achievement in deriving a sharp quantitative remainder term for the ACF monotonicity formula. Additionally, we demonstrate applications of these findings to free boundary problems.

Gaussian processes (GPs) are established methods for modeling dependent data, finding widespread use in fields such as spatial statistics, time series analysis, and econometrics. This article introduces the R package `varycoef`, which facilitates estimation, prediction, and variable selection for linear models featuring spatially varying coefficients (SVC) defined by GPs, known as GP-based SVC models. These models provide significant flexibility alongside relative ease of interpretation. Through `varycoef`, we demonstrate diverse applications of (spatially) varying coefficient models across spatial and time series datasets, covering coefficient and model estimation, prediction, and variable selection. The package leverages advanced computational statistics techniques—including parallelization, model-based optimization, and covariance tapering—to ensure computational efficiency. Consequently, users can work with (S)VC models effectively, enabling the estimation of large datasets within a practical timeframe.

Despite significant recent advancements, numerous challenges remain in emotion recognition using physiological data. This study addresses two primary obstacles. First, to handle sparsely labeled physiological data, we decomposed raw signals via spectral analysis to extract complexity and energy features, a process that mitigated noise and enhanced feature extraction efficacy. Second, to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models, we employed Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) for prediction and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for model interpretation. Using eight peripheral physiological signals with cross-subject validation on the DEAP database, LightGBM surpassed XGBoost, achieving F1-scores of 0.814, 0.823, and 0.860 for binary classification of valence, arousal, and liking, respectively. Additionally, SHAP identified critical features and elucidated the relationships between predictors and responses through main and interaction effects. Consequently, the proposed approach not only delivers robust performance with peripheral physiological data but also provides deeper insights into the mechanisms underlying emotion recognition.

Colding and Minicozzi introduced the min-max construction of minimal spheres via harmonic replacement, a method later generalized by Zhou to conformal harmonic tori. We establish that the Morse index of these min-max conformal harmonic tori is at most one.

Given a nonnegative matrix $A=(A_{ij})$, the matrix scaling problem determines if $A$ can be transformed into a doubly stochastic matrix $XAY$ using positive diagonal matrices $X$ and $Y$. The Sinkhorn algorithm achieves this through an iterative process that alternately normalizes rows and columns: $A_{ij} \leftarrow A_{ij}/\sum_{j}A_{ij}$ followed by $A_{ij} \leftarrow A_{ij}/\sum_{i}A_{ij}$. This method converges to a doubly stochastic matrix if and only if the bipartite graph linked to $A$ possesses a perfect matching. Consequently, this property allows one to determine the existence of a perfect matching in a bipartite graph $G$, represented by its $0,1$-matrix $A_G$. Linial, Samorodnitsky, and Wigderson demonstrated that a polynomial number of Sinkhorn iterations on $A_G$ suffices to decide the existence of such a matching. In this paper, we extend this finding: if $G$ lacks a perfect matching, a polynomial number of Sinkhorn iterations identifies a Hall blocker, serving as a certificate for the nonexistence of a perfect matching. Our approach relies on viewing the Sinkhorn algorithm as alternating KL-divergence minimization (Csiszár and Tusnády 1984; Gietl and Reffel 2013) and analyzing its behavior for nonscalable matrices (Aas 2014). Furthermore, we connect the Sinkhorn limit to parametric network flow, the principal partition of polymatroids, and the Dulmage-Mendelsohn decomposition of bipartite graphs.

A numerical study examines the focusing of a rubidium Bose-Einstein condensate using an optical lattice potential. These results are contrasted with a classical trajectory model, which fails to accurately predict the full width half maximum (FWHM) of the focused beam. By incorporating interaction effects inherent to the Bose-Einstein condensate into the classical trajectory framework, we demonstrate that reliable FWHM estimates can be achieved, aligning closely with numerical solutions of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. Furthermore, an analysis of optimal focusing conditions reveals that a strongly interacting Bose-Einstein condensate could potentially achieve a focusing scale of approximately 20 nm.

This paper provides a straightforward and comprehensive framework for defining mass at null infinity using harmonic coordinates through three distinct methods, all of which adhere to the Bondi mass loss law. The first two approaches rely solely on limits of the metric (the Trautman mass) and the null second fundamental forms along asymptotically characteristic surfaces (the asymptotic Hawking mass), respectively, both of which depend exclusively on the ADM mass. The third method introduces an original approach by constructing special characteristic coordinates at null infinity (the Bondi mass). These findings are based on metric asymptotics established in [24].

We demonstrate that pre-trained Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), such as StyleGAN, function effectively as a latent bank to enhance the quality of large-factor image super-resolution (SR). Although most current SR techniques rely on adversarial loss to synthesize realistic textures, our proposed method, Generative LatEnt bANk (GLEAN), surpasses these approaches by directly utilizing the rich and varied priors contained within a pre-trained GAN. In contrast to common GAN inversion strategies that demand costly, image-specific optimization during execution, GLEAN requires only a single forward pass to produce the upscaled result. This method integrates seamlessly into a straightforward encoder-bank-decoder framework featuring multi-resolution skip connections. By switching the latent bank, GLEAN can handle images across diverse categories, including cats, buildings, human faces, and cars. Compared to existing solutions, images upscaled by GLEAN exhibit marked improvements in both fidelity and texture faithfulness.

We conducted an analysis of diffuse ultraviolet (UV) emission in the vicinity of the Taurus Molecular Cloud using data from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX). By applying a Monte Carlo dust scattering model, we determined that approximately 50% of the scattered flux stems from the molecular cloud itself, with the remaining 25% located in the foreground and 25% in the background. While the best-fit albedo for the dust grains is 0.3, the specific geometry of the system prevented us from constraining the phase function asymmetry factor (g).

This study investigates "nanoptera"—solitary waves that are non-localized and feature exponentially small yet non-decaying oscillations—within two types of singularly perturbed Hertzian chains subjected to precompression: woodpile chains (modeled as systems of Hertzian particles and springs) and diatomic Hertzian chains with alternating masses. We show that nanoptera emerge from Stokes phenomena, manifesting when special paths known as Stokes curves are crossed in the complex plane. Utilizing exponential asymptotics, we derive approximations for the oscillation amplitudes. Our analysis indicates that traveling waves in a singularly perturbed woodpile chain cross a single Stokes curve, triggering these oscillations. Numerical simulations confirm that our asymptotic predictions accurately capture the non-decaying oscillatory behavior in woodpile chains. In a similar analysis of diatomic Hertzian chains, we find that nanopteron solutions consist of two distinct exponentially small oscillatory components. We demonstrate that specific mass ratios allow these two contributions to cancel, resulting in localized solitary waves; this finding extends previous experimental and numerical observations regarding mass ratios that support localized solitary waves in diatomic Hertzian chains without precompression. Furthermore, comparing asymptotic and numerical results for a diatomic Hertzian chain with precompression shows that our exponential asymptotic approach accurately predicts oscillation amplitudes across a broad range of system parameters, though it fails to identify several mass ratios that correspond to localized solitary-wave solutions.

As infrared night vision vehicle assistance systems become increasingly integrated into autonomous driving, the precision of pedestrian infrared imagery has steadily enhanced. This study employs transfer learning to adapt the YOLOv3 model for pedestrian detection within infrared images. Specifically, YOLOv3 is transferred to the CVC infrared pedestrian dataset, where the original loss function is substituted with Diou loss to optimize hyperparameters and achieve superior transfer learning performance. Experimental results on the CVC dataset indicate that while the standard YOLOv3 model achieves an Average Precision (AP) of 96.35%, the Diou-YOLOv3 variant attains an AP of 72.14%; however, the latter demonstrates a significantly faster convergence rate in the loss curve. Comparing these two models confirms the efficacy of the transfer learning approach.

Within the de Sitter ambient space formalism, a massless minimally coupled scalar field is derived from a massless conformally coupled scalar field combined with a constant five-vector $A^{\alpha}$. Furthermore, the interaction Lagrangian for massless minimally coupled scalar and spinor fields incorporates an additional constant five-vector, $B^{\alpha}$. In interacting scenarios, these constant five-vectors can be determined within the null curvature limit. This work proceeds by calculating the tree-level $\cal S$ matrix elements for scalar-spinor field interactions; subsequently, $A^{\alpha}$ and $B^{\alpha}$ will be fixed by matching these results in the null curvature limit against their Minkowskian equivalents.

The global pandemic caused by COVID-19 has stalled future progress and persists without an immediate long-term cure. Vaccine distribution is lagging behind the virus's rapid spread, making it crucial for individuals to remain vigilant and take timely precautions rather than waiting to react after infection. Leveraging the widespread availability of internet-connected mobile devices, we propose a Fog Server (FS) architecture designed to raise awareness about local virus transmission. This system integrates Hidden Markov Models (HMM) with Bluetooth contact tracing to achieve polynomial computational efficiency. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is validated through real-world data analysis across various simulation parameters.

The objective of blind image deblurring is to reconstruct a sharp image from a motion-blurred source without knowledge of the camera's movement. Although current state-of-the-art techniques perform exceptionally well on noiseless or near-noiseless images, the assumption of noise-free data is unrealistic, as low-light conditions—often the primary cause of motion blur due to longer exposure times—necessitate the presence of noise. Consequently, motion blur and significant noise frequently coexist. Most existing approaches tackle this by first estimating the blur kernel $k$ and subsequently deconvolving the noisy image. In this study, we demonstrate that current state-of-the-art kernel estimation methods relying on the $\ell_0$ gradient prior can be modified to effectively manage high noise levels while maintaining efficiency. Furthermore, we show that a rapid non-blind deconvolution technique can be substantially enhanced by applying denoising to the blurry image beforehand. The proposed method achieves results comparable to those of far more computationally intensive approaches.

In supervised classification tasks, test sets can include samples from classes unseen during training, and the same units may be measured using additional variables collected later. To address this, the classifier must adapt to both potential unknown classes and increased dimensionality. We propose Dimension-Adaptive Mixture Discriminant Analysis (D-AMDA), a model-based discriminant method capable of identifying unobserved classes and adjusting to higher dimensions. Parameter estimation is performed using a full inductive approach grounded in an EM algorithm. This method is integrated into a broader framework for adaptive variable selection and classification designed for high-dimensional data. The framework's efficacy in handling complex scenarios is validated through a simulation study and an artificial experiment involving the classification of adulterated honey.

Research into modeling conservative systems using neural networks is currently very active. A prevalent method involves Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs), which operate under the premise that conservative systems obey Hamilton's equations of motion. While many recent studies aim to refine the integration schemes for training HNNs, this paper proposes enhancing them by incorporating a continuous-time trajectory estimate generated by an auxiliary neural network known as a deep hidden physics model. We show that this proposed integration approach performs effectively for HNNs, particularly when dealing with low sampling rates, noisy, and irregular observations.

Features within the inflationary landscape can introduce additional energy into inflation models, generating on-shell particles with masses significantly exceeding the Hubble scale. This capability expands the energy horizon of cosmological collider physics, a field where signals from such particles are typically suppressed by Boltzmann factors. We investigate the mechanisms behind this classical cosmological collider across two classes of primordial features.
