A classical trajectory Monte Carlo model successfully extracts this mechanism, which is subsequently validated through quantum mechanical simulations. These findings highlight the critical role of pulse duration in NSDI and enhance our comprehension of strong-field tunnel-recollision dynamics within mid-infrared laser environments.

Pre-trained image-text models such as CLIP have proven highly effective due to the robust vision-language representations learned from extensive web-scale data. Leveraging these strong visual features, some prior research has successfully adapted image representations to the video domain. Nevertheless, the application of image-language pre-trained models for video-language post-pretraining remains largely unexplored. This paper addresses two key questions: 1) what factors impede CLIP's performance in video-language tasks during post-pretraining, and 2) how can these limitations be addressed? Through comprehensive experiments and analysis, we identify that data scale and the domain gap between language sources are critical factors. Guided by these findings, we introduce CLIP-ViP, an Omnisource Cross-modal Learning method built upon CLIP that incorporates a Video Proxy mechanism. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances CLIP's performance in video-text retrieval and achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple datasets, including MSR-VTT, DiDeMo, LSMDC, and ActivityNet. We will make our code and pre-trained CLIP-ViP models available at https://github.com/microsoft/XPretrain/tree/main/CLIP-ViP.

By employing pedal coordinates, we analyze the trajectories of a free double linkage. We present a geometric method to construct these orbits and demonstrate an unexpected link between this mechanical system and orbits surrounding a black hole, as well as solutions to the Dark Kepler problem.

This paper proposes modeling an extended DC state estimation (SE) problem within an electric power system as a factor graph (FG), which is then solved using the belief propagation (BP) algorithm. While the standard DC model utilizes bus voltage angles as state variables, the extended DC model incorporates both bus voltage angles and magnitudes. By applying BP to this extended DC scenario, we establish a Gaussian BP framework and derive closed-form expressions for the BP messages exchanged across the factor graph. The efficacy of the BP algorithm is validated using the IEEE 14-bus test system. Furthermore, applying BP to the extended DC case offers critical insights into the fundamental structure of BP equations in more complex models, such as the AC model, a subject for our future research. Additionally, a secondary objective of this work is to provide a comprehensive and detailed exposition on applying BP to state estimation, thereby enhancing the accessibility and applicability of this powerful algorithm within the power engineering community.

This paper investigates two discretizations of the AKNS-ZS type nonlinear Fourier transform, denoted as ${\cal F}^E$ and ${\cal F}^D$. The ${\cal F}^D$ transformation is specifically designed for analyzing distributions of the form $u = \sum_{n = 1}^N u_n \, \delta_{x_n}$, where the poles $x_n$ are not equidistant. The primary contribution of this work is the development of recursive algorithms for the inverses of both transformations. However, the algorithm for $({\cal F}^D)^{- 1}$ requires greater numerical resources compared to that for $({\cal F}^E)^{- 1}$. Additionally, we detail a significant symmetry property inherent to ${\cal F}^D$. This property facilitates the simplification of nonlinear Fourier analysis for constant mass distributions, $u = \sum_{n = 1}^N u_c \, \delta _{x_n}$, allowing for the use of the more computationally efficient ${\cal F}^E$ and its inverse.

We investigate two distinct analytical frameworks for characterizing the metastable behavior of a Markov chain: one based on transition probabilities and the other on the large deviations rate functional. Consider a sequence of continuous-time Markov chains $(X^{(n)}_t:t\ge 0)$ defined on a fixed finite state space $V$. Assuming specific conditions on the jump rates, we demonstrate the existence of time scales $\theta^{(p)}_n$ and probability measures with disjoint supports $\pi^{(p)}_j$ (where $j\in S_p$, $1\le p \le q$). These satisfy: (a) $\theta^{(1)}_n \to \infty$ and $\theta^{(k+1)}_n/\theta^{(k)}_n \to \infty$; and (b) for any $p$, initial state $x\in V$, and $t>0$, the distribution of $X^{(n)}_{t \theta^{(p)}_n}$ converges as $n\to\infty$ to a convex combination of the measures $\pi^{(p)}_j$, with weights dependent on $x$ and $t$.

Let $I_n$ denote the level-two large deviations rate functional for $X^{(n)}_t$ as $t\to\infty$. Under the same jump rate hypothesis and assuming reversibility, we show that $I_n$ decomposes as $I_n = I^{(0)} \,+\, \sum_{1\le p\le q} (1/\theta^{(p)}_n) \, I^{(p)}$. Here, the rate functionals $I^{(p)}$ are finite if and only if their arguments are convex combinations of the measures $\pi^{(p)}_j$; specifically, $I^{(p)}(\mu) < \infty$ precisely when $\mu = \sum_{j\in S_p} \omega_j\, \pi^{(p)}_j$ for some probability measure $\omega$ on $S_p$.

DeepFake face-swapping technology poses a serious risk to online security and social media by enabling the replacement of a source face in any photo or video with that of a different individual. To mitigate such fraud, researchers have explored adversarial methods targeting DeepFakes or facial manipulation; however, current approaches often rely on white-box settings or black-box scenarios requiring numerous queries, which restricts their real-world utility. Addressing this limitation, we present a practical adversarial attack that operates without any queries to the facial forgery model. Our approach utilizes a substitute model designed for face reconstruction to generate adversarial examples and transfer them directly to inaccessible black-box DeepFake systems. Specifically, we introduce the Transferable Cycle Adversarial Generative Adversarial Network (TCA-GAN) to create perturbations that disrupt unknown DeepFake architectures. Additionally, we develop a novel post-regularization module to improve the transferability of these adversarial examples. To thoroughly evaluate our methods, we have established a challenging benchmark for DeepFake adversarial attacks to support future research. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed attack significantly degrades the visual quality of DeepFake images, making them more susceptible to detection by both humans and algorithms. Furthermore, we show that the algorithm can be generalized to protect face images against a wide range of face translation techniques.

This note examines the challenge of calculating fermion propagators across a wide range of strongly correlated systems that can be modeled as fermions interacting with an (over)damped bosonic mode. It reviews several existing methods and their outcomes, such as standard diagrammatic resummation and the eikonal technique, alongside "experimental" approaches like higher-dimensional bosonization and generalized (or "bottom-up"/"non-AdS/non-CFT") holographic conjectures. Currently, these results largely conflict with one another or remain incomplete, indicating that a definitive solution to this pervasive problem has not yet been discovered.

This work introduces the explicit formulation of a triad family of Liouville integrable maps in three variables and suggests a multi-field extension thereof. By enforcing variable separability on the invariants of this family, we demonstrate the emergence of the $H_{\rm I}$, $H_{\rm II}$, and $H_{\rm III}^A$ Yang-Baxter maps in general position with singularities. Furthermore, two distinct approaches for deriving entwining Yang-Baxter maps are outlined. The first method yields entwining maps linked to the $H_{\rm I}$, $H_{\rm II}$, and $H_{\rm III}^A$ Yang-Baxter maps, while the second produces non-periodic entwining maps corresponding to the entire $F$ and $H$ list of quadrirational Yang-Baxter maps. Finally, we illustrate how transfer maps associated with the $H$-list can be viewed as the $(k-1)$-iteration of simpler maps, termed extended transfer maps; these subsequently generate $k$-point alternating recurrences, which represent alternating versions of certain hierarchies of discrete Painlev\'e equations.

This paper examines the Cauchy-type problem for a nonlinear differential equation featuring the $\Psi$-Hilfer fractional derivative, establishing the existence and uniqueness of solutions within a weighted function space. We analyze the Ulam--Hyers and Ulam--Hyers--Rassias stability of this problem using the successive approximation method. Additionally, we explore the sensitivity of solutions to initial conditions and uniqueness through the lens of $\epsilon$-approximated solutions, concluding with an illustrative example to validate our findings.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has caused profound social and economic disruptions, alongside dramatic and abrupt changes in traffic patterns. This study examines how local government mandates and restrictions influenced road safety in New York City, Los Angeles, and Boston. Specifically, we analyzed the distribution of accident hotspots before and after the outbreak, revealing that traffic accidents shifted in both timing and location relative to prior years. Furthermore, we investigated the road network characteristics within these hotspot areas to better understand the underlying causes of these shifts.

E. J. Cockayne and S. T. Hedetniemi first introduced the concept of the domatic number for graphs. B. Zelinka later extended this notion to uniform hypergraphs. Furthermore, Zelinka defined the edge-domatic number and total edge-domatic number of graphs. This paper explores and proves several assertions regarding the vertex domatic number, edge-domatic number, and total domatic number within specific uniform hypergraphs.

Learning-to-rank methods have demonstrated significant value in prioritization tasks, where resources are allocated to items with the highest estimated probabilities. However, this study highlights a critical flaw in current learning-to-rank algorithms: their reliance on convex proxies results in suboptimal approximations. The paper subsequently explores "exact" reranking approaches grounded in mathematical programming. It establishes that a relaxed formulation of this exact problem yields the same optimal solution and supports these findings with empirical analysis.

Previous research (Amuru et al., 2015) demonstrated that online learning algorithms can effectively determine optimal physical layer parameters for jamming digital modulation schemes without prior knowledge of the victim's transmission strategy. However, this task entails solving a multi-armed bandit problem with a mixed action space that can expand significantly, leading to slow convergence toward the optimal jamming strategy, particularly when the victim and jammer are not perfectly synchronized. To address these sample efficiency challenges, this work introduces a linear bandit algorithm that leverages inherent similarities among actions. Furthermore, we propose context features tailored to the statistical characteristics of non-coherent jamming, showing markedly improved convergence compared to existing methods. Additionally, we illustrate how prior knowledge regarding the victim's transmissions can be seamlessly incorporated into the learning framework, while also discussing limitations within the asymptotic regime.

Building upon the foundational models and concepts from Part 1, this study develops data-driven methods to approximate dictionary representations of Koopman operators. While Part 1 established a framework for validating the subspace invariance of a Koopman dictionary using the state-inclusive logistic lifting (SILL) basis—an affine structure enhanced with conjunctive logistic functions where nonlinear components are homogeneous—this work explores alternative approaches. We demonstrate that combining heterogeneous dictionary functions from distinct nonlinear classes yields accuracy and dimensional scaling comparable to the deep-learning-based deepDMD algorithm. Specifically, by constructing a mixed dictionary that integrates SILL functions with conjunctive radial basis functions (RBFs), we achieve deepDMD-level performance with a tenfold reduction in parameters, all while retaining geometric interpretability. These findings reinforce the potential of dictionary-based Koopman models for addressing high-dimensional nonlinear learning challenges.

The 2020 announcement of the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) has renewed interest in deep-inelastic-scattering (DIS) data from $ep$ collisions recorded at the Hadron-Electron Ring Accelerator (HERA). The H1 detector, characterized by its hermetic and asymmetric design featuring tracking and fully instrumented calorimeters, is particularly well-suited for analyzing jet and event shape observables. Proposed studies of jets, global event shapes, and correlations within both HERA and EIC DIS experiments aim to refine the three-dimensional understanding of nucleon structure and hadronization, including their flavor dependencies, while enabling precision tests of QCD and Beyond-Standard-Model (BSM) theories. This contribution details recent findings on lepton-jet azimuthal decorrelation and 1-jettiness event shape measurements derived from high-$Q^2$ DIS data collected by the H1 detector at HERA.

Robotic operations, such as attaining a pre-grasp state, are defined in task space, while motion control occurs in joint space. Due to intrinsic actuation inaccuracies within the joint space, robots cannot precisely achieve their intended task space configurations. Additionally, various inverse kinematics (IK) solutions map joint space errors to task space differently. Consequently, for a specific task with a defined error tolerance, not all IK solutions are guaranteed to succeed. An IK solution that can reliably execute a task (potentially with high probability) regardless of specific joint space error realizations is termed a robust IK solution. This paper formulates and resolves the robust inverse kinematics problem for redundant manipulators subject to actuation uncertainties. We provide both simulation and experimental data from a $7$-DoF redundant manipulator applied to two scenarios: pre-grasp positioning and pre-insertion positioning. Our findings indicate that robust IK solutions yield higher success rates and enable the robot to self-assess its potential success across various application scenarios.

This study introduces an algorithm for generating robust, reliability-based topology optimized designs within a random-field material framework. The initial design domain consists of linear elastic material, where the Young's modulus is represented as a random field. To streamline calculations, the Karhunen-Loève expansion discretizes this random field into a limited set of random variables. Robustness is attained by optimizing a weighted combination of the mean and standard deviation of the quantity of interest, whereas reliability is enforced via a probabilistic constraint. To minimize computational expenses, the method employs Smolyak-type sparse grids and the stochastic response surface method. Additionally, an efficient inverse-reliability algorithm is implemented to resolve the double-loop structure inherent in reliability analysis. The proposed approach is evaluated on two standard benchmark problems found in existing literature, and Monte Carlo simulations are subsequently used to verify the robustness and reliability of the resulting optimized designs.

An amplitude analysis of $B^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$ decays, utilizing a data set of $3 \; {\rm fb}^{-1}$ from $pp$ collisions recorded by the LHCb detector, reports observations of $CP$ violation from various sources. A significant $CP$ asymmetry is detected in the decay amplitude associated with the tensor $f_2(1270)$ resonance, alongside notable $CP$ violation within the low invariant mass $\pi^+ \pi^-$ S-wave. Furthermore, the study confirms $CP$ violation arising from the interference between the $\pi^+ \pi^-$ S-wave and the P-wave $B^+ \to \rho(770)^0 \pi^+$ amplitude; while this interference generates substantial local asymmetries, it vanishes when integrated across the full decay phase space. These findings offer both qualitative and quantitative advancements in understanding $CP$-violation mechanisms in hadronic $B$ decays.

Let $G$ be a finite group, $\alpha$ a normalized 2-cocycle in $Z^{2}\big(G,{\mathbb S}^{1}\big)$, and $X$ a $G$-space where a normal subgroup $A$ acts trivially. We demonstrate that the $\alpha$-twisted $G$-equivariant $K$-theory of $X$ splits into a direct sum of twisted equivariant $K$-theories for $X$, indexed by the orbits of a $G$-action on the set of irreducible $\alpha$-projective representations of $A$. This result extends the decomposition previously established in [G\'omez J.M., Uribe B., Internat. J. Math. 28 (2017), 1750016, 23 pages, arXiv:1604.01656] for standard equivariant $K$-theory. Additionally, we examine specific instances of this decomposition for the dihedral groups $D_{2n}$, where $n \ge 2$ is an even integer.

This paper introduces a novel subclass $\mathcal{M}_p(\alpha,\beta)$ of $p$--valent functions and derives several coefficient inequalities for this class. Furthermore, utilizing the Hadamard product, we define a general operator and establish the conditions under which it remains within $\mathcal{M}_p(\alpha,\beta)$.

TORCH is a time-of-flight detector engineered to identify charged pions and kaons up to 10 GeV/c over a 10-meter flight path, necessitating a time resolution of 15 ps per particle. The system utilizes a 1 cm thick quartz plane to generate Cherenkov photons, which are directed onto square 53 x 53 mm² Micro-Channel Plate Photomultipliers (MCP-PMTs) segmented into an equivalent 8 x 128 pixel array. A small-scale demonstrator featuring a custom MCP-PMT and readout electronics was successfully tested in a 5 GeV/c mixed pion/proton beam at CERN's PS facility, yielding preliminary results of single-photon resolution under 100 ps. The anticipated performance of a full-scale TORCH detector for the LHCb Upgrade II is also outlined.

We investigate coupled dark energy (CDE) models, in which dark matter particles experience a force exceeding gravity due to a scalar field acting as dark energy and mediating a fifth force. For the first time, we conduct a tomographic analysis of CDE, parametrizing and constraining the coupling strength across various redshift bins. This approach identifies which datasets most effectively limit the coupling magnitude and determines how strong the coupling can be at different cosmic epochs. Initially, we utilize cosmic microwave background (CMB) data from the Planck satellite, along with the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and South Pole Telescope (SPT), to evaluate the effects of different dataset combinations. Subsequently, we apply a range of low-redshift probes to test both constant and tomographic CDE scenarios. Notably, we incorporate KiDS-1000 weak lensing data, BOSS galaxy clustering data, and their combination, including 3x2pt galaxy-galaxy lensing cross-correlations, marking the first use of these specific datasets for this purpose. Our results indicate that a tomographic CDE model allows for significant variations in coupling strength between epochs. However, when combining CMB data with low-redshift probes excluding weak lensing and galaxy clustering, the coupling at redshifts $z \leq 5$ remains largely unconstrained. Conversely, galaxy clustering and the resulting 3x2pt analysis impose tight limits on the coupling strength $\beta$, yielding $\beta \lesssim 0.02$ at the 68% confidence level for a constant coupling. These findings suggest that future galaxy surveys could serve as powerful tools for constraining such CDE models.

Extracting acronyms and their full forms is a critical task for numerous NLP applications. Although recent years have seen significant advancements in this area, current research remains constrained to English and specific fields like science and biomedicine, leaving challenges in other languages and domains largely unexplored. The scarcity of annotated datasets across diverse languages and sectors has been a primary obstacle to progress in this field. To overcome this gap, we introduce a novel dataset designed for multilingual, multi-domain acronym extraction. This dataset comprises 27,200 manually annotated sentences spanning six typologically distinct languages and two domains: Legal and Scientific. Our extensive experiments on this dataset reveal that acronym extraction presents unique challenges across different languages and learning configurations, underscoring the urgent need for further investigation into multilingual and multi-domain acronym extraction.

Recent research indicates that machine intelligence systems are susceptible to failures caused by adversarial attacks or natural distribution shifts. This vulnerability has sparked significant concern regarding the deployment of machine learning in real-world settings, particularly within safety-critical fields like autonomous driving (AD). Conversely, traditional AD testing on naturalistic scenarios demands hundreds of millions of driving miles to capture the high dimensionality and rarity of safety-critical events. Consequently, various AD evaluation methods have emerged, yet they typically rely on disparate simulation platforms, safety scenario types, generation algorithms, and route variations. Therefore, despite extensive efforts in AD testing, it remains difficult to compare and assess the effectiveness and efficiency of different scenario generation algorithms and testing mechanisms under comparable conditions. This paper introduces SafeBench, the first unified platform designed to integrate diverse safety-critical testing scenarios, generation algorithms, and variations such as driving routes and environments. Furthermore, we deploy four deep reinforcement learning-based AD algorithms using four distinct input types (e.g., bird's-eye view, camera) to facilitate fair comparisons on SafeBench. Our findings reveal that the generated scenarios are indeed more challenging and highlight the trade-off between AD agent performance in benign versus safety-critical contexts. We believe that SafeBench will serve as a catalyst for developing new scenario generation techniques and safer AD algorithms. SafeBench is accessible at https://safebench.github.io.

As network infrastructure expands and demands for reliability grow, disruptive incidents such as natural disasters, power failures, and malicious attacks have emerged as significant threats to modern communication networks. These events can obliterate all devices within a specific region, causing prolonged disruptions to numerous network-dependent applications. Consequently, developing disaster-resilient networks is crucial for ensuring future highly survivable communication services. This paper addresses the design of such resilient networks using Software Defined Networking (SDN). Rather than relying solely on the control plane (the controller) to manage all failures, we propose an integrated design that mitigates disaster risks by incorporating redundant functions directly into the data plane. Our solution combines a sub-graph based proactive protection mechanism on the data plane with a splicing strategy at the controller to ensure effective restoration. Implemented within the OpenFlow framework using the Mininet emulator and Nox controller, our systematic design demonstrates high robustness with minimal control overhead in numerical evaluations.

This paper addresses tabular infinite-horizon concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) subject to convex constraints. Since many constrained applications, including robotics, strictly prohibit policy violations, we introduce a model-based algorithm that guarantees zero constraint breaches. Our approach relies on the assumption that the concave objective and convex constraints admit a solution within the interior of the feasible set of occupation measures. By solving a refined optimization problem, we ensure constraints remain satisfied even in the presence of model uncertainty and stochasticity. Additionally, we develop a novel Bellman error-based analysis tailored for tabular infinite-horizon scenarios, enabling the evaluation of stochastic policies. Integrating this analysis with our tighter optimization formulation, we derive a regret bound for the objective that scales as $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ over $T$ environment interactions, ignoring other factors.

We present the discovery of 1,656 new star clusters located in the Galactic disk (|b|<20°) at distances greater than 1.2 kpc, identified through Gaia EDR3 data. Building on our prior research, we employed an unsupervised machine learning algorithm, DBSCAN, alongside a distinctive data preparation technique to derive clustering coefficients. This approach demonstrated high effectiveness for blindly searching for star clusters. We compiled tables detailing the physical parameters and member stars of these new clusters and highlighted several intriguing cases, including a potential globular cluster. The dataset, encompassing cluster parameters and stellar membership, is accessible via anonymous FTP at https://cdsarc.cds.unistra.fr/ftp/vizier.submit//he22c through the CDS. Our analysis of these findings explored their statistical properties, revealing that the proper motion dispersions and radii of the newly found clusters align with previously reported values. Furthermore, clusters beyond 1.2 kpc were found to be older than those in the solar neighborhood, while objects in the third Galactic quadrant exhibited the lowest line-of-sight extinctions. When combined with our earlier results, this method identified a total population of 2,541 new clusters, representing 55% of all newly published clusters during the Gaia era. Consequently, the total number of cataloged Gaia star clusters has risen to nearly six thousand. Future efforts must focus on unified confirmation and the determination of member stars for all reported clusters.

Within Wilsonian Renormalization, renormalization group (RG) flows are characterized by differential equations describing the dependence of coupling constants on energy scales. These equations exhibit a strong resemblance to thermodynamic relations governing systems and temperature, suggesting that thermodynamic-like structures within the flows are a natural area of inquiry. Dynamical Systems theory provides the mathematical framework for analyzing these equations, with applications already established in studying RG flows. Notably, Zamolodchikov's C-Theorem and its higher-dimensional analogues demonstrate a monotonically decreasing function along the flow, mirroring the second law of thermodynamics; this concept corresponds to a Lyapunov function in Dynamical Systems. Such a function helps exclude exotic asymptotic behaviors, such as periodic flows or limit cycles. Furthermore, bifurcation theory and index theories are investigated for their utility in analyzing RG flows: bifurcation theory aids in understanding couplings crossing marginality, while index theory extracts global information about the flow's underlying space. Finally, this dissertation explores applications in holographic RG flows to determine whether structural behaviors in holographic theories align with those in the dual field theory.

Current research into quantum computing algorithms centers on identifying specific quantum features that can enhance computational models. Among these approaches, quantum annealing effectively parallelizes quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) representations of linear equation systems. This paper streamlines these formulations by leveraging the congruence of real symmetric matrices to diagonal matrices. Additionally, we demonstrate the computational advantages of the proposed QUBO models, which show potential to surpass classical algorithms like QR and SVD decompositions.

Richmond and Richmond (Amer. Math. Monthly 104 (1997), 713--719) demonstrated that in any metric space containing at least five points, if every triangle is degenerate, the space must be isometric to a subset of the real line. We show that this condition is overly restrictive; specifically, only $\Theta(n^2)$ appropriately positioned degenerate triangles are required.

We present findings on the $\beta$-Mn-type chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, showing that the magnetic field-induced collapse of a room-temperature metastable topological skyrmion lattice involves a phase characterized by partial topological charge inversion. Employing Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, we directly visualized the magnetization distribution as the field was swept antiparallel to the skyrmion core (negative fields). Because of the inherent topological stability of skyrmions, the metastable lattice does not transition directly to the equilibrium helical state under increasingly negative fields. Instead, it gradually evolves into giant magnetic bubbles separated by $2\pi$ domain walls. Ultimately, these large structures transform into a nearly homogeneous magnetic medium that unexpectedly contains a sparse density of isolated skyrmions with inverted core magnetization, resulting in a total topological charge of opposite sign and reduced magnitude compared to the initial state. This phenomenon mirrors the "topological melting" previously observed in systems with dipolar-stabilized ordered bubble lattices. Supported by numerical simulations, we attribute this regime of partial topological charge inversion to the topological protection inherent in the initial metastable skyrmion state.

A growing approach in distributed multi-sensor fusion involves employing random finite set filters at individual nodes and algorithmically merging the resulting filtered distributions via their exponential mixture densities (EMDs), with methods extending covariance intersection and consensus techniques serving as prime examples. This article examines the variational principles governing EMDs, revealing that EMDs derived from finite set distributions do not invariably ensure consistent fusion of cardinality distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such inconsistencies can arise with high probability in practical scenarios, illustrated through examples involving Bernoulli, Poisson, and independent identically distributed (IID) cluster processes. We establish that pointwise consistency of EMDs does not guarantee consistency in global cardinality, nor does the reverse hold true. Consequently, we reformulate the variational problems foundational to fusion and propose iterative solutions, thereby creating a framework that ensures consistent fusion of cardinalities.

Device-independent randomness generation and quantum key distribution protocols are fundamentally grounded in the connection between the non-local nature of quantum theory and its inherent randomness. Typically, this relationship is framed as a trade-off between the likelihood of correctly guessing measurement outcomes on quantum systems and the degree to which a specific Bell inequality is violated. However, a more precise evaluation of the randomness generated in Bell experiments can be achieved by simultaneously considering multiple Bell expressions or by analyzing the complete set of probabilities that define the device's behavior. We present protocols for device-independent randomness generation that remain secure against classical side information, utilizing either the estimation of an arbitrary number of Bell expressions or the direct analysis of experimental measurement outcome frequencies. Asymptotically, this approach yields optimal randomness generation from experimental data (quantified by min-entropy) without the prerequisite assumption that the devices must violate a particular Bell inequality.

Traditional longest-chain blockchains, exemplified by Bitcoin, ensure liveness regardless of fluctuating user participation (adaptivity) but fail to provide safety during network partitions, meaning they lack finality. Conversely, classical protocols such as PBFT achieve finality but sacrifice adaptivity. According to the CAP theorem applied to blockchains, no single protocol can simultaneously guarantee both adaptivity and finality.

We introduce a novel protocol termed the "checkpointed longest chain," which empowers individual users to choose between finality and adaptivity rather than enforcing a system-wide constraint. Its key innovation is supporting two distinct confirmation rules: one ensuring adaptivity and another ensuring finality. The optimistic adaptive rule confirms any block marked as finalized by the conservative rule and may approve additional blocks under varying participation conditions. Clients select their preferred confirmation rule locally, while miners adhere to a unified block proposal strategy compatible with both rules. Additionally, the protocol offers intrinsic validity: finalized blocks always reside on a single chain, allowing miners to verify transaction validity during block proposals. This design leverages the concept of a finality gadget, a widely adopted method for integrating finality into longest-chain systems.

We introduce the Hybrid Hadron-String Dynamic (HydHSD) model, which bridges the Parton-Hadron-String Dynamic (PHSD) framework and a hydrodynamic approach incorporating shear viscosity via the Israel-Stewart formalism. The model's performance is evaluated using pion and proton rapidity and transverse mass distributions derived from Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions at AGS and SPS energies. Key factors examined include the transition time between transport and hydrodynamic phases, the viscous parameter, and the freeze-out timing. Given that Israel-Stewart hydrodynamics relies on the perturbative nature of the viscous stress tensor ($\pi^{\mu
u}$), which must not exceed the ideal energy-momentum tensor ($T_{m id}^{\mu
u}$), hydrodynamic codes typically rescale the shear stress tensor when the condition $\|\pi^{\mu
u}\|\ll \|T_{m id}^{\mu
u}\|$ is violated. Our results demonstrate that the specific formulation of this constraint significantly influences the sensitivity of hydrodynamic calculations to the shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$). Specifically, the constraints employed in the vHLLE and MUSIC models yield identical outcomes for observables, under which rapidity distributions and transverse momentum spectra exhibit the highest sensitivity to variations in $\eta/s$. Alternatively, a strict condition was applied. Global fits to the rapidity and transverse mass distributions of pions and protons were conducted, revealing that $\eta/s$ increases monotonically with collision energy from $E_{m lab}=6A$GeV to $E_{m lab}=40A$GeV before saturating at higher SPS energies. Furthermore, we note that simultaneously reproducing the rapidity distributions of both pions and protons proves difficult with the current equation of state, as it lacks a phase transition.

Executing a quantum program on actual hardware requires the compiler to map logical qubits to physical ones, which is the most critical phase of quantum circuit compilation. Since circuit fidelity relies heavily on this mapping, and the underlying qubit mapping problem is NP-complete, heuristic methods are necessary to identify high-fidelity solutions. This paper focuses on developing efficient heuristics that integrate real-time error feedback and device connectivity constraints to optimize quantum circuit mappings. Through extensive analysis and experimentation using two baseline algorithms across various error rates and heuristic combinations, we designed sophisticated techniques that account for both real-time error data and connectivity limits. Our results demonstrate that the best proposed heuristic approach outperforms one baseline by an average of **1.62x** and the other by **1.934x** on random benchmarks. Furthermore, when comparing our top heuristic (CAES) against the current state-of-the-art algorithm on representative benchmarks, CAES achieved a **1.7x** average improvement in success rate.

Research indicates that online toxic behaviors, including harassment, trolling, and hate speech, correlate with increased offline violence and adverse psychological impacts on victims. This study investigates the effect of toxicity on user online behavior by analyzing a dataset of 79,800 Twitter conversations. Over a nine-week longitudinal period, we tracked and compared the behavioral responses of authors targeted by toxicity against those who were not. The findings reveal that victims exhibit a mix of avoidance, revenge, countermeasures, and negotiation. Through statistical analysis that accounted for confounding variables—such as conversation structure and user account visibility, identifiability, and activity levels—we determined the significance of toxic replies on user behavior. Interestingly, compared to random authors, victims are more prone to engaging in conversations, responding toxically, and unfollowing instigators. Even when toxicity targets other participants, the original authors remain more likely to engage and respond toxically. However, victims with verified accounts are less inclined to participate in these exchanges or reply with toxic comments. Furthermore, replies are more frequently removed in contexts featuring a high proportion of toxic nested replies or when toxicity is directed at third parties. These results offer valuable insights for future research aimed at creating more effective detection and intervention strategies to mitigate the negative effects of toxicity on social media platforms.

NGC 2915 is a distinctive nearby galaxy categorized as an isolated blue compact dwarf by its optical characteristics, yet it possesses a highly extended H i gas disk featuring prominent Sd-type spiral arms. To investigate the mystery behind its starburst activity, we conducted a thorough analysis of deep VLT/MUSE integral field spectroscopic data covering the star-forming core within the central kiloparsec. Our findings indicate that bursty star formation has occurred repeatedly in various locations across the central region, with the most recent peak happening approximately 50 Myr ago. While this episodic star formation has significantly disrupted the kinematics of ionized gas, it has left the neutral atomic gas kinematics largely unaffected, suggesting that these two gas phases are spatially decoupled along the line of sight. Classical line-ratio diagnostic diagrams reveal no evidence of an active galactic nucleus. Furthermore, the ionized gas metallicities display a positive radial gradient, confirming earlier studies based on individual H ii regions and likely resulting from a combination of stellar feedback-driven outflows and the inflow of metal-poor gas. Indications of metal-poor gas infall include high-speed collisions between gas clouds of differing metallicities, localized drops in gas metallicity, and unusually small metallicity discrepancies between gas and stars. Finally, the central stellar disk appears to counter-rotate relative to the extended H i disk, implying that recent bursty star formation episodes have been sustained by externally accreted gas.

This work introduces two novel interpolation techniques for the sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$. The initial section presents a straightforward method called \textit{Spherical Interpolation of orDER} $n$ (SIDER-$n$), which generates a $C^{n}$ interpolant for any $n \geq 2$, extending the concept of B\'{e}zier curves from $\mathbb{R}$ to spherical geometry. The subsequent section integrates the ENO philosophy to create a \textit{Spherical Essentially Non-Oscillatory} (SENO) scheme. This approach effectively mitigates spurious oscillations during high-order reconstruction when the curve on $\mathbb{S}^2$ exhibits kinks or sharp discontinuities in its higher derivatives. Multiple examples are provided to illustrate the accuracy and efficacy of these proposed methods.

Retrieving judicial decisions pertinent to specific legal inquiries constitutes case law retrieval, a process that consumes a substantial portion of a lawyer's time and is essential for delivering accurate counsel while minimizing workload. This survey examines retrieval methodologies from the last two decades and highlights the challenges anticipated in evaluating future case law retrieval systems. Although research has been scarce regarding ranking improvements in ad-hoc case law retrieval, significant advancements have occurred in other facets of case law and legal information retrieval generally. This disparity likely stems from commercial legal search providers being reluctant to disclose their competitive advantages. Consequently, most existing evaluations rely on small datasets and concentrate on related tasks like question-answering or recommendation systems rather than Cranfield-style assessments. The absence of publicly available test collections and established baselines for case law retrieval methods presents a major hurdle. However, the severity of this issue may be overstated within commercial contexts; even without standardized test collections, the efficacy of natural language systems and query expansion techniques demonstrated by commercial providers suggests promising results. As machine learning increasingly permeates legal search tasks, it clearly represents the future trajectory of case law retrieval.

The coherent superposition of quantum states serves as a vital resource for quantum information processing, fundamentally distinguishing it from classical dynamics and information. This study examines the coherence necessary for transmitting quantum information by utilizing hybrid random circuits as a model system. These circuits exhibit a phase transition in both quantum and classical channel capacities. The circuits are constructed through a quantum information game between two adversaries, Alice and Eve, who apply random unitaries and measurements to a fixed set of qubits. Alice employs unitaries to preserve quantum channel capacity, whereas Eve utilizes measurements to degrade it. By restricting the coherence-generating or coherence-destroying operations available to each player, we can determine the game's winner and adjust the phase transitions in entanglement and quantum channel capacity. These transitions enable us to pinpoint the coherence requirements for quantum communication and specifically demonstrate that coherence in any local basis establishes an upper limit on the quantum code distance of any stabilizer quantum error correction code. Consequently, this bound offers a rigorous quantification of the coherence resources needed for quantum error correction.

An infinite square lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet with discrete disorder, initialized in a N\'eel state, is evolved using the neighborhood tensor update (NTU) algorithm for infinite projected entangled pair states (iPEPS), as detailed in Phys. Rev. B 104, 094411 (2021). Ancillary spins facilitate averaging over 2 or 5 discrete disorder configurations. Employing a bond dimension of up to 20, the simulation achieves sufficient evolution times to detect a many-body localized regime under strong disorder. Additionally, the same Hamiltonian undergoes periodic spin flips. Floquet dynamics simulations indicate that the system can maintain a time-crystalline phase when the disorder is sufficiently strong.

A superconducting-compatible on-chip microwave circulator is essential for scaling up superconducting circuits. Previous integration methods relied on external driving requiring additional microwave lines or strong magnetic fields that could damage superconductivity. This work reports the first proof-of-principle demonstration of a passive on-chip circulator constructed from a superconducting loop interrupted by three nominally identical Josephson junctions, tuned solely via DC control fields. Our experimental findings indicate nonreciprocal scattering and align closely with theoretical simulations. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of quasiparticle tunneling using a hidden Markov model. By minimizing junction asymmetry and applying established protection techniques against quasiparticles, we expect Josephson-loop circulators to become a standard component in superconducting circuits.

A data commons functions as a cloud-based platform equipped with governance frameworks that enable communities to manage, analyze, and share their data. These platforms empower research groups to handle large datasets by leveraging the elastic scalability of cloud computing, facilitating secure and compliant data sharing that ultimately accelerates research progress. Over the last ten years, numerous data commons have been established, and this discussion highlights key lessons derived from those initiatives.

This study introduces a framework for multi-robot systems (MRS) that integrates human-robot trust into task allocation and motion planning for concurrent operations. By combining parallel task specifications with the MRS, a task allocation automaton is synthesized, where each transition reflects the aggregate trust level humans place in the relevant robots. This trust model, built using a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN), factors in individual robot performance, safety coefficients, human cognitive workload, and the overall assessment of task allocation. Consequently, the system searches for a task allocation path that maximizes encoded human-robot trust based on current trust values within the automaton. Once robots receive their action sequences, symbolic motion planning (SMP) is executed for each unit. Furthermore, this DBN-based trust model allows for the intermittent updating of the task allocation path. The proposed strategy is validated through a simulation involving five robots and three parallel subtask automata.

Over the last few decades, unified correspondence has emerged as a broad extension of Sahlqvist theory, applicable across all signatures of normal and regular (distributive) lattice expansions. This framework introduces a general definition of Sahlqvist and inductive formulas and inequalities for every such signature, grounded in order theory, which encompasses all (bi-)intuitionistic modal logics. These logics have been extensively examined for seventy years alongside classical polyadic modal logics, primarily utilizing adaptations of Goedel-McKinsey-Tarski translations. Consequently, two questions arise: (1) Can a unified view of Goedel-McKinsey-Tarski translations be established, relying on order-theoretic principles similar to those defining Sahlqvist and inductive formulas, thereby covering existing translations and applying uniformly to all signatures of normal (distributive) lattice expansions? (2) Can this unified perspective facilitate the transfer of correspondence and canonicity theorems for Sahlqvist and inductive formulas and inequalities across all aforementioned signatures via these translations? This paper addresses these inquiries. We affirmatively answer the first question. Regarding the second, we demonstrate the transfer of the correspondence theorem for inductive inequalities within arbitrary signatures of normal distributive lattice expansions. Furthermore, we establish the transfer of canonicity for inductive inequalities, though currently limited to arbitrary normal modal expansions of bi-intuitionistic logic. We also examine the obstacles preventing a broader transfer of canonicity beyond this specific context and outline a potential path toward extending canonicity transfer to all signatures of normal distributive lattice expansions.

We conduct a finite-time scaling analysis centered on the detrapping point of a three-state quantum walk on a line. The coin operator is defined by a parameter $\rho$, which governs the velocity of wavepacket spreading. The initial state, prepared at the origin, is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates characterized by a mixing angle $\theta$; specifically, one component corresponds to full spreading at the critical angle $\theta_c(\rho)$, where no wavepacket fraction remains trapped near the starting position. We demonstrate that key metrics, including survival probability and the participation ratio, exhibit single-parameter scaling forms near the detrapping angle $\theta_c$. Notably, we find that the participation ratio increases linearly with time, accompanied by a logarithmic correction, thereby clarifying earlier observations of sublinear dynamics.

We propose a new methodology to explain phenomena currently ascribed to the theoretical constructs of `dark energy', `dark matter', and `dark flow'. Rather than postulating these entities, we redefine the nature of inertial motion and inertial reference frames within flat space-time. Our framework retains only the stipulation that special and general relativity serve as local approximations of our revised inertial systems. Implicitly, we assume that at sufficiently large scales, objects within these systems behave as point particles with negligible impact on space-time curvature. We further posit that time and space are fundamentally linked, meaning that translational invariance in both time and space is not an intrinsic symmetry of flat space-time (i.e., clock rates vary based on relative velocity and spatial position). Under this premise, inertial motion is characterized by geodesics in the radial Rindler chart. This approach allows us to model the effects of `dark energy', `dark matter', and `dark flow' exclusively through inertial motion. Additionally, we investigate the theory's observable consequences in a gravitational system confined within an inertial frame, interpreting the Pioneer anomaly as evidence for our redefined inertial motion. Finally, we extend this analysis to quantum mechanics by quantizing a real scalar field, offering a potential explanation for matter-antimatter asymmetry within our redefined framework.

The majority of baryonic matter in the universe resides in gaseous states, primarily located within galactic halos and the low-density intergalactic medium. Proposed X-ray spectroscopy missions like Athena, Arcus, and Lynx possess the ability to detect absorption lines in the spectra of bright active galactic nuclei (AGNs), serving as a means to investigate this elusive matter. In this research, we analyze the optical environments around 15 primary targets to identify foreground galaxies and groups that could act as absorption sources. We document the fundamental characteristics of these potential hosts and measure their angular and physical distances from the AGN line of sight. This procedure involves locating various galaxies and groups on optical images surrounding the targets and plotting their angular separation against redshift to assess physical proximity to the background source. We categorize these surrounding objects based on whether their redshifts have already been measured or still need to be determined.

Animation is a pervasive feature of visualization systems, with transitions serving as a standard method for generating them. This technique involves smoothly interpolating a visual attribute from a starting point to an endpoint over a set duration. While effective when transitions complete sequentially, this approach struggles when new transitions are initiated before the current one concludes. Specifically, such interruptions cause abrupt changes in velocity and can degrade animation performance. To address these issues, we frame animation as a signal processing challenge. Our method generates animations by transforming time-based signals: converting an input signal that maps time to target attribute values into an output signal representing the displayed values. We demonstrate that established signal processing methods can be utilized to create animations that remain free of velocity discontinuities, even during interruptions.

The Collatz conjecture posits that every natural number $n$ serves as a node in the Collatz tree, linked to $1$ via the Collatz function, which maps even numbers to $n/2$ and odd numbers to $3n+1$. The conjecture is validated if a binary subtree $T_{\ge 0}$ exists, comprising all branching numbers within the congruence classes ${\left[4,16\right]}_{18}$ at a density of $2/18$. For every branching number, the "upward" and "rightward" functions create arrows pointing to two other branching numbers in the directions of $2n$ and $(n-1)/3$. Within the automorphism graph of tree $T_{\ge 0}$, the iterates and conjugates of these functions form outer paths extending from the root to two infinite sequences of nodes that contain nested subtrees and disjoint cotrees. The nodes and conjugate inner arrows inside each subtree and cotree correspond one-to-one with those in tree $T_{\ge 0}$. Ultimately, the cumulative density of the congruence classes found in the disjoint cotrees of $T_{\ge 0}$ equals the $2/18$ density of all branching numbers, thereby proving the conjecture.

We introduce a novel approach to adapt a pretrained denoising diffusion speech model for generating speech in the voice of unseen individuals. This method requires only a brief (~3 seconds) sample from the target speaker and steers generation during inference without any additional training steps. Central to our approach is a sampling process that merges the denoising model's estimation with a low-pass filtered version of the new speaker's sample. Both objective and subjective evaluations demonstrate that this training-free sampling technique produces a voice frequency similar to the target speaker, achieving accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

While coreference resolution has seen significant advancements in recent years within a single document using end-to-end models, the more complex task of cross-document (CD) coreference resolution remains largely under-explored, with existing recent approaches limited to gold-standard mentions. This work introduces the first end-to-end model capable of performing CD coreference resolution directly from raw text by adapting a leading within-document model to the cross-document context. Our approach yields competitive performance for both entity and event coreference on gold mentions and, crucially, establishes the first baseline results for CD coreference resolution over predicted mentions using the standard ECB+ dataset. Additionally, our model is simpler and more efficient than recent CD coreference systems and operates without relying on any external resources.

Bayesian mixture models are commonly employed for clustering high-dimensional data with proper uncertainty quantification; however, as dimensionality rises, posterior inference frequently overestimates or underestimates the number of clusters. This paper elucidates this phenomenon by examining the random partition posterior in a non-standard context where sample size remains fixed while data dimensionality increases. We demonstrate conditions under which the finite-sample posterior converges to either assigning each observation to its own cluster or grouping all observations into a single cluster as dimensions grow. Notably, these conditions are independent of the specific clustering prior, provided that every possible partition has positive prior probability, and they remain valid regardless of the true data-generating process. Consequently, we introduce a class of latent mixtures for Bayesian clustering (Lamb) defined on low-dimensional latent variables that induce a partition on observed data. This model supports scalable posterior inference and effectively circumvents the challenges of high dimensionality under reasonable and mild assumptions. Simulation studies and an application to cell type inference using scRNA-seq data confirm the robust performance of this proposed approach.

Out-of-distribution detection for graph classification remains an unsolved challenge, with current models often exhibiting excessive confidence on OOD samples or neglecting the task entirely. This study examines the issue through the lens of uncertainty estimation and evaluates several recent methodologies. Our experimental results indicate that no single universal solution exists for OOD detection, highlighting the necessity of integrating both graph representations and predictive categorical distributions.

This study proposes extending the Deep BSDE solver developed by Han and Jentzen (2017) to address Forward-Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (FBSDEs) involving jumps. Following the methodology of the original solver, the approach discretizes the BSDE and parametrizes high-dimensional control processes using a family of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). By framing the BSDE as a model-based reinforcement learning task, the ANN parameters are optimized to minimize a specific loss function. The framework accommodates both finite and infinite jump activity; for the latter, it employs an approximation of the forward process that utilizes a finite number of jumps.

We demonstrate that Feynman integrals, regardless of the number of loops involved, are entirely determined when linear relationships among them are established. Consequently, the computation of Feynman integrals transforms conceptually into a linear algebraic task. Examples up to five loops are presented to confirm this finding. As an additional benefit, this approach yields a robust method for calculating perturbative corrections in quantum field theory.

This paper investigates whether self-supervised learning introduces unique advantages to Vision Transformers (ViTs) that surpass those of convolutional networks (convnets). While acknowledging that self-supervised methods adapt exceptionally well to this architecture, we highlight two key findings: first, self-supervised ViT features explicitly encode semantic segmentation information, a capability less evident in supervised ViTs or convnets; second, these features serve as highly effective k-NN classifiers, achieving a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet even with a small ViT. Our research also emphasizes the critical roles of momentum encoders, multi-crop training, and small patch sizes in ViTs. Building on these insights, we developed DINO, a straightforward self-supervised approach interpreted as label-free self-distillation. We demonstrate the powerful synergy between DINO and ViTs by attaining 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet through linear evaluation with ViT-Base.

NGC 300 ULX1 is a pulsating ultraluminous X-ray source (PULX) characterized by the longest spin period observed among confirmed PULXs ($P\simeq31.6\,\rm s$) and a notably high spin-up rate ($\dot P\simeq5.56\times10^{-7}\,\rm s\,s^{-1}$). Following its initial detection of pulsations, recent observations indicate an inferred magnetic field of approximately $3.0\times10^{14}\,\rm G$. Simulations of the magnetic field and spin period evolution suggest that, given constraints on companion mass and accretion rate, this object could evolve into a recycled or millisecond pulsar. We propose that NGC 300 ULX1 is an accreting magnetar, a classification that explains its super Eddington luminosity. Furthermore, we suggest that other confirmed PULXs may also be accreting magnetars. Studying these sources will provide valuable insights into magnetar evolution and the formation of millisecond pulsars with magnetic fields exceeding $\sim10^{9}\,\rm G$.

Low-energy scattering between vector mesons and nucleons provides a crucial avenue for investigating non-perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), with the vector meson-nucleon scattering length ($|\alpha_{VN}|$) serving as a key parameter in understanding hadronic interactions. Recent photoproduction experiments and quasi-data have yielded numerous values for $|\alpha_{VN}|$. Furthermore, determining the trace anomaly's contribution to the proton mass has become a significant focus in hadron physics and non-perturbative QCD; however, direct experimental measurement of this trace anomaly remains challenging, leading to inconclusive results to date. In this study, we derived a connection between the vector meson-proton scattering length ($|\alpha_{Vp}|$) and the proton mass's trace anomaly contribution ($T_{A}$). Utilizing scattering length values obtained via the Vector Meson Dominance model, we calculated $T_{A}$ to be (22.8% $\pm$ 1.2%), a result consistent with the approximately 23% predicted by Lattice QCD. We hypothesize that the nucleon's trace anomaly contribution is independent of the specific vector meson probe used. Consequently, we anticipate that high-precision measurements of the vector meson-nucleon scattering length will enhance our ability to uncover the origins of nucleon mass.

This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to address the minimum dominating set problem. We provide theoretical proofs demonstrating that for specific network types, our algorithm yields a constant approximation factor relative to the optimal solution. Given the problem's natural occurrence in social networks—such as in news dissemination, rumor mitigation, and recommendation propagation—we implemented the algorithm on large-scale social networks to benchmark it against state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we extended the approach to tackle the $k$-distance dominating set problem and conducted experimental analyses of its efficiency. Our proposed method is characterized by its speed, ease of implementation, and adaptability to dynamic networks where vertices and edges are continuously added or removed. Crucially, experimental results indicate that the algorithm offers both reasonable solution quality and runtime performance, making it practically viable for distributed environments.

Automating the manipulation of compliant objects is a leading challenge in robotics, driven by its ability to enable numerous critical applications. Although significant strides have been made recently, the 3D shaping of such materials remains an unresolved issue. This paper introduces a novel vision-based controller designed to autonomously regulate the form of compliant objects using robotic arms. Our approach employs an efficient online surface and curve fitting algorithm that characterizes the object's geometry through a compact feature vector; this feedback-like representation facilitates the creation of an explicit shape servo-loop. To align robot motion with these computed features, we propose a receding-time estimator that approximates the sensorimotor model while adhering to specific performance criteria. Furthermore, a deep adversarial network is developed to robustly handle visual occlusions within the camera's view, allowing the shaping task to proceed even with partial object visibility. Model predictive control is applied to calculate the robot's shaping movements while respecting workspace and saturation constraints. Finally, a comprehensive experimental study is provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed control framework.

This paper initiates an investigation into motivic homotopy theory at infinity. By employing the six functor formalism, we provide an intrinsic definition of the stable motivic homotopy type at infinity for algebraic varieties. Key computational instruments utilized include cdh-descent for normal crossing divisors, Euler classes, Gysin maps, and homotopy purity. Upon $\ell$-adic realization, the motive at infinity reproduces Rapoport-Zink's formula for vanishing cycles, with analogous findings applicable to Steenbrink's limiting Hodge structures and Wildeshaus' boundary motives. Under topological Betti realization, the stable motivic homotopy type at infinity of an algebraic variety corresponds to the singular complex at infinity of the associated analytic space. We introduce the concept of homotopically smooth morphisms relative to a motivic $\infty$-category and apply it to generalize Morel-Voevodsky's purity theorem to virtual vector bundles, resulting in an enhanced form of Atiyah duality with compact support. Additionally, we examine a quadratic refinement of intersection degrees that maps to motivic cohomotopy groups. For relative surfaces, we demonstrate that the stable motivic homotopy type at infinity reflects a quadratic adaptation of Mumford's plumbing construction for smooth complex algebraic surfaces. These primary results extend to $\ell$-adic sheaves, mixed Hodge modules, and, more broadly, motivic $\infty$-categories.

Calculating molecular energies efficiently represents a promising application of quantum computing within quantum chemistry; however, the limitations of current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware—specifically their inability to run deep circuits—restrict existing variational algorithms to small molecules, as these methods typically demand deep entangling circuit ansatzes to model correlations. In this work, we introduce a variational algorithm optimized for NISQ devices that constructs a collection of mean-field Hartree-Fock (HF) ansatzes using multiple shallow circuits with a depth scaling linearly with the number of qubits. This approach estimates electronic correlation energies up to second-order perturbation theory. We validated the algorithm on various small molecules through both noisy classical simulations and execution on cloud-based quantum processors. Results indicate that the method successfully reproduces equilibrium molecular energies and accurately captures perturbative electronic correlation effects even at extended bond distances. As quantum processor fidelities advance, this algorithm will facilitate the investigation of larger molecules compared to alternative approaches that necessitate higher-order polynomial circuit depths.

We forecast the trajectory of ongoing susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) epidemics across regular, Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi, and Barab\'asi-Albert networks. Since the contact network structure dictates epidemic spread within a population, population-level observations inherently reveal information about the underlying network topology. This insight proves valuable for forecasting future epidemic dynamics. To operationalize this within a prediction framework, we approximate the exact high-dimensional stochastic SIS model with a lower-dimensional surrogate model. This surrogate, grounded in a birth-and-death process, characterizes the network's influence through a parametric model of birth rates. Empirical results demonstrate that once the epidemic passes the extinction threshold, the surrogate model effectively captures its intrinsic stochasticity. Bayesian parameter inference integrates uncertainty regarding both model parameters and the network class directly into probabilistic forecasts. Scenario evaluations indicate that, in most instances, the resulting prediction intervals adequately quantify uncertainty. Provided that population-level data spans a sufficiently long duration—even if infrequently sampled—the model yields excellent predictions when the network structure is correctly identified, with prediction uncertainty primarily reflecting the epidemic's inherent stochasticity. Conversely, for shorter observational windows, uncertainty regarding parameters and network class becomes the dominant factor. The proposed approach requires minimal data and is computationally efficient, making it a compelling standalone inference and prediction tool or a complementary method alongside other techniques.

Segmenting abdominal organs is a complex and labor-intensive process, making fully automated solutions essential for alleviating the workload of medical professionals. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) currently dominate this field, their high computational demands and reliance on extensive datasets hinder practical adoption. Our method addresses these challenges by developing a compact, custom 3D CNN, compiling the model, and optimizing its computational graph. This approach achieves high segmentation accuracy (Dice Similarity Coefficient: Liver 97.3±1.3%, Kidneys 94.8±3.6%, Spleen 96.4±3.0%, Pancreas 80.9±10.1) in just 1.6 seconds per image. Most importantly, inference runs exclusively on a CPU, eliminating the need for GPUs and enabling straightforward, widespread deployment without specialized hardware.

Face recognition is a prevalent challenge in machine learning that has become deeply integrated into daily life, exemplified by Facebook's automatic image tagging and the use of biometric security on mobile devices. However, face images often exhibit variations in background, lighting, expressions, and occlusions. While numerous recognition approaches exist, they are frequently tested on single-type databases, limiting their effectiveness across diverse datasets. Eigenfaces, a fundamental technique, offer simplicity and efficiency but perform best under controlled conditions. Consequently, this paper evaluates the experimental performance of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Normalized PCA (NPCA). Experiments were conducted using the ORL (ATT) and Indian Face Database (IFD), both characterized by variability in expression, pose, and facial details. The study compares the results of these two methods by adjusting the number of training images, with algorithms implemented using MATLAB.
We investigate embeddings of symmetric groups into the Cremona group.

In recent years, Knowledge Distillation (KD) has emerged as a pivotal approach for compressing and accelerating models. Typically, KD involves training a compact student model to mimic a large teacher model by minimizing the divergence between their probabilistic outputs. However, our experiments reveal that conventional KD methods often fail to transfer the teacher's critical explainable knowledge, resulting in inconsistent explanations between the two models. To address this, we introduce XDistillation, a novel framework that facilitates the transfer of both performance and explanation information from the teacher to the student. By leveraging convolutional autoencoders to approximate teacher explanations, XDistillation ensures that the student model not only achieves superior predictive accuracy compared to traditional KD methods but also maintains higher faithfulness to the teacher's reasoning.

The dynamic core hypothesis suggests that consciousness arises from assemblies of brain regions that are transiently synchronized, integrated, and differentiated simultaneously. To evaluate the integrity of this dynamic core, we utilized dynamic brain networks to model time-dependent functional interactions, specifically measuring network flexibility and the size of the largest multilayer module. Initially, we refined parameter selection by employing a novel benchmark designed for module detection in heterogeneous temporal networks. Subsequently, we applied a multilayer modularity maximization algorithm to dynamic brain networks derived from fMRI data collected during deep sleep and propofol anesthesia. Our findings indicate that unconsciousness alters network flexibility and diminishes the size of the largest spatiotemporal module, which corresponds to the dynamic core. These results offer the first characterization of modular brain network dynamics during unconscious states measured via fMRI, thereby providing further support for the dynamic core hypothesis regarding human consciousness.

The literature contains multiple versions of the Mean Value Theorem. By applying Flett's Mean Value Theorem to the Extended Generalized Mean Value Theorem, a novel result emerges, which has been developed through dedicated effort and is designated as the Extended Generalized Flett's Mean Value Theorem.

Object detection for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) remains a difficult endeavor due to the sparse nature of recordings and the presence of small objects. This study introduces a straightforward tiling approach that enhances detection capabilities in remote sensing scenarios without altering the underlying model. By mitigating background bias and allowing for higher-resolution images during training, this method significantly boosts model performance. The technique was tested across three distinct datasets, demonstrating superior performance and speed compared to similar existing methods.

This study examines two-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topologically ordered phases, specifically the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code and the modified surface code, situated on a simple hyperbolic lattice. By constructing a 2D lattice as the product of a 1D Cayley tree and a 1D conventional lattice, we analyze two key topological metrics for these phases: the ground state degeneracy on a closed surface and the topological entanglement entropy. Our findings indicate that both metrics vary with the number of branches and the generation level of the Cayley tree. We ascribe these dependencies to the existence of a vast number of anyon superselection sectors.

Speech recognition systems face significant challenges due to accent diversity, a problem that is particularly acute in India. This region presents a unique difficulty due to its vast linguistic diversity coupled with a scarcity of research detailing pronunciation variations. The rising population of L2 English speakers in India further underscores the necessity of investigating accent characteristics and the interaction between native languages (L1) and English (L2). This study examines the accents of Indian English (IE) speakers, documenting both region-specific and universal observations. Specifically, we analyze phonemic variations and phonotactics inherent in speakers' native tongues and trace their impact on English pronunciation. By comparing native language data with IE speech from existing literature and phonetically annotated recordings of 80 speakers, we demonstrate how 18 distinct Indian languages influence IE. This approach validates hypotheses regarding Indian language influences by deriving pronunciation rules directly from Indian phonology. Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive characterization of IE that encompasses both universal traits and regional nuances, thereby enabling the development of accent conversion and the adaptation of current Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems for diverse Indian accents.

Recent classical kernel methods have been enhanced through the integration of specialized tensor kernels designed to encourage sparsity in regression solutions. These approaches tackle an lp-norm regularization problem where $p = m/(m-1)$ and $m$ is an even integer, a formulation closely resembling the lasso problem. Nevertheless, a significant limitation of this method is the substantial memory required to store tensors, which restricts its practical application. This study addresses this challenge by introducing two key advancements. First, we propose a novel, more efficient data layout to directly lower memory consumption. Second, we employ a Nystrom-type subsampling strategy that reduces the number of data points needed during training, thereby decreasing computational costs. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of these improvements. Furthermore, we implemented the code in C++ to achieve additional performance gains.

The newly identified class of pulsar haloes is potentially numerous and sufficiently bright in the TeV spectrum to represent a significant portion of the sources detected by the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting and characterizing these haloes within the projected Galactic Plane Survey (GPS) by employing a simplified phenomenological diffusion model for both individual haloes and the Milky Way's population. Using a comprehensive spatial-spectral likelihood analysis of simulated survey data, alongside the latest instrument response functions and science tool prototypes, we assess our capacity to reveal pulsar haloes and constrain their primary physical parameters. For a model configuration mirroring the Geminga halo, we estimate that approximately 300 objects could produce detectable emission in the GPS. However, only about one-third of these could be distinguished via their energy-dependent morphology, and merely one-tenth would permit robust constraints on critical physical properties, such as the strength or spatial scale of suppressed diffusion near the pulsar. Additionally, we present a catalog of known pulsars potentially hosting detectable (Geminga-like) haloes and evaluate the stability of our results against various systematic uncertainties.

Grasping human-object interactions is essential in First Person Vision (FPV). Algorithms that track objects handled by the camera wearer offer valuable insights for modeling these interactions effectively. Although visual tracking techniques in computer vision have markedly enhanced their efficacy across diverse targets and scenarios over recent years, a rigorous evaluation of state-of-the-art trackers specifically within FPV contexts remains absent. This paper addresses that omission by introducing the inaugural systematic investigation into object tracking for FPV. We comprehensively evaluate recent visual trackers and baseline FPV methods across various dimensions, utilizing a novel performance metric. This analysis relies on TREK-150, a new benchmark dataset featuring 150 densely annotated video sequences. Our findings indicate that object tracking in FPV presents significant challenges, underscoring the need for further research to enhance tracking capabilities and, consequently, improve FPV tasks.

We investigate the topological characteristics of superconducting phases arising in a $\mathcal{C}_4$-symmetric Dirac semimetal analogous to Cd$_3$As$_2$, featuring two four-fold degenerate Dirac points separated along the $k_z$ axis. Contrasting with simple Weyl semimetals where all pairing orders are topologically constrained and nodal, we demonstrate that in Dirac semimetals, topological obstructions to pairing depend critically on the specific pairing symmetry. Specifically, we examine odd-parity $B_{1u}$ and $B_{2u}$ pairing states, which can be driven by Ising ferromagnetic fluctuations. These states retain the topological obstruction present in the normal state, ensuring they host four Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Dirac point nodes protected by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ monopole charge. Through Wannier state analysis, we reveal that this superconducting obstruction is of higher-order nature. Consequently, within a rod geometry possessing gapped surfaces, arcs of higher-order Majorana zero modes emerge on the hinges between the BdG Dirac points across certain $k_z$ regions. Unlike the Fermi arcs found in Weyl semimetals, these higher-order Majorana arcs remain stable against self-annihilation due to an additional $\mathbb{Z}$-valued monopole charge of the BdG Dirac points safeguarded by $\mathcal{C}_4$ symmetry. Furthermore, we observe that $B_{1g}$ and $B_{2g}$ channels carry the same $\mathbb{Z}$-valued charge; in these channels, the BdG spectrum contains bulk "nodal cages"—structures formed by nodal lines—that are robust against symmetry-preserving perturbations.
