We present a novel, practical, and broadly applicable definition for local symmetry-preserving operations on polyhedra. These operations are effective on any plane graph and yield graphs that retain the original symmetry. By incorporating specific additional properties, we can constrain connectivity to focus exclusively on polyhedra. Utilizing a set of fundamental structures alongside a catalog of 10 extension rules enables the generation of all possible local symmetry-preserving operations in an isomorph-free manner.

We define the concept of an eigenstate for an operator within an abstract C*-algebra and establish several associated properties. Notably, we demonstrate that if an operator is self-adjoint, every point in its spectrum corresponds to an eigenstate.

We analytically investigate the characteristics of an s-wave holographic superconductor incorporating exponential nonlinear electrodynamics within a four-dimensional Lifshitz black hole background. By assuming that scalar and gauge fields backreact on the background geometry, we compute both the critical temperature and the condensation operator. Utilizing the Sturm-Liouville method, we demonstrate that the critical temperature declines as the strength of the exponential nonlinear electrodynamics and the Lifshitz dynamical exponent ($z$) increase, implying that condensation becomes more challenging. Furthermore, we observe that backreaction effects play a more significant role in determining the critical temperature and condensation operator when the Lifshitz dynamical exponent is close to unity. Additionally, we examine the upper critical magnetic field within the Lifshitz black hole background using the Sturm-Liouville approach to map out the phase diagram of the corresponding holographic superconductor in the probe limit. Our results indicate that the critical magnetic field diminishes with an increasing Lifshitz dynamical exponent ($z$) and vanishes at the critical temperature, a behavior that remains independent of the specific value of $z$.

We investigate a unified dissipative dark fluid framework comprising an adiabatic component and a bulk viscous component. The adiabatic segment allows the equation of state to asymptotically approach two distinct power laws, effectively interpolating between dust and dark energy regimes at early and late cosmic epochs. The dissipative component features a bulk viscosity with a constant coefficient. Utilizing phase space analysis, we robustly characterize the model's dynamical behavior without relying on explicit system solutions. Model parameters are constrained by both asymptotic behaviors and extensive observational data. We numerically solve the Hubble parameter equation, plotting results against the latest Hubble data. Furthermore, the $Om(z)$ test confirms that, despite being quintessence-like, the model traverses the phantom barrier. We examine the universe's evolution by analyzing the deceleration parameter, cosmic density, the effective equation of state, and the underlying dark energy properties. The estimated present-day viscosity coefficient is $8 \times 10^6 Pa.s$, consistent with previous studies by Velten and Schwartz [26], Wang and Meng [27], and Sasidharan and Mathew [29]. We conclude that this model successfully accounts for the observed evolution of the universe.

Driven by LHC searches for leptonic scalars and the recent Tevatron measurement of the $W$ boson mass, we re-examine the Zee-Babu model's phenomenology for neutrino masses and its distinguishability from the Type II Seesaw model at the LHC. Our findings indicate that this differentiation is far more challenging than previously thought. Assuming identical inputs for both scenarios, we observe that the total and differential production rates for doubly and singly charged scalar pairs exhibit identical shapes, differing only in normalization. This normalization depends on the ratio of hadronic cross sections and may equal unity; consequently, cross-section differences are minimal and could be obscured by uncertain branching ratios. This similarity persists across Drell-Yan, $\gamma\gamma$, and $gg$ fusion processes, as well as LO and NLO QCD observables. This resemblance enables us to reinterpret Run II constraints on the Type II Seesaw and project sensitivities for the HL-LHC. Incorporating updated neutrino oscillation data, we note that certain collider observables, such as lepton flavor-violating branching ratios, have reached a precision sufficient to offer a viable path forward, alongside other potential discrimination methods. Additionally, as a supplementary contribution, we announce the release of new Universal \texttt{FeynRules} Object libraries, specifically the \texttt{SM\_ZeeBabu} UFO, which facilitate fully differential simulations up to NLO+LL(PS) using tool chains like \texttt{MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO}.

The prevalence of Inverter-Based Generators (IBGs) in power systems is rising rapidly. However, the thermal limitations of their associated Power Electronics (PE) result in a significantly lower Short Circuit Current (SCC) contribution compared to conventional Synchronous Generators (SGs), thereby weakening system strength and creating challenges for protection and stability. To address this, the paper introduces a Unit Commitment (UC) model incorporating SCC constraints for high IBG-penetration scenarios. This approach aims to minimize operational costs while ensuring adequate SCC levels at every bus. The formulation explicitly models SCC contributions from both SGs and IBGs, resulting in a constraint involving a decision-dependent matrix inverse. To manage the high nonlinearity of this constraint, it is conservatively reformulated into a linear format. Finally, simulations on IEEE 30- and 118-bus systems demonstrate the impact of the SCC constraint on system operations and its interplay with frequency regulation.

Mutual information (MI) quantifies the dependency between two random variables using information theory. Various approaches have been developed to estimate MI from samples where the underlying probability distributions are unknown. Recent techniques employ parametric distributions or neural network critics to approximate unknown density ratios, utilizing these approximations to calculate variational lower bounds of MI. Although these methods yield reliable estimates when the true MI is low, they exhibit high variance when the MI is high. We attribute this high variance to the uncontrolled complexity of the critic's hypothesis space. To substantiate this claim, we analyze the generalization error bounds of these variational lower bound estimates using the data-driven Rademacher complexity of the critic's architectural hypothesis space. In this work, we demonstrate that the high variance can be mitigated by constraining the critic's hypothesis space to a Reproducing Hilbert Kernel Space (RKHS), corresponding to a kernel learned via Automated Spectral Kernel Learning (ASKL). By examining these generalization error bounds, we incorporate an effective regularization term into the overall optimization objective. Empirical results on four variational lower bounds—NWJ, MINE, JS, and SMILE—confirm the efficacy of this regularization in enforcing an appropriate bias-variance tradeoff.

Learning generalized policies from visual inputs amidst distractions remains a significant challenge in reinforcement learning. Recently, there has been a resurgence of interest in bisimulation metrics as a solution; these metrics facilitate the learning of representations that are theoretically invariant to irrelevant distractions by assessing behavioral similarity between states. However, obtaining an accurate, unbiased, and scalable estimation of these metrics in continuous state and action spaces has proven difficult. We introduce entangled bisimulation, a metric that permits the specification of state distance functions and can be estimated without bias within continuous environments. We demonstrate that entangled bisimulation significantly outperforms prior methods on the Distracting Control Suite (DCS), even when combined with data augmentation techniques.

Within the $\varepsilon$-regime of chiral perturbation theory, random matrix theory (RMT) allows for the calculation of spectral correlations of the Euclidean QCD Dirac operator near the origin. To account for temperature effects, an RMT ensemble was introduced that adds a constant, deterministic matrix to the Dirac operator. The resulting eigenvalue correlation functions are expressed as the determinant of a temperature-dependent kernel. Leveraging recent advances in polynomial ensembles—characterized by this deterministic additive shift—we have determined the limiting kernels and correlation functions for this class. We establish the equivalence between this novel determinantal formulation of microscopic eigenvalue correlations and prior results expressed via determinants of varying sizes. This holds for any number of quark flavors, with and without temperature, and extends to non-zero topological sectors. These findings are mutually consistent and exhibit universality when scaled by the temperature-dependent chiral condensate, provided the system remains below the chiral phase transition.

We derive specific value results for convolutions of Goss and Pellarin $L$-series associated with Drinfeld modules, which yield values within Tate algebras. By utilizing Demeslay's class module formula on specific rigid analytic twists of one Drinfeld module by another, we generalize the special value formula for the Pellarin $L$-function linked to the Carlitz module and the Anderson-Thakur function to Drinfeld modules of any rank and their rigid analytic trivializations. Through the framework of Schur polynomials, these identities manifest as specializations of Rankin-Selberg type convolutions.

We examine the behavior of orthogonal non-holomorphic Eisenstein series at their harmonic points through the application of theta lifts. Specifically, for singular weights, we demonstrate that those orthogonal non-holomorphic Eisenstein series expressible as theta lifts possess a simple pole at $s = 1$; the residues of this pole generate holomorphic orthogonal modular forms that are Eisenstein series on the boundary, and we provide a sufficient condition ensuring the surjectivity of this construction.

This study addresses the challenge of tracking an adversarial state sequence within a linear dynamical system affected by adversarial disturbances and loss functions, extending previous literature. We introduce three distinct techniques, each valuable in its own right. First, we propose a comparator-adaptive algorithm for online linear optimization that accounts for movement costs; without parameter tuning, it nearly replicates the performance of optimally tuned gradient descent in hindsight. Second, addressing the related problem of online learning with memory, we design a novel strongly adaptive algorithm that leverages our first contribution as a foundational component. Finally, we establish the first reduction from adversarial tracking control to strongly adaptive online learning with memory. Collectively, these methods yield an adversarial tracking controller that offers robust performance guarantees, even when the reference trajectory involves extensive movement.

The rise of deep learning has spurred the development of specialized processors known as TensorCore Units (TCUs), which are designed for matrix multiplication on small matrices (typically 4x4 or 16x16) to accelerate convolutional and recurrent neural networks. This paper demonstrates how to utilize NVIDIA's TCUs to implement both reduction and scan operations using matrix multiplication, highlighting improvements in program simplicity, efficiency, and performance. By activating TCUs that would otherwise remain idle, our approach reaches 89%–98% of peak memory copy bandwidth and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by orders of magnitude for small segment sizes common in machine learning and scientific computing—achieving speedups of up to 100x for reduction and 3x for scan. Furthermore, this method reduces power consumption by up to 22% for reduction and 16% for scan.

This paper examines the behavior of a moving end mirror within an optomechanical setup comprising a Fabry-Perot cavity filled with a dilute condensate and excited by a single-mode optical field. We demonstrate that the quantum mechanical effect of dynamical localization manifests in both position and momentum spaces for this moving mirror. Furthermore, we analyze the parameter dependencies governing this localization and present a specific set of conditions that render the phenomenon experimentally achievable.

The census of Milky Way open clusters is currently undergoing an unprecedented period of flux. While recent studies utilizing Gaia's exceptional astrometric precision have identified hundreds of new clusters, others argue that many pre-Gaia discoveries are merely associations. This study compares various clustering algorithms designed to detect open clusters, aiming to statistically evaluate their strengths and weaknesses by calculating their sensitivity, specificity, precision, and true positive rates against a comprehensive sample. We focused on DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, and Gaussian mixture models due to their computational efficiency and suitability for Gaia data, adapting them through a specialized preprocessing pipeline and algorithmic refinement. Our analysis covers detection rates for all 1,385 open clusters in the study area, with detailed performance metrics for a subset of 100 clusters. DBSCAN demonstrated sensitivity between 50% and 62% for true positive clusters, maintaining generally high specificity and precision. In contrast, HDBSCAN prioritized sensitivity—reaching up to 82%—over precision, performing well across varying distances and cluster scales. Gaussian mixture models proved to be computationally slow and only detected 33% of the sample, largely limited to larger objects. Furthermore, we report 41 new open cluster candidates identified by HDBSCAN, including three within 500 pc. With additional post-processing to address false positives, HDBSCAN emerges as the most sensitive and effective tool for recovering open clusters in Gaia data. Our findings indicate that numerous previously unreported and known open clusters remain undetected in the current Gaia dataset.

Chemical patent literature encompasses diverse applications containing critical reaction and compound details, including chemical structures, reaction formulas, and molecular characteristics. These entities must first be detected within text segments before they can be applied to downstream tasks. Text mining facilitates the extraction of pertinent data from chemical patents using information extraction methods. Specifically, within the Information Extraction component of the Cheminformatics Elsevier Melbourne University challenge, this study evaluates the efficacy of contextualized language models for identifying reaction data in these patents. We examined transformer architectures trained on both general and domain-specific corpora to develop a novel ensemble model. Our top-performing model, utilizing a majority voting ensemble strategy, attained an exact F1-score of 92.30% and a relaxed F1-score of 96.24%. These findings demonstrate that ensembles of contextualized language models offer a robust approach for extracting information from chemical patents.

This study introduces a secure transmission protocol designed for flexible load balancing in two-hop relay wireless networks, operating without knowledge of eavesdropper channels or locations. Existing physical layer secrecy protocols relying on relay cooperation fail to offer such flexible load control, thereby restricting their practical applicability. To address this, the paper proposes a generalized transmission protocol that integrates load balancing by randomly selecting a relay from the top $k$ preferred candidates situated within a circle of radius $r$ centered between the source and destination (termed 2HR-($r,k$)). This framework encompasses existing methods as specific instances: it includes optimal relay selection ($r=\infty$, $k=1$) and random selection ($r=\infty$, $k=n$) under equal path-loss conditions, as well as selection from a specific region ($r \in (0, \infty), k = 1$) under distance-dependent path-loss. Furthermore, theoretical analysis determines the maximum number of eavesdroppers a network can withstand while maintaining target performance levels regarding secrecy outage and transmission outage probabilities. The results demonstrate that by appropriately configuring $r$ and $k$, the proposed protocol effectively balances load distribution among relays while satisfying specified security and reliability constraints.

Modeling serves as a critical step in the analysis and control of logical dynamic systems (LDS). It has been demonstrated that deterministic LDS can be represented as linear-like systems through algebraic state space formulations. However, obtaining an algebraic expression for stochastic LDS is challenging due to their inherently non-linear nature. This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing transitions in LDSs exhibiting both deterministic and stochastic dynamics. The discussion begins by reviewing the modeling of deterministic LDS, followed by an examination of stochastic LDS modeling, where the non-equivalence between subsystems and the global system is proposed. Subsequently, the rationale behind this non-equivalence is explained, and finally, consistency conditions are established for both independent and conditionally independent models.

We present extensions of the elliptic WP Bailey transform and lemma for $A_n$, $C_n$, and $D_n$ types, where the $n=1$ case was originally established by Andrews and Spiridonov. Our research relies on extending the terminating, balanced, and very-well-poised ${}_{10}V_9$ elliptic hypergeometric summation formula of Frenkel and Turaev to multiple series, building upon results by Rosengren and Rosengren with Schlosser. Within this study, we identify two novel $A_n$ ${}_{12}V_{11}$ transformation formulas; these reduce to new $A_n$ versions of Bailey's $_{10}\phi_9$ transformations when the nome $p$ vanishes, alongside two additional multiple series extensions of the Frenkel and Turaev sum.

This study assesses Beer-Lambert (BL) ray-tracing and Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) photon tracking simulations for predicting and comparing X-ray imaging system performance. These tools facilitate the systematic design of laboratory-scale X-ray particle image velocimetry (XPIV) experiments and tracer particles by forecasting image quality, with the particle image signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) serving as the performance metric. We compare simulated and experimental data for hollow, silver-coated, glass sphere tracer particles (AGSF-33). As the simulations indicate, AGSF-33 particles are visible with an SNR exceeding unity in 100 ms exposure images, highlighting their viability as tracers for X-ray PIV or particle tracking velocimetry (XPTV). The BL method offers computationally efficient prediction of image contrast, allowing for the exploration of extensive parameter spaces in system design. Conversely, while MCNP simulations provide slightly more accurate predictions of experimental images, they require more than an order of magnitude greater computational resources than BL simulations. For most practical XPIV system design applications, the significant computational cost of MCNP is likely not warranted given the modest accuracy gains over BL.

Predicting survey response rates with both accuracy and interpretability is crucial for operational efficiency. The US Census Bureau's ROAM application currently employs principled statistical models trained on the Census Planning Database to pinpoint difficult-to-reach areas. Although a previous crowdsourcing contest found that an ensemble of regression trees offered superior performance in forecasting response rates, these models were unusable for the Census due to their lack of interpretability. This paper introduces new, highly accurate, and interpretable statistical methods for predicting survey response rates. Specifically, we investigate sparse nonparametric additive models incorporating pairwise interactions through $\ell_0$-regularization, along with hierarchically structured variants that further enhance interpretability. While these models have robust theoretical foundations, they pose computational challenges; consequently, we develop new scalable algorithms to learn them and establish novel non-asymptotic error bounds for the resulting estimators. Experiments utilizing the US Census Planning Database confirm that our approach yields high-quality predictive models that offer actionable insights across various population segments. Notably, our methods achieve significant interpretability improvements without sacrificing the predictive performance of state-of-the-art black-box techniques like gradient boosting and feedforward neural networks. The Python code implementation is available at https://github.com/ShibalIbrahim/Additive-Models-with-Structured-Interactions.

The absence of specialized data presents significant hurdles in developing multi-domain neural machine translation systems. While recent studies on low-resource languages show promise, current state-of-the-art models typically rely on millions of sentences. Furthermore, most existing multi-domain adaptation strategies depend on complex architectures ill-suited for real-world deployment. To date, no scalable approach has outperformed the straightforward yet effective strategy of mixed-finetuning, which involves fine-tuning a general model with a combination of specialized and generic data. This paper introduces a novel training pipeline leveraging knowledge distillation from multiple specialized teachers to efficiently fine-tune models without incurring additional inference costs. Experimental results indicate that this pipeline enhances multi-domain translation performance compared to standard fine-tuning across configurations with 2, 3, and 4 domains, achieving BLEU score improvements of up to 2 points.

Transferring quantum information across distinct locations is fundamental to numerous quantum information processing applications. While single-qubit state transfer has been widely studied, moving the configuration of a many-body system has remained a significant challenge. This work tackles the problem of transferring the state of $n$ interacting qubits, a task complicated by the exponentially growing Hilbert space and the effects of interactions, which drastically increase the difficulty of achieving high-fidelity transfer. By utilizing random matrix theory and the framework of quantum dynamical maps, we establish a general formula for the mean and variance of fidelity for any quantum state transfer protocol involving $n$ interacting qubits. Furthermore, applying a weak-coupling scheme within a spin chain, we determine the specific conditions required for high-fidelity transfer of 3 and 4 interacting qubits.

Curiosity serves as a crucial metacognitive ability in education, fostering creativity and a passion for learning. Although many educational systems inadvertently diminish curiosity by prioritizing test preparation, educators are increasingly focused on methods to stimulate it, recognizing the necessity of lifelong learning and reskilling in the future. Despite this, the influence of peers in triggering curiosity remains underexplored. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework offering an integrated socio-cognitive perspective that links observable peer behaviors to internal curiosity states. We distinguish between individual and interpersonal functions that drive curiosity, along with the multimodal behaviors that fulfill them. Using a longitudinal latent variable modeling approach, we validated the framework, confirming that both individual and interpersonal functions positively predict curiosity, with interpersonal factors exerting a notably stronger impact. Furthermore, we identified key behavioral manifestations of these functions through data-driven analysis. We have developed specific strategies and tactics based on this framework, which can be integrated into learning technologies to signal, inspire, and support curiosity. This research advances the design of systems capable of detecting and evoking real-time curiosity within social learning environments, contributing to more comprehensive multimodal learning analytics. The principles established here are broadly applicable for enhancing computer support for various other metacognitive and socio-emotional competencies.

Driven by advancements in data and computing, scientific practice now increasingly relies on machine learning and AI-driven methods, necessitating specialized capabilities at the system, science, and service levels alongside traditional high-capacity supercomputing. Recent distributed architectures, centered on the composability of data-centric applications, have spawned a new ecosystem for container coordination and integration. Nevertheless, a gap persists between the development pipelines of existing supercomputing environments and these emerging dynamic systems, which utilize accessible, portable, and reprogrammable interfaces to disaggregate fluid resource pools. To further advance data-driven science with more efficient computing and domain-specific tools, new approaches for dynamically composing heterogeneous systems are required. This paper introduces a novel approach for leveraging composable systems at the intersection of scientific computing, artificial intelligence, and remote sensing. We detail the architecture of a functional composable infrastructure that federates Expanse, an NSF-funded supercomputer, with Nautilus, a Kubernetes-based, geo-distributed GPU cluster. Additionally, we summarize a wildfire modeling case study that illustrates the application of this infrastructure in scientific workflows, creating a composed system that unites edge sensing insights, AI, and computing capabilities with physics-driven simulations.

Precise simulation of soft mechanisms during dynamic actuation is essential for designing soft robots. We bridge this gap with a differentiable simulation tool that learns the material parameters of our soft robotic fish. Using a soft robotic fish as a case study, we demonstrate an experimentally validated, rapid optimization pipeline for deriving material parameters from quasi-static data through differentiable simulation, subsequently applying these parameters to predict dynamic performance. Our approach identifies physically realistic Young's moduli for the various soft silicone elastomers and stiff acetal copolymers utilized in constructing three distinct robotic fish tail designs. Furthermore, our method accommodates varying internal actuator geometries, such as the number of hollow cavities. Our framework enables high-fidelity prediction of dynamic behavior for composite bi-morph bending structures in physical hardware, achieving millimeter-level accuracy with less than 3% error normalized to actuator length. Additionally, we provide a robust and differentiable estimate of thrust force via a neural network predictor, facilitating accurate modeling of our experimental setup for measuring bollard pull. This work addresses a prototypical hardware and simulation challenge using our differentiable framework, which is applicable to higher-dimensional parameter inference, control policy learning, and computational design owing to its differentiable nature.

This work addresses a fully decentralized stochastic multi-armed bandit framework involving multiple players who lack communication capabilities and can only observe their individual actions and rewards. The environment is heterogeneous, meaning reward distributions for specific arms vary across players. We allow colliding players (those selecting the same arm simultaneously) to receive non-zero rewards. Unlike traditional settings, the time-horizon $T$ is unknown to the agents. We propose a policy capable of operating in scenarios where the number of players exceeds the number of arms, achieving a near order-optimal expected regret of $O(\log^{1 + \delta} T)$ for some $0 < \delta < 1$ over the duration $T$. This paper has been accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory.

This study examines an uplink mobile-edge computing (MEC) network utilizing non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). The primary goal is to minimize a weighted sum of task completion times for all users and their total energy usage, which encompasses both local computation and transmission energy, while adhering to constraints on computation latency, data upload rates, time allocation, and edge cloud capacity. This approach aims to substantially enhance energy efficiency and reduce end-to-end latency for applications in upcoming wireless networks. To address the general minimization problem, the work first converts it into an equivalent formulation, followed by the development of an iterative algorithm that yields a closed-form solution at each iteration. For the specific scenario focusing solely on minimizing completion time, a bisection-based algorithm is introduced to derive the optimal solution. Additionally, in the case of infinite cloud capacity, the original problem is demonstrated to be transformable into an equivalent convex optimization problem. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed algorithms outperform conventional methods regarding both completion time and energy consumption.

The one-dimensional lattice Schwinger model has recently been implemented using bosons within optical lattices. This system exhibits both confinement and deconfinement phases, with its phase diagram governed by the matter field's mass and the topological angle. While experimentally adjusting the matter field mass is straightforward, we propose a method to tune the topological angle, thereby enabling access to the full phase diagram. We suggest that direct experimental confirmation of confinement and deconfinement can be achieved by measuring whether a physical charge localizes near a fixed gauge charge to screen it. Additionally, we examine the PXP model realized in Rydberg atom arrays, which is equivalent to the lattice Schwinger model when all local gauge charges are set to zero. Even with fixed gauge charges, confinement and deconfinement in the PXP model can be investigated by analyzing the relative motion of a physical charge-anti-charge pair. These proposed schemes are directly applicable to current ultracold atom quantum simulator platforms.

This study evaluates the sufficiency and representativeness of physical domain testing for adversarial machine learning (ML) attacks targeting computer vision systems with human participants. Although numerous studies claiming to deploy such attacks label themselves as "real-world," our analysis reveals that actual physical testing is often scant, lacks detailed information regarding test subjects, and is frequently treated as an afterthought or mere demonstration. The absence of representative trials in adversarial ML research constitutes an ethical, scientific, and health/safety concern capable of causing tangible harm. We outline the problem and our methodology, critique the physical testing approaches currently used in the field, examine obstacles to more inclusive physical testing in adversarial ML, and provide recommendations to enhance such testing despite these hurdles.

Contemporary mathematical epidemiology, especially within COVID-19 studies, frequently employs a specific subclass of compartmental models categorized into three groups: "(x, y, z)" representing "susceptible/entrance," "diseased," and "output" (corresponding to the single classes found in the classic SIR framework). These models are characterized by ordinary differential equations containing exclusively linear terms, except for the products between x and y variables. It has been established for some time that the basic reproduction number $R$ possesses a straightforward formula (3.3) based on the defining matrices, alongside an explicit first integral formula (3.8). These foundational results, dating back to at least [ABvdD+07] and [Fen07], represent the "basic laws of SIR-type epidemics," yet numerous studies continue to unnecessarily rederive them using methods like the next-generation matrix or direct computation. Consequently, this work aims to highlight these fundamental principles and offer a comprehensive reference of associated formulas for (x, y, z) models. We propose renaming this class "matrix SIR epidemic models," or SYR, to underscore its resemblance to the traditional SIR case. For scenarios involving a single susceptible class, we suggest the term "SIR-PH," reflecting a probabilistic interpretation where the exponential infection time is substituted with a PH-type distribution. We observe that every SIR-PH model corresponds to a scalar quantity $Y(t)$ that adheres to "classic SIR relations," as detailed in (3.8). When multiple susceptible classes are involved, this extends to equation (5.10); in forthcoming research, we will demonstrate how (3.8) and (5.10) can yield approximate control policies that perform comparably to the optimal control of the original models.

This letter introduces a novel time-domain absorption technique aimed at mitigating speech masking within noisy and reverberant environments. The approach leverages the non-stationary characteristics of corrupted signal segments to identify masking distortions using a specific threshold, with these non-stationarity metrics objectively quantified to guide the absorption process. Notably, the method operates without requiring prior knowledge of speech statistics or room acoustics. Performance was assessed using three intelligibility metrics (ESII, ASIIST, SRMRnorm) alongside a perceptual listening test, with experimental results demonstrating that the proposed scheme achieves superior intelligibility gains compared to existing methods.

Unlike typical software quality attributes, code testability cannot be assessed exclusively through source code characteristics. Instead, it is significantly influenced by the assigned test budget and the effectiveness of the test suite. While test suite size dictates effort and cost, coverage metrics reflect effectiveness; consequently, testability is quantified by the number of test cases and their coverage relative to the budget. This paper introduces a novel equation to estimate testability based on test suite size and coverage. This method was applied to label 23,000 classes across 110 Java projects, which were then vectorized using 262 metrics. These vectors served as input for supervised regression machine learning algorithms to predict testability from source code metrics. The resulting regression models achieved an R² of 0.68 and a mean squared error of 0.03, demonstrating practical suitability. Feature importance analysis on the trained model identified fifteen software metrics that most strongly affect testability predictions. Compared to a relevant study on predicting branch coverage, the proposed models reduced mean absolute error by 38% by leveraging new criteria, metrics, and data. Furthermore, an application of this prediction technique showed that automating refactoring for 42 "smelly" Java classes, specifically targeting the 15 influential metrics, could increase their testability by an average of 86.87%.

The study begins by establishing the conditions under which early exercise of an American option is suboptimal, regardless of whether interest rates are positive or negative. It then provides a brief examination of the geometry of the exercise region specifically under negative rates. Subsequently, the paper introduces a novel integral equation that determines both the option price and the two early exercise boundaries in this context. The authors demonstrate how to solve this equation by adapting the efficient Andersen and Lake algorithm, modifying it from initial boundary guesses to refined adjustments within their fixed-point method to ensure stability. Finally, the accuracy and performance of this proposed algorithm are evaluated against a state-of-the-art finite difference method.

Determining the thermal architecture of protoplanetary disks is essential for interpreting observational data, forecasting the disk's physical and chemical evolution, and simulating planet formation. This research constrains the two-dimensional temperature distribution of the disk surrounding the Herbig Ae star HD 163296. By employing the RAC2D thermo-chemical code, we developed a thermal model that successfully reproduces spatially resolved ALMA data (spanning ~0.12 arcsec [13 au] to 0.25 arcsec [26 au]) for various CO isotopologues (J = 2-1, 13CO J = 1-0, 2-1, C18O J = 1-0, 2-1, and C17O J = 1-0), the upper limit on HD J = 1-0 flux, the spectral energy distribution (SED), and continuum morphology. The resulting model integrates a radial CO depletion driven by a timescale shorter than standard gas-phase chemistry (0.01 Myr) and elevated temperatures in the inner disk's surface layers (z/r ≤ 0.21). This configuration aligns with most empirically derived temperatures and emitting surfaces observed via J = 2-1 CO data. Utilizing the upper limits of the HD J = 1-0 and J = 2-1 fluxes, we establish an upper bound for the disk mass of 0.35 solar masses. Furthermore, using this final thermal structure, we investigated how gaps influence the observationally constrained temperature profile. Introducing a large gap in both gas and small dust increases the gas temperature within the gap by merely 5-10%. This work is included in the MAPS special issue of the Astrophysical Journal Supplement.

This study examines warped AdS$_3\times $S$^2\times$M$_5$ configurations within type II supergravity that maintain small ${\cal N}=(4,0)$ supersymmetry. We demonstrate that enforcing this supersymmetry requires between zero and three a priori isometries on the internal manifold $M_5$. Our analysis concentrates on solutions where $M_5$ possesses no such pre-existing isometries, thereby introducing further restrictions. In type IIA, resolving these constraints necessitates that $M_5$ carries an SU(2)-structure, a scenario previously explored in arXiv:1908.09851. Conversely, in type IIB, we identify two distinct new classes characterized by identity structure, which we simplify into local formulations for the physical fields and associated partial differential equations.

This paper introduces a family of neural networks known as multi-layer perceptrons, along with the training algorithms employed, aiming to provide sufficient mathematical rigor and precision. We then explore the application of these networks to a challenge within information security: the remote identification of operating systems, a key component of the information gathering phase in penetration testing. The primary contribution of this work lies in applying classic artificial intelligence techniques to a classification problem, yielding superior results compared to traditional methods previously used.

This study examines noncommutative principal bundles that exhibit equivariance under a triangular Hopf algebra. We provide concrete examples of infinite-dimensional braided Lie and Hopf algebras representing the infinitesimal gauge transformations of bundles defined on noncommutative spheres. The braiding within these algebras is determined by the triangular structure of the symmetry Hopf algebra. Furthermore, we offer a systematic examination of compatible $*$-structures, including the quasitriangular scenario.

This study addresses personalized dose guidance through Bayesian optimization, which determines an optimal, individualized drug dosage to enhance therapeutic results. Patient safety is secured with high probability via a safe learning approach utilizing the interior point method. The proposed method is validated on the task of learning the optimal bolus insulin dosage for individuals with type 1 diabetes to mitigate the impact of food intake. Beginning with no prior knowledge of the patients, the algorithm successfully improves therapeutic outcomes—measured as the percentage of time-in-range—while maintaining patient safety. Additionally, other potential applications within healthcare are explored.

We introduce a framework of exponential bounds designed to estimate the probability that a martingale sequence exceeds a time-varying linear threshold. Our central finding is that expressing exponential concentration inequalities in this manner is both intuitive and highly effective. We demonstrate this approach by offering a unified theorem and a single assumption that consolidate and enhance numerous tail bounds for martingales. This framework encompasses classical results from the 1960s and 1980s by Bernstein, Bennett, Hoeffding, and Freedman; significant contributions from the 1980s to 2000s by Shorack and Wellner, Pinelis, Blackwell, van de Geer, and de la Peña; and modern advancements post-2000 by Khan, Tropp, Bercu and Touati, Delyon, and others. In every instance, we provide the most robust and general formulations available, characterizing time-uniform concentration for scalar, matrix, and Banach-space-valued martingales across discrete and continuous time under diverse nonparametric conditions. Furthermore, this work connects existing line-crossing inequalities with the sequential probability ratio test, the Cramér-Chernoff method, self-normalized processes, and other relevant areas of research.

A significant outcome of the Banach Fixed Point Theorem is Hutchinson's theorem, which guarantees the existence and uniqueness of fractals within complete metric spaces. This paper aims to generalize that theorem to semimetric spaces by leveraging the work of Bessenyei and Páles from 2017. The study investigates specific properties of both semimetric spaces and fractal spaces. Furthermore, it adapts Hausdorff's theorem to define compactness and modifies Blaschke's theorems to define completeness within the fractal space. Building on these foundational elements, the authors prove a semimetric analogue of Hutchinson's theorem and subsequently establish error estimates and stability for fractals.

This study investigates the conditions under which multinational corporations (MNCs) demonstrate resilience in the face of natural disasters. To address this, we construct a straightforward model that examines the input-output relationships between foreign MNCs and domestic firms within the host nation. Our analysis indicates that when disasters severely impact local enterprises, driving up the costs of sourcing local intermediate inputs, the majority of MNCs may withdraw from the host country. Conversely, MNCs are more likely to remain if they maintain strong supply chain connections with local suppliers and encounter low trade barriers for importing foreign intermediates. Additionally, we extend the baseline model to account for variations such as heterogeneous productivity levels among MNCs and the processes involved in disaster reconstruction.

This paper addresses the recovery of $n$-dimensional signals from $m$ binary measurements affected by noise and sign flips, assuming the target signals possess a low generative intrinsic dimension. Specifically, these signals can be approximated by an $L$-Lipschitz generator $G: \mathbb{R}^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$ where $k\ll n$. Despite the high nonlinearity of the binary measurement model, we introduce a least squares decoder and demonstrate that, with high probability, it achieves a sharp estimation error of $\mathcal{O} (\sqrt{\frac{k\log (Ln)}{m}})$ up to a constant factor $c$, provided $m\geq \mathcal{O}( k\log (Ln))$. Extensive numerical experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art techniques confirm the decoder's robustness against noise and sign flips, as predicted by our theoretical analysis. Furthermore, we validate the (approximately) deep generative prior by constructing a ReLU network with appropriately selected depth and width, a result of independent interest.

We examine a precisely defined heterostructure featuring magnetic iron (Fe) layers positioned between graphene (Gr) and an iridium (111) substrate. The difficult challenge of preventing Fe-C solubility and Fe-Ir intermixing was successfully overcome through atomic-level controlled Fe intercalation at moderate temperatures below 500 K. When a single ordered Fe layer is inserted into registry with the Ir substrate, the intermixing of Gr bands and Fe d-orbitals disrupts the Dirac cone symmetry, causing an energy shift of the apex downward by approximately 3 eV and generating well-localized Fe states just below the Fermi level. First-principles electronic structure calculations indicate significant spin splitting of the Fe states, leading to a majority spin channel that is nearly fully occupied and strongly hybridized with Gr $\pi$ states. X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements on the Gr/Fe/Ir heterostructure demonstrate an ordered spin configuration with a ferromagnetic response from the Fe layer(s), exhibiting enhanced spin and orbital characteristics compared to bcc-Fe bulk values. Furthermore, the magnetization orientation shifts from a perpendicular easy axis when the single Fe layer is lattice-matched to the Ir(111) surface to a parallel axis when the Fe thin film is nearly commensurate with the graphene.

We introduce a learning-based navigation system designed to reach visually specified goals, validated on a real mobile robot. Learning offers a compelling alternative to traditional navigation methods; rather than relying on geometric reasoning and maps, it allows robots to grasp navigational affordances, distinguish between traversable obstacles (like tall grass) and non-traversable ones (like walls), and generalize environmental patterns. However, unlike standard planning algorithms, modifying the goal for a learned policy during deployment is more challenging. We propose a technique for learning to navigate toward a goal image representing the desired destination. By integrating a learned policy with a topological graph built from prior observations, our system can locate the path to a visually indicated goal despite variations in appearance and lighting. Three core insights—waypoint proposal, graph pruning, and negative mining—enable our approach to navigate real-world environments using only offline data, a scenario where previous methods often fail. We implemented this method, named ViNG, on a real outdoor ground robot, demonstrating that it surpasses prior goal-conditioned reinforcement learning approaches, including those combining reinforcement learning with search. Additionally, we investigated ViNG's generalization to unseen environments and its capacity to adapt through accumulated experience. Finally, we showcase ViNG in practical applications such as last-mile delivery and warehouse inspection. Readers are invited to visit our project website, sites.google.com/view/ving-robot, for videos of our experiments and demonstrations.
We address a question recently raised by B. Lovitz and F. Petrov, establishing the conjectured sufficient conditions for both minimality and uniqueness in 3-tensor decomposition.

Large-scale image processing serves as a potent mechanism for generating new datasets, merging them with established ones, and conducting analysis and quality assurance. Workflow managers provide significant benefits in this context, which typically entails numerous data access and processing stages. Typically, they facilitate workflow automation by identifying data and resources, enabling failure recovery, and tracking performance. This demonstration showcases how the Pegasus Workflow Manager Python API utilizes the Montage Image Mosaic engine to execute image processing tasks that create mosaics. Developed and maintained at USC/ISI since 2001, Pegasus was originally designed and optimized using Montage, which was among its first applications. Over time, Pegasus has been applied across various scientific domains; for instance, LIGO leveraged it to detect black holes, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory utilized it to evaluate cloud-based image processing costs and performance. Although these instances represent large-scale endeavors, small teams conducting research on local machine clusters can also derive substantial benefits from Pegasus.

Grant-free radio access IoT networks, such as SigFox and LoRa, provide cost-effective and robust communication within unlicensed frequency bands. Their popularity is driven by the growing demand for ultra-durable IoT systems characterized by extended battery life. While most existing research assumes the deployment of a single radio access technology, this paper examines the effects of competing technologies coexisting within the same network. We consider $K$ technologies, each defined by their time and frequency activity factors, bandwidth, and power consumption, all sharing a common pool of radio resources. By deriving closed-form expressions for successful transmission probability, expected battery lifetime, and latency as functions of distance to the access point, our analytical model—validated through simulations—serves as a tool to assess coexistence scenarios. This analysis reveals how introducing a new technology can degrade system performance regarding success rates and battery duration. Furthermore, we explore mitigation strategies to counteract these negative impacts, such as network densification and the implementation of joint reception techniques.

This paper investigates how the localization length of eigenstates depends on system size within a specific non-Hermitian model exhibiting a critical skin effect, characterized by a discontinuous energy spectrum transition in the thermodynamic limit. We analytically demonstrate that the eigenstates display remarkable scale-free localization, where the localization length scales linearly with the system size. These findings provide theoretical validation for the previously numerically proposed concept of scale-free localization.

We have developed a field-theoretic framework to address the non-linear and non-local responses of structured liquid dielectrics. These systems consist of dipolar solvent molecules alongside simple salt cations and anions. Our model employs two distinct order parameters: a polarization field representing the solvent and a charge density field for the ions. This approach explicitly and consistently incorporates the non-electrostatic interactions. We demonstrate the derivation of functionals for both the polarization and electrostatic fields across increasingly finer scales and solve the corresponding mean-field saddle-point equations within the linear regime. Furthermore, we establish solution criteria dependent on solvent polarity and structural lengths. Ultimately, our methodology offers a systematic route to developing generalized polarization theories.

By applying a metallicity-dependent conversion factor for CO luminosity to molecular gas mass and utilizing a star formation efficiency per free-fall time that varies with the virial parameter of molecular clouds, the observed star formation rate of the Milky Way can be accounted for. These methods also successfully predict the trend of star formation rate surface density relative to Galactocentric radius. The variation in efficiency per free-fall time as a function of the virial parameter is primarily responsible for aligning theoretical predictions with the total observed star formation rate, whereas the metallicity dependence of the CO-to-mass conversion factor most significantly influences the variation with Galactocentric radius. Implementing these adjustments resolves a discrepancy exceeding a factor of 100 between observed and theoretical star formation rates that has persisted for nearly half a century.

This paper offers a detailed examination of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models, covering their primary assumptions and rationales, key theoretical results, and insights through elementary examples. A specific focus is placed on the significance of singular ARMA models within both the theoretical framework and practical applications of these models. The study prioritizes the structural theory and classification of model types over detailed estimation techniques. Rather than providing an exhaustive survey, the objective is to highlight promising avenues for future research and underdeveloped applications.

This paper examines hamiltonicity in planar cubic graphs G that possess a facial 2-factor Q, utilizing (quasi) spanning trees of faces within the quotient graph G/Q and investigating the algorithmic complexity of identifying such structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if Barnette's Conjecture does not hold, then determining hamiltonicity in 3-connected planar cubic bipartite graphs is NP-complete.

We examine the spectrum of a $U(1)$ quantum link model, where gauge fields are represented by $S=1/2$ spins, to reveal a novel mechanism for creating quantum many-body scars—high-energy eigenstates that defy the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis within a constrained Hilbert space. The study of many-body dynamics under local constraints has gained significant traction following the observation of non-ergodic behavior in Rydberg atom-based quantum simulators. Lattice gauge theories serve as natural constrained systems because physical states must remain gauge-invariant. In our specific model, the Hamiltonian $H={\cal O}_{\rm kin}+\lambda {\cal O}_{\rm pot}$ features exact mid-spectrum zero modes at $\lambda=0$, with the number of these modes growing exponentially as system size increases. Although this extensive degeneracy is broken for any non-zero $\lambda$, specific linear combinations that simultaneously diagonalize both ${\cal O}_{\rm kin}$ and ${\cal O}_{\rm pot}$ persist as quantum many-body scars, indicative of an ``order-by-disorder'' phenomenon within the Hilbert space. We provide evidence for these scars and illustrate their dynamical effects on two-leg ladders comprising up to $56$ spins, results that could be verified using existing quantum simulator proposals. Furthermore, findings on broader ladders suggest that such scars likely exist in two-dimensional systems as well.

As distributed generation expands, traditional passive consumers in distribution networks are transforming into "prosumers" capable of both generating and consuming energy. When energy imbalances occur, trading with the main grid or among prosumers becomes necessary. Consequently, this study examines the peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading market, modeled as a generalized Nash game. We first demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE). Subsequently, a distributed online algorithm is developed to track this equilibrium within time-varying environments. It is proven that the algorithm's regret is bounded by a sublinear function of learning time, suggesting acceptable practical accuracy. Finally, numerical simulations involving six microgrids confirm the algorithm's effectiveness.

Knowledge distillation (KD) is frequently employed to generate synthetic training data for non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, a divergence in low-frequency word distribution between the distilled and original datasets often results in increased prediction errors for these rare terms. To mitigate this, we integrate raw data directly into NAT training via pretraining. Our analysis of directed alignments reveals that while KD forces low-frequency source words to align deterministically with targets, it fails to adequately align sufficient low-frequency target words back to sources. Consequently, we introduce reverse KD to recover additional alignments for low-frequency target words. By combining these complementary strategies to maximize the utility of both authentic and synthetic data, we propose a novel training framework designed to enhance NAT performance. Experiments across five translation benchmarks utilizing two advanced architectures demonstrate that this approach universally and significantly boosts translation quality, specifically by reducing errors on low-frequency words. Notably, the method achieves BLEU scores of 28.2 and 33.9 on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. The corresponding code, data, and trained models are accessible at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

This paper introduces a Hilbert-style axiomatisation for the crisp bi-G\"{o}del modal logic $\KbiG$, demonstrating its completeness with respect to crisp Kripke models where formulas are evaluated using the standard bi-G\"{o}del algebra on $[0,1]$. We further examine a paraconsistent extension of $\KbiG$, incorporating a De Morgan negation $\neg$, which we name $\KGsquare$. By developing a Hilbert-style calculus for $\KGsquare$ and utilizing a conservative translation from $\KbiG$ to $\KGsquare$, we establish its completeness relative to crisp Kripke models featuring two valuations over $[0,1]$ linked by $\neg$. For both logics, we prove that decidability and validity are $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete. Additionally, we investigate the semantic properties of $\KbiG$ and $\KGsquare$, showing that the Glivenko theorem applies exclusively to finitely branching frames. We also analyze the classes of formulas that characterize identical frame classes in both the classical modal logic $\mathbf{K}$ and the crisp G\"{o}del modal logic $\KG^c$. Specifically, we demonstrate that, among other cases, all Sahlqvist formulas and all implications $\phi\rightarrow\chi$ where $\phi$ and $\chi$ are monotone define the same frame classes in $\mathbf{K}$ and $\KG^c$.

This work presents a straightforward proof demonstrating that the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ($d\ge3$) is ill-posed within critical Sobolev spaces, thereby generalizing previous results by Bourgain and Li that addressed the specific case of $d=3$. Additionally, ill-posedness is established for specific critical Lorentz spaces.

Online reinforcement learning (RL) methods are becoming more prevalent for tailoring digital interventions in mobile health and online education. However, developing and validating RL algorithms in these contexts presents significant hurdles, such as maintaining stability and learning efficiency under real-time constraints and navigating complex environments lacking precise mechanistic models of user behavior. To address these issues, we adapt the PCS (Predictability, Computability, Stability) framework—originally a data science approach for supervised learning—to guide the design of RL algorithms for digital interventions. Additionally, we offer specific guidelines for creating simulation environments, which are essential for assessing RL candidates using the PCS framework. We demonstrate this application by designing an RL algorithm for Oralytics, a mobile health initiative launched in late 2022 aimed at enhancing tooth-brushing habits through personalized messaging.

Future $e^+e^-$ colliders like the FCC-ee are poised to deliver high-precision experimental data on the Higgs boson (approximately 125 GeV) and electroweak observables, including the W-boson mass and the effective weak leptonic mixing angle. To meet this anticipated experimental accuracy, theoretical predictions for these quantities must be refined to a comparable level. This overview briefly details the current status of Standard Model (SM) predictions and the computational tools employed. Furthermore, we discuss the necessary enhancements required to achieve the target precision and provide an overview of the simulation frameworks utilized for the Higgs and electroweak precision programs.

This study employs exploratory factor analysis to examine whether established community-level patterns of social capital variance persist online within the U.S. context. Specifically, we analyze Facebook groups that link users within the same local areas, investigating the link between county-level social capital metrics and participation patterns in corresponding online groups. Our findings identify four distinct factors characterizing Facebook group engagement by county: the first represents small, private groups dense with friendships; the second comprises very local, small groups; the third includes non-local, large, public groups with greater age diversity; and the fourth consists of partially local groups of medium to large size. While the first and third factors correlate with offline community social capital measures, the second and fourth do not. Both collectively and individually, these factors predict offline social capital even after controlling for county demographics. Ultimately, our analysis uncovers significant correlations between traditional social capital indicators and online interaction patterns in local Facebook groups. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic investigation into the association between regional offline social capital and online community engagement within the same areas.

We have identified stationary thin-brane configurations that correspond to far-from-equilibrium steady states of two-dimensional holographic interfaces. The boundary heat flux aligns with CFT predictions and established energy-transport coefficients within the thin-brane framework. We propose that the interface generates coarse-grained entropy at its maximum rate by entangling outgoing excitations, while highlighting both parallels and distinctions relative to double-sided black funnels. In our solutions, the non-compact, non-Killing event horizon—which is far from equilibrium—matches the local (apparent) horizon on the cooler side but remains situated behind it on the warmer side. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermal conductivity of an interface pair undergoes a transition at the Hawking-Page phase shift, moving from a regime governed by classical scatterers to a quantum regime where heat flows without obstruction.

We examine critical systems responsible for distributing limited resources to meet fundamental needs, such as housing programs for the homeless. Since these systems frequently serve communities marginalized by systemic injustices related to race, gender, or other factors, it is essential to integrate fairness principles into their design. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a framework for assessing fairness in contextual resource allocation, drawing inspiration from machine learning fairness metrics. This approach enables the evaluation of historical policies and the imposition of fairness constraints during the creation of new, counterfactual allocation strategies. Our study concludes with a series of incompatibility findings that explore the relationships between our proposed metrics. Specifically, we demonstrate that: 1) fairness in the allocation process and fairness in final outcomes are typically mutually exclusive; 2) policies relying on vulnerability scores often produce unequal outcomes across groups, even when those scores are perfectly calibrated; 3) incorporating contextual data beyond baseline risk and treatment effects can yield fairer outcomes than using only the latter; and 4) policies that include group status alongside baseline risk and treatment effects achieve the highest possible fairness given all available information. Ultimately, our framework aims to assist stakeholders in navigating discussions about which fairness metrics to apply when allocating scarce resources.

The recent emergence of pre-trained Transformer models has significantly advanced effective text mining for diverse biomedical applications. Nevertheless, these models, which are predominantly trained on textual data, frequently lack specific domain knowledge regarding entities, limiting their ability to capture context beyond individual sentences. To address this, we present a novel framework that allows models to learn comprehensive multi-omics biological information about entities, specifically proteins, by incorporating additional multi-modal cues such as molecular structures. Instead of creating separate architectures for each modality, we developed a generalized and optimized graph-based multi-modal learning mechanism. This approach leverages GraphBERT to encode both textual and structural data, utilizing the inherent features of various modalities to facilitate end-to-end learning. We assessed our proposed method on the Protein-Protein Interaction task within a biomedical corpus, demonstrating that our generalized approach yields significant benefits from the inclusion of this additional domain-specific modality.

Grasping the quantitative connections among urban components is vital for numerous applications. Macroscopic observations reveal that aggregated urban metrics, such as gross domestic product, scale systematically with city populations, a phenomenon termed urban scaling laws. Yet, at the mesoscopic level, it remains unclear whether these simple scaling relationships persist within individual cities, representing a core inquiry into the spatial origins of scaling in urban systems. By examining four large-scale datasets encompassing millions of mobile phone users and urban facilities, we explore scaling behaviors inside cities. Our findings indicate that while infrastructure volume scales sub-linearly with the active population, socioeconomic activity scales super-linearly. Furthermore, even for identical scaling phenomena, the exponents differ among cities with comparable population sizes. To account for these empirical findings, we introduce a conceptual framework that incorporates the heterogeneous distributions of populations and facilities alongside their spatial interactions. Both analytical and numerical results demonstrate that, despite the myriad complexities affecting urban activities, straightforward interaction rules can effectively explain the observed regularities and heterogeneities in scaling behaviors within cities.

Comprehending how the cladding tube architecture influences the guiding efficiency is essential for developing single-mode, wide-band, and ultra-low-loss nested hollow-core anti-resonant fibers (HC-ARFs). This study comprehensively examines the effect of realistic, non-ideal nested element geometries on propagation loss. Surprisingly, the size of these nested elements, rather than their shape, plays a decisive role in determining the final loss performance. We discovered a distinct "V-shaped" pattern for mitigating higher-order mode losses by optimizing the free design parameters of HC-ARFs. Our findings indicate that a 5-tube nested HC-ARF offers a broader transmission window and superior single-mode operation compared to its 6-tube counterpart. Furthermore, we demonstrate that propagation loss can be substantially reduced by employing anisotropic nested anti-resonant tubes elongated radially. Simulations reveal that this innovative fiber design can achieve a propagation loss as low as 0.11 dB/km at 1.55 $\mu$m. These results offer valuable design insights for fully harnessing the potential of single-mode, wide-band, and ultra-low-loss HC-ARFs. Additionally, the exceptional optical properties of this proposed fiber could benefit various applications, including future optical communication systems, high-energy light transport, extreme nonlinear optics, and beyond.

Low-distortion metric embeddings aim to map a complex "hard" metric space into a simpler target space, such as a tree metric, while approximately maintaining pairwise distances. While tree metrics are ideal, embedding them directly often causes significant distortion. Two established approaches to mitigate this are stochastic embeddings, which achieve logarithmic expected distortion, and Ramsey-type embeddings, which guarantee low distortion only for a subset of points. However, neither method ensures a worst-case distortion guarantee on all pairs within a single tree. This paper introduces a novel third approach termed \emph{clan embedding}. In this framework, each point $x$ maps to a subset of points $f(x)$, known as a \emph{clan}, which includes a designated \emph{chief} point $\chi(x)\in f(x)$. An embedding exhibits multiplicative distortion $t$ if, for every pair $(x,y)$, there exists a point $y'\in f(y)$ in the clan of $y$ that is within distance $t\cdot d(x,y)$ of $\chi(x)$ (i.e., $\min_{y'\in f(y)}d(y',\chi(x))\le t\cdot d(x,y)$). Our primary result establishes a clan embedding into a tree with multiplicative distortion $O(\frac{\log n}{\epsilon})$, where each point has an expected $1+\epsilon$ copies. Furthermore, we present a "spanning" variant of this theorem for graphs, leading to the development of the first compact routing scheme utilizing constant-size routing tables.

Subsequently, we examine minor-free graphs with a diameter parameterized by $D$. These graphs are known to admit stochastic embeddings into bounded treewidth graphs with expected additive distortion $\epsilon D$. We develop both Ramsey-type and clan embedding counterparts to these stochastic embeddings. Leveraging these new embeddings, we construct the first bicriteria quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme for the metric $\rho$-dominating set and metric $\rho$-independent set problems within minor-free graphs.

We investigate a natural class of refinements of the Ehrhart series for closed polytopes, originally introduced by Chapoton. Employing commutative algebra, we derive these refined series in complete generality for a $d$-dimensional simplex, a $d$-dimensional cross-polytope, and a $d$-dimensional hypercube where $d < 4$. These results yield summation formulas for products of $q$-integers with distinct arguments, extending a well-known identity attributed to MacMahon and Carlitz. Furthermore, we provide an algebraic characterization of a specific refined Eulerian polynomial.

Time series data underpins numerous real-world applications, where detailed analysis through forecasting and anomaly detection enhances our understanding of temporal events. While Time Series Analysis (TSA) traditionally relies on visual plots and standard statistical models, Machine Learning (ML) approaches have recently advanced the state of the art in forecasting and anomaly detection, offering comparable performance when data and computational constraints are satisfied. Although various toolboxes exist that provide rich interfaces for specific models like ARIMA or neural networks, or handle isolated tasks such as feature extraction and classification, open-source ML capabilities for time series remain constrained, often suffering from library incompatibility. Consequently, this paper aims to deliver a concise, user-friendly overview of essential open-source tools for TSA, focusing on two key areas: forecasting and anomaly detection. It outlines a typical TSA framework's architecture and features, categorizing the tools by their analysis tasks, data preparation methods, and result evaluation techniques. Through a quantitative analysis of the current landscape of actively developed open-source frameworks, the study evaluated 60 tools, identifying 32 with forecasting modules and 21 with anomaly detection capabilities.

The bulk and spectroscopic characteristics of 4He are investigated using an equation of motion phonon approach. This technique constructs a basis of n-phonon states (where n ranges from 0 to 3...) through tensor products of particle-hole Tamm-Dancoff phonons, subsequently solving the complete eigenvalue problem within this framework. The method operates without approximations and eliminates center-of-mass contamination by employing a singular value decomposition procedure on rectangular matrices. Two potentials, both originating from chiral effective field theory, are utilized in a self-consistent calculation limited to a basis of up to three phonons, with the latter states treated under a simplifying assumption. A comparison with experimental results highlights the varying efficacy of the two potentials and reveals that while the calculation only partially captures spectroscopic properties, it offers a pathway for future enhancements.

Visual localization, defined as estimating a camera's pose within a known environment, serves as a fundamental element for technologies like autonomous driving and augmented reality. Current leading methods typically employ image retrieval techniques to either generate an approximate pose or identify visible scene regions in a query image. While standard practice involves using advanced retrieval algorithms trained to recognize landmarks across vast viewpoint variations, such robustness is not always beneficial for localization. This study investigates the function of image retrieval across various localization tasks, introducing a benchmark setup and evaluating state-of-the-art retrieval representations on multiple datasets. The findings reveal that performance on traditional landmark recognition tasks correlates with localization success only in specific cases, underscoring the necessity for retrieval methods specifically tailored to localization. The associated benchmark and evaluation protocols can be accessed at https://github.com/naver/kapture-localization.

Algorithmic fairness has become a critical domain focused on identifying and reducing bias within machine learning models. While extensive research exists regarding fairness in regression and classification tasks, the application of these principles to survival analysis remains underexplored. Survival analysis involves estimating the probability of an event occurring over time, a capability that is vital for sensitive applications like patient diagnosis and prognosis. This study investigates the adaptation of existing survival metrics to assess bias using group fairness criteria. Through an empirical analysis involving 29 survival datasets and eight different measures, we observed that discrimination metrics effectively capture bias, whereas calibration and scoring rules offer less clarity. We recommend future research directions, particularly the development of prediction-based fairness metrics tailored for distribution predictions.

The explicit verification of integrability for classical and quantum rational Calogero-Moser systems with $n=3$ is achieved through the Lax pair method. We offer a comprehensive overview of reflection groups and root systems. Using Dunkl operators linked to root systems, we construct Olshanetsky-Perelomov operators for general root systems. The integrability of the quantum rational Calogero-Moser system is examined through these Olshanetsky-Perelomov operators, which yield a collection of commuting integrals of motion. Additionally, classical counterparts to both the Dunkl and Olshanetsky-Perelomov operators are presented.

High-resolution inelastic x-ray scattering experiments were conducted on molten NaI near its melting point of 680$^\circ$C at SPring-8. The study detected small, damped signals of longitudinal optic excitation modes on the tails of longitudinal acoustic modes at low momentum transfers ($Q\sim5$ nm$^{-1}$). The measured spectra align well with *ab initio* molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in terms of both frequency and linewidth, whereas they do not match classical MD results. The presence of these modes at small $Q$ and their strong agreement with simulations allow for a definitive identification as collective optic modes characterized by well-defined phasing among different ionic motions.

This study analyzes microlensing observations from the 2017–2019 seasons targeting peripheral Galactic bulge fields to detect planetary signatures within light curves that have sparse monitoring. By visually inspecting non-prime-field events for weak short-term anomalies, we identified two previously unknown planetary candidates: KMT-2017-BLG-0673 and KMT-2019-BLG-0414. The signal for KMT-2017-BLG-0673 resulted from the source crossing a planet-induced caustic, which was previously undetected due to sparse data coverage. Conversely, the potential signal for KMT-2019-BLG-0414 occurred without caustic crossing and was missed because of its weakness. For KMT-2017-BLG-0673, we determined a unique planetary model. In contrast, KMT-2019-BLG-0414 yields two pairs of planetary solutions, each subject to the close-wide degeneracy, alongside a less favored binary-source (xallarap) scenario where a single lens magnifies a rapidly orbiting binary source. Bayesian analysis estimates that KMT-2017-BLG-0673Lb is a planet with a mass of $3.7^{+2.2}_{-2.1}~M_{\rm J}$ orbiting a late K-type star of $0.63^{+0.37}_{-0.35}~M_\odot$. Under the planetary interpretation for KMT-2019-BLG-0414, the host star has a mass of $0.74^{+0.43}_{-0.38}~M_\odot$ and hosts a planet with a mass between $\sim 3.2$ and $3.6~M_{\rm J}$, depending on the specific solution. We also discuss how future adaptive-optics observations on 30-meter class telescopes might resolve the planet-xallarap degeneracy in KMT-2019-BLG-0414.

Through the analysis of data from $Gaia$ EDR3, SDSS/SEGUE DR16, and LAMOST DR8, we have identified 11 member stars belonging to the NGC 5466 tidal stream, seven of which are new discoveries. To eliminate contaminants, we applied stringent cuts based on sky position, color-magnitude diagrams, metallicity, proper motion, and radial velocity. Our findings were compared against a simulated stream created by modeling the cluster's disruption within a smooth Galactic potential, augmented by the influence of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The consistent phase-space trends between the model and observations suggest that the stream may have been perturbed by the LMC. Additionally, the two most distant detected members extend the known stream length to $60^\circ$ across the sky, thereby supporting and expanding upon the previously established $45^\circ$ length. Considering NGC 5466's considerable distance and the possibility of a longer tail than previously recognized, we anticipate that its tidal stream will serve as a valuable instrument for constraining the Milky Way's gravitational field.

Recent advancements in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) have leveraged domain-conditioned attention modules to achieve notable progress. However, since the specific type and placement of these attention mechanisms significantly influence performance, it is more effective to automatically optimize attention configurations tailored to arbitrary UDA scenarios. This paper introduces EvoADA, a novel framework designed to evolve attention configurations for specific UDA tasks without human input. The approach defines a new search space encompassing diverse attention setups. To assess these configurations and ensure the search process aligns with UDA objectives (balancing transferability and discrimination), the method employs a straightforward evaluation strategy: first, training network weights on source and target domains using standard domain adaptation techniques, and second, evolving attention configurations guided by the target domain's discriminative capability.
