Quantum systems present significant challenges when measuring operators and determining system states. In this Letter, we introduce a technique to determine the average value of a specific operator within a given state by observing the instantaneous variation in the average of another operator, utilizing a known reference state. We designate this approach as the instantaneous indirect measurement method. Through analysis of typical models, we demonstrate that this method enables the measurement of arbitrary quantum states. Notably, the process does not significantly alter the system's wave function or induce wave function collapse. Additionally, our research indicates that when two independent systems are coupled, information transfer occurs instantaneously. Finally, we explore the application of this method to quantify quantum Fisher information, which defines the precision limits for estimating parameters from quantum states.

This study introduces proLab, a novel colour coordinate system created through a 3D projective transformation of CIE XYZ. Our findings indicate that proLab significantly outperforms the commonly used CIELAB system (although it falls short of CAM16-UCS) regarding perceptual uniformity, as measured by the STRESS metric relative to the CIEDE2000 colour difference formula. Furthermore, angular errors in chromaticity estimation—typically associated with linear colour spaces—remain applicable in proLab because projective transformations maintain manifold linearity. Unlike in linear spaces, angular errors across different hues in proLab are normalized based on human colour discrimination thresholds. Additionally, we demonstrate that shot noise in proLab exhibits greater homoscedasticity compared to CAM16-UCS and other standard colour spaces, making proLab an ideal coordinate system for conducting linear colour analysis.

This paper presents a signal processing framework for networks that operates without explicit knowledge of the network topology. Instead, it leverages information regarding the distribution of operators across the network, rendering the approach flexible and effective even when precise graph topology data is missing. Furthermore, standard graph signal processing emerges as a specific instance of our framework when utilizing the delta distribution. The core components of this theoretical framework encompass the Fourier transform, filtering theory, and sampling theory.

This study investigates the critical behavior of the $3d$ $O(2)$ universality class within bounded domains by performing Monte Carlo simulations on the clock model. We employ an enhanced variant of this model featuring eight spin orientations and vacancies, specifically selected to reduce finite-size effects at the critical point. The simulations utilize a slab geometry with fixed boundary spins. Our findings yield the universal critical magnetization profile and two-point correlations, which align well with predictions derived from the critical geometry approach using the Yamabe equation. The primary conclusion is that, after removing dimensionful factors via the critical magnetization profile, the correlations depend exclusively on the inter-point distance defined by a metric obtained from solving the fractional Yamabe equation. We also present and discuss a quantitative comparison with critical Ising model results. Furthermore, the critical exponent $\eta$ is extracted from the magnetization profiles and agrees reasonably well with current state-of-the-art values.

Fluorescence microscopy is indispensable for investigating biological structures and dynamics; however, current systems face a compromise among field-of-view (FOV), resolution, and complexity, failing to meet the demand for miniaturized platforms capable of micron-scale resolution over centimeter-scale FOVs. To address this, we created the Computational Miniature Mesoscope (CM$^2$), a miniaturized system utilizing computational imaging for single-shot, 3D high-resolution imaging across wide FOVs. We now introduce CM$^2$ V2, which enhances both hardware and computational capabilities. By integrating a novel hybrid emission filter with the existing 3$\times$3 microlens array, we achieve a 5$\times$ improvement in imaging contrast, while a 3D-printed freeform collimator for the LED illuminator boosts excitation efficiency by 3$\times$. To facilitate high-resolution reconstruction within the large imaging volume, we developed an accurate and efficient 3D linear shift-variant (LSV) model to characterize spatially varying aberrations. A multi-module deep learning model, CM$^2$Net, was then trained exclusively using this 3D-LSV simulator. Our results demonstrate that CM$^2$Net generalizes effectively to experimental data, delivering accurate 3D reconstruction over a $\sim$7-mm FOV and 800-$\mu$m depth with $\sim$6-$\mu$m lateral and $\sim$25-$\mu$m axial resolution. Compared to the previous model-based algorithm, this approach offers approximately 8$\times$ better axial localization and is roughly 1400$\times$ faster. We anticipate that this simple, low-cost computational miniature imaging system will significantly impact numerous large-scale 3D fluorescence imaging applications.

This study demonstrates that integrating within-layer recurrent connections into feed-forward neural networks enhances neural response prediction in early visual regions by up to 11% across various datasets and tens of thousands of model configurations. To explain this superior performance, we hypothesize that recurrent computation functions as an ensemble of feed-forward pathways with varying lengths but shared parameters. By redefining recurrent models as multi-path architectures and analyzing them through this ensemble lens, we determined that recurrent models surpass their feed-forward counterparts because they utilize a compact, implicit multi-path ensemble. This structure efficiently approximates the complex functions inherent in recurrent biological circuits. Furthermore, we observed that performance variations among recurrent models strongly correlate with differences in their multi-path ensembles regarding path length and diversity, indicating that an optimal balance of paths with different lengths is essential for peak performance. Ultimately, our research illuminates the computational benefits and rationales of recurrent circuits for both neural modeling and broader machine learning applications.

We introduce an all-optical anti-waveguide approach for steering, splitting, and cloning optical beams that surpasses the diffraction limit. This method employs a spatially inhomogeneous pump beam to generate an anti-waveguide within a Doppler-broadened N-type four-level Raman gain medium, specifically for a co-propagating weak probe. Our findings indicate that a transverse modulation of the refractive index and gain, driven by the spatially varying pump, enables these beam manipulation techniques. Additionally, we demonstrate that an auxiliary control field allows an optical beam to propagate through a typically unstable gain medium without diffraction or instability. Finally, we explore how adjusting the detuning and intensity of the control field can enhance the finesse of the resulting cloned images.

The escalating complexity of deep neural network (DNN) architectures and the growing size of datasets have necessitated the development of strategies to minimize the time and memory demands of both training and inference. These optimizations are especially critical in resource-constrained training environments or time-sensitive inference applications. This survey offers a comprehensive overview and classification of current state-of-the-art methods for reducing the computational and spatial complexities of DNNs, with a specific emphasis on architectural adaptations.

This work introduces a fiber-diffraction interferometer designed for optical testing in uncontrolled environments, utilizing a coherent fiber optic taper. The system employs a coherent fiber optic taper alongside a single-mode fiber with a thermally expanded core. In this setup, a portion of the measurement wave from the test target is focused by the taper and spatially filtered through the single-mode fiber to generate the reference wave. Since vibrations affecting the cavity between the target and the probe impact both the reference and measurement waves equally, the interference fringes remain optically stabilized. Consequently, the reference wave generation remains stable despite target movement, while the coherent fiber optic taper renders the system insensitive to focus shifts in the input measurement wave.

Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) represent a category of modular, porous crystalline materials with significant promise for transforming fields including gas storage, molecular separation, chemical sensing, catalysis, and drug delivery. The Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) catalogs 10,636 synthesized MOF crystals alongside approximately 114,373 MOF-like structures. Given the vast quantity of existing and potentially synthesizable MOF architectures, researchers must employ computational strategies to effectively screen and identify promising candidates. This demonstration paper outlines our initiative to utilize knowledge graph methodologies to enhance MOF prediction, discovery, and synthesis. We detail the challenges and present case studies regarding (1) the assembly of a MOF knowledge graph (MOF-KG) derived from both structured and unstructured data sources, and (2) the application of this MOF-KG to uncover new or previously missing insights.

The collision terms within spin transport theory are examined using the Kadanoff-Baym formalism for systems near equilibrium. Non-equilibrium fluctuations in the spin distribution encompass both damping and polarization; the latter results from the exchange between orbital and spin angular momenta. Both the damping and polarization rates, or equivalently the relaxation times, are formulated in terms of various Dirac components of the self-energy. Contrary to the commonly employed Anderson-Witting relaxation time approximation, which assumes a uniform time scale across different degrees of freedom, the polarization effect is driven by thermal vorticity, resulting in a thermalization time scale that differs from that of damping. Numerical calculations performed within the Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model indicate that charge thermalizes before spin does.

Living and artificial active matter frequently interact with substrates within strongly confined environments, where quadrupolar active stresses become significant alongside dipolar ones. This study numerically examines how these non-equilibrium quadrupolar stresses influence self-organizing patterns in non-momentum conserving active nematics. Our findings indicate that beyond their stabilizing role, quadrupolar active forces can drive diverse modes of topological defect motion. Specifically, we observe the emergence of both polar and nematic defect ordering, along with novel self-organization phases characterized by topological defect chains and asters. These results deepen our understanding of collective motion patterns and non-equilibrium self-organization in active matter.

We calculate generating functions for elliptic genera valued in line bundles over Hilbert schemes of points on surfaces. Furthermore, as an application, we determine generating functions for elliptic genera valued in determinant line bundles on the moduli spaces of sheaves defined on K3 surfaces.

This paper examines the quasi-stationary dynamics of absorbed one-dimensional diffusions. It establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the exponential convergence to a unique quasi-stationary distribution in total variation, holding uniformly across all initial distributions. A key instrument in this analysis involves one-dimensional strict local martingale diffusions that descend from infinity. Under mild assumptions, we demonstrate that the expectation at any positive time remains uniformly bounded relative to the starting position. The study includes various examples and extensions, covering sticky Brownian motion as well as certain one-dimensional processes characterized by jumps.

In measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC), operations are executed through a series of measurements and corrections applied to an entangled state. Flow and associated concepts serve as potent tools for analyzing how corrections depend on prior measurement outcomes. We present flow-based approaches for continuous-variable (CV) graph state MBQC, termed CV-flow. These methods draw inspiration from, yet differ from, the concepts of causal flow and g-flow used in qubit MBQC. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an MBQC utilizing CV-flow can approximate any unitary operation with arbitrary precision in the infinite-squeezing limit, thereby resolving convergence challenges inherent to infinite-dimensional systems. Our proofs introduce a technique to transform CV-MBQC computations into circuit form, mirroring the extraction method proposed by Miyazaki et al., alongside an efficient algorithm for identifying CV-flow when it exists, adapted from the qubit-based approach by Mhalla and Perdrix. Finally, our findings and methodologies readily generalize to MBQC scenarios involving qudits with prime local dimensions.

We demonstrate that eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator defined on the half-line with a square-summable potential are Ces\`aro bounded. This result relies on the theory of Krein systems, specifically utilizing a continuous adaptation of a theorem established in 1991 by A. Mate, P. Nevai, and V. Totik.

The study investigates the physics of molecular-scale mixing within light-heavy element mixtures, a phenomenon critical to inertial confinement fusion and planetary science, by validating equation of state (EOS) properties. Thermodynamic state characteristics for pure xenon, ethane, and several compressed mixture ratios were derived via density functional theory molecular dynamics (DFT-MD) simulations under high temperature and pressure conditions, specifically along their principal Hugoniots. To verify these computational results, shock compression experiments were conducted using the Sandia Z-Machine. A bond tracking analysis revealed that the abrupt increase in the Hugoniot curve corresponds to the completion of ethane dissociation. The DFT-based simulation outcomes align closely with experimental data along the principal Hugoniots, offering valuable insights into dissociation processes and temperature variations relative to mixture composition along these curves.

Recent investigations have extensively explored theories extending the standard model that introduce a sub-GeV vector mediator, $Z_d$, to account for experimental anomalies in the magnetic moments of muons and electrons. Driven by Fermilab's recent measurement of the anomalous muon magnetic moment, this study derives constraints on such models based on magnetic moment data alongside low-energy transfer measurements of the weak charge, $Q_W$, for protons and cesium. To achieve this, we re-examine the determination of cesium's $Q_W$ from atomic parity violation experiments, which heavily relies on the average neutron root-mean-square (rms) radius of $^{133}\text{Cs}$. We establish this radius through a nearly model-independent extrapolation from the recent average neutron rms radius of $^{208}\text{Pb}$ reported by the PREX-2 Collaboration. By performing a combined fit of all relevant experimental results, we establish precise limits on the $Z_d$ boson's mass and kinetic mixing parameter ($\varepsilon$), finding $m_{Z_d} = 47{}^{+61}_{-16} \, \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\varepsilon = 2.3{}^{+1.1}_{-0.4} \times 10^{-3}$ after marginalizing over the $Z-Z_d$ mass mixing parameter $\delta$.

This study employs the first Born approximation to conduct a semirelativistic theoretical analysis of the inelastic excitation ($1s_{1/2}\longrightarrow 2s_{1/2}$) of a hydrogen atom via electron impact. Within this framework, incident and scattered electrons are modeled using free Dirac spinors, while the hydrogen target is represented by the Darwin wave function. The investigation thoroughly examines relativistic and spin effects across the relativistic regime, with particular attention given to both the nonrelativistic and moderate relativistic regimes. Furthermore, the work explores the dependence of these factors and the dynamic behavior of the differential cross-section (DCS) within the relativistic domain.

Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are extensively utilized in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era with the potential to achieve quantum advantage; however, their training is hindered by challenges such as barren plateaus (BPs), a phenomenon where cost function gradients vanish exponentially as qubit count increases. Drawing inspiration from transfer learning, where solutions to pre-solved tasks enhance efficiency in related problems, this paper introduces a parameter initialization strategy to alleviate BPs. This approach involves solving a small-scale task using a VQA, then transferring the resulting ansatz and optimal parameters to larger-scale tasks. Numerical simulations confirm that this method effectively mitigates BPs and boosts training efficiency. Additionally, a brief analysis explains the underlying mechanisms of this approach. By offering a viable reference for BP mitigation, this work facilitates the application of VQAs to a broader range of practical problems.

We examine whether a specific class of models representing F-theory compactifications supports a particular type of flux vacuum characterized by an exponentially small superpotential vacuum expectation value, by extending a technique recently introduced for Type IIB flux compactifications. Initially, we demonstrate that limiting the selection of $G_4$-flux components simplifies the general flux superpotential, thereby facilitating supersymmetric vacua with a single flat direction at the perturbative level. Subsequently, we apply mirror symmetry techniques to calculate one-instanton corrections to the potential and conduct a detailed analysis of the vacuum solutions within a specific model.

Recent discoveries in cuprate superconductors and related materials include unconventional symmetry breaking without spin order, such as rotational symmetry breaking (nematic or smectic phases) and spontaneous loop-current orders. These phenomena are theoretically described by non-$A_{1g}$ symmetry breaking in the self-energy, denoted as the form factor $f_{k,q}$. In this study, we apply the renormalization-group (RG) method to typical Hubbard models and demonstrate that diverse unconventional ordering arises from quantum interference among spin fluctuations. Consequently, both nematic ($q=0$) and smectic ($q \ne 0$) bond orders featuring a $d$-wave form factor ($f_{k,q}\propto \cos k_x - \cos k_y$) emerge in both cuprates and $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$X. These derived bond orders provide a natural explanation for the observed pseudogap behaviors in these compounds. Furthermore, this quantum interference mechanism induces various current orders with odd-parity form factors; specifically, we identify the appearance of charge and spin loop-current orders with $p$-wave form factors in geometrically frustrated Hubbard models. Ultimately, rich quantum phase transitions characterized by $d$- and $p$-wave form factors are driven by paramagnon interference across many low-dimensional Hubbard models.

We present a complete theoretical framework for conducting in-sample statistical inference regarding ROC curves derived from predicted values of a first-stage model with estimated parameters, such as logit regression. The designation "in-sample" denotes the utilization of identical data for both model training (estimation) and the subsequent evaluation phase, specifically the construction of the ROC curve. Our findings demonstrate that estimation error from the first stage exerts a generally non-negligible influence on the asymptotic distribution of the ROC curve, prompting the development of corresponding pointwise and functional limit theories. Furthermore, we introduce techniques for simulating the distribution of the resulting limit process and illustrate their practical application in comparing ROC curves.

Suspension of non-isothermal particles within a fluid generates intricate dynamics, as the particles react to fluid currents while simultaneously altering those flows through their thermal anomalies. This study presents a new numerical proof-of-concept using tracer particles thermally coupled to the surrounding fluid. These particles are modeled to adjust their internal temperatures based on local fluid conditions while adhering to straightforward, pre-programmed active control strategies. Specifically, we investigate a scenario where particle temperatures switch between hot and cold states contingent on whether the particle is rising or falling. Depending on the count of active particles and their specific excess positive or negative temperatures, the system undergoes a macroscopic shift from stable to unstable convective flow. The stable regime is defined by low turbulent kinetic energy, a robust temperature gradient, and an absence of large-scale structures. In contrast, the convective regime exhibits elevated turbulent kinetic energy, self-sustaining large-scale convection, and a weakly stable temperature gradient. While individual particles contribute to maintaining stable temperature gradients, their collective influence drives large-scale convection. When the Lagrangian temperature scale is small, the system evolves into a weakly convective laminar state. Furthermore, this Lagrangian method was compared against uniform Eulerian bulk heating with an identical mean injection profile, yet no such transition occurred in the latter. Our empirical findings demonstrate that thermal convection can be regulated via pure Lagrangian forcing, paving the way for additional data-driven, particle-based protocols to either amplify or suppress large-scale motion in thermal flows.

This study examines the spectral characteristics of a bounded self-adjoint operator defined on $L_2(\mathds R^d)$, which consists of a convolution operator with an integrable kernel combined with a multiplication operator by a continuous potential that vanishes at infinity. The analysis covers both the essential and discrete spectra. It is demonstrated that the essential spectrum of the sum comprises the union of the convolution operator's essential spectrum and the range of the potential. Furthermore, the paper establishes several sufficient conditions for the presence of discrete spectrum and derives both lower and upper bounds for the count of discrete eigenvalues. Particular emphasis is placed on operators with a countable set of discrete spectral points, and the results are contrasted with those of classical Schrödinger operators.

Parameter-efficient tuning seeks to distill knowledge for downstream tasks by optimizing a limited set of introduced parameters while keeping pretrained language models (PLMs) frozen. Among these techniques, continuous prompt tuning, which prepends trainable vectors to input embeddings, has garnered significant attention for its efficiency and effectiveness. These methods function by applying nonlinear transformations to hidden states within PLMs. However, a fundamental question remains unaddressed: can hidden states be utilized directly for classification without modification? This paper proposes a straightforward tuning approach using only three trainable vectors to address this inquiry. The method integrates hidden states from all layers via these vectors and then feeds the resulting integrated states to a task-specific linear classifier for category prediction. While this approach resembles how ELMo utilizes hidden states (though ELMo feeds them into LSTM-based models), our method achieves performance comparable to advanced prompt tuning techniques like P-tuning and P-tuning v2. This success confirms that original hidden states inherently contain valuable information for classification. Furthermore, our approach offers advantages over prompt tuning regarding both computational time and parameter count.

Semiflexible or stiff polymers, including most biopolymers, exhibit inhomogeneous deformation under shear, with non-affine effects significantly more pronounced than in flexible polymer systems. Currently, understanding of non-affinity in these networks is restricted to simulations or specific two-dimensional models of athermal fibers. We introduce a general effective medium theory (EMT) for non-affine deformation applicable to semiflexible polymer networks across both 2D and 3D dimensions, as well as in thermal and athermal regimes. Our model's predictions align well with previous computational and experimental findings regarding linear elasticity. Furthermore, this framework is extensible to investigate nonlinear elasticity and network dynamics.

We present Proof-of-Steak (PoS), a foundational net-zero block generation method typically paired with Non-Frangipane Tokens. By gradually heating and minting the Genesis cut with the proper sauce, miners can channel extracted gold and dissipated heat back into the furnace, establishing the first fully circular economy powered by blockchain technology that utilizes tamper-evident steak hachée. This paper outlines the essential components for constructing Proof-of-Steak, evaluates its worldwide impact, and explores potential opportunities to save the world and beyond.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the fluctuation theory of continuous-time skip-free Markov chains, building upon Choi and Patie's recent findings for their discrete-time counterparts. Our primary application involves deriving a comprehensive collection of fluctuation identities concerning the exit times from finite or infinite intervals for Markov branching processes with immigration, which yields numerous new insights into this well-established class of continuous-time Markov chains. Additionally, the proposed framework enables a straightforward recovery of fluctuation identities for skip-free downward compound Poisson processes.

Research into countering physical adversarial attacks within deep learning and computer vision is expanding quickly. Although prominent physical attacks, such as adversarial patches and objects, share traits with digital counterparts, they are often easily detectable by humans. This observation suggests that detection methods previously deemed ineffective against adaptive digital adversarial examples might still work against physical attacks. We tested this hypothesis using an autoencoder-based detector on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10 datasets against both CNN and two CapsNet architectures. Additionally, we introduced two enhancements to the EM-Routed CapsNet architecture—Affine Voting and Matrix Capsule Dropout—to boost classification accuracy. Our findings indicate that the detector maintains partial effectiveness even when facing adaptive adversarial patches. However, detection performance generally declines across all architectures as dataset complexity increases.

Consider a CW-complex $X$ that is 2-connected and 6-dimensional, with the condition that $H_{3}(X)\otimes\Z_2=0$. This work seeks to characterize the quotient group $\E(X)/\E_{*}(X)$, where $\E(X)$ represents the self-homotopy equivalences of $X$ and $\E_{*}(X)$ is the normal subgroup of equivalences inducing the identity on homology. By utilizing the Whitehead exact sequence for $X$, denoted as WES$(X)$, we introduce the group $\Gamma\mathcal{S}(X)$ consisting of $\Gamma$-automorphisms of this sequence. We subsequently establish the isomorphism $\E(X)/\E_*(X)\cong \Gamma\mathcal{S}(X)$.

Recent research has increasingly focused on robotic weed control for its potential to enhance agricultural productivity. However, while most efforts target croplands, the specific challenges of weed management in rangelands for stock farmers have been largely overlooked. A primary barrier to the widespread adoption of robotic weed control is the ability to robustly classify weed species within natural environments. Given the exceptional success of deep learning in such tasks, it is well-suited for identifying diverse weeds in complex rangeland settings. This study introduces the first large-scale, public, multiclass image dataset of weed species from Australian rangelands, providing a foundation for developing reliable classification methods essential for viable robotic weed control. The DeepWeeds dataset comprises 17,509 labeled images of eight nationally significant weed species collected from eight locations across northern Australia. This paper establishes a baseline for classification performance using benchmark deep learning models, Inception-v3 and ResNet-50, which achieved average accuracies of 95.1% and 95.7%, respectively. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the real-time capabilities of the ResNet-50 architecture, recording an average inference time of 53.4 ms per image. These promising results indicate a favorable outlook for the future deployment of robotic weed control systems in Australian rangelands.

This study seeks to illustrate the utility of mathematical models in cybersecurity policy discussions by analyzing phishing, vulnerability discovery, and the interplay between patching and exploitation. We modify these models' parameters to reflect potential technological advancements. Our findings suggest that while AI's influence on phishing might be exaggerated, it could result in increased undetected attacks. Furthermore, improvements in vulnerability discovery may benefit attackers more than defenders. Additionally, automated exploit generation offers greater utility to adversaries than automated patch writing, though faster patch deployment capabilities hold the most significant potential impact.

Utilizing the Liouville-von Neumann equation, we derive a closed set of equations describing a single qutrit or coupled qutrits under an arbitrary time-dependent external magnetic field. The analytical and numerical study examines how dynamics depend on initial states and magnetic field modulation. We compare the evolution of relative entanglement in a bi-qutrit system possessing permutation particle symmetry. Specifically, we identify magnetic field modulation strategies that preserve entanglement within a system of two coupled qutrits. Furthermore, we present analytical formulas for entanglement measures in chains ranging from two to six qutrits.

We examine two parametric families of special functions: the first is a power series that extends the classical Mathieu series, and the second is a generalized Mathieu-type power series where factorials appear in the coefficients. Applying criteria established by Fejer and Ozaki, we establish sufficient conditions for these functions to be close-to-convex or starlike within the unit disk, thereby ensuring they are univalent.

We introduce a precisely engineered sequence of two Gaussian pulses designed to achieve flawless population transfer via Stimulated Raman Adiabatic Passage (STIRAP). Our theoretical investigation examines the ideal timing and positioning of the Stokes and pump pulses, as well as determining the necessary power and duration for a specified pulse width. Notably, the time required to reach a target fidelity scales only logarithmically with the infidelity. Under conditions of optimal pulse truncation and referencing the point of maximum transfer speed, we derive a novel adiabaticity criterion that is both strikingly simple and highly effective.

`gym-saturation` is a Python-based OpenAI Gym environment designed for reinforcement learning agents to tackle theorem proving. It currently supports theorems expressed in the TPTP library's formal language, specifically in clausal normal form (CNF). The environment implements the 'given clause' algorithm, which mirrors methods used by provers like Vampire and E. Drawing inspiration from PyRes, `gym-saturation` diverges from the monolithic design of standard Automated Theorem Provers (ATPs) by allowing agents to independently select clauses and learn from their experiences. When paired with a specific agent, the system functions as an ATP; notably, even an untrained agent relying on heuristics can successfully refute 688 out of 8,257 CNF problems from TPTP v7.5.0.

The spectrum of a finite group consists of the orders of its elements. We demonstrate that for any $m>5$, the group $L_{2^m}(2)\times L_{2^m}(2)\times L_{2^m}(2)$ is uniquely characterized by its spectrum within the class of all finite groups.

We present evidence for a holographic correspondence linking superconformal quantum mechanics defined on the moduli space of Yang-Mills instantons to M-theory within specific asymptotically $AdS_{7}\times S^{4}$ backgrounds featuring a plane-wave boundary metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the gravitational background supports a supersymmetric black hole solution, the entropy of which is exactly matched by the superconformal index of the dual quantum mechanical theory.

Classical double-mode pulsators, including RR Lyrae stars and delta Cepheids, are crucial because they oscillate simultaneously in low-order radial modes, allowing for strict constraints on their physical properties. This study utilizes 30 luminous galactic double-mode RR Lyrae (RRd) stars to calculate their luminosities and compare them with values derived from the parallaxes in the recent Gaia EDR3 data release. By combining pulsation and evolutionary models with observationally determined effective temperatures, we derived the fundamental stellar parameters. After removing six outliers, likely due to blending issues, a strong correlation was found between RRd and Gaia luminosities. Adopting a temperature zero point from infrared flux method studies, we determined that increasing Gaia parallaxes by 0.02 mas is necessary to align the luminosities; this adjustment aligns with findings from binary star studies involving Gaia. Additionally, we analyzed the resulting period-luminosity-metallicity (PLZ) relation in the 2MASS K band based on RRd parameters, which confirmed two independently derived PLZ relations without significant zero-point discrepancies. Furthermore, the predicted K-band absolute magnitudes agreed within a range of $\sigma=0.005-0.01$ mag.

This study investigates the aging transition within a network of globally coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators subjected to discrete, time-dependent coupling. In this framework, inter-oscillator connections are systematically switched ON and OFF, utilizing either symmetric or asymmetric time intervals. Our findings reveal that the aging region contracts significantly within the parameter space as a function of the ON-OFF period and duty cycle, thereby facilitating the recovery of oscillatory dynamics from an aging state. Specifically, under symmetric discrete coupling (where ON and OFF durations are equal), the aging zone diminishes substantially as the period of these intervals increases. Conversely, with asymmetric coupling (unequal ON and OFF durations), the aging dynamics are governed by the ratio of these intervals; notably, the aging state is reversed more effectively when the OFF interval exceeds the ON interval. Furthermore, we examined the aging transition via discrete pulse coupling, highlighting the critical influence of the pulse interval on the aging region. Across all discrete time-dependent coupling scenarios, the aging regions shrink while rhythmicity is enhanced in a controlled fashion. These results indicate that such coupling mechanisms offer a noninvasive approach to restoring oscillatory dynamics in networks of coupled oscillators that have entered an aging state.

We demonstrate a dual formulation for conformal blocks within $d=2$ rational conformal field theories (CFTs), utilizing Hecke eigenfields and eigensheaves. Specifically, partition functions, conformal characters, and lattice theta functions can be derived from the action of Hecke operators. This approach extends to: 1) rings of integers in Galois number fields under trace or anti-trace forms; 2) root lattices associated with affine Kac-Moody algebras and WZW-models; 3) Belavin-Polyakov-Zamolodchikov minimal models and related $d=2$ spin-chain/lattice systems; and 4) vertex algebras linked to Leech and Niemeier lattices, among others. Furthermore, leveraging Witten's original concept, we construct 3-dimensional quantum gravity as the AdS/CFT dual of the $c=24$ Monster vertex algebra by Frenkel, Lepowsky, and Meurman. Regarding geometric Langlands duality, our work draws upon findings by Beilinson-Drinfeld, Frenkel-Ben-Zvi, Gukov-Kapustin-Witten, and others (see references).

The spin Hall effect of light (SHEL), characterized by a spin-dependent transverse displacement of light at optical boundaries, is inherently sensitive to the polarization of the incident beam. While a recent method aimed at removing this polarization dependence by balancing reflection coefficients for two linear polarizations was proposed, it is restricted to scenarios where the beam waist significantly exceeds the wavelength. In this study, we demonstrate that an interface where both the reflection coefficients of the two linear polarizations and their derivatives with respect to the incident angle are identical supports a polarization-independent SHEL, even when the beam waist is comparable to the wavelength. Furthermore, we introduce an isotropic-anisotropic interface that maintains this polarization-independent SHEL across the full spectrum of incident angles. Monte-Carlo simulations confirm that spin Hall shifts remain degenerate regardless of polarization and reach half the beam waist under unpolarized incidence. We propose utilizing this beam-waist-scale SHEL as a tunable beam-splitting device responsive to incident polarization. Additionally, a spin Hall shift that remains independent of incident polarization at all angles will enable diverse applications, ranging from practical spin-dependent components to active beam splitters.

The discontinuous Galerkin (DG) finite element method offers high-order accuracy through its alignment with quadrature and orthogonal polynomial theories, while also being conservative and well-suited for parallel computing. When utilizing an orthogonal discretization, such as a rectilinear grid, the DG method can be efficiently ported to GPUs using concise high-level code like Python. This study presents such an implementation by formulating the DG semi-discrete equation in tensor-product form and leveraging open-source GPU libraries for computation. The approach is validated through a plasma physics simulation of an instability within the magnetized Vlasov-Poisson system. Furthermore, given DG's intrinsic link to spectral methods via orthogonal bases, a transformation to a distinct set of global eigenfunctions can be computed for analytical purposes or additional operations; this transformation is also structured as a tensor product to enable GPU acceleration. As an example, a Fourier series is calculated (though not surpassing the discrete Fourier transform) to resolve the Poisson component of the Vlasov-Poisson system with $\mathcal{O}(\Delta x^{n+1/2})$ accuracy.

This study investigates the applicability of neural network classifiers for real-time detection of field-potential biomarkers within next-generation responsive neuromodulation systems. Unlike traditional filter-based approaches, neural networks facilitate easier patient-specific tuning, potentially alleviating the programming workload for clinicians. Specifically, the research examines a compact feed-forward architecture comprising merely dozens of units designed to classify seizure states in refractory epilepsy. While maintaining accuracy comparable to filter classifiers on clinician-annotated data, the proposed method significantly lowers detection latency. To address the computational limitations inherent in implantable pulse generators, the study prioritizes minimizing architectural complexity, trading off the features of classical methods for greater efficiency.

Although the Machine Learning (ML) field is advancing quickly, the development of "learning systems" required for widespread adoption has lagged behind, with few systems catering to the specialized needs of scientific ML. This paper introduces the Data and Learning Hub for science (DLHub), a multi-tenant platform focused on scientific applications that offers both a model repository and serving capabilities. DLHub tackles two major gaps in existing systems. First, its self-service repository enables users to share, publish, verify, reproduce, and reuse models; it ensures reproducibility by packaging and distributing models along with all their constituent components. Second, it provides scalable, low-latency serving features that utilize parallel and distributed computing resources to democratize access to published models via an intuitive web interface. Unlike other frameworks, DLHub can store and serve any Python 3-compatible model, processing function, or multi-function pipeline. Comparisons with systems like TensorFlow Serving, SageMaker, and Clipper reveal that DLHub offers superior capabilities, comparable performance without memoization or batching, and significantly improved performance when these techniques are applied. The text also outlines early scientific applications of DLHub.

Protecting privacy and security is critical when transmitting speech signals to cloud-based services like Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Speech Emotion Recognition (SER). Current speech anonymization methods primarily rely on voice conversion or modification to alter identity information while retaining content. However, sharing speech data through privacy-preserving representations remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces a novel anonymization framework that ensures privacy by applying noise perturbation to a specific subset of high-utility representations derived from a pre-trained speech encoder. This subset is identified using a Transformer-based privacy-risk saliency estimator. We evaluate the framework across four tasks: Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV), ASR, SER, and Intent Classification (IC) to assess both privacy and utility. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves utility comparable to or superior to baselines from the VoicePrivacy2022 Challenges while maintaining equivalent privacy levels. Furthermore, the framework's easily adjustable perturbation level enables a flexible privacy-utility trade-off without requiring any re-training.

Optical turbulence significantly impacts the quality of astronomical observations conducted from the ground. Accurate and reliable turbulence forecasts are essential for optimizing observation schedules, thereby enhancing data quality and scientific productivity at observatories. However, generating forecasts precise enough to support the operations of large observatories remains a notoriously challenging task. Various strategies have been explored, ranging from detailed physical atmospheric modeling to empirical, data-driven methods. This work introduces an empirical approach that leverages spatial diversity through simultaneous measurements at two nearby locations in Chile: Cerro Paranal, home to the Very Large Telescope (VLT), and Cerro Armazones, the future site of the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). The study focuses on the correlation between high-altitude turbulence as detected at these two sites. This research contributes to ongoing efforts by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) to develop short-term turbulence forecasts that will streamline VLT operations and prepare for the ELT's operational mode.

Many methods investigate network susceptibility to social contagion, with graph burning specifically examining the speed at which a contagion, represented as fire, propagates through a graph. This process occurs in synchronous, discrete rounds where a fire ignites at a chosen vertex and spreads to all adjacent burning vertices in each step. The sequence of ignition vertices constitutes a schedule determining the total rounds needed to burn the entire graph. The goal for an algorithm is to identify a schedule that minimizes these rounds; however, finding the optimal schedule is NP-hard, even for trees or disjoint paths. Currently, the only existing solution is an approximation algorithm for disjoint paths with a ratio of 1.5.

Recent advancements in encoder-decoder neural network architectures have substantially enhanced performance across diverse medical image segmentation tasks. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art models for specific tasks can be computationally intensive, often requiring affordable hardware users to adopt practical modifications such as input image downsampling or reducing network depth to satisfy memory limitations. This study examines the impact of these adjustments on segmentation outcomes and demonstrates that image complexity serves as an effective criterion for selecting optimal configurations. We evaluated four statistical metrics to quantify image complexity across ten public datasets. Additionally, we introduced two novel encoder-decoder architectures designed to be more memory-efficient, representing shallow and deep network variants. Our findings indicate that median frequency is the superior metric for determining appropriate input downsampling factors and network depth. Specifically, for high-complexity datasets, a shallow network processing original-resolution images may outperform a deep network using downsampled inputs, while the reverse holds true for low-complexity images.

We present Object-Guided Localization (OGuL), which utilizes an innovative local-feature matching technique. While direct local feature matching struggles with drastic illumination shifts, object detection remains robust under severe lighting variations. Our approach begins by detecting semantic objects and establishing their correspondences across images, which yields a planar homography for coarse local alignment. These homographies subsequently guide the matching of local features. Experiments conducted on standard urban localization datasets (Aachen, Extended-CMU-Season, and RobotCar-Season) demonstrate that OGuL significantly enhances localization accuracy using simple features like SIFT, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art CNN-based methods trained specifically for day-to-night scenarios.

We present an extension of L\^e's stochastic sewing lemma [Electron. J. Probab. 25: 1 - 55, 2020]. The original lemma establishes $L_m$ convergence for Riemann-type sums $\sum_{[s,t] \in \pi} A_{s,t}$ associated with an adapted two-parameter stochastic process $A$, contingent upon specific moment conditions for $A_{s,t}$ and their conditional expectations given $\mathcal{F}_s$. Our extension substitutes the conditioning on $\mathcal{F}_s$ with conditioning on $\mathcal{F}_v$ where $v < s$. Furthermore, it incorporates a singularity in $(s-v)$ to exploit asymptotic decorrelation between $A_{s,t}$ and $\mathcal{F}_v$. We demonstrate three applications where L\^e's original lemma appears inadequate. First, we prove the convergence of It\^o or Stratonovich approximations for stochastic integrals driven by fractional Brownian motion under low regularity conditions. Second, we derive novel representations of local times for fractional Brownian motion through discretization. Third, we strengthen a regularity requirement on the diffusion coefficient of a stochastic differential equation driven by fractional Brownian motion to ensure pathwise uniqueness and strong existence.

Typically, a thin disk with a crease exhibits bistability because the crease can be forced through to create a stable, cone-like inverted state featuring an elastic singularity at the cone's vertex. In our recent research, we discovered that this bistability can be eliminated by removing the singularity via a hole cut around the vertex, with the outcome dependent on the hole's dimensions and shape. This paper builds upon that work, analyzing tabletop models of creased disks with circular holes through three key observations: (i) excising an annular sector to reduce the disk's circumference allows the hole to expand to the size of the entire disk while maintaining bistability; (ii) a single crease permits a circular hole as large as the disk itself without compromising bistability; and (iii) a spectrum of stable inverted states can be achieved by inverting the disk at nearly any point along the crease. To investigate these phenomena, we employ an inextensible strip model. We formulate the minimal facet of the creased disk as a two-point boundary value problem, treating creases as nonlinear hinges, and utilize numerical continuation for parametric analysis. Our focus lies on geometric parameters such as the angle deficit (dictating disk circumference), the rest crease angle, the count of evenly spaced creases, and an eccentricity defining the hole's position relative to the crease. Our numerical findings validate the qualitative observations in points (i) through (iii) and uncover unexpected outcomes arising from the coupling of these geometric parameters. Ultimately, our results show that varying the geometry of a simply creased disk yields surprisingly rich nonlinear behaviors, offering new insights into the mechanics and design of origami, kirigami, and morphable structures.

Recent studies have demonstrated significant performance in 3D shape segmentation using supervised learning approaches across various benchmark datasets. However, these supervised techniques rely heavily on extensive annotated data to train deep neural networks, which is necessary to ensure robust generalization on unseen test sets. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a meta-learning framework designed for few-shot 3D shape segmentation, enabling effective segmentation with only a limited number of labeled samples for unseen classes. We conceptualize shape segmentation as a point labeling task within a metric space. First, we develop a meta-metric learner that maps input shapes into an embedding space, allowing the model to learn a tailored metric space for each object class based on these embeddings. Subsequently, for every class, a dedicated metric learner extracts prototype representations specific to parts from a small set of support shapes. Segmentation of query shapes is then performed by assigning each point to its nearest prototype within the learned metric space. A metric-based loss function dynamically adjusts distances between point embeddings to enhance intra-part similarity while reducing inter-part similarity. Furthermore, a dual segmentation branch leverages support information fully and implicitly promotes consistency between support and query prototypes. Experimental results on the ShapeNet part dataset under few-shot conditions demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms established baselines and state-of-the-art semi-supervised techniques.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have attracted significant attention due to their ability to produce high-fidelity images from text prompts alone. However, achieving superior results typically cannot be accomplished in a single attempt. Instead, text-guided image generation usually requires users to make numerous minor adjustments to inputs iteratively to refine the desired image. Unfortunately, small modifications to the prompt often result in drastically different outputs, thereby limiting the artist's ability to exercise precise control. To address this need for flexibility, we introduce Stable Artist, an image editing framework that facilitates fine-grained manipulation of the generation process. Its core component, semantic guidance (SEGA), directs the diffusion process along varying numbers of semantic vectors. This mechanism enables subtle image edits, alterations in composition and style, and the optimization of overall artistic intent. Moreover, SEGA allows for the exploration of latent spaces to better understand how the model represents concepts, including intricate ones like "carbon emission." We validate Stable Artist across multiple tasks, demonstrating its capability for high-quality image editing and composition.

The low-energy band structure of few-layer MoS$_2$ is critical for diverse experiments spanning optics to electronic transport, yet its characterization is complicated by complex multi-band behavior. We examine the conduction band of dual-gated three-layer MoS$_2$ using magnetotransport experiments, where the total carrier density is controlled by voltages applied to both top and bottom gate electrodes. Under asymmetric biasing, electrons accumulate in the layer nearest the positively biased electrode, allowing the three-layer system to mimic the electronic properties of a monolayer. Conversely, applying a positive voltage to both gates results in the occupation of all three layers. By analyzing Shubnikov–de Haas oscillations from distinct bands, we assign carrier densities to the top and bottom layers. Our findings reveal a twofold Landau level degeneracy for each band, indicating that conduction band minima reside at the $\pm K$ points of the first Brillouin zone, which contradicts zero-layer-asymmetry calculations predicting minima at the $Q$ points. Although interlayer tunnel coupling appears to leave the low-energy conduction band unchanged, we detect electron scattering between the outermost layers when layer asymmetry is zero. The middle layer stays decoupled because spin-valley symmetry is inverted in adjacent layers. However, when the bands of the outermost layers achieve energetic resonance, interlayer scattering occurs, causing increased resistance and magneto-interband oscillations.

Nonlinear terahertz (THz) spectroscopy involves the interaction of matter with few-cycle THz pulses possessing electric field strengths reaching megavolts per centimeter (MV/cm). Within condensed-phase molecular systems, both resonant interactions with low-frequency elementary excitations, such as intra- and intermolecular vibrations, and nonresonant field-driven processes play significant roles. Two-dimensional THz (2D-THz) spectroscopy serves as a pivotal technique for tracking the dynamics and nonequilibrium behavior of excitations to elucidate fundamental interactions and molecular couplings. This article reviews the current state of 2D-THz spectroscopy by outlining core concepts and supporting them with recent findings. These findings encompass the response of vibrational excitations in molecular crystals under nonperturbative light-matter interaction regimes, as well as field-driven ionization and electron transport phenomena in liquid water.

Heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) and a singlet scalar $s$ that mixes with the Higgs boson represent appealing minimal extensions of the Standard Model. When both exist, it is natural for HNLs to couple with $s$. For a light singlet, the decay channel $N\to s\nu$ may become dominant compared to standard weak HNL decays. We reinterpret current limits on HNL mixing derived from DELPHI, CHARM, and Belle experiments for HNL masses ranging from 0.5 to 100 GeV, incorporating this new decay mode. While constraints are often relaxed, they can also tighten in specific scenarios due to detectable $s\to\ell^+\ell^-$ signatures. This approach allows for recasting limits from other historical experiments without relying on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, we correct and update certain inaccuracies in the original analysis that excluded the singlet.

This work examines quasilinear reaction-diffusion systems based on the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto model, where the external force is represented by a nonlinearity that induces mass dissipation. Bounds for the solution across multiple norms are established, contingent upon constraints regarding diffusion coefficients, the reaction's growth rate, and the spatial dimension.

Commonsense Question Answering (CQA) evaluates a model's ability to address inquiries based on universal commonsense knowledge. Although previous studies integrating external knowledge bases have yielded promising outcomes, these databases are costly to build and typically restricted to specific relations. This paper shifts focus toward more effectively leveraging the \textit{implicit knowledge} inherent in pre-trained language models. While prior research demonstrates that such embedded knowledge can be extracted via carefully crafted prompts for tasks like relation extraction and text classification, it is uncertain whether this approach translates to CQA, where inputs and outputs vary significantly in flexibility. To address this, we explore four translation techniques that convert natural language questions into cloze-style sentences to elicit commonsense knowledge from models, comprising a syntactic-based approach, an unsupervised neural model, and two supervised neural models. Furthermore, we propose a method to enhance consistency across predictions generated by different translation strategies using unlabeled data. Our approach proves effective across three CQA datasets in zero-shot scenarios. We demonstrate that our methods complement knowledge-base-enhanced models, with their combination achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance. Additionally, our analysis highlights the unique characteristics of each cloze translation method and offers insights into why integrating them yields substantial improvements.

We examine the Abdesselam-Rivasseau (AR) model, which transforms the Jacobian Conjecture (JC) into a challenge within perturbative quantum field theory. In this framework, the inverse map of the JC is expressed as a formal integral that generates the tree expansion for the map. By assigning a specific color to the single outgoing edge at each vertex of the AR model, we execute selective Gaussian integration and demonstrate the termination of the tree series for the inverse map. This termination confirms the validity of the JC.

We recently introduced a Varying Speed of Light (VSL) framework to address several late-time cosmological issues \cite{Lee:2020zts}. This model utilizes a single free parameter, $b$, to describe how the speed of light evolves with the scale factor according to the relation $c = c_0a^{b/4}$. To maintain consistency with established local physics—specifically special relativity, thermodynamics, and electromagnetic interactions—various physical constants and quantities exhibit scale factor dependencies determined by powers of $b$. Built upon the Robertson-Walker metric, the model adheres to the cosmological principle's requirements for an isotropic and homogeneous three-dimensional space. Adiabaticity is essential for preserving this homogeneity and isotropy; a net energy flux could disrupt isotropy by introducing a preferred direction or compromise homogeneity if the flux is isotropic yet directed outward or inward. Consequently, a viable VSL model must satisfy an adiabatic expansion condition. Furthermore, this requirement offers an additional constraint for determining physical constants.

Millimeter-wave wireless communication has gained significant interest for enabling high-speed connectivity for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). However, acquiring the necessary channel measurements at these frequencies remains difficult due to the strict power and payload limitations inherent in commercial UAVs. This study introduces a new, lightweight (about 1.3 kg) 28 GHz channel measurement system mounted on an off-the-shelf UAV. The setup consists of a ground station using a horn antenna to transmit sounding signals to a UAV fitted with a compact spectrum analyzer. Results indicate that the UAV's frame significantly distorts the antenna pattern, necessitating a calibration procedure to compensate for angular gain variations. Finally, the measurement configuration was validated during actual flights from an airstrip, achieving distances greater than 300 meters.

Observations conducted with the Yebes 40 m radio telescope at TMC-1, covering the 31.0–50.3 GHz frequency range, revealed a set of unidentified spectral lines forming a complex pattern characteristic of an open-shell molecule. The specific frequencies detected, along with the resemblance of the spectral pattern to the 2$_{0,2}$-1$_{0,1}$ rotational transition of H$_2$CCN, suggest these lines originate from the deuterated cyanomethyl radical, HDCCN. By employing Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy alongside electric discharge experiments, we successfully synthesized HDCCN in the laboratory and recorded its 1$_{0,1}$-0$_{0,0}$ and 2$_{0,2}$-1$_{0,1}$ rotational transitions. Based on our data and assuming a rotational temperature of 5 K, we calculated an abundance ratio of H$_2$CCN/HDCCN = 20$\pm$4. The elevated abundance of the deuterated species is consistent with standard gas-phase models, where deuteration occurs via deuteron transfer from the H$_2$D$^+$ molecular ion.

We introduce a topological framework designed to analyze the progression of Alzheimer's disease, the predominant neurodegenerative condition. Our approach models the disease by representing brain connectivity as a graph and initiating the spread of toxic proteins from a specific vertex. Over time, a dynamical system simulates the accumulation and propagation of these proteins along the graph's edges, establishing an edge ordering based on the damage caused by high protein concentrations. This ordering creates a graph filtration, which we analyze across various seeding locations using a novel combinatorial and topological method. Specifically, a filtration corresponds to a maximal chain within the partially ordered set of spanning subgraphs arranged by inclusion. To identify graph similarities and construct a topological signature, we quotient this poset by graph homotopy equivalence, resulting in maximal chains within a reduced poset. We present an algorithm to calculate this direct quotient efficiently, avoiding the computation of all subgraphs, and establish bounds for the total number of graphs up to homotopy equivalence. Furthermore, we extend Kendall's $d_K$ metric for permutations to broader graded posets to compare the resulting maximal chains and define bounds for this metric. Finally, we validate the framework's effectiveness using real brain graphs by examining tau protein dynamics on the structural connectome, demonstrating that the proposed topological brain chain equivalence classes can effectively distinguish between different simulated subtypes of Alzheimer's disease.

Within the Standard Model, the Higgs boson's coupling to fermions represents its most delicate aspect. The decay of the Higgs into a tau pair ($H\rightarrow \tau\tau$) was confirmed using LHC Run 1 data. This report details recent measurements and searches concerning Higgs decays into two fermions, with a specific focus on results from the LHC Run 2 collected by the ATLAS experiment. These results cover decays to third-generation fermions ($H\rightarrow b\bar{b}$) and second-generation fermions ($H\rightarrow c\bar{c}$, $H\rightarrow \mu\mu$).

Object detection models often struggle in open or novel domains and typically demand expensive, exhaustive annotations from fully labeled datasets. Our goal is to leverage multiple datasets with diverse categories without requiring further labeling, thereby expanding the range of detectable objects, utilizing transfer learning, and improving domain independence. Our dataset merging approach begins by training several initial Faster R-CNN models on distinct datasets while incorporating images from complementary sources for domain adaptation. Mirroring self-training techniques, the predictions from these initial detectors help address the lack of annotations in the supplementary datasets. The final OMNIA Faster R-CNN is then trained on the union of all datasets, enriched with these generated predictions, across every category. This joint training process manages unsafe targets through a novel SoftSig classification loss applied in a softly supervised manner. Experimental results demonstrate that merging Modanet with COCO for in-the-wild fashion detection boosts mAP from 45.5% to 57.4%. Furthermore, applying our soft distillation to address domain shifts between GTA and Cityscapes allows the model to surpass the state-of-the-art by 5.3 points. This methodology holds the potential to enable object detection for real-world applications without relying on massive datasets.

In Europe, the bacterium *Xylella fastidiosa* (Xf) is primarily spread by the spittlebug *Philaenus spumarius*, resulting in substantial economic losses for olive and almond crops. Comprehending the drivers of disease dynamics in similar pathosystems is crucial for developing control measures that disrupt transmission chains. This study presents a compartmental model for Xf in Europe that incorporates key epidemiological mechanisms, including the seasonal fluctuations of *P. spumarius*. Validated against data from two major European outbreaks—the Olive Quick Decline Syndrome (OQDS) in Apulia, Italy (subspecies *pauca*), and Almond Leaf Scorch Disease (ALSD) in Majorca, Spain (subspecies *multiplex* and *fastidiosa*)—the model accurately replicates observed field trends using a Bayesian inference approach. Global sensitivity analysis identified vector-plant and plant-vector transmission rates, alongside the vector removal rate, as the most critical factors influencing the timing of infection and incidence peaks, as well as the ultimate mortality of host populations. Furthermore, simulations of various vector-centric interventions indicate that a combined strategy maximizing vector removal while reducing the annual influx of new vectors offers the most effective approach to disease management.

This work generalizes the classical Otal-Peign\'e's Theorem to encompass packed, Gromov-hyperbolic spaces equipped with a convex geodesic bicombing. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a group acting discretely and freely via isometries on such a space, the critical exponent is identical to the topological entropy of the geodesic flow on the corresponding quotient metric space. A key component of this proof involves a refined version of the classical Bishop-Jones' Theorem.
We categorize maximal arc systems on the 4-punctured sphere that intersect no more than once.

This work investigates weighted edge coloring in undirected, edge-weighted general multi-graphs $G := (V, E)$ with weights $w : E \rightarrow [0, 1]$. The objective is to determine a proper weighted coloring using the minimum number of colors. A proper weighted coloring is defined such that the sum of weights of edges incident to any vertex sharing the same color does not exceed one. In the online scenario, edges are revealed sequentially and must be colored irrevocably immediately upon arrival. We demonstrate that $3.39m+o(m)$ colors suffice when the maximum degree is $o(m)$, where $m$ represents the maximum, across all vertices, of the minimum number of unit-sized bins required to pack the weights of incident edges. We also establish the tightness of this analysis, improving the prior best upper bound of $5m$ established by Correa and Goemans [STOC 2004]. Regarding the offline case, we prove that for simple graphs containing edge-disjoint cycles, $m+1$ colors are adequate, and for multi-graph trees, $1.693m+12$ colors are sufficient.

For integers satisfying $k>t>0$ and $n>2k-t$, the generalized Kneser graph $K(n,k,t)$ is defined by taking all $k$-subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ as vertices, with adjacency occurring precisely when two subsets share fewer than $t$ elements. This study establishes the treewidth of $K(n,k,t)$ for $t\ge 2$ under conditions where $n$ is sufficiently large relative to $k$, offering a notably tighter bound on $n$ than previously established. A key implication of this finding is that for every integer $c\ge 1$, there exists a constant $K(c)\ge 2c$ such that whenever $k\ge K(c)$ and $t=k-c$, the equality $tw(K(n,k,t))=\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n-t}{k-t}-1$ holds if and only if $n\ge (t+1)(k+1-t)$.

Satellite communication holds the promise of delivering ubiquitous, scalable, and continuous services to areas that are currently underserved or unreachable. Nevertheless, realizing these advantages requires overcoming significant hurdles, as managing resources, network control, security, spectrum allocation, and energy consumption in satellite networks is considerably more complex than in terrestrial systems. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI)—encompassing machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning—has emerged as a rapidly expanding research domain with proven success across various applications, particularly in wireless communications. AI has demonstrated immense potential when applied to diverse satellite communication tasks, such as beam hopping, anti-jamming, traffic forecasting, channel modeling, telemetry mining, ionospheric scintillation detection, interference management, remote sensing, behavior modeling, space-air-ground integration, and energy optimization. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of AI, its sub-fields, and current state-of-the-art algorithms. It further examines specific challenges within satellite communication systems and presents both proposed and potential AI-driven solutions. Finally, the work outlines future directions and suggests key steps for advancing the field.

Because humans frequently rely on imprecise language, vague concepts with ill-defined boundaries are common in communication. This paper investigates whether models trained on the distributional statistics of language align with fuzzy membership patterns. By applying a state-of-the-art model to the natural language inference task, we examine its ability to map temperature data to fuzzy perceptions like "cool" or "hot." Our results reveal that the model exhibits patterns resembling classical fuzzy-set theoretic formulations of linguistic hedges, despite significant noise. This suggests that models trained exclusively on language hold promise for encoding fuzziness.

This paper addresses the online influence maximization (OIM) problem within social networks, where a learner iteratively selects seed nodes to trigger cascades, observes the resulting feedback, and progressively identifies the most effective seeds for maximizing cascade size across multiple rounds. Aligning with real-world constraints, we utilize node-level feedback rather than the edge-level feedback standard in existing literature. While edge-level feedback exposes every edge traversed by information in a cascade, node-level feedback discloses only the activated nodes and their timestamps. This approach is considered more realistic because, in practice, identifying who is influenced is feasible, whereas tracing the specific relationships (edges) responsible for influence propagation is often difficult. Although a nearly optimal algorithm with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$-regret has previously been developed for the OIM problem under the linear threshold (LT) diffusion model with node-level feedback, it remained an open question whether such an algorithm exists for the independent cascade (IC) diffusion model. In this work, we resolve this gap by introducing an $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$-regret algorithm for OIM under the IC model with node-level feedback.

Effective drone-to-drone communication, functioning similarly to traffic signals, is essential for the success of advanced air mobility (AAM) in both urban and rural environments. Large-scale AAM applications, including air taxis and air ambulances, depend on robust point-to-point and broadcast channels connecting multiple aircraft. Ensuring high reliability within such dynamic settings necessitates communication systems characterized by agility and efficiency. This paper outlines the fundamentals for creating and sustaining reliable communication links among various aircraft in distinct AAM scenarios. Furthermore, it explores concepts and findings regarding wireless coverage and mobility for AAM services when leveraging cellular networks as ground infrastructure. Additionally, the study evaluates wireless localization performance within three-dimensional AAM corridors utilizing cellular networks, examining factors such as corridor altitude and base station density. The manuscript concludes by identifying future research avenues and unresolved challenges aimed at enhancing wireless coverage and localization.

The Bethe-Salpeter equation's ladder kernel is modified by incorporating distinct flavor dependencies for dressing functions within the heavy-quark sector. Unlike previous studies, this approach enables the unified computation of the mass spectra and leptonic decay constants for light pseudoscalar mesons ($D_u$, $D_s$, $B_u$, $B_s$, $B_c$) and heavy quarkonia ($\eta_c$, $\eta_b$) at a physical pion mass using a single framework. Furthermore, the resulting Bethe-Salpeter amplitudes are projected onto the light front to reconstruct the mesons' distribution amplitudes within the full theory, followed by a comparison with the first inverse moment of the heavy meson distribution amplitude derived from heavy quark effective theory.

A primary limitation of football event data, widely utilized in recent analytics, is its reliance on manual collection, which restricts its accessibility to only a few tournaments. This study introduces a deterministic decision tree-based algorithm designed to automatically derive football events from tracking data through a two-stage process: first, a possession phase that identifies the ball holder in each frame and analyzes player configurations during dead-ball periods to facilitate set piece recognition; second, an event detection phase that integrates these possession shifts with the official laws of football to identify in-game occurrences and set pieces. We benchmarked the automatically generated events against manual annotations, demonstrating that the proposed method achieves a detection rate exceeding 90% across various tournaments and data providers for most event categories. Furthermore, we illustrate how contextual information from tracking data can enhance the granularity of auto-detected events and showcase the framework's potential for conducting diverse football data analyses.

Social reputations serve as a potent tool for maintaining cooperation, as people tend to collaborate with those who hold high social standing. However, determining how moral reputations should evolve based on observed behavior and when a population will settle on a unified standard of moral evaluation remains an open question. This study introduces a mathematical framework modeling reputation-dependent cooperation within a stratified population where groups adhere to distinct norms for assessing reputations. Consequently, these norms compete as individuals migrate between groups. We demonstrate that a minority group can eventually dominate the entire population, particularly if it adopts the "Stern Judging" norm, which penalizes cooperation with individuals of poor standing. Conversely, if group membership remains static, dividing reputation information into separate groups generally undermines cooperation, unless individuals are highly insular and prioritize interactions within their own group. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings regarding information flow structures within populations and the evolutionary trajectory of social norms governing moral judgment.

This paper investigates the weak amenability of weighted measure algebras, demonstrating that $M(G, \omega)$ is weakly amenable precisely when $G$ is discrete and all bounded quasi-additive functions are inner. Furthermore, we examine the weak amenability of $L^1(G, \omega)^{**}$ and $M(G, \omega)^{**}$, establishing that these Banach algebras are weakly amenable if and only if $G$ is finite. These findings provide a resolution to the inquiry regarding the weak amenability of $L^1(G, \omega)^{**}$ and $M(G, \omega)^{**}$.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have fundamentally transformed reversible steganography. While predictive modeling via deep neural networks serves as a core component of this field, it often struggles with significant errors when processing noisy or out-of-distribution data. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian deep learning framework to incorporate uncertainty into predictive models. We conceptualize Bayesian neural networks as self-aware systems capable of recognizing their own limitations. By utilizing Monte Carlo sampling with stochastic forward passes, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution to quantify uncertainty. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components, both of which can be learned without supervision. Our experimental findings indicate that integrating Bayesian uncertainty analysis enhances the capacity-distortion performance of steganographic systems.

We conducted a reanalysis of visible and near-infrared (0.3–2.5 microns) data from Uranus and Neptune, collected by various instruments, applying the Minnaert limb-darkening approximation. Our findings reveal a unified model for vertical aerosol distribution that aligns with the observed reflectivity spectra of both planets. This model comprises three components: (1) a deep aerosol layer with a base pressure exceeding 5–7 bar, presumed to be a mixture of H₂S ice and photochemical haze; (2) a photochemical haze/ice layer situated at the methane condensation level (1–2 bar) where high static stability occurs; and (3) an extended photochemical haze layer, likely of similar composition to the 1–2 bar layer, rising from that level into the stratosphere, where these particles are generated. For Neptune specifically, we determined the necessity of adding a thin layer of micron-sized methane ice particles at approximately 0.2 bar to account for increased reflection at longer methane-absorbing wavelengths. We propose that methane condensing onto haze particles at the base of the 1–2 bar layer creates ice/haze aggregates that rapidly grow and immediately "snow out" (as predicted by Carlson et al., 1988), only to re-evaporate at deeper levels, thereby releasing core haze particles to serve as condensation nuclei for H₂S ice. Furthermore, our results indicate that the spectral properties of "dark spots," including the Voyager-2/ISS Great Dark Spot and the HST/WFC3 NDS-2018, are effectively modeled by a darkening or potential clearing of the deep aerosol layer alone.

Enhancing the comprehension of vortex formation and propagation within pulsatile flows offers critical insights into mixing, transport mechanisms, and the transition to turbulence in such systems. For instance, analyzing pulsatile flow in obstructed artery models stimulates research into flow-induced effects related to morphological changes, blood viscosity, wall elasticity, and flow rate. This study employed an axisymmetric rigid model to investigate flow patterns under varying degrees of constriction ($d_0$), mean Reynolds number ($\bar{Re}$), and Womersley number ($\alpha$).
