However, for a generic location within the ergoregion, a condition for the existence of a black-hole bomb arises, linking the mass ratio before and after decay to the velocity of the fragment in the center-of-mass frame.

We introduce a novel, reference-free metric for assessing summary quality that prioritizes faithfulness. This metric is engineered to detect and quantify even the slightest inconsistencies between a summary and its source document. Named ESTIME (Estimator of Summary-to-Text Inconsistency by Mismatched Embeddings), our approach demonstrates a stronger correlation with expert ratings on the SummEval dataset compared to other standard measures, outperforming them in both Consistency and Fluency. Additionally, we present a technique for generating subtle factual errors within human-generated summaries. Our findings indicate that ESTIME exhibits greater sensitivity to these nuanced errors than existing evaluation metrics.

The influence of an external electric field on exchange coupling parameters was examined using first-principles electronic structure calculations via the KKR Green function method. These simulations focused on a one-monolayer (ML) free-standing Fe film and Fe deposited on two distinct substrates, with the 1 ML thickness chosen to mitigate field screening effects common in metallic systems. By contrasting the free-standing Fe ML results with those of Fe on the various substrates, the study elucidated the origins of field-induced variations in exchange interactions. Notably, the Fe/Pt(111) system exhibited significantly pronounced changes compared to the free-standing Fe ML. This is attributed to localized electronic states at the Fe/Pt interface, which are highly sensitive to the electric field and critically influence Fe-Fe exchange interactions.

We employ time-resolved x-ray absorption spectroscopy to measure molecular vibrations with femtometer-scale accuracy. As a proof of concept, a Raman process excites the A$_{1g}$ mode in gas-phase SF$_6$ molecules to an amplitude of approximately 50 fm, which is subsequently probed by a time-delayed soft x-ray pulse targeting the sulfur L$_{2,3}$-edge. Interpreting the minute energy shifts observed as changes in internuclear distances necessitates insights into electronic contributions derived from many-body ab initio simulations. This study demonstrates that core-level spectroscopy serves as a high-precision instrument for monitoring time-dependent molecular structures.

This work presents ATLAS collaboration results from LHC proton-proton collisions, analyzing charged-particle multiplicity and average transverse momentum distributions scaled to the KNO variable. Measurements cover center-of-mass energies ranging from 0.9 to 13 TeV within the absolute pseudorapidity range of |η| < 2.5, utilizing two event samples with charged-particle transverse momenta exceeding 100 MeV and 500 MeV, respectively. The study examines how multiplicity distributions evolve with collision energy using KNO scaling variables. On the KNO scale, these multiplicity distributions maintain a similar shape while decreasing as energy increases, approaching energy independence at the highest energies. Conversely, average transverse momentum distributions on the KNO scale exhibit a consistent shape that increases with rising collision energy.

Computational imaging has recently embraced artificial intelligence, where deep neural networks (DNNs) enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of reconstructed images that would otherwise be degraded by low sampling rates or noisy conditions. This study introduces a novel computational imaging framework utilizing a transformer network based on sequence transduction. Supported by a simulation database to develop signal translation capabilities, the system processes end-to-end data from a single-pixel detector to generate 2D images. This approach retrieves high-quality, noise-free images even at sampling ratios as low as 2%, accommodating both well-designed speckle patterns for sub-Nyquist imaging and random speckle patterns. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness against noise interference. This translation mechanism establishes a new pathway for DNN-assisted ghost imaging and is applicable across diverse computational imaging scenarios.

Accurately tracking the respiratory rate of premature infants is critical for triggering necessary medical interventions. Traditional wired monitoring methods are often invasive and disruptive to these fragile patients. Consequently, we introduce a Deep Learning-based wearable system designed for newborns, utilizing wireless signals from a non-invasive Bellypatch to predict respiratory arrest. Our proposed five-stage development pipeline encompasses data collection and labeling, feature scaling, model selection with hyperparameter optimization, training and validation, and final testing and deployment. The core model employs a 1-D Convolutional Neural Network (1DCNN) architecture, comprising one convolutional layer, one pooling layer, and three fully-connected layers, which achieves 97.15% accuracy. To mitigate the energy constraints typical of wearable devices, we investigated various quantization techniques, analyzing their impact on both performance and power consumption. Furthermore, we developed a novel Spiking Neural Network (SNN) approach for respiratory classification, optimized for event-driven neuromorphic hardware. We devised a method to translate the analog operations of our baseline 1DCNN into their spiking equivalents. Through design-space exploration using the converted SNN parameters, we generated inference solutions with varying trade-offs between accuracy and energy usage. We selected a specific configuration that delivers 93.33% accuracy while consuming 18 times less energy than the baseline 1DCNN model. Additionally, this proposed SNN solution maintains comparable accuracy but reduces energy consumption by a factor of four.

The parallels between shallow water dynamics and astrophysical phenomena have provided significant theoretical and experimental insights. To structure these investigations, we systematically examine the hydrodynamic characteristics of backwater profiles in the shallow water equations under 2D radial symmetry. Unlike the standard 1D scenarios common in hydraulics, even under isentropic conditions, solutions featuring a minimum-radius horizon emerge, mirroring black hole and white hole horizons; here, critical conditions characterized by a unitary Froude number create a unidirectional barrier for surface waves. Beyond these time-reversible solutions, a wider range of scenarios appears when accounting for dissipation via turbulent friction and shock waves (hydraulic jumps) in both convergent and divergent flows. This taxonomy of base-flow cases offers a foundation for a more systematic study of higher-order effects, such as wave propagation, instabilities, capillarity, variable bed slopes, and rotation.

Recent research utilizing city-level time series data indicates that various crimes decreased globally following the implementation of COVID-19 containment measures. Drawing on community-level data from Chicago, this study seeks to deepen the understanding of how public interventions influenced criminal activity at a more granular spatial resolution. The investigation employs a two-stage methodology. Initially, it utilizes Structural Bayesian Time-Series to estimate the causal impact of Chicago's social distancing and shelter-in-place policies across four crime categories: burglary, assault, narcotics offenses, and robbery. After the models identify the direction, magnitude, and statistical significance of these trend shifts, Firth's Logistic Regression is applied to examine the factors linked to the statistically significant reductions observed in the first phase. The statistical findings reveal that crime trend variations differ across both communities and crime types, indicating that aggregate models obscure a complex landscape of diverging patterns. Furthermore, the regression analysis yields mixed results regarding the correlates of significant crime reduction; while several relationships exhibit opposite directions across different crimes, population remains the sole factor consistently and positively associated with notable crime declines.

Snowball sampling refers to methods for human populations where participants are asked to distribute questionnaires to their social connections. While estimates from this method are generally considered biased, the extent of that bias depends on both the sampling design and the characteristics of the target population. Hybrid Probabilistic-Snowball Sampling Designs (HPSSD) seek to mitigate the primary source of snowball bias by randomly oversampling the initial stage of the chain. To evaluate HPSSD's performance, an algorithm was created that simulates an assortative network of tobacco smokers by integrating stochastic blockmodel edges into a graph of cliques, alongside various HPSSD outcomes. Analysis of 8,000 simulation runs suggests that HPSSD does not enhance the reliability of samples that are already representative. However, when population homophily is sufficiently low, the unadjusted mean from HPSSD performs slightly better than random sampling from a smaller population. Finally, adjusting HPSSD estimates to correct for bias yields performance improvements, indicating that an adjusted HPSSD estimator is a valuable advancement.

This study reports on a VLA HI imaging survey designed to investigate the formation of long extraplanar H$\alpha$ tails in extreme jellyfish galaxies. The survey focuses on five such galaxies, which were optically identified via the WINGS and OmegaWINGS surveys and verified to possess extended H$\alpha$ tails using MUSE data; each resides in a distinct cluster. Within the 40'x40' field of view and across a 6500 km s$^{-1}$ bandwidth, 88 additional spiral galaxies are present. We successfully detected 13 of these, along with one previously uncatalogued spiral, exhibiting HI masses between 1 and 7 $\times$ 10$^{9}$ M$_{\odot}$. Many of these detections feature extended HI disks, with two showing clear signs of ram pressure stripping and others potentially influenced by tidal forces or ram pressure. By stacking the 75 non-detected spirals, we determined an average HI mass of 1.9 $\times$ 10$^{8}$ M$_{\odot}$; given their stellar masses, these galaxies are highly HI deficient. Comparisons reveal that extreme jellyfish galaxies possess higher stellar masses than nearly all disk and HI-detected galaxies, while also being located closer to cluster centers and moving at higher relative velocities compared to both HI detections and most non-detections. We conclude that their substantial stellar mass enables them to penetrate deeply into the cluster before stripping occurs, and the surrounding intracluster medium pressure drives the formation of their distinctive star-forming tails.

This study theoretically investigates how interband transitions, altered by gate voltage-induced changes in carrier concentration, affect the modulation of transmitted or reflected radiation. Calculations were conducted for heavily doped graphene placed on high-K dielectrics (Al₂O₃, HfO₂, AlN, ZrO₂) or SiO₂ substrates under normal radiation propagation. Results indicate a modulation depth exceeding 10%, varying with wavelength, gate voltage (carrier concentration), and substrate characteristics. Consequently, structures combining graphene, a dielectric substrate, and doped silicon as a gate demonstrate potential as efficient electro-optical modulators for near-IR and mid-IR radiation, specifically when utilizing high-K and SiO₂ substrates, respectively.

We investigate the collective driven dynamics of a colloidal monolayer settling down an inclined plane. Gravity acting parallel to the base generates flow around individual colloids, and hydrodynamic interactions between them accelerate sedimentation as local density rises. This process produces a universal "triangular" inhomogeneous density profile featuring a traveling density shock at the leading front that moves downhill. Unlike density shocks in colloidal monolayers driven by applied torques rather than forces [Phys. Rev. Fluids, 2(9):092301, 2017], the sedimentation density front remains stable over extended periods despite developing roughness spanning tens of particle diameters. Using both experimental measurements and particle-based computer simulations, we demonstrate that the Burgers equation remarkably well models the density profile along the sedimentation direction as a function of time, with a modest improvement achieved when the nonlinear conservation law incorporates the sub-linear dependence of collective sedimentation velocity on density.

We establish a sufficient condition for the monogamy inequality of multi-party quantum entanglement across arbitrary dimensions using the entanglement of formation. By examining classical-classical-quantum (ccq) states—where the quantum components are derived from the two-party reduced density matrices of a three-party quantum state—we demonstrate that the additivity of mutual information for these ccq states ensures the monogamy inequality for three-party pure states in terms of EoF. Following an illustration of these findings with specific examples, we extend our results from three-party systems to general multi-party systems of arbitrary dimensions.

Small-angle X-ray or neutron scattering (SAXS/SANS/SAS) is extensively utilized to determine the structural properties of biomolecules and soft-matter complexes in solution. Translating scattering signals into molecular insights necessitates algorithms capable of generating SAS patterns from specific atomistic models. These predictions are complex due to the influence of the solute's hydration shell, excluded solvent volume, and thermal fluctuations. While many computationally efficient approaches rely on simplified, implicit models for hydration and solvent exclusion—introducing uncertainties and requiring experimental fitting of free parameters—explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations offer a more robust solution despite higher computational demands. To justify the use of explicit-solvent methods, we first examine the approximations inherent in implicit-solvent approaches. Subsequently, we outline the theoretical framework for explicit-solvent SAS predictions, which are readily accessible through the WAXSiS web server. We also detail a workflow for calculating SAS patterns from MD trajectories using a freely available, modified version of GROMACS termed GROMACS-SWAXS, which incorporates the WAXSiS methodology. Finally, we address practical aspects for executing routine explicit-solvent SAS simulations.

Drawing inspiration from humans, who navigate vehicles by leveraging contextual and spatial cues via their senses, current research primarily aims to develop robust and efficient driving policies. These efforts generally fall into two categories: modular systems and end-to-end architectures. While modular approaches exist, they often suffer from scalability issues due to the need for manual supervision of individual components. Consequently, this study concentrates on the end-to-end paradigm to establish a framework for autonomous driving policy learning. To emulate human driving capabilities, we introduce a system utilizing three RGB cameras (left, right, and center) to replicate the human field of view, combined with top-down semantic data to enhance contextual understanding. This sensor information is fused and processed through a self-attention mechanism, followed by an auto-regressive module for waypoint prediction. Experimental validation using the CARLA simulator demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving the highest driving scores during evaluation.

This paper provides an error analysis and additional numerical studies of the Parameterized-Background Data-Weak (PBDW) method for variational Data Assimilation, originally introduced by Maday, Patera, Penn, and Yano. As a state estimation technique utilizing reduced models, PBDW seeks to approximate an unknown function $u^{\rm true}$ within a high-dimensional Hilbert space using $M$ linear measurements of the form $y_m = \ell_m(u^{\rm true})$. The approximation $\hat{u}$ is constructed as the sum of a background component $\hat{z}$ from an $N$-dimensional reduced model space $\mathcal{Z}_N$ and an update term $\hat{\eta}$ from the space $\mathcal{U}_M$ spanned by the Riesz representers of the measurement functionals. While the standard PBDW approach works for noise-free data, it lacks robustness when noise is present ($y_m = \ell_m(u^{\rm true})+\epsilon_m$); specifically, increasing $N$ can degrade reconstruction accuracy. To resolve this, we propose an extension that searches for the background $\hat{z}$ over the entire space $\mathcal{Z}_N$ in noise-free scenarios, but restricts the search to a carefully selected subset $\mathcal{K}_N \subset \mathcal{Z}_N$ when noise exists. This restriction introduces nonlinearity, which is essential for significantly enhancing the algorithm's robustness against noise. Furthermore, we provide an *a priori* error and stability analysis and demonstrate the method's effectiveness through various numerical examples.

The magnetic structure of antiferromagnetic $\alpha$-Mn has remained unresolved for nearly seven decades since its discovery. By measuring zero-field nuclear magnetic resonance spectra below the Néel temperature ($T_{\text{N}} = 95$ K), we gained new insights into its magnetism. The site II spectra exhibited splitting into two sites with five subpeaks due to quadrupole interaction, indicating that the ordered moments at site II are slightly tilted from the $[001]$ direction. Furthermore, site III spectra revealed a division into four sites below $T_{\text{N}}$. These results clearly establish that the symmetry of antiferromagnetic $\alpha$-Mn is lower than previously believed.

The lack of annotated images impedes the development of reliable, automated systems for diagnosing and evaluating COVID-19 using CT scans. To address the challenges of data annotation, we introduce a label-free method for segmenting COVID-19 lesions in CT images by leveraging pixel-level anomaly modeling that extracts relevant patterns from normal lung scans. This approach is based on the observation that high-intensity structures, such as tracheae and vessels where lesions typically appear, display distinct patterns. To enable pixel-level learning of these patterns, we generate synthetic "lesions" using simple operations and insert them into normal CT scans to create training pairs. From these pairs, we train a Normalcy-Converting Network (NormNet) that restores "abnormal" images to a normal state. Experiments across three datasets confirm the effectiveness of NormNet, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms various unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) techniques.

This paper aims to present and analyze comprehensive-constructed subclasses of normalized analytic and bi-univalent functions within the unit open disc. We investigate the bounds for the second and third Taylor-Maclaurin coefficients of functions within these subclasses. Additionally, we highlight certain refinements and connections to previously established results.

This article introduces a novel definition of the linear canonical Stockwell transform (LCST), examines its fundamental properties, inner product relations, and reconstruction formula, and characterizes the transform's range as a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Additionally, we develop a multiresolution analysis (MRA) linked to this transform and construct an orthonormal basis for $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

To ensure dependable navigation on city streets, the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) must not only accurately derive positions from pseudorange data but also reliably assess when those positions are safe for use. However, urban settings introduce biases and faults in multiple GNSS signals due to building blockage and signal reflection, making it difficult to estimate position and availability. This paper introduces a novel particle filter framework utilizing a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) likelihood for GNSS measurements to robustly estimate vehicle position even under multiple measurement faults. By leveraging the probability distribution tracked by the filter alongside the designed GMM likelihood, the system evaluates localization accuracy and risk to determine availability at every time step. Experimental results from both simulated and real-world urban driving scenarios demonstrate that this method yields smaller horizontal positioning errors compared to existing filter-based state estimation techniques when faults are present. Additionally, simulations confirm that the proposed approach determines system availability with a lower probability of false alarms and reduced integrity risk than current particle filter-based integrity monitoring methods.

This paper investigates the Huq-centrality of morphisms within a framework adapted from pointed categories where binary products commute with coequalizers. The primary findings demonstrate that the core behaviors of Huq-centrality observed in unital categories persist in this new setting, encompassing both (weakly) unital categories and those existing outside the unital framework.

Models forecasting future trends often utilize heterogeneous data, yet existing approaches frequently overlook inconsistencies and flaws within this data while neglecting spatial correlations between monitoring points or generating predictions for the entire study area. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces a deep learning framework that employs graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fuse heterogeneous data from various monitoring points, specifically evaluated within an air quality prediction context. The core strategy involves (1) integrating collected data based on the spatial correlations of monitoring locations and (2) utilizing global information for prediction instead of relying solely on local data. The methodology proceeds in three stages: first, constructing a fusion matrix via a proposed RBF-based approach; second, generating spatially and temporally correlated inputs from the fused data; and third, applying a spatiotemporal graph convolutional network (STGCN) to forecast observation trends. In the air quality application, results demonstrate that (1) data fused through the RBF approach exhibit high consistency, (2) models trained on fused data outperform those using raw data, and (3) the STGCN surpasses all baseline models in performance. This method is suitable for scenarios involving continuous heterogeneous data gathered from multiple monitoring sites dispersed across a specific region.

DreamFusion has recently showcased the effectiveness of using pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models to refine Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), yielding impressive text-to-3D synthesis outcomes. Nevertheless, the approach suffers from two fundamental drawbacks: (a) prohibitively slow NeRF optimization and (b) reliance on low-resolution image-space supervision, which results in poor-quality 3D models requiring extensive processing times. This paper tackles these issues through a two-stage optimization framework. Initially, we generate a coarse model using a low-resolution diffusion prior, accelerating the process with a sparse 3D hash grid. Building on this coarse representation as an initialization, we further refine a textured 3D mesh by employing an efficient differentiable renderer in conjunction with a high-resolution latent diffusion model. Our proposed method, Magic3D, produces high-fidelity 3D mesh models in approximately 40 minutes—twice as fast as DreamFusion's average 1.5-hour runtime—while delivering superior resolution. User evaluations indicate that 61.7% of participants preferred our approach over DreamFusion. Coupled with its image-conditioned generation features, our method offers novel control mechanisms for 3D synthesis, paving the way for diverse creative applications.

This paper clarifies and generalizes the ant on a rubber rope paradox, a mathematical puzzle known for its counterintuitive solution. We demonstrate that the ant can still reach the end of the rope even when the ant's step length and the rubber rope's stretching length are treated as random variables.

This paper introduces a modified formal Lagrangian formulation by incorporating dummy dependent variables, demonstrating that such a formulation exists for any system of differential equations. The resulting Euler--Lagrange equations, which comprise the original system alongside its adjoint system relative to the dummy variables, simplify back to the original system through a straightforward substitution of these dummy variables. This approach is utilized to investigate conservation laws via Noether's Theorem, specifically yielding a nontrivial conservation law for the Fornberg--Whitham equation through its Lie point symmetries. Furthermore, the study establishes a correspondence between the conservation laws of the incompressible Euler equations and the variational symmetries of the associated modified formal Lagrangian.

Large-scale weakly supervised product retrieval is a practically useful yet computationally demanding challenge. This paper presents a novel approach for the eBay Visual Search Challenge (eProduct), which was part of the Ninth Workshop on Fine-Grained Visual Categorization (FGVC9) at CVPR 2022. The competition addressed two key difficulties: (a) the e-commerce domain is extremely fine-grained, featuring numerous products with subtle visual distinctions; and (b) a scarcity of target instance-level labels for training, relying instead on coarse category labels and product titles. To address these issues, we developed a robust solution through several specialized designs: (a) rather than utilizing text data directly, we extracted thousands of pseudo-attributes from product titles to serve as ground truths for multi-label classification; (b) we integrated powerful backbone architectures with advanced training strategies to enhance discriminative representation learning; and (c) we implemented various post-processing methods, such as whitening, re-ranking, and model ensemble, to improve retrieval performance. By achieving a mean average recall (MAR) of 71.53%, our solution, "Involution King," secured the second position on the leaderboard.

This paper investigates sharp isoperimetric comparison theorems and sharp dimensional concavity properties of the isoperimetric profile within non-smooth spaces possessing lower Ricci curvature bounds, specifically $N$-dimensional ${\rm RCD}(K,N)$ spaces $(X,\mathsf{d},\mathscr{H}^N)$. To address the lack of standard Geometric Measure Theory tools and the potential non-existence of isoperimetric regions in non-compact settings, the authors introduce a novel approach. This method estimates the first and second variations of area for isoperimetric sets without relying on regularity theory, complemented by an asymptotic mass decomposition result for perimeter-minimizing sequences. Many of these findings are new even for smooth, non-compact manifolds with lower Ricci curvature bounds and Alexandrov spaces with lower sectional curvature bounds. Furthermore, these results extend several established theorems applicable to compact manifolds, non-compact manifolds with uniformly bounded geometry at infinity, and Euclidean convex bodies. Additional implications of these findings are examined in a companion paper by the authors.

Wide-field magnetometry is achieved through imaging the optically detected magnetic resonance of ensembles of nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. However, inhomogeneities within these NV ensembles substantially constrain the sensitivity of magnetic field measurements. We introduce a double-double quantum (DDQ) driving method to enable wide-field magnetic imaging of dynamic fields at the micron scale. This DDQ approach utilizes four-tone radio frequency pulses to mitigate variations in the NV resonant response caused by inhomogeneity. As a proof-of-concept, we applied the DDQ technique to image the direct-current magnetic fields generated by individual magnetic nanoparticles tethered via single DNA molecules to a diamond sensor surface. This study confirms the effectiveness of the diamond NV ensemble system for high-frame-rate magnetic microscopy and single-molecule biophysics.

We present a protocol for categorizing three-qubit pure states into distinct entanglement classes, which has been successfully executed on an NMR quantum processor. This approach is engineered so that the experimental procedures used for classification simultaneously quantify the degree of entanglement within the states. The classification process involves reconstructing correlation matrices through the application of 13 operators; the rank of these matrices serves as the criterion to assign states to one of five categories: separable, three types of biseparable, and two types of genuinely entangled states (GHZ and W). To measure entanglement, a concurrence function is defined using the same 13 operators to assess global entanglement, which registers as zero for separable states and non-zero for all others. We validate the protocol's effectiveness by applying it to states selected from each of the six inequivalent classes under stochastic local operations and classical communication, as well as to randomly chosen states from the three-qubit pure state space.

We introduce Contrastive Neighborhood Alignment (CNA), a manifold learning technique designed to preserve feature topology by ensuring that data points proximal in the source (teacher) model's representation space remain neighbors in the target (student) model's space. By employing a contrastive loss, the target model replicates the local structure of the source representation. As an unsupervised algorithm, CNA operates without requiring ground-truth labels for individual samples. The method is demonstrated across three contexts: manifold learning, which retains the local topology of original data within a reduced-dimensional space; model distillation, where a compact student model emulates a larger teacher; and legacy model updates, involving the replacement of older models with more advanced ones. Experimental results indicate that CNA effectively captures high-dimensional manifolds and outperforms competing methods within their respective domains.

Climate model experiments depend on extensive sets of spatio-temporal boundary conditions, which define both the system's initial state and the external forcings driving the simulation. Although these conditions are usually fixed using existing reconstructions, they carry significant, unquantified uncertainty that can substantially alter experimental outcomes. This study introduces an efficient method to quantify such uncertainties by integrating data from multiple models and observations. Building on the coexchangeability model, we create a coexchangeable process model designed to handle multiple correlated spatio-temporal variable fields. By applying further exchangeability assumptions to the parameters within this framework, we derive a Bayes linear analogy of a hierarchical model. We apply this approach to jointly reconstruct sea-surface temperature and sea-ice concentration boundary conditions for the Last Glacial Maximum (19–23 ka), subsequently using these reconstructions to drive an ensemble of ice-sheet simulations via the FAMOUS-Ice coupled atmosphere and ice-sheet model. Our results show that standard boundary conditions currently employed in such experiments are implausible when accounting for these uncertainties, and we illustrate the resulting impacts on ice-sheet simulations when utilizing more plausible conditions.

Cellular-V2X (C-V2X) facilitates communication among vehicles and other transportation entities using the 5.9GHz spectrum. It employs direct communication modes to broadcast safety packets via periodic Basic Safety Messages, while reserving adequate resources within the pool for advanced services. Although numerous Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) applications are currently in development, identifying and optimizing the pertinent network parameters remains critical. This paper proposes an infrastructure-assisted transaction procedure executed entirely by C-V2X, optimized specifically for service parameters. To realize the utility of a transaction class, two C-V2X entities must exchange a sequence of multiple messages. Based on this concept, our proposed application prototype can be adapted to support any vehicular service by establishing connections dynamically. We determine appropriate activation zones for vehicles and evaluate their influence on service efficiency. The findings reveal diverse potential service configurations and parameter settings suitable for various use cases, thereby establishing a foundation for future research.

A recently developed, broadly applicable system of hyperbolic partial differential equations allows for the deterministic calculation of a complete heterogeneous stress field from a measured deformation field, such as a strain field derived from digital image correlation. This capability facilitates the determination of material properties, offering an alternative to finite element model updating or the virtual fields method. This paper details the creation of a finite volume discretization for this equation system to mitigate instabilities caused by violations of the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition. The resulting discretization supports application to irregular geometries and finite deformations. We also establish how boundary tractions can be converted into appropriate boundary conditions to accommodate various loading scenarios. Additionally, we examine the solution structure during deformation discontinuities, applying these findings to manage discontinuities at finite volume interfaces, which is relevant for applications like composite materials; notably, these discontinuities induce reflection and transmission of principal stresses. The finite volume discretization is validated using data from commercial finite element software and applied to an experimental uniaxial tension test involving plastic deformation and necking. Strain fields are acquired via digital image correlation, while stress fields are computed using the new discretization, jointly yielding the stress-strain behavior for individual material elements.

Oscillating electromagnetic effects arise near external electric and magnetic fields when gravitational waves (GWs) pass through them. This study examines this phenomenon, specifically reinterpreting findings from axion haloscope experiments that utilize lumped-element detectors to search for GWs within the 100 kHz to 100 MHz frequency band. Although current measurements from ABRACADABRA and SHAFT already constrain GWs, their strain sensitivity remains limited. However, we show that the sensitivity of these instruments scales significantly with volume—more rapidly than axion detection capabilities—promising swift advancements soon. Without alterations, DMRadio-m$^3$ is projected to achieve a GW strain sensitivity of $h \sim 10^{-20}$ at 200 MHz. Furthermore, a straightforward modification to the pickup loop used for reading induced magnetic flux could parametrically boost GW sensitivity, especially at lower frequencies.

Grasping novel, previously unseen objects remains a persistent challenge in robotic manipulation. While numerous approaches have been developed over recent decades for specific robotic hands, the recently introduced UniGrasp framework, though capable of generalizing across various gripper types, fails with closed-loop constrained grippers and is data-inefficient for hands with multigrasp configurations. This paper introduces EfficientGrasp, a generalized method for grasp synthesis and control that operates independently of specific gripper model specifications. By utilizing gripper workspace features instead of UniGrasp's gripper attribute inputs, EfficientGrasp reduces training memory consumption by 81.7% and extends generalization capabilities to include closed-loop constrained grippers. Evaluated through both simulation and real-world object grasping experiments, EfficientGrasp outperforms UniGrasp even when restricted to grippers without closed-loop constraints, achieving a 9.85% higher accuracy in contact point generation and a 3.10% higher grasping success rate in simulation. In real-world tests involving a closed-loop constrained gripper—where UniGrasp fails—EfficientGrasp attained an 83.3% success rate. The study concludes by analyzing the primary causes of the proposed method's grasping failures and identifying strategies to improve performance.

The growing scale and intricacy of contemporary machine learning systems have enhanced their predictive power but simultaneously rendered their decision-making processes more opaque. Although numerous methods for explaining models have emerged, there are currently no definitive standards for evaluating them. This paper reframes model explanation as a causal inference task: estimating the causal impact of real-world concepts on ML model outputs using actual input data. We present CEBaB, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate concept-based explanation techniques in Natural Language Processing. CEBaB comprises brief restaurant reviews paired with human-created counterfactual versions where specific dining aspects—such as food, noise, ambiance, or service—have been altered. Both original and modified reviews feature sentiment annotations at the aspect and review levels, validated through multiple methods. The robust structure of CEBaB enables an analysis that extends beyond surface-level input features to examine how abstract, real-world concepts influence model behavior. By applying CEBaB, we compare the performance of various concept-based explanation approaches across different theoretical frameworks and aim to define natural metrics for their comparative assessment.

Recent years have witnessed significant progress in controlling artificial limbs, where advancements in sensor and control technologies have enhanced their utility, enabling complex actions like grasping to a degree. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have yielded the most successful outcomes so far, prior research in artificial hands was restricted to non-mobile wrists, thereby limiting overall prosthesis functionality. This paper introduces, for the first time, empirical findings on gesture recognition utilizing both mobile and non-mobile wrist configurations. We demonstrate that RNNs equipped with simple recurrent units (SRUs) achieve superior gesture recognition accuracy compared to standard RNNs across both scenarios, using data captured via an arm band that detects electromagnetic signals from arm muscles through surface electromyography (sEMG). Additionally, we illustrate that integrating domain adaptation techniques into continuous gesture recognition with RNNs enhances transferability between individuals, allowing a limb controller trained on one person's data to effectively operate on another's.

Identifying influential training examples facilitates the debugging of datasets and the explanation of model behavior. Current methods rely on tracking how data influence propagates through model parameters, but this is often computationally prohibitive for large NLP models, leading practitioners to focus solely on the final layer. However, we observe that activations connected to this final layer contain "shared logic," causing data influence calculations to suffer from a "cancellation effect." In this phenomenon, conflicting high-magnitude influences from different examples negate each other, reducing the discriminative power of the influence scores and rendering the deletion of such examples ineffective. To address this, we introduce TracIn-WE, a modification of TracIn that operates on the word embedding layer rather than the last layer, where the cancellation effect is less pronounced. Although one might worry that embedding-based influence lacks high-level semantic information, we find that gradients avoid this issue, likely because they propagate through higher layers. Our results demonstrate that TracIn-WE significantly outperforms existing last-layer methods on case deletion evaluations across three language classification tasks and various models. Furthermore, TracIn-WE generates influence scores not only for entire training inputs but also for individual words within them, offering additional utility for debugging.

Extensive research confirms that the Bayesian optimization framework is highly efficient and effective for analog circuit synthesis. Nevertheless, prior studies have predominantly concentrated on creating informative surrogate models or efficient acquisition functions, largely overlooking the challenging task of finding the global optimum within the acquisition function surface. This paper introduces a fast and robust Bayesian optimization approach for analog circuit synthesis that utilizes one-dimensional subspaces. By optimizing only one-dimensional subspaces at each iteration, we significantly reduce the computational burden of the framework while ensuring the acquisition function is maximized safely. Furthermore, we combine various dimension selection strategies to adaptively balance between global and local search. Leveraging a batch Bayesian optimization framework allows us to fully utilize hardware resources, thereby accelerating the optimization process. Quantitative experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm speeds up the optimization procedure by up to 9x compared to LP-EI and by 38x compared to REMBOpBO when the batch size is set to 15.

We investigate solutions to the Lippmann-Schwinger equation within systems composed of multiple subsystems characterized by distinct dynamical timescales or energy scales. We establish two theorems demonstrating that: 1) scattering from slow to fast subsystems is unexpectedly suppressed, and 2) a method for calculating the scattering wavefunction exists in the limit where the ratio between these scales diverges. These theorems depend on broadly applicable assumptions, rendering them valid for a vast array of systems. Such results are particularly valuable for analyzing scattering at resonantly Floquet-driven impurities. As an illustration, we apply the theorem to study pair breaking in a Fermi-Hubbard chain situated at a resonantly Floquet-driven impurity.

Simulating the time evolution of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) for large-scale systems is vital across various scientific and engineering fields, including fluid dynamics, weather prediction, and their associated inverse optimization tasks. Nevertheless, traditional solvers and contemporary deep learning-based surrogate models remain highly computationally demanding due to their local evolution nature, which necessitates updating the state of every discretized cell at each inference step. To address this, we present Latent Evolution of PDEs (LE-PDE), a straightforward, rapid, and scalable approach designed to accelerate both PDE simulation and inverse optimization. LE-PDE constructs a compact, global representation of the system and propagates it entirely within the latent space using learned latent evolution models. This method achieves significant speed-ups by updating a substantially smaller latent dimension over extended rollouts rather than operating in the full input space. We propose novel learning objectives to capture these latent dynamics effectively, ensuring long-term stability. Additionally, we introduce methods to accelerate the inverse optimization of boundary conditions via backpropagation through time in the latent space, alongside an annealing strategy to mitigate issues related to boundary condition non-differentiability and sparse interactions. Evaluations on a 1D benchmark of nonlinear PDEs, 2D Navier-Stokes flows transitioning to turbulence, and inverse boundary condition optimization in 2D Navier-Stokes demonstrate that LE-PDE reduces the update dimension by up to 128x and improves speed by up to 15x compared to state-of-the-art deep learning surrogates and other strong baselines, while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Although numerous technologies have emerged recently to display audiovisual data, creating interfaces for tactile information remains a significant challenge. We introduce a wearable tactile device featuring an omnidirectional pressure system driven by pneumatic actuators. Specifically, this system utilizes a choker worn around the neck that incorporates a pneumatic actuator capable of applying pressure in any direction. This allows the user to receive haptic cues regarding the direction to walk, as well as signals to begin or cease movement. The paper details the device's construction, the results of evaluation experiments, our assessment of the prototype, and future development plans.

The most significant challenge to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model is the tension between the Hubble constant $H_0$ values derived from the local distance ladder and those inferred from the cosmic microwave background. Although numerous models have been suggested to alleviate or resolve this issue, no fully satisfactory solution has emerged to date. In this study, we examine Hubble parameter $H(z)$ data using the Gaussian process (GP) method and report a late-time transition in $H_0$, where it shifts from a lower value in early cosmic epochs to a higher one at later times. This discovery mitigates the Hubble tension by approximately 70\%. Our findings align with the decreasing trend of $H_0$ observed in time-delay cosmography of lensed quasars at the $1\sigma$ confidence level and support the hypothesis that the Hubble crisis stems from new physics beyond the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework. Furthermore, we find that neither the $\Lambda$CDM nor the $w$CDM models exhibit such a transition behavior.

This numerical investigation examines the interaction of two fuzzy dark matter solitons lacking explicit self-interaction, yielding an effective cross-section for velocity dissipation. The resulting cross-section exhibits an inverse cubic relationship with velocity, a finding supported by an analytic interpretation. Leveraging this result, we approximate the spatial displacements occurring during head-on mergers of fuzzy dark matter halos, a phenomenon potentially linked to observed offsets between dark matter and stars in colliding galaxy clusters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gravitational cooling is a critical factor during these collision events.

This study examines boundary feedback control for single-input-single-output (SISO) one-dimensional linear hyperbolic systems featuring anti-located sensing and actuation. A primary challenge in output feedback stabilization is the necessity for dynamic control laws incorporating delayed output values (either directly or via state observers), which often lack robustness against infinitesimal uncertainties in characteristic velocities. This paper aims to elucidate key aspects of this problem by analyzing the feedback stabilization of an unstable open-loop system composed of two interconnected transport equations with anti-located boundary sensing and actuation. The central contribution demonstrates that robustness against delay uncertainties is restored once even a minimal amount of diffusion is introduced into the system. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that diffusion's impact on stability is not self-evident, illustrated by a simple alternative example where diffusion actually induces destabilization.

We have developed an experimentally feasible model that generates twin beam states, allowing the individual photon statistics to transition from thermal to Poissonian while maintaining non-classical mode correlations. We investigated the utility of these states for loss measurement by evaluating three distinct estimators against correlated thermal twin beam states produced via spontaneous parametric down-conversion or four-wave mixing. Furthermore, by integrating photon subtraction into the model, we demonstrated its superiority in loss estimation compared to un-subtracted states, regardless of whether squeezing or per-photon exposure of the absorbing sample is held constant. For example, at fixed squeezing, two-photon subtraction yields up to a threefold advantage. While the benefit of photon subtraction largely diminishes in standard regimes under per-photon exposure, an unexpected finding reveals that in specific operating conditions, this scheme can still offer up to a 20% improvement over correlated Poisson beam results. Additionally, we conducted a comparative analysis of these estimators to identify the optimal method for loss estimation, presenting outcomes across all model parameter values that span the statistics of twin beam states from thermal to Poissonian.

The ALICE Collaboration has recently measured charm-hadron production at midrapidity in proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 5.02 and 13 TeV. The findings indicate that the ratios of baryon to meson yields deviate from predictions based on hadronization models tuned to data from $\rm e^{+}e^{-}$ and ep collisions for various charm-baryon types. These observations imply that charm fragmentation fractions are not universal and that the baryon-to-meson ratio varies depending on the collision system. The study also compares these results with predictions from Monte Carlo event generators and theoretical calculations.

This article focuses on Pickup and Delivery Problems with Transfers (PDP-T). We will first introduce the foundational Pickup and Delivery Problem (PDP), then provide a detailed description and mathematical formulation of PDP-T to clarify the challenge at hand. Finally, we will present various approaches used to solve this type of problem.

This paper investigates various weighted norm inequalities concerning the Opdam--Cherednik transform. We derive multiple forms of the Heisenberg--Pauli--Weyl inequality applicable to this transform, including an extension that utilizes weights with distinct exponents and a variant incorporating $L^p$-norms for the transform. Additionally, we establish a version of the Hardy--Littlewood inequality for the Opdam--Cherednik transform. Furthermore, we present further modifications of the Heisenberg--Pauli--Weyl inequality, specifically the Nash-type and Clarkson-type inequalities tailored to this transform.

To ensure greater reliability and extend battery life, it is crucial for both users and manufacturers to grasp the nuances of charging quality and smartphone battery performance; however, the wide variety of devices and varying user habits make this a significant challenge. This study examines a substantial dataset comprising battery analytics from 30,000 devices across 1,500 distinct smartphone models. By investigating battery properties and state of charge during the charging process, we uncover the characteristics of various power management system components, including charging mechanisms, state of charge estimation methods, and inherent battery traits. Furthermore, we explore the diverse charging patterns exhibited by both devices and their users.

**Context.** High-resolution imaging of the solar photosphere identifies fine structures, notably magnetic bright points (MBPs), which are small-scale features linked to strong kilogauss magnetic fields. Investigating these ubiquitous elements across all solar cycle phases is crucial for understanding their impact on solar atmospheric dynamics and their potential role in coronal heating. **Aims.** This study characterizes the size and velocity distributions of MBPs using two datasets of quiet Sun images captured by the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT/Hinode) and the High-resolution Fast Imager (HiFI/GREGOR) in the G-band (4308 Å). **Methods.** We employed an automatic segmentation algorithm to detect MBPs, tracked them to measure proper motions, and conducted a statistical analysis of hundreds of features to generate histograms of area, diameter, and horizontal velocity. **Results.** The findings indicate that MBP areas and diameters follow log-normal distributions best fitted by two components, while velocity vector components adhere to Gaussian distributions and vector magnitudes to a Rayleigh distribution, both also revealing a two-component structure. **Conclusions.** These results suggest the existence of two distinct MBP populations in the photosphere: one associated with stronger network magnetic flux and another with weaker intranetwork flux. Furthermore, the study highlights how the differing spatial resolutions of the GREGOR and Hinode instruments influence detection rates and average measured values.

Identifying semantic data types is a vital component of data science, supporting applications such as automated data cleaning, schema alignment, data discovery, type normalization, and the detection of sensitive information. Current approaches, which rely on regular expressions or dictionary lookups, struggle with unclean or unseen data and are restricted to a narrow range of semantic types. While existing machine learning techniques often depend on extracting numerous engineered features to train models like logistic regression, random forests, or feedforward neural networks, this paper presents DCoM. DCoM utilizes a suite of multi-input, NLP-driven deep neural networks that bypass extensive feature engineering by feeding raw column values directly to the model as text. Trained on 686,765 data columns from the VizNet corpus covering 78 distinct semantic types, DCoM significantly outperforms contemporary methods on the same dataset.

Driven by cold-atom experiments and the goal of elucidating far-from-equilibrium quantum transport, we perform an analytical investigation into the dynamics of spin helices within the one-dimensional $XX$ model. By employing a Jordan-Wigner transformation, we map the spin chain to a non-interacting Fermi gas characterized by straightforward equations of motion. Despite this simplification, the resulting dynamics are complex, as the initial spin-helix state maps to a highly nonequilibrium fermion distribution. Our analysis reveals a separation of timescales between in-plane and out-of-plane spin behaviors, supported by insights from both a uniform spin chain and a semiclassical model. A principal finding is that spin correlation functions exhibit a $t^{-1/2}$ decay at long times, contrasting with the exponential decay typically observed in experiments.

Media-based modulation (MBM), which leverages the rich scattering characteristics of transmission environments through distinct radiation patterns of a single reconfigurable antenna (RA), offers fresh perspectives for future communication systems. Building on this innovative transmission principle, this study presents SimMBM, a realistic, two-dimensional, and open-source channel simulator designed to support diverse applications of MBM systems within sub-6 GHz frequency bands across various environments.

Language models designed for historical language states are growing in significance for optimizing the digitization and analysis of ancient texts. Given that these historical forms are both more complex to process and less abundant in available corpora, specialized efforts are required to train natural language processing (NLP) tools tailored to such data. This paper details our work in developing NLP resources for Early Modern French (spanning the 16th to 18th centuries). We introduce the $\text{FreEM}_{\text{max}}$ corpus of Early Modern French and D'AlemBERT, a RoBERTa-based model trained on this corpus. We assess D'AlemBERT's utility by fine-tuning it for part-of-speech tagging, where it surpasses prior results on the test set. Crucially, we demonstrate the model's transfer learning capabilities, as its performance on less-resourced time periods improves when leveraging data from more abundant ones. We make D'AlemBERT and the open-access portion of the $\text{FreEM}_{\text{max}}$ corpus available.

Training robust and diverse GAN-based models for video generation is challenging due to the three-dimensional complexity and high stochasticity of the data space. Learning disentangled representations enhances robustness and offers control over the sampling process. Recent advancements in this field address video generation by treating motion and appearance as orthogonal components, utilizing architectures that efficiently separate them. These existing methods depend on manually designed structures that impose specific priors on the generator to decompose latent motion and appearance codes. Drawing inspiration from recent autoencoder-based image generation techniques, we introduce AVLAE (Adversarial Video Latent AutoEncoder), a two-stream latent autoencoder that learns the video distribution through adversarial training. Specifically, we propose autoencoding the motion and appearance latent vectors within an adversarial framework. Our results demonstrate that this approach successfully disentangles motion and appearance codes without requiring explicit structural composition in the generator. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method.

This paper offers a concise overview of meta-learning's evolution and outlines its role in advancing general artificial intelligence. By enhancing a model's ability to generalize, meta-learning creates versatile algorithms capable of handling both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. General AI aims to substitute task-specific models with broad algorithmic frameworks, thereby increasing automation across diverse problem-solving tasks. This work summarizes meta-learning's key contributions to general AI, such as memory modules, meta-learners, coevolution, curiosity, forgetting, and AI-generating algorithms. Furthermore, it explores the relationship between meta-learning and general AI, detailing how meta-learning can be leveraged to design general AI algorithms.

QuasinormalModes.jl is a Julia library designed to calculate quasinormal modes for any General Relativity model where the perturbation equation takes the form of a second-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation (ODE). Beyond this, it can also determine discrete eigenvalues for any second-order homogeneous ODE, such as energy eigenstates in the time-independent Schrödinger equation, assuming these eigenvalues exist. The package offers a flexible and user-friendly API, requiring users only to input the coefficients of the target ODE along with its boundary and asymptotic conditions. Users have the option to perform calculations using either machine or arbitrary precision arithmetic and can choose to run computations sequentially or in parallel via threads. Furthermore, the API is designed to avoid imposing a specific workflow, allowing researchers to integrate and adapt its functionality into their existing pipelines without disruption.

We examine a scenario involving two parties, Alice and Bob, who hold $X_{1}^{n}$ and $X_{2}^{n}$, respectively, where these samples are independently and identically distributed (IID) according to a joint probability mass function (PMF) $P_{X_1 X_2}$. Alice and Bob transmit information to Charles via noiseless communication channels with capacities $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively. The objective is for Charles to generate samples $Y^{n}$ such that the joint distribution of $(X_{1}^{n},X_{2}^{n},Y^{n})$ approximates the target product distribution $\prod P_{X_1 X_2 Y}$ in terms of total variation distance. Furthermore, the three parties may utilize pairwise shared common randomness at rates $C_1$ and $C_2$. This work aims to characterize the achievable region of rate quadruples $(R_1,R_2,C_1,C_2)$. We establish both sufficient conditions, represented as an inner bound, and necessary conditions, represented as an outer bound, for this three-party configuration. Our approach employs a joint-typicality-based random coding argument that incorporates specific encoding and decoding strategies to achieve soft covering, alongside a relevant relaxation of the PMF constraints for the encoders.

Due to global social distancing measures, social media has become the primary communication channel for most people. However, millions of individuals suffering from mental health conditions have faced increased isolation, hindering their access to in-person support. Consequently, they are increasingly turning to online platforms to express themselves and seek guidance on managing their disorders. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately 450 million people are affected by these conditions, which, including depression and anxiety, significantly impact physical well-being. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been introduced to assist mental health professionals, such as psychiatrists and psychologists, in making decisions based on authentic patient data, including medical records, behavioral patterns, and social media usage. AI innovations have shown significant success in various real-world applications, ranging from computer vision to healthcare. This study examines unstructured user data from Reddit to classify five prevalent mental illnesses: depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, ADHD, and PTSD. By training multi-class models using traditional machine learning, deep learning, and transfer learning techniques, we aim to detect these disorders. This initiative seeks to enhance the public health system by automating detection and alerting relevant authorities about individuals requiring urgent assistance.

Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) isolates the primary modes that define a system's inherent dynamics from measurement data. To accurately identify these dominant modes, the DMD algorithm requires high-quality input sequences. Consequently, this paper introduces two criteria to validate dataset suitability for DMD: the Persistence of Excitation (PE) condition and the Granger Causality Test (GCT). Virtual data sequences are constructed using Hankel matrix representations, where adding new state variables expands the dimensionality of the subspace containing essential system modes. The PE condition establishes a minimum trajectory length, while GCT determines the model order. While satisfying PE allows for the estimation of an approximate linear model, the temporal causality verified by GCT is necessary to ensure the predictability of the identified model. The proposed methodology is validated through its application to coherency identification (CI) in a multi-machine power system (MMPS), a critical aspect of transient stability analysis. The importance of both PE and GCT is further illustrated through various case studies conducted on a 22-bus, six-generator system.

This study investigates protoplasmic streaming in plant cells, specifically *Chara braunii*, by modeling the flow as a two-dimensional Couette flow with Brownian motion occurring between parallel plates. Protoplasmic streaming is a subject of significant interest across various fields, including agriculture and biotechnology. Since plant dimensions are influenced by streaming velocity and the driving force generated by molecular motors, understanding the detailed mechanics of this velocity is crucial. Although recent studies have simulated experimentally observed peaks in velocity distributions using a 2D Langevin Navier-Stokes (LNS) equation based on vortex and flow functions, accurately simulating actual 3D flows requires the standard Navier-Stokes equation for velocity. It is important to note that for 2D flows, the equations governing velocity are not always equivalent to those for vorticity and stream function. In this paper, we demonstrate that a 2D LNS equation formulated for velocity and pressure effectively simulates protoplasmic streaming, with results matching both experimental data and previous 2D LNS simulations based on vorticity and flow functions. Furthermore, dimensional analysis reveals how numerical outcomes depend on the strength ($D$) of the Brownian random force and physical parameters like kinematic viscosity and cell size. This analysis elucidates how the position of the peak in the normalized velocity distribution shifts in response to these varying parameters.

This paper explores and compares three prominent control theories applied to the simulation of a two-wheeled self-balancing robot using Robot Operating System (ROS) and Gazebo. Two-wheeled self-balancing robots represent a compelling application of the inverted pendulum system. The study examines PID, LQR, and fuzzy logic controllers, alongside the modeling and algorithms underlying the robot simulation. The primary objectives are to detail the construction of a robot model within ROS and Gazebo, test various control strategies, document the entire process, and provide an analysis and comparative evaluation of the different control theories on the system.

We examine how extended radio sources, specifically Centaurus A and Galactic supernova remnants (SNRs), impact the detection of the statistical $21\,\rm{cm}$ signal from the Epoch of Reionisation (EoR) using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). Although these sources are usually disregarded due to their location in heavily attenuated regions of the MWA primary beam, their combined flux densities reach $10\,\rm{Jy}$ on angular scales relevant to $21\,\rm{cm}$ detection. We developed custom 2D Gaussian multi-component models for Centaurus A and Galactic SNRs to simulate visibilities from two MWA snapshot observations. After gridding these visibilities, we performed a Fourier transform with respect to frequency, applying both spherical and cylindrical averaging to generate 1D and 2D power spectra. Comparing the simulated 1D power spectra to the anticipated $21\,\rm{cm}$ spectrum reveals that, despite their position in low-gain areas of the primary beam, these sources collectively possess sufficient power ($\sim10^4-10^5\,\rm{mK^2}\,\it{h^{-3}} \,\rm{Mpc^{3}}$) on EoR-relevant modes ($|\mathbf{k}| \leq 0.1 h \rm{Mpc}^{-1}$) to mask the $21\,\rm{cm}$ signal ($10^4\,\rm{mK^2}\,\it{h^{-3}} \,\rm{Mpc^{3}}$). Our results indicate that removing $50-90\%$ of these sources is necessary to reduce leakage to $10-20\%$ of the $21\,\rm{cm}$ power spectrum on EoR significant modes. Consequently, the influence of widefield extended sources will significantly affect the detectability of the $21\,\rm{cm}$ signal for both the MWA and the future Square Kilometre Array (SKA).

High-quality machine translation (MT) systems and other multilingual NLP applications rely on parallel text, yet such data is scarce for many South Asian languages. This paper introduces PMIndia, a new publicly available corpus containing parallel sentences that pair 13 major Indian languages with English, with up to 56,000 sentences per language pair. We detail the construction process, including an evaluation of two automatic sentence alignment techniques, and share preliminary Neural Machine Translation results derived from this corpus.

This study computes the cross section for inclusive dijet photoproduction in ultraperipheral heavy-ion collisions at the CERN Large Hadron Collider using next-to-leading order perturbative QCD, showing that the results accurately describe ATLAS experimental data. By applying Bayesian reweighting, we analyze how this data constrains nuclear parton distribution functions (nPDFs), demonstrating a potential reduction of small-$x$ uncertainties by a factor of two. Additionally, we forecast outcomes for diffractive dijet photoproduction in such collisions and assess its capacity to clarify the debated mechanism of QCD factorization breaking within diffraction.

This paper proposes utilizing color coding to differentiate between syntax and semantics as a pedagogical aid in logic courses. This distinction also provides a basis for examining certain philosophical questions related to semantics.

Since the geometric effects induced by passing gravitational waves cannot be detected locally due to the relationship between proper and coordinate distances, we investigated electromagnetic wave equations within this gravitational background. Our findings indicate that the expansion and contraction of wavelengths occur synchronously with the objects being measured. The presence of gravitational waves introduces dissipation and dispersion into electromagnetic wave propagation, where the gravitational wave phase governs both the dissipation and dispersion terms in the telegrapher's equation. A linearly polarized laser beam traveling in the same direction as incoming gravitational waves could potentially provide a local metric measurement. In scenarios involving pulsed beats, if the relaxation time exceeds the gravitational wave period, the detector would only register the modulation of the beats. Finally, we propose a non-local interference experiment to detect high-frequency gravitational waves, analogous to measuring gravitational redshift. Combined with conventional detectors, this approach would yield further and mutually complementary measurements of gravitational waves.

Higgs pair production offers a distinct method for determining the strength of the Higgs self-interaction and limiting the form of the Higgs potential. Among future proposed facilities, a circular 100 TeV proton-proton collider is projected to yield the most accurate measurement of this vital parameter. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the most viable decay modes and calculates the anticipated sensitivity of their combined results, based on an integrated luminosity of 30 ab$^{-1}$. Depending on the assumed systematic uncertainties, the precision for measuring the Higgs self-coupling at a 68% confidence level is expected to fall between 3.4% and 7.8%.

Parker Solar Probe (PSP) observations in the inner heliosphere reveal abundant wave activity, with ion and electron cyclotron modes being particularly significant. Despite their importance, the origins and evolution of these waves near the Sun remain unclear, specifically whether they originate as emissions from the solar atmosphere or grow locally via plasma instability within the heliosphere. To resolve this debate, it is essential to analyze the energy change rate of the wave modes. This study introduces a novel technique for measuring the energy change rate of plasma waves and applies it to electromagnetic field data collected by PSP. Our analysis of the wave Poynting flux in the solar wind frame identifies the waves as outward-propagating fast-magnetosonic or whistler modes, rather than sunward-propagating ones. Furthermore, we present the first evidence of local growth for these fast-magnetosonic/whistler waves in the inner heliosphere, derived from the spectra of the real and imaginary components of the wave frequencies. The energy change rate increases and remains positive within the same wavenumber range where electromagnetic field power spectral densities show peaks, clearly demonstrating that the observed fast-magnetosonic/whistler waves grow locally to large amplitudes.

This study introduces novel ensemble models for classifying multivariate functional data, constructed by combining weak learners based on semi-metrics. These models expand existing semi-metric approaches from univariate to multivariate contexts, introduce fresh semi-metrics for calculating inter-function distances, and employ stacked generalization to offer more adaptable strategies for integrating weak learners. We utilize these ensembles to detect respondents' struggles with survey items, aiming to enhance survey data quality. To predict difficulty, we analyze mouse movement trajectories generated during web survey interactions, where specific questions were altered to establish two scenarios with varying difficulty levels.

Multidimensional population balance models (PBMs) characterize chemical and biological systems that exhibit distributions across two or more intrinsic attributes, such as size and age or independent spatial coordinates. Adding further intrinsic variables to a PBM enhances its descriptive power and is often essential for capturing specific phenomena of interest. Since most relevant PBMs lack analytical solutions, researchers typically rely on computationally intensive high-order finite difference or finite volume methods to derive accurate numerical results. This paper introduces a finite difference approach utilizing operator splitting, where each sub-problem is solved at the limit of numerical stability. This method yields a zero discretization error for specific PBM classes and sufficiently low error for others. By combining specially designed meshes and variable transformations, the scheme leverages the commutativity of differential operators found in many PBM categories. Consequently, the proposed approach incurs minimal computational cost—potentially limited only to memory reallocation—and multiple case studies validate its performance.

Transfer learning (TL) is emerging as a vital technique for applying neural networks (NNs) to scientific domains like weather/climate forecasting and turbulence modeling. TL facilitates out-of-distribution generalization, such as parameter extrapolation, and allows for the effective integration of diverse training sources, including both simulations and observations. In this process, specific layers of a pre-trained NN, originally developed for a base system, are fine-tuned using a limited dataset from a target system. To optimize TL, two critical questions must be addressed: 1) which layers should be re-trained, and 2) what underlying physics are acquired during this transfer? This work introduces a novel framework and analyses to answer these questions across various multi-scale, nonlinear systems. Our method integrates spectral analysis of system data with the spectral characteristics of convolutional NN activations and kernels, thereby elucidating the mechanics of TL through the lens of the system's nonlinear physics. Applying this to 2D turbulence setups via subgrid-scale modeling, we demonstrate that learned kernels function as combinations of low-, band-, and high-pass filters, with TL acquiring new filters that align with the spectral disparities between base and target systems. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the shallowest layers are optimal for re-training in these scenarios, challenging the conventional wisdom prevalent in machine learning literature. This framework enables the pre-identification of the most suitable layers for re-training based on physics and neural network theory. Collectively, these insights clarify the physics captured by TL and offer a structured approach to guide its application in broad scientific and engineering fields, such as climate change modeling.

Deep neural networks currently dominate modern vision systems, delivering superior performance at the expense of higher computational complexity. Given the critical need for real-time operation and minimal energy consumption in applications like wearable devices, autonomous vehicles, edge IoT, and sensor networks, various optimization strategies—including quantization, pruning, and specialized lightweight architectures—are employed. Due to the logarithmic distribution of weights within neural network layers, Power-of-Two (PoT) quantization offers a method to achieve high performance with significant reductions in computational precision, utilizing 4-bit weights or fewer. This approach enables the replacement of standard Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) units with more energy-efficient Bitshift-Accumulate (BAC) units. This paper demonstrates that a hardware neural network accelerator featuring PoT weights, implemented on the Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC ZCU104 SoC FPGA, achieves at least a 1.4x improvement in energy efficiency compared to uniform quantization. Furthermore, to further lower power requirements by skipping computations for zero weights, we introduce a novel pruning technique tailored for logarithmic quantization.

For Bayesian inference sampling, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)—which autonomously determine trajectory duration—are widely used. However, these methods can be computationally expensive due to the need for numerous numerical gradients of the target density. We introduce Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) integrated with HMC and NUTS; once trained, HNNs eliminate the requirement for numerical gradients during sampling. Furthermore, they maintain critical properties like perfect time reversibility and Hamiltonian conservation, ensuring stationarity and suitability for these samplers. We also present Latent HNNs (L-HNNs), an extension capable of predicting latent variables, which provide greater expressivity and lower integration errors than standard HNNs. Additionally, we apply L-HNNs within NUTS alongside an online error monitoring mechanism to mitigate sample degeneracy in low-probability regions. Testing on complex, heavy-tailed, and high-curvature densities demonstrates that this approach successfully infers target distributions. Specifically, L-HNNs with online error monitoring reduced the number of required numerical gradients by 1–2 orders of magnitude compared to traditional NUTS and increased the effective sample size (ESS) per gradient by an order of magnitude.

This study addresses the challenge of augmenting an undirected graph with a specific number of new edges to reduce the graph's diameter, subject to the constraint that each vertex receives a limited number of additional edges. This problem is driven by network design scenarios where the goal is to minimize maximum communication latency without overburdening individual nodes. We introduce three distinct algorithms for this purpose, each offering unique advantages. Particular attention is given to the matching augmentation scenario, where each vertex is connected to at most one new edge; for this case, we demonstrate an inapproximability result and establish bounds on the minimum achievable diameter when applied to paths. Additionally, we conduct an empirical evaluation comparing these algorithms across various real-world network types.

Variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods (SGLMs) have previously been realized using the Nordsieck technique; however, this paper presents variable stepsize SGLMs formulated directly on nonuniform grids. We derive the order conditions for these methods, specifically targeting order $p$ with stage order $q=p$, and provide explicit examples achieving up to fourth-order accuracy. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed methods in addressing nonstiff problems and validate their theoretical convergence orders.

Computational feasibility is a central concern that directs how biological and artificial intelligence systems are framed and modeled. Often, the defined capacities of cognitive systems are influenced by unexamined intuitions regarding the complexity and search space of specific subcomputations.
