Ultimately, the tail risk metric derived from our model offers significant insights for asset allocation and portfolio insurance.

The expansion of cyber networks and the growing complexity of cyber-attacks have created significant hurdles for intrusion detection systems. The foremost challenge lies in identifying intricate, multi-stage attacks in real-time while managing the massive volume of traffic generated by modern networks. This paper introduces PRISM, a hierarchical intrusion detection architecture that leverages a novel attacker behavior model-based sampling technique to reduce real-time processing overhead. PRISM features a distinctive multi-layered design that distributes network traffic monitoring to enhance processing efficiency and system modularity. It utilizes a Hidden Markov Model-based prediction mechanism to detect multi-stage attacks and determine attack progression for proactive countermeasures. Additionally, PRISM incorporates a stream management procedure that resolves alert reordering issues arising from distributed alert reporting. To assess PRISM's performance, various metrics were proposed and experiments were conducted on a multi-stage attack dataset. The results demonstrate up to a 7.5x reduction in processing overhead compared to standard centralized intrusion detection systems, without compromising prediction accuracy, while also showing the capability to promptly identify different stages of an attack.

Alloys of the Si$_{y}$Ge$_{1-x-y}$(C,Sn,Pb)$_{x}$ composition have garnered considerable interest as a pathway to creating direct-gap group-IV semiconductors. By utilizing density functional theory (DFT) with both the local density approximation and hybrid Heyd-Scuzeria-Ernzerhof exchange-correlation functionals, we calculated lattice parameters, relaxed and internal elastic constants, and Kleinman internal strain parameters for both elemental diamond-structure group-IV materials and zinc blende IV-IV compounds. Our DFT results corroborate a lesser-known experimental reassessment of $\alpha$-Sn elastic constants while refuting a recent prediction of dynamic instability in certain IV-IV compounds. We combined these DFT-derived structural and elastic properties with a recently developed analytical parametrization of a harmonic valence force field (VFF) [Phys. Rev. B 100, 094112 (2019)] to generate comprehensive VFF potentials for Si$_{y}$Ge$_{1-x-y}$(C,Sn,Pb)$_{x}$ and Si$_{x}$Ge$_{1-x}$ alloys. This analytical approach precisely replicates relaxed elastic constants and Kleinman parameters without requiring numerical fitting, thereby facilitating accurate yet computationally efficient lattice relaxation. The validity of these VFF potentials was verified by comparing them against DFT supercell relaxation results for: (i) ordered Si (Ge) alloy supercells with substitutional C, Ge (Si), Sn, or Pb impurities, including comparisons to a model analytical VFF, and (ii) disordered Si$_{x}$Ge$_{1-x}$ alloy supercells. The presented VFF potentials facilitate accurate and low-cost relaxation of large-scale supercells modeling bulk-like group-IV alloys or heterostructures. These tools provide essential inputs for first-principles or empirical electronic structure calculations and support structural analysis and strain field computations in heterostructures for device applications.

Dark sectors featuring Abelian gauge symmetries can couple to standard matter through kinetic mixing. In these frameworks, magnetic monopoles originating from a broken dark $U(1)$ manifest within our sector as confined milli-magnetically charged entities under ordinary electromagnetism. Constraints derived from halo ellipticity impose significant limits on the interaction strength of dark magnetic Coulomb monopoles. Although the monopole ground state remains stable in a vacuum with zero magnetic charge or moment, it becomes quantum mechanically unstable when exposed to an external ordinary magnetic field. Should such states constitute a substantial portion of the local dark matter density, their decay within a galactic timeframe could drain considerable energy from the galactic magnetic field. We update and broaden this "Parker Bound" regarding galactic magnetic energy loss for milli-monopoles, yielding the most stringent constraints available for these states across a broad spectrum of monopole masses, while remaining consistent with our halo ellipticity limits.

Recent years have witnessed substantial advancements in video frame interpolation; however, most current approaches rely on standard metrics to evaluate results, with only a few exceptions utilizing time-intensive user studies. Since interpolated videos often contain distinctive artifacts, these conventional metrics frequently fail to align with human perception. Although some recent deep learning-based perceptual metrics show better consistency with human judgment, their effectiveness on videos is limited because they overlook temporal dynamics. To address this, we introduce a specialized perceptual quality metric designed specifically for video frame interpolation. Unlike methods that analyze frames in isolation, our approach learns perceptual features directly from video sequences. It utilizes pyramid features derived from video frames and integrates Swin Transformer-based spatio-temporal modules to capture both spatial and temporal information. We trained this metric using a newly curated dataset for video frame interpolation quality assessment. Experimental results demonstrate that our dedicated metric surpasses state-of-the-art methods in evaluating video frame interpolation. Our code and models are publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/hqqxyy/VFIPS}.

This study examines the Randall-Sundrum (RS) framework not as a solution to the hierarchy problem, but as a theory of flavour offering an alternative to Froggatt-Nielsen models. We analyze a modified RS setup situated between the GUT and Planck scales, a configuration that mitigates constraints from flavour physics. Fermion masses and mixing angles are fitted at the GUT scale, with the ranges of bulk mass parameters derived via a $\chi^2$ fit that accounts for $\mathcal{O}(1)$ parameter variations. In the hadronic sector, the heavy top quark necessitates large bulk mass parameters that localize the right-handed top near the IR brane. We evaluate two scenarios for neutrino masses: Planck-scale lepton number violation and Dirac neutrino masses. Unlike weak-scale RS models, both scenarios yield reasonable data fits, with the Planck-scale lepton number violation case performing marginally better than the Dirac scenario. In the supersymmetric extension, the fits remain largely unchanged except for variations in $\tan\beta$. If the Higgs superfield and the SUSY breaking spurion are localized on the same brane, sfermion mass structures are dictated by the zero-mode profiles of bulk hypermultiplets, while trilinear terms mirror the Yukawa matrices. The resulting squark spectrum, estimated at $\sim 2\text{--}3 \text{TeV}$, satisfies the requirement for a $125 \text{ GeV}$ Higgs mass and adheres to flavour-violating constraints.

This study presents an N-Body method for calculating Fock exchange matrices, evaluating both scenarios with and without permutational symmetry. By utilizing an embedded metric-query, the approach attains an O(N lg N) computational complexity and enables the hierarchical application of direct self-consistent field (SCF) criteria. While permutational symmetry yields a fourfold advantage in small systems, this benefit diminishes as system size grows or as neglect criteria become more permissive. The research lays the groundwork for two future developments: (1) integrating range queries into multi-level multipole schemes to achieve rank reduction, and (2) implementing recursive task parallelism.

This study presents the precise localization of X-ray emission from two strongly lensed active galactic nuclei (AGN): CLASS B0712+472 at redshift $z=1.34$ and CLASS B1608+656 at $z=1.394$. By integrating parametric lens modeling with Bayesian analysis, we developed a new technique to achieve milliarcsecond X-ray astrometry. Our results place the X-ray sources in CLASS B0712+472 and CLASS B1608+656 within 11 mas and 9 mas of their radio counterparts, respectively. In CLASS B0712+472, the X-ray emission aligns spatially with both radio and optical emissions. Conversely, in CLASS B1608+656, the X-ray emission matches the radio source but is offset from the optical emission at the $1\sigma$ level, identifying it as a potential offset AGN. This level of astrometric precision surpasses current X-ray instrument capabilities by two orders of magnitude. The validated methodology enables the search for offset and binary AGN at redshifts greater than 1 and offers a direct means to test supermassive black hole formation models in a previously underconstrained redshift regime.

Following the introduction of GAIL, adversarial imitation learning (AIL) has garnered significant research attention. Among the various methods developed, ValueDice stands out for its notable advancements: it outperforms the traditional Behavioral Cloning (BC) approach in offline settings and demands fewer interactions than GAIL in online scenarios. The question arises whether these gains stem from more sophisticated algorithmic designs. We address this with three key findings. First, we demonstrate that ValueDice can be reduced to BC within the offline context. Second, we confirm that overfitting is a critical issue in data-scarce environments and that regularization is essential; specifically, we show that applying weight decay allows BC to nearly match the expert performance achieved by ValueDice. These two points clarify the source of ValueDice's superior offline results. Third, we reveal that ValueDice fails when the expert trajectory is subsampled; its success relies on having a complete trajectory, under which conditions it behaves similarly to the highly effective BC. Finally, we explore the broader implications of these insights for imitation learning research beyond ValueDice.

We conducted a systematic investigation of X-ray cavities by analyzing archival Chandra data from nearby galaxy clusters identified through their Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) signatures in the Planck survey. This selection method yields a nearly unbiased, mass-complete sample ideal for examining the full AGN feedback duty cycle. Through X-ray image analysis, we identified cavities in 30 out of 164 clusters, representing a detection fraction of 18%. When adjusting for spatial resolution to align with the high-redshift SPT-SZ sample, this fraction drops to 9%, matching the high-z results and suggesting that AGN feedback has remained stable over nearly 8 billion years. This observation aligns with previous findings regarding the non-evolution of cool-core cluster fractions. Furthermore, our calculations of cavity power ($P_{\rm cav}$) indicate that the majority of systems in our sample possess sufficient AGN heating to counteract the radiative cooling losses of the intracluster medium.

Soft X-ray transients are identified during outbursts, where their X-ray luminosity rises by several orders of magnitude. These events signal a poorly understood transition in the system's spectral state from a low/hard to a high/soft configuration. This study examines the spectral characteristics of the transient MAXI J0637$-$430, utilizing data from the \textit{SXT} and \textit{LAXPC} instruments aboard the \textit{AstroSat} mission. The source was monitored for approximately 60 ks across two observations conducted on November 8th and 21st, 2019, shortly after its discovery. Flux-resolved spectral analysis reveals a multi-colour blackbody component attributed to the accretion disk alongside a thermal Comptonization component. The blackbody's stable low temperature of roughly 0.55 keV suggests a cool accretion disk with an inner radius of a few hundred kilometers. Furthermore, we detect a relativistically broadened Gaussian line at 6.4 keV. The disk-dominated flux, a photon power-law index of $\gtrapprox 2$, and a constant inner disk radius confirm that the source is in the soft state. Based on these findings, we conclude that MAXI J0637$-$430 is a strong candidate for a black hole X-ray binary.

Carbon dioxide (CO₂) ice is predominantly found on Ariel's trailing hemisphere but is largely missing from the leading side. This hemispherical asymmetry supports the theory that CO₂ is produced radiolytically through charged particle bombardment of water ice and carbon-rich materials in the regolith. While previous studies mapped this longitudinal distribution using 13 near-infrared spectra taken at low sub-observer latitudes (30°S to 30°N), this research expands the investigation with 18 new spectra: two at low latitudes, five at mid-latitudes (31°–44°N), and eleven at high latitudes (45°–51°N). The analysis confirms that CO₂ ice is mainly concentrated on the trailing hemisphere, yet the spectral band strengths weaken at mid and high latitudes. This latitudinal gradient may indicate that CO₂ is generated radiolytically at high latitudes and subsequently migrates to cold traps at lower latitudes. Furthermore, a subtle feature near 2.13 microns was identified in two high-latitude spectra, potentially representing a 'forbidden' CO₂ ice transition mode that intensifies in well-mixed CO₂ and H₂O substrates, suggesting radiolytically formed, regolith-mixed ice grains. Finally, a 2.35-micron feature observed in some low-latitude spectra may signify carbon monoxide (CO) produced within the CO₂ radiolytic cycle.

Recent studies have detailed the thermodynamic and electronic transport characteristics of trigonal EuMg2Bi2 under ab-plane magnetic fields (Hx) within its A-type antiferromagnetic structure. Below the Néel temperature (TN > 1.8 K), Eu magnetic moments (spin S = 7/2) are confined to the ab plane until they reach the critical field Hxc = 27.5 kOe, at which point they align parallel to Hx. New low-field measurements reveal an additional spin-reorientation transition at Hc1 = 465 Oe, where moments stay in the ab plane but orient perpendicularly to Hx. As the field increases further, the moments tilt toward Hx, producing magnetization proportional to Hx up to Hxc. Comparable findings were observed in EuMg2Sb2 single crystals, with a corresponding Hc1 of 220 Oe. A theoretical framework has been developed to model the low-field magnetic behavior of both compounds, calculating their associated anisotropies; notably, the ab-plane trigonal anisotropy in EuMg2Sb2 is substantially weaker than in EuMg2Bi2.

The group $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ is constructed by forcing every element $g$ from the first free factor of $G\ast G$ to commute with its corresponding copy in the second free factor. This work expands the known list of properties preserved by the functor $\mathfrak{X}$ and explores both the geometric and complexity aspects of the word problem for $\mathfrak{X}(G)$. Subtle characteristics of $\mathfrak{X}$ are captured within a normal abelian subgroup $W<\mathfrak{X}(G)$, which functions as a module over $\mathbb{Z} Q$ where $Q=H_1(G,\mathbb{Z})$. We derive a structural theorem for this module and demonstrate its effectiveness by showing that $\mathfrak{X}$ preserves virtual nilpotence, the Engel condition, and growth types—whether polynomial, exponential, or intermediate. Furthermore, we apply these findings to prove isoperimetric inequalities for $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ when $G$ belongs to a class encompassing Thompson's group $F$ and all non-fibered K\"ahler groups. The solvability of the word problem in $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ is equivalent to its solvability in $G$. Additionally, if $G$ maps onto a non-abelian free group, the Dehn function of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ is bounded below by a cubic polynomial.

This paper addresses the novel and demanding challenge of controllable video captioning using an exemplar sentence. Specifically, given a video and a syntactically correct exemplar, the objective is to produce a single caption that captures the video's semantic content while adhering to the grammatical structure of the provided sentence. To achieve this, we introduce a new Syntax Modulated Caption Generator (SMCG) within an encoder-decoder-reconstructor framework. The SMCG accepts video semantic representations and uses the encoded syntax of the exemplar to conditionally modulate the gates and cells of a long short-term memory network. Consequently, the SMCG regulates word prediction states to generate captions customized for specific syntactic requirements. We evaluated the method by gathering auxiliary exemplar sentences from two public video captioning datasets. Comprehensive experimental results confirm the approach's effectiveness in producing captions that are both semantically accurate and syntactically controllable. Furthermore, by varying the exemplar sentences, our method can generate captions with diverse syntactic structures, demonstrating a promising avenue for enhancing the diversity of video captioning.

Although optical frequency standards currently offer superior accuracy and stability, they have not yet been utilized for generating time scales, unlike conventional systems that combine atomic frequency standards with reliable local oscillators to deliver precise timestamps and intervals. In this study, we achieved the continuous generation of an "optically steered" time scale, TA(Sr), for six months by modulating an oscillator's frequency through the intermittent operation of a $^{87}$Sr optical lattice clock. The resulting time scale matched the stability of International Atomic Time (TAI) and reached an accuracy level of $10^{-16}$. We further compared TA(Sr) with TT(BIPM16), a time scale computed annually in January as a weighted average of TAI frequency evaluations derived from primary and secondary standards. Over a five-month period, the variation in the difference between TA(Sr) and TT(BIPM16) remained at 0.79 ns, indicating the feasibility of employing optical clocks for time scale generation. Additionally, the steady signal enabled the evaluation of one-month mean scale intervals for TAI across all six months with uncertainties comparable to those of primary frequency standards (PFSs).

We establish that the probability $p(t,x)$—defined as the likelihood that the fraction of time up to $t$ during which a random walk $S$ with i.i.d. zero-mean increments (taking finitely many values) remains non-negative exceeds $x$ for all $s \in [1,t]$—decays according to the power law $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$. In this expression, $\phi(x,b) = \mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$, where the parameter $\kappa(x,b)$ is given by $\frac{\sqrt{1-x} b - \sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x} b + \sqrt{1+x}}$. The coefficient $b=b_S \geq 0$ quantifies the asymptotic asymmetry between positive and negative excursions of the walk, taking the value $b_s=1$ when the increments are symmetric.

A reduced version of the Dirac equation has previously been examined within the Center of Mass reference frame. In this study, we demonstrate that the equation can be expressed in a covariant form applicable to any reference frame by employing specific momentum variables, which are also consistent with the model's interaction in the retarded form.

This study introduces an event camera as a key element of a vision system designed to count rapidly moving objects, specifically falling corn grains. Unlike traditional cameras, these sensors detect brightness changes at the pixel level, offering advantages such as minimal latency, the absence of motion blur, adaptability to varying lighting, and extremely low power usage. The developed counting algorithm processes incoming events in real time. The system's performance was validated using a test rig featuring a chute and a vibrating feeder to regulate the flow of grains. A PID controller was employed to stabilize the average rate of falling objects. Extensive testing confirmed the method's accuracy, thereby supporting the viability of event cameras for counting small, fast-moving items and highlighting their broad potential across industrial applications.

Movement serves as a common response for humans and animals seeking improved conditions in dynamic environments, a topic extensively explored within social dilemmas where individual and collective interests clash. Building upon the traditional public goods game, where agents are stationary and fixed as either unconditional cooperators or defectors, we introduce two new strategies allowing agents to adjust their dependence on local cooperation levels. These "sophisticated" players incur an additional cost to sustain the ability to continuously assess their surroundings and adapt accordingly. Consequently, four strategies compete, with successful ones spreading through imitation by neighbors. The introduction of costly mobility yields a strongly biased outcome for the primary strategies. Across most of the parameter space, movement harms defectors and significantly boosts cooperation when the population is sparse. However, at intermediate population densities—where immobile systems typically perform optimally—mobile actors can be detrimental if interaction patterns shift slightly, potentially obstructing optimal information flow. Within this specific range, sophisticated cooperators may exhibit a "Moor effect," initially avoiding defectors before transitioning into a stationary cooperative state. Paradoxically, the added expense of movement can prove advantageous for achieving higher overall income, particularly for rare populations that would otherwise remain isolated in subgroups.

The increasing adoption of telemedicine suggests that automatically evaluating health status through telephone speech could greatly benefit public health. This study presents initial results on the automatic identification of respiratory distress by analyzing standard acoustic and prosodic features. Data were gathered from anonymized telemedicine calls originating from a healthcare provider in Bangladesh, consisting of patient-doctor conversations where individuals exhibited mild to severe respiratory distress or asthma. We propose that respiratory distress influences speech characteristics such as voice quality, speaking patterns, volume, and pause lengths. To detect these changes, we employed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier using established acoustic and prosodic features. Experiments utilized a 3-fold cross-validation method with patient-independent data splits, achieving an overall accuracy of 86.4% in identifying respiratory distress based on the acoustic feature set. Correlation analysis identified loudness, voice rate, voice duration, and pause duration as the most effective features.

The Earth Observatory represents an expanding research domain that can leverage artificial intelligence for short-term forecasting, specifically within the "Now-casting" context. This study addresses weather prediction by utilizing a video transformer network. Although vision transformers have been applied across various fields, they are often hindered by the high computational cost of attention mechanisms and their reliance on large datasets for training. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a Video Swin-Transformer integrated with a specialized augmentation strategy. Additionally, the model incorporates gradual spatial reduction in the encoder and cross-attention in the decoder. The proposed method was evaluated on the Weather4Cast2021 dataset, which involves predicting future frames eight hours ahead (four frames per hour) based on hourly weather sequences. To ensure compatibility with evaluation metrics across different datasets, the data was normalized to a 0-1 range. The model achieved a Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 0.4750 using training data and 0.4420 during transfer learning without additional training data.

This paper extends trend filtering theory by integrating the Wasserstein metric to regulate spatiotemporal variation in filtered time series. Although standard trend filtering employs regularization to generate piecewise linear estimates via $\ell_1$ norms or temporally smooth estimates via $\ell_2$ norms, it overlooks the spatial topology of the signal distribution. By leveraging the underlying metric space of the pixel arrangement, the Wasserstein metric serves as an effective regularizer for uncovering spatiotemporal trends. We present a globally optimal algorithm for efficiently estimating these filtered signals using a Wasserstein finite differences operator. The algorithm's ability to maintain spatiotemporal trends in time series video is validated through simulations and fluorescent microscopy footage of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, with performance compared against conventional trend filtering methods.

We introduce a device comprising a graphene sheet coupled with a Weyl semimetal, enabling the experimental investigation of tunneling between two-dimensional and three-dimensional massless Dirac fermions. Due to its reconstructed band structure, this system functions as a robust valley filter for electrons within the graphene layer. By aligning the components appropriately, the Weyl semimetal selectively extracts current from one of the two graphene valleys while permitting the other to flow without obstruction. Unlike other proposed valley filters, this mechanism operates within the bulk of the graphene sheet, eliminating the requirement for precisely shaped edges or specific dimensions.

This study examines an imperfect hardware hybrid satellite-terrestrial network (HSTN) where ground user equipment (UE) communicates with satellites via multiple amplify-and-forward (AF) three-dimensional (3D) mobile unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) relays. All transceiver nodes in this setup are affected by radio frequency hardware impairments (RFHI). A stochastic mixed mobility (MM) model is utilized to determine the instantaneous positions of the 3D mobile UAV relays within a cylindrical cell, with the UE located at the center on the ground plane. Considering the aggregate RFHI model for both satellite and UAV relay transceivers, along with random 3D distance-based path loss for the UAV relay-to-UE links, we analyze the outage probability (OP) and its asymptotic behavior. This analysis is conducted in a unified framework for shadowed-Rician satellite links, Nakagami-$m$ terrestrial links, and Rician terrestrial links, under an opportunistic relay selection scheme. Theoretical findings are validated through simulations.

We examine the low-energy characteristics of an effective local model featuring a flipped $SU(5)\times U(1)_{\chi}$ gauge group, developed within the F-theory framework. This model originates from $SO(10)$ symmetry, linked to a geometric singularity in the compactification manifold, which is broken by an internal flux activated along the seven-brane in the $U(1)_{\chi}$ direction. The massless spectrum, dictated by topological properties and flux parameters, comprises the minimal flipped $SU(5)$ content plus an additional right-handed electron-type state and its complex conjugate ($E^c+\bar E^c$), alongside neutral singlets. Symmetry breaking down to the $SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1)_Y$ gauge group is mediated by a Higgs pair in $10+\overline{10}$ representations of $SU(5)$. Phenomenological analysis reveals that the $E^c+\bar E^c$ pair gains a mass in the few TeV range, potentially addressing the $g_{\mu}-2$ anomaly. Furthermore, neutrino interactions with extra neutral singlets facilitate an inverse seesaw mechanism, yielding a light state viable as dark matter. The model's predictions for ${0\nu}\beta\beta$ decay rates are testable in upcoming experiments, and non-unitarity deviations in the lepton mixing matrix ($U_{PMNS}$) could account for the recent CDF II measurement of the W-boson mass.

Wearable technologies like the ActiGraph have become standard tools in health research for tracking physical activity, addressing the increasing demand to evaluate how such activity impacts health outcomes like obesity. When analyzing the link between these device-derived activity measures (functions) and health indicators such as body mass index (scalar), scalar-on-function regression (SoFR) is the appropriate modeling framework. However, most existing SoFR estimation techniques assume functional covariates are observed without error or treat measurement errors as random; violating these assumptions can result in biased parameter estimates and suboptimal analysis. Currently, the literature offers few non-Bayesian measurement-corrected approaches for SoFR, and virtually no Bayesian alternatives. This study proposes a fully nonparametric Bayesian SoFR model that relaxes restrictive assumptions typically found in such models. By utilizing an instrumental variable (IV) to identify the measurement error structure, our method also introduces an IV quality scalar parameter estimated jointly with all other model parameters. We demonstrate that this approach is straightforward to implement and validate its finite sample performance through extensive simulations. Finally, the proposed method is applied to National Health and Examination Survey data to examine the relationship between wearable device-based physical activity measures and body mass index among U.S. adults.

This study tackles policy learning in non-stationary settings and games involving continuous actions. Instead of relying on traditional reward maximization, we introduce PORL, a no-regret reinforcement learning algorithm for continuous action tasks, drawing inspiration from follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) and mirror descent (MD) update principles. We demonstrate that PORL offers last-iterate convergence guarantees, a critical feature for adversarial and cooperative games. Empirical results indicate that in stationary environments, such as MuJoCo locomotion control, PORL matches or surpasses the soft actor-critic (SAC) algorithm. Conversely, in non-stationary contexts—including dynamic environments, adversarial training, and competitive games—PORL outperforms SAC by achieving superior final policy performance and a more stable training process.

The proliferation of very-high-resolution sensors and satellites with short revisit times has led to a continuous surge in available remote sensing data, making computational complexity in Earth Observation data extraction an increasingly significant challenge. High Performance Computing (HPC) has emerged as a standard solution, offering environments and tools that accelerate processing. Specifically, clusters provide flexible, cost-effective systems capable of handling data-intensive tasks to meet diverse computational needs. However, utilizing clusters often requires substantial coding effort to implement specific processing pipelines. This paper introduces a generic framework for developing remote sensing image processing applications designed for cluster computing. Built upon common open-source libraries, it enables the transparent parallelization of a wide range of image processing pipelines. Performance evaluations on typical remote sensing tasks implemented through this framework demonstrate its strong potential for the efficient and timely processing of large datasets.

Suitable feedback is essential for the proper functioning of numerous natural and artificial systems. This study examines how additional complex conjugate feedback influences globally coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators. We discover that this feedback induces symmetry-breaking and out-of-phase clusters. Notably, we also observe explosive amplitude death alongside distinct multistable states. By utilizing the amplitude order parameter, we characterize the first-order transition to explosive death, demonstrating that the shift from oscillation to a death state exhibits hysteresis. Furthermore, we map global dynamical transitions across parametric spaces. To elucidate the origins of multistability and their transitions, we analyze bifurcation scenarios in a reduced model and investigate basin stability. Ultimately, our research provides insights into emergent dynamics arising from additional feedback.

We utilize systematic density functional theory calculations to simulate the infrared reflectivity of CaS and MgS. Our findings indicate that accurate spectral modeling necessitates incorporating anharmonic effects alongside the standard harmonic approximation. CaS and MgS serve as ideal test systems due to their conceptual simplicity, allowing us to explicitly account for anharmonicity via a perturbative method that extends to three-phonon scattering and isotopic disorder. All requisite physical parameters, including Born effective charges and the dielectric constant for the Lorentz model, are derived directly from our first-principles computations. By comparing our predicted optical modes, transverse modes, and reflectivity spectra against existing experimental data, we confirm strong overall agreement. This validation underscores the critical role of including anharmonic terms when modeling infrared optical properties.

Effective risk management is essential for maintaining the competitiveness of financial institutions and ensuring economic stability. While Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a common metric, linear and parametric models often produce biased results or underestimate risk because they fail to account for time-varying volatility, skewness, and leptokurtosis in financial returns. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a nonlinear, nonparametric framework driven entirely by data to forecast VaR. In this approach, mean and volatility are estimated using Support Vector Regression (SVR), with the volatility component inspired by the standard Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH) structure. Value-at-Risk is subsequently calculated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). This hybrid method offers flexible tail shapes for profit and loss distributions, adapts to various tail events, and captures complex patterns in both mean and volatility.

The proposed SVR-GARCH-KDE model is evaluated against standard, exponential, and threshold GARCH models paired with different error distributions. Forecasts for one-day and ten-day horizons were generated across multiple financial indices to assess performance in diverse markets. Using a likelihood ratio-based test for interval forecasts and a test for superior predictive ability, the study finds that the SVR-GARCH-KDE hybrid performs competitively against benchmarks and significantly reduces potential losses, particularly for ten-day-ahead predictions. Notably, models assuming a normal distribution are consistently outperformed by the proposed approach.

Multi-view registration presents a fundamental yet difficult challenge within 3D reconstruction and robot vision. While the original motion averaging algorithm offers an effective solution for this problem, it fails to account for the reliability and accuracy of individual relative motions. To address this, this paper introduces a novel motion averaging algorithm specifically designed for multi-view registration. The method begins by using a pair-wise registration algorithm to estimate the relative motion and the degree of overlap for each scan pair. Leveraging this overlap data as a weight, the proposed weight motion averaging algorithm prioritizes reliable and accurate relative motions. By distinguishing between different relative motions, this weighted approach achieves more precise registration results when applied to multi-view range scans. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques regarding accuracy, robustness, and efficiency.

This paper investigates the upper bound for the lifespan estimate of the compressible Euler system featuring time-dependent damping and small initial perturbations. By utilizing techniques derived from the blow-up analysis of nonlinear wave equations, we introduce tools from Orlicz space theory to manage the nonlinear term arising from the pressure function $p \equiv p(\rho)$. This approach accounts for the distinct asymptotic behaviors of the pressure for both large and small values of $\rho-1$, where $\rho$ represents density. Consequently, we establish unified upper bounds for the lifespan in high dimensions ($n \in \{2, 3\}$) that depend solely on the dimension $n$ and the damping strength, remaining independent of the adiabatic index $\gamma > 1$. We conjecture these results to be optimal. Furthermore, the proposed method not only enhances existing upper bounds for $n \in \{2, 3\}$ but also holds potential for addressing related problems.

Research indicates that in various overparameterized nonlinear models, particularly during neural network training, the behavior of the loss function near a minimum significantly influences performance. Specifically, flat minima—regions where the loss increases gradually—are associated with superior generalization. This study advances the understanding of this relationship by examining the most fundamental category of such models: those involved in low-rank matrix recovery. The analysis covers overparameterized matrix and bilinear sensing, robust PCA, covariance estimation, and single-hidden-layer neural networks with quadratic activations. In each scenario, we demonstrate that flat minima, quantified via the trace of the Hessian, achieve exact recovery of the ground truth under standard statistical assumptions. While matrix completion yields weak recovery theoretically, empirical results suggest exact recovery is also attainable. The paper concludes with synthetic experiments that validate these observations.

The Ion cyclotron Sheath Test ARrangement (IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 0.1 meters in length and 0.4 meters in diameter, generates the required plasma environment ahead of the ICRF antenna. This source, which features a helical antenna, was engineered to achieve a helicon discharge mode. Although it was previously unconfirmed whether the source could reach this mode, achieving helicon operation is crucial for maximizing the source's capacity and producing high-density plasma. Consequently, a comprehensive study was conducted to attain helicon mode. This involved characterizing key plasma parameters—such as electron temperature, density, and plasma potential—and implementing a global model for particle and power balance. The study confirmed the existence of helicon mode at magnetic fields below 35 mT. To achieve the maximum possible plasma density, an optimization strategy was proposed to enable helicon mode operation at the highest available magnetic field.

Deciphering the intrinsic semantics of performing arts, particularly dance, presents a significant challenge due to the medium's multimedia nature and its extension across both time and space. Capturing and analyzing this content is vital for preserving cultural heritage, developing video recommendation systems, and enhancing tutoring tools for learners. To create applications for dance analysis, three core aspects must be addressed: (1) segmenting dance videos to isolate representative action elements, (2) recognizing or matching these detected elements, and (3) identifying dance sequences formed by combining multiple actions according to specific rules. This paper aims to resolve these three fundamental issues to better understand the underlying semantics of dance forms, with a specific focus on the Indian Classical Dance (ICD) style known as Bharatanatyam. Since dance is intrinsically linked to music, our approach utilizes both musical and motion data to extract key postures. We then employ machine learning and deep learning techniques to recognize these postures, followed by the use of Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to identify the overall dance sequences. Furthermore, we capture multi-modal data of Bharatanatyam using the Kinect sensor and construct an annotated dataset to support research in this field.

This article introduces MuMuPy, a computational library and cloud-based tool designed to calculate cross sections for dimuonium (true muonium) interactions with matter. MuMuPy computes relevant form factors and determines the probabilities of dimuonium transitions within a nuclear electric field. The development of MuMuPy was driven by the $\mu\mu$-tron facility project, a proposed low-energy electron-positron collider for producing and experimentally studying dimuonium at the Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics. The tool's reliability has been confirmed through three independent verification methods, one of which was previously created by the authors.

Fractal Clifford Spaces (FCS) offer a promising yet difficult framework for unifying micro-physics and macro-physics. Within these manifolds, trajectories are characterized by distinct poly-vectors that define paths and deviation equations for a variety of entities, including test particles, as well as charged, rotating, and rotating charged objects. This methodology relaxes the requirement of differentiability for all extended objects within the manifold. Consequently, this paper will examine a specialized Bazanski Lagrangian designed to describe the fractal analogues of extended objects in a fractal space-time.

We characterize the local form of every non-closed Lorentzian Weyl structure $(M,c,\nabla)$ possessing a recurrent curvature tensor. For manifolds with a dimension exceeding 3, the conformal structure is flat, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between these recurrent structures and the solutions to the Riccati equation. Furthermore, the recurrent curvature tensor is identified as a weighted parallel tensor.

This study introduces a method that combines ensemble Kalman filtering with Fourier series approximations to estimate time-varying parameters within deterministic dynamical systems. We validate this approach by estimating both sinusoidal and polynomial forcing parameters in a mass-spring system. The results highlight how critical the selection of frequencies in the approximation model is for accurately determining the corresponding time-varying parameters.

Conventional robust recommendation approaches typically treat atypical user-item interactions as noise, employing filtering techniques to mitigate their influence; however, this strategy often faces two significant limitations. Firstly, in real-world scenarios, these atypical interactions frequently reflect a user's transient interests distinct from their overall preferences, meaning that indiscriminate removal can harm recommendation personalization. Secondly, identifying such transient interests is challenging due to the lack of explicit supervisory signals indicating whether an interaction is atypical. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce Temporary Interest Aware Recommendation (TIARec), a novel model capable of distinguishing atypical from normal interactions without supervision, while simultaneously capturing both users' general preferences and temporary interests. Specifically, we propose a reinforcement learning framework comprising a recommender agent and an auxiliary classifier agent, jointly trained to maximize the cumulative return of recommendations. During this joint training, the classifier agent evaluates whether interactions with items recommended by the recommender agent are atypical, transferring insights on learning from these interactions to the recommender agent. This enables the recommender agent to independently generate recommendations that effectively balance general preferences with transient interests. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of TIARec.

Eigenstate thermalization in quantum many-body systems suggests that high-energy eigenstates resemble random vectors, making the identification of systems containing non-thermal eigenstates a significant open problem. This study demonstrates that interacting quantum models possessing a nullspace—a degenerate subspace of zero-energy eigenstates, or zero modes, corresponding to infinite temperature—offer a pathway to non-thermal states. We analytically prove the existence of a zero mode representable as a matrix product state for specific classes of local Hamiltonians. In broader scenarios, we employ a subspace disentangling algorithm to construct an orthogonal basis of zero modes exhibiting increasing entanglement entropy. Our findings indicate area-law entanglement scaling for the least entangled zero mode across a wide parameter range, leading to the conjecture that all local Hamiltonians with a nullspace feature zero modes adhering to area-law scaling; consequently, these states violate the strong thermalization hypothesis. Furthermore, we identify zero modes in constrained models and propose experimental setups to detect their signatures.

In the traditional firefighter game, a fire ignites at a vertex in a graph $G$ during the first turn, followed by the deployment of $k$ firefighters to secure $k$ vertices. In every subsequent turn, the fire expands to all currently unburnt neighbors of the burning set, while firefighters again protect $k$ vertices. Once a vertex is either burnt or protected, its status remains permanent. A standard goal for infinite graphs $G$ is to identify the minimum number of firefighters needed to contain the fire within a finite number of turns. This work introduces a distance-restricted variant where firefighters can only travel a fixed maximum distance $d$ per turn, rather than moving freely. We examine the general properties of this modified game compared to the original version and analyze specific instances on infinite square, strong, and hexagonal grids. We conjecture that two firefighters are inadequate to contain the fire on the square grid when $d = 2$, and we raise questions regarding the number of firefighters required in general when $d = 1$.

Additive and generalized additive models serve as powerful semiparametric approaches for analyzing multidimensional data. This article introduces an online smoothing backfitting algorithm designed for generalized additive models that utilize local polynomial smoothers. The core methodology employs a second-order expansion to approximate nonlinear integral equations, thereby maximizing local quasilikelihood. The resulting coefficients are retained as sufficient statistics, which can be dynamically updated in real-time using a candidate bandwidth method. This updating process relies solely on the stored sufficient statistics and the incoming data block. We establish the asymptotic normality and derive lower bounds for the relative efficiency of these online estimates, offering insights into the trade-off between estimation precision and computational costs dictated by the candidate bandwidth sequence length. Furthermore, simulations and real-world data applications are presented to corroborate our results.

This paper examines the semi-linear, defocusing wave equation $u_{tt}-\Delta u=-|u|^{p-1} u$ in higher dimensions under sub-conformal conditions, focusing on initial data that possess finite energy and exhibit rapid decay. We establish decay estimates for solutions when the initial data diminish at a specific rate as the spatial variable approaches infinity. By combining these estimates with the method of characteristic lines, we demonstrate scattering results for initial data satisfying the energy condition:
$$E_{\kappa}\left(u_{0}, u_{1}\right)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(|x|^{\kappa}+1\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\left|\nabla u_{0}(x)\right|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left|u_{1}(x)\right|^{2}+\frac{1}{p+1}\left|u_{0}(x)\right|^{p+1}\right) d x<+\infty,$$
where $\kappa=\frac{(2-d)p+(d+2)}{p+1}$.

Two families of surfaces emerge from examining cyclic branched covers of $\mathbb{P}^{2}$ defined by smooth quartic curves: degree 2 del Pezzo surfaces possessing a $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ action and $K3$ surfaces featuring a $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ action. We determine the monodromy groups for both families. For the del Pezzo surfaces, the group is the Weyl group $W\left(E_{7}\right)$, which aligns with the automorphisms of the 56 lines residing on such a surface. For the $K3$ surfaces, the group is an arithmetic lattice: the unitary group $U\left(h_{L_{-}}\right)$ associated with a type $\left(1, 6\right)$ quadratic form over $\mathbb{Z}\left[i\right]$, a result extending the work of Kondo and Allcock, Carlson, and Toledo.

Recent years have seen growing research interest in skeleton-based action recognition. However, a prevalent limitation in current popular methods is that sparse skeleton data alone often fails to fully capture human motion. This constraint causes several existing approaches to misclassify action categories that differ only subtly. To address this, we introduce JOLO-GCN, a novel framework that integrates human pose skeletons with joint-centered, lightweight information within a two-stream graph convolutional network. Specifically, the model utilizes Joint-aligned optical Flow Patches (JFP) to extract local, subtle movements around each joint as key visual cues. Compared to pure skeleton-based baselines, this hybrid approach significantly enhances performance while maintaining low computational and memory costs. Experiments conducted on the NTU RGB+D, NTU RGB+D 120, and Kinetics-Skeleton datasets confirm that the proposed method achieves notable accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art skeleton-based techniques.
